one_line_reasoning: Weighted MSE misaligns with the unweighted RMSE metric: it biases predictions darker on the ambiguous edge and background pixels that dominate the error count, so a slight regression is likely, though the effect is small.

Training for roughly 10-20x more steps with the same annealed cosine schedule should substantially reduce underfitting of the small U-Net; the median-background input already captures much of the stains, so I expect a solid but not dramatic RMSE drop, tempered slightly by overfitting on 105 images.

L1 optimizes the median rather than the mean, which biases toward sparse text/background extremes and slightly hurts RMSE on ambiguous stroke-edge pixels; with a short budget, the effect is likely a small regression or a wash.

Train and test noise come from the same synthetic distribution, so jittering only the inputs removes absolute-intensity cues the model uses (stain and paper levels vs. ink), and the clipping also wipes out detail near white; expect a moderate RMSE regression.

Multi-scale resampling blurs sharp text edges and white-background plateaus (interpolation down/up loses precision at ~0.015 RMSE level), and the net was trained only at native scale, so 0.75x/1.25x passes are out-of-distribution; averaging likely hurts.

The model is likely underfit at this short 2000-step budget rather than overfit, so Dropout2d on the skip and bottleneck features probably slows convergence and adds noise, giving a modestly worse RMSE.

Dropout2d in every U-Net block injects noise into a pixel-precise regression that's limited by the time budget rather than overfitting. It will likely slow convergence and raise the final RMSE somewhat.

A larger receptive field helps the model remove large stains and background texture. The fixed 180 s budget means fewer training steps, so the gain should be modest; the result is already strong at 0.0087.

A median-23 background channel gives the 3-level U-Net (receptive field ~40px) the large-scale stain context it otherwise lacks, so it should help modestly; with only ~2000 steps and a single seed, the result is noisy.

A deeper U-Net with larger context can help with stains, but batch 8 with BatchNorm, the same 2000 steps, and a much bigger model trained on only 105 images likely make it noisier and less converged, giving a slight regression or roughly equal score.

The model was trained with random horizontal and vertical flips, so it should be roughly equivariant to them; averaging the 4 flip variants cuts prediction variance and bf16 noise, typically a modest 3–5% RMSE gain.

The diff sets TRAIN_SECONDS to 180 instead of the specified 360, but even 180 s on a GPU likely gives several times the baseline's 2000 steps, and a small U-Net that is far from converged should see lower RMSE.

The metric is RMSE, and an L1-style loss optimizes a median rather than the mean; on documents with many near-saturated white pixels plus hard stroke/edge pixels, this usually costs some RMSE (bf16 in the sqrt adds a little noise), so I expect a slight to moderate regression rather than a gain.

Test noise follows the same synthetic distribution as train, so extra Gaussian noise creates a train/test mismatch; it also eats capacity and blurs fine text edges, which likely hurts an already low RMSE in a short training run.

GroupNorm removes BN's crop-vs-full-page statistic mismatch, but it also normalizes away global brightness per sample, so I expect a small net gain with moderate variance (GN training is also a bit slower and noisier).

SSIM+L1 no longer optimizes RMSE directly; white backgrounds are exact, but mean-level bias from SSIM's luminance insensitivity and L1 median behaviour on gray stroke edges usually costs a few thousandths of RMSE relative to MSE training.
8-view TTA averaging usually helps, but rot90 views were never seen in training (flip-only augmentation), which partly offsets the gain.

Pure SSIM loss barely penalizes small luminance offsets on the near-white background that dominates the pixels, so global intensity bias creeps in and per-pixel RMSE worsens versus direct MSE optimization.

Residual learning helps less here than in Gaussian denoising because the noise is structured (stains, backgrounds) and the clean targets are near-binary, so the sigmoid's saturation toward white actually fits them well; expect a roughly neutral to slightly worse score.

The RMSE loss's gradient is renormalized, which likely fixes little, and the SSIM term moves the objective away from pixel RMSE; on flat white backgrounds the variance terms are tiny, so SSIM is noisy there. The net effect is probably neutral to slightly worse on the RMSE metric.

Clean targets are mostly saturated at 1.0, where a sigmoid output fits more easily than a linear residual; background noise (stains) is large, so learning the residual gives little benefit, and the missing output bound likely makes results slightly worse or leaves them about the same.
Synthetic pairs dominate ~86% of samples with a noise distribution mismatched to real test noise, diluting real-data training under a fixed step budget, so RMSE likely worsens.
4.5x more training steps for an undertrained small U-Net on 105 images should reduce RMSE meaningfully (fine text edges), with mild overfitting risk limiting gains; runtime fits budget.

Dihedral TTA is implemented with correct inverses and should give a modest ensemble-style RMSE gain. Text isn't rotation-invariant, but the model was trained with flips, so the transposed views still help somewhat; training is unchanged.

The L1 loss is mismatched with the RMSE metric: it pushes predictions toward the median and down-weights large text-edge and stain residuals. Most pixels are exactly 1, so L1 may help the background a little, but I expect a mild net RMSE regression overall.

Reweighting away from the MSE objective that matches the metric shifts the fit toward dark pixels; on this data the white background dominates the RMSE, so a small regression is likely, with seed noise on a short CPU run.
Weighting ink 10x misaligns training with the unweighted RMSE metric, which is dominated by background pixels; the model drifts toward darker background predictions, giving a mild regression.

Zero-initialised residual learning starts from the identity map and makes background removal easy, and clamping at inference absorbs overshoot past 1, so expect a small gain or roughly no change versus the sigmoid output.

L1 on a mostly-white target tends to sharpen outputs and reach a similar optimum, but it no longer directly optimizes the RMSE metric and its gradients are weaker near convergence, so expect a similar or slightly worse RMSE.

Residual learning helps somewhat with fine detail, but losing the sigmoid's saturation at white (background ~1.0) makes it harder to hit clean white exactly under a short CPU budget, so a mild regression is most likely.

Halving the width cuts capacity to roughly a quarter, and with a fixed 2000-step budget the model is underfitting rather than overfitting (random crops give plenty of samples), so RMSE likely gets modestly worse.
The weighted loss no longer matches the RMSE metric, and the metric is dominated by background pixels; the extra weight on strokes gives little benefit, so expect a slight regression within noise.
The closing-based illumination-normalized channel should help the U-Net remove stains, giving a modest gain; the forced-CPU execution config adds a large risk of timeout or slower training.

An fp32 head alone would do roughly nothing, but the applied diff also adds an unrequested runtime.toml that forces CPU-only (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""), which likely makes the 2000-step U-Net run exceed the 15-min kill; this number assumes it somehow completes.

Flip TTA alone would give a small gain (about 0.0158), but the diff also adds a runtime.json that sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' and forces CPU; 2000 U-Net steps plus 4x TTA validation each epoch will very likely exceed the 15-min hard kill (run fails), and the number given is only a fallback guess for the case where it somehow completes.
The diff forces CPU with no AMP, so 2000 steps of the NAFNet risk timing out; if it finishes, this small from-scratch residual NAFNet likely converges worse than the tuned U-Net in this budget.

The ImageNet head was trained on the Stanford Dogs source images, so it is very confident on exactly this label set; blending it in with w and T tuned on the holdout should cut log loss substantially, with some risk from breed-name mapping mismatches.

PCA without whitening to 256 dims keeps most discriminative variance and L2-regularized LR already handles collinearity; C gets re-selected, so the log loss should come out roughly unchanged, possibly slightly worse from discarded low-variance fine-grained directions.

Heavy Mixup/CutMix at full probability over only 6 epochs on a pretrained in22k model mostly slows fitting and underfits; temperature scaling recovers some calibration, but clean-image log loss likely gets slightly worse.

With only 6 epochs of short fine-tuning from a strong in22k backbone, underfitting outweighs memorisation; very aggressive 0.08 crops add label noise (crops miss the dog) and train/test scale mismatch, so log loss slightly worsens.

ConvNeXt-V2 Large with IN-22k pretraining gives much stronger fine-grained dog features than ResNet-50 V1 (~85% vs ~76% IN-1k top1), and linear probes on such features typically reach 0.2–0.3 log loss on Stanford Dogs. Download and runtime risk is modest.
The ImageNet log-proba block encodes 118 dog-class predictions from a head trained on far more dog data, and it helps the LR, so dropping it likely raises the log loss somewhat.

Ridge probe scores with temperature-tuned softmax are usually slightly less well-calibrated than multinomial LR for log loss on 120 classes, since a single global T cannot fix per-sample calibration; expect a modest regression.

PCA to 128/block loses some discriminative fine-grained info and re-normalization changes scale so C grid may be suboptimal; LR on 2560-d with tuned C is already well regularized, so expect a slight regression.

ConvNeXt-Base pretrained on in22k gives much stronger frozen features for fine-grained dog classes than ResNet50 V1, and re-tuning C on a holdout should cut log loss substantially, to roughly 0.3–0.35.

Fine-tuning ConvNeXt-Tiny (pretrained on in22k) for 6 epochs with flip TTA and temperature scaling should reach about 89-91% accuracy and a calibrated log loss near 0.3, beating the frozen ResNet50+LR baseline; the risk is the 7-minute time guard truncating training.

ImageNet head log-probs over the 120 dog classes carry strong breed signal, likely helped by Stanford Dogs overlapping ImageNet training; standardization plus holdout-tuned C should use them well, though noise from the ~880 non-dog columns caps the gain.

Swapping ResNet-50 for concatenated features from ConvNeXt-B in22k, CLIP and DINOv2 should raise frozen-feature accuracy on Stanford Dogs, and DINOv2 in particular is very strong here. L2-normalised concatenation plus C tuning should push log loss down to roughly 0.25-0.35, with runtime still within budget.

Focal loss with gamma=2 shrinks gradients on confident examples, so the unscaled softmax outputs come out systematically underconfident; this likely costs more log loss than removing label smoothing saves, and accuracy should be similar or slightly lower.

ImageNet already covers these dog breeds, so freezing conv1–layer3 keeps strong pretrained features and cuts overfitting on ~9k images, likely a modest log-loss gain; label smoothing and BN running-stat drift in the frozen stages limit it.
Hflip TTA averaging on frozen ViT+logreg typically gives a small calibration/accuracy gain; runtime with 0 workers still within budget.

CLIP ViT-B/32 linear probe on Stanford Dogs is clearly weaker than an IN21k-to-IN1k ViT-B/16 (dog breeds are ImageNet classes, and the coarse patches hurt fine-grained detail), and C=0.3 is untuned for CLIP's feature scale, so log loss will likely go up.

PCA to 256 dims (no whitening) keeps most discriminative variance, but with C=0.3 tuned for 2048-d the effective regularization shifts slightly; fine-grained info in low-variance directions is lost, so expect a small regression or near-neutral change.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 linear probes on Stanford Dogs reach roughly 85-88% accuracy versus about 82% for ResNet50 features, so I expect a clearly lower log loss. Runtime of about 114k ViT-B forwards in fp16 should fit the budget, and the C re-selection keeps calibration reasonable.

Whitening scales the tiny L2-normalised features up to unit variance, so C=1.0 becomes far weaker regularisation. It also boosts noisy low-variance components, which makes the classifier overconfident and raises log loss.

kNN votes are poorly calibrated; test images whose true breed has no neighbour among the 10 get only about 1e-3 probability (about 6.8 nats each), which should roughly double the log loss versus logistic regression.

Fine-tuning ResNet-50 on only about 9k images at lr 0.01 for 10 epochs probably lands near or below the accuracy of the already-strong frozen ImageNet dog features. Label smoothing of 0.1 also flattens the softmax, which raises log loss even when accuracy is fine, so the score likely gets worse.
ViT-B/16 in21k-pretrained features are much stronger for fine-grained dogs than RN50 v1 features, though C=0.3 was tuned for ResNet features; linear-probe log loss should drop to roughly 0.3–0.4.

Averaging 10-crop TTA probabilities over a frozen ResNet-50 plus logistic regression usually gives a small log-loss gain; corner crops can clip the dog, which limits it, and the implementation looks correct.

ConvNeXt-Tiny in22k features are much stronger for dog breeds than ResNet-50, but at C=1.0 on L2-normalised unit-norm features the logistic regression is likely under-confident, which eats most of that gain.

The pretrained ImageNet dog head was trained on overlapping Stanford Dogs/ImageNet images, so it is strong and complements the logistic regression; the tuned temperature fixes the underconfidence from V2 label smoothing, so blending should cut log loss noticeably.

Unwhitened PCA-256 keeps most of the variance, but it discards some discriminative low-variance directions for fine-grained breeds; with the same C, regularization is effectively similar, so a small regression is likely.

The fc head was trained on avg-pooled features, so max-pooled ResNet-50 activations are shifted off-distribution and much larger in magnitude; with C=0.3 on the raw, unstandardized features, the logistic regression will likely be less well calibrated, and fine-grained linear-probe accuracy usually drops, so log loss likely gets worse.

IMAGENET1K_V2 was trained with label smoothing, mixup/cutmix and long schedules, which tend to produce less transferable penultimate features for linear probing, so frozen-feature logistic regression on fine-grained dog breeds likely gets worse despite higher ImageNet top-1.
C=0.03 underconfident init on unstandardized ResNet features raises log loss; short low-LR fine-tune only partly recovers sharpness.

Dropping from 224 to 192 resolution discards fine detail that fine-grained breed recognition depends on, and the pretrained resnet50 was trained at 224, so frozen features get noticeably worse and log loss should rise by roughly 10-20%.
PCA to 256 dims on ResNet-50 features discards some discriminative variance while the effective L2 regularisation stays roughly the same (projection is orthogonal), so log loss likely rises slightly.
Moving ResNet-50 from 224 to 192 px lowers resolution below its training scale, which usually hurts fine-grained features; I expect logloss to rise by roughly 10-20%.

ResNet-50 V2 weights were trained with heavy regularization (label smoothing, mixup/cutmix, long schedule), and those penultimate features usually linear-probe worse and give less calibrated results than V1. Their norm scale also differs, so C=0.3 is untuned; expect higher log loss. The run also carries a small risk of failing, because the removed TORCH_HOME setting sends the weight download to the default cache.

C was already tuned for log loss, so the model is probably close to calibrated and a single temperature gives only a small gain. The diff also dropped the TORCH_HOME override, a minor risk to fetching the pretrained weights.

Two epochs of small-LR SGD on unaugmented cached activations, starting from an already well-fit LR head, mostly lowers training loss and sharpens confidence, so test log loss is expected to be slightly worse.

Averaging center-crop probabilities with the horizontal-flip view usually gives a small, consistent log-loss gain for frozen-feature logistic regression; the MLflow and tempdir additions don't touch predictions.

Throwing away 90-99.7% of negatives (threat keeps ~480 negatives) loses most of the information about hard negatives; with C unchanged this raises variance, so rare-label AUC drops noticeably and toxic drops slightly.

Adding char n-grams should strengthen NB-LogReg on the obfuscated and rare labels, but it makes branch B more like branch A so the blend gains little; the larger liblinear fits also raise some timeout risk.

Undersampling throws away most negatives (e.g. threat trains on ~1k rows), so rare-label models lose a lot of information; balancing doesn't help AUC, which is insensitive to class priors, so the net effect is a modest loss.

MultinomialNB on TF-IDF is much weaker than NB-LogReg (~0.94-0.96 AUC, poor on rare labels), dragging the 50/50 rank blend down; its stacked features also add less information than the NB-LogReg OOF predictions did.

Mean-pooled self-trained W2V (~0.95-0.96 AUC alone) is weaker than word+char TF-IDF LR (~0.978); it now drives 2 of 3 rank-blend members, so the blend drops despite NB-LR staying strong; time also increases but likely fits.

Undersampling throws away 80-99% of the negative training data (e.g. threat is fit on only ~1k rows), and AUC does not depend on calibration, so balancing buys nothing while the smaller data raises variance, especially for rare labels; the MLP also gets far less training.

A sparse TF-IDF MLP should reach about 0.975–0.98 AUC alone and add some non-linear diversity to the blend, but equal 1/4 weight and possibly tight time guards (D may be skipped or cut to 1–2 epochs) limit the gain to a small one.
Undersampling discards 70-99% of negatives (and threat trains on only ~956 rows), which loses information and hurts ranking AUC; rare labels degrade most, so expect a clear drop below 0.981.

Vectorizers already lowercase and char n-grams capture obfuscation; normalization of this kind typically yields ±0.0005 on linear TF-IDF models, and repeat-collapsing and shorthand rewrites could slightly hurt, so I expect roughly no change.

Adding branch B's out-of-fold predictions as inputs to branch A gives it cross-label signal that may help the rare labels, but it also makes A more like B, so the final blend loses diversity; net effect is likely a small gain, and the 30 extra fits add some timeout risk.

The added MLP should be a reasonably strong and fairly diverse model (~0.975 AUC) on the same TF-IDF features. In an equal-weight rank blend it likely gives only a small gain, with the rare labels adding noise, and it should finish within the time budget.

An NB-LogReg on word+char features is typically stronger than B alone and adds some diversity, so the three-way rank blend should gain a small amount; runtime risk is modest since the vectorizers are fit once.

Shrunk per-label rank-blend weights tuned on a holdout usually give only a tiny AUC gain over an equal 0.5/0.5 blend; the main risk is runtime, since refitting both branches roughly doubles the cost and could push the run near the 15-minute kill.
LSA with 300 components discards the rare discriminative n-grams (slurs, threats) that sparse TF-IDF/NB-LR exploit; Jigsaw LSA+LR typically lands ~0.95-0.96 vs ~0.98 for sparse ensembles.

Negative subsampling discards most clean comments (e.g. threat keeps only ~5k of 159k rows), which hurts rare-label AUC through lost negative diversity and noisier NB ratios/fastText vocab, and the rebalancing buys nothing since AUC is rank-based.

One softmax model over all labels gives smoother, less saturated scores than six overfit binary models, so branch F should rank a bit better in the blend; the change to the column mean is small and noisy.

ComplementNB on raw word counts is a standalone NB ranker with no discriminative weights; its scores are distorted by comment length and saturate. Typical Jigsaw NB scores are about 0.93-0.95, well below the NB-LR/TF-IDF ensemble's 0.9816.

Mean-pooled corpus Word2Vec + logistic regression typically scores ~0.95-0.965 AUC on Jigsaw, well below NB-LogReg/TF-IDF ensembles (~0.98), since averaging dilutes sparse toxic-token signal; runtime should fit within budget.
Mean-pooled corpus Word2Vec with linear LR loses the sharp lexical/char signals (slurs, obscenities) that TF-IDF captures; typically ~0.95-0.96 AUC vs ~0.98 for TF-IDF blends.
Char NB-LogReg adds diversity (obfuscated profanity) giving a small AUC gain, partly offset by noisy per-label 3-way weight tuning on a small holdout for the rare labels; runtime stays within budget.
Public kernels found word+char TF-IDF LR peaks around C≈0.1–1 (~0.978-0.979 alone); C=4 overfits, especially on rare labels, slightly hurting branch A and the blend.

fastText without pretrained vectors (epoch=20, lr=0.5) overfits and scores ~0.96-0.97 AUC on rare labels; an equal 1/3 weight on this weaker branch likely dilutes the 0.980 linear blend slightly, and the extra ~3-4 min adds some timeout risk.

A char NB-LogReg branch adds a feature view the other branches lack, so a three-way rank blend typically gains about +0.0005 to +0.001 AUC; the main risk is runtime, since a second char_wb 3-7 vectorizer on ~313k docs plus primal liblinear fits could push the run near the 15-minute kill.

Losing 10% of the training data costs about 0.0005–0.001 AUC. Per-label weights tuned on a small holdout, which is noisy for threat and identity_hate, gain little over 0.5/0.5, so the net effect is roughly flat to slightly negative.
NB weighting may help branch A a little, but it makes branch A more like branch B and so reduces blend diversity; I expect roughly no change, possibly a slight drop.

min_df=1% of ~313k docs (~3.1k docs) collapses the word vocab to a few hundred tokens and char to a few thousand, dropping rare but highly discriminative profanity/slur/threat terms, so AUC falls clearly, especially for the rare labels.

Undersampling discards most negatives (e.g. threat keeps ~478 positives plus ~478 negatives), which hurts ranking quality under fixed C, especially for the rare labels; AUC drops noticeably but the result stays reasonable.

Centroid (Rocchio) classifiers on TF-IDF are much weaker than tuned logistic regression. The dominant negative-class centroid and the tiny score range (in [-2,2], with differences near zero) waste discriminative weighting. NB weighting in branch B helps ordering, but the AUC should still land around 0.92-0.95.

char_wb drops cross-word n-grams. In Jigsaw kernels char and char_wb score about the same, and the NB-LogReg branch dilutes the effect in the blend, so I expect a negligible, slightly negative change.
ComplementNB on TF-IDF gives decent but clearly weaker ranking than LR/NB-LR on Jigsaw (typically ~0.94-0.96 AUC); rank-averaging two NB branches won't recover the gap.
Compressing 60k TF-IDF features to 32 SVD dims badly weakens branch A (likely ~0.93 AUC alone), and the equal-weight rank average with fastText then falls below the current blend.

Collapsing the vocabulary to the 2k most frequent tokens erases rare obscene words, misspellings and obfuscations that the char n-gram and fastText branches rely on (e.g. for threat and identity_hate), so AUC should drop noticeably.

Stop words only take ~300 of the 10k word features, and the char 2-6-grams already capture those tokens; Branch B is unchanged and the blend is rank-averaged, so the effect should be negligible (±0.0002).
Logit averaging effectively overweights the higher-confidence NB-LR branch (C=4) relative to the heavily regularized branch A, reducing ensemble diversity benefit; small AUC drop vs rank average.

char vs char_wb with top-50k features is near-equivalent in Kaggle kernels (char captures cross-word ngrams but top-k selection shifts slightly); expect a tiny change, possibly slight drop, and a runtime risk from slower char fitting.

fastText trained from scratch for 5 epochs with ova loss typically reaches ~0.96-0.97 AUC on Jigsaw, weaker than NB-LogReg (~0.977), so the rank blend with branch A likely drops slightly, though diversity cushions the loss.

Removing 64 descriptors from LR typically hurts on leaf data (all features informative, LR is already well-regularized and separable); the LR component gets somewhat worse, though the NN blend dampens the effect.
Label smoothing caps the NN's confidence near 0.9, so the already-accurate 50/50 blend gets underconfident and log loss worsens.

OvR binary LR with only 10 positives per class at C=1 yields poorly separated, underconfident scores after normalisation; power calibration recovers much of it but multinomial is typically notably better on leaf, so the loss likely rises.

Bagged MLPs on standardized leaf descriptors are strong and diverse from LR; a CV-chosen blend before calibration should moderately lower log loss, with a fallback to LR-only (w=0) limiting the downside.
Averaging the five fold models softens the overconfident high-C probabilities, which usually helps log loss slightly and offsets the 20% less data per model, so expect a small gain.

Image size/aspect/moment features are known to add complementary info on leaf data (top solutions used them), likely reducing logloss moderately, though high C and small data risk some overconfidence.

L2-penalized logistic regression is rotation-invariant, so PCA to 95% variance only drops low-variance directions; with 99 classes those directions often still discriminate, so log loss likely rises modestly.

Fold models are trained on 80% of the data, so they are less confident and a bit less accurate than a single refit on 100%. Averaging the folds smooths the probabilities, but with C fixed this likely raises log loss slightly overall.

The NN on the features plus the silhouette should be reasonably accurate. Arithmetic blending with the LR mainly cuts confident-wrong errors, which should lower log loss. Timing is fine, but the gain depends on how well the NN is calibrated.

LR at C=1 on the standardised 192 features is heavily underconfident, so OOF-tuned power sharpening (a well above 1) should roughly halve the log loss; the eps floor guards against overconfident misses, and applying a tuned on 792-row folds to the more confident full-data refit costs only a little.

On standardized leaf features, logistic regression is well known to prefer much weaker regularisation (C around 100–2000), which drives log loss from about 0.12 down to about 0.04–0.07. The 55 fits should finish within the time budget using 4 parallel jobs.

Image geometry features (aspect ratio, solidity, circularity, Hu moments) add information that complements the 192 precomputed descriptors, and scaled LR at C=1 should use them, likely cutting log loss moderately. The risks are small: some noise from the image size columns, and MLflow is best-effort.
Stronger L2 shrinkage (C=0.2) makes the LR probabilities less confident on well-separated leaf classes, which raises log loss.
Training on 80% instead of 100% leaves roughly 12.8 instead of 16 samples per class for 99 classes, which likely raises the log loss by around 15-30%.

LR is already strong (~0.059); a convex blend with distance-weighted kNN and shrinkage LDA, with weights fit on OOF predictions, usually gives a modest log-loss gain, and SLSQP can fall back to mostly-LR weights if the other models don't help.

GBDT on 99 classes with ~8 samples per class after the 15% holdout (min_samples_leaf=10 is too restrictive) is known to do far worse than logistic regression on leaf features; expect log loss around 0.3–0.8 versus 0.06.

Swapping LR for Platt-calibrated OvR LinearSVC should hurt: 3-fold calibration leaves only 2-3 positives per class per fold, which yields poorly fit sigmoids. The 99-way OvR sigmoid probabilities are also flat and underconfident compared with softmax LR, so this weakens a strong member of the uniform soft-vote.

HGB with only ~9 samples/class likely gave overconfident but often-correct probs; RF with 99 classes gives very diffuse vote-fraction probabilities (max ~0.3-0.5), which diluted by 1/4 raises logloss on correct predictions, though it also removes HGB's catastrophic errors — net likely slightly worse.

An MLP early-stopped on accuracy, with only ~990 samples for 99 classes and 10% held out internally, tends to give less well-calibrated and noisier probabilities than a well-regularised linear softmax on these near-linearly-separable descriptors; the uniform shrinkage recovers some of that, so I expect a modest regression.
On leaf features, a standardised LR with larger C (~30–100) typically reaches log loss around 0.04–0.08 vs ~0.12 at C=1, and the OOF shrinkage will still guard against overconfidence.

Image features add some complementary shape information (area/aspect are informative since images aren't size-normalized), but LR at C=1 on already strong 192 descriptors gains only modestly, and the extra noisy histogram features partially offset the gain.

C=1 on standardized leaf features underfits; CV typically picks C~10-100, which on this dataset gives a noticeably lower log loss (~0.04-0.08), with an 8-9 minute lbfgs runtime risk for 25x10 fits being the main uncertainty.

Uniform soft-voting mixes the strong LR (0.124) with an HGB that is poorly calibrated on ~9 samples/class and an overconfident LDA, and uniform averaging dilutes LR's confident correct predictions, so log loss likely gets worse, though kNN adds some smoothing.
The log loss is dominated by a few confidently wrong predictions, so small out-of-fold-tuned shrinkage toward uniform (alpha ~0.01–0.03) should cut those penalties and modestly lower test log loss.

Fixing shrinkage at 0.9 pushes LDA toward a near-spherical nearest-centroid model, so it discards most of the useful within-class correlation structure. Ledoit-Wolf auto shrinkage is probably much lower here, so accuracy likely drops while the probabilities stay sharp, which raises log loss.

Each family on its own is much weaker than LDA on all 192 features, and arithmetic averaging of the three probability sets keeps the ensemble underconfident, so log loss probably gets worse even though the families carry complementary evidence.

Keeping only 90% of the variance probably drops low-variance components that still separate species, which would likely hurt log loss slightly even with C re-tuned; the leaf descriptors are not very redundant, so the regularization gain is small.
Shrinkage LDA classifies this data well, but its Gaussian posteriors are overconfident, and a few confident misses under log loss likely push it above the well-calibrated tuned logistic regression.

PCA at 95% variance on standardized leaf descriptors drops low-variance but discriminative directions (especially margin/texture fine detail); with C=1 L2 already regularizing, the rotation alone does nothing and the truncation mildly hurts log loss.

Shrinkage LDA is accurate on these features but its decision_function logits are very large, and a temperature capped at 4 cannot fully tame the overconfidence, so the few errors are heavily penalized and log loss likely gets worse than the well-calibrated LR.

C=1 logistic regression is already soft, so few test samples have true-class probability below the ~5e-5 floor; the fixed log(0.995) penalty on confident correct rows (~+0.005) likely outweighs the small tail gains.

With ~1267 training rows, dropping to 384 Nyström landmarks gives a slightly coarser kernel approximation, so log loss should be a little worse or about the same; the added regularization is unlikely to make up for the lost fidelity.

Shrinkage LDA should be about as accurate as logistic regression on these features, or slightly more, but its posteriors are very overconfident, so a few confident misclassifications will likely roughly double the log loss.

On this dataset, standardized-feature logistic regression usually favours weak regularization (C≈100–1000); the CV search will likely pick a high C, roughly halving log loss, and MLflow failures are caught so they won't break the run.

C=1 L2 logistic regression on standardized leaf descriptors is typically underconfident at near-perfect accuracy, so out-of-fold temperature scaling likely picks T<1 and sharpens probabilities, cutting log loss substantially; the MLflow wrapper is best-effort and shouldn't affect results.

An RBF Nyström map with gamma=1/192 on standardized data is nearly linear, but re-standardizing the 512 components and applying C=1 on ~1267 samples makes the fit weaker. The resulting probabilities will likely be less sharp or slightly overfit, so log loss probably worsens a bit.

Adding time trend, length, image, reciprocity and similar features gives a known modest lift on RAOP. With LR on top of TF-IDF the gain is likely around 0.01, and the 31 standardized dense columns may dominate the l2 penalty a little.
RF with sqrt max_features over ~8k sparse columns rarely samples the 9 informative numeric features and splits poorly on sparse TF-IDF, so it typically underperforms linear TF-IDF LR on RAOP.

The random forest will rarely pick the 10 useful dense columns: with max_features='sqrt' it samples about 71 of roughly 5,010 mostly sparse TF-IDF columns per split. It also handles high-dimensional sparse text worse than logistic regression, so AUC likely drops.
On RAOP, 50 LDA topic proportions usually carry less discriminative signal than sublinear TF-IDF unigrams, and the metadata plus giver features dominate either way, so I expect a small AUC drop.
Replacing the supervised TF-IDF LR logit (text AUC ~0.63-0.65) with 20 unsupervised LDA topics loses most text signal; metadata+timestamp alone gives ~0.66-0.68, topics add little.
In RAOP the success rate falls over time, so the timestamp carries real signal that transfers to a randomly split test set; hour and weekday are weak, noisy replacements, so AUC should drop slightly.

A GBM on the requester-history, time, and text-stat features typically lands around 0.66-0.69 AUC, and rank-blending it with the TF-IDF logistic regression adds modest diversity, so I expect a small gain of roughly one AUC point.

RF with max_features=sqrt over ~5000 sparse TF-IDF columns mostly samples uninformative text terms. Fully grown trees on ~4k noisy rows overfit, so it likely underperforms a regularized LR on this text-heavy problem, though the metadata signal limits how far it falls.

Subreddit bag-of-words is known to be weak and noisy on RAOP; the extra 3k sparse features under C=0.3 likely add little signal and may slightly dilute the model, leaving AUC roughly flat to slightly lower.

giver_username_if_known is kept in the test schema and is a near-perfect leak for positives, so the flag should rank a sizable share of test positives at the top; the gain collapses if the test values are mostly 'N/A'.
Stacking OOF text logits with LightGBM on the raw numerics and timestamp (a known useful drift signal) should modestly beat the single LR; the MLflow tracking is best-effort and harmless.

Known-useful RAOP signals (the request-time trend, body length, imgur links, prior RAOP activity) add modest lift to the TF-IDF+LR model; the MLflow wrapper is best-effort and doesn't change predictions.

LR on ~5.4k features with C=0.3 likely overfits (0.62); ExtraTrees with sqrt features will lean on the numeric and dense embedding columns, which are the most informative here, giving comparable or slightly better AUC.

Standardized 384 embedding dims already dominated the weakly regularized LR; dropping sparse TF-IDF removes some noise but also some lexical signal, so expect a small change, likely a slight gain; the mlflow additions are wrapped in try/except, so they are harmless.

In RAOP, length, money, gratitude and link features carry known signal that length-normalized TF-IDF misses, and the scaled dense columns get meaningful weight at C=0.3, so a modest AUC gain is likely.
Request-time metadata alone typically gives about 0.60-0.63 AUC on RAOP; dropping the text signal likely loses a few points versus the text-plus-metadata model.

On RAOP, mean-pooled Word2Vec trained on only ~5.7k short docs is noisy and loses the discriminative token signal (e.g. 'imgur', 'paycheck') that TF-IDF captures, so text contributes about as much or slightly less; with metadata and text stats unchanged, AUC should land roughly flat to slightly lower.

On RAOP the text signal is weak. Adding bigrams with min_df=2 mostly contributes sparse noise, and at C=0.3 the TF-IDF weight gets spread thinner while the dense numeric/stat features carry most of the AUC, so expect roughly flat to slightly worse; the mlflow calls are wrapped in try/except and should be harmless.

On RAOP, the request-time metadata alone reaches roughly 0.60–0.63 AUC. The SVD text features added a small amount, so dropping them should cost a little, though a GBM with num_leaves=63 on 9 features may also overfit less.

An RF on 309 dense SVD+numeric features is roughly comparable to an early-stopped LGBM; it is slightly noisier because sqrt feature sampling mostly picks weak SVD dims and dilutes the strong numeric signals.

MiniLM embeddings add some semantic signal (need, gratitude, reciprocity), but standardized 384-dim dense features at C=0.3 on about 4k samples risk overfitting, so expect only a small gain, assuming the model download succeeds.
Adding many sparse bigrams at C=0.3 with ~4k samples mostly dilutes the TF-IDF signal. The numeric features carry most of the AUC, so the change is likely neutral to slightly worse.

Text length and lexicon statistics are known useful RAOP signals (body length, reciprocity, money mentions), so they should add a small gain over the unigram TF-IDF with LR at C=0.3; the dense features are few relative to 5k sparse columns, which limits the lift.

On ~4k samples, LightGBM with num_leaves=63 over 300 noisy SVD components tends to overfit and usually matches or trails a TF-IDF+LR baseline; the numeric features help GBMs a little, but the SVD text signal is weak, so expect a similar or slightly lower AUC.

In RAOP, success rate declines over time, so the monotonic trend captured by the splines carries more signal than an annual seasonal cycle; replacing the splines with sin/cos loses that trend and should give a small AUC drop.
With C=30 on 5k TF-IDF unigrams and only ~2.3k training rows, the model will overfit badly to text noise and swamp the useful numeric signal, so AUC should drop noticeably.

Success rate in RAOP declines over time, so a smooth spline on request date adds a modest, known signal; test dates fall within the train range after a random split, so the gain is small but positive.

kNN with cosine distance over high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF, where the numeric block dominates the geometry, gives noisy neighborhoods; it typically underperforms logistic regression on RAOP and lands at roughly 0.56–0.61 AUC.

A distance-weighted KNN on nine skewed metadata features gives a noisier, weaker signal than CatBoost, and many near-duplicate zero-activity requesters make the distance weighting erratic, so the blend likely drops slightly.

With ~4.5k samples and 5k unigram features, C=30 overfits the text badly and hurts LR's ranking quality; the 50/50 CatBoost metadata blend dampens the damage but the net effect is still a moderate AUC regression.
Success rate declined over time in RAOP, so date splines add a modest real signal; test is a random split so the effect is small but positive.

BernoulliNB over 5000 binarized n-grams is overconfident, and its many weak text features drown out the useful numeric signal, which is also reduced to above/below-mean indicators; expect AUC somewhat below the LR baseline.

Success rate in RAOP declines over time, so the spline date features add a small real signal. The gain is modest, and the test period overlaps the train range, so constant extrapolation causes little harm.

Subreddit indicators are weakly predictive on RAOP and add roughly 1-2k noisy binary columns at C=0.3, so AUC should move only marginally and probably slightly down; the removed holdout and the best-effort MLflow logging leave predictions unchanged.

The metadata-only CatBoost adds a little nonlinear signal from requester history (AUC around 0.60–0.62 alone), and a 50/50 probability blend with the TF-IDF logistic regression usually gives a small gain; the extra mlflow/psutil dependencies and tracking wrapper don't change predictions.

Bigrams under a fixed 5000-feature cap displace some unigrams and add little signal on RAOP; the numeric features dominate AUC here, so expect roughly no change (±0.005). The added mlflow tracking is best-effort, and removing the holdout split doesn't affect the final full-data fit.
Stop words are strongly author-discriminative in stylometry; char_wb partly recovers them but losing function-word bigrams mildly hurts log loss.

Stacking NB on word and char counts with the TF-IDF LR is a well-known strong combo on Spooky (NB word counts reach about 0.40–0.45 alone and are complementary), so the log-prob meta-LR should cut loss by roughly 10–15%; the fold-averaged test predictions do lose a little from not refitting.

Stop words are highly discriminative for authorship; removing them weakens the word-level LR and NB (NB word is typically the strongest base model), and the char models plus stacker only partially compensate, so log loss worsens modestly.

An LR stacker fed raw probabilities (not log-odds) plus scaled meta-features can't sharpen NB's extreme probabilities nonlinearly the way the GBM can, so it typically loses slightly on this task; its lower variance only partly offsets that.
Punctuation (semicolons, commas, quotes) is a known strong authorial signal in the spooky data, so removing it from the char n-grams loses information and raises log loss.

Current LR at C=1 on the hstacked features is underfit at 0.439. Stacking a C=10 word/char LR with word/char NB and an LR meta-learner typically lands around 0.33-0.36 on this task. The added mlflow tracking is best-effort and doesn't change the model, and runtime should fit the budget.

Keeping only 10k of ~130k TF-IDF columns via chi2 drops useful rare n-gram signal. With C=1 the LR is already underfit rather than overfit, so it will likely get somewhat worse. The NB blend absorbs part of the loss, so the regression should be mild.
Stop words are strong stylometric signals in authorship attribution; removing them hurts NB heavily and LR somewhat (char block partially compensates), so log loss likely worsens.

With C=1 this TF-IDF logistic regression is over-regularized; 5-fold CV will likely pick C around 10–30, which typically lowers log loss to about 0.38–0.40, and 25 explicit fits run 5-way parallel should still finish within the time budget.

An OOF stack of NB on word/char counts with LR at C=10, fed into LightGBM, is known to reach about 0.33-0.36 on Spooky versus 0.43 for a single LR; the mlflow wrapper is best-effort and runtime should be fine.

Cross-boundary, case-sensitive char n-grams add useful stylometric signal. The gain should be small, though: LR at C=1 is already underfit, and spreading the L2-normalized TF-IDF mass over ~400k columns shrinks each feature's weight, which partly offsets the gain.

On this dataset, MultinomialNB on word counts is strong (~0.45 at a well-tuned alpha) and makes errors that differ from the LR's. An OOF-tuned arithmetic blend of the two typically improves log loss by several percent over the underfit C=1 TF-IDF LR.

In authorship attribution the function words carry much of the stylistic signal, so dropping them should hurt; fastText at 0.605 already overfits, and removing stopwords shortens sentences and throws away the frequent bigram cues, so log loss probably rises moderately.

The imbalance is mild, so oversampling adds little. Duplicated rows make fastText (already overconfident at lr 0.5 and 25 epochs) overfit further, and the prior shift miscalibrates probabilities, so log loss likely worsens.

ComplementNB's probabilities are poorly calibrated, but because w is chosen out-of-fold the blend can fall back to near-pure LR (w≈0.8–1.0), so the expected gain is small; the extra 5 parallel fits stay within the time budget.

MNB on stacked sublinear TF-IDF word+char features gives overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities; on Spooky it typically lands around 0.40–0.45 log loss even with tuned alpha, which is worse than the tuned LR's 0.355.
Char n-grams carry strong stylometric signal on this task; word-only NB-SVM with C=4 typically lands around 0.43-0.46 vs 0.409 with the word+char stack.

ComplementNB on TF-IDF gives decent accuracy, but its predict_proba is poorly calibrated: it is a softmax over weakly separated complement log-likelihoods. That should push log loss far above the NB-SVM logistic's 0.41.

TF-IDF LR at C=1 is heavily over-regularized for this task. CV will likely pick C≈10–31, which usually cuts log loss noticeably. Runtime should fit the budget, and MLflow is best-effort, so it shouldn't break the run.

MultinomialNB on word+char TF-IDF typically scores about 0.45–0.55 on this task. Correlated char n-grams double-count evidence and the MinMax-scaled style features distort the likelihoods, so it should be worse than the tuned logistic regression at 0.425.

fastText with lr=0.5 and epoch=25 on ~17k sentences badly overfits and gives overconfident softmax probabilities, which hurts log loss a lot even though accuracy stays decent; TF-IDF+LR is better calibrated.
Word+char TF-IDF logistic regression is under-regularized at C=1, so CV should pick C around 4–8 and lower log loss by about 5–8%; the parallel fits should finish within the time budget.
NB-SVM on TF-IDF with C=4 typically beats plain LR (C=1, underfit) on spooky; one-vs-rest renormalization adds slight miscalibration, but net gain is still likely.
14 MaxAbs-scaled dense style features add weak signal mostly already captured by char n-grams (punctuation); with C=1 LR they get small weights, so expect only a marginal change.

NB feature weighting sharpens the discriminative TF-IDF features and stretches their scale, so C=1 becomes effectively weaker regularization; this usually improves on an underconfident multinomial LR at 0.44, though OvR renormalization may cost a bit of calibration.
TF-IDF logistic regression at C=1 is already underfit on this task (the best C is usually well above 1), so dropping C to 0.25 should flatten the probabilities and push log loss up noticeably.
Dropping the word uni/bigram block removes complementary lexical signal; char_wb 2-5 alone with NB-LR at C=1 typically gives a slightly worse log loss than the word+char combination.

Plain OvR logistic regression at C=1 on L2-normalized TF-IDF is heavily underfit and underconfident, typically landing near 0.55-0.65 log loss. Removing the NB ratios takes away the sharpening that helped the current model, so the loss should get worse.

TF-IDF+LR on spooky typically benefits from higher C (weaker regularization); lowering C to 2 underfits and softens probabilities, raising log loss. Telemetry additions are best-effort and don't affect predictions.

NB-LR one-vs-rest usually helps on text, but independent OvR sigmoids renormalized are less calibrated for log loss, and C=4 on NB-scaled features tends to overfit, giving overconfident probabilities, so a slight regression is more likely than a gain.
Stop words are strong stylometric signals for authorship, so removing them from both the word and char branches discards key features and should noticeably worsen log loss.
TF-IDF LR on spooky typically benefits from larger C (weaker regularization); C=0.25 underfits, and temperature scaling only partially recovers sharpness, so the loss likely worsens modestly.

'char' analyzer captures cross-word punctuation/spacing patterns that help stylometry; the 60k cap limits gains, so expect a small improvement (the removed holdout and added telemetry don't change the final fit).

NB log-ratio scaling amplifies discriminative features, which acts like weaker regularization for the under-fit C=1 LR; that typically helps on Spooky, but OvR renormalization limits calibration, so expect a modest gain.
LR on TF-IDF with C=1 is typically underfit (log loss ~0.43); raising C to 4 sharpens probabilities and usually lowers log loss to ~0.38-0.41 before overfitting sets in.

TF-IDF LR at C=1 is typically underconfident, so the fitted temperature should come out below 1; sharpening the probabilities lowers log loss by a few percent, somewhat less than on the holdout because the full-data refit is already slightly more confident.

A log1p target with expm1 inversion predicts the conditional median rather than the mean, which slightly biases predictions low, and early stopping on log-scale RMSE doesn't target dollar RMSE; RMSE on valid rows likely rises a bit, while the invalid-row floor is unchanged.
Four times more training data should modestly lower error on the valid rows, but the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the gain, and the run should still fit the time budget.

The airport-distance features help with the flat JFK fares and the EWR surcharges. The gain is diluted by the noise floor from roughly 2.8% corrupt test rows, and trees can partly learn airport locations from the raw coordinates already.

Log1p targets with L2 loss predict the conditional geometric mean, which underestimates expensive trips. RMSE is dominated by high-fare outliers and by corrupt rows that fall back to NaN features, so the in-dollar RMSE usually worsens slightly.

Monotone constraint on distance mostly holds already. But the default 'basic' method restricts splits, and airport flat fares plus noisy short trips make the true fare non-monotone given the raw coordinates, so the RMSE should come out about the same or slightly worse.
Log target with expm1 back-transform biases predictions low (geometric vs. arithmetic mean) and underfits high fares, so dollar RMSE should get slightly worse.

In-sample encoding leaks each row's own fare into its encoding. For rare route keys, the trees can recover the fare exactly from fare_mean and count, so they overfit a pattern that is absent at test time; early stopping only partly limits the damage.

Taking expm1 of a log-space fit yields the conditional geometric mean, which biases predictions low. Under an RMSE metric this typically hurts slightly on high-fare tail trips, while the variance-stabilization benefit is small at 1M rows; the score is also dominated by the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows.
Airport distances help trees isolate flat-rate and surcharge trips, trimming the valid-row RMSE a bit, but the fixed floor from corrupt rows dilutes the gain.

Invalid-coordinate rows (~2.8%) dominate error; learning the fare distribution of that subpopulation from training data (instead of the global mean of valid rows) gives a modest gain, while valid rows are barely affected.
Four times more data gives a modest gain for the GBM on valid rows (about 3.6 to 3.53), but the roughly 2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the overall improvement.

OOF route/cell target encodings add modest signal (JFK flat fares, tolls) beyond raw coordinates that GBM already partly exploits; the 2.1 corrupt-row floor dilutes gains, so expect a small improvement.
Log target optimizes geometric mean under RMSE, biasing predictions low (especially fallback rows with high variance, where median << mean), slightly worsening dollar RMSE.
Manhattan distance and bearing give a small, consistent gain on valid rows (~3.6→~3.55), but total RMSE is dominated by the ~2.1 floor from corrupt rows, so the overall improvement is small.
Landmark distances help trees capture airport flat fares, a modest gain on valid rows while the corrupt-row floor dilutes it.

The L1 objective fits the conditional median, which sits below the mean on right-skewed fares, so predictions are biased low for RMSE. L1 gradient boosting also converges more slowly and handles long airport and toll trips worse, so RMSE on the valid rows rises modestly while the error floor from corrupt test rows stays the same.

Log target with expm1 predicts the geometric rather than arithmetic mean, so predictions are biased low; RMSE is dominated by the high-fare tail, so this usually slightly hurts RMSE on taxi fares, and the 2.1 floor from invalid rows is unchanged.
An L1 objective predicts the conditional median rather than the mean, so RMSE usually gets slightly worse on right-skewed fares; L1 boosting in LightGBM also converges more slowly within 1000 rounds.

Huber with delta=$1 targets something closer to the conditional median; RMSE is scored on heavy-tailed labels (airport flat fares, tolls), so predictions biased low on the tail likely raise RMSE slightly, plus slower convergence at lr 0.05.

A log-target model predicts roughly the conditional median rather than the mean, which biases fares low (expm1 of E[log]); RMSE on raw dollars usually gets slightly worse on the taxi data, and the 2.1 corrupt-row floor dilutes the effect.
Airport distances help the tree capture JFK flat fares on valid rows (~3.6→~3.5), but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows dominates, so overall gain is small.
4x data modestly lowers RMSE on valid rows, but the corrupt-row floor and the 1000-tree/lr 0.05 cap limit the gain; should fit in time.
5-fold bagging of identical LGBM models reduces variance slightly on the ~97% valid rows, but the corrupt-row floor dominates RMSE so the gain is small.
An out-of-fold pickup-cell target encoding adds little on top of raw coordinates, which the GBM already splits finely; the 2.1 floor from corrupt rows dominates, so expect a tiny gain or no change.
Snapping coordinates to a 0.01° grid (about 1 km) makes distance_km coarse, which throws away the dominant fare signal on short Manhattan trips, so RMSE on the valid rows should rise noticeably.

L1 loss predicts the median rather than the mean. Taxi fares are right-skewed, so this biases predictions low and raises RMSE. L1 gradient boosting also converges more slowly in 1000 rounds, so a small regression is expected.

L1 targets the conditional median rather than the mean, and fares are right-skewed, so the metric (RMSE) gets slightly worse on valid rows. L1 boosting also converges more slowly within 1000 rounds, which likely outweighs any gain from robustness to outliers.

Airport-distance features give LightGBM a cleaner signal for flat-rate and surcharge airport trips than raw coordinates alone, but the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the gain, so expect a modest improvement.

An L1 objective predicts the conditional median, which sits below the mean for right-skewed fares, and it trains more slowly with eval on RMSE, so RMSE on the valid rows likely worsens slightly while the ~2.1 floor from corrupt rows stays the same.

Two-decimal rounding (~1km grid) removes fine location detail, such as airport pinpointing, that LightGBM with 2M rows could exploit; the haversine distance is kept, so the loss should be slight, and the RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dampens the change.

An L1 objective predicts the conditional median, which sits below the mean for right-skewed fares, so RMSE on valid rows rises slightly; L1 in LightGBM also converges slower, and the invalid-row floor is unchanged.
Rotated Manhattan distance adds a small but real signal beyond haversine and raw coordinates; the invalid-row floor dominates the total RMSE, so the gain is tiny.

An OOF-smoothed route target encoding on 0.01° cells is sparse at 900k rows, so it adds only modest route and airport-flat signal beyond the raw coordinates plus distance; the corrupt-row floor dominates the total RMSE, so expect a small gain.

Rotated Manhattan distance adds modest signal beyond haversine+raw coords, but the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes gains; the diff only adds MLflow logging and removes a print, so the model is otherwise unchanged.

Doubling data gives a small gain on the ~3.6 valid-row RMSE, but the fixed ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows mutes the effect; MLflow/logging additions don't touch predictions, and 2M rows fits the time budget.

Airport route flags help a bit with the JFK flat fare and Newark surcharges, but the raw coordinates already let the trees approximate these regions, and the RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the gain, so expect a small improvement.

Without engineered interaction or unique-character-count features, LightGBM needs many trees to approximate the linear-combination interactions, and at 2000 rounds (lr 0.05) it is likely still improving, so it should land slightly below the MLP's 0.9866, around 0.978–0.984.

TPS May 2022 depends on precise continuous thresholds and cross-feature interactions such as f_21+f_02 and f_22+f_05; decile binning discards within-bin resolution on the floats, and one-hot inputs make those linear-sum interactions harder to learn, so AUC should drop noticeably.

TPS May 2022 features are nearly uncorrelated, so PCA whitening is essentially an arbitrary rotation that smears the key f_27 char / f_29-f_30 integer structure and axis-aligned interactions across all components, hurting trees; the linear leaves partly compensate but can't fully recover it.

f_27 strings are nearly unique (~700k distinct of 800k), so the whole-string target encoding collapses to roughly the prior and carries almost no signal, while the per-character information that drives much of the AUC is discarded.

f_27 is almost unique per row, so a whole-string target encoding collapses to roughly the prior. Dropping the per-position character columns removes a key signal, leaving only nunique and the numeric columns, so AUC should fall noticeably.

These are the known TPS-May22 interaction features (famous ternary indicators); GBDT with 3000 trees already partially captures them, and nunique is already present, so expect a modest ~0.001 AUC gain.
Logistic regression scores only ~0.78 AUC on this interaction-heavy data, so an equal-weight rank average with it substantially degrades the 0.984 LightGBM ranking.

The known 64-64-64-16 SiLU MLP recipe for TPS May 2022 captures its smooth interactions better than LightGBM (about 0.997 with unique-char counts), and without those counts it should still land around 0.993–0.995; 80 CPU epochs should fit inside the time budget.

A SiLU MLP picks up the linear-combination interactions in this data (f_00+f_01, f_21 and similar) better than trees. Without the unique-character count feature it should land only slightly above the 0.977 LightGBM score, around 0.98, well inside the time budget.

Linear leaves suit the oblique sum-threshold boundaries and should add a small AUC gain over the still-improving 3000-tree baseline, but the gain is modest because the missing f_27 unique-char and interaction features dominate the remaining error. Linear-tree fitting also risks slowing the run toward the timeout.

In TPS May 2022, the unique-character count of f_27 is known to be a very strong feature that trees struggle to reconstruct from per-position ordinals, so it typically lifts LightGBM AUC from about 0.977 to about 0.988-0.99.

These three sums are the known planted interactions in TPS May 2022. Exposing them directly lets the trees split on boundaries they otherwise approximate poorly, which should give a solid AUC gain even without the unique-character-count feature.

f_27 is almost unique per row, so LightGBM's categorical handling (min_data_per_group=100, max_cat_threshold) finds nearly no usable splits on it; dropping the per-position characters loses real signal, partly offset by the letter counts that remain.

Bigram categoricals with 676 levels add little signal beyond per-position ordinals and counts, and high-cardinality categorical splits in LightGBM tend to overfit slightly; expect roughly flat to a small regression.

The continuous features are nearly independent, so PCA factors are arbitrary rotations that miss the key sum interactions (e.g. f_21+f_02, f_00+f_01+f_26); losing the mined products probably costs a little AUC.
Hashing whole near-unique f_27 strings into 64 buckets destroys the strong per-position character signal, so AUC drops substantially.

ExtraTrees without engineered f_27 or interaction features is much weaker than LightGBM on this dataset (roughly 0.92 AUC versus 0.978). The added 5-fold CV runs before the submission is written, so the run may also be killed for exceeding the time limit.

NNs capture this dataset's smooth continuous interactions better than axis-aligned trees. The sklearn MLP without unique-char features, plus accuracy-based early stopping that may stop training early, should still land about level with or slightly above the LightGBM score of 0.978.
The f_27 unique-character count is a known strong signal in TPS May 2022, and adding it plus the letter counts should lift a GBDT with no interaction features by about 0.003–0.004 AUC.
Per-position f_27 characters carry strong signal and most full strings are near-unique, so a frequency count can't replace them; AUC should fall to roughly numeric-only levels.
f_27 unique-char count is a known strong feature in TPS May 2022 that trees can't derive from positional ordinals; I expect a moderate AUC gain.

The known TPS-May interactions are sums involving f_21, f_22 and f_26, which fall outside f_00..f_15 (and f_07..f_15 are integer columns), so the mined products mostly add noise and dilute colsample, giving a tiny change or slight regression.
Early stopping never fires, so stage 2 refits on 100% of rows with ~3333 trees; the extra data and extra trees give a small AUC gain, assuming two fits still finish within the time budget.

Categorical splits give only a marginal gain here: many f_27 positions are low-cardinality and near-ordinal, so trees already handle them well, and the key signal (unique-char count) is still missing.
The f_27 unique-char count is a well-known strong feature in TPS May 2022 and is hard for trees to derive from ordinal positions, so expect a gain of roughly +0.003 to +0.004 AUC.
TPS May 2022 depends on high-order interactions (f_27 chars, f_21/f_22 etc.), so depth-2 trees with 3000 rounds at lr 0.05 can't capture them and AUC drops substantially, landing around 0.94-0.95.
Small LightGBM (600 trees, 31 leaves, no interaction/unique-char features) captures TPS-May interactions far worse than the MLP, likely ~0.93-0.94 AUC.

A small LightGBM (600 trees, 31 leaves) with no interaction features badly underfits the f_00–f_28 interactions that the MLP captures; typical TPS-May scores for such a model are about 0.93–0.95 versus the MLP's 0.982, and selecting on logloss instead of the specified AUC changes little.

Quartile-binning all 16 continuous features throws away most of the fine-grained linear interaction signal (for example f_21+f_02 and f_00+f_01+f_20). The integer features and f_27 characters still carry a good share, so AUC should drop well below the baseline but not collapse.
TPS May 2022 depends on high-order interactions that small trees capture poorly; with only 7 leaves and 3000 trees at lr 0.05, the model will likely underfit, even with categorical char columns.

4-leaf trees can only model 2–3-way interactions per tree, and even 3000 rounds at lr 0.05 won't fully recover the multi-feature interactions this dataset relies on, so AUC should fall substantially from 0.9915.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known planted interactions in TPS May 2022; making it explicit lets trees split on it directly, giving a meaningful AUC gain, though the other two interactions remain unexposed.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the known TPS-May-22 planted interactions; trees split on the explicit sum far more efficiently than on the three raw columns, giving a modest AUC gain. The other interactions (f_21+f_02, f_22+f_05) and the unique-character count are still missing, which caps the gain.

In TPS May 2022, SiLU MLPs are known to learn the linear-combination interactions (f_00+f_01 etc.) far better than depth-limited GBDT, so a scaled MLP should beat 0.977 even without unique-char features. Around 50 epochs should fit in the CPU time budget.

Categorical splits on char positions (≤20 levels) allow grouping of letters, which could slightly help, but most signal comes from missing interaction and unique-char features, so the effect is marginal.
In TPS May 2022, the unique-character count of f_27 is a known strong feature that is hard for trees to reconstruct from per-position ordinals, so it should give a gain of roughly +0.01 AUC.

Weighting pixels by target darkness mismatches the unweighted RMSE metric, and the optimum shifts toward darker predictions on uncertain pixels, which adds error on the dominant white background; expect a small regression.

Moving from 2000 steps to a 330 s wall-clock budget should give roughly 10-20x more steps with a proper cosine anneal to zero; the small U-Net is clearly undertrained at 2000 steps, so RMSE should drop substantially, tempered by some overfitting risk on only 105 training images.

L1 should push the background to exactly 1.0, but it optimizes for the median rather than the mean on ambiguous stroke-edge pixels, which slightly hurts RMSE; I expect roughly neutral to a small regression, within the noise of a single run.

Train and test noise come from the same synthetic distribution, so absolute intensity is a strong cue; input-only brightness/contrast jitter (±0.1, ×0.8–1.2) destroys that cue and makes exact gray-level reconstruction harder, likely raising RMSE slightly rather than helping generalization.

The model was trained at a single scale, so the resampled passes are out of distribution. The 0.75x down/up round trip and the antialiased resizes blur sharp text edges, and pixel RMSE penalises that heavily, so averaging those passes with the good 1x prediction likely makes it worse.

The model is undertrained rather than overfit after only 2000 steps of dense pixel regression, so Dropout2d on the deep features and on the e2 skip adds noise and slows convergence, which likely hurts RMSE modestly.

Dropout2d in every block, including the final decoder block that feeds the 1x1 output conv, adds noise to a pixel-precise regression task that is time-limited and underfit rather than overfit; that costs fidelity and convergence speed, so RMSE is likely to rise moderately.

A larger receptive field helps capture stains and background gradients. Baseline val RMSE is already very low and training is time-bounded, so fewer steps partly offset the gain; expect a modest improvement.

A full-image median-23 background channel gives the 128px-crop U-Net global stain context that it can't infer easily from its limited receptive field, which likely helps a bit; since the baseline is already at 0.016, the gain should be modest, and the diff looks correct.

A larger receptive field and 256px context should help remove large-scale stains and backgrounds, so I expect a modest gain. The gain is tempered by batch 8 with BatchNorm, less crop diversity and the short 2000-step schedule for a bigger net.

The model was trained with random flips, so averaging over 4 flips should cut prediction variance and give a small, reliable RMSE gain. Unflipping before cropping is geometrically correct, and eval-mode BatchNorm makes the batch of 4 safe.

A 180s time budget (the implementation defaults to 180s, not the specified 360s) likely gives several times more than the baseline's 2000 steps on GPU, so the undertrained U-Net should reach noticeably lower RMSE, with diminishing returns.

Charbonnier fits a median-like target that doesn't match the RMSE metric, and its sign-like gradients near zero under bf16 and Adam give little gain on an already clean white background, so expect a slight RMSE regression.

The model is already near a 0.015 RMSE floor, and the injected Gaussian noise (sigma 0.05) creates a train/test distribution mismatch; test images have no such noise, so the augmentation mostly wastes capacity and blurs fine stroke edges, likely a modest regression.

GroupNorm still computes its statistics over the input's spatial extent, so it trades BN's consistent running stats for a crop-vs-full-page statistics mismatch, and it discards absolute intensity levels that matter for regressing pixel values; expect similar or slightly worse RMSE.

SSIM+L1 no longer optimizes the RMSE metric directly. SSIM's luminance term barely penalizes small offsets on the near-white background, which is most of the pixels, and L1 only partly compensates, so RMSE likely degrades somewhat.

Eight-way TTA averages away prediction noise, including bf16 noise. The 90° rotations were never seen in training, which only used flips, but local stroke and background features transfer reasonably, so expect a small net gain rather than a regression.

Pure SSIM loss barely penalizes small brightness offsets in the near-white flat background (its luminance term is almost flat near mu=1, and C2 dominates when local variance is near zero). Background pixels dominate the RMSE, so dropping MSE lets background bias build up and roughly doubles the per-pixel RMSE despite sharper strokes.

The residual head drops the sigmoid, which was already pinning the white background near 1; the final clamp recovers much of that, but bf16 quantization of larger noise residuals and the loss of the easy prior likely make it about the same or slightly worse.
Adam largely cancels the sqrt rescaling, so the change mostly adds an SSIM term that grows dominant at low RMSE and isn't aligned with the pixel metric; expect a neutral to slightly worse score.

Documents here are mostly clean white background plus stains, so the residual is large and structured rather than small noise. That removes the sigmoid's easy saturation at 1.0, so the linear output must hit the background exactly, and training penalizes overshoot even though the output is clamped at inference; expect roughly similar or slightly worse RMSE.

Synthetic noise (whole-image blur, ellipse stains, speckle) doesn't match the real noise, and real pairs drop to ~14% of samples under the same 2000-step budget, so the model under-fits the true distribution.

At 2k steps the small U-Net is clearly undertrained, so 4.5x more steps with the cosine schedule stretched to match should cut RMSE meaningfully; 9k small-batch GPU steps should still fit comfortably within the time budget.

The TTA inverses are correct, and averaging 8 views of a fully-convolutional denoiser usually cuts variance and bf16 noise for a few-percent RMSE gain; the transposed views were never seen in training (only flips), which slightly limits the benefit.

L1 targets the median rather than the mean, which mismatches the RMSE metric; at this low error level most error sits on ambiguous text-edge pixels, so L1 likely gives a slightly worse RMSE, partly offset by cleaner saturated backgrounds.
Weighting dark targets 3x pushes uncertain edge pixels darker, which no longer matches the unweighted per-pixel RMSE metric, so expect a small regression rather than a gain.

Weighting pixels by the target makes the per-pixel optimum a target-weighted mean, which pulls ambiguous edge and background pixels darker. That mismatch with plain RMSE probably causes a small regression, partly offset by better-fitted ink strokes.

Residual learning with zero-init output starts from identity and makes the easy background correction explicit. The inference clamp keeps the sigmoid's saturation benefit, so expect a modest gain or parity under the same budget.

L1 pushes background harder toward exactly 1.0, which helps, but it targets the median rather than the mean at anti-aliased stroke edges, which RMSE penalizes; I expect roughly neutral to slightly worse over this short CPU schedule.

The clean targets are mostly saturated white, which the sigmoid reaches easily; the residual head must instead learn large, image-dependent corrections (1 - x) for structured stains, and training penalizes overshoot, so under the same short CPU budget it will likely do slightly worse, partly offset by clipping at inference.
Halving the width cuts parameters about 4x under the same short 2000-step budget; the model is likely capacity-limited rather than overfitting on patch training, so RMSE should get moderately worse.

Weighted MSE misaligns the training objective with the uniform-RMSE metric; the model gets more accurate on strokes but slightly worse on the dominant white background, so the net effect is a small regression or roughly neutral with run-to-run noise (the runtime.json now pins CPU, and the parent result presumably ran on the same setup).

A background-normalized input from a 31x31 grey closing is a strong hand-made feature for removing stains, so a modest RMSE gain is likely; the main risk is that the diff forces CPU with 8 threads, which could make 2,000 steps slow or push the run toward the time limit.

Likely no score at all: the applied diff adds an out-of-scope runtime.toml that sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="" and forces CPU execution, and 2000 steps of batch-32 128x128 U-Net training (~700 TFLOP) on 8 CPU threads would far exceed the 15-minute hard kill; the metric shown is only what the requested fp32 head alone would give (≈0.0162, essentially unchanged), and that CPU-forcing file should be removed rather than trusted.

If the run completes, four-view flip TTA typically cuts RMSE by about 1–3%. But the diff also adds a runtime.json that sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="", which forces CPU training (about 2000 steps at batch 32 on 128px U-Net crops). That is very likely to exceed the 15-minute hard kill, so the most probable outcome is a failed run with no score.

The residual NAFNet has fewer FLOPs than the U-Net but is less expressive at 16 base channels, and its many LayerNorm/elementwise ops make it slow on the CPU the new runtime.json forces, so after 2000 steps it probably lands roughly on par to slightly worse, with some timeout risk.

ConvNeXt's pretrained ImageNet head already classifies exactly these 120 breeds, and many Stanford Dogs images were probably in its training data, so blending it with the LR at a holdout-tuned weight and temperature should cut log loss substantially.

Unwhitened PCA is a rotation plus truncation, and the L2 penalty is rotation-invariant, so the only effect is discarding the 768 low-variance directions; for fine-grained breeds these carry small but real signal, so expect roughly equal or slightly worse log loss.

Full-strength Mixup/CutMix (prob=1.0) over only 6 epochs on ~8k images slows convergence of an already strong in22k-pretrained model and leaves it underconfident; temperature scaling recovers only part of the calibration loss, so log loss likely gets slightly worse.

In a short 6-epoch fine-tune of a strong in22k backbone, the more aggressive 0.08 crops add train/test distribution shift and slow convergence (tiny crops often miss the dog), so val/test log loss likely worsens slightly despite the extra regularization.

ConvNeXt-V2-L (IN-22k to IN-1k) frozen features plus its ImageNet logits are much stronger than ResNet-50 V1 on dog breeds, which are an ImageNet subset, so linear-probe log loss should roughly halve; runtime stays well within budget.

The log-softmax block is a nonlinear function of the pooled vector, not a redundant one. It encodes ImageNet's own 118 dog-class heads, which map almost directly onto these breeds and whose training overlaps these images, so dropping it should noticeably worsen the linear probe's log loss.

A ridge (least-squares) probe with a single global temperature usually gives less calibrated probabilities than a tuned multinomial logistic regression on strong frozen features, so log loss likely gets somewhat worse even though the classification boundaries are similar.

Keeping 128 PCA components per block drops some low-variance directions that still help separate fine-grained breeds, and L2-regularised LR already handles 2560-d well, so expect a mild log-loss regression, partly offset by centering and a tighter C search.

Frozen ConvNeXt-Base features (ImageNet-22k pretrained, fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k) are much stronger than ResNet-50 V1 features for fine-grained dog breeds, and choosing C on a holdout should cut log loss substantially, to roughly 0.28–0.34; runtime should stay well within budget.

Fully fine-tuning an ImageNet-22k ConvNeXt-Tiny with flip TTA and temperature scaling should reach roughly 89-91% accuracy and a lower log loss than frozen ResNet-50 features with logistic regression; 6 epochs fit within the time budget.

The ImageNet head's log-probabilities over the 120 breed classes are very strong features (Stanford Dogs images likely overlap ImageNet train), so standardizing them and retuning C should cut log loss meaningfully, though the 880 non-dog noise dims and scaling artifacts limit the gain.

ConvNeXt-in22k, CLIP and DINOv2 features are each much stronger than ResNet-50 on fine-grained dogs, where ImageNet overlap also helps. Concatenating the L2-normalised blocks with a tuned-C logistic regression should cut log loss substantially, though the linear probe and possible underconfidence limit the gain.

Focal loss with gamma=2 shrinks gradients, so at the same LR the 10-epoch fine-tune learns more slowly; it also tends to give underconfident softmax outputs, much like label smoothing, so accuracy likely drops a little with no calibration gain and log loss gets slightly worse.

Stanford Dogs overlaps ImageNet, so freezing conv1–layer3 limits forgetting and overfitting at lr=0.01, giving a modest gain; label smoothing still keeps log loss inflated, and frozen BN layers still update running stats in train mode.

Horizontal-flip TTA with probability averaging on frozen ViT features usually gives a small, reliable log-loss gain of about 1–3%, and NUM_WORKERS=0 slows loading but should still finish well within the time budget.

CLIP ViT-B/32 linear probes are weaker on fine-grained dog breeds than an in21k→in1k ViT-B/16, whose ImageNet-1k fine-tune already includes these 120 dog classes. The coarse patch grid and a C value tuned for different feature scales likely increase log loss.

PCA without whitening only rotates the features and drops low-variance directions, and the L2-regularised logistic regression already shrinks weight on those directions; so the main effect is losing some fine-grained breed signal that lives outside the top 256 components (roughly 20-25% of the variance), which should slightly worsen log loss.

A frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 linear probe should beat a frozen ResNet-50 on fine-grained dog breeds, even though ResNet-50's supervised ImageNet training already covers these classes, so I expect a moderate log-loss gain. The run should stay well within the time budget, and C re-selection keeps the logistic regression well calibrated.

Whitening gives the 256 components unit variance.
