Before, the L2-normalised features were tiny per dimension, so C=1.0 now regularises far more weakly and the logistic head should overfit into overconfident probabilities; the truncation also drops some discriminative signal, so log loss likely gets worse.

k-NN vote probabilities are poorly calibrated. When the true breed gets none of the 10 neighbour votes (roughly 5–10% of test images), the 1e-3 prior leaves it with about 9e-4 probability, costing about 7 nats each. Near-uniform distance weights also make the other probabilities coarse, so log loss should rise well above logistic regression's 0.54.

Frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 features are already very strong on this ImageNet dog subset, so fine-tuning the whole network at lr 0.01 on about 9k images for 10 epochs likely lands near the same or slightly lower accuracy, and label smoothing of 0.1 caps confidence, which inflates log loss relative to the calibrated logistic regression.

ViT-B/16 features pretrained on ImageNet-21k and fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k give a much stronger frozen linear probe for fine-grained dog breeds than ResNet-50 V1, so log loss should drop substantially even with C=0.3 left untuned.

Averaging probabilities over 10 crop-and-flip views usually lowers log loss modestly. The gain is tempered because the classifier was trained only on center-crop features, so corner crops are off-distribution and can cut off parts of the dog.

ConvNeXt in22k features add real signal, but on unit-norm features C=1.0 regularises far more heavily than C=0.3 did on raw ResNet features (norms around 30), so predictions will be badly underconfident and log loss will rise despite good accuracy.

The pretrained ResNet-50 head restricted to the 120 dog classes is strong (Stanford Dogs overlaps ImageNet), and a temperature-scaled blend with the logistic regression, tuned on a held-out split, should cut log loss noticeably.

A non-whitened PCA is just a rotation plus truncation, and the L2 penalty is rotation-invariant, so the only real effect is dropping the discriminative low-variance directions beyond the top 256; that cost matters for 120 fine-grained breeds, so log loss should get modestly worse.

ResNet-50 was trained with average pooling, so max-pooled features are off-distribution and noisier. They are also larger in scale, which effectively weakens C=0.3 regularization. A linear probe on them typically loses some accuracy, and temperature scaling only partly recovers calibration, so log loss likely gets worse.

The V2 weights were trained with a heavy recipe (label smoothing, mixup/cutmix, long schedule), which is known to make penultimate features transfer worse for linear probes; that likely outweighs its higher ImageNet accuracy, even though these dog classes overlap ImageNet, so I expect a mild regression.

C=0.3 already won the holdout sweep over 0.03, so C=0.03 gives an underconfident head with shrunken logits; two short, low-learning-rate fine-tuning epochs only partly restore confidence, so log loss likely gets worse.

Running the ImageNet-224 ResNet50 at 192px shrinks objects further from their training scale (a FixRes-style mismatch) and loses fine detail that fine-grained breed classification relies on, so log loss should rise noticeably; the short, BN-frozen fine-tune of the last block cannot adapt enough to recover it.

Since the L2 penalty is rotation-invariant and the intercept is unpenalized, unwhitened PCA only discards the low-variance directions beyond 256, which lose a bit of fine-grained signal and slightly raise log loss.

Lowering the input from 224 to 192 for a frozen ResNet-50 trained at 224 shrinks the object scale relative to what the backbone expects and discards fine texture detail, and fine-grained breed features are sensitive to that. I expect a moderate log-loss regression.

V2 weights reach higher ImageNet accuracy, and the dog breeds are ImageNet classes, but V2's training with label smoothing, mixup and cutmix tends to hurt linear-probe transfer and calibration, and C=0.3 was tuned on V1 features, so I expect only a small log-loss gain; the removed TORCH_HOME setting also adds download-location risk.

One temperature fitted on the holdout should only fix a small miscalibration left by the L2-regularised logistic regression, so expect a gain of a few percent; there is a small risk from the dropped TORCH_HOME cache path.

Two short epochs at low learning rates, starting from the already-regularised logistic-regression head with no augmentation, should move the last bottleneck and head only slightly, so the log loss changes marginally and probably ends a little better.

Averaging probabilities over the original and flipped views of frozen ResNet-50 features usually cuts log loss by a few percent; the MLflow/tempdir wrapper is fault-tolerant, so it should not break the run.

1:1 undersampling discards most negatives: threat keeps ~960 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k and severe_toxic ~3.2k. That leaves the rare-label models and their NB ratios noisy and overfit, especially NB-LogReg at C=4. AUC does not need rebalancing, so the rare columns should lose AUC and pull the mean down about 0.01.

Adding char_wb n-grams to NB-LogReg usually lifts that branch by a few thousandths of AUC, but both branches then share the char block, so the blend loses diversity and should net only a small gain, around +0.0004. Runtime is the main risk: six liblinear fits on ~136M nonzeros could push the run toward the 15-minute kill, partly offset by fitting the char vectorizer once.

Undersampling to 1:1 throws away most negatives; for threat and identity_hate that leaves about 1-3k training rows. That starves the high-dimensional sparse models and noisily estimates the NB ratios, and since AUC is insensitive to class prior, there is no gain to offset the loss, so rare-label AUCs fall noticeably.

MultinomialNB on TF-IDF is much weaker than NB-LogReg on this task (per-label AUC roughly 0.93-0.95, and poorly ranked on rare labels), so a 50/50 rank average with it, plus weaker stacked OOF features for branch A, should drag the ensemble below branch A alone.

Mean-pooled corpus Word2Vec plus linear LR likely scores only about 0.95-0.96 AUC; that is well below the word+char TF-IDF branch it replaces (about 0.977), which also removes the strong char n-gram signal. The MLP on 200 dense dimensions is also weaker, so the equal-weight rank blend with NB-LR should drop by about 0.5 point.

AUC ignores class priors, so balancing brings no ranking benefit. Discarding 80-99% of negatives, down to about 1k rows for threat, loses negative-side diversity. With C fixed, the effective L2 on the small subsets is much stronger, so every branch gets weaker and the score drops moderately.

A sparse TF-IDF MLP (about 0.976–0.978 alone) adds some non-linear, shared-hidden-layer diversity to three fairly correlated linear branches, so an equal-weight rank blend likely gains about 0.0005; the time guards make a skip (no change) the main downside risk.

Balanced undersampling throws away 80-99% of the negatives. That hurts AUC because ranking depends on modelling the negative background, and rare labels like threat (~956 rows) and identity_hate lose the most. The expected result is a drop of roughly 0.5-1 AUC point, with no calibration benefit to offset it under a rank metric.

TF-IDF already lowercases, and the char n-grams already catch most obfuscations, so the de-obfuscation gains are small and roughly offset by the signal lost from collapsing repeated characters and punctuation; expect a near-zero net change.

Branch A gains an informative cross-label OOF signal from B, but that makes A more correlated with B, so the rank blend loses diversity; expect a small net gain, with some runtime risk from the 30 extra liblinear fits.

A 3-epoch shared-hidden-layer MLP on the TF-IDF features should reach roughly 0.975-0.98 AUC on its own and add some nonlinear diversity, so the equal-weight rank blend probably gains slightly; weaker rare-label heads and a plausible fit time of a few minutes cap the gain and add some risk.

Branch C is an NB-LogReg on word plus char n-grams, a strong model that adds some diversity, so an equal three-way rank blend should give a small gain; the capped liblinear iterations should keep runtime within budget.

Per-label holdout blend weights, shrunk halfway toward 0.5, only nudge an already near-optimal rank average (expected gain about +0.0001 AUC, within rare-label noise); the extra 80% refit, including the costly char vectorizer, adds a few minutes but should still finish under the 15-minute kill.

A 300-d LSA compression discards the rare, highly discriminative profanity and slur n-grams and the char features. Dense LR on those factors typically scores about 0.94–0.96 on this task, well below the sparse NB-LR/char ensemble, and the drop is largest on threat and identity_hate.

Toxic keeps nearly all rows, but threat, identity_hate and severe_toxic lose about 90% of negatives, so the rare-label models see fewer hard negatives and their AUC drops; rank-based AUC gains nothing from rebalancing, so expect a modest regression.

Guessing a small gain. The 0.883 parent is far below what the TF-IDF branches alone should reach, which points to the six per-label fastText models (20 epochs) giving overfit, saturated or tied probabilities that drag down the rank blend. A single softmax model over 7 classes should give smoother, better-ordered scores for the rare labels, but it only changes one of three branches, and I can't pin down why the parent score is so low.

On binary labels, ComplementNB ranks the same as multinomial NB, and NB on raw bigram counts is dominated by comment length and overconfident likelihood sums, so it typically scores only ~0.93–0.95 mean AUC here, well below the 0.98 NB-LogReg and TF-IDF LogReg ensemble.

Linear heads on mean-pooled, corpus-trained word2vec usually land around 0.95–0.96 AUC on Jigsaw, well below the ~0.98 of NB-LR and char TF-IDF, because averaging dilutes the few decisive abusive tokens in long comments and loses the n-gram and misspelling signal.

Mean-pooled corpus Word2Vec with a linear classifier dilutes the signal from a few toxic tokens, especially in long comments, and loses the char-n-gram and NB-weighted lexical signal, so it typically scores around 0.95-0.96, below the tuned TF-IDF blend at 0.980.

A char NB-LogReg branch adds real diversity, mainly on obfuscated spellings, so the three-way blend should gain a small amount (~+0.0005 to +0.001). Holdout weight-tuning noise on threat and identity_hate caps the gain, and the extra char vectorization makes runtime tighter but should stay under 15 min.
C=4 may help common labels slightly but likely overfits the rare threat and identity_hate labels on 60k TF-IDF features; diluted by the rank blend, the net effect is roughly flat to a slight loss.

A fastText model trained from scratch for 20 epochs at lr=0.5 tends to overfit, scores only ~0.96-0.97 on its own, and produces saturated, tied probabilities. Giving it an equal 1/3 weight in the rank blend likely dilutes the stronger A and B branches slightly rather than adding useful diversity.

A char-level NB-LogReg view adds real diversity to the blend (about +0.001 AUC), but a second char vectorizer fit on 313k docs pushes wall-clock toward the 15-min kill limit, so there is some risk the run fails.

Losing 10% of the training data costs about as much as per-label weight tuning gains, and the holdout is noisy for threat/identity_hate (few positives), so weights may overfit; net result is roughly flat to slightly worse.

NB weighting makes branch A look more like branch B, so the blend loses diversity; that roughly cancels any single-model gain, and the rescaled features may slow sag convergence, so I expect little net change or a slight drop.

min_df=0.01 means a term must appear in about 3.1k of the 313k docs, which cuts vocabularies to a few hundred or a few thousand features. That drops the rarer slurs, threat terms and bigrams that carry signal for the rare labels. Char n-grams keep partial coverage, so the drop is moderate rather than catastrophic.

Balanced undersampling discards most negatives, leaving only about 1k rows for threat and about 3k for identity_hate and severe_toxic. That starves the high-dimensional sparse linear models and the NB ratios, which hurts rare-label AUC most; since AUC is already insensitive to class imbalance, rebalancing brings no ranking benefit.

Swapping discriminatively trained logistic regression for Rocchio-style centroid-difference scoring removes learned per-feature weighting. Common n-grams dominate the centroids, so AUC should drop to roughly 0.93-0.95 per branch. The NB weighting partly rescues branch B, and the logit blend still works because the scores are small and near-linear.

char vs char_wb with 50k capped features gives near-identical single-model AUC on Jigsaw (~0.978-0.979); after rank-blending with NB-LogReg, the difference is within noise, maybe a hair lower since char captures cross-word patterns.

ComplementNB on binary labels is roughly multinomial NB, which trails regularized logistic regression and NB-LogReg on Jigsaw sparse n-grams by several AUC points, especially on toxic, obscene and insult; rank-averaging two weaker NB branches recovers little.

Compressing 60k TF-IDF features to 32 SVD dimensions throws away most of the discriminative lexical signal; logistic regression with C=0.1 on those dense features likely lands near 0.92-0.94 AUC, and averaging it with equal weight against the fastText branch should pull the blend below the current 0.973.

Capping vocabulary at 2,000 tokens maps obfuscated profanity, misspellings and rarer slurs to one shared unknown token, which strips most of the char n-gram branch's advantage; the common toxic words survive, so AUC drops moderately rather than collapsing.

Keeping stop words mostly swaps a few hundred low-weight features in the 10k word vocab. The char n-grams and branch B already cover function words (e.g. 'you'), so the rank-blended AUC should barely move, within noise.

The logit average probably lands slightly below the current rank average. NB-LogReg at C=4 produces much wider logits than the heavily regularized C=0.1 branch, so a 0.5/0.5 logit average effectively weights the NB branch more. That loses a bit of the diversity the equal-weight rank average captured, so AUC should dip slightly.

Switching char_wb to char adds cross-word n-grams but still caps at 50k top features, so the rank-averaged ensemble should move by at most a few 1e-4 AUC, likely slightly negative; runtime rises somewhat but should stay within budget.

Without pretrained vectors, a short-trained fastText OVA model usually scores around 0.965–0.972 AUC on its own, weaker than NB-LogReg at about 0.977, so the rank blend with branch A likely drops slightly despite added diversity.

On the leaf data nearly every descriptor carries useful signal, and L2-regularised LR already handles the redundancy, so dropping 64 columns likely removes discriminative information (especially margin/texture) and makes the LR's log loss worse; the 50/50 blend with the unchanged NN softens but doesn't cancel the regression.

On this nearly separable task, label smoothing caps the NN's confidence at about 0.9, so the 50/50 blend gives up log-loss on the many easy correct rows. That cost is likely larger than the small gain from softer mistakes.

OvR fits 99 heavily imbalanced binary problems (about 8–10 positives each), which gives poorly calibrated, less sharp probabilities than the joint softmax; the power calibration recovers some of this but not all, so log loss likely gets worse.

A bagged MLP on standardized leaf descriptors is roughly as strong as the LR and makes different errors, so an OOF-tuned blend before calibration should modestly cut log loss; w=0 in the grid limits the downside, and the 80 small MLP fits fit comfortably in the time budget.

Averaging the five fold models softens overconfident high-C mistakes, which log loss punishes heavily, but each model sees only ~80% of an already tiny set (~7 samples/class), so I expect a roughly neutral to slight gain.

The provided 192 descriptors are scale-normalised, so absolute size, aspect ratio, solidity and Hu moments add real discriminative signal for confusable species; CV-tuned C should limit overfitting, giving a moderate log-loss drop, assuming the images folder is found.

An L2-penalised logistic regression gives the same fit under an orthogonal rotation, so unwhitened PCA only helps by dropping components. Keeping 95% of variance throws away the low-variance directions, and fine species distinctions in this data often live there, so log loss likely gets worse.

Each fold model sees only 8 samples per class instead of 10, so with fixed C=1 the regularisation weighs relatively more and the models are less confident. Averaging a stable linear model adds little variance reduction, so dropping the full refit likely raises log loss slightly.

LR at C=1 is under-confident, so blending it 50/50 with a well-regularised two-branch NN trained on images plus features (with augmentation and rotation TTA) should sharpen correct probabilities and cut log loss substantially; both training runs should fit the time budget.

LR at C=1 on 99 well-separated classes is likely underconfident, so an OOF-fitted power sharpening (a≈2–3) plus a small eps floor should cut log loss sharply, though a mismatch against the more confident full-data refit may give up a little of the gain.

Standardised leaf features are nearly separable, so C=1 over-regularises the logistic regression and its probabilities are underconfident; 5-fold CV will likely pick C in the hundreds to thousands, and such models typically score around 0.04–0.06 log loss on this dataset, with runtime fitting in budget using 4 parallel jobs.

Image-size and shape descriptors (aspect ratio, solidity, Hu moments) add species-discriminative information the 192 precomputed features lack, so the loss should drop modestly; a small risk of added noise or slight overfit at the fixed C keeps the gain moderate.

On standardized leaf features the 99 classes are nearly separable, so log loss rewards confident probabilities; stronger L2 shrinkage (C=0.2) mainly flattens the softmax outputs, which should roughly double the loss rather than fix overfitting.
Training on 80% of the data (about 10-11 samples per class instead of about 13, for 99 classes) makes the model less confident and less accurate, so log loss likely rises by roughly 15-30%.

An OOF-weighted convex blend is unlikely to do worse than logistic regression alone on the OOF data. Shrinkage LDA and distance-weighted kNN make somewhat different errors on the leaf features, so they should cut the tail loss, probably by about 10% in test log loss.

With 99 classes and about 8 training samples per class after the 15% validation split, min_samples_leaf=10 trees barely fit; GBDT is known to do far worse than scaled logistic regression on this dataset, so log loss likely lands around 0.5 to 1.5.

LR is probably the strongest, most confident member; the calibrated SVM replacing it uses one-vs-rest Platt scaling fitted on only ~2-3 positives per class per fold across 99 classes, which gives diffuse probabilities, so the soft-vote average gets less sharp and the log loss likely rises.

HGB with 99 classes and about 800 rows is a weak member that is often wrong. A random forest is more accurate on leaf features, though its vote-fraction probabilities are underconfident, so swapping it in should modestly lower the averaged log loss rather than change it dramatically.

On about 990 samples across 99 classes, the MLP is likely to do slightly worse than the logistic regression. Early stopping holds out 10% of the data and triggers on validation accuracy, which saturates early, so the probabilities are not well converged or calibrated. OOF shrinkage recovers part of the gap but not all of it.

On standardised leaf features, logistic regression is known to be under-fit at C=1 and does much better at large C (100–1000); CV should pick a high C, and the retuned shrinkage alpha guards against overconfidence, so log loss should drop substantially.

The image features add information the precomputed descriptors lack, namely absolute size, aspect ratio and solidity, which should modestly help the logistic regression; noisy Hu-moment signs and the distance histogram may partly offset the gain.

C=1 over-regularises standardised leaf features, and CV on log loss will likely pick a much larger C (~10-100); on this dataset that is known to cut log loss to roughly 0.03-0.07, and 25 Cs x 10 folds with lbfgs fits easily in the time budget.

An equal-weight soft vote averages in a weak, diffuse HistGradientBoosting model (about 8 samples per class across 99 classes) and a near-hard kNN, which should pull down the true-class probability that logistic regression and LDA get right and so raise log loss.
Out-of-fold tuning will likely pick a small alpha (about 0.01–0.02), which caps the few confident misclassifications at a modest cost to correct predictions, giving a small gain or none.

Fixed 0.9 shrinkage is far above the likely Ledoit-Wolf value, so the model behaves almost like Euclidean nearest-centroid. That throws away the strong within-class correlations in the margin, shape and texture histograms, which should cut accuracy and produce confident errors that raise log loss.

Each single-family LDA is much weaker than joint LDA (shape especially), and arithmetic averaging dilutes confident correct predictions, so typical log loss rises despite tempering overconfident errors.

Keeping only 90% of standardized variance (roughly 40–60 components) likely throws away low-variance but discriminative margin and texture directions. With 99 classes, that information loss probably outweighs any stabilization, since the grid can already pick a well-regularized C, so log loss likely gets worse.

Shrinkage LDA classifies leaves about as accurately as the logistic model, but its Gaussian posteriors are overconfident with about 10 samples per class and 192 features, so rare misclassifications should dominate the log loss and roughly double it versus the well-calibrated logistic regression.

An L2 penalty is unchanged by an orthogonal rotation, so the only real effect is discarding the low-variance 5% of directions, which likely still carry fine species-discriminative detail, so log loss probably worsens moderately.

Shrinkage LDA should classify about as accurately as the current logistic regression, but its decision scores are much larger and sharper. The temperature cap of 4 probably can't soften them enough, so the few misclassified leaves will cost more and log loss likely gets worse.

Mixing in 0.5% uniform adds about -log(0.995)≈0.005 loss per confident-correct sample. The floor it creates (≈5e-5) only pays off on catastrophic misses, which are unlikely with C=1 logistic regression at 0.094 loss, so expect a slight regression.

Fewer Nyström landmarks (384 vs 512 of ~990 train rows) gives a slightly coarser kernel approximation with a different landmark sample; with C=1 already regularizing, this likely nudges log loss up modestly or leaves it roughly unchanged.

Shrunk LDA classifies about as accurately as LR (~98%), but its pooled-Gaussian posteriors are very overconfident, so a few misclassified leaves carry huge log-loss penalties. Uncalibrated probabilities should score clearly worse than the LR baseline's 0.124.
On standardized leaf descriptors, weakly regularized logistic regression (C=100–1000) usually cuts log loss a lot versus C=1, so the CV grid search should pick a large C and land around 0.04–0.07.

LogisticRegression at C=1 on well-separated leaf descriptors is likely underconfident, so an out-of-fold temperature below 1 should sharpen probabilities and cut log loss, with some risk of over-sharpening the full-data model and occasional heavily penalised misclassifications.

Standardizing all 512 Nyström components boosts the noisy small-eigenvalue directions, and with only ~990 rows, 99 classes and weak C=1 regularization the model likely overfits and gets overconfident, so log loss probably rises a little rather than falling.

Several of the added standardised dense features are known to be predictive on RAOP: the time trend, text length, the image/evidence flag, reciprocity and prior-RAOP activity. Because they are standardised, they carry real weight under C=0.3 alongside the sparse TF-IDF blocks, so I expect a modest AUC gain of about 1–2 points rather than a large one.

With max_features='sqrt' over about 8k mostly sparse TF-IDF and subreddit columns, the 9 informative numeric features are rarely among a split's candidates, so fully grown trees mostly overfit noisy text and AUC likely lands a bit below the linear baseline.

A random forest over 5k sparse TF-IDF columns with sqrt feature sampling will rarely pick the nine numeric features at a split, and it handles weak sparse text signal worse than logistic regression, so AUC likely drops to roughly 0.66–0.70.

Most of the score likely comes from the giver_known indicator and the requester-history features, and 50 LDA topics carry less discriminative text signal than 5k TF-IDF unigrams on RAOP, so expect a small drop rather than a gain.

Swapping the supervised TF-IDF logistic-regression text logit for 20 unsupervised LDA topic proportions throws away most of the text signal, since LDA topics are weak predictors on RAOP, so LightGBM falls back mostly on metadata and timestamp, costing roughly 0.03 to 0.04 AUC.

RAOP success rate falls steadily over time, and the test set is likely a random split from the same period, so the raw timestamp carries real signal. Hour-of-day and weekday are weak substitutes, so dropping the epoch column probably costs a little AUC.

A gradient-boosted tree model on the raw numeric, time and text-statistic features captures nonlinear effects that TF-IDF + logistic regression misses, so a CV-weighted rank average should add roughly 0.01 AUC; the gain stays small because both models share most of the signal.

With max_features='sqrt' over ~5,000 mostly-zero TF-IDF columns, each split rarely samples the ~30 informative dense features, so the forest captures little text signal and should land a bit below the linear model's 0.70.
Subreddit bag-of-words adds weak but real signal; it's l2-normalized, and C=0.3 limits overfitting, so expect a small gain, possibly noise-level on ~1.1k test rows.

giver_username_if_known is kept in the test schema and is a known leak: a named giver almost always means the request succeeded, so it covers a large share of positives. Even with C=0.3 shrinking its weight, those rows jump to the top of the ranking, which should lift AUC substantially.

An out-of-fold text logit plus raw history features plus the UTC timestamp (success rate on RAOP drifts over time), fed to a heavily regularised early-stopped LightGBM, should modestly beat the single linear model; text signal is weak, so the gain is limited.

Request time (success rate falls over time), text length/imgur/URL counts and RAOP-history flags are known modest signals on RAOP, and adding them as a small standardized block to the linear model should lift AUC by about 1–2 points; the MLflow wrapper is best-effort and should not affect the output.

ExtraTrees avoids the logistic regression's overfitting on the 384 dense embedding dimensions. But with sqrt feature sampling, most splits fall on embedding or sparse TF-IDF columns and rarely on the 9 informative numerics, so I expect only a small change, roughly on par to slightly better.

The standardized 384-dim embedding block already dominates the TF-IDF block, whose values are small in scale, so the tiny TF-IDF signal removed nets roughly zero change; the mlflow wrapper is harmless.

On RAOP, length, money, gratitude and link cues carry real signal, and as standardized dense columns they get strong weights next to the weak TF-IDF. The 9 history numerics already capture much of the signal, so the likely gain is only about 0.01 AUC.

On RAOP, logistic regression on only the nine request-time metadata features typically scores about 0.60-0.62 AUC; dropping the TF-IDF text removes real signal (need, gratitude, and reciprocity words), so a modest regression is likely. The mlflow wrapper falls back safely if tracking fails, so it shouldn't affect the run.

On RAOP, most of the signal comes from the metadata and text-stat features. Mean-pooled Word2Vec trained on only about 5.7k short documents is noisy, so it should score close to unigram TF-IDF, and its 200 standardized dense dims under C=0.3 probably add a little overfitting, giving a flat to slightly worse score.

RAOP's text signal is weak, so adding bigrams at min_df=2 mostly adds sparse noise. Spreading L2-normalized TF-IDF mass across more features weakens the text signal under C=0.3, leaving the dense features to dominate, so expect roughly flat to slightly worse; the mlflow calls are wrapped in try/except and should not affect the result.

The request-time history features alone typically reach only about 0.60–0.63 AUC on RAOP, and dropping the text removes some real signal (even though the SVD+LGBM text features were weak), so I expect a slight regression.

RF on 309 dense SVD features: the sqrt split (~17 features per split) mostly lands on noisy SVD components, which dilutes the few informative numeric columns; this likely ends up roughly on par with LightGBM or slightly worse, with AUC in the 0.60–0.64 range.

MiniLM embeddings add some semantic signal, but with only ~4k training examples, 384 standardized dense dimensions under weak regularisation (C=0.3) mostly add noise, so expect a small gain; there is also some risk the run fails if the model can't be downloaded.
On about 2–3k short requests, bigrams with min_df=2 add mostly noisy sparse features; under C=0.3 they spread the TF-IDF mass more thinly, so AUC stays essentially flat, perhaps a hair lower.

Length, readability and lexicon counts are known useful signals on RAOP, and unigram TF-IDF only partly captures them, so the scaled dense block should give a modest gain of about +0.01 AUC under the unchanged logistic regression.

LightGBM should fit the nonlinear requester-history features better, but 300 noisy SVD text components with num_leaves=63 on about 2.9k rows will likely overfit, so the net result is roughly flat versus the logistic-regression baseline.

RAOP success falls steadily across 2010–2013, so the spline on absolute time captured a real signal; annual sin/cos cannot encode that trend and adds only weak seasonal signal, so AUC likely drops a little.
On about 4k noisy RAOP samples with 5k TF-IDF unigrams, C=30 overfits the text badly, and the weak signal from the numeric features gets diluted, so AUC should fall noticeably.

RAOP success rate falls steadily over the 2010–2013 collection window, so a smooth spline of request time adds real signal on a random split. Only 5 standardized columns are added, so overfitting risk is low and a modest AUC gain of about 0.01–0.015 is likely.

Distance-weighted 25-NN with cosine similarity will likely underperform the logistic regression and give about 0.575 AUC. The dense subreddit indicators and standardized numeric features dominate the cosine geometry and swamp the unit-norm TF-IDF. With only 25 noisy neighbours on a weak, imbalanced signal, the probability scores will be coarse and noisy.
Distance-weighted KNN on nine weak, zero-heavy metadata features gives noisier and less well-ranked probabilities than CatBoost, so the fixed 50/50 blend likely loses some AUC.
C=30 on ~4k samples with 5k unigram TF-IDF features badly overfits, and its extreme probabilities dominate the 50/50 blend over the moderate CatBoost outputs, so AUC likely drops slightly.

RAOP success rate falls steadily over the 2010–2013 collection period, and a random train/test split shares that time distribution, so standardized date splines should add a modest real signal to the weak TF-IDF+LR baseline, worth roughly +0.01 AUC.

BernoulliNB over about 5,000 noisy presence and absence features double-counts correlated n-grams and throws away tf-idf magnitude and numeric scale, so its ranking should be somewhat worse than the regularized logistic regression.

RAOP success rates drop over time, so a spline on the request date should add a modest, real signal on top of weak TF-IDF plus numeric logistic regression, likely a gain of about 0.005–0.01 AUC; the MLflow wrapper is best-effort and should not affect predictions.

Binary subreddit indicators are a weak, noisy signal on RAOP. With C=0.3 and ~1k extra columns the effect is roughly neutral to a slight gain, and the MLflow wrapper and removed holdout don't change predictions.

Metadata-only CatBoost (~0.60–0.63 AUC alone) adds some nonlinear signal from the requester-history features, so the fixed 50/50 average with the text-plus-metadata LR should give a small gain, though the partly redundant features limit it.

Bigrams under the same 5000-feature cap mostly displace rare unigrams with noisy, stopword-stripped bigrams, which on about 4k short requests changes little. The best-effort mlflow telemetry and the removed holdout don't affect the test predictions, so I expect roughly flat AUC with a slight downside.
Function words and bigrams are key stylometric signals for authorship; dropping them from the word view hurts somewhat, partly offset by the char_wb view that still captures them.

On Spooky, NB word/char count models are strong and complementary to the TF-IDF LR (well known ~0.30-0.33 when stacked), and the log-prob meta-LR calibrates the overconfident NB outputs, so expect a solid improvement from 0.354 to ~0.32; fold-averaged test preds cost a little vs a full refit.

In spooky author ID, function words and their bigrams carry most of the stylometric signal, so removing stop words weakens the word-level LR and NB (NB especially). The char_wb models keep only part of that signal, so the stacked log loss gets moderately worse.
A linear LR on raw (not log) OOF probabilities plus scaled meta-features can't model the nonlinear calibration and interactions that LightGBM captured, so it likely does slightly worse.

Punctuation (semicolons, commas, quotes) is a genuinely strong authorial signal in Spooky (e.g., EAP/MWS semicolon use); removing it from the char n-grams loses discriminative features, so log loss likely worsens modestly.

Stacking a word-NB model, which is strong on this dataset, with LR at C=10 on word and char TF-IDF typically lands in the 0.33–0.37 range, well below the single C=1 LR's 0.439. The runtime should fit the budget because the char-LR folds run in parallel, and the mlflow logging is best-effort, so a missing mlflow won't break the run.

Keeping only 10k of ~130k columns drops real signal and shrinks the L2-normalized row norms, so the C=1 logistic regression underfits more; the naive-Bayes blend cushions it, giving a slight regression.
Function words are key stylometric signals for authorship; removing them hurts NB and word TF-IDF badly (char_wb partially compensates), so the blend degrades noticeably.

On stacked word and char TF-IDF features, C=1 is over-regularized, so cross-validation will likely pick C=10 or 30 and cut log loss by roughly 0.03-0.05; the explicit 5-fold x 5-C loop should still finish within the time budget.

Out-of-fold stacking of word and char LR (C=10) with word and char NB, plus a LightGBM meta-learner with stylometric features, typically brings Spooky log loss down to about 0.33-0.37 from a single-LR 0.43, and the run should fit in the time budget.

Cross-boundary, case-sensitive char n-grams add some signal. But going from 60k to about 400k uncapped columns spreads each row's L2-normalized TF-IDF mass thinly. With C=1 fixed, that makes the LR more strongly regularized and less confident, so log loss likely rises slightly or stays flat.

The LR at C=1 on TF-IDF is underconfident (about 0.43), while MultinomialNB on word 1-2gram counts at low alpha is overconfident but strong (about 0.45). Their errors complement each other, so an OOF-tuned arithmetic blend should give a solid gain, to roughly 0.36-0.38.

Function words are key stylometric signals for authorship, so dropping them should reduce accuracy; the already overconfident fastText model (lr 0.5, 25 epochs) will then make more confident mistakes, raising log loss modestly.

The baseline's 0.607 already points to overconfident fastText (lr=0.5, 25 epochs). Duplicating minority rows adds more memorization of those rows and shifts the class prior away from the test distribution, so log loss likely gets somewhat worse.

ComplementNB on TF-IDF is a weaker, differently calibrated model that complements the underconfident logistic regression, and choosing the weight by OOF log loss guards against harm, so a modest gain is likely.

Public Spooky kernels show MultinomialNB on TF-IDF scoring about 0.45–0.58 even with alpha tuned; stacking correlated char n-grams makes NB double-count evidence and become poorly calibrated, so it likely lands around 0.42–0.45, worse than the tuned LR at 0.355.
Char n-grams carry strong stylistic signal on this dataset (word+char typically beats word-only by ~0.03-0.05 logloss), so dropping them should hurt the NB-SVM.

ComplementNB with alpha=1.0 on L2-normalized TF-IDF gives heavily smoothed, poorly calibrated, near-flat softmax probabilities, so log loss likely lands around 0.85-0.95, far worse than the NB-SVM's 0.41 despite reasonable accuracy.

C=1 is likely under-fitting on sparse word and char TF-IDF features, so CV should pick a larger C (about 3–10) and lower the log loss; the run should finish in time with 3 folds in parallel, though large C values may converge slowly.

Naive Bayes on the stacked word and char TF-IDF features is usually worse than logistic regression on this task: TF-IDF scaling hurts its calibration, and the correlated char n-grams double-count evidence. MinMax-scaled style features read as pseudo-counts add noise, so log loss likely rises to about 0.5.

fastText with lr=0.5 and 25 epochs on ~17.6k sentences will overfit and produce overconfident softmax probabilities; accuracy may be comparable, but log loss should be clearly worse than the calibrated TF-IDF+LR baseline (0.432).
TF-IDF LR on this data is over-regularized at C=1, so CV will likely pick C=4–8 and cut log loss to roughly 0.38–0.40; parallelizing the 30 fits should keep the run within budget.

The baseline LR at C=1 is likely over-regularized on these TF-IDF features; NB count-ratio weighting plus C=4 sharpens the discriminative n-grams, which usually lands around 0.37–0.40 on this task, though renormalizing one-vs-rest probabilities costs a little calibration.

14 MaxAbs-scaled dense style features added to ~100k+ TF-IDF columns under C=1 LR carry little extra signal (punctuation already captured by char n-grams), so expect a negligible change, perhaps a tiny gain.

The current C=1 TF-IDF multinomial logistic regression is underfit, and NB log-count-ratio scaling amplifies the discriminative n-grams, much like a larger effective C with a better prior; NBSVM-style models typically beat plain LR on this task, though one-vs-rest renormalization costs some calibration.

TF-IDF with logistic regression at C=1 is already over-regularized (on this task log loss usually improves at C of 10 or more), so dropping C to 0.25 flattens the predicted probabilities and makes log loss noticeably worse.
Dropping the word uni/bigram block removes distinctive lexical and name features that char_wb 2-5 grams only partly capture (and the 60k cap limits coverage), so NB-LR log loss should rise modestly.

Without the NB log-count ratios, plain TF-IDF logistic regression at C=1 has no class-specific feature scaling and gives underconfident probabilities on this task, so log loss should get worse, from about 0.52 to roughly 0.56–0.60.

L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF logistic regression on this task tends to underfit rather than overfit, so halving C should soften probabilities and raise log loss. The added tracking code is best-effort and should not affect the predictions.

NB weighting amplifies features, so C=4 acts as weaker regularization, and one-vs-rest probabilities renormalized by row sum are less calibrated than multinomial LR; that likely makes predictions overconfident and worsens log loss despite similar accuracy.

Function words are highly discriminative stylometric signals for authorship; removing them from both word and char branches (char n-grams lose most function-word patterns) should noticeably hurt log loss.

On sparse TF-IDF features for this task, logistic regression usually does best with weaker regularization than C=1, so C=0.25 over-regularizes and loses discriminative power; temperature scaling fixes the resulting underconfidence but cannot recover the lost ranking quality.

The plain 'char' analyzer captures cross-word and punctuation n-grams such as '; ' and ', and', which are stylistically informative for this task, so expect a small gain, partly offset by the 60k max_features cap; removing the holdout and adding MLflow telemetry don't change the final full-data model.
NB log-count-ratio scaling boosts discriminative n-grams relative to the underfit C=1 multinomial LR, likely a modest gain; OvR normalization costs a little calibration.

Logistic regression at C=1 on TF-IDF features for this data typically underfits and gives soft probabilities, so C=4 should sharpen them and lower log loss by several percent without heavy overfitting; removing the holdout print does not affect the submission.

Logistic regression at C=1.0 on TF-IDF features tends to be underconfident; fitting a temperature below 1 on the holdout should sharpen the probabilities and cut log loss by a few percent. Refitting on all the data narrows the gain slightly, and the MLflow tracking is guarded, so it shouldn't affect the result.

Log1p target optimizes log-scale error and expm1 back-transform predicts a geometric rather than arithmetic mean, adding downward bias and hurting dollar RMSE slightly on the high-fare tail, while the invalid-row floor (~2.1) is unchanged.

Four times more data gives a modest improvement on the valid rows (roughly 3.57 to 3.47 RMSE), but the fixed ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows and noisy outliers dilute the overall gain; runtime should fit the budget.

Airport-distance features usually cut RMSE on the valid rows (fixed JFK fares, airport surcharges), but about 2.8% of test rows have corrupt coordinates that the change can't help, and those dominate the total error, so the overall gain stays small.

An L2 fit on log1p followed by expm1 predicts roughly the conditional geometric mean, which sits below the mean, so predictions are biased low for a dollar-RMSE metric. That hurts most on the expensive and corrupt, heavy-tailed rows that dominate RMSE, so expect a small regression.

Distance is already close to monotone and the default 'basic' method restricts splits, so expect a small loss (flat airport fares, zero-distance round trips) against an RMSE largely set by the corrupt-row floor.

Training on log1p(fare) while scoring RMSE in dollars shrinks predictions toward the conditional median and under-predicts the high-fare tail (airport and long trips), so dollar RMSE usually gets slightly worse; the fixed error from corrupt test rows dilutes the size of the change.

In-sample encoding leaks each row's own fare into its encoding: for a rare route key with count 1, the smoothed mean is (y + 20·global)/21, so the fare is recoverable from the mean and count. The trees will overfit on these low-count keys, while validation and test rows lack that leak, so RMSE should get somewhat worse; early stopping on the validation set limits the damage.

Training on log1p(fare) and scoring RMSE in dollars pulls predictions toward the median. That shrinks predicted fares on high-fare trips (airport, long rides), which dominate squared error, so RMSE on the valid rows likely rises slightly. The ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows mutes the effect on the total score.

Airport-distance features usually cut error on the valid rows by about 3-5% (for example, 3.6 to 3.45-3.5), but the roughly 2.8% of corrupt test rows add a fixed error term, so the overall RMSE should fall only modestly from 4.14 to about 4.05-4.07.

Modest improvement, about 1%. Test rows with good coordinates but a passenger count of 0 no longer get the mean fare; the model now predicts them from their real coordinates. Rows with one valid endpoint can also use that location. Rows with fully corrupt coordinates stay mostly unpredictable, so the roughly 2.1 floor barely moves, and the NaN branches keep the corrupt training rows from hurting the valid ones.

Four times as much data should cut RMSE on the valid rows from about 3.6 to about 3.5, but gains are muted because the 1000-tree cap binds at lr 0.05, and the fixed corrupt-row floor (about 4.5 of the squared error) dilutes the improvement on the total RMSE; the run should stay within the time budget.

Out-of-fold route and cell target encodings should help a little on valid rows (roughly 3.6 to 3.5), since LightGBM already learns much of the spatial signal from raw coordinates; the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the overall gain.

Training on log1p(fare) with expm1 back-transform predicts something closer to the median than the mean, so under RMSE it biases predictions low. That hurts most on the unpredictable invalid rows, where the fallback drops from about $11 to about $8.5, and slightly on long-tail valid rides, giving a small net regression.
Manhattan distance and bearing usually give LightGBM a modest gain on the valid rows (about 3.6 → 3.55 RMSE), but the corrupt-row floor of about 2.1 dilutes the overall improvement to around 1%.

Distances to the airports and to Manhattan help the trees isolate flat-fare and surcharge regimes that raw coordinates only approximate, so RMSE on valid rows might drop from about 3.6 to about 3.47; the roughly 2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes this to a small overall gain.

An L1 objective predicts the conditional median, which sits below the mean for right-skewed fares, so RMSE is biased upward. L1 boosting also converges more slowly per tree. RMSE on the valid rows likely rises from about 3.53 to 3.65, and the fixed floor of about 2.1 from corrupt test rows dilutes that into a modest overall regression.

Training on log1p and inverting with expm1 targets the conditional median (geometric mean), so predictions are biased low; that bias costs dollar-scale RMSE on the high-fare tail, and the invalid-row floor dilutes the change, giving a small regression (the MLflow logging does not affect the score).

An L1 objective fits the conditional median, but taxi fares are right-skewed and the metric is RMSE, so predictions will be biased low and long or airport trips will be underpredicted; that likely raises RMSE on the valid rows from about 3.6 to about 3.7-3.8, while the roughly 2.1 floor from corrupt rows stays the same.

With delta=$1, Huber is close to median regression, while fare residuals are right-skewed (tolls, airport flat fares), so predictions shrink below the conditional mean. Clipped gradients also slow the fit on long trips within 1000 rounds, so RMSE on valid rows should get worse, partly diluted by the ~2.1 floor from invalid rows.

Training on log1p and back-transforming with expm1 targets something close to the conditional median or geometric mean, which sits below the conditional mean, so high fares are under-predicted and dollar RMSE usually gets slightly worse; the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes this, so the total rises a little from 4.13.

Airport distances and flags modestly help the valid rows (~3.6 to ~3.55 RMSE) since trees already approximate airports from raw coords; the corrupt-row floor dominates the total and the fallback model is unchanged.

Four times more data should cut RMSE on the valid rows by roughly 0.05–0.1, from about 3.6. The corrupt-row floor, around 4.5 of the squared error, is unchanged, so the total RMSE falls only modestly, and it should still run within the time budget.
Averaging five fold models cuts variance slightly, but the score is dominated by the roughly 2.1 RMSE floor from invalid test rows, so any gain should be small (about 0.3-0.6%).

An OOF pickup-cell target encoding adds little over raw coordinates, which the trees already split finely on 1M rows. It might give a small gain in sparse areas such as the airports. The overall score is dominated by the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor, so I expect a marginal change.

Snapping coordinates to a 0.01° grid (~1 km) throws away distance precision on the dominant feature, especially for short trips, while the route encoding already captures the neighbourhood pooling; expect a modest RMSE regression partly masked by the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows.

An L1 objective fits the conditional median, which sits below the mean for right-skewed fares; on an RMSE metric that downward bias, plus slower convergence within 1000 rounds, likely costs a little RMSE rather than helping.

An L1 objective learns the conditional median, but RMSE rewards the conditional mean. Taxi fares are right-skewed (airport flat rates, tolls), so the median will systematically underpredict. L1 boosting also converges more slowly at lr 0.05, so RMSE on the valid rows likely worsens by about 0.1–0.2, while the fixed floor from corrupt rows dampens the change in the overall score.

Airport distances help with flat-rate JFK and Newark fares, but the raw coordinates already let the trees approximate them, and about 2.1 RMSE comes from invalid rows the model can't fix, so the gain should be modest.

An L1 objective predicts the conditional median, which sits below the mean for right-skewed taxi fares, and L1 boosting also converges more slowly. Both raise RMSE on the model-predicted rows, while the fixed floor from the corrupt rows dilutes the overall change.

LightGBM's quantile histogram bins already give finer spatial resolution than 0.01° (~1 km), so rounding mostly throws away location detail (for example near airport and bridge boundaries); distance stays exact, so expect a slight worsening, diluted by the fixed ~2.1 floor from invalid test rows.

L1 targets the conditional median of right-skewed fares, so predictions are biased low under an RMSE metric; with lr 0.05 and 1000 rounds, L1 boosting also converges more slowly, so RMSE on the valid rows likely rises by about 0.1–0.2 while the corrupt-row floor stays unchanged.
A rotated Manhattan distance adds little beyond haversine plus raw coordinates in a GBM; the RMSE floor of about 2.1 from invalid test rows dominates, so expect a small gain or noise.

Out-of-fold smoothed route means add some signal (mainly airport and common Manhattan routes), but the sparse 4-D keys and heavy k=50 smoothing leave most values near the mean. LightGBM already sees the raw coordinates, and the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes any gain, so expect a small improvement.

A street-grid-aligned Manhattan distance gives the trees a slightly better trip-length signal than haversine alone, so valid-row RMSE should drop a little. The ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows limits the overall gain, and the MLflow logging does not change the model.

Doubling the training sample to 2M rows should modestly improve the fit on valid rows. The gain is small because the model still stops at the 1000-tree cap and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dominates the total. The extra rows should still fit within the time budget.

The explicit airport-route category should help the model learn JFK flat fares and airport surcharges faster than raw-coordinate splits can, but LightGBM already captures much of this from the coordinates; with the roughly 2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows, the overall gain should be small.

The data's key interactions are additive (e.g. f_21+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26), which an MLP learns easily but axis-aligned trees only approximate. With no engineered sums or unique-char count, 2000 rounds at lr 0.05 (likely still improving at the cap) should land LightGBM a bit below the 0.9866 MLP, around 0.975-0.98.

The key TPS-May interactions are linear combinations of continuous floats (for example f_02+f_21 and f_00+f_01+f_26), and 10-bin quantile one-hot throws away the within-bin resolution the MLP needs to model those boundaries, so AUC should drop noticeably even though the integer columns lose little.

The TPS May 2022 features are nearly uncorrelated, so whitening PCA amounts to an almost arbitrary rotation that smears the discrete f_27 characters, the integer counts and the axis-aligned interactions across all components. Linear leaves recover some of the lost signal, but splits become much less effective, so AUC should drop noticeably.

f_27 is nearly unique per row (~740k distinct strings in 900k rows), so a whole-string target encoding collapses to the prior for almost every row. It also discards the per-character information that drives the key interactions, so AUC should drop sharply.

Most f_27 strings are unique or near-unique, so the whole-string target encoding collapses to the prior and carries almost no signal. Dropping the ten per-position character columns throws away important structure, and only f_27_nunique is left to recover it, so AUC should drop noticeably.

These are the known TPS-May-2022 interaction features (AmbrosM ternary sums); trees struggle to learn additive boundaries from the raw columns, so exposing them explicitly typically lifts GBDT AUC from about 0.991 to about 0.993.

The logistic regression can't capture the strong feature interactions and should only reach about 0.83–0.85 AUC; equal-weight rank averaging with a model that much weaker should drag the 0.984 LightGBM down noticeably.

The proposed 64-64-64-16 SiLU MLP matches the architecture that did well on this competition, and it tends to capture the smooth continuous interactions better than LightGBM. Missing the unique-character count feature caps the gain, but training should finish well within the time budget, so I expect roughly 0.99.

The key signals in this dataset are linear-combination interactions (f_00+f_01, f_02+f_21, f_22/f_26/f_28 sums), which a standardized SiLU MLP learns more easily than untuned trees. The 10 ordinal character columns, including the unique-character signal, stay hard for an MLP, so the gain over 0.977 should be modest rather than reaching the ~0.998 that engineered-feature solutions achieved.

Linear leaves can capture the oblique sum-threshold interactions in this dataset better than constant leaves, so I expect a small AUC gain; the main risk is that linear trees run several times slower than the baseline, which could push the run toward the 15-minute kill.

In TPS May 2022, the count of distinct characters in f_27 is a known strong signal that trees can't rebuild from per-position ordinals, so expect a clear gain (~+0.008 AUC). The interaction features that drive most of the remaining gap are still absent.

These three sums are the known key TPS-May-2022 interaction directions (f02+f21, f05+f22, f00+f01+f26). Exposing them lets the trees split cleanly on those boundaries, which historically lifted AUC from about 0.977 to about 0.99 even without the unique-character feature.

Most f_27 strings are unique, so native categorical splits on the raw string (min_data_per_group=100) carry almost no signal; dropping the per-position ordinals loses positional information that letter counts only partly recover.

The key signal in this dataset comes from interactions among the numeric columns and from the f_27 unique-letter count, which are already modelled; adjacent-character bigrams carry little extra signal. Declaring nine 676-level columns as native categoricals adds some risk of overfitting and slower training, so expect a flat or slightly worse AUC.

f_00..f_15 are nearly independent, so PCA only yields arbitrary linear rotations that trees gain little from, and dropping the mined products loses whatever interaction signal they carried, so expect a small regression.

Hashing the whole f_27 string, which is nearly unique per row, into 64 one-hot buckets throws away all the per-position character information (a major signal in TPS May) and just adds noise, so AUC should fall to roughly numeric-only levels.

Fully grown ExtraTrees on the raw ordinal f_27 characters, with only about 6 of 41 features tried per split, capture the dataset's key interactions much worse than 3000-round LightGBM, so AUC should land around 0.91-0.93. There is also real risk that the extra 5-fold CV pushes the run past the time limit.

The key TPS-May-22 interactions are linear-sum thresholds among the continuous features, which an MLP captures much better than LightGBM does from raw columns, so AUC should rise above 0.978. The gain is capped because sklearn's MLP stops early on noisy accuracy and cannot easily learn the unique-character-count signal from ordinal inputs.

In TPS May 2022 the unique-character count (and the letter counts) of f_27 is a known strong signal that per-position categoricals can't easily express, so AUC should rise a few thousandths; the missing numeric interaction features cap the gain well below ~0.99.

Dropping the per-position f_27 letters removes most of the key signal (the letter composition and unique-character count); since most full sequences are near-unique, a frequency count recovers little, so AUC should fall back toward the numeric-only level of about 0.93–0.94.

The unique-character count of f_27 is a known strong signal in TPS May 2022, and the trees can hardly reconstruct it from per-position ordinals, so adding it plus the letter counts should give a clear gain, from about 0.977 to about 0.983.

The known interactions are sums involving f_21, f_22 and f_26, none of which are in f_00..f_15, and f_07..f_15 are integer counts, so the 25 mined products are mostly noise and should leave AUC roughly unchanged or slightly lower.

The holdout curve is still rising at 3000 trees, so refitting on 100% of rows with about 3333 trees gives a small gain from more data and more rounds; runtime roughly doubles but should stay under the 15-minute kill.

Categorical splits on the f_27 character positions add little here: the ordinal codes are already informative, and the key signal is unique-character counts, which neither encoding captures, so AUC should stay flat or dip slightly from categorical-split overfitting.

The unique-character count of f_27 is a known strong signal in TPS May 2022. It is hard for trees to reconstruct from 10 separate ordinal columns, so it should add a few thousandths of AUC on top of the existing sum feature.

Depth-2 trees (4 leaves) cannot capture the high-order interactions this dataset depends on. These include the diagonal boundaries on f_21+f_02 and f_22+f_05, and the unique-character count of f_27, which spans all 10 positions. Even with 3000 rounds, the model ends up close to a pairwise GAM, so AUC should drop well below the deep-tree baseline of 0.982.

A 600-tree, 31-leaf LightGBM lacks the capacity and interaction features (e.g. f_27 unique-character count, f_21+f_02 style sums) that trees need on TPS-May-22, so it likely lands around 0.95 AUC, well below the MLP's 0.982.

A small LightGBM (600 trees, 31 leaves, lr 0.05) with no interaction or unique-character features captures the additive feature interactions poorly and is still underfit when it stops, so it should land below the MLP's 0.982, around 0.96.

Cutting the 16 continuous features down to four quartile bins throws away the fine-grained values behind the key sum-style interactions (e.g. f_21+f_22, f_00+f_01, f_28), so AUC should drop well below 0.977. The integer columns and f_27 characters still carry a lot of signal, so it shouldn't collapse.

This dataset's signal comes from multi-feature interactions (for example f_21+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26, and the f_27 characters), so 7-leaf trees at lr 0.05 capped at 3000 rounds should underfit clearly compared with 127 leaves.

This dataset depends on several multi-feature interactions (f_27 character positions, linear combinations of f_00/f_01/f_26 and f_21/f_02, among others), and 4-leaf trees capture these only slowly, so even 3000 rounds at lr 0.05 should underfit clearly compared with 127 leaves.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known TPS-May-22 interaction sums; trees find a single linear sum hard to approximate, so exposing it directly should give a solid gain of roughly one-third of the total interaction-feature improvement.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known planted interactions in TPS May 2022; making it explicit gives the trees a clean split they otherwise approximate poorly. That should yield a clear gain, though smaller than adding all three interactions together.

The key interactions in this dataset are linear sums of continuous features, which an MLP learns far more easily than trees, and 50 cheap CPU epochs fit the budget; the missing unique-character count over f_27 still caps it well below about 0.998.

Treating the per-position character codes as categorical lets LightGBM use set-based splits instead of ordinal thresholds. Most positions have only a few levels (A–B or A–T), so these splits add little over ordinal splits with 127 leaves and 3000 trees, and the gain should be tiny; categorical overfitting risk is small with 800k rows and min_child_samples=100.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is a known strong signal in TPS May 2022, and trees cannot easily build it from ten ordinal columns, so AUC should rise clearly. The gain stays capped because the continuous-feature interaction terms are still missing.

Weighting by target darkness no longer matches the unweighted RMSE metric: on ambiguous edge and stain pixels the optimum shifts toward darker values, which costs slightly more on the dominant white background than it gains on strokes, so expect a small regression.

The baseline stops at 2000 steps, far from converged; a time-based cosine over 330 s gives roughly 10-20x more steps with the same annealing. With random crops and flips on 105 images, overfitting risk is modest, so RMSE should drop meaningfully. The gain is capped by the small U-Net, and the run should still finish within the time limit.

The metric is RMSE, and MSE optimizes it directly; L1 targets the median, which cleans the white background slightly better but makes harder commitments on ambiguous stroke-edge pixels, and those edge pixels dominate the residual squared error, so expect a small regression or roughly no change.

Train and test share the same synthetic noise, so there is no exposure shift for input-only brightness/contrast jitter to cover. The jitter corrupts the absolute-intensity cues the model uses to map background to white and ink to dark, which makes training harder and likely raises RMSE moderately.

At 0.0154 RMSE most remaining error sits on sharp stroke edges. The 0.75x and 1.25x passes carry 2/3 of the weight and add resampling blur and off-scale inputs the single-scale model never saw, so edge error rises and outweighs any stain-removal gain.

Random-crop patch regression with only 2000 steps is not overfitting-limited, so channel dropout on e2 (and its skip into d2) mostly adds training noise and slows convergence of fine pixel-level reconstruction; expect a mild RMSE regression.

Dropout2d is placed ahead of later BatchNorm layers, so BN running statistics are computed under dropout and no longer match eval-time activations (the variance-shift problem). Channel dropout on the final 32-channel decoder map also adds output noise to a pixel-precise regression task. With a 180s budget it slows convergence too, so RMSE will likely rise from the strong 0.0085 baseline.

A larger receptive field and more capacity should help with large stains and background gradients, which should outweigh the roughly 25% fewer steps under the fixed 180s budget, but the gain at an already-low RMSE is likely modest and within seed noise.

A large-kernel median background channel gives the shallow U-Net, which has a small receptive field, explicit context about stains and fades; that usually helps on this dataset, but the gain should be modest because the baseline is already strong.

The deeper 5-level U-Net on 256px crops gets a much larger receptive field and more context for large stains and wrinkles, likely a modest gain; the same pixel budget, batch-8 BatchNorm noise and only 2000 steps for a model roughly 15x larger limit the improvement.
The trained model is unchanged, and it already saw flips during training, so 4-way flip TTA should average out prediction noise for a modest 2–5% RMSE gain with negligible runtime cost.

The diff sets TRAIN_SECONDS to 180 instead of the proposed 360; even so, a small U-Net at batch 32 on a GPU likely fits several thousand steps in 180s versus the baseline's 2000, and a time-based cosine schedule should lower RMSE meaningfully, though less than 360s would have.

Charbonnier approximates L1 and aims for the median, while RMSE is dominated by large errors at stroke edges and stains, which L1 down-weights; with near-binary targets the difference is small, so expect a modest regression rather than a collapse.

Gaussian noise does not resemble the structured stain and wrinkle noise in the test set, so it adds a train/test input mismatch. Clipping at 1.0 on white backgrounds also biases the noisy inputs downward, and the extra denoising task on a 2000-step budget encourages over-smoothing of text edges, so RMSE likely gets modestly worse.

GroupNorm right after the first conv strips each sample's absolute brightness level, which this intensity-sensitive denoiser needs to push stained backgrounds to white, and its per-image statistics still differ between 128px crops and full pages, so RMSE likely gets slightly worse rather than better.

The SSIM+L1 loss no longer matches the per-pixel RMSE metric: SSIM barely penalizes small background brightness offsets and L1 targets medians rather than means, so val RMSE likely drifts slightly worse despite crisper strokes.

Training is unchanged, and averaging 8 dihedral TTA passes cuts prediction variance and bf16 noise; half the views (rot90 variants) are outside the flip-only training distribution, so I expect a modest gain of about 3–6% rather than a large one.

With pure SSIM loss, small brightness offsets on the mostly white background are barely penalized (the luminance term is about 0.9998 for a 0.02 shift near 1.0). With no MSE anchor, the background will likely settle slightly gray and text intensities will drift, so per-pixel RMSE will probably get clearly worse than the 0.0108 MSE baseline, even if edges look sharper.

Residual learning with a zero-initialized linear head, plus the final clamp, avoids sigmoid saturation and bf16 quantization near 1.0 for the background. This likely gives a small gain, but the U-Net already has a skip path to the input, so the benefit is modest and within seed noise.
Under Adam, an RMSE loss behaves much like MSE, and the 0.1-weighted SSIM term pulls the model slightly away from optimizing pixel RMSE, so expect a roughly neutral to slightly worse score.

The noise here (stains, faded backgrounds) is large and structured, so the clean-minus-noisy residual isn't small and DnCNN-style residual learning gives little advantage. Dropping the sigmoid also loses easy saturation to white, so training MSE penalizes overshoot even though inference clamps it; net effect is roughly neutral to slightly worse.

About 86% of sampled crops become synthetic pairs whose noise (blurred ellipse stains, mild shading, speckle) does not match the real test backgrounds, which reuse the train noise textures, so the fixed 2000-step budget sees about 7x less real data and learns partly off-target deblurring, likely raising RMSE.

4.5x more steps with a stretched cosine schedule should help an undertrained small U-Net on random crops. Overfitting risk on about 105 images is modest, and the run should still fit comfortably in the time budget on GPU.

The inverse transforms are correct, so averaging the 4 flip views (seen in training) should give a solid small gain and smooth out bf16 noise, but the 4 transposed views were never seen in training and may be slightly worse, which dilutes the gain to a few percent.

L1 optimizes a median-like target rather than the RMSE metric, so predictions at ambiguous anti-aliased text edges tend to snap to one side, inflating squared error; the robustness gain against stains is small because the illumination-normalized channel already handles most of them, so expect a mild regression.

Upweighting dark pixels misaligns the training loss with the uniform per-pixel RMSE metric, which is dominated by the large white background areas, so a small regression is likely, though strong edge and glyph errors may partly offset it.

Weighting the loss by target intensity pulls the optimum toward the weighted mean, which biases uncertain pixels darker. Since the metric is unweighted MSE and dominated by background pixels, this should give a mild regression, though extra focus on ink edges may partly offset it.

A zero-initialised residual head starts training from the identity mapping. Clamping at inference lets background pixels reach exactly 1.0 without sigmoid saturation, which should give a modest RMSE gain with the same training budget.

Most clean pixels are pure-white background. L1's constant gradient pushes the sigmoid output fully to 1 there, where MSE's gradient vanishes near the target. Image-restoration work often finds L1 matches or beats L2 even on RMSE/PSNR. The mean-vs-median mismatch on stroke-edge pixels partly offsets this, so I expect only a small gain.

The clean targets are near-binary and saturated at white, which suits the sigmoid output; a residual head has to regress (1 - x) over varying stains with no output bound during training, so under the same 20-epoch CPU budget it probably lands slightly worse.

Halving the width cuts parameters by about 4x. With only 2000 training steps, the model is capacity- and optimization-limited rather than overfitting, so the smaller NAFNet should restore text strokes and edges less well and RMSE will likely rise modestly.

The weighted loss no longer matches the uniform per-pixel RMSE metric. Upweighting dark pixels threefold slightly biases predictions toward darker, sharper strokes at the expense of the dominant white background. Residual errors already sit mostly at stroke edges, so the net effect is roughly neutral to a small regression, within seed noise.

The closing-based background-normalized channel gives the shallow U-Net (receptive field of only ~40px) wider illumination context, so large stains should clean up better; since the baseline is already strong, I expect a modest gain, with some risk that the implemented CPU-only execution config makes 2,000 steps too slow for the time budget.

The run will most likely be hard-killed before producing a score. The applied diff adds a runtime.toml that sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to empty, forcing CPU-only execution; the proposal did not ask for this. On CPU, about 2000 steps of batch-32 128x128 U-Net training at roughly 11 GFLOP per sample is well past the 15-minute limit. The float32 1x1 head plus sigmoid on its own is essentially neutral (about 0.0162), and that is roughly what you would get with the runtime.toml removed.

4-view flip TTA matches the flip augmentation used in training and usually cuts RMSE by a few percent, but the diff also adds an unrequested runtime.json that sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' and forces CPU, which risks a timeout if the parent actually ran on GPU.

The compact NAFNet (width 16) uses mostly 1x1 and depthwise convs and needs about 5x fewer FLOPs than the baseline U-Net, so it should fit the budget even on CPU. But with less spatial 3x3 capacity, no sigmoid to saturate the white background, and only 2000 steps from scratch at lr 2e-3, it will probably land slightly worse than the 0.0162 U-Net.

Stanford Dogs images come from ImageNet train, so the pretrained 1k head, restricted to the 120 dog classes, is already a strong, partly memorized classifier for this exact label set; blending it with the LR, with weight and temperature tuned on the holdout, should cut log loss well below 0.31.

Without whitening, PCA is just a rotation plus truncation, and L2-penalised LR is invariant to the rotation. The low-variance directions it drops are already heavily shrunk by the penalty, so the net effect should be near-neutral, with a slight loss of fine-grained discriminative signal.

With only 6 epochs of fine-tuning on about 8.3k images, strong Mixup/CutMix (prob=1.0) makes the network underfit and costs some accuracy on these fine-grained breeds. Temperature scaling (grid down to T=0.5) can correct the resulting underconfidence, so I expect a mild log-loss regression rather than a gain.

With only 6 epochs of fine-tuning a strong in22k backbone, harsher crops (down to 8% of the image) make training noisier and widen the gap to whole-dog center-crop test images, so the model underfits slightly; temperature scaling recovers only part of the calibration loss.

ConvNeXt-V2-L (IN-22k→1k) features and its IN-1k dog-class logits are much stronger than ResNet-50 V1's, and the model has likely seen these ImageNet images, so this linear probe should roughly halve the log loss while running comfortably within budget.

The log-softmax block is a nonlinear function of the pooled features, and it carries the ImageNet classifier's dog-breed scores; ImageNet covers most of these breeds and Stanford Dogs overlaps with ImageNet train, so dropping it should weaken the linear probe and raise log loss.

A least-squares probe with one global softmax temperature is usually a bit less well calibrated and less sharp than multinomial logistic regression on strong frozen features, so log loss likely gets somewhat worse.

Unwhitened PCA gives no extra regularisation beyond what the L2-penalised LR already applies to low-variance directions, and truncating each block to 128 components discards some fine-grained discriminative signal; post-PCA centering and renormalisation may partly offset this, so a small regression is most likely.

ConvNeXt-Base pretrained on ImageNet-22k and fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k (which contains these 120 dog breeds) gives much stronger linear-probe features than ResNet-50 V1, and re-tuning C on a holdout accounts for the different feature scale, so log loss should drop substantially while staying well inside the time budget.

Fully fine-tuning ConvNeXt-Tiny (pretrained on ImageNet-22k, then fine-tuned on 1k) should beat a frozen ResNet-50 with logistic regression by a wide margin, likely around 91% accuracy. Flip test-time augmentation plus temperature scaling should undo the calibration cost of label smoothing, putting log loss near 0.30. Six epochs should fit the time budget.

The ImageNet log-softmax is a nonlinear, near-direct breed classifier (these Stanford Dogs images were likely seen during ImageNet training), so the standardized concatenation with a re-tuned C should cut log loss noticeably, partly offset by noise from the ~880 irrelevant log-prob dimensions.

Concatenating frozen ConvNeXt-in22k, CLIP and DINOv2 features gives much stronger, complementary features than ResNet-50, which should lift accuracy to about 92%. The C grid capped at 30 on L2-normalised features may leave the classifier slightly under-confident, which limits the log-loss gain.

Focal loss with gamma=2 shrinks gradients on the well-classified examples, which acts like a lower effective learning rate and may cost a little accuracy. Its (1-p_t)^2 weighting also leaves predictions underconfident, much as label smoothing does, so there is no calibration gain for log loss; I expect a similar or slightly worse score.

The dog classes come from ImageNet, so freezing conv1 through layer3 keeps strong pretrained features and cuts forgetting while layer4 and the head still adapt; the gain should be small because label smoothing already sets a floor on log loss, and frozen-layer BN stats still update in train mode.

Averaging hflip probabilities on frozen ViT features with a logreg head usually gives a small, reliable log-loss gain of about 1–3%; the NUM_WORKERS=0 change only slows loading of ~11k images, which still fits the time budget.

This swaps a ViT-B/16 that was fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k, whose label set already includes these 120 dog breeds, for a coarser CLIP ViT-B/32 whose linear-probe features are weaker for fine-grained dog breeds, so log loss should get clearly worse (roughly 0.75–0.9).

L2-regularized LR already suppresses low-variance directions, so hard-truncating 2048-d ResNet-50 features to 256 PCs mainly discards some fine-grained discriminative signal. With C left at 0.3, log loss probably worsens modestly rather than improving.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings are much stronger than ResNet-50 features for fine-grained classes like dog breeds, and C is re-tuned for them, so a linear probe with 10-view TTA should cut log loss by about a quarter, and the extra forward passes still fit the time budget.

Whitening to 256 unit-variance components greatly enlarges feature scale, so C=1.0 becomes far weaker regularization and amplifies low-signal components; that likely gives overconfident predictions and worse log loss, on top of the information lost by truncation, despite the parent likely being over-regularized.

A k=10 distance-weighted kNN gives coarse, overconfident vote fractions. Whenever the true breed gets no neighbour votes, the 1e-3 prior leaves it about 9e-4 probability, costing roughly 7 nats. A few percent of such misses plus diluted confidence on correct cases should push log loss well above the calibrated logistic regression's 0.54.

Fine-tuning at a fairly high SGD lr (0.01) for 10 epochs on about 9k images likely erodes the strong ImageNet dog features, which may partly overlap with these images, while label smoothing of 0.1 leaves predictions underconfident; accuracy should be similar or lower and log loss higher than the well-regularized logistic regression on frozen features.

The ImageNet-21k pretrained ViT-B/16 gives stronger frozen features for fine-grained dog breeds than ResNet50 V1 (about 81% vs 76% ImageNet top-1), so log loss should drop, but C=0.3 was tuned on ResNet features and may be off for the 768-d ViT features, which limits the gain.

Ten-crop plus flip TTA with probability averaging usually cuts log loss a few percent on frozen-feature linear probes, though corner crops that miss parts of the dog reduce confidence and limit the gain.

ConvNeXt features should help accuracy, but C=1.0 on L2-normalized, mostly-positive features (norm about 1.4 versus about 30 raw) is roughly 100x more regularization than the tuned raw setup, so probabilities come out underconfident and log loss likely gets worse despite similar or better accuracy.

Stanford Dogs images come from the ImageNet train set, so the pretrained ResNet-50 V2 dog head has effectively seen them. Its temperature-tuned probabilities over the 120 dog classes should therefore be strong and fairly complementary to the LR head. A validation-tuned blend should cut log loss by roughly 15-30%.
