PCA is an orthogonal projection, so the same L2-penalized logistic regression is now limited to the top-256 variance subspace. That drops some low-variance but discriminative fine-grained directions and should give a slightly higher log loss, while the 120-class structure is mostly kept.

ResNet-50 was trained with average pooling, so max-pooled features are off-distribution for it, and this usually lowers linear-probe accuracy; they are also larger and noisier, which weakens the fixed C=0.3 regularization, so log loss likely gets worse even with temperature scaling.

V2 weights reach 80.9% vs 76.1% ImageNet top-1, and the 120 dog breeds are themselves ImageNet classes (likely overlapping images), so better dog logits should carry over; the gain is tempered because features from a label-smoothing/mixup-trained model are known to linear-probe worse and the fixed C=0.3 was tuned for V1, with temperature scaling recovering part of any calibration mismatch.

C=0.03 was already rejected on the holdout in favour of C=0.3, so the head starts over-regularized and underconfident; the short fine-tune (about 290 SGD steps at a small head learning rate) only partly restores confidence, leaving log loss moderately worse.

At 192px, apparent object size drops further below what ImageNet-trained ResNet50 expects (FixRes effect), which degrades frozen features. That usually costs a few points of accuracy on fine-grained dog breeds, which translates to a noticeably higher log loss; the fine-tuning procedure itself is unchanged.

PCA is an orthonormal projection, so the L2 penalty behaves the same as before. The only real effect is dropping the low-variance directions beyond 256 components, which lose some fine-grained breed signal, so expect a small log-loss regression.

ResNet-50 V1 already prefers 224px or higher test resolution (the FixRes effect), so dropping to 192px loses fine-grained breed detail and shifts feature statistics, likely raising log loss by roughly 8–12%.

V2 weights score higher on ImageNet, and dog breeds are ImageNet classes, so in-domain features should be somewhat better; this is partly offset because label smoothing, mixup and cutmix in V2 change feature scale, which hurts calibration, and C=0.3 was tuned for V1.
C was already tuned for log loss, so the fitted temperature should land near 1 and give only a small calibration gain; applying the 85%-split temperature to the full refit adds slight noise.

Continuing unregularized training of the tuned-C logistic-regression head on the same training images, plus a tunable final bottleneck, with no augmentation and a fairly aggressive head learning rate on raw feature scales, should overfit and make test predictions overconfident, so log loss likely rises (dropping the TORCH_HOME setting also risks a weight-download failure).

Horizontal-flip TTA with probability averaging on frozen ResNet-50 features plus LR usually gives a small, consistent log-loss gain of about 1–3%, because averaging slightly smooths overconfident predictions; the added tracking and tempdir code is fault-tolerant and should not affect the output.

Balanced 1:1 undersampling discards most negatives (down to about 950 rows for threat and about 3k for identity_hate), leaving noisy NB ratios and over-regularised fits; that hurts AUC most on the rare labels, and the rank blend does not recover the lost information.

Adding char_wb n-grams usually lifts NB-LogReg by a few thousandths on its own, but it also makes branch B more correlated with branch A (which already uses the same char block), so the rank-blend gain should be small, about +0.0005, with some risk that the heavier liblinear fits run close to the time limit.

AUC ignores class priors, so 1:1 undersampling only throws away 80–99% of the negatives. Rare labels like threat (about 1k training rows) and severe_toxic/identity_hate lose the most, and the C values tuned for 160k rows now over-regularize while the NB ratios get noisier, so expect a clear drop.

MultinomialNB on TF-IDF is much weaker than NB-LogReg for these labels (about 0.94–0.95 AUC, poor on rare labels, and saturated probabilities that tie at the top), so its OOF stack features add little to branch A and the equal-weight rank blend drags the mean AUC down.

Mean-pooled corpus Word2Vec loses the strong char n-gram signal: a logistic regression on it scores only about 0.96-0.965 AUC. The MLP on the same 200-d features adds little diversity, so two-thirds of the rank blend comes from weaker, correlated branches and drags NB-LogReg down to below the current 0.9808.

1:1 undersampling throws away 90-99% of the negatives, and AUC is insensitive to class imbalance, so it gains nothing. The rare labels are fit on only ~1-3k rows (threat about 956), which hurts the heavily regularized C=0.1 LR, the NB ratios and the MLP, so expect a clear regression of roughly 0.005-0.01 AUC.

A sparse TF-IDF MLP should reach roughly 0.975–0.98 held-out AUC and add some non-linear diversity, so an equal-weight rank blend likely gains a little. The epochs are cheap enough that the time guards probably won't trigger, but equal weighting with a somewhat weaker model caps the upside.

1:1 undersampling throws away 80-99% of the negatives. Threat (~956 rows) and identity_hate (~2.8k) lose the most. The fixed C values become relatively stronger regularization on the smaller sets, and AUC doesn't benefit from prior balancing, so every branch should lose a little AUC and the blend lands about 1 point lower.

TfidfVectorizer already lowercases and char n-grams already capture much obfuscation, so repeat-collapsing and profanity de-obfuscation should give at most a marginal gain, within noise on this near-saturated linear AUC.

Adding B's out-of-fold predictions for all six labels lets A use cross-label signal, which should improve A on its own; but the weak effective L2 penalty (C=0.1 on 160k rows) means A will lean heavily on B's view, so A and B become more correlated and the rank blend loses diversity, leaving the net change near zero (the 30 extra liblinear fits also push runtime toward the limit).

A 3-epoch shared-hidden MLP on the same TF-IDF features probably reaches about 0.970–0.975 on its own, is weaker on threat and identity_hate, and is only moderately diverse from branch A, so an equal-weight rank blend should give a tiny gain or break even; runtime (~1–2 extra min) should stay within budget.

A third NB-LogReg branch on word plus char features is strong but highly correlated with A and B, so an equal rank blend likely adds only a small gain of about +0.0003 to +0.0005 AUC; the extra liblinear fits push wall-clock close to the limit, but the run should still finish.

Per-label rank-blend weights from an 80/20 holdout, shrunk halfway to 0.5, can only move the blend slightly off equal weighting. The gain on test AUC should be tiny, roughly +0.0001 to +0.0003, with noise from the rare labels. The extra holdout vectorizer and LR fits add runtime but likely stay under the 15-minute kill.

Compressing to 300 LSA factors discards the discriminative individual profanity and insult n-grams and all char features, and it drops the ensemble, so AUC should fall to about 0.95–0.96, with the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) hit hardest.

Keeping 10 negatives per positive leaves toxic unchanged but drops about 90–97% of the negatives for severe_toxic, threat and identity_hate. That loses hard-negative diversity, adds noise to the NB ratios and effectively strengthens regularization, so the rare-label AUCs should fall and pull the mean down modestly.

A single softmax fastText over 7 classes gives less saturated, more rankable per-label scores and shares signal across co-occurring labels. It is only one third of the rank blend, and the parent's anomalously low 0.883 points to noise elsewhere, so I expect a small gain within noise.

For binary labels, ComplementNB ranks test comments exactly as plain multinomial NB does (the prior only shifts scores by a constant, which AUC ignores), and NB on raw 1-2-gram counts is length-sensitive and poorly ranked compared with the LR/NB-LR rank blend, so expect a mean AUC around 0.92-0.95.

An unweighted mean of 200-d corpus-trained word2vec vectors fed to a linear head loses the sparse lexical signal. Mean pooling dilutes toxic tokens in long comments and removes n-gram and char-level evidence, so the score should land around 0.96, well below the 0.9816 three-branch sparse ensemble; the run should still fit the time budget.

Averaging corpus-trained Word2Vec vectors per comment washes out the few strongly toxic tokens, and a plain logistic regression on 200 dense dimensions loses the n-gram and char-level signal that the NB-LR and TF-IDF blend relies on, so AUC typically falls to around 0.95–0.96.

A char-level NB-LogReg adds real diversity against the word NB branch, so a small gain is likely, partly offset by noisy 3-way holdout weight tuning on the rare labels; the run should still finish within the time budget.

C=0.1 is somewhat underfit for word+char TF-IDF LR, so C=4 likely helps the common labels slightly, but it risks overfitting the rare labels (threat, identity_hate); it also makes branch A more similar to branch B, so the gain is largely diluted in the rank blend and the net change should be near zero, slightly positive.

A fastText model trained from scratch with 20 epochs at lr=0.5 likely overfits, landing around 0.96–0.97 AUC with many saturated, tied probabilities; giving it a full 1/3 of the rank blend probably dilutes the stronger linear branches slightly rather than helping.

An NB-LogReg on char_wb 3-7-grams is a strong, fairly decorrelated view, so a three-way rank average should add about +0.001 AUC. The main risk is runtime: a second char vectorizer, fit and then transformed separately on ~313k docs, plus six primal liblinear fits on 100k features, could push the run past the 15-minute kill and produce no score at all.

Training both branches on only 90% of the data costs a little AUC, and per-label blend weights tuned on a 10% holdout (about 48 threat positives) are noisy and gain at most a few 1e-4, so the net effect is roughly flat to slightly negative.

NB rescaling may help branch A alone at C=0.1, but it makes A more like the NB-LogReg branch B, cutting blend diversity, and heavy smoothing inflates weights on rare features, adding noise on threat and identity_hate, so the net is roughly flat to slightly worse.

A 1% document-frequency cutoff (about 3,100 docs) shrinks the vocabularies from roughly 260k features to a few thousand. That drops rare slurs and threat words, which hurts the threat and identity_hate AUCs most. The NB-LogReg branch should degrade badly, while the char n-grams in branch A partially compensate.

Balanced undersampling throws away 80-99% of the negatives (for threat it leaves only ~960 training rows), so the NB ratios get noisy and the fixed C is effectively over-regularized; since AUC gains nothing from rebalancing, every label loses ranking quality, the rare labels most.

Swapping the logistic regressions for cosine class centroids (Rocchio) removes discriminative weight fitting; the NB-weighted branch still behaves like a reasonable naive-Bayes-style linear scorer, but plain TF-IDF centroids are clearly weaker, so AUC likely drops a few points to about 0.95.

On Jigsaw, char_wb and char 2-6-grams at 50k features perform about the same; losing the cross-word n-grams costs a little, and the NB-LogReg rank blend dampens any difference, so expect a negligible change, at most slightly negative.

In the binary case ComplementNB with norm=False ranks comments the same way as plain multinomial NB with no prior, which is a much weaker ranker than LogReg or NB-LogReg on TF-IDF n-grams (typically ~0.94-0.96 mean AUC on this task, and weakest on the rare labels), so the blend should drop by a few AUC points.

Compressing 60k TF-IDF features into 32 SVD components discards most of the discriminative lexical signal, especially for rare labels, so branch A falls to roughly 0.92 AUC. Rank-averaging it at equal weight with the fastText branch then drags the blend well below the current 0.9734.

Collapsing everything outside the 2,000 most frequent tokens into 'raretoken' removes the rarer slurs, obfuscated or misspelled profanity and subword signal that the char n-gram and fastText branches rely on, so every label should lose AUC, with threat and identity_hate losing the most.

Removing stop words only swaps a few hundred low-signal tokens into a 10k-vocab word branch that is already dominated by 50k char n-grams and then rank-blended with NB-LogReg (which already keeps stop words), so the effect should be within noise (~±0.0003).

Branch B (C=4) produces much wider logits than the heavily regularized branch A (C=0.1), so a logit average effectively weights B more heavily than the balanced rank average does; I expect a slight AUC loss, within about ±0.0005.

In public kernels, switching char_wb to char with a 50k feature cap barely changes a single model's AUC. Cross-word n-grams add some noise under the cap, and in a rank blend with the NB-LR branch the net effect should be near zero or slightly negative, with the runtime increase staying within budget.

Standalone, a 5-epoch, dim-64 fastText with no pretrained vectors is weaker than NB-LogReg on Jigsaw (about 0.965–0.972 AUC versus about 0.977), and saturated OVA sigmoid outputs make it noisier on the rare labels, so the rank blend with the char branch should drop slightly despite the added diversity.

On leaf data, all 192 descriptors carry complementary signal, and standardised LR at C=1 is already well regularised. Dropping 64 of them with ANOVA ranking (which favours redundant high-F bins and discards weaker but complementary ones) should raise the LR's log loss. The unchanged NN in the 50/50 blend only partly dampens that, so the blended score should get slightly worse.

With eps=0.1 over 99 classes, the NN's predicted probability for the true species tops out around 0.9, and TTA averaging lowers it further. On this near-separable task that confidence cap puts a floor on the blend's log loss for correct predictions, so it likely rises from 0.074 to around 0.09–0.10 rather than improving calibration.

In one-vs-rest, each binary fit has only 10 positive specimens against about 780 negatives, so the per-class scores are poorly calibrated and less discriminative than the joint softmax; the power/floor calibration should recover part of this but not all, so log loss likely rises from about 0.045 to about 0.07.

On standardized leaf descriptors a regularised 5-seed MLP bag is competitive with logistic regression and makes different errors, so the CV-chosen blend before calibration should lower log loss moderately; the small test set adds noise, and w=0 guards against a large regression.

Averaging the five fold models softens the sharp high-C probabilities on the few misclassified test leaves. That roughly offsets losing 20% of the data per model, so I expect about the same score, perhaps a marginal improvement.

The 192 provided descriptors are scale-normalised, so absolute size, aspect ratio and convexity should help separate the few confusable species pairs, and CV selection of C limits overfitting on the 21 extra columns; the small test set makes the size of the gain noisy.

An L2-penalized logistic regression gives the same fit on any rotation of the features, so PCA's only real effect is dropping the lowest-variance directions (the last 5% of variance). With just 10 samples per class, those directions often still carry discriminative signal, so the log loss likely rises moderately.

Each fold model trains on only 792 of 990 rows, and with the same C that means relatively stronger regularisation and softer probabilities; averaging these five linear models buys little variance reduction, so it probably doesn't beat the full-data refit, and the log loss rises slightly.

A dropout-regularised two-branch NN on image plus features should reach roughly 0.05–0.12 log loss alone; averaging it with the under-confident C=1 LR sharpens correct predictions while the LR limits confident NN errors, so the blend likely lands near 0.07–0.09 and fits the time budget.

Logistic regression at C=1 on this data is accurate but underconfident; a power/temperature sharpening of about 2–3x, fitted on out-of-fold predictions, should cut log loss sharply, with a small risk of over-sharpening when applied to the full-data refit.

On standardised leaf features, logistic regression is known to do much better with weak regularisation (large C); CV will likely pick C≈1000–3000, cutting test log loss from 0.124 to roughly 0.04–0.05, and the 55 lbfgs fits should run comfortably within budget.

The image-derived features (image height and width, area, eccentricity, Hu moments) add shape information that the 192 precomputed descriptors don't fully capture, and on this dataset image size is known to be informative. Standardised logistic regression should use them for a moderate log-loss gain, with some overfitting risk from 27 extra columns on about 990 rows.

On Leaf, standardized features are nearly separable and log loss is dominated by calibration and confidence, not accuracy; stronger L2 shrinkage (C=0.2) flattens the softmax probabilities, so loss should roughly double even though accuracy barely changes.
Dropping the full-data refit leaves the model trained on only ~8 of ~10 samples per class, so it is less confident and makes more mistakes on test, raising log loss.

Blend weights learned from OOF predictions let the ensemble use LDA's strong but sharp leaf-feature probabilities and kNN's diverse errors. Logistic regression still limits the damage from overconfident mistakes, so a modest log-loss gain over LR alone is likely.

With 99 classes, only about 8 training samples per class after the 15% hold-out, and min_samples_leaf=10, histogram GBDT is data-starved; it typically gets 0.3–1.0 log loss on this dataset, far worse than well-tuned L2 logistic regression at about 0.06.

The logistic regression was likely the sharpest, best-calibrated member; Platt-calibrated one-vs-rest LinearSVC with 3-fold CV (only 2-4 samples per class in each fold, 99 classes) gives much flatter probabilities after renormalisation, lowering the averaged true-class probability and worsening log loss.

With about 9 samples per class, min_samples_leaf=10 and a noisy early-stopping split, HGB likely gives weak, miscalibrated probabilities; a 600-tree forest is more accurate on these descriptors, though its diffuse vote fractions (true class often 0.3–0.6) limit the gain, so I expect a modest improvement.

An MLP on about 800 samples across 99 classes, early-stopped on validation accuracy rather than loss, tends to be overconfident. The OOF shrinkage helps calibration, but accuracy gains over well-regularised logistic regression on these features are likely small, so I expect a slight regression in log loss.

On standardized leaf descriptors, multinomial logistic regression is known to be under-fit at C=1, so a CV search will likely pick C≈100–1000; with alpha shrinkage guarding against overconfidence, log loss should roughly halve, though the small test set makes the result noisy.

Scale-aware contour features (area, perimeter, axes) and the radial histogram add real signal that complements the 192 descriptors, so near-separable classes should get more confident correct predictions; noisy Hu and orientation features plus the untuned C=1 should cap the gain.

C=1 over-regularises these 192 standardised leaf features. CV on log loss should pick a much larger C (around 100 to 1000), and known results in that range give log loss near 0.03 to 0.06. The run fits well inside the time budget.

LDA, LR and kNN are strong on these features. But the equal-weight HGB is probably the weakest and least confident member: it has 99 classes, only 6–10 samples per class, and min_samples_leaf=10. Averaging it in with uniform weights likely pulls down the probability on the correct class, so log loss probably gets worse than the tuned-free LR's 0.124, even though averaging trims the worst misses.

Logistic regression at C=1 is already fairly soft, so its loss mostly comes from moderately underconfident correct predictions; the out-of-fold search will likely pick alpha at or near 0, leaving the score essentially unchanged.

Fixed 0.9 shrinkage makes the model close to nearest-centroid on standardized features. It would ignore the strong correlations within the margin, shape and texture histograms and double-count correlated evidence, which should lower accuracy and increase overconfidence, so log loss likely worsens versus Ledoit-Wolf auto shrinkage.

Each per-family LDA is weaker than the joint model; shape alone is especially poor. Arithmetic averaging throws away the sharpening that multiplying joint evidence gives, so predictions become under-confident and log loss likely rises, even though catastrophic errors are softened.

L2-regularized logistic regression is unaffected by PCA's rotation, so the only real change is dropping the directions that hold the last 10% of standardized variance, and those low-variance directions often carry fine discriminative signal among 99 species, so log loss likely gets worse.

Shrinkage LDA classifies leaves very accurately, but its Gaussian posteriors are much more overconfident than logistic regression's, so a few confident test errors should roughly double log loss even with shrinkage tuned on CV log loss.

Unwhitened PCA is only a rotation plus truncation, and the L2 penalty is rotation-invariant, so the only real effect is dropping the low-variance 5% of directions; for leaf data those directions often still carry discriminative signal, so log loss likely gets somewhat worse.

Shrinkage LDA is accurate on these descriptors, but its logit gaps across 192 dimensions are very large. With T capped at 4, the few misclassified test leaves still get near-zero probability, so log loss likely ends up worse than calibrated LR's 0.045.

The uniform mix puts a floor of about 5e-5 under every class, which only pays off if the true class sometimes gets probability far below that. Moderately regularized LR (C=1) likely rarely does that, so the roughly uniform -log(0.995) ≈ +0.005 cost on confident correct rows probably dominates, giving a slight regression.

Cutting the Nyström landmarks from 512 to 384 on about 990 training samples slightly coarsens the RBF kernel approximation, and C=1 already regularizes, so expect a small log-loss regression or roughly no change.

Shrinkage LDA classifies leaves accurately (about 98%), but its Gaussian posteriors are much more overconfident than a C=1 logistic regression, so the few misclassifications among roughly 99 test rows get near-zero probability and should inflate log loss well above 0.124.

On standardized leaf descriptors, weak regularization (C≈100–1000) usually beats C=1 by a lot on log loss, so the 3-fold search should pick a large C; the MLflow wrapper swallows its own failures and won't affect the result.

Logistic regression at C=1 on the leaf descriptors tends to be underconfident, so the out-of-fold temperature fit should sharpen the probabilities (T<1) and cut the log loss, though a small train/refit mismatch limits the gain.

An RBF kernel at a moderate gamma (1/192 on standardized features, about the 'scale' default) keeps the problem nearly linear-separable. Re-standardizing the 512 Nyström coordinates lets C=1 logistic regression reach larger margins, which should ease the baseline's under-confidence and cut log loss modestly. Overfitting risk with ~790 training rows keeps the gain moderate.

Standardised temporal features (the success rate declines over time), text length, and history flags are known useful RAOP signals that complement the unigram TF-IDF, likely adding about 1.5–2.5 AUC points given the small 5.7k dataset and noisy test.

An RF over about 8k mostly sparse TF-IDF and subreddit columns samples the 9 informative numeric features in only a small fraction of splits (sqrt ≈ 90 of 8k), and fully grown trees tend to overfit sparse text; on RAOP this usually scores slightly below a regularised linear model.

A random forest over 5k sparse TF-IDF columns plus 9 numeric ones picks mostly weak text columns at each split (sqrt gives about 71 candidate features, almost all text), and trees handle sparse TF-IDF far worse than regularised logistic regression, so AUC will likely fall to around 0.68–0.71.

Most of the score likely comes from the giver_known leak plus the requester metadata. Fifty LDA topics fit on about 4.5k short posts are noisy and usually carry a bit less discriminative text signal than regularised TF-IDF unigrams, so expect a small regression rather than a gain.

Twenty unsupervised LDA topic proportions carry much less outcome signal than the supervised TF-IDF LR logit on RAOP. Dropping that logit leaves LightGBM mostly on metadata plus noisy topic columns, so AUC should fall a few points.

In RAOP the success rate drifts down over time, and the test split is likely random, so the raw timestamp carries real transferable signal; hour and weekday are weak substitutes, so a small AUC drop is expected.

A shallow HistGradientBoosting model on metadata, time and text statistics should reach about 0.66–0.68 AUC. It captures nonlinear effects that the LR misses and is only moderately correlated with it, so a CV-weighted rank blend typically adds about 0.01 AUC on RAOP.

With max_features='sqrt' (~71 of ~5,030 columns per split), the ~34 informative dense metadata features rarely compete against noisy sparse TF-IDF columns, and fully grown trees on ~4k rows give noisy rankings, so the random forest likely underperforms the regularized linear model on AUC.

The subreddit bag carries a weak signal about user activity and community type, and it partly overlaps with the existing subreddit-count and activity numerics; with C=0.3 and an L2-normalised block, expect a small gain of about +0.003 to +0.006 AUC, with some risk of noise.

In this prepared split the test rows probably keep giver_username_if_known, as the original Kaggle test schema did. That makes the flag a near-perfect leak for roughly a quarter to a third of positives, and ranking them at the top lifts AUC to about f + (1-f)*0.657 ≈ 0.74–0.77.

The out-of-fold text logit plus raw requester history and the UTC timestamp (success rate falls over time in RAOP) in a well-regularised, early-stopped LightGBM should beat the single linear model by a few AUC points; the text signal itself stays weak.

Time-of-request trend, text length, imgur/link and karma-ratio features are known useful RAOP signals that complement unigram TF-IDF, so a modest AUC gain is likely; the MLflow wrapper is best-effort and should not affect the score.

ExtraTrees with sqrt feature sampling over ~5.4k mostly-sparse TF-IDF columns will waste most splits on near-empty word features, which dilutes the modest signal in the numerics and embeddings. That roughly offsets the gain from escaping the linear model's overfitting to the embeddings, so AUC should land about where it is now, around 0.62.

The standardized 384-dim MiniLM block plus the numerics likely already drives most of the signal at C=0.3, and sparse unigrams add little on RAOP, so dropping TF-IDF should make the score roughly flat to slightly better; the added MLflow calls are wrapped in try/except and should not break the run.

Body length and some style cues carry real RAOP signal that length-normalised TF-IDF discards, and the scaled dense columns get meaningful weight at C=0.3, so a modest gain is likely; many of the flags are noisy or duplicate the TF-IDF tokens, which limits the upside.

On RAOP, logistic regression on the nine log-scaled request-time requester features usually lands around 0.60–0.64 AUC; dropping the TF-IDF text removes the modest signal it adds, so the score likely falls a little rather than improving (the mlflow wrapper is guarded and should not affect results).

Mean-pooled skip-gram vectors trained on only ~5.7k short docs are noisy and dominated by common words, so they carry roughly as much weak text signal as heavily regularised unigram TF-IDF (most of the AUC comes from the metadata and length stats), giving about the same result or slightly worse.

On a few thousand RAOP docs, sparse bigrams with min_df=2 mostly add noise, and at C=0.3 the dense numeric and text-stat features dominate, so the score should stay roughly flat or dip slightly; the mlflow telemetry is wrapped in try/except and won't affect it.

The nine request-time history features alone usually reach about 0.60–0.63 AUC on this task, and the SVD text features carry some complementary signal even when LightGBM uses them poorly, so dropping them probably causes a small regression.

With max_features='sqrt', each split considers about 17 of 309 features, so the 9 informative numeric columns are rarely available against 300 mostly noisy SVD components; the forest is more stable than the overfit-prone 63-leaf LGBM but lacks its focused split selection, so expect roughly similar or slightly worse AUC.

MiniLM embeddings add some semantic signal, but 384 standardized dense columns at C=0.3 on about 2.9k rows will dominate the heavily down-weighted TF-IDF block and partly overfit, so the net gain should be small.

Adding bigrams at min_df=2 mostly adds sparse, noisy features on about 4k weak-signal documents. It also spreads each row's L2-normalized TF-IDF weight thinner, so at C=0.3 the text contributes even less and the numeric features keep dominating; expect a flat to slightly lower AUC.

Text length, gratitude, reciprocity and hardship statistics are known modest signals in RAOP, and TF-IDF misses them. With scaled dense features, the LR at C=0.3 should use them for a small AUC gain, though some of it overlaps with the unigrams.

On about 4k samples, LightGBM over 300 dense SVD components with num_leaves=63 is noisy and likely to overfit; it loses sparse lexical signal that logistic regression uses well, while the gain from the numeric features is modest, so the result should be roughly flat to slightly worse.

The quantile spline captured RAOP's strong secular decline in success rate over 2011–2013, which matters on a random test split. Annual sin/cos features drop that monotonic trend and keep only weak seasonality, so AUC likely falls slightly.
On a few thousand noisy RAOP requests, raising C 100x to 30 lets 5k sparse unigram weights overfit and drown out the weak but reliable requester-history and time signals, so AUC should drop.

RAOP success rates drift down over time, so a smooth time spline adds real signal the text and history features lack; the test split likely shares the train time range, so expect a modest AUC gain of about 0.01–0.015.

KNN with cosine distance on this mixed, high-dimensional sparse matrix is likely to be dominated by the subreddit and numeric blocks, giving noisy neighbour votes; on small RAOP data it typically scores well below a regularised logistic regression, with ROC AUC around 0.55–0.60.

A distance-weighted KNN on nine heavy-tailed, log-scaled metadata features is noisier than CatBoost, and exact-duplicate rows give it hard 0/1 outputs; with an unweighted 50/50 blend, this should pull AUC down somewhat.

At C=30, the logistic model on 5,000 TF-IDF unigrams and about 4,000 samples will overfit noisy text, and its more extreme probabilities will dominate the 50/50 blend, likely diluting CatBoost's metadata signal and lowering test AUC.
RAOP success rates fell steadily over the collection period, so a smooth date spline adds a real signal on a random split, likely a modest AUC gain of about 0.01.

Swapping to BernoulliNB will likely lower AUC to about 0.615: its independence assumption breaks down on 5,000 correlated unigram and bigram presence indicators, and the 9 binarized requester-history features get swamped by the text features.

RAOP success rates fall over time, so a spline on the request date adds a real but small signal; with C=0.3 and only about five bounded spline columns next to 5k TF-IDF features, expect a modest gain of roughly +0.005 to +0.01 AUC.
Subreddit-membership indicators carry only weak signal on RAOP, and adding about 1,000 unscaled binary columns at C=0.3 adds some noise, so the net AUC change should be roughly zero.

A 50/50 blend with a CatBoost model on the nine metadata features (which alone reach roughly 0.60–0.63 AUC) adds some non-linear signal the logistic regression misses, so expect a small gain, though the fixed equal weighting may dilute the text signal.

Bigrams must share the fixed 5000-feature budget with unigrams (after stop-word removal) and tend to add only noisy, sparse signal on RAOP, so AUC should barely move and may dip slightly; the numeric features and model are unchanged, and the added telemetry is best-effort and shouldn't affect predictions.

Function words are among the strongest authorship signals. Dropping them loses stop-word unigrams and phrases like 'of the', and creates noisy bigrams from non-adjacent words; the char_wb view only partly compensates, so log loss should get modestly worse.

Stacking MultinomialNB on word and char counts with TF-IDF LR, using a log-prob meta-LR, is a known strong recipe on Spooky (about 0.30–0.32); it's partly offset by fold-averaged test predictions from 80%-data models instead of a full-data refit.

On spooky, function words and bigrams built on them are strong author signals, so the word-level LR and NB base models get noticeably worse; the char_wb models and the stop-word meta-feature recover part of that loss at level 2, leaving a modest net regression.

A linear softmax on standardized raw (not log) probabilities can't recalibrate the near-0/1 NB outputs or model the nonlinear interactions between base models that LightGBM captures, so the loss likely regresses slightly despite the lower variance.

In Spooky, punctuation is a known strong authorial signal (semicolons and commas for MWS and EAP, quote and dash habits), and char n-grams capture it, so stripping punctuation from the char block likely removes useful features and raises log loss by a few percent.

Stacking a less-regularised word LR, a char LR and alpha-tuned NB models under a CV-tuned LR meta-learner typically brings Spooky log loss to about 0.33–0.36, well below the single C=1 LR's 0.439; 5-way parallel char-LR folds should fit the time budget.

Keeping only the top 10k chi2 columns throws away useful n-gram signal. Because the selected rows are not re-normalized, their TF-IDF norms shrink, which makes C=1 regularize even harder on an LR that is already underfit, so its OOF gets worse. The NB blend absorbs part of the loss, giving a mild regression.

Function words are strong stylometric signals for authorship, so stripping them hurts NB and the word block noticeably; the char_wb n-grams still partly capture them, which limits the damage to a moderate regression.

C=1 under-fits these L2-normalized word and char TF-IDF features, so a 5-fold CV search should pick C around 10–30 and lower log loss to about 0.38–0.39; the explicit 25 fits run 5 in parallel and should finish within the time budget.

Stacking diverse word/char LR and MultinomialNB out-of-fold predictions with LightGBM is a known strong recipe on Spooky; NB count models add signal that complements the TF-IDF models, so expect roughly 0.33–0.37, with small extra gains from the meta-features and the fold-averaged test predictions.

Cross-word, case-sensitive char n-grams add real stylistic signal, but spreading the L2-normalized char block over roughly 400k columns dilutes each feature's value, so an already under-confident C=1 logistic regression gets effectively stronger regularization; I expect these to roughly cancel, with a slight regression.

The strongly regularized LR (C=1) is underconfident while count-based MultinomialNB is sharp and overconfident, so an out-of-fold-tuned arithmetic blend should cut log loss substantially; the MLflow wrapper is best-effort and shouldn't affect the run.

Function words ('the', 'of', 'and', 'upon') carry much of the stylometric signal for telling these authors apart, so removing them should lower accuracy; since fastText at lr=0.5 and 25 epochs is already overconfident, the extra errors should push log loss up.

The fastText model (lr=0.5, 25 epochs) is already overfit and overconfident; oversampling adds duplicated minority examples (more memorization) and shifts the prior away from the natural test distribution, so log loss should get slightly worse.

The blend weight is chosen by out-of-fold log loss with w=1.0 (plain LR) available as a fallback, so a regression is unlikely; NB-style models on n-gram TF-IDF are known to complement LR on this task, but ComplementNB's soft, pooled-complement probabilities limit the gain to a modest few percent.

On Spooky, MultinomialNB over TF-IDF features usually scores about 0.42–0.48 log loss even with alpha tuned, because the calibration is poor. Stacking highly correlated char n-grams breaks the independence assumption, so it very likely loses to the CV-tuned logistic regression (0.355).
On Spooky, character n-grams carry strong stylistic signal such as punctuation and morphology that complements word n-grams, so a word-only NB-SVM usually loses a few hundredths of log loss.

ComplementNB with alpha=1 on a TF-IDF stack of roughly 160k features is heavily smoothed and adds no class prior; each class's complement mixes two authors, so the logits are compressed and the probabilities badly underconfident. Expect log loss near 0.8–0.9, far worse than NB-SVM's 0.41.

C=1.0 over-regularizes a high-dimensional word+char TF-IDF logistic regression, so CV on log loss should pick C of roughly 3–10, which typically cuts Spooky log loss by a few hundredths; runtime should fit the budget with parallel folds.

Multinomial NB on stacked word and char TF-IDF (my estimate from recalled Spooky kernel results, nothing run here) is typically about 0.45–0.58 log loss, worse than the tuned LR's 0.425, because overlapping char n-grams double-count evidence and make it overconfident.

fastText is run with lr=0.5 and 25 epochs on about 17.6k short sentences, so it will nearly memorize the training set; its accuracy (~80–83%) is comparable to the current model, but its probabilities will be extremely confident, and the ~17% wrong predictions will carry heavy per-row loss, making log loss much worse than the calibrated TF-IDF+LR score of 0.43.

C=1.0 underfits sparse word+char TF-IDF features on this task, so CV will likely pick C=4 or C=8 and cut log loss to roughly 0.37-0.39, assuming the parallel CV search finishes within the time budget.

The baseline LR at C=1 is under-fit on L2-normalized TF-IDF. Weighting features by NB log-ratios with C=4 sharpens the probabilities and usually cuts log loss on spooky to about 0.38-0.40, though heavy alpha=1 smoothing over ~150k features and one-vs-rest renormalization limit the gain.

14 MaxAbs-scaled dense style features added to ~100k+ TF-IDF columns under C=1 LR carry little signal beyond what char n-grams (which already capture punctuation) encode, so expect a tiny improvement or near no change.

NB log-count-ratio scaling amplifies discriminative word and character n-grams, which effectively loosens the underfit C=1 regularization on TF-IDF and usually beats plain logistic regression on this task; renormalizing the three one-vs-rest probabilities costs a little calibration, so I expect a moderate gain to about 0.39-0.40.

TF-IDF with logistic regression is already underconfident and underfit at C=1 on this task (larger C usually lowers log loss), so C=0.25 shrinks the logits further and makes probabilities softer, which sharply worsens log loss.
Dropping the word uni/bigram block removes complementary lexical signal, and the char_wb block at C=1 is already underfit, so the log loss should get somewhat worse.

Removing the NB log-ratio scaling leaves unit-norm TF-IDF inputs, so C=1 regularizes much harder and the model underfits (spooky TF-IDF logistic regression at C=1 usually scores about 0.58-0.65), losing the supervised feature boost.

On L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF, logistic regression is already under-confident at C=4. Halving C to 2 tightens regularization further, so predicted probabilities flatten and log loss rises (the optimal C here is usually well above 4). The added tracking code does not affect the predictions.

My guess is this gets worse. NB log-ratio scaling at C=4 weakens regularization and makes the models overconfident, and renormalized one-vs-rest probabilities are usually less calibrated than multinomial logistic regression, so log loss likely rises to around 0.39–0.42.

Stop words carry much of the author's style, so removing them from both word and char features should raise log loss by roughly 0.06–0.09; content words, punctuation and temperature scaling limit the damage.

Stronger L2 regularization should hurt here. With L2-normalized TF-IDF on spooky, logistic regression typically does better at higher C, so C=0.25 likely costs discrimination. Temperature scaling corrects the resulting underconfidence but cannot recover the lost ranking quality.

Switching the character TF-IDF from 'char_wb' to 'char' lets n-grams span word boundaries and punctuation (for example ', and' or '; the'), which carry authorship style, so I expect a small gain; the 60k max_features cap drops more of the larger 'char' vocabulary, which limits it, while removing the holdout and adding MLflow tracking don't change the final fit.

NB log-count-ratio scaling sharpens the most discriminative n-grams and effectively weakens regularization for the underfit C=1 TF-IDF model, which usually cuts log loss by a few points on Spooky; heavy +1 smoothing and one-vs-rest renormalization, which hurts calibration somewhat, limit the gain.

C=1 is likely over-regularized for L2-normalized TF-IDF features in the 100k+ range, so raising C to 4 sharpens the predicted probabilities and should cut log loss meaningfully without overfitting badly; dropping the holdout print does not affect the submission.

Logistic regression with C=1 on stacked TF-IDF features is usually underconfident, so the fitted temperature will likely be below 1. Sharpening the probabilities should cut log loss by a few percent. The full-data refit is slightly more confident, which trims the gain a little.

Training on log1p and inverting with expm1 predicts roughly a conditional median rather than the mean, which biases predictions low on skewed fares and slightly hurts dollar RMSE; the corrupt-row floor of about 2.1 RMSE dilutes the effect, and the MLflow logging is best-effort and should not change the score.

Four times more data should help the capacity-limited LightGBM a little on the valid rows (about 3.55 to 3.50 RMSE), but the roughly 2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the gain, so expect only a small improvement that should still fit the time budget.

Airport-distance features give the trees an easier way to find JFK flat fares and airport trips, which should trim clean-row RMSE by a few percent. The corrupt-row floor dominates the total, though, so the overall gain stays small (~1-2%).

A log1p target makes the L2 model predict a conditional geometric mean, which expm1 turns into a low-biased dollar prediction, while the grader scores RMSE in dollars. The bias costs most on noisy long trips and on the ~2.8% corrupt, high-variance rows, so expect a slight regression rather than a gain.

Distance is already the dominant, well-sampled split feature with 4M rows, so there is little spurious non-monotonicity to remove, while real non-monotone structure exists: near-zero-distance round trips with high fares, and flat-rate airport fares. The default 'basic' monotone method also restricts splits, so I expect a slight regression.

Training on log1p(fare) and back-transforming with expm1 predicts roughly a conditional median, which sits below the conditional mean, so high fares like airport and out-of-town rides get under-predicted. That usually worsens dollar RMSE a little, and the fixed floor from corrupt test rows dampens the overall change.

In-sample encoding puts each row's own fare into its key's mean. For sparse ~2 km route keys, the model can recover the fare from the low-count fare_mean and log_count, but at test time those keys are unseen or unleaked, so it overfits and generalises worse; early stopping on the clean holdout only partly limits the damage.

Fitting on log1p and back-transforming with expm1 gives a median-like prediction that runs low. That bias hurts dollar RMSE most on the high-fare tail (airport and long trips), so the score should get slightly worse; the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows stays unchanged.

Airport-distance features help LightGBM isolate flat-rate JFK and Newark fares, which it currently has to learn from raw coordinates. That should lower RMSE on valid rows from about 3.6 to about 3.5. The fixed ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the overall gain to around 1%.

Valid rows are essentially unchanged because NaN branches isolate the corrupt rows. The corrupt ~2.8% of test rows gain a little: passenger_count=0 rows keep usable coordinates, half-valid pickups still carry information, and year/hour trends help. Most zero-coordinate fares remain unpredictable, so the gain is small.

Four times the training data should modestly lower RMSE on the valid test rows (about 3.6 to 3.5), but roughly 2.1 RMSE of error from corrupt test rows is fixed, and the 1000-tree cap limits the gain, so the overall score improves only slightly.

The out-of-fold route and cell target encodings are implemented correctly and add some toll, airport and flat-fare signal, but LightGBM already learns a lot of spatial structure from the raw coordinates. I expect a modest gain on valid rows (about 3.6 to 3.5), while the roughly 2.1 floor from corrupt test rows caps the overall improvement.

The model will be trained with squared error in log space, which estimates the geometric rather than the arithmetic mean after expm1, so predictions shift slightly low. That hurts dollar RMSE on the valid rows (about 3.6 to 3.65–3.7). The fallback rows lose more, about $2 each, because of their wide fare spread, so the overall score gets modestly worse.

Manhattan distance and bearing give LightGBM a small gain on the valid rows (for example, airport and bridge directions). The fixed floor from corrupt rows and the unchanged fallback model limit the overall improvement.

Distances to the airports and Manhattan help the trees isolate flat-rate and surcharged airport trips, likely cutting valid-row RMSE by about 0.1–0.2. The overall gain is diluted by the fixed ~2.1-RMSE floor from corrupt test rows, and by the raw coordinates already capturing much of this signal with 4M rows.

Switching to an L1 objective makes the model predict the conditional median, which sits below the mean for right-skewed fares, so it systematically underpredicts the long and airport trips that dominate squared error. L1 boosting also converges more slowly under this fixed learning rate and tree budget. I expect RMSE on the valid rows to rise from about 3.6 to about 3.85, while the error floor from the corrupt test rows stays the same.

A log1p target makes the model predict something close to the conditional geometric mean, which runs low on high fares such as airport and long trips. That hurts dollar-scale RMSE, but the fixed floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the regression.

An L1 objective fits the conditional median, but taxi fares are right-skewed with real high-fare modes (airport flat rates, long trips), so the median sits below the mean and RMSE on the valid rows rises by roughly 0.1–0.2. The ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows is unchanged, so the overall score worsens modestly.

LightGBM's Huber loss with delta=$1 clips each gradient at 1, so a leaf moves at most about $0.05 per iteration and the model has to crawl from the mean toward high fares like the ~$52 airport trips. It also pulls predictions toward the conditional median of a right-skewed target, which RMSE penalises. Expect underfitting on long trips and a slightly worse score, with the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor unchanged.

Training on log1p and back-transforming with expm1 predicts roughly the geometric mean, which is biased low. It also down-weights high-fare tail rides (e.g. airport flat fares) that dominate dollar-scale RMSE, so error on the valid rows likely rises a few percent, diluted by the ~2.1 floor from corrupt rows.
Airport distance features help LightGBM on valid rows (JFK flat fares), maybe 3.6 to ~3.47; the fallback rows are unchanged and dominate the error floor, so the overall gain is diluted to about 2%.

Four times the training data should cut clean-row RMSE by a few percent (about 3.6 to 3.48), but the roughly 2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the gain on the total RMSE, and the run should still fit the time budget.

Averaging 5 fold models trims a little LightGBM variance on the valid rows. Each fold trains on 800k rows instead of 900k, and about 2.8% corrupt test rows fix a noise floor, so the net gain should be small.

The model already sees the raw coordinates, so an out-of-fold ~100m pickup-cell mean fare adds only a little extra spatial signal (airports, tolls); the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes any gain, so expect a small improvement.

Snapping to a 0.01° grid (~1 km) adds roughly 0.4 km of error to each trip's distance, the dominant fare predictor, which hurts short trips most. The coarser route cells add little over the existing 0.01 floor-based encoding, and the fixed ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dampens the change, so expect a modest regression.

An L1 objective fits the conditional median, but the metric is RMSE. Taxi fares are right-skewed (tolls, airport and long trips), so the median underpredicts them. With 1000 capped rounds, the sign-based gradients may also converge more slowly, so RMSE likely rises modestly.

The L1 objective fits the conditional median, which sits below the mean for right-skewed fares, and L1 boosting converges more slowly, so RMSE on the valid rows should get slightly worse; the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row floor dampens the overall change.

Airport-distance features are a known useful signal for flat-rate and long airport fares, but the trees can already partly locate airports from the raw coordinates on 1M rows, and about 2.8% of corrupt test rows fix a floor on the score, so I expect only a small overall gain.

An L1 objective estimates the conditional median, which sits below the mean for right-skewed fares, so predictions are biased low and RMSE rises on valid rows (~3.6 to ~3.7). The mean-fare fallback for corrupt test rows is unchanged, so their ~2.1 RMSE floor still dominates, which limits the overall loss.

LightGBM's quantile histogram bins already pool locations, so rounding to 0.01° (~1 km) mostly throws away finer resolution in dense Manhattan while distance stays exact; expect a slight loss masked by the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor.

The L1 objective fits the conditional median, but taxi fares are right-skewed and the metric is RMSE, so predictions shrink below the mean and RMSE on valid rows likely rises from about 3.6 to about 3.8; L1 also converges more slowly in LightGBM, while the invalid-row floor stays unchanged.

A 29°-rotated Manhattan distance is a well-known small win for taxi-fare GBMs, but it is highly correlated with the existing haversine distance and the corrupt-row floor dominates RMSE, so expect only a slight improvement.

A leak-safe route-mean fare adds a little signal on frequent routes such as airport flat fares, but the heavy smoothing (50) and sparse 1 km cells shrink most routes toward the mean, the trees already learn much of this from raw coordinates, and the ~2.1 floor from corrupt rows dilutes any gain, so expect only a small improvement.

A rotated-grid L1 distance adds a fairly informative feature on top of haversine and the raw coordinates, so RMSE on valid rows should drop slightly (~1%); the corrupt-row floor dilutes this to a small overall gain, and the MLflow logging changes don't touch predictions.

Doubling the training rows should give a small gain on the valid rows (~3.6 → ~3.56), but about 2.1 RMSE of the floor comes from the corrupt test rows, so the overall improvement is diluted; the MLflow additions don't affect predictions.

LightGBM already partly learns airport zones from the raw coordinates, so an explicit airport-route categorical should give only a small gain on the valid rows (JFK flat fares, Newark surcharge), diluted by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows.

Without engineered features, LightGBM struggles more than the MLP with this dataset's linear-combination interactions (f_21+f_02, f_22+f_05, etc.); with only 2000 rounds at lr 0.05 it is likely still improving when it stops, so it probably lands slightly below the MLP's 0.9866.

The key TPS-May interactions are thresholds on linear sums of continuous features (e.g. f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26); decile one-hot binning destroys the fine resolution needed to form those sums, and it also merges integer count levels, so AUC should drop noticeably despite a wider first layer.

The 41 features are close to uncorrelated, so whitening PCA is essentially a random rotation. It smears the discrete f_27 character codes and integer counts across every component, which destroys the axis-aligned structure the trees rely on, and it does not specifically expose the known pairwise sum interactions, so AUC should drop noticeably.

Most f_27 strings are unique, so the out-of-fold target encoding collapses to the prior for nearly every row. That throws away the strong per-position character signal, and the unique-letter-count interaction the trees could partly recover, so AUC should drop substantially.

f_27 has roughly 700k+ unique strings across 900k rows, so the whole-string target encoding is almost always the prior and carries little signal. Dropping the ten per-position character columns throws away the strong character-level signal the trees relied on, leaving only f_27_nunique, so AUC should fall noticeably.

These are the known TPS-May-2022 ternary interaction features (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26). They encode the diagonal boundaries that trees struggle to learn from axis-aligned splits, so LightGBM should gain roughly 0.001 AUC over the 0.9915 baseline.

A linear model scores only about 0.83 AUC here, since the key interactions are nonlinear and threshold-like. Giving it equal rank weight with a 0.984 LightGBM should noticeably degrade the ordering rather than add useful diversity.

This is the proven TPS-May MLP recipe (64-64-64-16 SiLU, Adam 0.01, batch 4096), which models the smooth continuous interactions far better than 3000-tree LightGBM; it still lacks the unique-char-count feature, so I expect roughly 0.992-0.994 rather than 0.998.

In TPS May 2022 the key interactions are linear sums of features that a SiLU MLP learns easily, which the LightGBM baseline captures poorly. A 64-64-64-16 MLP on standardized raw features plus per-character ordinals should reach about 0.99 even without a unique-character-count feature, and 60 epochs of a tiny net on CPU fits the time budget.

Linear leaves can represent the oblique sum-threshold boundaries, but boosting with 127-leaf trees already approximates them well; the run should roughly match the baseline, and linear trees slow training enough that runtime, not accuracy, is the main risk.

The distinct-letter count of f_27 was a known strong signal in this competition, and trees can't easily rebuild it from ten separate per-character ordinals, so one new column should give a clear gain; the linear interactions between numeric columns are still missing, which caps the improvement.

These three sums are the known hidden decision boundaries in TPS May 2022, and giving them to the trees raw lets LightGBM split on them directly, which should add about 1pt of AUC; the missing unique-character count and the cap at 3000 trees keep it below the ~0.992+ top range.

Most of f_27's ~740k values are unique, so LightGBM will lump nearly all of them into an 'other' bin and the categorical column carries almost no signal; dropping the per-position ordinal columns loses real positional information that the letter counts only partly recover, so AUC should fall.

The dominant signal in this dataset is the numeric interactions (f_21/f_02, f_05/f_22, f_00/f_01/f_26) plus the f_27 unique-letter count, and the per-position chars are already given. So 676-level categorical bigrams add little new information and carry some overfit risk from LightGBM's categorical splits; I expect roughly no change, possibly a tiny regression.

f_00..f_15 are nearly independent, and some are integer-valued, so PCA gives roughly arbitrary rotations that miss the key sum interactions (e.g. f_21/f_02, f_00+f_01+f_26); swapping the mined products for these latent factors should be roughly neutral to slightly negative.

f_27 is almost unique per row, so hashing the whole string into 64 buckets gives a random one-hot that is essentially noise. That throws away the per-character position and letter information, which is among the strongest signals in this dataset, so AUC should drop sharply toward the numeric-only level.

Fully grown ExtraTrees with max_features='sqrt' and no engineered interaction features struggle to capture this dataset's additive-sum interactions (for example f_21+f_22 and f_00+f_01+f_26), which boosting with 3000 rounds captures well, so AUC likely drops to about 0.92–0.93. There is also a real risk that the added 5-fold CV pushes the run past the time limit.

An MLP picks up the key linear-sum interactions (f_21+f_02, f_22+f_05, f_00+f_01+f_26) that trees only approximate, so it should beat the untuned LGBM, but sklearn MLP gets limited epochs with accuracy-based early stopping and cannot easily learn the f_27 unique-character equality structure, so the gain is only modest.
The f_27 distinct-character count is a known strong signal in TPS-May-2022 that per-position categoricals can't easily express, and the letter counts add more, so expect roughly a 0.977 to 0.99 jump.

The per-character f_27 codes carry much of the signal in TPS May 2022 (letter identities, and the interactions built from them). Most full f_27 strings are unique, so a frequency count keeps only a weak duplicate-signature signal, and AUC should drop sharply toward a numeric-only model.

The f_27 unique-character count is a known strong signal in TPS May 2022 that trees can't easily reconstruct from positional ordinals; per-letter counts add more, so AUC should rise by roughly 0.01, assuming the run still finishes within budget with about twice as many features.

The known TPS-May-22 interactions are sums involving f_21, f_22 and f_26, which fall outside f_00..f_15, so these products are mostly noise that dilutes colsample; expect a tiny change, likely slightly negative.

Early stopping never fires, so best_iter stays at 3000 and the refit trains about 3333 trees on 11% more rows; the curve is still rising, so expect a small AUC gain, with some risk that roughly double the runtime approaches the time limit.

The ten f_27 positions have few letters and a roughly ordered frequency, so threshold splits already capture most of their signal, while categorical splits add some overfitting. With the main gains coming from unique-char and interaction effects that neither encoding captures, I expect a roughly neutral to slightly negative result.

In TPS May 2022 the distinct-character count of f_27 is a known strong signal. Trees cannot easily reconstruct it from the ten per-position ordinals, so adding it should give a clear gain of a few thousandths AUC over the current 0.9818.

TPS May 2022 depends on higher-order interactions: the f_21/f_02 and f_05/f_22 hidden sums, plus f_27 character structure. With max_depth=2, each tree has at most four leaves and captures only pairwise effects, so even 3000 rounds at lr 0.05 should lose much of the deep-tree signal. The engineered sum covers only one of those interactions, so AUC should drop substantially.

In this competition the key signal comes from smooth linear interactions (such as f_21+f_22 and f_00+f_01), which an MLP captures well; a small LightGBM (600 trees, 31 leaves, max_bin 63, no engineered or unique-character features) will not converge in that budget and should land around 0.93–0.95, well below the MLP's 0.982.

With no interaction features, a small LightGBM (31 leaves, 600 trees at lr 0.05) will still be underfitting the diagonal f_21/f_02 and f_22/f_05 interactions and should land around 0.94–0.95, well below the MLP's 0.982; the diff also early-stops on logloss instead of AUC, but that barely matters.

Cutting the roughly 16 continuous sensors (f_00–f_06, f_19–f_26, f_28) to 4 quartile codes removes most of their fine-grained signal, which matters for the known linear-combination interactions. The strong integer columns and f_27 character features stay, so AUC should drop well below 0.977 but not collapse.

Seven-leaf trees can only express shallow interactions, and this dataset is driven by multi-way ones (f_27 character patterns, sensor combinations); with lr 0.05 and a 3000-tree cap the model will still be underfit when training stops, so AUC should fall noticeably below the 127-leaf baseline.

TPS-May-2022's signal depends on multi-way feature interactions, and 4-leaf trees can capture only about 2-way splits per tree, so 3000 rounds at lr 0.05 would underfit badly compared with 127 leaves.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known TPS-May-2022 sum interactions that trees struggle to learn from raw features, so adding it should lift AUC; the gain is only partial because the f_21+f_02 and f_22+f_05 interactions are still missing.
The f_00+f_01+f_26 sum is one of TPS-May-22's known linear-boundary interactions, which trees approximate poorly on their own, so exposing it directly should give a modest but real AUC gain.

An MLP should capture the linear-sum interactions (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22) more easily than trees, but it still cannot easily learn unique-character counts from scaled ordinals, and 50 epochs of 4096-row batches limits fitting, so the gain over LightGBM's 0.977 should be small.

Each f_27 position has low cardinality and the letters are near-ordinal, so switching them to categorical splits (with 720k rows, little overfitting risk) should change little, maybe a small gain from grouping letters more flexibly while training is still under-converged at 3000 trees.

The f_27 distinct-character count is a known strong signal in TPS May 2022 that is hard for trees to rebuild from the per-position ordinals, so it should add roughly 1 AUC point; no interaction features are added, which limits the gain.

Weighting the loss by how dark the target is biases predictions darker wherever the model is unsure, mostly at stroke edges and faint areas; that mismatches the unweighted RMSE metric, so with a baseline already at 0.016 the likely outcome is a small regression rather than a gain.

At 330 s of training, a modern GPU should get through roughly 15–25k steps instead of 2k, with a proper time-based cosine anneal. That should materially lower the error on this small U-Net with its background-channel input, since random crops limit overfitting. The job should still finish within the time limit, though gains taper off, so I expect about 0.012–0.013.

L1 targets the median rather than the mean, so it snaps ambiguous anti-aliased stroke-edge pixels to one side; those edge pixels dominate the remaining squared error at RMSE of about 0.0165, so this should outweigh the small gain from a whiter background under the sigmoid head, giving a slight regression that is within seed noise.

Test scans share the training set's exposure and noise statistics, so input-only brightness/contrast jitter adds no helpful variation; it forces invariance to absolute gray levels that are actually informative for exact background (1.0) and anti-aliased stroke values, which likely costs precision under the fixed 2000-step budget.

At 0.0154 RMSE the remaining error sits mostly on sharp text-stroke edges. The 0.75x pass (downsample, predict, upsample) and to a lesser extent the 1.25x pass blur those edges, and the model is off its training scale. Averaging them in with equal 1/3 weights adds systematic edge error, so RMSE should get worse.

The short 2000-step run is more likely underfitting than overfitting, since the noise patterns repeat across images; dropping whole channels on the e2 skip adds noise to a precise pixel regression and causes a train/eval variance shift with the downstream BatchNorm, so RMSE likely rises modestly.

Channel dropout adds gradient noise and a BatchNorm train/eval variance mismatch in a pixel-precise regression U-Net whose 180s budget is already tight, and the test pages reuse the training noise templates so memorizing them is not really overfitting; expect a clear regression.

The 4th level roughly doubles the receptive field, which should help with large stains and wrinkle textures. That gain is partly offset by about 25–30% fewer optimizer steps in the fixed 180s budget, so I expect a modest improvement within run-to-run noise.

A 23px median background channel gives the small 3-level U-Net (limited receptive field) direct large-scale stain and shading context, a known-useful feature on this dataset, so a modest gain over an already-strong baseline is likely, though run-to-run noise could mask it.

Two more U-Net levels grow the receptive field from about 50 px to about 200 px, which should help the net model large stains and background gradients. Same pixels per step, so only a moderate gain, tempered by noisier batch-8 BatchNorm, a bigger model at a fairly high LR on a short schedule, and bf16 output quantization.

The model was trained with flip augmentation and its BatchNorm layers run in eval mode, so averaging the four flip variants is a valid ensemble that mainly smooths residual noise near text edges; this typically gives a modest 2-4% RMSE gain, and training itself is unchanged.

The diff sets TRAIN_SECONDS to 180, not the proposed 360, but even 180s should give a small bf16 U-Net at batch 32 on 128px crops several thousand steps versus the baseline's 2000, so the undertrained model should gain a meaningful RMSE drop.

The metric is RMSE, and MSE training already optimizes it directly; Charbonnier/L1 targets the conditional median instead, so it tends to snap background to exactly 1.0 but make larger errors on ambiguous anti-aliased stroke edges, which dominate RMSE, giving a small net regression.

Injected Gaussian noise (σ=0.05, clipped at white) does not resemble the real stain/wrinkle noise, and it destroys fine text-edge information the model needs. That creates a train/test mismatch where the net over-smooths clean-ish test inputs. Memorizing the shared noise patterns actually helps on this dataset, so RMSE likely worsens moderately.

At inference, BatchNorm's running statistics act as a fixed per-channel affine, so it has no real crop-vs-page mismatch; GroupNorm computes statistics per image over space, which creates a new mismatch between near-blank or text-heavy 128px crops and full pages, and partly discards absolute intensity levels, so expect a small regression or no gain.

The graded metric is pixel RMSE, which MSE training optimizes directly. SSIM+L1 instead rewards structure and median-like, snapped stroke edges, and weakly penalizes small intensity offsets, so RMSE likely gets slightly worse (a moderate regression, not a collapse).

Training already covered h/v flips, so rot180 and the two flips are in-distribution and their averaging should help. The four 90° variants show vertical text the net never saw and are likely somewhat worse individually. The denoiser is fairly local and the noise is roughly isotropic, so averaging should still give a small net gain rather than a regression.

An SSIM-only loss barely penalizes absolute intensity and contrast offsets in text and edge regions, which dominate the remaining RMSE. Autocast also runs the SSIM convs in bf16, so the variance terms carry quantization noise several times larger than C2. Both effects should make RMSE worse than the MSE baseline, not better.

The clean targets are nearly binary with a constant white background, so direct sigmoid regression is the natural fit. Residual prediction forces the net to reproduce the structured background texture pixel-exactly (x-1), and bf16 precision limits make that harder. Clamping and the linear head partly offset this, so I expect a roughly neutral to slightly worse RMSE.

The SSIM term is not aligned with the RMSE metric, and because F.conv2d runs under bf16 autocast (pred.float() does not prevent the cast), the variance terms suffer cancellation noise on near-white backgrounds where variance is far below the rounding step. That noisy gradient is on the order of c2 and roughly as large as the RMSE gradient, so I expect a mild regression rather than cleaner edges.

A linear residual head avoids the gradients that vanish in a saturated sigmoid on the mostly-white background, and the clamp at inference then zeroes out any overshoot, so a modest gain is likely; the residual here is structured stains rather than small noise, though, so the benefit is limited and the result stays close to baseline.

Real pairs drop to about 14% of sampled crops (105 real vs 630 synthetic). The synthetic stain, blur and shading noise does not match the fixed real background textures shared by train and test, and it forces the model to learn deblurring of text edges, so it gets far less exposure to the real distribution in the same 2000 steps and RMSE likely gets worse.

At 2,000 steps the small U-Net is likely under-trained, so 4.5x more steps with a stretched cosine schedule should cut RMSE noticeably (estimated ~0.013–0.015); with only 105 training images the gain will taper off, and a small GPU U-Net at 9k steps should fit in the time budget.

The inverse transforms are correct, so 8-fold dihedral TTA should average away some variance and bf16 noise. The flip views match the training augmentation. The four transposed views are out of distribution, since training used flips but no 90° rotations, so they likely add only a small gain or slightly dilute it. Net result: a modest improvement of a few percent.

Swapping in L1 aims the model at the median rather than the mean. On the ambiguous antialiased text edges, which dominate the remaining error at 0.0158 RMSE, that slightly raises RMSE. This is only partly offset by L1 pushing the white background harder toward 1, so a mild regression is expected.

The weighted loss no longer matches the unweighted RMSE metric: its optimum pulls uncertain edge and background pixels darker, which likely costs more than the extra glyph signal gains over 2000 steps, so a small regression is expected.

Weighting by the target makes the loss optimum for uncertain edge pixels E[w·y]/E[w], which is biased darker than the MSE-optimal E[y], and it down-weights background stain removal. With RMSE already near 0.016, where most error sits at stroke boundaries, this mismatch with the evaluation metric should cause a mild regression rather than a gain.

The sigmoid head makes near-binary white backgrounds easy to hit through saturation, whereas an unbounded residual must reproduce 1−x exactly on about 85% of pixels, from bf16 decoder features and with no output bound during training. The [0,1] clamp at inference and the identity skip for text edges only partly offset this, so I expect roughly neutral to slightly worse RMSE.

At an RMSE of about 0.015 the remaining error sits mostly on ambiguous stroke edges and stain residue, where L1's median estimate is not the RMSE-optimal mean, so RMSE likely gets slightly worse; Adam normalizes gradient scale and L1 helps saturate the background, which keeps the loss small.

Residual linear output with inference clipping helps bright backgrounds hit exactly 1.0, but large, structured stain deltas and the loss of sigmoid's easy saturation under a short 2000-step CPU budget roughly offset that, so expect near-neutral to a slight regression.

Halving the width cuts capacity about 4x, and training is still a fixed 2000 steps; the receptive field stays the same, but since random-crop training is not overfitting-limited, the model will likely underfit more and RMSE should rise.

The weights depend on the target, so the loss pulls ambiguous stroke-edge pixels darker than the conditional mean. That misaligns training with the unweighted RMSE metric, and any gain from focusing on text under this short schedule probably won't offset it, so expect a small regression.

A 31x31 closing background-division channel gives the shallow 3-level U-Net stain and illumination context at a larger scale than its receptive field, so a modest gain is likely; this assumes the run finishes, though the diff forces CPU with 8 threads, which puts 2,000 steps at risk of the time limit.

The fp32 head is neutral, but the diff also adds an unrequested runtime.toml that sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' before torch is imported, so 2000 steps of a batch-32 128px U-Net would run on 8 CPU threads (~700 TFLOPs), far past the 15-minute kill. Likely no graded score; 0.0162 is the expected result only if that override is removed.

Most likely outcome is a failed run, not this number: the unrequested runtime.json sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' before torch is imported, forcing about 2000 fp32 U-Net training steps onto 13 CPU threads at a few seconds per step, which would hit the 15-minute hard kill. The figure given only applies if the run finishes; there, 4-way flip averaging of a flip-trained U-Net should cut RMSE by roughly 2-4%.

A width-16 NAFNet with one block per stage has much less full-resolution capacity than the 32-channel BN U-Net, and it trains in fp32 on CPU for the same 2000 steps (which risks the time limit). Its residual output with clamping and global channel attention help, but likely end up at slight parity or a small regression.

The ImageNet-1k head was fine-tuned on images that largely overlap Stanford Dogs, so after temperature tuning its 120-way dog softmax should be a strong, well-calibrated predictor. Blending it with the LR on the same features should noticeably cut log loss, though label-smoothing and mixup in the head's training and the correlation with the LR features limit the gain.

Unwhitened PCA only rotates and centres the features, which L2-penalised LR is already invariant to, so the only real effect is dropping 768 low-variance directions that already carry little weight; that removes a little fine-grained signal, so expect roughly neutral to slightly worse.

With only 6 short epochs, prob=1.0 Mixup/CutMix mostly slows convergence of a backbone that already knows these ImageNet breeds, likely costing a little accuracy; temperature scaling will fix most of the added underconfidence, so expect a small regression rather than a gain.

With only 6 epochs of fine-tuning a strong in22k backbone, whose pretraining already covers these ImageNet dog images, tiny 8% crops often cut the dog out or give ambiguous partial views; that adds label noise and a train/eval scale mismatch, likely slightly worsening calibrated log loss rather than reducing overfitting.

ConvNeXt-V2-L (IN-22k→IN-1k, about 87% top-1) gives far more discriminative frozen features and much better ImageNet dog-breed log-probs than ResNet-50 V1 (76%), so the linear probe log loss should roughly halve; fp16 GRN is safe because norm runs in fp32 under autocast, and runtime stays well within budget at about 10k images.

The 1000-d ImageNet log-proba block is not redundant. All 120 Stanford Dogs breeds are ImageNet classes, and the fc head was trained on about 1300 images per class, many of them the same images. Its log-softmax output is a strong, nonlinear, near-ready classifier that an L2-regularised LR fit on about 77 samples per class cannot recover from the pooled features alone, so dropping it should noticeably worsen log loss.

A ridge probe with a single global temperature usually matches logistic regression on accuracy for strong frozen features. Its least-squares scores are less well calibrated per class than a model trained directly on log loss, especially on fine-grained confusable breed pairs, so I expect log loss to be moderately worse, not better.

Keeping only 128 PCs per block drops some fine-grained breed signal from low-variance directions that the regularised LR on 2560-d features was already using, so log loss likely gets slightly worse; the gain from centring and re-normalising only partly offsets that.

ConvNeXt-Base (in22k pretrained, in1k fine-tuned) gives much stronger fine-grained dog features than ResNet-50 V1, since its ImageNet top-1 is about 85.8% versus 76.1%; the re-tuned logistic regression on its 1024-d layer-normed features should cut log loss substantially, and runtime stays well within budget.

Fine-tuning an ImageNet-22k-pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny for 6 epochs fits the time budget easily and should reach roughly 92-94% accuracy (Stanford Dogs overlaps ImageNet), well above frozen ResNet-50 plus logistic regression; flip-averaged predictions and temperature scaling largely offset the calibration cost of label smoothing, so log loss should land around 0.25-0.32.

The ImageNet head's log-probs are a linear function of the pooled features, but they encode a classifier trained on about 1000 images per breed (plus Stanford Dogs/ImageNet overlap), so standardizing them and tuning C on a holdout makes that strong prior cheap for the logistic regression and should lower log loss noticeably; it won't be dramatic, since the information is already in the features.

Replacing ResNet-50 with three much stronger and complementary frozen backbones (IN22k ConvNeXt-B, CLIP ViT-B/16, DINOv2 ViT-B/14), L2-normalising each block and tuning C on a holdout should cut log loss substantially, to roughly 0.22-0.30, and the run should comfortably fit the time budget.

Focal loss (gamma=2) is not a proper scoring rule, so like label smoothing it leaves predictions underconfident; it also shrinks the effective gradient in a short 10-epoch fine-tune that is not overfitting, so accuracy may dip slightly and log loss will be similar to slightly worse.

The Stanford Dogs classes are a subset of ImageNet, so the pretrained low- and mid-level features are already close to ideal; freezing conv1 through layer3 limits forgetting at lr=0.01 on a small dataset, so accuracy and calibration should improve a little. Label smoothing still sets a floor on how low the log loss can go.

Averaging probabilities over each test image and its mirror should smooth overconfident mistakes for a flip-invariant task on ViT features, a small but reliable log-loss gain; train features and the classifier are unchanged, and switching to NUM_WORKERS=0 only slows loading without affecting the result.

I expect this swap to hurt: all 120 breeds are ImageNet-1k classes, which gives the supervised in21k→in1k ViT-B/16 features a large edge, while OpenAI CLIP ViT-B/32 (coarser patches, weaker fine-grained features) typically reaches only ~75-80% linear-probe accuracy on Stanford Dogs, so log loss should rise to about 0.8.
