L2 is rotation-invariant, so PCA's only real effect is dropping the 1792 low-variance directions (roughly 20-30% of the variance), which L2 already shrank and which likely carry some fine-grained breed signal; with C fixed, expect a small loss of accuracy and calibration and a slightly worse log loss.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 CLS embeddings are much stronger fine-grained features than ResNet-50 V1 (accuracy likely ~86% to ~89-90% on Stanford Dogs), and the logistic-regression head re-tuned on a holdout should stay calibrated; the gain is capped by using only the 224px CLS token and by ResNet-50's own ImageNet overlap, so I expect a moderate drop in log loss rather than a dramatic one. Runtime is fine, since the real forward count is about 19k, not 113k.

Whitening scales the tiny L2-normalised features up to unit variance, so C=1.0 goes from heavily regularising (the current underconfident fit) to barely regularising. The classifier then fits noise that whitening amplified in the low-variance components, and cutting to 256 dimensions drops some fine-grained breed detail, so predictions come out overconfident and log loss should get worse.

A k=10 neighbour vote on L2-normalised concatenated features is less accurate than the tuned logistic regression and poorly calibrated. The smoothing caps the top probability at about 0.894, which adds roughly 0.11 of loss even to perfect predictions. When the true breed is absent from all 10 neighbours, which I expect for about 5–7% of test images, each such image costs about 7.0 nats (the probability is only about 9e-4). Together these should push log loss well above 0.54.

ResNet-50 pretrained features already separate these ImageNet dog breeds well, so 10 epochs of fine-tuning at lr 0.01 should give about the same accuracy, around 83-86%. But 0.1 label smoothing over 120 classes caps confidence near 0.9 and leaves test probabilities poorly calibrated, so log loss likely gets somewhat worse, not better.

The ViT-B/16 augreg in21k→in1k backbone scores about 84.5% ImageNet top-1, versus 76% for ResNet50 V1, and in21k pretraining gives much stronger fine-grained dog features. The 768-d pre-logit feature scale is roughly comparable, so C=0.3 should still be reasonable, and a linear probe on these features should cut log loss by about a third.

10-crop+flip TTA with probability averaging on frozen ResNet-50 features usually gives a modest gain: it smooths overconfident errors and adds a little accuracy, partly offset by corner crops that differ from the center-crop training features and sometimes cut off the dog.

ConvNeXt-Tiny in22k→in1k features are much more discriminative for ImageNet dog breeds than ResNet-50 (accuracy likely rises from ~86% to ~92%), but C=1.0 on L2-normalized ~√2-norm features is roughly 100x more regularization than the tuned raw-feature C, so probabilities come out underconfident and give back much of the log-loss gain.

The pretrained ImageNet head is in effect a linear classifier on the same features but trained on about 10x more dog images, many of which overlap Stanford Dogs. Tuning temperature and blend weight on an internal split should therefore cut log loss noticeably, though both models share one feature space, which limits the gain from diversity.

Orthogonal PCA leaves the L2 penalty unchanged, so the only real effect is dropping 1792 low-variance directions that still carry fine-grained breed signal; with C=0.3 already tuned, the extra truncation should cost a bit of accuracy and log loss rather than help.

ResNet-50 was trained with average pooling, and its average-pooled features already line up almost directly with ImageNet's dog classes; max-pooled layer-4 activations lose that alignment and are larger in scale, so fixed C=0.3 overfits more and accuracy likely drops a few points, with temperature scaling only partly offsetting the worse log loss.

The dog breeds are ImageNet classes, so V2's stronger ImageNet accuracy (80.9 vs 76.1 top-1) should mostly carry over to a linear probe here; its label-smoothing, mixup and cutmix features transfer worse in general, but that matters less on in-distribution classes, and temperature scaling limits any calibration drift.

C=0.03 was already worse than 0.3 on the holdout for plain logistic regression: its head is underconfident and over-shrinks the low-variance discriminative directions. The 2-epoch, 90s fine-tune will restore much of the confidence along the dominant directions but only partly close the gap, so log loss likely ends slightly worse.

Frozen ImageNet ResNet50 features lose fine-grained detail at 192px, and objects appear smaller than the train-time 224 RandomResizedCrop scale (the FixRes effect), so dog-breed accuracy likely drops about 1.5–2.5 points and log loss rises noticeably; the brief last-block fine-tune cannot recover this.

An unwhitened PCA is only a rotation plus centering, and the L2 penalty and unpenalized intercept are unchanged by that, so the only real effect is cutting to 256 components; since between-breed variance dominates these all-dog ResNet-50 features, this should cost a small amount of discriminative detail and slightly raise log loss.

Frozen ResNet-50 features are best at the 224px training resolution; cutting to 192px drops fine detail and makes the train/test object-scale mismatch worse, so fine-grained dog-breed separability falls. Expect roughly a 1–3 point accuracy loss and about 8–14% higher log loss.

Stanford Dogs is a subset of ImageNet's own classes, so V2's higher top-1 (80.9% vs 76.1%) should carry over to the frozen features and outweigh the usual transfer penalty from label smoothing and mixup. The untuned C=0.3 may leave the log loss slightly miscalibrated, so I expect a modest rather than large gain; this assumes the V2 weights download succeeds now that the TORCH_HOME override was removed.

C was already tuned for log loss on a similar holdout, so the fitted temperature should land near 1 and give only a small gain, slightly muted because T is fit on the 85% model but applied to the full-data refit; the removed TORCH_HOME line is a small risk to the weight cache.

Starting from the LR head and applying a low learning rate to only the last bottleneck, trained for 2 epochs on un-augmented cached activations, moves the model only slightly; mild feature adaptation roughly offsets overconfidence from fitting in-sample residuals, so expect a small improvement at best.

Averaging each test image with its horizontal flip on a frozen ResNet-50 plus logistic regression usually gives a small, consistent log-loss gain from smoother probabilities; the extra MLflow and tempdir wrappers fail safely and should not affect the result.

1:1 undersampling discards 80-99% of negatives, down to about 950 rows for threat, which also inflates regularization at fixed C and makes the NB ratios noisy; rank-based AUC gains nothing from rebalancing, so expect clear drops led by threat, identity_hate and severe_toxic.

Adding char_wb n-grams to NB-LogReg is a known gain on its own (roughly +0.003 standalone), but branch B then overlaps more with branch A, so the rank-blend gain shrinks to a few ten-thousandths of AUC, and the run should still fit inside the time limit.

AUC is unaffected by class prior, so 1:1 undersampling gains nothing and throws away 80–99% of the negatives. The rare labels (threat at ~960 rows, identity_hate, severe_toxic) are hit hardest: NB ratios get noisy, and the fixed C now regularizes much more heavily relative to the smaller data, so each column's AUC should drop.

Plain MultinomialNB on TF-IDF bigrams is much weaker than NB-LogReg (likely ~0.94-0.95 AUC, with overconfident, tie-prone probabilities), so both the stacked features going into branch A and the equal-weight rank blend get worse, pulling the mean AUC down by roughly half a point.

Mean-pooled corpus Word2Vec plus logistic regression typically reaches only about 0.95–0.965 AUC on Jigsaw, well below word+char TF-IDF (about 0.978), so branch A gets clearly weaker. The MLP on 200-d dense inputs is also weaker than on the sparse n-grams. Rank-averaging two weaker, mutually correlated branches at 2/3 total weight with NB-LR should pull the blend down by about half a point, while runtime should stay within budget.

1:1 undersampling discards 90–99% of negatives. AUC does not need balancing, so this is mostly lost information, and the loss hits the rare labels hardest: threat drops to ~956 rows, and C=0.1 over so few rows becomes much stronger regularization. The NB ratios also get noisier, and the MLP gets far fewer update steps, so every branch degrades and the blend loses roughly 0.01 AUC.

A sparse TF-IDF MLP should finish in about 1–2 min, pass the 0.97 sanity check and enter the blend. As a somewhat weaker (~0.977–0.979) but non-linear model fit on 90% of train, at 1/4 weight it adds modest diversity to three correlated linear branches, for a small gain partly offset by weaker rare-label (threat/identity_hate) ranking.

AUC does not depend on the class prior, so balancing buys nothing, while undersampling throws away 90–99.7% of the negative rows; with fixed C, the much smaller training sets (about 956 rows for threat) change how strongly the models are effectively regularized and hurt the rare labels most, so AUC should drop about 0.005–0.015 across labels.

The TF-IDF vectorizers already lowercase, and the char_wb n-grams already capture most obfuscations and elongations. That leaves de-obfuscation and the u/ur→you/your mapping with only small gains, which are likely offset by losing the timestamp/(utc) non-toxic signal and repeat-intensity cues, so the net is roughly neutral within rare-label noise.

Branch A can freely use the six dense OOF NB-LR columns, since the L2 penalty on one well-supported dense weight is tiny against a C·n data term, and the cross-label signal helps rare labels. But stacked A now mostly re-encodes B, so the 50/50 rank blend loses diversity and overweights B, leaving a small net gain (~+0.0005); the 30 extra liblinear fits also add real timeout risk.

A 3-epoch shallow MLP on the word+char TF-IDF should land a bit below the linear branches (roughly 0.975-0.978 AUC). Its nonlinear, multi-task errors should still be diverse enough that an equal-weight rank blend gains a few ten-thousandths. The extra runtime (~2-3 min of Adam steps over 3.8M dense params) should fit under the 15-minute kill.

A third NB-LogReg branch on word 1-2-gram plus char_wb features is a somewhat diverse, individually decent (~0.978-0.980) model, so an equal rank-blend should give a small gain of a few ten-thousandths; the gain is limited by its high correlation with A and B, and the extra char-feature liblinear fits add some runtime risk.

The per-label weights will likely land around 0.55–0.65 toward the stronger word+char branch after shrinkage, so the blend moves only slightly from 50/50; expect a tiny gain of about +0.0001 to +0.0002 AUC, within noise. The extra holdout fits should still finish under the hard 15-minute kill.

Squeezing the sparse n-gram space into 300 LSA factors discards the specific profanity, slur and threat n-grams (and all char n-grams) that drive AUC on the rare labels, and it drops the NB-LR/rank-blend ensemble; dense LSA plus logistic regression usually lands around 0.95–0.965 on this task.

At 10:1, toxic keeps essentially all its rows, but severe_toxic, threat and identity_hate drop to roughly 5–17k training rows. That discards hard negatives, makes the NB ratios and fastText noisier, and effectively over-regularizes C=0.1 LR, so the rare-label AUCs should fall and pull the mean down modestly.

A single softmax fastText model splits probability mass across co-occurring labels, so heavily toxic comments get diluted P(toxic/obscene/insult) and rank below borderline ones, which likely lowers branch F's per-column AUC. That branch has only 1/3 weight in the rank average, and shared embeddings may help the rare labels slightly, so the net effect should be a small regression.

For binary labels ComplementNB ranks exactly like multinomial NB on raw counts, which suffers from document-length bias and, on rare labels (~0.3–1% positive), heavy smoothing over 200k features that rewards rare vocabulary; that should land well below the tuned three-branch LogReg/NB-LogReg rank blend (~0.93 versus 0.98).

Averaging corpus-trained skip-gram vectors dilutes the few decisive abuse tokens, especially in long comments. With only 200 dimensions and a linear head, this pipeline typically scores about 0.95–0.96 mean AUC on Jigsaw, well below sparse NB-LR/char TF-IDF ensembles at around 0.98. The rare labels (threat, identity_hate) should suffer most.

Averaging Word2Vec vectors trained on the corpus for only 5 epochs, then fitting a linear model, washes out the few toxic tokens in long comments and loses the char and n-gram signal for misspellings. This typically lands around 0.94–0.96 AUC, well below the 0.98 TF-IDF/NB-LR blend, with the rare threat and identity_hate labels hit hardest.

A char_wb NB-LogReg branch adds real diversity against the word-level NB branch and the lightly weighted char LR, so a tuned three-way rank blend should gain roughly +0.0005–0.001 AUC. Noisy holdout weights on rare labels and the no-refit 90% fit cap the gain; runtime rises to about 10–12 min but should stay under the 15-min kill.

C=4 probably helps branch A on frequent labels, but it likely overfits the rare threat/identity_hate labels and makes branch A more like branch B (also C=4), costing blend diversity; net effect should be roughly flat to slightly negative.

Scratch-trained fastText at epoch=20 and lr=0.5 overfits and saturates its probabilities, so it scores about 0.955–0.965 AUC on its own (weakest on threat and identity_hate); giving that weaker branch an equal 1/3 rank weight roughly cancels the gain from its diversity, so expect flat to slightly worse.

A char-level NB-LogReg view should add some diversity to the rank blend (typically +0.0003 to +0.0008 AUC on this competition), but a second char_wb vectorizer (3-7-grams on ~313k docs) plus primal liblinear fits adds roughly 5-7 minutes, which puts the run near the 15-minute kill. So I expect only a small gain, with a real risk of a timeout.

Training both branches on only 90% of the data likely costs a few ten-thousandths of AUC, and per-label weights tuned on a noisy 10% holdout (the threat label has only about 50 positives there) rarely beat a 0.5/0.5 rank blend by more than that, so I expect a small net regression.

NB log-count weighting may strengthen branch A slightly, since NB features usually help linear text models; but it also weakens regularization at C=0.1 and makes branch A more like branch B, reducing blend diversity, so the net change is roughly neutral to slightly negative.

min_df=0.01 on about 313k documents means a term must appear in at least ~3.1k documents. That cuts the word vocabularies to roughly 1k terms and removes rare slurs, threat and identity-hate cues, so the NB-LogReg branch degrades sharply. The char branch keeps a moderate set of frequent n-grams and softens the loss, but the blend still regresses.

Per-label balanced undersampling throws away most negatives, down to about 956 rows for threat and about 3k for severe_toxic and identity_hate, so both the linear models and the NB log-count ratios become noisier; the rare labels should lose 1–3 AUC points and the common labels a few tenths, dropping the mean by roughly 0.01.

Swapping the tuned logistic regressions for a cosine difference-of-centroids classifier discards all discriminative weight fitting. Its weights are dominated by frequent n-grams, it is noisy on rare labels, and NB smoothing inflates weights on rare features. This is typically several AUC points below logistic regression on this task, though the strong lexical toxicity signal keeps it around 0.92-0.94.

char_wb drops cross-word n-grams (and with max_features=50k the kept vocabulary shifts toward within-word fragments). Char and char_wb TF-IDF+LR usually score within about ±0.0005 AUC of each other, and rank-blending with the NB-LR branch dampens the effect further, so the expected result is roughly neutral to slightly worse.

In binary tasks ComplementNB ranks exactly like MultinomialNB, so both branches lose the discriminative logistic fit. With alpha=1 on fractional TF-IDF mass over 60k–200k features, the rare classes (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) are swamped by smoothing: rare and unusual words get spurious positive weight and correlated char n-grams are double-counted, so per-label AUCs fall to roughly 0.90–0.96 and the rank blend lands around 0.94.

Compressing about 60k TF-IDF features to 32 SVD components discards most of the discriminative lexical signal, especially for rare labels, and C=0.1 underfits the dense features further. Branch A likely drops to about 0.91–0.93 AUC, and an equal rank-average with the weaker fastText branch pulls the blend down noticeably.

Capping the vocabulary at 2,000 tokens turns misspellings, obfuscated profanity, concatenated insults and rarer slurs into one 'raretoken', which guts the char n-gram signal in branch A and the fastText vocabulary; the common toxic words survive, so AUC drops moderately rather than collapsing.

Keeping stop words restores pronouns like 'you' and 'your', which carry signal for insults, but the char_wb 2-6-grams and the NB-LogReg branch already capture them. It also displaces only about 300 of the 10k vocabulary slots, so expect a negligible, possibly slightly positive shift.

Averaging logits instead of ranks shifts weight toward branch B, whose C=4 fit spreads logits much wider than branch A's heavily regularized C=0.1 fit; branch B is usually the slightly weaker branch, so expect a small loss or no change rather than a gain.

Switching char_wb to char in the 50k 2-6-gram TF-IDF adds cross-word-boundary fragments, which the Jigsaw kernels using analyzer='char' found about as good or slightly better; halved by the rank blend with NB-LR, the net effect should be within noise (roughly ±0.0005).

A 5-epoch, 64-dim fastText model without pretrained vectors is expected to score about 0.965–0.97 AUC on Jigsaw, below NB-LogReg (~0.977), and it will be especially weak on the rare labels threat and identity_hate. Rank-averaging it at equal weight with the ~0.979 word+char branch should therefore pull the blend slightly down, and the added model diversity will probably not make up for that.

The 192 leaf descriptors are nearly all informative and near-linearly separable once standardized, so dropping 64 of them (mostly low-F texture and shape bins) makes the C=1 logistic regression less confident and slightly less accurate; the blend then gets modestly worse rather than better.

The NN is already highly accurate, so eps=0.1 label smoothing caps its true-class probability near 0.9 (a NN log-loss floor of about 0.1). That under-confidence carries straight into the 50/50 arithmetic blend and outweighs any calibration gains on the few hard Quercus/Acer cases, so log loss likely gets worse.

With only about 8–10 positives per species, each OvR binary model gives poorly calibrated scores that don't compete with each other. After normalizing across classes, the confidence is spread unevenly, and a single power-and-floor calibration can only partly correct that. Accuracy should stay similar, but the joint softmax of multinomial LR usually yields clearly better log loss, so expect a moderate regression.

A 512-unit MLP bag on the scaled 192 descriptors is usually competitive with or better than LR on this dataset, and blending two different models before OOF-tuned calibration (with w=0 as a fallback) should lower log loss moderately, though the small test set keeps the gain noisy.

The five fold models are highly correlated, since each pair shares about 80% of the training rows, so averaging gives only modest smoothing. Each fold model also loses about 20% of the roughly 8–10 samples per class, which likely costs slightly more than the ensembling gains and makes log loss a little worse than the full-data refit.

The pre-extracted shape descriptor is scale-normalised, so absolute size, aspect ratio, solidity and Hu moments add real complementary signal; they should resolve a few of the confusions that dominate a high-C logistic regression's log loss on a small test set. I expect a meaningful but noisy gain, with some risk from outlier features or the images folder being absent, in which case the score would be unchanged.

An unwhitened PCA rotation does not change the L2-penalised logistic regression, because the L2 penalty is rotation-invariant; the only real effect is dropping the ~100+ low-variance directions (5% of variance), and these are barely shrunk at C=1 with n=990, so they still carry discriminative margin/texture/shape detail and removing them should make the classifier less confident and raise log loss moderately.

Logistic regression is a convex, low-variance model, so bagging it gains little, while each fold model trains on 8 instead of 10 samples per class with the same C (effectively stronger regularisation); the averaged fold models are likely slightly less accurate and less sharp than the full refit, giving a mild log-loss regression.

The image-plus-feature NN should reach roughly 0.04-0.07 log loss on its own, with the feature branch doing most of the work. Averaging it arithmetically with the underconfident LR (0.124, C=1) should cut the loss substantially, though the LR's softness limits the gain to around 0.07-0.08. Runtime is close to the 9-minute guard, but a truncated full-data run would still be adequate.

LR at C=1 on standardized leaf features is strongly underconfident (~98% accuracy, but log loss 0.124). OOF-fitted power sharpening (a≈2–3) plus a small uniform floor should roughly halve the log loss. The gain is slightly tempered because the full-data refit is more confident than the fold models, so the chosen a may overshoot a little.

C=1 over-regularises these nearly separable standardised leaf features; cross-validation should pick C around 100–2000, which typically gives about 0.03–0.06 log loss for logistic regression on this data, and the 55 lbfgs fits should finish within the 10-minute budget.

Image size, aspect ratio, solidity and eccentricity add species signal that the 192 descriptors lack, so this should give a modest gain. Log-transformed Hu moments (sign flips, some tiny values) and the count and Euler features add noise, which limits the gain for untuned LR at C=1.

Leaf classes are nearly linearly separable on standardized features, so a stronger L2 penalty mostly shrinks the logits and makes predictions underconfident, which inflates log loss; this setup usually does better with weaker regularization (larger C).

Dropping the refit trains on ~8 instead of ~10 samples per class across 99 classes, and makes the fixed C=1 penalty relatively stronger. That should give less confident and slightly more error-prone probabilities, so test log loss likely rises.

Blend weights fit on OOF predictions will likely stay LR-dominant, with small weights on distance-kNN and shrinkage LDA; that adds some diversity for a modest log-loss gain, though the small test set adds noise and LDA overconfidence limits the upside.

With 99 classes, only about 9 training samples per class, and a further 15% held out for early stopping, histogram GBDT with min_samples_leaf=10 cannot isolate classes cleanly, so it stays far less calibrated and accurate than the tuned linear logistic regression on standardised descriptors; GBDT on this dataset typically lands around 0.5–1.5 log loss.

With only 2-3 positives per class in each 3-fold calibration split, Platt's smoothed targets cap each one-vs-rest probability near 0.8 and give every wrong class a small floor, so the calibrated SVC's predictions are much softer than C=1 softmax LR's; averaging it in lowers the true-class probability in the soft vote, so log loss likely gets worse.

The RF (600 trees, fully grown, 99 classes) will be more accurate than the overfit, near-0/1 HGB, but its vote-fraction probabilities are strongly underconfident (true-class probability around 0.5). Under uniform soft voting, that dilution on the many easy test rows roughly cancels or slightly outweighs the tail rescue on hard rows, so expect a near-tie with a slight regression on this noisy 99-row test set.

An MLP on about 800 effective samples of 99 classes, early-stopped on validation accuracy from about 89 unstratified samples, likely restores underconfident or noisy weights, so the OOF shrinkage cannot sharpen it; expect it to be about as accurate as the logistic regression but worse calibrated, around 0.13–0.25.

On standardized leaf features, C=1 over-regularizes multinomial LR; CV should pick C around 100–1000, and with the OOF-tuned uniform shrinkage kept as a safety net, log loss should drop to roughly 0.04–0.07.

Hu moments, size and elongation scalars, and the radial histogram add discriminative global-shape and scale information that the 192 descriptors only partly cover; with StandardScaler and the same C=1 logistic regression this should sharpen the correct-class probabilities modestly, though some features duplicate the shape descriptor and the small test set keeps variance high.

C=1 over-regularises this near-separable 99-class problem; I expect 10-fold CV log-loss tuning to pick C around 100–1000, which usually brings standardised-feature LR to about 0.03–0.06 log loss, and the run should fit well inside the time budget.

Equal-weight soft voting pulls the strong, confident models (LR and shrinkage-LDA) toward weaker members. Distance-weighted kNN gives diffuse-to-sharp probabilities. HGB on about 8 samples per class and 99 classes becomes overconfident from large Newton leaf steps and has much lower accuracy. So wherever kNN or HGB is wrong, the correct-class probability is capped near 0.6–0.7, which likely raises log loss above the 0.124 baseline despite some error-averaging benefit.

LR at C=1 is heavily regularised and likely under-confident rather than over-confident, so the OOF grid (0.01 steps) probably picks alpha=0 or 0.01, leaving the test log loss essentially unchanged or very slightly worse.

Auto shrinkage fits Ledoit-Wolf per class (about 10 samples each) toward that class's own feature variances, so it keeps per-feature within-class weighting. A fixed 0.9 blend toward one pooled variance for every feature drops that weighting and makes the model close to Euclidean nearest-centroid, so accuracy probably falls a few points. Errors will likely still be near-certain and heavily penalised, so log loss probably rises, though the change could also damp spikes from very low-variance features.

Each single-family LDA is much weaker than the full model (margin ~80-85% accuracy, texture ~75%, shape ~55-65%). Averaging their probabilities avoids a few catastrophic near-zero errors but caps confidence at about 2/3 whenever one family, usually shape, misses. It also discards the cross-family covariance, so the net log loss likely rises.

A 90% PCA on the standardized descriptors keeps roughly 50–70 components and drops the low-variance directions. For these near-separable leaf features, those directions often still separate species, and plain L2 regularization already handles the redundancy. So PCA likely removes useful signal and raises log loss moderately rather than stabilizing the fit.

LDA on 192 features across 99 classes should be accurate (about 98%), but its posteriors are extremely sharp, so each of the one to three likely test misclassifications (in roughly 99 test rows) costs about 20–34 nats, and shrinkage tuning won't fix that the way the smoothly calibrated LR did.

An unwhitened PCA is only a rotation, and the L2 penalty ignores rotations, so the change's only real effect is to drop the lowest-variance directions (notably the many collinear shape components); those carry some fine discriminative signal the C=1 LR was using, so I expect a modest loss increase partly offset by temperature recalibration.

Shrinkage LDA probably matches or beats logistic regression on accuracy for these features. Its discriminant scores are huge, though (Mahalanobis gaps in 192 dimensions), so even T=4 leaves them overconfident, and each rare test error costs a lot of log loss, likely making the score worse than the calibrated LR's 0.045.

Mixing in 0.005 of the uniform distribution adds about -log(0.995) ≈ 0.005 nats to every confidently correct prediction. The added floor of 5e-5 per class only helps when the true-class probability is below about 1e-3, and a C=1 logistic regression with a 0.094 loss is unlikely to have many such errors, so a small regression is most likely.

Cutting the Nyström landmarks from 512 to 384 on roughly 900 training rows gives a coarser RBF kernel approximation with fewer standardized features and the same C, so the model loses some separability and logit scale; expect a slight log-loss regression, though the effect is noisy.

Shrinkage LDA should classify these descriptors about as accurately as logistic regression, but its generative probabilities are far more extreme (with class-separated 192-dim standardized features); an uncalibrated error or two costs tens of nats each and should inflate log loss well above 0.124.

On standardized leaf descriptors, logistic regression is known to be strongly under-fit at C=1, so 3-fold CV should select C=100 or 1000, which typically brings log loss down to roughly 0.03–0.07; the MLflow wrapper is fault-tolerant and the runtime is small.

L2-regularised LR at C=1 is underconfident on this highly separable 99-class problem, so the out-of-fold temperature will likely come out around 0.4–0.6 and sharpen the probabilities, cutting log loss substantially; the gain is limited because the full-data refit is slightly more confident than the fold models and any misclassified test rows get penalised harder.

Nyström RBF features at gamma=1/192 act like linear plus polynomial features, and standardizing them makes the effective scale larger. That weaker effective regularization may give sharper probabilities, but the high-order parts are distance-based and treat every descriptor equally. They add noisy, memorization-like capacity and weaken the linear part that already works well here. With only 99 test rows, a mild regression is more likely than a gain.

In RAOP, request length and posting time are known useful signals, and the l2-normalised TF-IDF block cannot see length or time, so the new dense block should give a modest AUC gain over the 0.671 baseline.

With max_features='sqrt' (about 90 of roughly 8k mostly-sparse columns per split), the forest rarely sees the few informative numeric columns and wastes splits on rare tokens, so its AUC should land a bit below the tuned-free linear model on this small, text-heavy dataset.

RF with max_features='sqrt' over about 5k sparse TF-IDF columns rarely sees the nine numeric columns or the strong giver_known indicator as split candidates; that dilutes both the leak and the text signal, and RF on sparse unigrams usually ranks worse than logistic regression, so AUC likely drops by a few points.

Most of the 0.748 likely comes from the giver_known leak and the requester metadata, and neither changes; 50 unsupervised LDA topic proportions typically carry less discriminative signal than 5k TF-IDF unigrams on RAOP (topics alone reach roughly 0.58–0.60 AUC versus about 0.63 for TF-IDF), so I expect a small regression rather than a gain.

Swapping the supervised out-of-fold TF-IDF LR logit, a compact and strong text signal, for 20 weak unsupervised LDA topic proportions loses most of the text signal on ~4k rows, so AUC should fall toward the metadata-only level plus a small topic contribution.

On RAOP the success rate falls steadily over the collection period, and the test split is likely a random split within the same window, so the raw timestamp is a genuinely predictive in-distribution feature; hour and weekday carry only weak signal, so swapping them in should give a small net loss.

A shallow, well-regularized HistGradientBoosting model on the requester-history, time and text-statistics features (roughly 0.63–0.66 AUC alone) adds nonlinear signal that is fairly decorrelated from the text-heavy logistic regression; a rank blend with the weight picked by 5-fold CV should typically add about 0.005–0.02 AUC over 0.7007, with limited downside.

The strong features are about 42 dense metadata columns buried among 5000 sparse TF-IDF columns, so with max_features='sqrt' most split candidates are near-useless sparse text terms and fully grown trees overfit that noise on about 4.5k rows. A random forest on RAOP typically lands around 0.64–0.68, below this linear TF-IDF+metadata model.

A bag of subreddits on RAOP carries weak signal that largely duplicates the activity and subreddit-count numerics already in the model. Adding about 1–2k sparse l2-normalized columns under C=0.3 mostly adds noise that competes with the text block, so I expect a roughly neutral result within about ±0.01 AUC, leaning very slightly negative.

giver_username_if_known leaks the label: it is non-'N/A' for roughly a quarter to a third of successful requests and almost never for failed ones, and the prepared test keeps that field, so the unscaled indicator puts those positives at the top of the ranking (AUC ≈ p + (1-p)·~0.64 ≈ 0.72–0.75); if the field were missing from test, the result would stay near 0.66.

Stacking an out-of-fold text logit with raw requester-history numbers and the UTC timestamp in a heavily regularised, early-stopped LightGBM should add modest non-linear signal, mainly from the time trend, over the linear baseline. The weak unigram LR logit caps the gain at around +0.01–0.02 AUC, and the best-effort MLflow code should not break the run.

In RAOP, time trend (success rate declines over time), body length, imgur/link presence and RAOP-history flags are known weak-to-moderate signals, and they are properly scaled next to TF-IDF in the linear model. Expect a modest gain of about 1–3 AUC points; the best-effort MLflow wrapper shouldn't affect the output.

Logistic regression at C=0.3 likely overfits the thousands of TF-IDF columns plus 384 dense embedding columns. Averaged extra-trees should be more robust and pick up some nonlinear signal from the numerics and embeddings. The gain is capped because only about 0.12 of the ~73 features sampled per split are the informative numerics, and random thresholds on sparse TF-IDF are weak, so expect a modest gain.

The TF-IDF rows are L2-normalized with small values, so under C=0.3 they carried little weight next to the 384 standardized embedding dims. The weakly regularized embedding block is the main source of both signal and overfitting, so dropping TF-IDF should change the AUC only marginally, likely a small loss of lexical signal. The added MLflow wrapper doesn't affect the score.

Length, evidentiality ($/links/digits) and gratitude features are known weak but real signals in RAOP; when scaled into a heavily regularized TF-IDF logistic regression they should add a modest AUC gain of about 1–2.5 points, and the main risk is noise from the extra features.

On RAOP, request-time metadata alone usually scores about 0.60–0.64 AUC, and even heavily regularized TF-IDF text adds a few points on top, so removing the text block most likely costs roughly 0.02–0.03 AUC rather than improving generalization.

Mean-pooled skip-gram vectors trained on only ~5.7k short posts are mostly topical and length signal, carrying about as much signal as, or slightly less than, sparse unigram TF-IDF on RAOP. The 200 standardized dense dims also add some overfitting noise to the metadata- and stats-driven LR, so expect roughly flat to slightly worse AUC.

RAOP text signal is weak and train is small; sparse bigrams at min_df=2 add noise and spread each document's L2-normalized TF-IDF mass across more features, so at fixed C=0.3 the result is roughly flat to slightly worse (the mlflow logging is try-wrapped and harmless).

The current 0.633 likely comes mostly from the requester-history features, since 300-dim SVD text gives LightGBM only weak, noisy signal. Dropping the text removes a small real contribution but also removes noise, so metadata-only (about 0.60–0.64 on RAOP) should land slightly below the current score.

Swapping in a random forest should land roughly level, slightly lower. With sqrt(309)≈17 features per split, the few informative numeric columns get picked rarely among ~300 mostly-noisy SVD components, which dilutes the signal. The forest's variance averaging roughly offsets the overfit-prone num_leaves=63 LightGBM, so the net change is about flat to slightly negative.

MiniLM embeddings add some semantic signal (roughly 0.60–0.63 AUC alone on RAOP), but 384 standardized dense columns under a weakly regularized LR (C=0.3, about 3k rows) will partly overfit and swamp the small TF-IDF values, so the net gain should be small, assuming the model download works and encoding fits in the time budget.

With about 4k training samples, bigrams at min_df=2 add tens of thousands of sparse, noisy features. L2 normalization spreads each row's weight across more terms, which effectively regularizes the text part harder at the fixed C=0.3. The text signal in RAOP is weak anyway, so expect roughly flat to a slight AUC drop.

Request length and narrative cues such as hardship and reciprocity are known RAOP predictors. L2-normalised unigram TF-IDF discards length, so adding scaled dense stats should give a modest AUC gain, though several features overlap with the unigrams and the data is noisy.

With only about 2.9k training rows, LightGBM on 300 noisy SVD text components loses most of the sparse unigram signal that logistic regression uses. It may extract slightly more from the 9 numeric columns, but num_leaves=63 plus the noise columns likely nets a small regression versus 0.657.

The quantile spline on absolute time captured RAOP's strong monotonic decline in success rate over 2010–2013, which annual sin/cos cannot represent; the seasonal signal is weak, so AUC likely drops slightly.
With about 4.5k noisy samples and 5k sparse unigrams, C=30 lets the text coefficients overfit, and that noise swamps the requester-history and date signal that carries most of the AUC at C=0.3.

RAOP success rate falls steadily over the collection period, and the test split likely covers the same span, so a smooth, standardized time spline adds real signal that complements text, history and subreddits for a modest gain of about +0.01 AUC.

Cosine KNN over high-dimensional mixed features is noisy. The standardized numerics (norm ~3) and binary subreddit indicators dominate the unit-norm TF-IDF text, and a 25-neighbor vote on about 4k samples ranks far worse than regularized logistic regression, so AUC likely drops to about 0.58–0.61.

Distance-weighted KNN (k=25) on nine weak metadata features gives noisy, coarse probabilities whose spread is wider than the low-variance LR output, so it dominates the 50/50 blend with a weaker ranking signal than CatBoost and lowers AUC.

With C=30, about 5k sparse unigrams on only about 4k noisy RAOP samples will overfit. The logistic regression's probabilities also become more extreme, so they dominate the 50/50 average and weaken CatBoost's metadata signal, which should lower AUC.

RAOP success rates fall steadily over time, and the test split is probably random, so standardized splines on the request date should add a small but real signal on top of the weak TF-IDF+history logistic model.

BernoulliNB sums independent log-likelihood terms, including absence terms, over roughly 5,000 noisy binarized n-grams with limited positives, so the text noise likely drowns out the nine coarsened above-mean numeric indicators; this should rank worse than the regularized LR (C=0.3), which uses the continuous numeric features.

RAOP success rates fall steadily over time, so a quantile spline on the request date adds a real temporal signal, but its seven unscaled columns are only lightly used by a C=0.3 logistic regression on top of text and history features, which should give a small gain of roughly +0.005 to +0.01 AUC.

Subreddit membership carries weak signal that largely overlaps with the activity counts already in the model, and roughly 1–2k unscaled binary columns at C=0.3 on ~4k samples add noise, so the net effect is roughly flat, possibly a small gain.

CatBoost on the nine request-time metadata features should reach about 0.62–0.64 AUC and capture nonlinearities the logistic regression misses, but it overlaps heavily with the numeric features the logistic regression already uses, so a fixed 50/50 average should only nudge AUC up by about a point.

On a weak-text dataset like RAOP, adding stopword-stripped bigrams under a shared 5000-feature cap mostly swaps rare unigrams for frequent bigrams, so AUC should barely move; the MLflow telemetry is best-effort and removing the holdout doesn't change the final fit.
Stop words and their bigrams are strong stylometric signals for author attribution. The char_wb view only partly recovers the lost function-word patterns, so log loss should get modestly worse.

On Spooky, a log-prob meta-learner stacked over MultinomialNB word and char count models plus the TF-IDF LR is a known strong combination (~0.29-0.32). NB's overconfidence gets rescaled by the meta-LR, so expect a solid gain over the single LR's 0.354, slightly tempered by fold-averaged test inputs and 1e-6 clipping.

In authorship attribution, function words and the bigrams around them carry much of the stylistic signal, so dropping them weakens both word-level base models; the char_wb models and the stacker should recover part of that loss, leaving a small net regression.

A linear softmax stacker on raw (not log) probabilities cannot express the nonlinear recalibration that LightGBM does, especially for the extreme NB outputs and the unscaled-count meta-features, so log loss likely gets slightly worse rather than better.

Punctuation is genuinely discriminative in this corpus: Shelley's semicolons, Poe's heavy commas, dashes and quotes, and Lovecraft's style all differ. Because the word block already ignores punctuation, the char n-grams are the only features carrying that signal, so stripping it should raise the log loss moderately rather than help.

Stacking the diverse word and char NB and LR models with a calibrated meta-LR typically gets ~0.33–0.36 on Spooky, well below the single C=1 LR (0.439); runtime fits the budget since the char-LR folds run in parallel and mlflow failures are handled.

LR at C=1.0 is already over-regularized on TF-IDF; keeping only 10k chi2 columns strips row mass and the correlated n-grams that L2 shares weight across, so the LR out-of-fold loss gets worse, and the NB blend-weight search only partly compensates.

Function words carry strong author style (EAP, HPL and MWS differ in how they use 'of', 'which', 'upon', 'and' and in their bigrams), so removing them hurts the naive Bayes model sharply. The logistic regression is only partly protected, because its char_wb n-grams still see those words. The blend loss should therefore rise by several percent.

C=1 on two stacked L2-normalized TF-IDF blocks underfits; CV will likely pick C≈10 (or 3–30), which typically lowers logloss by about 0.03–0.04. The explicit per-fold fits should still finish within the budget.

Stacking LightGBM on out-of-fold probabilities from diverse models (word/char LR and word/char MultinomialNB) typically lands around 0.33-0.37 on this task, calibrates the overconfident NB outputs, and adds a little from meta-features; averaging the fold models for test costs little, and the runtime fits the budget.

Word-crossing, case-sensitive char 1-5 grams add real stylistic signal (punctuation-in-context, capitalization), but with C=1.0 the LR is already over-regularized. The extra uncapped rare n-grams mostly spread the unit-norm char block thinner rather than adding independent evidence, so expect only a small improvement.

The LR at C=1 is underconfident and count-based MNB is overconfident, and the two use diverse features, so an OOF-tuned arithmetic blend should correct calibration and cut log loss from about 0.43 to about 0.37-0.39.

Function words like the, of, and upon are strong stylistic signals for telling authors apart, so dropping them lowers accuracy; this already overconfident, overfit fastText (lr=0.5, 25 epochs) then pays heavily in log loss on the extra mistakes.

The imbalance is mild, so balancing has little to fix. Duplicating minority rows under 25 epochs at lr=0.5 adds more passes and makes the already overconfident fastText model more confident, and the balanced prior is slightly miscalibrated against the natural test distribution, so log loss likely gets a bit worse.

ComplementNB is a diverse, reasonably strong model on this TF-IDF text, so an OOF-tuned convex blend with the CV-tuned logistic regression (w likely around 0.6–0.8, and never worse than w=1.0 on OOF) should cut log loss by a few percent. The gain is limited by NB's poor calibration, and the few extra fold fits should stay within the time budget.

On L2-normalized TF-IDF, MultinomialNB is miscalibrated and weaker than tuned logistic regression (public spooky kernels show about 0.47–0.58 for word TF-IDF NB). Adding char n-grams and a tuned small alpha helps, but it likely still lands around 0.42–0.45, well behind the 0.355 LR.

On Spooky, char n-grams reliably add stylistic signal (punctuation, morphology, rare-word fragments) on top of word 1-2 grams, so dropping the 60k char features from the NB-SVM should cost a few hundredths of log loss rather than help.

Swapping the discriminatively trained NB-SVM heads for a single ComplementNB(alpha=1) on 160k TF-IDF features should hurt: NB probabilities are poorly calibrated, the large alpha smooths over thin TF-IDF counts, and the complement normalization biases scores away from the majority class, so log loss likely lands around 0.55–0.65, well above 0.409.

Tuning C with log-loss-scored cross-validation should pick a larger value (around 3–10), because C=1 underfits TF-IDF features whose rows are L2-normalized per vectorizer; that likely cuts log loss by several percent, and the lbfgs cross-validation should still finish inside the time budget.

MultinomialNB on L2-normalized TF-IDF plus heavily correlated char n-grams is usually worse than LR on this task (historically ~0.48-0.58 versus about 0.43 for LR): with alpha=0.1, the independence assumption double-counts the correlated char-gram evidence, which hurts calibration, and the min-max style features add mass but almost no signal.

fastText with lr=0.5 and 25 epochs will likely reach similar or slightly lower accuracy (~80-83%) than the TF-IDF+LR baseline, but its predictions will be much more confident, so wrong answers will be penalised heavily and log loss will get worse.

Stacked L2-normalised TF-IDF blocks with C=1 are typically under-regularised for this task, so CV should pick a larger C (about 4–8) and give a moderate log-loss gain; the 4-way joblib parallelism should keep the run within budget, with a small timeout risk.

The NB log-ratio weighting boosts discriminative n-grams, and C=4 undoes the underfitting of the baseline's C=1 logistic regression; the heavy +1 smoothing on small TF-IDF sums and the one-vs-rest renormalization's weaker calibration should cost back only part of that gain.

The char_wb n-grams already capture most punctuation signal (semicolons, commas, quotes), and the 14 MaxAbs-scaled dense features are few and weak next to ~100k+ TF-IDF columns under C=1, so the length and word-length stats should add only a marginal, near-noise gain.

Naive Bayes feature weighting on top of logistic regression (NB-LR) scales up the discriminative word and character n-grams, which effectively loosens regularization where it helps. The current model at C=1 is probably underconfident, so this should sharpen predictions and cut log loss by a few hundredths; renormalizing the three one-vs-rest outputs costs a little calibration.

At C=1.0 this TF-IDF logistic regression is already over-regularized and gives soft, under-confident probabilities (typical optimum is C≈10–30). Cutting C to 0.25 shrinks the coefficients much further, pushing predictions toward uniform and raising log loss substantially.

Dropping the word n-grams removes discriminative whole-word and bigram signals (names, collocations), and it halves the row norm at a fixed C=1, so the already underfit liblinear NB-LR likely gets less confident and worse on log loss.

Dropping the NB log-count ratio removes both the author-evidence prior and the effective feature rescaling. On L2-normalized TF-IDF with C=1, the logistic regression becomes over-regularized and its probabilities too soft, so log loss should regress toward the ~0.58–0.62 range typical of plain TF-IDF logistic regression on Spooky.

Word+char TF-IDF with logistic regression on this task usually wants weak regularization (best C is often around 10 or higher), so halving C from 4 to 2 should underfit and flatten the probabilities, raising log loss; the added tracking code is best-effort and shouldn't affect the score.

At C=4, NB log-ratio scaling (magnitudes about 1–4) weakens effective regularization and makes predictions overconfident, and renormalizing one-vs-rest outputs calibrates worse than multinomial LR, so log loss likely rises modestly from 0.369.

Function words such as 'the', 'of', 'upon' and 'which' are among the strongest stylometric cues for telling these authors apart, and stripping them from both the word and the char_wb branches removes that signal. Kaggle kernels that used stop-word-filtered TF-IDF with logistic regression landed around 0.5-0.57, so the loss should rise noticeably, and the char n-grams on content words plus temperature calibration only partly offset it.

On sparse TF-IDF features with many n-grams, this logistic regression is already over-regularized at C=1; dropping C to 0.25 shrinks the weights further and hurts ranking quality, and temperature scaling (which may hit its 0.25 floor) can't fully recover the lost confidence.

Plain 'char' n-grams add cross-word and punctuation-spacing patterns that carry style information, but the 60k feature cap and the strong C=1 regularization limit the gain, so expect a small improvement; the MLflow and holdout-removal edits don't change the submission.

The NB log-count-ratio scaling acts like a discriminative prior: it boosts author-indicative n-grams and loosens the too-strong C=1 regularization on them, which usually beats plain TF-IDF logistic regression on Spooky by a few hundredths of log loss; normalizing the three one-vs-rest probabilities costs a little calibration, so the gain is only partial.

At C=1.0, L2 logistic regression on stacked word and char TF-IDF features is noticeably over-regularized for this task, so C=4.0 should sharpen the probabilities and lower log loss by several percent; removing the holdout print does not affect the submission.

At C=1.0, logistic regression on sublinear TF-IDF word+char features is heavily regularized and underconfident, so the fitted temperature should be below 1 (about 0.5–0.7), which sharpens the probabilities and should cut log loss by roughly 5–8%; the refit on the full training set slightly dilutes that gain.

Training on log1p and inverting with expm1 predicts roughly the median rather than the mean, so fares come out biased low. It also weakens the fit on expensive tail and airport rides that dominate dollar RMSE. Expect a slight regression on the valid rows, diluted by the fixed ~2.1 floor from invalid rows; the MLflow logging is best-effort and harmless.

Four times more rows should cut RMSE on the valid rows by roughly 1-3% (about 3.57 to 3.49). The mean-fare corrupt rows add a fixed error of about 2.1 RMSE that more data can't reduce, so the total improves by only about 1%. The 1000-tree cap limits the gain further, and the run should finish within budget.

Airport-distance features help LightGBM capture flat-rate JFK fares and airport surcharges more cleanly than raw coordinates do, probably cutting clean-row RMSE by about 0.1. The roughly 2.1 floor from corrupt rows dilutes the overall gain to a modest improvement.

Fitting L2 loss on log1p fares with a plain expm1 back-transform predicts something close to the conditional median, not the mean. That biases dollar predictions low on long, noisy trips and on the NaN-coordinate corrupt rows, where heavy-tailed fares matter most, so dollar RMSE likely worsens slightly.

Fare is not monotone in haversine distance at the low end: about 1% of rows are zero-distance trips (pickup equal to dropoff) with near-mean fares, which is well above the fare for 0.3–1 km trips. The constraint forces those predictions down and pools them with short trips. On top of that, LightGBM's default 'basic' method over-constrains the tree structure on the dominant feature, and the regularization benefit on rare long trips is small, so RMSE probably rises slightly.

Back-transforming a log1p target with expm1 predicts a conditional geometric mean or median, which sits below the conditional mean. That biases RMSE-relevant predictions low on high-variance long trips and airport fares, so the valid-row RMSE should rise slightly (~3.6 to ~3.65-3.7); the ~2.1 floor from corrupt rows is unchanged, giving a small overall regression.

In-sample encoding leaks each training row's own fare into its key's mean; for rare route keys (count 1–2), the fare mean plus count pins down the label almost exactly, so trees overfit to a pattern that is absent at validation and test time; early stopping on the honestly encoded holdout and the ~2.1 invalid-row floor limit the damage to a modest regression.

Fitting squared error on log1p(fare) and back-transforming with expm1 predicts something closer to the geometric mean than the mean, so predictions run slightly low and large fares (airport and long trips) lose weight; that usually costs a little dollar RMSE, and the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the regression.

Airport-distance features give the trees a cleaner split for flat-rate JFK and surcharged EWR rides; that should trim valid-row RMSE by about 0.05–0.1 (1M rows and raw coordinates already capture much of this), while the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the overall gain.

About 2.8% of test rows are invalid and account for roughly 4.5 of the ~17.1 total MSE. The biggest gain is passenger_count=0 rows with valid coordinates, which now get a real, distance-based prediction instead of the mean fare. Rows where only one endpoint is bad also gain a little from the other endpoint and from year/time trends. Fully 0,0 rows stay mostly unpredictable, and predictions for valid rows barely change, so the net improvement is small, about 1%.

Quadrupling the training rows while keeping the 1000-tree cap should trim the valid-row RMSE from about 3.6 to about 3.5, but roughly 2.8% corrupt test rows fix a large irreducible part of the error, so the total gain is only about 1–2%; runtime (~5–7 min) should fit the budget, and the float32 dtypes, explicit timestamp format and MLflow logging are neutral.

Out-of-fold route and cell fare encodings add some toll and flat-JFK-fare signal that raw coordinates only partly capture, but the 2.1 floor from corrupt test rows and noisy outlier fares keep the gain small (valid-row RMSE ~3.6 → ~3.53).

Back-transforming a log1p target gives median-like predictions that sit below the conditional mean, which RMSE penalizes; on valid rows the fit is roughly unchanged or slightly worse, and the fallback on the ~2.8% corrupt rows drops from about $11 toward about $9, adding a little squared error, so a mild regression is expected.

Bearing and delta/Manhattan features give the trees direction information they can't easily build from raw coordinates, a modest gain (valid-row RMSE ~3.6→~3.5); the ~2.1 floor from corrupt rows and the unchanged fallback dilute the overall improvement.

Airport and Manhattan distances help the trees find the flat-fare and surcharge airport trips faster than raw coordinates do. That should cut the valid-row RMSE from about 3.58 to about 3.45, but the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the overall gain.

The L1 objective fits the conditional median of a right-skewed fare target, which biases predictions low and pays heavily on large residuals under RMSE; convergence is also slower, and early stopping now also watches the L1 metric, so RMSE on the valid rows likely rises from about 3.58 to about 3.7, while the roughly 2.1 floor from invalid rows is unchanged.

Training on log1p and back-transforming with expm1 predicts roughly the conditional median, which sits below the conditional mean, so fares come out biased low. Airport and long-ride fares get shrunk most, which slightly worsens dollar-scale RMSE on the ~3.6 valid-row portion. The ~2.1 floor from corrupt rows, which still get the mean-fare fallback, dilutes the change.

An L1 objective fits the conditional median, which sits below the conditional mean for right-skewed taxi fares, so predictions shift low and RMSE on the valid rows rises from about 3.6 to about 3.8. The 2.1 floor from corrupt test rows is unchanged, so the overall RMSE gets modestly worse.

With Huber delta=$1 the gradients are clipped to ±1, so at lr 0.05 each tree moves a leaf by at most about $0.05. That leaves high-fare trips like the $52 airport flat fare badly underfit within 1000 trees. The loss also pulls predictions toward the median of a right-skewed fare distribution, which hurts RMSE.

A model trained on log1p(fare) and back-transformed with expm1 predicts roughly the geometric-mean fare rather than the arithmetic mean, so it systematically underpredicts high-variance long and airport trips. That hurts raw-dollar RMSE slightly, and the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the effect on the total score.

Explicit airport distances and flags should help the trees capture JFK flat fares and airport surcharges better than raw coordinates do, cutting valid-row RMSE by about 0.1–0.2 (3.6 to about 3.45), but the roughly 2.1 floor from invalid rows is unchanged, so the overall gain is diluted.

Four times more rows should give LightGBM finer spatial splits on the raw coordinates, cutting clean-row RMSE from about 3.6 to about 3.5; the roughly 2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows is unchanged, so the overall gain is modest.

Averaging five fold models slightly lowers variance on the valid rows (about 3.6 to 3.57 RMSE), but the roughly 2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the gain, so expect under 1% improvement overall.

The out-of-fold smoothed pickup-cell mean fare mostly duplicates location information the trees already learn from raw coordinates plus distance, with some added help for airport and landmark pickups; expect a small gain on the clean rows (~3.6 to ~3.57), diluted by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows.

Snapping coordinates to a 0.01° grid (about 0.85–1.1 km) adds roughly 0.4 km of error to distance_km, the dominant feature, which is worth about $0.5–0.6 of fare noise in quadrature; the route encoding is essentially unchanged, so expect a modest regression.

The L1 objective fits the conditional median, but RMSE rewards the conditional mean; with right-skewed fares (tolls, airport flat rates) this biases predictions low and learns high-fare trips worse, while the roughly 2.1 floor from invalid rows predicted at the mean is unchanged, so RMSE should rise modestly.

L1 loss predicts the conditional median, which sits below the mean for right-skewed fares, and its sign-gradient boosting converges more slowly at lr=0.05, so RMSE on valid rows likely worsens by about 0.1–0.2 while the roughly 2.1 floor from corrupt rows is unchanged.

Airport-distance features help GBMs capture JFK flat fares and EWR surcharges that raw coordinates only partly encode, cutting valid-row RMSE by roughly 0.05–0.1; the fixed ~2.1 floor from corrupt rows dilutes the total gain to about 1%.

An L1 objective fits the conditional median, which sits below the mean for right-skewed fares (tolls and long trips), so it adds downward bias and under-predicts expensive rides, while the corrupt-row floor is unchanged; valid-row RMSE rises by roughly 0.1-0.2.

LightGBM already bins coordinates into histograms, so rounding to 0.01° (~1 km) adds little regularization with 2M rows and discards some fine Manhattan and airport detail; since the corrupt-row floor dilutes any change, expect a slight regression.

The L1 objective fits the conditional median, which sits below the mean for right-skewed fares, and its sign-only gradients give weaker splits, so RMSE on valid rows likely rises from about 3.6 to 3.75; invalid rows are still predicted as the mean fare, so their roughly 2.1 floor stays fixed.

A grid-rotated Manhattan distance is a mildly useful complement to haversine that trees can only partly rebuild from raw coordinates, but about 2.8% of test rows are corrupt and put a fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor under every score, so the total improves only slightly.

Heavily smoothed (m=50) directional route encoding on ~1km cells is sparse for most routes, so the feature stays near the global mean. It mainly adds signal on dense corridors like airport runs, which the GBM already partly learns from raw coordinates, and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows is untouched, so expect only a small gain.

The rotated-grid Manhattan distance adds a little signal beyond haversine plus raw coordinates, maybe 0.02–0.04 RMSE on the valid rows, but about 2.8% corrupt test rows dominate the total error, so the overall gain shrinks to a fraction of a percent; the MLflow logging does not affect predictions.

Doubling the training data gives a modest RMSE gain on the valid rows (about 3.60 to 3.54), while the unpredictable corrupt test rows keep the overall floor near 2.1. The 1000-tree cap also limits how much the extra data can be used, so the overall improvement should be about 1%.

An explicit airport-route categorical helps capture JFK flat fares and airport surcharges that the raw-coordinate trees only approximate, but the trees can already partly isolate airports from 1M rows, and about 2.1 RMSE of the total comes from corrupt test rows no feature can fix, so expect only a modest overall gain.

With only 2000 rounds at lr 0.05, no interaction or unique-character features, and the holdout AUC probably still climbing at the cap, LightGBM has to build the linear-sum interactions and the letter-count signal out of axis-aligned splits, so it likely ends slightly below the SiLU MLP's 0.9866 rather than above it.

The key interactions in this data are thresholds on sums of continuous features (f_21+f_02, f_22+f_05, f_00+f_01+f_26); decile one-hot coarsens these into staircases and merges tail integer values, so the gain from outlier robustness is outweighed and AUC should drop noticeably.

After standardization the columns are nearly uncorrelated, so the correlation matrix is close to identity and PCA returns an essentially arbitrary, noise-driven rotation. That rotation smears the discrete f_27 characters, the integer counts and f_29/f_30 across all 41 components, which destroys the axis-aligned structure the trees rely on. It also does not align with the target-relevant sum interactions, so AUC should drop noticeably, with linear leaves recovering only part of the loss.

f_27 is nearly unique per row (~700k+ distinct strings in 800k rows), so an out-of-fold smoothed target encoding of the whole string sits close to the prior and carries little signal; dropping the ten strong per-character features removes most of what f_27 contributes, so AUC should fall to roughly the numeric-only level.

In this dataset about 740k of the 900k f_27 strings are unique and repeats are rare. With m=20 smoothing the target encoding is almost always just the prior, so it adds very little. Meanwhile the change drops the ten per-character columns, which carry much of the signal, leaving only f_27_nunique, so AUC should fall substantially.

These are the known TPS-May-22 hidden-interaction ternary features (f02+f21, f05+f22, f00+f01+f26). Trees struggle to learn additive thresholds, so exposing them explicitly typically lifts LightGBM from about 0.9915 to about 0.993.

Plain logistic regression on these mostly interaction-driven features should only reach about 0.83–0.85 AUC, so giving it equal rank weight with the ~0.984 LightGBM model will pull the blend down to roughly 0.95–0.97 rather than add useful diversity.

An MLP of this shape (64-64-64-16, SiLU) is known to work well on TPS-May22, and at roughly 1–3 s per epoch it should finish all 80 epochs inside the budget; it should capture the continuous interactions (f_21/f_02, f_05/f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) more smoothly than 3000-tree LightGBM, but without a unique-character count for f_27 it should stay below the ~0.998 top scores.

This follows the well-known TPS-May-22 SiLU 64-64-64-16 MLP recipe, which learns the linear-combination interactions such as f_21+f_02 that trees miss, so it should clearly beat the LightGBM baseline (0.977). Without the unique-character feature and with only 60 epochs, it likely lands near 0.99 rather than the ~0.998 of the full recipe.

Linear leaves let the boosted logit follow the smooth, sum-of-features structure in the continuous columns better than constant-leaf staircases, which should give a modest AUC gain, but they cannot create oblique step boundaries or supply the missing f_27 unique-count feature, so the gain is limited; there is also a real risk of slow training or overfit instability with small linear_lambda.

The distinct-letter count of f_27 is a known strong signal in TPS May 2022, and trees struggle to reconstruct it from ten per-character ordinals, so this one column should lift AUC by roughly 0.005–0.008 even without the other interaction features.

These three sums are the known key interactions in TPS May 2022; exposing them as raw sums lets LightGBM find the ~±5 thresholds with single splits instead of approximating diagonal boundaries, so AUC should jump about a point, though the missing unique-char count still caps it below ~0.99+.

Most raw f_27 strings are unique (about 740k distinct values in 900k rows), so no category reaches LightGBM's cat_smooth/min_data_per_group thresholds and the new categorical column is effectively unsplittable. The net effect is losing the per-position character features, and the letter counts only partly recover that positional signal, so AUC should drop moderately. Scanning the huge number of categorical bins also adds runtime risk.

The per-position ordinals and letter counts already capture most of the signal in f_27, so nine high-cardinality categorical bigram features add little new information and some overfitting and dilution risk; expect roughly neutral to slightly worse.

f_00..f_15 are nearly independent, so PCA returns fairly arbitrary rotations that don't align with the known sum interactions (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22). Swapping the 25 mined products for 8 near-random projections should be roughly neutral to slightly negative for an unconverged 3000-tree LightGBM.

Hashing the whole f_27 string as one token scatters about 740k mostly unique codes into 64 random one-hot buckets, which is effectively noise. That throws away the strongly predictive per-position character signal, and the model falls back on numeric features and products only, with a small extra overfit penalty from the 64 noise columns.

Swapping LightGBM for 300 fully grown ExtraTrees on the same raw features should lose accuracy (my estimate is an AUC of about 0.92–0.93). Boosting with thousands of trees is much better at modelling the continuous sum interactions (f_21+f_02 and similar) and the f_27 character interactions, while randomized, sqrt-feature, fully grown trees on noisy labels plateau near 0.92–0.93. There is also a real risk that the added 5-fold CV of 300-tree models pushes the run past the time limit.

In TPS May 2022 the signal comes from linear-combination interactions such as f_21+f_02 and f_05+f_22 feeding into thresholds, which an MLP on standardized inputs captures more easily than 3000 trees of LightGBM, so a (256,128) MLP should beat 0.978 even without the unique-character count; sklearn's accuracy-based early stopping and constant learning rate cap the gain at roughly 0.985–0.99.

In this competition the distinct-character count of f_27 is a known strong signal that per-position categoricals cannot express, and letter counts add some more, so AUC should rise by about a point; the unexploited continuous-feature interactions cap the gain below ~0.99.

In TPS May 2022 most f_27 strings appear only once, so the whole-string count carries little signal, while the per-character positions and their unique-letter composition are among the strongest predictors; dropping them should push AUC down toward numeric-only LightGBM levels (~0.93).

In TPS May 2022, the unique-character count of f_27 (plus per-letter counts) is a known strong signal that trees cannot easily recover from per-position ordinals, so the score should rise from about 0.977 to about 0.99. Without the explicit f_21+f_02 / f_22+f_05 / f_00+f_01+f_26 interaction features, it will likely stay short of about 0.998.

The known TPS-May-2022 interactions are sign-of-sum patterns (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) involving columns outside f_00..f_15, and about half of f_00..f_15 are integer counts, so the gain-ranked products mostly add noise and dilute colsample. The result should be roughly flat to slightly worse.

Early stopping never fires, so the model is still improving at 3000 trees. Refitting on all 800k rows with about 3333 trees adds about 11% more data and more rounds, giving a small but reliable AUC gain. Total runtime should be about 2.2x the baseline, which likely stays within budget.

In this synthetic data the letter codes of f_27 carry real ordinal meaning, and the key signal (unique-character counts and cross-position interactions) is not something categorical splits capture; LightGBM's many-vs-rest categorical splits on 26 letters add a bit of overfitting risk with no real gain, so AUC should end up roughly flat to slightly lower.

The distinct-character count of f_27 was one of the strongest engineered signals in TPS May 2022, and trees cannot easily rebuild it from 10 separate ordinal columns, so it should add a noticeable AUC lift (about +0.003 to +0.005), with no runtime concern.

Depth-2 trees (4 leaves) restrict the model to pairwise effects. That removes the higher-order f_27 character interactions and the fine staircase approximations of diagonal sums like f_21+f_02 and f_22+f_05. With only 3000 rounds at lr 0.05 the model will also be heavily underfit, so a large AUC drop from 0.982 is likely.

With only 600 shallow trees (31 leaves, max_bin=63) and no engineered interaction or unique-character features, LightGBM struggles to learn the additive continuous interactions (like f_21+f_02, f_22+f_05) that the MLP captures naturally, so AUC should land around 0.93–0.95, below the MLP's 0.982.

Without engineered interaction or unique-character features, a small LightGBM model (600 trees, lr 0.05, 31 leaves, max_bin 63) cannot capture the continuous-feature interactions that the MLP learns, so AUC should land around 0.93–0.94, a clear drop from 0.982 (early stopping on logloss instead of AUC is a minor deviation).

The 16 floats (f_00–f_06, f_19–f_26, f_28) carry the main signal through continuous interactions such as f_21+f_02 and f_22+f_05. Cutting each to 4 quartile bins throws away most of the resolution those interactions need, so AUC should drop sharply, cushioned only by the f_27 characters and the integer count columns.

This task depends on multi-way feature interactions (e.g. f_21/f_02, f_22/f_05, f_00+f_01+f_26, the f_27 unique-character pattern), and 7-leaf trees can represent only about 2–3-way splits each. With 3000 rounds at lr 0.05 they will underfit badly compared with 127 leaves, so AUC should drop noticeably.

In this dataset, AUC depends on multi-way interactions: hidden linear-combination thresholds like f_00+f_01+f_26 and f_21/f_22 sums, plus character-position interactions in f_27. Four-leaf trees can capture at most about 2–3-way splits each, so even 3000 rounds at lr 0.05 will underfit relative to 127 leaves, likely costing several AUC points.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the known planted TPS-May-2022 interactions; trees struggle to learn a three-way linear sum, so exposing it directly should give a clear gain (still missing the f_02/f_21 and f_05/f_22 pairs).

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known threshold-style interactions in TPS May 2022. As an explicit continuous sum, trees can split on it directly instead of approximating a diagonal boundary with axis-aligned splits, so AUC should rise modestly (about +0.003 to +0.004). The other two interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22) and the unique-char count are still missing, which caps the gain.

An MLP picks up the linear-sum interactions in this dataset (f_21+f_02, f_22+f_05, f_00+f_01+f_26) far more easily than depth-limited trees, and 50 cheap CPU epochs fit comfortably inside the budget, so it should beat the 0.977 LightGBM baseline; it will likely fall short of 0.995 or higher because there is no unique-character-count feature and training is short.

Categorical splits on ten low-cardinality (≤20 levels) char columns can only mildly outperform ordinal splits on ~720k rows. The tree is still improving at 3000 iterations, and the letter codes are already near-monotonic in effect, so I expect a tiny gain or noise-level change.

In TPS-May-22 the distinct-character count of f_27 is a well-known strong signal, and trees struggle to reconstruct it from ten ordinal position columns, so adding it should lift AUC noticeably (roughly +0.005 to +0.008) even without the column-interaction features.

Weighting pixels by target darkness moves the loss away from the metric: the weighted-MSE optimum is E[wy]/E[w], which pulls predictions darker wherever text-vs-background is uncertain (stroke edges, stains, faint text), and those pixels carry most of the residual error; plain MSE gradients on well-fit background are already near zero, so there is little dilution for the reweighting to fix, and a small RMSE regression is expected.

At an estimated 10–25 ms per step, a 330 s time-based cosine schedule gives roughly 15k–30k steps, about 8–15x the undertrained 2000-step baseline. Train and test share the same backgrounds and texts and the fully convolutional U-Net is small (~0.47M params), so overfitting risk is low and longer training should cut pixel RMSE by about 2 dB. Capacity and diminishing returns probably stop it short of ~0.010, and the run stays well within the time limit.

Under Adam, MSE's small gradients near the target don't stall training. Background pixels already snap to 1.0 through bf16 sigmoid rounding and consistent Adam updates, so L1's cleaner-paper benefit is small. L1 fits the conditional median rather than the mean the RMSE metric rewards, so it snaps uncertain stroke edges and stain pixels on this bimodal black/white data, and it puts less weight on the large residuals that dominate RMSE; net effect is roughly neutral to slightly worse, within run-to-run noise.

Test scans come from the same synthetic process as train, with the same backgrounds, fonts and exposure. Input-only brightness/contrast jitter therefore adds a mismatch that does not exist at test time. It forces the net to become invariant to intensity when absolute gray levels are informative, and clipping destroys anti-aliased stroke-edge detail. Edges dominate the error at an RMSE of about 0.017, so with only 2000 training steps I expect a moderate regression rather than a regularization gain.

The model is unchanged, so only inference changes. On thin (about 1.5-2 px) high-contrast text strokes, the 0.75x down/up round trip should cost about 0.04-0.05 RMSE, and the 1.25x path about 0.02-0.03. These are systematic edge blurs in the same direction, so equal-weight averaging only dilutes them by a third, adding about 0.02 of edge error on top of the 0.0154 native-scale error, which outweighs any variance reduction.

The small U-Net (about 470k params, not 1.9M) gets only 2000 steps on train/test data that share the same noise backgrounds, so it is more likely under-trained than overfit. Channel dropout mid-network in a pixel-regression model usually hurts (as in 'Reflash Dropout' for super-resolution), because it slows convergence and causes train/test variance shift in the following BatchNorm layers, and it also degrades the e2 skip path, so I expect a mild RMSE regression.

Test pages share fonts and noise templates with train, so memorizing them helps and there is little overfitting for dropout to fix; spatial dropout before every BN (train/eval variance shift) and on the full-resolution skip and final features blurs the precise edge regression and slows convergence in the fixed 180s budget, so RMSE should get moderately worse.

The receptive field grows from about 41 px to about 89 px and capacity roughly quadruples, which helps tell large stains, folds and creases apart from text strokes; the baseline already gets tens of thousands of steps in 180 s, so the ~25% fewer steps costs little, but the unchanged 32-channel full-resolution path still limits text-edge precision, so the gain should be modest.

The diff is correct: the background is computed on the full image before cropping, flips stay consistent, and predict handles the 2-channel input. The edge-preserving 23x23 median gives this small (~470K params) U-Net a robust full-resolution background estimate, which should mainly clean up stain edges and low-contrast text. The U-Net's own max-pool context and init noise between runs limit the gain, so I expect a modest improvement rather than a large one.

The 5-level U-Net has a receptive field of about 200 px and roughly 16x the parameters, which should better separate large-scale stains, creases and wrinkles from text. Larger crops at the same pixel budget are neutral to slightly helpful. Compute roughly doubles but stays well within the time limit. Batch-8 BatchNorm and only 2000 steps limit the gain, so expect a moderate improvement of about 10-15% rather than a large one.

The diff is correct: it flips the reflect-padded tensor, un-flips each output before averaging, then crops, and the multiple-of-8 size keeps the pooling grid flip-symmetric. Training is unchanged and already used random h/v flips, so all four orientations are in-distribution and averaging them acts as a cheap correlated ensemble. For a small (~470k-param) U-Net trained for only 2000 bf16 steps, that typically gives about 0.15-0.3 dB of PSNR, roughly a 2-3% RMSE reduction. Most error is bias-like ambiguity at text edges and stains, so the gain stays modest. Nondeterministic CUDA backward ops (e.g. bilinear upsampling) will make the retrained model differ slightly, adding about ±1-2% noise.

The diff sets TRAIN_SECONDS to 180, not the proposed 360, but on an A100/H100-class GPU a step of this small bf16 U-Net takes about 10–20 ms, so 180 s still gives roughly 9k–18k steps versus 2k.
