The cosine schedule keeps the same shape, the model is clearly undertrained at about 50 pixel-epochs, and the test backgrounds and texts are shared with train, so longer training and more memorization should cut RMSE noticeably. Gains are capped by the small 470k-param, 3-level model and bf16 output precision.

Charbonnier loss targets the median rather than the mean, which mismatches the RMSE metric; MSE already optimizes RMSE directly. On bimodal document pixels this makes ambiguous edge and halo pixels commit instead of hedging, and it spends gradient on already-good background, so a small regression is most likely, within seed noise, with maybe a 35-40% chance of a slight improvement from L1's better convergence.

Test documents share the same background and stain patterns as training, so memorizing the training corruptions helps rather than hurts, and a ~470k-param net on about 24M training pixels over 2000 steps barely overfits. Injecting σ=0.05 Gaussian noise on the input only creates a train/test mismatch: the residual head learns to subtract high-frequency detail, which oversmooths anti-aliased text edges on the clean test inputs. It also raises the loss floor, which slows convergence within the fixed step budget. Expect a moderate RMSE regression, roughly 0.0165–0.019.

In eval mode, BatchNorm with batch-32 crop statistics is just a fixed affine map, so the claimed train/test mismatch doesn't exist; GroupNorm actually creates one, because it normalizes over 128x128 crops in training but over whole pages at full-image inference (the global-statistics inconsistency the TLC paper documents). Expect a mild regression, with no gain in optimization or regularization to offset it.

The loss becomes SSIM-dominant, which weights leftover background texture far more than errors at text-stroke edges (normalized by local variance). Those edge errors are what drive per-pixel RMSE, and the L1/SSIM terms push toward median-like, decisive outputs rather than the RMSE-optimal mean. L1 may clean backgrounds and gray stain patches somewhat better, so I expect near-neutral to a slight RMSE regression.

8-view dihedral TTA averages away some view-specific edge errors in this MSE-trained U-Net, which should give a small gain. Training used only h/v flips, so the four transposed (rot90-type) views are out-of-distribution for horizontal text and share a common bias, which offsets part of the gain. The implementation is correct and fits the time budget, so I expect a modest ~1-2% RMSE improvement with a real chance it comes out neutral or slightly worse.

I expect a sizable regression, with uncertain magnitude. Pure SSIM no longer optimizes per-pixel error: it strongly weights flat regions, barely penalizes small background offsets near 1.0, and relaxes accuracy at text edges, which is where most RMSE comes from. It is also computed inside the bf16 autocast block, so the variance terms are corrupted by rounding errors of a few thousandths, larger than C2=0.0009, giving near-zero or negative denominators and erratic, heavy-tailed gradients in background and halo windows. The likely result is slower, noisier convergence and imperfect background saturation.

Predicting the residual keeps anti-aliased text edges through the identity path, and clamping removes overshoot at 0 and 1. That likely trims the edge errors that dominate the sigmoid baseline's error. It is partly offset by having to cancel background stain and wrinkle texture exactly, so I expect a small gain near run-to-run noise.

Using sqrt(MSE) keeps gradients from shrinking as the loss falls 500x from initialisation, so Adam's second-moment memory throttles later steps less and optimisation in the 2000-step budget likely improves slightly. That gain is partly offset because conv2d under autocast recasts the SSIM inputs to bf16, making the variance and C2 terms quantisation-noisy. The 0.1 SSIM term also mostly just reweights halo and background flatness, so the net effect should be a small change within seed noise, leaning slightly better.

The clean targets are near-binary with a background of exactly 1.0, so the baseline's sigmoid gets background right for free by saturating, while x+r must cancel dense, textured stains pixel-exactly (only partly rescued by the inference clamp); the identity path and linear output may help text edges and hard pixels, so I expect a small net regression.

Only 105 real images get 6x synthetic copies, so about 86% of the fixed 2000-step budget goes to mismatched synthetic noise, and training on the real distribution is diluted about 7x. The whole-image sigma 1-4 blur also forces the small U-Net to spend capacity on an irreducible text-deblurring task that the sharp-text test images never need. Test backgrounds are shared with train, so real exposure matters most, and I expect a moderate regression rather than a gain.

The 470k-param U-Net is still clearly undertrained at 2,000 steps (about 50 pixel-epochs); 4.5x more steps with a stretched cosine schedule should keep cutting edge and stain error, since test shares fonts and backgrounds with train and overfitting risk is low; runtime stays around 3-6 min, so no fallback to 45 epochs is needed, and gains taper toward the capacity/receptive-field and bf16 floor.

Training is unchanged, so the 8-view average should cut prediction variance and give a small gain. The four flip views are in-distribution because training used h/v flips. The four transposed views are mildly out-of-distribution, since text lines become vertical, but the denoising is mostly local and isotropic (background estimation, stroke contrast). That makes them only slightly worse and adds useful diversity. Net expected RMSE reduction is about 2-4%, with some risk of a regression if the transposed views degrade more than expected.

L1 targets the conditional median, not the mean. On near-binary document targets this snaps ambiguous light anti-aliased edge pixels to white and down-weights the large residuals that dominate RMSE. That likely outweighs L1's stronger push to saturate the background through the sigmoid, so I expect a small regression.

Weighting dark targets 3:1 pulls predictions darker wherever the model is uncertain, especially at glyph edges where most of the remaining error sits, while the plain-MSE objective already matches the RMSE metric; expect a modest regression (assuming the run finishes on hardware comparable to the parent's — the new execution.json pins CPU, which at 2000 steps could otherwise risk the time limit).

Weighting dark targets 10x moves the optimum to roughly E[y] - 9Var/(10-9E[y]). That biases uncertain near-white pixels (stain remnants, the white side of strokes) toward dark and cuts the relative weight on the ~85-90% background pixels that dominate unweighted RMSE. Better text fitting only partly offsets this, so expect a modest regression.

A residual output with a clamp removes overshoot errors and gives stronger gradients on badly wrong pixels, but it gives up sigmoid saturation on the roughly 85% of pixels that are pure-white background: every background pixel now needs a precise absolute 1-x correction, computed from BatchNorm-normalized features that don't preserve absolute brightness, plus bf16 activation noise on GPU, so a small regression is the likely net effect.

L1 on sigmoid outputs pushes the dominant white background closer to exactly 1.0, a small RMSE gain. But it fits the conditional median rather than the mean, which hurts at anti-aliased edges and heavily stained pixels whose large residuals drive RMSE. It also down-weights exactly those residuals, so I expect a near-neutral to slightly worse score.

Residual output starts at the identity (RMSE about 0.2 rather than 0.5). It also removes the sigmoid's undershoot on exactly-white background: clipping after flip-TTA discards overshoot, whereas sigmoid plus MSE leaves a systematic gap of about 0.003-0.008. Working against that, the net must cancel background texture exactly instead of just saturating a classifier-like logit. Net expected effect is a small gain, within about seed-noise range.

Halving the width cuts parameters about 4x (roughly 640K to 160K) and leaves only 8 channels at full resolution. The test images closely match training (same noise backgrounds and texts), so the 'regularization' has little overfitting to fix. At the same 2000 steps, the narrower net should underfit text edges and stains more, giving a moderate regression of about 5-15% in RMSE rather than a gain. It runs faster, so there is no timeout risk.

The competition scores plain RMSE, but the new loss weights errors by how dark the target pixel is, so it no longer matches the metric. The loss-minimizing prediction becomes E[w·y]/E[w] instead of the conditional mean, which darkens uncertain pixels (stroke edges, text versus stain) and trades background accuracy for text, likely costing a few percent of RMSE with only a small chance that extra focus on hard strokes in this undertrained small NAFNet makes up for it.

The implementation matches the proposal. A 31x31 closing-normalized channel adds explicit flat-field and background information from a wider area than the U-Net's roughly 48px receptive field, so it should modestly reduce stain and edge residuals. It cannot remove thin ring or fold lines, the baseline is already strong, and seed noise is likely ±3-5%, so I expect a small gain. Caveat: forcing CPU fp32 for 2,000 batch-32 steps risks timing out; this prediction assumes the run completes.

The fp32 head by itself would be roughly neutral (about 0.0161), but the applied diff also adds an unrequested runtime.toml that hides the GPU (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='') and caps CPU threads at 8. The ~700 TFLOP fp32 training run (2000 steps x batch 32 x 128^2 U-Net) would need about 30-60 min, so it is hard-killed at 15 min before any submission is written; the result is a failed run, and 1.0 is a worst-case placeholder.

The 4-view flip TTA is implemented correctly and leaves training unchanged; on a flip-augmented U-Net it usually cuts RMSE by about 1.5-3.5%. The main risk is that the new runtime.json sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES to empty, so all 2000 fp32 training steps run on 13 CPU threads and may exceed the 15-minute kill; if the run completes, expect about 0.0158-0.0159.

NAFNet-16 has a larger receptive field, global context and a residual output with clamping, but about 5.5x fewer FLOPs and much weaker full-resolution capacity where text-edge error dominates; it also gets only 2000 steps at lr 2e-3, a patch-vs-full-image mismatch in its channel-attention pooling, and the runtime.json change forces fp32 CPU training (a timeout risk, not a quality hit), so I expect roughly parity to a slight regression.

The implementation looks correct: every breed maps to its ImageNet index, the LR path is unchanged and w=0 is in the grid. The model's in1k head was trained on about 1,300 images per dog class, and Stanford Dogs images are ImageNet images, likely in its training set. So the dog-restricted, temperature-tuned head should match or beat the LR fitted on 77 images per class, and the holdout-tuned blend should cut log loss substantially (roughly 0.12–0.29, centred near 0.21).

L2-regularised LR already shrinks the low-variance directions, so a hard cut to 256 PCs mostly duplicates that; ImageNet-trained features should keep most breed information in the top PCs, but losing the small signal for confusable breed pairs likely makes log loss slightly worse (about neutral to a few percent).

Full-probability Mixup/CutMix is a strong regularizer designed for long recipes. Here it is added on top of label smoothing in a 6-epoch (~775-step) fine-tune on 9k fine-grained images whose features the in1k-trained backbone already knows. That likely slightly slows or noisifies head fitting, and CutMix may cut out the discriminative parts that separate confusable breeds. The resulting underconfident, harder-to-calibrate outputs are only partly fixed by one validation temperature, so expect a mild log-loss regression rather than a gain.

In a short 6-epoch fine-tune of a backbone that already knows ImageNet dog breeds, dropping the minimum crop scale to 0.08 turns about 29% of training crops into small or partial views. That slows convergence of the new head and widens the train/test object-scale gap versus the 224 center crop, while overfitting is not the bottleneck (label smoothing, drop path, short schedule). Expect roughly 0.5–1% lower accuracy and a slightly worse log loss, with temperature scaling absorbing most of the calibration shift.

ConvNeXt-V2-L (IN-22k→1k, ~87% IN-1k top-1 versus 76% for ResNet-50 V1) gives much stronger frozen features. Its 1000-d head covers exactly these 120 dog synsets, and the Stanford Dogs images were very likely seen during its IN-22k/IN-1k training. With the same StandardScaler+LR and holdout-tuned C, I expect about 95-97% accuracy and log loss around 0.1-0.16, well below 0.449. The implementation looks correct: norm/LayerNorm run in fp32 under autocast, forward_head(pre_logits) plus head.fc are wired properly, and the runtime fits the budget.

All 120 breeds are ImageNet-1k classes and Stanford Dogs images largely overlap ImageNet train, so the dropped logp block is not noise but ImageNet's own trained dog classifier, a low-norm, highly discriminative signal that an L2-regularised LR on pooled features alone (about 77 images per class) can't fully recover, so log loss should get clearly worse.

Ridge on one-hot targets behaves roughly like LDA, so accuracy should stay close to logistic regression. But one global temperature over bounded least-squares scores cannot both suppress the 119 background classes and calibrate confusable breeds the way directly fitted log-loss logits can. Confident background-type mistakes become far more extreme, and float32 clipping on the holdout hides part of that cost when picking T. So log loss most likely gets moderately worse.

Truncating each block to 128 PCs is like principal-components regression versus an already tuned ridge penalty: it discards the low-variance directions that separate similar breed pairs (Norfolk/Norwich, husky/eskimo, the poodles), and renormalising the centred projections removes useful per-image confidence scaling. Centring, balanced block widths and the effectively larger C range may recover a little, so a modest log-loss regression is most likely.

Swapping to a frozen ConvNeXt-Base (IN-22k pretrained, IN-1k fine-tuned) with C tuned on a holdout should roughly halve the log loss versus ResNet-50 V1. Its ImageNet top-1 is about 10 points higher, and Stanford Dogs images overlap the backbone's pretraining data, so the 120 breeds are nearly linearly separable. The runtime additions (timm, HF cache, fork workers, 5 LR fits on 1024-d features) should fit within the budget.

Fully fine-tuning an ImageNet-22k-pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny is a much stronger model than frozen ResNet-50 features, and Stanford Dogs overlaps ImageNet, so the pretrained features already fit these images well; 6 epochs (~129 steps each, about 2 minutes, well inside the 7-minute guard), flip TTA and temperature scaling (which offsets label-smoothing underconfidence) should give roughly 91-93% accuracy and log loss around 0.22-0.30, versus 0.45 now.

The 120 breeds are ImageNet classes and Stanford Dogs overlaps ImageNet train, so the pretrained head's log-probs give the probe a much better-estimated breed signal (about 1300 images per class versus 77 here), which should help most on confusable pairs; with standardization and a re-tuned C (the likely optimum of 0.03-0.1 is inside the grid) this acts like stacking two similar-strength predictors, but L2 on standardized logp limits how fully the head is used, so I expect a solid rather than dramatic drop from 0.45 to about 0.38.

Three much stronger complementary frozen backbones should lift accuracy from about 86% to about 94–95%: a ConvNeXt pretrained on ImageNet-22k and fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k (whose training data likely already contains these ImageNet-derived dog images), DINOv2 and CLIP. With per-block L2 normalisation and C tuned on a holdout over {1,3,10,30}, which covers the confident regime these normalised features need, log loss should fall to about 0.17–0.22; the main risks are LR convergence at max_iter=500 and download/runtime, not the metric.

Near a coin flip with a slight lean to improvement: LS=0.1 over 120 classes caps easy predictions near 0.9 and flattens the non-target mass, and FL gives similar easy-case confidence while keeping residual mass on look-alike breeds (softening mistakes), but FL's non-proper underconfidence on medium cases and a possible small accuracy loss eat most of that gain.

Stanford Dogs is a subset of ImageNet, so the pretrained features are already close to optimal. Full fine-tuning at a fairly high learning rate (0.01 at batch 64 with momentum) tends to erode them, and freezing conv1–layer3 is known to help on Dogs, so I expect a modest gain; the effect is capped because layer4 still gets the same distortion and the schedule is short.

Averaging probabilities over an image and its mirror can only lower log loss relative to the mean of the two views' losses, and the flipped view should score about the same as the original since the ViT was pretrained with flips. The gain comes mostly from the few hard, view-disagreeing test images, so expect a modest improvement of about 2%. The switch to NUM_WORKERS=0 only slows extraction (~2–3 min total) and leaves the results unchanged.

The current in21k→in1k ViT-B/16 was supervised on these exact ImageNet dog-breed images and labels, and its 16px patches keep fine detail. CLIP ViT-B/32 has neither advantage: its 7x7 patch grid loses fine detail, CLIP's linear probes lag badly on fine-grained animal sets (e.g. Birdsnap), and timm's .openai variant runs GELU instead of the native QuickGELU. I expect roughly 75-80% probe accuracy on about 77 images per class, so log loss should rise to about 0.8 even though C=0.3 suits CLIP's feature scale.

An unwhitened PCA only zeroes out the classifier's weights outside the top 256 directions. With C already tuned, L2 was handling the noisy low-variance directions softly, so hard truncation mainly removes some fine-grained breed signal (about 20-25% of variance dropped) and lowers accuracy on confusable breed pairs. C is also not retuned for the smaller space. I expect a small-to-moderate log-loss regression.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 CLS features are far stronger than ResNet-50 for fine-grained breeds (ImageNet linear probe 84.5% vs 76%, Pets 96% vs 92%). ResNet-50's supervised memorization of these ImageNet-derived images narrows the gap, so I expect roughly a 30–35% log-loss reduction; the C re-search and runtime fit the budget.

C=1 on per-block L2-normalised features, which are tiny in scale, is heavily over-regularised: equivalent C is roughly 100x stronger than the root's tuned C=0.3 on raw features. The current model is therefore underconfident and mostly uses only the top-variance directions. PCA whitening rescales the features so that C=1 becomes weak regularisation. That should sharply cut log loss on correctly predicted images, partly offset by overconfident errors and noise-fitting on similar breeds with ~77 images per class in 256 dimensions. Net result is a moderate improvement.

Smoothing puts a floor of about 0.11 on every sample's loss, since even a 10/10 vote gives the true class at most 0.894. Any test image with no true-class neighbour among its 10 costs about 7.0, and that should happen for roughly 4-6% of images (confusable breeds, label noise). That outweighs the gain on easy samples over the somewhat underconfident C=1 logistic regression, so log loss should get worse, to roughly 0.62-0.85.

Stanford Dogs images are ImageNet-train images, so the frozen ResNet-50 features plus logistic regression already benefit from memorization. Uniform-LR SGD fine-tuning (lr 0.01, momentum 0.9, 10 epochs) likely erodes that advantage and leaves test accuracy flat or lower, around 83-86%. Label smoothing 0.1 puts a floor of about 0.1 on loss even for easy correct examples, so log loss probably rises to roughly 0.5-0.6.

The ViT-B/16 augreg in21k-ft-in1k backbone is much stronger than ResNet-50 V1 (about 84.5% vs 76.1% ImageNet top-1), and in21k pretraining helps fine-grained dog breeds; the pipeline is implemented correctly and runs fast, so log loss should drop by roughly 30-40%, with some loss from C=0.3 not being retuned for the 768-d features.

The implementation matches the spec: the center view is identical to the baseline and the view reshapes are ordered correctly, so the run should finish well within budget. Flip views are equally good in expectation, and the shifted FiveCrop views at 256->224 overlap heavily with the center crop and come from a crop-robust backbone that likely saw these ImageNet images. Averaging 10 probability views should give a modest log-loss gain (~2-5%), partly offset by the 80% weight on slightly worse shifted crops and some underconfidence from averaging a classifier fit only on center crops.

ConvNeXt-T (in22k→in1k) features are much stronger than ResNet-50 features and should cut errors a lot, but C=1.0 on L2-normalized blocks is roughly 100x+ more regularized than the tuned C=0.3 on raw ResNet features (norm ~30). That shrinks logits to margins of about 6 and leaks around 15–20% probability to the other 119 classes on every sample, which cancels most of the gain and leaves the result close to baseline.

The Stanford Dogs images almost certainly overlap the ImageNet-1k train set, so the pretrained ResNet-50 V2 dog-restricted head has effectively been trained on these images and labels, including noisy ones, and should beat the 77-per-class LR. A validation-tuned probability mixture with temperature scaling covers each model's confident mistakes, so a substantial log-loss drop is likely (plausible range 0.15-0.27); all 120 breed names should map cleanly, so the run should not crash.

Centering and rotation are no-ops for L2-regularized LR with an unpenalized intercept, so the only real effect is dropping the 1792 lowest-variance directions; L2 already shrinks those, which leaves little denoising gain, but they hold some of the fine-grained breed-pair signal that dominates log loss. Expect a modest regression with C fixed at 0.3.

ResNet-50 was trained with average pooling, and its frozen features for the ImageNet dog breeds are tuned to that pooling, so swapping in max pooling is a noisier, misaligned descriptor. It is also roughly 3-6x larger in scale, which makes C=0.3 effectively much weaker regularization. That should cost a few points of accuracy and some overconfidence that temperature scaling only partly repairs, pushing log loss up by about 20-35%.

The 120 breeds are exactly ImageNet-1k classes, and Stanford Dogs images come largely from ImageNet's training set, so the V2 checkpoint (80.9% vs 76.1% top-1, trained 600 epochs) should give clearly more separable breed features; its label-smoothing and mixup training mainly hurts transfer to non-ImageNet classes, so any 'confidently wrong' loss penalty should only partly offset the gain.

C=0.3 was already the best value on the holdout grid, so C=0.03 gives an under-confident head (margins roughly 0.5-0.6x). The head barely moves during fine-tuning because at the logistic-regression optimum its gradient is only -λW, and 288 SGD steps at lr 1e-3 grow it by about 1%. The frozen-BN bottleneck fine-tune at lr 1e-4 over 2 epochs sharpens predictions only partially, so log loss should get worse, not better.

ResNet50 was trained at 224 with random-resized crops, which already makes 224 center crops slightly too small (FixRes). Testing at 192 shrinks dogs further and removes fine fur and texture detail, so frozen features for this fine-grained task get noticeably worse (~1.5-3 pt accuracy drop). Refitting the LR and the brief last-block tune cannot recover the lost information, so log loss should rise about 8-12%.

Unwhitened PCA is an orthogonal rotation, and centering is absorbed by the unpenalized intercept, so this just restricts the C=0.3 logistic regression to the top-256 subspace. The dropped 1792 low-variance directions likely carry some of the fine-grained cues for confusable breed pairs, and C was tuned for the full space, so expect a mild log-loss regression rather than a gain.

ResNet-50 V1 was trained with RandomResizedCrop at 224, so objects in a 224 center crop already look smaller than in training; dropping to a 192 crop shrinks them further and discards fine detail, which matters for fine-grained breeds. On ImageNet this costs about 1.5–2 top-1 points, and refitting the logistic regression only partly offsets the loss in feature quality, so I expect roughly a 7–12% rise in log loss.

The 120 breeds are themselves ImageNet classes (Stanford Dogs is drawn from ImageNet), so V2's much stronger ImageNet accuracy (80.9% vs 76.1%) and its tighter, label-smoothing-induced class clusters should outweigh the usual 'V2 transfers worse' effect; the main risk is that C=0.3 was tuned for V1 feature scale, which could shrink the gain.

Scalar temperature scaling is implemented correctly: at T=1 it reproduces sklearn's multinomial predict_proba exactly, it is fitted on a clean 15% holdout, and it is applied to the refit on all data; but because C=0.3 was already chosen for log loss, the model is probably already close to calibrated, so the optimal T is likely near 1 (about 0.9–1.2) and the log-loss gain should be small, roughly 0.5–2%.

The run starts from exactly the baseline linear-probe solution, and the updates are too small to matter. Conv updates at lr 1e-4 with frozen BN over about 288 steps barely move the weights, far less than one late-stage ImageNet step. The head SGD at lr 1e-3 on raw, large-norm features stays near the LR optimum but adds small per-class logit noise, so log loss comes out essentially unchanged or slightly worse.

Averaging the probabilities of two views can only lower the log loss relative to the mean single-view loss (Jensen). Mirrored views are in-distribution and ImageNet features are nearly flip-invariant, so the two views mostly agree and the gain is small. It comes mainly from the ~5–10% of hard images where they disagree, giving roughly a 2% drop. The extra 1,023-image forward pass is cheap, and the MLflow/tempdir wrappers are exception-guarded, so a failed run is unlikely.

Undersampling to 1:1 throws away 90–99.7% of the negatives. That includes nearly all the hard negatives, such as toxic comments that aren't threats, severe or identity hate, and benign comments with violent or identity words. For L2 logistic regression that roughly halves the effective sample size and makes the negative-side estimates much noisier, while class balance itself only moves the intercept, which rank-AUC ignores. The rare labels should drop most (about 0.005–0.01 each) and toxic, obscene and insult modestly. Recomputing the Naive-Bayes ratios on balanced data removes the odd log(n_neg/n_pos) scaling of rare features, which may partly offset the loss in branch B, so I expect a net drop of about 0.004.

Adding the shared char_wb block to the NB-LR branch should make branch B stronger on its own, by roughly +0.002, mainly from subword robustness on toxic, threat and identity_hate. But branch A is already dominated by those same char features, so B becomes much more correlated with A and most of the rank-blend's diversity gain is lost. Net effect is a small gain, around +0.0003, that is comparable to the rare-label noise. Runtime should land around 10-12 minutes, inside the 15-minute limit.

AUC depends only on ranking, so the class-imbalance 'bias' this targets costs nothing; the real effect is throwing away 90–99.7% of negatives, including most of the hard toxic-but-not-this-label comments. A and B also use the same subsample, so the blend cannot average that noise out. Threat (956 rows), identity_hate and severe_toxic should lose roughly 0.5–1.5 pts and the common labels 0.2–0.5, dropping the mean by about 0.6 pts.

MultinomialNB with alpha=1 over 200k TF-IDF features is heavily over-smoothed, especially for the rare labels, so its scores mostly penalise document length and common vocabulary; its mean AUC should land around 0.93–0.95. Rank-averaging that at 50% weight with branch A (~0.979), whose stacked OOF inputs also get weaker, should pull the blend below the parent despite the added diversity.

This drops the strongest branch (word+char TF-IDF LR, about 0.978) and turns the MLP from strong sparse n-gram input into weak inputs. Mean-pooled self-trained Word2Vec with LR or a 3-epoch MLP likely scores only about 0.955-0.965, since it dilutes toxic tokens and loses char-level obfuscation handling. These two correlated weak models now hold 2/3 of the rank-average weight next to NB-LR (about 0.977), so any diversity gain probably won't offset the loss.

A 1:1 undersample keeps only about 0.3–10% of negatives per label (just 478 for threat). That discards most hard negatives, such as toxic-but-not-threat comments and benign identity or violent-word mentions, and makes the linear models 5–167x more regularized relative to the data. AUC should drop most on threat, identity_hate and severe_toxic. The MLP keeps all rows with any positive label, so it partly buffers the rare labels, but it now gets about 5x fewer Adam steps. Net loss is roughly 0.006–0.007 in mean AUC.

The sparse TF-IDF MLP is probably about as strong as the linear branches on its own (~0.975-0.978 on test) and adds some non-linear, multi-task diversity. But it uses the same features, its errors will be highly correlated with the linear branches, and the time guards will likely cut it to 1-2 epochs (or skip it entirely if branch C ends late), so a 1/4-weight rank-average gives only a small expected gain.

Balanced 1:1 undersampling throws away 90–99.7% of the negatives: only 478 of about 159k are kept for threat, and about 1.4–1.6k for identity_hate and severe_toxic. AUC depends only on ranking, so rebalancing the class prior gains nothing, while losing the hard negatives (toxic-but-not-X comments and benign 'kill'/'jew'-type contexts) and adding variance to the NB ratios and weights hurts most on the rare labels. Expect a clear drop of about 0.005–0.012, driven mainly by threat, identity_hate and severe_toxic.

The vectorizers already lowercase and handle whitespace, and char_wb n-grams already catch most obfuscated profanity, so only a handful of rare comments gain from de-obfuscation. That small gain is roughly cancelled by signal the cleaning throws away: register markers (u/ur/wtf become generic you/fuck), 'U.S.' turning into 'you', the (utc) signature timestamps that mark civil comments, and the intensity of '!!!!' runs. Net effect is about zero, leaning slightly negative, and the change is within the noise from the rare labels.

Stacking NB-LR out-of-fold predictions for all six labels into the char+word LR gives the rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) a strong toxicity signal they currently lack, but the final 50/50 rank blend with B then counts B twice and loses some diversity, so I expect only a small net gain.

A 64-unit sparse MLP trained 3 epochs on branch A's features should score about 0.975-0.978 on its own. Its nonlinear, multi-task errors are only partly correlated with the two linear branches (error correlation around 0.9), so an equal 1/3 rank blend should give a small gain, most likely on toxic and insult, partly offset by weaker rare-label (threat, identity_hate) AUCs from the shared bottleneck. Epoch-3 overfitting with essentially no regularization is a risk. Runtime rises by about 3-5 minutes (roughly 1,870 dense Adam updates over 3.84M params), likely still under the 15-minute kill.

Branch C is an NB-LogReg on word bigrams plus char n-grams, so on its own it should roughly match or beat A and clearly beat B. It is still strongly correlated with both, so an equal 3-way rank average should add only a few 1e-4 AUC. There is some risk C=4 overfits the rare labels (threat, identity_hate), and the extra liblinear fits on about 143M nonzeros push wall-clock toward the 15-minute kill, but a small gain is most likely.

Full-data branch predictions are deterministic and unchanged, so only the per-label rank-blend weights move; the flat blend curve plus 50% shrinkage (w in [0.25,0.75]) should give a small gain from up-weighting the stronger char+word branch on high-count labels, partly offset by noisy holdout weights on threat and identity_hate and by train/test shift (the extra holdout pass also adds runtime risk but should not change the score if it completes).

This projects the sparse n-gram space onto 300 unsupervised LSA directions, dropping the char n-grams and the NB-LR branch. Most of the capacity goes to topic and template variance rather than the specific abusive words and obfuscated spellings that separate toxic, insult, threat and identity_hate. The post-SVD L2 normalization also discards how much of each comment the subspace actually captures. Expect a clear regression to roughly 0.94–0.96 mean AUC, with the largest losses on toxic, insult and the rare labels.

Toxic is unchanged because it has fewer than 10 negatives per positive, and obscene/insult keep about half their negatives, so the loss comes mainly from threat, identity_hate and severe_toxic, which keep only 3-10% of their negatives. Those labels lose most of their hard negatives (toxic comments without the sub-label, benign identity mentions), their NB ratios get noisier, and fastText gets many more unseen words and untrained bigram buckets. All three branches degrade in the same direction on the same subsample, so I expect a clear drop of about 0.002-0.004 in mean AUC.

The parent's 0.883 is far below the ~0.978 a word/char TF-IDF plus NB-LogReg blend should score, and the likely cause is a numpy-2 bug: old fasttext-wheel builds run under numpy 2 return every probability in a predict row equal to the top one, so the parent's fastText branch output the model's confidence rather than P(toxic) and was anti-correlated with the labels; the child's numpy<2 pin should remove that bug, so the three-way rank blend should recover to about 0.977-0.98 even though softmax multi-label fastText is somewhat weaker than per-label models (if the pin were not applied, the score would drop below the parent instead).

With only two classes, ComplementNB ranks documents exactly like multinomial NB minus its prior, so the promised imbalance correction never kicks in. Scoring raw counts with no length normalization rewards short texts and repeated words and penalizes long ones, so long toxic comments sink. alpha=1 smoothing over 200k features dominates the rare labels (threat, identity_hate), and predict_proba saturates at exactly 1.0 for heavily profane texts, creating ties. The expected result is a plain naive Bayes baseline around 0.92-0.94 mean AUC, well below the 0.98 logistic-regression ensemble.

Unweighted mean-pooled skip-gram vectors with a linear head lose the sparse token and char-level weighting that toxicity detection relies on. Averaging dilutes isolated insults in long comments, and a 200-d projection of unsupervised embeddings is coarser than per-token weights, so this typically lands around 0.94-0.96 against about 0.98 for the tuned TF-IDF/NB-LR ensemble (the run should still fit the time budget).

Averaging unsupervised corpus Word2Vec vectors dilutes the few decisive toxic tokens across every word in a comment. The per-label linear model then sees only 200 fixed dimensions instead of per-token weights over 60k–200k sparse n-grams. Mean-embedding plus logistic-regression baselines on Jigsaw typically land around 0.94–0.96 test AUC, versus about 0.978 for TF-IDF and NB-LR. The pipeline fits the time budget, so expect a clear regression of roughly 0.025–0.03 AUC.

A character-level NB-LogReg shares char features with branch A and the NB-weighted, weakly regularized setup with branch B, so it is only moderately diverse; a third linear model like this usually adds about +0.0003 to +0.0006 AUC. Tuning three weights per label on a 10% holdout (only about 48 threat and 140 identity_hate positives) adds noise that eats part of the gain. The branch probably adds 4-5 minutes (char vectorization plus slow liblinear fits on dense char features), so runtime is near the 15-minute kill limit but most likely finishes.

Weaker regularization (C=4) on the word+char TF-IDF logistic regression likely helps the frequent labels (toxic, insult, obscene) a little but hurts the rare, noisy labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic), where the community-tuned C=0.1 is safer; it also makes branch A more like the already weakly regularized NB-LogReg branch, so the rank blend gains less from diversity. Net effect is roughly flat to slightly negative, with some added runtime risk from liblinear converging slowly at C=4.

A working per-label fastText (unregularized SGD on mean-pooled word uni/bigrams, 20 epochs) should score about 0.968-0.973, weaker than both branches and highly correlated with NB-LR, so an equal 1/3 rank weight is roughly neutral to slightly harmful. There is also a real (~1/3) tail risk of a large drop: an old-pybind11 fasttext-wheel under numpy 2 would return duplicated k=2 probabilities, making the F branch a confidence score rather than P(label=1).

Assuming the run finishes, a char_wb 3-7 NB-LogReg branch should score about 0.977-0.979 alone and add a little diversity, but it overlaps heavily with branch A's char features and branch B's NB weighting, so the three-way rank average gains only about +0.0003 to +0.0006. The main risk is runtime: a second char vectorizer on 313k docs plus six fully converged primal liblinear fits on roughly 90M nonzeros could push the run past the 15-minute kill.

Losing 10% of training data, with no full-data refit, costs roughly 0.0003-0.0005 mean AUC, mostly on the rare labels. Per-label weights tuned on a 16k holdout (only about 48 threat positives) recover little, since the rank-blend AUC surface is flat near 0.5, and they risk overfitting noisy extreme weights. Net effect is a slight regression.

NB log-count scaling at C=0.1 relaxes regularization on discriminative char/word n-grams and should modestly help branch A, especially on rare labels, but it makes A more similar to the NB-LR branch B, which shrinks the blend's diversity gain, so the net effect is roughly flat to slightly positive (the slower sag convergence adds runtime, but it should still fit the budget).

A 1% document-frequency floor (about 3.1k of 313k docs) shrinks the vocabularies to roughly 600 words, 10-15k char n-grams, and about 1.2k word 1-2grams for NB-LR, dropping most rare but highly discriminative profanity, slurs, identity terms and threat words (bitch, cunt, gay, nigger, moron, murder, etc.); only 'fuck'/'stupid' plus a few borderline terms survive, so AUC falls noticeably on toxic, insult, threat and identity_hate.

Balanced undersampling doesn't help AUC for logistic regression. It mainly throws away negatives, keeping ~0.3–10% of them. The biggest loss is the hard negatives, such as toxic comments that aren't threats or identity hate, which the rare-label models need to separate those labels from generic profanity. On top of that, branch A becomes heavily over-regularized on ~1–3k rows, so its logits get compressed and the blend is mostly branch B. Expect small drops on toxic, obscene and insult (~0.003–0.005) and larger drops on threat and identity_hate (~0.01).

A cosine class-centroid (Rocchio) score is a mean-difference linear classifier. It weights features by average mass rather than discriminative power, under-weighting rare but strong cues and over-weighting common and register features. The NB weighting in branch B helps for obvious profanity, slur and threat words, but subtle toxic and insult positives and profane non-threat negatives degrade the ranking. Expect mean AUC roughly 3-5 points below the LR blend (0.98), around 0.94.

Switching char to char_wb only drops cross-word n-grams. Branch A's word block is unigram-only with stop words removed, so it loses a little phrase signal (e.g. 'k you', 'kill y'). The freed 50k slots mostly go to within-word fragments that duplicate the word block. Branch B's word bigrams restore most of the phrase information in the rank blend, so the net effect should be near zero, possibly slightly negative, and within the noise from the rare labels.

Binary ComplementNB with norm=False ranks documents exactly like prior-free multinomial NB, so it drops logistic regression's discriminative reweighting. Alpha=1 on fractional TF-IDF counts is also heavy smoothing: the smoothing mass (about 60k in branch A, 200k in branch B) swamps the positive-class mass for the rare labels. That flattens their distribution and adds a strong length and rarity bias. Expect toxic, obscene and insult to lose about 2-4 AUC points and threat and identity_hate to lose about 7-15, pulling the mean from 0.980 down to roughly 0.92-0.93.

A 32-component SVD keeps only the highest-variance directions of the 60k-dim TF-IDF space. Those directions are mostly generic character statistics and talk-page templates, with perhaps one or two profanity or second-person axes. That drops branch A from about 0.978 to roughly 0.90–0.93 AUC, because rare, keyword-driven labels like threat, identity_hate and non-profane insults are lost. Branch A was the strong half of the blend; the fastText branch is only about 0.95–0.96 alone. The equal-weight rank blend should land near the weaker fastText level, roughly 0.945–0.96, rather than the current 0.973.

Cutting the vocabulary to about 2,000 tokens keeps common profanity but collapses mid-frequency insults, slurs, compound or misspelled profanity and char-n-gram subword signal into 'raretoken' in both branches, making them weaker and more correlated, so AUC should drop about 0.008, mostly on insult, identity_hate and threat.

Keeping stop words puts useful pronoun and modal tokens back into branch A's word block (you/your/i/will matter for insult and threat), but char_wb 2-6-grams already capture them, only ~300 low-rank vocab slots are displaced, and the change is diluted by the 50/50 rank-average with the unchanged NB-LR branch, so expect a tiny, slightly positive shift (~+0.0001).

Averaging logits instead of ranks gives each branch weight in proportion to its logit spread. The weakly regularized NB-LogReg branch (C=4, NB-scaled features, overconfident) has a much wider spread than the C=0.1 char+word branch, especially on the rare labels. That shifts the blend toward the weaker, overconfident branch and loses some of the equal-weight diversity gain, so expect a small drop.

Switching to 'char' under the same 50k-feature cap fills roughly half the vocabulary with cross-word n-grams, which mostly duplicate the phrase information branch B already has from word bigrams, and it pushes out mid-frequency within-word n-grams; branch A's own AUC should move by no more than about ±0.001, the equal-weight rank blend halves that, and the added overlap with B slightly reduces blend diversity, so I expect essentially no change with a slight lean negative (the run should finish in about 10–12 minutes, under the 15-minute kill).

A 5-epoch, dim-64 fastText word/bigram model (ova loss, no subwords, no pretrained vectors, mean pooling) will probably score around 0.965-0.972 alone, below the NB-LogReg branch (~0.976); rank-averaging it at equal weight with the word+char branch likely gives a smaller gain than NB-LogReg did, so the blend should drop slightly despite some added diversity.

At C=1 on standardised features the LR is over-regularised rather than high-variance (Kaggle tuning favours C around 1000). Dropping the 64 lowest-F columns, which still carry real, non-redundant margin/texture signal while the redundant high-F shape bins survive, shrinks the achievable margin, so the LR becomes less confident and slightly less accurate. The NN is unchanged, so roughly half to three-quarters of the LR's relative loss increase passes through the 50/50 blend.

Label smoothing at 0.1 over 99 classes caps the NN's true-class probability at about 0.9, down from about 0.98–0.99 with one-hot targets. That removes the sharpness the 50/50 blend relies on on top of the softer C=1 logistic regression, so each correct sample costs roughly 0.03–0.05 more log-loss. The blend already limits the damage from confident NN errors, so the calibration gain on hard samples is small and the net result should be a clear regression.

One-vs-rest with only about 7–9 positives per class gives worse-calibrated scores that vary from class to class. Normalising the 99 sigmoid outputs also adds leakage from the 98 negative classes. When two confusable species both score high, the sigmoids saturate near 1, so the power exponent cannot sharpen the tie. The single global power-plus-floor calibration therefore only partly recovers what multinomial softmax already gets right. I expect log loss to get worse (roughly 1.3–2x), though the 99-row test set makes the exact number noisy.

A 5-seed MLP bag (alpha=0.1 is actually about LR C=1 strength, since sklearn divides the penalty by batch size) is decorrelated from the LR and comparable or better on these features, so the OOF-tuned blend plus calibration should cut log loss noticeably. The ~99-row test set, where a couple of hard rows dominate, adds a lot of variance; w=0 fallback and runtime (~3-5 min) are safe.

This is a few-shot setup with roughly 9 training rows per class, so each fold model loses about 20% of the data and becomes softer and slightly less accurate; averaging five highly correlated linear models only partly makes up for that. The averaging should cap a few confident errors but raise the loss on the many easy test points, and with only about 99 test rows the net effect is small, noisy and leans slightly worse.

The new features add absolute leaf size (image height and width, area, axis lengths), which the scale-normalised 64-dim shape descriptor lacks, so the tuned logistic regression should break some species confusions. The gain is tempered by noisy features (Hu-moment sign flips, heavy-tailed Euler number) and a possibly inverted threshold, since the files may be white leaves on black. The 99-row test set is also very noisy, and there is roughly a 10-15% chance the images folder or libraries are missing, which would give an identical score.

The L2 penalty is unchanged under rotation and the data is already centred, so PCA alone gives the same fit. The only real effect is dropping the lowest-variance ~5% of directions (likely ~100 of 219, keeping ~110-125). At C=1 the model already shrinks those heavily, but they still carry some signal (fine shape detail, redundant geometric features, histogram contrasts) on a dataset that rewards weaker regularisation, so expect a mild increase in log loss.

Averaging five fold models, each trained on 80% of the data, behaves roughly like the full-data logistic regression at a slightly lower effective C, about 0.8, so its logits are a few percent smaller. At C=1 this model is already under-confident, so that softening costs a few percent of log loss. The probability-averaging (Jensen) bonus on the few misclassified samples should recover part of that, leaving a small net regression that sits within test-set noise.

The image+feature CNN, like the known Kaggle Keras ConvNet, should be accurate (~98-99%) and confident, and averaging it with the under-confident C=1 LR roughly halves the LR's loss on correct samples; the blend is still limited by the LR's probability mass, and by any NN errors (the >50% leaf-coverage inversion heuristic weakens the image branch), so the result lands around 0.06-0.075 rather than NN-alone levels.

LR at C=1 on near-separable standardized leaf features is strongly underconfident (0.124 loss despite roughly 98-99% accuracy), so OOF-fitted temperature sharpening (likely a≈2.5-4, small eps) should remove most of the loss on correctly classified samples; the result on the roughly 99-row test set is then dominated by the 0-2 misclassified leaves, which the sharpening makes costlier, so the outcome is noisy (about 0.02-0.12) but very likely a large improvement.

The leaf features are nearly linearly separable, so C=1 is heavily over-regularised and gives soft probabilities (0.124). Out-of-fold CV should pick a large C (about 300 to 3000), which typically brings multinomial LR log loss down to roughly 0.03 to 0.06; the small (~99-row) test set makes the exact value noisy because one or two misclassified leaves dominate it. The 55 lbfgs fits in parallel should finish within the time budget.

The added size columns (image h/w, log area, perimeter, axes, bbox) carry new information, since the 192 precomputed descriptors are scale-invariant, and they still track leaf size on inverted images. At a fixed C=1.0 the model is regularization-limited and underconfident, so extra informative standardized features act like a modestly larger C and should lower log loss. Gains are limited by noise from three sources: the fill>0.5 inversion heuristic, which will often flip tightly cropped round leaves onto background corners; random-sign Hu moments; and the roughly 99-row test set. Expect a moderate rather than dramatic improvement.

Standardized leaf features are nearly linearly separable, and multinomial LR here is known to reach its best log loss at very large C (around 1e2 to 1e3), so the C=1 loss is mostly under-confidence on correctly classified samples. Cutting C 5x shrinks the logits by roughly 25%, which raises the loss on easy and medium samples about 2 to 4x, especially where mass leaks to the many similar Quercus classes. Only slightly less loss on the rare wrong predictions offsets this, so the loss roughly doubles.

Dropping the full-data refit means the submitted model trains on only about 712 of 891 rows (roughly 7 instead of 9 samples per class for 99 classes); at fixed C=1 this also regularizes harder, so predictions get less confident and a few extra confusions are likely, raising log loss about 20-30% on the roughly 99-row test set.

The LR component is effectively the same model as before. Shrinkage LDA is very accurate (~98%) but nearly hard, and kNN is weak but diverse. Blending them with weights tuned on out-of-fold predictions should put most weight on LR (~0.7) and most of the rest on LDA. That rescues some of LR's confidently wrong samples and pays a small -log(1-w) cost where LDA errs, so I expect a modest gain, though the ~99-sample test set makes it noisy.

Log loss should get several times worse: boosted trees handle 99 classes with about 7-8 training samples each poorly, especially since min_samples_leaf=10 forbids pure class leaves and there is no subsampling for diversity. The model also trains on only 85% of the data and keeps 30 extra rounds past its best point, so expect roughly 90-95% accuracy with soft probabilities, about 0.3-0.5 log loss, versus about 0.06 for the tuned linear model.

Sigmoid calibration with only 2-4 positives per class in each 3-fold calibration split caps positive targets near 0.75-0.8, and 99 one-vs-rest calibrators each spread about one unit of mass over negatives, so the calibrated SVC gives the true class roughly 0.7-0.8 versus about 0.85-0.9 from weakly regularised C=1 logistic regression; since the equal-weight ensemble already looks underconfident (log loss 0.29 at about 98% accuracy), a less confident member lowers the average true-class probability by about 0.03 and raises log loss by about 0.03-0.04.

Given the underconfident kNN (the log-loss CV pushes k toward 20) and C=1 logistic members, the observed 0.29 implies HGB is supplying fairly confident, mostly correct probabilities; a 600-tree forest spreads its votes on 99 classes (mean true-class probability around 0.5–0.6), which lowers the averaged true-class probability on easy samples by more than its stability saves on HGB's occasional confident errors, so log loss likely rises moderately.

The baseline LR at C=1 is over-regularised and underconfident; the achievable score on these features is about 0.04. The nearly unregularised Adam MLP, early-stopped on accuracy with patience 30, should stop mid-refinement with fairly confident, roughly 97-98% accurate predictions. That gains on correct samples, but errors cost more and 10% of training data goes to the internal split, so expect a modest, noisy improvement (99 test rows) with a fat tail toward regression.

C=1 leaves standardized multinomial LR underconfident on this nearly separable 192-feature, ~9-samples-per-class data, so OOF selection should pick a large C (about 100–1000) and cut log loss to roughly 0.04–0.06, as tuned-LR results on leaf data suggest; with only about 99 test rows, one or two now-overconfident errors add a lot of variance, only partly offset by the alpha shrinkage.

The leaf images should be white silhouettes on black, so the extraction is valid. The regularisation stays fixed at C=1, which leaves the model under-confident. Adding 48 standardised features that are fairly informative and partly redundant (Hu moments, solidity/eccentricity, a radial histogram, and new absolute-size information from area and axes) acts like a modestly larger effective C and adds some genuinely new signal. That should sharpen probabilities for a moderate log-loss gain, with only minor harm from noisy features like orientation and the sign of hu_7.

With C=1 on standardized features the model is underconfident even though accuracy is about 98–99%, and 10-fold log-loss CV will select a high C (tens to hundreds, where lbfgs's mean-scaled tolerance plateaus), cutting the loss on correct samples several-fold. One or two confident misses on the small test set keep the result near 0.04–0.05 rather than about 0.01. This assumes every CV fold contains all 99 classes; if the prepared training set has fewer than 990 rows, the neg_log_loss scorer will likely raise and the run will crash.

The LR component is identical to the current model, which is under-confident but accurate (p_true about 0.9 on most samples). Averaging it with equal weight against three weaker models (distance-weighted kNN with CV-picked k around 8-12, capped near 0.6-0.8 on classes with 6-9 training samples; near-one-hot HGB at roughly 85% accuracy that struggles with ~8 samples/class and min_samples_leaf=10; and near-one-hot shrunk LDA at ~97%) should dilute true-class mass on the many easy samples. That likely outweighs the gains on LR's few hard cases, so a moderate regression is expected rather than an improvement.

At C=1 on standardised leaf features, LR is underconfident: accuracy is about 98–99%, and its log loss mostly comes from correct predictions with p≈0.85–0.95, not from confidently wrong ones, which is why much larger C scores far better on this data. Shrinking toward uniform would therefore raise out-of-fold loss even at the smallest grid step (0.01 costs about +0.01 nats per correct sample). The search should pick alpha=0, making the test predictions bit-identical and the score unchanged.

sklearn applies shrinkage per class, so 'auto' (Ledoit-Wolf on ~9 standardized samples) already acts like a diagonal-preserving, correlation-shrunk LDA that weights reliable low-variance features heavily; fixed 0.9 toward scaled identity makes it near nearest-centroid, overweighting noisy sparse histogram bins and underweighting discriminative shape features, so accuracy likely drops from ~98% to ~93-96%; softer logits make each error cheaper, which only partly offsets the extra errors on a ~99-row test set where each error costs several nats.

Joint shrinkage LDA effectively multiplies evidence from the three descriptor families, so its ~0.36 loss comes from a few confident errors. Arithmetically averaging three 64-feature LDAs (roughly margin ~83%, texture ~78%, shape ~55-65% accuracy on their own) caps confidence. Whenever one family, especially the weak shape model, disagrees, the true-class probability falls to about 2/3 (~0.4 nats), which costs more across the ~99 test rows than it saves on the rare catastrophic errors.

Unwhitened PCA is just a rotation, so the L2 penalty is unchanged and the only real effect is dropping the low-variance tail (probably about 100 of 192 dimensions, including fine shape detail that is consistent within species); with near-separable 99-class data and weak regularization (C around 1000) the model uses that tail, so separation and confidence should drop, making log loss moderately worse, and the ~99-row test set keeps the result noisy.

Shrinkage-LDA on 192 standardized leaf features gets roughly 98-99% accuracy with about 9 samples per class, below tuned logistic regression. Its softmax posteriors come from the Gaussian model rather than being fitted for calibration, so they are overconfident. With 99 test rows, even one confident error costs about 0.1-0.35 in log loss. The most likely outcome is about one error, giving roughly 0.2, though there is about a 30% chance of zero errors and a score near 0.01.

Truncating to 95% of standardized variance removes low-variance directions (fine shape modes, contrasts between correlated histogram bins) that the L2 logistic regression was already using, because n*C is large; on leaf, weaker regularization and more directions help, so truncating likely costs some discrimination on the hard confusable species, and re-fitting the temperature only restores calibration, so expect a moderate worsening, with high noise from the ~99-row test set.

sklearn's shrinkage='auto' applies Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage to each class separately, and with only about 7-9 samples per class and 192 features that shrinkage is heavy (roughly 0.7-0.9). This makes the model close to a diagonal LDA and probably slightly less accurate than the standardized LR baseline. Its logits are sharp, so easy samples cost almost nothing. However, on a 99-row test set, each extra mistake costs roughly 2-3 nats even after temperature scaling, which is capped at T=4. That likely outweighs the gain, giving a modest but noisy regression.

Mixing 0.5% uniform mass across 99 classes adds about -log(0.995) ≈ 0.005 of loss to every sample whose true-class probability is above about 0.01. It only helps samples with p below about 1e-4. With roughly 99 test rows and a total loss sum of only about 9.3, even one worst-case error can recover at most about 0.4 of the roughly 0.49 total cost, so the net result is almost certainly a small regression of about +0.001 to +0.005.

Two effects both likely push log loss up slightly. First, with the same random_state the 384 landmarks are a subset of the original 512, so the kernel span only shrinks and a few classes lose landmark coverage. Second, after the post-Nystroem StandardScaler the feature-space scale grows with n_components, so cutting to 384 acts like roughly 20-25% lower effective C. That matters because this nearly separable dataset favours weak regularization, and C=1 is probably already under-confident.

Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage caps the extreme overconfidence of plain LDA (which scores about 0.9 on this data), and with about 98.5-99% accuracy it removes the underconfidence that dominates LR C=1's 0.124, so it likely wins slightly; but on only about 99 test rows each confident error costs about 5-15 nats, so the outcome is high-variance and a regression is also plausible.

The model is unchanged apart from C. On these near-separable standardized leaf descriptors, C=1 is badly over-regularized, and 3-fold CV should pick C=100 or C=1000. That makes correct predictions far more confident and should cut log loss to roughly 0.03–0.06. The 99-row test set makes this noisy, since one confident misclassification adds about 0.03–0.05.

LogisticRegression with C=1 on this near-separable 99-class data is underconfident (much more held-out-accurate than its probabilities suggest, and it leaks mass to background classes), so a temperature fitted on out-of-fold scores should land around T≈0.4-0.6 and sharpen the correct predictions a lot, only partly offset by larger losses on the 1-2 likely misclassified samples among the ~99 test rows; the code is otherwise identical and T=1 would reproduce the baseline exactly.

Two effects roughly cancel. The second scaler blows the 512 whitened Nystroem coordinates up to unit variance, giving an effective RBF-kernel C of about 600–800. In the linear subspace that is about as regularized as the current C=1 model, so typical-point confidence stays about the same, since the RBF's large self-similarity term (partly memorizing training points) offsets its stronger same-class similarity. The isotropic RBF on standardized, heavy-tailed histogram features is also less robust than learned linear projections for atypical or confusable leaves, which dominate log loss. Net expectation is roughly flat to a mild regression, with high variance on a 99-row test set.

The added block brings real new signal that the L2-normalised TF-IDF and history counts cannot see, chiefly the success-rate decline over time (t_days) and request length, plus modest extras like images and reciprocity. With about 2.9k training rows and weak effective regularisation on 40 standardised dense columns, overfitting risk is low, so I expect a gain of roughly +0.01 to +0.02 AUC; the test set of about 1.1k rows adds around ±0.01 noise.

A fully grown sqrt-mtry forest on about 8k mostly sparse TF-IDF and subreddit columns dilutes the nine informative dense numeric features (considered at only about 10% of splits) and handles weak-signal bag-of-words worse than a regularized linear model, while RAOP's monotone count effects gain little from nonlinearity, so AUC likely drops a few points versus logistic regression.

The ~5k-dim sparse TF-IDF hurts the random forest: with max_features='sqrt' (~70 candidates per split), splits are mostly near-random rare-word cuts and the 9 numeric features are drawn at only ~12% of nodes, so non-leak ranking should fall from ~0.64 to ~0.59-0.61 AUC; the forest still exploits the giver_known leak fairly well (drawn at ~1.4% of nodes, but over ~40-level paths it isolates pure-positive leaves in ~35-45% of trees), so the overall drop is moderate rather than catastrophic.

About 30% of test positives are flagged by the giver_known leak and stay ranked at the top, so only the ~70% base (text+metadata) portion is affected; 50 unsupervised LDA topic proportions on ~2.9k short docs discard token-level discriminative signal (imgur/evidence words, edit remnants, specific narrative terms) that the TF-IDF LR exploits, likely lowering the base AUC by ~0.02 and the overall score by ~0.01-0.02.

Replacing the supervised out-of-fold TF-IDF logit (text-only AUC about 0.61–0.63) with 20 unsupervised LDA topic proportions throws away most of the discriminative text signal (topics alone reach about 0.55–0.58, lose length and word-level cues, and add noise dimensions on under 3k rows), so the model falls back mostly to metadata plus timestamp, giving a drop of roughly 0.02–0.04 AUC.

The prepared test set is a random split from the same 2010-2013 period, so the raw timestamp's declining success-rate trend (about 0.57-0.58 AUC on its own, and one of the top RAOP features) transfers to test. Dropping it loses real signal. Hour and weekday are weak or noisy features that the heavily regularized LightGBM gains little from, so I expect a net drop of about 0.01 AUC.

The LR already sees all of the dense features (linearly, log-scaled), so a GBM on metadata alone (likely ~0.65-0.67 OOF vs LR ~0.68-0.70) adds mainly nonlinearity and model diversity; the CV-chosen rank blend (w≈0.6-0.8 on LR) should give a small gain of about +0.005 to +0.01, with some chance of no change or a slight drop given about 1.1k test rows.

A random forest on about 4.5k sparse TF-IDF columns plus about 33 dense features (max_features=sqrt, roughly 67 candidates per split) will usually split on weak rare-word features. That dilutes the metadata and time signal that drives this weak-signal problem, and fully grown trees on about 2.9k rows add noise, so it should underperform the regularized linear model by several AUC points.

The binary IDF-weighted subreddit bag adds weak signal: niche gift and help communities, plus a rough proxy for posting era, which the model otherwise lacks because it ignores the timestamp. Most of the activity signal is already carried by the log-scaled count features, and about 1–1.5k sparse, noisy features under the fairly loose C=0.3 add prediction noise, so expect only a small net gain of roughly +0.003 to +0.008 AUC, with some risk of no change.

The MLE-bench test split is carved from the original labeled train and keeps giver_username_if_known. A known giver almost always means the request succeeded, and this covers roughly 30% of positives. LR with C=0.3 should give that flag a logit weight of about +4, ranking those rows above essentially every negative. AUC then comes out near 0.30 + 0.70 x ~0.65, about 0.75-0.76, instead of 0.657.

The stack adds a real new signal, the UTC request timestamp (RAOP success rate falls over time, and the random MLE-bench split keeps train and test in the same period), and lets a regularized LightGBM learn the text-versus-metadata weighting and nonlinear history effects; this should give about +0.01 to +0.02 AUC over 0.657, though the small ~1.1k-row test set adds roughly ±0.01 of noise.

The main gain should come from the request-time trend, since success rates fell steadily over RAOP's life and the random train/test split keeps that trend useful, plus the length features, which TF-IDF's L2 row normalisation mostly hides from the model. The other additions (imgur, [request], punctuation, hour, weekday, history flags and karma ratio) are weak or already covered by TF-IDF and the existing numerics. The implementation looks correct, and the MLflow logging fails safely. Combining two roughly independent signals suggests about +0.015 to +0.025 AUC, with noise from the roughly 1.2k-row test set.

With max_features='sqrt', ExtraTrees samples about 73 features per split, and ~93% of them are sparse TF-IDF words, so the 9 strong requester-history numerics are rarely considered. Axis-aligned random-threshold trees also capture the weak, diffuse, mostly linear embedding signal poorly. That should outweigh any gain from avoiding the near-unregularized LR's overfitting, leaving AUC slightly lower.

With C=0.3, the L2-normalized TF-IDF features are tiny in scale and heavily shrunk, while the 384 standardized MiniLM dims are fit nearly unregularized on ~2.9k rows and dominate both the model and its overfitting noise. Removing TF-IDF therefore drops a small, clean lexical signal and removes little noise, so AUC should fall slightly or stay near flat.

Explicit length and link (evidence) features add real signal that length-normalized TF-IDF misses; the Althoff paper also found length and evidentiality predictive. The lightly regularized LR pays an estimation-noise cost for the ~24 dense features, many of them weak (VADER, Flesch, pronouns, gratitude flags), which offsets part of the gain. Net is a modest improvement of about +0.005 to +0.012 AUC, within test-set noise of roughly 1.2k rows.

This drops the TF-IDF text block, which on RAOP carries roughly as much signal as the requester-history features. Nine log-scaled numeric features in a logistic regression typically reach only about 0.60-0.63 AUC, and the test split is random, so the temporal-drift argument doesn't apply. The mlflow wrapper is fail-safe and won't affect the result, so I expect a drop of about 0.03 AUC.

Swapping the heavily shrunk sparse TF-IDF block for 200 standardized dense mean-W2V dims under the same weak C=0.3 adds roughly 200 near-unregularized degrees of freedom on about 2.9k rows (about 3 positive events per variable). The resulting logit noise likely outweighs the modest synonymy and topic signal that noisy self-trained embeddings add on a weak-signal task, so AUC drops by about 0.02-0.03.

On ~2.9k training docs, bigrams and min_df=2 mostly add rare, high-IDF terms. These dilute the L2-normalised unigram weights, so at the fixed C=0.3 the already weak text block is regularised further and the model leans on the dense features, which carry most of the signal. The expected effect is flat to slightly negative, within the noise of this test set, and the mlflow logging does not change the metric.

The nine at-request history features are individually weak (roughly 0.55-0.58 AUC each) and correlated with each other; with no timestamp or text they should reach only about 0.60 with a 63-leaf LightGBM on ~2.9k rows, while the SVD text features, though noisy, carry real signal (unigrams alone reach about 0.62 in Althoff et al.) that early stopping was already using, so dropping them likely loses about 0.02-0.03 AUC.

In this 309-dim design only a few columns (the 9 numeric ones and a few SVD directions) carry signal, and the text signal is spread weakly across many SVD dimensions; a sqrt-mtry forest of fully grown trees is mostly splitting on noise and captures additive, distributed signal worse than greedy early-stopped boosting, so expect roughly parity or a slight drop, within test-set noise (about ±0.015 AUC on ~1.1k rows).

StandardScaler puts the 384 MiniLM dimensions at unit variance, so C=0.3 barely regularises them. With about 2.9k training rows and about 25% positives, that adds roughly 0.6–0.7 logit-variance of estimation noise, far more than the modest extra text signal the frozen embeddings carry beyond the TF-IDF and metadata features, so AUC most likely drops.

Many rare, high-IDF bigrams and df=2 unigrams take up most of each row's L2 norm. With C=0.3 fixed and the text weights already heavily shrunk, this roughly halves the unigram text contribution next to the standardized numeric features. The small extra phrase signal from bigrams (e.g. 'pay forward', 'imgur com') only partly makes up for that, so a slight drop within test-set noise is most likely.

Body length is a known predictor of RAOP success, and the L2-normalised TF-IDF discards it; the stripped pronouns and the lexicon counts add a little more, so with ~2.9k rows and only 15 standardised dense features this should give a modest ~+0.01 AUC with low overfitting risk, slightly dampened by redundancy with the unigrams and by Flesch/word-length outliers.

LightGBM with 63 leaves on about 3k rows of mostly noisy SVD components (300 of 309 features) will fit noise. Trees also approximate spread-out linear text signal worse than LR on sparse TF-IDF. The gains, a length proxy from the first SVD component and nonlinear handling of the numeric features, probably don't make up for this, so expect a small regression within test-set noise.

The test set is a random split drawn from the same period as training, so the date spline was capturing RAOP's real long-term decline in success rate. Swapping it for an annual sin/cos pair throws that trend away and keeps only a weak seasonal signal, so AUC should drop by about 0.005–0.015.

At C=30 the ~5k unigram TF-IDF weights are almost unregularized on only about 2.9k weak-signal RAOP samples. The text part will nearly separate the training set, and its test-time noise will swamp the well-fit numeric and date signal, so AUC likely drops about 4–8 points.

RAOP success rates fell steadily over time (early 2011 requests succeeded far more often), so a request-time trend alone gives roughly 0.57–0.59 AUC; that signal is mostly independent of the text, requester-history and subreddit features. With a random train/test split and weak effective regularization on 7 standardized spline columns, the trend should be captured well, adding about +0.01 to +0.015 AUC.

Cosine distance on the unweighted concatenation is dominated by subreddit indicators (norm ~sqrt(#subs)) and the 9 standardized numerics (norm ~3), with text contributing only norm 1, so the neighbors mostly reflect broad activity groups (throwaway, active, prior-RAOP) and lose most of the text signal. On top of that, k=25 on a ~25% base rate adds label noise of about ±0.09 in probability, comparable to the gaps between groups, so the AUC shrinks from the logistic model's 0.649 toward roughly 0.55–0.60.

A distance-weighted KNN on nine weak, zero-heavy log-count metadata features will be noisier and weaker (standalone AUC about 0.56–0.58) than the CatBoost it replaces. Its wide, near-1-NN probability spread gets outsized weight in the fixed 50/50 average, and the LR already captures most of the linear metadata signal, so the blend should lose roughly 1.5–3 AUC points.

C=30 is 100x weaker regularisation, so the logistic regression on ~5k sparse unigrams and ~3k weakly-labelled RAOP requests nearly separates the training set and its text logits become large and noisy; its extreme probabilities then dominate the 50/50 blend and push the metadata-driven CatBoost aside, and the extra text weight and model diversity only partly offset the overfitting, so expect a modest AUC drop.

In RAOP the success rate falls steadily over time (timestamp alone gives roughly 0.56–0.58 AUC) and is mostly independent of the text and requester-history features. Seven standardized spline columns are barely regularized at C=0.3 on a random split, so they should capture the decline cleanly and add about +0.01 AUC, with some noise from the small test set.

BernoulliNB reduces to a linear model on binary presence with noisy, double-counted, Laplace-biased weights. Its score is dominated by the number of distinct terms present (a length proxy, AUC ~0.58-0.60 on RAOP), which swamps the nine binarized requester-history features and discards the TF-IDF weighting, so it should land below the tuned-ish LR combo.

RAOP success rates fall steadily over community age (time alone gives AUC of roughly 0.57), the benchmark split is random so the trend carries over to test, and the 7-column spline is lightly regularised at C=0.3 on about 2.9k rows. The time signal is only partly covered by the text and history features, so expect a modest gain of about +0.01 AUC, within test noise of about ±0.007; the MLflow wrapper does not change predictions.

The change adds about 1–1.5k unscaled binary subreddit columns, roughly 15 active per user, to an LR with C=0.3 fitted on about 2.9k rows. That regularisation is weak for 0/1 features (effective df is in the hundreds), so rare and mid-frequency subreddit weights add about ±0.6 logit of noise for active users. The real signal they carry (activity and era proxies) is mostly already in the numeric features, so test AUC most likely falls slightly; the MLflow wrapper and removed holdout do not affect the submission.

The logistic regression already uses the same nine log-scaled metadata features at close to unregularized fit. A 50/50 probability blend with a metadata-only CatBoost (standalone AUC around 0.60-0.62, highly correlated with the linear metadata part, with similar or larger probability spread) mostly doubles the metadata weight relative to text. Any gain from nonlinearity or interactions is roughly cancelled by that reweighting, so I expect a change near zero with a slight downward lean, within about ±0.01 of test noise.

Keeping the 5000-feature cap means bigrams mainly replace rare df≈3-5 unigrams with frequent phrases that largely repeat their unigrams (e.g. 'pay forward', 'imgur com'); text is a weak signal next to the numeric features, so expect roughly no change, maybe slightly positive. The diff also adds unrequested mlflow telemetry and drops the holdout check; neither changes the test predictions unless tracking hangs.

Function words and function-word bigrams ('of the', 'upon the', 'my father') are classic authorship signals. The char_wb view keeps the unigram function words, but word-crossing bigrams are lost outright, and short sentences can end up with a sparse or empty word view. I expect a modest regression (~+0.01 log loss) rather than a gain from the lower dimensionality.

The diff implements the proposal correctly with no leakage or ordering bugs. Multinomial NB on word and char counts is strongly complementary to L2-regularized TF-IDF logistic regression on this authorship data, because it leans harder on rare names and phrases. A log-probability meta-logistic-regression can temper NB's overconfidence, including the mostly saturated NB-char votes, so I expect about 0.03 of CV gain. Replacing the full-data refit with fold-averaged test predictions should cost roughly 0.005, leaving the net test log loss near 0.33.

Function words are a strong authorship signal. Word bigrams like 'upon the' or 'of the' are the pipeline's only cross-word features, because char_wb n-grams stop at word boundaries. Dropping stop words weakens both word-level base models (and leaves short sentences nearly empty) while their content words become more redundant with the char models. The char models and the stop-word-ratio meta-feature keep function-word unigram information, so the stacked log loss should degrade moderately rather than collapse.

A linear LR stacker on raw, standardized probabilities cannot use the near-0/1 NB outputs beyond their votes, which LightGBM's rank binning exploits. It also misses LightGBM's length-by-confidence interactions and exposes heavy-tailed meta-features linearly. That means worse log loss, likely around 0.31–0.33 versus 0.2986.

Punctuation reaches the model only through the char block, since the default word token pattern already ignores it and the word bigrams stay identical. Stripping it discards real, test-consistent style signal (semicolon-heavy Shelley, Poe's quoted dialogue, comma and colon patterns and their contexts), and the slight regularization relief from a smaller char vocabulary won't offset that, so log loss should worsen by about 0.02-0.03.

Moving from an underfit C=1 logistic regression to C=10 base models should help on its own. Char LR is likely around 0.40 and word LR around 0.46. Temperature-scaled word NB adds rare-word evidence the LR under-uses, and char NB acts as a near-hard vote. A log-prob LR meta-learner on these 4 base models typically lands around 0.33–0.36 on Spooky, and the run should fit comfortably within the time budget.

Keeping only the top 10k of about 130k columns by chi2 cuts rare author-specific n-grams and many weakly skewed char n-grams that still help L2-regularized LR at C=1, so the LR component should get a few percent worse; the unchanged NB branch already carries the rare-word evidence, and the reweighted blend should absorb most of the loss, leaving a small regression.

Function words are strong authorship signals here, and sklearn's 318-word list also removes discriminative words such as 'upon', 'seemed', 'one', 'my', 'thus', 'however' and 'indeed'; the NB component loses them entirely, while the LR component keeps unigram function-word information through char_wb but loses cross-word function-word bigrams such as 'upon the', 'it is' and 'of my'; so the blend should get moderately worse, with a partial offset from NB being less overconfident.

C=1 underfits the two stacked L2-normalized TF-IDF blocks and gives underconfident probabilities, so 5-fold CV should pick C≈10 (possibly 30), which typically cuts log loss about 8-14%; the explicit per-C fold loop is valid and should finish in a few minutes, so I expect roughly 0.38-0.39.
