The stack should run cleanly in about 3-5 minutes and beat the single LR: the baseline is an underfit C=1 LR at 0.432; C=10 word and char LR fits plus NB on word and char counts give diverse, partly overconfident predictions, and LightGBM can recalibrate and combine them with weak stylometric features. SRK-style NB-plus-meta stacks reached roughly 0.30-0.33, but char_wb 2-5 capped at 60k features makes a weaker char NB and there are no SVD features, so I expect about 0.33-0.36.

The char analyzer adds moderately frequent cross-word n-grams that carry author-specific signal (punctuation plus conjunction, phrases like 'I was' and '; and', case cues) which the word and char_wb blocks miss, but at fixed C=1 roughly 1.5x more nonzeros per row, plus the rare uncapped n-grams, dilute the char block and reduce confidence, so I expect only a modest net gain.

The C=1 TF-IDF LR is underconfident and the word-count MultinomialNB (about 84% accurate) is overconfident; their errors partly differ because the LR also sees char/punctuation n-grams. An arithmetic blend with OOF-tuned weight and alpha should sharpen the many confident-correct cases, while each confident NB error only costs about -log(w), so log loss should fall from about 0.43 to about 0.37-0.39.

The model is already overfit and overconfident (0.607 log loss), and the test set follows the natural 40/29/31 class split. Oversampling shifts the model's prior toward HPL and MWS, so its probabilities no longer match that split. The duplicates also add about 20% more updates concentrated on minority rows, which sharpens predictions further. Both effects slightly worsen log loss, with some run-to-run noise from multithreaded training.

ComplementNB (alpha=0.1) on the same TF-IDF matrix is probably weaker alone (~0.45–0.55) but weights rare, author-specific tokens differently from L2-regularized LR; an OOF-tuned convex blend (likely w≈0.7–0.9) should shave a few percent off log loss, and falls back to the LR-only 0.355 if NB doesn't help. Runtime rises only ~4 LR-fit-times, so it should stay under the kill limit.

Multinomial NB on L2-normalized stacked word+char TF-IDF cannot learn per-feature weights the way LR can. It double-counts correlated char n-grams, and tuning alpha shifts smoothing and class bias rather than acting as a clean temperature control, so it lands around the spooky NB norm (~0.40-0.45), clearly worse than the C-tuned LR's 0.355.

Dropping the char_wb features removes punctuation, 'I'/'a' and subword/rare-word style signal, which matters a lot for authorship; word-only NB-SVM on spooky typically lands around 0.43-0.46, versus about 0.41 with word+char.

ComplementNB (alpha=1, no class prior) on l2-normalized TF-IDF rows spreads its evidence thinly: TF-IDF values of about 0.05–0.2, pooling two classes per complement, and heavy alpha=1 smoothing of rare features make its margins roughly half those of MNB. That gives a flat, underconfident, slightly EAP-biased softmax (typical sentence probabilities around 0.4–0.6) with a weaker ranking than the NB-SVM's tuned logistic heads. Log loss should land well above 0.41, near or somewhat worse than the known about 0.58 for MNB on word TF-IDF.

C=1 underfits l2-normalized stacked word+char TF-IDF. A log-loss CV over [0.1..31.6] will most likely pick C≈3–10 and cut log loss by about 0.03–0.04. The lbfgs warm-start path over 3 parallel folds (two CV fits) should fit comfortably in the time budget, and the best-effort MLflow additions shouldn't change the predictions.

Multinomial NB at alpha=0.1 on stacked word and char TF-IDF counts the same words many times over, because overlapping char n-grams are treated as independent evidence, which makes its probabilities overconfident, and its generative weights discriminate slightly worse than logistic regression's; low alpha on L2-normalized TF-IDF keeps it from being badly miscalibrated, so expect a moderate regression rather than a collapse (rough range 0.41-0.58).

fastText's word, bigram and subword features should reach about 85-87% accuracy, beating the C=1 TF-IDF LR. But lr=0.5 for 25 epochs with no early stopping or calibration will nearly memorize the ~16K sentences. Its softmax outputs then get very overconfident, with a probability floor of only 1e-5, so confident errors on ambiguous short sentences push log loss above the 0.432 baseline even though accuracy is similar or better.

LR at C=1 on L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF is underconfident because per-feature values are tiny, so 5-fold CV should pick C=4 or 8 (near the top of the grid) and cut log loss by roughly 0.03-0.04. Joblib parallelism should keep the run inside the time limit, and MLflow is best-effort only, so the C change is the only thing that affects the score.

Two things should help: the NB log-ratio weighting boosts distinctive words and char-grams, which is known to work well on short sentence-level text, and moving from C=1 to C=4 relieves the baseline's likely over-regularization; together these should outweigh a small calibration cost from one-vs-rest plus renormalization, giving a moderate gain rather than a large one.

The 14 MaxAbs-scaled dense features are mostly redundant with the char_wb n-grams, which already encode punctuation and word-length patterns. The genuinely new signals are absolute length and uppercase (the TF-IDF lowercases and L2-normalises), but these are weak, and a linear LR can only add them to the logits, not use them to modulate confidence. Expect a tiny gain, with a small risk that length or count outliers produce overconfident errors.

Scaling features by class log-count ratios acts like a per-feature C of r², so C=1 is less regularized on the discriminative n-grams (names, topical words) of this underconfident TF-IDF/C=1 baseline; this sharpens mostly-correct predictions, partly offset by one-vs-rest normalization and in-sample NB weights, for an expected drop to roughly 0.38–0.41.

At C=1, logistic regression on row-normalized TF-IDF for Spooky is already over-regularized and under-confident, with the best log loss usually at C of about 3–10. Dropping to C=0.25 shrinks the test logits to roughly 0.4–0.55 of their current size and costs a little accuracy, so log loss should get clearly worse (about 0.44 → ~0.55–0.61).

At C=1 the NB-LR is already underfit. Dropping the word block removes word bigrams, the only cross-word information since char_wb n-grams stay inside word boundaries, and it roughly halves the kernel mass, which acts like cutting C. Predictions should become less confident, so log loss likely worsens by about 0.04-0.07.

At C=1, plain OvR TF-IDF logistic regression on word+char features is over-regularized and assigns only small weights to author-exclusive names and rare words. The NB ratios partly offset this by amplifying those features. That gain is roughly cancelled by this implementation's smoothing offset, which suppresses mildly positive evidence for HPL and MWS, so removing the weighting probably leaves the score about the same or slightly worse.

Sublinear TF-IDF LR on the stacked word and char blocks is still underfit at C=4, so halving C shrinks the logits of mid-frequency discriminative n-grams (~20-25%) and makes predictions more underconfident, raising log loss by roughly 0.015-0.02; the mlflow telemetry is try/except-guarded and does not change the predictions.

NB log-count-ratio weighting boosts rare, author-specific lexical features, which suits a random sentence split from the same books, so discrimination should improve; one-vs-rest normalization, damping of common stylometric features, and C=4 not being retuned for the scaled features (risk of overconfident errors) offset most of that gain, so I expect a small net improvement.

Stripping sklearn's 318 stop words from both the word and char_wb inputs throws away the function-word signal (upon, the, of, which, I, my, her, though, seemed…), one of the strongest cues for telling these authors apart; content words, names and punctuation still carry a lot, and temperature scaling keeps the model calibrated, so expect a clear but not catastrophic regression of about 0.06–0.11 log loss.

C=1 is already heavily regularized for L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF on ~16k short sentences, so cutting C to 0.25 shrinks logits about 2-2.5x and shifts weight from rare lexical markers (names, distinctive words) to common stylometric n-grams. Scalar temperature can only undo the overall scale, not the direction loss. The needed temperature (~0.2) also sits at or below the 0.25 bound, and dividing logits by T inflates the class-prior bias too, so log loss should worsen by roughly 0.03-0.05.

Switching to the 'char' analyzer adds n-grams that cross word boundaries. These capture punctuation followed by the next word and sequences of function words, including 'I' and 'a', which the word tokenizer drops, so they are useful authorship style cues. Under strong regularization (C=1) this should help a little. The gain is limited because word bigrams already cover much of this, and the 60k feature cap now drops rarer within-word n-grams. Expect a small improvement of about 1-3%.

NB log-ratio scaling boosts frequent author-specific features such as names and 'upon', which helps the underfit C=1 model. That gain is partly offset by three things: one-vs-rest sigmoids plus normalization give worse probabilities than multinomial, alpha=1 smoothing on small TF-IDF sums suppresses the many moderately discriminative word and char features, and the class-size offsets skew which features get kept. Net result is a modest improvement.

L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF logistic regression at C=1 is over-regularized and under-confident on about 17.6k short sentences. Raising C to 4 should sharpen the probabilities and fit more discriminative n-grams, moving close to the usual log-loss optimum (C around 5 to 10) without clear overfitting, for roughly an 8-10% drop in log loss.

LR at C=1 on word+char TF-IDF is regularized heavily enough to be under-confident (mid-frequency words and names are shrunk hard), so the fitted temperature should land around 0.6-0.7 and sharpen predictions. Ranking and accuracy are unchanged, so the gain is only in calibration: roughly 3-6% lower log loss, with a small offset because T is fit on the 90% model but applied to the full refit.

Training on log1p and inverting with expm1 predicts roughly the conditional geometric mean, which sits below the conditional mean, and nothing corrects that bias; it also down-weights the expensive and noisy rides that dominate dollar RMSE, so the model gets slightly worse on valid rows (about 1-2% higher RMSE there), and the unchanged fallback rows (about 2.1 of the RMSE floor) dilute the overall change to roughly -1%.

Four times more rows (about 3.9M after cleaning), with the same 1000-tree, 63-leaf LightGBM, should cut the reducible error on the valid test rows by roughly 1.5–2.5%. The graded RMSE moves less because about 26% of test MSE comes from corrupt-coordinate rows predicted at the mean, which put a fixed floor of about 2.1 under the score. That gives an expected drop of about 4.10 to 4.04–4.06, assuming the run finishes within the time budget.

Airport distances are a known useful feature for this task (JFK flat fares, EWR surcharges, LGA tolls), but a 1M-row LightGBM that already has raw coordinates and haversine distance can mostly isolate airports with one or two splits (e.g. lon > -73.83 for JFK), so the valid-row RMSE gain is modest (about 3.65 to 3.60); it is further diluted by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt rows, which gives a small improvement of about 1%.

Fitting L2 on log1p makes expm1 return roughly the conditional geometric mean, not the mean, so predictions shift downward. That costs about 3% on typical rides and about $2.5 on the wide-spread zero-distance and corrupt-coordinate rows in this noisy, right-skewed test sample. Robustness gains only partly offset this, giving a small net RMSE regression.

The main cost is zero-distance rows (identical pickup and dropoff coordinates, about 1% of valid rows). Their mean fare is near the overall mean, well above short-trip fares, and LightGBM gives distance=0 its own bin, so the unconstrained model predicts them well. The constraint forces them to be pooled with short trips at about $6, adding several dollars of bias. The default 'basic' method also over-constrains subtrees under distance splits, and with 4M i.i.d. rows there is no extrapolation or regularization benefit to offset this. Valid-row RMSE should rise about 1–2%, diluted by the fixed 2.1 floor from corrupt rows, giving about a 1% regression.

The grader's test rows come from the same noisy, right-skewed distribution as training, so the raw squared-error objective is already the RMSE-optimal target. Training on log1p gives back-transformed predictions near the conditional median, which are biased low by a few percent. That loss is concentrated on high-fare and outlier rows, which dominate dollar RMSE. With 3.6M rows there is little variance for the transform to reduce. The invalid-row floor of about 2.1 RMSE is unchanged, so the net effect is a small worsening of about 1%.

This replaces out-of-fold target encoding with in-sample encoding, which leaks the target. For the roughly 5% of rows on rare route keys (about 1.7% singletons), fare_mean together with log_count lets the trees decode each row's own fare: a singleton's encoded value is (y+20·gm)/21, and smoothing does not stop monotone decoding. Unseen test keys (log_count=0, fare_mean=gm) fall outside anything the model saw in training and get treated like singletons with a fare near the global mean. These are high-variance, long or unusual trips, so their errors inflate the MSE. Honest-validation early stopping only partly limits this. The gain from removing the log(0.8) count offset on common keys is negligible.

Fitting on log1p and back-transforming with expm1 predicts roughly the conditional geometric mean rather than the mean, so predictions are biased low. The bias is large for the high-dispersion rows: near-zero-distance trips, out-of-town trips and airport outliers. The bulk of ordinary rides loses about 1-2% to the same bias, and with 900K rows variance stabilisation buys a GBDT little. I expect the valid-row MSE to rise by about 0.2-0.4, diluted by the unchanged ~4.4 MSE floor from the mean-filled corrupt test rows, so the RMSE gets slightly worse, about 4.20-4.23.

The airport distances let the trees isolate JFK flat-rate and Newark-surcharge trips with one split, but raw coordinates already allow partial capture, so I expect valid-row RMSE to drop only from about 3.6 to about 3.5 (MSE reduction of roughly 0.6-0.8), while the ~2.1 floor from corrupt rows stays fixed, giving a total near 4.05.

Main gain: about 30 test rows with passenger_count=0 but valid coordinates stop getting the mean fare (squared error ~90) and get normal model predictions (~15), cutting total MSE by ~0.25. Rows with both endpoints invalid gain little from time features, and valid rows lose slightly from the noisier training data, so RMSE improves modestly from 4.138 to about 4.11.

Four times more training rows with the same features and model should cut error on the valid-coordinate test rows from about 3.62 to about 3.53, but the 1000-tree cap limits the gain and the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows dilutes it; the float32 and parsing changes are neutral, and the run should finish in about 3-6 minutes.

The out-of-fold route and cell target encodings are implemented correctly with no leakage, and they capture tolls, airport flat fares and cross-river routes that the capacity-limited raw-coordinate GBM only partly learns; that likely cuts valid-row RMSE by about 0.07–0.1 (from roughly 3.6), but the fixed ~2.1-RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the gain to about 1–2% overall.

Log-space squared error back-transformed with expm1 predicts roughly the conditional geometric mean or median rather than the mean, so dollar-space RMSE worsens. The valid rows (right-skewed and heavy-tailed) lose about 1% from the Jensen-gap bias. The time-only fallback for the ~2.8% corrupt rows drops from about $11.3 to about $9.3, adding a bit more squared error. No capacity or robustness gain offsets this at 1M rows.

Bearing and absolute-delta/Manhattan features give the trees direction information they can't easily build from raw coordinates (grid orientation versus straight-line route ratio, slow crosstown trips), so valid-row MSE should drop by roughly 0.3–0.5 $², taking valid-row RMSE from about 3.6 to about 3.53; the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the unchanged fallback rows dilutes this to about a 1% overall gain.

Airport and Manhattan landmark distances are the classic high-gain features for this data: they give single-split access to the JFK flat-fare and EWR surcharge regimes, so RMSE on valid rows should fall by roughly 0.08-0.1 (from about 3.58 to 3.49); the fixed ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows, still predicted as the mean fare, dilutes the total gain to about 2%, and raw coordinates already let the trees approximate some of this.

The grader uses RMSE, which rewards predicting the conditional mean, but an L1 objective predicts the conditional median. Taxi fares given these features are right-skewed (traffic, detours, tolls, zero-distance GPS failures, and heavy positive-tail outliers), so median predictions sit systematically about $0.5–0.7 low. That adds roughly 4–7% MSE on the valid rows (valid-row RMSE about 3.58 to about 3.65–3.7). The ~2.1 RMSE floor from mean-filled corrupt rows dilutes the effect, giving an overall RMSE near 4.19 versus 4.104. Runtime stays well within budget.

Fitting on log1p and inverting with expm1 predicts roughly the conditional geometric mean, which sits below the conditional mean that raw-dollar RMSE rewards. That downward bias is largest in noisy, skewed segments such as zero or very short distance rides and airport trips, and it only partly cancels the gain from reduced outlier influence and more additive structure. Valid-row RMSE should rise by about 0.03-0.05, diluted by the unchanged ~2.1 floor from invalid rows, so expect a small regression.

An L1 objective makes the model predict the median fare for each kind of trip, not the mean that RMSE rewards. Taxi fares are right-skewed and sometimes bimodal (traffic time, tolls, airport flat fares plus tolls, zero-distance trips), so the model is biased low. That should add about 0.5–1.0 MSE on the valid rows. The fixed ~2.1-RMSE floor from invalid test rows and RMSE-based early stopping dampen the effect, so I expect roughly a 2% RMSE regression.

LightGBM Huber with alpha=1 clips gradients to ±1 with unit hessian, so predictions move at most lr·alpha = $0.05 per tree from the ~$11.3 start. After 1000 trees, long trips (Newark, suburbs, >$57) stay under-predicted, and JFK trips only just converge. It also targets values near the conditional median rather than the mean on right-skewed, noisy fares. Both effects raise RMSE on the valid rows, while the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows is unchanged.

Fitting log1p and back-transforming with expm1 predicts roughly the geometric mean rather than the arithmetic mean, so it under-predicts the heteroscedastic, heavy-tailed noisy and long rides, and it gives less weight to the high-fare rows that dominate dollar RMSE; the expected bias and misalignment add roughly 0.3–0.6 to the MSE on valid rows, while the invalid-row floor (~2.1) is unchanged, giving a small regression of about 1%.

The graded RMSE is roughly 12.6 MSE from valid rows (about 3.6 RMSE) plus a fixed floor of about 4.4 MSE from corrupt rows. The corrupt-row fallback model is unchanged, so only the valid part can improve. Explicit airport distances and flags make the JFK flat fare, the EWR surcharge and the LGA effects easy for LightGBM to isolate, which raw coordinates only approximate with several box splits. I expect valid-row RMSE to fall by about 0.08–0.12, which dilutes to roughly 4.03–4.07 overall.

Four times more rows helps LightGBM on raw coordinates, mainly by learning airport and toll areas more finely, so the valid-row RMSE should drop from about 3.62 to about 3.53. The constant ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dampens this to a small overall gain, and runtime (~3–5 min) stays within budget.

Averaging five fold models (each trained on 80% of the rows, with a 20% slice for early stopping) mainly cuts variance, so valid-row RMSE should drop about 0.5%. The fixed ~2.1 floor from the 2.8% corrupt rows dilutes this, so the total improves by only about 0.3-0.4%, and runtime stays well under budget.

The diff is correct: the encoding is strictly out-of-fold, cells map positionally, and x_test gets the new column last in the same order as x_all. Its signal mostly overlaps what LightGBM already learns from raw coordinates plus distance on 1M rows. The main gain is on pickup-driven effects such as airport and zero-distance trips. The corrupt test rows (~2.1 RMSE floor from mean-fare predictions) are untouched. So expect only a small improvement.

Snapping coordinates to a 0.01° grid (~0.84×1.1 km) throws away sub-cell position, which LightGBM's quantile bins were resolving to tens of metres, and that loss is irrecoverable. It leaves roughly 0.4 km SD of noise in distance_km (the dominant feature, ~$2–2.5 per km), adding about $0.9 SD of fare error. It also lumps exact zero-distance trips (about 1%, high mean fare) in with short same-cell trips. Together that adds about 0.8–1.1 $² MSE on the valid rows, with no offsetting regularization benefit at 900k rows. The corrupt-row floor of about 2.1 is unchanged, so the total RMSE rises from 4.126 to about 4.24.

L1 fits the conditional median, which sits below the conditional mean for right-skewed fares (tolls, traffic, zero-distance and airport trips, heavy positive noise tails). Because the test set is a noisy random sample, that bias adds about 0.4-0.6 to the valid-row MSE. The 2.8% mean-fallback rows are unaffected, so RMSE rises modestly instead of improving through robustness.

An L1 objective predicts the conditional median rather than the conditional mean. Fares are right-skewed (traffic time, tolls, flat airport fares, zero-distance and GPS outliers), so predictions shift down by roughly $0.3–0.5, with larger gaps in heavy-tailed regions. The test set contains the same outliers and is scored by RMSE, so this adds about 0.3–0.6 to the MSE (base MSE ≈ 17.1). The robustness gain against training outliers only partly offsets it, so RMSE likely rises from about 4.14 to about 4.2.

Airport distances make JFK flat fares and EWR surcharge trips reachable with one split instead of multi-split coordinate boxes. That should give a real but modest gain for a 1,000-tree LightGBM that likely hits its tree cap and already has raw coordinates. The fixed ~2.1 floor from mean-predicted corrupt rows and heavy fare noise dilute the gain (the Manhattan-distance addition barely moved the score), so I expect roughly 0.03-0.04 lower RMSE.

The L1 objective predicts the conditional median rather than the RMSE-optimal mean, and fares are right-skewed (traffic time, tolls, zero-distance and noisy rows), so predictions shift downward and add roughly 0.3–0.6 to MSE on valid rows. L1's robustness to outliers offsets only part of that, and the 2.8% fallback rows are unchanged, so expect a small regression of about 1–2%.

Keeping the unrounded haversine distance preserves the main fare signal. Two-decimal cells (~1 km) still identify airports and boroughs. Most of what is lost is Manhattan resolution: LightGBM's quantile bins there are ~0.0005° wide, about 20x finer than the new grid. That detail carries route/direction and congestion information that is worth a little on 1.8M rows. The loss is diluted by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from rows predicted as the mean fare, which this change does not touch, so expect a small regression.

The grader's test rows are drawn from the same noisy training data, so RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean; L1 instead targets the conditional median, which sits systematically lower for right-skewed fares (traffic time, bimodal tolls on airport routes, zero-distance rows, positive fare outliers). That bias adds roughly 0.3-0.7 MSE on the valid rows, only slightly offset by robustness to training outliers, while the invalid-row floor stays the same, giving a small regression of about 1-2%.

A street-grid distance rotated 29 degrees tells the trees how far the route runs along the grid versus diagonally, which they struggle to piece together from raw coordinates and haversine distance alone. That should cut the valid-row MSE by roughly 0.2–0.3, but the unchanged ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the gain to a small overall improvement.

The out-of-fold, smoothed route encoding is implemented correctly with no leakage. It gives the trees a pickup×dropoff interaction the baseline lacks, which partly captures bearing and grid detour, tolls and airport flat fares, so valid-row RMSE should drop roughly 1–2%. The unchanged ~2.1 floor from corrupt rows and the heavy-tailed label noise dilute the gain to about 1% overall.

A distance measured along Manhattan's street grid, rotated 29 degrees, carries direction information that the tree can't easily build from raw coordinates and haversine alone. On the valid rows this should cut RMSE by roughly 0.05-0.08, but the fixed ~2.1 floor from the corrupt test rows dilutes that to about a 1% total gain; the MLflow logging changes don't affect predictions.

Doubling the random-sample training data from 1M to 2M rows should lower the valid-row RMSE by roughly 1-1.5% (about 3.60 to 3.55); the tracking and logging edits do not change predictions. About 4.5 MSE units come from the corrupt test rows and cannot be reduced, so the total RMSE should fall by only about 0.9%, from 4.138 to about 4.10, with some test-sample noise.

An airport-route category lets trees isolate JFK flat-fare and Newark-surcharge trips in one split, a known useful signal, but the model can already find airports from the raw coordinates and the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows is untouched, so expect a modest gain of about 0.05–0.1 on valid rows.

LightGBM should model the per-position f_27 letters better as categoricals, but on this dataset trees must approximate the dominant diagonal tail interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) with axis-aligned staircases, which the existing SwishMLP learns natively; the README notes it is still improving at 3000 trees, and here only 2000 rounds at lr 0.05 are used, with no unique-character feature for either model, so it likely lands slightly below the MLP's 0.9866.

Decile one-hot bins erase within-bin position, which blurs the key tail-threshold sum interactions (f_21+f_02, f_22+f_05, f_00+f_01+f_26 around ±5) that the continuous MLP captured, since roughly half of that signal becomes unrecoverable inside the wide tail bins. Quantile binning also collapses binary f_29 to a single constant bin, dropping it entirely, and merges f_30 values 1 and 2. There is no compensating gain, so AUC should fall by about 1–1.5 points.

After standardization most of the 41 columns are nearly uncorrelated (integer counts, f_29/f_30, per-character ordinals), so their eigenvalues sit near 1 and full-rank PCA whitening becomes an essentially random rotation that ignores the target and does not align with the f_02+f_21-type interaction directions; this scrambles the axis-aligned discrete and nonlinear structure the trees rely on, and linear leaves only recover the linear part, so AUC should fall substantially.

Most f_27 strings are unique (roughly 740k distinct values in 900k rows), so a smoothed, out-of-fold target encoding of the whole string sits at the prior for about 80% of rows and carries almost no signal; the change mostly just deletes the per-character features, which carry a large share of the target signal (per-position effects and a partial proxy for the unique-letter count), so AUC should fall to roughly the level of a numeric-only model, around 0.94-0.955.

The ten per-position characters carry real signal (their letter order behaves like Poisson counts, so the ordinal encoding is not arbitrary), and f_27_nunique only captures part of it. About 740k of the 900k strings are unique, so the full-string encoding is almost always the prior or a very noisy 1–2 sample estimate shrunk by m=20; it can't replace the dropped columns, and AUC should fall well below 0.9915.

These are the known TPS-May-2022 threshold interaction features. Trees can only approximate the diagonal sum-threshold boundaries with many axis-aligned splits, so making them explicit should lift LightGBM from about 0.9915 to about 0.997-0.998 (the public-notebook GBDT range); 3000 trees at lr=0.05 may leave it slightly under-trained, so I expect a bit below 0.998.

A logistic regression on these features probably reaches only about 0.75–0.82 AUC, and its signal is the linear part LightGBM already captures, so an equal-weight rank average mostly adds its large within-class rank noise to the LightGBM ranking. A latent-Gaussian estimate puts the blend around 0.92–0.95, well below the 0.984 single model.

This swaps LightGBM for an MLP with the same 64-64-64-16 SiLU, Adam 0.01, batch-4096, L2 and cosine recipe that got about 0.998 on TPS May 2022. It should model the smooth continuous effects much better than the unconverged GBDT, and the raw sums give it the threshold interactions. But the unique-character count of f_27 is still missing, and a small MLP on per-position ordinals can barely learn that non-additive count. So I expect a clear gain over 0.984 that stays well short of about 0.998.

This SiLU MLP (64-64-64-16, L2 3e-5, Adam 1e-2, batch 4096) closely matches the known strong TPS-May-22 Keras setup and should learn the diagonal interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) that trees only approximate with axis-aligned splits, which should lift it clearly above 0.977; it still lacks the unique-character count of f_27, which an MLP cannot easily build from ordinal codes, and trains for only 60 epochs, so it should land well short of about 0.998, around 0.985-0.99.

Linear leaves on standardized, NaN-free inputs add little cost on this data (720k rows, about 10 path features per leaf), so the run should finish; they should partly capture the oblique f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22 and f_00+f_01+f_26 thresholds and the smooth continuous effects, and should converge faster than the constant-leaf baseline, which is still underfit at 3000 trees; the unique-character structure of f_27 stays unmodeled, so the likely gain is small (about +0.002 AUC), with some risk that noise from the lightly regularized per-leaf fits offsets it.

The count of distinct letters in f_27 is a well-known strong signal in TPS May 2022. Trees cannot easily build it from the 10 ordinal columns, because that needs pairwise equality checks across positions. Giving it directly to an under-converged LightGBM should add roughly +0.005 to +0.015 AUC, and there is essentially no risk of regression.

These three sums are the known TPS-May-22 diagonal interaction boundaries (at about ±5.2), which axis-aligned trees only approximate as a blurry staircase. Raw sums let LightGBM split cleanly at those thresholds and free capacity for other structure, which should give roughly +0.01 AUC. The unique-character feature for f_27 is still missing, which keeps the score well short of the ~0.998 reached with the full feature set.

f_27 has about 740k unique values, most appearing once, so LightGBM's categorical binning (min_data_in_bin=3, cat_smooth, min_child_samples=100) leaves only a few usable bins and the feature does nothing. The change therefore just removes the informative per-position ordinals, and the letter counts plus nunique keep only the position-independent part of that signal, so AUC should drop noticeably.

The adjacent-pair features are a deterministic function of the per-position ordinals, and the f_27 signal (per-character values and the unique-letter count) is already captured, so they add no new information. Declaring them as categoricals with a few hundred levels each lets LightGBM's gradient-sorted category splits win on noise at deep nodes of the 127-leaf trees. That wastes splits the model needs for the unengineered numeric interactions (f_02+f_21 etc.), so I expect a slight regression rather than a gain.

The known interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) mostly fall outside f_00..f_15, and those features are nearly independent, so PCA(8) on them gives near-random dense projections that neither product mining nor PCA can exploit much. Swapping out the gain-screened products (which likely helped slightly, e.g. f_00×f_01) for these roughly neutral oblique features should be a tiny net regression.

Each row's hashed list is [s], i.e. the whole string, so every row gets one pseudo-random bucket out of 64 carrying no target signal; this deletes all f_27 information (per-position letters and the unique-letter proxy), leaving LightGBM on the numeric columns plus noise, which historically lands around 0.93-0.94 AUC.

The error here is mostly approximation error, not noise: the target is near-deterministic and built from additive and diagonal interaction effects. Boosting fits that structure well; fully grown sqrt-feature ExtraTrees behave like adaptive kNN in about 40 dimensions and lose the many moderate additive effects, so AUC should fall from 0.978 to roughly the mid-0.94s, assuming the added 5-fold CV still finishes within the time limit.

In TPS-May22 the key interactions are linear-sum thresholds (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26), which a standardized MLP learns directly while GBDT only approximates them with staircases, so the MLP should beat LightGBM by roughly +0.005–0.01 AUC; the gain is limited because neither model gets the unique-character count of f_27, and sklearn's setup (constant lr, at most 40 epochs, early stopping on accuracy) leaves some performance unrealized.

In TPS-May22, the count of distinct characters in f_27 is a well-known strong feature. Trees working from ten per-position categorical columns can only approximate that count additively, so adding it directly (plus the order-invariant letter counts) should close a good share of the 0.023 AUC gap. The unmodelled continuous-sum interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) still cap the score well below about 0.998.

f_27 is almost always unique across rows (about 741k distinct values in 800k training rows), so the full-string count is 1 for about 85% of rows and carries little signal. Dropping the ten per-position letter features removes most of the f_27 information the trees used, including their partial approximation of the strongly predictive unique-character count, so ROC AUC should fall by about 0.015 to 0.03.

In TPS-May22 the unique-character count of f_27 is known to be a strongly predictive engineered feature. Trees cannot rebuild it from the 10 per-position ordinals because it depends on pairwise equality across positions, so adding it (plus the per-letter counts, which make it additively learnable) should cut a sizeable part of the ~0.023 AUC gap. The main missing structure that remains is the f_02/f_21, f_05/f_22 and f_00+f_01/f_26 diagonal interactions, so the expected gain is about +0.006 to +0.012 AUC. The runtime increase of roughly 1.5x on features stays within budget.

NUM_COLS=f_00..f_15 mixes 7 continuous and 9 integer features and leaves out f_21/f_22/f_26, so the known sum-threshold interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) are essentially not captured; f_00*f_01 is at best a weak proxy, and the other ~24 redundant products add mild split noise to a 720k-row GBDT, so the result is roughly flat within run noise.

Holdout AUC was still rising at 3000 trees, so best_iter is about 3000 and the refit uses about 3333 trees on 11% more rows. The model is underfit and data-hungry (it has to approximate diagonal and unique-character interactions with axis-aligned splits), so both extra data and extra trees should add a small gain, roughly +0.0005 to +0.001 AUC. The two-stage fit should still run in about 5-9 minutes, so a timeout is unlikely.

The letter codes are roughly ordinal, with frequency falling as the letter rises, and the A/B-only positions are unaffected, so the main effects barely change; with 720k rows and the model still improving at 3000 trees, LightGBM's gradient-sorted categorical splits should capture the collision structure behind the unique-character count a little more efficiently, giving a small gain.

In TPS-May-22 the distinct-character count of f_27 carries real signal. Trees cannot easily rebuild it from 10 per-position ordinal columns because it depends on equality between positions, so they only approximate it through letter rarity. Adding it directly should give a clear gain of about +0.005 to +0.009 AUC, though the two missing f_02+f_21 and f_05+f_22 interactions will still cap the score well below 0.997.

Capping trees at depth 2 (4 leaves) cuts per-round capacity about 30x. The model cannot represent higher-order structure such as f_27's unique-character count, and must build the f_02/f_21 and f_05/f_22 diagonal bands slowly out of rectangular steps. That leaves 3000 rounds at lr 0.05 heavily underfit, even though the sum feature is still captured as a main effect.

A small GBDT (600 trees, 31 leaves, max_bin 63, lr 0.05) without the unique-char or interaction features approximates the key diagonal interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) poorly with axis-aligned splits, which an MLP learns directly; the run finishes well inside the budget but should land around 0.94-0.955, below the MLP's 0.982.

A LightGBM with 600 trees, 31 leaves and lr 0.05 is badly underfit here, since it can only approximate the diagonal feature interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) with axis-aligned staircases; I expect it to land around 0.95 AUC, below the MLP (the implementation also early-stops on logloss rather than AUC, which barely matters because all 600 iterations will likely be used).

Binning all 16 continuous columns into quartiles throws away most of their fine-grained signal. These columns are among the strongest predictors, and the tail-based sum-threshold interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) become mostly unrecoverable, so AUC should drop well below the 0.977 baseline.

Cutting num_leaves from 127 to 7 removes most per-tree capacity. This dataset depends on high-order interactions (diagonal f_02+f_21 and f_05+f_22 boundaries, unique-character structure in f_27). The 127-leaf model was still improving at 3000 trees, so 3000 trees of 7 leaves at lr 0.05 will underfit badly, likely roughly doubling 1-AUC.

TPS May 2022 relies on sharp diagonal interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26). Trees with 4 leaves only approximate these as coarse staircases, and 3000 trees at lr 0.05 (about 9k splits in total, versus about 380k) will stay badly underfit, so AUC should drop well below 0.9915 while main effects keep it around 0.97+.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known TPS-May-22 hidden interactions, with a step at about |sum|=5. That boundary is an oblique 3-D plane, which axis-aligned splits approximate poorly, so exposing the exact sum should recover roughly a third to half of the ~0.006 AUC gap that the full interaction set closes. The other two interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22) are still missing, so the gain is a solid but partial improvement.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the known TPS-May-22 threshold interactions (step near ±5); trees approximate the 3-D diagonal boundary poorly, so the explicit sum lets them split once and should add about 0.001–0.002 AUC. The gain is modest because the dominant missing signal (unique-character count in f_27) is still absent.

On TPS-May-2022 an MLP can learn the diagonal linear-threshold interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) that trees only approximate with staircases, and the ~51k-param net on 720k rows should finish most or all of its 50 epochs inside the 420 s CPU budget; it still lacks the unique-character count and explicit interaction features, and a single under-tuned run at lr 1e-3 should land around 0.985–0.993 rather than the ~0.998 of fully feature-engineered NNs.

Positions 0, 2 and 5 hold only two letters, so their splits don't change. On the other seven positions (about 15–20 letters each), LightGBM's many-vs-many category splits can group non-adjacent letters, which may capture a bit more of the letter-coincidence (unique-character) interaction that ordinal thresholds miss. That gain is partly offset by noisier letter orderings at deep nodes with 127 leaves and by the cat_l2 shrinkage, so I expect a small net change, most likely a slight improvement.

In TPS May 2022 the count of distinct characters in f_27 is a known strong driver of the target, and trees cannot build it from 10 ordinal columns because that needs pairwise equality checks, so this is new signal and should recover a large share of the remaining AUC gap (the diagonal interaction features that reach about 0.998 are still missing).

The scoring metric is unweighted pixel RMSE, so darkness-weighting the loss pulls uncertain edge and stain pixels darker and fattens strokes. It also moves capacity away from the roughly 88% background pixels. Plain MSE already concentrates gradient where errors are large, so the 'dilution' fix buys little, and I expect a mild regression of a few percent.

A time-budgeted cosine run of about 330 s should give roughly 10-20x the original 2000 steps; that undertrained ~470k-param U-Net should keep refining text-edge reconstruction, and because test shares fonts and noise types with train, overfitting risk is low, so I expect a solid but diminishing-returns RMSE drop of about 15-20%.

The metric is RMSE and the targets are strongly bimodal (white paper, dark text). L1 trains toward the conditional median and gives small residuals as much weight as large ones, so it gives up some accuracy on the few large-residual pixels (stroke edges, text under stains) that dominate RMSE; with sigmoid plus Adam, MSE is already the metric-aligned objective, so any optimisation or saturation benefit from L1 is likely too small to offset this, and a mild regression within seed noise is the most probable outcome.

Train and test share the same synthetic noise backgrounds and gray-level statistics, and the 2000-step run shows little overfitting, so the extra regularization buys nothing; jittering only the noisy input removes a useful absolute-intensity cue, blurs stain-versus-faded-ink cases and slows convergence under a fixed step budget, though the large receptive field limits the damage to a moderate regression.

The 0.75x and 1.25x passes each resize the image and then resize back. Bilinear plus antialias low-passes the thin, dense, near-binary text strokes on a pure-white background. That roughly doubles the blur, from about 0.3 to 0.6 px² of variance, and gives per-scale round-trip errors of roughly 0.03–0.05 RMSE. Those errors are systematic edge-contrast loss with the same sign in both passes, so averaging cannot cancel them. Even at one-third weight they swamp the 0.0154 native-scale error, and decorrelating the model errors gains almost nothing. Expect a clear regression to about 0.025–0.03.

I expect a small regression. The model is small (~0.47M params, not 1.9M) and gets only 2000 steps on random crops, so it is more likely underfit than overfit. Train and test share the same synthetic noise types, so memorising stains is not penalised. Channel dropout before BatchNorm also creates a train/eval variance mismatch that blurs precise pixel outputs, so it should slow fitting and add error rather than help.

Dropout2d in every block will most likely hurt. This is precise pixel regression at about 41 dB, and test pages reuse the train noise templates and fonts, so memorizing them helps rather than hurts. Channel dropout also feeds the next block's BatchNorm, so running statistics gathered in train mode no longer match the eval-mode network. It slows convergence within the fixed 180 s budget as well, so expect a moderate rise in RMSE rather than a gain.

A 4th U-Net level roughly doubles the receptive field (~41 to ~89 px) and adds low-resolution capacity, which should help separate folds, speckle and stains from text strokes. The run is already heavily trained (likely tens of thousands of steps over about 105 images), so about 20-25% fewer steps should cost little. The remaining error is probably dominated by local text-edge reconstruction, which extra depth helps only indirectly, so I expect a modest gain rather than a large one.

A robust 23x23 median background channel gives the U-Net a direct estimate of the stain or background level under text, so it can compute x-bg more easily and converge faster within 2000 steps. The net already sees about 48 px of context and can approximate the background with max-pooling, and most of the remaining error is at antialiased text edges, so I expect only a modest gain of a few percent, comparable to run-to-run noise.

The 5-level U-Net grows the receptive field from about 44 px to about 200 px, which gives better background and stain context. The repeated noise patterns in this dataset make that extra context exploitable. Full-res capacity is unchanged, pixels per step stay equal, and the model trains easily within budget, so a moderate gain is likely. The 8-crop BatchNorm batches, noisier gradients and the crop-to-full-image shift cap the upside and leave some risk of a small regression.

The model was trained with random h/v flips, so flipped inputs are in-distribution, and averaging four orientations mainly reduces the model's orientation-specific variance at text edges and stains (eval-mode BN, so batching has no effect). Systematic errors such as background bias near 1.0 and ambiguous stains remain, so I expect a small but reliable gain of about 2-4% RMSE, not a large one.

On a modern GPU the baseline's 2000 steps likely take only about 30-80 s, so a 360 s budget gives roughly 5-15x more optimizer steps under the same cosine schedule; the small U-Net is clearly undertrained and the test split is in-distribution with little overfitting risk, so RMSE should fall substantially, with diminishing returns.

Charbonnier aims at the conditional median rather than the RMSE-optimal mean. Most remaining error sits on sparse, ambiguous text-edge and stain pixels with skewed distributions near the white point mass, so the short 2000-step run will probably lose slightly more there than it gains from crisper backgrounds, a small regression within seed noise.

The test noise likely uses the same background types as train, and 2000 steps leaves the small U-Net underfit, so there is little overfitting for this to fix; meanwhile sigma=0.05 input-only noise (about 3x the current RMSE) creates a train/test mismatch that makes the net over-smooth anti-aliased text edges and faint stroke tails, which dominate the error, and also slows convergence.

BatchNorm in eval mode with 32x128x128 batches already applies a fixed, size-independent transform, so there is little mismatch to fix; GroupNorm adds its own crop-versus-full-page statistics mismatch and usually optimizes slightly worse than BN at batch 32, partly offset by benign scale invariance and global context, so expect roughly neutral to a slight regression.

The 0.84-weighted SSIM term moves training away from the RMSE metric: it heavily rewards flat backgrounds (scaled by 1/C2) and contrast preservation, and the median-seeking L1 term makes ambiguous text-edge pixels in stained regions commit instead of hedging toward the mean, which raises squared error. The stronger push to saturate white backgrounds to exactly 1.0 recovers only about 2-3%, and computing SSIM in bf16 inside autocast is a further downside risk, so I expect a small net regression.

Training is unchanged, so the effect comes only from inference. The four flip views are in-distribution because the model was trained with h/v flips, so averaging them should cut RMSE by about 1.5-2.5%. The four rot90/transpose views put text lines vertical, which the model never saw, so they are probably 5-20% worse and partly correlated with the upright errors. Equal 50/50 weighting of good and somewhat-worse views lands near break-even, with a small expected gain and a fatter downside tail.

Pure SSIM no longer optimizes the pixel-RMSE metric: it down-weights luminance errors near white, normalizes errors in high-variance text windows and gives sharper, less hedged edges than the MSE-optimal mean, and its variance terms are noisy when run under bf16 autocast. The background still likely saturates to 1.0, so I expect a moderate regression rather than a collapse.

The clean targets are near-binary (pure-white background, dark text) while the noise is complex stains and texture, so predicting the residual adds no useful structure. It drops the sigmoid's saturation, which lets the baseline produce an exact 1.0 for the roughly 85% background pixels, and instead forces the network to cancel the input's background texture precisely. The leftover cancellation error and BN train/eval noise are only half removed by the inference clamp, so a small regression is likelier than a gain, though the effect is modest and close to seed noise.

The SSIM term mostly pushes for flat backgrounds, which are already near-saturated, and stays weak on the text edges that dominate RMSE, so it mainly misaligns the loss from the metric. The sqrt(MSE) switch barely matters under Adam. As specified, SSIM sits inside the bf16 autocast block, so its convs run in bf16 and the near-white variance estimates (C2=9e-4, below the bf16 step) become noisy or spiky. Expect neutral to slightly worse RMSE.

The clean targets are nearly binary (pure-white background), so the sigmoid saturating to exactly 1.0 already handles the ~88% background pixels well. A linear residual head has to cancel the noise texture pixel by pixel, wasting capacity on overshoot errors that the inference clamp would remove anyway. The identity path may help a little on text grey levels, so I expect a small regression overall.

About 630 synthetic pairs against 105 real ones means roughly 86% of the fixed 2000-step budget goes to mismatched noise, including whole-image Gaussian blur of the text that turns training into a deblurring task. The real wrinkle, fold and coffee-stain backgrounds are already covered by the training set, so the dilution and the higher-loss synthetic gradients should hurt fitting to the real distribution more than the extra diversity helps.

At 2k steps the ~470K-param U-Net is still undertrained. Moving to 9k steps with the stretched cosine schedule should keep the runtime well under budget, since the small net trains on 128px crops on GPU. Random crops, flips and backgrounds shared between train and test limit the overfitting risk. Edge and stain errors should shrink by a moderate ~15-20% before the model's limited capacity and ~50px receptive field cap the gains.

Averaging over the four flip views, which the model saw in training, reduces variance in this small, undertrained U-Net; the four transposed views are out of distribution but probably only slightly worse for a local denoising task, so the 8-way average should still give a modest gain of about 3-5%.

The targets are near-binary (pure-white background, dark anti-aliased strokes) and the metric is RMSE. L1 fits the conditional median rather than the mean, which snaps uncertain stroke and edge pixels toward an extreme. It also stops emphasising the large residuals that dominate RMSE, so it should cost slightly more on edges than it gains by pushing the saturated background closer to 1.

Weighting the loss by the target pulls the optimum to the weighted conditional mean, biasing ambiguous edge and faint-stroke pixels darker; it also slightly down-weights the dominant white background, a mismatch with symmetric RMSE that dark pixels (plentiful in the data) won't offset, so expect a small regression.

Weighting by target intensity pulls predictions darker wherever ink and background are ambiguous (stain edges, anti-aliased stroke borders); that bias is largest on the near-white pixels that dominate the plain RMSE metric, so a well-converged uniform-MSE baseline should lose a moderate amount.

Predicting a correction is likely a small net gain: the network gets the exact input for free (good for edges and faint fringes), and the linear MSE gives full gradients on large errors. This is partly offset by losing sigmoid saturation on the ~88% pure-white background, which must now be cancelled precisely under BN/bf16 (the inference clamp halves that cost), so the result is close to neutral with a mild improvement.

With a sigmoid output and mostly pure-white targets, L1 avoids MSE's quadratically vanishing gradient near saturation (it behaves like BCE there), so background and faint stain residue get pushed closer to exactly 1.0. Much CNN restoration work also finds L1 matches or beats L2 even on PSNR/RMSE; this is partly offset by weaker pressure on the few large edge or stain errors that dominate RMSE, so I expect a small net gain.

On this dataset noisy text is close to the clean text, so the identity prior keeps text intensities with no logit to approximate. The linear output also avoids sigmoid+MSE gradient decay near 0 and 1, and inference clipping plus flip averaging remove background overshoot. Against that, the net must now cancel large structured background texture precisely rather than just saturating to white. Net effect is roughly neutral to a slight gain.

Halving the width cuts parameters about 4x (~620k to ~155k). The test set reuses the same noise backgrounds and text styles as train, so capacity matters more than regularization, and at a fixed 2000 steps the narrower net should land roughly 0.7-1.2 dB worse in PSNR, a moderate regression rather than a gain.

Target-dependent weights shift the loss optimum from the conditional mean by about -2σ²/(3-2μ). This darkens ambiguous edge and stain pixels, and the unweighted RMSE metric penalizes that bias. Capacity also moves toward text at the background's expense, which any faster stroke learning only partly offsets, so I expect a small regression.

A background-normalized channel from a 31px closing is a well-known strong feature for this dataset: it flattens broad stains and the grey paper and normalizes text contrast, which is close to a division the ~41px-RF U-Net struggles to learn in 2000 steps, so expect a moderate gain (wrinkle textures and narrow stain edges remain, and seed noise is about ±3-5%).

Running only the head in fp32 removes bf16 output rounding (about 0.004 steps near white, roughly 0.001 RMS, added in quadrature to a 0.016 RMSE) and the gradient dead zone above logit 6.2. Background pixels contribute almost nothing either way, so the systematic gain is about 0.1–0.3% and the result is dominated by trajectory noise from the changed numerics.

The model was trained with symmetric h/v flip augmentation, so averaging the four flip views is in-distribution and reduces view-specific error variance (Jensen), mainly at text edges and stains; flip-view errors are highly correlated, so expect only a small ~2-3% RMSE gain, with training otherwise unchanged apart from GPU nondeterminism noise.

This NAFNet uses about 5x less compute per pixel than the baseline, with only width-16 single blocks at full resolution. It also outputs a residual with no sigmoid on near-binary targets, and its global-pool attention is trained on 128px patches but run on full pages. Those costs should slightly outweigh its gains from a larger receptive field and multiplicative gating, giving a small regression within the 2000-step budget.

The test images are almost certainly in ImageNet-1k train (Stanford Dogs is drawn from ImageNet), so the 1k head was trained on them. That head was fit on about 1300 images per class, against the LR's 77, and its labels match the competition's. Restricted to the 120 dogs and temperature-tuned, it should be several points more accurate and more confident than the LR. Errors stay correlated because both share the same features, so blending should cut log loss from about 0.31 to about 0.19. This assumes the implementer catches the 'cardigan' collision with the sweater class (474), which the assert would flag.

PCA without whitening only rotates, centres and truncates the features, and L2-regularised logistic regression is unaffected by rotation and centring. So the only real effect is dropping 768 low-variance directions that ridge already shrinks, and those still carry some signal for confusable breed pairs, giving a small regression rather than a gain.

Heavy Mixup/CutMix on every batch (prob 1.0, alpha 0.8/1.0) is a long-schedule from-scratch regularizer: ConvNeXt's own in22k→in1k fine-tune recipe and BiT's rule for datasets under 20k images both turn it off. Here it would dilute only ~775 fine-tuning steps on features that already separate these leaked ImageNet dog classes. Mixup also tends to make models harder to fix with temperature scaling, so I expect a 1–2 point accuracy drop and a modestly worse log loss after calibration.

Under a short 6-epoch fine-tune from strong in22k features, about 29% of crops become very tight (scale <0.35). This replaces informative whole-dog views with noisier part views and widens the train/test object-scale gap against the center-crop eval, so the most likely result is a small regression within noise, not a regularization gain (milder crops like 0.35 usually win on short schedules).

Swapping ResNet-50 (76% ImageNet top-1) for ConvNeXt-V2-L in22k→in1k (87% top-1, 198M params) should raise frozen-feature 120-way dog accuracy from about 87% to about 95%. Stanford Dogs images sit inside ImageNet training data, so the in1k head's log-probs are near-memorized labels and the larger model memorizes much more. LR with holdout-tuned C should land log loss around 0.12–0.18, up to ±0.03 test noise; fp16 GRN and pipeline risks look small.

The 120 breeds are exactly ImageNet dog classes, and these Stanford Dogs images likely overlap ResNet-50's training set. So the dog-class log-probs carry an fc classifier fit on roughly 17x more data, which a 76-per-class linear probe on pooled features can't fully recover. Dropping them should hurt by about 10-25%.

Ridge on ±1 targets should match LR's accuracy on these strong frozen features, but a single global temperature cannot fix the score geometry for 120-class log loss: fine-grained pairs need T near 2/K≈0.017, while the compressed true-vs-bulk gaps, noisy wrong-class scores and outliers need a larger T, so the result is underconfident on confusable breeds and worse than the directly log-loss-optimised LR.

L2-regularised LR with a tuned C already shrinks low-variance directions, so truncating each block to 128 of 768-1024 PCs (near the 119-d between-class rank) mainly loses some fine-grained breed directions; the gains from centring, renormalising and rebalancing blocks (an effective C rescale the grid absorbs, plus giving the anisotropic CLIP block more weight) only partly offset this, so expect a mild log-loss regression.

ConvNeXt-B in22k-ft-in1k is about 10 ImageNet top-1 points stronger than ResNet-50 V1, carries in22k fine-grained dog knowledge, and was trained on these same ImageNet images, so its frozen LN pre-logit features should push linear-probe accuracy from roughly 87% to roughly 94-95%; with the holdout-selected C that roughly halves log loss to about 0.15-0.22, and the run should comfortably fit the time budget.

Fine-tuning ConvNeXt-T (in22k→in1k, a much stronger backbone whose pretraining data already overlaps Stanford Dogs) with sensible LRs, augmentation, flip TTA and temperature scaling should lift accuracy from roughly 86% to roughly 92-94% and comfortably finish in about 2-3 minutes. Label smoothing (only partly undone by temperature scaling) and the 10% holdout give up a little, so log loss lands around 0.22-0.28 rather than the 0.45 baseline.

Stanford Dogs images come from ImageNet and probably overlap its training set, so the 1000-way head's log-probs give near-training-set, precisely fit class directions that a 77-shot logistic regression cannot recover. Standardised stacking lets the regression recover a temperature-scaled 120-way head plus corrections, so I expect a sizable drop from 0.45 rather than a marginal one.

ConvNeXt-B in22k-ft-in1k was supervised on these exact ImageNet dog images, so on its own it should give a log loss of roughly 0.17-0.2 against ResNet-50 V1's 0.45; per-block L2-normalised DINOv2 and CLIP features add modest complementary gains, and the C grid {1, 3, 10, 30} sensibly covers normalised features, so expect about 0.16 (the timm GELU-vs-QuickGELU mismatch in the CLIP tower only slightly weakens that block).

Focal loss with gamma=2 is not a proper scoring rule. It biases predictions toward underconfidence in the 0.9–0.99 range, which is worse than LS-0.1's cap there, and on balanced fine-grained tasks it usually costs about 0.5–1.5% accuracy versus LS. Partly offsetting this, it drops LS's uniform probability floor and keeps more mass on look-alike breeds, so expect a small log-loss regression rather than a gain.

Stanford Dogs images come from ImageNet, so adapting the early layers gains almost nothing, while lr=0.01 everywhere with Nesterov momentum causes some feature drift. Freezing conv1 through layer3 removes that drift, but those layers move little anyway and layer4, where most of the change happens, still trains at the aggressive LR. I expect a small gain of about 1 accuracy point, roughly the size of run-to-run noise.

Averaging the probabilities of an image and its mirror never raises per-sample log loss above the mean of the two views (Jensen), and a mirrored dog photo is as in-distribution as the original. The flip-trained ViT's mirror features disagree only modestly, so expect the typical small 2-4% log-loss reduction from flip TTA, give or take about ±0.005 of test-set noise.

The current ViT-B/16 was trained on ImageNet-21k and then ImageNet-1k, which contain these exact 120 dog breeds and likely many of the same Stanford Dogs/ImageNet images. CLIP ViT-B/32 gets no such label or taxonomy advantage, and its coarse 7x7 patch grid weakens fine-grained detail (it trails CLIP B/16 and ImageNet-supervised models on Pets and Birdsnap linear probes). I expect breed accuracy to drop from roughly 88-90% to about 77-81% under the same C=0.3 linear probe, pushing log loss to roughly 0.8-0.95.

Unwhitened PCA only restricts the L2-regularised LR weights to the top-256 PCs (about 65–75% of variance), because centering is absorbed by the unpenalised intercept. ImageNet ResNet-50 features concentrate the dog-breed signal in high-variance directions, so the loss is small, but C=0.3 beating C=0.1 suggests the discarded tail carries some fine-grained signal for confusable pairs, giving a mild log-loss regression rather than a gain.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 CLS features are much more linearly separable on fine-grained pets/dogs than supervised R50 (e.g. Pets linear ~96% vs ~92%). The gain is partly offset because R50 has label-leak on these ImageNet-derived Stanford Dogs images. Expect roughly +3-5 points of accuracy and a ~20-30% lower log loss. This assumes the engineer adds img_size=224 or dynamic_img_size to get around timm's 518 strict-size assert, and the run time fits the budget easily.

C=1 on per-block L2-normalised features (feature variance ~1e-3 to 1e-4 per direction) is heavily over-regularised and underconfident; whitening to unit-variance PCs cuts the effective regularisation by 1-3 orders of magnitude, so predictions become much more confident and log loss should drop, though it overshoots (nearly unregularised in 256-d with about 77 images per class), and overconfident errors plus the truncation keep it above the roughly 0.3 a tuned C could reach.

A 10-NN distance-weighted vote gives sparse, discrete probabilities, which hurts log loss in two ways. First, the 1e-3 uniform mix puts about 10.7% of mass on the other classes, so every sample costs at least about 0.11. Second, the roughly 3-5% of test images whose true breed gets no neighbor votes (atypical photos, confusable breeds, label noise) cost about 7.0 each. kNN accuracy will likely be similar to or slightly below the logistic regression's, so log loss should get clearly worse, to roughly 0.6-0.8.

The 120 Stanford Dogs breeds and many of these exact images are in ImageNet's training set, so frozen ResNet-50 features with a calibrated logistic regression are already near-optimal; full fine-tuning at a fairly high learning rate (SGD lr 0.01, momentum 0.9) for 10 epochs on 9.2k images likely gives similar or slightly lower accuracy through forgetting, and label smoothing 0.1 caps confidence near 0.9, adding about 0.05 to log loss, so expect roughly 0.50-0.60.

Stanford Dogs images overlap ImageNet train and the 120 breeds are ImageNet classes. The in21k-pretrained, in1k-finetuned ViT-B/16 (~84.5% ImageNet top-1, vs 76.1% for ResNet-50 V1) gives much more separable breed features. That should lift linear-probe accuracy from about 86% to about 92-93%, roughly cutting log loss from 0.45 to about 0.25-0.27, with C=0.3 still in a sensible regime for LayerNorm'd 768-d features.

Standard 10-crop TTA on ResNet-50 usually adds about 1% top-1 accuracy, and averaging probabilities mainly helps the confidently wrong, heavy-tail cases; this is partly offset because the LR's C was tuned for center crops, so averaging makes it underconfident, and because the corner crops after aspect-preserving Resize(256) are shifted a lot. Net result: a modest gain of about 3-4%.

The in22k ConvNeXt-T features are much more discriminative than ResNet-50 on these ImageNet-derived dog images, which should lift accuracy into the low 90s. However, C=1.0 on per-block L2-normalised features is roughly 30x or more stronger regularisation than the tuned C=0.3 on raw ResNet features (raw ResNet feature norm is about 30). That leaves typical correct-class probabilities near 0.75-0.85, so underconfidence takes back part of the gain; a well-tuned C would likely reach about 0.25.

Stanford Dogs images come from the ImageNet train set, so the pretrained 1000-way head (restricted to the 120 dog logits, temperature-tuned) is effectively a memorization-backed classifier at least as accurate as the 77-shot LR on the same features. Blending the two with alpha and T picked on a holdout should cut log loss well below 0.309, with no mapping or runtime risk.

Centering plus orthogonal projection is otherwise equivalent for LR with an unpenalised intercept, so the only change is truncating to the top 256 PCs. That is likely mildly lossy: the backbone's breed directions mostly sit in high-variance PCs, but subtle fine-grained cues in the discarded tail are lost, and with C=0.3 already tuned, hard truncation rarely beats L2 shrinkage, so expect a small rise in log loss.

ResNet-50 was trained with average pooling, so global max pooling of its frozen layer4 maps gives noisier features that are less linearly separable, and they no longer match the space where ImageNet already separates these exact dog classes. The max-pooled features are also about 4-5x larger in scale, so C=0.3 becomes much weaker regularization (more overfitting). Temperature scaling only partly corrects that, so I expect a moderate regression of a few accuracy points, with log loss rising from about 0.45 to about 0.6.

The 120 Stanford Dogs breeds are ImageNet classes, and these images were likely in ImageNet's training set, so the stronger V2 recipe (+4.7 top-1 points, plus a FixRes-matched eval transform) should give more linearly separable dog features; label smoothing and mixup typically hurt only out-of-distribution linear transfer, though tighter class clusters and a C value tuned for V1 temper the gain.

C=0.3 was already the best value in the holdout grid, so C=0.03 gives a 120-class head with logits roughly 25-35% too small, which makes it underconfident and raises log loss by about 15-25% from the classifier alone. The fine-tune cannot undo this: at the classifier's optimum the head's training-loss gradient is only -W/(Cn), so with lr 1e-3 over 2 epochs the head scales up by about 1%. Smaller head weights also shrink the conv-driven logit changes, so the bottleneck tuning recovers only a few percent.

Shrinking the crop from 224 to 192 while keeping the same crop ratio makes dogs about 14% smaller in pixels. That pushes further from the apparent object size ResNet50-V1 was trained on (FixRes effect, roughly a 2% ImageNet top-1 drop) and loses fine-grained fur and face detail. The brief last-block fine-tune with frozen BN will barely compensate, so frozen-feature log loss should rise by about 10%.

PCA-256 without whitening is an orthogonal projection, so with the same L2-penalised logistic regression (C=0.3) it amounts to the same model restricted to the top-256 subspace, which should keep most of the roughly 119-dimensional between-breed signal for these in-domain ImageNet dogs; dropping the 1,792 low-variance directions (plus approximation error from randomized SVD) likely removes some fine-grained signal, so I expect a mild log-loss regression rather than a gain.

ResNet-50 was trained at 224 and already sees objects too small at test time, so a 192 crop shrinks objects further and drops fine detail, usually costing about 1.5–2% ImageNet top-1; on fine-grained breeds this means roughly a 8–12% rise in log loss, only partly recovered by refitting the linear probe on the 192 features.

Dog breeds are exact ImageNet classes and are likely in ImageNet's training images, so V2's much higher ImageNet accuracy (80.9 vs 76.1) should carry over to a linear probe, despite the usual transfer penalty from label smoothing and mixup/cutmix; there is some risk from the feature scale changing under the fixed C=0.3, but log loss probably improves.

The final model is unchanged and only its logits are divided by a single temperature. C=0.3 was already tuned for log loss on the same kind of 15% holdout, which largely calibrates the scale, so the fitted T should land near 1 (about 0.9–1.2). That leaves a small gain from finer scale tuning than the coarse C grid allowed, partly lost to transferring T from the 85% model to the full-data model and to noise on a 1,023-image test set.

Two epochs (~288 steps) of SGD at lr 1e-4 on the last bottleneck should only nudge features slightly: the head starts at the calibrated LR optimum, the train loss is already low, and these dog images overlap ImageNet. The likely result is a small first-order gain in breed discrimination with little added overconfidence, so log loss should be roughly unchanged or slightly better.

ResNet-50 was trained with random flips and dog photos are roughly mirror-symmetric, so the flipped view scores about as well alone as the original. Averaging the two views' probabilities then gives a Jensen-style gain on samples where they disagree, typically 1–4% relative log-loss improvement for hflip TTA on a linear probe, at negligible runtime cost.

AUC ignores the intercept, so rebalancing gains little; discarding 80–99.7% of negatives (threat trains on 956 rows) removes hard negatives such as toxic non-threats, toxic non-identity-hate comments and clean identity mentions, and zeroes the NB ratio for unseen features. The rare labels lose roughly 0.01–0.02 AUC each and the common ones about 0.003–0.005, so this is a clear regression.

Adding char_wb features to the NB-LogReg branch likely lifts it by about 0.002–0.003 AUC on its own, but it now shares the same char block with branch A, so the two branches are more correlated and the blend gains less from mixing them. Net effect on the rank-averaged blend is a small gain of roughly +0.0003 to +0.0008, with some downside risk from C=4 overfitting on the rare labels (threat, identity_hate). Runtime should stay within budget if fit_transform is used.

Imbalance barely biases logistic-regression rankings, so 1:1 undersampling mostly just discards 80-99% of negatives, including the toxic-but-not-label-j hard negatives that separate threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic and insult from general toxicity. That raises coefficient variance, weakens both branches and the stacked out-of-fold features, and should cut mean AUC by roughly 0.005-0.008.

MultinomialNB with alpha=1 on fractional TF-IDF over a 200k vocabulary is dominated by smoothing for minority labels, leaving it with a strong length bias and inflated weights on rare words, so alone it likely scores only ~0.91-0.93 mean AUC (rare labels worst); a 50/50 rank average with the ~0.979 branch A, which also loses its stronger NB-LR stack features, should drop the blend by roughly 0.006-0.010.

Unsupervised mean-pooled skip-gram embeddings give up the char n-grams, IDF weighting and keyword precision, and they dilute a single toxic word in a long comment, so the LR and MLP on them should land around 0.95-0.96 test AUC; two such correlated weak branches then take 2/3 of the equal rank-average weight, which pulls the blend below NB-LogReg alone (~0.977) and well below the current 0.9808.

Undersampling only shifts the intercept in expectation, so it cannot help AUC; what it does is throw away 90-99.7% of negatives, including nearly all the hard negatives. For threat, identity_hate and severe_toxic, branches A and B would see only about 45-140 toxic-but-not-this-label comments instead of about 14k. Those columns should lose roughly 0.5-1.2 points each, with toxic, obscene and insult losing roughly 0.3-0.6. The MLP keeps all label-positive rows and degrades less, but it gets about 5x fewer Adam steps, so the blend should still fall by about 0.6-0.7 points.

A shared-hidden-layer sparse MLP on the same TF-IDF features should be a reasonably strong and fairly diverse fourth model; at 1/4 rank weight it likely adds roughly +0.0005 to +0.001. Runtime is the main risk: the A+B+C run plausibly ends near 600 s, so D may get only one or two epochs, or none under the 690 s guard, in which case the score stays 0.98099, so the expected gain is shrunk.

AUC does not depend on the class prior, and LR already balances the positive and negative gradients on its own, so 1:1 undersampling helps nothing. It just throws away 80-99.7% of the negatives. That roughly doubles the variance of the weight estimates. It also leaves the subset labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) with only dozens of hard negatives (toxic comments without that label) to learn from, so profanity gets over-weighted. Expect small drops on toxic, obscene and insult and drops of about 0.01-0.02 on threat and identity_hate, a mean of about -0.007.

Several steps change nothing because TfidfVectorizer already lowercases and char_wb already normalizes whitespace; the rest roughly cancel: de-obfuscation and the u→you mapping help Branch B's bigrams a little, while deleting timestamps (a signed-comment cue), collapsing IPs and URLs, collapsing repeated characters, and turning u/ur/r into stop words that Branch A drops lose small amounts of signal, so the net change is expected near zero with a slight negative lean.

A will lean heavily on B's out-of-fold predictions, because those six features cost almost no regularization at C=0.1 while A's n-gram weights are strongly shrunk, especially for the rare labels. The final 50/50 rank-average with B then counts B twice, giving roughly 25–35% A and 65–75% B, and loses the diversity behind the current +0.0011–0.0016 blend gain. Cross-label gains (mostly threat, identity_hate and severe_toxic) and joint residual fitting are diluted by half in the blend and only partly offset this, so I expect a roughly neutral to slightly negative result.

A 64-unit multi-task MLP on the existing word+char TF-IDF should score about 0.975-0.978 alone, likely a bit below the C=0.1 logistic regression because the MLP is barely regularized and is stopped at 3 epochs without tuning; it sees the same features as branch A, so its errors overlap heavily with A's, and an equal 1/3 rank weight should give only a small gain (roughly -0.0001 to +0.0015). There is some risk the extra ~3-5 min of dense Adam updates pushes the run toward the 15-min kill.

Branch C (NB-LR on B's word 1-2gram block plus A's char_wb block, C=4) is probably individually a bit stronger than B and on par with A, but it overlaps heavily with both. An equal three-way rank average should therefore add only a small diversity gain (~+0.0002-0.0004 AUC). It also shifts weight toward the NB-word style. The extra ~4-6 min of liblinear fits on ~100M nonzeros raises some runtime risk, but the run should most likely finish under the hard kill.

The full-data predictions are identical; only the per-label blend weights change, and shrinkage keeps them in [0.25, 0.75]. AUC is flat near an equal rank blend, so the expected gain is about +0.0001. The 20% holdout has few threat and identity_hate positives, and train-to-test shift may favour the char branch, which could cancel the gain. Runtime grows about 1.5x and may approach the 15-minute kill.

With roughly 160k labeled rows, the sparse linear models are not meaningfully overfitting, so compressing to 300 unsupervised SVD factors and dropping char n-grams discards the discriminative long-tail lexical and bigram signal. Main profanity directions survive, but toxic, insult, threat and identity_hate ranking degrades, giving an expected mean AUC around 0.95-0.96, well below the 0.980 blend.

Only the rare labels lose much data: toxic keeps every row, obscene and insult keep about half their negatives, but threat, severe_toxic and identity_hate keep just 3-11%. Branch A barely moves because its strongly regularized LR (C=0.1) acts almost like a centroid classifier that ignores class ratio. Branches B and F should lose some AUC on rare labels: they get fewer hard negatives, fastText's vocabulary shrinks, and NB smoothing changes. The rank average dilutes this, so the mean AUC should fall slightly.

A single softmax fastText model trained on randomly sampled labels splits probability mass across co-occurring labels, so p(toxic), p(severe_toxic) and p(insult) get diluted for heavily multi-label comments; this makes branch F somewhat worse per label, but F is only one third of the rank average and A+B dominate those pairs, so I expect a small net regression within run noise. The 0.883 baseline is far below the ~0.98 typical for this TF-IDF/NB-LR blend, which points to a quirk in the grader or data rather than in F, so changes to F should be compressed further.

For binary labels ComplementNB ranks documents exactly like plain MultinomialNB minus the prior, so its imbalance fix does nothing here. On raw counts with alpha=1 over 200k features, the rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) are dominated by smoothing, carry a strong length bias, absorb train-spam artifacts and saturate at 1.0, so they should trail the ~0.982 tuned LR/NB-LR rank blend by roughly 3–5 AUC points.

Mean-pooled unsupervised skip-gram vectors with a linear head reduce to an average of per-token scores. Those scores are limited to 200 dimensions, and the setup drops bigrams, char n-grams, IDF and out-of-vocabulary obfuscated spellings. Averaging also dilutes a single insult in a long comment.
