Depth-2 trees (4 leaves) can only represent main effects and pairwise terms. That loses the high-order f_27 unique-character structure and other multi-way interactions this interaction-themed dataset relies on. The full 127-leaf model was still improving at 3000 rounds, so 3000 tiny trees at lr 0.05 will be badly under-fit. AUC should drop by several points even though the sum feature and the f_02/f_21 and f_05/f_22 pairs remain partly learnable.

A 600-tree, 31-leaf, max_bin-63 LightGBM on raw features plus ordinal chars has no unique-character count and no interaction features. It will be heavily underfit, since the README says even 3000x127 is still improving at the last iteration, and it approximates the diagonal f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22 and f_00+f_01+f_26 boundaries poorly. It should land in the GBDT-without-feature-engineering range, around 0.94-0.96, below the 0.982 MLP, which learns the linear interactions directly.

A small LightGBM (600 trees, 31 leaves, lr 0.05, max_bin 63) on raw features plus per-character ordinals is badly undertrained here: the README notes even 3000x127-leaf boosting is still improving. Trees approximate the diagonal f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22 and f_00+f_01+f_26 interactions only with coarse staircases, especially with 63 bins in the tails, while the MLP learns these linear sums directly. Without the unique-character count, I expect the result to land several points of AUC error below the MLP's 0.982.

Reducing the 16 continuous sensors to quartile codes discards within-bin variation: about 14% of a linear effect, much more of any curved effect, and most of the tail-driven sum interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26). Because the near-deterministic target makes AUC very sensitive to extra noise, this roughly doubles or triples the baseline's error, giving a sizable regression to about 0.93–0.95.

The 127-leaf model is still improving at 3000 trees, so it is capacity-limited. With 7 leaves, the same 3000 trees at lr=0.05 have about 20x fewer splits and much shallower interactions per tree. That makes it hard to learn the diagonal f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22 and f_00+f_01+f_26 boundaries and the f_27 unique-character structure, so it underfits badly.

This dataset depends on diagonal 2- and 3-way interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26), and even the 127-leaf model is still improving at 3000 rounds. Capping trees at 3 splits each leaves only about 9k splits over 3000 rounds at lr 0.05, so main effects get fit but the interaction staircases stay coarse. The result should be clear underfitting, landing around 0.97 AUC.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known TPS-May22 threshold interactions; it gives a diagonal 3D boundary that axis-aligned trees only approximate with staircases, and the model is still under-trained at 3000 trees, so supplying the sum directly should close a meaningful share of the roughly 0.005 AUC that all three interactions are worth, around +0.002.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known sharp diagonal interactions in this competition, with thresholds near ±5 that put about 8% of rows in the outer regions; axis-aligned trees can only approximate this 3-way boundary with blurry staircases, so a single explicit sum split should cut boundary errors noticeably, a gain of roughly +0.002 to +0.004 AUC.

In this competition, MLPs beat GBDTs because they learn the oblique sum-threshold interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) directly from scaled inputs; the gain should outweigh the missing unique-character feature (only partly learnable), the roughly 50-epoch CPU budget, and the single unensembled model, landing near 0.993.

Native categorical splits make it easier to isolate individual letters, and the f_27 signal is mostly equality/unique-count based, so the underfit 3000-tree model should gain a little; this helps only the f_27 part, and the continuous interactions it cannot fit stay the bottleneck, so the gain is small with some noise or overfitting risk.

In TPS May 2022 the unique-letter count of f_27 is a strong signal. Trees on ordinal per-position characters can't easily compute it, because it depends on equality checks across positions, so adding it should close much of the gap toward about 0.99 even without the interaction features.

Train and test share one distribution and the same pages, so plain MSE already matches the RMSE metric. Weighting dark targets 5x pulls predictions darker wherever the model is uncertain (stain residue, stroke edges), and that likely costs slightly more than the extra emphasis on strokes gains, giving a small regression within seed noise.

On a GPU, a fixed 330 s budget gives roughly 7–15x more steps than 2000, and a small U-Net denoiser is far from converged at 2000 steps; because the test pages are re-noised copies of the training pages, extra fitting should carry over to test, so I expect about 15–25% lower RMSE, with no timeout risk (~8 min total) and little overfitting risk.

L1 should pull the sigmoid's white background, which is 83% of pixels, closer to exactly 1.0, but it optimizes the conditional median while RMSE rewards the mean: at uncertain stroke borders next to the point mass at white, L1 snaps to 1.0 and down-weights large residuals, so I expect a small net regression within run-to-run noise.

The test scans are i.i.d. re-noisings of the same 36 pages, and the model is limited by the 2000-step budget rather than overfitting. Input-only ±0.1 brightness and 0.8–1.2 contrast jitter widens the training distribution and adds clipping-induced edge ambiguity, so stroke-edge precision likely drops a little, giving a mild regression (seed noise ~±3%).

Training and the model are unchanged; only inference changes. The 0.75x and 1.25x passes are resampled back with bilinear interpolation, which blurs the near-binary, pixel-aligned text edges. That blur error is systematic, so averaging three views does not cancel it the way flip TTA cancels orientation errors. With roughly 0.04 edge-px per pixel and thin strokes, it should add about 0.013–0.016 RMSE in quadrature to the current 0.0154, with little offsetting gain on stains.

The roughly 470k-parameter U-Net has a ~44px receptive field and only 2000 steps to learn a local mapping, and the test pages and noise types are the same ones seen in training, so it is more likely under-trained than overfit. Mid-network Dropout2d (which also degrades the e2 skip) mostly adds gradient noise and a train/eval mismatch with the following BatchNorm layers, so I expect a modest regression in precise pixel regression rather than a gain.

The baseline is not overfitting: test pages are re-noised copies of training pages, so memorizing them helps. Channel dropout in every block, including the skip paths and right before the output conv, therefore only adds training noise and limits the precision of a small U-Net in a fixed 180 s budget. Dropout feeding into BatchNorm also causes a train/test variance shift. Together these should raise pixel-precise RMSE by roughly 15-30%.

Test scans reuse the 36 training pages and the same few noise types, so this is mostly memorization and extra capacity helps. The 4th level adds about 4x parameters and doubles the receptive field cheaply, which should help with large stains and folds. Its cost is concentrated at low resolution, so the roughly 25% fewer steps in the 180 s budget should not offset the gain, giving a modest improvement within ±3-5% run noise.

A full-resolution median background channel is a principled cue for this task: it lets even the shallow layers normalize stains and tint per pixel, which helps text-edge accuracy and convergence within the short 2000-step budget. The U-Net (receptive field about 50 px, with max-pooling that already approximates local background) partly covers this, so I expect a modest gain of roughly 4-8% rather than a large one, with roughly ±3% single-seed noise.

Growing the receptive field from about 50 px to about 230 px gives more context to separate large stains, folds and tint from text and to push background pixels confidently to 1.0. Capacity also rises about 17x for only about 2x the compute, so it fits the budget. The gain should be modest because local cues already handle most pixels, and batch 8 makes BatchNorm and gradients noisier.

The model was trained on all four flip orientations, so averaging those four predictions can only lower the MSE relative to a typical single orientation (Jensen's inequality), but the errors on stroke edges and stain residue are highly correlated across flips, so the gain from this small, briefly trained U-Net should be modest (about 2–4% RMSE) and comparable to run-to-run GPU nondeterminism.

The diff actually defaults TRAIN_SECONDS to 180, not 360. The baseline's 2000 steps of this tiny 470K-param U-Net likely took only ~20-40s on an Ampere-class GPU, so 180s of time-based cosine at the same LR gives roughly 5-10x more steps. Test pages and noise types are both seen in training, so the extra steps should reduce RMSE substantially, with diminishing returns as the small model nears its capacity.

The test metric is RMSE and the clean targets are strongly skewed (83% pure white, sparse ink). Charbonnier fits the conditional median and gives equal weight to the many background pixels with tiny errors, which shifts effort away from the few edge and stain pixels that dominate RMSE. MSE optimizes the metric directly, and Adam already cancels L1's gradient-scale advantage over these short 2000 steps, so I expect a mild regression within seed noise rather than the gains reported in the natural-image literature.

The test set is the same 36 pages under the same structured noise types, so the 2000-step baseline is closer to underfitting than overfitting; always-on sigma=0.05 Gaussian input noise adds little useful regularization, makes the pixel-precise residual task harder, and causes a train/test mismatch (mild edge over-smoothing, shifted BatchNorm statistics) on the text strokes where most remaining error sits, so I expect a mild regression.

In eval mode, BatchNorm with batch-32 crops already behaves almost identically at train and test time, and each output pixel depends only on its local ~40px receptive field, so the proposal's mismatch argument is weak here. GroupNorm with 4 channels per group is close to instance norm and adds a real mismatch of its own: its statistics come from 128x128 crops in training but from whole pages at inference. Patch-trained restoration nets with spatial-statistic normalization are known to lose some accuracy from this, and GroupNorm also tends to converge a little slower than BatchNorm at batch 32 over 2000 steps. Exact invariance to global intensity scaling may help slightly on tinted pages, so I expect a small net regression of a few percent.

Swapping MSE for an SSIM-dominated loss moves the objective away from the RMSE metric: SSIM barely penalizes shifts in local brightness, normalizes errors by local variance (it heavily punishes faint texture in flat white areas but under-weights intensity errors on stroke cores and edges, which dominate RMSE), and L1 favors committing to one value over hedging toward the mean. Cleaner stain removal and L1's push toward pure white may offset part of this, so I expect a modest regression rather than a collapse.

Training only augmented with flips, so the four flip-group TTA views are in-distribution and should help by a few percent. The four rot90/transpose views show vertical text lines and rotated glyphs, noise and folds the model has never seen. They should be noticeably worse (the U-Net is roughly flip-equivariant, so all four share the same out-of-distribution bias), and averaging them at 50% weight with highly correlated errors likely cancels the flip gain and adds a small net regression.

Pure SSIM stops optimizing the graded per-pixel MSE. It weights mean-intensity errors in bright background only about Δ²/2 and down-weights high-contrast stroke edges, which is where most of the baseline's RMSE comes from. It also rewards extra contrast where the target is uncertain. The SSIM convs also run in bf16 under autocast despite the .float() casts, so the E[x²]−μ² variance terms suffer cancellation noise larger than C2 in bright windows, giving erratic SSIM values and gradient spikes. Training should still converge to a usable denoiser with a mostly saturated white background, but with a moderate RMSE regression.

Here the clean target is simpler than the noise: mostly white, and the sigmoid saturates it to exactly 1.0. Predicting the residual forces the net to reproduce absolute background intensity (x-1), but the U-Net applies BatchNorm right after a bias-free first conv, so batch-dependent statistics inject coherent offset noise during training and a small offset at eval. This, plus imperfect cancellation of background texture, should slightly outweigh the gains from a linear head and clamping.

The SSIM term mainly acts as a smoothing penalty in flat background, where most pixels are already saturated at exactly 1.0 by the bf16 sigmoid. That background contributes little RMSE, while text edges, where most of the error is, are dominated by the RMSE term (SSIM gradient there is about 5% as large). SSIM is also computed in bf16 because autocast covers its conv2d calls, so its variance estimates and gradients are noisy. Switching MSE to sqrt(MSE) mostly just raises Adam's effective learning rate. Net effect is about neutral within seed noise, with a slight tilt toward degradation because the loss no longer matches the metric.

The clean targets are nearly binary (83% pure white), so the sigmoid head can saturate background to exactly 1.0, while the residual x+r head must cancel the stain and paper texture pixel by pixel; the clamp at inference only removes overshoot above 1, so small regression errors over most pixels outweigh the likely modest gains at text edges and on confidently-wrong stain pixels, giving a slight regression.

Synthetic pairs are about 86% of sampled crops (630 synthetic vs 105 real), and their whole-image Gaussian blur (sigma 1-4) turns most of the 2000 fixed steps into a hard text-deblurring task. Real noisy scans are sharp and test noise uses the same backgrounds as train, so this dilutes real-noise training (blur-heavy synthetic loss dominates the gradient) and risks the model turning faint wrinkle and stain lines into ink, so RMSE likely rises noticeably.

At 2,000 steps this ~470k-parameter U-Net is still optimization-limited, so 4.5x more steps with the same cosine anneal should keep refining text edges and the stain textures that recur across pages; overfitting risk is low because test pages and noise are re-noised copies of train, and the run should fit the time budget, so I expect a roughly 15-25% RMSE drop rather than a plateau.

Training is unchanged and the TTA inverses are implemented correctly. Averaging over the 4 in-distribution flips should give a small variance reduction (about 2-4%), but the 4 transposed views are out of distribution because the model never saw vertical text lines or transposed noise textures. Those views are probably about 10-20% worse and their errors overlap the hard stain and edge regions, which roughly cancels the gain, so I expect a near-neutral result with a heavier downside tail.

L1 targets the per-pixel median and does not up-weight large residuals, and combined with the sigmoid output it gives little push to confidently wrong pixels such as stain rings, fold lines and faint strokes, which dominate RMSE; it should drive near-white background closer to 1, offsetting part of that, so I expect a mild net regression.

The 3:1 dark-pixel weighting no longer matches the unweighted RMSE metric. It shifts gradient share from the background, which is about 83% of pixels and holds most of the stain error, toward text, and pushes uncertain edge and stain pixels slightly darker. The likely net is a small regression, about the size of run-to-run noise.

Weighting dark targets 10x shifts the optimal prediction away from the conditional mean, toward ink by roughly 10:1 odds wherever the model is unsure. That darkens uncertain near-white pixels like residual stains and stroke halos, which raises the unweighted RMSE the competition scores; the baseline is already well fit after 2000 steps, so extra emphasis on ink buys little to offset this, giving a modest regression.

Zero-initialised residual output plus a clamp at inference keeps exact text detail and removes the one-sided sub-1.0 background error that sigmoid with MSE leaves behind; losing sigmoid saturation and still having to cancel large structured stains offsets much of that gain, so I expect a small improvement close to seed noise.

L1 through a sigmoid keeps pushing the 83% pure-white background toward exactly 1.0, where MSE's gradient fades out, and L1 often matches or beats L2 on PSNR in image restoration. Against that, it gives less weight to the stain and edge tail errors that RMSE punishes, so I expect roughly neutral to a slight gain within seed noise.

The clean target is nearly binary (83% pure white, 5% ink) and much simpler than the stain and tint noise, so a residual output has to cancel that noise pixel by pixel. That loses the sigmoid's free saturation to exact white. Clipping at inference and a linear output on edges recover only part of this, so I expect a small regression rather than the gain residual learning gives on natural images.

Halving NAFNet width (about 640k to 160k params, 8 channels at full resolution) leaves a short, likely capacity- and step-limited 2000-step run with less ability to reconstruct anti-aliased text edges, where most of the error sits. Every test page reuses a training page, so capacity regularization brings little benefit and memorizing the pages actually helps, so expect a moderate regression of roughly 0.5-1 dB.

Weighting the loss by the target pulls uncertain pixels darker and moves training effort away from the residual background-stain removal that unweighted RMSE rewards, though the bias is small at errors this low, so I expect a slight regression (about 1-3%) that sits near run-to-run noise.

Assuming the run finishes (execution.json pins it to 8 CPU threads, which risks timing out), the 31px-closing illumination-normalized channel gives the 44px-receptive-field U-Net a background-divided view, which helps it remove stains and tint and recover edge intensities; the gain is modest because the baseline is already strong and wrinkle and stroke-edge errors are untouched, and it sits near seed-level variance.

The fp32 head by itself would be roughly neutral (about 0.0162), but the applied diff also adds a runtime.toml that the proposal did not ask for: it sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' and 8 threads before torch is imported, so the roughly 700 TFLOPs of fp32 training (2000 steps x 32 patches of 128^2 through the U-Net, forward and backward) runs on 8 CPU threads, needs an estimated 20-60 min, and should be hard-killed at 15 min with no submission; 1.0 is a failure placeholder, not a real RMSE.

The 4-view flip TTA is implemented correctly; by convexity it can only reduce or match error, and it typically trims RMSE by about 2-4% on a flip-augmented, short-trained small U-Net whose errors sit at text edges and stains. The big risk is the added runtime.json: it sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='', which forces fp32 CPU training (about 350 GFLOPs per step x 2000 steps on 13 threads) plus 4x CPU validation inference, so the run could exceed the 15-minute hard kill. This prediction assumes the run completes; if it does, fp32 vs bf16 training should be roughly neutral, giving about 0.0158.

Assuming the run finishes (the new runtime.json forces CPU fp32 at 13 threads, so there is a real risk it exceeds the time limit), this tiny 16-width NAFNet uses about 5x fewer MACs than the 32-channel U-Net, has a thin full-resolution stage for text strokes, uses an unbounded residual output instead of a saturating sigmoid on the 83% pure-white targets, and its channel attention sees 128px patches in training but full pages at test; the larger receptive field, clamping and fp32 recover some of that, so I expect a slightly worse RMSE after the same 2000 steps.

Stanford Dogs images are in ImageNet's training set, so the pretrained ConvNeXt head restricted to the 120 dog classes (trained on about 1300 images per class plus these very images) should be clearly more accurate than an LR fit on 77 images per class, and temperature tuning fixes the label-smoothing calibration; the breed-to-index mapping and the fallback look correct, and w=0 caps the downside, so expect a large but not total drop from 0.31 to about 0.2.

Non-whitened PCA is a rotation plus truncation. The L2 penalty is rotation-invariant and the intercept is unpenalised, so the only real change is dropping 768 low-variance directions. These features come from a network trained on these exact breeds, so most class signal sits in the top 256 PCs and the change should be small. Truncation still removes some fine-grained, look-alike-breed information that the tuned L2 already handled softly, so expect a slight log-loss regression.

Full-strength Mixup/CutMix (prob=1.0) is unlikely to pay off in a 6-epoch (~775-step) fine-tune of a backbone that already knows these ImageNet dog classes: it slows head and backbone adaptation and costs some accuracy, and the official ConvNeXt 22k-to-1k fine-tuning recipe turns mixup/cutmix off; stacked with label smoothing it also compresses confidence in a way temperature scaling only partly recovers, so log loss likely worsens modestly, though the 1k-image test set is noisy enough that a small improvement is possible.

Over only 6 epochs of fine-tuning, a ~29% share of crops under 35% area, often fur or background, dilutes the full-dog views that match the 256/224 center-crop test, and widens the train/test object-size mismatch (~1.36x vs ~1.10x); with label smoothing and drop path already regularizing a strong in22k backbone, expect a small regression within noise rather than a gain.

ConvNeXt-V2-L (IN-22k to IN-1k, 87.3% top-1) has very likely trained on these Stanford Dogs/ImageNet images, so its pre-logits and logprobs should be far more discriminative than ResNet-50's (roughly 95% vs 87% accuracy), cutting log loss from about 0.45 to about 0.15; fp16, download and runtime risks look small.

The 120 dog-breed ImageNet log-probs come from an fc head trained on about 1300 images per class, and Stanford Dogs is heavily contained in ImageNet training, so that head is already a strong classifier on these exact images. An LR fitted on 77 images per class cannot recover it under L2, so dropping that block should lose a few points of accuracy and raise log loss by roughly 0.08–0.12.

Ridge regression on 120 one-hot targets compresses score gaps within groups of similar breeds, saturates gaps between groups, and scales scores with class size (58-118 images per class). One softmax temperature cannot calibrate all three at once, so accuracy may hold roughly steady while log loss gets clearly worse than the logistic regression that optimises it directly.

Truncating each block to 128 PCs likely drops some low-variance directions that separate look-alike breeds, and re-normalising after centering removes some confidence information, which mildly hurts log loss; the rescaling it implies may partly offset this if the parent was pinned at C=30, so I expect a small regression.

Swapping to an in22k-pretrained ConvNeXt-B (85.8% ImageNet top-1 vs 76.1%) should cut error on these ImageNet-overlapping dog classes from about 14% to 7-8%, because its frozen features are much more breed-discriminative and it has likely memorised these images more strongly. The holdout C grid should cover the optimum, so log loss should drop from 0.45 to roughly 0.2, with runtime well inside budget.

Fully fine-tuning an ImageNet-22k ConvNeXt-T should complete all 6 epochs well inside the 7-minute guard on a modern GPU. That backbone is far stronger than a frozen ResNet-50 V1, and its pretraining has already seen these Stanford Dogs/ImageNet images. Flip test-time averaging and temperature scaling on the validation split largely undo label smoothing's underconfidence. Expected accuracy is about 91-93%, giving a log loss near 0.25-0.30 (vs 0.45). Holding out 10% of the data and keeping label smoothing cost a little.

These images come from ImageNet, so ResNet-50's head was likely trained on them, labels included. Its standardized log-probs give the LR a well-estimated breed direction, which should help most on look-alike pairs and memorized noisy labels. The logits are almost linear in the pooled features and the C grid regularizes fairly hard, so I expect a moderate gain (~0.45 to ~0.36), not a collapse to ~0.1.

ConvNeXt-B (IN-22k, then IN-1k) is a much stronger backbone than ResNet-50 and was trained on these very ImageNet dog images and labels, so it carries a large leakage benefit; DINOv2-B and CLIP-B/16 add complementary features, and per-block L2 normalisation with C tuned on a holdout should keep calibration good. Expected accuracy is roughly 94-95%, giving a log loss of about 0.19, down from 0.45; the code looks correct and should fit in the time budget.

Focal loss probably won't sharpen breed discrimination or raise accuracy much, but it drops label smoothing's 0.9 confidence cap and uniform non-target mass, so look-alike breeds keep more probability on errors. That modestly helps log loss, partly offset by focal loss's improper, underconfident bias on moderately easy examples, so the net is a small, noisy gain.

These images come from ImageNet, so pretrained features already separate them well and full fine-tuning at an effective step of 0.1 (lr 0.01, momentum 0.9) likely erodes that; freezing conv1–layer3 keeps the mid-level features intact and should modestly cut test log loss, but layer4 still carries most of the drift and label smoothing caps confidence, so the gain stays small.

Hflip TTA on frozen ViT features with the same LR head can only help, since averaging probabilities is never worse than the mean of the two views' losses and the mirrored view is as in-distribution as the original. The gain comes mostly from softening confident errors on hard look-alike breeds, typically a 2–3% relative drop in log loss. NUM_WORKERS=0 only slows loading and leaves the features unchanged.

CLIP ViT-B/32 is a weaker probe backbone here than the current ViT-B/16 (ImageNet-21k pretrained, ImageNet-1k fine-tuned): its ImageNet linear probe is about 76% vs about 84%, and its coarse 7x7 patch grid hurts fine-grained breed cues. It also lacks the current model's training on these exact 120 ImageNet dog classes and images, and timm's non-QuickGELU variant slightly distorts the weights. Expect roughly 76-80% probe accuracy and a log loss near 0.8.

Unwhitened PCA only rotates and truncates, so this is the same L2-regularized LR (C was tuned for the full 2048-d features) but restricted to the top-256 variance subspace; the low-variance, low-within-class-noise directions it drops are the ones most useful for look-alike breed pairs, so expect a small accuracy loss and a mild log-loss regression rather than a denoising gain.

DINOv2 ViT-B/14 features are generally much stronger than ResNet-50's, but Stanford Dogs images come from ImageNet. The supervised ResNet-50 has effectively already seen these test images with their labels, while label-free DINOv2 has not. Its CLS-token linear probe at 224px should land near or a little above the baseline's roughly 86% accuracy, so expect a small, uncertain log-loss gain.

C=1 on L2-normalized concat features is very strongly regularized (roughly 200x stronger than the tuned C=0.3 on raw ResNet), so the current model is likely underconfident; whitening to 256 unit-variance PCs makes the same C=1 far weaker (logit-variance penalty), sharpening correct predictions a lot, but it also lets the model fit noise in the amplified mid-variance directions, so errors get more confident and part of the gain is lost: net moderate improvement, with real regression risk.

LR at C=1 on per-block L2-normalised features is probably heavily over-regularised and underconfident, so 0.54 likely hides about 90% accuracy. A 10-NN head on these supervised, ImageNet-seen dog features should be nearly as accurate. Pure neighbourhoods give about 0.11 loss each, versus about 0.4 for the soft LR, which should outweigh the roughly 2–3% of zero-hit test images that each cost about 7.0 under the 1e-3 floor. The net is a modest gain, but it is very sensitive to the zero-hit rate.

Stanford Dogs is a subset of ImageNet, so frozen ResNet-50 features with a tuned logistic regression are already close to optimal. A short, untuned full fine-tune (lr 0.01, random head) gains little accuracy and risks some feature drift. Label smoothing at 0.1 also caps confident predictions near 0.9, adding roughly 0.1 nats on the many easy test images, so log loss likely gets somewhat worse.

Frozen ViT-B/16 (in21k pretrain, then in1k fine-tune, about 84.5% in1k top-1) gives much more discriminative fine-grained dog features than ResNet-50 V1 (76.1%), and the backbone has likely already seen these ImageNet-derived images in training; the timm config call and C=0.3 should still behave sensibly at a similar feature scale, so I expect roughly a 30-45% log-loss reduction, to about 0.25-0.32.

The diff correctly averages probabilities over 10 Resize(256)+FiveCrop(224)+hflip views. That mainly softens confidently wrong look-alike-breed predictions. The backbone has largely seen these ImageNet dog images under random crops and flips, so corner and flip features stay in-distribution for the center-crop-trained LR head. Expect a modest log-loss gain of about 3-6%, partly offset by slight under-confidence on correct predictions and some corner crops cutting off the dog.

ConvNeXt-T in22k features are much stronger than ResNet-50 for these ImageNet-derived dogs, so a tuned linear probe on the concatenation could reach roughly 0.22-0.28, but C=1 on L2-normalised features is about 100-200x more regularisation than the C the baseline found optimal, so predictions will be under-confident and give back much of the gain, landing around 0.33-0.45.

The pretrained IMAGENET1K_V2 head is a linear classifier on the same features, fit on roughly 1300 images per breed that likely include these Stanford Dogs images, so after restricting it to the 120 dog classes and temperature scaling it should match or beat the LR fit on 9k images; blending two moderately correlated, differently calibrated classifiers, tuned on a 1.8k-row stratified split, should cut confident errors and lower log loss by roughly 15-25%, with little risk of regression since alpha=0 is in the grid.

Without whitening, PCA is just a rotation plus truncation, so the only real change is dropping the lowest-variance directions. Label-smoothed V2 features on ImageNet-overlapping dog images are strongly class-collapsed, so the top 256 components should hold nearly all of the 119-dimensional between-breed signal. Ridge-style L2 logistic regression already shrinks the dropped directions, and C was tuned for the full features, so hard truncation most likely costs a little residual signal for little gain against overfitting: a small regression.

ResNet-50 was trained with average pooling, so its final features are built to be averaged and its memorised ImageNet dog-class evidence lies along linear directions of the averaged features; max pooling replaces this with a noisier, nonlinearly distorted readout. Max-pooled features are also about 4-5x larger in magnitude, so a fixed C=0.3 is effectively several times weaker regularisation. That likely produces a more overfit classifier, which temperature scaling only partly corrects, so I expect a moderate log-loss regression.

The 120 breeds are ImageNet classes, so the V2 features' stronger in-domain discrimination (80.9 vs 76.1 top-1, much better top-5) should carry over to the linear probe; the usual transfer penalty from label smoothing and mixup mostly hits non-ImageNet tasks, and temperature scaling absorbs most of the calibration and fixed-C mismatch, giving a moderate log-loss gain.

With 2048-d raw ResNet features and about 77 images per class, the training set is nearly separable: C=0.3 already reaches a training loss of roughly 0.005, so the lr=1e-4, 2-epoch bottleneck tune is close to a no-op and cannot recover the confidence lost to 10x stronger L2. The run is therefore roughly LR-only at C=0.03, which the holdout already ranked below C=0.3; its test logits shrink by about 0.7-0.8x, and that underconfidence is costly for a 120-class log loss (expected several percent worse).

Testing an ImageNet ResNet50 (trained with RandomResizedCrop at 224) at 192 px shrinks dogs further below the scale it learned and discards fine-grained detail, costing about 2% ImageNet top-1. Refitting the logistic regression on 192-px features recovers part of that. Even so, dog breeds are resolution-sensitive, so accuracy should drop about 1.5–2.5 points and log loss rise about 10–15%. The 90 s fine-tune budget is not binding at either size, so fine-tuning has the same effect in both runs.

Centred, unwhitened PCA is a rotation plus truncation, and the L2 penalty does not change under rotation. So this is the same C=0.3 logistic regression restricted to the top-256 subspace, which is approximated cheaply here with 2 power iterations in float32. The penalty already shrinks the low-variance tail heavily, and breed structure for these ImageNet classes sits mostly in the top components, so the loss should be small. Still, some fine-grained, look-alike-pair signal and the tuned fit are lost. Expect a slight log-loss increase rather than a gain.

Shrinking frozen ResNet-50 V1 inputs from 224 to 192 px loses fine detail and makes objects look smaller than they did in training. On ImageNet that costs about 2 points of top-1, and fine-grained dog breeds are hurt at least as much. Refitting the linear probe and the flip TTA only partly offset this, so log loss should rise about 10%.

The 120 breeds are ImageNet classes, so the V2 weights (80.9% vs 76.1% ImageNet top-1) should give more class-separable features and higher probe accuracy. The usual transfer penalty from label smoothing and mixup mostly hits non-ImageNet classes. Some of the gain is likely lost to C=0.3 being tuned for V1's feature scale and to sharper, overconfident errors from tight clusters.

The final classifier is unchanged from the baseline; only one scalar temperature is applied, fitted on a 1,380-image holdout where C=0.3 was already chosen by log loss, so T should land near 1 (about 0.9–1.15) and the gain should be small, roughly 0.2–1%, with a slight chance of no gain because of estimation noise and val-to-test transfer.

The head starts as an exact copy of the converged C=0.3 LR on the same training images. The training residuals are small, and the remaining gradient mostly comes from the regularization gap (wd 1e-4 vs the LR's ~3.6e-4), so 288 SGD steps at 1e-4/1e-3 shift logits by only about 0.1% and leave the bottleneck weights almost unchanged. Test predictions should therefore be nearly identical to the baseline, so log loss stays about 0.452 ± 0.005.

The flipped view comes from the same distribution as the training features because the backbone was trained with flip augmentation, so averaging the two views' probabilities gives a small Jensen-style ensemble gain that mostly softens the hard and confidently wrong cases that dominate log loss; the implementation looks correct and costs little runtime, so expect a modest gain of about 2–4%.

Undersampling to 1:1 discards most of the negatives (down to 478 for threat, about 1.4k for identity_hate and 1.6k for severe_toxic). AUC is unaffected by base rate, so the only real effect is lost negative-side information: toxic-but-not-X and neutral identity or 'kill' mentions. Branch A's fixed C=0.1 also becomes far more regularized on the tiny sets, so rare-label AUCs should drop about 1.5–2 points and common labels about 0.3–0.5 points, a clear net regression.

Adding the char_wb block should make NB-LogReg a stronger single model (about +0.002–0.003, since char n-grams catch obfuscated and sub-word cues), but branch B then becomes much more correlated with the char-dominated branch A, and C=4 is weakly regularized on that block, so the gain in the rank-average shrinks to a small net improvement; runtime (~10–11 min) should stay under the hard kill.

AUC ignores calibration, so a 1:1 undersample only discards data. It also removes almost all hard negatives (toxic comments that are not threat, identity_hate or severe_toxic), leaving the rare-label models with under 1-3k rows. Combined with the effectively much stronger regularization at fixed C, I expect drops of about 0.01-0.02 AUC on the rare labels and about 0.003-0.005 on toxic, obscene and insult, so the mean falls by roughly 0.007.

MultinomialNB(alpha=1) on 200k L2-normalised TF-IDF features is a poor ranker, around 0.93-0.95 mean AUC versus about 0.976 for NB-LogReg. Here α·V dwarfs the positive-class mass, so rare n-grams look 'toxic' and profanity is even down-weighted for rare labels like threat. Its weak OOF logits add little to branch A's stack, and a 50/50 rank average with this much weaker model should pull the blend down by about 0.005-0.008.

Mean-pooled corpus Word2Vec features are a much weaker ranker (~0.95–0.965 AUC) than word+char TF-IDF LR (~0.979): averaging dilutes single insults in long comments and drops all char-level signal, and these features now drive two of the three equal-weight branches (LR and MLP), so the extra diversity only partly offsets the quality loss and the blend should land at or below NB-LR alone.

Logistic regression ranks correctly without balancing, so 1:1 undersampling only throws data away: about 81% of rows for toxic, and 99.7% of negatives for threat, whose fit drops to 956 rows; most n-gram features are rare among negatives, so their weights become much noisier and C is effectively stronger, and the few remaining hard negatives (toxic comments that are not threat, identity_hate or severe_toxic) mainly hurt the rare columns; branches A and B share the same subsets so their errors correlate, while the MLP keeps hard negatives but loses about 80% of its updates, giving an expected blend drop of about 0.004-0.007 AUC.

A TF-IDF sparse MLP should train correctly (each epoch roughly 1–1.5 min, held-out AUC well above 0.97) and should land near the linear branches (~0.977–0.979 on test); because it is non-linear with a shared hidden layer, it adds some diversity, so a 1/4-weight rank blend gives a small gain of about +0.0003 to +0.0008, while time guards may limit it to 1–2 epochs or occasionally drop it entirely (leaving 0.98099).

Balanced 1:1 undersampling discards 89-99.7% of the negatives, and AUC does not suffer from class imbalance in the first place. For logistic regression, case-control sampling only shifts the intercept in expectation, so the change mostly adds variance. That costs a little on toxic, obscene and insult (~0.002-0.004), which keep 8-15k negatives. It costs more on threat, identity_hate and severe_toxic, which keep only 0.5-1.6k negatives and so lose most of the hard toxic-but-not-label negatives and the benign identity mentions. All three branches share the same subsample, so the blend cannot average this out. The expected net effect is roughly a 0.005-0.008 drop in the column mean.

The vectorizers already lowercase and split on whitespace, and char_wb 2-6-grams already absorb most obfuscation, so the real changes are small: canonicalizing variants slightly helps the word-level NB-LR branch, while losing intensity, register and signature cues (u→stop-word 'you' in branch A, 'U.S.'→'you', collapsed '!!!!', deleted timestamps, generic IPs) slightly hurts. Expect a net change near zero, within the noise of the rare labels.

A becomes a stronger, cross-label-aware stacker, which should help the rare labels (threat, identity_hate), but A now leans heavily on B's OOF logits. Re-blending it 50/50 with B double-counts B and cuts the char-n-gram diversity that drove the original blend gain, so the gains and losses roughly cancel, with a slight negative lean. The extra 30 liblinear fits also push runtime toward the 10–15 min range.

Over 3 epochs, a 64-unit multi-task MLP on branch A's word+char TF-IDF features should land near 0.975-0.978 on its own, close to the linear branches but correlated with A because it shares A's features. Giving it equal 1/3 rank weight probably helps slightly on the main labels and is roughly neutral or slightly negative on threat and identity_hate, for about +0.0003 net. Small chance of hitting the time limit, since the MLP adds about 3-4 minutes.

Branch C (NB-LogReg on 200k word 1-2-grams plus 50k char_wb features) should be about as strong as A or B alone (~0.978-0.980) but is highly correlated with both, so an equal three-way rank average likely adds only ~+0.0004 AUC, mostly on the noisy rare labels; it also adds ~4 min of 100-iteration liblinear fits on a ~100M-nonzero matrix and ~11 GB peak memory, which probably stays under the 15-min kill but carries some risk.

Per-label blend weights from a train holdout, shrunk halfway to 0.5, can only nudge two similar-strength models off an already near-optimal flat AUC curve, so the gain is about +1e-4 at most and may not transfer because of train/test shift and noisy rare labels; the main risk is runtime, since the holdout adds a half-size char-vectorizer fit plus 80% LR refits (roughly 1.5x current wall-clock) and could approach the 15-minute kill.

Toxicity signal lives in a long tail of specific lexical n-grams and character variants (obfuscated profanity, slurs, threat bigrams), and a 300-d variance-driven SVD of word-only TF-IDF throws much of it away. The change also drops the char n-gram branch and the rank-average ensemble, so it should lose about 2 AUC points, mostly on toxic, threat and identity_hate. The run should still finish well within budget.

AUC does not depend on class balance, so undersampling buys nothing. It only discards data: toxic is unchanged (10x its positives exceeds the negative count), obscene and insult lose about 45% of their negatives, but threat, identity_hate and severe_toxic keep just 3-10% of theirs, which is where the hard negatives live (non-threat toxic comments, benign identity or violent wording). All three branches share the same subsample. NB-LR's C=4 fits and fastText's vocabulary, now built from about 5k documents, are hurt most, so expect a small regression concentrated in the rare labels.

The parent's 0.883 is far below what the word+char TF-IDF LR and NB-LR blend usually gets (about 0.978). That gap fits a known break: fasttext-wheel is built with old pybind11, and under numpy 2 it returns every top-k probability equal to the top one. That turned branch F into an anti-informative 'confidence' score. The child pins numpy<2, which should restore correct fastText probabilities. The multi-label softmax F (about 0.95 AUC) then blends to roughly 0.975-0.98. Risk: if the pin does not apply, the same bug gives every column the max-class probability, F becomes strongly inverted, and the score would drop to about 0.77.

For two classes, sklearn's ComplementNB (no TF transform or normalization, and no prior in the score) ranks test rows exactly as MultinomialNB with alpha=1 on raw counts does, so this swaps a 0.98 three-branch linear ensemble for plain NB. Plain NB's score grows linearly with comment length, so long comments with one insult rank low. Spreading alpha=1 over 200k features also distorts the weights for rare labels like threat and identity_hate. Expect a mean AUC of roughly 0.93-0.955 instead of 0.98.

Replacing the tuned sparse n-gram ensemble with mean-pooled 200-d Word2Vec trained on the corpus plus logistic regression should regress the score. The mean pooling dilutes the few toxic tokens in longer comments, and the linear head can only weight words through a rank-200 projection. It also loses bigrams and char n-grams (obfuscation), and the rank-blend diversity is gone. Averaged-embedding LR typically lands around 0.94–0.96 AUC on this test set, versus about 0.977 for a single TF-IDF LR and 0.982 for the current blend.

Averaging frozen 200-d CBOW vectors trained without labels dilutes rare toxic tokens, especially in long comments. It also gives up the char n-grams, bigrams and 200k-feature capacity of TF-IDF, so this model is weaker than unigram TF-IDF LR or fastText-supervised (~0.97). Expect roughly 0.94-0.95 mean AUC, with the biggest losses on toxic and identity_hate.

A char_wb NB-LogReg is a decent model that differs from the existing branches: its NB weighting and much weaker regularisation set it apart from branch A's heavily regularised char LR. A per-label 3-way blend should gain roughly +0.0003 to +0.0005 AUC, partly eroded by noisy holdout tuning on threat and identity_hate. A and B are reproduced exactly, so the blend cannot drop much. Main risk is runtime: the extra char vectorizer plus six denser liblinear fits likely adds about 4–5 min, not the claimed 1–2, putting the run near 12–13 min, with an estimated 10–20% chance of hitting the 15-min kill.

Raising C 40x (0.1 to 4) likely helps the frequent labels (toxic, insult, obscene) slightly, but probably over-fits the rare labels (threat, severe_toxic, identity_hate) on 60k features and makes branch A more like the weakly-regularized NB-LR branch, which cuts blend diversity, so the net is roughly flat to slightly negative (runtime should still fit the budget).

The fastText branch has no char n-grams, is overfit (20 epochs at lr=0.5) and averages its features, so I expect it to score only about 0.965-0.97 alone and to correlate strongly with the word-bigram NB-LogReg branch; giving it an equal third weight cuts the stronger char branch from 1/2 to 1/3, so its extra diversity roughly cancels its weakness, a flat-to-slightly-negative change (this assumes the run finishes despite runtime being close to the cap).

A char_wb 3-7 NB-LogReg is probably about as strong as branch A (~0.978 alone) and only moderately decorrelated from A and B, so an equal three-way rank average should add roughly +0.0003 to +0.001 mean AUC; the main risk is runtime, since a second char vectorizer (~4 min) plus six fully converged liblinear primal fits on a ~90M-nonzero matrix could push the run to 13–16 min, close to the 15-minute kill.

Dropping 10% of the training data costs roughly 3-5e-4 mean AUC, mostly on the rare threat and identity_hate labels. That outweighs the small, noisy gain from per-label weights tuned on a 16k holdout with only about 48 threat positives, since the two branches are diverse enough that 0.5 is already near-optimal, so the net effect is a slight regression.

NB log-count weighting at C=0.1 loosens regularization on discriminative char and word n-grams and suppresses neutral ones, which probably helps branch A on toxic, obscene and insult; rare labels risk mild overfit from the smoothing offset, and A becomes more correlated with the NB-LR branch B, so the blend gain is roughly flat to slightly positive (assumes sag still converges within the 15-minute limit).

A 1% min_df means a term must appear in at least ~3.1k of the 313k documents, which leaves roughly 900 of the 10k word features, about 20k of the 50k char features, and only about 3k of branch B's 200k NB features. That removes the long tail of moderately rare profanity and identity/threat terms (cunt, faggot, nigger, rape, murder, often even bitch and suck) that the linear models rely on, especially for the rare labels. Branch B is gutted and branch A is weakened, so I expect a clear drop of about 0.6–1.0 AUC points.

Balanced 1:1 undersampling keeps every positive but discards 90–99.7% of the negatives (threat trains on only 956 rows, identity_hate on 2.8k, severe_toxic on 3.2k). That leaves very few hard negatives, such as toxic comments without the specific label or neutral uses of identity and threat words, so the nested rare-label models collapse toward generic toxicity or keyword detectors with noisy NB ratios. Class rebalancing gives no compensating AUC gain, so the rare labels likely drop about 0.01–0.015 each and the common labels about 0.005, for a mean loss of roughly 0.008.

Swapping trained logistic regression for a cosine difference-of-centroids classifier (an untrained, Rocchio-style direction) loses the learned feature weighting: generic and length-correlated n-grams leak into the score in branch A, and moderately rare cue words get under-weighted. The NB weighting keeps branch B reasonable at roughly 0.95-0.96, and the code itself looks correct, so expect a clear regression from 0.980 to around 0.95.

Switching char to char_wb only swaps the cross-word n-grams in the 50k frequency-capped vocabulary for rarer within-word pieces, so Branch A changes by a few 1e-4 AUC at most. Rank-averaging with the NB-LogReg branch, which already has word bigrams, halves that, giving a near-zero blended change with a slight lean negative from losing cross-word context.

For a binary label, ComplementNB with norm=False ranks documents exactly like Laplace-smoothed multinomial NB. With alpha=1 on small L2-normalised TF-IDF values, the smoothing swamps the positive-class mass for rare labels, so rare neutral n-grams get weights close to threat and identity-hate cue words. NB also over-counts correlated char n-grams and lacks discriminative weighting, so frequent labels likely land near 0.94-0.96 and threat and identity_hate near 0.88-0.91, pulling the column mean to roughly 0.93 (no probability-saturation ties are expected).

Squeezing 60k word and char TF-IDF features into 32 roughly fitted SVD components (n_iter=2) throws away most of branch A's lexical detail, so A probably falls from about 0.977 AUC to about 0.89, keeping only coarse profanity and style directions; the weaker fastText branch (about 0.95, as the current 0.973 blend implies) then dominates, and equal rank-averaging with the degraded A should land around 0.93 to 0.95.

Collapsing every token outside the top 2,000 by document frequency into 'raretoken' throws away the long tail: misspelled or obfuscated profanity, rarer insults and slurs, and most of the subword signal the char_wb n-grams relied on. It also cuts Branch A's word features from 10k to about 1.7k and pollutes common char n-grams like 'are' and 'en'. Both branches should lose roughly 0.005–0.012 AUC, hitting threat and identity_hate hardest, and the name-overfitting regularization will not make up for it.

Keeping stop words gives branch A pronoun signal ('you', 'your', 'off', 'up', 'will'), which helps insult and threat. But char_wb n-grams already encode those tokens and branch B already keeps stop words, so after rank-blending the gain should be tiny and within noise (slightly positive).

Expit is monotonic, so the ranking depends only on the sum of the two branches' logits. The NB-LogReg branch (C=4, NB-scaled features, very weakly regularized) has a much wider logit spread than the word+char LogReg branch (C=0.1), especially on rare labels like threat, identity_hate and severe_toxic. The unweighted logit average therefore effectively up-weights the weaker NB branch, losing part of the gain from the balanced rank blend. Better tail resolution from logit averaging only partly offsets this, so I expect a small regression.

Switching to 'char' adds cross-word n-grams such as 'k you', 'you a' and 'ill kil'. These give branch A phrase-level insult and threat cues it lacks, since its word part is stopword-filtered unigrams. The 50k cap pushes out some rarer within-word n-grams, and branch B's bigrams already cover part of the new signal, so the blend should gain only slightly (about +0.0002 to +0.0004). Vectorizing should take about 1.5-2x longer, roughly 11-13 minutes in total, which is likely still under the 15-minute kill.

A from-scratch fastText model with mean-pooled embeddings, 5 epochs, heavily hashed bigrams, and a quantized/saturating sigmoid lookup table likely scores about 0.965–0.97 alone, below NB-LR's ~0.976, so the equal-weight rank blend with the word+char branch probably drops slightly under the current 0.9801.

At C=1 the multinomial LR on the 192 standardised leaf descriptors is under-confident (the log-loss optimum for this dataset is around C≈1000), and nearly every column is informative. Dropping the 64 lowest-F columns shrinks the class-mean separation available under the L2 penalty. That makes the LR softer and loses some margin/texture detail that separates similar species, which outweighs the small benefit of removing sparse noisy bins. The NN half is deterministic and unchanged, and the blend loss moves at about 0.7x the LR's relative change, so I expect a modest regression.

Label smoothing at 0.1 over 99 classes caps the network's probability on the true species at about 0.9, down from about 0.98–0.99. The 50/50 blend with the logistic regression already protects against confident mistakes, so the main effect is a lower true-class probability on the correctly classified majority. That adds about 0.05–0.06 nats on most of the 99 test samples, and any small accuracy or calibration gain on the few hard leaves cannot offset it.

Independent sigmoids over 99 extremely imbalanced binary fits (about 7 positives against 700 negatives each) are misspecified compared with the joint softmax and give inconsistent scales across classes. The single power-plus-floor calibration fixes the overall under-confidence but not those per-class distortions near class boundaries, which is where the log loss is concentrated. Accuracy should stay similar while log loss gets moderately worse, though with only 99 test rows the result is noisy.

A bagged 512-unit MLP is a nonlinear, fairly diverse partner for the linear LR, and blending their probabilities before the power/floor calibration (with w=0 as a fallback) should cut out-of-fold log loss by roughly 15-25%; the run fits the time budget (about 80 MLP fits run 5 in parallel, plus a grid search of about 26k log-loss evaluations), but with only 99 test rows a couple of hard samples dominate the score, so the expected test gain is more modest and noisy.

Averaging the five fold models' probabilities should soften the few confidently wrong test predictions that dominate the log loss of this sharp, high-C model, but each fold model sees only about 7 instead of 9 samples per class, which adds errors of its own, so the expected net effect is close to zero with a slight lean toward improvement on a noisy 99-row test set.

The 192 provided descriptors are scale-normalised histograms and contours, so the image's absolute size (log H/W, area, perimeter, axis lengths) is genuinely new and discriminative for similar-shaped species. C is still re-selected by CV, so OOF and test log loss should drop moderately. The gain is damped by a few noisy features (signed Hu moments, Euler number) and a possible mask-polarity inversion: the Kaggle JPGs may be white-on-black, which would put the features on the background, though they would stay informative through H/W. The 99-sample test is very noisy.

An L2 penalty is unchanged by rotation, so PCA without whitening has only one real effect: it drops the lowest-variance directions (5% of variance, roughly half the dimensions). With 99 classes and 9 rows each, those directions likely carry fine distinctions between similar species, such as the many Quercus and Acer, and C=1 already under-weights them, so the result is probably a modest log-loss increase rather than a gain.

At C=1 this LR is under-confident (the known optimal C for this data is much higher), so the five fold models, each trained on about 7 instead of 9 samples per class, are effectively more regularised and less confident; averaging a stable linear model recovers little variance, so log loss should rise modestly.

The C=1 LR is under-confident (geometric-mean p_true ≈ 0.88), so averaging 50/50 with a confident, roughly 98–100%-accurate feature-dominated CNN+MLP should roughly halve the log loss (a perfect NN gives a floor of about 0.05–0.06). The likely NN errors on 99 test rows are cushioned by the LR, and the min(fill, 1-fill) inversion quirk only weakens the image branch; runtime (~1 s/epoch) is well under the guard.

LR at C=1 on standardised leaf features is about 98–99% accurate but underconfident (test true-class probability averages ~0.88), so OOF-fitted power sharpening (a≈2–3) should cut log loss sharply on correct predictions; the full model's test probabilities are unchanged, and over-sharpening from refitting on more data is minor, but with only 99 test rows each misclassification now costs ~0.03–0.05, so the result is noisy (roughly 0.02–0.10).

C=1 is heavily over-regularised for these near-separable standardised features. 5-fold OOF tuning should pick C around 300-3000, matching known Kaggle results where tuned multinomial logistic regression reaches about 0.03-0.05 log loss. Correct predictions become much more confident while the roughly one expected error costs only a few hundredths. The 55 fits should finish in about 5-8 minutes with 4 jobs. The 99-row test set adds variance.

Image height and width add genuinely new leaf-size information that the scale-normalised precomputed features lack, which should sharpen the under-confident C=1 logistic regression; but the images are likely tight crops, so many leaves fill more than half the frame and the 'mask.mean()>0.5' polarity flip would describe background corners instead of leaves, making about 25 features bimodal and noisy, plus Hu5-7 sign noise, so expect only a modest net gain with wide variance on 99 test rows.

Standardized leaf features are almost linearly separable, so LR at C=1 is already underconfident (the best C on this data is typically around 1e2–1e3). Cutting C 5x shrinks the logits by roughly 0.75, which about doubles the loss on correctly classified samples, while the few hard or misclassified samples barely change, so log loss should rise to about 0.15–0.18.

Skipping the refit means the submitted model trains on about 7 rows per class instead of 9 (712 vs 891 rows). That leaves less class coverage, and with fixed C=1 the regularization becomes relatively stronger, so predictions are less confident and there are more hard misses. This should raise log loss by roughly 20–40%.

The kNN probabilities are spread over many classes, so the OOF optimizer should give kNN a weight near zero, leaving an LR plus shrinkage-LDA blend. LDA is about 97-99% accurate and very confident, so it sharpens LR's correct but not fully confident predictions. LR's weight caps the extra cost of LDA's confident errors at roughly 0.5-0.7 per sample. The expected gain is about 15-25%, though the 99-row test set is noisy.

This should get much worse: with about 7.6 training rows per class after the 15% early-stopping holdout, min_samples_leaf=10 means no leaf can isolate a class, and axis-aligned trees on 192 histogram features generalise far worse than a well-tuned linear model here (tree boosters typically score around 0.4-1.0 log loss on this dataset versus about 0.05 for LR), with overconfident errors and no refit on the held-out 15% making it worse.

The swap will likely make the ensemble worse. Per-class Platt calibration with only 2-3 positives per class per fold uses smoothed targets of about 0.8 for positives and about 1/296 for negatives. Summed over 98 classes, that negative floor caps the normalized true-class probability near 0.6-0.7, and each base SVM sees only 2/3 of the data. That is clearly less confident than the C=1 multinomial LR it replaces, which is probably near 0.9 on easy samples. In a uniform 4-way average that is already underconfident, this lowers the ensemble's true-class probability by roughly 0.05-0.08, so log loss rises by about 0.06-0.12.

With 99 classes and about 9 samples per class, a fully grown RF spreads its votes, giving roughly 0.4–0.6 on the true class. The early-stopped Newton-step HGB, when right, puts roughly 0.9 or more on it. Swapping HGB for RF therefore lowers the uniform soft-vote's typical true-class probability. That outweighs the RF's steadier mass on samples HGB misclassifies, so I expect a moderate log-loss regression.

The MLP early-stops on validation accuracy from a 10% split (about 90 samples, 99 classes) and restores the weights from the first epoch that hits peak accuracy. Accuracy plateaus long before log loss converges on this highly separable data, so the restored model stays soft. It also trains on only about 801 rows and comes from a single seed, so on 99 test rows it will likely land near or above LR C=1's 0.124 rather than at the roughly 0.03-0.05 a well-trained net reaches.

At C=1 the multinomial LR is under-confident for its roughly 98-99% accuracy (0.124 loss comes mostly from soft correct predictions), so CV will almost surely pick a large C (>=31.6); modern lbfgs with gtol=1e-4 then gives a model about 1.5-2x sharper, which should cut log loss by roughly 40-55%, though with only 99 test rows one or two errors that get more confident could eat much of that gain.

The 48 OpenCV features add information the 192 scale-invariant descriptors lack, such as absolute leaf size, solidity, eccentricity, Hu moments and a rotation-invariant radial histogram, and adding standardized features loosens the effective regularization of the underconfident C=1 model, so the loss should drop moderately; a few noisy columns (signed log-Hu h5-h7, wrap-around ellipse orientation) and the 99-row test set limit and add variance to the gain.

The data has 891 training rows, roughly 9 per class (not 10), so 10-fold StratifiedKFold leaves about 10 classes missing from every validation fold. The neg_log_loss scorer inside LogisticRegressionCV then raises the 'y_true and y_pred contain different number of classes' ValueError, or StratifiedKFold refuses outright if every class has exactly 9. The run should therefore crash before writing a new submission, leaving the score at the baseline. If it did run, a tuned C of about 100-1000 would likely give roughly 0.04-0.05.

Uniform soft voting averages the baseline LR, which already puts about 0.9 on the true class, with two much less confident members. The CV-tuned distance-weighted kNN will likely pick a large k (log loss punishes misses at about 36 nats each), so with only 6-10 samples per class its true-class probability is diluted to about 0.5. HGB, trained on about 8 samples per class, makes large Newton-step jumps and reaches maybe 70-80% accuracy with spiky probabilities. LDA (near-diagonal because shrinkage is applied per class) is sharp but cannot offset this. The ensemble's mean true-class probability drops to about 0.75-0.8, so log loss should land around 0.25-0.3, roughly double the baseline.

Logistic regression at C=1 is underconfident on this data (raising C toward 1000 is known to reach about 0.04) and its errors are soft, so the out-of-fold search will almost certainly pick alpha=0, which is in the grid, and produce an identical submission; any alpha of 0.01 or more would add roughly +0.01 per step on the test set, but that would need extreme out-of-fold errors (p_true below 1e-6), which are unlikely.

In sklearn, 'auto' is a per-class Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage (about 0.7 with 9 samples/class) toward a diagonal of per-feature within-class variances, while fixed 0.9 shrinks toward the trace-scaled identity and keeps only 10% of the correlation structure; that weights noisy, sparse and correlated shape directions almost equally with discriminative features, so errors among similar species should rise. Lower logit scale makes each error somewhat cheaper, but log loss on a 99-row test set is still dominated by a few confident mistakes, so a moderate regression is most likely, with a real chance of a small gain.

Per-family LDAs are much weaker (roughly 85% margin, 80% texture, 60% shape) and still near one-hot, so the arithmetic mean pays about 0.4 nats on every sample where one model (usually shape) is wrong and about 1.1 nats where only one is right. That outweighs removing the combined model's one or two catastrophic confident errors, which likely dominate the current 0.364.

The L2 penalty is rotation-invariant, so non-whitened PCA only matters by dropping the low-variance tail (likely 100+ of the 192 standardized components). That tail holds fine margin and texture detail used to separate confusable species such as the many oaks, and tuned L2 already handled the redundancy, so expect higher log loss with large noise on a 99-row test set.

Shrinkage LDA should match logistic regression on accuracy (about 98-99%), but its plug-in Gaussian posteriors are overconfident: the sparse margin/texture bins and noisy 6-9 sample class means mean any error on the 99-row test costs roughly 5-35 nats, so one error likely roughly doubles the log loss even though an error-free run could beat 0.06.

PCA without whitening is just a rotation, which leaves the L2-penalized LR unchanged, so the only real effect is dropping roughly 90 low-variance directions. C=1 with about 712 rows per fold is weak regularization, so the baseline still uses those directions for fine-grained species splits. Cutting them should slightly lower held-out separability, making the temperature-scaled predictions somewhat less confident, though the 99-row test set makes the result noisy.

sklearn's 'auto' shrinkage is computed per class from about 7 samples, so it shrinks hard toward diagonal and gives up some of the LDA whitening that makes LDA accurate on leaf; its generative scores also make outlier-driven errors very confident, so the OOF temperature will likely hit the T<=4 cap, and with accuracy similar to or slightly below LR, a few confident test errors probably make log loss modestly worse than 0.045, though zero test errors could improve it.

The 0.0943 baseline over 99 test rows caps any single loss at about 9.3, so no prediction has a true-class probability below about 1e-4; the 5e-5 floor therefore rescues almost nothing, while scaling by 0.995 adds about -log(0.995) ≈ 0.005 to the loss of every confident row, a net regression of roughly 0.005.

With per-coordinate re-standardization, Nyström features have roughly 1/d variance each. Cutting components from 512 to 384 therefore shrinks the effective kernel scale, much like lowering C by about 25%, and it also coarsens the kernel approximation, with about 3.9 vs 5.2 landmarks per class. On this nearly separable dataset, where log loss rewards confident predictions and the model already looks under-confident, both effects should modestly raise the loss.

Shrunk LDA should be about as accurate as LR here (~98–99%), but its Gaussian plug-in posteriors are much sharper than C=1 LR's. It saves the softness loss on easy samples, but each of the expected ~1–2 test errors would cost about 8–15 nats instead of ~2. Per-class Ledoit-Wolf over-shrinks toward the diagonal, which overcounts the correlated shape features and inflates confidence. Net, it is probably somewhat worse than 0.124, with high variance (about 0.03 if there are zero errors, 0.3+ if there are three).

Leaf features are nearly linearly separable, so 3-fold CV will likely pick C=100 or 1000; the more confident model should cut test log loss from 0.124 to about 0.04–0.06, though one confident miss among the 99 test rows could add roughly 0.05.

The final model's logits are unchanged from the baseline, so only the temperature differs. At C=1 the L2-regularised LR is clearly underconfident (mean p_true is about 0.88 at roughly 98% accuracy), so the out-of-fold temperature should come out around 0.4–0.6. That sharpening cuts the loss on correctly classified rows sharply, while the 1–2 likely test errors get more costly, giving a net drop to roughly 0.06–0.09.

After the second StandardScaler, Nyström-RBF plus LR(C=1) is roughly kernel LR at about the same effective scale as the linear baseline, so typical test confidence is similar; the RBF's free memorization of the 512 landmarks, its isotropic sensitivity to sparse standardized histogram noise and the 512/891 landmark coverage likely make test predictions slightly less confident or reliable than the linear model, giving a small regression (high variance on 99 test rows).

The new block adds real information the model cannot see now: the request timestamp (success rates declined over the subreddit's life) and text length (lost to L2-normalised TF-IDF), plus image, gratitude and reciprocity flags. The dense features are nearly unregularised at C=0.3, so the extra 31 columns cost little in overfitting, giving an expected gain of roughly +0.01 to +0.025 AUC on a random split.

With max_features='sqrt' over about 6,000 sparse word and subreddit columns, a split sees one of the 9 informative numeric features only about 10% of the time, so the fully grown trees are mostly weak word splits that overfit. A random forest on sparse TF-IDF with weak signal and about 2.9k rows usually trails L2 logistic regression on AUC, so expect roughly a 0.04–0.07 regression.

The test set's giver_known field is a near-perfect leak (about 30% of positives), and LR's large coefficient ranks those rows above every negative, whereas the RF samples about 70 of 5010 features per node and so applies the giver split on only roughly 20-35% of trees' paths, letting some leak rows slip below negatives. RF on 5k sparse TF-IDF words also dilutes the few numeric signals and usually ranks text slightly worse than LR, so expect a modest drop.

The giver_known leak supplies roughly 30% of the AUC and is unchanged. Swapping 5k TF-IDF unigrams for 50 noisy LDA topic proportions, fit on only ~2.9k short documents, usually loses some lexical signal (for example imgur, job or paycheck words). That should cut the non-leak AUC by about 0.01–0.02, a small net regression.

Swapping the supervised out-of-fold TF-IDF logistic-regression logit (text AUC around 0.61) for 20 unsupervised LDA topic proportions keeps only a weak, diffuse text signal (roughly 0.56–0.58) on short RAOP posts, so the gain from text over the metadata and timestamp features (about 0.66–0.67 alone) shrinks, and the 20 noisy columns add some overfitting risk on about 2.9k rows.

The test split is a random sample from the same 2010–2013 window, so the raw timestamp carries a real, transferable signal (RAOP success rates fell steadily as the community aged); dropping it should cost roughly 0.01 AUC, and the weak, noisy hour-of-day and weekday features will likely recover only a fraction of that.

The GBM uses only the meta and text-statistic features the LR already sees, so it can add only non-linearity, such as a non-quadratic time trend and length thresholds. A meta-only GBM probably scores around 0.64–0.66 out-of-fold against about 0.69 for the LR. A CV-weighted rank blend (w≈0.6–0.8) therefore likely gives a small gain of roughly +0.003–0.01 AUC. If w=1 is chosen, the output reproduces the baseline exactly.

Fully grown sqrt-feature random forests do poorly on 5000 mostly-noise sparse TF-IDF columns. Only about 37% of split candidate sets even include one of the roughly 33 strong dense features, so their signal gets diluted. The forest also cannot pool the weak distributed word signal the way the linear model does, so it most likely lands near 0.64-0.67, below the 0.70 baseline.

The subreddit list is available at request time, but beyond the subreddit count and prior RAOP activity it carries only weak signal. The l2-normalised binary-idf block is heavily shrunk under C=0.3, so it adds a mild, mostly redundant kernel term: expect a small gain within test-set noise (about ±0.01).

In the MLE-bench split the test rows come from the original train file and keep their giver_username_if_known values. A known giver appears only on successful requests, roughly 30-35% of positives, so the flag gets a large coefficient (about 4) and puts those positives above every negative. Expected AUC is about f + (1-f)*0.645, which gives roughly 0.75-0.77.

The code should run cleanly: MLflow is wrapped best-effort, the OOF text logits avoid leakage, and LightGBM is heavily regularized and early-stopped. The main real gains are the newly added UTC timestamp (RAOP success rates fell over time and the split is random, so the trend carries over) and a learned weighting of the text score against the requester history. Trees gain nothing from the raw-versus-log change, and the text model is the same C=0.3 LR. Expect a modest lift of about +0.01 to +0.02 AUC, which is within the roughly ±0.016 test noise.

The implementation looks correct (the MLflow wrapper only does logging and fails safe), and it adds real signal TF-IDF misses: the downward success-rate trend over time and request length, which L2-normalised TF-IDF discards, plus image-link evidence. The standardised dense columns are barely constrained by C=0.3 at n≈2.9k, so the model will use them. The extra features are near-collinear (t² with t, word count with character count) but harmless. I expect a gain of roughly 0.01–0.025 AUC, within the noise of a 1,162-row test set.

With max_features='sqrt' over about 5.4k features (93% sparse TF-IDF), ExtraTrees rarely gets to split on the 9 useful requester numerics, and axis-aligned random splits extract the weak linear signal in the text and embeddings less well than LR. Fixing the LR's overfitting does not make up for that, so expect a small drop (test-set noise is about ±0.02).

The TF-IDF block was barely contributing: its rows are L2-normalised and unscaled, so against 384 standardised embedding dims at C=0.3 it is effectively about 400x more regularised and makes up only a small share of the decision function. Removing it drops a little lexical signal (e.g. imgur/evidence and money words) along with a little noise, while the dominant, near-unregularised embedding and numeric model stays the same, so expect a roughly neutral to slightly negative change of about ±0.007.

TF-IDF rows are L2-normalized, so the model currently has almost no document-length signal; length (univariate AUC ~0.58) and link/evidentiality flags are known RAOP predictors and fairly independent of requester history, so they should add about 0.01–0.02 AUC, though the buggy money regex, exact-match gratitude flags, weak VADER/style features and Flesch/count outliers dilute the gain and the 1162-row test split is noisy.

On RAOP, the request-time history counts on their own reach only about 0.60-0.62 AUC, and the text signal (evidence, job and family words) is complementary to them. The train/test split is random, so the time-drift argument doesn't apply, and removing TF-IDF should cost about 0.03-0.04 AUC compared with the 0.650 text+meta baseline.

Swapping the strongly shrunk sparse TF-IDF block for 200 standardized dense mean-Word2Vec dims (trained on only ~400k tokens) at C=0.3 adds roughly 200 almost unregularized parameters on 2.9k rows, a weak-signal setting. The extra coefficient variance should outweigh the modest, partly length-redundant signal the averaged embeddings add, so expect an AUC drop of about 0.02 to 0.04.

Bigrams and the min_df=2 rare terms take roughly half of each row's L2-normalised TF-IDF norm, and C=0.3 is kept, so the unigram signal is shrunk further while the bigram signal is sparse and largely redundant with unigrams and the reciprocity/gratitude stats; on about 2.9k weak-signal requests that usually gives a neutral to slightly worse AUC.

On RAOP, request-time requester-history features alone are weak (univariate AUCs of roughly 0.55 to 0.58, and Althoff's status features alone score about 0.58). Dropping the text SVD also removes topic and length cues, and deep 63-leaf trees on 9 zero-inflated features overfit, so I expect test AUC to fall to about 0.60 rather than improve.

A default forest of fully grown trees with sqrt(309)≈17 candidate features per split often never sees the informative numeric columns among the 300 weak SVD text dimensions, which roughly cancels its variance-reduction edge over the overfit-prone 63-leaf LightGBM. I expect a near-identical, slightly lower AUC, within the roughly ±0.02 noise of a 1162-row test set.

The 384 MiniLM dimensions are standardized to unit variance, so C=0.3 barely regularizes them. With only ~715 positives (about 1.8 events per dense feature), estimation noise of roughly 384/(n·π(1−π)) ≈ 0.7 in logit variance swamps the weak incremental text signal on RAOP (frozen-embedding text-only AUC is around 0.60–0.63). Expect a net AUC drop of a few points rather than a gain.

Rare bigrams and the extra min_df=2 unigrams take roughly half of each L2-normalised TF-IDF vector's norm, which roughly halves the effective C on the shared unigram signal and adds sparse noise, while RAOP's text signal is topical rather than phrase-level, so expect a slight AUC drop or no change.

Request length is a known RAOP signal (univariate AUC about 0.59) that row-normalised TF-IDF mostly discards, and pronouns and 'please' are new because they are stop words; these near-unregularised dense features should add about +0.01 AUC, minus slight noise from collinear counts and mean_wlen/Flesch outliers.

With only about 2.3k rows per fold, a 63-leaf LightGBM over 300 mostly noisy SVD components keeps less text signal than L2-regularised LR on sparse TF-IDF; the trees' nonlinear handling of the 9 numeric features only partly offsets that, so expect a slight regression (test AUC noise is about ±0.02).

The train/test split is random, and RAOP success rates decline steadily from 2010 to 2013, so the absolute-time spline captures a real trend worth about 0.01 AUC; annual sin/cos cannot represent that trend (it absorbs only about 6% of a linear trend over 2.8 years), and RAOP seasonality is likely weak, so expect a small regression.

At C=0.3 the dense standardized requester-history and date features are already effectively unregularized while the roughly 5k unigram weights are heavily shrunk. Raising C to 30 on 2,878 nearly separable rows leaves the numeric part about the same but lets the text block nearly memorize the training set, so a noisy, overweighted text score dilutes the numeric and time signal; I expect AUC to fall by about 0.04 to 0.08.

Success rates in this data fell steadily from about 30% or more early on to about 20% by 2013, and the split is random, so a smooth time spline adds a real, mostly independent signal (about 0.57 AUC on its own). Combined with the 0.649 model, that should give roughly +0.01 to +0.02 AUC, minus a little to finite-sample noise.

Cosine distance on the stacked matrix is dominated by the standardized numeric part (norm about 3) and the binary subreddit part (norm up to about 10), while unit-norm TF-IDF barely matters, so KNN mostly separates new accounts from established ones and loses most of the text signal; with k=25 on roughly 2.9k noisy samples at a 25% base rate, the estimates stay noisy and should land well below the regularized LR's 0.649.

A distance-weighted 25-NN on nine weak-signal, duplicate-heavy metadata columns gives much noisier probabilities than CatBoost (standalone AUC roughly 0.56-0.58 versus about 0.60). Because its spread is wider than the logistic model's, it dominates the fixed 50/50 average and mostly adds noise, so the blend drops by about 0.02-0.03 AUC.
