At C=30, roughly 5000 sparse unigram features fit on 2878 weak-signal samples nearly separate the training set, so rare words take large noisy weights. The resulting extreme LR probabilities then dominate the 50/50 probability blend and drown out the metadata signal that C=0.3 kept balanced, so AUC most likely drops a few points.

RAOP's success rate falls steadily as the community ages (roughly 0.56–0.58 AUC on its own), and the test set is a random split covering the same dates; seven standardized B-spline columns let the mildly regularized LR fit that trend with little overfitting risk, and it is largely independent of the text and karma features, so expect about +0.01–0.02 AUC, with ±0.01 noise from the small test set.

BernoulliNB's score is a sum of log-odds weights over thousands of binarised n-grams, so it is dominated by document length and noisy, upward-biased weights on rare n-grams. That swamps the nine binarised requester-history indicators, which carry much of LR's 0.654, and leaves a mostly text- and length-driven ranking at about 0.60–0.63.

On RAOP, success rates fall over time, and the date alone gives an AUC of about 0.56–0.58. Because MLE-bench splits train and test at random, test dates match the training range, so a 7-basis spline under weak L2 (C=0.3, n≈2900) should add roughly +0.01 AUC to the text and numeric LR with little overfitting risk. The MLflow wrapper is best-effort and does not change the predictions.

Adds roughly 1000 unscaled 0/1 subreddit columns under a C=0.3 tuned for L2-normalised TF-IDF, so they are only lightly regularised. Niche subreddits seen in 5–50 requests pick up noise weights of about 0.25 logit each, totalling about 0.5 per active user, comparable to the baseline's whole logit spread. Most of the activity signal they carry is already in the numeric features, so the extra noise likely outweighs any small gain (for example a weak time proxy).

The run should complete fine (CatBoost on 2.9k×9 takes seconds, MLflow failures are caught), but the 50/50 probability average adds a second, likely more spread-out and mildly overfit (600 iters on weak-signal data) model built only on the nine metadata features the LR already uses near-unregularized; this roughly halves the relative weight of the TF-IDF text signal while adding only modest tree-vs-linear diversity on log-linear-friendly counts, so the net effect is about neutral to slightly negative.

The only change that affects predictions is adding bigrams under the shared 5000-feature cap: frequent bigrams (formed after stop-word removal) replace a few hundred rare unigrams, and the logging and holdout edits do not touch the test fit; on this small, weak-signal text task that usually means a near-zero, slightly positive AUC shift inside test-set noise of about ±0.005.

Function words are strong authorship cues; the char_wb view still covers stop-word unigrams, but word bigrams like 'of the', 'upon the' and 'my father' are lost, so the stacked LR should regress modestly (about +0.01 log loss) rather than improve.

On Spooky, MultinomialNB on raw word and char counts is strongly complementary to tf-idf LR: it weights rare names and raw function-word frequencies differently. A log-linear meta-LR on clipped log-probs recalibrates the overconfident NB outputs, so meta-CV should drop by about 0.03-0.04. Part of that is lost on test: there is no full-data refit (base models see only 80% of rows), and with min_df=1 the NB-word out-of-fold features carry a singleton-n-gram class bias that test features lack. Expected net result is about 0.32-0.33.

On Spooky, function words and their bigrams ('of the', 'at length', 'upon', 'it was') are strong author cues. Dropping them weakens both word-level base models. The char_wb models still cover single function words but cannot see cross-word bigrams. The stacker should absorb some of the damage, so expect a moderate regression rather than any gain from added diversity.

A linear logistic stacker on raw probability columns cannot use the log-odds magnitude carried by the overconfident MultinomialNB outputs (near 0/1, with informative tiny minority-class probabilities). LightGBM, which is invariant to monotone transforms, can split on those, so the linear combiner effectively sees the NB models as hard votes, distorts the calibrated LR inputs in probability space, and gains little from the meta-features. Expect a moderate regression of about 0.01–0.025 log loss rather than an improvement.

The word block is essentially unchanged, because sklearn's token pattern already ignores punctuation and its bigrams already span it. The char block, however, loses strong and fully transferable signals: semicolons (14/19/32%), quotes (17/6/13%), apostrophes and comma patterns, all reliably learnable as frequent features. Train and test are a random split of the same novels, so even edition-specific punctuation conventions help on the test set. The slight renormalization 'regularizer' gain is small, so I expect a modest regression of about +0.01 to +0.015 log loss.

Stacking four diverse base models (word and char LR at C=10, plus word and char count NB) with a log-prob logistic-regression meta-learner should fix the under-regularised C=1 single LR and add NB diversity, which typically lands Spooky at about 0.33-0.36. Runtime fits the budget, and the fold-averaged test predictions and the 1e-5 clipping are benign.

The L2-regularized LR at C=1 is already underconfident on this task, and chi2 on TF-IDF keeps the high-mass and strongly skewed columns. Cutting 130k columns to 10k mainly drops weak char and rare word n-grams that still add margin, plus a small offsetting gain from removing memorization-like rare features. The LR branch should get slightly worse, and the unchanged NB branch plus the re-tuned blend weight absorb most of that, so the blend degrades only mildly.

This change should make the score worse. In authorship attribution, function words such as upon, her, toward/towards, seemed and thus are strong style cues, and sklearn's 318-word stop list also strips the stop-word bigrams like 'upon the' and 'of the'; removing them should cost the naive Bayes model about 0.05 log loss. The logistic regression keeps some of this signal through its unchanged character n-grams, so it loses only slightly, which suggests the blend rises by about 0.02 to roughly 0.38.

C=1 is over-regularized for stacked word+char TF-IDF, so 5-fold CV should pick C≈10 (possibly 3 or 30). That sharpens the under-confident probabilities and typically cuts log loss to about 0.38-0.40 on this data. The worst case is bounded near the current 0.432 because CV can still pick C=1, and the explicit per-C cold-start fits avoid the warm-start issue and fit the time budget.

Stacking four diverse base models gives large gains on this dataset. LR at C=10 on word and char TF-IDF is better tuned than the current C=1 model, and multinomial NB on word and char counts adds complementary ranking signal from rare words and names. A LightGBM meta-learner with length and stylometric features can recalibrate the overconfident NB outputs. Comparable public NB+meta+GBM stacks reached about 0.30-0.35, and the code looks correct and fits the time budget, so I expect about 0.33-0.35 rather than 0.43.

Cross-word, punctuation-in-context and case-sensitive char n-grams add real authorship signal that the word block (which drops punctuation and 1-char tokens like 'I') lacks, but leaving the vocabulary uncapped puts about a third of each row's L2 norm on rare df 2-5 n-grams; at fixed C=1 that dilution makes predictions less confident, so the net effect should be a small gain.

The C=1 LR on TF-IDF is underconfident, while MultinomialNB on word (1,2)-gram counts is a strong, overconfident and complementary model that captures rare name cues; an arithmetic blend with alpha and weight picked on 17.6k OOF rows should transfer reliably to test and give roughly a 7-12% log-loss gain, and the implementation looks correct and fits the time budget.

Function words are key authorship cues here: upon/which/however point to EAP, she/her/my point to MWS, and toward vs towards separates HPL from MWS, and sklearn's 318-word list removes all of them along with words like seemed and found. Accuracy should drop a few points, and the heavily overconfident fastText model (lr=0.5, 25 epochs) turns each extra error into a costly confident miss, so log loss should rise noticeably.

The current fastText model (25 epochs, lr 0.5) is already overfit and overconfident; duplicating minority-class rows means about 21% more updates and harder memorization of the duplicates, and balancing on a mildly skewed (40/29/31) dataset adds a prior mismatch that log loss penalizes, so expect a small regression, partly hidden by hogwild run-to-run noise.

Out-of-fold selection of w protects against harm, since it can fall back to w=1, which is LR alone. ComplementNB on the same TF-IDF features with alpha=0.1 is probably a weaker (~0.45-0.5) and less sharp model, but its errors are partly independent of LR's, so the selected w should land around 0.7-0.9 for a modest gain of ~2-4%. The 5 extra LR fits should stay under the 15-minute kill.

Multinomial NB with tuned alpha (likely 0.05–0.1) ranks texts about as well as logistic regression on these short sentences, but it is worse calibrated. The independence assumption over-counts the heavily redundant stacked char and word n-gram evidence, and alpha is only a crude confidence knob, so expect roughly 0.42–0.45 log loss versus the parent's 0.355.

Dropping the char_wb 2-5 block loses most of the stylistic signal (punctuation like ; and ", the single-letter words I/a that the default token pattern discards, and subword cues for out-of-vocabulary words), and char n-grams are consistently strong on Spooky, so a word-only NB-SVM should land around 0.44-0.47 rather than 0.41.

ComplementNB(alpha=1) on L2-normalized TF-IDF (~130k features) gives over-smoothed, complement-diluted log-odds (roughly 0.5-0.7x MNB's) and has no class prior, so its probabilities are underconfident and uncalibrated; its ranking is NB-level, below the LR-calibrated NB-SVM, so log loss should regress to about 0.5-0.6.

C=1 is likely too much regularization for L2-normalised word and char TF-IDF scored on log loss, so 3-fold CV should pick C≈3–10, sharpening predictions and using weak n-gram cues better, for roughly 0.03–0.04 lower log loss; two CV fits should finish in time, with a small risk of a slow run.

Multinomial NB with alpha=0.1 on the same word+char TF-IDF features should reach roughly the same accuracy as the logistic regression, but it counts the correlated evidence from unigrams, bigrams and char n-grams more than once, so its probabilities come out somewhat overconfident and log loss likely ends slightly worse than the C=1 LR (about 0.43-0.47), while the MinMax-scaled style features are negligible.

fastText with char n-grams and bigrams should match or beat the over-regularized C=1 TF-IDF LR on accuracy, but 25 epochs at lr=0.5 with no early stopping or regularization makes its softmax overconfident on 17.6k short sentences, so misclassified rows cost a lot and log loss most likely ends up worse (~0.45–0.55).

At C=1, logistic regression on two stacked L2-normalized TF-IDF blocks is over-regularized: it gives soft predictions and under-weights strong cues like character names, so 5-fold CV should pick C≈4–8 (likely 8, the top of the grid), and on Spooky that usually lowers log loss by about 8–12%; running the 30 fits in parallel with joblib should keep the run inside the time limit.

The NB log-ratio scaling acts like a per-feature C_eff = 4*r^2. That gives class-specific words, names and char n-grams much weaker regularization than the likely underfit C=1 baseline, while neutral features are suppressed. Adding alpha=1 smoothing on TF-IDF-scale sums keeps rare-feature ratios modest, which limits overconfidence. One-vs-rest fitting plus renormalization costs a little calibration, so I expect a moderate net improvement to about 0.40.

The added features carry little new signal, so expect a small gain of about 0.002. Punctuation and word-shape cues are already in the char_wb n-grams. The '!', hyphen and digit columns are probably all-zero in this normalised text. MaxAbs scaling against extreme train outliers (4663 chars) shrinks the length and count features toward zero under C=1's L2 penalty. Only capitalisation (lost to lowercase=True) and the word-length stats add new information, with no real overfitting risk from about 28 extra weights on 17.6k rows.

NB log-count-ratio scaling loosens regularization on discriminative n-grams such as names and author-specific phrases and shrinks non-discriminative ones, which helps the underfit C=1 TF-IDF model; renormalized one-vs-rest probabilities and the down-weighted char block give some of that gain back, so I expect a moderate net improvement.

L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF logistic regression at C=1 is already on the underfit, underconfident side for this data (optimum is likely around C=3–10). Cutting C 4x roughly halves the test logits and shrinks the weights on rare author cues like character names and dialect, so the 3-class log loss should rise substantially rather than improve.

At C=1 the NB-logistic model is underfit; dropping the word block removes word-bigram and whole-word cues and roughly halves the NB-scaled feature mass, so predictions get softer and somewhat less accurate (an estimated 0.03–0.08 log-loss regression); char_wb still keeps names, punctuation and single-letter words, so it does not collapse.

Removing the NB log-count ratios takes away the per-feature boost on strongly author-exclusive words (r^2 of about 2-15), so at C=1 plain unit-norm TF-IDF LR is the familiar over-regularized, under-confident model (word-only gives about 0.57-0.60 on Spooky), and the extra effective scale from stacking the char block only partly offsets this.

Stacked L2-normalised word and char TF-IDF features have small values, so they need large weights. C=4 is probably at or a little below the log-loss optimum for LR here, so halving C should make predictions more under-confident and push loss up by about 0.015–0.025. The mlflow tracking and dtype edits do not affect predictions.

NB log-count weighting is known to help on short-sentence, vocabulary-driven text like this: it shifts regularization toward author-specific words and names and away from uninformative n-grams, which should beat the C=4 multinomial LR; the gain is partly offset by one-vs-rest normalization and some overconfidence from rare features whose ratios and weights both come from the same training rows; the code looks correct and should finish well within the time limit.

At C=1 this sublinear-TF-IDF model is likely already under-fit, since the useful C range for these features is about 2–10. Cutting C to 0.25 pushes the weights toward a class-centroid direction and shrinks the rare discriminative n-grams (names, dialect words) the most. Temperature scaling can fix the overall confidence but not that direction loss, and the needed temperature may hit the 0.25 floor. Expect a moderate log-loss increase of about 0.03.

The 'char' analyzer mostly keeps what 'char_wb' captures and adds n-grams that span word boundaries, i.e. punctuation and function-word sequences such as '; and' and ', which', which are useful style cues for telling these authors apart. The 60k max_features cap now drops rarer within-word fragments, but the word TF-IDF block still covers names and rare words, and C=1 leans on frequent features anyway. Net effect should be a small improvement.

The C=1 TF-IDF LR baseline is clearly underfit (per-feature contributions are tiny), and NB log-count-ratio scaling loosens regularization on discriminative cues like names and dialect words by roughly r² while shrinking rare and neutral n-grams. I expect a real discrimination gain, partly given back by one-vs-rest sigmoid renormalization and mild overconfidence from computing r on the training data, for a net of about 0.40-0.41.

At C=1 the L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF logistic regression is over-regularized: char features (~0.04 each) and rare cue words like character names are shrunk, so predictions come out underconfident. C=4 should sharpen probabilities and use those features while staying below the C≈10-20 range where this task usually starts to overfit, so I expect roughly a 7-11% log-loss gain.

LogisticRegression at C=1 on L2-normalized TF-IDF is heavily regularized, so its probabilities are likely too soft; a temperature below 1 (around 0.65-0.8), fitted on the 1.76k-row holdout, should sharpen them and cut log loss by about 0.01-0.03, with little lost when reused on the slightly more confident full-data refit and accuracy unchanged.

The metric is RMSE in dollars, so training on log1p and inverting with expm1 predicts roughly the conditional geometric mean, which sits below the conditional mean. That downward bias hurts most in high-variance groups such as zero-distance and airport trips, while the multiplicative-structure and outlier-robustness gains are small. The fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from invalid test rows dilutes the change, so expect a small regression of about 1%.

Using 4x more data from the same shuffled distribution should cut LightGBM's estimation error. Since the model is capped at 1000 trees x 63 leaves and was probably already near 1000 iterations at 1M rows, I expect only about 0.3-0.6 lower MSE on valid rows. The ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows (predicted as mean fare) is unaffected, so overall RMSE should fall modestly, from 4.10 to about 4.05. Runtime should stay around 3-5 minutes.

Airport distances turn JFK flat fares and EWR/LGA long trips into single clean splits, which raw-coordinate trees can only approximate. I expect this to cut error on the ~5.5% of test rows that touch an airport, reducing valid-row RMSE by about 0.06-0.10 (total MSE down about 0.5-0.7). Corrupt rows keep NaN features and still cost about 2.1 RMSE, which dilutes the gain to roughly 1-2.5% overall.

Training L2 on log1p fares and mapping back with expm1 predicts something close to the conditional median rather than the conditional mean, so with no smearing correction every prediction is biased low (a few percent on normal rides, and about $2-3 on the wide-spread NaN-coordinate and zero-distance rows); because the test is a random sample of the training data with the same outliers, this bias adds roughly 0.3-0.6 to the MSE and outweighs any robustness gain, raising RMSE from about 4.19 to about 4.24.

About 1.1% of trips have zero distance but roughly $11 mean fares, far above the ~$5 fares of short trips; the non-decreasing distance constraint stops the model isolating that spike, and LightGBM's basic constraint method also over-restricts distance-location interactions, while 3.6M rows give little regularization benefit, so RMSE should get modestly worse.

Back-transforming log1p predictions gives roughly a conditional median rather than a mean, so predictions are biased low for this right-skewed fare distribution (zero-distance trips, long or airport trips); the bias adds about 0.2-0.35 MSE on valid rows, partly offset by less outlier-chasing, and the 2.1-RMSE floor from invalid rows is unchanged, so RMSE degrades slightly.

In-sample encoding leaks each row's own fare: for singleton route keys (about 1-2% of rows), (y+20*gm)/21 is an exact function of y, so the trees learn to trust the encoding on rare keys. Test and validation rows on unseen keys (count 0, never seen in training, mean equal to gm) then look like 'cheap singleton' trips, and those are mostly long or unusual high-fare rides. The removed log(0.8) count offset was a negligible mismatch, so the net effect is a regression concentrated on rare-route rows.

Fitting squared error on log1p(fare) and back-transforming with expm1 without a smearing correction predicts roughly the conditional geometric mean, which sits 2-4% below the conditional mean that RMSE rewards; the gap is largest on long, airport and zero-distance trips with heavy-tailed fares, which dominate the squared error, while the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from mean-predicted corrupt rows dilutes the change, so expect a small regression of about 1% rather than a gain.

Explicit airport distances let the trees isolate the high-variance, high-fare JFK flat-fare, EWR surcharge and LGA trips (about 5% of rows) and add non-axis-aligned spatial splits, which should cut valid-row MSE by roughly 0.5–0.8 (valid RMSE about 3.6 to 3.5). The fixed corrupt-row floor (about 4.5 MSE) dilutes this, so total RMSE drops only about 0.07.

The biggest gain should come from the roughly 45 test rows with passenger_count=0: their coordinates are valid but they currently get the mean fare (per-row MSE about 95), and the model should predict them at about 15, cutting total MSE by roughly 0.35. The roughly 232 zero or out-of-box coordinate rows should gain only a little, since without location only the subgroup bias and time effects can be learned and the heavy-tailed noise dominates. Training on the NaN rows may cost the valid rows slightly, so net MSE goes from about 17.1 to 16.7 and RMSE to about 4.09.

About 2.1 RMSE of the total comes from the 2.8% corrupt test rows, which keep the mean-fare prediction, and a few extreme fares among the valid rows also stay. Four times more data with the same 1000-tree, 63-leaf cap should cut the valid-row RMSE by roughly 0.05-0.07 (from about 3.62 to 3.56). The float32 read, explicit timestamp format and n_jobs=4 change nothing functionally, and the run fits easily in the time budget, so expect a modest gain of about 1%.

The change should help a little. The out-of-fold encoding is implemented correctly with no leakage, but LightGBM already learns most spatial and airport structure from the raw coordinates, so the route and cell encodings likely improve the valid rows only about 1.5-2.5% (3.62 to about 3.54). The roughly 2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows (predicted as the unchanged mean fare) is untouched, which shrinks the gain in the graded score to about 1.3%.

Training on log1p and back-transforming with expm1 targets the conditional geometric mean, not the arithmetic mean, so predictions are biased low under a raw-dollar RMSE metric; the bias is largest on high-uncertainty rows such as zero-distance trips and on the fallback rows, where the fallback drops from about $11.3 to about $9, so a small net regression is likely.

Bearing, Manhattan distance and the absolute deltas give the tree model trip direction and grid-detour information it could otherwise only approximate from raw coordinates, so RMSE on valid rows should drop by about 1.5-2% (roughly 3.6 to 3.54). The corrupt rows' contribution (a floor of about 2.1 RMSE) is unchanged because the fallback model's features and data split stay the same, which dilutes the overall gain to about 1%.

Distances to the airports and Manhattan let the trees isolate the high-variance airport trips (JFK flat fare, Newark surcharge plus tolls, LaGuardia) with single splits instead of coordinate boxes, so I expect valid-row RMSE to drop about 3% (roughly 3.58 to 3.47). The fixed about 2.1 RMSE floor from mean-predicted corrupt rows dilutes this to about a 2% overall gain, and the extra features add only about a minute of training, well within budget.

RMSE is minimised by the conditional mean, but an L1 objective fits the conditional median, which sits below the mean for right-skewed fares (tolls, traffic, bimodal airport and borough routes, GPS-failure zero-distance trips). That adds roughly 0.4–0.6 to the MSE on valid rows, while the mean-fare fallback for invalid rows is unchanged, so the overall RMSE should rise modestly and not improve.

Fitting on log1p and inverting with expm1 estimates the conditional geometric mean rather than the mean, so predictions are biased low, mostly where fares are noisy and right-skewed (zero-distance rides, outliers in the uncleaned test labels); for raw-dollar RMSE this adds bias² that outweighs any small robustness gain, and the ~2.1 floor from mean-fare fallback rows is unchanged, so expect a small regression.

The grader's test rows are a random sample of the same noisy training data, so the conditional mean (L2) is RMSE-optimal. L1 instead predicts the conditional median, which sits low in the right-skewed fare distributions (traffic time, tolls, zero-distance GPS failures, airport mixtures), adding a squared-bias term of roughly 0.4–0.9 to the valid-row MSE of about 13. The invalid-row mean-fare floor is unchanged and RMSE-based early stopping limits other damage, giving an overall regression of about 1–3%.

LightGBM's Huber objective with alpha=1 is nearly L1 here (median residual size is about $1–1.5), so it fits close to the conditional median of right-skewed fares rather than the RMSE-optimal mean. Its clipped gradients with unit Hessian also cap movement at about $0.05 per tree, so after 1000 trees starting from $11.3, high fares (Newark, long trips, post-2012 JFK) stay underpredicted; the small robustness gain does not offset either bias, giving a moderate RMSE regression.

Training on log1p(fare) and back-transforming with expm1 and no smearing correction predicts roughly the conditional geometric mean, which sits below the conditional mean that raw-dollar RMSE rewards. It also shifts model capacity away from the expensive rides that dominate squared error, so expect a small loss (~+0.2–0.5 MSE on the valid rows), diluted by the unchanged ~2.1 floor from corrupt rows.

Airport distances and flags make the airport flat-fare/surcharge effects (JFK, EWR) and some oblique spatial structure easier for a 1000-tree LightGBM to learn, which likely cuts valid-row RMSE by about 0.1 (from ~3.6 to ~3.5). The fallback model and its predictions for the ~2.8% corrupt rows are unchanged, so the ~2.1 RMSE floor dilutes the total gain to about 2%.

About 2.1 RMSE of the score comes from corrupt test rows that more data cannot fix; on the valid rows (about 3.62 RMSE), 4x more data should cut the learnable excess error (better spatial, airport and Newark structure, less noise-fitting per tree), but the 1000-tree cap limits the gain, so valid-row MSE drops by roughly 0.4-0.7 and total RMSE lands near 4.06-4.08.

Averaging five 800k-row fold models instead of using one 900k-row model gives a modest variance reduction on the valid rows (about 3.62 to 3.59 RMSE); the corrupt test rows are still predicted as the mean fare and keep a fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor, which dilutes the gain to roughly 0.4-0.5% overall.

The leak-free out-of-fold pickup-cell target encoding is mostly redundant with raw pickup coordinates plus distance, since the GBM already learns airports and other coarse spatial effects; it adds only a small, finer-grained spatial and GPS-failure signal, and the roughly 2.1 RMSE floor from mean-filled corrupt test rows dilutes any valid-row gain further, so expect only a ~0.5% improvement.

Snapping every coordinate to a 0.01° grid (about 0.84 x 1.1 km) before computing haversine distance destroys the main signal: distance error has roughly 0.4 km std, which at about $2.4/km adds about 1 $² of MSE. Same-cell short trips also merge with the 1.1% identical-coordinate trips, and the route encoding gains nothing at the same resolution, so overall MSE rises by about 1.2 (17.0 to about 18.2) while the 2.1-RMSE floor from invalid rows stays fixed.

An L1 objective makes the model predict the conditional median, and taxi fares are right-skewed (traffic time, tolls, zero-distance and airport trips), so the median sits below the mean. Under RMSE that bias likely adds about 0.4–0.6 to the clean-row MSE, while the ~2.1 RMSE floor from mean-filled corrupt rows stays fixed, giving roughly a 1–2% regression.

The test labels contain the same anomalies as training, so RMSE is minimised by the conditional mean. The L1 objective instead learns the conditional median, which is biased low on skewed or bimodal cases such as tolls, airport flat fares, zero-distance GPS failures and traffic delays. That extra error outweighs the small robustness gain from 1M rows with min_child_samples=100, and the 2.8% of test rows predicted as the mean fare stay unchanged and dilute the effect.

Distances to JFK, LGA and EWR let the trees isolate flat-fare and surcharge airport trips with one split each, but raw coordinates already approximate these regions; the gain lands only on the ~5% of test rows that are airport trips, and the 2.1 floor from the mean-fare fallback rows stays fixed, so expect a modest gain of about 0.03-0.07 RMSE.

An L1 objective targets the conditional median, but RMSE rewards the conditional mean, so this should make the score worse. Taxi fares are right-skewed and often bimodal given the features (traffic, tolls, airport flat fares plus tolls, zero-distance trips). That should add roughly 0.5–0.8 to MSE on the valid rows. The fixed floor of about 2.1 RMSE from corrupt rows, which still get the unchanged mean fallback, dilutes the effect. Net result: about 4.13 → about 4.21.

Rounding to 0.01 degrees (about 1 km) throws away sub-km Manhattan detail, such as trip direction against the street grid and river or park edges, but costs few dollars because distance stays exact and the big location effects (airports, NJ, boroughs) are coarse; with little overfitting at 2M rows there is no regularization gain, and the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row floor dilutes the change, so expect a small degradation.

Training on L1 targets the conditional median, but RMSE is minimised by the conditional mean. Taxi fares are right-skewed given the features (traffic delays, tolls, airport extras, zero-distance GPS-failure trips), so predictions will be biased low. That should add roughly 0.5-0.8 to the valid-row MSE, while the mean-fare floor on the 2.8% invalid rows stays the same, giving a modest regression of about 1-3%.

A grid-rotated (29°) Manhattan distance gives real new information about route length that LightGBM can't easily build from four raw coordinates plus haversine, so valid-row MSE should drop by roughly 0.2–0.5, but about 4.4 MSE from corrupt test rows predicted at the mean fare dilutes this to a total-RMSE gain of only ~0.03–0.04.

The out-of-fold, smoothed directional route fare adds pickup-by-dropoff interaction information the baseline lacks (airport flat fares, tolls, and grid direction or traffic per cell pair), and the cross-fitting avoids leakage, so the 97% valid rows should improve by about 0.05–0.15 RMSE; the roughly 2.1 RMSE floor from the about 2.8% invalid rows, which get the mean fare either way, is unchanged, so the total moves only modestly.

The 29° rotation is correctly aligned with Manhattan's avenues and streets, so the grid L1 distance tracks driving distance better than haversine for most trips, a direction effect that trees struggle to learn from raw coordinates. It mainly reduces error on ordinary trips, though, while about half the valid-row MSE comes from outliers and the roughly 2.1 floor from invalid rows is unchanged, so I expect only a modest total gain of about 0.03–0.04 RMSE.

Doubling the clean training prefix to about 1.95M rows mostly cuts variance, but the tree budget stays capped at 1000 and the 255-bin coordinate resolution is unchanged, so valid-row RMSE should fall only by about 0.02-0.04 (from roughly 3.6). The unchanged corrupt-row floor of about 2.1 RMSE dilutes that gain, the added MLflow and logging code does not affect predictions, and runtime stays well within budget.

The implementation is correct: fixed categories in train and test, and the categorical column is passed to LightGBM properly. The airport-route flag gives one clean split for JFK flat fares, the Newark surcharge and LGA trips, which raw coordinates only approximate with several axis-aligned splits. However, raw coordinates already capture much of this, airport trips are only about 5.5% of test rows, and the roughly 2.1-RMSE floor from corrupt rows (predicted as the mean either way) is untouched. I therefore expect a modest gain of about 0.3 MSE, taking overall RMSE from 4.138 to about 4.10.

In this competition the key signal is diagonal sums such as f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22 and f_00+f_01+f_26, which the MLP learns directly but axis-aligned trees only approximate, and neither model gets the unique-character count. LightGBM at 2,000 rounds with lr 0.05 is also still under-converged (the README notes it was still improving at 3,000), and declaring the letters categorical is roughly neutral versus ordinal, so the score should land around 0.98, slightly below the MLP's 0.9866.

Decile one-hot coding throws away within-bin precision on the continuous features, which carry most of the signal. It also prevents the linear first layer from computing exact diagonal sums such as f_02+f_21, whose thresholds sit in the widest tail bins. Duplicate quantile edges also collapse f_29 to a single constant bin and merge f_30=1 with f_30=2, so those features lose information too. At AUC around 0.987 this kind of quantization noise should cost roughly 1–2 AUC points.

After standardization, the many uncorrelated features (count columns, the f_27 character ordinals, f_29/f_30) all have variance 1, so PCA picks arbitrary, noise-driven eigenvectors and effectively applies a random rotation. That blurs the discrete, axis-aligned character and unique-letter-count signal and the threshold-on-sum interactions that boosted trees depend on, leaving mostly the weak linear signal plus some additive nonlinearity, so AUC should drop sharply, somewhere around 0.78–0.88.

f_27 is almost unique per row (about 72% of test strings never appear in train), so the out-of-fold target encoding equals the prior for most rows and holds only a weak signal from a single repeat. Dropping the per-character ordinals loses the per-position effects and the model's partial proxy for the distinct-letter count, which separates rows at roughly 9% vs 91% positive. Expect a drop of about 2–4 AUC points.

f_27 is close to unique per row: about 72% of test strings never appear in train, and the rest have counts of at most 10, so with m=20 the smoothed full-string target encoding is nearly the prior and adds only a weak, slightly train/test-shifted frequency signal. Dropping the ten per-position character columns removes real per-position main effects (for example position 6), and keeping f_27_nunique recovers only its ternary tail signal, so AUC should drop by roughly 1.5–3 points.

These are the known TPS-May-22 interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26 with thresholds near ±5). Trees can only approximate diagonal sum boundaries with axis-aligned staircases, and the baseline was still improving at 3000 trees, so giving the model the sums and ternary indicators directly should cut the remaining ranking error substantially (roughly 30-40%) without any change to the model.

A logistic regression on these features (linear correlations at most 0.13, with the signal living in interactions) should reach only about 0.70-0.76 AUC, and its information is a subset of what LightGBM already uses; equal-weight rank averaging gives it as much say as the 0.984 model, so its rank noise flips many correctly ordered pairs, and binormal estimates put the blend near 0.92-0.94.

The 64-64-64-16 SiLU MLP on standardized inputs with Adam at lr 0.01 and batch 4096 is close to the known strong TPS-May-22 setup. It models the linear and threshold-on-sum structure better than an under-trained 3000-tree LightGBM. The unique-character count is still missing and has to be inferred indirectly from the letter positions, and training is only 80 epochs on a single holdout. So I expect a modest gain to about 0.989, not the ~0.998 reached with the full features.

A swish MLP picks up the linear-sum threshold interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) and the smooth additive structure far better than trees, so it should clearly beat the 0.977 GBDT. It still lacks the non-additive unique-character signal it can't compute from ordinals, and 60 epochs is fewer than the ~200 of the reference recipe, so it lands below the ~0.998 of fully engineered NNs.

The data is nearly deterministic and the baseline is still limited by under-fitting (still improving at 3000 trees), and the signal largely comes from functions of feature sums, so linear leaves should speed convergence and fit oblique boundaries better; the run should also finish within budget (about 1.5x slower). The gain is likely small because the missing unique-character-count signal stays hard to learn, and the near-unregularized leaf fits (lambda 0.01, at least 100 rows, about 10 branch features) add noise, which may also trigger early stopping on logloss sooner.

Counting distinct letters across 10 ordinal columns is very hard for axis-aligned trees, and the count carries a strong signal (9% positive at 2-3 letters vs 91% at 7-8), so supplying it directly should close roughly half of the gap to about 0.998, with the diagonal f_02+f_21-type interactions still missing.

These three sums are the known TPS-May-2022 diagonal interactions; I recall that giving them explicitly to GBDTs helped a lot, since axis-aligned trees only approximate the f_00+f_01+f_26 plane and the two 2-D lines with a staircase, but the gain is capped because the much bigger missing signal (distinct-letter count of f_27) is still absent, so I expect about +0.004 to +0.006 AUC.

The new f_27 categorical will almost certainly never be split on: its ~670k near-unique strings collapse into LightGBM's 'other' bin, and no category clears cat_smooth=10 or min_data_per_group=100, so the change mostly just deletes the 10 per-position ordinals; the letter counts and nunique cannot recover position-specific effects (binary positions, position 6), so I expect a moderate AUC drop.

Adjacent-pair bigrams are deterministic functions of the per-position ordinals, which the trees already combine, and the letter counts plus nunique already capture f_27's real signal, so the bigrams add no new information. The remaining error comes from the diagonal continuous interactions (f_02/f_21, f_05/f_22, f_00/f_01/f_26), which bigrams do not address. LightGBM's gradient-sorted categorical splits on 30-255-level features tend to pick up some noise in deep nodes late in boosting, so I expect roughly a wash with a slight downward drift. The run should finish well inside the time budget.

f_00..f_15 is mostly independent unit-variance continuous and count features, so PCA(8) gives near-arbitrary rotations; neither those nor the dropped products touch the f_19-f_26 sum interactions that matter, so the change is roughly neutral, with a slight dip expected because the parent was kept as the best run so far (likely partly by luck).

Wrapping each string as [s] makes FeatureHasher hash the whole 10-char code into 1 of 64 buckets. These are effectively random one-hot noise columns: about 10k unrelated strings share each bucket and 72% of test strings are unseen. So all f_27 signal (per-position letters, the unique-letter-count tails at 9% and 91%) is lost and only the numeric features and products remain. That should give a sizeable regression to roughly 0.93-0.95, with the noise columns themselves costing little.

On this synthetic data the signal is spread across about 30 weakly-marginal features, with diagonal pair/sum interactions and the f_27 distinct-letter count. Fully grown ExtraTrees with sqrt(41)≈6 random features and random thresholds act like a coarse adaptive nearest-neighbour vote. That captures far less of this structure than 3000 boosted 127-leaf trees, so AUC should land around default-GBDT level (~0.92-0.94) rather than 0.978. The runtime is also borderline: the 5-fold CV runs before the submission is written, which risks the hard kill at 15 minutes.

This dataset is known to favour neural nets, because the f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22 and f_00+f_01+f_26 diagonal step interactions, plus sums of letter values that stand in for the unique-letter count, are linear combinations a standardized MLP learns easily and trees only approximate with staircases. That gain is roughly cancelled by sklearn MLP's limits: constant LR, at most 40 epochs (about 14k Adam steps), noisy accuracy-based early stopping, training on 90% of rows, and no explicit unique-count feature. The run should finish in time, and I expect a roughly flat result with a wide spread of about ±0.007.

The distinct-letter count of f_27 is a strong signal (about 9% positive rate at 2-3 distinct letters vs about 91% at 7-8). Trees can only approximate it from the per-position categoricals, so supplying it directly should close much of the gap toward the roughly 0.99-0.993 seen with chars + nunique and no interaction features. The letter counts add little extra, and the run stays well within the time budget.

Dropping the ten per-position f_27 features removes the most informative feature group. Rare and high letters, and position-6 letters, swing the positive rate from 0.10 to 1.00, and the letters implicitly carry the unique-letter signal. The full-string count is mostly 1 (about 70% of rows are singletons) and only weakly tracks letter rarity, so it recovers little. The result should fall to roughly the numeric-only LightGBM level of about 0.93, versus 0.977 now.

The distinct-letter count of f_27 is a strong signal that trees struggle to build from the per-position ordinals: ~9% positive at 2-3 unique letters vs ~91% at 7-8, a step-like effect on ~7.6% of rows. Adding it explicitly, plus the mostly redundant per-letter counts, should give a solid gain. The missing diagonal sum-threshold interactions still cap the GBDT around ~0.98.

The products only cover f_00..f_15 (7 continuous plus 9 count features) and miss f_19..f_26, so none of the dataset's known sum-type interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) can be represented; the 25 added columns are mostly redundant or noise, so 65 features instead of 40 should cost the not-yet-converged 3000-tree model a little through wasted splits, with runtime still well within budget.

The holdout AUC is still rising at 3000 trees and this raw-feature GBDT is data-hungry, so refitting on all 800k rows with about 3333 trees should add a modest +0.0005 to +0.001 AUC with no overfitting risk. Runtime is about 2.2x the baseline training, which likely still fits the budget.

LightGBM's gradient-sorted categorical splits on the 14-20 letter positions can capture equality and distinct-letter patterns more efficiently than threshold splits, but the letter codes are already roughly ordinal (rarer letters push the target up). Also, cat_l2 and cat_smooth regularize the categorical splits, and the dominant missing signal is the continuous-feature interactions, so I expect only a small gain.

The distinct-letter count is a real step-like signal (about 9%, 48% and 91% positive rate in its three bands, covering roughly 7.6% of rows strongly). Trees on per-position ordinals cannot compute set cardinality because it depends on equalities between positions, so they only approximate it; making it explicit should cut 1-AUC by roughly 25-35% (about 0.018 to 0.013), the size of gain this feature gave in the original competition.

Capping trees at depth 2 (four leaves) turns the model into main effects plus pairwise terms. That cannot represent the higher-order f_27 unique-character structure, and it fits the oblique f_02+f_21 and f_05+f_22 bands only slowly. The 127-leaf model is still improving at 3000 trees, so 3000 four-leaf trees will be badly underfit and AUC should drop to roughly 0.90.

A small LightGBM (600 trees, 31 leaves, lr 0.05, max_bin 63) on raw features has no unique-character count and no sum interactions, so axis-aligned splits approximate the diagonal f_02+f_21-style boundaries slowly. It should finish all 600 trees well inside the budget but land around 0.94–0.95, below the MLP's 0.982, which learns linear-combination interactions natively.

A small LightGBM (600 trees, 31 leaves, lr 0.05, max_bin 63) on raw features plus f_27 ordinals has no distinct-letter count and no sum-interaction features, so it has to approximate the diagonal decision boundaries with staircases and stays far from converged; on this dataset such GBDTs land around 0.92–0.95, well below the MLP that learns the linear combinations directly.

In TPS-May-22 much of the signal comes from interactions among the 16 float columns, including oblique, tail-located boundaries such as f_02+f_21 and f_00+f_01+f_26, and only an estimated ~25-30% from f_27, so cutting them from about 255 histogram bins to 4 quartile codes should keep roughly half of that signal (only ~25-35% for the tail boundaries), dropping AUC from 0.977 to around 0.90 (plausible range 0.85-0.95).

This dataset's signal comes from interactions: diagonal sum thresholds such as f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22 and f_00+f_01+f_26, plus the multi-position f_27 unique-letter count. Trees with 7 leaves allow only about 6 splits each, so they approximate these much more coarsely than 127-leaf trees, and 3000 trees at lr 0.05 (about 18k splits in total) leave the model badly underfit, given the 127-leaf model was still improving at 3000. Expect a clear drop of several AUC points, to roughly 0.94-0.955.

4-leaf trees can only represent interactions among about 3 features each. This data's signal comes from interactions (diagonal threshold ridges and other continuous-feature interactions), and even the 127-leaf model was still improving at 3000 rounds, so a 4-leaf model at lr 0.05 will be heavily underfit at the same 3000-tree cap and should lose roughly 2–3 AUC points.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known diagonal threshold interactions in TPS May 2022 (target probability jumps when the sum passes about ±5). Trees can only approximate a 3-D diagonal boundary with many axis-aligned splits, and this model is still undertrained at 3000 trees, so making the boundary a single split should clearly help. I put the gain at roughly a third to half of the ~0.005 AUC the full interaction set is known to add, about +0.002.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known threshold interactions in TPS-May22, with steps near ±5. Axis-aligned trees only roughly approximate a 3-way diagonal boundary, and the model is still undertrained at 3000 trees. Giving it the raw sum lets it split at the thresholds directly, which should be a solid gain of about +0.003–0.004 AUC. The gain stays modest because this is only one interaction, and the missing nunique feature and the other two interactions still limit the score.

An MLP picks up the linear-combination interactions in this dataset (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) that trees only approximate, and it can partly learn the distinct-letter count from the ordinals through pairwise-difference units. But it gets no explicit unique-count feature and only 50 epochs at lr 1e-3 with an aggressive plateau schedule, so it should beat the 0.977 LightGBM baseline without reaching the ~0.997+ of fully engineered models.

LightGBM's gradient-sorted categorical splits can group arbitrary letter subsets, which helps a little with the equality-based distinct-letter interaction that ordinal thresholds model poorly. The gain should be small: the letters are count-like, so ordinal order already fits well; the binary positions are unaffected; rare-letter handling and cat_l2 add slight noise; and the continuous diagonal interactions, which limit this model most, are untouched.

The distinct-letter count is a step-like signal (positive rate ~9% at 3 or fewer letters, ~91% at 7 or more), but trees cannot build it from 10 per-position ordinals because it needs equality checks across positions; adding it directly should recover a large share of the missing f_27 signal, though the sum-threshold interactions stay unmodeled, so I expect roughly +0.005 to +0.009 AUC.

Weighted MSE misaligns the training objective with the unweighted RMSE metric; the model trades slightly more background/stain error for stroke fidelity, and on a dataset where background dominates the metric this typically yields a small regression rather than a gain.

Training ~5-10x more steps with a properly annealed cosine schedule on a small U-Net that was clearly undertrained at 2000 steps should give a solid gain; every-100-step full-image validation eats some budget but the net effect is a meaningful RMSE reduction, with diminishing returns limiting it to roughly 0.013-0.015.
L1 vs MSE on this denoising task typically yields near-identical RMSE; L1 may sharpen edges slightly but the metric is RMSE which MSE directly optimizes, so expect a wash within seed noise.

Input-only brightness/contrast jitter creates a train/test distribution mismatch (test scans share the exact photometric statistics of train, and absolute intensity is a strong cue for paper vs. ink in this synthetic-noise task), so the augmentation mostly adds label noise and slightly hurts RMSE rather than helping.

Multi-scale TTA on a network trained at a single scale for this near-binary text denoising task tends to blur thin strokes (downscale/upscale resampling of the 0.75x and 1.25x maps) and introduce scale-mismatch errors that averaging doesn't cancel, so a slight regression is more likely than a gain.

Dropout2d at p=0.2 in a short 2000-step denoising run mostly injects train/eval mismatch and slows convergence; pixel-regression denoisers rarely benefit from dropout, so expect a small regression rather than a gain.

Channel dropout in every block of a small regression U-Net adds noise to dense pixel prediction and slows convergence within the fixed 180s budget; this task is not overfitting-limited, so RMSE likely worsens modestly.

Larger receptive field helps model background/stain gradients that the 41px RF struggles with, and per-step cost rise is modest under a 180s wall-clock budget; expect a small gain, with some risk of neutral outcome from fewer steps.

A median-filter background channel gives the 128px-receptive-field U-Net explicit global background context it otherwise lacks, which typically helps on this dataset's smooth stains/shading, though the effect is modest since the net already captures most local structure; implementation is correct and cost negligible.

Deeper U-Net with larger receptive field should better model low-frequency stains/background in this dataset, likely a modest gain; but batch 8 with BatchNorm and only 2000 steps adds variance and the 5-level net could slightly overfit 105 images, so improvement is small.
Flip TTA on a model trained with flip augmentation gives a small, reliable variance reduction on a regression metric; typically a few percent RMSE improvement with negligible runtime cost.

180s wall-clock budget likely gives several times the 2000 baseline steps for this tiny UNet on a GPU, with cosine-to-zero annealing intact; longer training typically lowers RMSE moderately on this small-data denoising task, with diminishing returns and some overfit risk on 105 train images.

Charbonnier/L1 typically gives sharper images but the metric is RMSE, which MSE directly optimizes; with a strong residual U-Net already at 0.0152, the mismatch between L1 objective and L2 metric plus the 1e-3 epsilon making gradients near-constant for small errors likely yields a slight RMSE regression, though noise across seeds could swamp the difference.

Adding sigma=0.05 Gaussian noise to inputs creates a train/test mismatch: test images have no such noise, so the model learns to over-smooth fine text strokes (residual head now must also suppress high-frequency detail), slightly raising RMSE; the dataset's noise is structured stains, not iid Gaussian, so the regularization benefit is small.

GroupNorm removes the BN train/test stat mismatch but typically converges slower and slightly worse than BN under a short 2000-step Adam budget on small U-Nets, so I expect a small regression or roughly neutral result rather than a gain.

Metric is RMSE, so training directly on MSE is already Bayes-optimal for it; SSIM+L1 tends to produce crisper but not MSE-optimal outputs (L1 pushes toward median, SSIM ignores small luminance offsets), typically costing a few percent RMSE on this task.

8-fold dihedral TTA on a U-Net trained with flip augmentation typically gives a small but consistent variance-reduction gain (~2-4% RMSE); rotations by 90 are unseen in training but text/noise statistics are fairly orientation-agnostic for the denoising target, so the average still helps modestly.

Metric is RMSE; pure SSIM loss is insensitive to low-frequency luminance offsets and background level bias in large flat white regions, so predictions drift from exact intensities and per-pixel RMSE typically worsens versus direct MSE optimization despite sharper strokes.

Residual learning with linear head removes sigmoid saturation on the near-white background and starts from identity; typically a modest gain for document denoising at this training budget, though the baseline is already strong and TTA averaging limits headroom.

Switching from MSE to sqrt(MSE)+0.1*(1-SSIM) changes gradient scaling (RMSE gradient blows up near small errors with 1e-8 eps) and adds a term misaligned with the RMSE metric; with the existing setup already at ~0.0165 the mismatch likely costs slightly, though effect is small.

Residual learning removes the sigmoid's natural saturation toward the white/black extremes that dominate this task's targets; the noise here is large-scale (stains, folds) rather than small additive noise, so identity init and unbounded output give little stabilization benefit and tend to yield slightly worse RMSE with the same short schedule.

Synthetic corruptions (blurred ellipse stains, bicubic shading, speckle) don't match the competition's real noise and dilute real pairs 6:1 under a fixed 2000-step budget, so the model spends most of its capacity on off-distribution examples and mildly regresses.

4.5x more steps with stretched cosine schedule on a small U-Net typically yields a modest but real gain in this regime (baseline at 2k steps is undertrained); risk of overfitting on 105 images is low with random crops, so expect ~0.0145 unless the run times out.

Dihedral TTA is a reliable small win for denoising regression (variance reduction on a fully convolutional net); transpose views are slightly out-of-distribution for text but flips were trained, so expect a modest ~3-5% RMSE drop with negligible runtime cost.

L1 with sigmoid outputs on a near-binary target pushes toward median-like sharp predictions and gives constant-magnitude gradients that don't shrink near convergence; on an RMSE-graded task with only 2000 CPU steps this typically trains slightly worse than MSE, so a small regression is most likely.

Weighting the loss away from the evaluation metric (plain MSE) typically hurts slightly: the model trades accuracy on the dominant white-paper pixels for glyph pixels, and with a small effective weight change (3x) the shift is modest but net negative under per-pixel RMSE; the CPU execution.json also risks a slower run but same epochs.

Weighting ink 10x misaligns the training objective with the unweighted RMSE metric; background pixels dominate the score, so slightly worse background reconstruction likely outweighs ink gains, yielding a small regression.

Residual (noisy + correction) parameterization with zero-init head starts at identity and typically speeds/improves denoising convergence with a short 2000-step budget; removing the sigmoid risks slight overshoot but clamping at inference handles it, so a modest RMSE gain is most likely (assuming the run finishes under the same CPU/GPU setup as the parent).

L1 loss on a metric graded by RMSE typically hurts slightly: it optimizes the median and de-emphasizes the large residuals that dominate squared error, though for near-binary document targets the gap is small; expect a mild regression.

Residual output without sigmoid loses the saturating output that helps hit exact 0/1 pixel values; document denoising involves large deviations (dark stains, faded text) rather than small residuals, so zero-init residual on CPU with only 2000 steps likely converges slightly worse or comparable.
Halving channel width cuts capacity roughly 4x; the CNN is not overfitting at 2000 steps, so the smaller net converges to a somewhat higher RMSE, a modest regression.

Weighted MSE misaligns training objective with the unweighted RMSE metric; upweighting dark pixels trades background accuracy for stroke accuracy, typically yielding a small regression given the metric is dominated by abundant white pixels; the runtime.json also forces CPU, though the loss change itself is the main driver.

Grey-closing background-normalized channel gives the U-Net an explicit illumination-corrected view that a 3-level net with limited receptive field struggles to derive, typically yielding a modest RMSE gain; risk factors are the forced CPU execution (timeout if a GPU was previously used) and that the net already learns much of this, so improvement is small rather than dramatic.

The runtime.toml forces CPU-only execution, so autocast was/is disabled and the fp32 head is a no-op; expect essentially the same score with only run-to-run noise (risk of timeout if the hill was previously on GPU).

Flip TTA with flip-augmented training gives a small, reliable variance reduction (~1-3% RMSE), though the sneaky runtime.json forcing CPU-only training adds real risk of slowdown/timeout without changing the metric if it completes.

A compact residual NAFNet with zero-init branch scales should train stably in 2000 steps and match or slightly beat the 32-ch U-Net, but width-16 capacity, short schedule, patch-vs-full-image global-pool attention mismatch, and forced CPU execution (timeout risk) limit the gain to a small improvement.

The in1k-fine-tuned ConvNeXt head already classifies these exact 120 breeds (and saw many of these ImageNet images in training), so its temperature-tuned dog softmax is a strong, decorrelated predictor; blending with LR tuned on the holdout should cut log loss meaningfully, with w=0 as a safe floor.

PCA to 256 dims on layer-normed ConvNeXt features discards discriminative low-variance directions useful for fine-grained breeds; L2-regularized LR already handles the 1024-d case well, so a mild regression is most likely.

Mixup/CutMix with prob=1.0 over only 6 short epochs on a small dataset slows fitting and adds bias for a pretrained model; temperature scaling recovers some calibration but expected slight regression in log loss.
With only 6 short epochs, aggressive 0.08 crops add train/eval distribution mismatch and noisy tiny crops that slow convergence more than they regularize; expect a slight regression or no change.

ConvNeXt-V2 Large with IN-22k pretraining gives far more linearly separable features than ResNet-50 V1 on Stanford Dogs (ImageNet-22k models typically reach ~0.15-0.25 log loss with frozen linear probes here); runtime and code path look sound, so a large improvement is expected.

The 1000-d log-softmax block is not redundant in practice: ~118 ImageNet classes are exactly these dog breeds, so the fc layer trained on 1.2M images injects strong breed-discriminative information that a 10k-sample LR on pooled features cannot recover; dropping it should noticeably worsen log loss.

Ridge/least-squares probe with softmax temperature scaling on L2-normalised features is typically somewhat worse-calibrated than a well-tuned multinomial logistic regression for log loss; LR at C up to 30 with lbfgs on 2560-d features converges adequately, so expect a modest regression.

PCA to 128 dims per block discards fine-grained discriminative directions that L2-regularised LR on 10k samples already handles well; unsupervised compression on high-quality frozen features typically slightly hurts log loss, and re-normalisation changes the effective scale so the fixed C grid may be suboptimal.

ConvNeXt-Base in22k-pretrained features are far stronger than ResNet-50 V1 on Stanford Dogs (a subset of ImageNet-22k, so near-leakage); frozen-feature logistic regression typically lands around 0.18-0.25 log loss, with C tuned on holdout.

Fine-tuning an ImageNet-22k pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny with flip TTA and temperature scaling typically reaches ~0.2-0.3 log loss on Stanford Dogs, a large gain over frozen ResNet-50 features; risk is the 7-min guard truncating epochs, but even 3-4 epochs should beat 0.45 comfortably.

The 1000-d ImageNet log-probabilities are a direct breed classifier signal (all 120 breeds are ImageNet classes), and standardization plus re-tuned C on 3048-d features typically cuts log loss noticeably versus raw pooled features; modest risk from the 15% holdout selecting a slightly off C.

Stanford Dogs is in ImageNet-22k/CLIP/DINOv2 pretraining; frozen ConvNeXt-in22k + CLIP + DINOv2 features with L2-norm and tuned C typically reach ~0.12-0.20 log loss versus 0.45 for ResNet-50 V1, and runtime fits the budget.

Focal loss removes label smoothing's calibration benefit and downweights gradient from most examples, yielding somewhat worse-calibrated probabilities; log loss likely regresses modestly (~0.70-0.72).

Stanford Dogs is a subset of ImageNet so the pretrained features are already near-optimal; freezing conv1-layer3 reduces forgetting/overfitting from full fine-tuning at lr=0.01 on ~9k images, likely giving a modest log-loss improvement (layer4+fc still has enough capacity), with BN running stats still adapting.

Horizontal-flip TTA on frozen ViT features with a linear head gives a small, consistent variance reduction; typical gains for log loss at this level are 1-4%, with no plausible regression path since the flipped view is in-distribution for the augreg-trained backbone.

CLIP ViT-B/32 is a weaker fine-grained feature extractor than IN21k-pretrained ViT-B/16 (coarser patches, no exposure to the 120 ImageNet dog classes that IN models were trained on), and the raw un-normalised CLIP feature scale with a fixed C=0.3 is unlikely to be well matched, so the linear probe log loss should regress.

L2-regularized logistic regression already suppresses noise directions, so truncating to 256 unwhitened PCs discards fine-grained discriminative signal (variance-ranked, not label-aware) and typically hurts linear probes on ResNet features; expect a modest log-loss regression.

DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings are far stronger than ResNet-50 for fine-grained breeds; frozen linear probes on Stanford Dogs reach ~90%+ top-1 and roughly halve log loss, with C reselection and 10-view TTA retained.

PCA-256 with whitening amplifies low-variance noise directions and discards discriminative information from the L2-normalized concatenated embeddings; with C=1.0 on whitened unit-variance features the LR is effectively under-regularized, so log loss likely worsens moderately.

Distance-weighted 10-NN yields overconfident, sparse vote probabilities; the ~1e-3 floor makes each misclassified test image (~12-15%) cost ~6-7 nats, so log loss roughly doubles versus the well-calibrated logistic regression.

Full fine-tuning with augmentation and label smoothing typically beats frozen ResNet-50 features on Stanford Dogs, but lr=0.01 on all layers for only 10 epochs with 9k images plus smoothing-induced under-confidence limits the gain; expect a modest improvement to ~0.40.

ViT-B/16 augreg in21k→in1k features are far stronger for fine-grained dogs than ResNet-50 V1 (Stanford Dogs is in ImageNet, in21k pretraining helps a lot); frozen linear probe typically drops log loss substantially, though C=0.3 was tuned for 2048-d ResNet features and may be slightly suboptimal for 768-d ViT features, limiting the gain.

10-crop+flip TTA averaging on frozen ResNet-50 features with a linear head typically gives a modest but reliable log-loss gain (~3-6%); corner crops are slightly off-distribution vs center-crop training but averaging smooths overconfident errors, and runtime stays well within budget.

ConvNeXt-Tiny in22k-pretrained features are far stronger for fine-grained dogs than ResNet-50 V1, and L2-normalized concatenation with C=1.0 logistic regression should cut log loss substantially (roughly 0.45 -> ~0.29), well within the time budget.

The pretrained ResNet-50 V2 ImageNet dog head is a strong, independently trained classifier on the same features; blending it with the LR (with temperature tuned on a holdout) typically gives a meaningful log-loss reduction, though the V2 head is label-smoothed so temperature < 1 will be picked and gains are moderate.
Unwhitened PCA to 256 dims drops discriminative low-variance directions useful for fine-grained breeds, and C=0.3 was tuned for the raw 2048-d features, so log loss likely worsens modestly.

Max-pooled ResNet-50 features are far larger-scale, sparser, and off-distribution from what the final layers were trained for; with unscaled logistic regression at fixed C=0.3 they typically underperform average pooling noticeably for frozen transfer, so log loss should worsen despite temperature calibration.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 features are substantially stronger (80.9 vs 76.1 top-1) and transfer well to fine-grained dog breeds; with C=0.3 and temperature refit, expect a clear log-loss drop, though V2 features have different scale so the gain may be somewhat less than the top-1 gap suggests.

C was already tuned on a holdout (0.3 chosen over 0.03 among the grid); tenfold stronger L2 on unstandardized ResNet features yields an underfit, overly flat initial head, and the short 90s fine-tune at low head LR cannot fully recover the sharpness, so log loss likely worsens modestly.

Dropping input from 224 to 192 reduces fine-grained detail that pretrained ResNet50 features rely on for similar breeds; the rest of the pipeline is unchanged, so log loss likely worsens by roughly 5-15%.

Unwhitened PCA to 256 dims discards fine-grained discriminative variance in ResNet50 features; with C=0.3 tuned for 2048-d raw features, the logistic regression on compressed components typically loses a bit of log loss (roughly +0.01 to +0.03), so a mild regression is expected.
Lower 192px resolution reduces fine-grained detail and shifts the frozen ResNet-50 away from its native 224px training scale, degrading feature quality and worsening log loss by roughly 8-12%.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 is ~5 points stronger on ImageNet (which contains these very dog classes), so frozen pooled features should be more discriminative for a linear probe; gain is tempered because C=0.3 was tuned for V1 feature scale and V2 features are known to transfer only modestly better in linear-probe setups.

C was already tuned for log loss so the LR is nearly calibrated; a single temperature fit on a 15% holdout (from an 85%-data model, applied to the full-data model) yields only a small calibration gain, likely T slightly >1 giving ~1-2% improvement.

Head starts at the regularized LR optimum; two short unregularized, unaugmented CE epochs mostly sharpen already-fit training logits (worse calibration) while tiny-lr conv tuning with frozen BN changes features little, so expect a small log-loss regression rather than a gain.

Horizontal-flip TTA with probability averaging is a reliable small gain for frozen-feature LogReg (typically 2-4% log loss reduction); added mlflow/tempdir scaffolding is fault-tolerant and shouldn't affect the metric.

Balanced undersampling throws away 90-99% of negatives (threat: ~950 rows total), hurting sparse linear models' ranking of the huge negative test population and degrading NB ratios; rare-label AUCs drop most, common labels slightly, so the column mean falls by roughly a point.

Adding char_wb n-grams to the NB-LogReg branch typically lifts that branch a few tenths of a point (char features help on obfuscated/rare-label cases), and the blend gains a modest fraction of that since branch A already has char features; risk of timeout with liblinear on ~136M nnz is real but the diff follows the memory hygiene, so small positive gain expected.

1:1 undersampling throws away 90-99% of negatives per label (threat fits on ~1k rows), degrading ranking of hard negatives and adding variance; AUC does not benefit from rebalancing linear models, so mean AUC drops noticeably, most on rare labels.

MultinomialNB on TF-IDF is much weaker than NB-LogReg (~0.95-0.96 AUC vs ~0.978), and both the 50/50 rank blend and the stacked OOF features into branch A will degrade, so the ensemble drops noticeably despite branch A carrying most of the weight.

Mean-pooled Word2Vec (~0.95-0.96 AUC) is much weaker than word+char TF-IDF LR (~0.98) for toxicity, and the MLP on 200-d dense inputs no longer adds the sparse-feature diversity; NB-LogReg branch B holds the blend up but the rank-average still regresses.

1:1 undersampling throws away 90-99.7% of negatives (threat fits on ~950 rows), degrading ranking of the large negative test tail and NB ratios; imbalance is not a problem for AUC with regularized linear models, so expect a ~1% AUC drop driven by rare labels.

A sparse TF-IDF MLP typically reaches ~0.98 alone and adds nonlinear/shared-hidden diversity to three highly correlated linear branches, giving a small blend gain (~+0.0005-0.001); risk that time guards skip D (no change) or the rare-label noise dilutes it tempers the estimate.

Discarding most negatives removes the information the linear models need to rank the huge benign majority; rare labels (threat, identity_hate) trained on ~1-3k rows will be noisy and overfit, so the mean AUC drops from 0.981 to roughly 0.972-0.975 despite faster fits.

Profanity de-obfuscation, repeat collapsing and IP/URL/timestamp tokens are known small wins for TF-IDF linear models on this data (~+0.0003-0.001), though lowercasing removes the char branch's case signal and shorthand expansion is roughly neutral, so expect a marginal gain.

Feature-level stacking of OOF NB-LogReg into branch A gives A cross-label information and a stronger word-ngram view; with scale /20 and C=0.1 the stacked columns get modest weight, so a small but real gain is likely, though the final blend still re-adds B so the improvement is partly redundant; runtime rises by ~30 liblinear fits but stays within budget.

A 3-epoch multi-label MLP on 60k sparse TF-IDF features adds a modestly diverse nonlinear view; sklearn MLP on sparse CSR is slow but ~2k steps should fit in budget, and equal-weight rank blending of a slightly weaker third model typically yields a small gain (~+0.0005-0.001) on this metric.

Adding an NB-LogReg branch on word+char features gives a third correlated-but-distinct linear view; rank-averaging three linear models typically yields a small AUC gain (~0.0005-0.001), with runtime risk on the 250k-column liblinear fit but capped at 100 iterations.

Per-label holdout-fitted weights shrunk toward 0.5 will deviate only modestly from equal blending; the two branches are similar-strength so gains are tiny, with small risk from noisy rare-label weights, plus runtime roughly doubles but should stay under budget.

Replacing sparse word+char TF-IDF ensembles with a 300-dim LSA + C=1 LogReg discards the lexical precision (specific slurs, misspellings, char n-grams) that drives toxicity AUC; LSA on this task typically lands around 0.94-0.96, a clear regression from 0.980.

Capping negatives at 10:1 throws away 90-97% of training negatives for the rare labels (threat, severe_toxic, identity_hate), degrading hard-negative ranking and NB log-odds estimates in the linear/fastText branches; AUC on rare columns drops, giving a modest overall regression.

Single softmax multi-label fastText shares n-gram weights but forces labels to compete for probability mass and keeps the same saturated/tied low-probability floors on rare labels (threat, identity_hate) that likely drag the current blend; expect roughly neutral effect on the rank average.
Replacing a strong 3-branch TF-IDF LogReg/NB-LogReg rank blend with a single ComplementNB on raw counts drops to classic Naive Bayes territory (~0.92-0.95 mean AUC on this task), a clear regression.

Mean-pooled from-scratch 200d word2vec with a linear head loses the exact-token and char n-gram signal that drives the sparse ensemble; such pipelines historically score ~0.95-0.96 on Jigsaw versus ~0.98 for TF-IDF/NB-LR blends.

Average-pooled corpus Word2Vec into a single logistic regression loses the sparse lexical precision of TF-IDF n-grams and NB-LR; on Jigsaw such dense mean-pooled baselines typically land around 0.94-0.96 AUC, a clear regression from 0.98.

A char-level NB-LogReg adds genuine diversity (obfuscated spellings) to word-heavy branches and rank-blending with holdout-tuned simplex weights typically yields a small but real gain of ~0.0005-0.001 AUC; some overfitting risk on rare labels from the coarse 3-way search, but the added branch is strong enough that net effect should be positive.

Moving branch A from C=0.1 to C=4 matches the reference kernel setting for word+char TF-IDF (~0.978-0.979 alone) and should modestly strengthen the weaker branch; rare labels may overfit a bit more, so blend gain is small and could be near zero.

Supervised fastText with bigrams on this task typically scores ~0.975 AUC alone; as a diverse third member in an equal-weight rank blend it should add a small gain (~+0.0005-0.001), though rare labels (threat) with epoch=20/lr=0.5 may overfit and dilute part of the benefit.

NB-LogReg on char n-grams is a well-known strong diverse view (~0.98 alone) that blends well with word NB-LR and the sag word+char model; small but real gain, with runtime risk from a second char vectorizer on 313k docs plus 6 liblinear primal fits on 100k features.

Losing 10% of training data slightly hurts both linear branches; per-label weights tuned on ~16k holdout rows give small gains on common labels but are noisy for threat/identity_hate, so net effect is roughly neutral to marginally negative.

NB-weighting branch A makes it more correlated with the NB-LogReg branch B, reducing ensemble diversity, and with C=0.1 sag on NB-scaled features the regularization becomes mismatched (sag may also converge poorly on rescaled features), so a small net regression is most likely.

min_df=0.01 on ~313k docs requires ~3,100 document occurrences, pruning vocab to a few thousand common terms and discarding most profanity/slur/threat tokens that drive the rare labels, so AUC drops substantially especially for threat and identity_hate.

Balanced undersampling throws away the vast majority of negatives (e.g. ~159k -> ~1k rows for threat), degrading the ranking of negatives and NB log-count estimates; AUC only needs ranking so imbalance was never a problem, expect a clear regression especially on rare labels.

Cosine class-centroid (Rocchio) classifiers discard discriminative weight learning; on sparse TF-IDF they typically trail logistic regression by 2-4 AUC points, partly mitigated by the NB log-count weighting in branch B and the rank-preserving blend.

char_wb vs char with 50k max_features on 2-6 grams is a near-wash; the original kernel used char_wb and typically scores within ~0.0002 AUC, and the rank blend with branch B further dampens any difference.

Replacing tuned logistic regression with plain ComplementNB on TF-IDF features loses discriminative fitting; NB on this task typically scores ~0.94-0.96 mean AUC, a clear regression from 0.9797 even with rank blending of two branches.

A 32-dim SVD of 60k TF-IDF features discards the sparse lexical cues (profanity tokens/char n-grams) that drive branch A's AUC, so branch A drops from ~0.97 to roughly 0.93-0.95 and its equal-weight rank blend with fastText pulls the ensemble below the current score.

Collapsing everything outside the top-2k tokens to 'raretoken' removes many discriminative obscenities, slurs, and misspellings and neuters the char_wb branch's ability to model them, so AUC drops noticeably, especially on rare labels like identity_hate and threat.

Removing English stop words from the 10k word unigram vocab in branch A adds a few function words (e.g. 'you', 'your') that are mildly toxicity-informative, but char n-grams already capture them and branch A is half of a rank blend, so the effect is a tiny, likely noise-level gain.

Logit averaging weights branches by their calibration spread; NB-LogReg with C=4 produces much more extreme logits than the C=0.1 branch, so the blend tilts toward branch B and loses some of the rank-average's balanced diversity, giving a tiny regression.

Switching char_wb to char with a 50k-feature cap yields slightly different but comparable n-gram sets (cross-word n-grams add a little context, lose some word-boundary padding); in this competition the two analyzers are known to perform nearly identically, and the branch is half of a rank blend, so the net effect is essentially noise-level.

fastText OVA with 5 epochs and no char n-grams is a weaker second branch than NB-LogReg on this task (typically ~0.96-0.97 alone), so the equal-weight rank blend with branch A likely drops slightly below the current 0.9801.

Leaf features are all weakly informative and the LR at C=1 is already well-regularised; dropping 64 of 192 descriptors by univariate F-score discards complementary histogram bins and typically worsens LR log loss on this dataset, which then degrades the 50/50 blend modestly (NN half is unchanged).
