OvR binary fits with 10 positives vs 780 negatives at C=1.0 produce weaker, less separable per-class scores than the joint softmax on this near-linearly-separable data; row-normalisation plus power calibration recovers some but OvR logistic typically loses to multinomial on leaf log loss.

Bagged MLPs on standardized leaf descriptors typically reach ~0.03-0.05 OOF logloss and are diverse from LR; blend with CV-chosen weight and calibration should give a modest improvement, with w=0 fallback limiting downside.

With only 16 samples/class, each fold model sees ~13 per class instead of 16; the lost data hurts more than fold-averaging helps, so slight regression versus the full-data refit, though averaging softens over-confident high-C probabilities and keeps it close.

Absolute size, aspect ratio, convexity and Hu moments are genuinely new information relative to the scale-normalised descriptors and are known to help on this dataset; with C re-tuned by CV, logloss should drop modestly, though the risk of images dir missing (no change) or noisy features tempers the gain.

Unsupervised PCA to 95% variance drops low-variance but class-discriminative directions in the margin/texture histograms; with 99 classes and only 990 rows, this reliably worsens logistic-regression log loss (regularisation on the full standardised features already handles collinearity).

Averaging five logistic models each fit on only 8 samples per class loses training data relative to the full 10-per-class refit; probability averaging smooths estimates slightly but for a linear model with fixed C this typically nets a small log-loss regression rather than a gain.

A two-branch NN using the 192 features plus silhouette typically reaches ~0.03-0.05 log loss on this task; a 50/50 arithmetic blend with the weaker LR (0.124) caps the gain, landing around 0.06-0.07, with runtime safely inside budget at 64x64.

LR with C=1.0 is strongly underconfident on this near-separable dataset; power/temperature sharpening fitted on OOF (a likely ~2-3) with a small uniform floor should roughly halve the log loss, with the full-data refit only slightly more confident than the fold models so the OOF-tuned a transfers well.
Tuning C via 5-fold CV on this near-separable 990x192 problem will pick a large C (~1000-3000), a well-known lever on Leaf Classification that drops logreg log loss from ~0.12 to roughly 0.03-0.04.

On this dataset (990 samples, 99 classes, 10/class) linear models are known to dominate; GBDT with 15% internal validation overfits, is poorly calibrated, and typically lands around 0.3-1.0 log loss, a large regression from 0.061.

Platt-sigmoid OvR calibration with ~6 positives per class on 3 folds yields flat, under-confident probabilities that dilute the ensemble more than the well-calibrated multinomial LR did; expect a modest regression.

RF vote-fraction probabilities are diffuse but rarely near-zero on the true class, so swapping it for a fragile early-stopped HGB in a uniform soft vote should be roughly neutral to slightly better, with the ensemble still dominated by LR/LDA calibration and kNN's harsh zeros.

Leaf features are nearly linearly separable; C=1 is far over-regularized and CV will select C~100-1000, which historically yields ~0.03-0.06 log loss on this competition, with shrinkage alpha guarding against overconfidence.

Averaging three weaker per-family LDAs (shape alone is quite weak) yields flatter, less confident probabilities than one joint 192-feature LDA that fuses complementary evidence, so log loss should worsen substantially.

PCA to 90% variance discards discriminative low-variance directions in the margin/texture histograms that logistic regression at high C exploits; on this near-separable 99-class problem, lossy compression typically raises log loss noticeably.

Uniform mixing at 0.5% adds ~0.005 loss on the ~90% of confident correct predictions while only modestly capping the few overconfident errors; the LR model at C=1 is already regularized, so the net effect is a small regression or wash.

C=1 logistic regression is underconfident on this 990-row/99-class dataset; an OOF-fitted temperature well below 1 sharpens probabilities and should roughly halve the log loss, similar to tuning C upward.

Nyström RBF features (512 standardized components) give the C=1 logistic model more capacity to make confident correct predictions on this easy, near-separable 99-class dataset, likely lowering log loss moderately, though C=1 remains under-tuned so gains are limited.

Random forest on ~5000 sparse TF-IDF columns with sqrt feature sampling dilutes the strong metadata signals and loses the linear text signal that LR exploits; on this small noisy dataset RF typically underperforms tuned LR by a few AUC points.

Bag-of-subreddits is a known useful signal in RAOP (e.g. prior RAOP/assistance subreddit presence correlates with success); with min_df=5 and L2 rows, LR at C=0.3 should gain a modest ~0.01 AUC, though the block partly duplicates the numeric history features so the lift is small.

giver_username_if_known is a known leak present in the test schema: ~5% of rows are flagged and nearly all of those received pizza, so LR will push them to the top of the ranking and lift AUC substantially.

Stacking a text logit with raw history numerics and the request timestamp in a GBM captures the strong nonlinear/temporal signal (RAOP success rate drifted over time and history features are skewed) that a single linear model on scaled log features misses; typical RAOP LightGBM-on-metadata scores land around 0.67-0.70, so a moderate gain over 0.657 is likely.

Time trend, text-length stats, and RAOP-history indicators are known strong signals in this dataset (success rate drifted over time; longer posts and prior RAOP activity help), so adding them to LR should give a modest AUC gain over the weak text+numeric baseline; mlflow logging is best-effort and harmless.

ExtraTrees with sqrt feature subsetting over ~5.4k mostly-sparse TF-IDF columns dilutes the informative numeric/embedding signal per split and generally underperforms linear models on high-dimensional text; the numeric-history nonlinearities help a bit but not enough, so roughly flat-to-slightly-worse around 0.61-0.62.

MiniLM embeddings plus behavioral numerics carry most of the signal; dropping the noisy 5k unigram block at C=0.3 on ~4.5k rows likely reduces variance slightly, giving a small AUC gain, while local-file MLflow logging is harmless.

Adding ~24 scaled document statistics (length, gratitude flags, sentiment, readability) to a TF-IDF+LR model on 4k rows typically yields a small but real AUC gain of ~0.01, since length and politeness signals are known predictors in this dataset and the dense block is regularized alongside the sparse features.

The nine requester-history features alone give roughly 0.60-0.62 AUC on RAOP; the TF-IDF block carries genuine signal (about +0.03-0.05), so removing it regresses the score, and the mlflow additions are inert.

Mean-pooled skip-gram vectors trained on a ~5.7k-doc corpus are noisy and lose the specific lexical cues TF-IDF captures; standardized 200-dim dense features with C=0.3 tend to slightly underperform sparse unigrams on this task, so expect a small regression with metadata/text-stats carrying most of the signal.

Adding bigrams with min_df=2 and a 60k vocab on only ~4k training rows inflates the sparse block relative to the dense numeric features under fixed C=0.3, typically adding noise rather than signal for this small dataset; expect a small regression or flat result.
Nine requester-history features alone typically yield ~0.60-0.62 AUC on RAOP; dropping text removes weak but real signal (SVD text + meta got 0.633), so a modest regression is expected.

MiniLM embeddings add modest semantic signal over unigram TF-IDF on this small, noisy dataset (~0.65-0.68 ceiling for text+history), but 384 standardized dense columns with untuned C=0.3 add some overfitting; expect a small net gain, with a risk of no-op or slight regression.

Success rate in RAOP drifted over the collection period and the train/test split is random in time, so a smooth spline over request date adds a small but real signal; modest gain expected on top of the weak text+history baseline.

kNN with cosine over a mixed feature space (5000 sparse TF-IDF dims dominated by 9 dense standardized numerics and binary subreddits) discards the linear signal LR exploits; kNN on noisy short text with ~25% positives typically yields AUC in the 0.55-0.62 range, a clear regression.

C=30 on 5000 sparse TF-IDF features with ~4000 training rows will heavily overfit the text model (near-separable), degrading its held-out ranking; the 50/50 blend with CatBoost dampens but does not eliminate the hit, so AUC likely drops modestly.

Request date is a known strong signal in RAOP (success rate shifted over time as the subreddit grew and the temporal split matters); a smooth spline block adds modest, low-risk lift on top of TF-IDF and history features, though extrapolation='constant' limits gains if test dates lie outside the training range.

BernoulliNB on binarized TF-IDF discards term weighting and badly handles the strong numeric requester-history features (only above-mean indicators, naive independence), and this dataset's text signal is weak, so AUC likely drops several points versus the tuned-enough logistic regression.

Request date is a known strong signal in RAOP (success rate drifted over time as the subreddit grew), and spline features let the L2 logistic regression capture it; test set spans same period so a modest but real AUC gain is likely, with mlflow overhead irrelevant to the metric.

Binary subreddit membership features add modest signal about requester history beyond the nine numeric counts; unscaled binaries with C=0.3 fit reasonably alongside TF-IDF, so expect a small AUC gain, though the added sparse block may partly overfit with ~2800 training rows.

Metadata-only CatBoost captures nonlinear requester-history signal (RAOP activity, account age) that the linear model underuses; a 50/50 blend with the weak text LR typically lifts AUC a couple of points on this dataset, with small risk since the metadata-only model alone is roughly on par with the baseline.

Adding bigrams under a fixed 5000-feature cap mostly displaces useful unigrams with sparse bigrams; with C=0.3 on ~4k docs the effect is roughly neutral, tiny noise either way, and the mlflow telemetry is best-effort so it shouldn't break the run.

Author identification is stylometric: function-word usage and stop-word bigrams are strongly author-discriminative, so removing them from the word view discards real signal that char_wb only partially recovers; expect a modest regression.

Function words are core authorship signals; dropping stop words weakens both word-level base models (especially NB word counts) and the char_wb models only partially compensate, so stacked log loss worsens modestly.

Linear stacker on scaled OOF probs + meta features is competitive but LightGBM's nonlinear use of raw meta-features (length, punctuation) typically gives a small edge on Spooky; expect slight regression, roughly 0.30-0.31.

Punctuation patterns (commas, semicolons, dashes, quotes) are among the strongest stylometric signals for these three authors in this competition; removing them from char n-grams discards real signal, so log loss should worsen by a few percent.

Stacking word/char LR with tuned MultinomialNB on counts is a well-known strong combo for this competition; NB adds complementary signal and the meta-LR calibrates well, typically moving TF-IDF LR baselines from ~0.44 to the 0.36-0.39 range.
Aggressive chi2 selection (130k->10k) discards useful rare n-grams that L2 LR already exploits well; LR OOF worsens, NB blend partially cushions, net modest regression.

Function words are strong authorship signals (stylometry); removing them from both word TF-IDF and NB count features weakens both models, only partly offset by the intact char_wb block, so log loss worsens from ~0.361 to ~0.385.

Cross-boundary case-sensitive char n-grams add punctuation/capitalization style signal that helps author ID; with C=1.0 LR on many more L2-normalized TF-IDF columns the gain is modest but real, likely a few percent.

Test set shares the natural ~40/29/31 class prior, so balancing shifts predicted priors away from truth and duplicated rows add overfitting for a 25-epoch fastText model; log loss likely worsens slightly.

MultinomialNB on stacked TF-IDF features is poorly calibrated and overconfident relative to tuned logistic regression; on this competition NB typically scores ~0.40-0.48 log loss, a clear regression from 0.355.

Dropping char n-grams removes complementary stylistic/punctuation signal that is genuinely predictive of author on this dataset; word-only NB-SVM typically loses a few hundredths of log loss versus the word+char stack.

TF-IDF + LR on this dataset typically prefers much weaker regularization (C≈10-30) than C=1.0; CV over logspace(-1,1.5) will pick a higher C and cut log loss noticeably, with modest risk of runtime or mlflow side effects.

MultinomialNB with alpha=0.1 on word+char TF-IDF yields overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities (char n-grams violate independence heavily), so log loss worsens from 0.425 to roughly 0.5-0.55 despite comparable accuracy.

fastText supervised with lr=0.5/epoch=25 on ~17k short sentences overfits and yields poorly calibrated softmax probabilities; on Spooky, fastText historically scores ~0.5-0.6 log loss versus ~0.43 for TF-IDF+LR, so this is a regression.

NB log-count-ratio weighting on word+char TF-IDF is a known strong boost on this dataset (typical NB-SVM kernels ~0.39-0.41), partially offset by less-calibrated one-vs-rest renormalized probabilities and C=4 on ~100k features.

Adding 14 MaxAbs-scaled stylometric features to a ~200k-dim TF-IDF logistic regression adds weak, mostly redundant signal (punctuation already captured by char n-grams); expect a tiny improvement or near no-op, roughly 0.002 log loss.

Dropping word unigrams/bigrams removes the strongest author-discriminative lexical features (proper nouns, vocabulary); char_wb 2-5 alone with NB-LR typically scores noticeably worse than the concatenation on Spooky, so log loss rises.

Halving C on TF-IDF word+char LR for Spooky typically slightly hurts: this task rewards weak regularization (high C, even 10+), so C=2 will flatten probabilities a bit and raise log loss marginally; tracking code is inert.

Stop words are strong stylometric signals for author identification (function-word usage distinguishes Poe/Lovecraft/Shelley), and removing them from both word and char branches degrades features, so log loss likely worsens.

Switching char_wb to char adds cross-word-boundary and punctuation n-grams (useful for author style), but with a 60k feature cap and unchanged C the effect is marginal; expect a tiny improvement or near-zero change.

LogisticRegression with C=1 on high-dim TF-IDF is underconfident on this task; fitting a temperature <1 on the holdout sharpens probabilities and typically cuts log loss by a few hundredths, with minor mismatch from the full-data refit.

Log1p target optimizes relative error while the metric is dollar RMSE dominated by expensive/tail rides; expm1 of a log-scale mean predictor is biased low on high fares, so LightGBM on this data typically scores slightly worse (or flat) in RMSE versus the raw-scale L2 fit, with the mlflow addition having no effect on the score.

4x more training rows with a capped 1000-tree LightGBM gives a modest gain on the predictable rows, but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows and the fixed model capacity limit the improvement to a few percent; timing risk is low.

Log1p target optimizes geometric-mean-like predictions and underpredicts expensive rides, hurting dollar-scale RMSE slightly despite cleaner training; typical outcome for this competition is a small regression.

Monotone constraint on distance is a mild regularizer but taxi fares are not strictly monotone in haversine distance (airport flat fares, tolls, traffic), so the constraint slightly hurts fit; effect small, likely near-neutral to slightly worse, with the corrupt-row floor dominating.

Log-target training optimizes the wrong loss for RMSE in dollars: expm1 of a log-space mean predicts roughly the geometric mean, systematically underpredicting high fares that dominate squared error, so RMSE typically gets slightly worse despite the 2.1 floor from corrupt rows.

Fitting log1p optimizes a different loss than the dollar RMSE metric; expm1 predictions underestimate the conditional mean on high fares that dominate RMSE, so expect a small regression despite variance stabilization.

Airport distance features are a well-known strong signal for flat-rate JFK and surcharged Newark trips; with 1M rows and unchanged LightGBM they typically shave a modest amount off RMSE, though the 2.8% corrupt-row floor caps the gain.

NaN handling lets LightGBM learn the fare distribution of the corrupt-coordinate population (and use time features), shaving a bit off the ~2.1 RMSE floor those 2.8% of rows impose, while valid-row performance stays roughly unchanged; modest improvement expected.

Out-of-fold route/cell target encodings add genuine toll/airport signal on top of raw coordinates that trees already partially exploit; expect a modest gain, with the 2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows and irreducible noise limiting the improvement.

Training on log1p optimizes relative error and back-transform yields a median-like estimate that underpredicts the large fares dominating RMSE; the 2.8% corrupt-row floor is unchanged, so expect a small regression rather than improvement.

Manhattan distance, deltas and bearing are well-known modest gains for this competition on top of haversine plus raw coords; with a ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows the improvement is small, roughly 0.03-0.08.

Airport-distance features are a known solid gain for this task (JFK flat fare, airport surcharges), but with 4M rows and raw coordinates already available to trees, the improvement is modest and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the visible change.

L1 objective fits the conditional median while the metric is RMSE; it under-predicts the heavy right tail (airport/toll fares) and L1 boosting converges more slowly, so RMSE typically degrades by several percent.

Fitting log1p(fare) and inverting with expm1 optimizes relative error and underestimates the conditional mean on high fares, which dominate raw-scale RMSE; on this taxi task log targets typically cost ~0.05-0.2 RMSE versus direct MSE fitting, and MLflow logging does not affect the score.

L1 targets the conditional median, underpredicting skewed high fares that dominate RMSE, and L1 boosting converges slower within 1000 trees; the noisy ~2.8% invalid rows are already handled by the mean fallback, so robustness gains are small and the metric mismatch dominates.

Huber with delta=$1 makes the objective near-L1 for most rows, pulling predictions toward the conditional median rather than mean; RMSE evaluation rewards mean estimation, and taxi fares are right-skewed, so the metric will likely worsen slightly despite early stopping on RMSE.

Optimizing log1p loss and back-transforming predicts the conditional median-ish rather than the mean, underpredicting expensive rides that dominate RMSE; the 2.8% corrupt-row floor is unchanged, so expect a small regression (~4.2-4.3).

Weighting by target darkness shifts the optimal predictor toward darker values in ambiguous stain/stroke regions, misaligning the objective with the unweighted RMSE metric; expect a small regression rather than a gain.

5-10x more optimizer steps with a proper cosine anneal to zero should let the small U-Net converge further; overfitting risk on 105 images is modest with random crops/flips, so expect a moderate RMSE reduction rather than a large one.

L1 trains fine and gives crisper edges, but the metric is RMSE where L2 is the matched objective; L1 pushes ambiguous stroke-boundary pixels toward the median (0 or 1) instead of the hedged mean, which slightly hurts RMSE, so expect roughly no change to a small regression.

Test noise is drawn from the same synthetic generator as train, so input-only brightness/contrast jitter adds label ambiguity (same target for shifted inputs) without matching any real test shift; with only 2k steps this slightly wastes capacity and regresses RMSE a little.

Denoising is a pixel-exact regression task; the 0.75x/1.25x passes see off-distribution stroke widths and the downscale/upscale round trip blurs thin text edges, so averaging those with the scale-1 map most likely adds edge error rather than cancelling it, giving a small RMSE regression.

Dropout2d p=0.2 on both e2 (also feeding the skip) and e3 in a short 2000-step run of a pixel-regression task adds noise and slows convergence; the task is not strongly overfitting (dense per-pixel supervision on crops), so regularization likely costs a bit of RMSE, with train/eval BatchNorm-dropout variance shift adding slight degradation.

Denoising is a dense per-pixel regression where the model is under- rather than over-fitting in a 180s budget; Dropout2d(0.1) in every block (including skip connections and the final decoder block) injects noise into the pixel-precise reconstruction path, slows convergence, and the BN train/eval variance shift adds a small mismatch, so RMSE most likely worsens modestly.

A deeper U-Net with ~89px receptive field helps remove large-scale noise (stains, shading) and typically gives a modest RMSE gain on this dataset; the ~30% fewer steps within the 180s budget partly offsets it, so expect a small improvement.

Median-filter background is a well-known strong feature for this dataset; giving the U-Net an explicit global background estimate beyond its 128px receptive field should modestly help on large-scale stains and shading, yielding a small RMSE gain.

Larger receptive field (5 levels, 256px crops) helps model low-frequency stains/background gradients that the 3-level net can't see; same pixel budget and 2000 steps still converge, so expect a modest gain, with some risk from noisier batch-8 gradients and less crop diversity.

Flip TTA on a model trained with random flips gives a small, reliable variance reduction on this smooth-target regression task; typically a few percent RMSE gain with negligible risk, and inference cost stays tiny.

Baseline's 2000 steps likely take ~60-90s on GPU, so a 180s cosine wall-clock budget gives roughly 2-4x more optimizer steps with a smooth decay, yielding a modest RMSE improvement for this small UNet; risk is a regression if the node is slow (CPU or contended GPU) and 180s yields fewer than 2000 steps.

The metric is RMSE, which MSE directly optimizes; Charbonnier/L1 pushes toward median-like sharper predictions that under pixel uncertainty (stain edges, faint strokes) incur larger squared errors, so expect a small regression or at best neutrality, with noise from a single run.

Input-only Gaussian noise (σ=0.05) creates a train/test mismatch (test scans have no such noise) and pushes the residual U-Net toward smoothing fine text strokes, which typically hurts pixel RMSE on this already low-noise-floor task rather than regularizing helpfully.

GroupNorm with 4 channels/group in a small U-Net typically converges a bit slower than BN under Adam 2e-3 for 2000 steps, and its per-sample spatial statistics still shift between 128px crops and full pages, so expect a small regression rather than the hoped-for gain.

The metric is RMSE, which MSE directly optimizes; SSIM+L1 favors sharper/median-like outputs and misallocates capacity to structure over squared error, so a small regression is more likely than a gain.

Pure SSIM loss is nearly indifferent to small intensity offsets in flat white background regions (luminance term ≈1 for mu near 1, contrast term ≈C2/C2) so the net is weakly constrained on exactly the pixels dominating per-pixel RMSE; Zhao et al. also found SSIM-alone typically trails L2 on PSNR/RMSE, so expect a clear regression despite sharper strokes.

Residual formulation is roughly equivalent in expressivity for this U-Net with BN; losing the sigmoid removes the clean saturation to exactly-white background that helps most pixels, so expect near-neutral to slightly worse RMSE within seed noise.

Replacing MSE with sqrt(MSE)+0.1*(1-SSIM) moves the objective away from the graded per-pixel RMSE, and the SSIM convs run under autocast in bf16 (variance via E[x^2]-mu^2 is noisy in bf16), adding gradient noise; expect a small regression rather than a gain.

Residual formulation with identity init is a well-trodden swap that trains slightly faster but the U-Net already regresses this task well; the noise here is large structured background so the residual is not small, and losing the sigmoid's saturation toward pure white roughly offsets the gain, yielding a near-neutral tiny improvement.

Synthetic pairs outnumber real ones ~8:1 so most of the fixed 2000-step budget goes to a mismatched noise distribution (whole-image Gaussian blur smears the text, unlike the sharp-text real scans), diluting learning of the actual stain/crease artifacts; modest regression expected.

8-fold dihedral TTA averages out per-view errors for a small U-Net; flips were seen in training so those views are strong, transposed views (unseen orientation) are somewhat weaker but still coherent for local stroke/noise textures, so expect a small net RMSE reduction, partly obscured by seed-to-seed variance.

L1 loss targets the median rather than the mean; for an RMSE-graded task with mostly-white targets and few text/stain pixels, MAE tends to sharpen but slightly under-optimize squared error, usually yielding a small regression versus MSE in a short 2000-step CPU run.

Multinomial LR on raw 2048-d features is typically overconfident on test even with C tuned for log loss; a holdout-fitted temperature (likely T≈1.2-1.5) should shave a few percent off log loss without changing accuracy, with slight bias since T was fit on an 85%-data model.

Head starts at the already-optimal regularized LR solution; two epochs of unaugmented SGD on cached deterministic activations with negligible weight decay mostly pushes it toward an overconfident unregularized fit, while lr 1e-4 on three convs for ~290 steps barely changes the features, so expect a small log-loss regression rather than a gain.

Horizontal-flip TTA with probability averaging on frozen ResNet-50 features gives a small but reliable log-loss reduction (~2-4%); the extra pass over 1,023 test images is cheap, and the MLflow/tempdir scaffolding is inert with respect to the metric.

Balanced 1:1 undersampling discards 90-99.7% of negatives, so rare labels (threat ~950 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k) train on tiny sets with 60k-200k features and the NB ratios become noisy; ranking quality on the ~64k graded rows degrades, especially for threat/identity_hate, outweighing any gain from class balance.

Adding char n-grams to NB-LogReg typically gives a small standalone gain, but it makes branch B more correlated with branch A so the rank blend gains little; expect a marginal improvement, with some risk of a wash from liblinear hitting the 100-iter cap on the larger matrix.

AUC is ranking-based and insensitive to class-prior bias, so undersampling gives no upside while discarding 80-99% of negatives (threat fits on ~950 rows, NB ratios become noisy), degrading rare-label AUCs and the overall mean.

MultinomialNB on TF-IDF is a much weaker per-label ranker (~0.95-0.96 AUC vs ~0.978 for NB-LogReg), so both the 50/50 rank-average blend and the stacked OOF features degrade, dragging the ensemble below branch A alone.

Mean-pooled Word2Vec + logreg typically scores ~0.96-0.97 AUC on this task, well below the word+char TF-IDF branch it replaces (~0.978), and losing char n-grams hurts obscene/insult misspellings; two of three blend components get weaker so the rank average drops modestly despite NB-LogReg holding it up.

1:1 undersampling discards 80-99.7% of negatives, so high-dimensional sparse linear models (esp. for threat with ~950 training rows and identity_hate) lose the negative-vocabulary signal and overfit; AUC is ranking-based and does not benefit from rebalancing, so expect a clear regression concentrated in rare labels.

A sparse TF-IDF MLP is a genuinely different (non-linear, shared-hidden) model that alone reaches ~0.98 and adds diversity to three near-duplicate linear branches, so an equal-weight rank blend should gain a little; the main risk is the 690/720 s time guard triggering after the slow char-vectorizer plus branch C, in which case the score is unchanged.

Throwing away 90-99.7% of negatives starves the linear TF-IDF models of vocabulary coverage of benign text and makes the NB ratios and rare-label fits (threat ~956 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k) very noisy; AUC for sparse linear models typically drops noticeably under 1:1 undersampling, so expect a clear regression rather than a gain.

Regex normalization (repeat-collapse, de-obfuscation, IP/URL tokens) adds slight signal for word models but char_wb n-grams already capture most obfuscation and timestamp/shorthand removal drops some informality/signature cues, so expect a near-neutral, marginally positive change.

OOF B-logits scaled by 1/20 under C=0.1 give branch A a modest cross-label boost, but the stacked A becomes more correlated with B so the rank blend gains little; expect a small positive change (with some runtime risk from 30 extra liblinear fits).

A 3-epoch multi-task MLP on the same 60k TF-IDF features adds a modestly diverse nonlinear view that usually helps a rank blend by ~0.0005-0.001, but equal 1/3 weight and weak rare-label (threat) performance from joint BCE limit the gain and add timeout risk.

Branch C (NB-weighted word+char) is a slightly stronger single model but highly correlated with A and B, so an equal-weight rank blend yields a small AUC gain of roughly half a point in the fourth decimal, assuming the extra liblinear fits stay within budget.

Per-label holdout-tuned weights (shrunk toward 0.5) can only shift the rank blend modestly; the two branches are near-equal in strength so gains are tiny but likely slightly positive, with the main risk being the added runtime from re-fitting both branches on the 80% split.

Replacing sparse 260k-feature n-gram ensemble (incl. char n-grams and NB weighting) with 300-d LSA discards discriminative rare tokens; LSA+logreg on Jigsaw typically scores ~0.95-0.96, a clear regression especially on threat/identity_hate.

Capping negatives at 10:1 discards ~90% of training data for the rare labels (threat ~5k rows, severe_toxic/identity_hate ~16k), removing discriminative negative evidence for linear/NB/fastText models; toxic is barely affected but the rare-label AUCs, which dominate the column mean's variance, should drop measurably.

A 7-way softmax forces the six co-occurring labels to compete for probability mass (a toxic+obscene+insult comment gets a lower 'toxic' score than a toxic-only one), degrading per-column ordering of branch F, and with 1/3 rank weight this drags the blend down slightly; runtime improves but the metric likely regresses a bit.

Swapping a rank-averaged trio of tuned NB-LogReg/TF-IDF branches for a single ComplementNB on raw word counts (which for binary labels reduces to an MNB log-count-ratio scorer) drops the discriminative fitting entirely; NB alone on Jigsaw typically lands around 0.93-0.95 mean AUC, with rare labels like threat and identity_hate suffering most.

Replacing a strong sparse n-gram NB-LR ensemble (0.9816) with unweighted mean-pooled 200d corpus word2vec + linear head loses lexical precision and char-level robustness; such pipelines historically score ~0.95-0.96 on Jigsaw, a clear regression.

Averaged corpus-trained Word2Vec + logistic regression is a known weak baseline on Jigsaw (~0.94-0.96 mean AUC); it discards char n-grams and NB-weighted features that drive the 0.98 sparse blend, so a clear regression is expected.

A char-level NB-LogReg adds modest diversity (NB weighting on char n-grams differs from branch A's plain char TF-IDF), and 3-way per-label rank blending typically yields a small but real AUC gain; the coarser 0.1 weight grid and holdout noise on rare labels cap the upside, and runtime should stay under the 15-minute kill.

C=0.1 was the tuned value for the plain word+char TF-IDF kernel; raising to C=4 under-regularizes branch A (especially rare labels threat/identity_hate), likely dropping it ~0.002-0.003 AUC, partly dampened by the rank blend with branch B, so a small net regression.

Supervised fastText (bag of word bigrams, epoch=20/lr=0.5 overfits rare labels, saturated softmax probs create rank ties) is weaker (~0.97 AUC) and not very diverse from the NB-LogReg branch, so an equal-weight 1/3 rank blend roughly breaks even or slightly regresses.

NB-LogReg on char n-grams is a strong, partly diverse view; equal 3-way rank blend should add ~+0.001 AUC, though the extra char_wb vectorizer pushes wall-clock toward the limit and the gain is modest given overlap with branch A's char features.

Training on 90% of data costs a small amount of AUC (especially for rare labels like threat), and per-label weights tuned on a 16k-row holdout with few positives are noisy; the gain from optimal weights over 0.5/0.5 is tiny, so net effect is roughly neutral to slightly negative.

NB-weighting branch A makes it near-redundant with the NB-LogReg branch B, cutting ensemble diversity, and the strong C=0.1 sag regularization with rescaled features plus noisy log-ratios on rare labels (threat) likely nets a small AUC loss.

min_df=0.01 on ~313k docs requires ~3.1k document occurrences, pruning word vocab to ~2k terms and eliminating rare slurs/threat words that drive threat and identity_hate AUC, so rare-label AUCs drop and the column mean falls noticeably.

Balanced undersampling discards ~90-99% of negatives per label (threat trains on ~1k rows), and AUC does not benefit from class balance with logistic regression, so rare-label AUCs (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) drop materially and drag the column mean down.

Cosine class-centroid (Rocchio) classifiers are far weaker than tuned logistic regression on sparse n-gram features; the NB weighting in branch B helps somewhat, but expected mean AUC drops from 0.980 to roughly 0.95-0.96.

Switching char to char_wb in branch A is a near-neutral swap; the README already describes the baseline as char_wb (the well-known kernel), char_wb loses cross-word n-grams which sometimes hurt slightly on toxic text with spacing tricks, so expect essentially flat to marginally worse.

Swapping tuned logistic regression for ComplementNB on TF-IDF removes discriminative training; NB on n-gram TF-IDF for Jigsaw typically lands near 0.94-0.96 mean AUC (weak on rare threat/identity_hate), so rank-averaging two NB branches gives roughly 0.955, a clear regression from 0.9797.

Collapsing 60k sparse TF-IDF features to 32 SVD components cripples branch A's linear separability (likely ~0.93 AUC), and equal-weight rank blending with fastText then pulls the ensemble well below the current sparse-logreg blend.

Collapsing everything outside a 2,000-token vocabulary to a single placeholder destroys the char n-gram and rare-word signal (obfuscated profanity, slurs, misspellings) that drives threat/identity_hate AUC, so both branches lose discriminative information and the blend regresses noticeably.

Removing English stop words from the 10k word unigram vocabulary in branch A adds pronouns like 'you' which are mildly informative for toxicity, but char n-grams already capture them and the rank blend with branch B dilutes the effect, so expect a negligible, slightly positive change.

Logit averaging of two differently-calibrated branches (C=0.1 sag vs C=4 NB-LR with much sharper logits) effectively upweights branch B, so the blend drifts from the balanced rank average; expect a tiny, near-noise change, slightly negative.

Switching char_wb to char at 50k capped features yields nearly identical n-gram vocabulary (mostly within-word grams) with slightly more cross-word context; branch A is half a rank-average so the effect is a tiny, roughly neutral wobble.

A 5-epoch dim-64 word-bigram fastText model (~0.965-0.97 AUC alone) is weaker than the NB-LogReg branch it replaces (~0.977), so the rank blend with the unchanged word+char branch drops slightly despite some diversity gain.

The 192 leaf descriptors are nearly all informative and L2 at C=1 already controls variance; dropping a third of columns via univariate F-scores discards complementary information and typically raises LR logloss, so the 50/50 blend regresses modestly.

With eps=0.1 over 99 classes the NN's confident predictions are capped near 0.9 (a log-loss floor of ~0.105 for the NN alone), and since the current blend is already at 0.074 with mostly correct, confident predictions, the mandated under-confidence should push the blended log loss up rather than improve calibration.

OvR with 10 positives vs 980 negatives per binary problem yields poorly separated, weakly informative per-class scores; row-normalisation plus power calibration recovers most of the scale but the decoupled decision geometry typically ranks slightly worse than the joint softmax on this dataset, so a mild regression is expected.

A bagged 512-unit MLP on standardised leaf descriptors is a well-known strong learner here (OOF logloss typically ~0.02-0.05) and is fairly diverse from LR, so an OOF-tuned blend plus power calibration should cut logloss meaningfully, with the w=0 fallback bounding downside; some optimism shaved for grid-selection overfit on 990 rows.

Fold-averaging five 80%-data high-C logreg models smooths overconfident probabilities (helping logloss) but each model sees ~3 fewer samples per class; net effect is roughly neutral to slightly positive.

The 21 geometric image features (absolute size, aspect ratio, solidity, Hu moments) add genuinely new information beyond the scale-normalised descriptors and are cheap to compute; with CV-tuned C the logreg should gain modestly, though the gain is capped by an already low baseline and the fallback to 192 features if images are missing.

L2 logistic regression is rotation-invariant so PCA only acts by discarding the low-variance directions; on this 99-class fine-grained problem those directions still carry discriminative signal, so truncation at 95% variance (roughly 130 of 219 columns) is likely to cost log loss rather than help.

Each fold model sees only 8 instead of 10 samples per class, so averaged fold models are less sharp than the full refit; probability averaging softens a few overconfident errors but on a 0.088-logloss, mostly-correct predictor the loss of 20% training data dominates, giving a modest regression.

The two-branch NN (features + silhouette, 80 epochs) should reach roughly 0.06-0.10 on its own; averaging with the underconfident C=1 LR is a Jensen-favourable blend, giving ~0.07-0.09, with some risk the 9-minute guard truncates the full-data run on CPU.

C=1.0 LR on 99 well-separated classes is systematically underconfident; OOF-fitted power sharpening (a≈2-3) with a tiny uniform floor is essentially temperature scaling and should cut log loss substantially with little overfit risk from two scalars on 990 rows.

On this dataset standardised multinomial logistic regression is heavily over-regularised at C=1; CV will pick C in the ~1000-3000 range, which known kernels show yields ~0.03-0.05 log loss versus 0.124 now, a large improvement.

Image size, aspect, Hu moments and solidity are known to be informative and only partly redundant with the precomputed shape descriptor; with 990 rows and C=1 the extra 27 standardized columns should give a modest log-loss gain rather than overfit, and the mlflow wrapper is failure-guarded so runtime risk is low.

This dataset is nearly linearly separable and the known optimum for LR is a large C (weak regularization); cutting C from 1.0 to 0.2 flattens the predicted probabilities, so log loss rises substantially rather than improving.

Dropping the refit means the submitted logistic regression sees only ~13 instead of 16 samples per class; with 99 classes and 240 features, fewer training rows sharpen nothing and reduce calibration/accuracy, so test log loss worsens noticeably.

OOF-weighted blend of a well-tuned LR with shrinkage LDA and distance-weighted kNN typically trims log loss modestly on this dataset by improving calibration and diversity, though gains are limited since LR already dominates and kNN/LDA are individually weaker.

With only ~10 samples per class across 99 classes, tree ensembles are known to badly underperform well-regularised logistic regression on this dataset (typical GBDT/RF log loss 0.4-1.0 vs ~0.05 for linear models); min_samples_leaf=10 with ~8 training samples per class after the 15% holdout further cripples the splits, so a large regression is expected.

Platt-sigmoid OvR calibration with only ~2-3 positives per class per fold yields diffuse, underconfident probabilities across 99 classes, so the swapped member is weaker than the standardised multinomial LR it replaces and drags the uniform soft-vote average down.

RF vote fractions are less confident than HGB but more robust with 6-10 samples/class and no reliance on a ~99-row early-stopping split; in a uniform 4-way soft vote this mostly softens the hard misses from kNN/LDA, so I expect a small improvement rather than a large shift.

Kaggle kernels show small MLPs on the 192 standardised leaf descriptors reach ~0.03-0.08 log loss, beating an untuned C=1 logistic regression; noisy 10% early-stopping split on 99 classes and overconfidence limit gains, but the OOF uniform-shrinkage calibration caps the damage, so a moderate improvement to ~0.07 is expected.

Known result on this dataset: standardized multinomial LR is heavily under-regularized-sensitive; CV will pick a large C (~100-1000) which drives OOF log loss from ~0.12 to ~0.04-0.06, and the uniform-shrinkage step keeps the test score robust, so roughly halving the loss.

Hand-crafted contour/Hu/radial features add some complementary shape signal beyond the 192 descriptors, but with only 990 samples, C=1.0 fixed, and several noisy columns (orientation, raw area/perimeter, redundant radial histogram) the gain for logistic regression should be modest, likely a small log-loss improvement rather than a large one.

On standardized leaf features, multinomial logistic regression is heavily under-regularized-optimal (well-known kernels use C~1000-2000 reaching ~0.03-0.05 logloss); 10-fold CV over logspace(-3,3) will select a large C and substantially cut the 0.124 loss, with 990x192 data fitting easily in budget.

Uniform soft-voting adds a strong shrinkage-LDA and a decent kNN/HGB to the C=1 LR; averaging calibrated-ish confident models usually cuts logloss on this dataset (LDA/LR alone reach ~0.03-0.1), but kNN's near-zero true-class probs on its few errors and HGB's softer outputs limit the gain, so a moderate improvement to ~0.08-0.09 is most likely.

LogReg at C=1.0 on this dataset is underconfident (larger C is known to cut logloss substantially), so OOF search will pick alpha≈0 and the uniform-shrinkage step leaves test probabilities essentially unchanged.

Forcing 90% spherical shrinkage discards the informative feature correlations that Ledoit-Wolf auto (likely ~0.1-0.3) preserves with 891 residual degrees of freedom for 192 dims; predictions get flatter/less discriminative, so log loss likely worsens moderately.

Each 64-feature family alone is much weaker than the concatenated 192-feature LDA (shape especially), and arithmetic averaging of three soft-max outputs dilutes confident correct predictions instead of combining evidence multiplicatively, so log loss likely roughly doubles.

Truncating to 90% of standardized variance discards low-variance but class-discriminative margin/texture dimensions; with 99 classes and already-tuned L2 regularization, PCA adds no needed stabilization and typically raises log loss noticeably.

Shrinkage LDA is a strong fit for these 192 Gaussian-like descriptors with 10 samples/class, and CV-tuned shrinkage on log loss should calibrate it near or slightly better than the coarse-C logistic regression, though LDA overconfidence on a few test errors caps the gain.

Truncating to 95% variance (~110 of 192 dims) discards low-variance but discriminative histogram directions that L2-regularized LR was already handling well, so log loss should worsen noticeably despite the OOF temperature partially compensating.

Shrinkage LDA is strong on these 192 leaf descriptors (~97-98% accuracy) and the temperature fixes its overconfidence, but its confident errors and noisier class means with 10 samples/class likely leave log loss slightly worse than the already well-regularized logistic regression.

Mixing 0.5% uniform costs ~-log(0.995)=0.005 on every confidently-correct row while only helping rows where true-class prob is below ~0.005, which are rare for a well-regularized LR at 0.094 logloss, so a slight regression is most likely.

Fewer Nyström landmarks (384 vs 512 out of ~990 training points) reduces kernel approximation fidelity and model capacity for a 99-class problem; with logistic regression already regularized at C=1 the compactness gain is unlikely to offset the loss, so expect a small regression.

LDA on the 192 leaf descriptors classifies accurately (~98%) but its Gaussian posteriors are severely overconfident; each of the handful of test misclassifications incurs a near-clipped ~34 penalty, so log loss likely regresses well above the tuned-free LogisticRegression's 0.124 despite Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage softening it somewhat.
On this dataset logistic regression is badly under-regularized-fit at C=1; CV will pick C in the 100-1000 range, which is known to drop log loss to roughly 0.03-0.05 on the Kaggle leaderboard.

C=1.0 logistic regression on this dataset is strongly underconfident (heavily regularized), so an OOF-fitted temperature will sharpen logits (likely T near the 0.25 lower bound), substantially reducing log loss toward what less-regularized models achieve.

Nyström RBF with smooth gamma=1/192 and 512 standardized components acts like a mildly nonlinear expansion of an already well-separable 192-D problem; with C=1 the extra capacity likely sharpens probabilities modestly rather than overfitting badly, giving a small log-loss gain over the linear baseline.

Temporal drift (t_days), text-length, reciprocity/gratitude and prior-RAOP flags are known strong signals in this dataset and are largely absent from stopword-filtered TF-IDF plus raw counts, so a modest standardised dense block under an L2 logistic model should lift AUC by roughly 1-3 points.

RF with max_features=sqrt over ~8000 mostly-sparse TF-IDF/subreddit columns dilutes the strong numeric history signal (each split sees ~90 mostly-noise text columns) and fully-grown trees on 4k rows overfit sparse text, so it typically underperforms the regularised linear model on this dataset.

Random forest with max_features='sqrt' over ~5000 sparse TF-IDF columns dilutes splits on the few strong metadata/giver columns and handles sparse text worse than linear models, so it likely underperforms the tuned logistic regression despite capturing nonlinearities.

Collapsing 5k TF-IDF unigrams into 50 LDA topic proportions loses the specific lexical signal (money, pay, student, thanks, etc.) that logistic regression exploits on this small corpus; LDA topics on 4.5k short posts are noisy and typically underperform sparse text features, so the text block weakens while metadata/giver_known carry the rest.

Dropping the supervised OOF TF-IDF logit for 20 unsupervised LDA topics on short noisy requests discards most of the text signal; LGBM on metadata plus weak topic features likely lands near the metadata-only level, a modest regression.

In RAOP the test split is random within the same collection window and the base rate drifted strongly over time, so the raw timestamp is one of the most predictive level-2 features; replacing it with weak hour/weekday signals removes that period information and should lower AUC.

Adding a GBM on the numeric/time/text-stat features and rank-blending with CV-selected weight typically adds a modest 1-2 AUC points on RAOP, since the tree captures nonlinear requester-history and time effects the linear model misses; risk of overfitting the blend weight is small with 21 candidates.

Random forest with max_features=sqrt on ~5000 sparse TF-IDF columns dilutes the informative dense/history features among noisy word columns, and fully grown unpruned trees on ~4k rows overfit; RF on this feature set typically lands a few AUC points below a tuned-ish logistic regression.

Bag-of-subreddits adds genuine signal about requester activity/community (known useful in RAOP work), but l2-normalized sparse block with C=0.3 on ~4k rows yields a modest, noisy gain over the 0.657 baseline.

giver_username_if_known is a known leak in the original RAOP test schema (nearly 100% positive when non-N/A, covering a meaningful slice of positives), so if the prepared test.json retains it the AUC jumps substantially; hedged downward because the prepared split may have stripped the column, in which case the effect is ~zero.

Stacking OOF text logit with raw requester-history numerics and the request timestamp in a well-regularized LightGBM lets nonlinear effects (RAOP prior activity, time drift in success rate) be exploited, which typically lifts RAOP at-request-feature AUC from the mid-0.60s to ~0.70; runtime is well within budget.

Time-of-request (community success rate declined over years), text length/link indicators and RAOP-activity flags are known strong signals in this dataset; added dense features are well-scaled and fed to the same LR, so a modest gain over 0.657 is likely, with mlflow overhead irrelevant to score.

ExtraTrees handles the strong nonlinear requester-history numerics and dense embedding block reasonably, but random sqrt feature subsetting over ~5k sparse TF-IDF columns dilutes signal, so only a small gain over the weak LR baseline is expected.

TF-IDF block is L2-normalized and already dominated by the standardized embeddings under C=0.3, so dropping it loses a small complementary lexical signal (specific words like 'pay it forward', 'broke', 'kids') and likely nudges AUC slightly down rather than up.

Length, money/link mentions and gratitude flags are known modest predictors in RAOP that length-normalized TF-IDF discards; adding ~24 scaled dense features to the LR should give a small but real AUC gain, with sentiment/readability mostly redundant.

Dropping the TF-IDF block removes the strongest signal; nine log-scaled requester-history features in a linear model typically yield ~0.60-0.62 AUC on this task, below the 0.65 text+meta baseline, and the mlflow wrapper is best-effort so it won't break the run.

Mean Word2Vec vectors trained on a ~5.7k-doc corpus are noisy and lose the sparse lexical cues TF-IDF captured; metadata and text-stats blocks carry most of the signal so the result stays near baseline, likely slightly lower.
Bigrams and a larger vocab add some phrase signal but on ~4.5k rows with L2-normalized TF-IDF and fixed C=0.3 the extra sparse features mostly dilute; expect a marginal, near-neutral gain.

Dropping text removes real signal (title/body wording carries ~0.02-0.03 AUC on this task); the nine requester-history features alone with LightGBM typically land around 0.60-0.62 AUC, and num_leaves=63 on 9 features adds some overfitting even with early stopping.

RF with 400 deep bagged trees on 309 dense features is roughly on par with an overparameterized LGBM (num_leaves=63) on ~4k noisy samples; sqrt feature sampling dilutes the informative numeric columns among noisy SVD components, so gains are marginal and within noise.

MiniLM embeddings add some semantic signal beyond unigram TF-IDF, but 384 standardized dense columns under C=0.3 LR on ~4.5k rows mostly overlap with existing text signal and add variance, so expect only a small AUC gain (assuming the model download succeeds).

Bigrams with min_df=2 and up to 100k features roughly triple the sparse text dimensionality on only ~4k training docs; with fixed C=0.3 (untuned) the added noisy features dilute the informative numeric block, typically yielding a small AUC drop or wash on this dataset.

Adding 15 scaled text-statistic features (length, gratitude/reciprocity/hardship lexicons, money mentions) to a TF-IDF+numeric logistic regression typically gives a small but real AUC gain on RAOP; length and reciprocity are known predictors, though TF-IDF already captures much of the lexicon signal, so the lift is modest.

LightGBM captures nonlinear interactions in the requester-history numerics (the strongest signal here) and early-stopped CV picks a sane round count, but 300 SVD components on ~4k rows with num_leaves=63 are noisy and largely lose the sparse lexical signal LR used, so expect only a small net gain over 0.657.

The spline captured the strong monotone decline in pizza success over the community's lifetime (the dominant temporal signal under a random split); annual sin/cos discards that trend and keeps only weak seasonality, so AUC should drop modestly.

C=30 with ~4000 training rows and 5000 TF-IDF unigrams plus unscaled-magnitude spline/numeric features will overfit the text; logistic regression on this small noisy dataset typically peaks near C~0.1-1, so weakening regularization 100x should drop AUC by a few points.

RAOP success rate drifts strongly over calendar time (community grew, success fell), and with a random train/test split a smooth spline over request date is a genuinely informative, well-regularized feature that logistic regression can exploit, giving a modest AUC lift.

Distance-weighted cosine kNN on a concatenation of L2-normalized TF-IDF, large-magnitude standardized numerics, and binary subreddit flags gives a noisy, poorly calibrated neighborhood signal that typically underperforms a regularized linear model on this small, text-heavy dataset.

Distance-weighted KNN on nine standardized metadata features yields noisier, weaker rankings (~0.58-0.60 AUC alone) than CatBoost (~0.63-0.65), so the fixed 50/50 blend with the logistic model loses a bit of signal and AUC drops modestly.

C=30 on 5000 TF-IDF features with ~4500 samples overfits the text model (weak, noisy lexical signal on RAOP), degrading the LR half of the blend; the metadata CatBoost half limits the damage, so expect a modest AUC drop.

Request date is a known strong signal in RAOP (success rate fell as the subreddit grew) and the split is random in time, so quantile splines on the timestamp should give a modest AUC gain over the weak 0.654 baseline.

BernoulliNB discards TF-IDF magnitudes and coarsens the nine requester-history features (the strongest signal) to above/below-mean bits, and its independence assumption over 5k unigram+bigram indicators typically yields ~0.60-0.63 AUC on this dataset, below the tuned-ish logistic baseline.

Request date is a known strong signal in RAOP (success rate declined markedly over the subreddit's life), and a quantile-knot cubic spline lets the logistic model capture that nonlinear trend; with a random train/test split this should add a couple of AUC points on top of the weak TF-IDF+metadata baseline.

Subreddit membership indicators are a known useful signal in RAOP (community/activity proxy); unscaled binary block with C=0.3 adds modest lift on top of TF-IDF and numeric features, with some risk of noise from ~hundreds of sparse columns.

A nonlinear CatBoost model on the nine requester-history features captures interactions the linear model misses and is diverse from the TF-IDF-dominated logistic; a 50/50 blend should give a modest AUC gain, though a metadata-only model is itself only ~0.62-0.65 so the lift is limited.

Adding bigrams under a fixed 5000-feature budget (with stop words removed) displaces informative unigrams and adds sparse, noisy bigram features on a 4k-row set; text signal is weak here, so expect roughly neutral to slightly worse AUC, with the mlflow telemetry being a no-op for the metric.

Function words are a core stylometric signal for authorship (Poe vs Lovecraft vs Shelley differ in usage of 'the', 'of', 'upon', 'which'); removing them and all stop-word-containing bigrams from the word view loses signal that char_wb only partially recovers, so log loss should worsen modestly.

MultinomialNB on word/char counts is a strong, diverse complement to TF-IDF LR on this competition (top kernels stack exactly these to reach ~0.30-0.32); a log-linear meta blend on OOF log-probs should cut log loss noticeably, with only a small penalty from 80%-data fold-averaged test predictions.

Function words are among the strongest authorship signals; dropping them degrades both word-level LR and NB OOF probabilities (especially bigrams like 'of the', 'which I'), and while char_wb models and the stacker partially compensate, the ensemble loses discriminative information and log loss modestly worsens.

Linear stacker on raw (not log) OOF probabilities loses LightGBM's ability to recalibrate overconfident NB outputs and exploit nonlinear meta-feature interactions, so a modest regression is more likely than a gain despite the early-stopping optimism argument.

Punctuation (comma/semicolon density, quotation style) is a well-known strong authorial signal in this corpus, especially for Poe vs Lovecraft; stripping it removes discriminative char n-grams and worsens log loss.

OOF stacking of word/char LR with tuned MultinomialNB on raw counts is the classic strong recipe for this competition; NB word model alone reaches ~0.40 and the log-prob meta LR typically lands in the 0.34-0.38 range, a clear gain over the single C=1 LR at 0.439.

Chi2 truncation to 10k of ~130k TF-IDF columns discards useful long-tail word/char signal that L2-regularized LR exploits well; LR OOF degrades and the blend leans more on NB, so the ensemble gets worse, though NB partially cushions the loss.

Function words are among the strongest stylometric signals in authorship attribution (Poe/Lovecraft/Shelley differ markedly in their use of 'upon', 'which', 'the', etc.), so removing them from both the word TF-IDF and the NB count features discards discriminative information; the char_wb block partially recovers it for LR, but NB degrades and the blend worsens overall.

C=1 is under-fit for high-dimensional word+char TF-IDF on this task; CV will likely pick C≈10–30, which historically drops LR log loss from ~0.43 to ~0.40, with the explicit per-fold fitting fitting comfortably in the time budget.

OOF stacking of LR and MultinomialNB (NB on counts is notably strong on this dataset) with a LightGBM meta-learner is the classic recipe that took public kernels from ~0.43 to ~0.32-0.36; four diverse base models plus meta-features should land around 0.34-0.35 with some noise from the ~2k-row test set.

Weighting black target pixels 3x moves the optimum away from the unweighted RMSE the leaderboard uses, biasing uncertain boundary pixels darker; the model already handles text well, so this mismatch likely yields a small regression rather than a gain, within run-to-run noise.

The metric is unweighted RMSE dominated by background pixels; 10x ink weighting shifts capacity toward strokes and away from cleaning stains on white-target regions, so the mismatch between objective and metric likely yields a small regression.

Residual prediction with zero-init head starts at the identity and converges faster under the short 2000-step budget; losing the sigmoid costs little since the inference clamp handles background overshoot, so expect a small improvement rather than a large one.

L1 targets the conditional median rather than the mean, so on ambiguous stroke-edge/noise pixels it commits to 0 or 1 and pays a larger squared penalty under the RMSE metric; expect a small regression with unchanged optimizer/schedule.

Residual (DnCNN-style) parameterization with zero-init identity start removes sigmoid saturation/vanishing-gradient issues on the mostly-white targets and converges faster within the short 2000-step CPU budget, likely giving a small gain, though sigmoid's natural crispness on bimodal pixels means the difference is modest.

Halving base channels cuts NAFNet capacity ~4x; with the same 2000 training steps the small model likely underfits fine text strokes slightly, giving a modest RMSE regression rather than any regularization benefit on this fairly clean synthetic task.

Upweighting dark pixels 3x misaligns the training objective with the plain-RMSE metric dominated by background pixels; stroke fidelity may improve slightly but background/residual noise errors typically grow, giving a small net regression.

The background-normalized second channel gives the shallow U-Net an explicit stain/illumination-removed view, which typically trims a few percent of RMSE on this dataset; however the diff also hard-pins execution to CPU with 8 threads, so if the node normally offers a GPU or more cores the 2,000 updates risk slowing or timing out, capping the expected gain.

The diff's runtime.toml forces CPU (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""), so autocast is already disabled and the float32 head is a no-op; if the hill was already CPU-only the metric is unchanged up to thread-count nondeterminism, though if the parent ran on GPU the CPU run risks a timeout.

4-view flip TTA on a flip-augmented U-Net typically gives a small but consistent RMSE reduction (~1-3%) from averaging out per-view noise; note the diff also adds runtime.json forcing CPU (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""), which adds inference cost and raises timeout risk but if the run completes the metric should modestly improve.

A compact residual NAFNet (~5x fewer FLOPs than the U-Net, LayerNorm + gated blocks, zero-init residual scales) should train stably in 2000 steps and match or slightly beat the U-Net, but the diff hardcodes device=cpu via runtime.json, making the run slow and at real risk of hitting the 15-minute kill, so gains are modest and uncertain.

The pretrained ConvNeXt-B in1k head is already a strong 120-breed classifier (and these Stanford Dogs images were in its fine-tuning set), so a holdout-tuned temperature+weight blend with the LR should cut log loss noticeably with w=0 as a safe floor; compute cost unchanged.

Unwhitened PCA to 256-d on already-L2-regularised LR mostly discards low-variance but still discriminative directions for fine-grained breed separation; C re-selection limits damage, so expect a small regression rather than a gain.

Mixup/CutMix at prob=1.0 for only 6 fine-tuning epochs on a small dataset slows convergence and underfits the clean distribution; the calibration benefit is already captured by temperature scaling, so expect a small regression rather than a gain.

With only 6 epochs of fine-tuning and eval at full center crop, the much more aggressive 0.08 lower bound mostly adds train/test scale mismatch and underfitting on tiny crops rather than useful regularisation, so log loss likely gets slightly worse.

ConvNeXt-V2 Large IN-22k features (plus its 1000-way logits, which already contain the 120 dog classes) are far more separable than ResNet-50's; frozen strong backbones with logistic regression typically land near 0.15-0.2 log loss on this task, with runtime well within budget.

The 1000-d ImageNet log-softmax includes the network's own pretrained 120 dog-class outputs (Stanford Dogs = ImageNet dog classes), a nonlinear, near-optimal readout that a 9k-sample L2-regularised LR cannot fully relearn from pooled features alone; dropping it should noticeably worsen log loss toward the typical ~0.5-0.6 ResNet-50 linear-probe level.

Least-squares one-hot regression with a single global temperature is a weaker probabilistic head than tuned multinomial LR on well-separated features; the coarse T grid and per-class miscalibration of ridge scores typically cost ~10% log loss.

Unsupervised PCA to 128 dims per block discards discriminative low-variance directions that matter for fine-grained 120-way separation; the L2-regularised LR already controls overfitting on 2560-d normalised features, so compression most likely costs a modest amount of log loss rather than helping.

ConvNeXt-Base pretrained on ImageNet-22k (which contains many dog breeds) yields far more discriminative frozen features than ResNet-50 V1 for fine-grained Stanford Dogs, and C is re-tuned for the new feature scale; expect log loss to drop from ~0.45 to roughly 0.2-0.27.

End-to-end fine-tuning of an ImageNet-22k-pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny with augmentation, flip TTA and temperature scaling should substantially beat frozen ResNet-50 features (typical ~90%+ accuracy on Stanford Dogs), landing around 0.25-0.30 log loss within the 7-minute guard.

The ImageNet head is a strong breed classifier that has effectively seen these Stanford Dogs images (both Kaggle train and test derive from ImageNet train), so appending its log-probs and standardizing with re-tuned C should meaningfully cut log loss, though sklearn LR on 3048 standardized dims caps the gain.

ConvNeXt-in22k, CLIP and DINOv2 features are far stronger than ResNet-50 on Stanford Dogs (DINOv2 alone linear-probes ~90%+ top-1), and L2-normalised concatenation with tuned C typically drops log loss into the ~0.15-0.25 range, assuming downloads and the timm models load correctly within budget.

Focal loss (gamma=2) down-weights the bulk of examples once they're moderately confident, slowing effective learning in a short 10-epoch fine-tune and yielding under-confident, flatter softmax outputs; dropping label smoothing helps slightly but focal loss typically matches or trails CE on accuracy and its systematic underconfidence costs log loss, so a modest regression is most likely.

Full fine-tuning at lr=0.01 on ~9k images overfits and drifts from ImageNet features that are already near-optimal for this ImageNet-subset task; freezing conv1..layer3 and tuning only layer4+fc regularizes strongly and should lower log loss noticeably, though not to SOTA levels since single-model no-TTA ResNet-50 at 224px is still limited.
Hflip TTA on frozen ViT features gives a small but reliable log-loss gain by averaging two near-independent probability estimates; features still un-normalised so improvement modest (~1-3%).

CLIP ViT-B/32 linear-probe features are weaker on fine-grained dog breeds than an ImageNet-21k/1k-supervised ViT-B/16 that was trained on exactly these 120 ImageNet dog classes at finer patch resolution; plus unnormalized CLIP features with the same hardcoded C=0.3 are a mismatched regularization, so expect a noticeable regression.

Truncating 2048-d ResNet GAP features to 256 unwhitened PCs discards low-variance but breed-discriminative directions that fine-grained classification relies on; with C fixed the linear probe is already well regularised, so PCA is more likely to mildly hurt than help log loss.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings are far stronger than ImageNet-1k ResNet-50 for fine-grained breeds (linear-probe accuracy on Stanford Dogs ~92-94% vs ~86%), and with C re-tuned plus 10-view TTA the log loss should drop substantially, likely into the 0.22-0.32 range.

Whitening rescales features from norm ~1.4 to ~16, so C=1.0 becomes far weaker regularization while whitening amplifies noisy tail components and truncation to 256-d drops some discriminative signal; the resulting overconfident logreg should increase log loss noticeably despite similar accuracy.

k-NN vote probabilities are poorly calibrated for log loss: whenever the true breed gets zero of the 10 neighbor votes (likely ~8% of test images among 120 fine-grained classes), the 1e-3 floor incurs ~7 nats each, swamping the gains and roughly doubling the loss versus the calibrated logistic head.

Full fine-tuning at lr 0.01 on 9k images gives accuracy similar to frozen ImageNet features (which already encode dog breeds), while label smoothing 0.1 imposes a calibration floor on log loss, so expect roughly flat-to-slightly-worse log loss around 0.45-0.5, with some timeout risk from 10 epochs of JPEG decoding.

ViT-B/16 augreg in21k->in1k features are far stronger for fine-grained dog breeds (in21k covers these classes) than frozen ResNet-50 V1; linear probe log loss typically drops to ~0.2, though the un-retuned C=0.3 on differently scaled 768-d features leaves some slack.

Averaging LR probabilities over 5 crops + flips of frozen ResNet-50 features smooths overconfident single-view predictions; corner crops are slightly off-distribution vs center-crop training but the ensemble effect typically yields a modest 3-7% log-loss gain, and the extra 10k forward passes are cheap.

ConvNeXt-Tiny in22k features are much stronger for fine-grained dog breeds than ResNet-50 v1 and complement it; L2-normalised concat with C=1.0 may be slightly under-confident but should still cut log loss substantially, roughly to ~0.30.

Stanford Dogs images are in ImageNet train, so the pretrained fc head's dog-restricted softmax is a strong, leak-boosted classifier; a validation-tuned temperature/alpha blend with the LR should cut log loss substantially, though V2 label smoothing and heavy-aug training limit memorization so it won't approach zero.

Projecting 2048-d ResNet-50 features to 256 unwhitened PCA dims discards low-variance but discriminative directions needed for fine-grained 120-breed separation, and C=0.3 was tuned for the full space, so log loss likely worsens modestly.

Global max pooling on a frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 generally yields noisier, larger-magnitude descriptors than the avg-pooled features the network was trained to feed its classifier; the linear probe with fixed C=0.3 will overfit more and lose fine-grained breed discrimination, so log loss likely worsens despite temperature calibration.

V2 weights are ~4.7pt stronger on ImageNet (which contains these dog classes) so penultimate features should separate breeds better, though heavy-aug/label-smoothing recipes sometimes transfer worse under linear probes, so the gain is modest and uncertain; temperature refit absorbs any logit-scale shift.

C=0.03 was already tested and lost to 0.3 on the holdout; the tenfold stronger L2 yields an underconfident, lower-norm head, and the short 90s/2-epoch fine-tune at head lr 0.001 cannot fully recover the sharper logits, so log loss regresses moderately.

Lowering input resolution from 224 to 192 degrades frozen ResNet50 feature quality (roughly 1-2% ImageNet top-1 drop), which for fine-grained breeds translates into noticeably worse log loss; faster fine-tuning steps within the 90s budget only partially offset this.
Unwhitened PCA to 256 dims discards fine-grained discriminative variance in the 2048-d ResNet-50 features, and C=0.3 was tuned for the raw feature space, so log loss likely worsens modestly.

Lowering input resolution from 224 to 192 for a frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 degrades feature quality (known ~1-2% top-1 drop, worse for fine-grained breeds), so log loss should worsen moderately with no offsetting gain.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 features (~80.9% vs 76.1% top-1, and dog breeds are ImageNet classes) should be more discriminative for a linear probe; C=0.3 was tuned for V1 feature scale so gains may be partly offset, and dropping the TORCH_HOME cache dir adds some download-failure risk, but expect a moderate log-loss improvement.

LR on raw unnormalised features with C=0.3 fits training data nearly perfectly and is overconfident on held-out data, so a holdout-fitted temperature (likely T~1.2-1.5) should trim log loss modestly; slight mismatch from calibrating on the 85% model limits gains to a few percent.

Head starts at the LR optimum so it barely moves; 2 epochs of tiny-lr SGD on the last bottleneck's convs without augmentation gives only marginal adaptation, so expect a small improvement (or a wash) with mild overfitting risk from the lower effective weight decay.

Horizontal-flip TTA on frozen ResNet-50 features with probability averaging reliably gives a small log-loss gain (roughly 1-4%) by reducing per-image feature variance; the mlflow/tempdir scaffolding is guarded and should not affect the score.

AUC is ranking-based so class imbalance does not hurt L2 logistic regression; discarding 90-99.7% of negatives (threat trains on ~950 rows over 60k-200k sparse features) throws away the information needed to rank the huge negative pool, so rare-label AUCs degrade noticeably and the mean drops.

Adding char_wb n-grams to the NB-LogReg branch is a known strengthening of NB-SVM-style models on this task (better handling of obfuscated/rare tokens), which should lift branch B individually enough to raise the blend slightly despite reduced branch diversity; runtime risk from liblinear on the larger matrix is capped by max_iter.

Balanced undersampling throws away 90-99% of the data per label (threat trains on ~950 rows, NB ratios estimated from tiny subsets), and AUC is ranking-based so imbalance was never hurting it; expect a clear regression concentrated on rare labels.

MultinomialNB on TF-IDF is a markedly weaker classifier (~0.93-0.95 AUC on this data, with overconfident near-0/1 probabilities that also weaken the stacked features), so replacing the ~0.978-AUC NB-LogReg branch and blending it 50/50 by rank with branch A drags the ensemble down noticeably.

Mean-pooled Word2Vec + logreg/MLP (~0.965-0.97 AUC) is clearly weaker than word+char TF-IDF logreg (~0.98), and it now carries 2/3 of the rank blend weight against the strong NB-LogReg branch, so the diversity gain does not offset the loss and the blend regresses modestly.

AUC is rank-based so balancing gives no calibration benefit, while discarding 90-99.7% of negatives leaves rare labels (threat ~950 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k) with far too few examples for 60k-200k sparse features and makes the NB log-count ratios very noisy; expect a clear regression concentrated in threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic.

A sparse TF-IDF MLP is a genuinely different (non-linear, label-shared) model and usually blends positively with NB-LR/LR at equal rank weight, but with only 1-3 short epochs before the 690s guard it will reach ~0.98 held-out AUC, roughly on par with the linear branches, so the gain is small (~+0.0005) and there is some fallback/undertraining risk.

1:1 undersampling discards 80-99.7% of negatives, so the linear models lose most of the hard-negative information that drives ranking AUC; rare labels (threat ~956 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k) will degrade the most, and NB ratios computed on tiny balanced sets become noisy, outweighing any prior-balancing benefit.

Lowercasing is already done by TfidfVectorizer, so only the repeat-collapse, IP/URL/timestamp tokens and profanity de-obfuscation add signal; char_wb n-grams already capture much of this, so expect a tiny gain (~+0.0002–0.0005) with small risk of neutral/slightly negative.

Feature-level stacking of B's OOF logits into A gives A a cross-label view and a stronger word-ngram signal, but the /20 scaling plus C=0.1 limits how much A can use it and it makes A more correlated with B, shrinking blend diversity; expect a small gain (~+0.0004) with meaningful timeout risk from 30 extra liblinear fits.

A 3-epoch shared-hidden-layer MLP on the same 60k TF-IDF features is a diverse nonlinear learner that alone likely scores ~0.975-0.978 (weaker than A/B, rare labels undertrained), so an equal-weight rank blend gives a small net gain from decorrelation, with modest risk of being neutral or slightly negative.

NB-LogReg on word+char TF-IDF is a strong, somewhat decorrelated third linear branch; three-way rank average should give a small but real lift (~+0.0005), with the main risk being wall-clock from the 250k-column liblinear fits rather than metric regression.

Per-label holdout-fitted blend weights shrunk toward 0.5 will move weights only modestly from equal blending between two similarly-strong branches, giving a tiny but likely positive AUC gain (~+0.0001), with some time-budget risk from the extra holdout vectorizer fits.

Compressing 100k TF-IDF n-grams to 300 LSA factors discards the discriminative rare profanity/threat tokens that sparse LR exploits; LSA+LR on this dataset historically lands around 0.95-0.96, a clear regression from the 0.98 two-branch sparse ensemble (and the SVD adds timeout risk).

Capping negatives at 10:1 discards ~90% of negatives for severe_toxic/threat/identity_hate (threat trains on ~5k rows), throwing away hard-negative evidence that linear n-gram models and fastText need; rare-label AUCs drop noticeably while toxic/obscene/insult barely change, so the column mean regresses.

The fastText branch is already dragging the A+B blend (~0.98 alone) down to 0.883 via overfit/saturated probabilities and ties; a single 7-class softmax model shares embeddings but makes rare labels (threat, severe_toxic, identity_hate) compete against dominant classes and saturate to the 1e-5 floor even more often, and softmax competition among co-occurring labels distorts per-column ordering, so I expect roughly unchanged to slightly worse rather than a fix.

Swapping a strong three-branch NB-LR/LR TF-IDF rank ensemble for a single ComplementNB on raw word counts drops to classic Naive-Bayes territory (~0.93-0.95 mean AUC), with saturated predict_proba ties on long comments and weak rare-label ranking hurting further.

Mean-pooled 200d corpus word2vec loses the exact-token and char n-gram signal that drives the strong TF-IDF/NB-LogReg ensemble; such dense-average baselines on Jigsaw typically land around 0.95-0.96 AUC, a clear regression from 0.9816.

Mean-pooled corpus-trained Word2Vec fed to a linear classifier loses exact lexical n-gram signal (profanity, char-level misspellings) that drives this task; such embedding-average baselines historically land around 0.94-0.96 mean AUC versus 0.98 for TF-IDF/NB-LR blends, so a clear regression.

A char-level NB-LogReg is a genuinely different view (obfuscated spellings) and 3-way rank blending of strong linear branches typically adds a few tenths of a thousandth in AUC; holdout-tuned weights at step 0.1 add little overfit, though the extra char vectorizer plus dense char liblinear fits push wall-clock toward the 15-min kill limit.

C=0.1/sag is the tuned setting from the original word+char TF-IDF kernel (C=4 comes from the NB-SVM kernel, a different feature set); raising C 40x on l2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF over-fits rare labels and makes branch A more correlated with branch B, so the rank blend likely loses a little AUC while staying within budget.

Supervised fastText alone scores ~0.965-0.975 here (softmax saturation and overfitting at epoch=20/lr=0.5 hurt rare labels), but it is diverse from the two sparse-linear branches, so an equal-weight rank blend should give a small net gain rather than a regression; runtime lands ~11-13 min, under the hard kill.

A char-ngram NB-LogReg is a moderately diverse, strong-ish linear view (~0.98 alone) and equal-weight rank blending of three correlated linear models typically yields a small gain of ~0.0005-0.001; the main risk is the extra char_wb 3-7 vectorizer pushing wall-clock near the 15-min kill.

Training on only 90% of the data costs a small amount of AUC, and per-label blend weights tuned on a 10% holdout (only ~48 threat positives) add mostly noise, so the net effect is roughly neutral to slightly negative.
