NB-weighting branch A makes it more similar to branch B (loss of blend diversity) and the noisy log-count ratios on rare labels (threat, identity_hate) plus sag convergence issues on rescaled char n-grams likely offset any single-branch gain, yielding a small net regression.

min_df=0.01 on ~313k docs requires each term to appear in ~3100+ documents, collapsing word vocab to a couple thousand common words and dropping most bigrams and rare slurs/threat terms, which hurts the rare labels (identity_hate, threat) most; char n-grams partially compensate so the drop is moderate rather than catastrophic.

Discarding ~90-99% of negatives per label (e.g. threat keeps 478 of 159k negatives) throws away the hard negatives that drive AUC ranking on 150k test rows and makes the NB log-count ratios noisy, so all six columns regress, with the rare labels (threat, severe_toxic, identity_hate) hit hardest.

Rocchio/centroid classifiers on TF-IDF are a much weaker discriminator than tuned logistic regression (no per-feature weighting, negative centroid dominated by bland high-frequency n-grams); NB weighting in branch B helps but overall AUC should drop several points to the mid-0.95s.

Switching char to char_wb on a capped 50k vocabulary marginally reduces cross-word noise n-grams but loses cross-token patterns; in this rank-blended two-branch setup the effect is essentially neutral, likely within ±0.0003 AUC.

Swapping discriminative logistic regression (and the NB-LogReg trick) for pure ComplementNB on TF-IDF features drops to generative NB quality, which on this task typically lands around 0.94-0.96 mean AUC, well below the 0.98 of tuned linear models; the rank blend of two NB branches recovers only a little.

Collapsing 60k sparse lexical features into 32 SVD components discards most of the discriminative signal (linear TF-IDF logreg thrives on high-dimensional sparsity), so branch A drops from ~0.978 to roughly 0.92-0.93 AUC and the equal-weight rank blend with fastText is dragged below the fastText branch alone.

Collapsing everything outside the top 2,000 tokens to 'raretoken' erases most slurs, obscene variants, and threat vocabulary that drive the rare labels, and neuters the char n-gram features and fastText subword signal, so expect a clear regression concentrated in identity_hate/threat/severe_toxic.

Removing English stop words from the 10k word unigram vectorizer adds a few hundred function words (e.g. 'you', 'your' are strong toxicity cues) that the char branch and NB branch already capture, so the rank-averaged ensemble shifts only marginally, likely a tiny gain.

Logit averaging weights the branches by their logit spread; the sharp NB-LogReg (C=4) branch dominates the compressed C=0.1 sag branch, so the blend loses some of the equal-weight diversity the rank average captured, giving a small regression.

Switching char_wb to char adds cross-word-boundary n-grams but with a 50k feature cap and a 50/50 rank blend with the untouched NB-LR branch, the effect on mean AUC is marginal, likely within a few ten-thousandths either way.

A 5-epoch dim-64 fastText with bigrams and no char n-grams typically reaches only ~0.96-0.97 AUC on Jigsaw, weaker than the NB-LogReg branch it replaces, so the equal-weight rank blend with branch A should drop slightly below the current 0.980.

L2-regularised multinomial LR on leaf descriptors already handles redundancy well; discarding a third of the columns by univariate F-score throws away complementary low-marginal-F bins, so the LR component gets slightly worse and the 50/50 blend regresses modestly.

Label smoothing at 0.1 caps the NN's true-class probability near 0.9 (floor ~0.105 logloss for the NN alone) on a dataset where classes are nearly perfectly separable, so the 50/50 blend loses confidence on correct predictions and log loss likely rises modestly despite any calibration gain on the few ambiguous cases.

OvR at C=1.0 with 10-vs-980 imbalanced binaries yields flatter, less discriminative score geometry than the joint softmax; power/floor calibration recovers most of the scale but not the ranking quality, so OOF log loss likely degrades modestly.

A 5-seed relu MLP bag on the 192 standardized descriptors is a strong, decorrelated complement to LR on this dataset; blending before the power/floor calibration with CV-chosen w typically trims OOF log loss by ~15-25%, with some optimism from the larger selection grid but w=0 fallback bounding downside.

Fold-averaging smooths high-C probabilities but each fold model sees only ~13 of 16 samples per class; with such tiny per-class counts the lost data slightly outweighs the variance reduction, so expect a small regression or near-neutral result.

Absolute size, aspect ratio and Hu moments are genuinely new signal on top of the scale-normalised descriptors and are known to help on this dataset; with C re-tuned by OOF CV the 21 extra columns should give a modest log-loss gain, tempered by the risk that the images folder is absent (no change) or that a few noisy features add little.

Unwhitened PCA is just an orthogonal rotation for the isotropic L2 penalty, so the only real effect is truncating ~90-120 low-variance directions, which on a 99-class problem with 10 samples/class discards discriminative signal and typically raises log loss.

Logistic regression at fixed C=1.0 is already underconfident on this 99-class, 10-per-class problem; each fold model sees only 8 samples per class under effectively stronger regularisation, and averaging convex linear models gives little variance reduction while further flattening probabilities, so log loss should worsen modestly versus the full-data refit.

The two-branch NN on features+silhouettes should reach roughly 0.05-0.09 holdout log loss (features branch alone is a decent MLP; augmentation/dropout keep it calibrated enough), and a 50/50 blend with the underconfident C=1 LR at 0.124 typically lands near or below the better model, so ~0.07; runtime fits comfortably under the 9-minute guard.

LR at C=1.0 on this near-separable 99-class problem is heavily under-confident (the famous leaf trick is C>>1); OOF-tuned temperature sharpening (a likely ~3-5) with a tiny uniform floor recovers most of that gain, roughly halving log loss, though not quite matching a properly tuned C.

Standardised 192-feature logistic regression on this dataset is heavily over-regularised at C=1; CV will pick a large C (~1000-3000) which on Kaggle historically gives ~0.03-0.06 log loss, a large gain with modest overconfidence risk.

Image size and shape descriptors (Hu moments, solidity, circularity) carry real species signal in this dataset and add only ~27 columns to a 192-feature LR, so with fixed C=1.0 the log loss should drop moderately without overfitting; mlflow wrapper is fail-safe and runtime stays well within budget.

This dataset is near-separable and logistic regression logloss falls steeply with larger C (known best C in the thousands); cutting C from 1.0 to 0.2 flattens the predicted probabilities and materially worsens log loss.

Dropping the full refit trains the submitted logistic regression on only 792 rows (~8 per class instead of ~10) with no other change, and with such tiny per-class counts the loss of 20% of the data noticeably worsens calibrated probabilities, so log loss should rise from ~0.081 to roughly 0.10-0.12.

OOF-optimized convex blend of LR with distance-weighted kNN and shrinkage LDA is unlikely to hurt (weights can collapse to LR) and typically shaves a bit off log loss via calibration diversity on this well-separated feature set, so modest improvement expected.

With only 10 samples per class across 99 classes, GBDTs are known to badly underperform regularised logistic regression on the leaf dataset (typical XGBoost/GBM log loss ~0.3-0.6 vs ~0.05 for LR), and the tiny 15% early-stopping split plus min_samples_leaf=10 makes trees coarse and poorly calibrated.

Platt-sigmoid calibration of OvR LinearSVC with 3-fold CV leaves only ~2-3 positives per class per fold, so calibrated probabilities are capped/under-confident (~0.6-0.7 on the true class) and each base fit sees only 2/3 of the data; this member is likely slightly worse than the C=1 multinomial LR it replaces, nudging the uniform soft-vote loss up a little rather than down.

A 600-tree RF gives smoother, better-calibrated vote-fraction probabilities than an early-stopped HGB with a ~1-row/class validation split on 99 classes, so the uniform soft vote loses a somewhat noisy member; RF is still diffuse on this data, so the gain is modest rather than large.

A (256,128) ReLU MLP on standardised leaf descriptors typically beats an untuned C=1 logistic regression on this dataset, but early stopping on a 99-sample accuracy-based validation split leaves the softmax somewhat underconfident and adds seed noise, so expect a moderate rather than dramatic gain.
The leaf features are nearly linearly separable so CV will pick a large C (~100-1000), which on this dataset is known to drop LR log loss from ~0.12 to ~0.04-0.07; shrinkage alpha adds minor safety.

Hu moments and contour scalars add modest complementary shape information to the provided descriptors, but the radial histogram largely duplicates the shape feature and C=1.0 on 240 dims with 990 samples limits gains, so expect a small log loss improvement (or no change if images are missing and features zero out).

Standardized leaf features are near-separable, so CV over log loss will select a much larger C (~30-300) than 1.0, sharply reducing under-confidence; known Kaggle results for tuned-C logistic regression on these features land around 0.03-0.06.

Uniform soft averaging pulls in poorly calibrated kNN (near-hard probabilities) and HGB (weaker on 99 classes with ~9 samples each), diluting the confident correct predictions of LR/LDA; the ensemble's true-class probability is capped by the weakest member, so log loss lands near or slightly above the 0.124 baseline rather than approaching the ~0.03 a tuned LR/LDA alone could reach.
LogisticRegression at C=1.0 is over-regularised (underconfident) on this dataset, so OOF selection will pick alpha at or near 0; shrinkage toward uniform yields at most a negligible change.

Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage on these correlated descriptors is small, leaving overconfident posteriors that dominate the log loss; fixing shrinkage at 0.9 heavily regularizes the within-class covariance, softening probabilities on the few errors while class means remain well separated enough to keep accuracy high, so log loss should drop noticeably.

Per-family LDA models are individually much weaker (shape alone is poor) and arithmetic averaging of probabilities dilutes confidence rather than combining evidence multiplicatively, so log loss will likely worsen noticeably versus the joint 192-feature shrinkage LDA.

Standardized leaf features are already well-conditioned and LR with large C exploits low-variance discriminative directions; truncating to 90% variance (~70-90 components) discards class-separating signal, so log loss likely roughly doubles rather than improves.

Shrinkage-regularized LDA is a strong, well-calibrated fit for these 192 Gaussian-like descriptors with 99 classes and few samples per class; with shrinkage tuned on neg_log_loss it should roughly match or slightly beat tuned logistic regression, though the gain is uncertain and could be neutral.

L2-regularized logistic regression is rotation-invariant, so PCA only truncates ~40% of low-variance standardized directions, which on sparse margin/texture histograms carry discriminative signal; expect a mild log-loss regression rather than a gain.

Shrinkage LDA is a known strong fit for these 192 low-noise descriptor features (many Kaggle kernels reported LDA beating logistic regression on this dataset), and OOF temperature scaling should tame LDA's overconfident scores, so a moderate log-loss improvement is likely though not guaranteed.

Mixing 0.5% uniform costs ~-log(0.995)≈0.005 on every confident correct prediction, while the C=1 logistic model is already soft (avg p_true≈0.91) so very few test rows have p_true below the 5e-5 floor where the prior would help; net small regression.

Dropping Nyström components from 512 to 384 on a 990-sample train set loses kernel fidelity (already well below the 990-landmark exact kernel) with no matching regularization gain, so log loss likely worsens modestly, though randomness in landmark selection makes it partly a seed-dependent shift.

Ledoit-Wolf shrunk LDA fits the near-Gaussian standardized leaf descriptors well and typically beats untuned C=1 logistic regression here, but its sharp posteriors risk a few catastrophic clipped-probability errors, so gain is moderate rather than large.
Leaf descriptors are nearly linearly separable so CV log loss keeps falling with weaker regularisation; grid should pick C=100-1000, which public kernels show yields ~0.04-0.05 versus 0.124 at C=1.

C=1.0 LR on 192 standardized features is heavily over-regularised and underconfident on this easy 99-class task, so the OOF-fitted temperature will land well below 1 (sharpening toward the 0.25 bound) and cut log loss substantially, though not as much as properly tuning C (~0.04-0.05) since sharpening cannot fix the shrunk weight directions.

Nyström RBF (gamma=1/192 on standardized data) expands to 512 standardized features, giving the C=1 LR more effective capacity and sharper, still well-calibrated logits on this near-separable 99-class problem, so log loss should drop modestly from the over-regularized 0.124 baseline, though tail-eigenvalue noise components after re-standardization limit the gain.

Adds the known-strong RAOP signals the current model lacks (request length, imgur/image link, reciprocity/gratitude cues, time-of-request trend, prior RAOP activity) as properly standardized dense columns into the same LR; these features reliably add ~0.02-0.04 AUC on this dataset with negligible runtime risk.

Fully-grown RF on ~8k mostly-sparse TF-IDF columns with max_features=sqrt rarely splits on the informative numeric features and overfits sparse word noise; RF typically underperforms L2 logistic regression on bag-of-words text, so expect a small regression despite bagging over 500 trees.

Random forest with max_features='sqrt' over 5000 noisy sparse TF-IDF columns dilutes the few strong dense features and handles text far worse than linear TF-IDF models, so text signal degrades; the strong requester-history/giver indicator features keep it from collapsing but it likely lands a few AUC points below the logistic baseline.

Replacing 5k sparse TF-IDF unigrams with 50 standardized LDA topic proportions typically loses discriminative lexical signal (money/job/student words) that a linear model exploits directly; the metadata block carries most of the AUC so the drop is modest, but topic features rarely match TF-IDF for text classification at this scale.

Twenty unsupervised LDA topic proportions carry far less discriminative signal than a supervised out-of-fold TF-IDF logit, so LightGBM ends up close to a metadata-only model plus a small topic boost, likely a regression of roughly 0.01-0.03 AUC.

In RAOP the success base rate drifted strongly over the collection period and the test split is random in time, so the raw timestamp is a genuinely useful feature; hour/weekday are known to be near-noise here, so swapping them in should modestly lower AUC.

A GBM on the requester-history/time/text-stat features captures nonlinear interactions (e.g. RAOP prior activity, account age, request date) that the linear model misses, and rank-blending it with the TF-IDF LR on this small noisy dataset typically lifts AUC by a few points.

RF with sqrt max_features over ~5000 mostly sparse noisy TF-IDF columns dilutes the strong dense time/history signals and loses the additive text signal LR exploits; fully grown unregularized trees on ~4k rows will likely land a bit below the linear baseline.

Bag-of-subreddits is a known modest signal (account activity type, prior RAOP/giving communities) for this dataset; with l2-normalised binary tf-idf and C=0.3 it should add ~0.01 AUC to the linear model without overfitting.

giver_username_if_known is a known label leak (non-N/A rows are almost all positives, covering roughly a third of positives); if present in test.json, the logistic model will rank those rows at the top and AUC should jump from ~0.66 to the high 0.7s, with no change only if the column is absent in the prepared test split.

GBM on raw requester-history numerics plus the UTC timestamp (a known strong drift feature in this competition) captures nonlinear metadata signal the linear model missed, and the OOF text logit avoids leakage; expect a solid gain from 0.657 toward ~0.69, with MLflow wrapped in try/except so it won't break the run.

Time trend (success rate drifts over years), text length, image-link and prior-RAOP-activity indicators are known strong signals on RAOP that word TF-IDF alone misses; with a random train/test split they generalize, so a modest but real AUC gain (~+0.02-0.03) is likely, while mlflow tracking is best-effort and shouldn't break the run.

ExtraTrees with sqrt feature subsetting over ~5.4k mostly-sparse noisy TF-IDF columns rarely samples the informative numeric/embedding features at each split, so random splits on sparse text dilute signal; tree ensembles on this dataset without retrieval-time leaks typically land near 0.60, slightly below the linear model that exploits the dense embedding block well.

The unit-norm TF-IDF block contributes little coefficient mass next to the standardized 384-dim embeddings and numerics at C=0.3, so dropping it removes a bit of noisy signal and a bit of real lexical signal; expect roughly a wash with a slight edge from lower variance, and the MLflow additions do not affect the metric.

Length, gratitude and readability stats are known modest predictors in this dataset that length-normalized TF-IDF discards; with a regularized LR they add a small but real lift, while sentiment/flag features partly duplicate TF-IDF tokens so the gain stays modest.

Dropping the TF-IDF block removes the text signal that carries a real chunk of the AUC; a nine-feature requester-history logistic regression on this dataset typically lands around 0.60-0.62, below the current 0.65 text+metadata score.

Mean-pooled skip-gram vectors trained on only ~1.7M tokens are noisy and lose the sparse exact-token cues TF-IDF captures; with metadata and text stats retained the drop is bounded, but 200 standardized dense dims plus C=0.3 on 5.7k rows likely gives a small regression rather than a gain.

Bigrams with a 60k vocabulary on ~4.5k training docs add mostly sparse noise to an L2-normalized TF-IDF block whose signal is already weak relative to the standardized requester-history features; with fixed C=0.3 the effect is roughly neutral to slightly negative, and the mlflow telemetry is guarded so it should not break the run.

Dropping text removes real signal; the nine at-request history features alone typically yield ~0.60-0.62 AUC on RAOP, and num_leaves=63 on 9 features adds little, so expect a modest regression from 0.633.

On ~4k noisy rows a 400-tree RF over the same 309 dense features should be roughly on par with LightGBM(num_leaves=63) which likely overfits; sqrt feature sampling dilutes the few informative numeric columns among 300 weak SVD dims, so expect only a small, near-neutral change.

MiniLM embeddings add some semantic signal beyond unigram TF-IDF, but text is a weak predictor here and 384 standardized dense columns under C=0.3 LR on ~4k rows add overfitting noise, so expect only a small net gain.

Expanding to 100k uni+bigrams with min_df=2 on ~4k samples mostly adds sparse noisy features that dilute the L2-normalised text vector; with weak text signal and the numeric block carrying most of the AUC, the net effect is roughly flat to slightly negative.

Length, reciprocity, gratitude and hardship lexicon counts are known weak-but-real signals in RAOP (Althoff et al.) that unigram TF-IDF only partly captures; 15 scaled dense features in a C=0.3 logistic regression should add a modest ~0.005-0.015 AUC gain without overfitting risk.

LightGBM captures nonlinearities in the strongly predictive skewed requester-history numerics better than logistic regression, while SVD-300 dense text loses some of the sparse lexical signal; on ~4k samples with early-stopped CV the net is a modest gain over 0.657.

The spline captured the strong multi-year decline in RAOP success rate (a trend the test split shares); two annual sin/cos terms discard that trend and only model weak seasonality, so AUC should drop slightly.

A 100x weaker L2 penalty on ~5000 sparse TF-IDF unigrams with only ~4000 training rows lets the text coefficients memorize training noise; RAOP text is weakly predictive and strong regularization is what kept the current model generalizing, so AUC should drop by a few points.

RAOP success rate drifts strongly over calendar time (community growth diluted success) and the Kaggle split is random rather than temporal, so a smooth spline of request date should add real signal on top of the weak text+history baseline, likely a modest AUC gain.

KNN with cosine on a heterogeneous sparse feature mix (unit-norm TF-IDF swamped by unscaled subreddit indicators and standardized numerics) is far weaker than regularized logistic regression on this noisy, small dataset; expect a clear AUC drop to roughly 0.58-0.62.

Distance-weighted 25-NN on nine noisy, heavily-tied metadata features yields coarser and noisier probabilities than CatBoost (exact-match ties collapse weights onto few neighbors), so the 50/50 blend with logistic regression likely loses a bit of AUC.
C=30 with 5k TF-IDF features on ~4k rows overfits the weak text signal, and its extreme near-0/1 probabilities dominate the 50/50 average with CatBoost, degrading the blend's ranking.

Success rate on RAOP drifts strongly over calendar time (high in 2011, low by 2013), and the current model has no time signal, so quantile-knot date splines on a presumably random train/test split should add a few AUC points.

BernoulliNB with 5000 correlated unigram/bigram presence features will be dominated by noisy text likelihoods, and the nine strong requester-history features are collapsed to above/below-mean bits, so ranking quality drops below the tuned-ish logistic baseline.

RAOP success rate drifted strongly over the subreddit's lifetime and the test split is random in time, so a smooth spline over request date is a known useful signal for this competition; modest gain on top of TF-IDF plus history numerics, with no leakage risk from the fit-on-train protocol.

Binary subreddit-membership features add modest signal about requester community history (known to help on RAOP), and with C=0.3 regularization the ~1k sparse columns should give a small AUC gain rather than overfit; the mlflow wrapper is inert for scoring.

A nonlinear CatBoost on the nine requester-history features adds diversity to the linear TF-IDF model; metadata-only GBMs score ~0.62-0.65 AUC here, so a 50/50 average should give a modest gain despite unequal probability scales.

Adding bigrams under the same 5000-feature cap mostly swaps low-frequency unigrams for frequent bigrams; with C=0.3 logistic regression on ~4k docs this is roughly neutral, perhaps a tiny gain, and the mlflow telemetry is best-effort and won't affect predictions.

Authorship attribution is stylometric, and function-word usage (stop words, their bigrams) is among the strongest author signals; removing them from the word view discards useful features and only partially survives via char_wb, so log loss should get modestly worse.

Stacking log-probs of the strong TF-IDF LR with two diverse MultinomialNB models (word/char counts, typically ~0.40-0.45 OOF on Spooky) via a calibrated log-linear meta-learner usually yields a solid few-hundredths gain on this task, partly offset by fold-averaged (80%-data) base test predictions instead of a full refit.

Function words are among the strongest stylometric signals for authorship; removing them degrades the word-level NB and LR base models noticeably, and although the char_wb models and stacker recover part of the loss, the ensemble's overall log loss most likely worsens modestly.

A linear softmax on raw (not log-odds) standardized probabilities cannot recalibrate the overconfident NB columns or exploit meta-feature interactions the way LightGBM does, and the LightGBM early-stopping optimism mostly affects the printed CV rather than the averaged test predictions, so expect a modest regression.

Punctuation (commas, semicolons, dashes, quotes) is a well-known strong authorial signal in Spooky; stripping it removes discriminative char n-grams from the dominant feature block, so log loss should worsen modestly.

OOF stacking of word/char LR (C=10) with tuned MultinomialNB on word/char counts is the classic strong recipe for this competition; NB word features alone reach ~0.42 and the log-prob meta-LR typically lands near 0.37-0.40, a clear gain over the 0.4386 single-LR baseline, with mlflow guarded so no runtime failure risk.

Dropping ~92% of TF-IDF columns via chi2 removes long-tail discriminative n-grams that L2-regularized LR was already handling well, so the LR branch degrades and the NB blend only partially compensates; expect a modest regression in log loss.

Function words are among the strongest stylometric signals for authorship attribution, so dropping them from both the word TF-IDF and the NB count features removes discriminative information; the char_wb block still captures some of it, limiting but not preventing a regression.
Word+char TF-IDF LR on spooky is under-regularized at C=1; CV will likely pick C≈10-30, which typically drops log loss from ~0.43 to ~0.40-0.41 on the same features.

OOF stacking of NB-on-counts (strong on this dataset) with LR word/char models plus a LightGBM meta-learner with stylometric features is the classic winning recipe for Spooky, historically pushing log loss from ~0.43 down into the 0.33-0.37 range; runtime fits the budget and mlflow is best-effort.

Cross-boundary case-preserving char n-grams add punctuation/capitalization style signal that distinguishes these authors, and uncapped features with LR C=1.0 on L2-normalized TF-IDF typically yield a small gain (~0.005-0.01) rather than a large one, with some risk of extra regularization dilution offsetting it.

MultinomialNB on word counts is a strong, diverse complement to TF-IDF LR on this dataset (NB alone ~0.42-0.45), and an OOF-tuned arithmetic blend with clipping reliably drops log loss by several points; implementation is faithful and mlflow is safely wrapped, so a ~0.40 result is expected.

Function words are among the most discriminative stylometric signals for authorship attribution, and removing them also destroys informative word bigrams, so stopword removal should noticeably worsen log loss rather than help.

Imbalance is mild and the test distribution matches train, so oversampling only shifts predicted priors away from the true ones and adds duplicate rows that make the already-overconfident 25-epoch fastText softmax more overfit on minority classes; log loss is calibration-sensitive, so expect a small regression rather than a gain.

LR+NB probability blends on TF-IDF are a classic win in this competition, and the OOF-selected weight guards against harm (w=1 recovers the current model); ComplementNB with fixed alpha=0.1 and no calibration limits the gain to a modest ~0.01 improvement.

MultinomialNB on stacked word+char TF-IDF is a known weaker model for this task (Kaggle kernels typically land ~0.40-0.48 even with tuned alpha); its poorly calibrated, overconfident probabilities hurt log loss relative to the tuned logistic regression at 0.355.

Char n-grams capture author-specific punctuation/morphology that complements word features; removing them from the NB-SVM stack loses a well-known complementary signal on this dataset, so log loss should worsen from ~0.41 to roughly 0.43-0.45.

ComplementNB with alpha=1.0 on ~110k small-valued TF-IDF columns is heavily oversmoothed and its predict_proba is poorly calibrated, so probabilities collapse toward uniform-ish outputs; expect a large regression from 0.409 toward roughly 0.85-1.0 log loss.
TF-IDF+LR on this task is under-regularized-tuned at C=1; CV over log loss will likely pick C≈3-10, giving a modest but real gain, with the MLflow additions being inert best-effort telemetry.

MultinomialNB on stacked word+char TF-IDF is poorly calibrated and overconfident; NB on this dataset typically lands around 0.45-0.55 log loss vs ~0.42 for tuned LR, so expect a regression despite faster training.

fastText with lr=0.5, 25 epochs, softmax and bigrams+subwords on only ~17k sentences overfits and yields overconfident probabilities, so accuracy is comparable but log loss degrades noticeably versus the calibrated TF-IDF+LR baseline.

TF-IDF LR on this task is under-regularized-optimal at C=1; CV will most likely pick C=4 or 8, which historically drops stacked word+char LR log loss by a few points (~0.43 -> ~0.41), with modest risk of timeout from the 30 parallel fits.

NB log-count-ratio weighting on already L2-normalized TF-IDF plus one-vs-rest binary LR at C=4 (weaker regularization, OvR renormalized sigmoids) tends to give overconfident, less calibrated probabilities than the tuned multinomial LR, so log loss likely worsens modestly rather than improves.

14 MaxAbs-scaled stylometric features (sentence length, punctuation counts) add modest orthogonal signal to a TF-IDF LR that already captures most of this via char n-grams; expect a small improvement, with risk of near-zero effect from scale mismatch with L2-normalized TF-IDF blocks.

NB log-count-ratio scaling amplifies discriminative word/char n-grams and effectively reduces regularization on them, which historically helps on Spooky (NB-LR ~0.40-0.43), but the OVR-then-renormalize scheme is less well calibrated than multinomial softmax, so only a modest gain is expected.

L2-normalized TF-IDF rows already yield small logits at C=1; the known optimum for this feature set is at higher C (~10), so cutting C to 0.25 underfits and squashes probabilities toward uniform, raising log loss noticeably.

Dropping word 1-2 gram TF-IDF removes the most discriminative vocabulary features for this task; char_wb 2-5 alone with NB-LR is typically slightly worse than the concatenated representation, so a modest regression is expected.

Dropping NB log-count-ratio scaling leaves plain OvR L2 logistic regression on raw TF-IDF with C=1, which is underfit/overregularized on ~200k sparse features and typically lands around 0.55-0.62 log loss on this task, worse than NB-LR's 0.518.

With L2-normalized TF-IDF features, LR on spooky benefits from weak regularization (higher C); halving C to 2 underfits and makes predictions less confident, historically worsening log loss by a few percent, and the mlflow telemetry is best-effort and metric-neutral.

NB log-ratio scaling amplifies feature magnitudes (weakening effective L2 at C=4) and OvR binary probabilities renormalized are less well-calibrated than multinomial softmax, so log loss likely rises slightly despite similar accuracy.

Function words are among the strongest stylometric signals for authorship attribution; stripping them from both word and char_wb branches removes discriminative features (and word bigrams spanning stopwords), so log loss should worsen noticeably.

TF-IDF logistic regression on this task is already under-regularized-limited at C=1 (optimal C is typically higher); quartering C shrinks and blurs the decision function, temperature scaling can partly recover sharpness but not the lost discriminative signal, so log loss likely worsens modestly.
Switching to 'char' adds cross-word-boundary n-grams (punctuation/spacing style cues useful for author ID) but the 60k feature cap dilutes them; expect a small, near-neutral improvement in log loss.

NB log-ratio scaling effectively reduces regularization on the underfit C=1 TF-IDF LR and adds a strong NB prior, which historically helps on this task, but one-vs-rest sigmoid normalization is less calibrated than multinomial softmax, so expect only a modest net improvement.

C=1.0 is over-regularized for sparse high-dimensional word+char TF-IDF on ~17k sentences; loosening to C=4.0 sharpens probabilities and typically lowers log loss by a few points on this dataset, with only mild overconfidence risk.

LogisticRegression with C=1.0 on stacked TF-IDF is over-regularized and underconfident, so holdout-fitted temperature (T<1) sharpens probabilities and should trim log loss by ~0.02, similar to raising C.

Log1p target optimizes a geometric-mean-like fit and systematically underpredicts expensive/tail rides, which dominate dollar-scale RMSE; on this competition log targets typically give a slight RMSE regression rather than an improvement, and the added MLflow tracking is best-effort and won't affect the score.

4x more training rows with identical LightGBM config gives a modest but real gain (more trees used, lower variance), though the corrupt-row floor (~2.1 RMSE) and unchanged features cap the improvement to a few hundredths; mlflow logging is best-effort and shouldn't break the run.

Airport distance features are a known win here (JFK flat fare, LGA/EWR surcharges) that raw coordinates capture only coarsely with 1M rows and 63 leaves; expect a modest RMSE drop, bounded by the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows.

Fitting L2 on log1p and inverting with expm1 predicts roughly the conditional geometric mean, which under-predicts expensive/long and corrupt-coordinate rows that dominate dollar RMSE; on this competition log targets typically give similar-to-slightly-worse RMSE, so expect a small regression.

Fare is already nearly monotone in distance so the constraint adds little signal, while LightGBM's default 'basic' monotone method is restrictive and prevents the model from learning that very long in-box GPS distances are often corrupt low-fare rows, so expect a small regression.

Optimizing squared error in log space yields conditional-median-like predictions that systematically underpredict the dollar mean on high-variance long trips, so the dollar RMSE metric typically gets slightly worse (a known result for this competition), with early stopping on log RMSE adding no help.

In-sample encoding leaks each training row's own fare into its route/cell mean (self-weight 1/(c+20), large for the many sparse 2 km route keys), so trees learn to trust the TE features more than they deserve; validation/test rows lack that leak, early stopping fires earlier and the model degrades relative to the OOF scheme.

RMSE rewards the conditional mean; fitting log1p and back-transforming with expm1 yields a median-like estimate that systematically underpredicts high fares (airport/long trips), which dominate squared error, so the dollar-scale RMSE typically worsens slightly despite better-behaved training.

Airport distance features are a well-known strong signal for JFK/EWR flat-rate and surcharge rides; with 1M rows the trees can exploit them cheaply, but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the visible gain to a modest ~0.05-0.1 improvement.

The ~2.8% corrupt-coordinate test rows dominate the error floor; letting LightGBM learn the missing-coordinate population's mean plus year/hour adjustments (and using partially valid endpoints) should trim that contribution modestly, while valid-row predictions stay essentially unchanged, yielding a small improvement.

4x more training rows with the same LightGBM config gives a modest but reliable gain on the predictable rows (tree cap of 1000 likely binds), while the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the overall improvement; float32 coords and n_jobs change are neutral.

OOF-smoothed route/cell target encodings add some signal on tolls and airport flat fares, but LightGBM on raw coordinates already captures most spatial structure, and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the visible gain, so expect a small improvement within the noise of a 9.9K-row test set.

Training on log1p and back-transforming yields geometric-mean-style predictions that systematically underpredict large fares and the mean-optimal fallback for the corrupt-coordinate rows, which hurts squared-error RMSE; expect a small regression rather than a gain.

Manhattan distance, abs deltas, and bearing are well-known helpful features for this competition (typically ~0.1-0.2 RMSE gain on the valid rows with 1M rows), but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the relative improvement, so expect a modest gain.

Airport/landmark distance features are a well-known win for NYC taxi fares (JFK flat fare, EWR surcharge), letting trees isolate those regimes; expect a modest but real improvement, tempered by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows.

Optimizing L1 fits the conditional median, which systematically underpredicts the mean on a right-skewed fare target and converges slower with sign gradients; since the metric is RMSE, mismatching the training loss typically worsens RMSE by a few percent, and the MLflow wrapping is a no-op for the score.

Log-target fitting optimizes relative error and expm1 inversion yields median-like predictions biased low on the expensive tail (airport/long rides), which hurts dollar-scale RMSE; a small regression is more likely than a gain, with the corrupt-row floor unchanged.

L1 objective fits the conditional median of a right-skewed fare distribution, biasing predictions low on expensive trips and misaligning with the RMSE metric; expect a modest regression despite RMSE-based early stopping.

Huber with delta=$1 is effectively L1 for nearly all residuals, pulling predictions toward the conditional median and under-predicting the heavy-tailed high fares that dominate RMSE; with slower clipped-gradient convergence and early stopping on RMSE it will likely regress by a few percent.

Optimizing squared error in log space yields conditional-median/geometric-mean predictions that are biased low on the high-fare tail that dominates raw-dollar RMSE, so the metric typically worsens slightly despite the cleaner target distribution.

Airport distance/flag features are a known modest win for LightGBM on this task (JFK flat fares), but raw coordinates already let trees carve airport regions and ~2.1 RMSE of the score is an irreducible corrupt-row floor, so expect a small improvement of a few hundredths.

4x more training rows gives LightGBM a modest but real gain on the valid rows (roughly 3.6 to ~3.5 RMSE), but the ~2.8% corrupt test rows contribute a fixed error floor that damps the overall improvement; runtime stays comfortably within budget.

5-fold bagging of identical LightGBM models on the same 1M sample reduces prediction variance slightly and each fold sees 80% vs 90% of the data; the 2.8% corrupt test rows dominate the error floor, so expect only a small improvement of ~0.02-0.04 RMSE.

OOF-smoothed pickup-cell mean fare adds a little spatial signal (airport/hotspot pickups) but LightGBM on raw coordinates already captures most of it and the OOF/full-encoding mismatch adds noise, so expect only a marginal gain.

Snapping all four coordinates to a ~1 km grid injects up to ~1.5 km of error into haversine distance (the strongest fare predictor) and erases street-level/airport-scale location detail that LightGBM already exploits via fine splits, while the route encoding was already at 0.01-degree cells and gains nothing; expect a clear regression.

L1 objective targets the conditional median while the metric is RMSE; on right-skewed fares with heavy tails (airport flat rates, outliers) median predictions are systematically biased on the mean-square criterion and L1 leaf updates converge slower, so RMSE degrades modestly.

L1 objective targets the conditional median on a right-skewed fare distribution, biasing predictions low and converging slower (sign gradients), which hurts a mean-squared metric like RMSE despite RMSE-based early stopping.

Airport-distance features are a known useful signal for flat-rate JFK fares and airport surcharges; LightGBM can partly learn this from raw coordinates already, so expect a modest but real improvement, limited by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows.

L1 targets the conditional median of a right-skewed fare distribution and converges slower with sign gradients, so the mean-squared-error metric worsens relative to the L2 objective; the 2.1 floor from corrupt rows is unchanged but the fitted rows lose accuracy on high-fare outliers.

Rounding to 0.01 degrees (~1 km) coarsens location well below LightGBM's quantile-binned resolution in dense Manhattan, losing fine-grained pickup/dropoff signal (bridges, tunnels, toll zones) that distance alone doesn't recover; airports remain roughly identifiable so the hit is modest but likely negative.

L1 optimizes the conditional median on a right-skewed fare distribution while the grader uses RMSE, so predictions are biased low on expensive trips and LightGBM's sign-only L1 gradients converge slower; expect RMSE to degrade by a few percent.

Rotated Manhattan-grid distance is a known modest gain in this competition, but the tree model can already approximate it from raw coordinates and haversine, and the 2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows limits the impact, so expect a small improvement.

Cross-fitted route target encoding at 1km cells is mostly shrunk to the global mean with only 900k rows and adds little beyond raw coordinates plus distance already in the trees; expect a marginal, noise-level improvement.

A rotated Manhattan-grid distance is a genuinely informative feature that trees approximate poorly from raw coordinates alone, so expect a small gain on the ~97% valid rows, but the 2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows and the existing haversine feature cap the improvement to well under 2%; the MLflow tracking additions are best-effort and should not affect the result.

Doubling the training sample from 1M to 2M rows with identical features and hyperparameters gives LightGBM a modest generalization gain (typically 0.02-0.05 RMSE at this scale), while the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows and unchanged feature set cap the improvement; telemetry additions do not affect predictions.

Airport-route categorical helps LightGBM isolate JFK flat-fare and Newark surcharge trips that raw coordinates only partially capture, giving a modest gain on the ~97% clean rows while the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the visible improvement.

LightGBM with num_leaves=127 on raw numerics plus per-char f_27 typically lands around 0.987-0.99 on this dataset (the big gains to ~0.998 need explicit interaction features, which are excluded); treating letters as nominal rather than ordinal costs a little, and early stopping is unlikely to fire before 2000 rounds, so expect a small edge over the unengineered MLP's 0.9866.

The key signal in this dataset is sharp thresholds on additive sums of continuous features (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26); coarse 10-bin quantile one-hots destroy the within-bin resolution the MLP needs to reconstruct those sums, and binning the integer count columns collapses categories, so AUC should regress noticeably despite the wider first layer.

The raw features are nearly uncorrelated in this synthetic set, so full-rank PCA acts as an arbitrary rotation that scrambles the highly informative axis-aligned f_27 character ordinals and known integer-feature interactions; boosted trees (even with linear leaves) lose much of their split efficiency on rotated coordinates, so AUC should drop noticeably.

f_27 is almost unique per row (~740k distinct in 900k), so a smoothed target encoding collapses to the prior for nearly every row and discards the highly informative per-character signal, causing a large AUC regression.

f_27 has ~700k unique strings across 900k rows, so a smoothed full-string target encoding (m=20 vs counts of ~1) collapses to near the prior and carries almost no signal, while the dropped per-position character columns are among the strongest features in this dataset; removing them should cost a sizable chunk of AUC.

The f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, and f_00+f_01+f_26 sums with their ternary thresholds are the known key interactions in this synthetic dataset; exposing them directly lets LightGBM capture the additive structure trees struggle to learn from raw columns, typically lifting AUC from ~0.991 to the ~0.996-0.997 range.

Logistic regression on these raw features (no interaction terms, ordinal f_27 chars) will score only ~0.80-0.85 AUC on this interaction-heavy synthetic data, and an unweighted 50/50 rank blend lets the weak model's ranking noise substantially corrupt the 0.984 LightGBM ordering, so the blend regresses well below the single-model score.

MLPs are known to strongly outperform GBDTs on this dataset when given the three additive interaction sums and ordinal f_27 chars (Keras notebooks hit ~0.998 with extra unique-char count and fold ensembling); this single-model 80-epoch CPU MLP without unique_characters should land around 0.995, a clear gain over LightGBM's 0.984.

This is the known Ambros-style 64-64-64-16 SiLU MLP for TPS May 2022; even without the interaction/unique-char features, MLPs learn the additive feature interactions that trees miss, so holdout AUC should jump from ~0.977 to the low-0.99s (feature-engineered versions reach 0.998), and the tiny network trains 60 epochs on CPU well within budget.

Linear leaves can represent the oblique sum-of-features boundaries in this synthetic data more directly than staircase constant leaves, giving a modest AUC gain, but overfitting risk with 127 leaves and the real chance of exceeding the 15-minute kill (linear trees are often 3-5x slower, not 2x) cap the expected improvement.

The f_27 unique-character count is the well-known key interaction feature in TPS May 2022; trees cannot easily reconstruct it from ten per-position ordinals, so adding it typically lifts GBDT AUC from ~0.977 to ~0.985+.

These are the well-known true generative interactions for this synthetic dataset (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22); giving LightGBM the raw sums lets it split along oblique boundaries it could not represent, which in the original competition lifted GBDT AUC from ~0.977 to the low 0.99s.

f_27 has ~700k near-unique values, so the native categorical is mostly useless (min_data_per_group filters singletons, unseen in test) and very slow, while dropping the per-position ordinals removes the strongest known positional signal; letter counts + nunique retain part of it, so a clear regression (and real timeout risk).

Trees already capture per-position char interactions from the ordinal columns; 676-level native categorical bigrams add marginal signal at 800k rows and may slightly overfit, so expect near-neutral, tiny positive change.

The 16 continuous columns are nearly independent synthetic Gaussians, so unsupervised PCA yields essentially arbitrary rotations that carry no target-aligned interaction (the known important interactions are sums like f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21 involving columns outside the block); dropping the supervised product features loses a small but real signal, leaving the score around the no-interaction baseline.

f_27 has ~700k near-unique strings, so hashing the whole string into 64 buckets is effectively a random partition with no target signal, while the deleted per-position character columns carried substantial information in this competition; the model falls back to roughly numeric-only performance.

This dataset's signal lives in additive/interaction structure (f_27 char combos, sums of continuous groups) that boosting learns well but fully-grown sqrt-feature ExtraTrees on raw columns capture poorly; RF/ET on this data historically lands ~0.90-0.93 vs 0.978 for LightGBM, and the post-fit 5-fold CV of 300-tree ET on 800k rows before the submission is written also puts the run at real risk of hitting the 15-minute kill.

This dataset's key interactions are additive/diagonal (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22) which an MLP on standardized inputs captures far better than axis-aligned trees, so a 256-128 sklearn MLP should modestly beat the untuned LGBM baseline, though ordinal-encoded f_27 characters, no unique-char count, and sklearn's plain Adam/accuracy-based early stopping keep it well short of the ~0.998 top NNs.

f_27 unique-character count and per-letter bag-of-letters counts are known strong features in this competition that per-position categoricals cannot express; LightGBM with 3000 trees should exploit them for a clear but sub-1% AUC gain, still short of the interaction-feature gains (f_02+f_21 etc.) that top solutions rely on.

f_27 is ~80% unique across train+test so its frequency is almost constant (1 or 2) and carries little signal, while the per-character categorical columns it replaces are among the strongest features in this competition; dropping them should cost several AUC points.

The f_27 unique-character count is a known strong signal in this competition that trees cannot easily reconstruct from per-position ordinals, and per-letter counts add order-invariant bag-of-letters info; expect a clear AUC gain with negligible runtime cost.

The known TPS-May-2022 interactions are additive (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22) and involve f_27 unique-char counts, not pairwise products within f_00..f_15; z-score products add mostly noise that trees can already approximate, so expect roughly neutral to a hair worse from feature dilution under colsample_bytree=0.8.

Refitting on all 800k rows with ~3333 trees (holdout AUC still rising at 3000) adds both data and rounds, giving a small but consistent AUC gain typical of full-data refits on this synthetic task; main risk is wall-clock doubling, not accuracy.

Declaring the 10 low-cardinality f_27 letter columns as categorical lets LightGBM find letter-subset splits directly instead of approximating them with many ordinal thresholds, which typically gives a small but real AUC gain on this dataset (with 800k rows overfitting risk is minimal), though the dominant interaction/unique-count signal remains unmodeled so the gain is modest.

The f_27 unique-character count is a known strong interaction feature in TPS May 2022 that trees cannot easily reconstruct from per-position ordinals; public notebooks show a clear AUC gain of roughly +0.002 to +0.003 when adding it to GBDT models.

This dataset's signal lives in higher-order interactions (f_27 character combinations, multi-feature sums like f_21+f_22 and f_19+f_20+f_23 not yet engineered); capping trees at depth 2 leaves only one engineered sum exposed and severely underfits relative to 127-leaf trees, so AUC should drop substantially despite the full 3000 rounds.

On TPS May 2022 the MLP captures the smooth f_27/numeric interactions better than trees without engineered features; a small LightGBM (600 rounds, 31 leaves, max_bin 63) will still be improving when it stops and should land noticeably below the 0.982 MLP, around 0.96.

TPS May 2022 is dominated by additive interactions (sums of features, f_27 unique counts) that MLPs learn easily but trees struggle with on raw features; a small 600-tree/31-leaf LightGBM without engineered interactions typically lands around 0.90-0.92 AUC, well below the MLP's 0.982.

Collapsing each of the 16 continuous sensors to 4 quartile codes destroys the fine-grained continuous interactions (e.g. sum-type interactions between f_00/f_01/f_26, f_02/f_21, f_05/f_22) that drive most of the AUC above what integers and f_27 provide; the model keeps integer and character signal but loses several AUC points.

Trees with 7 leaves badly underfit this interaction-heavy dataset even at 3000 rounds with lr 0.05; early stopping won't fire and the model lacks capacity for the multi-way sensor/f_27 interactions that deep trees exploited, so AUC drops noticeably.

num_leaves=4 severely underfits a dataset whose signal lies in multi-way feature interactions (f_27 characters, f_02/f_21/f_00 sums); 3000 depth-2 trees at lr 0.05 cannot recover the capacity of 127-leaf trees, so AUC drops noticeably.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known key additive interactions in TPS May 2022 that trees struggle to learn axis-aligned; exposing it directly typically lifts GBDT AUC by several tenths of a percent, though only one of the three interactions is added here.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the known ground-truth interaction features in TPS May 2022; giving trees the sum directly lets them threshold it cleanly instead of approximating an oblique boundary, so a modest but real AUC gain is expected.

This dataset's key interactions are linear sums (e.g. f_02+f_21+f_26) that MLPs capture natively while trees struggle; ordinal f_27 chars were used successfully in top MLP notebooks, and the small CPU MLP will comfortably complete ~50 epochs in 420s, so expect a clear gain over LightGBM though short of the ~0.998 achievable with unique-char-count features.

Per-position f_27 codes have low cardinality (~10-20 letters) and 800k rows, so LightGBM's native categorical splits can capture arbitrary letter subsets in fewer splits than ordinal thresholds; effect is small since deep ordinal trees already approximate this, expect a marginal gain with slight overfit risk.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is a known strong signal in this dataset that trees cannot easily reconstruct from ten independent ordinal columns, so a modest but real AUC gain is expected with no runtime risk.

The graded metric is unweighted RMSE; up-weighting dark pixels biases the sigmoid regressor toward darker predictions on ambiguous edge/stain pixels (optimum becomes a weighted mean rather than the conditional mean), trading background/edge accuracy for stroke accuracy, which typically nets a small regression against the unweighted metric with only run-to-run noise as upside.

~10x more optimizer steps (roughly 15-25k vs 2000) with a properly annealed time-based cosine should let the small U-Net converge further on this denoising task; overfitting risk on 105 images is modest with random crops/flips, so expect a solid but not dramatic RMSE drop from 0.0161 to ~0.013-0.014.

The metric is RMSE, which MSE optimizes directly; L1 drives ambiguous pixels (stroke edges under stains) toward the conditional median instead of the mean, raising squared error exactly on the pixels that dominate RMSE, and with Adam the 'vanishing L2 gradient' argument mostly disappears, so expect a roughly neutral to slightly worse result within run-to-run noise.

Test noise/paper statistics match train exactly here, so input-only brightness/contrast jitter (80% of crops) adds a train/test mismatch and makes the exact stroke gray levels ambiguous (same target for inputs spanning ~0.04-0.36 with identical clipped background), forcing the MSE-optimal net to hedge on text/edge pixels; the large-receptive-field U-Net can partly recalibrate from context, so I expect a modest regression rather than a collapse.

The U-Net is scale-dependent and the targets are near-binary text; the 0.75x (downsample-predict-upsample) and 1.25x views add resampling blur and scale-mismatched stroke handling at text edges, and averaging them with 2/3 weight against the sharp 1x prediction will most likely raise RMSE rather than cancel errors as flips do.

Dropout2d on e2/e3 (including the skip) injects feature noise into a pixel-regression U-Net that isn't strongly overfitting, slows convergence in a short 2000-step run, and creates a BatchNorm variance-shift mismatch at eval, so RMSE most likely worsens slightly rather than improving.

Dropout2d in every block (including skip paths and the final feature map before the 1x1 output conv) injects channel-level noise into a pixel-regression network that is time-budget-limited rather than overfitting, plus the BN-after-dropout variance-shift mismatch at eval; restoration nets typically lose fine-detail accuracy with dropout, so expect a modest regression.

A 4th U-Net level roughly doubles the receptive field (41→89 px), which helps model the large-scale stains/shading that dominate residual error in this dataset; the ~1/3 higher per-step cost cuts steps under the fixed 180 s budget but the small model still converges, so expect a modest gain within run-to-run noise (~0.0002–0.0004).

An explicit 23x23 median background channel is a known strong feature for this dataset (stains/shadows become locally subtractable), which a small 3-level U-Net trained for only 2000 steps cannot easily synthesize itself; expect a modest but real gain, tempered by single-run seed noise.

Two extra U-Net levels give a receptive field large enough to model stain/fold backgrounds on 256px crops at unchanged pixels-per-step, which typically helps this task modestly; compute stays well under budget, though batch-8 gradient diversity and a ~4x parameter count over only 2000 Adam steps cap the gain and add run-to-run variance.

Model was trained with random h/v flips so flipped inputs are in-distribution; averaging 4 flip variants reduces prediction variance for a small but reliable RMSE gain (typically 1-3%), with training itself unchanged and no risk to the time budget.

On a GPU the small UNet at batch 32/128px runs ~20-40ms per step, so a 180s wall-clock budget gives roughly 4-8k steps versus the baseline's 2000 with a cosine decay to zero; the model is under-trained at 2000 steps and more optimization with a proper anneal should reduce RMSE noticeably, with modest overfitting risk on 105 training images.

Charbonnier optimizes toward the per-pixel median and equalizes gradient weight across the mostly-clean background and the few high-error stroke/stain pixels, while the metric is RMSE, so committing to one mode at ambiguous edge pixels and under-weighting large errors typically costs a little RMSE despite sharper-looking output; expect a small regression within noise-to-modest range.

Train/test corruption processes are already identical, so the injected sigma=0.05 Gaussian noise mostly creates an input-distribution mismatch: the denoiser learns mild spatial smoothing it then applies to the cleaner test scans, slightly blurring text edges and anti-aliased strokes, which outweighs any regularization benefit at this already-low error floor.

At batch 32 BN's running stats are already stable and the crop-vs-page mismatch is mild, whereas GroupNorm discards per-sample absolute intensity information (critical for a regression-to-intensity task) and introduces its own crop-vs-full-page statistics shift at inference, so I expect a small regression rather than a gain.

The graded metric is RMSE, which MSE training optimizes directly; the 0.84-weight SSIM term is insensitive to low-frequency luminance offsets (residual faint stains) and pushes uncertain edge pixels toward committed 0/1 values rather than the RMSE-optimal hedge, so I expect a small regression (within noise of neutral) rather than a gain.

8x dihedral TTA averages out variance in a strong per-pixel regressor; flips/rot180 are in-distribution (trained with H/V flips) and rot90 variants are mildly OOD for text but low-level stroke/stain features largely transfer, so expect a modest RMSE gain (~3-5%) with negligible runtime cost.

SSIM-only loss is inherently weaker than MSE at the RMSE metric (half-sensitivity to luminance bias, Zhao et al. found SSIM alone trails L2/L1 on PSNR), and worse, the SSIM convs run in bf16 under autocast so sigma = blur(x^2) - mu^2 suffers catastrophic cancellation in the flat white background (rounding noise ~±0.004 vs C2=0.0009), making the structure term and its gradients heavy-tailed noise once the background gets flat; training will be noisy and plateau well above the baseline, with some risk of much worse or NaN.

Residual (stain) target is smoother/low-frequency than the sharp text image, which suits the 2000-step budget and removes sigmoid saturation, but the U-Net skip already learns near-identity and the current 0.0165 is close to this architecture's plateau, so expect only a small gain within seed noise.

MSE is already metric-aligned and sqrt(MSE) under Adam is nearly equivalent, so the only real change is the 0.1*(1-SSIM) term; it is computed inside the bf16 autocast block, so F.conv2d runs in bf16 and the variance terms (conv(x*x)-mu^2) suffer catastrophic cancellation in flat background regions (noise ~0.004 vs C2=0.0009), making most of the SSIM map noisy garbage, while at text edges it pushes for more contrast/commitment which tends to raise per-pixel RMSE slightly under uncertainty; expect a small regression within run-to-run noise.

Residual learning with zero-init output is stable and converges fine, but it drops the sigmoid's free saturation to exact white/black on the ~90% background pixels; net effect is roughly neutral with a small regression more likely than a gain at this already-converged 2000-step budget.

With a fixed 64k-patch budget, ~88% of samples become synthetic noise (blurred-whole-image stains, mild shading, pixel speckle) that poorly matches the real paper-texture/coffee-stain/crease artifacts, so real-noise exposure drops ~8x and the blur-then-sharp target teaches an off-distribution deblurring mapping; expect a moderate regression rather than a gain.

4.5x more Adam steps with a stretched cosine schedule lets the small U-Net converge further on this low-noise regression task; overfitting risk is low with random crops/flips over 105 images, so expect a modest but real RMSE drop rather than a large one.

8-fold dihedral TTA averages out edge/uncertainty noise in an undertrained U-Net; flips match training augmentation and should help, while the 4 transposed views are slightly out-of-distribution (model never saw rotated text) which caps the gain, yielding a modest few-percent RMSE reduction with negligible runtime risk.

L1 keeps constant-magnitude gradients on the many small background/edge residuals that MSE lets vanish, sharpening near-binary document outputs (the Zhao et al. L1-beats-L2-on-PSNR effect); slight over-confidence on ambiguous stain pixels costs a bit under RMSE, so net a small improvement within run-to-run noise.

Weighting dark pixels 3x moves the training target away from the plain-RMSE-optimal conditional mean (biasing ambiguous boundary pixels darker) while the metric stays unweighted MSE; with ~90% white pixels this typically costs a little background accuracy for no metric gain, so expect a small regression within noise.

The graded metric is unweighted RMSE; a target-weighted MSE (10x on ink) biases predictions darker in uncertain edge/gray regions (weighted-mean optimum instead of conditional mean), so background/edge errors rise slightly and the mismatch between training objective and metric yields a small regression.

Residual (DnCNN-style) prediction with a zero-init head starts at identity and removes MSE+sigmoid gradient saturation, which typically speeds convergence within the short 2000-step budget; the loss of the sigmoid's saturating prior for the near-binary target offsets part of the gain, so I expect a small improvement roughly within seed noise.

L1 targets the median rather than the mean so it is slightly misaligned with the RMSE metric on antialiased stroke edges and mid-gray stain residues; with sigmoid outputs and short CPU training it will likely land close to the MSE baseline but a touch worse.

Residual (DnCNN-style) parameterization with zero-init output starts at identity, converges faster within the short 2000-step CPU budget and removes sigmoid saturation on the near-binary targets; the U-Net skip connections already approximate this, so expect a modest gain rather than a large one, with some risk of a slightly less crisp linear output.

Halving NAFNet width to 8 cuts capacity ~4x with the same short 2000-step schedule; document denoising is simple enough that the tiny net still works, but the reduced channels (especially 8-wide gates at full resolution) will lose fine text-edge fidelity, giving a mild regression rather than the hoped-for regularization gain.

The graded metric is unweighted RMSE dominated by white-background pixels; a 1-3x foreground reweighting mismatches the objective and biases predictions slightly darker in ambiguous/background regions, so expect a small regression or at best noise-level change rather than a gain.

The morphological-closing illumination-normalized channel hands the small U-Net an explicit background estimate over a ~31px window, which with only 2,000 updates speeds convergence on stains/shading and typically yields a modest RMSE gain; compute cost is unchanged (only the first conv widens), though the unrequested CPU/8-thread execution.json adds some timeout risk that tempers the expected improvement.

The fp32 output head is numerically near-neutral (would land ~0.0162 ± 0.5%), but the added runtime.toml hides CUDA and caps torch at 8 CPU threads before import; 2000 steps × 32 × 128² through this U-Net is ~700 TFLOP fwd+bwd in fp32, which 8 CPU threads cannot finish inside 15 min, so the run is hard-killed before submission.csv is written and is recorded as a failure (no valid score).

4-way flip TTA on a flip-augmented U-Net is a cheap variance-reducing ensemble that typically trims a few percent RMSE (also smooths per-view border-padding artifacts); training is untouched so the gain is small but reliable, with the caveat that the added runtime.json forcing CPU (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES="") risks a timeout if the parent ran on GPU.

A tiny width-16 NAFNet (only depthwise spatial mixing at full res, GAP-attention trained on crops but applied to full images) trained from scratch for just 2000 steps at lr 2e-3 should converge to roughly U-Net-level quality but likely slightly worse on crisp text edges; the residual/no-sigmoid output helps a bit, while the added runtime.json forcing CPU with 13 threads makes the run borderline on the 15-minute kill and removes any GPU advantage, so I expect a modest regression around 0.0175 conditional on finishing.

The pretrained in1k head is a linear classifier on the same 1024-d features but trained on ~17x more dog images per class (which include the Stanford Dogs/test images themselves), so once temperature-calibrated its 120-way softmax should rival or beat the 77-per-class LR; blending two partly-decorrelated linear heads with w,T tuned on a 1.4k holdout should give a solid gain (~0.31 -> ~0.25), with low risk since w=0 recovers the baseline and the name mapping/asserts should pass.

Unwhitened PCA is a rotation plus truncation, so the L2-regularised LR is unchanged except for losing the 768 low-variance directions; those carry some fine-grained breed signal, so expect a small regression (roughly 0.31 to 0.32) rather than a gain.

Full-probability Mixup/CutMix on a ~780-step, 6-epoch fine-tune of an already strongly-regularized (label smoothing + drop path) ImageNet-22k ConvNeXt slows convergence and typically costs 1-2 points of accuracy on fine-grained 120-class data; the calibration benefit is largely redundant with the existing temperature scaling, so log loss likely worsens modestly.

The (0.08,1.0) scale is a from-scratch/long-schedule recipe; with only 6 fine-tuning epochs on ~8k images it makes the model underfit and widens the train/eval scale mismatch (eval is Resize256+CenterCrop224), so many crops become uninformative fur/background patches and val log loss likely worsens slightly.

ConvNeXt-V2-L IN22k->IN1k is a vastly stronger backbone than ResNet-50 (86%+ vs 76% top-1) and its 1000-class log-probs directly cover all 120 dog breeds on images it effectively saw during ImageNet training, so the linear probe should drop log loss from ~0.45 to roughly 0.15-0.25; pipeline is otherwise unchanged and runtime fits comfortably.

The 1000-d ImageNet log-proba block is not redundant in practice: the fc layer was trained on 1.2M images (including these very Stanford Dogs images) with ~118 breed classes matching the targets, so it encodes a far better 2048->breed map than L2-regularised LR can learn from ~9k samples; dropping it removes strong signal and should worsen log loss noticeably despite the cleaner feature space.

Ridge-regression scores on one-hot targets with a single global temperature are less well calibrated than multinomial LR probabilities on these strong features; accuracy should be similar but log loss typically comes out several to ~15% worse.

Unsupervised PCA to 128 dims per block (barely above the 120-class count) discards fine-grained breed-discriminative directions that L2-regularised LR on the full 2560-d already handles well, so expect a modest log-loss regression rather than a gain.

ConvNeXt-Base in22k-ft-in1k frozen features are far more discriminative on ImageNet-derived dog breeds than ResNet-50 (Stanford Dogs images overlap the pretraining data), and the holdout C selection on layer-normed 1024-d features should yield a well-calibrated LR; expect roughly 0.15-0.22 log loss with runtime comfortably inside budget.

Full fine-tuning of an in22k-pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny with flip TTA and temperature scaling should reach ~93% val accuracy on this ImageNet-subset task, cutting log loss roughly in half versus frozen ResNet50 features; 6 short epochs comfortably fit the 7-minute guard on a modern GPU, with small risk from weight download or slower hardware truncating the cosine schedule.

The ImageNet head is already a breed classifier (and the competition images overlap ImageNet train), so its 1000-d log-probs are highly discriminative extra features; combined with standardisation and a re-tuned small C, expect a solid drop in log loss, tempered somewhat by noise from standardising 1000 mostly-irrelevant class log-probs.

ConvNeXt-B in22k, CLIP and DINOv2 frozen features (L2-normalised, C tuned) are far stronger than raw ResNet-50 on this ImageNet-derived fine-grained task; expect ~95% accuracy and log loss around 0.2, with runtime comfortably inside budget.

Focal loss (gamma=2) sharply damps gradients once p_t exceeds ~0.5, which in a short 10-epoch fine-tune with a strong pretrained backbone leaves the model under-trained and systematically under-confident on the ~80% of correctly classified test images; the reduced penalty on confidently-wrong cases partly offsets this, but net log loss is likely to worsen modestly versus label-smoothed CE.

Freezing conv1-layer3 preserves ImageNet features that already encode these dog classes well and regularizes against overfitting on ~9k images, so with the same aggressive lr=0.01 recipe the model should generalize slightly better than full fine-tuning; layer4+fc is still ~60% of parameters so capacity is ample and the run stays well within budget, yielding a modest log-loss improvement.

Averaging probabilities over the image and its mirror gives a small but reliable log-loss reduction for frozen-feature classifiers (smoother, slightly less overconfident predictions); no training changes, so expect a modest ~2-4% gain.

CLIP ViT-B/32 features are a weaker fine-grained dog-breed probe than an ImageNet-1k-finetuned ViT-B/16 that was trained on these exact 120 classes (and likely saw these ImageNet-sourced images); coarser 32px patches and un-normalised CLIP features with untuned C=0.3 should push log loss noticeably up.

Unwhitened PCA-256 is just an orthogonal subspace constraint on the already L2-tuned (C=0.3) logistic probe, so it can only remove capacity; fine-grained breed cues (e.g. Norfolk vs Norwich) partly live in low-variance directions that get discarded, so log loss likely worsens by ~0.03-0.08.

DINOv2 ViT-B/14 frozen CLS embeddings are far stronger than supervised ResNet-50 features for fine-grained breeds (linear-probe accuracy typically jumps from ~87% to ~92-94% on Stanford Dogs), and with holdout-tuned C plus the same 10-view TTA the log loss should drop roughly in half, assuming the HF weight download and DataLoader fixes work in the batch job.

PCA-whitening to 256 unit-variance components raises the feature norm from ~1.4 to ~16, making C=1.0 roughly 100x weaker in effective regularization and inflating low-variance noise directions, so the head becomes overconfident on test images; likely a modest log-loss regression rather than the hoped-for stabilization.

10-NN vote probabilities are coarse and near-hard; with 1e-3 smoothing any test image whose true breed gets zero of 10 neighbours costs ~7 nats, and on 120 fine-grained breeds with confusable pairs that happens for several percent of images, so log loss degrades substantially versus the calibrated logistic head.

Full fine-tuning with RRC/flip aug, label smoothing and warmup+cosine SGD should lift accuracy a few points over the frozen linear probe (Stanford Dogs is in ImageNet so frozen features are already strong, limiting the gain), and LS keeps confidence tempered, giving a modest log-loss improvement; run comfortably fits the time budget.

ViT-B/16 augreg in21k→in1k pooled features are far more linearly separable on fine-grained ImageNet-derived dog breeds than ResNet-50 V1 features (linear-probe accuracy ~93-95% vs ~85-88%), so even with the un-retuned C=0.3 the log loss should roughly halve; extraction of ~10k images at 224px fits easily in budget and the mlflow wrappers are fail-safe.

10-crop+flip TTA with arithmetic probability averaging on frozen ResNet-50 features typically gives a modest log-loss gain (flip is near-free, corner crops add diversity and smooth overconfident errors), though corner crops are slightly off the center-crop training distribution so the gain is limited to a few percent.

ConvNeXt-T in22k_ft_in1k features are far more discriminative for these (ImageNet-sourced) dog images than ResNet-50, so concatenation should help substantially, but row-L2-normalising both blocks shrinks feature scale ~30x so C=1.0 is roughly two orders of magnitude more regularised than the tuned raw setting, which will leave predictions under-confident and cap the gain well short of what the features could deliver.

Stanford Dogs images are ImageNet training images, so the pretrained ResNet-50 head restricted to the 120 dog classes is a strong, partly complementary linear classifier on the same features; a temperature-calibrated blend selected on a stratified holdout should cut log loss noticeably (roughly 0.31 -> ~0.24), with the name-mapping assertion very likely passing given torchvision's WordNet-style category names.

Unwhitened PCA to 256 dims drops ~1800 low-variance directions that carry some fine-grained breed signal; L2 regularization already downweights those, so the loss is modest, but truncation still slightly hurts log loss rather than helping.

ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 features are linearly separable in the avg-pooled space the fc was trained on; max-pooled descriptors are noisier, larger-scale (effectively weakening the C=0.3 regularisation on unstandardised features) and typically give a few points lower linear-probe accuracy, so log loss should regress noticeably despite temperature calibration.

V2 weights raise ImageNet top-1 from 76.1% to 80.9% and the 120 breeds are literal ImageNet classes, so frozen penultimate features should separate them better; some risk that heavy-aug/label-smoothing training and an untuned C=0.3 blunt the gain, so a moderate improvement to ~0.41 is expected.

C=0.3 was already holdout-selected for these frozen features, so a 10x over-regularized init starts softer and worse; two epochs of head fine-tuning at lr 0.001 will recover much of the gap (and the lower-norm start mildly counters overconfidence), leaving a small net regression.

Running an ImageNet ResNet50 pretrained at 224 on 192-px crops loses fine-grained detail and creates a train/test resolution mismatch, typically costing 1-2% accuracy and noticeably worse calibrated log loss; the small fine-tune speedup doesn't compensate since two epochs already fit in 90s.

Unwhitened PCA to 256 dims is just an orthogonal restriction of the same C=0.3 logistic regression to the top-variance subspace; on a dog-only dataset the breed-discriminative directions are mostly high-variance so the loss is modest, but dropping 7/8 of the dimensions still discards some fine-grained signal (Norfolk vs Norwich style) that the raw-feature probe was using, so expect a small log-loss regression rather than a gain.

Testing a 224-trained ResNet-50 at 192px reduces ImageNet accuracy by ~3 points (train/test resolution discrepancy), and fine-grained breed features lose discriminative detail, so frozen-feature log loss should worsen moderately with no offsetting benefit beyond speed.

V2 weights are ~4.7pt better on ImageNet (whose classes include these 120 breeds), so frozen features should separate breeds better; gain is tempered by C=0.3 being tuned for V1 feature scale and V2's heavy regularization (label smoothing/mixup) which can hurt linear-probe calibration, plus the diff removes TORCH_HOME which risks a download failure but likely still runs.

Temperature scaling is a single-parameter post-hoc calibration; since C=0.3 was already chosen on a holdout by log loss (coarse 3x grid), the fitted T will be near 1 and yield only a small calibration gain (~0.005-0.015), with slight mismatch from fitting T on an 85% model but applying it to the full-data refit.

The head starts at the LR optimum so its mean gradient is ~zero, and with lr 1e-4 for the convs and 1e-3 for the head over only ~288 SGD steps the weights move by well under 1%, so the fine-tune is effectively a no-op; predictions match the baseline LR up to fp16 logit rounding and tiny stochastic drift, leaving log loss essentially unchanged.

Horizontal-flip TTA with probability averaging on frozen ResNet-50 features gives a small, reliable log-loss gain (smoothing overconfident predictions and a modest ensemble effect); the flip is correctly applied on the width axis and the extra tracking/tempdir code is fail-safe, so expect roughly 2-3% improvement.

Balanced 1:1 undersampling throws away 80-99% of negatives per label; linear models on sparse n-grams are already robust to imbalance for AUC, so discarding data (threat trains on ~950 rows, identity_hate on ~2.8k, and NB log-count ratios become noisy/zero for unseen features) degrades ranking quality, especially for the rare labels that dominate the column mean, yielding a clear regression despite the rank-average blend.

Adding char_wb n-grams to the NB-LR branch typically lifts that branch by ~0.002-0.003 AUC (char features capture obfuscated profanity and rare-label cues), and although sharing the char block with branch A reduces blend diversity, the stronger branch B should net a small gain in the rank average; runtime rises but likely stays under the 15-minute kill.

AUC is ranking-based and unweighted LR on all rows is already near-optimal; 1:1 undersampling discards ~80-99% of the data (threat fits on ~950 rows, NB ratios from tiny subsets become noisy), so rare-label AUCs (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) degrade noticeably and toxic/obscene/insult slip slightly, giving a clear regression despite faster runtime.

MultinomialNB with alpha=1 on 200k sparse TF-IDF features is heavily over-smoothed and gives saturated, tie-prone probabilities (~0.92-0.95 mean AUC, worse on rare labels); the 50/50 rank average with the ~0.979 branch A drags the ensemble below branch A alone, and the weak OOF stack features add little.
