Mean-pooled self-trained Word2Vec + logreg (~0.955-0.965 AUC) and a small MLP on the same 200-d vectors (~0.965-0.97) are both clearly weaker than the TF-IDF word+char branch they replace, and with 2/3 blend weight on these weaker branches the rank average drags below the NB-LogReg branch's ~0.978 despite some diversity gain; the run should fit the budget with lbfgs.

AUC is threshold-free so imbalance was not hurting ranking; 1:1 undersampling discards 80-99.7% of informative negatives (threat fits on ~950 rows, NB ratios from ~480 negatives become noisy, C effectively far stronger), so rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) lose several AUC points and the blend cannot fully recover.

A sparse MLP on the same TF-IDF blocks should reach ~0.98 alone within the 1-3 epochs the time guards allow and adds the blend's only non-linear, shared-hidden-layer view, so a 1/4-weight rank average should lift the mean AUC by roughly +0.001; the guards make the downside near-zero (fallback writes the unchanged 0.98099) but also cap how well D can train, so the gain is modest.

Discarding 90-99.7% of negatives starves the linear models of the negative-background information that AUC ranking depends on; rare labels (threat ~956 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k) on 60k-250k sparse features will overfit badly and the NB log-count ratios become noisy, so expect a clear regression concentrated in the rare columns.

Lowercasing is already done by the vectorizers and char_wb n-grams already catch most obfuscation, so the de-obfuscation/repeat-collapse mostly helps only the rare identity_hate/threat columns marginally, while stripping '(utc)' timestamps and merging 'u'/'r' shorthand removes weak but real non-toxic/toxic cues; net effect is a small, noisy positive on the order of a few 1e-4.

Feature-level stacking of OOF NB-LogReg logits into branch A adds little beyond what the existing 50/50 rank blend already captures (A_stacked becomes B-like, reducing diversity, and fold-averaged test logits are shrunk relative to single-model OOF), so expect only a marginal gain of a few 1e-4 AUC, with real risk that the 30 extra liblinear fits push wall-clock near the kill limit.

A shallow multi-task MLP on the same word+char TF-IDF adds a nonlinear, differently-biased third view (~0.975-0.980 standalone); equal rank-averaging with two ~0.978 linear branches typically yields a small +0.001 gain, with the main risk being ~2-3 extra minutes of Adam steps over 3.8M sparse-input weights rather than a metric regression.

NB-LogReg on word+char TF-IDF is a strong linear branch (~0.980 alone) but highly correlated with A and B, so the equal 3-way rank blend should yield a small, positive gain of roughly +0.0005 AUC, assuming the denser 250k-column liblinear fits finish within budget.

Per-label holdout-fitted weights (shrunk to the 0.25-0.75 range) can only nudge the ordering slightly versus an already-balanced rank average of two comparably strong branches; NB-LR tends to win on toxic/obscene/insult and char-grams on the rare labels, so a small consistent gain of a few 1e-4 is likely, with holdout noise and the extra ~3-4 min of fitting as the main downside risks.

Compressing 100k word n-grams to 300 SVD factors discards the rare lexical cues (profanity variants, char patterns) that drive AUC on this task; LSA+LR on Jigsaw typically lands ~0.95-0.96 mean AUC, well below the sparse TF-IDF/NB-LR rank blend at ~0.98, with rare labels (threat, identity_hate) hurt most.

Undersampling negatives never helps AUC for linear/TF-IDF models (ranking, not calibration, is scored) and here it discards ~97% of negatives for threat and ~90% for severe_toxic/identity_hate, including most of the hard toxic-but-not-X negatives; all three branches share the same subsample so the blend can't compensate, and the rare labels drive the column mean down by roughly 0.005-0.008.

A single softmax multi-label fastText (random one-of-labels target per row) spreads probability mass across co-occurring labels and gives rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) fewer effective updates than dedicated binary models, so branch F's per-label ranking quality drops slightly; at 1/3 rank-blend weight this yields a small regression rather than a gain.

For binary labels ComplementNB reduces to plain multinomial-NB log-odds on raw counts; heavy smoothing over a 200k 1-2gram vocab biases rare labels (threat, identity_hate) toward long/rare-vocab docs, predict_proba saturates to exact 1.0 creating large ties, and dropping the three tuned LR branches loses the ~0.98-level discrimination, so expect a big regression to roughly 0.90-0.92.

Mean-pooled corpus-trained Word2Vec + linear head loses exact-token/char n-gram signal that drives the strong NB-LR TF-IDF ensemble; on Jigsaw such dense-average baselines typically land around 0.95-0.965 mean AUC, with rare labels (threat, identity_hate) hurt most, so a clear regression from 0.9816.

Mean-pooled corpus-trained Word2Vec + unscaled LR loses the exact-token/char-n-gram signal that drives toxicity AUC (dilution of single slurs in long comments, weak rare-label discrimination), so this well-known weaker baseline should land around 0.95, a clear regression from the 0.980 TF-IDF/NB-LR rank blend.

A char-level NB-LogReg is a genuinely diverse third linear branch and 3-way per-label rank blending typically adds ~0.0005-0.001 AUC on Jigsaw; gain is capped by shared linear/n-gram nature and slight holdout overfit on rare labels, with a real risk that the second char_wb vectorizer plus liblinear fits on ~70M-nnz matrices pushes the run past the 15-minute kill (the proposal's 1-2 min estimate is optimistic).

C=0.1/sag is actually the CV-tuned reference config for this word+char TF-IDF set (C=4 belongs to the NB-weighted branch), so a 40x weaker penalty on 60k l2-normed features will mildly overfit the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) and make branch A more similar to branch B, costing roughly 0.0005-0.0015 in the rank blend; liblinear primal on 159k x 60k with C=4 is also slow enough that a timeout is a real risk.

Supervised fastText on this corpus typically lands around 0.965-0.975 mean AUC (weaker than each existing branch, worst on threat/identity_hate, with saturated/tied probabilities), so giving it a full 1/3 rank weight adds some low-rank diversity but is roughly a wash: expect a small gain of about +0.0003 to +0.001 if it completes, with a meaningful risk that the extra ~5-7 min of six 20-epoch fastText fits pushes the run past the 15-minute kill limit.

A char-ngram NB-LogReg branch adds a genuinely different feature view and rank-averaging three decent linear models typically nudges mean AUC up by a few tenths of a point (0.980 -> ~0.981), though the extra ~5 min char vectorizer fit plus primal liblinear on dense char matrices pushes the run near the 15-min kill limit.

Optimal per-label rank weights typically sit near 0.5 for two comparably strong branches (gain ~+0.0002 at most), while training on only 90% of the data costs more than that, especially for rare labels (threat has ~48 holdout positives, so its tuned weight is noisy and may land on an extreme); net effect is a small regression.

NB log-count-ratio weighting acts as an informative-feature prior that usually helps char+word linear models slightly, but it makes branch A more correlated with the already NB-weighted branch B and changes effective regularization under C=0.1/sag, so the rank-blend gain is mostly offset; expect roughly flat, marginally positive, with some timeout risk from slower sag convergence on unnormalized rows.

min_df=0.01 on ~313k docs requires ~3.1k document frequency, pruning nearly all bigrams and most discriminative rarer slurs/threat words (nigger, faggot, cunt, kill, jew, etc.) from both word and char vocabularies; common profanity survives so toxic/obscene hold up moderately, but threat and identity_hate lose their key features and drag the column mean down substantially.

Balanced undersampling discards ~90-99% of negatives per label (threat trains on ~950 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k), so the models lose the hard-negative structure (toxic-but-not-threat comments) that drives AUC ranking, and NB log-count ratios become noisy from tiny samples; AUC is prior-invariant so balancing buys nothing while the data loss costs 1-3 points on rare labels and ~0.5-1 on common ones.

Replacing discriminatively trained logistic regression with mean-difference (Rocchio) centroids removes weight learning over 60k-200k sparse features; centroid/NB-style scoring on TF-IDF typically lands ~0.94-0.96 AUC on this task, with the NB-weighted branch partly compensating, so a clear regression from 0.980 is expected.

Switching to char_wb drops cross-word character n-grams (useful for multi-word profanity patterns) but adds boundary-padded within-word grams; in the Kaggle kernels the two variants scored within ~0.0002 of each other, and after rank-blending with the unchanged NB-LogReg branch the effect is near-zero, likely a hair negative.

Swapping discriminative logistic regression for ComplementNB on TF-IDF loses substantial AUC (NB on n-gram TF-IDF for Jigsaw typically lands ~0.93-0.95 vs ~0.98 for NB-LR/LR); rank-averaging two NB branches recovers a little but cannot close the gap.

Collapsing 60k sparse TF-IDF features into 32 LSA components discards the discriminative rare tokens/char n-grams that drive branch A (~0.978 alone), likely dropping it to ~0.92; equal-weight rank blending with the ~0.96 fastText branch then pulls the ensemble down well below the current 0.9734.

Collapsing everything outside the top-2,000 tokens into a single 'raretoken' neuters the char_wb branch's main strength (subword generalization over profanity variants, obfuscations, and rare slurs) and starves fastText of vocabulary, costing signal especially on threat and identity_hate; the mild regularization benefit does not offset the information loss.

Keeping pronouns like 'you'/'your' in the word unigram TF-IDF adds weakly useful second-person signal for toxicity, but char_wb 2-6-grams and branch B already capture these tokens, so the blended gain is tiny and positive at most.

Logit averaging lets the weakly-regularized NB-LogReg branch (C=4, large logit spread) dominate the heavily-regularized branch A (C=0.1, compressed logits), so the blend loses the equal-influence benefit rank averaging gave; expect a small regression toward branch B's standalone AUC.

Swapping char_wb for char in a 50k-capped 2-6-gram vectorizer changes which n-grams survive (cross-word spans vs. padded within-word), a near-neutral tweak for a branch that is only half of a rank blend; expect a difference within ±0.0003 AUC, essentially noise.

fastText supervised without subwords, with a small 200k bucket for hashed bigrams, only 5 epochs, and fastText's table-quantized/saturating sigmoid (ties on rare labels) is a clearly weaker standalone model (~0.96-0.97) than NB-LogReg (~0.977); an equal-weight rank blend with the ~0.979 word+char LR branch should land slightly below the current 0.9801, roughly 0.977-0.979.

Univariate ANOVA selection drops 64 descriptors that are individually weak but collectively useful for the 99-class linear model (sparse margin/texture bins specific to a few species), so the LR component gets slightly worse and the 50/50 blend regresses modestly; the NN is unchanged.

With 99 classes, eps=0.1 caps the NN's correct-class probability near 0.90 (loss floor -log 0.901 ≈ 0.10 for the NN alone); since the blend is a 50/50 arithmetic average with a moderately confident C=1 LR, the many easy correct rows lose ~0.03-0.05 nats each, outweighing the small gain from softening overconfident mistakes, so log loss regresses to roughly 0.10-0.11.

OvR at C=1 fits 99 imbalanced 8-vs-792 hyperplanes whose scores are not jointly comparable and resolve confusable species pairs worse than the coupled softmax; the single global power/floor calibration cannot fix misranked rows, so OOF/test log loss should worsen from ~0.045 to roughly 0.06.

A 5-seed 512-unit MLP bag is a genuinely different, reasonably strong learner on these 192 descriptors; blending with the LR before the same power/floor calibration typically cuts OOF and test log loss by 10-25% on this dataset, with w=0 as a safe fallback and only mild grid-selection optimism.

Averaging five high-C fold models smooths the near-one-hot probabilities that dominate log loss on the few hard test leaves, which typically outweighs the loss from each fold model seeing 8 rather than 10 samples per class; expect a small-to-moderate improvement, not a large one.

Absolute size/aspect/convexity from the binary images is genuinely new information not in the scale-normalised descriptors and is known to help LR on this dataset; C is re-tuned by CV so 21 extra standardised columns add little overfitting risk, though noisy Hu-moment log transforms and the possibility of a missing images dir cap the expected gain to a moderate improvement.

L2 logistic regression is rotation-invariant, so PCA only matters via truncating the low-variance ~5% of directions; on this well-separable dataset where the optimal C is far larger than 1.0 (i.e. the model is already over-regularised), those low-variance directions of the margin/texture histograms carry fine-grained class information, so discarding them adds effective regularisation and modestly worsens holdout/test log loss rather than helping.

Each fold model sees only 8 of 10 samples per class, which hurts a 219-dim logreg; averaging five near-identical convex lbfgs solutions gives little variance reduction beyond mild probability smoothing, so I expect a small net regression versus the full-data refit.

The feature branch alone is an MLP that typically reaches ~0.04-0.08 on this data, the image branch adds mild diversity, and arithmetic 50/50 blending with the underconfident C=1 LR is bounded above by the mean of the two losses and usually beats it, so expect roughly 0.06-0.09 unless the 9-minute guard clips the full-data run badly.

C=1.0 LR is heavily under-confident on this ~98%-accurate task, so OOF-fitted power/temperature sharpening (a likely 2-4) plus a small uniform floor should cut log loss substantially, with modest risk from OOF models (792 rows) being less confident than the full-data refit.

C=1 heavily over-regularises this well-separated 192-feature problem; CV will pick C in the ~1000-3000 range where standardised multinomial logistic regression is known to reach ~0.03-0.06 log loss on this dataset, a large improvement over 0.124.

Image size/aspect and shape descriptors (height, width, solidity, eccentricity, Hu moments) are known to be discriminative in this competition and are partly complementary to the 192 precomputed features; with fixed C=1.0 the extra standardized signal should sharpen margins and lower log loss moderately, with low runtime risk.

The leaf dataset is near-perfectly separable with standardized features, so log loss is dominated by under-confidence; on this competition log loss falls monotonically with larger C (C=1 ~0.08-0.1, C=10 ~0.04), so shrinking C to 0.2 will flatten the predicted probabilities and roughly double or triple the log loss.

Dropping the full-data refit trains the submitted logistic regression on only 80% of an already tiny dataset (~13 vs 16 samples per class across 99 classes), which reliably raises test log loss; the 'consistency with holdout' rationale doesn't change the fact that less data hurts.

LR stays dominant, but OOF-optimized blending with shrinkage LDA (a strong, differently-biased model on this data) typically shaves ~10-15% off LR-only log loss; kNN will get near-zero weight and the 3-weight SLSQP fit on ~990 OOF rows carries little overfitting risk, so a modest gain to ~0.05 is the most likely outcome.

With only ~8-9 training samples per class after the 15% holdout, min_samples_leaf=10 and l2=1.0, gradient-boosted trees cannot produce the sharp well-calibrated probabilities that tuned logistic regression already gets on these near-linearly-separable descriptors; tree ensembles on this competition historically score ~0.2-0.6 log loss versus ~0.05 for linear models, so this is a large regression.

Platt-sigmoid calibration in 3-fold CV with only ~2-3 positives per class per fold uses heavily smoothed targets (~0.8 for positives), so the calibrated LinearSVC member is systematically less confident than the C=1 multinomial LR it replaces; with uniform soft voting the ensemble's mean true-class probability drops, raising log loss despite similar accuracy.

Random forest vote-fraction probabilities on 99 classes are diffuse (true-class share often ~0.5-0.6), so under uniform soft voting it lowers the ensemble's confidence on the ~95% of correctly classified test rows more than it softens the few confident HGB errors, giving a modest log-loss regression.

MLP with early stopping on accuracy over a tiny (~70-80 sample) unstratified validation split will likely stop at a moderately under-trained/over-confident point with ~2-3% errors on 99 classes; with only ~640-710 effective training samples per fit the MLP's OOF/test logloss should land around 0.15-0.25, somewhat worse than the already well-calibrated C=1 logistic regression, though variance is high.

C=1 is badly over-regularised for this near-separable 192-feature/99-class problem; CV will pick C in the 30-1000 range where LR on standardised leaf features is known to score ~0.04-0.07, and the retained OOF uniform-shrinkage guards against the rare confident miss, so log loss should roughly halve from 0.124.

Hu moments and contour scalars add some complementary shape signal to the 192 descriptors under strong C=1 L2 regularization, so a modest gain is likely; the radial histogram is largely redundant with the provided shape descriptor and orientation/area are noisy, capping the improvement, and if images fail to load the features are all-zero and the score is unchanged.

On this near-separable standardized 192-feature problem, C=1 is heavily under-regularized in the wrong direction; CV on neg_log_loss will pick a large C (~300-1000), and tuned multinomial LR on these features is known to reach ~0.03-0.06 logloss, so a large gain from 0.124 is expected with runtime well within budget.

Uniform soft-voting dilutes the well-calibrated LR with a soft distance-weighted kNN (CV on neg_log_loss pushes k large, giving p_true ~0.6-0.8 on easy rows), an overconfident LDA, and a noisy HGB (early-stopped on ~1 sample/class); it caps the worst-row losses but raises the loss on the ~90% of easy rows, netting a modest regression around 0.15.

LogReg at C=1.0 on this dataset is over-regularized and underconfident (loss dominated by ~0.88-ish correct probabilities, ~98% accuracy), so shrinking toward uniform only hurts; the OOF grid includes alpha=0 and will almost surely select it, leaving test probabilities unchanged.

Fixed 0.9 shrinkage makes the pooled covariance nearly isotropic (0.1*S + 0.9*mean-var*I), which discards the strong within-class correlation structure of the 64 contiguous shape descriptors and homogenizes per-feature weights; the model becomes near nearest-centroid with badly overconfident log-odds along high-variance shape directions, so accuracy drops a few points and errors remain confident, likely worsening log loss versus the per-class Ledoit-Wolf model that keeps the within-class diagonal.

Each 64-feature family LDA is far weaker alone (shape especially, ~60% accuracy), and arithmetic averaging dilutes confidence rather than multiplying evidence, so the ensemble loses the joint-covariance discrimination of the full 192-feature LDA and log loss rises to roughly 0.5-0.6.

Truncating standardized 192-dim leaf descriptors to 90% variance (~70-100 PCs) discards low-variance but class-discriminative margin/texture directions that near-separable multinomial LR exploits, so CV-selected log loss degrades noticeably rather than improving.

Shrinkage-LDA with CV-tuned shrinkage is known to be one of the strongest classical models on the leaf descriptors (typically ~0.01-0.03 log loss vs ~0.04-0.06 for tuned multinomial LR), since classes are near-Gaussian with shared covariance; main risk is LDA's extreme softmax probabilities turning any single misclassification on the small held-out split into a large penalty, so expected gain is roughly halving the loss with wide variance.

L2 logistic regression is rotation-invariant so PCA only acts by discarding the ~5% tail variance across many low-variance directions, which on leaf descriptors still carry class-discriminative detail; truncation typically raises log loss for this dataset.

Shrinkage LDA matches or slightly beats LR in accuracy on these near-Gaussian leaf descriptors, but its Mahalanobis-scale logits are far more overconfident; a single temperature capped at 4.0 cannot fully soften the few confident OOF errors, so log loss likely lands somewhat worse than the softly-regularized LR baseline.

LR at C=1 on 512 standardized Nystroem features is near-separable and overconfident, so a few catastrophic test errors likely dominate the 0.094 loss; 0.5% uniform mixing caps those tails (big gains when true-class p << 0.01) at a cost of only ~0.005 nats per correct sample, netting a small expected improvement, though it could mildly hurt if errors are not extreme.

Cutting Nyström landmarks 512→384 gives a coarser RBF kernel approximation for a 990-sample, 99-class problem where capacity (not overfitting) limits confidence; with C=1 L2 already regularizing, fewer components should slightly reduce separability and raise log loss modestly.

Shrinkage-LDA is known to be one of the strongest tabular models on the leaf descriptors (~98-99% accuracy, far better calibrated than C=1 logistic regression which is badly under-fit), so log loss should drop substantially toward the ~0.02-0.05 range, with residual risk from LDA's over-confident errors.

On this dataset logistic-regression log loss drops sharply as C grows (C≈100-1000 is far better than C=1), and 3-fold CV should select a large C; expect roughly 0.04-0.07 with some variance from a few confident errors on the small test set.

C=1.0 LR on this nearly separable 99-class data is badly under-confident (most of the 0.124 loss is calibration, accuracy ~98-99%), so an OOF-fitted temperature will sharpen logits (T≈0.4-0.6) and recover a large chunk of the gap toward tuned-C results (~0.03-0.04), though residual misclassifications get pricier and the fold-vs-full confidence mismatch limits the gain.

RBF/Euclidean geometry on the standardized 192 descriptors is far weaker than linear separation on this dataset (KNN/RBF-SVM ~89% vs LR/LDA ~98%), and standardizing the Nyström coordinates whitens away the kernel's smoothness so the C=1 LR fits landmarks near-perfectly and makes sharp, sometimes confidently wrong test predictions; expect a clear regression to roughly 0.3-0.5 log loss.

Adds known-strong RAOP signals (request length, community age/t_days, image/URL evidence, reciprocity, prior RAOP activity flags) that l2-normalised TF-IDF and the log-scaled numerics don't capture; standardised dense block in a regularised LR should give a modest, reliable lift, though some regex/temporal one-hots add noise.

Fully-grown RF with max_features=sqrt over ~8k mostly-rare sparse TF-IDF/subreddit columns rarely samples the 9 strong numeric features and splits on noisy rare tokens, so it typically underperforms a regularised linear model on small bag-of-words data; expect a drop of roughly 0.02-0.04 AUC despite 500 trees.

Random forest with max_features='sqrt' over 5000 sparse TF-IDF columns dilutes the few strong signals (nine history numbers and the giver_known indicator get sampled at only ~1.4% of nodes each), so the leak-like giver feature is exploited less sharply than LR's near-deterministic coefficient and the weak text signal becomes noisy deep splits; RF typically trails linear models on sparse bag-of-words, so expect a modest regression despite better handling of numeric non-linearities.

Replacing 5k sparse TF-IDF unigrams with 50 noisy LDA topic proportions estimated from ~4.5k short posts typically loses discriminative lexical signal for a linear model (LDA is unsupervised and optimizes likelihood, not the label), so the text block's contribution shrinks while the metadata/giver features carry the rest, yielding a modest regression.

Swapping the supervised OOF TF-IDF logit (the strongest text signal, ~0.61-0.63 AUC alone) for 20 unsupervised LDA proportions loses most of the direct word-level predictiveness; topics add only a little over metadata-plus-timestamp (~0.67-0.68), so the stack should regress modestly.

In RAOP the success base rate drifts strongly over the collection period and the test split is drawn from the same period, so the raw timestamp is a genuinely predictive (if non-stationary) feature; replacing it with weak hour/weekday signals removes that period information and should cost roughly 0.01 AUC.

A regularized HistGradientBoosting on time/history/text-stat features captures nonlinear meta signal the linear model misses; rank-averaging two diverse ~0.67-0.70 AUC models typically yields a modest but real gain of ~0.01-0.02 AUC, with CV-selected weight limiting downside.

Random forests with max_features='sqrt' over ~5000 mostly-zero TF-IDF columns waste most splits on noisy sparse word features and fully grown trees overfit ~4000 rows; the metadata/time signals partly survive, but RF on high-dimensional sparse text typically trails a regularized linear model by several AUC points.

Bag-of-subreddits is a known useful requester-history signal on this dataset that the count-only numerics don't capture; l2-normalised binary tf-idf with min_df=5 keeps it well-conditioned for C=0.3 LR, so expect a modest but real gain of roughly 1.5-3 AUC points rather than noise.

giver_username_if_known is a well-known label leak (non-N/A only when pizza was received) that the Kaggle-style test schema retains; LR will assign it a large weight so the ~25-30% of positives with a known giver rank at the top, lifting AUC to roughly f + (1-f)*0.657 ≈ 0.74 (if the column were stripped from test the change would be ~neutral).

Stacking an OOF text logit with raw requester-history counts and the request timestamp into a small, well-regularized LightGBM captures the nonlinear numeric and temporal effects (success rate drifts over time, RAOP activity thresholds) that a linear model on scaled features misses, which on this dataset typically lifts AUC by roughly 0.03-0.04.

Time-of-request trend (success rate drifted strongly over RAOP's history) plus text-length/link/imgur stats are known strong meta-features for this dataset and are largely orthogonal to unigram TF-IDF; with LogReg C=0.3 they should lift holdout AUC by a few points, while the mlflow tracker is best-effort and unlikely to break the run.

ExtraTrees with sqrt(5.4k)≈73 random candidates per split dilutes the nine strong requester-history numerics among thousands of sparse, noisy TF-IDF columns and dense embedding dims, and random-threshold splits on sparse text are weak, so the forest is likely a bit worse than the linear model that already leans on numerics+embeddings; expect a small regression, not a gain.

TF-IDF unigrams carry real lexical signal (reciprocity/need words) on RAOP, though its L2-normalized small-scale values were already muted by C=0.3 relative to the standardized dense blocks, so dropping it should cost only a little; the mlflow wrapper is best-effort and shouldn't affect the run.

Request length (lost by l2-normalized TF-IDF), gratitude/money flags and mild sentiment signal are known modest predictors on RAOP, so adding them as standardized dense features to the same LR should give a small but real AUC gain (~+0.01-0.02) with little downside risk.

Dropping the TF-IDF block removes the text signal that carries most of the discriminative power here; nine log-scaled requester-history features in a linear model typically land around 0.58-0.62 AUC on this dataset, so expect a clear regression from 0.650.

Mean-pooled skip-gram vectors trained on only ~5.7k short documents are noisy and dominated by frequent function words, so they carry less discriminative text signal than sublinear TF-IDF with stop-word removal; the 200 standardized dense dims at C=0.3 also regularize less effectively than the small-norm sparse block, so I expect a modest drop toward the metadata+stats-only level.

Adding bigrams and a much larger vocabulary to L2-normalized TF-IDF on ~4k docs recovers some phrase-level signal but text is a secondary signal here relative to the requester-history features, so expect a small net gain (with real risk of neutral/slight regression from rare-feature noise at C=0.3); the mlflow additions are metric-neutral.

Dropping text removes real signal (wording like 'pay it forward', money/paycheck cues that TF-IDF captures); the nine at_request history features alone typically yield ~0.60-0.62 AUC with a GBM on this dataset, so expect a modest regression from 0.633, not an improvement.

On ~4k noisy samples with 309 dense SVD+numeric features, a 400-tree bagged forest is roughly on par with early-stopped LightGBM; smoother averaged probabilities and lower variance likely give a small AUC gain, but the weak signal in SVD text components caps improvement near a point or so.

MiniLM embeddings add semantic signal beyond sparse unigrams and typically give a small AUC lift when concatenated with TF-IDF+numeric features in LR; the standardized 384-dim block will dominate the C=0.3 model on ~4k rows so gains are modest (~+0.01) with some overfit/noise risk, assuming the model download succeeds within budget.

Bigrams with min_df=2 add a little phrase signal ('pay it forward', 'will pay') but on ~4k docs the 100k sparse features are mostly noise and L2-normalized TF-IDF spreads mass thinner; with C=0.3 and numeric history features dominating, expect a marginal change, roughly +0.00 to +0.01 AUC.

Dense length/gratitude/reciprocity/hardship stats add signal that L2-normalised sublinear TF-IDF cannot express (especially request length, a known predictor per Althoff et al.), so a small but real AUC gain is likely with LR at C=0.3; the 15 scaled columns are low-risk for overfitting.

GBM handles the 9 numeric features' nonlinearity better, but SVD-300 compresses away much of the sparse lexical signal and num_leaves=63 on ~3-4k rows with 300 dense noisy components overfits despite early stopping, so the net is roughly flat to slightly below the TF-IDF+LR baseline.

The quantile spline captures the strong monotonic decline in pizza-success rate over the collection period (a known, sizable signal in this random-split data); two annual sin/cos terms discard that trend and encode only weak seasonality, so the date block loses most of its value and AUC should drop by roughly a point.

C=30 on ~4k samples with 5k sparse TF-IDF columns near-interpolates the training text, drowning the genuinely predictive requester-history/date signal in noisy word weights; overfitting should cut AUC by several points.

RAOP success rate drifted down substantially from 2011 to 2013 and the split appears random, so a standardized 7-column time spline gives the weak TF-IDF+history logistic model a genuinely new, dense, well-scaled signal worth roughly +0.015-0.025 AUC; risk of no gain only if the holdout is time-ordered (constant extrapolation would collapse the feature).

KNN with cosine on a heterogeneous sparse space (unit-norm TF-IDF plus unscaled standardized numerics and many-hot subreddit flags) on ~4k noisy samples is a weak learner here; neighbor votes wash out the linear signal LR exploits, so AUC likely drops into the high 0.5s/low 0.6s.

Distance-weighted 25-NN on nine standardized metadata features yields noisy, coarsely quantized probabilities (many exact-duplicate zero-history points) that are weaker than CatBoost's ~0.64-level metadata AUC, and at 50/50 with higher variance it dilutes the LR signal, so the blend likely slips a couple of points.

C=30 on 5000 TF-IDF features with ~4k rows makes the LR badly overfit and output extreme probabilities that dominate the 50/50 average, dragging the blend toward the weaker, overfit text ranking and below the current CatBoost-supported score.

RAOP success rate declined strongly over calendar time (~40% early to ~20% late), and with a random train/test split a 7-column standardized quantile spline of request date captures this trend that neither TF-IDF nor the requester-history features encode, so a moderate AUC gain is expected; if the split were temporal the constant extrapolation would make it neutral instead.

BernoulliNB on 5000 binarized TF-IDF presence indicators discards term weighting, models absence noise, and swamps the 9 informative requester-history indicators among thousands of correlated weak word cues, so ranking quality drops well below the discriminative LR baseline.

Request date is a known moderately strong signal in RAOP (success rate declined as the subreddit grew), and a 7-column quantile cubic spline lets the L2 logistic regression capture that nonlinearity cleanly with negligible overfitting risk, so expect a modest gain of roughly +0.01 to +0.02 AUC assuming a random (not time-based) train/test split.

Binary subreddit-membership features carry real signal in RAOP (activity in giving/assistance communities correlates with success) and the moderately regularized LR should absorb ~1-2k sparse extra columns without much noise, giving a modest AUC gain; the mlflow additions are best-effort and do not affect predictions.

Metadata-only CatBoost captures nonlinear requester-history effects (repeat RAOP posters, karma, account age) that the linear LR misses; a fixed 50/50 blend with the 0.657 text+meta LR should add a modest ~0.01 AUC, with small downside risk from the untuned equal weighting.

Bigrams under the same 5000-feature budget displace some unigrams with sparser, mostly redundant phrase features; on this small, numeric-dominated task the net effect is near zero, likely a marginal AUC gain, and the mlflow telemetry is best-effort so it should not break the run.

Authorship attribution is stylometric, and function words like 'upon', 'which', 'the' and their bigrams are among the strongest author signals; dropping them from the word view removes discriminative features, only partly compensated by the char_wb view, so log loss should worsen modestly.

Stacking NB word/char count models with the TF-IDF LR via a log-linear meta-learner is a well-known strong combination on this dataset (NB and LR errors are complementary and the meta-LR recalibrates NB overconfidence), typically cutting log loss from ~0.35 to ~0.31; fold-averaged test predictions cost little, so a solid improvement is expected.

Function words are a core authorship signal on this dataset; dropping them (and archaic list entries like 'whence','whither','thereupon') degrades both word-level base models' OOF log loss, and although the char_wb models and stacker partially compensate, the ensemble loses information and diversity of strong signals, so a modest regression is likely.

A multinomial LR on raw (not log) OOF probabilities cannot recalibrate the overconfident NB/LR-C=10 columns or exploit nonlinear length/meta interactions the way the tree stacker does, so despite being cleaner it should land a few hundredths worse, roughly 0.32-0.33.

Punctuation (semicolons, commas, dashes, quotes) is a well-known authorial stylistic signal in this corpus and the char n-gram block exploits it; stripping it removes discriminative features, so log loss should worsen by several percent.

Stacking diverse LR (word/char TF-IDF, C=10) and tuned-alpha MultinomialNB (word/char counts) base models via a log-prob meta-LR is a well-established win on Spooky (NB adds strong complementary signal), typically dropping log loss from ~0.44 to the high 0.30s; mlflow is best-effort-guarded so the run should complete within budget.

Cutting ~130k word+char TF-IDF columns to 10k via chi2 discards much of the diffuse stylistic signal that L2 LR already handles well in high dimensions; LR OOF likely worsens by several points, the blend shifts weight toward the unchanged NB branch and partially compensates, netting a modest regression.

Function-word frequencies are a core stylometric signal for authorship (Poe's 'upon', Shelley's 'my'/'I', etc.), so stripping them from both the word TF-IDF and especially the NB count model discards discriminative evidence; the char_wb block partially preserves it for LR and the blend-weight search will lean on LR, but the net effect is a noticeable regression rather than a gain.

L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF features are underfit at C=1; CV over [1,3,10,30,100] will most likely select C≈10-30, which historically drops word+char TF-IDF LR log loss on this task from ~0.43 to ~0.39-0.41, with the mlflow wrapper being best-effort and unlikely to break the run.

OOF stacking of NB-on-counts (strong for this task) with word/char LR plus stylometric meta-features through an early-stopped LightGBM is the classic mid-to-upper recipe here and typically lands around 0.32-0.36; runtime (~10 parallel LR fits, tiny LGBM) is comfortably within budget, so a substantial improvement over the single C=1 LR is expected.

Cross-boundary, case-sensitive char n-grams with no vocab cap add stylometric punctuation/capitalization signal that helps author ID; with fixed C=1.0 LR and l2-normalized blocks the gain is modest (rare high-idf n-grams dilute common features), so expect a small improvement around 0.42-0.43 rather than a large jump.

Tuned-alpha MultinomialNB on word 1-2gram counts scores ~0.40-0.44 on Spooky and is decorrelated from the TF-IDF LR (which is under-regularized-C limited at 0.43), so an OOF-selected arithmetic blend should yield a solid few-hundredths gain; MLflow tracker is best-effort and runtime is well within budget.

Function words are core stylometric signal for authorship attribution (this competition's kernels consistently found stopword removal hurts), and stripping them also destroys informative word-bigram features like 'of the'/'in which' that fastText's wordNgrams=2 exploits, so log loss should worsen noticeably.

Test prior matches the imbalanced train prior, so oversampling to uniform miscalibrates probabilities slightly, and duplicated minority rows make the already-overfitting 25-epoch fastText softmax more overconfident; expect a small log-loss regression rather than a gain.

ComplementNB on the same TF-IDF matrix is overconfident and weaker than LR, so OOF selection will likely land on w≈0.7–0.9; a small-weight blend with a moderately accurate but differently-shaped model typically yields a modest log-loss gain (~0.005–0.015), with w=1.0 as a no-regression floor.

MultinomialNB on l2-normalized word+char TF-IDF gives overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities (highly correlated char n-grams violate independence), and even with alpha tuned by CV it historically lands ~0.42-0.50 on this competition versus ~0.35 for tuned logistic regression, so log loss should regress noticeably.

Char n-grams carry strong stylistic/punctuation signal on this dataset and are complementary to word 1-2 grams; dropping them from the NB-SVM stack reduces useful features and typically raises log loss by several hundredths.

ComplementNB(alpha=1.0) on L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF word+char features is heavily smoothed and weakly discriminative with poorly calibrated softmax-of-jll probabilities; NB on TF-IDF for this task typically lands ~0.55-0.60 log loss, far worse than the 0.409 NB-SVM/logistic hybrid it replaces.

C=1.0 underfits L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF features; 3-fold CV on neg_log_loss will likely pick C around 3-10, which typically drops LR log loss on Spooky noticeably (~0.42 -> ~0.40), and the added MLflow calls are guarded so runtime and correctness are unaffected.

MultinomialNB on TF-IDF word+char features is a well-known weaker, poorly calibrated model on this competition (historical kernels show ~0.5-0.6 vs ~0.4 for LR); the 60k char n-grams plus alpha=0.1 will make posteriors overconfident, so wrong predictions get heavily penalized under log loss and the score regresses noticeably.

fastText supervised with lr=0.5/epoch=25/2M hashed bigram+char buckets on ~17.6k sentences memorizes training data and yields overconfident softmax probabilities; historically on this competition it scores ~0.5-0.6 log loss, clearly worse than the calibrated TF-IDF+LR baseline at 0.432.

L2-normalized TF-IDF with C=1 is underregularized-side-of-wrong (underfit); CV will almost certainly pick C=4 or 8 on this ~20k-row sparse setup, which historically drops log loss by several hundredths, though the parallel 30-fit search adds some timeout risk.

NB log-count-ratio weighting on the same word+char TF-IDF stack usually gives a modest gain over plain LR on spooky (strong class-discriminative features amplified, neutral ones suppressed), but alpha=1 smoothing on fractional TF-IDF sums flattens r for rare features and the one-vs-rest C=4 binaries with row renormalization lose some calibration, so expect only a small improvement (~0.41-0.42) rather than a large one.

Sentence-length and punctuation-count features add modest author signal not fully captured by L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF (length is removed by normalization), but punctuation is largely redundant with char_wb n-grams and MaxAbsScaler shrinks long-tailed counts toward zero, so expect only a small gain of a few thousandths in log loss.

NB log-count-ratio weighting sharpens discriminative word/char features and effectively loosens the C=1 regularization, typically giving a modest gain over plain TF-IDF LR on this task, but the one-vs-rest liblinear probabilities are less jointly calibrated than multinomial softmax, so the log-loss improvement is likely small rather than large.
TF-IDF rows are L2-normalized so LR at C=1 is already on the under-confident side for this task; quartering C shrinks coefficients further, softening probabilities and raising log loss noticeably.

Dropping the word 1-2gram block removes vocabulary-choice signal that complements character fragments on this task; char_wb alone with the same NB-LR setup typically scores a few hundredths worse than the concatenation, so a modest regression is expected.

Dropping the NB log-count-ratio weighting removes both the generative prior and the implicit feature scaling that reduced effective L2 regularization; plain OvR LR with C=1.0 on L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF is known to be underconfident on Spooky (typically ~0.55-0.60 log loss), so expect a clear regression.

TF-IDF+LR on this task is typically under-confident rather than overfit at C=4; halving C to 2 increases shrinkage and should slightly raise log loss (~+0.005-0.012), with the added mlflow tracking being a no-op for the metric.

NB log-count-ratio scaling heavily down-weights common stylistic function-word/char features that drive authorship signal, and normalizing three OvR sigmoids is less calibrated than a multinomial softmax, so with C=4 untuned for the new geometry I expect a small log-loss regression rather than a gain.

Function words (upon, which, whom, whither, hence, thence, etc.) are among the strongest stylometric signals for distinguishing Poe/Lovecraft/Shelley; stripping them from both word and char branches removes discriminative features and should noticeably worsen log loss.

Quadrupling L2 regularization on sparse TF-IDF LR with ~17.6k samples underfits and reduces discrimination; temperature scaling recovers the logit scale but not the lost ranking quality, so log loss likely worsens modestly.

Plain 'char' n-grams add cross-word punctuation/spacing patterns (e.g. ', the', ';') that are complementary to the word TF-IDF and author-discriminative, whereas char_wb mostly duplicates word prefixes/suffixes; with the 60k cap the frequent boundary n-grams survive, so expect a small gain (~0.003-0.005) rather than a large shift; telemetry changes are behavior-neutral.

NB log-count-ratio scaling of the same word+char TF-IDF typically gives a small gain on short-text author ID, but OvR-normalized liblinear probabilities are slightly worse calibrated than multinomial softmax and the +1 smoothing on TF-IDF sums shrinks tail features, so net effect is a modest improvement around 0.42-0.43 with real risk of no change.

L2-normalized sparse word+char TF-IDF with LR at C=1 is underfit on this dataset; raising C to 4 typically lowers log loss noticeably (best C for such stacks is usually 3-10), with overfitting only appearing at much larger C.

L2-regularized LR (C=1) on unit-norm TF-IDF is systematically underconfident; a single temperature fitted on the ~1.76k-row holdout will land well below 1 (sharpening) and should recover a good chunk of the gap to a higher-C model, with only minor mismatch from the 90%-vs-100% refit.

Log1p target optimizes the conditional geometric mean rather than the mean, so expm1 predictions systematically underpredict expensive/long rides that dominate raw-dollar RMSE; on this competition with GBMs the log transform is typically neutral-to-slightly-worse, and the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor damps any change, so expect a small regression (~4.15-4.22).

4x more training rows gives LightGBM a modest gain on the predictable rows (valid-row RMSE ~3.6 -> ~3.5), but the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows and the 1000-tree cap limit the overall drop to a few hundredths.

Airport distances help LightGBM capture flat-rate JFK fares and toll-heavy EWR/LGA trips that raw coordinates approximate only coarsely; a modest gain on the ~97% valid rows (~3.63 -> ~3.53) is partly diluted by the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows.

L2 on log1p targets the conditional geometric mean, so expm1 predictions are biased low by roughly exp(sigma^2/2) on the dollar scale, and RMSE rewards conditional-mean predictions; the log fit is more robust to the $500-tail outliers and early-stops on the wrong metric, so I expect a small net regression, with the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows unchanged.

Distance is already a deterministic function of the four raw coordinates the model sees, so the constraint mostly restricts splits (LightGBM's default 'basic' method is crude and slightly lossy) while adding little new information; fares are also genuinely non-monotone at near-zero distances, so expect a roughly neutral-to-slightly-worse result, damped further by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows.

RMSE in dollars rewards conditional-mean estimates; fitting log1p and back-transforming with expm1 yields geometric-mean-like predictions that systematically underpredict skewed high fares and downweight the tail errors that dominate squared error, so despite variance stabilization the graded RMSE typically ends slightly worse than the direct dollar-space fit (2.8% corrupt-row floor unchanged).

In-sample encoding leaks each row's own fare into its route/cell mean (exactly invertible for singleton keys, only mildly damped by m=20 for rare keys), so LightGBM learns leaky splits on rare-route rows that don't transfer to validation/test rows encoded without their own fare; early stopping on the clean holdout limits the damage but unusual-route, high-fare test rows will be predicted worse, so RMSE regresses.

Optimising squared error in log space then exponentiating yields a geometric-mean-style estimator biased low on the fare tail (airport/long trips) that dominates dollar RMSE, so the metric-mismatched log target typically costs a few percent of RMSE on this competition despite the variance stabilisation.

Airport-distance features are a well-known win in this competition (flat JFK fare, Newark surcharge) and let trees isolate those high-fare rides with one radial split, but raw coordinates already capture much of it with 1M rows, and the corrupt-row floor (~2.1) dilutes gains, so expect a modest ~0.05-0.1 RMSE improvement.

The ~2.8% corrupt-coordinate test rows dominate the error (RMSE ~12.5 under the mean fallback); letting LightGBM predict them from year/hour, passenger_count, and any single valid endpoint (plus properly predicting passenger_count=0 rows that have fine coordinates) should trim their MSE modestly while leaving valid-row accuracy essentially unchanged, giving a small but real gain rather than a large one since most of that error is irreducible fare variance/outliers.

4x more training rows with identical features/hyperparameters gives LightGBM a modest but real gain (clean-row RMSE ~3.6 -> ~3.45), while the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the total improvement; float32/usecols/n_jobs=4 changes are neutral and the run should fit the budget.

Proper 5-fold OOF smoothed target encoding of ~1km cells and 2km route pairs adds route/toll/airport signal that trees on raw coords+haversine only partially capture; gains in this setting are typically modest and diluted by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows, so expect a small improvement (~4.14 -> ~4.09) with low regression risk.

Log-target training optimizes relative error and expm1 back-transform yields a median-like, downward-biased estimate of the conditional mean; since the metric is dollar-space RMSE dominated by large fares and the ~2.8% corrupt rows (whose fallback now predicts near the geometric rather than arithmetic mean), the change most likely slightly worsens RMSE.

Manhattan distance, abs deltas and bearing are well-known modest wins for this competition on top of raw coords + haversine; the corrupt-row floor (~2.1 RMSE) is unchanged since the fallback model is untouched, so a ~0.05-0.1 gain on valid rows translates to only ~0.05 on the total RMSE.

Airport/landmark distance features are a well-known win on this competition (JFK flat fare, Newark surcharges) and let trees isolate those regimes better than raw coordinates; expect a modest RMSE drop on valid rows, diluted by the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows.

The metric is RMSE, so an L1 objective fits the conditional median of a right-skewed fare distribution and systematically underpredicts high-fare (airport/long) trips; L1 gradients also converge slower under the same lr/round budget, so RMSE should worsen by a few tenths of a dollar rather than improve.

Log1p target makes LightGBM optimize relative error, and expm1 of a log-space mean systematically underpredicts the expensive tail (airport/long trips) that dominates dollar-scale RMSE; on this competition raw-target training is usually slightly better for RMSE, so expect a small regression.

L1 objective fits the conditional median of a right-skewed fare distribution and converges slowly with sign-only gradients, so predictions systematically undershoot high fares and RMSE (which rewards the conditional mean) worsens; early stopping on RMSE can't fix the objective mismatch.

Huber with delta=$1 is effectively L1 for most residuals (typical |residual| ~$2-3), so the model targets the conditional median of a right-skewed fare distribution (biased low vs the RMSE-optimal mean) and LightGBM's clipped gradients with hessian=1 cap each leaf step at lr*alpha=$0.05/iter, leaving high-fare tail rides (airport, long trips) underfit even at 1000 trees; RMSE-based early stopping can't fix an objective mismatch, so the RMSE gets noticeably worse.

The metric is RMSE in raw dollars; fitting L2 in log space and back-transforming with expm1 yields roughly the conditional median, systematically under-predicting expensive rides where squared errors are largest, and the 2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows is untouched, so expect a small regression rather than a gain.

Airport distance/flag features are a known meaningful gain for NYC taxi fares (JFK flat fares), but LightGBM on raw coordinates already captures some of it and ~2.1 RMSE of the score is an irreducible floor from corrupt test rows, so expect a modest ~1-2% improvement.

4x more training rows reduces variance for the GBDT and should trim valid-row RMSE by a few percent, but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows and noisy target outliers dilute the overall gain, and the run should still fit the budget (~5-8 min) with 1000 trees on 3.6M rows.

5-fold bagging averages out per-model variance from subsample/colsample and the early-stopping split, giving a small but usual RMSE gain; each fold trains on slightly fewer rows (800k vs 900k) and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the visible improvement, so expect a modest ~0.5-1% drop.

OOF-smoothed pickup-cell target encoding adds a weakly informative spatial prior the trees can already approximate from raw coordinates; with heavy smoothing (m=30) on sparse ~100m cells and a 9.9k-row test dominated by a ~2.1 corrupt-row floor, expect a marginal, near-noise improvement rather than a step change.

Snapping to a 0.01-degree (~1 km) grid injects up to ~0.7 km of endpoint error into the haversine distance and removes fine spatial splits the trees already exploit, which typically adds ~$1 of noise on short trips and outweighs any pooling benefit, so RMSE should worsen modestly.

L1 objective targets the conditional median while the metric is RMSE; taxi fares are right-skewed (airport/long trips), so predictions bias low on the expensive tail and L1 gradients converge slower, raising RMSE on valid rows from ~3.55 to ~3.75 on top of the fixed ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows.

L1 objective targets the conditional median of a right-skewed, heavy-tailed fare distribution while the metric is RMSE (minimized by the conditional mean), so predictions systematically underestimate high fares; plus LightGBM's L1 converges slower within the 1000-tree cap, so expect a modest regression.

Airport distance features are a well-known strong signal here (JFK flat-rate and airport surcharges) that trees struggle to carve cleanly from raw coordinates; with 1M rows this should yield a modest but real gain, bounded by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows.

L1 objective targets the conditional median while the metric is RMSE on a right-skewed fare distribution, so predictions systematically undershoot on high/outlier fares and LightGBM's L1 also converges more slowly; expect a modest RMSE regression.

Rounding coordinates to ~1 km cells coarsens location far below LightGBM's native 255-bin quantile resolution in dense Manhattan, losing fine spatial cues (airport terminals, bridge/toll approaches) that trees already exploit; haversine keeps trip length so the hit is small, but the 2M-row model isn't overfitting location enough for the regularization to pay off, so expect a slight regression.

L1 objective targets the conditional median of a right-skewed fare distribution while the metric is RMSE (minimized by the mean), so predictions will be systematically biased low on high-variance/long trips and the sign-gradient boosting converges more slowly; expect a moderate RMSE regression despite RMSE-monitored early stopping.

A grid-rotated Manhattan distance is a well-known complementary feature to haversine for NYC fares and trees can't easily synthesize the |rotated dx|+|rotated dy| form from raw coords, so a small real gain is likely, but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows and single-run noise cap the improvement at a fraction of a percent.

A cross-fitted smoothed route-mean fare adds a modest route-level interaction signal (flat-rate/airport-ish pairs) on top of coordinates+distance the trees already model well; heavy smoothing (50) and sparse 0.01° cell pairs on ~880K rows limit the gain, and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the visible effect, so expect a small improvement rather than a large one.

Rotated Manhattan grid distance is a well-known modestly useful feature for NYC fares, but it is largely redundant with haversine plus raw coordinates for a 1000-tree LightGBM, and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the visible gain, so expect a small improvement within noise.

Doubling the random sample to 2M rows gives LightGBM modestly better coordinate/distance resolution (model-portion RMSE ~3.6 -> ~3.5), but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the gain to roughly a 0.04-0.05 improvement; the MLflow tracking is best-effort and should not affect the score or the ~4-minute runtime.

Explicit JFK/LGA/EWR route flags help the model isolate flat-fare and surcharge trips that raw coordinates only approximate with 1M rows, but the tree model already partially learns airports, and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes gains, so expect a small improvement.

LightGBM with num_leaves=127 on raw numerics plus categorical f_27 letters is a strong native interaction learner at 720k rows; in this competition plain GBDT without engineered features landed around 0.987-0.990, slightly above the small raw-feature MLP, though trees approximate the linear-sum interactions (f_02+f_21 etc.) imperfectly so gains are modest.

Decile one-hot binning destroys the precise continuous values the MLP needs to reconstruct the additive interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26), collapses the tails into single bins, and quantile edges on f_29/f_30 collapse so f_29 becomes a constant column and f_30 loses a level; the raw standardized inputs already represented sums exactly, so this should regress noticeably rather than help.

The features in this synthetic dataset are nearly uncorrelated, so full-rank PCA whitening is essentially an arbitrary rotation that smears the axis-aligned signals (per-character f_27 ordinals, integer counts, sign-interaction features) across all 41 coordinates, badly hurting tree splits; linear leaves recover only linear structure, so expect a clear regression.

f_27 is near-unique per row (~740k distinct strings per 900k in this dataset), so an out-of-fold smoothed TE with m=20 collapses to the prior for almost every row and discards the strong per-position character signal that the ordinal columns carried; the model effectively becomes numeric-only and loses several AUC points.

f_27 is nearly unique per row (~82% singleton strings in train, most test strings unseen), so the OOF smoothed target encoding collapses to almost the prior everywhere and carries near-zero signal, while the removed per-position character ordinals are among the strongest features in this dataset (the letters were generated from ordinal values, so alphabetical order is meaningful); keeping only nunique salvages part of the f_27 signal but the net effect is a substantial regression.

These are the well-known ground-truth additive interactions of this synthetic dataset (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26 with ±5 thresholds); trees struggle to learn additive sums axis-aligned, so exposing them explicitly typically lifts GBDT AUC from ~0.991 to ~0.996-0.998 with no runtime risk.

The logistic regression on ordinal char codes and raw sums cannot capture the strongly nonlinear f_27 and threshold interactions, so it will score roughly 0.75-0.85 AUC; an unweighted 50/50 rank blend injects that weak model's ranking noise into a 0.984 model and should drag the combined AUC down to the mid-0.94s rather than help.

This dataset is famously well-suited to small SiLU MLPs (the 64-64-64-16 architecture reached ~0.998 with full FE and 5-fold ensembling); a single-split, 80-epoch CPU run without the unique-character count feature should still land around 0.995-0.997, well above the 0.984 LightGBM baseline.

This dataset's target is driven by smooth linear-combination interactions (e.g. f_02+f_21, f_00+f_01+f_26) that trees approximate poorly but an MLP learns naturally, so a standardized SiLU MLP on the same 40 features should beat LightGBM's 0.977 and land near 0.99, while still missing the unique-char count and one-hot chars needed for the 0.998 regime.

Linear leaves can rank points correctly within boxes straddling the diagonal sum-threshold boundaries (f_02+f_21 etc.) that constant leaves smear into staircases, so a modest AUC gain is likely; gains are capped because the unique-char count and char ordinals aren't helped, weak linear_lambda adds leaf noise, and there is a nontrivial risk of earlier overfitting or a near-timeout from 2-3x slower training.
The f_27 unique-letter count is a known strong feature in TPS May 2022 that trees cannot easily reconstruct from ten per-char ordinals, so a clear but moderate AUC gain is expected.

These three additive sums are the known key feature interactions in TPS May 2022; axis-aligned trees only crudely approximate sum boundaries, so exposing them directly lets LightGBM jump from ~0.977 to the ~0.99+ range (short of ~0.997 since the f_27 unique-character count is still missing).

f_27 has ~700k+ distinct strings in 800k rows, so LightGBM's categorical binning (min_data_in_bin/min_data_per_group, 255-bin cap) collapses it to a near-useless feature; dropping the per-position ordinal columns removes real positional signal that the letter-count and nunique columns only partially recover, so AUC should fall modestly.

Adjacent-char bigrams add little signal beyond per-position ordinals in this synthetic task, and 676-level native categoricals in LightGBM tend to be picked greedily and mildly overfit, so expect roughly neutral to slightly negative AUC.

The 16 columns are near-independent synthetic features, so PCA on them is essentially a random orthogonal rotation carrying no target information and missing the known additive interactions (which involve f_21/f_22/f_26 outside this block); it should be roughly neutral to slightly worse than the gain-mined products, which at least selected target-relevant nonlinear terms.

f_27 has ~740k unique strings out of 900k rows, so hashing the whole string into 64 buckets yields essentially random noise columns; this throws away the strong per-position letter signal that the ordinal columns captured, leaving the model with only numeric features plus 64 noise dims, causing a large AUC drop.

This dataset's signal is dominated by oblique additive interactions (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22) and high-order f_27 character interactions that boosting approximates far better than sqrt-feature random-threshold ExtraTrees, so ET on the same raw features should land ~2-3 AUC points below LightGBM's 0.978; there is also a real risk the added 5-fold CV (4x extra fitting compute on ~800k rows) pushes the run past the 15-minute kill, in which case no score is produced at all.

This dataset's known structure (additive/multiplicative interactions like f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21) is what NNs capture natively while raw-feature LightGBM plateaus near 0.978; an sklearn MLP on standardized numeric + ordinal f_27 chars should land around 0.985-0.99 despite the crude accuracy-based early stopping, no lr schedule, and missing unique-character feature that keep it well short of the ~0.998 Keras solutions.

The f_27 unique-character count is a well-known strong feature in TPS May 2022 (typically lifts GBDT from ~0.977 to ~0.98+), and per-letter counts add order-invariant information the per-position categoricals cannot express; expect a modest but real AUC gain.

f_27 is ~80% unique strings so its full-sequence frequency is nearly constant (mostly 1-2) and carries almost no signal, while the discarded per-position letters (and the implied unique-letter count) are among the strongest predictors in this dataset; losing them should cost several AUC points, leaving mostly the numeric-interaction signal the trees can approximate.

The f_27 unique-character count is a well-known strong signal in this competition (a key hidden interaction), and per-letter counts add modest extra information; LightGBM should gain a few thousandths of AUC, with some runtime risk from doubling the feature count but likely still within budget.

The known interactions in this dataset are additive sums (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) mostly involving columns outside f_00..f_15, so standardized products of f_00..f_15 capture little new signal; a few products (e.g. f_00*f_01) give a marginal boost while 25 extra correlated columns slightly dilute colsample, netting a near-neutral tiny gain.

Refitting on all 800k rows with ~3333 trees (holdout AUC was still rising at 3000) adds 11% more data and more boosting rounds, giving a small but real AUC gain for a non-saturated GBDT; runtime roughly doubles but should stay under the kill limit.

The f_27 per-position letter effects are largely smooth/monotonic in ordinal order (NNs using scaled ordinals reach ~0.998), so LightGBM's many-vs-rest categorical splits mostly reproduce the threshold splits it already finds with 127 leaves and 3000 trees; the missing signal (unique-char count, f_02+f_21+f_26 interactions) is untouched, so expect a near-neutral result within noise.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is a known strong interaction feature in TPS May 2022 that trees cannot easily reconstruct from 10 per-position ordinals; adding it to LightGBM typically lifts AUC by roughly half a point.

Depth-2 trees cap each learner at pairwise interactions, but this dataset's signal (f_27 character combinations, unique-char structure, multi-feature sums like f_02+f_21 and f_05+f_22) is higher-order; 3000 four-leaf trees at lr 0.05 will underfit relative to 127-leaf trees, so AUC should fall noticeably.

A small LightGBM (600 trees, 31 leaves, max_bin 63, lr 0.05) on raw features will underfit this 800k-row dataset whose key structure is additive threshold interactions and f_27 character combinations; the README notes even 3000x127-leaf LGBM is still improving, so this capacity-limited config likely lands slightly below the 0.982 MLP rather than above it.

On TPS May 2022 the target depends on additive sum-threshold interactions (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22) that an MLP captures naturally but a modest GBDT (600 trees, 31 leaves, max_bin=63, no engineered features) approximates poorly with axis-aligned splits; plain-feature LightGBM historically lands ~0.96-0.97 here, below the MLP's 0.982.

Collapsing the continuous sensors (f_00–f_06, f_19–f_26, f_28) to 4-level quartile codes destroys the fine-grained sum/threshold interactions that drive this dataset, so the trees lose most of the float signal and AUC drops well below the raw-feature baseline.

This dataset is interaction-heavy (f_27 chars, f_02/f_21, f_00+f_01+f_26 sums) and the 127-leaf model was still improving at 3000 rounds, so cutting to 7 leaves (~depth-3 trees, ~20x fewer splits total) removes capacity the data needs; 3000 rounds at lr 0.05 partially compensates but the model will underfit, likely losing ~2-4 AUC points.

num_leaves=4 trees are far too shallow to capture the strong multi-feature interactions this synthetic dataset is built on (sums of 3 numerics, f_27 character combos); 3000 trees at lr 0.05 will still be underfitting at the cap, so AUC drops noticeably below the 127-leaf baseline.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the known strong linear interactions in this synthetic dataset that trees approximate poorly on their own; exposing it directly should lift AUC noticeably, though less than adding all three known interaction sums.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the known strong additive interactions in this synthetic dataset; trees approximate the sum threshold poorly from separate columns, so exposing the sum directly should give a clear AUC gain (roughly +0.008), though smaller than adding all interaction features.

This dataset's key interactions are linear sums of continuous features (e.g. f_02+f_21) that trees approximate poorly but an MLP learns natively, so a plain scaled MLP on raw features typically beats raw LightGBM here (~0.99 vs ~0.977); it still misses the unique-character-count signal, so it won't reach the 0.998 of engineered-feature NNs, and the small model/50-epoch budget fits easily in 420s.

Native categorical splits let LightGBM partition letter subsets at each f_27 position in one split rather than via monotone ordinal thresholds, a mild gain on 800k rows with low overfitting risk, but the big missing pieces (unique-char count, f_00+f_01+f_26-style interactions) remain absent so the change is small.

The unique-character count of f_27 is a known strong feature in this competition that trees cannot easily derive from per-position ordinals, so a solid AUC gain (roughly +0.005 to +0.01) is expected with the same LightGBM config and budget.

Weighting dark targets 5x mismatches the unweighted-RMSE metric: the weighted optimum is a darkness-biased conditional mean, so ambiguous stain/edge pixels (the bulk of the residual error) get systematically pushed darker and background fit is deprioritized; any gain on thin strokes is likely offset by this bias, yielding a small regression within run noise.

Roughly 5x more optimizer steps (~9-11k vs 2000) with a proper cosine anneal to zero should let the still-undertrained 470k-param U-Net fit the text/background reconstruction noticeably better; overfitting risk on 105 images with random crops/flips is low for pixel regression, so I expect a solid but diminishing-returns gain from 0.0161 to about 0.014.

L1 keeps non-vanishing gradients on the ~90% near-white background and text interiors, driving the sigmoid output to saturate closer to exact 0/1 and giving crisper strokes, which in short 2000-step training typically yields a small PSNR/RMSE gain as in Zhao et al./EDSR; this is partly offset by the loss/metric mismatch on genuinely ambiguous pixels under heavy stains (median vs mean hedging), so expect only a modest improvement near run-to-run noise rather than a large jump.

Test scans come from the same synthetic noise distribution as train, so brightness/contrast invariance buys nothing while input-only jitter (with clipping) decouples absolute intensity from the regression target and acts like label noise on anti-aliased stroke intensities; expect a small regression roughly comparable to seed variance.

Scale TTA is not a lossless self-ensemble like flips: the 0.75x path's bilinear upsample and the 1.25x path's antialiased downsample both blur the thin anti-aliased text strokes that dominate RMSE, and with 2/3 of the weight on these systematically edge-softened maps the averaged output regresses (train/test share one scale distribution, so there is little scale-mismatch error for the extra views to cancel).

This small U-Net is optimization-limited rather than overfit (2000 steps, random-crop/flip augmentation over ~20M training pixels, flip TTA), and pixel-wise regression rarely benefits from mid-network dropout; Dropout2d(0.2) on e2/e3 (including the e2 skip) adds gradient noise within a fixed budget plus a dropout-before-BatchNorm variance shift at eval, so expect a modest regression of roughly 0.001 RMSE.

Test pages share the same fonts/noise templates as train so there is little overfitting to fix; Dropout2d(0.1) in every block (including the e1 skip and the features right before the output conv) injects noise into a precise pixel-regression target, slows convergence within the fixed 180s budget, and creates a dropout-before-BatchNorm variance shift between train and eval mode, so RMSE should rise moderately rather than fall.

Adding a 1/8-resolution stage roughly doubles the receptive field (41->73+ px) and quadruples capacity, which helps separate large-scale stains/folds from text strokes on this same-distribution split; the ~30% fewer steps in the fixed 180 s budget is a mild cost since the baseline already runs thousands of steps over ~21M training pixels, so I expect a modest single-run improvement rather than a large one, with some risk of a small regression from step count and crop/full-image padding mismatch.

An explicit 23x23 median background channel hands the small, briefly-trained U-Net (RF ~41px) the local paper-intensity normalization that classical solutions relied on, easing text-vs-stain disambiguation in heavily shaded regions; negligible runtime cost, so I expect a modest improvement (~5-10%) with seed noise of a few percent, and no crash risk since medianBlur on uint8 supports large kernels.

The noise (stains, creases, uneven illumination) is low-frequency and structured, so a 5-level U-Net with a ~3x larger receptive field and ~15x more parameters should model backgrounds and text edges better; the same pixel budget (2000 steps, 8x256^2) and ~2x compute keep it well inside the time limit, though batch-8 gradient noise and fewer distinct crops per step limit the gain to a modest ~10% improvement rather than a large one.

4-way flip TTA is a pure variance-reduction ensemble of views the model was already trained on (random h/v flips), so by convexity of MSE it can essentially only help; gain equals inter-view prediction variance, which for a small, moderately-trained U-Net is a few percent of MSE, giving a modest ~2-4% RMSE reduction with negligible runtime cost.

The applied diff uses a 180s wall-clock budget; on an Ampere+ GPU the tiny UNet(32) at batch 32x128^2 runs roughly 10-20 ms/step, so ~9k-18k optimizer steps replace the baseline's 2000 (4-9x more training) under the same cosine shape and LR, and this small, under-trained denoiser with 105 train images still has substantial headroom before its ~0.011-0.012 capacity floor, so val/test RMSE should drop meaningfully with diminishing returns.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean, and MSE trains exactly that; Charbonnier/L1 targets the conditional median, which for near-binary document targets makes ambiguous pixels (text under stains, faded strokes) get pushed decisively to 0/1 and down-weights precisely the high-error pixels that dominate RMSE, so despite L1's optimization robustness in natural-image restoration I expect a modest regression of roughly 4-8%.

Test scans contain structured stain/fold noise, not white Gaussian noise, so sigma=0.05 input corruption is a train/test shift that mainly teaches the U-Net to smooth high-frequency detail (slightly blurring anti-aliased text edges, which dominate the residual MSE at this 0.015 level) and raises the loss floor within a short 2000-step budget; the model is not strongly overfitting, so the regularization upside is small, netting a modest regression.

BN with batch 32 x 128x128 crops already has well-converged running stats and a tiny train/eval gap, so the stated mismatch is largely illusory; GN instead introduces its own crop-vs-full-page statistics shift (per-sample normalization over 128x128 crops at train time vs whole pages at test) and typically converges a bit slower in a short 2000-step budget, so I expect a roughly neutral-to-slightly-worse result within run-to-run noise.

The metric is RMSE, so MSE is the matched objective; the SSIM-dominated (0.84) + L1 composite spreads gradient uniformly and encourages committed, median-like outputs on ambiguous stain/text pixels, which raises squared error there, while the structure term mostly helps regions that already contribute little to RMSE — with Adam normalizing loss scale the optimization-advantage argument from Zhao et al. is weak, so I expect a small regression (roughly within seed noise), not a clear gain.

Training is untouched so the model is the same; 8-view dihedral TTA averages out model variance at stroke edges (the dominant error source) — the 4 flip views are in-distribution (trained with h/v flips) and should give ~2-3% RMSE gain, while the 4 rot90 views show vertical text the net never saw, but denoising is a local stroke-vs-stain task so they should be only mildly worse and roughly neutral in the average, netting a small improvement.

Pure SSIM loss is nearly blind to uniform luminance offsets in the large flat white background that dominates per-pixel RMSE (Zhao et al. themselves note SSIM-only causes brightness shifts, hence their L1 mix), and here the F.conv2d Gaussian blurs run in bf16 under autocast so blur(x^2)-mu^2 variance estimates carry rounding errors (~4e-3) larger than C2 (9e-4), corrupting the SSIM map/gradients in flat regions; expect a clear regression on RMSE even if text edges look sharper.

Residual/linear-head formulation is a standard, low-risk denoising trick: it removes the sigmoid's saturation floor on the ~90% white background (clamp can now hit exactly 1.0) and slightly speeds convergence in the short 2000-step budget, but the U-Net's skip connections already make identity easy, so the gain should be small (a few percent) and within seed noise.

The SSIM convs run inside bf16 autocast, so the E[x²]−μ² variance estimates on the ~90% flat-white document background are quantization garbage (s_x jumps in ±1/256 steps vs C2=9e-4), turning the 0.1-weighted structural term into a noisy local-smoothing gradient with occasional large spikes rather than a clean signal; sqrt(mse) is direction-neutral under Adam, and SSIM offers little for an exactly-MSE metric, so expect roughly unchanged-to-slightly-worse RMSE dominated by run noise.

Residual output with zero-init identity start and a linear (unsaturated) head gives cleaner gradients than MSE-through-sigmoid and preserves text via the input skip, but the U-Net already has full-res skips and the stain 'residual' is as complex as the clean target here, so expect only a small gain (~3%) with real risk of a wash.

Synthetic pairs make up ~86% of sampled patches but their noise model mismatches the real textured/wrinkled backgrounds, and the whole-image Gaussian blur (sigma up to 4) turns most of the training signal into a hard deblurring task the test data doesn't need, so with a fixed 2000-step budget the real-data mapping gets far fewer effective updates and val/test RMSE likely worsens modestly rather than improving.

4.5x more Adam steps (2k→9k) with a stretched cosine schedule on a small ~0.5M-param U-Net over random crops should converge further with little overfitting risk (test noise comes from the same generator), fits comfortably in budget (~3-5 min on GPU), so expect a moderate but diminishing-returns gain from 0.0162 to roughly 0.014.

8-fold dihedral TTA is correctly implemented (exact inverses, padded dims stay multiples of 8) and averaging reduces prediction variance at ambiguous text-edge/noise pixels; flips are in-distribution from training augmentation, transposed views are slightly out-of-distribution for a text-denoising U-Net but the task is mostly local/isotropic, so expect a modest few-percent RMSE reduction with negligible runtime cost.

L1 on sigmoid outputs gives BCE-like non-vanishing gradients near saturation, pushing the ~90% background/text-core pixels closer to exact 0/1 and converging faster in the short 2000-step budget (consistent with L1>L2 PSNR results in restoration literature), but the median-vs-mean mismatch makes confidently wrong calls on ambiguous stain/text pixels that dominate RMSE, so I expect only a small net gain with real risk of being neutral or slightly worse.

Target-dependent weighting (3x on dark pixels) makes the weighted-MSE optimum a dark-biased conditional mean, so in ambiguous regions (stains over/near text, antialiased edges) predictions skew darker and residual noise is kept, which the unweighted RMSE metric penalizes; any gain from crisper stroke interiors is likely offset, yielding a small loss/metric-mismatch regression within seed-noise range.

The metric is uniform RMSE, but a target-dependent 10:1 weighting makes the optimal predictor E[w·y|x]/E[w|x], biasing uncertain boundary/faint-stain pixels darker (thicker strokes, residual gray on background), so the mismatch between training objective and the graded uniform MSE should modestly worsen RMSE despite crisper ink.
