Residual (identity-init) output removes the sigmoid's interior bias on the ~90% pure-white background and gets free error reduction from the inference clamp on overshoot, and converges faster in the short 2000-step budget; but the network must now precisely cancel structured stain texture rather than just classify it, so the net effect is a small improvement with real downside risk.

L1 targets the conditional median rather than the mean, so on the bimodal text-vs-stain pixels that dominate RMSE it commits to 0/1 and pays full squared error when wrong; the offsetting gain from pushing background to exactly 1.0 is small since MSE+sigmoid already gets background to ~0.995, so I expect a slight regression within seed noise.

Linear residual output removes sigmoid saturation bias on the ~90% near-white background (clipping at inference turns overshoot into exact 1.0) and the zero-init identity start converges faster within the short 2000-step budget; the residual form is no harder for a skip-connected U-Net on this structured noise, so expect a modest gain, though seed noise (~±0.001) and the less natural residual target for near-binary outputs make a small regression possible.

Halving NAFNet width (~4x fewer params/FLOPs) removes capacity on a task where val tracks train closely (little overfitting to regularize away), so fine text/stain detail degrades modestly; run stays well within budget, but RMSE likely rises ~0.0015 from 0.0173 to ~0.019.

Target-dependent weighting shifts the optimum away from the conditional mean (biasing ambiguous stain/faint-text pixels darker), and since the metric is plain uniform RMSE this mismatch typically costs a little more than the extra emphasis on stroke pixels gains; expect a small regression within trajectory noise.

The 31x31 grey-closing ratio channel is a near-clean text/background proxy with 61px context (vs the U-Net's ~44px receptive field), so within the fixed 2000 steps the net converges to a slightly lower error (~5% gain, within ~2x seed noise); big caveat: the added execution.json forces device=cpu with 8 threads, which for ~350 GFLOP/step x 2000 steps very likely blows the 15-minute kill limit, so this estimate is conditional on the run actually completing.

Running the 1x1 head and sigmoid in fp32 only removes bf16 output quantization (ULP ~0.004 near white), which in quadrature contributes ~1e-5 to a 0.0162 RMSE, so the metric is essentially unchanged (bit-identical if the hill was already CPU/fp32); the real risk is the added runtime.toml forcing CPU-only with 8 threads, which could push 2000 steps of batch-32 U-Net training past the 15-minute kill rather than change the score.

Flip TTA on a flip-augmented U-Net is a low-risk variance-reduction ensemble (Jensen guarantees MSE of the mean ≤ mean of view MSEs); with an under-trained small model and per-view padding-phase diversity, expect a modest ~2-3% RMSE gain, training unchanged and the ~5% extra inference compute fits the budget.

The residual NAFNet (LayerNorm + SimpleGate, zero-init blocks, dirty+correction output with clamp) should learn stain removal at least as quickly as the BN U-Net in 2000 steps and gets text edges nearly for free, but it has ~5x fewer FLOPs, only 16 channels at full res, an untuned 2e-3 LR, and the channel-attention patch-vs-full-image mismatch; forced CPU fp32 training only affects speed, so I expect a modest, not dramatic, improvement.

The in22k_ft_in1k head is a linear classifier on the very same 1024-d features but fitted on ~1300 ImageNet images per breed (including these exact Stanford-Dogs/ImageNet test images), so it should be at least as accurate as the 77-img/class LR and partly memorizes noisy labels; with T and w tuned on holdout (w=0 as a safe floor) the blend should cut confident LR errors and drop log loss from ~0.31 to roughly 0.19-0.24.

Unwhitened PCA to 256-d is just the original L2-regularised LR constrained to the top-variance subspace; since ridge already down-weights low-variance directions, truncation mainly discards the subtle fine-grained breed-pair signal (Norfolk/Norwich, husky/malamute) that lives in small-eigenvalue directions, so expect a small but real log-loss regression rather than a gain.

Mixup/CutMix at prob=1.0 is a heavy regularizer designed for 300-epoch recipes; official ConvNeXt/Swin/BiT fine-tuning recipes drop it for short fine-tunes and small (<20k) datasets because it slows convergence, so in 6 epochs (~775 steps) the model likely underfits slightly (val acc down ~0.5-1%), while its calibration benefit is largely already captured by the existing temperature scaling, netting a small regression or near-neutral result.

With only 6 epochs (~770 steps) and a center-crop eval transform, dropping the min crop scale to 0.08 adds many near-background/zoomed-in views that the model has too little time to exploit and widens the train/test scale mismatch; expect a slight underfit and a small log-loss regression (~+0.01–0.03), within noise of neutral.

ConvNeXt-V2-L (IN-22k→IN-1k, 88% top-1) gives far more separable dog features than ResNet-50, and since these Stanford-Dogs images were in its labeled training set its 1000-d log-probs nearly memorize the breed; frozen features + tuned LR should reach ~95-97% accuracy, cutting log loss from ~0.45 to roughly 0.15-0.22 (with ~±0.03 test-set noise), and the implementation (forward_head pre_logits + head.fc, timm eval transform, fp16) is correct and comfortably within budget.

The premise that log-softmax adds nothing is wrong for a linear probe: the 120 dog-class log-probs are a nonlinear, ImageNet-head-distilled summary (trained on ~1300 imgs/class of these very breeds, largely seen in ImageNet train) that the heavily L2-regularised LR can exploit at low norm cost, whereas re-learning that map from 2048-d pooled features with ~77 imgs/class generalises worse; dropping the 880 near-constant non-dog columns removes only mild noise, so the net effect is a moderate regression (~0.50-0.55).

Ridge on ±1 one-hot targets gives LDA-like boundaries that on these strong 2560-d features are close to but typically ~1% less accurate than the cross-entropy-optimal LR, and a single global temperature cannot reproduce LR's per-class logit shaping (ridge scores saturate near ±1 with class-dependent shrinkage), so log loss should land modestly worse, roughly 0.35-0.40, with a fair chance of near-parity.

L2-regularised LR already ridge-shrinks low-variance directions optimally per the holdout C search, so hard truncation to 128 PCs per block mainly discards the subtle low-variance directions that separate confusable breed pairs (Norfolk/Norwich, husky/malamute, poodle sizes) which dominate log loss; the renormalisation's effective-C boost and parameter reduction only partly offset this, so expect a modest regression.

ConvNeXt-B in22k→in1k (85.8% top-1) pre-logit features are far more linearly separable for the 120 ImageNet dog classes (which the in1k head was trained on, including these very images) than torchvision ResNet-50 V1 features; frozen-feature LR on such backbones typically lands ~0.12-0.2 on this competition, with C re-tuning on a holdout guarding against the LayerNorm feature-scale shift.

End-to-end fine-tuning of an in22k-pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny (whose ImageNet-1k training already covered these Stanford-Dogs images) with flip TTA and temperature scaling should reach ~94-95% val accuracy, roughly halving the log loss versus frozen ResNet-50 features + LR; 6 epochs at 224px fits comfortably in the 7-minute guard, so the main residual risks are a failed weight download or noisy T selection on the ~920-image val split.

The ImageNet fc head is a linear readout of the same 2048-d features but trained on ~1300 images/class (and the Stanford Dogs images largely overlap ImageNet train), so its dog-class log-probs act as a strong, precisely-estimated classifier the 77-image/class probe can stack on; standardisation plus a sensible C grid keeps the 3048-d fit well regularised, giving a moderate log-loss drop rather than a dramatic one since both classifiers share the same feature-level confusions on the hard breed pairs.

ConvNeXt-B in22k (trained on these very ImageNet dog images), DINOv2 and CLIP features are far more separable than ResNet-50 V1; per-block L2 normalisation plus a tuned C fixes calibration, so log loss should drop from 0.45 to roughly 0.12-0.20 as seen with strong-backbone linear probes on this dataset.

Focal loss (gamma=2) is not a proper scoring rule and yields systematically under-confident softmax outputs while its vanishing gradients on already-correct examples slow late-epoch fine-tuning; on a balanced 120-class task with ~80-85% accuracy the extra log-loss paid on correct predictions roughly cancels the softer (less costly) errors, so I expect a small net regression versus label-smoothed CE.

Stanford Dogs is literally an ImageNet subset, so pretrained features are near-optimal and full fine-tuning at lr=0.01/momentum 0.9 is known to drift too far (the 0.67 log loss implies only ~82-84% accuracy, below a good linear probe); freezing conv1-layer3 keeps the generic features intact while layer4+fc (still ~15M params, so no underfitting) adapts, which should recover a few accuracy points and cut log loss to roughly 0.55-0.62, though layer4 still drifts at the same LR so the gain is partial rather than dramatic.

Hflip TTA on a flip-augmented ViT backbone gives highly correlated features, so probability averaging yields only a small variance-reduction gain; expect a modest 2-4% log-loss improvement (~0.51 -> ~0.50), with NUM_WORKERS=0 affecting only runtime, not the metric.

All 120 breeds are ImageNet classes and these images are ImageNet-train images, so the supervised in21k/in1k ViT-B/16 features are near-optimal for this task; CLIP ViT-B/32 (coarse 7x7 patch grid, no label supervision, GELU/QuickGELU mismatch in the non-quickgelu timm variant) is known to lag supervised models on ImageNet-covered fine-grained sets like Pets (90.0 vs ~94.5) and Birdsnap, so linear-probe accuracy should drop from ~86% to roughly 77-80%, inflating log loss to ~0.7-0.9 with the untuned C=0.3.

Unwhitened PCA is an orthogonal projection, so with the same C=0.3 the L2-regularized probe is equivalent to the original model constrained to the top-256 PC subspace; L2 already tames noise directions, so the constraint mostly discards some residual fine-grained breed signal (the hard terrier/spaniel pairs), yielding a small-to-moderate log-loss regression rather than a denoising gain.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 CLS features are far more linearly separable for fine-grained breeds than supervised ResNet-50 pooled features (roughly halving error on breed-style benchmarks like Pets), the holdout-selected C keeps the LR calibrated, and 10-view TTA is retained, so log loss should drop substantially, tempered only by ResNet-50's existing ImageNet-memorization advantage on these images.

Whitening to unit-variance components multiplies the effective feature scale ~200x, so C=1.0 becomes 10-1000x weaker regularization per direction than now; the near-separable 256-d fit turns overconfident and confident test errors inflate log loss more than the sharper correct predictions and modest truncation gains recover.

kNN top-1 on these frozen features should be roughly comparable to the logreg (~83-85%), but 10-neighbor vote probabilities are coarse and overconfident: the tiny 1e-3 uniform mix caps any true class with zero neighbor votes at ~7.0 nats, and even perfectly-voted correct cases pay ~0.11 each, so the ~5-7% of test images whose breed is absent from its 10 nearest training images alone adds ~0.4 to the loss, pushing it well above the calibrated logistic regression.

Full fine-tuning with a solid recipe (RRC+flip, label smoothing, warmup+cosine SGD) should lift test accuracy from ~86-87% to ~88-90% and stay well-calibrated, giving a moderate log-loss gain; the leak-friendly frozen ImageNet features and lr=0.01 on the whole backbone cap the upside, and label smoothing's ~0.1-nat floor on correct predictions limits how low it can go.

ViT-B/16 augreg in21k→in1k features are far more discriminative for the 120 in1k dog classes than ResNet-50 V1 (85% vs 76% top-1, and the backbone saw these images during in1k fine-tuning), so a linear probe should jump from ~86% to ~93% accuracy; C=0.3 was not retuned but feature scale is comparable and 768-d limits overfitting, so log loss should roughly halve to ~0.22-0.28.

10-crop+flip TTA with probability averaging is a cheap ensemble over near-in-distribution views of a frozen ResNet-50; it typically trims a few percent of log loss (reducing overconfident errors), with only mild dilution risk from corner crops the LR never saw, and the extra 10k forward passes fit easily in budget.

ConvNeXt-Tiny in22k features are far stronger than ResNet-50 V1 for these ImageNet-derived dog images, but per-block L2 normalization shrinks feature norms ~30x while C only rises 0.3→1.0, so with sklearn's sum-loss and ~77 samples/class the multinomial LR is heavily over-regularized (centroid-like, under-confident, typical p≈0.8); the under-confidence tax on easy samples eats most of the gain from fewer/less-confident errors, leaving only a modest net improvement.

The Stanford Dogs images are ImageNet training images, so the pretrained V2 fc head restricted to the 120 dog classes is a strong, largely memorized classifier trained on ~15x more dog data than the 9k-sample LR; temperature-tuned and blended (alpha likely 0.5-0.7) it should cut log loss meaningfully, though V2's heavy regularization (label smoothing/mixup/cutmix) limits memorization so the gain is moderate rather than dramatic.

PCA-256 without whitening is just L2 logistic regression constrained to the top-256 principal subspace with a C tuned for the full 2048-d space; ImageNet-trained ResNet features make class variation dominant so most signal survives, but the discarded lower-variance channels carry breed-specific fine-grained cues (Norfolk vs Norwich etc.), so expect a modest regression of a few percent in log loss rather than a gain.

ResNet-50's final conv features were trained to be linearly separable under average pooling (and ImageNet-1k V1 saw these very dog images), so swapping to max pooling yields noisier, larger-scale descriptors (background patches dominate individual channels, effective C grows ~10x with raw unstandardised features); temperature scaling fixes the calibration but not the 2-5pt accuracy loss typical of max-vs-avg linear probes, so log loss should rise moderately.

Dog breeds are literally 120 ImageNet-1k classes (and Stanford Dogs images sit in the ImageNet train set), so the V2 checkpoint's much stronger in-domain classification (80.9% vs 76.1% top-1, better top-5 on fine-grained confusions) should translate fairly directly into more separable pooled features and a lower log loss; the known 'regularized recipes (label smoothing/mixup/cutmix) transfer worse as frozen features' effect mainly bites on out-of-domain targets, not on an ImageNet subset, though the untuned C=0.3 and possible feature-scale shift likely eat some of the gain, so I expect a solid but not dramatic improvement rather than the ~0.25 a naive accuracy-scaling would suggest.

C=0.03 was already measured worse than the holdout-selected C=0.3 for the frozen-feature head, and the short 2-epoch fine-tune barely moves the head from its LR optimum (the mean-CE gradient there is only W/(nC), negligible at lr 1e-3), so the under-confident, lower-margin init largely persists; slightly larger residuals give the last-bottleneck convs more signal and recover part of the gap, but net expect a modest regression.

Dropping the crop from 224 to 192 (ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 evaluated below its training resolution, with FixRes-style apparent-object-size mismatch worsening) degrades fine-grained breed features by roughly 1.5-2.5% top-1; the 2-epoch fine-tune already fits within 90s so the speedup buys no extra updates, giving a moderate log-loss regression rather than a neutral change.

Unwhitened PCA is an orthogonal projection, so with C=0.3 the classifier is effectively unregularized on the 256 kept directions while losing ~800+ lower-variance directions that the tuned full-dim LR was actually using; for 120 fine-grained breeds the pairwise-discriminative directions for confusable pairs are low-variance and partly discarded, so expect ~1% accuracy loss and a modest log-loss regression (roughly +0.03) rather than a gain.

Feeding a frozen ResNet-50 trained at 224 a 192px center crop (~27% fewer pixels) worsens the train/test apparent-object-size mismatch and discards fine texture/face detail that fine-grained breed discrimination depends on; ImageNet top-1 drops ~1.5-2 pts at 192 and the dog subset is hit harder, so the linear probe's log loss should rise noticeably (roughly 0.45-0.50), with flip TTA and C=0.3 unchanged offering no offset.

V2 weights lift ImageNet top-1 from 76.1% to 80.9% and the 120 breeds are literally ImageNet classes (images largely in the pretraining set), so frozen 2048-d features should separate breeds noticeably better; heavy V2 regularization (label smoothing/mixup/cutmix) and an un-retuned C=0.3 on differently-scaled features blunt the gain, so expect a moderate rather than dramatic improvement.

C=0.3 was already tuned for log loss on a holdout, so the LR is roughly calibrated; a single temperature fit on 1380 val samples (T likely 0.9-1.1) decouples logit scale from the coarse C grid and typically yields a small ~0.5-1.5% NLL gain, slightly diluted by the 85%->100% train-size mismatch and 1023-sample test noise.

Head is initialized exactly at the LR optimum so the network starts at the baseline's 0.4525; two epochs (~288 steps) of SGD at lr 1e-4 on the last bottleneck convs (head lr 1e-3 barely drifts from its optimum) moves weights only ~0.1-0.5% with frozen BN and no augmentation, giving a small early-fine-tuning gain that transfers partially to test, so expect a modest improvement of roughly 0.005-0.015 rather than a large one.

Horizontal-flip TTA with probability averaging is a cheap two-member ensemble over a frozen backbone; features are near flip-invariant so gains are modest, but averaging reliably tempers the overconfident LR probabilities, giving a typical 2-4% log-loss reduction with negligible runtime cost on 1,023 test images and no correctness risk in the diff.

AUC is threshold-free so 1:1 balancing buys nothing in ranking, while it throws away 80-99% of the training rows (threat keeps ~956 of 159k, identity_hate ~2.8k) for 60k-200k-feature sparse LR, removing the hard negatives and making the NB ratio q-estimates noisy; expect small drops on toxic/obscene/insult and 0.02-0.04 drops on threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic, with both branches sharing the same negative subset so errors are correlated.

NB-weighted LR on word 1-2gram + char_wb 2-6 features was a known stronger single model (~0.980-0.981) than word-only NB-LR (~0.977) in this competition; branch B improves by ~0.002-0.003 alone, but since branch A already carries the same char block the rank-blend gain shrinks from added correlation, netting roughly +0.001 to the mean AUC. Main risk is runtime: six liblinear dual fits on a ~136M-nnz matrix (~40-60 s each) plus predict/multiply overhead may push the run to 12-14 min, so a timeout failure (~15% chance) is possible; conditional on finishing, a small improvement to ~0.9814 is most likely.

AUC is threshold-free so 'majority-class bias' is not a real problem for this metric; 1:1 undersampling just discards 80-99% of the negatives (threat fits on ~950 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k, severe_toxic ~3.2k) for regularized linear models on 60k-200k sparse features, and the NB log-count ratio is estimated from the same tiny subset, so every per-label model gets noisier and the rare labels lose the toxic-but-not-X negatives that teach context; expect small drops on toxic/obscene/insult and 1-3 point drops on threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic, pulling the column mean down by roughly 0.008.

MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0) on L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF with 200k features is heavily over-smoothed for the rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic), giving branch B roughly ~0.92 mean AUC vs ~0.977 for NB-LogReg; the fixed 50/50 rank average then drags the strong ~0.978 branch A down on the rare columns, and the weaker MNB OOF stack features also remove the small stacking gain A got from NB-LogReg, so the blend falls by a few thousandths despite some complementarity.

Mean-pooled corpus-trained Word2Vec + LR/MLP typically scores ~0.95-0.965 on Jigsaw (dilution of profanity signal, loss of char n-gram robustness to misspellings), so replacing the ~0.979 TF-IDF branch and its MLP twin with two correlated weaker models that carry 2/3 of the equal-weight rank blend drags the ensemble below the ~0.977 NB-LogReg branch alone; run should still finish within budget.

1:1 undersampling discards 80-99% of negatives (threat keeps only ~478 negatives, identity_hate ~1.4k, severe_toxic ~1.6k), so each label's model no longer sees toxic-but-not-this-label negatives and degenerates toward a generic toxicity/keyword scorer with poorly sampled negative class; AUC rewards more data not balance, and since all three branches share the same systematic loss the rank blend can't recover it, with the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) dragging the column mean down by roughly a point.

A sparse TF-IDF MLP is the first non-linear/multi-task model in an otherwise all-linear, highly correlated blend, so even at 1/4 weight and only 1-2 epochs (time guards likely cut it short given the ~80s/epoch SparseAdam cost and the ~550-650s pipeline) it should add ~+0.001-0.002 diversity gain; ~20% risk the 720s guard skips D entirely (no change) and small crash/OOM risk temper the estimate.

AUC is a ranking metric that logistic regression already handles fine under imbalance, so 1:1 undersampling only discards information: frequent labels lose ~90% of their negatives (small AUC drop), while threat (956 rows) and identity_hate (2.8k rows) are fit on <2% of the data with 60k-250k sparse features, so benign comments containing 'kill'/identity terms get ranked high and those columns drop by 0.02-0.04; all three branches share the same subsample so rank-averaging cannot average the noise away.

Text cleaning is historically near-neutral for TF-IDF+LR on Jigsaw: de-obfuscation helps branch B on a few hundred rare test comments (char n-grams in A already cover most), but mapping u/ur/r→you/your/are and wtf→'what the fuck' erases strong chat-register toxicity markers (and 'you'/'your'/'are' are stop words in A), timestamp deletion and !!!-collapse drop mild signals, so I expect a small net regression within noise.

Feature-level stacking of proper 5-fold OOF NB-LogReg logits (scaled so sag still converges) gives branch A a complementary bigram/NB view plus cross-label priors that mainly help the noisy rare labels, but the final 50/50 re-blend with B double-counts B's weaker signal and the OOF-vs-fold-averaged test mismatch adds noise, so expect only a small net gain (~+0.0004) if the ~30 extra liblinear fits keep the run under the 15-minute kill.

A 3-epoch 64-unit multi-task MLP on the word+char TF-IDF should land near the linear branches (~0.977-0.980 alone) and adds nonlinear/multi-task diversity, so the 1/3 rank blend likely gains a small ~+0.0005-0.001; main risks are the MLP being undertrained on rare labels (neutral outcome) and the extra ~4-5 min of sklearn sparse Adam updates pushing the run toward the 15-min kill.

Branch C (NB-LogReg on word 1-2gram + char_wb) is a solid single model (~0.979-0.980 alone) but is highly correlated with both A (char block) and B (NB-scaled word block), so an equal-weight 3-way rank blend should give only a small lift (~+0.0003 to +0.0008) over the current A+B blend; main risk is runtime, since six liblinear dual fits on a ~95M-nnz, 250k-column matrix add ~4-6 min and push the run near the 15-min kill, and a slight overfit on rare labels from C=4 with the extra features could make the gain a wash.

Per-label blend weights between two highly correlated linear n-gram branches move the AUC only second-order from the 0.5/0.5 optimum; with 50% shrinkage toward equal blending and noisy holdout argmax on rare labels, the expected gain is tiny (+0.0001 to +0.0003), while the extra ~5 min of holdout vectorizer/LogReg fitting adds some risk of hitting the 15-min kill but likely finishes around 11-13 min.

Toxicity is driven by specific rare lexical cues (profanity, slurs, 'kill') that a 300-component variance-maximizing SVD over 100k word n-grams dilutes into generic talk-page topic factors; dropping the char n-gram and NB-weighted sparse branches and the blend gives a well-known ~2-3 AUC-point regression (LSA/doc-embedding + LR on Jigsaw typically lands ~0.95-0.96), with the largest hits on toxic, threat and identity_hate.

Toxic is untouched (10x positives exceeds negatives) but the rare labels lose most of their negatives (threat keeps ~3% of the data, severe_toxic/identity_hate ~10%), and for high-dimensional sparse linear models plus fastText the discarded negatives carry real information about non-toxic n-grams; with the same subsample seed shared across all three branches the errors correlate, so expect a modest regression concentrated in threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic.

The parent's 0.883 is far below what A+B alone gives (~0.98), which is explained by fasttext-wheel's old pybind11 returning duplicated (max) probabilities under NumPy 2 so branch F ranked by confidence and was anti-correlated; the child pins numpy<2, restoring valid fastText outputs, and the single multi-label softmax model is a slightly weaker but genuine ranker (~0.94 alone), so the 1/3-weight rank blend should recover to roughly the A+B level near 0.98 (if the venv is not rebuilt, the k=7 duplicated-prob bug would instead push it down toward ~0.85).

In binary settings sklearn's ComplementNB reduces exactly to MultinomialNB's log-count-ratio scorer; on raw (unnormalized) 1-2gram counts with 200k features the score becomes length-dominated (long toxic comments with sparse markers rank below short clean ones) and the alpha*200k smoothing mass swamps the tiny positive classes (threat, severe_toxic, identity_hate), so per-label AUCs fall to roughly 0.76-0.87 versus ~0.98 for the TF-IDF LR/NB-LR ensemble — a large regression.

Mean-pooled from-scratch Word2Vec + LR is a well-known weak baseline on Jigsaw (~0.94-0.96 mean AUC vs ~0.976-0.98 for TF-IDF/NB-LogReg): averaging dilutes single-keyword profanity signal in long comments and discards the char n-gram views, so replacing the tuned three-branch sparse ensemble with it should regress by roughly 2-3 points, assuming the ~6-10 min skip-gram training fits the budget.

Mean-pooled corpus-trained Word2Vec (200d, 5 CBOW epochs on ~20M tokens) + plain LR discards the exact-token/char-ngram evidence that drives toxicity AUC and dilutes rare-label signal words (threat, identity_hate) in long comments; such embedding-average baselines typically land ~0.95-0.96 versus ~0.98 for the TF-IDF/NB-LR blend, so a clear regression is expected.

A char-level NB-LogReg is a genuinely different regularization/weighting of char n-grams than branch A and should add ~+0.0005 via the holdout-tuned 3-way rank blend, but it is partly redundant with A's char_wb features so gains are small; main risk is runtime, since a second char vectorizer plus six liblinear fits on ~4x denser rows likely adds 5-7 min (not 1-2) and pushes the run toward the 15-min hard kill.

C=0.1 in the word+char TF-IDF LR was a CV-tuned choice from the reference kernel (0.9788 LB); raising C 40x to 4.0 under-regularizes the 60k-feature model, mostly hurting the rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) and making branch A more correlated with the already-C=4 NB-LogReg branch, so the rank-blend should slip slightly rather than gain.

Supervised fastText (word/bigram only, no char n-grams, bucket=500k collisions, lr=0.5/epoch=20 overfits) should land around 0.96-0.97 mean AUC, notably weaker on threat/identity_hate; an equal 1/3 rank weight on a moderately-correlated weaker word model roughly cancels its diversity gain, so expect a flat-to-slightly-negative change (~-0.001). Also note a real risk that 6 labels x 20 epochs (~270M tokens each at dim=64 on 4 threads) adds 6-10 min on top of the ~7-9 min baseline and trips the 15-min hard kill.

If it finishes, an NB-weighted char_wb 3-7 view is genuinely complementary to A (heavily regularized 50k chars) and B (words) and a 3-way rank blend should add ~+0.0005-0.001 (≈0.981); but a second char_wb vectorizer (~4-6 min on top of the existing ~4 min) plus six fully-converged primal liblinear fits at C=4 on ~80M-nnz NB-scaled features (TRON with sklearn's tight scaled tol, no iteration cap in practice) very plausibly pushes the run past the 15-min hard kill, so I hedge the point estimate toward no gain.

Per-label weight tuning on a 16k holdout yields at most a few 1e-4 of AUC (and is noise-driven for threat/identity_hate with ~50-140 positives), while permanently training both branches on only 90% of the data costs a comparable or slightly larger amount, especially on the rare labels; net expected effect is a small regression.

NB log-count-ratio scaling on the word+char branch mostly re-shapes regularization (C_eff = 0.1·r²): roughly neutral-to-slightly-positive on toxic/obscene/insult, but for the rare labels (threat, severe_toxic, identity_hate) the smoothing asymmetry gives most tail n-grams r≈3-5, i.e. ~10-20x weaker regularization and more overfitting; on top of that branch A becomes more correlated with the NB-LR branch B, shrinking the rank-blend's diversity gain, so net a small regression (plus some timeout risk since sag's step shrinks ~15x on the unevenly scaled rows).

min_df=0.01 on ~313k docs means df>=3128, which shrinks branch B's 200k word/bigram vocab to ~1.5k common terms and prunes the rare-but-decisive slurs/threat words (nigger, faggot, cunt, jew, moron, murder, etc.) plus most 5-6 char n-grams; coarse profanity signals (fuck, shit, stupid, hate) survive so toxic/obscene/severe_toxic degrade only modestly, but identity_hate and threat lose most of their discriminative features, dragging the column mean down by roughly 0.025-0.03.

Balanced 1:1 undersampling discards ~90% of negatives (threat trains on only ~956 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k, severe_toxic ~3.2k); AUC is ranking-only so balancing brings no benefit for logistic regression, while the tiny, noisy training sets and NB ratios computed from a few hundred negatives degrade discrimination, especially on the rare labels that dominate the column mean.

Rocchio-style mean-difference classifiers are a valid but much weaker linear model than discriminatively trained LR/NB-LR on sparse n-grams: they cannot zero out non-discriminative common features, over-weight correlated char n-grams, and let generic profanity swamp rare labels (threat, identity_hate), so expect NB-level AUCs (~0.94-0.98 per label) and a mean around 0.96 despite a valid, fast run.

char_wb vs char is a near-noise swap for TF-IDF+LR on this data; under the 50k feature cap char_wb spends less capacity on cross-word junk n-grams and covers more within-word obfuscated slurs, so branch A likely gains a few 1e-4 that dilute to ~+0.0002 after the rank blend with unchanged branch B (direction could easily flip within ±0.0003).

For binary labels ComplementNB reduces to a plain multinomial-NB log-count-ratio score with no discriminative fit on top; with alpha=1 against L2-normalized TF-IDF (tiny per-doc mass vs. 60k–200k-feature smoothing) the weights collapse toward a rarity/length signal, so common labels drop to ~0.94–0.96 and threat/identity_hate to ~0.8–0.85, giving a mean well below the LR/NB-LR blend.

Collapsing 60k sparse word+char TF-IDF features to a 32-dim LSA space discards the specific lexical cues (profanity, slurs, threat words) that make branch A the strong ~0.978 member of the blend; a 32-component LR will likely land around 0.91-0.93 mean AUC (much worse on threat/identity_hate), so the equal-weight rank blend with the already-weaker fastText branch drops to roughly 0.945-0.955 rather than improving.

Collapsing everything outside the top-2000 DF tokens to a single 'raretoken' discards the misspelled/obfuscated profanity and mid-frequency slurs/threat words that the char_wb n-grams and fastText bigrams were capturing (hurting identity_hate, threat and insult most), and both branches degrade into near-identical ~2000-word bag-of-words models with less blend diversity; core frequent profanity survives so the drop is moderate rather than catastrophic.

Keeping stop words adds 2nd-person pronouns and negations ('you', 'your', 'not') that carry toxicity signal, but this is already captured by the char_wb block and Branch B's unfiltered 1-2 grams, and the ~300 displaced rare words in the 10k vocab matter little; the change affects only one of two feature blocks in one of two rank-averaged branches, so expect a near-zero, marginally positive shift.

Logit averaging is not scale-invariant: the NB-LogReg branch (C=4, near-unregularized, NB-scaled features) has 2-3x the logit spread of the C=0.1 word+char branch, so the blend effectively tilts ~70/30 toward the weaker, overconfident branch B instead of the 50/50 ordering weight the rank average gave; blend curves are flat near the optimum so the loss is small, likely a few 1e-4 with extra noise on the rare labels.

char vs char_wb is a near-wash for toxicity: cross-word n-grams add phrase cues (e.g. 'ck you', 'kill y') that branch A's stop-worded unigrams lack, but they dilute the 50k vocab and overlap with branch B's word bigrams, so the rank-blend moves only ~±0.0002; slight lean positive per the original 0.9792 kernel using analyzer='char', with a modest runtime/timeout risk.

Dropping the strong NB-LogReg branch (esp. good on rare labels) for a 5-epoch fastText ova model is a downgrade, and fastText's ova sigmoid is a 512-bin lookup table that saturates to exactly 0/1 beyond |logit|>8, so the branch emits heavily tied probabilities (most rows at 1e-5 for rare labels) that blend poorly in a rank average and pull hard positives below fastText's confident false alarms; expect the blend to land near or slightly below Branch A alone (~0.977).

At C=1 the standardised-feature LR on leaf data is regularisation/underconfidence-limited (empirically optimal C is ~1000+), so dropping a third of the mostly-informative, correlated descriptors both removes signal and effectively tightens the L2 penalty, making the LR less confident and slightly less accurate; since the blend's loss is ~half-sensitive to LR's absolute loss change, expect roughly +0.01 on the final log loss with the NN branch unchanged.

With ~98% accuracy the optimal confidence on correct examples is ~0.97, but label smoothing 0.1 trains the NN to cap true-class probability near 0.9, imposing a ~-log(0.9) floor per correct example; even diluted 50/50 with the LR this adds ~0.03-0.04 to the blend log loss while the gain on the few overconfident errors (already tempered by the LR in the blend) is negligible, so a clear regression.

OvR with 8-vs-784 imbalanced binary fits gives heterogeneous per-class scales/intercepts that a single power exponent cannot reconcile, so ranking among confusable Quercus/Acer species degrades slightly versus the jointly-fit softmax; with ~99% baseline accuracy each extra confident error costs ~4 nats, so a few added mistakes push calibrated log loss from ~0.045 to roughly 0.06.

A 5-seed MLP bag adds a nonlinear, diverse base model to an under-confident C=1 LR; blending before the power calibration with OOF-selected (alpha, w, a, eps) and a w=0 fallback should modestly cut the few confident errors that dominate log loss on 594 test rows, though the gain is limited by overlapping hard samples and OOF-selection noise.

Fold-averaging five high-C logistic models hedges the few confident test mistakes that dominate log loss (loss capped near the least-wrong fold), but each fold model sees ~20% less data with only ~8 samples per class, adding small hedged losses on borderline samples; for a stable linear model these effects roughly cancel, so expect a near-wash with a slight edge to the ensemble on this noisy small test set.

Absolute leaf size (log H/W/area) and convexity are genuinely new signal not in the scale-normalised 192 descriptors and historically helped LR on this dataset; CV-selected C limits overfit from the 21 extra (partly noisy Hu/euler) columns, so expect a moderate log-loss drop rather than a large one, with some risk of a couple of confident test errors offsetting gains.

PCA is a rotation (L2-invariant) so the only effect is dropping the ~5% low-variance tail; with 99 classes and 10 samples each, directions that separate a few confusable species pairs have tiny total variance and get discarded, while the weak effective L2 (alpha~1/(nC)) was already using them, so the hard pairs that dominate log loss get slightly worse; the clean, low-noise precomputed descriptors offer little denoising upside, so expect a modest regression rather than a gain.

Averaging 5 fold models each trained on 792 rows acts like a full-data fit with effective C≈0.8 plus probability smoothing; at C=1.0 this LR is already underconfident on Leaf (optimal C is in the thousands), so the softer, less-trained fold models lose a few percent on the ~98% correctly-classified test rows, only partly offset by Jensen/tempering gains on the handful of confident errors — expect a small regression, roughly a wash within noise.

The final submission is the LR's unchanged (under-confident, ~0.124) probabilities averaged with a features+silhouette NN; the 192 standardised descriptors alone let a small MLP reach ~0.05-0.12 log loss, and Jensen's inequality on the 50/50 arithmetic blend caps the result below the mean of the two, so the blend should land around 0.08-0.10 — the image branch adds little (fill-ratio-based polarity heuristic will invert many tightly-cropped leaves inconsistently, and 8-rotation TTA mostly just smooths it), and the main tail risks are an over-confident NN or the 9-min guard truncating the full-data run on a slow CPU.

C=1 multinomial LR on 99 classes is strongly under-confident (most correct predictions at p~0.9 dominate the 0.124 loss); OOF-tuned power sharpening (a~2) drives those toward ~1 at the cost of making the ~1-2% soft errors more expensive, netting roughly a 35-50% log-loss reduction, so ~0.07 on test with some variance from a few severe errors.

C=1 is far too much regularisation for this near-separable 192-feature/99-class problem; CV will select C in the ~1000-3000 range, which in this competition is well known to drop standardised logistic regression from ~0.12 to roughly 0.03-0.05 log loss, so expect ~0.04.

Image dimensions add genuinely new size information absent from the normalized 192 descriptors and the hu/solidity/eccentricity features help where consistent, so the C=1.0 logistic regression should get modestly more confident; but the mask.mean()>0.5 polarity heuristic will flip many tightly-cropped ovate leaves (fill ~0.5-0.7) so a chunk of the shape features describe background blobs and are bimodal within species, and the sign*log Hu transform is noisy for near-zero moments, capping the gain at a modest improvement rather than a large one.

With 240 standardized features, 99 classes and ~10 samples/class the data is near-separable, so LR log loss on this dataset is dominated by regularization-induced underconfidence (known leaf-competition behavior: loss keeps improving up to C~1000); cutting C from 1.0 to 0.2 shrinks the logit scale by ~30%, inflating the soft-correct-prediction losses roughly 2x on top of a small irreducible floor, giving a clear regression to ~0.13-0.20.

Dropping the full-data refit trains the submitted classifier on only ~12.8 instead of 16 samples per class (792 vs 990 rows) in a 99-class, 240-feature problem, which reliably worsens log loss on a data-starved dataset; the holdout-measured model is simply a weaker model, not a better-calibrated one.

Blend weights are fit by a convex SLSQP problem on OOF log loss, so the blend cannot be worse than LR alone in-sample and with only 3 parameters transfers well; distance-weighted kNN and shrinkage LDA are overconfident (poor standalone log loss) but confident-correct on many samples where LR is uncertain, so a small weight on them typically trims LR's tail losses by ~15-25%.

On this dataset (99 classes, ~8-9 training samples per class after the 15% holdout, highly linearly separable descriptors) tree ensembles are well known to lag linear models badly: axis-aligned splits with min_samples_leaf=10 cannot isolate a 9-sample class, accuracy drops to roughly 92-96%, and the resulting misclassifications plus mushier calibration push log loss to the ~0.25-0.45 range typical of GBDT/RF here, a large regression from 0.061.

Platt-sigmoid calibration with only 2-4 positives per class per 3-fold split caps the SVC member's true-class mass near (N+1)/(N+2)≈0.8 before normalisation over 98 hedged wrong classes (~0.7 after), so it is systematically less confident than the C=1 multinomial LR it replaces on the ~95% of easy test leaves; with uniform soft voting that lowers the ensemble's mean correct-class probability by ~0.03-0.04 and raises log loss by roughly 0.03-0.05, with no offsetting gain on the few hard samples since both are linear models with correlated errors.

RF vote fractions on 99 classes with ~9 samples/class are diffuse (true-class prob ~0.55-0.65) while HGB's Newton-step multiclass boosting is sharp (~0.95 when right); in a uniform soft average the lost confidence on the ~90% easy test rows outweighs RF's better hedging on the few hard rows, so log loss should rise modestly.

MLP with weak weight decay and accuracy-based early stopping on ~10% held-out rows will be far more confident than the strongly regularised C=1 LR, cutting the ~0.09/sample underconfidence cost on the ~98% correct predictions, but its ~1.5-2.5% errors become confidently wrong (loss ~3-5 each) and uniform shrinkage only partly caps them, so net is a modest improvement to roughly 0.09-0.14 with high single-run variance.

Standardised leaf features are near-separable, so the C-search will pick a large value (~300-1000) that sharpens the multinomial LR probabilities; known results on this dataset show scaled LR log loss dropping from ~0.12-0.2 at C=1 to ~0.03-0.06 at C≈1000-2000, and the OOF-selected uniform shrinkage caps the damage from the few confident errors, so expect roughly 0.04-0.06.

C=1 LR is heavily over-regularized on this near-separable 99-class data, so adding 48 mostly-informative shape features (Hu moments, contour scalars, radial histogram) spreads weight and raises effective margin, giving a modest log-loss drop; gains capped by redundancy with the provided shape descriptor, a few noisy features (hu5-7, orientation), and some chance the image path resolves wrong yielding zero features and no change.

C=1 is far too much regularisation for these 192 standardised, nearly separable features; CV over C up to 1e3 with neg_log_loss should pick a large C (~100-1000), which on this dataset is known to bring multinomial LR from ~0.12 down to roughly 0.03-0.05 log loss, with 10-fold CV guarding against overconfident extremes.

Uniform soft-voting averages the decent LR (0.124) and a very confident ~98%-accurate LDA with two weaker, poorly calibrated members: distance-weighted kNN whose CV-on-logloss picks a large k (zeros dominate the scorer) and so yields diluted ~0.5-0.7 true-class probabilities, and a 99-class HGB with ~8 samples/class and min_samples_leaf=10 that makes aggressive Newton steps and confident errors on ~10% of the 99 test rows; the LDA boost on easy rows is roughly offset by kNN/HGB dilution, while HGB/kNN errors each cost ~0.3-0.5 per row, so the ensemble most likely lands around 0.18-0.25 rather than improving.

LR at C=1.0 is already under-confident on this dataset (log loss keeps improving as C rises to ~1000), so shrinking toward uniform only raises OOF loss on the ~97% correctly-classified samples; the grid search will pick alpha=0.0, and the clip at 1e-15 plus renormalization is a no-op, leaving the identical full-data model and unchanged test probabilities.

sklearn applies the shrinkage per class before pooling, so 'auto' already yields ~0.5 shrinkage toward a per-feature diagonal target (0.5*S_w + diag), while fixed 0.9 toward a spherical target collapses to 0.1*S_w + ~0.3*I, i.e. a near nearest-centroid classifier on standardized features that overweights noisy/rare-bin features and top-variance correlated directions; this likely costs 1-3% accuracy on similar-species pairs with similarly confident errors, so log loss most likely rises moderately (uncertain, could improve if it tempers single-feature outlier errors).

Per-family LDAs are much weaker (margin ~85%, texture ~82%, shape ~60% accuracy), and equal-weight arithmetic averaging caps p_true near 2/3 whenever the weak shape model disagrees and ~1/3 when only one model is right; this hedging loss roughly offsets the savings from softening the joint model's few extremely confident errors, giving a near-wash, slightly worse log loss.

Keeping 90% of standardized variance likely drops to ~80-90 of 192 dims; the nearly separable 99-class LR at high C loses discriminative low-variance margin/texture bin directions, giving less confident predictions and a moderately worse log loss rather than a gain.

Shrinkage-LDA matches or slightly beats tuned LR in accuracy on the leaf descriptors (~98-99%), but its softmax sharpness is fixed by the pooled covariance rather than tuned like LR's C, so the 1-3 residual errors on the ~200-sample test split tend to be penalized more heavily; expect a similar-to-slightly-worse log loss around 0.06-0.09 with high variance.

On this near-linearly-separable 99-class problem the best models are weakly regularized (large-C LR), and the current ridge at C=1 with n=990 barely shrinks low-variance directions, so hard-truncating ~80-100 low-variance PCs (5% of standardized variance, which for fine-grained species discrimination still carries between-class contrasts among correlated margin/texture bins) removes usable discriminative signal; OOF temperature recalibration limits the damage, but expect a moderate regression rather than a gain.

Shrinkage LDA (sklearn applies Ledoit-Wolf per class on ~8-10 samples, so it is heavily diagonal-shrunk) should reach similar ~98.5-99% accuracy to LR, and OOF temperature scaling fixes global overconfidence, but LDA's distance-based scores give heavier-tailed confident errors than NLL-trained LR logits, so log loss likely lands slightly worse, around 0.05-0.06.

Mixing 0.5% uniform costs ~-log(0.995)=0.005 nats on every non-extreme sample and only pays off for true-class probabilities below ~1e-3; a C=1 LR on whitened Nyström features at 0.094 logloss is mostly moderately confident with few catastrophic misses, so the flat ~0.005 penalty likely dominates, giving a small regression (with some chance of a gain if a couple of test rows are extremely overconfident).

Fewer Nyström landmarks (384 of 990 samples, ~3.9 per class vs ~5.2) both coarsens the RBF feature map and, via the post-Nyström StandardScaler (column std ≈ 1/sqrt(m)), tightens the effective RKHS regularization by ~25%; the model is already under-confident at 0.094 with C=1, so extra shrinkage and reduced coverage should raise log loss modestly rather than denoise.

Shrinkage LDA is highly accurate (~99%) on the 990x192 leaf descriptors and far sharper than the over-regularised C=1 logistic regression, so most correct rows cost ~0 while the handful of confusions between sibling species cost several nats each; net effect is a modest gain over 0.124 but with real risk of overconfident errors pushing it above baseline.

Leaf descriptors are nearly linearly separable, so CV over C will pick 100-1000 (known kernels select C~1000-2000 with LB ~0.03-0.05); weaker regularization sharpens the already-accurate multinomial LR probabilities, cutting log loss roughly 2.5-3x from the C=1 baseline, tempered by small-test-set noise from a few confidently wrong predictions.

C=1.0 multinomial LR on 192 standardized features is heavily over-regularized and under-confident (LL 0.124 at ~98% accuracy); an OOF-fit temperature will land around T≈0.5-0.7 and sharpen the logits, cutting loss on the many correct predictions far more than it inflates the few confident errors, recovering a large share of the gap to tuned-C LR (~0.04) though not all since the weight direction stays shrunk.

Standardizing the 512 Nyström coordinates whitens the RBF kernel (effective kernel K(x,B)K_BB^-2 K(B,x)), turning the model into a weakly-regularized soft-nearest-basis classifier: basis rows become one-hot, tail eigen-directions get amplified, and with C=1 on features of norm ~22 the LR fits training nearly perfectly, so test predictions are confident; on this near-linearly-separable 99-class dataset with ~5 basis points per class the RBF-interpolation representation is noisier than the linear model (block-level kernel shifts plus tail noise give signal/noise ~7 against 98 competitors), yielding a few percent of confident errors and softer correct-class probabilities, so log loss most likely lands around 0.15-0.25 versus the 0.124 linear baseline, though a well-behaved outcome near 0.08 is possible.

The dense block adds genuinely new signal the l2-normalised lowercase TF-IDF cannot see (community-age trend via t_days, request length, first-person/caps/punctuation rates, upvote ratio) plus partially redundant flags; with a random train/test split and only 31 standardised columns in an L2 LR, the ~14 calendar one-hots add little noise, so expect a modest but real AUC gain of roughly +0.01 to +0.02.

RF with sqrt(~8k) candidates per split on a mostly-sparse TF-IDF/subreddit matrix dilutes the 9 informative dense features and exploits the diffuse linear text signal far less efficiently than the L2 logistic model; the modest gain from nonlinear thresholds/interactions on the count features is unlikely to offset the text-handling loss on a ~3k-row, weak-signal task, so expect a moderate AUC drop rather than a gain.

RF with sqrt(5010)≈71 features per split handles the sparse TF-IDF block much less efficiently than L2 logistic regression (text signal diluted into near-random word splits), and the modest non-linear gain on the 9 requester numerics doesn't offset it; the giver_known leak is mostly retained via deep fully-grown trees, so the drop is limited to a couple of AUC points rather than a collapse.

Replacing 5k sparse TF-IDF unigrams with 50 LDA topic proportions on ~4.5k short noisy posts typically loses text signal for a linear model (specific lexical cues like reciprocity/evidence words get smeared into coarse topics, and length information is normalized away); the giver_known leak and requester-history features carry most of the AUC so the drop is modest, but the text block's marginal contribution shrinks from roughly 0.03-0.04 to 0.01-0.02.

Replacing a supervised OOF TF-IDF/LR logit (the single strongest text feature) with 20 noisy unsupervised LDA topic proportions on ~3k short training docs loses most of the discriminative lexical signal; LightGBM with num_leaves=8/min_child_samples=50 can only recover a little of it via topic-metadata interactions, so the result lands near metadata-only performance plus a small topic bump, i.e. ~0.68-0.69.

The test split is a random (not temporal) sample from the same Dec-2010..Sep-2013 window, so the raw timestamp legitimately captures the well-known decline in RAOP success rate over the period and transfers to test; dropping it removes a genuinely predictive column, while hour-of-day/weekday effects in ~3-4k rows are weak and noisy, so the net is a small regression.

Rank-blending a well-regularized HGB on ~34 dense meta/time/text-stat features (typically ~0.66-0.68 OOF AUC alone, capturing nonlinear temporal/history interactions LR misses) with the existing 0.70 LR, using a CV-chosen weight that falls back toward LR if the GBM is weak, is a low-risk diversity gain worth roughly +0.01 on a ~1k-row test set with noise of ±0.015.

A sqrt-max_features random forest over ~5,000 sparse TF-IDF columns plus only ~33 dense columns dilutes the strong metadata/time signals (expected <1 dense feature per split), fragments the ~4k training rows on noisy word splits, and loses most of the linear text signal that LR exploits; RF's nonlinear gains on metadata are small versus this dilution, so expect a clear regression to roughly the mid-0.6s.

Bag-of-subreddits is a known modestly useful signal on RAOP (help-seeking/drug subreddits, prior-activity profile) that the 9 numeric counts only partly capture; l2-normalised binary block plus C=0.3 l2 penalty bounds the noise from ~2k sparse extra features, so expect a small gain of roughly +0.01 AUC on a noisy ~1k-row test split, with downside risk limited to a few thousandths.

giver_username_if_known is in the Kaggle/MLE-bench test schema and is a near-perfect leak (known giver => received pizza, ~8% of rows, roughly a third of positives); the unscaled 0/1 column gets a large LR coefficient (~4) pushing those rows to the top of the ranking, so AUC ≈ f + (1-f)*base ≈ 0.33 + 0.67*0.63-0.66 ≈ 0.75, with the rest of the model unchanged.

Well-regularized LightGBM on an out-of-fold text logit plus raw requester-history numerics and the request timestamp (success rate drifts over time, and a random test split lets trees exploit it) should beat the single linear model by roughly +0.02 AUC; runtime is trivial and the mlflow wrapper is fail-safe, so the main risk is only test-set noise on ~1k rows.

Random train/test split makes the request timestamp (success rate fell as the subreddit grew) a genuinely new, fairly strong signal for this LR, and length/imgur/RAOP-prior indicators add small complementary gains that L2-normalized TF-IDF lacks; ~27 standardized dense columns on 4k rows won't overfit, so expect a modest +0.01 to +0.03 AUC lift rather than a regression.

ExtraTrees with max_features=sqrt(5393)≈73 samples mostly sparse TF-IDF columns at each split, so the 9 strong requester-history numerics appear in only ~11% of nodes and random thresholds on rare words add noise; the forest ends up mostly splitting on weak MiniLM dims, which typically ranks worse than the linear model on this weak-signal task, so expect a modest regression of a couple of AUC points with sizeable test-set noise.

Dropping the TF-IDF block removes a low-variance (heavily shrunk at C=0.3 given row-normalized tf-idf) lexical signal that is only partly redundant with MiniLM, while the real problem — a nearly unregularized 384-dim standardized embedding block on ~4.5k noisy rows — is untouched, so the model loses a bit of complementary signal and AUC slips slightly rather than improving.

Adding ~24 standardized dense doc statistics to a ~4-5k-sample LR is low-risk, and explicit length/structure signal (known to be predictive in RAOP and lost under L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF) plus gratitude/link flags should lift AUC modestly; VADER and Flesch add little, so expect roughly +0.01 to +0.02.

Dropping the TF-IDF block removes real signal (need/hardship words are predictive on this dataset); the nine log1p requester-history features under plain logistic regression typically land around 0.60-0.63 AUC here, below the current text+metadata 0.65, so this is a regression rather than the hoped-for generalization gain.

Mean-pooled skip-gram vectors trained on only ~5.7k short docs (~0.5M tokens) are noisy, dilute strong sparse cues like imgur/http and specific hardship words under unweighted stop-word-heavy averaging, and 200 dense standardized columns at C=0.3 overfit more than the L2-normalized TF-IDF block, so the text contribution shrinks and the combined AUC likely slips a point or two below the TF-IDF baseline.

Bigrams and a 12x larger vocab add a little phrase-level signal but on ~3-4k training docs most df>=2 n-grams are noise and the L2-normalized TF-IDF rows dilute unigram weights under fixed C=0.3, while the strong metadata/text-stat dense block dominates the AUC anyway, so the net effect is roughly neutral to marginally positive.

The nine at_request history counts carry only modest signal (~0.60-0.63 AUC in known RAOP analyses; no timestamp feature), while the SVD text components in the current model add real, if inefficiently used, signal; dropping text with an over-capacity 63-leaf GBM on 9 features should land slightly below the current 0.633.

On ~4k noisy samples with 300 mostly-noise SVD components, a 400-tree RF's bagging/feature-subsampling regularizes about as well as the early-stopped but fairly deep (num_leaves=63) LGBM; sqrt feature sampling dilutes the 9 strong numeric features somewhat, but averaged deep trees still recover them, so expect roughly the same AUC with a small edge from lower variance, within test-set noise of ±0.02.

MiniLM embeddings add complementary semantic/narrative signal on top of unigram TF-IDF and the nine history features, but the 384 standardized dense dims are nearly unregularized at C=0.3 with only ~4k samples and largely overlap the TF-IDF content, so expect a modest gain of roughly +0.01 AUC with real risk of a flat or slightly negative result from overfitting.

Bigrams add a few useful phrase features (reciprocity/gratitude) but with ~3k docs, min_df=2, and fixed C=0.3 the extra ~30k mostly-rare features dilute the L2-normalized unigram signal and effectively strengthen regularization, so the net effect is roughly flat with a small expected gain well within test-split noise.

Request length and first-person/reciprocity stats are known modest predictors on RAOP that L2-normalized TF-IDF plus requester-history numbers don't capture; 15 standardized dense features under C=0.3 LR should add roughly +0.01 AUC, with some noise from heavy-tailed features like uppercase fraction and Flesch on empty bodies limiting the gain.

On ~4k rows the LR on sparse TF-IDF already captures the weak, diffuse word signal well; SVD(300)+LightGBM with num_leaves=63 will overfit noisy dense components despite early stopping, and gains from nonlinear handling of the 9 meta features are too small to offset the lost text signal, so expect a small regression.

RAOP success rate has a strong monotone decline over 2010-2013 that the absolute-time spline captures and that generalizes to a random test split; annual sin/cos features discard year identity and only weakly alias that trend (via uneven month coverage), while genuine seasonality is weak and noisy at ~3k rows, so expect a modest AUC loss rather than a gain.

With ~4k rows and ~5k TF-IDF columns the design is near-separable, so C=30 (100x weaker L2) lets thousands of moderate/rare-word coefficients fit label noise while the already near-unregularized numeric features gain nothing; RAOP text signal is weak, so the overfit text logits swamp the requester-history signal on the test split and AUC should drop several points.

RAOP success rates fell markedly as the subreddit grew (2010→2013), and nothing in the current TF-IDF + requester-history + subreddit features encodes calendar time explicitly; with a random train/test split the 7 standardized quantile-spline columns are a low-variance, well-regularized addition that should lift LR AUC by roughly 0.01–0.03, tempered by partial redundancy with account-age/RAOP-tenure proxies and small-test-set noise.

Cosine KNN on the concatenated matrix is dominated by the unit-variance numeric z-scores and unnormalized binary subreddit indicators (norms ~3-7) while the L2-normalized TF-IDF block (norm 1) barely affects distances, so the text signal LR exploited is largely lost; distance-weighted k=25 local averaging on ~4k noisy 25%-base-rate samples is high-variance and typically lands around 0.58-0.62 AUC on RAOP, a clear regression from 0.649.

Distance-weighted k=25 KNN on nine standardized metadata columns yields noisy, coarse probability estimates (effective k ~15-20, likely ~0.58 AUC alone) whose variance rivals its signal; at a fixed 50/50 weight this injects substantial ranking noise into the logistic model, so the blend should land below the smoother CatBoost blend and near or slightly under LR-alone.

C=30 on ~5000 TF-IDF unigrams with only ~4k rows is near-unregularized (features > samples, weak lexical signal), so the LR overfits the text and emits extreme probabilities that dominate the 50/50 blend, dragging the blend toward the degraded LR ranking rather than gaining from CatBoost; a modest C bump might help, but a 100x jump most likely costs a few AUC points.

RAOP success rate declined strongly as the community grew (roughly 40%+ in 2011 to under 20% by 2013), a signal largely orthogonal to text and requester-history features and absent from the current model; with a random train/test split the 7 standardized spline columns let the LR capture that multi-year trend, which typically adds ~0.015-0.025 AUC, tempered by small-test-set noise and mild correlation with RAOP-history features.

BernoulliNB on 5k binarized n-grams is noisier than regularised LR, its ranking gets dominated by document length via smoothing bias, and the 9 informative numeric features are reduced to crude above-mean indicators that get drowned out by text terms, so expect a clear regression to roughly 0.60-0.62.

RAOP success rate declined strongly over 2010-2013 and the prepared test split is random in time, so an 8-column quantile cubic spline on the request date adds a largely orthogonal signal to TF-IDF plus requester-history features; implementation is leak-free and consistent (fit on full train for final model), regularization is mild enough for bounded [0,1] spline bases, so expect a modest but real gain of roughly +0.01 to +0.03 AUC.

Subreddit membership carries only modest signal beyond the existing activity/count numerics, while ~1000 unscaled binary columns (min_df=5) at C=0.3 are far less regularized than the L2-normalised TF-IDF block, so noisy coefficients on mid/rare subreddits add logit noise for established users that roughly offsets or slightly outweighs the gain; expect near-flat to slightly worse AUC.

A CatBoost model on the nine at-request history features captures nonlinear metadata signal (RAOP prior activity, karma, account age) that the linear LR only models additively; alone it likely scores ~0.62-0.64, and a 50/50 blend with the 0.657 text+meta LR is diverse enough to add roughly 0.01 AUC, with small risk of being neutral given the weak metadata-only model and noisy ~1k-row test set.

Adding bigrams under the same 5000-feature budget swaps ~1k rare, mostly-noise unigrams for frequent phrases (pay forward, food stamps, job interview) that add a little signal beyond unigrams; text is the weaker component next to the numeric features and the final model is refit identically, so expect a small, near-noise gain (roughly +0.002 AUC) with real chance of a slight regression; the mlflow telemetry is try/except-wrapped and should not affect predictions.

Authorship attribution is driven largely by function-word style; dropping stop words removes stylistic word unigrams and, more importantly, cross-word function-word bigrams ('of the', 'it was') that char_wb (2,5) cannot span, so the word view loses discriminative signal that the char view only partially compensates for, giving a modest log-loss regression.

NB on raw word/char counts is a strong, decorrelated complement to TF-IDF LR on this dataset (rare-vocabulary evidence), and the log-prob meta-LR re-temperatures NB's overconfidence, so a clean OOF stack typically cuts log loss by ~5-10% here; implementation looks correct with no leakage or runtime risk.

Function words (I/my/upon/which, and bigrams like 'of my', 'which had') are among the strongest authorship signals in this dataset and sklearn's stop list also removes content words like 'fire', 'cry', 'found', so the word LR and word NB base models will each lose roughly 0.04-0.06 OOF log loss; the char_wb models retain function-word frequencies but not cross-word bigrams, so the LightGBM stacker only partially compensates and the final score regresses modestly.

A linear stacker on raw (standardized) probabilities cannot nonlinearly recalibrate the overconfident MultinomialNB and C=10 LR base outputs or exploit meta-feature interactions the way the regularized 5-fold LightGBM does; the GBM is not meaningfully overfitting (15 leaves, early stopping, 5-model average), so swapping it for multinomial LR should cost roughly 0.01-0.03 log loss.

Punctuation (semicolons, commas, quotes, exclamation/question marks) is a strong, well-documented authorial signal in this dataset and is consistently present in train and test; the word block is essentially unchanged by the stripping, so the change mainly removes dense, robust punctuation-bearing char n-grams from the char block, which under C=1.0 regularization were among the most exploitable features, so expect a moderate regression of roughly 0.02-0.04 log loss.

Stacking word/char TF-IDF LR (C=10) with tuned MultinomialNB on word/char counts via a log-prob meta LR is a well-known strong recipe on Spooky (NB and LR errors are fairly decorrelated); base models individually land ~0.42-0.46 and the linear blend typically reaches ~0.35-0.38 CV, the code is correct and runs well within budget (char matrices are small), so expect roughly 0.36-0.38 on the test split.

Chi2 keeps only ~8% of columns and is frequency-biased, so the L2-regularized LR (already underfit at C=1.0) loses the rare-token/long-tail signal that individual short sentences depend on and gets smoother and worse; the OOF blend weight will shift toward NB and limit the damage, but the blend still ends up modestly worse than 0.361.

Authorship attribution is a stylometry task where function words (including sklearn's stop list entries like 'upon', 'whence', 'thence', 'amongst') are among the most author-discriminative tokens; removing them from both the NB count features and the word TF-IDF block weakens NB noticeably (~0.43 to ~0.46-0.48 OOF) and mildly hurts LR (char_wb partially retains unigram function-word signal but loses function-word bigrams), so the blend regresses from ~0.36 to roughly 0.38-0.40.

With L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF (word+char stacked) on ~17.6k rows, C=1 is over-regularized; 5-fold CV over [1,3,10,30,100] will almost surely pick C≈10–30, which typically cuts log loss from ~0.43 to ~0.38–0.40 for this feature set, and the explicit parallel fold loop plus final refit fits comfortably in the time budget.

Proper OOF stacking of two LR (word/char tfidf) and two MNB models plus 16 stylometric meta-features into an early-stopped LightGBM recalibrates and combines diverse ~0.43-0.48 base models; comparable NB/LR-stack kernels on this task land around 0.32-0.37, so a solid drop from 0.432 to roughly 0.35 is expected, with small risk from the fold-averaged test vs single-model OOF probability shift and the ~2k-row test noise.

Case-sensitive cross-word char n-grams add real stylometric signal (punctuation context, capitalization) for LR, but the uncapped rare high-IDF n-grams dilute L2-normalized rows and are largely redundant with the word block, so at fixed C=1 the net effect is a small improvement (~0.005), well within the range where it could also be neutral.

MultinomialNB on 1-2gram counts with tuned alpha scores ~0.42-0.45 OOF on this data and its overconfident errors are fairly decorrelated from the underconfident C=1 TF-IDF LR, so an OOF-tuned arithmetic blend (likely w~0.5-0.6) should land around 0.39-0.40; implementation is correct and fits within the time budget.

Function words are the strongest stylometric signal for authorship attribution (sklearn's list even drops 'upon', a hallmark Poe token, plus archaic 'whence/thence/hence'), so stripping them removes discriminative unigram and bigram features and shortens inputs, leaving an already-overconfident fastText model to overfit content words; expect a clear regression rather than a gain.

The test set shares the natural ~40/29/31 class prior, so balancing removes a correct prior and duplicated minority rows give an already-overfit fastText (25 epochs, lr 0.5, char+word n-grams) extra passes that make its wrong predictions more overconfident; expect a small log-loss regression on the order of 0.01-0.03 on top of fastText's run-to-run noise.

ComplementNB(alpha=0.1) on the stacked TF-IDF is a weaker, overconfident but decently accurate (~82-85%) model whose rare-feature memorization is partly decorrelated from L2-regularized LR; the OOF-selected weight (likely w≈0.7-0.9, with w=1.0 as a safe floor) should sharpen LR and buy a modest ~0.005-0.015 log-loss gain rather than a regression.

MultinomialNB on L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF is a known step down from tuned LR on this task (Spooky kernels show tuned NB on TF-IDF at ~0.43-0.50 vs LR ~0.35-0.40): NB's generative probabilities are poorly calibrated and the stacked, highly correlated char/word blocks double-count evidence, so even the best alpha on the grid yields noticeably higher log loss.

Dropping the char_wb 2-5 gram block removes punctuation/subword stylistic signal that is highly discriminative for author attribution (and the only coverage of rare/unseen words given min_df=2 word tokens), so the word-only NB-SVM should lose roughly 0.02-0.04 log loss; the 'chunking artifact' argument is unconvincing since those artifacts are shared across authors and the head is regularized.

Replacing the NB-SVM head (ratio-weighted logistic regressions with proper probability calibration) by a plain ComplementNB(alpha=1.0) on L2-normalized TF-IDF gives NB-style probabilities: alpha=1 smoothing is huge relative to fractional TF-IDF mass (muting the rare discriminative word features), the redundant char n-gram block and missing class prior distort calibration, and no C/alpha tuning is done; MNB/CNB with default alpha on TF-IDF for this competition historically lands around 0.55-0.65 log loss versus ~0.41 for NB-SVM, so expect a clear regression.

C=1 is over-regularized for L2-normalized sublinear word+char TF-IDF; 3-fold CV on neg_log_loss will almost surely pick C≈3-10, sharpening under-confident probabilities for a modest log-loss gain (~0.40), with the grid including C=1 as a floor and only a small timeout risk from the two lbfgs CV paths.

MultinomialNB on L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF is far less calibrated than LR: the ~300 highly redundant char_wb n-grams per sentence plus rare-word features with alpha=0.1 produce very sharp posteriors (margins of several nats), so the ~16% misclassified sentences incur 3-5 nat penalties; word-only TF-IDF NB with alpha=0.1 historically gives ~0.49 on this data and the char block makes it more overconfident, so expect a clear regression to roughly 0.55-0.70.

fastText with lr=0.5/epoch=25 plus word bigrams and char 2-5-grams on ~17.6K sentences drives training loss near zero and yields overconfident softmax outputs (~80-83% accuracy but wrong predictions with p_true often <0.05), so log loss degrades substantially versus the well-regularized TF-IDF+LR (0.432); expect roughly 0.55-0.70.

C=1 is over-regularized for L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF with lbfgs multinomial LR (the small-magnitude char_wb block is under-utilized at low C); 5-fold CV on ~20k rows will reliably select C=4 or 8, typically cutting log loss to ~0.39-0.41 on this dataset, and since C=1 remains in the grid the CV selection makes a regression unlikely.

NB log-count-ratio weighting amplifies author-specific vocabulary (which is why MNB does well on Spooky) and C=4 relaxes the underfit C=1 baseline, typically buying ~0.02-0.03 log loss on word+char TF-IDF; OvR renormalization costs a little calibration versus multinomial, so expect a moderate net gain to roughly 0.40-0.41 rather than a large one.

The 14 MaxAbs-scaled stylometric features add weak but genuinely new signal (raw length, case fraction, punctuation counts lost under lowercasing/L2-normalized TF-IDF) to a well-regularized LR; implementation is correct and cheap, so expect a small gain of roughly 0.001-0.004 log loss rather than a large shift.

NB log-count-ratio scaling amplifies discriminative features and effectively loosens regularization on them (the C=1 multinomial LR on L2-normalized TF-IDF is over-regularized), which typically helps on author-ID lexical cues, but the switch to OvR liblinear binaries with row-sum normalization gives up some joint calibration, so expect a modest net log-loss improvement (~0.02), not a large one.

L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF with ~125k features on ~17.6k rows is already under-regularized-limited at C=1 (optimal C for log loss on this setup is typically 3-10), so quartering C shrinks the logits further, makes predictions markedly under-confident, and log loss should rise by roughly 0.06-0.10.

Dropping the word (1,2) block removes vocabulary-level cues (names, archaic words, bigrams) that matter most for author ID on this dataset and shrinks the NB-scaled row norm, making the C=1 L2 logistic even more under-confident; char_wb alone typically trails word+char by ~0.03-0.06 log loss, so expect a regression to roughly 0.55-0.58.

Dropping the NB log-count-ratio scaling removes the informative sign/magnitude prior, so a C=1 L2 OvR logistic on L2-normalized TF-IDF is heavily over-regularized and underconfident (Abhishek-style TF-IDF+LR C=1 baselines land ~0.55-0.63 on this task); stop words and char n-grams soften but don't erase the hit, so expect a modest regression to roughly 0.53-0.58.

TF-IDF + L2 logistic regression on this data is typically on the under-regularized-is-better side (C=1 is badly underconfident; optimum for stacked word+char is around C≈4-10), so halving C to 2.0 softens probabilities and modestly raises log loss rather than lowering it.

NB log-count-ratio scaling is a well-suited informative regularizer for short-sentence, high-dimensional word+char TF-IDF (suppresses uninformative common n-grams, emphasizes class-skewed ones), which historically made NB-LR/NBSVM among the strongest single linear models on Spooky; the gain is partly offset by switching from multinomial softmax to normalized one-vs-rest liblinear sigmoids at an untuned C=4, so I expect a modest net improvement rather than a large one.

Function words (the, of, which, upon, thus, yet, whence...) are the strongest stylometric author markers in this dataset and sklearn's 318-word list removes them from both the word and char_wb branches, discarding roughly half of all tokens; expect a clear regression (roughly +0.05-0.08 log loss), partly cushioned by retained punctuation/affix char n-grams and temperature scaling.

C=1.0 is already on the over-regularized side for L2-normalized TF-IDF text features; cutting C to 0.25 shrinks rare-but-discriminative word/char n-gram weights toward a centroid-like classifier, costing ~1.5-2 points of accuracy that temperature scaling (which only fixes confidence, not ranking, and may even hit its 0.25 lower bound) cannot recover, so log loss worsens by roughly 0.03-0.04.

Switching to 'char' adds cross-word-boundary n-grams (punctuation-to-next-word and function-word transitions) that are stylometrically informative for authorship and largely overlap the existing char_wb vocabulary, so with the same strongly-regularized LR (C=1.0) I expect a small gain; the 60k cap displaces some rare within-word 5-grams but those carry little weight at C=1, and the telemetry/holdout-removal changes don't affect the refit-on-all submission, so net a modest ~1% improvement.

NB log-count-ratio scaling amplifies class-exclusive/discriminative TF-IDF features and effectively loosens regularization on them, which should help since C=1 multinomial LR on L2-normalized TF-IDF is under-confident here; but switching to one-vs-rest liblinear with post-hoc normalization costs a little calibration versus true multinomial softmax, so net a modest improvement (~0.42) with real risk of being roughly neutral.

L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF rows make LR at C=1 clearly under-regularized-in-reverse (overly smooth, underconfident probabilities); on Spooky the log-loss-vs-C curve keeps improving until roughly C=10-20, so C=4 should sharpen calibration and cut ~0.03 log loss without overfitting, with no runtime risk.

L2-regularized LR at C=1 on l2-normalized TF-IDF is typically under-confident, so a holdout-fit temperature (likely T≈0.7-0.85) sharpens the softmax and recovers part of the gain that C-tuning would give; T=1 exactly reproduces the baseline, so downside is limited and a modest ~2-5% log-loss improvement is the most likely outcome.

RMSE on raw dollars is optimized by the conditional mean, but training on log1p and inverting with expm1 yields a geometric-mean (median-like) predictor that is biased low on right-skewed fares and down-weights the expensive rides that dominate squared error; the flexible GBDT gains little from the multiplicative structure, so expect a small regression (~2-3%), with the 2.8% corrupt-row floor unchanged.

4x more training rows (1M→4M) with the same LightGBM config reliably lowers RMSE on this dataset by a few percent on the predictable rows, but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows and unpredictable fare outliers dampens the total gain; the timestamp-format and n_jobs changes are result-neutral and the run should fit the budget.

Airport distances are a well-known strong feature here (JFK flat fare, EWR surcharge, LGA tolls) and let trees isolate airport trips in one split instead of several; raw coords already capture part of this and the ~2.1 RMSE corrupt-row floor dilutes any gain, so expect a modest but real drop of roughly 0.1 RMSE.

The metric is RMSE in dollars, so the optimal prediction is the conditional mean; fitting L2 on log1p and inverting with expm1 yields the conditional geometric mean, which systematically underpredicts wherever fare variance is large (long trips, mis-recorded fares, and especially the ~2.8% corrupt-coordinate test rows that already dominate the MSE), and with 1M rows and min_child_samples=100 the raw-scale model's outlier-chasing variance is too small for the log model's smoother fit to offset that bias, so I expect a modest regression (~+0.05-0.10 RMSE), consistent with the Kaggle consensus that log targets hurt on this RMSE-scored competition.

LightGBM's default 'basic' monotone method over-restricts leaf outputs (mid-point bounding), slightly slowing per-tree fit at a fixed 1000 rounds, and the data has genuine non-monotonicities in haversine distance (zero/near-zero-distance rows with high mean fares, corrupt long-distance rows with low fares) that the constraint forces the model to mispredict; with 4M rows regularization gains are negligible, so expect a small net regression, muted by the 2.8% corrupt-row floor.

The metric is RMSE in dollars, so the raw-target L2 fit already targets the conditional mean; log1p training yields expm1 predictions near the conditional geometric mean, which are biased low (most so on high-variance long/airport trips that dominate squared error) and under-weight expensive-trip errors during fitting, so the ~3.6 valid-row RMSE degrades by roughly 3-4% while the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor is unchanged, giving ~4.25 overall.
