In-sample TE with the count feature lets LightGBM invert the m=20 smoothing for singleton/rare route keys (enc=(y+20gm)/21 with log_count=log2 is an exact function of the row's own fare), so it learns 'enc≈gm & rare key → fare≈gm' from corrupt long-distance rows and over-trusts single-neighbor fares; at test time unseen keys get enc=gm exactly and rare keys get neighbor-driven predictions, inflating errors on the few percent of unusual, high-fare trips that dominate squared error, while early stopping on the clean holdout cannot undo the interleaved leak fitting.

Metric is raw-dollar RMSE, so the conditional mean is optimal; fitting log1p and back-transforming with expm1 yields median-like predictions biased low by roughly 3-6% on the high, noisy fares that dominate squared error, and it down-weights those high-fare rides during training, while the 2.8% corrupt rows (mean-fare floor) are unchanged — the outlier-robustness gain is minor at 1M rows with min_child_samples=100, so expect a small regression.

Airport-distance features are one of the most reliable gains in this competition: they let the trees isolate flat-rate JFK and surcharged Newark trips (high-fare tail that dominates RMSE) with one radial split instead of sparse coordinate splits, typically cutting valid-row RMSE by ~0.15-0.2; the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows is untouched, so the total should drop from ~4.14 to roughly 3.95-4.05.

The ~2.8% invalid test rows dominate the error (RMSE ~12.7 around the constant mean); letting LightGBM learn the missing-coordinate population's conditional mean from year/hour/passenger features, plus properly predicting passenger_count=0 rows that have perfectly valid coordinates (previously wasted on the mean fallback), should trim overall MSE by roughly 0.3-0.8 with negligible harm to valid-row predictions, giving a modest ~1-2% gain.

4x more training rows (3.6M clean) with identical features and a 1000-tree cap should trim the reducible error on clean test rows by ~3% (3.6 -> ~3.48), but the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows and fat-tailed fare noise dilute the overall gain; float32 coords, format-specified datetime parsing, and n_jobs=4 are neutral, and runtime (~5 min) stays within budget.

OOF-smoothed route/cell target encodings are implemented correctly (index-aligned, leak-free, seconds of overhead) and give LightGBM an explicit toll/flat-fare route signal, but with 1M rows the tree already learns most spatial structure from raw coordinates and ~2.1 RMSE of the score is an irreducible corrupt-row floor, so expect only a modest ~1% gain (4.138 -> ~4.09), within test-set noise.

Metric is dollar RMSE, so an L2 fit on the raw target already estimates the RMSE-optimal conditional mean; training on log1p and back-transforming with expm1 yields a geometric-mean-like predictor that systematically underpredicts (retransformation bias, ~3% of fare) and down-weights the high-fare errors that dominate RMSE, while the log-space fallback shifts the ~2.8% corrupt rows from ~$11.3 toward ~$9, adding bias there too; expect a modest regression of roughly 0.05-0.15 RMSE rather than an improvement.

Manhattan distance, axis-aligned deltas and bearing are well-known modest gains for tree models on this task (raw coords + haversine already capture most of the signal); expect ~3-4% lower RMSE on the valid test rows, but the unchanged fallback rows impose a ~2.1 RMSE floor, diluting the overall improvement to roughly 2%.

Airport/landmark distances are a well-known win on this competition (they let trees isolate JFK/EWR flat-fare and surcharge regimes far more sample-efficiently than raw lat/lon boxes), but with 4M rows the model already partly captures those regions and ~2.1 RMSE of the score is an unfixable floor from corrupt test rows, so the gain shows up as a modest ~0.05-0.1 drop rather than the 0.15-0.2 seen on Kaggle's cleaned test set; runtime rises but stays within budget.

The metric is RMSE, which is minimized by the conditional mean; an L1 objective fits the conditional median of a right-skewed fare distribution (systematic under-prediction, larger gaps on long/airport trips) and LightGBM's sign-based L1 gradients isolate high-magnitude tail rows less effectively, so the ~3.6 RMSE on valid test rows should degrade to roughly 3.8 while the fixed ~2.1 floor from corrupt rows stays, giving about 4.3 overall; runtime remains within budget.

The metric is raw-scale RMSE, whose optimal predictor is the conditional mean; training on log1p and inverting with expm1 yields a median-like, systematically low prediction (Jensen gap) that is worst exactly on the high-fare/airport/outlier rows that dominate squared error, and in this competition log-target models were repeatedly reported to score worse than raw-target ones, so valid-row RMSE likely drifts from ~3.6 to ~3.75 while the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor is unchanged, giving ~4.26 overall.

The metric is RMSE, whose optimal predictor is the conditional mean; an L1 objective targets the conditional median, and taxi fares are right-skewed conditional on features (traffic, tolls, long trips), so predictions will be systematically biased low by roughly $0.5-2 depending on trip length, adding ~1 to the valid-row MSE; the 2.8% corrupt rows (mean-fare fallback, unchanged) dilute the effect, giving roughly a 3% regression rather than an improvement.

With alpha=1.0 LightGBM's Huber uses gradients clipped to ±1 and unit hessians, so each tree can move a prediction by at most lr*alpha=$0.05; over 1000 rounds from the ~$11 mean the model cannot reach fares above ~$55-60 and effectively fits the conditional median (below the mean for right-skewed fares with tolls/surcharges), so the RMSE-dominating high-fare tail (JFK/EWR/long trips) is systematically under-predicted and overall RMSE worsens by several percent despite the modest robustness gain on the bulk.

Metric is raw-dollar RMSE, so the log target's back-transformed predictions approximate a geometric-mean (below the MSE-optimal conditional mean, especially given the heavy right tail of noisy fares) and de-emphasize the expensive rides that dominate squared error; with 1M rows LightGBM already fits the raw target well, so the retransformation bias and tail underweighting should slightly outweigh any outlier-robustness gain, diluted by the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows.

Airport distance/near flags are a well-known strong signal here (JFK flat fares, EWR surcharges) that trees on raw coordinates only partially capture; expect a modest real drop on the ~97% valid rows (~3.57 to ~3.45), diluted by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows (unchanged fallback), landing around 4.03-4.06.

4x more training rows gives LightGBM a steadily better fit on the ~97% valid test rows (roughly 3.57 -> ~3.40 on that portion), but the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows and the 1000-tree cap dilute the overall gain to a modest ~3% improvement; runtime (~3-6 min) stays within budget.

Averaging 5 fold-models trained on 80% subsets reduces GBM variance (MSE of the average <= mean MSE by Jensen), typically a 0.3-1% RMSE gain on the model-attributable error, but the ~2.8% corrupt test rows put a fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor that dilutes the relative gain, and 80% vs 90% per-model data slightly offsets it, so expect a small but consistent improvement to roughly 4.11-4.12.

The OOF smoothed pickup-cell mean fare is correctly implemented and leak-free, but LightGBM already has the raw pickup coordinates and the dropoff/distance that dominate fare, so the encoding adds only a modest, noisy fine-scale spatial prior (~100 samples per Manhattan cell); expect a small gain on the valid rows, damped further by the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows, for roughly a 0.5% improvement.

Snapping all four coordinates to a ~1 km (0.01°) grid before computing haversine distance injects ~0.4 km of random distance error (≈$1 of fare noise at ~$2.5/km) on trips whose median length is ~2 km, and coarsens coordinate resolution 10x below LightGBM's native histogram bins, while the route encoding (already at 0.01°) gains nothing; the added ~1.0 MSE on valid rows pushes overall RMSE from ~4.13 to ~4.24.

L1 objective targets the conditional median of a right-skewed, heavy-tailed fare distribution while the test set (same distribution, including noisy high fares and zero-distance rows) is scored by RMSE which rewards the conditional mean; sign-based gradients also make trees slower to isolate high-magnitude subgroups (airports, long trips), so valid-row RMSE should rise a few percent and the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row floor dilutes but does not offset that.

L1 fits conditional medians while the metric is RMSE on a right-skewed fare distribution whose test labels carry the same anomalies as training, so the L2 model's mean-tracking is already optimal; the median bias (largest on long/airport trips) adds roughly 0.4-0.8 to MSE, worsening RMSE by about 0.05-0.1 with no offsetting robustness gain.

Airport distances (esp. JFK flat-fare and EWR surcharge trips) are a well-known strong feature in this competition and make airport trips separable in one split instead of several axis-aligned coordinate splits, but raw coordinates already let the trees approximate this, airport trips are only ~4-5% of rides, and the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows compresses the gain, so expect a modest improvement of roughly 0.05-0.1 RMSE.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean; fares given distance are right-skewed (traffic, tolls, label noise), so an L1/median model systematically under-predicts and, with sign-based split gains, fits the high-fare tail less well; with 2M rows the L2 model's variance from outliers is small, so L1's robustness gain does not offset its bias, and only the 97% valid rows can change (the 2.8% invalid-row floor is untouched), giving a modest ~3-5% regression.

Rounding to 0.01° (~1 km cells) throws away within-neighborhood location detail that LightGBM's quantile bins (~40 m in Manhattan) already exploit on 2M rows with early stopping and min_child_samples=100, so the added 'regularization' is redundant while blurring river/Manhattan boundaries and fine location–distance interactions; distance stays unrounded and the 2.1 RMSE floor from invalid test rows dampens the effect, so expect a small regression roughly at the noise level.

L1 targets the conditional median while the metric is RMSE; taxi fares are right-skewed conditional on features (traffic/tolls/waiting, heavy-tailed errors), so median predictions are systematically low and RMSE gets a bit worse despite the robustness gain; the run itself is unaffected in cost.

A rotated Manhattan-grid distance is a genuinely new geometric signal that trees can't easily build from raw coordinates plus haversine, so it typically yields a small valid-row RMSE gain (~0.03-0.05) in this competition; diluted by the fixed ~2.1 RMSE corrupt-row floor, that translates to roughly a 0.02-0.04 improvement overall, with run-to-run noise from colsample/early-stopping making it a modest but likely positive change.

Out-of-fold smoothed route target encoding adds a precomputed pickup×dropoff interaction (tolls/airport flat fares/typical route fare) that trees on raw coords only approximate; leakage-safe and fast, so expect a small gain on valid rows, compressed by the ~2.1 RMSE corrupt-row floor to roughly 0.5-1% overall.

Grid-rotated Manhattan distance is a well-known compact routing proxy that trees can't easily synthesize from four raw coordinates, so expect a small but real gain on the learnable ~3.57 RMSE portion; the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor caps the visible improvement and the best-effort MLflow additions don't affect the model.

Doubling the LightGBM training sample from 1M to 2M rows with the same features typically trims valid-row RMSE by ~1-2% (3.6 -> ~3.54); the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes this, so the graded RMSE should drop modestly to ~4.09, with mlflow tracking being metric-neutral and runtime staying well under budget.

Airport-route categorical is a genuinely informative feature (JFK flat fare, Newark surcharge) that lets trees isolate airport trips in one split, but raw coordinates already capture most of it and ~2.8% corrupt test rows fix a ~2.1 RMSE floor, so expect a small, diluted gain of roughly 0.03-0.06 RMSE; the MLflow wrapper is inert without the env var and should not affect the run.

On this synthetic data the decisive signals are additive 'sum' interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) whose diagonal boundaries an MLP learns natively but axis-aligned trees only staircase-approximate; with the same 41 raw features (no unique-char count, no interaction features) LightGBM at 2000 rounds should land a few thousandths below the MLP, around 0.98, consistent with the hill having replaced the LightGBM baseline with this MLP; categorical f_27 handling and lambda_l2 are near-neutral and the run comfortably fits the 9-minute guard.

Decile one-hot binning throws away within-bin resolution on the ~15 Gaussian float columns whose sum-threshold interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) drive this dataset, so the diagonal boundaries become coarse 10x10 staircase averages; quantile edges on integer/binary columns also collapse tail values and likely drop f_29 entirely, and the 2-3x wider first layer may trip the 9-min guard before the cosine anneal finishes — net a clear regression versus standardized raw inputs.

The 41 standardized columns are nearly uncorrelated (synthetic, independently generated features), so the covariance spectrum is flat and full-rank PCA whitening amounts to an essentially arbitrary dense rotation; this destroys the axis-aligned, tree-friendly structure of the per-character f_27 codes, the integer count features and f_29/f_30, forcing staircases of oblique splits to recover simple per-feature effects (the classic GBDT-under-random-rotation degradation), while the oblique sum interactions it hoped to expose are not variance-dominant directions and so are not found by unsupervised PCA; linear leaves salvage the monotone/linear parts, limiting but not preventing a sizeable AUC drop.

f_27 is nearly unique per row (~740k distinct strings per 900k rows), so a smoothed whole-string target encoding collapses to the prior for most train/val/test rows and carries almost no signal; dropping the ten per-character ordinals (which encode the strongly informative letter effects and let trees partially recover the unique-character count) effectively reduces the model to numeric-only features, which on this dataset lands in the low 0.9s rather than 0.98.

In this dataset ~80% of f_27 strings are unique (and the rest appear 2-3 times), so with m=20 the whole-string target encoding collapses to the prior (or prior ±0.02 noise) for nearly every row, while the ten per-position ordinal characters it replaces are among the strongest signals in the data (letter order is genuinely ordinal here, and per-position letters were key to the 0.99+ scores); keeping f_27_nunique retains part of the f_27 information, but dropping the per-char columns should cost several AUC points, landing around 0.94-0.95.

These are the well-known AmbrosM interaction features for TPS May 2022; giving the trees the raw sums f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26 (plus ternary thresholds) lets LightGBM split directly on diagonal decision boundaries it could only staircase-approximate before, which historically lifted GBDT from ~0.991 to ~0.994-0.996 AUC, so I expect a clear gain of roughly +0.0035.

Plain logistic regression on ordinal chars + raw numerics (no unique-count, ramps instead of the ±5 step interactions) should land around 0.90-0.95 AUC; its signal is essentially a subset of what the 0.984 LightGBM already captures, so a fixed 50/50 rank average mostly re-weights redundant linear components and injects the weaker model's ordering errors, giving a modest drop rather than a gain.

This dataset's target is a smooth function of feature sums that trees approximate poorly; the AmbrosM-style 64-64-64-16 SiLU MLP with the f_27 ordinals and interaction sums is known to reach ~0.997-0.998 here, so even without the unique-character count, with only 80 epochs, and a single model, a standardized MLP should land around 0.996, a clear jump from LightGBM's 0.984; CPU training of this tiny net is ~1-2 s/epoch so the 8-minute guard is unlikely to bite.

This is essentially AmbrosM's TPS-May22 Keras-quickstart MLP (64-64-64-16 swish, L2 3e-5, cosine LR) which natively learns the additive f_02+f_21 / f_05+f_22 / f_00+f_01+f_26 interactions that trees struggle with, so it should clearly beat the 0.977 LightGBM; but it lacks the unique-character-count feature (hard for a small MLP to synthesize from ordinals), uses only 60 epochs and a single split, so it lands well short of the ~0.997-0.998 that full-feature NNs reached.

Linear leaves can represent the oblique sum-threshold interactions (f_02+f_21 etc.) better than axis-aligned staircases and converge faster than the still-improving 3000-tree baseline, but those tail regions are a small share of rows, the dominant residual error (f_27 unique-count structure) is untouched, and linear terms on ordinal/integer columns add noise plus earlier logloss-driven early stopping, so expect only a marginal gain (with some risk of the 2-3x slower run hitting the time limit).

Unique-character count of f_27 was a well-known strong, non-redundant feature in TPS May 2022 (trees cannot reconstruct cross-column equality/collision counts from per-position ordinals), so a strong LGBM should gain a solid ~0.5-0.8 AUC points, short of the ~0.99 that additionally needs the ternary sum-interaction features.

These three sums are the known generative interactions in TPS May-22 (diagonal step boundaries that axis-aligned trees can only staircase); giving LightGBM the raw sums removes that burden, so the still-underfit 3000-tree model should jump roughly +0.01 AUC, though it stays below the ~0.995 level because the unique-character count of f_27 is still missing.

f_27 is almost unique per row (~1.2 rows per string), so LightGBM's native categorical binning (min_data_in_bin/cat_smooth filters on a 200k sample) collapses nearly all strings into the 'other' bin and the column carries almost no signal; meanwhile the dropped per-position ordinals are genuinely informative (letters are binned counts with position-specific target effects), and the retained 26 letter-count + nunique columns only recover the position-agnostic part, so AUC should fall noticeably rather than improve.

Adjacent-char bigram categoricals are largely redundant with the per-position ordinals that 127-leaf trees can already combine; LightGBM's native categorical splits on 676-level codes may give a marginal gain (faster convergence within the 3000-tree budget) but no known strong adjacent-position interaction exists in this DGP, so expect a near-neutral, slightly positive change.

f_00..f_15 are mutually uncorrelated synthetic features, so PCA on the standardized block is near-degenerate and yields 8 essentially random oblique projections that trees gain little from, while dropping the 25 target-screened products (which included partial proxies like f_00*f_01 for the true sum interactions) removes a small but real signal; expect a small regression of roughly 0.0005-0.001 AUC.

f_27 is nearly unique per row (~740k distinct values in 900k), so hashing the whole string into 64 buckets yields pure noise columns and effectively deletes the per-character signal that is one of the strongest predictors in this dataset (per-position letters and unique-char count); the model regresses to numerics + products only, which historically scored around 0.88-0.92 AUC, with the 64 noise binaries hurting slightly further.

ExtraTrees with random thresholds and sqrt feature sampling is much less sample-efficient than 3000-round LightGBM at carving the sum-threshold interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) and per-position f_27 effects that drive this synthetic target, so expect a clear regression to roughly the RF/ET tier (~0.94-0.96); additionally, running 5-fold CV of 300 fully-grown trees on 800k rows before the submission is written makes the run borderline for the 15-minute kill, which is a real failure risk on top of the metric drop.

TPS May 2022 is the canonical case where standardized MLPs beat GBDTs: the signal is diagonal/sum thresholds (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22) plus per-position f_27 effects that a relu net learns directly, so even an undertrained sklearn MLP (40 epochs, constant lr, no unique-char feature, ordinal chars) should land around 0.99, above the 0.978 LightGBM staircase approximation but short of the ~0.998 achieved by tuned Keras nets with unique_characters and LR schedules.

The f_27 distinct-character count is the well-known key feature in TPS May 2022 (strongly predictive, not derivable from per-position categoricals with few splits), and the 26 order-invariant letter counts help trees express 'letter present anywhere'; GBDTs with these features typically reach ~0.985-0.99 AUC versus ~0.977 without, so expect a solid gain with negligible runtime cost.

The per-character f_27 codes are the strongest signal in this dataset (splitting f_27 is what lifts GBDTs from ~0.9 to ~0.98); ~82% of full strings are unique so a train+test count is mostly 1s/2s and carries only a weak proxy for letter typicality, leaving essentially a numeric-only LightGBM around 0.90-0.92 AUC.

In TPS May 2022 the f_27 unique-character count is a well-known strongly predictive feature that axis-aligned trees cannot reconstruct from per-position ordinals, and the 26 letter counts add cross-position information; with 720k rows and min_child_samples=100 the extra low-cardinality columns pose little overfitting risk, so expect a solid gain (roughly +0.008-0.010 AUC), while the remaining gap to ~0.996 stays due to the missing f_02+f_21 style diagonal interactions.

The dataset's true numeric interactions are additive sums (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22), not products, and the screening scope f_00..f_15 excludes f_21/f_22/f_26 and mixes in 9 integer columns; the 25 gain-selected products (likely including f_00_x_f_01) give trees a marginally useful extra split direction but mostly add near-redundant columns, so expect a near-flat, slightly positive change within run-to-run noise, with runtime still comfortably under budget.

Refitting on all 800k rows with ~3333 trees (holdout AUC was still rising at 3000, so more trees/data cannot overfit here) should give a small but real gain of roughly +0.001 AUC; main risk is wall-clock (~2.2x baseline training) but it should finish under the 15-minute kill.

The f_27 letters are essentially ordinal bins of latent variables and the model's bottleneck is approximating continuous-feature interactions (still improving at 3000 trees), so declaring the ten low/moderate-cardinality char columns categorical lets LightGBM carve letter groups slightly more efficiently without meaningful overfitting risk on 720k rows; expect a near-neutral, marginally positive change.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is a known strong signal in this dataset that axis-aligned trees on per-position ordinals cannot easily reconstruct (it needs cross-position equality comparisons), so adding it directly should give LightGBM a solid boost, likely on the order of +0.004-0.006 AUC.

Capping trees at depth 2 (4 leaves) turns the ensemble into a main-effect + pairwise model; it can staircase the sum-threshold interactions but can no longer approximate the high-order f_27 structure (unique-character count, multi-position char interactions) that the 127-leaf trees were partially learning, and 3000 tiny trees at lr 0.05 will also underfit somewhat, so AUC drops a couple of points from 0.9818.

This dataset's signal is dominated by additive sum-threshold interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) that an MLP learns directly but axis-aligned trees only approximate with staircases; a small LightGBM (600 trees, 31 leaves, max_bin=63, no unique-char or interaction features) is also undertrained relative to the README's 3000x127 config that was still improving, so expect a clear regression from the MLP's 0.982 to roughly 0.955-0.972.

Swapping the MLP for a low-capacity LightGBM (600 trees x 31 leaves, lr 0.05, max_bin 63) on raw features drops the model's ability to capture the additive f_02+f_21 / f_05+f_22 / f_00+f_01+f_26 interactions that the MLP learns natively; the README notes even 3000x127 trees were still improving, so this underfit GBDT (logloss early stopping won't fire, all 600 trees used, runs in ~1-2 min) should land around 0.96-0.975, below the 0.9822 MLP.

Collapsing all 16 continuous columns (f_00–f_06, f_19–f_26, f_28) to 4 quartile codes discards most of the fine-grained signal the trees use, especially the known diagonal sum interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) whose thresholds lie in the tails far beyond the 75th percentile; integers and f_27 chars keep a strong backbone so it is not catastrophic, but a clear regression of roughly 0.015–0.025 AUC is expected.

This dataset's signal is dominated by feature interactions (diagonal sum boundaries across float pairs/triples, joint f_27 character structure) that 127-leaf trees were still learning at 3000 rounds; 7-leaf trees at the same lr/rounds are ~18x lower capacity and will badly underfit those interactions, so holdout/test AUC should drop by roughly 1-2 points to ~0.96.

num_leaves=4 (3 splits/tree) at lr=0.05 for 3000 rounds severely underfits this dataset, whose signal depends heavily on diagonal 2-way/3-way sum interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) and f_27 character interactions that deep trees carve efficiently; the model will still be improving at 3000 rounds and land well below the 127-leaf baseline, roughly 0.975-0.985.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known planted sum-interactions in this synthetic dataset (thresholds near ±5); a 3-way planar boundary is the hardest for axis-aligned trees to staircase, so exposing the sum directly should recover a sizable chunk (~0.002-0.003) of the ~0.005 gap to a fully feature-engineered LightGBM, while the other two pairwise interactions remain unaddressed.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the known linear interactions in this synthetic dataset (target saturates beyond |sum|~5); axis-aligned trees approximate a 3-way diagonal boundary poorly, so exposing the raw sum should yield a solid gain (~+0.005-0.007 AUC), though still well short of the ~0.99 reachable with the full interaction/unique-char feature set.

On TPS May 2022 the target hinges on additive threshold interactions (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22) that an MLP on standardized inputs learns natively but trees approximate poorly, so a plain 256-128-64 SiLU MLP should clearly beat the 0.977 LightGBM; without the unique-character count or explicit interaction features and with only ~50 epochs at lr 1e-3 (~8.8k steps) it will land around 0.99 rather than the 0.998 of fully feature-engineered, long-trained NNs, and the 420 s budget comfortably fits the run.

Native categorical splits on 10 low-cardinality (≤26 letters, mostly A–D) char columns with 720K rows are well-regularized (cat_smooth/min_data_per_group) and slightly more expressive than contiguous ordinal thresholds, but the letters are count-like/near-ordinal and the model's remaining error is in unmodeled interactions (unique-char count, numeric sums), so expect a tiny gain within noise, roughly +0.0003 AUC.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is a known strong signal in this dataset that trees cannot reconstruct from the per-position ordinals (it needs cross-position equality logic), so giving it explicitly should lift LightGBM from ~0.977 toward the ~0.99 range typically seen for char-split + unique-count GBDTs, with the remaining gap to ~0.996 belonging to the sum-interaction features that are still absent.

The graded metric is unweighted RMSE, for which plain MSE is the exactly aligned objective; target-darkness weighting shifts the optimal prediction below the conditional mean (bias ≈ -4·Var[y|x]/(5-4E[y|x])) precisely at the uncertain edge/faint-stroke/stain pixels where the error lives, so predictions get systematically darker there and unweighted RMSE should worsen slightly, with no capacity or optimization bottleneck for the reweighting to relieve in this already-easy 2-channel setup.

Training ~8-10x more steps (≈15-25k vs 2000) with a proper cosine anneal lets the small U-Net converge much further on this low-noise synthetic task; gains are real but diminishing since 2000 steps already covers the ~21M training pixels dozens of times, so expect roughly 0.016 → 0.013 rather than a halving, assuming the run finishes under the 15-min kill.

L1 through the sigmoid head keeps pushing the dominant near-white paper/stain pixels and text interiors to their targets where MSE's residual-scaled gradient vanishes, which typically yields a small PSNR/RMSE gain (as in Zhao et al./EDSR), but the metric is RMSE and L1 targets the conditional median, so confident snapping on genuinely ambiguous stroke/stain pixels claws back most of that gain, leaving a modest, noise-level improvement.

Train and test share the same synthetic noise backgrounds and exposure statistics, so there is no photometric shift to be robust to; input-only brightness/contrast jitter (±0.1 shift, 0.8-1.2 contrast with clipping) breaks the precise intensity correspondence at anti-aliased stroke edges and stain/text overlaps, adding target ambiguity that an already well-fit U-Net (0.0166 RMSE) cannot fully resolve from context, so I expect a small regression rather than a regularization gain.

Multi-scale TTA is a segmentation trick that does not transfer to pixel-exact regression: the 0.75x pass (and to a lesser extent 1.25x) pushes a scale-non-invariant U-Net out of distribution and the resize-in/resize-out round trip adds ~0.5-0.7 px of systematic blur on text edges, where almost all of the residual 0.0154 RMSE already lives; with equal 1/3 weights this correlated edge blur (plus thinner, fainter strokes at 0.75x) outweighs the small decorrelation gain over the already-strong flip ensemble, so RMSE rises by roughly 15-30%.

Dropout2d inside a BN-heavy encoder of a pixel-regression denoiser injects feature noise and a train/test BN variance shift (dropout before the next Conv-BN), which low-level vision work consistently finds hurts PSNR, and with only 2000 training steps the model is under-trained rather than overfit, so the regularization gain on unseen stains is unlikely to offset the slower, noisier fit; expect a modest regression.

A small-receptive-field fully-convolutional U-Net on same-distribution crops barely overfits, so Dropout2d in every block (including skips, bottleneck and the pre-output features) mostly costs capacity, slows convergence within the fixed 180s budget, and introduces BN variance-shift at eval; dense regression nets at ~41 dB PSNR typically lose ~1 dB from such regularization, i.e. RMSE rises from 0.0085 to roughly 0.0095-0.0100.

A 4th U-Net level roughly quadruples parameters and doubles the receptive field, which helps with large-scale stains and faded text; with ~20k+ steps already available in 180s the ~25% step reduction is in diminishing-returns territory, so I expect a small net RMSE improvement rather than a regression, though gains are limited because the 3-level model is already near the task's floor on this in-distribution split.

The 23x23 median background channel gives the small, briefly-trained U-Net an explicit local-contrast reference (x - bg) that disambiguates dark stains from text; this classic trick for this competition should modestly reduce errors around stained regions, with median blur cost negligible and no training-budget impact, though seed noise could mask part of the gain.

A 5-level U-Net raises the receptive field from ~45 px to ~190 px, which is what this task's large-scale stains and wrinkle shading need, and the 16x larger model still trains comfortably in 2000 steps at equal pixels/step (~2x compute, well within budget); batch 8 adds some gradient noise and a single seed adds variance, but a moderate RMSE gain (roughly 0.016 to 0.014) is the most likely outcome.
Flip TTA on a flip-augmented U-Net denoiser averages out residual prediction noise; typical gain is ~0.1-0.2 dB PSNR, i.e. a 1-3% RMSE reduction, with run-to-run training noise of similar magnitude.

A 360s budget on a GPU yields roughly 5-15x more optimizer steps than the current 2000 with a properly annealed cosine LR, and this small U-Net is far from converged at 2000 steps; pixel-dense supervision on 105 images limits overfitting, so val/test RMSE should drop meaningfully though not to top-leaderboard levels.

The metric is RMSE and targets are bimodal (white background/black text), so Charbonnier/L1 pushes the net toward conditional-median outputs that commit on ambiguous pixels (text under stains, creases, faint strokes) which dominate the squared error; its literature advantage comes from unimodal natural-image noise and mostly perceptual sharpness, so with the same 2000 Adam steps I expect a small regression within noise rather than a gain, with cleaner background partially offsetting.

Baseline training noise already matches the test corruption exactly, so injecting sigma=0.05 Gaussian noise creates a train/test mismatch that biases the U-Net toward over-smoothing anti-aliased text edges and snapping faint gray pixels to white; with ~64k random crops from 105 large images overfitting is mild, so the regularization gain is small and the net effect is a modest RMSE regression.

BN here is in a healthy regime (batch 32 x 128^2 pixels gives stable running stats, eval mode is a fixed affine so crop-vs-page mismatch is negligible), while GroupNorm introduces instance-dependent statistics whose spatial extent changes from 128x128 crops at training to whole pages at inference and typically converges slightly slower under the same 2000-step budget, so I expect a small regression within or just beyond seed noise rather than the hypothesized gain.

The metric is RMSE, which MSE optimizes directly; SSIM+L1 pushes ambiguous stroke-edge/faint-text pixels toward committed rather than hedged values and SSIM's luminance term is nearly blind to background offsets, so expect a small regression (SSIM-based losses typically cost ~0.1-0.3 dB PSNR vs L2/L1), though training will remain stable and the change stays within seed-noise range.

Flip-TTA members match the training augmentation and should give a modest variance-reduction gain (~2-4%), but the four rot90/rot270 members feed the net vertical text it never trained on, so those predictions are individually worse and partially cancel the gain; net effect is a small improvement with real downside risk.

The metric is RMSE, which MSE optimizes directly; pure SSIM tolerates small luminance offsets in the dominant flat-white regions and favors sharper-than-conditional-mean edges, and computing blur(x^2)-mu^2 under bf16 autocast suffers heavy cancellation noise (even NaN risk), so expect a clear regression rather than a gain.

Pure output-reparameterization with identical capacity, data, and schedule: unbounded residual output plus zero-init removes bf16 sigmoid saturation (where σ rounds to exactly 1.0 and gradients vanish) and lets inference clamping absorb overshoot, but the U-Net skip already provides a near-identity path and the quasi-binary clean target suits a sigmoid, so the net effect is small and near seed noise, with a slight lean toward improvement.

sqrt(MSE) is gradient-direction-equivalent to MSE under Adam, and a 0.1-weight SSIM term mostly adds background-smoothing pressure that is roughly RMSE-neutral; but the SSIM convs run under bf16 autocast (the .float() casts don't prevent conv2d downcasting), making local-variance terms near the C2 scale numerically noisy, so expect a small regression within run-to-run noise rather than a gain.

Residual learning with identity init trains stably and preserves text strokes, but this task's target is nearly binary (mostly exact-white background), where the sigmoid saturation is a strong prior; a linear residual output must precisely cancel background texture (1 - x) and tends to leave faint haze, so I expect a small net regression within seed noise rather than the DnCNN-style gain seen on Gaussian denoising.

Synthetic noise (whole-image Gaussian blur sigma 1-4 also blurs the text into a deblurring task absent from test, smooth ellipse stains and speckle don't match the textured crumpled-paper/stain noise shared by train and test) makes up ~86% of samples under a fixed 2000-step budget, so real-distribution exposure drops ~7x and capacity is spent on off-distribution artifacts; expect a mild regression rather than a gain.

2,000 steps leaves this small U-Net clearly under-trained; stretching the cosine schedule to ~9,000 steps (or 6,750 if time-capped) on a pixel-dense denoising task with crop/flip augmentation typically keeps lowering val RMSE with little overfitting, giving a moderate ~10-15% gain rather than a dramatic one since the baseline already learns most of the local mapping quickly.

8x dihedral TTA is a variance-reducing ensemble of the same model: the 4 flip variants match training augmentation and should give a reliable ~2-4% gain, while the 4 transposed variants are out-of-distribution for horizontal text but the denoising task is mostly local and the noise is roughly isotropic, so they likely dilute rather than cancel the gain; net small improvement, not a large one, since the dominant error is systematic (residual stains, soft edges) which averaging does not fix.

L1 removes the residual-proportional weighting that makes MSE match the RMSE metric: with near-binary targets and a sigmoid head, L1 shifts gradient mass toward already-white background pixels and pushes genuinely ambiguous stain/text pixels toward the median instead of the RMSE-optimal mean, so I expect roughly neutral-to-slightly-worse RMSE (sharper text edges may partly offset, but the hard pixels that dominate RMSE get less attention).

Target-dependent weights (3x on dark pixels) bias predictions darker at ambiguous boundary/stain pixels where the unweighted-MSE optimum is the plain conditional mean, and they de-emphasize background stain removal, so the train objective drifts from the graded unweighted RMSE; expect a small regression within noise rather than a gain.

Weighting dark targets 10x mismatches the unweighted RMSE metric: the weighted-MSE minimizer is a darkness-biased conditional mean, so anti-aliased stroke edges and ambiguous stained background get predicted too dark (over-inking), and the slight extra focus on ink pixels is unlikely to offset that bias plus the deprioritized stain-removal on background, giving a small regression.

Global residual with zero-init output starts at identity (initial RMSE ~0.1 instead of ~0.5), gives better-conditioned gradients than MSE-through-sigmoid (no saturation on the many exactly-white targets), and inference clamping turns overshoots into free perfect predictions; the U-Net already has skip paths so the gain is modest and within ~1 seed-noise of the current 0.0160, most likely a small improvement to ~0.0155.

L1 optimizes the per-pixel median, so on the near-binary targets the sigmoid outputs become crisper and the white background gets cleaner, but the metric is RMSE where hedged (mean) predictions on ambiguous text-under-stain pixels are optimal; L1's overconfident 0/1 commitments on those hard pixels plus its relative down-weighting of large residuals should slightly outweigh the background gains, giving a small regression within a few percent, partly softened by the 4-flip TTA averaging.

Identity-initialized residual output removes the vanishing-gradient problem of sigmoid+MSE on saturated pixels (e.g. faint text under stains) and gives a better starting point for the short 2000-step budget, so modest gains are likely, though the near-binary targets suited the sigmoid well, so the effect should be small and within a few percent.

Halving width quarters the parameter count (~620k to ~155k) in a regime where random crops from 105 images give effectively unlimited patches, so overfitting is not the bottleneck; the narrower 8-channel full-resolution stages lose fine stroke/edge detail, and width reductions in restoration nets typically cost ~0.3-0.5 dB, i.e. a small RMSE regression rather than a regularization gain.

The metric is plain RMSE, so target-dependent weighting shifts the optimum toward a dark-biased weighted conditional mean at ambiguous edge/faint-text pixels and de-emphasizes stain removal on the dominant background; with an already well-converged NAFNet there is little optimization upside to offset this, so I expect a small regression on the order of run-to-run noise.

The closing-based background-divided channel hands the under-trained (2k-step) U-Net a near-flat background and makes text-in-stain regions trivially separable, which should modestly speed convergence and cut errors in dark-stain areas; it does nothing for the dominant text-edge error and the net's 41px receptive field already infers local background, so expect a small gain (~3-6%) with a few-percent chance of a wash from init/seed noise.

Only the final 1x1 conv and sigmoid move to fp32; this removes bf16 output quantization (~1/256 ULP near white, which already nearly aligns with the 8-bit gray grid) while the whole encoder/decoder and its gradients stay bf16, so the effect is at most a few tenths of a percent and is swamped by run-to-run training noise.

Flip TTA averages four predictions from a model already trained with flip augmentation, so it is near-equivariant and the ensemble mainly reduces prediction variance; for a small briefly trained U-Net this typically yields a modest 2-4% RMSE reduction with no risk to training or budget.

A width-16 NAFNet with zero-init residual branches, linear (non-sigmoid) output and global-pool attention trained on 128px patches but applied to full images learns more slowly than the BN+ReLU U-Net in a 2000-step budget and has a train/test statistics mismatch, so it most likely lands slightly worse than the baseline rather than better.

Stanford Dogs images are ImageNet train images, so the in22k_ft_in1k head (trained on ~1300 imgs/class including the test images) restricted to the 120 dog classes is a strong, complementary classifier; holdout-tuned temperature and mixing weight (w=0 falls back to current) make a regression very unlikely, and blending should cut log loss roughly 15-25%.

L2-regularized LR is rotation-invariant, so PCA's only effect is hard-truncating 768 low-variance directions; L2 already shrinks those softly while keeping any fine-grained discriminative signal (e.g. Norfolk vs Norwich) that lives in low-total-variance directions, so unsupervised truncation to 256-d with the C grid capped at 1.0 should lose a little information and nudge log loss up modestly rather than help.

Full-probability Mixup/CutMix is a long-schedule regularizer; with only 6 epochs (~780 steps) of fine-tuning on a pretrained in22k ConvNeXt that already knows these breeds it mainly slows convergence and creates a train/eval distribution mismatch (ConvNeXt's own 22k->1k fine-tune recipe disables mixup/cutmix), and the calibration benefit is already captured by the existing temperature scaling, so I expect a mild regression rather than a gain.

With only ~770 optimizer steps (6 epochs) the run is schedule-limited rather than overfitting-limited; replacing ~29% of views with tiny 8-35% area crops (often fur/background with blurry upsampling) slows convergence and widens the train/eval apparent-object-size mismatch (FixRes effect) relative to the Resize256/CenterCrop224 eval, so I expect a small regression of ~0.01-0.02 log loss, within noise of a wash but more likely worse than better.

ConvNeXt-V2-L in22k->1k (87.3% top-1, trained on the very ImageNet dog images this dataset is drawn from) gives far more separable frozen features and sharper dog-class log-probs than ResNet-50 V1 (76%), so a C-tuned linear probe should drop from ~87% to ~96-97% accuracy, cutting log loss roughly 3x; small 1k-image test and confusable breed pairs keep it above ~0.1.

The 1000-d log-softmax block is not noise here: ImageNet's fc already contains a 120-way dog-breed classifier trained on ~1300 images/class (including many of these very Stanford Dogs images), so it injects strong supervised prior directions that a 9k-sample L2 linear probe cannot fully recover on its own; dropping it removes that implicit ensemble and should cost roughly 0.03-0.06 log loss, with holdout-tuned C having already protected against the extra columns overfitting.

Ridge decision boundaries plus a single global temperature usually trail a tuned multinomial LR on log loss by a few percent (squared loss is a weaker proxy and per-example calibration is cruder), but the current LR is likely mildly over-regularized on L2-normalised features with C capped at 30, so the free T largely offsets that; net expectation is a small regression, roughly a wash.

L2-tuned LR already shrinks low-variance directions softly, so a hard PCA cut to 128/block mostly discards some fine-grained breed-discriminative variance in the CLIP and DINOv2 blocks (ConvNeXt's ImageNet-supervised block survives better); the centering+renormalisation and faster convergence roughly offset only a little, so expect a small regression.

ConvNeXt-Base with ImageNet-22k pretraining (85.8% top-1 vs ResNet-50's 76%) has a far more discriminative, linearly separable pre-logit space for the 120 ImageNet dog classes (which it has effectively seen), and holdout-tuned C keeps LR calibrated, so frozen features + LR should drop log loss from ~0.45 to roughly 0.15-0.2 as seen with strong backbones on this competition.

Full fine-tuning of an in22k-pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny with augmentation, flip TTA and validation temperature scaling should reach ~93-95% accuracy on these ImageNet-derived dog images (the backbone has effectively seen them), cutting log loss from 0.45 to roughly 0.13-0.20; the recipe is standard, fits comfortably in the time budget, and temperature scaling (T in [0.5,2]) undoes the label-smoothing underconfidence, with residual risk only from weight download/time-guard truncation.

The ImageNet fc rows are well-estimated linear directions for the same 120 breeds (trained on ~1300 images/class, with partial memorization of these very images), so exposing them as log-softmax features gives the L2-regularized LR a cheap strong prior and reduces estimation variance; standardization and the 880 non-dog noise dims roughly wash out with C re-tuning, so expect a moderate log-loss gain rather than a dramatic one.

Swapping ResNet-50 for L2-normalised ConvNeXt-B(in22k), CLIP-B/16 and DINOv2-B features is a large backbone upgrade on a dataset that is literally ImageNet training images (strong leak benefit for the in22k/in1k model), so accuracy should climb from ~86% to ~95%; concatenation plus holdout-tuned C should land around 0.15-0.22 log loss, with some risk the C grid tops out too low or lbfgs underconverges.

Focal loss (gamma=2) sharply down-weights the already-correct majority after the first epoch or two, so the short 10-epoch fine-tune adapts the backbone less and ends under-confident on correct test predictions (mean true-class prob ~0.75 vs ~0.85 with LS=0.1); for log loss that under-confidence costs more than the modest gain from spreading mass on wrong predictions, and focal does not improve balanced fine-grained accuracy (it also chases noisy/ambiguous labels), so expect a small regression rather than the hoped-for sharper discrimination.

Stanford Dogs images are literally ImageNet-1k training images, so the pretrained low/mid-level features are near-optimal; full fine-tuning at a fairly aggressive lr=0.01 (batch 64) on 9k images likely drifted/overfit them, and freezing conv1-layer3 while still training the 15M-param layer4+fc preserves those features and regularizes, so I expect a moderate log-loss improvement (~0.60) rather than a large one, with residual risk of no change.

Flip TTA on a frozen ViT-B/16 gives two correlated but non-identical feature views; averaging probabilities slightly reduces overconfident errors from the C=0.3 logreg, which typically yields a small but reliable 2-4% log-loss gain with no risk of regression beyond noise.

CLIP ViT-B/32 is a much weaker frozen encoder for 120 ImageNet-class dog breeds than an IN21k->IN1k fine-tuned ViT-B/16 (coarser 32px patches, no label supervision on these exact classes, no IN1k train-image overlap, plus timm's non-quickgelu variant mismatches OpenAI's QuickGELU weights), so linear-probe accuracy likely drops from ~92% to ~80%; the smaller ln_post feature scale makes C=0.3 effectively stronger and partly offsets the overconfidence, but log loss still roughly climbs to ~0.8.

L2-regularized LR with a tuned C already shrinks noisy directions softly; hard-truncating 2048-d ResNet-50 features to 256 PCs discards low-variance but still breed-discriminative directions (fine-grained pairs like Norfolk/Norwich), so expect a mild regression of roughly 0.02-0.05 log loss rather than a gain.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 CLS embeddings are far more discriminative for fine-grained breeds than supervised ResNet-50 pooled features (e.g. Pets ~96% vs ~92%, CUB ~90% vs ~70% linear probe), so with a re-tuned C and the same 10-view TTA the linear probe should move from ~87% to ~91-92% accuracy and cut log loss by roughly a third, assuming the engineer handles timm's 518-vs-224 img_size assertion (img_size=224 or dynamic_img_size) so the run completes.

C=1.0 on L2-normalised (norm ~1.4) features is heavily over-regularised, so the whitened 256-d space (norm ~16) effectively loosens regularisation and sharpens the many easy, correct predictions; but whitening amplifies low-variance PCs and lets the head overfit confusable-breed pairs with 77 samples/class, producing overconfident errors that log loss punishes, so the net is only a small gain with substantial risk of a regression.

kNN top-1 on these in-domain ImageNet features will be close to the linear probe (~82-85%), but vote-count probabilities with only 1e-3 smoothing are badly calibrated: every test image whose true breed gets zero of the 10 neighbor votes (likely 5-8% of cases) costs ~7.0 nats, plus overconfident partial votes, so log loss regresses sharply to roughly 0.8-1.0 despite similar accuracy.

End-to-end fine-tuning of ResNet-50 on in-distribution ImageNet dog images should lift accuracy a couple of points over the frozen-feature LR (~86%→~88-89%), and label smoothing 0.1 keeps the 10-epoch model from becoming overconfident on its errors, but LS also caps correct-prediction confidence near 0.9 (~0.1 nat floor per correct image), so the log-loss gain is modest, roughly 0.45→0.41, with real risk the short lr=0.01 uniform-LR recipe only matches the baseline.

ViT-B/16 augreg in21k->in1k (84.5% top-1 vs ResNet-50's 76.1%, with in21k pretraining that is especially strong for fine-grained dogs and in1k fine-tuning that saw these very Stanford Dogs images) yields far more linearly separable 768-d features; by the Kaggle feature+LogReg scaling (IRv2 ~0.3, NASNet-L ~0.2) expect ~0.15-0.22, with a small penalty since C=0.3 was tuned for ResNet feature scale and stronger features may be slightly over-confident.

10-view probability averaging (5 crops x hflip) on frozen ResNet-50 features acts as a cheap ensemble; Jensen's inequality guarantees the mixture beats the average single-view loss, and flips/corner crops of a 256->224 resize are mild enough that the center-crop-trained LR stays well calibrated, so expect a modest ~4-7% log-loss reduction rather than a large jump.

ConvNeXt-T in22k features are far more discriminative for these ImageNet-derived dog breeds (well-tuned LR would reach ~0.2-0.25), but L2-normalizing to unit norm with C=1.0 is ~100-300x more regularization than the holdout-optimal raw-feature setting, which shrinks logit margins ~2-3x and leaves the model underconfident; net effect is a moderate improvement rather than the full gain, with real risk of landing near the current score.

Stanford Dogs images are ImageNet-1k train images, so the restricted pretrained fc head is a strong (memorization-boosted) 120-way classifier on the same features; a validation-tuned temperature/alpha mixture with the data-limited LR should fix many LR-specific errors and soften confident mistakes, giving a solid log-loss drop with little regression risk since alpha=0 recovers the baseline.

Unwhitened PCA to 256 dims is equivalent to restricting the already C-tuned L2 logistic regression to the top-variance subspace; it drops low-variance but class-specific ReLU directions that fine-grained breed discrimination relies on, so expect a mild-to-moderate log-loss regression (~+0.03) rather than a gain.

ResNet-50's final features were trained to be read through average pooling; max-pooled descriptors are noisier, less linearly separable, and ~4x larger in scale, which makes the hardcoded C=0.3 badly under-regularized (temperature scaling only partly repairs the resulting overconfidence), so log loss should worsen noticeably rather than improve.

Dog breeds are literally ImageNet classes, so the V2 checkpoint's much higher ImageNet accuracy (80.9 vs 76.1 top-1) should yield more linearly separable breed features and lower log loss; the gain is tempered because heavily regularized recipes (label smoothing/mixup/cutmix) shift feature scale and partly collapse within-class information, and C=0.3 was tuned for V1 features, so the improvement is likely meaningful but short of what an architecture upgrade would give.

C=0.3 was already chosen on a holdout over a grid that included 0.03, so the 10x more regularized head starts underconfident and underfit; the brief 2-epoch SGD fine-tune (head lr 1e-3 with momentum, negligible weight decay) will re-sharpen the dominant feature directions and recover part of the gap, but the low-variance discriminative directions stay over-shrunk, so a modest net regression (roughly 0.49-0.53) is the most likely outcome.

Running the 224-pretrained ResNet50 at 192 crop loses fine detail that fine-grained breed discrimination relies on (ImageNet top-1 drops ~1-1.5 pts at this test resolution), and the frozen-feature LR plus light bottleneck tuning cannot recover it, so log loss should degrade modestly while runtime shrinks.

Unwhitened PCA-256 followed by L2 LR is equivalent to the same ridge-penalised LR restricted to the top-256 principal subspace; the tuned C=0.3 already barely shrinks mid/low-variance directions, so hard-truncating 1792 dims discards some breed-discriminative signal (fine-grained differences partly live in lower-variance directions), giving a small-to-moderate log-loss regression, with only a modest chance that the reduced capacity improves calibration enough to offset the lost accuracy.

Shrinking inputs to 192px for a frozen ResNet-50 trained at 224 lowers feature quality (ImageNet top-1 drops ~1.5-2 pts at 192, worse train/test apparent-size mismatch per FixRes), and fine-grained breed cues like coat texture are lost first, so the linear probe's log loss should rise noticeably while flip-TTA and refit LR only partially compensate.

V2 weights raise ImageNet top-1 from 76.1% to 80.9%, and since the 120 breeds are ImageNet classes the penultimate features should separate them markedly better (as Inception-family features did on this task in 2017), outweighing the mild linear-probe penalty from label smoothing/mixup/cutmix and the V1-tuned C=0.3.

C was already tuned on holdout log loss (coarse x3 grid), so the LR is near-calibrated; a single temperature fit on ~1380 held-out samples fixes residual mild overconfidence with little estimation noise, but the 85%-fit T transfers imperfectly to the full refit, so expect only a small ~1-2% log-loss gain rather than a large one.

The head starts at the LogReg optimum so its mean CE gradient is ~zero, and lr 1e-4 SGD for only ~288 steps on the last bottleneck convs (training loss already ~0.05) changes weights by well under 1%; the result is essentially the same model as the baseline with at most a marginal feature-adaptation gain and tiny fp16/overconfidence noise.

Horizontal-flip TTA with probability averaging is a low-risk two-member ensemble that tempers overconfident errors on a frozen-feature LR classifier; ResNet-50 was trained with flips so mirrored features are in-distribution, giving a small but consistent log-loss gain (~0.01) rather than a large one since the two views are highly correlated.

AUC is threshold-free, so the imbalance was never hurting the ranking; 1:1 undersampling just discards 80-99% of the negatives (threat drops to ~956 training rows, identity_hate/severe_toxic to ~3k), adding variance and losing the negative-context signal that separates true positives from neutral uses of trigger words and from non-X toxic comments, so expect ~1 point loss on common labels and 2-3 points on the rare ones, with the same-subset blend giving no variance relief.

Adding the shared char_wb 2-6 block to NB-LogReg typically lifts the NB branch from ~0.977-0.978 to ~0.980-0.981 alone (community NBSVM word+char results), which should outweigh the lost blend diversity from sharing char features with branch A; convergence at max_iter=100 and C=4 on the larger separable problem is a mild risk, so expect a small net gain of roughly +0.0005 to +0.001 rather than a large one.

AUC only depends on ranking, so imbalance mainly shifts the intercept and the current full-data fits are not actually hurt by it; 1:1 undersampling discards ~90-99% of the negatives (threat drops to ~950 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k, severe_toxic ~3.2k), making the NB log-count ratios and the 60k/200k-feature logistic fits extremely noisy (unseen features get r=0 and vanish), so the rare labels lose ~2-3 AUC points and the big labels ~0.5 points, dragging the column mean down despite the faster runtime.

MultinomialNB(alpha=1) on L2-normalized TF-IDF with 200k 1-2gram features is massively over-smoothed for the rare labels (N_1 << alpha*n_features), so its ranking is driven by document length and rare-token content rather than toxic words; its mean AUC should land roughly 0.85-0.92 (threat/identity_hate far worse), and a fixed 50/50 rank-average with a ~0.979 branch A (whose stacked OOF features also become saturated and weak) drags the blend down to the mid-0.96s rather than helping.

Mean-pooled self-trained Word2Vec + LogReg typically reaches only ~0.955-0.96 mean AUC on Jigsaw (profanity signal is diluted by averaging and lexical n-gram precision is lost), and the MLP on the same 200-d features adds little diversity (~0.965), so the blend puts 2/3 of its rank weight on two correlated weaker branches and drops below the current 0.9808 toward roughly branch B's level despite some cross-feature diversity.

AUC is prior-invariant so balancing buys nothing for ranking, while 1:1 undersampling discards 80-99.7% of negatives (threat trains on ~950 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k) and loses the hard toxic-but-not-this-label negatives that separate rare labels, plus same-seed subsets give A and B no bagging diversity and the MLP gets 5x fewer steps; expect toxic/obscene/insult to lose ~0.003-0.005 and threat/identity_hate/severe ~0.01-0.025, a clear regression.

A sparse multi-task MLP on the same TF-IDF blocks is the only non-linear, differently-trained member, so rank-averaging it at 1/4 weight should add real diversity to three highly correlated linear branches (likely +0.0005 to +0.002 if it reaches ~0.98 test AUC after 2-3 early-stopped epochs); downside risks are the 690/720 s guards truncating or skipping D entirely (no change) and noisy rare-label heads (threat) slightly diluting the blend, so I expect a modest net gain rather than a large one.

1:1 undersampling discards 90-99.7% of negatives (threat trains on ~956 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k), losing the hard toxic-but-not-this-label negatives and making NB ratios and LR weights noisy; AUC is prior-invariant so balancing buys nothing, and the rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) should drop ~0.01-0.03 each, dragging the column mean down roughly a point.

OOF B logits give A a learned in-model blend plus cross-label signal that mainly helps the rare labels (threat, identity_hate), but A and B are already highly correlated linear n-gram models and the final 0.5/0.5 rank blend then over-weights B, so the net is a small positive gain of a few 1e-4 rather than a step change; runtime grows by only ~2-3 min of liblinear fits so it stays within budget.

A 64-unit multi-task MLP on the same 60k word+char TF-IDF matrix, 3 Adam epochs, should land around 0.975-0.979 standalone — slightly below the LR branches but nonlinear and jointly trained, so an equal-weight rank blend most likely adds a few 1e-4 (rare labels threat/identity_hate may get little from it and cap the gain); the bigger risk is wall-clock: ~1875 Adam steps each touching a dense 60k×64 weight/moment set (~15 elementwise passes over 3.8M floats) costs roughly 4-7 min on top of a ~7-9 min baseline, so there is a real (~30%) chance the run is hard-killed at 15 min.

NB-LogReg on word 1-2gram + char_wb TF-IDF is the strongest classical single branch (~0.980-0.981 alone, char n-grams catch obfuscated profanity that word-only NB misses), so equal rank-blending it with A and B should add a small but real gain over 0.9801; upside is capped by high correlation with the existing branches, and the main downside risk is runtime creeping toward the 15-min kill with a third set of liblinear fits on ~250k dense-ish features.

Per-label weights tuned on a 32k holdout and shrunk halfway toward 0.5 can only move within [0.25,0.75]; the two branches are similar in strength and AUC-vs-weight is flat near equal blending, so expect a tiny gain (~+0.0001 to +0.0003) mostly from threat/identity_hate leaning toward the char branch, with noise on rare labels capping upside; caveat: the extra holdout branch fits add ~5-7 min of char-vectorizer and liblinear time, a material risk of hitting the 15-min kill.

Compressing 100k TF-IDF features to 300 LSA components discards the rare lexical cues (slurs, threat verbs, specific profanity) that drive this task; dense LSA+LR on Jigsaw typically lands ~0.95-0.96 mean AUC versus ~0.98 for sparse n-gram LR, with threat and identity_hate degrading most, so dropping the two-branch sparse ensemble is a clear regression.

Capping negatives at 10:1 leaves toxic untouched but discards ~90-97% of training rows for severe_toxic, identity_hate and threat; linear TF-IDF/NB models and especially fastText lose negative-side evidence (noisier q estimates, spurious rare-feature weights, tiny 5k-doc fastText sets), and since AUC only needs ranking (imbalance was never hurting it), the rare-label columns degrade by ~0.005-0.02 each, dragging the six-label mean down by roughly 0.004-0.006.

fastText softmax with multi-label lines samples one label per update, so heavily co-labeled comments (toxic+obscene+insult) get per-label probabilities diluted to ~1/3 and overlap with borderline negatives, degrading F's toxic/obscene/insult ordering (~-1% in-branch) while rare labels gain little from shared embeddings; at 1/3 rank weight behind strong A/B branches this nets a small regression within run-to-run noise.

For binary labels ComplementNB reduces exactly to multinomial NB log-count-ratio scoring on raw counts (no discriminative weighting, strong length bias from add-one smoothing with V=200k vs tiny positive-class token mass), which historically lands around 0.90-0.94 mean AUC on Jigsaw versus ~0.98 for the TF-IDF LR / NB-LR blend, with threat and identity_hate degrading most.

Unweighted mean-pooled from-scratch skip-gram vectors + a single LR discard the exact-token evidence that drives this task (a lone slur in a long comment is diluted to near nothing, min_count=5 drops rare misspelled abuse terms, no IDF/sublinear weighting), and bag-of-embeddings + linear heads historically score ~0.94-0.96 on Jigsaw versus ~0.98 for TF-IDF/NB-LogReg ensembles; the run should finish in ~5-6 min but the metric regresses by roughly 0.025-0.03.

Mean-pooled unsupervised Word2Vec + linear LogReg loses the exact-token profanity signal that TF-IDF n-grams exploit and dilutes single insults in long comments; on Jigsaw this family of bag-of-embeddings baselines typically lands around 0.94-0.96 mean AUC, well below the ~0.98 sparse NB-LogReg/char-ngram ensemble it replaces.

A char-level NB-LogReg is a genuinely different third view (NB weighting on char n-grams vs. ridge-like LR and word-NB), and 3-way rank blends of linear models on this task reliably add a few e-4 AUC, mostly on the rare labels; gains are capped by correlation with branch A's char features and by weight-overfitting on the ~48-positive threat holdout, and the extra char vectorizer plus six liblinear fits on dense char matrices likely costs 4-7 min (not 1-2), so there is a real timeout risk, but conditional on finishing expect ~+0.0005.

The reference word+char TF-IDF kernel actually used C=0.1 (tuned; C=4 belongs to the NB-SVM word kernel), so jumping to C=4 on 60k dense char features overfits the rare labels (threat, severe_toxic, identity_hate), lowering branch A's mean AUC by ~0.002 and making it more correlated with the already weakly-regularized branch B, so the rank blend loses roughly 0.001.

Supervised fastText without pretrained vectors is effectively a mean-pooled hashed word/bigram linear model that scores ~0.965-0.975 alone on Jigsaw (weakest on threat/identity_hate), and its errors are highly correlated with the NB-LogReg word-ngram branch; giving it equal 1/3 weight dilutes the stronger char n-gram branch and the probability floor (p+1e-5) creates bottom ties, so I expect a roughly neutral-to-slightly-negative change, with a nontrivial risk the extra ~4-7 min of training pushes the run past the 15-minute kill.

High risk this never scores: a second char_wb vectorizer (3-7 grams, 100k) costs another ~7-8 min of pure-Python analysis plus six primal-liblinear fits at C=4 on a ~90M-nnz NB-weighted matrix (~1-2 min each), which on top of the existing ~8-11 min baseline very likely trips the 15-min hard kill; if it does finish, a char NB-LogReg (~0.978-0.979 alone) adds modest diversity to A's regularized char view and B's word-only view, so an equal three-way rank average should give a small gain of roughly +0.0005.

Per-label weight tuning gains only ~0.0002-0.0004 since the AUC-vs-weight curve is flat near 0.5 and the 16k holdout (~48 threat positives) makes rare-label weight picks noisy, while never retraining on the full set costs ~0.0004-0.0008 mean AUC, mostly on threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic; net slight regression.

NB log-count weighting on l2-normalized TF-IDF with fixed C=0.1 helps the frequent labels slightly but, for the rare labels (threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic), the +1-smoothed ratio uniformly amplifies rare noise features (effective C ~2-3) while suppressing common ones, risking overfit; combined with reduced diversity against the already-NB-weighted branch B, the rank blend likely ends roughly flat to slightly worse.

min_df=0.01 means a term must appear in ~3,100 of the 313k documents, which collapses the word vocabularies to roughly a thousand common words, deletes essentially all bigrams in the NB-LogReg branch, and prunes a large share of the char n-grams; the rare but highly discriminative tokens (idiot, gay, nigger, jew, kill, faggot) that drive threat and identity_hate AUC are removed, so those columns drop a few points while toxic/obscene/severe hold up via common profanity, yielding a clear regression.

AUC gains nothing from class balance, so 1:1 undersampling only discards information: toxic keeps ~31k of 160k rows but threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic shrink to ~1-3k rows, making NB log-count ratios and LR weights noisy on spurious words, inflating scores of easy negatives at test time; the rare-label columns (which dominate the column mean) should each lose 0.02-0.03 AUC and the common ones ~0.005-0.01, for a net drop of roughly 0.01 from 0.980.

Cosine centroid (Rocchio) scoring is equivalent to the first gradient step of logistic regression from the intercept-only solution, i.e. an extremely over-regularized linear model; it keeps the strong profanity/insult keyword signal (so AUC stays high-0.9s) but loses the discriminative reweighting that handles short clean comments, long toxic rants and rare-label cues (threat, identity_hate), costing roughly 2-3 AUC points per branch with the blend recovering only a little.

Switching char to char_wb at a 50k feature cap trades cross-word n-grams for denser within-word ones; on this task the two analyzers score nearly identically for the TF-IDF+LR branch, and the effect is further diluted by the equal-weight rank blend with the untouched NB-LogReg branch, so expect a change within noise, marginally positive.

In the binary case ComplementNB(norm=False) reduces exactly to MultinomialNB log-odds; with alpha=1 on tiny L2-normalized TF-IDF values the smoothing swamps class evidence, all neutral features get weight ~log(base rate), so scores become dominated by document length and feature rarity rather than toxicity — a classic failure on imbalanced text that hits threat/identity_hate hardest, and rank-averaging two such NB branches cannot recover the ~0.98 LR/NB-LR quality.

Collapsing 60k sparse word/char TF-IDF features to a 32-dim LSA projection discards the specific profanity/threat n-gram signal that makes branch A the strong (~0.978) model; a 32-component LR will land around 0.91-0.93 mean AUC, so the equal-weight rank blend is now dominated by the mediocre fastText branch (coarse sigmoid-table-quantized outputs with many ties) and should drop to roughly 0.955-0.96, a clear regression.

Collapsing the vocabulary to the 2,000 most document-frequent tokens keeps core profanity but wipes out the long tail of slurs, inflected forms, misspellings and obfuscations that the char_wb n-grams and fastText bigrams currently exploit, so both branches lose signal (especially for threat and identity_hate) and the rank blend loses diversity; expect a moderate regression rather than a collapse.

Keeping stop words (e.g. 'you', 'your', 'not') adds mildly toxic-predictive pronouns to the 10k word vocab at the cost of ~300 rare low-value words, but char_wb 2-6-grams and the NB branch already capture these tokens, so the rank-averaged ensemble moves only marginally, likely a hair up.

Logit averaging is scale-sensitive: branch B (C=4 NB-LR, liblinear dual) emits logits with roughly 2-3x the spread of the heavily regularized branch A (C=0.1 sag), so the blend becomes an effective ~70/30 tilt toward the weaker NB-LR branch (worst on rare labels like threat), losing part of the ~+0.001 diversity gain the equal-weight rank average captures; expect a small regression of a few 1e-4.

Switching to analyzer='char' under the same 50k cap trades rarer within-word subword n-grams (unique to branch A) for cross-word fragments that mostly duplicate branch B's word bigrams, so branch A changes little on its own and the rank blend loses a bit of diversity; expect a negligible-to-slightly-negative shift of a few 1e-4.

fastText supervised (count-averaged unigrams + 200k-bucket hashed bigrams, no IDF, 5 epochs) is a clearly weaker learner than NB-LogReg (~0.96 vs ~0.977 alone), and its ova sigmoid is table-quantized and clipped at |logit|>8 so most comments return the exact 1e-5 floor, creating huge tie blocks that the rank-average turns into a hard floored/non-floored split; the strong word+char branch still anchors the blend near its solo ~0.979, but the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) lose from floored positives, netting a small regression.

At C=1 the LR is already over-regularized (best C for this dataset is ~1000+), so dropping 64 of 192 features, mostly margin/texture bins that are weak individually but complementary jointly, removes signal and the ability to spread weight over correlated bins; the LR gets worse by ~20-30% and the unchanged, deterministic NN half of the blend only partly buffers it.

With ~99% achievable accuracy, eps=0.1 smoothing over 99 classes caps the NN's true-class probability near 0.85-0.9 on test (loss floor -log(0.9)=0.105 even when correct), and since the final probabilities are a linear 50/50 blend with the unchanged LR, this underconfidence directly lowers the blend's true-class probability on the ~95% of easy samples (from ~0.95 to ~0.90), adding roughly +0.04 to +0.06 log loss while offering no rescue on confident errors (other-class floor ~0.001).

OvR and multinomial LR produce similar rankings on this near-separable 99-class data, so accuracy barely moves, but normalised independent sigmoids are a worse-shaped surrogate for multi-class cross-entropy than softmax logits; the single power/floor calibration undoes OvR's under-confidence but not its heavier, less-informative wrong-class tails, so expect a modest regression (roughly 0.05-0.065) rather than the hoped-for gain.

A 5-seed bagged MLP on the standardized 192 descriptors is a strong, diverse complement to the heavily regularized LR (C=1) on this near-linearly-separable 99-class data; CV-selected blending before power calibration should sharpen confident-correct rows while softening the few confusions, with w=0 fallback limiting downside, so I expect a moderate log-loss gain (~0.045 -> ~0.033) tempered by small OOF-selection optimism and test-set noise.

Averaging five sharp high-C fold models caps the handful of confidently-wrong test predictions that dominate log loss on this near-separable 99-class problem, and errors made by a single fold cost only ~0.2 nats after averaging; the 20% less data per model partially offsets this, so expect a modest improvement (roughly 0.045-0.060 range) rather than a large one.

Absolute leaf size (area, axis lengths, H/W) is genuinely new information beyond the scale-normalised 192 descriptors and Kaggle kernels found image dimensions help LogReg on this task, so OOF-tuned C should yield a modest gain; but most of the 21 features are redundant with shape/margin, euler/n_comp/hu7 are noisy near-discrete outlier features risky in the weakly-regularised large-C regime, and the small test set makes the outcome swing on one or two confident errors, so expect only a small improvement (~0.057 -> ~0.048) with real chance of no change or slight regression.

L2 logistic regression is rotation-invariant, so unwhitened PCA only truncates the lowest-variance ~5% of directions (≈100 of 219 components dropped); on this near-separable 99-class problem the tail of margin/texture histogram components still carries some discriminative signal that C=1.0 was using, and the model is already over-regularized, so extra truncation yields a small-to-moderate degradation rather than a gain.

A C=1.0 L2 logistic regression on 219 standardized features is already underconfident (Kaggle leaf kernels show logloss dropping steeply as C rises), so each fold model trained on 792 rows (8/class, effectively ~20% stronger regularization) will be softer and slightly less accurate; averaging five highly correlated low-variance linear models recovers little of that loss, so the CV-bagged submission should land modestly worse than the single full-data fit, roughly 0.095-0.10.

The C=1.0 LR is underconfident (~0.91 on correct answers) rather than inaccurate, so averaging with a sharper feature+image NN that should reach ~97-99% accuracy sharpens correct predictions while the LR floor caps damage from the NN's few confident errors; the blend is bounded below by ~0.06 by the LR's softness and above by NN mistakes, landing around 0.08-0.10, with the tiny CNN easily fitting the time budget.

LR at C=1.0 on this near-separable 99-class data is strongly underconfident (well-known that raising C to ~1000 drops log loss from ~0.12 to ~0.04 with little accuracy change), so OOF-tuned temperature sharpening (a≈2.5-3.5) should cut the loss substantially; the gain is limited by the ~1-1.5% residual errors that get amplified, so expect roughly 0.06-0.08 rather than the high-C ~0.04.

C=1 heavily over-regularises this near-separable 990x192, 99-class problem; CV will pick C in the ~1000-5000 range, where a standardised multinomial LR on the raw 192 features is known to score roughly 0.03-0.05 on this test set (Kaggle kernels report ~0.04 with C≈2000), so expect a large drop from 0.124 to around 0.04.

Image height/width carry genuine new absolute-size signal and extra standardized features let the over-regularized C=1 LR spread weight and grow margins, but the polarity heuristic (mask.mean()>0.5) picks the background corners for the many tightly-cropped leaves that fill over half the frame, so most of the ~20 region descriptors are regime-mixed noise; net effect is a modest improvement, not a large one.

Leaf data with 240 standardized features is near-separable and on this dataset log loss keeps falling as C grows to ~1000, so cutting C 5x to 0.2 shrinks logit margins (~15-25%) and roughly triples the loss on correctly classified test rows while barely changing the few confident errors, pushing the score from ~0.08 to roughly 0.13-0.18.

Dropping the full-data refit trains the submitted model on only 80% of a tiny 99-class set (about 8 instead of 10 samples per class), losing information and effectively strengthening regularization at C=1.0, so test log loss should rise noticeably toward the holdout value rather than improve.

OOF-optimized blend of calibrated LR with a sharper (overconfident but ~98% accurate) shrinkage-LDA and a soft large-k distance kNN should tighten probabilities on the many agreed-upon easy leaves while LR keeps LDA's rare catastrophic errors bounded; weights fit on 990 OOF rows with only 3 params transfer well, so expect a modest ~15-25% log-loss gain rather than a dramatic one.

Leaf features are near-linearly separable with only ~8-10 samples per class, where tuned logistic regression is historically far better than tree ensembles (Kaggle GBM/XGBoost runs land ~0.15-0.5 logloss vs ~0.04-0.06 for LR); HGB additionally sacrifices 15% of training data to the early-stopping holdout, cannot form pure class leaves with min_samples_leaf=10, does not roll back to the best iteration, and its few misclassified test leaves get p_true~1e-3 (loss ~5-8 each), so ~4% errors plus ~0.95 confidence on correct rows gives roughly 0.2-0.4 logloss.

Platt-sigmoid OvR calibration with only 2-3 positives per class per 3-fold calibration split (and SVCs trained on 2/3 of the data) yields noisy, flatter probabilities after 99-way normalization (~0.6 bulk confidence, ~0.05-0.1 on confusable Quercus-type samples) versus the softer-tailed C=1 multinomial LR (~0.7 bulk, ~0.2-0.3 when wrong), so with a 99-row test set dominated by a handful of hard samples the uniform soft vote loses a bit on both bulk and tail; linear SVC adds little diversity over LR/LDA, so expect a modest regression.
