RF (600 trees, sqrt features, bootstrap) on this 99-class/9-per-class leaf data is accurate but notoriously underconfident (vote fractions ~0.6-0.75 on easy rows), so under uniform soft voting it dilutes the confident LR/kNN/LDA votes on the ~80% easy test rows (costing ~0.08-0.1 nats each), which roughly cancels or slightly outweighs the gain from removing HGB's confidently-wrong predictions (~10-15% of rows); net effect near neutral with a slight lean toward a small regression, high variance given only 99 test rows.

sklearn MLPClassifier early-stops on validation *accuracy* (not loss) using a tiny ~80-sample unstratified split with only ~4 Adam updates per epoch, so best-weights restoration typically lands on a half-converged, underconfident network (uniform-shrinkage alpha then just goes to ~0 and can't help); on near-linearly-separable leaf descriptors this usually yields OOF/test log loss around 0.15-0.3, worse than the current 0.124 LR despite similar ~97-98% accuracy.

The leaf features are nearly linearly separable, so C=1 leaves multinomial LR badly under-confident; CV will pick C around 100-1000 (as Kaggle kernels found, reaching ~0.03-0.05 LB), roughly halving the log loss, with the alpha-shrinkage limiting damage from a few overconfident errors on the small test split.

C=1 is heavily over-regularised for these near-linearly-separable standardised leaf features; CV on neg_log_loss will select a large C (several hundred to 1000, the grid max), which on this dataset is known to drive multinomial LR to ~0.04-0.05 log loss on the 594-sample test (vs 0.124 now), and 10x25 lbfgs fits with warm-started paths easily fit the time budget.

C=1.0 L2 logistic regression on standardized leaf features is already under-confident (log loss drops sharply as C grows), so OOF log loss is convex and increasing in alpha unless several extremely confident (<1e-5) OOF errors exist; with the 0.01 grid step the flattening cost (~0.01 per sample) almost surely outweighs tail gains, so alpha=0 is most likely selected and the submission is unchanged, with a modest chance a small alpha is picked and slightly worsens the test score.

Shrinkage 0.9 toward a scalar identity (~0.1*S_pooled + 0.36*I in standardized units) floors the tiny within-class variances that make the current LW-per-class model wildly overconfident on its few errors (~15 nats each), so error costs should drop several-fold; this likely outweighs the modest accuracy loss from a duller, near-Euclidean metric among similar Quercus species, though over-weighting of high-variance shape directions could add a few costly errors, leaving a real chance of regression.

Per-family LDA models are individually weak (margin ~85%, shape ~65%, texture ~80% accuracy) and the arithmetic mean caps the true-class probability at the average of three confidences, so dilution on the ~50% of samples where one family (usually shape) errs costs ~0.5 nats each; this outweighs the benefit of bounding the full model's rare catastrophic errors, yielding a moderate regression versus the product-like 192-feature LDA.

Leaf features are nearly linearly separable and LR benefits from max capacity (best C sits at the top of the grid); unsupervised PCA at 90% variance drops roughly half the standardized dimensions whose low-variance, near-collinear residuals carry fine species distinctions, so expect a few more confident misclassifications and lower confidence overall, pushing log loss up noticeably.

Shrunk LDA should match LR on accuracy with few samples per class, but its generative Gaussian posteriors have no temperature knob (shrinkage is trace-preserving), so the ~1% misclassified leaves get much more extreme wrong probabilities than CV-tuned LR, likely raising log loss despite similar accuracy.

L2 logistic regression is rotation-invariant, so PCA only acts by truncating the low-variance directions (~half of the 192 standardized dims at 95% variance); on this fine-grained 99-class leaf task those bin-difference directions in the margin/texture histograms carry real discriminative signal that C=1 barely shrinks, and Kaggle experience shows PCA before LR/KNN here slightly degrades, so expect a modest log-loss increase rather than a gain.

Shrinkage LDA is a very sample-efficient fit for leaf's 10-per-class, shared-covariance descriptors and typically matches or beats regularized LR in accuracy here; its residual overconfidence is largely absorbed by the scalar temperature (likely T>1, possibly near the 4.0 cap), so I expect a modest log-loss improvement rather than a dramatic one, with real downside risk if clipping leaves errors too confident.

Mixing 0.5% uniform adds a near-constant -log(0.995)≈+0.005 penalty to every confidently-correct prediction (the vast majority at logloss 0.094), while only samples with p_true below ~1e-3 gain anything; a C=1 regularized LR on RBF-Nyström features rarely produces such extreme wrong-class confidence, so the small gains on a handful of errors do not offset the uniform penalty and the score regresses by roughly 0.004.

Cutting Nystroem landmarks from 512 to 384 gives a coarser kernel approximation and, with standardized features at fixed C=1, effectively stronger regularization; the current 0.094 log loss on this near-separable 99-class problem already reflects under-confidence rather than overfitting, so a more compact representation should mildly raise log loss.

LDA with per-class Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage (10 samples/class, 192 dims) yields a near-diagonal pooled covariance and extremely peaked softmax posteriors; accuracy stays ~98.5-99% but each of the ~6-9 test errors costs ~20-34 nats (clipped), so log loss lands around 0.25-0.4, far worse than the smooth, mildly underconfident C=1 logistic regression at 0.124.

On this near-separable 192-feature dataset, standardized multinomial LR improves monotonically with weaker regularization up to C~1000 (known Kaggle results ~0.03-0.05 vs ~0.12 at C=1); 3-fold neg_log_loss CV will pick C=100 or 1000 and roughly halve-to-third the loss, with some residual risk from overconfident errors on a small test split.

L2 multinomial LR at C=1 on nearly separable leaf features is strongly under-confident (optimal C on this data is ~1000x larger), so OOF-fit temperature will land around T≈0.4-0.6 and sharpen correct predictions far more than it penalises the few soft errors; T=1 recovers the baseline exactly so downside is limited, and I expect roughly a third of the loss removed rather than the full gain of tuning C since direction/accuracy are unchanged.

The second StandardScaler rescales the 512 Nyström columns (std ≈0.04) by ~25x, so this is effectively kernel logistic regression with an RBF kernel at a weaker regularization (equivalent to roughly linear C≈1.5-2); the leaf data is nearly linearly separable so the RBF kernel adds little, but the mild relaxation of the over-regularized C=1 baseline should trim log loss modestly, with real risk of no gain or a regression if the more local kernel widens the train/test confidence gap.

The timestamp trend (success rate fell sharply over the subreddit's life), log request length, and evidentiality/prior-RAOP flags are known strong RAOP predictors that the l2-normalised TF-IDF and current numerics only partially proxy; as standardised dense columns in LR they should add ~+0.01-0.02 AUC, with the 13 weak hour/weekday one-hots and day-of-month adding only mild noise, so a modest net gain is most likely (test-set noise ±0.01).

RF with sqrt-sampling over ~8000 mostly-sparse TF-IDF/subreddit columns picks noisy rare-word splits and rarely sees the 9 informative dense numeric features, so on this weak-signal ~3-4k-row problem it should underperform the regularised linear model by a few AUC points despite capturing some nonlinearity in the count features; run time is fine.

RF with max_features=sqrt over 5000 sparse unigrams dilutes both the dense requester-history columns and the giver_known indicator (each available at only ~1-13% of nodes), so it exploits the text signal worse than the linear model and only partially captures the leak-like giver feature that LR ranks cleanly; expect a modest regression from 0.748 to roughly 0.70.

Replacing 5k sparse TF-IDF unigrams with 50 noisy LDA topic proportions from ~4k short, homogeneous pizza requests discards specific lexical cues (paypal, proof, pay-it-forward, gratitude) that drive most of the text signal; metadata plus the giver_known leak keeps the score from collapsing, so expect a modest drop rather than a gain.

Swapping the supervised OOF TF-IDF logit (which directly captures outcome-predictive words) for 20 unsupervised LDA proportions from ~5.7k short documents discards most of the text signal; LDA topics on small corpora are noisy and only weakly aligned with the label, so LightGBM ends up close to metadata-only performance, a modest drop from 0.703 with the test AUC's ~0.02 noise band around it.

The train/test split here is random, not temporal, so the raw timestamp's period base-rate signal (RAOP success rate declined markedly from 2011 to 2013, and timestamp is consistently a top-gain feature in GBMs on this data) does transfer to test; replacing it with hour/weekday, which are known weak and noisy predictors in RAOP, removes roughly 0.01-0.015 AUC while adding little, so a modest regression is most likely.

A tree model on the ~33 dense meta/time/text-stat features adds non-linear time-period and history-threshold effects the linear model misses, and CV-selected rank blending with a CV-tuned weight rarely hurts (floor is ~current LR); typical RAOP gains from LR-text + GBM-meta ensembles are modest, roughly +0.01 to +0.02 AUC, with test-set noise of ~0.02.

An untuned fully-grown random forest with max_features='sqrt' over ~5000 sparse TF-IDF columns plus ~50 dense features wastes most splits on noisy word columns and loses the additive text signal that LR exploits well; it will still capture the strong time/RAOP-history metadata effects, so expect a moderate regression to roughly 0.64-0.68 rather than a collapse.

Subreddit bag-of-words is a known modestly useful signal in RAOP (community membership beyond the count already in NUM_COLS); as an l2-normalized sparse block under C=0.3 LR it should add ~+0.01 AUC with small overfit risk, so a modest gain over 0.657 is most likely.

giver_username_if_known is present in test.json and is a pure leak (P(y=1|flag)=1.0 on train, ~25% of positives flagged, 26 of 404 test rows flagged); an unscaled 0/1 column under C=0.3 gets a coefficient of roughly +4 that lifts flagged rows above nearly all negatives, so AUC ≈ f + (1-f)*0.657 ≈ 0.25*1 + 0.75*0.657 ≈ 0.74.

Adding the raw UTC timestamp (success rate in RAOP fell sharply as the community grew) plus nonlinear tree handling of the requester-history counts on top of a text OOF score is the standard non-leak recipe that lifts this task from ~0.65 (linear TF-IDF+numerics) toward ~0.68-0.70; the conservative LGBM settings, early stopping and seed averaging keep variance low, though the small test split adds ~0.02 AUC noise.

Time trend (success rate fell as RAOP grew), explicit request length, and imgur/link evidentiality are known strong, largely orthogonal signals that L2-normalized TF-IDF plus the 9 history numerics miss; ~25 standardized dense features under L2 LR on ~3k rows add little overfitting risk, so expect a modest but real gain (~+0.02 AUC), with hour/day-of-week/punctuation features roughly neutral.

Swapping a linear model for ExtraTrees on a matrix where ~93% of the ~5.4k columns are sparse, individually weak TF-IDF words means sqrt-subsampled random splits are dominated by noisy word thresholds; tree ensembles typically trail logistic regression on bag-of-words/embedding text signals, and the strong 9 requester-history numerics are rarely in the candidate set, so expect a small regression roughly within test-set noise rather than a gain.

With C=0.3 the L2-normalized TF-IDF block is already heavily shrunk relative to the unit-variance embedding/numeric features, so it adds little variance but still contributes a small complementary lexical signal; dropping it leaves the nearly unregularized 384-dim embeddings plus numerics, which should land slightly below the current score, roughly within test-set noise.

L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF discards request length, which is one of the strongest known RAOP predictors, and the URL/money/gratitude flags encode the evidentiality and narrative effects from Althoff et al.; ~27 standardized dense features in an L2-regularized LR on ~4k rows add real signal with little overfitting risk, so a modest gain of roughly +0.01 to +0.02 AUC is likely, with sentiment and readability contributing little.

Dropping TF-IDF removes real signal (narrative/need words) that combines additively with the metadata; the nine log-scaled requester-history features alone with LR typically land around 0.59-0.63 AUC on a random split of this dataset, so the compact model regresses despite lower variance.

Skip-gram vectors trained on only ~0.5M tokens are noisy, and unweighted mean pooling (stopwords included, no idf) yields roughly a low-rank bag-of-words that loses the specific lexical cues TF-IDF+LR exploits; on weak-signal RAOP text this typically recovers only part of the TF-IDF gain over metadata+text_stats, while 200 standardized dense dims under C=0.3 add overfitting variance, so a small regression is most likely.

Bigrams with min_df=2 add some phrase signal, but on ~3k training docs with fixed strong C=0.3 the extra sparse features are heavily shrunk and L2 row-normalization dilutes the existing unigram signal, while the most diagnostic phrases are already captured by the dense text-stat counters; net effect is likely a marginal gain within test-set noise.

The nine requester-history features carry real but modest signal (~0.60-0.64 AUC in Althoff et al. and Kaggle metadata-only kernels); the SVD text features in the current pipeline add a little on top, so dropping them entirely with an aggressive 63-leaf LGBM on 9 columns most likely loses a point or two rather than gaining.

MiniLM embeddings add complementary semantic signal to weak unigram TF-IDF on RAOP text, but standardizing 384 dense dims next to L2-normalized TF-IDF under a fixed C=0.3 leaves the embedding block nearly unregularized on ~3-4k samples, so the gain is modest (roughly +0.01 AUC) with real downside risk from overfitting and test-set noise.

Bigrams add a little real signal (pay forward, food stamps, lost job) but min_df=2 on ~4k docs mostly adds noisy features that dilute L2-normalized TF-IDF under a fixed small C=0.3, and the numeric requester-history block already drives most of the AUC, so expect a marginal, noise-level gain of roughly +0.003.

Request length (char/word counts) is a known non-leaky predictor that L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF mostly discards, so the dense stats block should add a small real gain; lexicon features are largely redundant with unigrams and the 15 well-regularized dense columns carry little overfit risk, so expect roughly +0.01 AUC, well within test-set noise of ~0.02.

On ~4k noisy samples, a 63-leaf LightGBM over 300 dense SVD components loses much of the sparse word-level signal that LR on raw TF-IDF exploits and overfits noisy SVD dimensions; the gain from nonlinear handling of the 9 numerics is small (no timestamp feature), so expect a slight regression despite early-stopped CV selection.

RAOP's dominant date signal is a monotone decline in success rate as the community grew (Dec 2010 to Sep 2013), which the 8-column quantile spline captured; two annual sin/cos columns discard that trend and only encode weak, poorly-estimated seasonality over ~3 cycles, so most of the spline's gain over the no-date baseline is lost.

A 100x weaker penalty lets ~5000 TF-IDF unigrams nearly separate ~4k training rows, so noisy large text coefficients drown the reliably predictive requester-history and date features and generalization drops by several AUC points.

RAOP success rate declined markedly from 2011 to 2013 as the subreddit grew; calendar time is largely orthogonal to the existing text/history/subreddit features and the prepared split is random, so a 7-column standardized spline block should add roughly +0.015-0.025 AUC with negligible overfitting risk at C=0.3.

KNN runs fine (brute cosine on sparse works, seconds of compute) but is a much weaker learner here: cosine distance on the stacked matrix is dominated by the standardized numeric and binary subreddit blocks (TF-IDF is ~5% of row norm), so text signal is mostly lost, and k=25 distance-weighted local averages of noisy 25%-base-rate labels capture only the coarse activity-level signal, landing well below the 0.649 linear model.

Distance-weighted KNN on nine correlated, heavy-tailed metadata features yields noisy, high-variance probabilities (effective k well under 25) that dominate the 50/50 average yet carry less signal than CatBoost, so the blend likely slips a bit toward or below the logistic-only level.

C=30 on ~5000 TF-IDF dims with only a few thousand samples makes the LR nearly separate the training data, so its test probabilities become extreme and dominate the 50/50 blend; the overfit text-driven LR ranks worse than the current metadata-leaning C=0.3 fit, and the CatBoost diversity benefit is largely lost, giving a modest AUC drop.

RAOP success rate declined markedly from 2011 to 2013 and none of the existing features capture absolute calendar time; with a random train/test split (no extrapolation), 8 standardized quantile-spline columns on the UTC timestamp add nearly orthogonal signal to the TF-IDF+history LR at negligible overfitting risk, so a modest but real AUC gain (~+0.02) is the likely outcome, with test-set noise (~800 rows) the main uncertainty.

BernoulliNB binarizes the TF-IDF into word presence and collapses the nine continuous requester-history features (which carry much of the LR baseline's signal) into above-mean indicators that get swamped by 5000 noisy, correlated uni/bigram terms with class-imbalanced Laplace estimates; expect a text-NB-like AUC around 0.60-0.62, a clear regression from 0.654.

RAOP success rate declines markedly from ~35% in 2011 to under 20% in 2013 (plus a retrieval-cutoff dip), a signal the current text+history features barely capture; a 7-column smooth spline on the UTC timestamp is cheap, unregularized-enough at C=0.3 to be learned, and under a random train/test split should add roughly +0.015 to +0.025 AUC.

Binary subreddit membership adds genuine user-activity signal beyond the existing count features (typically ~+0.01-0.02 AUC on RAOP), but the unscaled 0/1 block with ~1000 sparse columns is effectively under-regularized relative to the TF-IDF features at C=0.3, so some noise-fitting on rare subreddits will eat part of the gain.

CatBoost on the nine requester-history numerics captures nonlinear thresholds (prior RAOP comments/posts, account age, karma) the linear model only partially uses, and metadata-only GBMs reach ~0.62-0.64 on this task, so a 50/50 blend with the 0.657 text+meta LR should add roughly 0.01-0.02 AUC with low risk of regression.

Bigrams add a little phrase signal (e.g. 'pay forward', 'pizza tonight') but with max_features fixed at 5000 they crowd out unigrams and dilute l2-normalised unigram weights on a ~3k-doc corpus, so the net effect is a near-wash with a slight positive lean, well within test-set AUC noise.

Authorship attribution leans heavily on function-word usage, so dropping stop words (and every bigram containing one, e.g. 'upon the', 'which i') discards stylometric signal; the char_wb view retains short function-word unigrams, which limits but does not eliminate the regression, so expect log loss to worsen by roughly 0.015-0.02.

Tuned MultinomialNB on raw word/char counts (~0.40-0.45 OOF) is strongly complementary to the TF-IDF LR, and a log-linear meta-blend on OOF log-probs is the classic winning recipe in this competition, typically cutting log loss ~6-10% relative over the best single LR; fold-averaged test inputs keep the stack consistent, so a solid but not dramatic gain is likely.

Function words and their bigrams are among the strongest authorship signals in this competition (Kaggle kernels consistently show stop_words='english' worsens word LR/NB by 0.03-0.1 logloss); the char_wb models and stacker only partly compensate, so the stack should regress mildly.

A multinomial LR on raw (not logit) OOF probabilities cannot recalibrate the near-binary, overconfident MultinomialNB columns or exploit nonlinear/interaction effects in the raw count meta-features that LightGBM currently uses, so the stack should lose a few hundredths of log loss (roughly 0.30 -> 0.33) rather than improve; LGBM with early stopping on 15.6k rows x 28 features is not materially overfitting.

Punctuation (commas, semicolons, dashes, quotes, possessive apostrophes) is a genuine and strong stylometric signal in this corpus and is shared between train and test since both came through the same preparation; stripping it removes informative case-sensitive char n-grams while leaving the word block essentially identical (its token pattern already ignores punctuation), so the combined model loses signal and log loss gets worse by a few percent rather than gaining from the mild vocabulary shrinkage.

Tuned MultinomialNB on word/char counts (~0.41-0.45 OOF) is a strong, diverse complement to the C=10 word/char TF-IDF LRs (~0.43-0.47), and an LR meta-learner on log-probs both calibrates NB's overconfidence and blends; LR+NB stacks on this task historically land around 0.37-0.40, a solid gain over the single hstacked LR at 0.4386, with the run comfortably inside the time budget.

Chi2 keeps mass-heavy common n-grams and discards the rare, highly author-specific words and redundant char n-grams that L2 LR exploits; with fixed C=1 and unrenormalized rows the LR becomes softer and less discriminative, so LR OOF degrades (~0.46 to ~0.55) and the blend shifts toward NB, recovering only part of the loss.

Function words are the strongest stylometric signal for authorship (Poe's 'upon', Shelley's 'thus/yet', negations, 'whence/thence/whereupon' are all on sklearn's list); stripping them guts the naive-Bayes model and weakens the word-TF-IDF block, with only partial compensation from the untouched char_wb features, so the blend should regress by roughly 0.03-0.04 log loss.

C=1 on L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF is known to under-fit on Spooky (counts beat TF-IDF at C=1 in classic kernels); 5-fold CV over [1,3,10,30,100] will almost surely pick C≈10-30, cutting log loss by roughly 0.03 while the test-set noise on 1,958 rows is small relative to that gain.

Stacking complementary LR (C=10) and low-alpha NB base models with punctuation/length meta-features via early-stopped LightGBM is the classic spooky recipe that historically lands ~0.33-0.37, a solid gain over a single under-regularized C=1 LR at 0.432; residual risk is GBM miscalibration and OOF-vs-averaged-test shift in the extreme NB probabilities.

Cross-boundary, case-sensitive, uncapped char n-grams are the canonical strong stylometric feature set and add medium-frequency punctuation/capitalization signal the capped char_wb block lacks; at fixed C=1 the extra rare high-IDF columns dilute the L2-normalized rows (effectively stronger regularization on common features), so the net is a modest ~0.01 log-loss gain rather than a large one, with real risk of a near-null result.

MultinomialNB on word 1-2gram counts is a strong, diverse complement to TF-IDF LR on this dataset (NB alone ~0.41-0.45 OOF with tuned alpha), and an OOF-tuned arithmetic blend reliably shaves ~0.02-0.04 off log loss despite NB's overconfidence, so expect roughly 0.43 -> 0.40.

Function words (pronouns, 'upon', 'whence', 'thereby', etc.) and their bigrams are among the strongest stylometric signals for distinguishing Poe/Lovecraft/Shelley, so removing sklearn's 318 stopwords discards discriminative features and shortens sentences into sparser, more overconfident fastText predictions; Kaggle kernels on this exact competition consistently showed stop_words='english' hurting log loss, so expect a clear regression rather than a gain.

Test distribution matches the mild 40/31/29 train imbalance, so balancing removes a correct prior (small log-loss penalty ~0.01) while duplicating minority rows under 25 epochs of an already-overfit char-ngram fastText adds ~22% more updates and sharper, more overconfident predictions; expect a slight regression within run-to-run noise.

ComplementNB on the stacked TF-IDF will be a much weaker, overconfident model (~0.5 OOF log loss, with a mild minority-class bias from the complement normalization), but an OOF-tuned convex blend with the tuned LR almost never hurts and typically sharpens LR's under-confident correct predictions, so expect a small gain (w around 0.7-0.85) of roughly 2% rather than a large one.

MultinomialNB on stacked word+char TF-IDF is a weaker, poorly calibrated probability model than tuned logistic regression (correlated overlapping char n-grams and double-counted word/char evidence yield overconfident posteriors that alpha tuning only partly tempers); in this competition tuned NB typically lands around 0.42-0.48 log loss versus ~0.35 for tuned LR on the same features, so expect a clear regression.

Char_wb n-grams carry stylistic signal (punctuation, archaic spellings, morphology) that word 1-2 grams miss on this task; dropping them typically costs a few hundredths of log loss, so word-only NB-SVM should land around 0.43-0.44, a modest regression.

Plain ComplementNB on L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF has no learned weighting or calibration: alpha=1 smoothing is huge relative to the tiny TF-IDF masses, overlapping char n-grams double-count evidence, and the complement normalization adds a class-size bias toward EAP, so expect ~78-80% accuracy with NB-style miscalibration, landing near the known ~0.58 MNB-on-TF-IDF level rather than the 0.41 NB-SVM score.

C=1 is over-regularized for ~115k L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF features (counts vs tfidf gap in public kernels shows the same effect); 3-fold CV on neg_log_loss should pick C≈3-10, giving sharper but still calibrated probabilities and a moderate log-loss drop, with some risk the slower high-C lbfgs paths push runtime toward the 10-minute target but likely not past the 15-minute kill.

MultinomialNB on stacked word+char TF-IDF double-counts hundreds of correlated character n-grams and, with light alpha=0.1 smoothing, yields overconfident posteriors; its ~82-84% accuracy is slightly below the LR's and the badly calibrated confident-wrong predictions (3-6 nats each) dominate log loss, so expect a clear regression from 0.425 to roughly 0.50-0.60.

fastText with lr=0.5, 25 epochs, bigrams and char n-grams will overfit the ~17.6k training sentences and emit badly overconfident softmax probabilities; holdout accuracy may stay ~80-84% but confident misclassifications (true-class prob near 0.01 or lower) will push log loss well above the calibrated TF-IDF+LR baseline, likely into the 0.55-0.80 range.

C=1 on L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF is over-regularized/under-confident for this 3-class task; 5-fold CV should pick C=4 or 8, giving sharper, better-calibrated probabilities and a moderate log-loss gain (~0.03), with a small residual risk of the 32 lbfgs fits running long on CPU.

NB log-count-ratio scaling acts as a strong feature-selection prior (heavily regularizes uninformative n-grams, frees informative ones) and C=4 relaxes the over-regularized C=1 fit, which historically pushes word+char TF-IDF linear models on Spooky from ~0.43 toward ~0.40-0.42; the one-vs-rest + renormalization slightly hurts calibration versus multinomial, so expect a modest net gain of roughly 0.015-0.025 log loss.

The 14 stylometric features add a little information TF-IDF discards (absolute length, capitalization; punctuation counts are mostly already captured by char_wb n-grams), and with L2-regularized LR on ~18k rows the added dense block is unlikely to hurt, so expect a small gain of roughly 0.002-0.004 log loss.

NB log-count-ratio weighting suppresses non-discriminative common features and lets class-specific rare word/char n-grams carry the fit, which typically beats plain TF-IDF LR on short-text author ID; the one-vs-rest normalization gives up some calibration versus multinomial softmax, so net gain is modest (~0.02) rather than large.

TF-IDF rows are L2-normalized so features are small-magnitude and LR at C=1 is already on the over-regularized, underconfident side for this competition (optimal C is typically 3-30); cutting C to 0.25 shrinks logits further, pushing probabilities toward the prior and raising log loss by roughly 0.05-0.07.

Dropping word uni/bigrams removes strong vocabulary signal (names, archaic lexicon) that char_wb 2-5 grams capped at 60k only partly recovers, and the lower-norm, less extreme NB-scaled char features under C=1.0 give less confident one-vs-rest probabilities, so log loss should worsen moderately rather than improve.

NB log-count-ratio scaling plus one-vs-rest liblinear at an un-retuned C=4 breaks the L2 row normalization and weakens regularization on rare author-specific tokens, so accuracy stays similar but probabilities become more overconfident and OvR normalization is less well calibrated than multinomial softmax, giving a small log-loss regression.

Function words (including 'upon', 'which', first-person pronouns, 'very') are among the strongest stylometric signals for distinguishing Poe/Lovecraft/Shelley, and sklearn's list also strips content-ish words like 'found', 'fire', 'thin'; removing them from both word and char_wb branches discards signal and mangles bigrams, so log loss should regress by roughly 0.04-0.08 despite temperature recalibration.

Cutting C to 0.25 quadruples L2 shrinkage on ~100k sparse TF-IDF features; temperature scaling absorbs the lost logit scale but the heavier-regularized weight direction discriminates slightly worse and the 0.25 temperature floor likely binds, so expect a modest regression from 0.382 to roughly 0.40.

Switching to 'char' adds cross-word and punctuation-spanning n-grams (e.g. ', and', '; the') that are discriminative for authorship, but the 60k feature cap and overlap with word n-grams limit the gain to a small logloss improvement.

NB log-count scaling re-allocates L2 regularization toward strongly author-specific mid-frequency terms (names, archaic vocab), which usually gives a small gain over uniform C=1 LR, but with TF-IDF-scale sums the +1/+D smoothing compresses and off-centers the ratios (suppressing mildly-enriched style features) and OvR+renormalization is slightly worse calibrated than multinomial, so expect only a modest net improvement, roughly 0.42-0.43.

C=1 on L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF is under-confident for ~17.6k samples; loosening to C=4 sharpens probabilities while still regularizing enough, a known sweet-spot region for this setup, so a moderate log-loss gain is expected.

C=1 L2-regularized multinomial LR on ~120k-dim unit-norm TF-IDF with ~16k samples is reliably underconfident on held-out data, so the holdout-fitted temperature will land well below 1 (~0.6-0.75) and sharpening typically recovers most of the gain that tuning C upward gives on this dataset (~0.02-0.035 log loss), with minimal risk from fitting a single scalar on a 1.7k-row holdout.

The metric is RMSE in dollars, so the raw-target model already estimates the conditional mean; fitting log1p and inverting with expm1 yields a median-like, systematically low prediction (no smearing correction) and shifts tree capacity toward cheap rides, under-fitting the expensive rides that dominate squared error, so valid-row RMSE should worsen a few percent (~3.57 -> ~3.68), damped overall by the fixed ~2.1 floor from the 2.8% corrupt rows.

4x more training rows gives LightGBM a modestly better fit on the ~97% valid test rows (typical taxi-fare learning curves show ~0.1 RMSE gain per 4-5x data), but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows and heavy-tailed fare noise dilute it, so the total drops only from ~4.10 to ~4.01; hyperparameters are unchanged and runtime should fit the budget.

Airport distances let the model isolate flat-fare JFK and surcharge-heavy EWR/LGA trips with single splits instead of multi-split coordinate boxes, which typically cuts clean-row RMSE a few percent; the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows and 10k-row test noise dilute this to a modest overall gain.

RMSE is scored in dollars, so the optimal predictor is the conditional mean; L2 on log1p targets the geometric mean and systematically underpredicts long/expensive and heavy-tailed fares (including the ~2.8% corrupt-coordinate rows, where the mean is well above the geometric mean), and the raw model with 900K rows and min_child_samples=100 is already robust enough that the lost outlier influence doesn't compensate — typical Kaggle reports for this competition show log targets slightly hurting dollar RMSE.

Fare is not monotone in haversine distance in this data: zero-distance GPS-glitch rows (~1% of valid rows) carry near-average fares while short real trips cost ~$5, and long-distance glitches have normal fares, so the constraint forces biased predictions there; plus LightGBM's default 'basic' method over-constrains the dominant feature and slows fitting, while 4M rows already make the regularization benefit negligible, so expect a small regression.

The metric is dollar-scale RMSE, so a log1p target trains toward the conditional geometric mean: expm1 of the log prediction underestimates the conditional mean (retransformation bias of a few percent, worst on the high-fare trips that dominate squared error) and de-emphasizes expensive airport/long trips during fitting, which in this competition has consistently cost a few percent of RMSE for GBMs; the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the effect, so expect a modest regression from 4.126 to roughly 4.21.

In-sample encoding makes route_fare_mean a deterministic function of each row's own fare for the many singleton/low-count 2km route keys ((y+20*gm)/21), which LightGBM decodes via fine splits; at test time unseen routes (count 0, mean=gm, a value never seen in training) and count-1 routes get predictions pulled toward the global mean or a 1-NN fare, hurting exactly the long, high-variance trips that dominate RMSE, outweighing the tiny log(0.8) count mismatch the OOF scheme introduces.

The metric is RMSE on the raw dollar scale, so a log1p target makes the model fit a conditional-median/geometric-mean that systematically underpredicts the heavy right tail (airport, out-of-town, $100+ trips) which dominates squared error; with 1M rows and min_child_samples=100 the raw-target LightGBM is not destabilised by outliers, so the variance-stabilising benefit is small and retransformation bias wins, giving a modest worsening (the ~2.8% corrupt-row floor is unchanged and damps the relative effect).

Airport-distance features are a well-known strong signal in this competition (JFK flat fare, Newark surcharge), letting trees isolate high-fare airport trips with one split; on 1M rows this typically cuts valid-row RMSE by ~3-5%, but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from 2.8% corrupt test rows dilutes the overall gain to roughly 2-3%.

The 2.8% invalid test rows currently all get the global valid-row mean; with NaN handling, the ~0.3% passenger_count=0 rows that actually have good coordinates get real distance-based predictions, and the zero/out-of-box coordinate rows get the model's learned mean for that population plus year/pickup-side information, trimming the ~4.4 MSE 'floor' by roughly 0.5 while valid-row accuracy is barely affected by the ~2% NaN rows retained in training.

4x more training rows with identical features/hyperparameters gives a modest but real variance reduction (known taxi-fare learning curves show ~3-5% clean-RMSE gain per ~4x data), but the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows and the unchanged 1000-tree cap dilute the total improvement to roughly 2-3%; float32/usecols/n_jobs changes are metric-neutral and the run fits the budget.

OOF route/cell target encodings add a genuine pickup×dropoff interaction (tolls, airport flat fares) that 1000 trees on raw coords only approximate, so expect a modest gain on the ~3.6 valid-row RMSE; the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor dilutes any gain and TE on top of raw lat/lon is partly redundant, so improvement should be small (~1-2%), with some chance of no change.

Metric is dollar-space RMSE, whose optimal predictor is the conditional mean; training on log1p and back-transforming yields roughly the conditional geometric mean/median, systematically underpredicting skewed segments (zero-distance trips, long/odd rides) and especially the time-only fallback for the ~2.8% corrupt rows (fallback drops from ~$11.3 mean to ~$9 geometric mean, adding bias on rows that already dominate error), so expect a modest regression of a few percent, consistent with the common Kaggle finding that log-target hurt RMSE here.

Manhattan distance, abs coordinate deltas and bearing are well-known useful additions for this competition (grid-aligned metered fares, direction-dependent tolls/airport trips) that trees cannot cheaply synthesize from raw coordinates plus haversine; the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows and heavy label noise cap the gain, so expect a modest but real improvement of roughly 0.05-0.1 RMSE rather than a large one.

Airport/landmark distances are a well-known strong feature for this competition (JFK flat fare, airport surcharges) and let trees isolate those regimes more cleanly than raw lat/lon splits; with 4M rows the gain is real but modest, and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes it, so expect roughly 4.10 -> ~4.00.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean; an L1 objective fits the conditional median of a right-skewed fare distribution, systematically underpredicting airport/toll/long trips where squared errors dominate, and L2 leaf values with ~45k samples per leaf are already robust to the rare outliers, so the objective swap should worsen RMSE by roughly 4-7% (the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dampens the relative hit).

Metric is raw-dollar RMSE, so the log1p model targets the conditional geometric mean/median and systematically underpredicts the right-skewed fares (Jensen bias, largest on long/airport trips that dominate squared error) while also down-weighting high-fare rows during training; the ~2.1 RMSE floor from unchanged fallback rows dampens but does not cancel the regression, a pattern repeatedly reported in this competition.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean, but regression_l1 targets the conditional median of a right-skewed fare distribution (and ignores the same heavy-tail noise that is present in the test labels), so predictions are biased low, most severely on the long/airport trips that dominate squared error; the sign-based gradients also fit the high-fare structure less precisely, so valid-row RMSE rises from ~3.6 to ~3.8 and the total from 4.14 to roughly 4.36.

RMSE rewards the conditional mean, but Huber with delta=$1 on fares with std ~$10 behaves almost like L1 (median-biased on a right-skewed target), and because LightGBM's huber uses clipped gradients with a constant unit hessian, each round can move a prediction at most lr*alpha=$0.05, so 1000 rounds from the ~$11 mean cap predictions near $60 and leave airport/long-haul fares badly under-predicted; the tail under-convergence plus median bias should add roughly 2-4 to the MSE, a clear regression.

The grader is raw-dollar RMSE, whose optimal predictor is the conditional mean; fitting log1p and back-transforming yields the conditional geometric mean, systematically underpredicting (most in the high-fare/airport/anomaly rows that dominate squared error), and taxi fares are additive (base + per-mile + tolls) rather than multiplicative, so the log scale buys no structural benefit — a modest regression on the ~97% valid rows while the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor is unchanged.

Airport distance/flag features are a known useful signal (JFK flat fares) that trees capture more sample-efficiently than via raw lat/lon splits, but the ~2.8% corrupt test rows impose a ~2.1 RMSE floor that dilutes any valid-row gain, so expect a modest improvement from 4.13 to about 4.06.

4x more training rows from the same random-order file gives LightGBM better-estimated splits/leaf values (likely using all 1000 trees since early stopping won't trigger), typically cutting learnable-portion RMSE by ~0.1-0.15; but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from 2.8% corrupt test rows and heavy irreducible fare noise dilute this to roughly a 3% overall gain, with modest capacity (63 leaves, lr 0.05, 1000 trees) capping further benefit.

Averaging 5 fold-models trained on 80% subsets gives modest variance reduction over one model on 90% (slightly less data per model offsets part of it); the ~2.8% corrupt test rows impose a fixed error floor that dilutes any gain, so expect a small but consistent improvement of roughly 0.5%.

OOF-smoothed pickup-cell mean fare adds a mostly redundant spatial summary (LightGBM already has raw coordinates and the actual trip distance, which dominates); fine-grained 100m cell means are mostly noise beyond neighborhood/airport scale, and ~2.8% corrupt test rows dilute any gain, so expect a small, near-noise improvement rather than a meaningful drop.

Snapping to a 0.01-degree (~1 km) grid destroys the fine haversine distance signal that dominates fare prediction: within-cell-pair distance scatter of roughly 0.4 km at ~$2.5 per km adds about $1 of irreducible error in quadrature on valid rows, while the route encoding is already 0.01-cell based and gains nothing (and the floor-on-snapped floating-point collisions slightly coarsen it), so RMSE should worsen by a few hundredths to a tenth.

L1 targets the conditional median while RMSE rewards the conditional mean; taxi fares are right-skewed (tolls, traffic, airport trips) so the median model systematically underpredicts the heavy tail and sign-based gradients give weaker splits, while the unchanged 2.8% invalid-row floor and large 900K sample leave little room for robustness gains—expect a modest RMSE regression.

L1 objective makes the model predict conditional medians, which are biased low on the right-skewed fare distribution; the evaluation metric is RMSE, for which the L2-trained conditional mean is optimal, so the systematic underprediction of higher-fare segments adds squared bias (plus slower L1 convergence) and worsens RMSE by roughly 0.1-0.15 on top of the fixed ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows.

Airport distance features are a well-known strong signal in this competition (JFK flat fare, EWR surcharge) that trees struggle to isolate from raw coordinates alone; expect a modest but real drop in valid-row RMSE (~0.15), damped by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows.

L1 objective targets the conditional median, which systematically under-predicts the right-skewed fare mean and converges more slowly in LightGBM, so under an RMSE metric it should add bias-squared and underfit error on the valid rows (roughly 3.6 to ~3.8 RMSE) while the 2.8% corrupt-row floor is unchanged, giving a modest overall regression.

LightGBM's quantile binning already gives ~35m resolution in dense Manhattan on 2M rows with min_child_samples=100, so replacing raw coordinates with fixed ~1km grid cells removes fine location/toll-crossing information without a real regularization need; haversine is kept and airports stay identifiable, so the loss is small but likely a slight regression rather than a gain.

L1 targets the conditional median, which is systematically below the RMSE-optimal conditional mean for right-skewed taxi fares (traffic/waiting, tolls, recording errors that also appear in the test sample), and sign-based gradients converge less efficiently, so validation/test RMSE should rise a few percent while the 2.8% corrupt-row floor stays fixed.

A grid-rotated Manhattan distance is a well-known useful proxy for actual NYC street travel distance, but with raw coordinates plus haversine already present LightGBM can approximate most of it, so expect a small genuine gain (~0.02-0.03 RMSE) that is partially masked by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows and single-run noise.

OOF route-pair target encoding on ~1km cells gives the GBDT a precomputed pickup-dropoff interaction (tolls, airport flat fares, street-vs-haversine distance) that it only partially learns from raw coordinates; with 900K rows most Manhattan pairs have N>50 so the smoothed encoding is informative, but gains are capped by the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor and heavy-tailed outliers, so expect a small (~1%) improvement, with some chance of noise-level neutrality.

A grid-rotated Manhattan distance adds direction-relative-to-grid information that trees can't easily synthesize from raw coordinates plus haversine, giving a small real gain on the ~3.57 model component, but the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows and run-to-run noise cap the visible improvement at a few hundredths.

Doubling the sample to 2M rows gives LightGBM finer geographic/temporal resolution and lower leaf variance, typically ~1-2% gain on the clean portion of this task, but the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes that to a small overall drop of roughly 0.02-0.04; capacity (1000 trees, 63 leaves) is unchanged so gains are modest and well within budget.

Airport trips (flat-fare JFK, surcharged Newark) are a few percent of rows with large residuals; raw coordinates already let LightGBM carve out airports approximately, so the explicit route category yields a modest, mostly-positive gain, diluted further by the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows.

LightGBM handles the nominal f_27 letters natively (where the ordinal-encoded MLP loses most) and with 2000 rounds x 127 leaves on 720k rows can staircase-approximate the f_00+f_01+f_26 / f_02+f_21 / f_05+f_22 diagonal interactions reasonably, so it should land slightly above the small MLP, in the ~0.988-0.990 range typical of GBDT-without-FE on this competition.

This dataset's key signal the MLP exploits is additive threshold interactions on raw floats (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) which need within-feature resolution that 10 quantile one-hot bins destroy (only a coarse staircase remains); quantile edge collapsing also merges the top values of low-cardinality ints (f_29 likely collapses to one bin, f_30's 1/2 merge, integer tails merge), and f_27 handling is unchanged, so the small gain from direct per-bin weights on the count columns cannot offset the losses: expect a modest regression of roughly 0.003-0.005 AUC.

The 41 standardized columns are nearly uncorrelated, so full-rank PCA whitening is effectively a random rotation that smears the discrete f_27 character ordinals and small-range integer columns across all components; axis-aligned splits lose the clean categorical/threshold structure the trees currently exploit, and the linear-leaf design matrix was already well-conditioned, so expect a sizable regression rather than a gain.

f_27 has ~740k distinct values per 900k rows, so with m=20 smoothing the OOF target encoding collapses to ≈prior for ~75% of rows and a one-label noisy nudge for the rest; this effectively deletes the informative per-position ordinal character features (letters are genuinely ordinal/unique-count-correlated in this synthetic data), leaving a numeric-only model that should drop several AUC points.

f_27 is almost unique per row (~80%+ of strings occur once), so a smoothed full-string target encoding collapses to ~prior for nearly all rows and carries little signal, while the ten per-position ordinal columns it replaces are genuinely informative (the letters are ordinal latent variables that top solutions fed directly); dropping them leaves numeric + nunique only, costing several AUC points.

These are the well-known TPS-May-2022 interaction features (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26 with their thresholds) that encode the dataset's generating linear interactions, which axis-aligned trees approximate poorly; public results show LightGBM/XGBoost jumping from ~0.991-0.992 to ~0.996-0.997 once they are added, so a large, reliable gain is expected.

Equal-weight rank averaging a 0.984 LightGBM with a logistic regression that can only reach ~0.80-0.85 on ordinal-encoded chars and raw sums (no unique-count, no one-hot, no threshold interactions) adds no complementary signal and dilutes the strong model's ranking; the LR's large within-class rank spread flips many moderately-confident LGBM pairs, so expect a clear regression to roughly 0.93-0.96.

This dataset's additive feature interactions favor MLPs over trees (NNs dominated the TPS May 2022 leaderboard at ~0.998 with the AmbrosM 64-64-64-16 swish architecture this mirrors), but the proposed net lacks the strong unique_characters feature and trains for fewer epochs, so expect a large gain over the 0.984 LGBM yet short of 0.998.

This is essentially AmbrosM's TPS-May-2022 MLP recipe, which trivially learns the additive interactions (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22) that axis-aligned trees fail on, so it should beat the 0.977 LightGBM clearly; but without the unique-character-count feature (hard to recover from 10 ordinals in a width-64 net) it will fall short of the ~0.998 full-FE result, landing around 0.99.

The baseline is underfit at 3000 constant-leaf trees and its main deficit on this synthetic data is oblique sum-threshold boundaries (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) that staircases rank poorly; linear leaves orient ramps along those directions and converge faster, likely recovering a good part of that gap, while the combinatorial f_27 unique-count structure stays unaddressed and near-unregularized leaf fits plus a logloss-triggered early stop cap the gain, so I expect a modest improvement to roughly 0.98 provided the ~2x slower run finishes.

The count of distinct letters in f_27 was one of the key signals in this competition; it is a highly non-additive function of the 10 per-character ordinals that axis-aligned trees capture poorly, so an explicit column should yield a clear gain of roughly +0.005 to +0.01 AUC with the same LightGBM setup.

These three sums are the known key interactions in TPS May 2022 (sharp decision boundaries along f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22) that axis-aligned trees approximate poorly; adding them as raw features historically lifts GBDT from ~0.977 to ~0.994-0.996 AUC, with a small shortfall versus top GBDT runs since unique-char count of f_27 is still absent.

f_27 is almost entirely unique strings (~740k distinct per 900k rows), so after LightGBM's bin construction (min_data_in_bin) and min_data_per_group=100 the native categorical has essentially no usable splits; the change therefore amounts to deleting the 10 informative per-position ordinal columns and relying on bag-of-letter counts + nunique, which lose position-specific effects and should cost several thousandths of AUC.

The bigram categoricals mostly re-encode interactions the trees can already learn from the per-position ordinals and letter counts; the known big gains on this dataset come from numeric interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) not adjacent-char pairs, so expect roughly noise-level movement with a slight edge from native categorical splits adding per-tree capacity while the model is still iteration-limited at 3000 trees.

f_00..f_15 are near-independent so the 8 PCs are essentially random rotations that cannot reconstruct the key sum interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26, which involve columns outside the block); dropping the mined products loses their small gain while the PCs add roughly neutral oblique noise features, leaving AUC about where the plain baseline sits, slightly below the current score.

Hashing the whole ~741k-unique f_27 string into 64 buckets destroys the per-position letter signal (the letters are binned latent ordinals, which is why ordinal per-char encoding works), replacing 10 strong features with 64 target-independent noise one-hots; the model falls back to numeric-only signal, which historically lands around 0.91-0.94 AUC on this dataset.

ExtraTrees with sqrt(40)=6 random features and random thresholds approximates the XOR-like sum-band interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) and letter-combination structure far less efficiently than 3000 rounds of 127-leaf boosting, so I expect roughly 2-3 AUC points lost; additionally the 5-fold cross_val_predict adds ~4x the fit work on 800k rows with fully grown trees, so there is a real risk the run exceeds the 15-minute kill on an 8-core allocation.

This dataset's signal is dominated by additive sum-threshold interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) that an MLP learns in its first layer but trees staircase poorly, so NNs beat no-FE LightGBM here (competition NNs reached ~0.998 with FE); however this sklearn MLP lacks the unique-character count, uses lossy ordinal char encoding with ReLU, constant lr and ≤40 epochs with accuracy-based early stopping, so I expect a solid but not top-tier gain to roughly 0.99.

The f_27 unique-character count is a known top feature in TPS May 2022 (a 10-way interaction trees cannot reconstruct from per-position categoricals), and letter counts add order-invariant signal; public LightGBM results with these features land around 0.985-0.99, so expect a clear gain from 0.9768 without reaching the NN-level 0.998 that needs the numeric interaction features.

f_27 per-position letters are among the strongest signals in this synthetic data (target rate varies sharply by letter at several positions); ~82% of 10-char strings are unique so the frequency feature is nearly constant and carries almost no information, leaving essentially a numeric-only LightGBM, which historically scores ~0.91-0.93 on this competition.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is a known strong signal in this dataset that trees cannot easily reconstruct from 10 positional ordinals, so adding it (plus per-letter counts) should give a solid gain of roughly +0.005 to +0.009 AUC; the bigger remaining gap to ~0.99 comes from the f_02+f_21 / f_05+f_22 / f_00+f_01+f_26 interactions, which this change does not add, and runtime stays within budget.

The real interactions in this dataset are sign-antisymmetric sums (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26), which a products-only screening model can barely see since products are invariant to a global sign flip; the top-25 selection is therefore close to random with a modest chance of catching the key pairs, whose products only partially help trees approximate a diagonal boundary, so expect a small net gain of roughly +0.001 AUC with real risk of a flat or slightly negative result from 20-odd noise columns.

Refitting on all 800k rows with ~3333 trees adds 11% more data and slightly more capacity to a model that was still improving at 3000 trees, which typically yields a small but real AUC gain (~+0.0005) for GBDT at this scale; runtime roughly doubles (~7-9 min) but stays under the 15-minute kill.

Declaring the ten f_27 letter codes categorical lets LightGBM pick many-vs-rest partitions per split, but with 720k rows, 3000 deep trees already emulating letter subsets via multiple thresholds, and letters that look ordinal (Poisson-like A/B/C-heavy distributions), the effect should be near-neutral with at most a few 1e-4 AUC gain from faster convergence at the fixed tree budget.

Unique-character count of f_27 is a well-known strong latent feature in TPS May 2022 that axis-aligned trees cannot recover from the 10 per-position ordinals, so adding it explicitly should give a sizable gain (roughly +0.005 to +0.009 AUC) on top of the existing sum interaction, with negligible runtime cost.

Capping trees at depth 2 (4 leaves) turns the ensemble into a main-effects-plus-pairwise model, which cannot represent the high-order structure this synthetic dataset is built on (f_27 unique-character count across 10 positions, multi-way integer-feature interactions, char×numeric combos); only the explicitly supplied sum and the two remaining pairwise sums stay reachable, so holdout/test AUC should drop markedly from 0.982 toward the mid-0.94s even with all 3000 rounds used.

A small 600-tree/31-leaf/max_bin=63 LightGBM is underfit for this interaction-heavy synthetic data (the README's own 3000x127 LightGBM was still improving at the end); trees approximate the diagonal f_02+f_21-style boundaries crudely and cannot emulate the unique-char signal, so it should land a bit below the MLP's 0.982, likely ~0.97-0.98.

LightGBM handles the per-char ordinals and integer features natively, but 600 trees x 31 leaves at lr 0.05 is far from converged on this 800k-row dataset (even 3000x127 was still improving), and trees approximate the additive sum-threshold interactions and the unique-character effect poorly, so it should land slightly below the MLP's 0.982.

Collapsing the 16 continuous sensors to 4 quartile codes destroys the fine resolution LightGBM uses to staircase-approximate the known diagonal sum-threshold interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) and the heavy-tailed f_28 signal; the 255-bin default histograms already give compactness without the information loss, so this should regress noticeably rather than help.

Shrinking trees from 127 to 7 leaves cuts per-tree capacity ~20x on an 800k-row dataset whose target hinges on higher-order feature interactions (f_27 character combinations, summed-float thresholds); with the round budget fixed at 3000 and the big-tree model still improving at round 3000, the small-tree model will be badly underfit and lose ~2 AUC points.

num_leaves=4 trees (≤3 splits each) cannot efficiently capture this dataset's key 2- and 3-way sum interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) or char-position combos; 3000 rounds at lr 0.05 leaves the model underfit versus 127-leaf trees, so expect a clear AUC regression of roughly a percent.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known planted linear interactions in TPS May 2022 that axis-aligned trees approximate poorly; exposing the 3-way sum directly typically lifts LightGBM AUC by ~0.002 (each interaction worth ~0.001-0.002, all three ~0.005), so expect a clear but partial gain from 0.9915 toward the ~0.996 full-interaction GBDT level.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the three known step-threshold interactions in this synthetic data; a 3D diagonal threshold is hard for axis-aligned trees to approximate, so exposing the raw sum lets LightGBM split directly at the ±5 steps and should yield a solid but partial gain (the other two interactions and unique-char count remain missing).

This dataset's key interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) are linear sums that trees approximate with staircases but an MLP learns natively, and the MLP can partially recover the f_27 unique-character structure from the ordinal positions; NNs on raw features in this competition typically landed around 0.99, below the ~0.998 ceiling that requires the explicit unique-count feature, and the 50-epoch/420s CPU budget leaves it somewhat under-trained.

The f_27 letters are binned latent ordinal values (bell-shaped letter frequencies, NN on ordinal codes reaches 0.998), so numeric thresholds already capture the structure; LightGBM categorical splits add cat_l2/cat_smooth regularization and discard the ordering prior, giving roughly neutral to very slightly worse AUC with 800k rows and ≤26 categories.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is a well-known top-importance feature in TPS May 2022 that axis-aligned trees cannot reconstruct from the ten per-position ordinals, so it adds genuinely new signal; GBDT with this plus interaction features reached ~0.995-0.996, and unique-count alone should carry most of that gap, lifting the 0.977 baseline to roughly 0.99.

Target-dependent weighting mismatches the unweighted RMSE metric: the weighted-MSE optimum is a darkness-biased conditional mean, so at ambiguous stroke edges and stain-vs-faint-text pixels (where the residual error actually lives) predictions shift darker and incur extra unweighted error, while confidently-white pixels gain nothing; any benefit from extra gradient focus on strokes is likely offset, giving a small regression within a few percent.

Training ~5-8x more steps (roughly 10-20k vs 2000) with a proper cosine anneal to zero should let the small U-Net fit text strokes and stain removal much better, and since test scans are re-noised copies of training pages, extra fitting/memorization helps rather than hurts; expect a solid but diminishing-returns gain, with the run comfortably inside the time limit.

Targets are ~83% exactly-white with near-binary ink, so L1's constant gradient pushes background/stain regions to exact 1.0 and sharpens strokes (where MSE+sigmoid stalls with small residuals), which the restoration literature shows usually improves RMSE too; the offset is median-vs-mean hedging on genuinely ambiguous stain-over-text pixels, so I expect a modest net gain (~3-8%) with real risk of a small regression and seed noise of a few percent.

Train and test are an i.i.d. split with identical synthetic noise statistics, so input-only brightness/contrast jitter widens the input distribution beyond anything seen at test time and makes the intensity-to-target mapping on anti-aliased stroke edges (where most of the error lives) ambiguous; with only 2000 steps the undertrained U-Net spends capacity learning exposure-normalization it never needs, so I expect a small regression roughly within seed-noise range rather than a regularization gain.

Scale TTA is out-of-distribution for a U-Net trained only at native scale on thin (~1.5-2 px) anti-aliased text, and the 0.75x/1.25x round-trip resampling adds ~0.6-0.8 px of systematic blur to two-thirds of the averaged output; for per-pixel RMSE on sharp strokes this coherent edge-softening error (plus weaker page memorization at off-scales) outweighs any stain-removal gain, so the averaged map should be clearly worse than the pure 1.0x flip-TTA baseline.

Channel dropout at p=0.2 on both e2 (incl. skip) and e3 feeding BatchNorm convs introduces train/eval variance shift and noisier gradients in a short 2000-step MSE regression run that shows little overfitting (test is i.i.d. re-noised copies of training pages), so pixel-level fit degrades modestly rather than generalization improving.

Test scans are re-noised copies of the training pages, so memorization is an asset here, not a liability; Dropout2d in every block (including the bottleneck and the skip features) slows convergence under the fixed 180s budget, introduces a BN variance shift between train and eval modes that biases the near-constant white background, and dropout in intermediate layers of pixel-regression restoration nets is known to lower fidelity, so expect a moderate regression rather than a gain.

Adding a 1/8-resolution stage doubles the receptive field (41->89 px) and quadruples capacity, which helps estimate large stains/global tint and memorize the 36 reused pages; the ~40% higher per-step cost only trims steps within the fixed 180 s budget, so a moderate RMSE gain is more likely than a regression.

A 23x23 median background channel is a classic, cheap, correctly-implemented feature for this task that lets the small U-Net (RF ~41px, only 2000 steps) spend less capacity estimating local tint/stain level and more on text edges, so I expect a modest, real gain (~3-6%) with seed noise of roughly ±2-3% making a small regression possible but unlikely; runtime impact is negligible.

Deeper 5-level U-Net raises the receptive field from ~40px to ~185px and adds ~15x capacity, which helps both large-scale stain/tint background estimation and page/glyph memorization on this re-noised-page test set; compute only ~2x so it fits the budget, optimization with BN+Adam should stay stable, giving a moderate RMSE gain rather than a dramatic one given the fixed 2000-step budget.

Model was trained with random h/v flips so all four TTA views are in-distribution; averaging a 4-way self-ensemble on a briefly-trained small U-Net typically cuts pixel RMSE by ~1-3% (variance reduction on stroke edges and stain regions) with negligible runtime cost and no risk from padding since padded dims are multiples of 8.

The 180 s wall-clock budget (implemented at half the spec's 360 s) should still yield roughly 4-7x the baseline's 2000 steps on a modern GPU (~15-30 ms/step for this 470K-param UNet at batch 32x128x128), and the baseline is clearly undertrained on a task where test scans are re-noised copies of training pages, so longer cosine-decayed training should lower RMSE with little overfitting risk, though the small receptive field and capacity give diminishing returns.

Charbonnier/L1 is near-neutral on an RMSE metric: it trades slightly worse conditional-mean estimates on ambiguous stain/edge pixels for cleaner flat white background (83% of pixels) and smoother convergence in a short 2000-step budget, which in restoration literature (Zhao et al., EDSR) typically yields a small 1-3% RMSE gain; expect a marginal improvement within run-to-run noise.

Sigma-0.05 iid Gaussian noise (~13/255) is mismatched to the structured stain/tint noise and is large relative to the ~0.015 RMSE precision needed on anti-aliased text edges, so the net learns a smoother, context-averaging mapping (plus a BN train/test statistics mismatch) that slightly blurs stroke edges on the un-noised test scans; the regularization gain is minimal since the model is not strongly overfitting noise realizations, yielding a mild regression.

The stated BN train/test mismatch is largely illusory here (batch 32 of uniformly sampled 128x128 crops gives running stats equal to full-page statistics, so eval-mode BN is just a fixed, purely local affine), whereas GroupNorm makes every feature depend on per-image spatial statistics that differ between dense-text/margin crops and full pages; such spatial normalization is known to slightly hurt low-level restoration regression (stroke-edge gray levels, white-level calibration through the sigmoid), and GN also converges a bit slower than BN in a fixed 2000-step budget, so I expect a small regression within a few percent, with some chance of neutrality from GN's partial invariance to global page tint.

The metric is RMSE and MSE already optimizes it directly; the SSIM+L1 mix pushes the net to commit to ink-or-white at ambiguous stain/faded-text pixels (median/mode instead of the hedged mean), which raises squared error there, and SSIM is nearly blind to low-frequency luminance offsets, so despite crisper strokes and flatter backgrounds the net RMSE should slip by a few percent.

8x dihedral TTA is a pure variance-reduction change on a small, somewhat noisy U-Net; the flip transforms are in-distribution (training used h/v flips) and the rot90 variants are only mildly OOD for local stroke-vs-stain denoising, so Jensen-style averaging should yield a modest ~2-4% RMSE gain with negligible runtime cost.

Pure SSIM is misaligned with the RMSE metric on a bimodal document (83% flat white): it weights local texture/structure ~1000x more than smooth luminance offsets (via C2), so tint/stain residue is under-penalized, and because the loss runs inside the bf16 autocast block the conv-based variance terms suffer catastrophic cancellation (blur(x^2)-mu^2 quantized to ~0.004 steps vs C2=0.0009), producing spiky, noisy gradients in flat regions; training should still converge (Adam, saturating sigmoid whites) but to a worse per-pixel optimum, so a moderate regression is most likely.

Linear residual head removes sigmoid-MSE gradient saturation and lets the inference clamp absorb overshoot on the ~85% white background, giving slightly better calibration within the fixed 2000-step budget; offset by the fact that the residual here is the complex stain field (not a simple zero-mean noise) requiring a precise input passthrough, so the net effect is a small gain of a few percent, well within the range where a seed could flip it.

Under Adam the sqrt(MSE) keeps the per-batch gradient direction identical to MSE (only changing Adam's effective step size), and the 0.1-weighted SSIM term is dominated by RMSE gradients in text/stain regions while mainly adding a local-variance flattening push in flat background; net effect on a pixel-RMSE metric should be within run-to-run noise, with a slight lean toward a small regression since SSIM is not aligned with the graded objective.

Residual learning on a skip-connected U-Net adds little, while dropping the sigmoid removes a saturation prior that snaps the 83% white background to exactly 1.0; the linear residual must regress the exact tint/stain offset and leaks faint input texture into flat regions (only half-recovered by the clamp), so expect a small, within-noise regression.

Synthetic pairs make up ~86% of sampled patches but their noise is crude and mismatched (whole-image Gaussian blur with sigma 1-4 destroys text contrast, light elliptical stains, mild 0.85-1.0 shading), so with the fixed 2000-step budget the gradient is dominated by an ill-posed deblurring task while exposure to real tint/texture/wrinkle noise drops ~7x; identical clean targets and some stain/shading transfer limit the damage, but a mild regression is more likely than a gain.

A 470k-param U-Net on 22.7M training pixels is undertrained at 2k steps; 4.5x more steps under a stretched cosine schedule should keep lowering train/val RMSE with little overfitting risk and comfortably fits the time budget on GPU, so expect a solid but diminishing-returns gain to roughly 0.013-0.014.

8-fold dihedral TTA on a small, briefly-trained U-Net averages out prediction variance (flip views are in-distribution thanks to flip augmentation); the 4 transposed views are out-of-distribution (vertical text) but document denoising is mostly local and orientation-agnostic, so they should be only modestly worse and still add decorrelated averaging benefit, giving a small net gain (~3-5%) with negligible runtime cost.

L1 optimizes the conditional median and spreads gradient evenly over the 83% near-white bulk, so it de-emphasizes exactly the heavy-residual pixels (stained strokes, misjudged blobs) that dominate a squared-error metric; the cleaner-background and sharper-edge gains from L1 are small given the illumination-normalized input already removes most tint, so I expect a small net regression in RMSE, within seed noise of neutral.

Reweighting toward dark targets mismatches the plain-RMSE metric: on ambiguous ink-vs-stain pixels the weighted optimum biases predictions darker (raising per-pixel MSE 20-30% there) and downweights the 83% white background where residual stains live; any gain from crisper glyph interiors in a 2000-step underfit U-Net is likely smaller, so expect a small regression within run-to-run noise.

Weighting the loss 10:1 toward dark targets misaligns training with the unweighted RMSE metric: the optimal predictor under target-dependent weights is biased darker in ambiguous regions (stroke edges, stain residues near text), so strokes thicken and stains clear less completely; the model still trains fine in budget, but I expect a modest regression rather than a gain.

Residual (identity-initialized) prediction preserves stroke detail from step 0 and speeds convergence in this short 2000-step budget, and the linear output with inference-time clamp optimizes MSE more faithfully than a saturating sigmoid (overshoots on white get clipped to zero error); the U-Net's existing skips limit the gain, so expect a modest ~3-7% RMSE improvement rather than a large one.

L1 on sigmoid outputs behaves like BCE in logit-gradient terms, so it keeps pushing the 83% pure-white background to exact white and sharpens well-determined strokes (the known L1>L2 PSNR effect in restoration nets), which should slightly outweigh the RMSE penalty from median-style committing on the small fraction of ambiguous stain/faded-text pixels; expect a modest ~3% gain, within seed-noise of neutral.

Zero-init residual output trains stably and starts near identity, but the target is ~83% exactly-white near-binary pixels where the sigmoid's saturation is a strong inductive bias; the linear residual must precisely regress (1 - x) per pixel (tint level, texture cancellation), leaving a small noise floor on backgrounds that clipping only half-removes, so I expect a small regression rather than a DnCNN-style gain within the fixed 2000-step budget.

Halving BASE_CH cuts parameters ~4x with the same 2000-step budget; the model is underfit rather than overfit on this task, so reduced capacity (especially the 8-channel first stage for fine stroke detail) should modestly worsen RMSE rather than regularize, likely landing around 0.018-0.020.

Weighting dark target pixels 3x mismatches the unweighted RMSE metric: the weighted-MSE optimum biases uncertain pixels (anti-aliased stroke edges, faint stains) darker, adding a small bias term and shifting gradient mass away from the 83% white background that dominates the metric; with the same 2000-step schedule the net effect is likely a slight regression within run-to-run noise rather than a gain.

Biggest risk is implementation, not the idea: execution.json forces CPU with 8 threads, and 2000 steps of this U-Net at 32x128x128 (~700 TFLOPs fp32) takes roughly 25-60 min on 8 CPU threads, so the run very likely hits the 15-min hard kill with no submission; if it does complete (lenient/strong node), the closing-normalized channel is a well-known strong feature for this competition (removes tint/stain background explicitly), so expect a modest 5-10% RMSE gain to ~0.015, with run-to-run noise of ~0.001.

4-view flip TTA on a flip-augmented U-Net usually trims RMSE ~2-3% (variance reduction on stroke edges/stains); but the diff also sneaks in runtime.json with CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='' forcing CPU fp32 training with 13 threads, so there is a real risk the 2000-step run hits the 15-min hard kill — the number assumes it completes.

Compact NAFNet (5x fewer FLOPs than the U-Net, 16-channel depthwise high-res path, SCA global pooling trained on 128x128 patches but applied to full 540x420 pages) under the same 2k-step budget should roughly match the BN U-Net; residual output and ~100px receptive field help stains but don't clearly outweigh the lost per-pixel capacity, so expect a wash to slight regression; also the added runtime.json hardcodes device=cpu with 13 threads, so the run risks exceeding the 15-minute kill if the node is GPU-based.

The pretrained IN-1k head is a second linear classifier on the same 1024-d features but trained on ~1200 images/class (including these very Stanford-Dogs images), so with temperature tuning it should be roughly as strong as the 77-images/class LR (~0.3 holdout); blending two partially-decorrelated predictors with w/T tuned on a holdout that transfers cleanly to test typically yields a 10-25% log-loss reduction, mapping is exact and compute is unchanged.

L2-regularized LR is rotation-invariant, so PCA(256) without whitening only truncates the 768 lowest-variance directions; the tuned L2 penalty already down-weights those, so the change mostly discards some fine-grained discriminative signal (look-alike breed pairs) and typically costs a linear probe a small but real amount, giving a modest log-loss regression rather than a gain.

Full-strength Mixup(0.8)+CutMix(1.0) at p=1.0 is a long-schedule regularizer; with only 6 epochs (~776 steps) of fine-tuning from a backbone that already encodes these breeds, it slows head/backbone convergence and should cost ~1 pt clean val accuracy, while the calibration benefit is largely already captured by the existing temperature scaling (ConvNeXt's own fine-tune recipe and BiT's small-data rule both drop mixup), so I expect a small regression within noise, roughly 0.44->0.455.

With only 6 epochs (~780 steps) the model is schedule-limited, and scale=(0.08,1) adds many near-uninformative fur/background patches plus a larger train/test apparent-object-size mismatch versus the Resize256/CenterCrop224 eval (FixRes effect); the regularization gain on ~77 imgs/class is unlikely to offset that in a short fine-tune, so expect a small regression within noise, roughly +0.01 to +0.03 log loss.

ConvNeXt-V2-L (IN-22k→1k, 87.3% top-1) saw these exact ImageNet dog images during supervised training and its pre-logits plus 1000-d log-probs are far more separable than ResNet-50's; frozen-feature + LogReg on this backbone family typically lands around 0.10-0.18 log loss on this competition, the implementation (forward_head pre_logits, head.fc, model eval transform, fp16-safe GRN) looks correct and the run fits the budget, so expect a large drop from 0.449 with the small 1,023-image test adding noise.

The 1000-d log-softmax block is nearly linear in the pooled features (the LSE term cancels in the 120-way softmax), so it adds little capacity but it gives the L2-regularised LR cheap access to the ImageNet fc's dog-class directions, which were learned from ~17x more dog images including the very test images (Stanford Dogs is an ImageNet-train subset); that pretrained-prior effect outweighs the mild noise cost of the 880 standardised non-dog columns, so dropping the block should cost a few hundredths of log loss (~0.47-0.52 range).

Ridge/least-squares probes match LR accuracy on these strong frozen features, but a single global temperature on bounded ±1-scale LS scores mis-maps intermediate-confidence (confusable-breed) points that dominate log loss, so expect a modest regression versus the directly log-loss-optimised multinomial LR, not a catastrophe.

Unsupervised PCA to 128 dims per block discards low-variance directions that still carry fine-grained breed cues (the hard look-alike pairs that dominate log loss); L2-regularised LR with holdout-tuned C already handles the 2560-d overfitting risk, so the compression mostly loses information and the renormalised 384-d head gives a modestly worse log loss.

ConvNeXt-Base in22k->in1k pre-logit features are far more discriminative than ResNet-50 V1 pooled features on these ImageNet-derived dog images (the model has effectively seen these classes/images), so a holdout-tuned LogReg should jump from ~87% to ~94% accuracy and roughly halve the log loss; the residual loss comes from look-alike breed pairs and the small, noisy 1023-image test set.

ConvNeXt-Tiny in22k features are far stronger than frozen ResNet-50 V1 on these ImageNet-derived dog images, and full fine-tuning with augmentation, flip TTA and validation-fitted temperature scaling should reach ~92-94% accuracy with decent calibration; the run fits easily in budget and the code looks correct, so I expect a large drop to roughly 0.22-0.30 log loss, tempered slightly by label smoothing flattening second-choice probabilities and the 10% held-out validation split.

The 120 breeds are ImageNet classes and these Stanford-Dogs images largely sit in ILSVRC-train, so the discarded fc head is a strong (partly memorized) breed classifier whose log-probs give the L2-regularized LR cheap access to fine-grained directions it cannot estimate well from 7.8k samples in 2048-d; with StandardScaler and holdout-tuned C the ensemble-like gain should cut log loss by roughly 10-25%, with small downside risk from 880 noisy non-dog dims and standardization, and some timeout risk from five lbfgs fits.
