ConvNeXt-B in22k frozen features alone are far stronger than ResNet-50 V1 on these ImageNet dog images it has effectively seen (~0.22-0.28 expected), and L2-normalised concatenation with complementary CLIP and DINOv2 features plus holdout-tuned C mirrors the multi-backbone LR recipes that reached ~0.2 on the original Kaggle LB; compute is a few minutes so it fits the budget, with residual risk from label noise and the small noisy test split.

Focal loss (γ=2) acts as an implicit entropy regularizer without label smoothing's hard 0.9 confidence cap, so it should give better refinement (confident on easy, soft on confusable breeds) and comparable calibration, while its reduced gradient on already-fit examples perturbs the strong pretrained backbone less at the aggressive lr=0.01; accuracy may dip slightly without LS, so net effect is a small, uncertain improvement in log loss.

Stanford Dogs is literally ImageNet data, so pretrained early/mid features need no adaptation and lr=0.01/m=0.9 full fine-tuning likely degrades them slightly (per Li et al. L2-SP / 'rethinking fine-tuning hyperparameters' findings on Dogs); freezing conv1-layer3 keeps those features intact and mildly regularizes layer4+fc, so I expect a small accuracy/calibration gain, though with a 1k-image test set and ~15M params still trainable the effect is modest and could be noise-level either way.

Horizontal-flip TTA on frozen ViT-B/16 features averages two highly correlated probability vectors, slightly softening overconfident errors; this reliably gives a small log-loss gain (~1-3%) with essentially no risk, and the NUM_WORKERS change is result-neutral.

The current ViT-B/16 augreg backbone was trained on ImageNet-1k/21k, which contains these exact 120 breeds (and these very Stanford Dogs images), so its frozen features are near-optimal for this task; CLIP ViT-B/32 has no breed-level supervision, a coarse 7x7 patch grid that hurts fine-grained fur/face cues, and a known linear-probe deficit on ImageNet-class fine-grained sets (e.g. Pets 90.0 vs ~94 for supervised ViTs, Birdsnap 58.5 vs ~74), so I expect accuracy to drop from roughly 86% to the mid-70s and log loss to rise substantially under the unchanged C=0.3 probe.

L2-regularized LR is rotation-invariant, so PCA(256, no whitening) is a pure hard truncation of ~1800 mid/low-variance directions (~20-25% of variance) that a C=0.3-tuned probe was still partly exploiting for fine-grained breed cues; ridge-style shrinkage already handles noise directions, so unsupervised truncation typically costs ~0.5-1% accuracy and a few percent log loss rather than helping, with C now also slightly over-regularizing the smaller space.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 CLS features are far more linearly separable on fine-grained breeds than ResNet-50 V1 pooled features (e.g. Pets linear probe 96.2% vs ~92%, ImageNet linear 84.5% vs 76%), so with holdout-tuned C and the same 10-view TTA the log loss should drop substantially, though intrinsic look-alike pairs (Norfolk/Norwich, husky/eskimo, poodle sizes) and CLS-only features at 224px with ~77 shots/class keep it well above the fine-tuned-ensemble regime.

The current head is heavily over-regularized (unit-norm 2816-d features with C=1 yields underconfident ~0.54 despite ~90%+ accuracy); whitening to 256 unit-variance components raises the feature scale ~100x, effectively loosening regularization to a regime that strong frozen dog features usually tolerate well (Kaggle raw-feature LR anchors ~0.3), but whitening amplifies nuisance low-variance directions and truncation drops some ResNet-specific signal, so part of the gain is eaten by overconfident errors on look-alike breeds; net expected modest improvement with real regression risk.

Distance-weighted 10-NN gives near-hard vote fractions; the 1e-3 uniform mix leaves any test image with zero true-class neighbors at p≈0.0009 (loss ≈7.0), and with ~3% such outliers/look-alike misses plus coarse 0.1-step probabilities on the ~15% partially-mixed neighborhoods, the heavy tail outweighs the 0.11 floor on clean hits, so log loss likely rises from 0.54 to roughly 0.6 despite similar top-1 accuracy to the linear probe.

End-to-end fine-tuning with RRC/flip augmentation, label smoothing and a cosine schedule should add a few points of accuracy over the frozen linear probe and calibrate errors better, but the ImageNet overlap means frozen ResNet-50 features are already near-optimal and LS 0.1 imposes a ~0.1-nat floor on confident correct predictions, so only a modest log-loss gain (roughly 0.45 -> ~0.41) is expected, with real risk of a neutral result.

ViT-B/16 augreg in21k→in1k (84.5% top-1, trained on these very ImageNet dog images) yields far more class-discriminative frozen features than ResNet-50 V1; on this Kaggle task stronger backbones historically map ~0.45 (ResNet50) → ~0.2-0.3 (Inception/NASNet-class), so with LR C=0.3 on raw 768-d CLS features expect ~93-95% accuracy and log loss around 0.2, floored by look-alike breed pairs and a little label noise.

10-crop+flip TTA on frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 features is a classic variance-reduction win (ResNet paper: ~2pt top-1 gain); averaging probabilities mainly softens the confidently-wrong center-crop predictions that dominate log loss, with only mild train/test crop mismatch for the LR head, so expect a modest ~4-7% improvement rather than a large one.

ConvNeXt-T in22k_ft_in1k features are far more discriminative than ResNet-50 V1 (and it has effectively seen these ImageNet dog images), so accuracy should rise to ~90%+, but row-L2-normalising to unit norm with C=1.0 and only ~77 samples/class is ~100x more regularised than the baseline's tuned regime, giving an underconfident nearest-centroid-like fit (typical p_correct ~0.8) that caps the log-loss gain; net a moderate improvement to roughly 0.35-0.45 rather than the ~0.25 a well-tuned C would reach.

The pretrained ImageNet head restricted to the 120 dog classes is a strong, differently-trained linear classifier on the same features (and has seen these ImageNet-derived images during pretraining), so a holdout-tuned temperature + convex blend with the LR should reliably cut log loss by roughly 10-20%, mainly by softening the LR's confidently-wrong fine-grained confusions; selection on an 80% LR and a 1.8k holdout adds only small bias/noise.

Unwhitened PCA to 256-d is an orthogonal projection, so with the same C=0.3 it is equivalent to constraining the already-tuned L2 logistic regression to the top-256 variance subspace; most between-class signal survives (near-neutral is plausible), but subtle low-variance directions that separate look-alike breeds are discarded and C is not retuned for the smaller space, so I expect a mild log-loss regression rather than a gain.

ResNet-50's ImageNet head was trained on average-pooled features (and these dog images overlap ImageNet train), so GAP features are near-optimally linearly separable; global max pooling discards that alignment, adds spatial-outlier noise, and its ~5x larger raw scale makes C=0.3 effectively 20-25x weaker regularization on unstandardized features, so accuracy drops a few points and log loss rises materially despite temperature scaling.

IMAGENET1K_V2 lifts ImageNet top-1 from 76.1% to 80.9%, and since the 120 breeds are ImageNet classes the regularized, class-separated V2 penultimate features should be markedly more linearly separable for this probe (Kaggle precedent: ~80%-top-1 backbones give ~0.25-0.30 log loss); gains are tempered by C=0.3 being tuned for V1 feature scale and label-smoothing-induced overconfidence that temperature scaling only partly fixes.

C=0.3 was already the holdout-selected optimum for this LR; 10x stronger L2 yields an underfit, underconfident head, and the gentle 288-step SGD fine-tune (head lr 1e-3, conv lr 1e-4) only partially re-sharpens it, so the run should land modestly worse than baseline.

Running a 224-trained ResNet50 at 192px discards ~26% of pixels and worsens the train/test apparent-object-size mismatch; fine-grained breed cues (fur texture, ear/muzzle shape) degrade, and the refit LR head plus light layer4[-1] tuning only partly compensates, so expect ~2 points lower accuracy and roughly 8-12% higher log loss, with no offsetting gain since both runs already finish 2 epochs well inside the 90s budget.

Unwhitened PCA-256 + LR with the same C=0.3 is just the raw-feature LR constrained to the top-256 variance subspace: it discards ~1800 directions the 2048-d model was actively fitting (L2 at C=0.3 barely touches mid-variance components), losing some fine-grained look-alike-breed signal while C was not re-tuned for the reduced space, so I expect a modest accuracy drop and slightly less confident correct predictions, pushing log loss up by a few hundredths rather than improving it.

Running an ImageNet-224-trained ResNet-50 at 192px shrinks apparent object size and discards fine texture detail (FixRes shows ~2-3pt ImageNet top-1 drop at 192); retraining the LR on the new features recovers some of it, but fine-grained breed discrimination still loses roughly 1-2 accuracy points, pushing log loss up a few hundredths.

V2 weights (80.9% vs 76.1% ImageNet top-1) give more class-discriminative pooled features for breeds that are themselves ImageNet classes; label-smoothing/long-schedule features cluster tighter so a 77-per-class LR recovers class templates better, outweighing the un-retuned C=0.3 and any feature-scale mismatch, so log loss should drop moderately rather than collapse.

C=0.3 was already tuned on holdout log loss so the LR is near-calibrated, but at the log-loss-optimal C a high-dim LR is typically still slightly overconfident (T≈1.1); a single scalar temperature fit on a 1380-sample stratified holdout is low-variance and the 85%→100% refit mismatch is small, so expect a modest ~1-3% log-loss gain, with some run-failure risk from the removed TORCH_HOME and the doubled LR fit time.

The head is copied from the converged LR optimum and the conv/head learning rates (1e-4 / 1e-3 SGD) over only ~288 small-batch steps move the weights by well under 1%, so the model stays essentially the frozen-feature LR solution with a tiny systematic descent; expect a marginal, noise-level improvement rather than a real fine-tuning gain.

Horizontal-flip TTA with probability averaging on near-flip-invariant frozen ResNet-50 features is a low-risk variance reduction; Jensen's inequality guarantees the averaged log loss is at most the mean of the two views' losses, and the flipped view is only mildly off-distribution for the LR, so expect a modest ~2-4% gain (not a large one) with negligible runtime cost.

1:1 undersampling discards 80-99.7% of negatives; for threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic the models train on ~1-3k rows with 60k-200k features, losing the ability to separate threats/hate from generic profanity and from benign uses of 'kill'/'jew'/'gay', while C values tuned for 159k rows become mis-scaled, so rare-label AUCs drop ~0.01-0.03 and common labels slip slightly, giving a net ~0.011 loss.

Char_wb n-grams reliably add ~0.002 AUC to linear models on this data (obfuscated profanity, rare labels), so NB-LogReg on word12+char should become the stronger single branch (~0.980+); the blend gains less than that because both branches now share the char block and become more correlated, and weak C=4 regularization adds mild overfit risk on threat/identity_hate, so expect a small net gain (~+0.0005 to +0.001) rather than a large one.

AUC is ranking-based so class imbalance does not bias linear-model rankings; 1:1 undersampling just discards ~90-99% of negatives (threat fits on 956 rows, identity_hate on 2.8k), removing hard negatives (non-threatening 'kill', non-hateful identity terms) and making the NB log-count ratio extremely noisy, so rare-label AUCs drop by 0.02-0.04 and common labels by ~0.005-0.01, degrading both branches and the stacked OOF features.

MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0) on 200k L2-normalised TF-IDF 1-2grams is heavily over-smoothed (positive-class mass for threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic is ~3-10k vs 200k pseudo-counts), so branch B drops from ~0.977 to roughly 0.90-0.93 mean AUC with rare labels worst; its probabilities also saturate so the stacked OOF features become near-binary and stop helping branch A, and the fixed 50/50 rank blend then pulls the strong word+char LR branch down by ~0.005-0.015, mostly via threat and identity_hate.

Mean-pooled self-trained Word2Vec + LR on Jigsaw typically lands ~0.94-0.96 mean AUC (pooling dilutes single-slur signal in long comments, rare labels suffer most), and the 3-epoch MLP on the same 200-d features is only modestly better and highly correlated with it; giving these two 2/3 of the rank-average weight drags the blend below the surviving NB-LogReg branch (~0.978), so the ensemble loses the strong word+char TF-IDF branch's gain and regresses to roughly 0.97 (assuming the ~9-11 min run finishes before the 15-min kill).

1:1 undersampling discards 95-99.7% of negatives; for sparse TF-IDF linear models that information loss (especially for threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic with ~1-3k training rows, noisy NB ratios, and a heavily overfit C=4 liblinear fit) degrades ranking of the diverse negative bulk and should cost roughly a point of mean AUC, with the MLP also undertrained on 5x fewer steps; run finishes well within budget.

A sparse TF-IDF EmbeddingBag MLP is roughly LR-quality (~0.978-0.981 standalone) but non-linear and multi-task, so a 1/4-weight rank blend should add a modest ~+0.0005-0.001; gain is capped because time guards likely allow only 1-2 epochs (and ~25% chance D never trains and the score is unchanged), with low but non-zero timeout risk.

Logistic regression's ranking is barely affected by class prior, so 1:1 undersampling just discards 80-99% of the negatives (hard negatives included); the big labels lose a few tenths of a point, while threat (956 rows), identity_hate and severe_toxic lose 1-2 AUC points because their models degrade toward generic toxicity detectors with noisy NB ratios and mis-scaled C, dragging the column mean down roughly 0.008.

Lowercasing/newline/whitespace steps are no-ops for TfidfVectorizer; de-obfuscation and IP/repeat canonicalization help the word branches slightly (esp. rare labels), but char_wb 2-6 grams already cover most obfuscation and the u/ur/r expansions plus suck/wtf/timestamp merges lose register signal, so net effect is near zero with a slight positive tilt.

Clean 5-fold OOF stacking of NB-LogReg into branch A (with cross-label columns and per-label learned weighting) should lift A_stacked above the current blend, but re-blending 50/50 with B double-counts the weaker branch and pulls the effective weighting B-heavy, so most of the stacking gain is given back; expect a near-neutral, slightly positive result (~+0.0003), with a real risk of the 30 extra liblinear fits pushing wall-clock toward the 15-minute kill.

A 3-epoch 64-unit multi-task MLP on the existing 60k TF-IDF matrix should train fine via sparse CSR in sklearn (~3-4 extra minutes, likely under the 15-min kill) and land around 0.975-0.978 alone; it adds nonlinearity and shared-representation signal for rare labels that the two linear branches lack, so an equal-weight rank blend most likely nudges the mean AUC up by roughly +0.0005 to +0.001, with modest downside if the undertrained MLP is weaker than expected.

Branch C (NB-weighted LR on word 1-2gram + char_wb) is a hybrid of A and B, likely ~0.979 alone and highly correlated with both, so the equal three-way rank blend should add a small diversity gain (+0.0003 to +0.0007) over 0.9801; main risk is runtime, since liblinear on a ~110M-nnz matrix for 100 iterations x 6 labels adds ~4-5 min on top of an already ~8-9 min run, and a weakly-regularized C=4 model could leave the blend flat.

Per-label holdout-tuned weights (shrunk toward 0.5) move the blend only slightly from the equal rank average; the AUC-vs-weight surface is flat near the optimum for two similar linear branches, so expect a tiny gain (~+0.0001) partly eroded by noise on threat/identity_hate — and the extra char-vectorizer fit on the 80% split adds ~50-60% runtime, so there is a real (~20-25%) risk of the run breaching the 15-minute kill limit.

Compressing 100k word n-grams into 300 SVD factors discards the sparse, highly specific profanity/slur/threat vocabulary that drives these labels; LSA+LR typically loses 2-4 AUC points vs full sparse TF-IDF (worst on threat and identity_hate), and dropping the char n-gram branch and NB weighting removes the obfuscation robustness, so expect a clear regression to roughly 0.95-0.96.

Toxic is untouched (10x positives exceeds the negative count) but threat keeps only ~3% of rows, severe_toxic/identity_hate ~10%, and obscene/insult ~55%; for AUC on sparse TF-IDF/NB-LR/fastText the discarded negatives carry the benign-context evidence (e.g. 'kill', identity terms in neutral Wikipedia talk), so the rare-label columns lose 1-3 AUC points with higher-variance weights, the same negative sample across all three branches gives the rank blend no diversity to average it out, and the net is a clear regression despite the faster run.

Single 7-way softmax fastText shares the clean-vs-toxic representation across labels, giving the rare columns (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) far more rank resolution than six overfit, floor-saturated binary models, while softmax dilution on co-occurring labels (obscene/insult) is mostly absorbed by the 1/3-weight rank blend with the strong A/B linear branches; expect a small net gain within run-to-run noise, runtime drops.

For binary labels ComplementNB's log-odds reduce exactly to plain multinomial NB (score_1 - score_0 = sum count*log(p1/p0)), so this is a raw-count NB ranker: length-dependent scores (short insults under-ranked, long argumentative docs over-ranked), probability saturation ties at 1.0, and the smoothing pathology that boosts rare-vocabulary docs for threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic typically land NB around 0.90-0.95 per column, far below a tuned TF-IDF LogReg ensemble at 0.9816.

Mean-pooled from-scratch 200d word2vec + LR discards the exact-token and char n-gram evidence that drives Jigsaw AUC and dilutes single-profanity signal in long comments; such dense-average baselines typically land ~0.95-0.965 versus ~0.98 for TF-IDF/NB-LR ensembles, so a clear regression is expected (run should still fit the time budget).

Mean-pooled corpus-trained Word2Vec (200-d, 5 epochs on ~20M tokens) plus plain logistic regression discards the exact profanity/char-n-gram evidence that drives this task and dilutes single-token signals in long comments; such setups historically land around 0.94-0.96 mean AUC on Jigsaw, well below the 0.980 TF-IDF/NB-LogReg rank blend, with rare labels (threat, identity_hate) hit hardest.

A char-level NB-LogReg is only moderately diverse from branch A (already char_wb) and branch B (already NB-LogReg), so the 3-way rank blend should add a small ~+0.0003-0.0006 gain, partly eaten by noisier simplex weight tuning on the 10% holdout for threat/identity_hate; big caveat: vectorizing 626k docs with char_wb 3-5 plus six liblinear fits on ~70M-nnz matrices is closer to 6-9 min than the claimed 1-2, so there is a real (~40-50%) risk the run exceeds the 15-min hard kill and fails outright.

C=0.1 was the tuned value for this dense char_wb+word TF-IDF set (C=4/liblinear is actually the NB-SVM kernel's config, where NB-scaled features justify weak regularization); jumping 40x in C will mildly overfit the rare labels (threat, severe_toxic, identity_hate) while gaining little on toxic/obscene/insult, and the rank blend with branch B halves whatever branch A loses, so expect a small net regression of roughly 0.0005-0.001 (plus some timeout risk since liblinear primal on ~110M nonzeros is slower than sag).

Supervised fastText (dim 64, bucket 500k with heavy bigram collisions, 20 epochs of high-lr SGD) is itself another bag-of-ngram linear model that typically lands ~0.965-0.972 on this shifted test set, i.e. ~0.01 below either linear branch; at equal 1/3 rank weight it adds little new signal to an already highly correlated A+B blend and tends to dilute the rare-label columns (threat, identity_hate), so I expect a flat-to-slightly-negative change; additionally six sequential ~270M-token-pass fastText trainings on 4 threads add roughly 6-10 minutes on top of a ~8-minute baseline, so a 15-minute hard-kill is a real risk.

If it finishes, an NB-weighted char 3-7-gram LR is a genuinely different view (~0.979 alone) and a 3-way rank blend of A/B/C should edge up ~+0.0005-0.001 over the 0.9801 two-way blend; but the second char_wb vectorizer (~5 min) plus six primal-liblinear TRON fits at C=4 on ~90M-nnz NB-scaled matrices (likely 1-2 min each) push the run toward 15-20 min, so there is a substantial chance it is hard-killed rather than scored.

Training on 90% of the data costs a few 1e-4 of AUC (most on the rare threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic labels), while per-label weight tuning on a 16k holdout with ~48-160 positives for the rare labels is noisy and the blend-vs-weight curve is flat, so the realized tuning gain (~+0.0002 on common labels) does not fully offset the data loss and there is no full-data refit.

NB log-count-ratio scaling on TF-IDF word+char features is roughly a wash for a well-regularized LR (frequent labels gain a little profanity sharpness, rare labels like threat see mostly a frequency-dependent amplification of rare features that weakens effective regularization at the untuned C=0.1), and making branch A NB-weighted like branch B reduces blend diversity, so the rank-average stays near 0.9796 with a slight downward lean; some timeout risk from slower sag convergence on rescaled features.

min_df=0.01 on ~313k docs requires df>=3,128, collapsing vocabularies to ~1k words, ~15k char-grams and ~1.5k word 1-2grams; most label-specific terms (idiot, gay, kill, die, nigger, faggot, bitch, dick, cunt, moron, loser...) fall below 1% df and vanish, so only fuck/shit/ass/stupid plus generic second-person cues remain — toxic/insult/obscene lose several points and threat/identity_hate lose their entire specific lexicon, dropping mean AUC by roughly 0.02-0.03.

Balanced undersampling discards 90-99% of negatives (threat keeps 956 rows, identity_hate 2.8k, severe_toxic 3.2k), so both LR branches lose the background/toxic-but-not-this-label contrast and the NB log-count ratios become noisy; AUC on the rare columns should drop ~1-2 points and on common columns ~0.5, giving a clear regression despite the faster fits.

Rocchio/mean-difference centroids are the C→0 limit of LR with no feature-covariance correction; they keep the strong lexical profanity signal (so AUC stays well above 0.9) but lose discriminative weighting for subtle insults, context words, and the toxic-vs-severe/threat/identity distinctions, so each column drops ~1.5-4 points and the mean lands near 0.95-0.96.

Switching to char_wb spends the 50k-feature budget on within-word n-grams (profanity stems, obfuscations) instead of frequent cross-boundary function-word combos, which typically gives branch A a tiny gain; lost cross-word phrase info is covered by branch B's bigrams, and the rank-average blend halves the effect, so expect a marginal (+0.0001 to +0.0003) improvement, essentially noise-level.

For binary targets ComplementNB(norm=False) reduces to ranking by the raw NB log-count-ratio sum, i.e. pure Naive Bayes instead of NB-weighted or regularised logistic regression; on l2-normalised TF-IDF with alpha=1 over 60k/200k features the positive-class likelihood is heavily flattened (especially for threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic), rare tokens become spurious positive evidence and long mildly-toxic comments are drowned by neutral n-grams, so per-label AUCs fall to roughly 0.87-0.95 (branch B worst) and the rank blend lands near 0.92, a large regression from 0.9797.

Collapsing 60k sparse word+char TF-IDF features to 32 LSA components destroys most of branch A's lexical signal (standalone ~0.979 -> roughly 0.92, with threat/identity_hate hit hardest), so the 50/50 rank blend is now anchored by the weaker fastText branch (~0.95) plus a lossy partner, landing well below the current 0.9734; runtime is not an issue.

Collapsing everything outside the top-2,000 tokens into a single 'raretoken' discards the mid-frequency slurs, insults, and obfuscated profanity (and neuters the char_wb n-grams, which were branch A's main strength), so both branches lose rare-word signal, hurting identity_hate/threat/insult the most; the regularization benefit is negligible since C=0.1 LR already handled rare tokens, so expect a clear drop of roughly 0.01-0.015 mean AUC.

Keeping pronouns like 'you'/'your' in branch A's word unigrams slightly helps toxic/insult ranking, but char_wb 2-6-grams already encode these tokens and the branch is only half of a rank blend, so the net effect is a tiny positive, near-noise shift.

Branch B (NB-LogReg, C=4, NB-scaled features) produces far wider logits than the heavily regularized branch A (C=0.1), so logit averaging effectively tilts the blend ~70-80% toward the weaker, overconfident NB branch (especially on threat/identity_hate where A's probabilities are most compressed), losing part of the equal-weight rank-blend gain; expect a small regression of a few 1e-4.

Switching char_wb to char adds cross-word character n-grams (e.g. 'kill you', 'fuck you' fragments) that the stop-word-filtered unigram branch lacks, which historically scored about the same or marginally better on this task; since branch A is only half of a rank blend with NB-LR (which already has word bigrams), the net effect is a tiny gain within noise, with modest runtime risk from the larger raw vocabulary.

fastText supervised (mean-pooled 64-d embeddings, hashed bigrams, 5 epochs, OVA with 512-bin quantized sigmoid outputs) should land around 0.965-0.97 standalone, clearly below the ~0.977 NB-LogReg it replaces; rank-averaging a ~0.979 branch A with a weaker, still highly correlated word-based model gives roughly branch-A-level performance, so the blend most likely slips slightly below the current 0.9801 while comfortably fitting the time budget.

The NN path is untouched, so only the LR changes; at the already-overregularized C=1.0 dropping 64 correlated/weak descriptors effectively tightens L2 shrinkage and removes some complementary signal, making the LR slightly less confident on correct predictions, which propagates to a small regression in the 50/50 blend on the noisy 99-row test set.

With 99 classes and eps=0.1 the NN's true-class probability is pinned near 0.9 even on confidently-correct leaves, so in the arithmetic 50/50 blend every easy test row loses ~0.03 of probability mass (loss ~0.05 -> ~0.08-0.1 each) while the LR floor already prevents the few hard rows from benefiting much; the task is near-perfectly classified so this underconfidence dominates and the log loss regresses by roughly 0.03.

OvR fits 99 heavily imbalanced (9 vs 882) binary problems whose logit gaps are not jointly optimized, so even after the global power/floor calibration the per-sample margins are less consistent than the softmax-trained multinomial and a confusable test leaf or two gets hedged or misranked; on this dataset tuned OvR LR historically lands around 0.07-0.1 vs ~0.04 for multinomial, so expect a moderate regression rather than a gain.

A 5-seed MLP bag is a genuinely diverse, roughly LR-strength model on these 192 descriptors; CV-selected blend weight (with w=0 fallback) plus re-tuned power calibration typically trims the few confident LR errors that dominate log loss, so a modest ~10-20% gain is expected, though the 99-row test makes the realized change noisy.

Averaging five high-C logistic fold models softens overconfident probabilities, which log loss rewards when the single refit has a confident error, but each fold model sees only ~7 instead of ~9 samples per class and the models are highly correlated, so the net effect on a 99-row test set is near-neutral with a slight lean toward a small improvement.

Absolute leaf size (log H/W, area, axis lengths), convexity and Hu moments are genuinely new, species-discriminative information on top of the scale-normalised 192 descriptors, and CV-selected C adapts to the 213-column matrix, so OOF and test log loss should drop modestly; gains are capped by the noisy 99-row test where a single confident error dominates, and the sign-flipping Hu-log features add some noise, so the improvement is likely moderate rather than dramatic (with a real chance of no change if the images dir isn't found, which falls back to the identical 0.0566 pipeline).

PCA without whitening is a rotation (irrelevant to L2 logreg) plus truncation; the ~100 dropped directions are mostly harmless shape-contour and geometric collinearity contrasts, but the margin/texture tail directions (eigenvalues ~0.2-0.4) still carried usable class contrasts that an already over-regularised C=1 model was exploiting, so expect slightly smaller margins and a confident miss or two more on 99 test rows, i.e. a modest log-loss regression rather than a gain.

LogReg at fixed C=1 on ~9 samples/class is already on the regularisation-limited part of the curve, so each fold model trained on 80% of the rows (7 per class, sum-loss objective so effectively 25% stronger regularisation) is softer and slightly less accurate; averaging five highly correlated linear models recovers only a little via Jensen smoothing on the few hard test rows, so the lost confidence on the ~95 easy rows dominates and the log loss worsens modestly rather than improving.

The feature branch alone should give a confident, ~97-99% accurate NN (likely 0.05-0.15 log loss), and averaging with the under-confident C=1 LR is guaranteed no worse than the mean of the two losses, so the blend should land around 0.07-0.09; the image branch adds little (the >0.5 inversion heuristic flips polarity for broad leaves that fill most of their crop) and timing is tight but should fit, with a small tail risk of regression if the 9-minute guard truncates the full-data run.

C=1 LR on standardised leaf features is systematically underconfident (the known Kaggle fix is C~2000), so an OOF-fitted power/temperature a≈2-2.5 plus a tiny uniform floor should roughly halve the log loss on the ~97-98% correctly-classified rows while only modestly hurting the few moderate-confidence errors; test set is only 99 rows so a confidently-wrong row could limit the gain, hence ~0.05-0.08 expected.

On the leaf dataset the 192 standardised descriptors are nearly linearly separable, so C=1 is badly over-regularised (underconfident ~0.9 probabilities give ~0.12 loss); CV will pick C in the ~300-3000 range where OOF loss roughly flattens, cutting test loss to the well-known ~0.03-0.06 LR regime, though with only 99 test rows a single confident error keeps the result noisy and right-skewed.

Image size/aspect features add genuinely new scale information the normalized 192 descriptors lack and effectively loosen the C=1 regularization, which should lower loss; but the polarity rule (invert when foreground >50%) makes many simple-leaf images compute features on the background, and sign-log Hu5-7 are near-random, injecting within-species inconsistency that can produce a few confident errors on the 99-row test, so the expected gain is modest and uncertain.

Leaf data is nearly separable with 99 classes and ~9 samples each, so logistic regression log loss is dominated by under-confidence and is known to keep improving up to C~1000; cutting C to 0.2 shrinks all logits ~20-30%, inflating loss on the many near-boundary correct predictions far more than it softens the one or two errors, so log loss should rise to roughly 0.12-0.16.

Dropping the full-data refit means the submitted LR is trained on ~7 instead of ~9 samples per class (713 vs 891 rows) in a data-starved 99-class/240-feature regime, so predictions get less accurate and less confident; log loss should rise noticeably (roughly 30-50% relative), with the validation rows never contributing to the final model.

Convex OOF-optimised blend can only match or beat LR alone in-sample and LDA (very accurate but one-hot-ish) plus smoothed distance-kNN add complementary mass on LR's low-confidence samples, so expect a moderate test gain; the 99-row test set makes the outcome noisy and confident LDA errors on hard species could partly offset the gain.

With ~7-8 training samples per class after the 15% holdout, 99 classes, min_samples_leaf=10 and axis-aligned splits, boosted trees generalize worse than the near-linearly-separable tuned logistic regression (known on this dataset: GBMs land ~0.2-0.5 vs ~0.03-0.06 for logreg); expect ~3-7 confidently wrong test samples plus hedged probabilities on held-out points, roughly 4-6x worse log loss.

Platt-sigmoid OvR calibration on 3-fold held-out sets with only 2-4 positives per class caps and noisily softens the SVC's true-class probabilities (~0.75-0.9 after normalisation) and leaves less mass on the true class when it errs, so the swapped linear member is slightly worse-calibrated than the multinomial LR it replaces while offering no new diversity (same standardised linear view as LDA); under uniform soft voting this lowers the averaged true-class probability on the easy majority and hard tail alike, a modest regression.

With uniform soft voting, swapping the sharp (near 0/1) HGB member for a 600-tree RF whose vote-fraction probabilities for the true class are diffuse (~0.5-0.7 even when correct on this 99-class, ~9-per-class problem) lowers the averaged true-class probability on the many easy samples; RF's higher accuracy and non-zero floor help the hard samples, but the net on log loss is a modest regression unless HGB's leaf-constrained boxes were generalizing much worse than expected.

An early-stopped (accuracy-monitored, tiny unstratified 10% val split) 256-128 MLP on ~800 samples/99 classes will be roughly as accurate as or slightly less accurate than LR but far more overconfident on its 2-3 expected test errors; uniform shrinkage can only partially cap those (~0.07 loss each), so the 99-sample test log loss most likely lands ~0.15-0.25, a regression versus the underconfident but rarely-wrong C=1 logistic regression.

On the leaf dataset standardized multinomial LR is badly under-regularized at C=1 (avg test confidence ~0.88); CV will pick a large C (~300-1000) where OOF log loss is typically ~0.04-0.06 versus ~0.13 at C=1, so test loss should drop substantially, tempered by the 99-row test variance and the risk of a confidently wrong sample.

The 48 CV features (Hu moments, solidity/eccentricity, scale-dependent area/axes which are informative in this dataset, and a radial histogram partly redundant with the shape descriptors) add real signal and effectively relax the over-regularized C=1.0 model, so predictions get more confident on an already near-perfectly-classified test set; a few noisy features (orientation, sparse histogram bins) and the 99-row test noise temper the gain, so expect a moderate ~15% drop rather than a large one.

The change almost certainly crashes before writing a submission: with 891 rows and 99 classes every 10-fold validation fold (~89 rows) is missing classes, so sklearn's neg_log_loss scorer raises 'y_true and y_pred contain different number of classes' inside LogisticRegressionCV (and if the split is exactly 9/class, StratifiedKFold(10) raises first); a successful run would have landed near 0.04-0.06 via a large selected C, but the most likely recorded outcome is no new submission, i.e. the parent's 0.1244 stands.

Uniform soft-voting dilutes the already well-calibrated LR with a diffuse distance-weighted kNN (CV on neg_log_loss will push k to ~8-14, giving p_true≈0.8 even when right) and adds sharp but ~2-6% error-prone LDA/HGB components whose confident misses (p_true≈0) each cost ~0.3-0.5 log loss on a 99-row test set, outweighing the gains on LR's few uncertain samples; expect a moderate regression from 0.124 to roughly 0.15-0.20.

C=1.0 multinomial LR on standardized leaf features is under-confident (typical held-out p_true ~0.85-0.95, errors mostly mild), so uniform shrinkage only helps samples with p_true below 1/99; the 0.01-step OOF grid most likely picks alpha=0 (score unchanged at 0.1244), but there is a meaningful chance a few confident OOF errors push it to alpha=0.01-0.02, which costs ~alpha per sample on the 99-row test set (0.134-0.144) since the test set's 12.3-nat total budget rules out catastrophic errors that shrinkage could rescue; expected outcome is a small regression.

Fixed shrinkage=0.9 toward a scaled identity discards most of the well-estimated pooled within-class correlation structure (792 df for 192 dims) and the per-feature within-class variance heterogeneity that the per-class Ledoit-Wolf target preserves; the classifier drifts toward a Euclidean nearest-centroid rule that overweights the dominant within-class noise directions, so expect a few more confident misclassifications on the 99-row test set and a noticeably worse log loss.

Each 64-feature LDA is much weaker (shape alone ~55-65% accurate, margin/texture ~80-85%), and equal-weight arithmetic averaging caps the true-class probability near 0.66 whenever one family model is wrong (~40% of rows, ~0.4 nats each) and near 0.33 when two are wrong; this systematic under-confidence outweighs the benefit of taming the joint model's few catastrophic errors, so a mild regression from 0.364 is most likely.

L2 logistic regression is rotation-invariant, so the only effect of unwhitened PCA is truncating the ~100 lowest-variance directions; on this near-separable 99-class problem the tuned high-C model relies on exactly those fine margin/texture distinctions between similar species, so unsupervised truncation to 90% variance should cost separability and roughly double the log loss (more errors and softer selected C), though CV-selected C limits the damage.

LDA on 192 standardized features with ~9 samples/class classifies well (~97-99%) but its softmax of Mahalanobis scores is extremely overconfident regardless of shrinkage (shrinkage reshapes the metric, it does not temper the scale), so the 1-3 expected misclassifications on the 99-row test set each cost several-to-tens of nats; expected log loss lands around 0.1-0.3, clearly worse than the calibrated, CV-tuned logistic regression at 0.060, with only a minority chance (zero test errors) of matching or beating it.

PCA at 95% standardized variance keeps roughly 90-110 of 192 dimensions; the L2 penalty is rotation-invariant so the only effect is unsupervised truncation of low-variance directions, which on this dataset (fine margin/texture histogram detail and shape high-frequency contour features) carry real species-discriminative signal that LR at C=1 was already exploiting, so OOF/test accuracy and confidence drop slightly and a few extra uncertain or misclassified test rows push the 99-row log loss up modestly.

Shrinkage LDA fits these near-Gaussian shared-covariance leaf descriptors well (historically ~98-99% accuracy on this data) and the out-of-fold temperature (likely landing near 2.5-4) tames most of LDA's usual overconfidence, giving sharper correct predictions than C=1 logistic regression; expect a modest gain, but with high variance on a 99-row test set and real tail risk if T hits the 4.0 bound on a confident error.

Training is unchanged and deterministic, so the only effect is the post-hoc mix; for any sample with p_true > ~0.01 the mix adds ≈ -log(0.995) ≈ 0.005 to its loss, and the current total loss (9.3 over 99 rows) bounds how extreme any mistake can be, so even the best case cannot recover enough from the single low-p sample to offset ~98 × 0.005, giving a near-certain regression of about +0.0048.

Dropping landmarks from 512 to 384 (a subset of the same permutation) yields a coarser kernel approximation with ~4 instead of ~5 landmarks per class and, after the post-Nystroem StandardScaler, effectively lowers the LR's capacity/implied C by ~25%; since the C=1 model is already in an under-confident (over-regularized) regime relative to what this dataset supports, the test log loss should rise modestly, with ±10% noise from the 99-row test set.

Shrinkage LDA on standardized leaf descriptors is a known strong, near-99%-accuracy fit with much sharper posteriors than the underconfident C=1 logistic regression, so most of the 0.124 'softness' cost disappears; the downside is 1-2 confidently wrong test rows (each adding ~0.05-0.2), giving a skewed outcome roughly in 0.01-0.2 with a median around 0.06.

On this dataset standardized multinomial LR improves sharply as C grows (classic kernels with C~1000-2000 reach ~0.03-0.05 vs ~0.12-0.2 at C=1); 3-fold CV will almost surely pick C=1000 or 100, the run finishes in a minute or two, so expect a large drop, tempered by variance from only 99 test rows where one confidently wrong prediction costs ~0.05-0.1.

LR at C=1 on standardized leaf features is well known to be under-confident (tuning C up to ~1000 cuts LB loss several-fold), so an OOF-fitted temperature well below 1 should sharpen the many correct, moderately-confident test predictions and recover a sizable share of that gap; gains are capped and noisy because the 99-row test set likely holds 1-3 misclassified leaves whose penalties get amplified by sharpening.

Nyström RBF (gamma=1/192) + re-standardization effectively weakens regularization, which should make typical predictions more confident than the underconfident C=1 linear model, but on this near-linearly-separable 192-dim data with 9 samples/class an isotropic RBF kernel is a worse inductive bias than linear (RBF SVMs historically trail LR by 1-2% accuracy here), landmark self-similarity encourages memorization, and per-point exp(-gamma||x||^2) attenuation hurts outlier test points; with 99 test rows each extra confident error costs ~0.03-0.05, so I expect a mild net regression.

The timestamp (community-age decline in success rate), request length, evidentiality (image/url) and reciprocity flags are the strongest non-text predictors in Althoff et al. and are currently absent; on a random split they should add roughly +0.015-0.02 AUC, partially offset by ~15 near-noise standardized columns (hour/weekday/day-of-month, punctuation) in a lightly regularized LR on 2.9k rows.

A fully-grown sqrt-mtry random forest on ~6500 sparse TF-IDF/subreddit columns plus only 9 dense numeric columns dilutes the strongest (numeric) predictors to ~10% of candidate sets and captures the weak, diffuse text signal far worse than L2 logistic regression, so expect a moderate AUC drop (roughly 0.60-0.66) rather than a gain.

RF with sqrt sampling over 5000 sparse, weakly informative TF-IDF columns dilutes the 9 dense history features and extracts text signal worse than L2 logistic regression; the giver_known leak is still mostly captured (the pure-positive split gets picked somewhere along most paths, and even partial capture ranks those rows above nearly all negatives), so the drop comes from the non-leak portion where fully grown trees on noisy text lose a few AUC points versus LR, netting roughly 0.70-0.75.

Score is dominated by the giver_known leak plus requester-history metadata; the TF-IDF block adds only a modest text increment, and 50 LDA topic proportions estimated from ~2.9k short posts typically carry less discriminative text signal than regularized sparse unigrams, so expect a small regression within noise rather than a gain.

Unsupervised 20-topic LDA on ~70-word posts is a lossy, noisy substitute for a supervised TF-IDF logit (which carries ~0.62-0.64 AUC of discriminative word signal like pay-it-forward/need cues); the metadata signal remains intact so the drop is modest, but 20 weak topic columns on 2.9k rows add variance rather than interactions LightGBM can reliably exploit, so expect a small regression.

The test set is a random (not temporal) split of the same 2010-2013 window, so the raw timestamp's era-specific base rates (RAOP success rate declined markedly as the community grew) are genuinely transferable signal; dropping it loses roughly 0.01-0.02 AUC, while hour-of-day/weekday on ~2.9k rows are weak, noisy features that recover little.

Adding a conservatively-regularized HistGradientBoosting model on the ~33 metadata/time/text-stat features captures the nonlinear time trend and interactions the linear model misses, and rank-blending a tree model with a text-LR is a reliably positive, low-variance change on this small dataset; expected gain is modest (+0.01 to +0.02 AUC) since the LR already uses the same dense features, and test-set noise (~0.019 SE) could mask it.

Random forest with sqrt(~5040) ≈ 71 candidate features per split sees the ~33 informative dense metadata/time columns in only ~37% of splits, so most splits land on sparse, individually weak TF-IDF unigrams; RF is known to underperform logistic regression on sparse text and the nonlinear gains on metadata are unlikely to offset the dilution, so expect a modest AUC drop (~0.65-0.69 range).

Bag-of-subreddits adds a weak (~0.60 AUC standalone) signal that is largely redundant with the activity-count numerics already present; with ~1500 idf-weighted sparse features on 2878 rows under C=0.3 LR, expect a small net gain (~+0.005 to +0.01) with real risk of noise-driven regression on the 1162-row test set.

giver_username_if_known is the well-known RAOP leak: ~7% of rows have a giver and essentially all of them received pizza (~25-30% of positives); the Kaggle 17-field test schema retains it, and the unscaled 0/1 column gets a large LR coefficient that puts those rows at the top, lifting AUC from ~0.657 to roughly f*1.0 + (1-f)*0.65 ≈ 0.74-0.75.

Stacking adds the raw UTC timestamp (a known informative feature in RAOP, success rate drifts over 2010-2013) and lets a well-regularized LightGBM model non-linear effects of requester-history counts, while the OOF text logit preserves the text signal; the 11-feature GBM on ~2.9k rows is low-risk and should modestly beat the linear baseline, though test AUC noise (~±0.015) and small-data variance cap the gain.

Temporal trend (success rate fell as RAOP grew), log text length (lost by L2-normalized TF-IDF), and image-proof/RAOP-history indicators are well-known independent predictors on this dataset; adding ~27 standardized dense columns to an L2 LR rarely hurts, so expect a modest gain of roughly +0.02 AUC, with ±0.015 test noise on 1162 rows.

ExtraTrees with sqrt feature sampling over ~5.4k mostly-sparse TF-IDF columns dilutes the 9 informative requester-history numerics and 384 embedding dims (only ~5 dense candidates per split), so trees are near-random and the ensemble is unlikely to beat a regularized LR on text-heavy features; expect roughly a wash to slight regression, as nonlinear interactions in RAOP are weak.

The TF-IDF block was already effectively ~50x more regularized than the standardized dense blocks (small L2-normalized values vs unit-variance features), so it contributed a small, mostly-signal perturbation; dropping it removes that modest lexical signal (edit-aware text still carries predictive unigrams like job/kids/paycheck) while leaving the 384 standardized MiniLM dims with the same overfitting tendency, so expect a slight regression rather than the hoped-for gain.

L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF discards request length, which is one of the strongest known non-leak predictors in RAOP; adding standardized length/gratitude/sentiment stats to a well-regularized LR should recover a modest ~0.01-0.02 AUC gain, consistent with the ~0.67 ceiling reported for text+metadata models on this data, though the 1162-row test set makes the gain partly within noise.

The test split is a random re-split of the same 2010-2013 corpus, so the drift argument doesn't apply; the nine requester-history features alone (RAOP prior activity, account age, karma) typically give ~0.60-0.63 AUC on this data, and dropping the TF-IDF block removes real complementary text signal (need/narrative words), so expect a ~0.03 AUC regression from 0.650.

Self-trained skip-gram on only ~4k short documents yields noisy vectors, and unweighted mean pooling (no stop-word removal or IDF weighting) dilutes the topical signal that sparse TF-IDF + LR already captured well; 200 standardized dense dims under C=0.3 also add overfitting surface, so the text block's contribution shrinks and the AUC likely dips slightly below the current 0.662 while metadata keeps it from collapsing.

On only ~2.9k training docs, min_df=2 bigrams add mostly noisy sparse features and dilute the L2-normalized unigram and dense-metadata signal under a fixed C=0.3, so I expect a roughly neutral-to-slightly-negative shift (text is a weak signal here and the metadata block, which carries most of the AUC, is unchanged); mlflow additions are try/except-wrapped and runtime stays trivial.

The nine requester-history columns carry real but modest signal (prior RAOP activity, account age, karma) and typically yield ~0.60-0.63 AUC alone on this dataset; the SVD text block in the parent was weak but still complementary, so dropping it should cost a few points rather than help, with the 63-leaf GBM on 9 features kept in check by early stopping.

Same 309-dim SVD+numeric features cap the signal (~0.63-0.65 for tree models here); a 400-tree sqrt-feature RF averages variance better than the over-complex num_leaves=63 LGBM but dilutes the strong 9 numeric features among 300 noisy SVD components, so I expect roughly a wash with a slight edge to the forest, well within test-set noise (~±0.015).

MiniLM embeddings capture the semantic narrative cues (family, job loss, reciprocity vs. craving) that 5k unigrams on 2.9k docs miss, and should add a modest ~0.01-0.03 AUC on top of the metadata-dominated baseline; gains are capped because text signal in RAOP is inherently weak and C=0.3 is under-regularized for 384 standardized dense dims, but runtime on CPU is comfortably within budget.

Bigrams add a few predictive phrases (pay forward, food stamps, lost job) but on 2.9k short docs the min_df=2 vocabulary explosion dilutes informative unigrams under L2 normalization with fixed C=0.3, so text signal barely changes while the metadata block still carries most of the AUC; expect a small, noisy gain near +0.003.

L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF discards request length, which is a known strong RAOP predictor (longer, more detailed requests succeed more), and the aggregated gratitude/reciprocity/hardship lexicons give lower-variance signals than individual unigrams under C=0.3, so 15 standardized dense features on 2878 rows should add roughly +0.01 AUC with LR, though test-set noise (~288 positives) and partial redundancy with TF-IDF keep the gain modest.

On ~2.9k docs, compressing TF-IDF to 300 SVD components and boosting with 63-leaf trees loses text signal relative to sparse L2 logistic regression, while the mostly monotone log-scaled requester-history features gain little from a GBM; expect roughly neutral-to-slightly-worse AUC (~0.64-0.66), with CV early stopping keeping it from collapsing.

RAOP's dominant temporal signal is the multi-year decline in success rate as the community grew, which the quantile spline over absolute days captured; annual sin/cos cannot represent that trend and genuine seasonality is weak, so the model loses roughly the ~0.01-0.015 AUC the spline contributed, partially offset by the Oct-Dec phase coincidentally proxying earlier years.

C=30 on ~5000 sparse TF-IDF unigrams with only 2878 rows makes the problem near-separable, so text coefficients blow up and inject high-variance noise that swamps the stable requester-history and date signal; expected drop of a few AUC points, not a gain.

Request time is a known strong meta signal in RAOP (success rate fell as the subreddit grew), the test split shares the training time range so the quantile spline generalizes, and 7 standardized smooth features add almost no overfitting risk under C=0.3, so expect a modest but real AUC gain of roughly +0.015 to +0.03.

Cosine KNN on the concatenated matrix is dominated by the z-scored numeric block (norm ~3.5) and subreddit indicators (norm sqrt(k)) rather than the unit-norm TF-IDF text, so it degrades to a crude requester-type similarity classifier; KNN is also generally weaker than regularized LR on this small noisy dataset, so expect a drop of several AUC points, though the strong zero-history vs. established-user split keeps it above 0.55.

Distance-weighted 25-NN on 9 weak metadata features is far noisier than CatBoost (label-sampling noise ~0.09 std, near-binary outputs for the many exact-duplicate zero-history requesters), and its wider probability spread dominates the 50/50 blend, so the mostly redundant metadata signal is swamped by noise and the blend likely falls below the LR-alone level.

A 100x jump in C on ~2.9k docs with 5k TF-IDF features puts LR in the near-separable, heavily overfit regime; its test probabilities become extreme and dominate the 50/50 probability blend, dragging the blend toward the degraded LR AUC (~0.59-0.61) despite CatBoost's steadier metadata signal.

RAOP success rate fell steadily as the subreddit grew (roughly 30%+ in 2011 to under 20% in 2013), and with a random train/test split the 7 standardized quantile-spline features of request date add a mostly orthogonal signal (time alone is ~0.58-0.61 AUC) that L2 logistic regression at C=0.3 can absorb cleanly, so expect a modest gain of roughly +0.015 to +0.025 AUC.

BernoulliNB on 5000 noisy, correlated uni/bigram presence indicators drowns the 9 strong requester-history signals (now crudely binarized at the mean), double-counts bigrams/unigrams, and effectively becomes a document-length-plus-noise ranker; length is only a weak positive cue on RAOP, so AUC should fall several points below the regularized LR's 0.654, landing around 0.60.

RAOP success rate declined markedly over 2011-2013 and the test split is random in time, so a 7-column cubic spline over the request date adds a real, low-variance signal (~0.56-0.58 AUC alone, largely orthogonal to TF-IDF/history features) that logistic regression at C=0.3 can exploit; expect a modest ~+0.01-0.02 gain, with MLflow wrapping being inert.

Bag-of-subreddits adds real request-time signal (location/community membership beyond the numeric count), but ~1000 unscaled binary indicators with min_df=5 under C=0.3 are weakly regularized relative to L2-normalized TF-IDF and add estimation noise for heavy users, so expect only a small net gain within test-set noise.

A metadata-only CatBoost on the nine requester-history features typically reaches ~0.62-0.63 AUC on RAOP and is complementary to the text-heavy logistic regression, so a fixed 50/50 probability average should add roughly +0.01 over the 0.657 baseline, with modest risk of near-neutral results if the tree model is weaker than expected.

Bigrams under the same 5000-feature cap swap rare unigrams for common bigrams like 'pay forward'; on ~2.9k docs with C=0.3 this is typically a small net gain, and the mlflow wrapper is try/except-guarded so the deterministic lbfgs fit on all data still produces the same-style submission.

Authorship attribution is driven largely by function-word usage (upon, which, whilst, 'of the', 'it was', etc.); dropping sklearn's stop list removes those unigrams and every bigram containing them from the word view, and char_wb n-grams never cross word boundaries so the collocation signal is lost entirely, yielding a clear regression partially cushioned by the char view.

LR-TFIDF plus tuned MultinomialNB on word/char counts are well-known complementary models on this dataset, and a log-linear meta-learner on log-probs acts as a calibrated NB-LR interpolation (NBSVM-like), typically cutting log loss by ~5-10%; the loss of the full-data LR refit (fold models on 80% data) costs a little, so expect roughly 0.354 -> ~0.33.

Function words are core stylometric fingerprints in authorship attribution (Poe's 'upon', Shelley's 'which'/'yet' patterns, Lovecraft's dialect), and function-word bigrams like 'of the'/'upon the' cannot be recovered by char_wb n-grams which don't cross word boundaries; dropping stop words will weaken both word-level base models by roughly 0.05-0.08 OOF, and although the char models partially compensate in the LightGBM stack, the ensemble should end up modestly worse (~0.31-0.32) rather than better.

A multinomial LR on standardized raw probabilities is a lossy combiner here: it cannot reproduce logit-style calibration of the LR base models, collapses the near-binary MultinomialNB outputs into votes (losing the informative tail magnitude the tree bins exploit), and cannot use the 16 meta-features to modulate confidence via interactions (e.g. length x agreement); LightGBM with early stopping on 28 features and ~14k rows is not materially overfitting, so the swap should cost roughly 0.02-0.04 log loss, landing around 0.32-0.33.

Punctuation here is a genuine, transferable authorial cue (MWS semicolons 32% vs EAP 14%, EAP quotes 17% vs HPL 6%, HPL apostrophes 16%) and train/test share the same editions, so stripping it removes informative char n-grams like ', and' / '; the' and comma-density signal; the mild regularization gain from a smaller char vocabulary won't offset the information loss, so log loss should worsen by roughly 0.01-0.02.

A proper 5-fold OOF stack of word/char LR plus word/char NB with a log-prob LR meta-learner is a well-known Spooky recipe; the calibrated NB models add strong, diverse signal over the single hstacked LR, historically dropping log loss from ~0.44 to the mid-0.30s, tempered by a slightly smaller train set and small-test variance.

Chi2 top-10k on TF-IDF keeps mostly frequent/skewed columns and discards the long tail of rare-but-discriminative words and char n-grams that L2 LR exploits; it also shrinks row norms so C=1.0 becomes effectively more regularized and softer. LR OOF likely worsens by ~0.05; the re-tuned NB blend absorbs part of it, so the final log loss regresses modestly to ~0.375-0.385.

Authorship attribution is stylometry: function-word rates and stop-word bigrams ('of the', 'and the') are among the strongest author cues (Shelley's 'and', Poe's 'of the'), so dropping them hurts both the word TF-IDF block and especially MultinomialNB; char_wb n-grams retain unigram function words and the OOF blend-weight search will lean harder on LR, limiting the damage to roughly +0.015-0.025 log loss.

C=1 on L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF is over-regularized and under-confident; 5-fold CV will almost certainly pick C=10-30, which on this dataset typically cuts LR log loss by ~0.03-0.05 (to ~0.39-0.40), with downside bounded near zero since C=1 stays in the grid and the refit/featurizer are unchanged.

Stacking diverse LR (word/char TF-IDF, C=10) and MultinomialNB (word/char counts) OOF probabilities plus stylometric meta-features into an early-stopped LightGBM is a well-trodden recipe on this competition that typically lands around 0.35-0.39 (NB and LR errors are complementary, the GBM recalibrates NB overconfidence), a solid gain over the single C=1 LR at 0.432; runtime should fit in budget with parallel folds.

Cross-word-boundary, case-sensitive char n-grams add punctuation/capitalization style cues that help authorship attribution, but at fixed C=1.0 the many rare uncapped high-IDF n-grams dilute the common features' L2-normalized mass (effectively stronger regularization on an already underfit LR), so the net is only a small gain of roughly 0.005-0.01 log loss.

Tuned-alpha MultinomialNB on word (1,2)-gram counts is a strong, diverse, overconfident complement to the under-confident C=1 TF-IDF LR on this dataset (NB alone ~0.45-0.47 OOF); OOF-selected arithmetic blend (w~0.5-0.7) historically moves LR-only ~0.43 down to ~0.39-0.41 on Spooky, with ~0.01-0.02 noise from the 1,958-row test set.

Authorship attribution is largely stylometric: function words and their bigrams ('upon', 'i/my', 'thus', 'whilst', 'hence' are all in sklearn's stop list) are strong author cues here, so stripping them removes signal fastText's word-bigram/char-ngram features were exploiting; content words and names remain, limiting the damage, but a clear regression is more likely than a gain.

Test prior matches train (40/31/29), so balancing removes a correctly-learned prior and duplicating minority rows just gives an already-overfit, overconfident fastText (25 epochs, lr 0.5, char n-grams) more memorization of those examples; expect a small log-loss regression on the order of 0.01-0.02, within fastText's run-to-run noise.

ComplementNB on stacked tf-idf is a weaker, overconfident model (OOF ~0.5-0.7 vs LR ~0.36), but its heavy weighting of rare author-specific words is complementary to a regularized LR, so the OOF-selected blend (likely w≈0.7-0.9) should give a modest, robust gain of ~0.01 log loss; small chance of w=1.0 (no change) or a near-timeout from the extra LR fits.

Dropping the char_wb 2-5 gram block removes all punctuation/morphology stylometric cues (semicolon, quote, apostrophe habits that the default word tokenizer discards), which are strong author signals here; word-only NB-LR typically lands ~0.42-0.45 on this task versus ~0.40-0.41 for word+char, so expect a clear regression despite faster runtime.

Plain ComplementNB with alpha=1 on L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF is a known step down from NB-SVM: the small feature values plus Laplace smoothing crush the rare-word/name evidence that LR exploits, sklearn's multiclass CNB drops the prior and its complement-count smoothing adds an undue EAP tilt, and NB probabilities are poorly calibrated, so expect ~80% accuracy and log loss in the 0.5-0.6 range rather than 0.41.

C=1 on two l2-normalized TF-IDF blocks with only 17.6k samples is over-regularized (under-confident probabilities); 3-fold neg_log_loss CV should pick C≈3-10, sharpening predictions and typically cutting log loss by ~0.02-0.03 on this dataset, with modest risk that the selected C is near 1 (no change) or the run approaches the time limit.

MultinomialNB on stacked word+char TF-IDF treats ~300 heavily overlapping char n-grams per sentence as independent evidence, re-counting each distinctive word several times, so posteriors become sharp (often >0.98) and the ~15% misclassified sentences are penalized at 3+ nats each; word-tfidf NB alone historically scores ~0.47-0.50 on this task and the char block adds overconfidence more than accuracy, so I expect a clear regression from the well-calibrated LR's 0.425 to roughly 0.5-0.55.

fastText with lr=0.5/25 epochs/no regularization on 16k sentences fits training nearly perfectly and emits extremely peaked softmax probabilities (down to the 1e-5 floor), so even at ~0.80-0.83 accuracy (roughly on par with or slightly below the TF-IDF+LR) the confidently-wrong tail dominates log loss; expect a clear regression versus the well-calibrated C=1 logistic regression.

L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF with LR is underfit at C=1; 5-fold CV will almost surely pick the top of the grid (C=4 or 8), which typically cuts Spooky log loss by ~0.03-0.04, while the parallelized 30 fits should finish within budget.

NB log-count-ratio weighting plus weaker regularization (C=4) amplifies the strong lexical cues (names, dialect, distinctive vocabulary) that make MNB competitive on this task and typically beats an under-tuned C=1 LR by a few hundredths; the one-vs-rest renormalization and heavy alpha=1 smoothing on small TF-IDF sums eat part of the gain, so expect a modest improvement from 0.432 to roughly 0.40-0.41 rather than a large jump.

Fourteen MaxAbs-scaled stylometric columns add a little genuinely new signal (sentence length lost by L2-normalized TF-IDF, uppercase fraction lost by lowercasing, semicolon/comma counts) but most punctuation info is already in the char_wb n-grams and several features are near-constant (no '!', few digits/hyphens), so a well-regularized LR on 17.6k rows gains only a couple thousandths of log loss, within test-set noise.

NB log-count-ratio weighting redistributes the (currently heavy, C=1) regularization toward the strongly class-specific lexical/char features that dominate this dataset (names, dialect, author-specific vocabulary), which historically lifts linear models on spooky from ~0.44 to ~0.38-0.41; the untuned C=1, in-sample r weights and OvR-normalized probabilities cost a little calibration, so a moderate improvement to ~0.40 rather than a large one.

L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF rows make C=1 already a fairly strong regularizer for a 17.6k-row 3-class problem (empirically the log-loss optimum for word+char TF-IDF LR sits around C≈2-5); quartering C shrinks logits ~35-50%, pushing predictions toward the prior and raising log loss noticeably, likely to roughly 0.49-0.51.

Word n-grams carry the strongest signal on Spooky (character names, rare archaic vocabulary); char_wb 2-5 grams capped at 60k features only partially recover these via fragments, and their smaller NB log-ratio magnitudes make C=1.0 effectively over-regularize, so dropping the word block should regress log loss by roughly 0.04-0.06.

Dropping the NB log-count-ratio scaling leaves plain L2-normalized TF-IDF with C=1 liblinear OvR, which is known to underfit on this task (classic word-TF-IDF+LR C=1 gives ~0.62); the added char block and doubled row norm help somewhat, but softer, less confident probabilities should still push log loss up from 0.518 to roughly 0.55-0.60.

L2-normalized TF-IDF features need fairly weak regularization for LR (community grids on Spooky put the log-loss optimum around C≈5-10 for a single block, ≈3-7 for stacked word+char), so halving C to 2.0 likely lands on the under-fit side of a flat U-curve: slightly less confident, slightly less accurate predictions, a small regression of roughly +0.005 to +0.01 log loss.

NB log-count-ratio weighting suits this single-sentence 'snippet' regime and amplifies rare author-specific vocabulary (names, dialect) that transfers across the random split, likely giving a small gain, but it is partly offset by the one-vs-rest normalisation being less calibrated than multinomial softmax for log loss and by shrinking weakly-informative stylometric char n-grams; net expect a modest improvement, roughly 0.355-0.372.

Function words (upon, thus, yet, which, of the...) are the core stylometric signal for authorship attribution and sklearn's 318-word stop list strips them from both word and char_wb branches, so the model is left with only content/theme cues and character names; expect a clear regression from 0.382 to roughly 0.45-0.52.

On L2-normalized TF-IDF the C=1 model is already under-regularized-side-of-optimal only in scale (which temperature scaling fixes); cutting C to 0.25 additionally shrinks rare discriminative n-grams (character names, dialect spellings) relative to common stylistic features, degrading ranking quality by ~1-2 accuracy points that a single global temperature cannot recover, so log loss worsens modestly.

Switching to 'char' adds cross-word n-grams that capture punctuation-context style cues (', which', '; and', ', but') invisible to both char_wb and punctuation-stripped word bigrams; the 60k cap drops mostly rare within-word fragments already covered by word unigrams, so expect a small net gain (~0.004) with final predictions unchanged otherwise since the full-data refit is retained.

With alpha=1 smoothing on TF-IDF-valued sums (sums ~0.2-20 vs +1 smoothing and D~120k in denominators) most log-count ratios compress to |r|~0.1-0.8, so X*r shrinks the feature scale and at fixed C=1 acts like a 3-5x stronger L2 penalty on the bulk of stylistic/medium-frequency features, making the already-underfit LR less confident on generic sentences; only name/exclusive-vocabulary features (|r|>1) get sharper, which helps ~15% of rows but also adds a few confidently-wrong tail rows, and OvR-normalized liblinear is slightly worse calibrated than multinomial softmax, so net a moderate regression from 0.432 to roughly 0.47.

C=1.0 L2-regularized LR on L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF is typically under-confident on this task; raising C to 4 sharpens probabilities and sits near the usual log-loss optimum (C~4-10) for ~17k samples with ~130k informative features, so a moderate improvement is expected, with no runtime or correctness risk from the diff.

LogisticRegression at C=1 on L2-normalized word+char TF-IDF with only ~16k samples is over-regularized and systematically under-confident (optimal C for this setup is ~5-10x higher), so the holdout-fitted temperature should land around T≈0.7-0.85 and sharpen the probabilities; applying it to the full refit costs almost nothing (flat loss curve near T*), yielding a modest but real log-loss gain of roughly 0.01, with no change to features or decision direction limiting the upside.

The metric is RMSE in raw dollars, so training on log1p targets optimizes relative error, deweights the high-fare rides that dominate squared error, and expm1 of the log-mean systematically underpredicts the conditional mean (Jensen bias); in this competition log targets were widely reported to hurt by a few percent, while the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows damps the total change.

4x more rows with the same 1000-tree/63-leaf LightGBM should modestly sharpen fine spatial and toll patterns (typical Kaggle experience: ~3-5% RMSE gain going 1M->4M), but the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from unpredictable corrupt test rows and heavy-tail noise on a 9.9k-row test set dampen the total improvement to roughly 0.1.

Airport distances let trees isolate flat-fare JFK/LGA/EWR trips (~5.5% of test rows, high-variance fares) in one split instead of several coordinate splits; raw coords already capture most of this, so expect a modest valid-row gain (~3.63 to ~3.55) on top of the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows, giving roughly 4.12-4.16 overall.

RMSE is scored in raw dollars, so the optimal prediction is the conditional mean; fitting L2 on log1p and inverting with expm1 yields geometric-mean-like predictions that systematically under-predict long/expensive trips and the unpredictable corrupt-coordinate rows (NaN branch now predicts ~$9 instead of ~$12), and down-weights exactly the high-fare rows that dominate squared error, so the metric gets slightly worse, as was the common finding in this competition.

Fare is not monotone in haversine distance in this data: ~1.1% of trips have identical pickup/dropoff (distance 0) yet normal fares (~$11), which the unconstrained model isolates via a distance split but LightGBM's basic monotone method forbids (violating splits get zero gain and leaf values are clipped), so those rows get pooled with cheap short hops and under-predicted by ~$5; that alone adds ~0.3-0.4 to MSE, plus the basic method over-constrains the dominant feature, while any gain from saner long-trip extrapolation on a same-distribution test set is small.

The metric is RMSE in raw dollars, so the optimal predictor is the conditional mean; fitting log1p and back-transforming with expm1 (no smearing correction) yields a geometric-mean-like prediction that systematically underpredicts right-skewed fares (especially airport/long trips and neighborhoods with occasional erroneous fares), and with 4M rows the raw model's outlier variance is already small, so the added bias dominates and the valid-row RMSE rises modestly (~3.60 to ~3.67) on top of the fixed ~2.1 floor from invalid rows.

In-sample TE leaks each row's own fare into its key statistics (weight up to 1/21 for singleton routes, and log_count=0 never occurs in training), so LightGBM over-trusts fare_mean on rare, high-fare routes and early-stops sooner; the OOF version already added ~nothing over raw coordinates, so the leak is pure loss, likely costing a few percent on the heavy-tailed rows.

The metric is dollar RMSE, so the optimal predictor is the conditional mean; expm1 of a log-space fit returns roughly the conditional geometric mean, which systematically underestimates fares in high-variance regions (zero-distance/GPS-failure trips, long and airport rides, tail fares) and down-weights exactly the large-dollar errors that dominate RMSE, a well-known loss on this competition; the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row floor dilutes the damage, so expect a modest regression of roughly 0.05-0.15 RMSE rather than a collapse.

Airport distance features are a well-established win on this task (flat-rate JFK and surcharge-heavy Newark trips get isolated with one split, plus radial geometry helps generally), but trees on 900k rows already partly learn airport boxes from raw coordinates and ~2.8% corrupt test rows impose a fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor, so valid-row RMSE improves roughly 3.6 to ~3.5, yielding a modest overall gain to about 4.05.

The ~45 passenger_count=0 test rows have valid coordinates and normal fares, so predicting them with the model instead of the global mean cuts their error from ~10 to ~4 RMSE (about -0.35 MSE), and the ~232 zero/out-of-box rows gain a little from the learned NaN-population conditional mean plus year/hour (their heavy-tailed fares remain mostly unpredictable); keeping 2% NaN rows in training barely affects valid-row predictions, so a modest overall improvement from 4.138 to roughly 4.06.

4x more training rows with identical features and a 1000-tree cap should cut the model's variance on the ~97% predictable test rows (roughly 3.6 -> ~3.47 RMSE there), but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes the gain, so the total drops only modestly from 4.14 to about 4.02; float32/usecols/format changes are numerically harmless and runtime stays ~5-6 min.

OOF smoothed target encodings (especially the pickup->dropoff route mean) hand the GBM a 4-way spatial interaction it struggles to learn from raw coordinates in 1000 trees, adding modest signal on tolls/detours/crosstown traffic; implementation looks leak-free, but much overlaps with what coordinates+haversine already capture, the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor is untouched, and train/test count-scale mismatch plus OOF noise eat part of the gain, so expect a small improvement within or just beyond test-set noise.

RMSE in dollar space is dominated by large fares; training on log1p and back-transforming with expm1 predicts roughly the conditional geometric mean, systematically under-predicting expensive trips (retransformation bias) and shifting model capacity toward cheap rides, while the time-only fallback drops from ~$11.4 to ~$9.2 on the 2.8% corrupt rows, so the standard Kaggle finding for this competition applies: log target slightly hurts RMSE.

Manhattan distance, abs lat/lon deltas and bearing are classic high-importance features for this competition that trees struggle to synthesize from raw coordinates plus haversine alone; expect a modest gain on the ~97% valid test rows (roughly 2-4% of their RMSE), diluted by the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows, giving a small overall improvement.

Landmark/airport distances let trees carve out JFK/LGA/EWR flat-fare regimes with non-axis-aligned boundaries that raw coords only approximate, a known modest win on this dataset (~0.1 RMSE on the ~3.6 valid-row portion); the ~2.1 RMSE floor from 2.8% corrupt test rows is untouched, so the overall gain shrinks to roughly 1-2%, with small run-to-run noise and a slight runtime increase from 18 features.

The metric is RMSE, whose optimal predictor is the conditional mean; an L1 objective fits the conditional median, which for right-skewed fare residuals (traffic time, tolls, GPS-glitch trips, long/airport rides) systematically underpredicts by roughly 0.5-1 dollar on average and by several dollars in the heavy-tail segments, adding ~1 to the valid-row MSE (3.58 -> ~3.72) while the 2.8% invalid-row floor is unchanged; sign-only gradients also allocate splits less toward the high-fare regions that dominate squared error, and with 3.5M rows and min_child_samples=100 the L2 model gains little from L1's outlier robustness, so expect a modest regression to ~4.26.

The metric is raw-dollar RMSE, so the optimal predictor is the conditional mean; expm1 of a log-space fit returns a geometric-mean-like estimate that is biased low (most on high-variance, high-fare rows that dominate squared error) and the log loss de-emphasizes exactly the expensive trips RMSE cares about, so expect a mild regression on valid rows, diluted by the unchanged ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows.

L1 trains toward the conditional median while RMSE rewards the conditional mean; taxi fares are right-skewed with a heavy upper tail (tolls, traffic, mis-metered rides, zero-distance GPS trips), so the L1 model will systematically under-predict by roughly $0.5-1.5 on the rows that dominate squared error, adding ~1-1.5 to the valid-row MSE; the unchanged ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows damps the relative hit to a few percent, so expect a modest regression rather than the hoped-for gain.

LightGBM's Huber uses clipped gradients (|g|<=alpha=1) with constant hessian 1 and no leaf renewal, so each tree can move a prediction by at most lr*alpha=$0.05; starting from the mean (~$11.3), 1000 trees can shift predictions by at most ~$50, so JFK/Newark/long-trip fares ($50-$150) converge slowly or are capped near ~$55-60, while the body converges to a median-like estimate below the conditional mean — both hurt RMSE on a heavy-tailed target evaluated with squared error, likely costing ~2-3 MSE on clean rows.

Metric is raw-dollar RMSE, whose optimum is the conditional mean; fitting log1p and back-transforming with expm1 yields a geometric-mean-like estimate that is systematically biased low, most severely on the long, airport, GPS-failure and heavy-tail trips that dominate the squared error, and the log loss also shifts tree capacity toward relative accuracy on cheap rides, so valid-row RMSE should degrade by roughly 0.15 (the 2.8% corrupt-row floor is unchanged), a pattern widely reported in this competition.

Explicit JFK/LGA/EWR distances and flags help LightGBM isolate flat-fare airport trips (~3-5% of rows, high fares that dominate squared error) more cleanly than raw coordinate splits, giving a modest valid-row gain (~3.6 to ~3.5) that is damped by the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows; low regression risk and runtime unaffected.

4x more rows (3.6M train) lowers variance in splits/leaf values and lets early stopping run the full 1000 trees, giving a typical GBM learning-curve gain of ~4-5% on the ~97% clean test rows (3.62 -> ~3.45), but the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows dilutes that to roughly 3% on the total; runtime (~5-7 min) should stay within budget.

5-fold bagging averages five highly correlated LightGBM models (800k rows each, 75% overlapping data), giving a modest variance reduction on the valid rows that is further diluted by the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows; expect a small gain of roughly 0.02-0.04 RMSE, with test-set noise on 9.9k heavy-tailed rows making a null or slightly negative result plausible.

A leak-free, well-smoothed OOF pickup-cell mean adds a modest fine-grained spatial prior that trees on raw lat/lon approximate only with many splits, but pickup location alone is a weak marginal signal once distance and coordinates are present and ~2.1 RMSE of the score is a fixed corrupt-row floor, so expect only a small gain (~0.03 on valid rows) with some chance of neutral or slightly negative noise-driven outcomes.
