Snapping to a 0.01-degree grid (~1 km cells) injects ~0.4 km RMS error into the dominant haversine feature (~$1+ of fare noise, especially on the many sub-2 km trips) and pools genuine short trips with high-variance GPS-failure zero-distance trips, while the route encoding already operated at 0.01 so gains nothing; expect roughly 1.2-1.5 extra MSE on the ~97% valid rows on top of the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row floor.

L1 objective targets the conditional median, but the metric is RMSE and fares are right-skewed (tolls, airport flat fares, traffic time, zero-distance trips), so predictions are systematically biased low exactly on the high-variance rows that dominate squared error; sign-only gradients also fit the tail less well, so expect a few percent worse RMSE rather than any robustness gain.

L1 objective targets the conditional median, which sits systematically below the conditional mean on right-skewed fares (tolls, traffic, zero-distance and airport trips), and RMSE rewards the mean; the test set carries the same label anomalies as train, so the robustness gain is small while the median bias and less informative sign-only gradients add roughly 0.5-0.9 to MSE on top of the fixed ~4.4 MSE floor from invalid rows.

Airport distances are the classic high-value feature here (JFK flat fare, EWR surcharges), but raw coordinates already let the trees partially isolate airports and 2.8% corrupt test rows impose a ~2.1 RMSE floor, so expect a modest, reliable gain of roughly 0.04-0.08 RMSE rather than a large jump.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean; L1 fits the conditional median, which for right-skewed, partly bimodal fares (traffic time, tolls, airport trips, GPS-mismatched outliers) is biased low by roughly $0.3-1 per region, adding ~0.5-0.8 to MSE with no offsetting label-noise benefit since test shares the same tail distribution; the 2.8% mean-fallback rows are unchanged, so expect a modest ~2% regression.

Rounding to 0.01° (~1 km cells) is far coarser than LightGBM's own 255-quantile bins in dense Manhattan, so fine location signal (route detour, toll/landmark specifics) is lost while airport and borough-scale effects and exact haversine are retained; with 1.8M rows and min_child_samples=100 there is little overfitting to regularize away, so expect a small regression (valid-row RMSE ~3.56→~3.63, total ~4.13→~4.19).

L1 targets the conditional median while RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean; taxi fares are right-skewed conditionally (tolls, traffic, GPS-failure round trips, recording errors that also exist in the random-sample test set), so predictions are biased low and the clean-row MSE rises by roughly 1 dollar-squared on top of less efficient sign-gradient fitting, while the ~2.1 RMSE corrupt-row floor is untouched, giving a modest regression from 4.14 to about 4.26.

Grid-rotated Manhattan distance is a classic complementary feature to haversine that trees struggle to synthesize from raw coordinates; expect a small but real gain on valid rows, heavily damped by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows, so overall RMSE drops only ~0.02.

Correctly cross-fitted directional route target encoding adds a kNN-like fare lookup that LightGBM only approximates from raw coordinates, but with ~877k rows, 0.01-degree cells and smoothing of 50 most routes are shrunk toward the mean and distance already carries most signal, so expect a small gain on valid rows (~3.62 to ~3.55) on top of the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows; run completes comfortably within budget.

Rotated-grid L1 distance is a better route-length proxy than haversine for Manhattan trips and hard for trees to synthesize from raw coordinates at 1M rows, so expect a small gain on the ~97% clean rows (~3.6 -> ~3.56), diluted by the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows; MLflow tracking is best-effort and shouldn't affect the score or budget.

Doubling the random sample to ~1.95M clean rows gives LightGBM (63 leaves, capped at 1000 trees) lower-variance leaves and better coverage of rare long/airport trips, typically ~2% RMSE gain on the predictable rows; the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows is untouched, diluting the total gain to roughly 1%, and runtime stays well inside budget.

The airport-route categorical is a clean single-split proxy for JFK/LGA/EWR flat fares and surcharges, but LightGBM already carves those regions out of the raw coordinates plus haversine, and ~2.8% corrupt test rows impose a ~2.1 RMSE floor that dilutes any gain, so expect only a small improvement (roughly 0.5-1.5%) with the implementation running fine within budget.

In TPS May 2022 the key signals are additive sum interactions (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22) and the f_27 unique-letter count; GBDT without engineered features must staircase-approximate the diagonal boundaries and was typically stuck around 0.98 in the competition, while the MLP learns the linear sums natively, so swapping to LightGBM on the same raw features likely lands slightly below the current 0.9866 despite exact handling of the nominal letter columns.

This dataset's key signal is sharp thresholds on linear sums of continuous features (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22) living in the distribution tails, which a raw-input MLP learns trivially in its first layer; 10 equal-frequency bins make the tail bins very wide (within-bin sd ~1 raw unit on f_21/f_26), so the one-hot model can only output cell-averaged, blurred probabilities for the ~15% of rows in those determined regions and for neighboring middle rows, costing roughly 0.01 AUC, while gains on count/categorical columns are negligible and the weak f_27 ordinal side is unchanged; runtime and memory stay within budget.

The 40 standardized features are essentially mutually uncorrelated in this synthetic data, so full-rank PCA whitening is a near-Haar-random rotation that smears every discrete signal (f_27 letter effects, unique-letter structure, f_29/f_30, Poisson counts) and the oblique sum-threshold interactions across all PCs; axis-aligned splits can then only recover linear trends plus weak low-order interactions, a classic large GBDT-under-rotation regression, while PCA cannot find the supervised sum directions since they are not variance directions.

f_27 is near-unique (671k distinct in 800k rows, max count 10, ~72% of test strings unseen), so a whole-string target encoding with m=20 collapses to the prior for most rows and only ±0.02 for singleton matches; this effectively deletes the strongest feature block (per-position letters, which drive 0.10–1.00 positive-rate spreads and the 9%/91% distinct-count tails), leaving a numeric-only model plus a weak neighbor-label signal, so AUC should fall to roughly the mid/high 0.8s.

f_27 is near-unique (671k distinct in 800k rows, 72% of test strings unseen), so with m=20 smoothing the OOF target encoding collapses to the prior for ~75% of train rows and ~72% of test rows and is only a faint signal elsewhere; meanwhile the per-position ordinals carry strong, roughly monotone letter effects (position 6 rates 0.10→1.00, rare letters →1.00) that nunique only partially proxies, so the model loses the most informative feature group and falls back to numerics + nunique, costing several AUC points.

These are the well-known TPS-May-2022 'magic' additive interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26 with ±5 thresholds) that trees cannot learn efficiently from raw columns; in the competition they lifted GBDT models from ~0.991 to ~0.996-0.997, so this 3000-tree/127-leaf LightGBM should land around 0.9965 with negligible runtime cost.

The logistic regression on raw numerics plus ordinal f_27 codes cannot capture the non-monotone interaction sums or the unique-letter-count signal, so it should land around 0.72-0.78 holdout AUC; forcing a 50/50 rank average of that weak model with a 0.984 LightGBM injects its ordering noise into every near-boundary pair and should cost roughly 3-5 AUC points rather than help.

This is essentially the known AmbrosM-style 64-64-64-16 SiLU MLP recipe that reached ~0.998 on TPS May 2022; NNs dominate GBDTs on this smooth-interaction synthetic data, but the proposal omits the unique-character-count feature (which the MLP can only partially reconstruct from ordinals), uses a single model with 80 epochs, so expect a clear gain over LightGBM's 0.9842 but short of 0.998, around 0.993-0.996.

A median-filtered background channel supplies strong global illumination/stain context that helps the U-Net disentangle text from background noise, giving a modest but real RMSE improvement with identical training budget.
Deeper U-Net with 256px context captures larger stains/wrinkles and typically improves denoising RMSE, though batch 8 gives noisier gradients, so expect a modest ~5-8% gain over the 0.01626 baseline.
4-way flip TTA averages out per-orientation prediction noise on a well-converged U-Net; typically yields a small but reliable RMSE reduction (1-3%) with no training changes.

A 180s wall-clock budget with time-based cosine decay likely yields more optimizer steps than the original fixed 2000 (small UNet steps are fast on GPU), giving slightly more converged training with the same LR annealing shape, so a modest RMSE improvement.

Charbonnier/L1 training optimizes toward the conditional median rather than the mean, so it typically slightly degrades an RMSE-graded metric despite sharper outputs; with identical architecture and training budget, expect a small regression of a few percent.

Injecting sigma=0.05 Gaussian noise trains the model to remove corruption that doesn't exist in the test images (whose noise is stain-like, not Gaussian); at inference the model applies smoothing/denoising calibrated for the extra noise, biasing clean-pixel predictions toward over-smoothing, so RMSE likely regresses modestly.

GroupNorm removes the crop-vs-full-page BN statistics mismatch and batch coupling, which typically gives a small but real gain in image restoration; with identical training budget and architecture the effect is modest, so expect a ~2% RMSE improvement.

SSIM+L1 improves structural sharpness but is not aligned with RMSE; Zhao et al. show it typically trades a small amount of pixel MSE for perceptual/structural quality, so expect a slight RMSE regression over the MSE-trained baseline.
8-fold dihedral TTA averages out orientation-dependent errors and typically gives a modest but reliable RMSE improvement (~2-3%) for patch-regression denoisers with flip/rotation-ambiguous noise.

The metric is per-pixel RMSE, and pure SSIM loss optimizes local structural correlation rather than absolute pixel error — it typically sharpens strokes visually but increases MSE/RMSE versus L2-trained models (Zhao et al. found L2 wins on PSNR), so this likely regresses on the graded metric.

Residual learning with a linear, zero-initialized head avoids sigmoid saturation on the dominant white background, giving cleaner gradients and identity-mapping initialization, which typically yields a moderate RMSE improvement over direct image regression.

A small SSIM term on top of an RMSE-anchored pixel loss typically sharpens edges and improves structured-error RMSE slightly in document denoising, with only minor risk from the added sqrt/structural gradient scale change.

Residual prediction with zero-initialized final conv is a well-established win for denoising (DnCNN-style): the network only needs to learn the sparse noise component rather than regress the mostly-white image, speeding convergence and lowering RMSE, with the clamp preserving valid output range.

Adding ~800 synthetic corrupted-clean pairs from ground-truth targets diversifies the training distribution on a small 134-image dataset and should improve generalization, though domain mismatch between synthetic artifacts (stains/shading/speckle) and the real test noise plus the heavy blur limits gains to a modest ~4% RMSE reduction.

4.5x more Adam steps with stretched cosine decay on random 128px crops should reduce underfitting of the small U-Net; with abundant patch-level augmentation overfitting risk is low, so expect a modest RMSE improvement of roughly 5-8%.

8-fold dihedral TTA is a standard, low-risk win for patch-regression denoisers: averaging over self-consistent transforms reduces prediction variance and typically cuts RMSE by 1-3%; the inverse transforms are correctly implemented, and the modest 8x inference cost on 29 small images fits easily in the budget.

MAE optimizes the median rather than the mean, which biases predictions away from the RMSE-optimal conditional mean; since grading is RMSE, switching from MSE to L1 typically causes a small regression (~3-6%) in this regime.

Upweighting dark/text pixels (weight 3) in training better fits glyph interiors and edges, typically yielding a small but real RMSE improvement in document denoising; minor risk of biased white-pixel predictions caps the gain.

Up-weighting dark/ink pixels counters background dominance and typically gives a small RMSE gain on this denoising task, though the effect is modest since background errors already dominate RMSE and the model capacity/training budget are unchanged.

Residual (skip-from-input) prediction with a zero-initialized output layer makes the identity mapping the starting point, which stabilizes early training and typically yields a small but real RMSE gain for image denoising, with clamping at inference kept so predictions stay valid.

L1 optimizes the median rather than the mean, so it is misaligned with the RMSE grading metric; denoising results typically degrade slightly (a few percent) when switching from MSE to L1, though the robustness to severe corruption keeps the regression modest.

Residual prediction with zero-initialized head starts from the noisy input (already a strong baseline for denoising) and lets the network learn only the noise, typically converging faster and better than direct sigmoid prediction within the same 20-epoch budget, yielding a modest RMSE improvement.

Halving NAFNet width (16->8) cuts capacity ~4x on an already-thin model; document denoising is simple but the baseline was far from overfitting, so expect a modest RMSE regression from reduced representational power.

Foreground-weighted loss sharpens faint stroke reconstruction, which usually yields a small net RMSE gain since text pixels carry most of the residual error, though slightly worse background fits cap the improvement.

The illumination-normalized channel from grey-closing background estimation is a well-known effective feature for this dirty-documents task, giving the network an easier signal to separate text from stains, and should yield a solid RMSE improvement with the unchanged training budget.

Running the 1x1 conv + sigmoid in fp32 changes only the last layer's precision, so output values shift negligibly; the added runtime.toml forcing CPU-only execution mainly affects wall-clock (tight but likely feasible at 2000 small-patch steps) and slightly alters numerics, so RMSE stays essentially the same with a tiny regression risk from bf16-vs-fp32 rounding differences in the final layer.
4-view flip TTA averages out model noise without changing training; on this denoising task it reliably gives a small RMSE gain of ~1-3%, well within the time budget.

NAFNet is a better architecture, but runtime.json forces CPU-only training with 13 threads; 2000 steps of NAFNet on 128x128x32 batches will barely fit or be cut short of the budget, leaving an undertrained model that likely regresses slightly versus the well-converged U-Net baseline.

The pretrained ImageNet-1k head is already a strong classifier for exactly these 120 dog classes (Stanford Dogs images come from ImageNet), so blending it with LR probabilities — with w=0 available as a fallback — should cut holdout-tuned log loss substantially, roughly 0.31 -> 0.24-0.26.

PCA-256 retains the bulk of feature variance while decorrelating inputs and shrinking the LR parameter space 4x, which typically gives a small but real log-loss improvement for linear probes on frozen features with only ~85 samples/class.

Mixup/CutMix are strong regularizers well-suited to small fine-grained datasets and soften overconfident predictions on confusable breeds, which benefits log loss; with only 6 epochs gains are modest but likely net positive.

The (0.08, 1.0) scale range matches the backbone's pretraining augmentation and adds useful regularization for only ~77 images/class, likely giving a small log-loss improvement, though very tight crops occasionally discard breed context so gains are modest.

ConvNeXt-V2 Large with IN-22k pretraining is a vastly stronger feature extractor for fine-grained breed recognition than ResNet-50 V1, and IN-22k contains the exact 120 dog classes, so frozen features + logistic regression should cut log loss roughly in half; runtime and pipeline correctness are sound.

The 1000-d log-softmax block is a deterministic linear function of the pooled features, adding mostly collinear/noise dimensions (especially near-constant non-dog columns inflated by standardisation) that waste L2 budget; a clean linear probe on the 2048-d pooled features should modestly improve log loss.

Closed-form ridge boundaries are roughly equivalent to converged LR on these strong L2-normalized frozen features, and the joint (alpha, T) holdout search with temperature scaling directly optimizes calibration for log loss, typically shaving a few percent off the LR head's score.

Per-block PCA to 128 components retains nearly all breed-relevant variance on an all-dog distribution while discarding noisy low-variance directions, giving mild denoising and a better-conditioned LR fit; with 10k samples the 2560-d head was only mildly overfit, so expect a small improvement rather than a large one.

ConvNeXt-Base pretrained on IN-22k and fine-tuned on IN-1k produces far more discriminative features than ResNet-50 V1, and its feature space includes the actual ImageNet dog breeds, so a linear probe should cut log loss substantially; the re-tuned C adds a small extra gain.

Fine-tuning an ImageNet-22k ConvNeXt-Tiny (whose pretraining includes many dog breeds) with flip TTA and validation-calibrated temperature scaling should substantially beat frozen ResNet50 features; 6 epochs fits the 7-min budget for this small dataset, so log loss should drop from ~0.45 to roughly 0.25-0.32.

All 120 breeds are ImageNet classes, so the discarded fc head's log-softmax outputs add a strong, well-calibrated breed signal; combined with standardization and re-tuned C, log loss should drop roughly 15-25% from 0.4515.

Concatenating L2-normalized features from three diverse strong backbones (ConvNeXt-22k, CLIP, DINOv2) gives a much richer 2560-d representation than frozen ResNet-50 features, and this kind of multi-backbone ensemble typically cuts log loss on fine-grained Stanford Dogs from ~0.45 to ~0.2-0.3, with holdout-tuned C adding a small extra gain.

Removing label smoothing and adding focal loss typically yields higher accuracy on hard cases but worse-calibrated, more overconfident probabilities, which hurts a log-loss metric on a 120-class fine-grained task.

Last-stage-only fine-tuning is a well-matched regularizer for ~85 images/class: it preserves ImageNet low/mid features, cuts trainable params ~6x, and typically matches or slightly beats full fine-tuning on small fine-grained sets within a short 10-epoch budget, so I expect a modest log-loss improvement with some uncertainty.

Horizontal-flip TTA almost always reduces log loss slightly by averaging out pose/view noise in linear-probe predictions; the change is safe, within budget, and expected to give a modest ~2-4% improvement.

CLIP ViT-B/32 features are solid but the coarser patch grid and contrastive (non-ImageNet-supervised) features typically underperform an augreg ImageNet-21k-fine-tuned ViT-B/16 for fine-grained breed discrimination under a fixed linear probe, so log loss should regress modestly.
PCA to 256 components retains most discriminative variance of ResNet-50 GAP features and denoises the probe; with C fixed at 0.3 the effect is small, likely a marginal log-loss improvement (~0.002).

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings with a linear head are known to reach ~89-90% top-1 on Stanford Dogs (vs ~83% for ResNet-50 features), which typically translates to log loss in the 0.25-0.30 range; the C re-selection and unchanged TTA pipeline add small gains, though at 224px (below DINOv2's native 518) some fine-grained detail is lost, capping the improvement.

PCA-whitening to 256 components on L2-normalized deep embeddings equalizes noise directions and amplifies within-class variance, typically mildly hurting calibrated log-loss for an already well-regularized linear head, so a small regression is expected.

Distance-weighted 10-NN over 9k samples in 2816-d space produces coarse, poorly calibrated probabilities (multiples of ~1/10) with heavy log-loss penalties on confident wrong predictions, and is known to underperform a linear softmax head even on good embeddings (DINO-style kNN trails linear probes substantially), so expect a large regression from 0.54.

End-to-end fine-tuning of ResNet-50 on the Stanford Dogs subset (which overlaps ImageNet classes) with label smoothing typically reaches ~80% accuracy and clearly lower log loss than frozen features + linear probe; 10 epochs fp16 fits comfortably in the budget, though short training and confident softmax keep the gain moderate rather than dramatic.

ViT-B/16 augreg-in21k features are substantially stronger than ResNet50-V1 features for fine-grained dog breed classification (Stanford Dogs is a subset of ImageNet where this backbone excels), so the linear probe should cut log loss from ~0.45 to roughly 0.28, while keeping the identical sklearn head and runtime well within budget.

10-crop TTA averaging over probabilities on frozen ResNet features typically gives a modest log-loss improvement (5ish %) by reducing crop variance; the extra MLflow noise is best-effort and harmless, and runtime stays well within budget.

Adding stronger ConvNeXt-tiny (in22k→in1k) features, L2-normalizing blocks, and concatenating with ResNet-50 features is a well-established win for frozen-feature linear probes on fine-grained classification, typically cutting log loss substantially.

The pretrained ResNet-50's ImageNet dog-head logits (restricted to the 120 breeds and temperature-calibrated) are a strong complementary classifier for this ImageNet-subset task, and the CV-selected convex blend with the logistic regression should reduce log loss meaningfully.
PCA to 256 dims discards discriminative low-variance directions and C=0.3 was tuned for raw 2048-d features, so log loss typically regresses slightly (roughly 2-6%) with this projection.

Global max pooling on a frozen ResNet-50 keeps only the single strongest spatial response per channel, producing noisier, less calibrated features than average pooling, so log loss on fine-grained breeds typically degrades modestly.
IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 (80.9% top-1 vs 76.1% for V1) yields notably better frozen features, and with matched preprocessing (232px resize) this typically reduces transfer log loss by ~5-10%.

C=0.3 was already selected via holdout search over {0.03,...,3}, so dropping to C=0.03 over-regularizes the head init, yielding slightly underfit probabilities that the brief bottleneck fine-tuning won't fully recover — expect a modest log-loss regression.

Downscaling to 192px removes fine-grained detail critical for breed discrimination with an ImageNet backbone tuned for 224px inputs, degrading both feature quality and the fine-tuned layer4, so log loss worsens moderately while runtime savings are irrelevant to the metric.

PCA(256) keeps most discriminative variance, but the previously tuned C=0.3 doesn't transfer to the new feature scale (unwhitened PCs inflate early components, effectively under-regularizing), so log loss regresses modestly.
Downscaling inputs to 192px removes discriminative fine-grained detail the ImageNet-pretrained features rely on, so log loss should regress moderately while the pipeline still runs correctly.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 (80.9% vs 76.1% top-1) yields noticeably better frozen features for fine-grained transfer, and matching its documented 232/224 preprocessing should reduce log loss by roughly 8-10% with the same C=0.3 logistic head.

Scalar temperature scaling fitted on a stratified holdout typically yields a small but real log-loss improvement (~1-3%) for frozen-feature logistic regression, since the refit-on-all-data probabilities are slightly miscalibrated; risk of regression is low as the temperature is bounded and NLL-optimized.

Initializing the head from the fitted logistic regression and briefly fine-tuning only the last bottleneck (2 epochs, small LRs, frozen BN) on cached activations should gently adapt features to the breed task without overfitting, yielding a modest log-loss improvement over the frozen baseline.

Horizontal-flip TTA on the frozen ResNet-50 features typically yields a small but consistent log-loss improvement (~1-2%) by averaging out pose/asymmetry variance; the extra inference pass is trivial within budget and the training pipeline is unchanged.

Discarding 90-99.7% of negatives throws away ranking information; L2 logistic AUC is largely insensitive to class balance (only the intercept shifts), while the NB log-count ratio computed on the balanced subset is biased by the altered base rate, so rare-label gains are offset by small losses on the common labels.

Adding char_wb features to the NB-LogReg branch gives it access to subword patterns (crucial for obfuscated profanity and rare labels like threat/identity_hate), which historically lifts NB-LogReg AUC by ~1%; blended 50/50 with unchanged branch A, expect a ~0.5% net gain.

For logistic regression, 1:1 undersampling mainly shifts the intercept while leaving coefficient-driven ranking (and thus AUC) nearly unchanged, but fitting rare labels like threat/identity_hate on only ~1-3k rows adds variance to both the NB ratio and the classifier, likely costing a small amount of AUC on those noisy columns.

Plain MultinomialNB on TF-IDF is markedly weaker than the NB-ratio-weighted LogisticRegression it replaces, and since branch B carries half the rank-average blend (plus feeds the stack into A), the mean AUC drops by roughly 0.5-1 point despite faster fits.

Mean-pooled Word2Vec features are substantially weaker than word+char TF-IDF n-grams for toxicity classification (typical standalone AUC ~0.94-0.95 vs ~0.978), so two of the three equally-weighted rank-blend branches (A and the MLP) degrade, dragging the blend below the 0.9808 baseline even though strong branch B remains.

1:1 random undersampling discards 80-99.7% of training data per label; AUC-based ranking with linear models degrades with far less data (especially branch B's NB counts and the rare labels), and balanced sampling is unnecessary here since AUC is threshold- and calibration-insensitive, so expect a modest regression with a small speedup.

A 4-epoch sparse EmbeddingBag MLP on the same TF-IDF features will be individually weaker than the NB-LogReg branches (~0.975-0.98 held-out) but adds modest diversity; equal-weight rank blending a weaker fourth model typically leaves the mean AUC essentially flat, with a tiny gain at best.

AUC depends on ranking quality; discarding 84-99.4% of negatives (threat down to ~956 rows) degrades coefficient estimation and adds variance, especially for rare labels that dominate column-mean noise, so balanced undersampling likely costs a small amount of AUC despite faster fits.

De-obfuscation and repeat-collapsing unify sparse toxic-token variants (helping the rare labels like threat/identity_hate slightly), while lowercasing loses some CAPS signal that char n-grams could exploit; net effect on this strong linear baseline is a small positive gain, consistent with classic kernels that saw minor improvements from such cleaning.

Adding OOF NB-LogReg predictions as low-norm dense features lets branch A's logistic models exploit B's signal with proper interaction weighting rather than just rank-averaging; this typically yields a small but real AUC gain (~+0.0005-0.001), with minimal leakage risk since OOF folds and the /20 scaling keep the stack well-behaved.

A 3-epoch MLP on the same sparse TF-IDF is meaningfully weaker than the tuned linear branches, so diluting the 50/50 rank blend to 1/3 weight for it should slightly regress the mean AUC despite the small diversity gain.

Branch C is an NB-LogReg on B's word features plus A's char features, so it correlates heavily with B but adds complementary char-level signal; equal-weight rank blending of three branches typically yields a small gain (~+0.001 AUC) over the two-branch blend, and runtime stays within budget since all vectorizers are fit once and liblinear is capped at 100 iterations.

Holdout-fitted per-label blend weights with shrinkage toward 0.5 should give a tiny gain at best; the two branches are similarly strong so optimal weights are near 0.5, and holdout noise on rare labels mostly cancels out thanks to the shrinkage.

Compressing to 300 LSA factors and dropping char n-grams and NB-weighting loses substantial discriminative signal; dense LSA+LR baselines on this dataset typically land around 0.96-0.97, well below the 0.9798 sparse ensemble.

Keeping all positives preserves rare-label ranking, but discarding most negatives (up to 10:1 cap) degrades the linear models' decision boundaries and starves fastText of data, so AUC drops slightly on the common labels while rare labels stay roughly flat.

Softmax over 7 classes forces probabilities to sum to 1, coupling the labels and compressing per-label rankings (rare labels like threat/identity_hate get near-zero scores), so branch F's column-wise AUC drops relative to six independent binary fastText models, dragging the 1/3-weighted rank blend down by roughly half a point.

A single ComplementNB on raw word counts loses the TF-IDF weighting, the NB-LogReg discriminative boost, the char n-gram views, and the ensemble variance reduction — the 'correlated errors buy little' claim is wrong for this task, so the score should drop from ~0.9816 to a typical standalone-NB level around 0.96.

Mean-pooled from-scratch Word2Vec with a linear head is a well-known weaker baseline for this competition (~0.95-0.96 AUC): unweighted averaging destroys word-order and rare-token signal that the sparse TF-IDF/NB-LogReg ensemble exploits, especially hurting the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) that dominate column-mean noise.

Average-pooled Word2Vec trained only on the competition corpus with a linear head is well-documented on Jigsaw to underperform word+char TF-IDF NB-LogReg blends (~0.98) by 3-4 AUC points, since mean pooling loses word order/emphasis and the small corpus yields weaker embeddings than pretrained ones.

A char-level NB-LogReg branch adds diverse signal (catches obfuscated tokens the word branches miss) and is known to help Jigsaw linear blends, but gains are small at this score level since branch A already includes char features and holdout-tuned weights may slightly overfit rare labels; expect a modest net improvement of ~0.0004 AUC.

C=0.1 heavily over-regularizes branch A; C=4 with liblinear is the well-established configuration from top public kernels for this exact word+char TF-IDF setup and typically lifts branch A's standalone AUC by several thousandths, raising the rank-blended score from ~0.980 to ~0.985.

Supervised fastText (dim 64, bigrams) is a diverse, reasonably strong branch (~0.975 standalone) whose rank-average with the two TF-IDF branches typically adds ~0.002-0.003 to mean column AUC on Jigsaw.

Adding a char n-gram NB-LogReg branch is a well-known complementary signal in this competition's top kernels; rank-averaging word and char NB-LR views typically lifts mean AUC by ~0.004-0.005 over a two-branch baseline, and the 100k char_wb fit fits within the time budget.

Per-label weight tuning gains are tiny since the two branches are similarly strong, while training on only 90% of data and tuning weights on a noisy 10% holdout (rare labels like threat have ~30 positives) roughly cancels or slightly outweighs them, giving a near-neutral to slightly negative net effect.

NB log-count-ratio weighting typically helps linear TF-IDF models (it already powers branch B), so applying it to branch A should give a small but real lift that partially carries through the 50/50 rank blend.

min_df=0.01 (~3130 of 313k docs) is a very aggressive cutoff: it barely binds for the capped word/char branches (top-k by frequency already exceeds this df), but it prunes many mid-frequency bigrams from branch B's NB-LogReg vocabulary below the 200k cap, discarding discriminative rare-term signal and slightly hurting AUC.

Balanced undersampling discards ~90-99% of negatives per label, slightly hurting ranking quality (especially for rare labels like threat/identity_hate that dominate the column mean), though logit blending largely restores calibration, so expect a small net AUC drop.

Cosine nearest-centroid is a much weaker linear separator than regularized logistic regression (no learned discriminative weighting beyond class means, and expit of unbounded cosine-diff scores keeps poor ordering), so both branches lose several AUC points and the blend lands around 0.95.

char_wb character n-grams (word-boundary padded) are the standard choice in the original Toxic kernels and typically edge out plain 'char' slightly by avoiding spurious cross-word n-grams, so a small AUC gain on the blended rank average is expected.

Replacing regularized logistic regression (and the NB-weighted NB-LogReg branch) with raw ComplementNB discards the discriminative feature weighting that drives this benchmark's top linear scores; NB models are known to underperform NB-LogReg/logreg on Toxic Comment AUC, so both branches regress while retaining the same vectorizers.

Crushing 60k sparse TF-IDF features to 32 SVD components discards most discriminative lexical signal (especially for rare labels like threat/identity_hate), sharply weakening branch A; the 50/50 rank blend with unchanged fastText then drags the mean AUC down by roughly 1.5-2 points.

Collapsing every out-of-top-2000 token into a single 'raretoken' destroys exactly the rare-word and character n-gram signal (slurs, identity terms, unusual spellings) that drives AUC on the rare labels, so both branches lose discrimination and the blend regresses modestly.

Removing English stop words lets frequent function words ('the', 'is', 'a') consume slots in the fixed 10k word vocabulary, slightly diluting discriminative unigram coverage in branch A; effect is tiny since char n-grams and the unchanged NB branch dominate the blend.

Logit-averaging mixes the two branches' differing probability calibrations (sag LR vs NB-weighted liblinear), which distorts within-column orderings that rank-averaging preserves; AUC depends only on ordering, so expect a small regression of a few hundredths of a percent.

Switching char_wb to char lets n-grams span word boundaries, typically a tiny gain on short toxic text; with 50k features and equal rank blending the effect on mean AUC is very small, likely a marginal improvement.

NB-LogReg on word bigrams is a very strong per-label linear branch (~0.985 standalone); replacing it with a small fastText model (dim=64, 5 epochs, 256 tokens) yields a weaker (~0.97) but decorrelated model, so the equal-weight rank blend with branch A should land slightly below the original 0.9801.

Multinomial LR with lbfgs at C=1.0 on 990x192 is already well-regularized and not variance-bound, so discarding 64 F-ranked features mostly removes weak-but-real signal; expect a small (~1-2%) degradation of the LR half, which shows up scaled by the 50/50 blend weight.

Label smoothing prevents logit saturation and improves calibration of the NN half of the blend, which typically lowers multi-class log loss modestly on a tiny 99-class dataset, while the 50% LR blend damps the effect size.

OvR decouples the classifiers but with only ~10 positives per species the independent binary fits produce noisier, less mutually consistent probabilities than the joint softmax; the power/floor calibration can fix scale but not the lost cross-class coupling, so a modest regression from 0.045 is expected.

A 5-seed 512-unit MLP bag on the 192 descriptors is a genuinely competitive second model (~0.05-0.07 OOF alone); blending it with LR before calibration typically trims a few percent off a strong LR baseline, and the w=0 fallback plus OOF-only selection makes regression unlikely, though 990-row OOF selection noise limits the gain to a modest 2-4%.

Averaging five 80%-data fold models smooths probabilities (small bagging benefit) but loses the full-data refit's extra training signal; for a well-regularized convex logreg these roughly cancel, with a slight net regression typical — expect a score very close to the parent's ~0.057.

The 21 image-derived geometric features (size, aspect ratio, compactness, Hu moments) add genuinely complementary information to the scale-normalized shape descriptors, and this classic leaf dataset is known to benefit from such features; with proper scaling and CV-selected C, expect a modest but real log-loss improvement.

PCA retaining 95% variance decorrelates the collinear histogram bins making the isotropic L2 penalty better matched, likely giving a small improvement, but it also risks discarding discriminative low-variance directions so the gain will be modest (~0.088 -> ~0.086).

Averaging five stratified-fold logistic regression models (CV bagging) typically reduces variance and slightly improves log loss over a single full-data fit for this small 10-samples-per-class problem; expect a modest ~2-4% gain, with the OOF estimate also being more reliable.

The augmented CNN with rotation TTA on silhouettes plus standardized features should reach ~0.3-0.5 holdout log loss, and a 50/50 arithmetic blend with the well-calibrated LR (0.124) typically lands around 0.09 on this dataset, a solid improvement with low risk given the small, standard architecture and time guard.

OOF-fitted power/temperature + uniform-floor calibration on a strong LR baseline (logloss 0.124) typically yields a modest but real gain; grid search on OOF is low-risk for overfitting with only 2 scalars, so expect a few percent improvement to roughly 0.115-0.120.

Tuning C by 5-fold stratified CV on multinomial logistic regression over the 192 leaf descriptors typically finds a much better regularisation strength (large C, ~100-1000) than fixed C=1, cutting log loss from ~0.124 to roughly 0.07-0.09; implementation is faithful to the proposal and runs well within budget.

Geometric shape descriptors (Hu moments, eccentricity, solidity, etc.) add genuinely discriminative signal for leaf species beyond the precomputed margin/texture/shape histograms, and with 27 clean features fed to a regularized linear model, holdout and test log loss should drop meaningfully without overfitting risk.

With only 990 rows, 99 classes, and ~240 correlated standardized features, stronger L2 shrinkage (C=0.2) typically reduces overconfident probabilities and modestly improves multiclass log loss; effect is small since C=1.0 was already in a reasonable regime.

Training on only 80% of the small (~990 sample) training set instead of refitting on all data discards ~198 labeled examples, which slightly degrades the logistic regression's calibration and test log loss despite aligning with the internal holdout.

OOF-weighted blending of LR with complementary kNN/LDA learners on this classic dataset typically nudges log loss below the LR-only 0.059 baseline; LR will dominate the weights, so the gain is modest, and the implementation is leak-free and well within budget.

Gradient boosting on 99 classes with only ~990 samples and 16 samples/class typically overfits badly despite early stopping; the well-tuned multinomial LR (logloss ~0.06) is a very strong low-variance baseline for these pre-extracted descriptors, and HGB on this dataset usually lands around 0.15-0.3 log loss.

Replacing well-calibrated multinomial LR with a linear SVM whose Platt sigmoid is fit on tiny 3-fold splits (~3 samples/class per fold) yields noisier probabilities, and log loss punishes that; expect a modest regression in the ensemble.

RF vote-fraction probabilities are coarser and worse-calibrated than early-stopped HGB's log-loss-trained probabilities, so swapping it into the uniform soft vote likely degrades log loss modestly on this small 99-class problem.

With only ~990 samples across 99 classes, an MLP tends to produce overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities; uniform-shrinkage calibration partially compensates but typically cannot fully fix it, so log loss likely regresses versus the well-calibrated linear softmax baseline.

CV-tuning C on this small 990x192 dataset typically selects a less-regularized value (C~10-100) than 1.0, modestly sharpening OOF-calibrated probabilities and reducing log loss by roughly 10-15% while the rest of the pipeline (shrinkage alpha, clipping, scaling) stays identical.

The 48 classical shape/contour features are redundant with but complementary to the provided descriptors; with standardization and multinomial logistic regression they typically add a small but real signal, yielding a modest log-loss improvement, and the run completes well within budget.

C=1.0 is underregularized for 192 features/990 samples; CV-selected C (typically much smaller) plus neg_log_loss scoring and full-data refit meaningfully improves calibrated log loss, consistent with known leaf-classification LR results (~0.07-0.10).

The leaf dataset is near-linearly separable with shrinkage LDA and tuned distance-weighted kNN; a soft-voting ensemble of diverse, well-regularized classifiers on all 891 rows typically cuts log loss roughly in half versus a single fixed-C logistic regression.

Shrinking LR probabilities toward uniform almost always reduces log loss on this well-calibrated-ish leaf task; OOF-selected alpha will be small-to-moderate and the test score should improve a few percent, roughly matching the OOF loss (~0.08-0.12) vs. the unshrunk 0.1244.

Ledoit-Wolf 'auto' shrinkage already adapts well to the high-dimensional, few-samples-per-class setting; fixing heavy 0.9 shrinkage likely over-regularizes and slightly worsens log loss, though the effect is modest since standardized features make spherical covariance a decent prior.
Per-family shrunk LDAs average complementary evidence and soften overconfident probabilities, typically giving a modest log-loss gain over one concatenated LDA on this small dataset.

Multinomial logistic on the 192 standardized descriptors already works well with 16 examples/class; discarding 10% of variance via unsupervised PCA loses discriminative signal, so a modest log-loss regression is expected.

LDA with tuned shrinkage is a strong fit for this small-sample (16/class), moderate-dimensional Gaussian-like descriptor data and typically edges out tuned logistic regression on the leaf benchmark, so expect a modest log-loss improvement.

PCA at 95% variance on standardized descriptors discards low-variance but class-discriminative components and adds a rotation that doesn't help a well-regularized lbfgs logistic model, so log loss should regress modestly from the already-strong 0.045 baseline.

Shrinkage LDA with temperature scaling is a strong model on these 192 descriptors but typically slightly underperforms calibrated multinomial logistic regression, so expect modest regression from 0.045 to roughly 0.055-0.065.

A tiny 0.005 uniform shrink barely changes probabilities; with an already well-calibrated low-loss model it slightly softens confident correct predictions, yielding a near-zero, marginally negative effect.

Reducing Nystroem components from 512 to 384 is a mild change on a small (n~1267) dataset; the slightly more compact RBF approximation acts as weak regularization and typically yields a near-neutral result, likely a tiny improvement or tiny regression within noise.

LDA with lsqr auto-shrinkage is a well-known strong baseline on this 192-feature leaf dataset (16 samples/class, high-dim), typically achieving log loss ~0.05-0.07, roughly halving the untuned logistic regression's 0.124.

3-fold CV over C with fold-local scaling reliably picks stronger regularization for this dataset (typically C in 10-100), which is a well-known substantial log-loss improvement over the fixed C=1.0 baseline; runtime is trivial for 990x192 data.

Temperature scaling fitted on out-of-fold logits typically reduces log loss by a few percent for an already reasonably calibrated lbfgs logistic regression; the unchanged classifier keeps base accuracy the same, so a modest ~5-10% improvement from calibration is expected.

Nyström RBF features (512 components, gamma=1/192) give logistic regression a nonlinear decision boundary that historically improves leaf-classification log loss substantially (from ~0.12 to ~0.05-0.08); the pipeline correctly avoids leakage and fits comfortably within the time budget, with the MLflow/threading boilerplate not affecting the metric.

The 31 dense features (temporal decline, text form stats, first-person/reciprocity signals invisible to stop-worded TF-IDF, upvote ratio) are well-known predictive signals for RAOP and should add modest AUC to a strong linear baseline; a couple of overlapping features may be redundant with the existing numeric block, capping the gain at ~1-2%.

Random forests typically underperform regularized logistic regression on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF features (~8000 cols, ~4.5k rows): unpruned trees overfit rare tokens and dilute splits across many weak text features, while the strong linear signal in the requester-history features is captured less efficiently, so expect a modest AUC regression despite RF being the competition's benchmark.

Random forests on 5k-dim sparse TF-IDF with sqrt feature subsampling (~71 features per split) will be dominated by noise text features and underfit the smooth numeric signal; linear models consistently beat RF on this dataset, so expect a sizable AUC drop despite the Kaggle RF benchmark narrative (that benchmark used different features).

Replacing 5k TF-IDF unigrams with 50 unsupervised LDA topics discards most discriminative word-level signal; LDA on ~4.5k short documents yields blurry topics, so the text block adds little beyond the metadata, dropping AUC toward the metadata-only level.

Replacing the supervised TF-IDF+LR text logit (the strongest signal in the stack) with 20 unsupervised LDA topic proportions discards most predictive text information; LightGBM gains minor interaction ability but cannot recover the lost supervised signal, so AUC drops toward the metadata+weak-topics level.

Replacing the non-stationary absolute epoch with stationary hour-of-day and weekday features preserves the useful posting-time signal (giver activity patterns) while removing timeline memorisation; effect on a LightGBM that already had 10 other features is expected to be small but slightly positive, roughly +0.002 AUC.

The GBM on requester-history/dense features captures complementary non-text signal; rank-blending with the text-LR via CV-tuned weight typically adds ~0.01 AUC over the text-only baseline on this competition, with small risk of the blend weight overfitting OOF noise.

Random forests split greedily on single features, which works poorly on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF (rare word columns rarely win splits and each tree sees mostly noise), so despite good use of the dense metadata the model typically loses several AUC points versus a well-regularized linear model on this classic text classification setup.

Prior-subreddit presence (e.g. RAOP community participation) is a known predictive signal in this dataset; adding it as a binary idf-weighted block should give a modest AUC lift over the text+numeric baseline.

giver_username_if_known is a post-outcome leak field that the organizers removed from the test set, so the column will be absent in test.json and the fallback fills it with zeros; the flag helps slightly on train/holdout but contributes nothing to test predictions, leaving the graded AUC essentially unchanged.

Stacking OOF text logits with raw requester numerics in a small LightGBM typically beats plain TF-IDF+LR on RAOP by capturing nonlinear interactions; expect a modest gain to ~0.67 despite added variance from the timestamp feature and refit.

Adding request timing, text statistics, and RAOP-history indicator features to TF-IDF+LR is a well-known small win on RAOP; leakage-free and properly scaled, should lift AUC modestly (~0.01-0.015) without risk of regression.

ExtraTrees on ~5.4k high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF features with only ~5.7k rows typically underperforms a linear model on text; sqrt feature subsampling mostly picks noise n-grams, yielding a modest AUC regression versus logistic regression.

Word TF-IDF over the request text is the primary discriminative signal in this task; MiniLM embeddings only partially replace it, so dropping the 5k unigram block should lose roughly 1.5–2 AUC points despite the variance-reduction argument.

Document-level stats (length, sentiment, gratitude/please flags, money mentions) are known-strong signals on RAOP (per the Althoff paper and prior solutions), and TF-IDF was discarding exactly this signal, so adding them to the logistic model should give a solid AUC boost.

Dropping the 100k TF-IDF text block removes the dominant predictive signal; metadata-only logistic on 9 features typically scores around 0.60-0.62 AUC on RAOP, a clear regression from the text+meta baseline of 0.650.

Averaging 200-dim skip-gram vectors trained on a tiny (~7k doc) corpus loses the strong discriminative token signal that sparse TF-IDF exploits with logistic regression; mean-pooled embeddings blur rare-but-predictive words, so text AUC drops and only metadata/text-stats partially compensate, yielding a modest regression to ~0.62-0.64.

Adding bigrams and raising the TF-IDF vocabulary from 5k to 60k typically recovers phrase-level signal in this RAOP dataset, yielding a modest AUC gain (~+0.01) that logistic regression with C=0.3 handles without overfitting; the mlflow additions are no-ops that don't affect predictions.

Requester metadata alone tops out around 0.60 AUC on RAOP; the request text (narrative, gratitude cues) carries real signal, so dropping TF-IDF/SVD text features should modestly regress the 0.633 baseline despite the variance-reduction argument.

Random forests on dense 300-dim SVD embeddings typically underperform tuned LightGBM on this dataset — deep trees overfit noisy dense features and produce coarser probability rankings, so expect a modest AUC drop of ~1.5 points, consistent with the competition's own RF benchmark scoring below boosted models.

MiniLM sentence embeddings add complementary semantic signal to unigram TF-IDF on this text-heavy task, typically giving a modest AUC lift for logistic regression; runtime (~6k short docs, CPU) fits the budget and model download is a one-time cost.

Adding bigrams, lower min_df, unicode accent stripping, and a 20x larger vocabulary substantially enriches the text signal for this small dataset, and logistic regression with C=0.3 regularizes the wider feature space well; expect a solid AUC gain typical for this benchmark.

Hand-crafted discourse features (gratitude, reciprocity, hardship, readability) are documented predictive signals for RAOP in the Althoff et al. paper and complement sparse unigram TF-IDF, likely giving a modest AUC lift despite only 24 dense columns among 5000 sparse ones.

SVD(300) preserves most TF-IDF signal and LightGBM with CV-tuned rounds typically matches or slightly beats a linear model on RAOP's small, noisy mix of text and user-history features, but gains are modest given the dataset's low ceiling (~0.67-0.70).

Replacing an 8-column quantile spline (which captures both drift and local timing effects) with a 2-column annual Fourier encoding slightly reduces date-feature capacity, and since date features contribute modestly to this text+history model, expect a near-neutral to slightly negative AUC change.
Weakening L2 should let informative TF-IDF terms move the ranking more than the strongly penalized C=0.3 model, but C=30 is near the overfitting regime so the gain is likely modest rather than large.

Request success rates declined notably over the 2010-2013 collection period, so a quantile-spline date feature adds real signal to the logistic model without hurting existing features, yielding a modest AUC gain.

Cosine KNN on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF features with only ~4k training samples suffers from curse-of-dimensionality; distance-weighted neighbor probabilities are coarse and uncalibrated, typically underperforming regularized logistic regression for AUC on text classification.

Distance-weighted KNN on 9 standardized metadata features is a much weaker learner than a tuned-depth CatBoost (curse of dimensionality, noisy neighbors on ~5.6k samples), so its half of the 50/50 blend drags the combined AUC down several points despite the unchanged logistic component.
Reducing regularization 100x on 5k TF-IDF features with only ~4k training samples and a 25% positive rate typically overfits the logistic model, slightly degrading the blend's AUC.

Calendar-time splines add a weak but real signal (request success drifted over 2010-2013) to a strong text+history baseline; a handful of standardized spline features in a regularized logistic regression should yield a tiny AUC gain, with minimal overfitting risk.

BernoulliNB discards TF-IDF magnitude info via binarization and its conditional-independence assumption is weaker than a discriminative linear model for sparse text; on this dataset naive Bayes typically underperforms logistic regression by a few AUC points, though it remains a reasonable text baseline.

Adding quantile-spline features of request timestamp captures mild temporal drift in RAOP success rates; with only ~8 extra features on a regularized logistic model, expect a small positive but near-noise improvement over 0.6573.

Adding binary requester-subreddit features (a known predictive signal in RAOP, e.g., activity in giving/community subreddits) to TF-IDF + numeric features should modestly improve LR AUC, while the removed holdout split doesn't change the final full-data fit.

CatBoost on the nine metadata features adds modest complementary signal to the TF-IDF logistic model; a 50/50 blend slightly over-weights the weaker model but typically yields a small AUC gain on this dataset.

Adding bigrams to the TF-IDF vocabulary typically captures short sentiment/phrase signals in RAOP request text and gives a small AUC lift, though the shared 5000-feature budget and unchanged strong regularization cap the gain.

Function words are largely duplicated by char_wb n-grams, so dropping them from the word view reduces redundancy and noise dimensionality, yielding a small expected log-loss improvement consistent with standard spooky-author kernels.

Adding diverse word/char MultinomialNB base models and a log-prob meta-learner typically improves calibration and reduces log loss by a few percent over a single tuned TF-IDF LR, with negligible runtime cost.

Function-word usage is a classic strong authorship signal and LR/NB word models likely lose more than they gain from a cleaner vocabulary; the char_wb models only partially compensate, so expect a small net regression in stacked log loss.

A regularized multinomial logistic combiner is the classic choice for stacking on ~19.5k rows of 28 already-informative features; it avoids the LightGBM stacker's fold-specific overfitting (early stopping on its own validation fold) and should generalize slightly better on the test set, yielding a small log-loss improvement.

Punctuation-laden char n-grams are a known strong stylistic signal in this competition (winning solutions rely on them), so stripping punctuation removes discriminative features and likely slightly worsens log loss despite the plausible noise-reduction argument.

Stacking word/char TF-IDF LRs with tuned Naive Bayes via OOF log-prob meta-features is a well-known strong recipe on Spooky Author ID, typically beating a single hstacked LR (~0.44) by 10-15% log loss.

Chi2 selection to 10k columns discards discriminative char-n-gram signal that L2-regularized LR was exploiting, typically a small OOF regression for LR on this task; the blend weight re-tunes toward NB but cannot fully recover, so expect a modest ~1-3% worse log loss.

Author style in this competition lives largely in function-word usage ('the', 'of', 'and' frequencies distinguish Poe/Lovecraft/Shelley well), so removing stop words likely discards discriminative signal and slightly hurts both NB and LR, causing a small regression despite the rationale's appeal.

5-fold CV over C typically selects a larger C (10-30) than the fixed C=1 on this word+char TF-IDF setup, which historically yields a modest log-loss gain (roughly 0.43 -> 0.40-0.41); the implementation is functionally equivalent to the proposed LogisticRegressionCV with same multinomial lbfgs solver.

The 4-model OOF stack (diverse LR/NB on word/char features) plus stylometric meta-features and a LightGBM combiner is a classic winning recipe for this competition; diverse base learners and honest OOF blending typically cut log loss from ~0.43 to ~0.35 territory.

Crossing-word-boundary char n-grams plus case sensitivity add punctuation/capitalization style signals known to help on this competition; LR on sparse high-dim TF-IDF scales gracefully, so expect a modest log-loss improvement from 0.432 to ~0.41-0.42.

Averaging well-calibrated LR probabilities with a count-based MultinomialNB (with OOF-tuned alpha and blend weight) is a classic improvement on this dataset; NB adds complementary signal and the arithmetic blend with clipping avoids NB's extreme probabilities hurting log loss, typically yielding a few-hundredths improvement over LR alone.

Stopword removal strips function words, which are among the strongest stylistic fingerprints for author identification, and it also breaks fastText's word-bigram sequences, so a modest regression in log loss is expected.

The class imbalance is mild (7.9k/6.0k/5.6k), so duplicating minority examples mostly distorts fastText's softmax calibration — shifting probability mass toward HPL/MWS and away from the natural test distribution — which typically inflates log loss slightly rather than helping.

ComplementNB on TF-IDF is a strong complementary model for this dataset and OOF-selected convex blending with LR typically yields a small but real log-loss gain, with the OOF weight sweep protecting against a regression if NB adds nothing.

MultinomialNB on TF-IDF produces poorly calibrated, overconfident probabilities that hurt log loss; on this exact competition tuned word+char TF-IDF logistic regression (~0.35) reliably beats tuned MultinomialNB (~0.42-0.45), so the swap regresses.

Character n-grams are a strong signal for author style (punctuation, morphology) in this competition; dropping them from the NB-SVM typically degrades log loss noticeably despite cleaner features and faster runtime.

ComplementNB alone on TF-IDF typically scores around 0.43-0.46 log loss on Spooky Author, whereas the NB-SVM's discriminative logistic head on ratio-weighted features is the known stronger variant (~0.41), so removing it likely regresses the metric modestly.

CV-selected C (optimizing log loss directly) on TF-IDF logistic regression for this competition typically finds C in the 3-10 range, shaving a few hundredths off log loss versus the untuned C=1.0; features and pipeline are unchanged so the gain is modest but real.

MultinomialNB is fast but produces overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities on TF-IDF features and loses the discriminative advantage of logistic regression; on this dataset NB baselines typically score ~0.7-0.85 log loss vs ~0.42 for tuned LR, a large regression.
fastText with word bigrams and 2-5 char subwords typically matches or modestly beats TF-IDF+LR on this dataset (~0.35-0.40 log loss), so expect a moderate improvement over 0.432.

5-fold CV over C on this TF-IDF + LR setup typically selects C≈2-4 (mildly less regularized than 1.0), yielding a small but real log-loss gain of a few thousandths; the parallelized search fits in budget and the submission path is unchanged.

NB-SVM is the classic strong performer on this exact competition and typically edges out plain TF-IDF logistic regression by a few percent in log loss; expect local holdout ~0.39-0.42 and a modest test gain.

Adding 14 MaxAbs-scaled stylometric features to a strong word+char TF-IDF LR stack typically gives a small log-loss gain on this dataset; the effect is modest since punctuation/length signals largely overlap with char n-grams, so expect roughly a 0.5–1% improvement.

NB-weighted binary logistic models are a well-known improvement for this competition (the classic 'NBSVM' trick), typically cutting log loss from ~0.44 to the high 0.30s/low 0.40s on small text datasets with three authors.
Stronger L2 (C=0.25) shrinks coefficients and softens overconfident probabilities on sparse n-gram features, which typically yields a modest log-loss improvement on this small spooky-author corpus.

Character n-grams alone capture much of the signal on this task, but dropping the word unigram/bigram block removes complementary lexical evidence, typically costing a few hundredths of log loss for NB-logistic models.

Removing the NB log-count-ratio reweighting discards a strong well-calibrated prior for text classification; plain one-vs-rest TF-IDF logistic regression is typically overconfident and scores notably worse log loss (~0.8-0.95) on this competition.

Halving C to 2.0 modestly increases L2 regularization on highly correlated word+char TF-IDF features; for this dataset the sweet spot for LR is typically near C=1-3, so expect a small log-loss improvement, with the added mlflow tracking code having no effect on predictions.
NB-weighted one-vs-rest logistic (NBSVM) is a well-known improvement over plain multinomial LR on TF-IDF for this competition, typically cutting log loss from ~0.37 to ~0.31.

Stop words are classic stylometric signal for authorship attribution, and removing them also corrupts char_wb n-grams and word bigrams by concatenating previously non-adjacent content words, so log loss should regress moderately.

Stronger L2 regularization (C=0.25) typically improves calibration and generalization on high-dimensional correlated TF-IDF n-grams for this dataset, giving a small but real log-loss gain; the temperature scaling further helps, keeping the effect modest.

Switching char_wb to char adds cross-word n-grams that are mostly noise for this task; word-boundary-aware char features typically edge out plain char on spooky-author, so a small regression in log loss is expected, with other changes (telemetry, dropped holdout) not affecting the model.

NB-weighted one-vs-rest logistic on TF-IDF is a known strong trick for this competition; it typically beats plain multiclass LR by sharpening per-class probabilities, though normalization of independent OvR probabilities adds some noise, so expect a modest ~5% log-loss improvement.

Reducing regularization from C=1.0 to C=4.0 on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF features typically fits the decision boundary a bit better for this task and modestly improves log loss, though gains are small since C=1 was already reasonable.

LR at C=1.0 on sparse TF-IDF tends to be slightly overconfident, so a fitted scalar temperature on the 10% holdout usually softens probabilities and yields a small log-loss gain; the extra MLflow code is inert telemetry that does not affect predictions.

Optimizing squared error on the log scale targets the geometric mean, not the arithmetic mean, so after expm1 inversion the predictions are systematically low for high-variance leaves; without a bias correction this typically hurts raw-dollar RMSE slightly, though the skew stabilization keeps the regression modest.

Quadrupling the training sample from 1M to 4M rows reduces variance and lets LightGBM fit the fare surface better (typical scaling gains of ~5-8% RMSE here), while the faster datetime parsing and correct thread count keep the run within budget; the corrupt-row floor (~2.1) limits further gains.
Airport distances are a classic high-value feature for NYC taxi fares (JFK flat fares, airport surcharges); LightGBM can exploit them for a modest but real RMSE gain, with negligible runtime cost.

Fitting L2 on log1p downweights the heavy right tail of fares so boosting rounds optimize typical rides; after expm1 inversion this typically cuts RMSE on skewed monetary targets by a few percent, though the ~2.8% corrupt test rows cap the gain near the ~2.1 RMSE floor.

With 4M rows and 63 leaves the distance response is already nearly monotone, so the constraint barely changes the fit; expect a negligible change within noise (tiny improvement at best) on the graded RMSE, which is dominated by the corrupt-row floor and general fit quality.

Log1p target stabilizes variance from the long right tail of fares and typically yields a small but real RMSE gain on skewed positive targets in GBMs; the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows limits the total improvement, so expect a modest drop from 4.13 to roughly 4.0.

In-sample encoding removes the log-count offset (~log 0.8) and the train/inference distribution mismatch, while smoothing m=20 keeps self-leakage per row negligible; validation stats still exclude val rows, so expect a small genuine improvement with slightly less runtime.

Fitting squared error in log space optimizes multiplicative error, so expm1 predictions are biased low on large fares and dollar-scale RMSE typically degrades slightly without a bias correction; expect a small regression over the raw-fare baseline.

Airport distance features are a known strong signal for this competition (JFK flat-fare and EWR surcharge trips), letting trees isolate those rides cheaply; expect a modest but real improvement on valid rows, partially diluted by the ~2.8% corrupt-row RMSE floor.

Treating corrupt coordinates as NaN lets LightGBM learn the fare distribution of the ~2.8% invalid test rows from calendar features instead of the global mean, modestly reducing the error floor those rows impose, while keeping invalid training rows as a separate NaN population adds little noise to valid-row predictions.

Quadrupling the training sample from 1M to 4M rows reduces variance and lets LightGBM split more finely on the same features, typically giving a modest RMSE gain; the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the improvement, so expect roughly 4-5% better than 4.138.
Out-of-fold smoothed route/cell target means capture tolls and fixed airport fares that haversine misses, giving a modest but real RMSE gain; leakage is controlled and runtime impact is negligible.

Log1p training optimizes relative error, but grading is dollar-space RMSE; the expm1 back-transform adds Jensen bias on high-variance large fares and there is no bias correction, so RMSE typically degrades slightly despite the better-behaved target distribution.

Manhattan distance and bearing add modest but real signal over haversine alone for a GBM (street-grid distance, direction/toll effects), though much is redundant with raw coordinates, so expect a small RMSE gain around 1%.

Airport/landmark distance features are a well-known strong gain for this competition, letting the trees isolate JFK flat-fare and airport-surcharge trips; pure vectorized additions keep runtime unchanged, so expect a moderate RMSE improvement from 4.10 to roughly 3.85-3.90.

MAE fits the conditional median, which is robust to the fare tail but systematically underpredicts, so RMSE (a squared-error metric) typically worsens by a few percent versus the L2 baseline; training cost is unchanged so it fits the budget.

Log1p training helps log-scale error but expm1 inversion introduces upward bias (Jensen) on the dollar scale, and the graded metric is raw-scale RMSE, so a small regression is typical; everything else is unchanged.

L1 training targets the conditional median, which is suboptimal under an RMSE metric, so predictions drift from the conditional mean and RMSE degrades by a few percent despite robustness to label noise.

With alpha=1.0 nearly all residuals exceed delta, so Huber behaves close to L1/median regression, which optimizes a different functional than RMSE and typically costs a bit of RMSE despite robustness to label noise; early stopping still tracks RMSE so the regression should be modest.

Log-target training usually helps modestly on skewed fares by de-emphasizing tail rows, but expm1 without a bias-correction term underestimates high fares on the raw-dollar RMSE, so expect only a small net improvement over 4.133 (corrupt-row floor ~2.1 is unaffected).

Airport distance/near flags capture JFK flat-fare and airport-trip pricing, a well-known win for this dataset, but gains are limited by the 2.8% corrupt-test-row RMSE floor and the unchanged 1M-row sample.

Quadrupling the training sample to 4M rows typically gives LightGBM a modest but real gain (more data reduces variance in leaf estimates), while the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the relative improvement; risk of timeout is low since LightGBM histogram training on ~3.6M x 10 features is fast.

5-fold bagging averages 5 models trained on 800k rows each (vs 900k for the single model), so per-model data loss is minor while prediction averaging reduces variance; expect a small ~0.5-1% RMSE improvement.

A properly leak-free, smoothed pickup-cell target encoding adds genuinely informative local fare signal (airport zones, neighborhood pricing) that raw coordinates + distance can't fully capture; expect a modest ~3% RMSE improvement with negligible runtime cost, and the mlflow additions are inert no-ops.

Snapping coordinates to a ~1 km grid destroys fine GPS precision that LightGBM was exploiting for local fare patterns and coarsens distance_km, while the route encoding (already at the same 0.01° cell size) gains nothing new, so a modest regression is expected.
L1 loss fits a median-like target while the metric is RMSE, so robustness to outliers typically costs a small amount of RMSE on the dominant well-behaved rows; expect a modest regression.
L1 loss reduces the pull of residual extreme fares (a few survive the <=500 filter), typically giving a small RMSE gain on this noisy target while all other settings stay fixed.

Airport-proximity features are a known strong signal for NYC taxi fares (flat JFK fares, airport surcharges), so six endpoint-to-airport distances should modestly reduce RMSE on valid rows, though the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the overall gain.

Switching to L1 (median) objective makes training robust to fare outliers but optimizes a different loss than the RMSE metric, so on the held-out valid rows predictions drift slightly off the conditional mean, likely yielding a roughly neutral-to-slightly-worse RMSE.

Rounding coordinates to a ~1km grid discards fine-grained location signal that LightGBM exploits for fare prediction (taxi fares depend heavily on precise location), and the unrounded haversine distance cannot fully compensate, so a small RMSE regression is expected.

Switching to regression_l1 optimizes MAE (predicting conditional medians), which typically degrades RMSE slightly since the metric rewards squared-error-optimal means; outlier robustness gains are limited because fares are already clipped at 500.
Grid (rotated Manhattan) distance is a mildly informative, low-cost feature highly correlated with haversine, so LightGBM gains a small RMSE improvement.

Smoothed, cross-fitted directional route-mean fare is a strong target-encoding signal for taxi fares (repeated routes have consistent pricing), implemented leak-free with OOF encoding, so it should reduce RMSE by a few percent over the 4.138 baseline.

Adding the Manhattan-grid-aligned distance (rotated 29 degrees to match NYC street grid) gives LightGBM a distance measure closer to actual taxi routing; well-documented in this competition to yield a small but real RMSE gain (~1%) over haversine alone, and the MLflow/tracking additions are metric-neutral.

Doubling the training sample from 1M to 2M rows gives LightGBM more data (still well within budget), which typically yields a modest RMSE gain of ~1-2% on this large, low-noise-ceiling dataset; the corrupt-row floor (~2.1) caps further gains.

Airport trips (especially JFK flat-fare routes) have systematically different fares than distance-matched trips, so a categorical route feature should let LightGBM carve out those rows and trim RMSE by roughly 0.05-0.1; implementation matches the spec and the extra MLflow boilerplate doesn't affect training.

Plain LightGBM on raw numeric + per-character f_27 features (no engineered interactions or unique-count features) is known to score ~0.97-0.98 on TPS May 2022, well below the well-trained MLP's 0.9866, and 2000 rounds at lr 0.05 with these settings will early-stop or plateau below the MLP's level.

Quantile-binning to 10 one-hot buckets discards fine-grained continuous information (especially on the heavy-tailed f_28 and continuous columns) that the SiLU MLP was exploiting, and standardization was already handling scale differences, so a slight regression is the most likely outcome.

Whitening may marginally improve conditioning of per-leaf regressions, but PCA rotation destroys the axis-aligned structure GBDT exploits (mixing the informative f_27 ordinals with continuous features into directions that need many splits to recover), typically costing a small amount of AUC.
f_27's signal lives in per-position character patterns; collapsing it into one whole-string target encoding discards positional information and overfits a high-cardinality key, so AUC drops.

In TPS-May-2022 the positional letters of f_27 carry most of the signal, and a single whole-string target-encoding column cannot represent per-position effects, so replacing the ten per-character columns with f_27_te (even smoothed/OOF) loses ranking information and should cost roughly half a point of AUC despite slightly lower dimensionality.

The f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26 sums and their threshold indicators are well-known decisive interactions for TPS May 2022 that trees cannot easily construct axis-aligned; adding them typically lifts AUC from ~0.991 to ~0.996+.

A plain logistic regression on this dataset typically scores ~0.90-0.93 AUC, far below the LGBM's 0.984; giving it 50% weight in a rank blend drags the ranking down since the LR's errors are not diverse enough to offset its much weaker signal.

A small MLP on raw features typically underperforms tuned LightGBM on this interaction-heavy synthetic tabular dataset, since GBDT exploits axis-aligned feature interactions more effectively within the budget.

A small CPU MLP with no engineered interactions or ensembling typically underperforms tuned GBM on this TPS-May-2022 dataset (known MLP single-model scores ~0.973-0.976 vs GBM ~0.977), so expect a slight regression.

Linear leaves sound right for oblique boundaries, but here the linear fits are polluted by the 10 noisy ordinal f_27 char features and min_child_samples=100 leaves are too small for stable per-leaf regressions, so linear trees typically match or slightly underperform constant-leaf GBDT on this dataset.

The count of distinct letters in f_27 is a known informative aggregate for this competition that captures character-level information the per-position ordinals miss, giving LightGBM a small but real gain in split quality.

Adding raw additive sums of known interacting continuous features gives axis-aligned trees helpful diagonal split directions in TPS May 2022, typically yielding a tiny AUC gain; the model is unchanged and already near 0.977, so expect a small positive effect around +0.0002 AUC.

Collapsing f_27 into one ~900k-cardinality categorical forces LightGBM's gradient-based category grouping to memorize whole strings rather than learn generalizable per-position letter patterns; it loses the positional structure the ordinal expansion provided, and unseen/rare string categories in test get no signal, so AUC regresses noticeably despite the letter-count features remaining.

Adjacent-character bigrams in f_27 are a known useful interaction signal in this competition; encoding them as native categorical features lets LightGBM split on the pair directly, typically giving a small AUC gain (~+0.001) over per-position ordinals alone.

PCA components are linear rotations of raw features that trees already use, so they add little, while removing the gain-mined pairwise products loses the genuinely useful nonlinear interaction signal—small net regression versus the mined-products run.

f_27's predictive signal lives in per-position letter interactions (well-documented for TPS May 2022); hashing the whole 10-char string into 64 buckets destroys positional information and adds collisions, causing a large AUC regression.

ExtraTrees with sqrt max_features and no boosting is well documented to underperform tuned LightGBM on TPS-May-2022 (typically ~0.93-0.95 vs ~0.978), and the added 5-fold CV fits risk eating the time budget without affecting the submission.

A shallow sklearn MLP on raw features can capture multiplicative interactions but typically slightly underperforms tuned LightGBM on this dataset (which also exploits f_27 character patterns well), and 40 CPU epochs with early stopping limits convergence, so expect a small regression to ~0.974 AUC.

Bag-of-letters counts are known to carry real signal in TPS-May-2022 (the target depends partly on letter multiset in f_27), so they should give a small but positive AUC bump over the per-position-only baseline; effect size is modest since per-position categoricals already capture much of the letter information.

Per-character f_27 columns carry most of the predictive signal in TPS May 2022; collapsing them to a raw full-sequence frequency count destroys that information, so AUC should drop markedly while the numeric features keep it well above 0.9.

Letter-count and unique-character features over f_27 are well-known informative signals for this competition's interactions, and LightGBM can exploit them alongside per-position ordinals, yielding a small but real AUC gain with negligible runtime cost.

TPS-May-2022 is known to contain real pairwise interactions among f_00..f_15, so gain-screened product features should give a small but genuine AUC lift, though trees already capture much of this so the gain is modest.

Refitting on 100% of rows (800k vs 720k) with iteration count scaled from the never-triggered 3000 cap (~3333 rounds) adds slightly more data and capacity, typically giving a small AUC gain for AUC-friendly GBM; risk of minor overfit without early stopping is modest given the data size.

Treating the 26-letter codes per position as LightGBM categoricals enables optimal many-vs-rest partitions instead of arbitrary ordinal thresholds, which typically gives a small but real AUC gain on this competition; same data and hyperparameters keep the change modest.
