The unique-character count of f_27 is a known weakly useful aggregate for TPS May 2022; it complements the per-position ordinals and typically yields a small AUC gain (~+0.0003), though LightGBM may already capture much of it via tree interactions, so the effect is marginal.

TPS May 2022 is dominated by high-order feature interactions; max_depth=2 limits each tree to single pairwise splits, causing severe underfitting relative to 127-leaf trees despite the 3000-estimator budget.

LightGBM on the same features is a known-strong fit for this synthetic interaction-heavy dataset, but the reduced capacity (600 trees, 31 leaves, max_bin=63 vs. the README's 3000-tree/127-leaf config) keeps the gain modest over the MLP's 0.9822, likely landing around 0.984.

LightGBM with modest hyperparameters (31 leaves, 600 rounds, no subsampling/colsample) on per-char ordinal f_27 features typically reaches ~0.97-0.975 AUC on this dataset, slightly below the tuned MLP's 0.982, though trees handle the interaction structure well enough to stay close.

Quantizing continuous features to 4 ordinal bins discards fine-grained splits that gradient-boosted trees exploit, so the model loses some discriminative signal while gaining nothing it couldn't already learn from raw values; expect a small but real AUC regression.

Reducing num_leaves from 127 to 7 severely restricts each tree's capacity to capture the multi-feature interactions this dataset is built around, and the fixed 3000-tree budget won't fully compensate, so holdout/test AUC should drop noticeably below the 0.9768 baseline.

num_leaves=4 makes each tree nearly a stump (max ~2 splits), crippling the model's ability to capture the multi-feature interactions this dataset is built around; even 3000 boosting rounds won't recover the lost interaction capacity, so AUC drops well below the 0.9915 baseline despite faster training.

A simple sum of three existing continuous features is nearly redundant for gradient-boosted trees, which already model such interactions via splits; it should neither help nor hurt beyond run-to-run noise.

Gradient-boosted trees can already approximate an additive combination of f_00, f_01, f_26 through splits, so a single sum feature adds at most negligible signal; expect a change within run-to-run noise of the 0.97692 baseline.

A CPU MLP on raw numeric + ordinal f_27 chars misses the key character-count/interaction signal and trains only a few epochs in 420s, so it should land around 0.91-0.94 AUC, well below LightGBM's 0.977.

Treating f_27 character positions as native LightGBM categoricals enables many-way partitions of the 26 letter values instead of 25 binary ordinal splits, which better captures the known position-based categorical interactions in this dataset and typically yields a solid AUC gain.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is a well-known strong signal in TPS May 2022 that the per-position ordinals only partially capture, so adding it should give a small but real AUC boost (~+0.001-0.002).
Mild darkness weighting should shift limited capacity from easy white background to stroke/edge residuals and improve RMSE modestly, with alpha=4 unlikely to badly bias the dominant background.
Extending cosine-annealed training from about 2,000 to roughly 8,000–11,000 steps should substantially reduce underfitting, while augmentation and the held-out split should limit overfitting.

L1 loss is a well-established better default for pixel-wise restoration (Zhao et al. 2017, EDSR/RCAN) and typically yields crisper edges that reduce residual variance even under RMSE, so a small improvement over the MSE baseline is expected; the effect is modest since only 2000 training steps limits how much the loss choice matters.

Input-only brightness/contrast jitter should regularize the small training set and reduce reliance on exact scan intensity statistics, yielding a modest RMSE improvement despite some added train/test distribution mismatch.

Multi-scale flip averaging should cancel some scale-specific errors and reduce variance, but antialias resampling blur and the unchanged single-scale-trained model cap the gain to a small improvement.

Dropout2d p=0.2 on the two deepest encoder levels slightly reduces effective capacity during a short 2000-step schedule with already-low training error; on this denoising task the bottleneck features are mostly generic (text strokes/background) rather than stain-specific, so the regularization likely yields a small regression rather than a generalization gain, within noise of the baseline.

Dropout2d is disabled at eval but adds gradient noise and slightly degrades skip/high-frequency features in a dense regression U-Net that is already reasonably regularized by crops/BN, so a small RMSE regression is more likely than a gain.

The 4-level U-Net quadruples parameters and doubles the receptive field (~89px vs 41px), which helps disambiguate text strokes from noise using broader context; the ~33% higher per-step cost is absorbed by the wall-clock-bounded cosine schedule, so slightly fewer steps at better capacity should yield a modest RMSE improvement.

The median-filter background channel gives the U-Net an explicit local-background estimate that helps disentangle text from stain/shadow noise, a well-known effective trick for this competition; the extra input is cheap and the change is implemented correctly, so expect a modest but real RMSE gain of roughly 5-10%.

The 5-level U-Net adds useful context/receptive field for stain and background separation while keeping pixels-per-step constant, likely improving RMSE modestly despite higher overfit/instability risk.
4-way flip TTA averages out flip-asymmetric prediction errors and typically yields a small (~1-3%) RMSE gain for CNN denoisers at negligible extra inference cost, with no change to training.

The time-based cosine schedule preserves the LR anneal while likely allowing comparable or more optimizer steps after removing per-epoch validation overhead, yielding a small diminishing-returns gain rather than a large change.
Charbonnier loss should de-emphasize extreme stain/edge errors and produce slightly sharper, faster-converging restorations, giving a small RMSE gain despite the metric being L2-based.
The σ=0.05 input-only Gaussian noise creates a train/test mismatch and biases the MSE denoiser toward over-smoothing/blurred edges, likely outweighing any small-data regularization benefit.
GroupNorm removes BatchNorm's crop-training vs full-page running-stat mismatch while keeping optimization stable, so I expect a small RMSE gain rather than a large architectural effect.
SSIM+L1 should sharpen near-binary text/background and reduce sigmoid under-saturation from MSE, giving a modest RMSE gain despite some metric mismatch.

8-way dihedral TTA typically gives a small RMSE gain by averaging out prediction noise; flips are in-distribution from training augmentation while rot90 outputs are weaker (text is horizontal), so the net benefit is modest, roughly 1-2%.
SSIM may sharpen document structure, but it is locally contrast/luminance tolerant and not the RMSE/L2 optimum, so the graded per-pixel RMSE likely regresses modestly.

Residual (DnCNN-style) prediction with a linear head and zero-initialized output avoids sigmoid saturation on the mostly-white background, providing better-conditioned gradients and an identity initialization; this standard reformulation typically yields a modest but consistent RMSE gain over direct image regression with identical training budget.
The SSIM term should modestly improve stroke edges and local structure while the RMSE component preserves alignment with the graded metric.

Residual learning with zero-initialized output (DnCNN-style) makes the task much easier than regressing the full clean image through a sigmoid — the net starts as identity (already a decent solution since noise is sparse) and only needs to learn the noise, typically cutting RMSE by roughly 10-20% for this kind of document denoising.

Synthetic corruption of clean targets (stains/shading/speckle) closely mimics this dataset's known artifacts and is the classic winning strategy for this competition; a ~7x larger, more diverse training pool with unchanged compute should generalize better to real test noise, with only mild risk from the global blur step making synthetic inputs slightly off-distribution.

Extending training from 2,000 to 9,000 steps with the cosine schedule stretched accordingly typically yields a modest but real RMSE gain for a small U-Net that was still underfit at 20 epochs; expect roughly 5-10% improvement while staying well within the time budget.

8-fold dihedral TTA almost always reduces variance and smooths prediction noise for small patch-trained CNNs; even though transpose views weren't in training augmentation (only flips were), averaging typically nets a modest 1-2% RMSE gain, and inference cost (~8x on 29 test + 10 val images) fits well within the time budget.

L1 training optimizes the median, not the mean, and with a LR tuned for MSE it typically yields a slightly worse RMSE on clean-target denoising — the robustness gain against outlier stains usually costs a few percent on the RMSE metric being graded.
Mild 3:1 foreground weighting should better preserve underrepresented glyph interiors and antialiased edges without substantially degrading the dominant white-background predictions.
Ink/boundary upweighting should reduce the dominant high-error dark-stroke pixels with only a modest background tradeoff, giving a small RMSE gain within the same budget.

Zero-init residual prediction starts from the identity/noisy image and is better conditioned than direct sigmoid regression, likely preserving clean regions and converging a bit faster under the same budget.

The evaluation metric is RMSE, which MSE training directly optimizes; L1 targets the conditional median, producing slightly different (often marginally blurrier) outputs that typically trade a bit of RMSE for robustness, so expect a small single-digit-percent regression rather than an improvement.

Zero-initialized residual output starts the network at the identity mapping (already a strong baseline for denoising), so the fixed 20-epoch budget is spent only on learning the noise component, which typically converges faster and to a slightly better RMSE than a sigmoid-parameterized direct prediction; inference-time clipping still bounds the now-unbounded output.
Halving NAFNet width cuts capacity roughly fourfold while keeping depth/receptive field, so the simple document prior still fits but with mild underfitting and slightly higher RMSE.
Foreground weighting should reduce the largest errors on faint/dark strokes while keeping abundant background near weight 1, giving a modest RMSE gain with limited background tradeoff.

The background-normalized second channel (grey-closing division) is a well-established, strong feature for document denoising that should give the same U-Net a modest boost, though the forced-CPU execution config adds timing risk and the gain is limited by the unchanged 2k-step training budget.

The applied runtime.toml forces CPU-only execution (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""), where AMP/autocast is already disabled (amp=False), so running the head in float32 is a computational no-op and the score should be essentially identical to the baseline.

4-view flip TTA averages out independent prediction errors and typically yields a small (~1-2%) RMSE reduction on denoising tasks; the forced-CPU runtime config slows execution but doesn't change model outputs, and 2000 steps on ~260x420 images stays within budget.

The compact residual NAFNet should outperform the small sigmoid U-Net by preserving clean background through its identity path while learning structured local noise removal; the fixed update count should still fit the CPU budget.

The dog-restricted ImageNet head is a strong exact-label prior and the holdout-tuned blend/temperature should add a modest ensemble/calibration gain over LR, though same-backbone correlation caps the upside.

PCA-256 should retain most breed-discriminative variance while trimming noisy low-variance directions, giving a small log-loss gain; the arbitrary 256 cutoff and fixed C grid keep the improvement modest.

Mixup/CutMix is the canonical ConvNeXt regularizer and suits this small 120-class fine-grained setup: it combats overconfidence and improves calibration (helped further by the validation temperature scaling), so log loss should improve modestly, though the short 6-epoch schedule limits the full benefit since mixup-trained models converge more slowly.

Standard (0.08,1.0) RandomResizedCrop adds scale/part-view diversity that should reduce overfitting on ~77 images per breed while matching ConvNeXt pretraining, likely giving a modest log-loss gain despite slightly harder short-schedule optimization.

ConvNeXtV2-L IN22k->IN1k features plus label-aligned ImageNet logits should be substantially more discriminative than ResNet50 V1 under the same frozen LR pipeline, cutting log loss by roughly one-third while frozen/no-TTA keeps it from going near SOTA.

The 1000 log-softmax features are largely redundant and noisy after standardisation, but the dog-class ImageNet logits are a useful pretrained prior for these exact breeds, so removing the block should cause a slight regression.

Ridge probes on strong frozen features match LR decision boundaries, and the joint holdout temperature search explicitly optimizes calibration for log loss — something the LR head lacks — typically shaving a few percent off log loss; expect a modest improvement to roughly 0.31–0.32.
Per-block PCA to 128 likely keeps most breed-relevant variance while denoising/regularizing the linear probe, giving a small log-loss gain, though some fine-grained low-variance signal may be lost.

ConvNeXt-Base pretrained on IN-22k and fine-tuned on IN-1k produces substantially more discriminative features than ResNet-50 V1 (which already contains dog-breed-like classes), and the holdout-based C re-selection adapts regularization to the new feature scale, typically cutting log loss by ~25-30% on Stanford Dogs-style fine-grained tasks.

Fine-tuning ImageNet-22k ConvNeXt-Tiny with augmentation, flip-TTA, and temperature scaling is a well-proven recipe on Stanford Dogs (~88% top-1), far stronger than frozen ResNet-50 features; the 7-minute guard still allows ~4-6 epochs, enough to reach log loss around 0.28-0.33.

Adding the 1000-d ImageNet log-prob features (which directly encode breed predictions since all 120 breeds are ImageNet classes) alongside standardized pooled features, plus holdout-based C re-selection, should give a solid but modest log-loss gain over the 0.4515 baseline, though the small-C grid on standardized features limits how much better the linear head can get.

Concatenating L2-normalized frozen features from three diverse strong backbones (IN22k ConvNeXt, CLIP, DINOv2) dramatically improves linear separability of fine-grained breeds versus a single ResNet-50, and holdout-tuned C on normalized features further helps calibration; this combination typically cuts log loss by roughly a third on Stanford Dogs-style tasks.

Classes are roughly balanced, so focal loss mostly removes label-smoothing calibration and shifts capacity to hard/noisy examples, likely giving similar accuracy but less calibrated probabilities and worse log loss.
Freezing conv1 through layer3 should modestly reduce overfitting on the small dataset while retaining highly transferable ImageNet features, though limiting adaptation prevents a larger gain.

Horizontal-flip TTA averages out pose/orientation noise and softens overconfident predictions, which reliably yields a small (~1-3%) log-loss improvement on frozen-backbone + logistic-regression pipelines; the num_workers=0 change only affects loading speed, not the metric, and doubling test extraction stays well within budget.
CLIP B/32 is robust but less aligned with ImageNet's exact dog-breed taxonomy and its coarser 32px patches lose fine coat/face detail, so the unchanged linear probe should score worse.

PCA-256 is unsupervised and fairly aggressive for 120 fine-grained breeds, and with C left at 0.3 it likely discards some subtle low-variance breed cues, giving a small log-loss regression despite denoising.

DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings are dramatically stronger for fine-grained dog-breed discrimination (linear-probe accuracy ~87% vs ~80% for ImageNet1K ResNet-50 features), so a logistic head on frozen features with the same 10-view TTA should roughly halve the log loss; re-selecting C on a holdout adds a small calibration benefit.

PCA truncation to 256 components keeps ~90% of variance (mostly signal) and whitening equalizes feature scales so the fixed C=1.0 regularizes informative directions less harshly, typically a small net gain for linear heads on concatenated deep embeddings; whitening's noise amplification is limited by the truncation, so expect a modest improvement rather than a large one.

The frozen features stay strong, but distance-weighted 10-NN probabilities are coarse and sparse; whenever the true breed is absent from the top neighbors the tiny smoothed probability incurs large log-loss penalties, so the calibrated linear head should remain clearly better.

ImageNet already contains these 120 dog breeds, so the frozen baseline is strong, but end-to-end fine-tuning with augmentation, label smoothing, and a warmup+cosine schedule for 10 epochs typically lifts fine-grained accuracy a few points and improves logloss modestly (~10%), with label smoothing keeping probabilities slightly conservative and capping the gain.

ViT-B/16 augreg (in21k→in1k) features are far stronger than ResNet-50 IMAGENET1K_V1 for ImageNet-subset fine-grained classification like dog breeds, so a linear probe should cut log loss by roughly a third; C=0.3 may be slightly suboptimal for the new features but the dominant effect is the backbone upgrade.

10-view TTA (five-crop + hflip) with probability averaging is a well-established, low-risk improvement for frozen-backbone classifiers; it reduces prediction variance and typically cuts log loss by ~4-8% on fine-grained tasks like this, while the unchanged training path keeps everything else constant.

The stronger ImageNet-22k-pretrained ConvNeXt features should complement ResNet-50, and balanced L2-normalized concatenation should reduce log loss substantially while remaining well within the runtime budget.
The pretrained dog head is a correlated but useful second linear readout; CV can choose alpha near zero if unhelpful, so expect a small calibration/ensemble gain rather than a large shift.

PCA-256 should retain most useful embedding variance, but discarding lower-variance fine-grained breed cues and reusing the raw-feature regularization strength will likely cause a small log-loss regression.

Global max pooling discards most spatial evidence and yields noisier, poorly scaled descriptors for a linear probe; for fine-grained breed classification with frozen ResNet-50 + logistic regression, average pooling features are typically better calibrated, so log loss should regress modestly.

IMAGENET1K_V2 has a much stronger ResNet-50 training recipe and the matched 232->224 preprocessing should yield more separable frozen features, giving a moderate log-loss gain with the same architecture and runtime.

C=0.3 was already holdout-selected as optimal for these frozen features, so the C=0.03 head is a worse starting classifier; the 2-epoch bottleneck fine-tune only partially washes out the over-shrunk initialization (head lr is small, weight decay negligible), leaving slightly worse-calibrated final probabilities and a modest log-loss regression.

Dropping input resolution from 224 to 192 discards fine-grained detail (critical for distinguishing 120 similar breeds) and shifts features away from the ResNet's pretrained 224px distribution; the brief two-epoch fine-tune of only the last bottleneck with frozen BN statistics is unlikely to fully compensate, so a modest log-loss regression is expected.

256 PCA components should retain most breed-discriminative ResNet structure while decorrelating/denoising features and easing optimization, giving a small log-loss gain; fixed C and unwhitened truncation cap the improvement.

Dropping the crop from 224 to 192 px throws away ~26% of pixels for a ResNet-50 pretrained at 224, degrading fine-grained features (which matter a lot for 120 similar breeds), so log loss should worsen moderately while remaining in the same ballpark.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 weights are substantially stronger (~80.9% vs 76.1% ImageNet top-1) and the matched 232px preprocessing yields better frozen features for this fine-grained task, which typically translates to a ~8-12% log-loss improvement for a linear probe; the harness changes (config file, MLflow wrapper, dropped TORCH_HOME) are risk-neutral assuming TORCH_HOME is set in the environment.
Temperature scaling should mildly recalibrate an already cross-entropy-trained logistic head, giving a small log-loss gain with some holdout/refit noise.
Initializing the head from the tuned logistic model and briefly adapting the final bottleneck should improve features without severe overfitting, yielding a modest log-loss gain.

Horizontal-flip TTA with averaged probabilities on an ImageNet-pretrained frozen backbone is a well-established small win for fine-grained classification; features of flipped dog images stay in-distribution for the classifier, and averaging reduces per-view variance, typically shaving 1-2% off log loss.

1:1 undersampling discards most negative examples and strengthens effective regularization/variance, while AUC is rank-based and full-data linear models usually exploit the large negative pool better, so expect a small mean-AUC regression.
Adding the shared char_wb block should modestly strengthen branch B with complementary subword/obfuscation signal, while redundancy with branch A caps the gain to a small positive.

ROC AUC is ranking-based, so 1:1 undersampling mostly discards informative negatives and makes the NB ratios and rare-label fits much noisier, likely hurting severe/threat/identity columns while leaving frequent labels nearly flat.

Plain MultinomialNB on TF-IDF is a much weaker model than the NB-LogReg hybrid (standalone AUC ~0.95 vs ~0.98), so both its half of the 50/50 rank blend and the OOF stacking features fed into branch A degrade substantially, dragging the blended mean AUC down by over a point.

Mean-pooled Word2Vec loses much of the discriminative word/character n-gram signal, leaving two correlated weaker branches whose combined two-thirds weight is not fully offset by the unchanged NB-LogReg branch.

AUC is ordering-based and these sparse linear/NB models rely on abundant negatives for background statistics and stable L2 fits; 1:1 undersampling keeps positives but makes rare-label fits and NB ratios much noisier, likely causing a small mean-AUC regression.

Branch D is a guarded 'free option': the tight CPU time budget means it often starts too late (zero epochs) or trains only 1-2 epochs and risks falling below the 0.97 val-AUC keep-threshold, in which case the 3-branch blend is written unchanged; when it is kept, a shallow undertrained EmbeddingBag-MLP at 1/4 rank weight adds only modest diversity to three strong linear branches, so the blend stays essentially flat with a slight positive expected value.

AUC depends only on ranking, so the claimed class-prior benefit of 1:1 undersampling is largely moot, while discarding 80-99.4% of the negative rows (down to ~956 rows for threat) loses ranking information and adds per-label variance, typically costing a small amount of column AUC — roughly offset by minor gains from making C behave uniformly across labels, netting a tiny regression.

Canonicalizing obfuscated profanity/slurs and removing URL/IP/timestamp noise should slightly consolidate sparse n-gram signal and help rare labels, with minimal risk since vectorizers already lowercase.

OOF stacking is leakage-safe and may let branch A absorb some B/cross-label signal, but B is already in the rank blend and the /20 scaling keeps the added features weak, so only a tiny mean-AUC gain is likely.
The 3-epoch 64-unit MLP is underfit but adds a modest decorrelated nonlinear/multitask view, so equal rank averaging should roughly preserve the strong linear signal with a tiny net gain.

Branch C is essentially a stronger NB-LogReg (word 1-2gram + char_wb, the classic ~0.983-0.984 kernel), and it is diverse enough from B to help a rank blend; A and B are unchanged, so the 3-way equal rank average should gain roughly +0.002-0.003 mean AUC, with the liblinear max_iter=100 cap being a negligible risk to quality on these sparse NB-weighted features.

Holdout-fitted per-label blend weights with 50% shrinkage toward equal blending is a mild, low-risk form of stacking: the two linear branches differ modestly in per-label strength, so shrinking noisy holdout-optimal weights toward 0.5 should yield a tiny gain on common labels while the shrinkage largely neutralizes noise on rare labels (threat, identity_hate) — expect a change in the 4th decimal, most likely slightly positive.

Dropping the char_wb n-gram branch (critical for obfuscated profanity/misspellings) and the NB-weighted bigram branch for a 300-dim LSA loses substantial discriminative signal; dense SVD features with a plain LR typically score ~0.95-0.96 on this task, well below the 0.980 sparse ensemble, and the rare-label AUCs degrade most.

AUC depends only on ranking so common labels (toxic, insult) are nearly unaffected since their 10:1 caps barely bind, but rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) lose ~90% of their negative evidence — noisier NB log-odds and linear/fastText fits on those columns should cost a few thousandths of AUC each, dragging the column mean down slightly despite the faster runtime.

Replacing six independent binary fastText classifiers with one 7-way softmax (a mismatch for multi-label — 'ova' would be proper) lets the dominant 'clean' class and co-occurring common labels suppress per-label probabilities, badly hurting ranking on rare labels (threat, identity_hate) that dominate column-mean noise; the damage is diluted by F being only 1/3 of the rank blend, so expect a modest ~1% drop.

Dropping TF-IDF/char views and the discriminative NB-LogReg calibrations for a single raw-count ComplementNB should stay trainable and sane, but its generative length-sensitive scores will rank the rare/noisy labels worse, costing roughly 1.5–2 AUC points overall.

Replacing a strong 260k-feature TF-IDF/NB-LogReg ensemble with mean-pooled from-scratch Word2Vec (trained on only ~20M tokens, min_count=5 dropping rare abuse variants, no word order/char info) is a well-documented large downgrade on this task — mean-pooled embedding + linear models historically score ~0.93-0.94 vs ~0.98 for n-gram linear ensembles, with rare labels (threat, identity_hate) hurt most.

Average-pooled corpus-trained Word2Vec (dim 200, 5 epochs, min_count=5) with linear readout is a well-documented weaker representation for this task than high-dimensional word/char n-gram TF-IDF with NB-weighting; it loses the strong surface-token signal for slurs/misspellings, so mean AUC drops from ~0.980 to roughly 0.93-0.94.

Adding a diverse char-level NB-LogReg branch typically adds a small ranking signal the word branches miss, and the simplex search can only help on the holdout; but per-label weights tuned on a 10% holdout are noisy for the rare labels (threat, identity_hate), capping the expected gain to a small positive.

C=0.1/sag badly over-regularizes the 60k-feature word+char branch; switching to the canonical C=4/liblinear configuration lifts branch A by ~0.005-0.01 AUC, which carries through roughly half-weighted into the rank blend (whose weaker branch was A), moving the blend from ~0.9801 to ~0.986.

Supervised fastText alone scores ~0.975-0.978 on this competition, so as a third diverse branch in a rank-average it typically adds a small gain (~+0.002) over the 0.9801 TF-IDF/LR blend; it fits comfortably in the time budget and rarely hurts since rank averaging is robust to its weaker calibration.

Char n-gram NB-LogReg is a strong, diverse view (a classic ~0.98 standalone kernel branch), and equal three-way rank averaging adds complementary signal over the word-only NB branch and the lightly-regularized char view, giving a small but real gain; runtime stays within budget since the added char vectorizer fits in roughly the time of the existing one.

Per-label weight tuning on a 10% holdout offers little gain (the two branches are already well-matched so 0.5/0.5 is near-optimal) and the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) make the tuned weights noisy, while dropping 10% of training data slightly weakens both branches — small net regression.

NB log-ratio weighting should make branch A’s word/char features more discriminative and better aligned with branch B, but increased correlation and rare-label noise limit the gain to a small improvement.

min_df=0.01 (~3130 docs) is far more aggressive than min_df=3; word/char branches are barely affected since max_features caps them anyway, but branch B loses many rare yet discriminative bigrams that NB-LogReg exploits, hurting especially the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) that dominate column-mean noise — net small regression.

Keeping all positives preserves much of the ranking signal, but discarding most negatives while keeping the same C makes the high-dimensional per-label fits noisier and relatively under/over-regularized, especially for threat/identity_hate, so mean AUC should slip a few points.

Cosine class-centroid (Rocchio-style) classifiers on TF-IDF are reasonable but clearly weaker than regularized logistic regression for this task — they lose the discriminative reweighting of features, so both branches degrade, with the blend landing around 0.965-0.970 AUC.

char_wb pads word boundaries and avoids spurious cross-word character n-grams, which typically gives a small boost on toxic-comment TF-IDF logistic models (a well-known trick in the original Kaggle kernels); the word+NB-LogReg branches are unchanged, so expect only a modest gain in the rank-averaged blend, roughly +0.05–0.1%.

ComplementNB is fast and imbalance-aware, but its independent complement posterior is usually a weaker ranker than the tuned linear/NB-logreg heads on these TF-IDF features, so expect a small AUC regression.

Compressing 60k sparse TF-IDF features to 32 SVD components destroys most of the rare-token lexical signal that drives AUC on the sparse labels (threat, identity_hate), substantially weakening branch A (likely from ~0.975 to ~0.95 standalone), and since branch A contributes half the rank-average blend, the final mean column-wise AUC regresses noticeably.

A 2,000-token document-frequency vocabulary collapses exactly the rare slurs, insults, and identity/threat terms that carry the toxicity signal into a single 'raretoken', destroying discriminative power in both the char-n-gram TF-IDF branch and fastText, with the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) hit hardest in the column mean.

Keeping stop words adds potentially useful pronoun/auxiliary signals but also displaces a few rare content features under the 10k cap, so the ensemble AUC should change only negligibly, with a slight expected gain.

Logit/odds averaging lets the sharper, less-regularized NB-logreg probabilities dominate or veto the smoother word+char branch, whereas rank averaging equalized calibration, so a small AUC regression is likely.

Switching char_wb to char under a 50k feature cap mostly reshuffles which n-grams survive; boundary-crossing char n-grams add little signal for this task and slightly dilute the top-50k feature set, so expect a negligible-to-tiny regression in the rank-averaged blend.
fastText should be somewhat weaker than NB-logistic on sparse lexical cues, but its diversity in an equal rank blend with the unchanged TF-IDF branch should yield a small net gain.

The LR is already L2-regularized and the 192 descriptors are mostly informative; univariate k=128 filtering can drop complementary histogram bins and slightly hurt rare-class calibration, with the 50/50 NN blend diluting this to a very small regression.

Label smoothing should make the over-augmented NN less confidently wrong and better calibrated for log loss, but the fixed 50/50 blend with unchanged strong LR limits the overall gain to a small improvement.

OvR keeps similar rankings but replaces the metric-aligned joint softmax with 99 imbalanced binary surrogates whose scores are less commensurate, so the global power/floor calibration only partly recovers the lost log-loss.
The w=0 fallback bounds downside, and a regularized 5-seed MLP bag should add a little nonlinear diversity before calibration, but the LR score is already very low so gains are modest.

The five fold models are highly correlated and each sees only 80% of the data, so probability averaging gives little bagging benefit while losing the full-data refit; expect essentially flat to slightly worse log loss.
The 21 silhouette/size moments are partly redundant with the 64 shape bins, but should add some scale/compactness/compound-leaf signal that the CV-tuned linear model can exploit for a small gain.

Retaining 95% of variance should preserve the dominant discriminative directions while truncating noisy, highly correlated low-variance components, giving the fixed-C logistic regression a modest regularization benefit.

CV-bagging five logreg models trained on 80% subsets slightly reduces prediction variance versus one full-data fit; each fold model is marginally weaker from less data but averaging typically nets a small logloss gain on this stable, well-regularized linear model, so expect ~0.085 vs 0.0882.

The tiny 990-row/99-class from-scratch CNN is likely overfit or undertrained within the CPU budget, and the arithmetic 50/50 blend dilutes the well-calibrated LR probabilities, so log loss should worsen.
Two-scalar OOF temperature/floor calibration should slightly soften overconfident LR probabilities and cap rare catastrophic errors with low overfitting risk, giving a modest log-loss gain.
5-fold OOF tuning should pick a less-regularized C than 1 and the full-data refit should sharpen mostly-correct predictions, but the 10-samples-per-class limit and no C<1 keep the gain modest.
Mask geometry/Hu features should add some complementary shape signal but are partly redundant with the 192 descriptors, so fixed-C logistic likely gains only modestly.
Stronger but still moderate L2 should slightly improve calibration/generalization for 99 classes with correlated descriptors, trimming overconfident errors without much underfitting.

Training on only 80% of the data (8 instead of 10 examples per species) removes useful information from the submitted classifier, so test log loss should regress modestly despite unchanged validation semantics.

Tuned logistic regression should remain dominant; shrinkage LDA and distance kNN add only modest diverse signal, and the 3-weight OOF convex blend is low-variance, so expect a small log-loss gain rather than a large jump.

With only ~990 training samples across 99 classes (16 per class), multinomial logistic regression on these 192 well-behaved descriptors is exceptionally strong (0.061 log loss is near state-of-the-art single-model territory), while HistGradientBoosting on tiny per-class counts produces poorly calibrated, overconfident probabilities and typically scores several-fold worse (~0.4-0.7 log loss) on this dataset.

The SVM keeps a useful linear margin view, but 3-fold Platt calibration with only a few examples per 99 classes is less reliable than multinomial logistic probabilities for logloss, so the uniform soft vote should lose a little calibration.
The random forest trains on all rows and should be slightly stronger and more diverse than the early-stopped HGB member, though uniform four-model voting limits the overall gain.

A 256-128 MLP is far too high-variance for 990 samples/99 classes with noisy accuracy-based early stopping, so any interaction gain is likely outweighed by overconfident errors despite OOF uniform shrinkage.

Cross-validating C should find a somewhat less-regularized multinomial LR than C=1 while preserving the stable scaling and shrinkage pipeline, giving a modest log-loss improvement with limited model-selection overfitting risk.

The 48 extra features (Hu moments, shape scalars, radial histogram) add genuine shape signal to an already strong 192-feature logistic baseline, but much of it is redundant with the provided shape descriptors and the thresholding actually captures the white background (inverted polarity), so several contour features degenerate toward the image frame — net effect is a small improvement under L2 regularization rather than a large one.

CV-tuning C on this small 990x192 dataset reliably finds a better regularization level than the fixed C=1.0, typically shaving several percent off log loss; the model already refits on all training data in both versions, so gains come purely from C selection, which on the classic leaf benchmark usually moves multinomial LR from ~0.124 to ~0.11-0.12.
Soft-voting LR/LDA with CV-tuned KNN should add useful diversity over the strong LR baseline, while HGB/KNN calibration dilution keeps the gain modest rather than dramatic.

OOF-tuned uniform shrinkage should mostly leave confident correct probabilities intact while capping rare overconfident errors, giving a small log-loss gain with low downside because alpha=0 is in the grid.

Strong fixed shrinkage toward scaled identity should regularize the pooled-covariance LDA and calm overconfident probabilities with only ~10 labels per species, giving a modest log-loss gain rather than a large shift.

Block-wise LDAs should cut covariance-estimation noise versus 192-D LDA and probability averaging should smooth errors, while keeping nearly all discriminative signal, so expect a modest log-loss gain.

PCA(0.90) after standardization likely discards low-variance but species-discriminative descriptor directions, while the tuned multinomial logistic baseline already controls redundancy, so calibration/log loss should degrade modestly.

Shrunken LDA is fast and competitive on these 192 descriptors, but with only ~10 train samples per species its equal-covariance generative probabilities are usually a bit less calibrated than CV-tuned multinomial logistic regression, so I expect a modest log-loss regression rather than a large change.

PCA(0.95) on standardized descriptors will keep ~100 of 192 components, discarding ~5% of variance that carries some discriminative signal; the already near-optimal baseline (0.0452) has little headroom for regularization gains, so a slight regression is more likely than an improvement.

Shrinkage LDA should remain strong on these 192 descriptors, but logistic regression more directly optimizes the calibrated log-loss objective and is less tied to Gaussian/equal-covariance assumptions, so I expect a modest regression rather than a large change.
The 0.005 uniform mix lowers the already-high true-class probabilities on nearly all samples, adding roughly -ln(0.995)≈0.005 log loss with little chance of rescuing rare sub-1% confident errors.

Reducing Nyström components from 512 to 384 slightly degrades the RBF kernel approximation on ~990 training samples where 512 components were not yet over-parameterized, so a small log-loss regression is expected, though the effect is minor since both configs are in a reasonable rank range.
Shrunken LDA is well-suited to 192 descriptors with only ~10 labeled leaves/class, and leakage-free scaling should make it better calibrated than fixed-C logistic regression.
Fold-local scaling plus a small C grid should pick a slightly better-regularized logistic model than fixed C=1, but with only one hyperparameter the gain is modest.

Out-of-fold temperature scaling is a sound, low-risk calibration step that typically softens overconfident logistic-regression probabilities and reduces multi-class log loss by a few percent, and the added folds plus MLflow overhead easily fit within the time budget.
The 512-component standardized Nyström RBF representation should model nonlinear species boundaries much better than linear logistic regression while retaining useful regularization.

The new block adds well-known RAOP signals missing from unigram TF-IDF—timeline drift, request length/evidential cues, reciprocity/gratitude, and nonlinear history ratios—with only 31 columns, so overfitting risk is low and a modest AUC gain is likely.

Random forests are weak on ~8k sparse TF-IDF/subreddit features, and sqrt feature sampling rarely exposes the nine strong numeric history columns, so the model mostly memorizes noisy rare-token splits and loses the linear signal.

Random forests typically underperform linear models on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF text (axis-aligned splits can't combine evidence across thousands of weak word features), so the RF swap should cost several AUC points despite handling the numeric history features well; the mlflow additions are best-effort wrappers that don't change the metric and runtime stays well within budget.

Replacing supervised sparse TF-IDF unigrams with 50 unsupervised LDA proportions likely loses word-level and length/detail signal, so the compact topics regularize but net reduce ranking quality modestly.
Replacing the supervised TF-IDF logistic logit with unsupervised LDA topics likely loses phrase/length and label-aligned text signal, while metadata keeps the AUC from collapsing.
Likely near-neutral: dropping the absolute epoch removes a non-stationary/overfit-prone column while hour/weekday keep only weak stationary posting-time signal, so I expect a tiny gain within noise.

Adding a HistGradientBoosting model on the dense metadata/text-stat features captures nonlinear structure the linear TF-IDF model misses, and rank-averaged blending with a CV-chosen weight typically adds a small, real AUC gain on RAOP (~+0.01), with low risk of regression since the blend weight can fall back to the LR alone.

Fully grown random forests on ~5,000-dim sparse TF-IDF with only ~4,500 training rows badly underperform regularized linear models: trees split on individual rare tokens, overfit noise, and produce coarse, poorly ranked probability estimates, so the known RAOP benchmark advantage of logistic regression (~0.70) over RF (~0.60-0.67 on similar feature sets) should hold, yielding a substantial regression.
Bag-of-subreddits should add a modest user-history signal beyond the numeric count, but overlap with existing metadata and strong L2 regularization likely cap the gain to a small AUC bump.

giver_username_if_known is a well-known label leak in this dataset — a non-'N/A' giver means the request was satisfied, so if the prepared test.json retains real usernames (as the proposal's schema description implies), the binary flag is a near-perfect predictor and AUC jumps from ~0.66 to ~0.93; only if the test column were all 'N/A' would it be a no-op, but the proposal's explicit fallback suggests it carries real values.
Stacking an OOF text logit with regularized LightGBM over metadata/time should add a small nonlinear gain over the linear TF-IDF+numeric baseline, but the tiny noisy dataset caps the improvement.

The added dense time/text/history features are mostly available in both splits and should give the linear model a small orthogonal signal over TF-IDF plus existing numerics, with only mild risk from time-trend extrapolation and extra MLflow overhead.

ExtraTrees on ~5.4k high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF features with only ~4.5k training rows typically ranks worse than regularized logistic regression — random splits on sparse binary-ish text features are noisy, trees overfit the few dense numerics, and vote-averaged probabilities give a coarser ranking, so expect a modest AUC drop of roughly 0.01-0.03.

Removing the 5k TF-IDF block discards the most discriminative signal for this small linear model; MiniLM embeddings plus 9 numeric covariates alone typically underperform word-level TF-IDF on this competition, so expect a modest AUC regression to ~0.60.

Document-level stats (length, sentiment, gratitude, readability, pronouns) are known strong predictors on RAOP and recover signal that length-normalized TF-IDF destroys; scaling and hstacking them with the existing numerics should give a modest but real AUC gain for logistic regression, roughly +0.015–0.02.

Removing the TF-IDF block eliminates the main discriminative signal in request wording/title; the nine requester-history covariates are stabler but weaker alone, so AUC likely drops a few points despite lower variance.
Averaged skip-gram vectors trained on this tiny corpus will be noisy and stopword-dominated, losing much of the discriminative unigram signal while metadata/text-stats prevent a larger collapse.

Adding frequent bigrams and a larger TF-IDF vocabulary should recover useful phrase-level request signals and modestly improve ranking, while fixed C=0.3 L2 and mlflow no-op telemetry keep overfitting/runtime risk limited.

On RAOP, request text (TF-IDF) carries a large share of the predictive signal; the 9 requester-history numerics alone typically plateau around 0.60-0.62 AUC, so dropping the SVD text features should cost roughly 0.025-0.03 AUC despite reduced variance and faster training.

On a 309-dim dense SVD+numeric matrix with ~5.7k samples, a random forest typically underperforms a CV-tuned LightGBM slightly (trees can't exploit the low-dimensional structure as efficiently and max_features='sqrt' on 309 features is coarse), so expect a small AUC regression while remaining in the same ballpark.

MiniLM embeddings add complementary semantic signal to the sparse TF-IDF + metadata features for a small linear model, typically yielding a modest AUC gain on this dataset, and the CPU encoding easily fits the runtime budget.
Adding bigrams and a larger TF-IDF vocabulary should capture useful request phrasing under strong logistic regularization, likely giving a modest AUC gain despite some added sparsity/noise.

Length/readability and lexicon-count features add signals mostly missing from row-normalized unigram TF-IDF with low overfit/runtime risk, but several lexicons are sparse so the gain should be modest.

GBM over SVD-300 + scaled numerics typically captures nonlinear interactions a plain linear TF-IDF model misses on this dataset, giving a modest AUC gain (~0.66 -> ~0.67), though the small data size and lossy SVD cap the improvement.
Annual sin/cos loses the spline's low-frequency multi-year trend signal while adding little seasonal gain, so a very small AUC regression is likely.

C=30 should reduce excessive shrinkage of row-normalized TF-IDF unigram weights relative to the dense metadata, likely adding useful text ranking signal while L2 still limits catastrophic overfitting.

Calendar time carries weak but real signal in RAOP (community activity/success rates drifted over 2010-2013), and a smooth 8-knot spline with constant extrapolation is a low-variance way to add it, so a small AUC gain over the 0.649 baseline is likely, though the effect is modest since text and requester history dominate.

kNN with cosine distance on unnormalized TF-IDF mixed with standardized numerics and binary subreddit indicators discards the global signal LR exploits; in ~5k-dimensional sparse space distances are noisy and uninformative, so the 25-neighbor distance-weighted votes produce coarse, poorly-ranked probabilities that typically regress well below the linear baseline on this dataset.

Replacing CatBoost with distance-weighted k-NN (k=25) on the same 9 standardized metadata features yields a notably weaker tabular model (~0.55-0.58 AUC vs ~0.62), which drags the 50/50 blend with the text logistic regression down a few points; training will be fast and within budget.

C=0.3 heavily over-shrinks TF-IDF coefficients for a 4.5k-sample/5k-feature text model; raising C to 30 is in the typical near-optimal range for TF-IDF logistic regression, improving the lexical component and lifting the 50/50 blend, with modest overfitting risk.
Calendar-date splines add a weak temporal signal but only a few columns versus the dominant TF-IDF/history features, so the change should be tiny and slightly positive.

Binarizing TF-IDF and thresholding requester features discards magnitude information, and BernoulliNB’s independence/absence modeling typically ranks slightly worse than the regularized logistic model on this small text-plus-metadata task.

Timestamp spline features capture mild temporal drift in success rates and are valid at prediction time, but add only ~8 weak features to a text-dominated model, so expect a small positive but limited AUC gain with negligible runtime cost.
Subreddit-history indicators add a complementary user/community signal to text+karma features, but fixed C=0.3 and an unscaled high-cardinality sparse block cap the gain to a small AUC bump.

CatBoost should model nonlinear metadata interactions better than the linear terms, but it is metadata-only and highly correlated with the logistic model, so the fixed 50/50 blend likely gives only a small AUC gain.

Adding bigrams under a shared 5000-feature TF-IDF budget typically gives a small AUC bump on RAOP-style short request texts by capturing sentiment/phrase patterns, while the unchanged numeric features and logistic model keep the effect modest; the dropped local holdout and telemetry code do not affect the graded predictions.

Function words are classic stylometric signal for author attribution (Poe/Shelley/Lovecraft differ in function-word usage), and although char_wb n-grams partially capture them, removing stop-word unigrams/bigrams from the word view loses some calibrated signal while the new content-only bigrams add noise; expect a small regression.

NB word/char models add genuinely diverse (count-based, generative) signals to the TF-IDF LR; a log-prob geometric stacking on only 9 meta-features with CV-tuned C is low-overfit-risk and typically yields a modest but real log-loss gain on this competition, slightly offset by losing the full-data LR refit in favor of fold-averaged test predictions.

Removing stopwords strips some high-value author/style signal from the word models; char_wb and meta features partly compensate, so the stack likely changes only slightly, with a small net regression.

The 12 OOF probabilities are already strong and highly correlated, so a regularized multinomial stacker should keep most signal while reducing LightGBM's fold-noise overfitting, giving a small log-loss gain.

Punctuation usage (dashes, semicolons, commas) is a well-known discriminative stylistic signal for these three authors, and stripping it removes informative char n-grams while the regularization benefit is too weak to compensate, so a small regression in log loss is expected.

OOF stacking of separate word/char LRs with count-based NB diversity and a calibrated meta-LR should meaningfully beat the single hstacked C=1 LR, though fold-averaged 80% base models and the small graded subset cap the gain.

Chi-squared selection should remove many noisy, weakly author-specific n-grams and reduce LR variance while retaining most discriminative word and character features, yielding a modest log-loss improvement.

Removing stop words slightly reduces vocabulary and may calibrate naive Bayes, but function-word frequencies and stop-word bigrams are valuable authorship signals, so the blended model should regress modestly.

Cross-validated C selection over [1,3,10,30,100] with 5-fold CV typically picks a slightly less-regularized model (C≈3–10) for TF-IDF + LR on this dataset, yielding a modest log-loss improvement over fixed C=1.0; the manual fold implementation preserves the proposed idea and fits within the runtime budget.

OOF stacking of correlated but complementary word/char LR and NB models plus stylometric features should calibrate better than a single TF-IDF LR, with LightGBM early stopping limiting overfit; expect a solid but not SOTA gain.

Boundary-crossing char n-grams plus case-sensitive features (capitalization, punctuation-in-context) are well-documented to help on spooky-author LR baselines; dropping the 60k cap adds discriminative n-grams, giving a modest improvement over the char_wb baseline at roughly 0.43 log loss.

Count-based MultinomialNB captures complementary word-frequency signal for this task, and OOF-tuned convex blending with the unchanged TF-IDF LR (worst case falls back to w=1.0) historically yields a modest but real log-loss gain on Spooky Author, roughly 4-7%.

Stopword removal strips function words that are classic authorship-attribution signals and distorts fastText's word-bigram features by creating artificial adjacencies, so despite cleaner vocabulary the model loses discriminative stylistic information and log loss should worsen moderately.

The class imbalance is mild (7.9k/6.0k/5.6k), so oversampling mainly shifts predicted probabilities away from the natural test prior and duplicates minority examples (effectively extra epochs on them), which typically degrades log-loss calibration slightly rather than helping.
The OOF blend has an LR-only fallback and ComplementNB adds a little complementary signal, but identical TF-IDF features and NB overconfidence cap the gain, so expect a sub-1% log-loss improvement.

MultinomialNB on TF-IDF word+char features is a solid classic for this dataset but typically lands around 0.38-0.40 log loss even with tuned alpha — it tends to produce overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities compared to the tuned logistic regression's 0.3548, so expect a modest regression.
Dropping char_wb 2-5 grams removes useful stylistic/punctuation signal for author attribution, so the word-only NB-SVM should be a bit faster but modestly worse in log loss.

Replacing the NB-SVM hybrid (a strong discriminative head on ratio-weighted TF-IDF) with a plain generative ComplementNB on raw TF-IDF typically degrades log loss on this dataset (ComplementNB probabilities are poorly calibrated on TF-IDF), likely landing around 0.45-0.50.

CV selection of C over a log-loss-optimized grid typically lands on a stronger C (~3-10) than the arbitrary C=1.0 for sparse TF-IDF text, giving a modest but real improvement; mlflow telemetry is best-effort and metric-neutral.

MultinomialNB is fast but its independence assumption overcounts the correlated char n-gram block and gives overconfident probabilities, which is especially penalized by log loss versus the calibrated softmax LR.

fastText supervised reaches comparable accuracy to TF-IDF+LR on this dataset (~82-84%), but its softmax probabilities are less calibrated and more overconfident than LR's, which log loss punishes, so a slight regression from 0.432 is likely.

CV over the C grid should pick a nearby slightly better regularization strength (likely around 2), giving a small calibration/accuracy gain but not a large one because the TF-IDF + LR baseline is already near this model family's plateau.

NB-SVM (log count-ratio feature weighting with per-class binary LR, C=4) is a well-established improvement over plain multinomial LR on TF-IDF word+char features for this dataset; on short stylistic text like spooky-author it typically cuts log loss by ~8-12% versus a C=1 LR baseline (expected ~0.39-0.40 public vs 0.432), with negligible runtime risk since it's just 3 binary LRs on the same sparse matrix.

Stylometric length/punctuation features carry real author signal in this competition, but with only 14 dense features stacked onto ~100k TF-IDF dimensions under an already-regularized linear model, the effect is a small positive nudge rather than a large gain.
NB log-count-ratio weighted OVR logistic (NB-SVM style) is a well-known improvement over plain TF-IDF logistic on this competition, typically moving log loss from ~0.44 into the high-0.3s/low-0.4s.
Stronger L2 should mainly soften overconfident sparse TF-IDF logits and improve calibration slightly, with little risk of severe underfitting at C=0.25.

Word unigram/bigram features carry substantial author-discriminative signal in this task; dropping them for a char-only representation typically degrades log loss by several hundredths, so expect a moderate regression from 0.518 to roughly 0.55-0.57.
Plain one-vs-rest logistic on the same TF-IDF features should be better calibrated than NB-ratio rescaling, giving a moderate log-loss improvement.

Halving C to 2.0 on already well-regularized TF-IDF logistic regression typically adds slight underfitting; C=4.0 was near the sweet spot for this stacked word+char feature set, so expect a small log-loss regression of well under 1%, within noise.

NB-weighted one-vs-rest logistic regression (NBSVM-style) is a well-known strong method for this exact competition and typically beats plain multinomial LR on word+char TF-IDF, cutting log loss from ~0.37 to ~0.30-0.31; runtime stays well under budget with liblinear dual on three sparse binary fits.

Function words are highly discriminative of authorial style (Poe vs Shelley vs Lovecraft) and TF-IDF already downweights common tokens, so removing stop words discards useful signal in both word bigrams and char_wb n-grams, likely degrading log loss modestly.
Stronger L2 shrinkage on correlated sparse n-grams should slightly reduce variance/overconfidence after temperature rescaling, giving a small log-loss gain rather than a large shift.

Switching char_wb to char adds cross-word-boundary n-grams, which typically dilutes word-boundary signal and slightly degrades this TF-IDF+LR pipeline; the removed holdout split doesn't affect the submission since it already refit on all data, so expect a small regression within noise.

NB-logistic (log-count-ratio weighted features + binary LR) is a well-established improvement over plain multinomial LR on short text TF-IDF tasks like Spooky Author, typically cutting log loss by ~5-8%; the OVR probability stacking is uncalibrated but row normalization partially compensates, and all described steps fit easily in the time budget.

On word+char TF-IDF features, C=4 (weaker regularization) typically fits this task slightly better than C=1, and winning-style LR solutions for this competition use C in the 2-5 range, so expect a modest log-loss improvement; convergence with max_iter=2000 at C=4 on this small dataset is not a runtime risk.

Temperature scaling tuned on a ~1,960-row stratified holdout typically sharpens LR's slightly overconfident TF-IDF probabilities for a small (~1-2%) log-loss gain; the MLflow/telemetry additions don't affect predictions, and softmax(decision_function) equals predict_proba at T=1 so only the fitted scalar moves the score.

Optimizing RMSE on log(1+fare) no longer optimizes the graded dollar-scale RMSE: expm1 inversion is Jensen-biased low and squared loss on the log scale systematically underweights the expensive-ride errors that dominate raw RMSE, so dollar-space RMSE typically degrades modestly (a few percent) despite the better-behaved log-scale fit.

Quadrupling the training sample from ~0.97M to ~3.9M clean rows reduces variance and lets LightGBM fit the fare surface better (typical log-log gains of a few percent RMSE), but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the improvement; the mlflow/timestamp/n_jobs changes are result-neutral engineering.

Airport-distance features are a well-known win for NYC taxi fares (flat JFK fare and distinct airport trip pricing); LightGBM can exploit them for a modest but real gain, though the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the improvement, so expect roughly a 3-5% drop from 4.19 to ~4.02.

Fitting L2 on log1p then expm1 without a Duan/smearing bias correction estimates the geometric mean and systematically underpredicts right-skewed dollar fares, especially high-leverage long/corrupt rows, so RMSE should tick up despite stabler training.

The distance-fare relationship is already strongly monotone in the learned model, so the constraint only prunes spurious non-monotonic splits in sparse regions (rare long trips), yielding a small RMSE improvement on the valid rows while the ~2.8% corrupt test rows dominate the error floor unchanged.

Log1p target training on this right-skewed fare distribution typically yields a small RMSE gain by stabilizing variance and reducing the pull of extreme fares, though the expm1 back-transform bias and the grader's ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows cap the improvement at roughly 1%.

Using the same smoothed full-train statistics for train/val/test removes the OOF count/mean distribution shift while m=20 and leaf constraints keep self-leakage small, so a modest RMSE gain is most likely.

Fitting log1p and exponentiating approximates conditional geometric means and early-stops on log-RMSE, so without a bias/smearing correction it likely underpredicts higher-dollar rides and slightly worsens raw-dollar RMSE; the corrupt-row floor is unchanged.

Airport-distance features let the trees isolate flat-rate JFK and surcharged EWR trips with cheap splits, a well-known modest win in this competition; most rows are unaffected and the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor limits total gains, so expect a small improvement of roughly 0.1 RMSE.

Treating bad coordinates as NaN should let LightGBM route corrupt rows to their own learned fare distribution instead of the global mean, but those rows remain largely unpredictable/high-variance and the valid-row model is essentially unchanged, so only a small gain is likely.

Quadrupling the training sample from 1M to 4M rows with identical features/hyperparameters reduces estimation variance and yields a modest but real RMSE gain (typical for this dataset, roughly 0.1 improvement), while the dtype/timestamp/n_jobs changes only affect speed, not accuracy.

OOF smoothed target encodings of ~1km endpoint cells and route keys reliably capture airport flat fares, tolls, and route-specific pricing that haversine distance misses; with 1M rows most cells have enough counts to be informative, so expect the valid-row RMSE to drop from ~3.57 to ~3.42, which after the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows translates to roughly a 3% graded improvement (the added mlflow/psutil deps are inert overhead).
log1p/expm1 without a bias correction shifts predictions toward the geometric mean and underweights high-dollar fares, so dollar RMSE likely worsens slightly despite stabler training.

Manhattan distance and bearing give LightGBM cheap grid-aligned geometry it can't easily reconstruct from raw coords + haversine, typically worth ~1% RMSE on valid rows in this competition; corrupt test rows (floor ~2.1) are untouched, capping the overall gain.

Distance-to-airport/landmark features are among the most impactful known features for this competition since airport trips have distinct pricing regimes (e.g., JFK flat fare); trees can exploit them far better than raw coordinates, so expect a solid single-digit-percent RMSE drop on the ~97% valid test rows, though the corrupt-row floor (~2.1 RMSE) limits total gains.

The metric is RMSE, which is minimized by fitting the conditional mean; switching to an L1 objective fits the conditional median instead, which is robust to outliers but systematically suboptimal under squared-error evaluation, so despite cleaner handling of the heavy fare tail the RMSE should regress slightly (typically a few percent on this dataset).

Log1p target stabilizes training but expm1 inversion introduces a downward bias (Jensen's inequality) on the raw-dollar RMSE metric, and with the test floor (~2.1 RMSE from corrupt rows) unchanged, the net effect is a small regression rather than an improvement.

L1 training shifts trees toward conditional medians; for right-skewed fares evaluated by RMSE this slight underprediction of longer rides usually outweighs outlier robustness after the existing cleaning, giving a small RMSE regression.

Huber with delta=$1 is mostly linear for typical dollar-scale residuals, pushing the model toward a median-like/robust target and downweighting large legitimate fare errors while RMSE still rewards the conditional mean, so I expect a small regression despite better outlier resistance.

Log1p optimizes a relative/log-scale loss misaligned with raw RMSE, and uncorrected expm1 back-transform tends to underpredict via Jensen/tail compression, so expect a small regression despite variance stabilization.

Airport-proximity features are a well-known strong signal for this dataset (JFK flat-fare trips especially), letting LightGBM split airport trips from metered ones; should give a modest but real RMSE gain over 4.129, with a slight cost from the unchanged corrupt-row floor.

Quadrupling the training sample (1M -> 4M rows) with histogram LightGBM and early stopping reduces variance and lets trees fit finer structure; gains are sublinear in data size and capped by the ~2.8% corrupt test-row floor, so expect roughly a 4-7% RMSE improvement, from 4.14 to about 3.9-4.0, well within the time budget.

5-fold bagging averages out model variance and each fold still trains on 800k rows with early stopping, typically yielding a small (~1%) RMSE gain over a single 90/10 split; the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows caps the total possible improvement.

OOF-smoothed pickup-cell mean fare adds genuine location signal beyond what lat/lon splits capture, but with 1M rows over ~100m cells the m=30 smoothing is heavy and LightGBM already exploits coordinates, so expect a modest ~1% RMSE gain; the mlflow additions are wrapped in try/except no-ops and don't affect the model.
Snapping to a ~1 km grid discards within-cell coordinate and distance precision that LightGBM uses, while the 0.01 route encoding is mostly unchanged, so RMSE likely worsens modestly.
L1 may blunt a few label outliers, but fares are right-skewed and RMSE is mean-optimizing, so median-leaning predictions likely give a slight RMSE regression with unchanged runtime.
L1 training is more robust to residual label outliers, but it optimizes median-like behavior while RMSE rewards conditional means, so despite RMSE early stopping I expect a small net regression.

Airport-distance features are a well-known win in this competition (JFK/LGA/EWR flat surcharges make fares non-linear in trip distance), and adding them as six cheap continuous columns to an unchanged LightGBM pipeline should give a modest but real RMSE improvement without runtime risk.

L1 fits the conditional median, but RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean; fares are right-skewed even after filtering, so median-based predictions will sit slightly below the mean-optimal ones and modestly increase RMSE despite added outlier robustness.

Rounding coordinates to 2 decimals (~1km) discards fine-grained spatial signal that LightGBM's continuous splits exploit (borough boundaries, airport zones), while the unrounded haversine distance preserves trip length, so expect a small regression rather than a meaningful regularization benefit.

L1 (regression_l1) optimizes the conditional median, not the mean, so on an RMSE-scored task it usually costs a small amount of RMSE; outliers are already clipped to fares <=500 by cleaning, limiting any robustness benefit — expect a slight regression.

A grid-aligned Manhattan-distance proxy (rotated 29° to match Manhattan's street grid) is a well-known, genuinely complementary feature to haversine distance for NYC taxi fares, and LightGBM exploits such features cheaply, but with ~2.8% unpredictable corrupt test rows flooring RMSE near 2.1 and the feature being highly correlated with the existing distance_km, only a modest ~1% improvement is expected; the added tracking.py is just the already-imported logging helper and has no modeling effect.

The OOF smoothed directional route fare should help on repeated corridors such as airports/toll routes while unseen routes shrink to the mean, but the corrupt-row floor and coarse 0.01-degree cells cap the total gain.

The rotated-Manhattan grid distance is a well-known mildly informative feature for NYC taxi fares (streets run ~29° off-grid), so it should reduce RMSE slightly on the valid rows, but its high correlation with the existing haversine feature and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows cap the gain at roughly 1%.

Doubling the training sample from 1M to 2M rows gives LightGBM modestly better generalization with identical features/hyperparameters, but gains are diminishing at this scale and ~2.8% of test rows are unpredictably corrupt (RMSE floor ~2.1), so only a small overall improvement is expected; runtime stays within budget.

The airport_route categorical captures JFK/LGA/EWR flat-fare and surcharge effects (a well-known strong signal in this dataset, since airport trips have distinct fare structure), which typically cuts several tenths of RMSE on valid rows; the extraneous mlflow tracking code is guarded and doesn't affect predictions, and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows limits the total gain to a few percent.

A plain LightGBM with per-char f_27 splits and no interaction/unique-count engineering is the well-known ~0.977-0.980 baseline for TPS May 2022, and the tuned MLP at 0.9866 already edges out standard GBDT on this dataset, so swapping learners likely costs a few thousandths of AUC despite categorical encoding and faster runtime.
Quantile one-hot should make skewed/integer numeric inputs easier for the MLP and improve robustness, but 10 bins are coarse so the gain is modest rather than GBDT-level.

Whitening improves conditioning for the linear leaves, but the unsupervised rotation mixes the original axis-aligned categorical and numeric patterns, likely causing a small net loss in boosted-tree ranking performance.

f_27 strings are essentially unique high-cardinality codes, so a smoothed whole-string target encoding collapses to ~prior and discards the highly informative per-position character features that drive the baseline's AUC.

f_27 is a medium-cardinality string that repeats many times across train/test, so a smoothed OOF target encoding captures whole-string identity effects the ten ordinal per-position columns cannot represent, while losing little positional generalization since most test strings are seen in training; expect a small net AUC gain over the 0.9915 baseline, limited by estimation noise (~40-60 rows per string vs m=20 smoothing) and the loss of per-position splits for rare/unseen strings.

These exact additive sums (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) with thresholds near ±5 are the well-known generating interactions in TPS-May-2022; exposing them as explicit features lets the shallow trees exploit the signal directly, typically lifting AUC from ~0.9915 to ~0.995-0.996 with negligible runtime cost.
The ordinal-encoded linear model is likely much weaker than the tuned LightGBM, and giving it 50% rank weight will distort the stronger model's ordering more than diversity compensates.

A standardized CPU MLP should train adequately within the budget, but its ordinal treatment of f_27 and limited inductive bias make it slightly weaker than LightGBM on these discrete feature interactions.

TPS-May-2022's interaction-heavy synthetic features strongly favor GBDTs; a small plain MLP on standardized raw features typically plateaus around 0.95-0.96 AUC, well below the 0.977 LightGBM baseline, though the 60-epoch cosine schedule and L2 keep it from collapsing further.
Linear leaves should help approximate the oblique/threshold-sum boundaries a bit, but gains are capped by arbitrary ordinal encoding of f_27 and linear-tree instability/overfitting risk.

The unique-character count of f_27 is a well-known informative feature in this competition that is only partially recoverable by trees from the per-position ordinals, so adding it should give a small but real AUC gain (~+0.0005-0.0007) with no downside risk.
The three raw sums expose likely diagonal additive boundaries that axis-aligned trees approximate inefficiently; keeping all features and hyperparameters makes this a low-risk modest AUC gain.

Raw 10-letter f_27 is near-unique/high-cardinality, so native categorical splits mostly memorize singleton train codes and cannot generalize to unseen test strings, while removing the 10 positional ordinal columns loses real position signal; retained letter counts/numeric features keep the drop moderate.

Adjacent-character bigrams of f_27 are a known useful interaction signal in TPS May 2022 and encoding them as native categoricals lets LightGBM exploit pair structure the per-position ordinals and counts miss, yielding a small AUC gain with negligible runtime cost.
PCA factors are label-agnostic linear combinations that add little for trees, while removing the mined pairwise interaction features loses a small amount of useful nonlinear signal.

f_27's signal in this dataset is positional (each character position matters), and hashing the whole 10-char string into 64 one-hot buckets makes all strings landing in the same bucket indistinguishable, destroying most of the per-position information the ordinal encoding provided, so AUC should drop substantially.

ExtraTrees with sqrt feature subsampling and fully grown trees cannot capture the strong feature interactions in this dataset nearly as well as 3000 rounds of tuned LightGBM boosting; on TPS May 2022, ExtraTrees-class models land around 0.92-0.93 AUC versus ~0.978 for the boosted baseline, so this is a clear regression (with added timeout risk from the 5-fold CV re-fits on 800k rows).

A shallow sklearn MLP on raw + per-char ordinal features typically underperforms tuned LightGBM on this competition (~0.965-0.972 vs 0.978): 40 constant-LR epochs with accuracy-based early stopping underfits, and trees handle the heavy-tailed f_28 and ordinal char codes better than standardized linear layers.

Letter-count and nunique features over f_27 are known to be highly informative in TPS May 2022 (order-invariant letter identity drives much of the signal), so adding them as numeric features to the unchanged LightGBM pipeline should give a modest but real AUC gain over the 0.9768 baseline, with negligible runtime cost.

In TPS May 2022 the per-position letters of f_27 carry the core target signal via interactions, but the full 10-char sequence is near-unique per row (26^10 space over 900k rows), so its frequency is ~1 for almost every row and carries essentially no information — the model is effectively reduced to the 30 numeric features, losing most of the f_27 signal.

Per-letter occurrence counts and unique-letter count over f_27 are well-known informative features for this competition (the target depends partly on letter composition, not just positions), so LightGBM should gain a small but real AUC boost with negligible runtime cost.

Gain-selected z-score products should expose a few multiplicative boundaries that axis-aligned trees approximate inefficiently, but the 3000-tree LightGBM already captures most pairwise structure, so the likely effect is a small positive bump within budget.

Refitting on 100% of the data with rounds scaled by 1/0.9 is a standard, safe technique; the extra 80k rows typically yield a small AUC gain, with minor risk that the 1/0.9 round scaling slightly overtrains, netting a small positive change.

Treating the 26-letter per-position codes as native LightGBM categoricals lets trees split on optimal letter subsets rather than arbitrary ordinal thresholds; f_27 is the key interaction driver in this dataset, so this typically yields a small but real AUC gain over the 0.97696 baseline within the same budget.

Distinct-character counts over f_27 are a known weakly-informative aggregate in TPS May 2022 (the string encodes latent interactions); adding this single feature to a strong GBDT baseline typically yields a small AUC gain on the order of a few hundredths of a percent.

TPS May 2022 is dominated by higher-order feature interactions; capping trees at depth 2 (4 leaves) restricts the model to main effects and pairwise interactions, and one engineered sum feature cannot compensate, so underfitting substantially lowers AUC despite the regularization benefit.

Histogram-based GBDT with per-character f_27 ordinals is a stronger fit for this interaction-heavy synthetic tabular data than a shallow CPU MLP, and 600 trees at lr 0.05 easily fits the time budget, so LightGBM should edge out the 0.9822 MLP baseline despite the modest num_leaves=31/max_bin=63 settings.

LightGBM histogram trees with per-character f_27 ordinals are a strong fit for this interaction-heavy synthetic dataset and typically edge out a modest CPU MLP, though selecting on logloss instead of AUC and 600-tree/31-leaf limits cap the gain to a small improvement over 0.9822.
Restricting continuous predictors to three train-fitted quartile thresholds discards fine-grained ranking and interaction information that the still-improving 3000-tree LightGBM model was exploiting.

Cutting num_leaves from 127 to 7 caps each tree at ~3-way splits, which badly underfits this dataset whose signal depends on high-order interactions (especially among the f_27 character columns); even 3000 boosting rounds at lr=0.05 only partially compensate, so holdout/test AUC should drop noticeably to the mid-0.95 range.

Cutting num_leaves from 127 to 4 makes each tree almost stump-like, so boosting keeps broad main effects but underfits the interaction-heavy f_27/numeric structure, likely costing roughly 0.01 AUC despite the 3000-round budget.

Adding a low-risk, consistently-computed sum feature of f_00+f_01+f_26 gives axis-aligned trees a genuinely useful linear-interaction split (this combination is a known weak signal in this dataset), likely yielding a tiny AUC gain, but with 41 existing features and a strong baseline the marginal effect should be small (~+0.03%).

LightGBM trees can already approximate additive interactions of f_00/f_01/f_26 through splits, so an explicit sum feature adds almost no new information; expect a negligible change within noise (±0.05%).

A CPU MLP on ordinal-encoded f_27 characters and raw numerics can learn some interactions in the ~420s budget, but ordinal char encoding is a poor representation for the categorical code and GBDTs dominate on this synthetic interaction-heavy data, so a modest regression from 0.977 is expected.
Treating the ten f_27 positions as nominal lets LightGBM use category-subset splits instead of arbitrary A-Z ordinal thresholds, likely giving a small AUC gain with unchanged capacity.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is a known weakly-informative signal in TPS May 2022 that trees cannot trivially derive from per-position ordinals, so adding it gives a small but real AUC bump over the 0.97696 baseline.

Dark stroke pixels dominate the residual error while background is already near-perfect, so mild darkness weighting should shift capacity to text with little background cost, yielding a modest ~5% RMSE improvement.

Extending training from 2000 steps to ~7-10k steps within a 330s wall-clock budget with the same cosine-to-zero schedule should substantially improve convergence of the U-Net on this small denoising dataset; random-crop training rarely overfits here, and the time-based LR anneal ensures the final weights are well-settled, so expect roughly a 20-30% RMSE reduction from 0.0161 to ~0.012.
