L1 is metric-mismatched to RMSE but is robust to stain outliers and tends to give sharper text/background in restoration CNNs, so I expect a small single-run RMSE gain rather than a large change.

Input-only brightness/contrast jitter is a mild, well-matched regularizer for a ~105-image training set; it slightly discourages overfitting to specific scan intensity statistics, and since the test set comes from the same synthetic noise generation process the distribution shift risk is small, so a modest ~1-2% RMSE improvement is expected.

Multi-scale TTA averaging typically gives a small RMSE gain for single-scale-trained dense nets by canceling scale-specific errors, but the benefit is modest since the 0.75x/1.25x passes see out-of-distribution stroke widths, so expect ~1-2% improvement rather than a large one.
Moderate spatial dropout at the deepest encoder levels should provide a small regularization benefit on the very small training set without materially disrupting the U-Net or runtime.

Dropout2d in every block adds gradient noise and slows fixed-time convergence for a precise pixel-regression denoiser that is already performing very well, so a small RMSE regression is more likely than a generalization gain.

A 4-level U-Net roughly doubles receptive field (~41→89 px) and capacity for a modest extra per-step cost within a fixed wall-clock budget; larger context helps disambiguate noise from text strokes, typically yielding a small single-digit RMSE gain on this task, though slightly fewer optimization steps cap the benefit.

A 23x23 median-blur background channel is a classic, well-matched feature for this task: it explicitly exposes the slowly-varying stain/shading component, letting the U-Net separate background noise from text more easily, which typically yields a solid single-digit RMSE gain over a noisy-only input; the diff is correctly implemented and adds negligible runtime cost.
The 5-level U-Net adds capacity and global context while keeping pixel throughput constant, so it should modestly reduce RMSE; the short fixed schedule and near-full-height 256px crops cap the gain.
4-way flip TTA averages out asymmetric prediction errors and typically yields a small but reliable RMSE gain for image-to-image models trained with flip augmentation, at negligible compute cost.

The time-based budget with manual cosine decay trains to a fully annealed LR; on a GPU the small UNet likely completes more optimizer steps in 180s than the baseline's fixed 2000 steps, yielding a small improvement, though validation overhead and unchanged data/augmentation cap the gain.

The leaderboard metric is RMSE, which MSE directly optimizes (conditional mean); Charbonnier/L1 optimizes something closer to a conditional median and down-weights large residuals, so on this L2-aligned metric it typically trades a tiny bit of RMSE for perceptual sharpness — with identical budget/architecture, expect a small regression of roughly 1-4%.

Injecting fairly large Gaussian noise (sigma 0.05) shifts training away from the test corruption and pushes the fixed-capacity U-Net toward stronger smoothing/over-cleaning, likely outweighing any regularization benefit.

GroupNorm removes the train/inference statistics mismatch but typically converges slightly worse than BatchNorm in small denoising U-Nets at fixed lr/epochs, so expect a small regression of a few percent rather than a gain.
SSIM+L1 should sharpen stroke edges and robustly clean speckle/stains on near-binary documents, giving a small RMSE gain despite being less directly aligned with squared error than MSE.

8-fold dihedral TTA is a standard, reliable variance-reduction trick for fully-convolutional denoisers; averaging inverse-transformed outputs typically cuts per-pixel RMSE by a few percent (roughly 3-6%) on this benchmark, with the modest 8x inference cost adding well under a minute to the run.

RMSE is directly optimized by MSE/posterior-mean behavior, whereas pure SSIM is locally contrast/structure invariant and can trade exact intensity accuracy for sharper structure, so it should look cleaner but score modestly worse.

Residual (DnCNN-style) learning with a linear head and zero-init final conv removes sigmoid saturation near the dominant white background and eases optimization, typically giving a modest but real RMSE gain on document denoising with identical capacity and budget.

RMSE/MSE is already aligned with the leaderboard metric, and the small SSIM plus per-batch RMSE normalization likely shifts emphasis away from hard squared-error residuals, giving a neutral-to-slightly-worse RMSE.

Residual prediction with zero-initialized final conv is a well-established win for image denoising (DnCNN): the network starts at the identity (already a decent solution since noise is small relative to the mostly-white background), removes the saturating sigmoid bottleneck, and learns the sparse noise component, which converges faster and to lower RMSE than direct regression within the same 20-epoch budget.

Synthetic corruption-augmented pairs add artifact diversity that typically improves U-Net generalization on this benchmark, though the hand-crafted stains/shading/speckle only loosely match the real test noise, so expect a modest ~3% RMSE gain with identical training budget.

4.5x more Adam steps with a cosine schedule stretched to match typically yields a modest but real RMSE gain for a small U-Net on 105 training images before overfitting sets in, roughly 5-12% improvement over the undertrained 2k-step baseline.

The dihedral-8 TTA is correctly implemented (inverse transforms check out, batching by shape-preserving vs transposed groups works, training path and RNG consumption unchanged so the model is identical); flip/rot180 views are in-distribution due to training-time flip augmentation and transpose views are only mildly OOD for this local denoising task, so averaging 8 mostly-independent predictions should shave the variance component of the error, yielding the typical small ~1-3% RMSE gain with negligible runtime cost.

Since evaluation is RMSE, training with L1 optimizes the median rather than the mean and down-weights large residuals, so it typically yields slightly blurrier, RMSE-suboptimal reconstructions; expect a small regression of a few percent.
Foreground weighting should modestly improve reconstruction of glyphs and antialiased edges, with only a small penalty from slightly darker background predictions.

Intensity weighting should reduce the background's dominance and improve reconstruction of ink and boundaries, giving a modest unweighted-RMSE gain despite slightly darker biased predictions in ambiguous regions.

Residual prediction with zero-initialized final conv is a well-established improvement for image denoising: the network starts from the identity mapping (already a decent solution since noise is sparse) and only learns the correction, which eases optimization and removes the sigmoid's saturation constraints, typically yielding a modest but real RMSE gain under identical training budget.

Evaluation is RMSE, so directly optimizing MSE is metric-aligned; switching to L1 optimizes the conditional median and typically yields slightly worse squared-error performance (L1's constant-magnitude gradients also interact suboptimally with the unchanged LR schedule near convergence), though the degradation should be modest since L1 is a reasonable denoising objective.

Zero-initialized residual prediction starts the model at the identity (a strong prior for denoising since input and target are highly correlated) and eases optimization, typically giving a modest but real RMSE gain over direct sigmoid regression; dropping sigmoid saturation also helps fit near-extreme intensities.
Halving BASE_CH quarters most NAFNet capacity; with the same short 2000-step schedule this should mildly underfit fine stroke/noise detail, so RMSE likely rises rather than improving.

Upweighting dark/edge pixels should reduce the large squared errors from missed faint strokes while leaving easy white background nearly unchanged, giving a small RMSE gain with some risk of over-darkening.

The full-resolution background-normalized channel should help the U-Net suppress stains and uneven illumination while the unchanged target and training schedule limit the gain to a modest improvement.

The runtime.toml forces CPU-only execution (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=''), so AMP autocast is already disabled (amp = device.type=='cuda' is False); disabling autocast around the final conv+sigmoid is therefore a numerical no-op — the score should match the baseline within run-to-run noise.

4-view flip TTA with the same trained U-Net reduces prediction variance and edge artifacts, typically giving a modest 2-4% RMSE improvement on this denoising task; training is unchanged so model quality is the same, and the CPU-only runtime mainly affects wall-clock, not the metric.

The residual NAFNet is a stronger denoising architecture than the small direct-prediction U-Net and should train sufficiently within the 2,000-update budget, yielding a substantial but not order-of-magnitude RMSE gain.
The ImageNet head is an aligned, possibly leaky dog classifier on the same features, and temperature/weight tuning with a w=0 fallback should give a meaningful but not extreme log-loss gain.

PCA-256 without whitening on already layer-normed ConvNeXt features keeps most variance, but L2-regularized LR with holdout-tuned C already handles feature correlation well, so decorrelation gives little benefit while discarding low-variance directions that can carry fine-grained breed signal — expect a near-neutral to very slight regression in log loss.
Mixup/CutMix should act as strong regularization and improve probability calibration across 120 confusable breeds with negligible runtime cost, though the short 6-epoch schedule limits the gain.

Switching to the standard (0.08, 1.0) RandomResizedCrop matches the backbone's pretraining augmentation and adds useful view diversity for a 120-class problem with ~77 images/class, likely reducing overfitting enough for a small log-loss gain, though the more aggressive crops (occasionally missing the dog) cap the improvement.

ConvNeXt-V2 Large pretrained on ImageNet-22k is a far stronger feature extractor than ResNet-50 V1 for fine-grained dog breeds (its features are much more linearly separable and the IN-22k dog classes transfer directly), typically cutting log loss by ~25-35% in this frozen-features + logistic-regression setup; the timm head API usage and preprocessing are correct, so the main risk (runtime/download) is modest.

The 1000-d log-softmax block is a deterministic function of the pooled features, so after per-column standardisation it mostly adds inflated near-constant noise columns; removing it gives a cleaner homogeneous feature space for the L2-regularised linear probe, yielding a modest log-loss improvement (C selection may also shift slightly under the same grid).

Ridge boundaries should be close, but softmax-tempered one-vs-rest squared-error scores are less matched to multiclass log loss than CE-trained logistic regression, so calibration likely degrades slightly despite the alpha/T holdout search.

Per-block PCA to 128 keeps the dominant breed-related subspace, drops nuisance low-variance directions, equalizes block widths, and makes the linear head better conditioned, so I expect a small log-loss gain with negligible runtime risk.

ConvNeXt-Base pretrained on IN22k produces far more discriminative frozen features than ResNet-50 V1 (dog breeds are an ImageNet subset it saw more variants of), and the holdout re-selection of C adapts regularization to the new feature scale, typically cutting linear-probe log loss by roughly 25-30%.

Fine-tuning an ImageNet-22k ConvNeXt-Tiny with augmentation, flip TTA, and temperature scaling massively outperforms frozen ResNet50 features + logistic regression on this fine-grained task; the 7-minute budget allows roughly 4-6 epochs on a modern GPU, which is enough to reach ~0.25-0.35 log loss typical of fine-tuned ConvNeXt baselines on Dog Breed ID.
The pretrained ImageNet breed logits add a strong supervised signal while scaling and retuned regularization should improve optimization and calibration, with only modest added training cost.

Concatenating L2-normalized frozen features from three strong, diversely pretrained backbones (ConvNeXt-22k, CLIP, DINOv2) is substantially richer than a single ResNet50-V1 vector, and the holdout-tuned C on normalized features is appropriate; expect a large log-loss drop, limited only by the linear probe ceiling on 120 fine-grained classes.
On roughly balanced clean 120-class data, swapping smoothed CE for hard-target focal gamma=2 likely hurts calibration and overweights noisy hard examples, giving a small log-loss regression.

On ~10k images, freezing conv1-layer3 regularizes the 10-epoch fine-tune while keeping the lr/schedule valid for layer4+fc, typically yielding a modest log-loss gain over full fine-tuning at this scale.

Horizontal-flip TTA on frozen ViT features is a well-established, low-risk ensemble that reduces prediction variance and typically improves multiclass log loss by ~1-4%; the implementation is correct (post-transform flip is valid, train untouched, probabilities averaged and renormalized), so a modest improvement over 0.5126 is expected.

CLIP B/32 is robust but coarser and less aligned with the exact ImageNet dog synsets than the IN21k/IN1k ViT-B/16 features, so the fixed linear probe should lose fine-grained breed separation and log loss rises moderately.

PCA-256 should retain most discriminative ImageNet embedding structure and slightly denoise/regularize the linear probe, but keeping C fixed and discarding low-variance fine-grained directions caps the gain.

DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings are dramatically stronger than ImageNet-supervised ResNet-50 features for fine-grained breed discrimination (self-supervised ViT features routinely push dog-breed linear-probe accuracy into the high 80s/low 90s), so the same LR+10-view-TTA pipeline should cut log loss from ~0.44 to roughly ~0.30.

PCA-256 keeps most structure but whitening amplifies noisy mid/low-variance components and truncation discards low-variance fine-grained breed-discriminative directions; combined with a fixed C=1.0 (not re-tuned for the whitened space), this typically costs a small amount of log loss versus the already-strong 2816-d linear probe, though faster fitting keeps the run well within budget.

k-NN on sparse 120-way high-dimensional frozen features should keep reasonable nearest-neighbor signal but produce coarse, poorly calibrated vote probabilities versus the tuned linear head, so log loss regresses despite negligible runtime.

End-to-end fine-tuning of ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 with RRC+flip augmentation, label smoothing, and warmup+cosine schedule over 10 epochs (~1440 steps, well within budget on GPU) typically lifts accuracy over a linear probe on frozen features on this 120-class fine-grained task, yielding a modest log-loss improvement from ~0.453 to ~0.40; label smoothing limits overconfidence so the gain is moderate rather than large.

ViT-B/16 with ImageNet-21k augreg pretraining produces substantially more discriminative frozen features than ResNet-50 V1 (typically ~84-85% vs ~76% IN1k top-1), so a linear probe on the 768-d pooled features should cut log loss roughly 25-30%, from ~0.45 to ~0.32-0.34.

Averaging probabilities over 10 TTA views (5 crops × 2 flips) is a well-established, low-risk improvement for frozen-backbone classifiers, typically reducing multiclass log loss by a few percent through variance reduction and better invariance; runtime stays well within budget since only the 1023-image test set gets 10x forward passes.

Concatenating L2-normalized ConvNeXt-Tiny (in22k) features with ResNet-50 features adds complementary, higher-quality representations for fine-grained breeds, typically reducing multiclass log loss by roughly 15-20% over the single-backbone baseline.

The pretrained ImageNet dog-restricted classifier is a strong, decorrelated second signal (zero-shot top-1 ~75-85% on Stanford Dogs), and the honest CV-selected blend with the stronger LR head should shave a few percent off the 0.309 log loss rather than hurt, since alpha=0 is in the search grid as a safety fallback.

PCA to 256 unwhitened components preserves most variance but discards low-variance directions that carry fine-grained breed-discriminative signal, and C=0.3 was tuned for raw features, so log loss typically degrades modestly (~0.31 -> ~0.34) while fitting gets faster.

Global max pooling keeps only peak activations and discards averaged spatial/context evidence, shifting feature scale/regularization and making probabilities less smooth, so I expect a modest log-loss regression rather than a gain.

ResNet50 IMAGENET1K_V2 weights are trained with a substantially better recipe (80.9% vs 76.1% ImageNet top-1) and matched 232px preprocessing, yielding more discriminative frozen features that should reduce log loss by roughly 5-8% on this fine-grained task with everything else unchanged.
C=0.03 was already rejected for the same frozen 2048-d head, and the short last-block/head fine-tune is too light to fully undo the stronger shrinkage, so I expect a modest log-loss regression.

Dropping from 224 to 192 keeps the pipeline valid but removes fine-grained detail and shifts inputs away from ResNet50’s 224 operating point, so log loss should regress modestly despite lower compute/memory.

PCA(256) on ImageNet features retains nearly all discriminative variance while denoising correlated activations and adding implicit regularization, typically giving a small log-loss improvement with a linear classifier, though the effect is modest.

Dropping the crop from 224 to 192 removes fine detail the ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 was calibrated for, slightly degrading fine-grained breed features, so log loss likely worsens modestly (a few percent) while remaining in the same overall regime.

IMAGENET1K_V2 gives a stronger, better-aligned ResNet-50 embedding and the 232->224 eval preprocessing matches it, so the same logistic probe should separate the ImageNet-derived dog breeds somewhat better; fixed C/no fine-tuning keeps the gain moderate rather than dramatic.

Temperature scaling fitted on a proper holdout typically yields a small log-loss gain for an L2-regularized logistic regression that is already fairly well calibrated; expect T modestly above 1 and a ~1% improvement, with negligible runtime cost.

Conservative last-bottleneck tuning with BN frozen and a logistic-initialized head should slightly improve class separation without enough time or learning-rate to badly overfit, yielding a modest log-loss gain.

Horizontal-flip TTA on frozen ImageNet features reliably gives a small log-loss gain for fine-grained breed classification (dogs are roughly mirror-symmetric), and the extra test pass is cheap, so expect a modest ~1-2% improvement with no risk of runtime failure.

Random 1:1 undersampling discards most negative training signal (up to 170x for threat); for AUC-optimized linear TF-IDF models the richer negative pool aids ranking, so rare-label overfitting on ~1k-row fits and reduced data overall likely cause a small regression, only partly offset by faster convergence and better rare-label gradient balance.
Sharing the char_wb block into NB-LogReg should strengthen branch B on obfuscated profanity/slurs, but the unchanged branch A and equal rank blend cap the mean-AUC gain to a small bump.
AUC is largely prior/intercept insensitive, so 1:1 undersampling mostly discards negative evidence and adds variance—especially for threat/identity_hate and the NB ratios—yielding a small regression.

Plain MultinomialNB should rank noticeably worse than the NB-ratio + liblinear hybrid, and its weaker OOF stack also slightly degrades branch A, so the 50/50 rank blend drops despite some generative/discriminative complementarity.

Mean-pooled Word2Vec (200d) loses word/char n-gram specificity — a W2Vec-logreg branch typically scores ~0.95-0.96 vs ~0.978 for the TF-IDF branch it replaces, and the dense-input MLP stays weak, so two of the three rank-averaged branches degrade and drag the blend below the 0.9808 baseline.

1:1 undersampling discards nearly all negative evidence for the rare labels, increasing variance and overfitting while also sharply reducing MLP optimization updates; the common labels may be nearly unchanged, but severe_toxic, threat, and identity_hate should regress enough to lower the mean AUC.

Branch D likely runs and passes the 0.97 guard but is an under-trained CPU shallow NN on the same TF-IDF signal, so giving it 25% rank weight slightly dilutes the stronger linear A/B/C blend; time/quality guards prevent a larger failure.

AUC is largely class-prior insensitive, while 1:1 undersampling discards almost all negative evidence—especially for threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic—so ranking should degrade modestly despite faster fits.

Lowercasing is a no-op (TfidfVectorizer already lowercases), but collapsing repeated characters and de-obfuscating profanity consolidates sparse obfuscated variants into strong canonical tokens for both word and char TF-IDF branches, and URL/IP/timestamp removal cuts noise — consistent with small gains (+0.05–0.15%) from classic Jigsaw kernels using similar cleaning, with minimal risk since normalization is applied identically to train and test before fitting.
Leakage-free OOF branch-B probabilities should modestly enrich branch A, especially for correlated rare labels, while its information overlaps heavily with the existing rank blend.

The 3-epoch MLP on branch A's TF-IDF will be undertrained (~0.97-0.975 solo AUC) but adds genuine nonlinear/multi-task diversity to the two linear branches, and equal-weight rank blending of a moderately weaker but decorrelated model typically nets a small gain on mean column-wise AUC; slight risk of drag on rare labels (threat, identity_hate) keeps the expected gain modest.

A and B are unchanged; branch C should be slightly stronger than B by adding char n-grams to NB-LogReg, but it is highly correlated with B and equal blending still retains weaker A, so expect only a small mean-AUC gain.

The two branches are highly correlated and the 0.5/0.5 rank blend is already near-optimal; holdout-fitted per-label weights shrunk halfway toward 0.5 can only nudge the blend slightly, and weight-estimation noise on rare labels (threat, identity_hate) cancels most of any gain, so expect a change within noise of the baseline.

Compressing to 300 LSA factors and dropping the char n-gram branch and NB weighting discards most of the discriminative signal (misspellings/obfuscated slurs, rare bigrams) that the sparse linear models exploit; LSA+logreg typically lands ~0.955-0.96 on this task versus ~0.98 for the strong TF-IDF ensemble, and the loss is worst on the rare labels that dominate the column-mean noise.
Keeping all positives with a 10:1 negative cap mainly shifts class priors/intercepts while preserving ranking signal, so AUC should be nearly flat with a tiny gain from less-skewed fits.

The single softmax fastText makes the six independent labels mutually exclusive, lets the dominant clean class absorb mass, and dilutes rare/co-occurring labels, so branch F degrades while branches A/B limit the overall drop.

ComplementNB on raw counts is a solid single model but its per-label AUC ordering is consistently weaker than TF-IDF logistic regression (especially on rare labels like threat), and dropping the three-branch rank ensemble removes genuine diversity gains, so expect roughly a 0.01 AUC regression.

Mean-pooled from-scratch Word2Vec (200d) with a linear head is a well-documented mid-0.95 AUC approach on this dataset — it discards the exact-token and char n-gram signal that drives the 0.9816 sparse ensemble, and the rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) lose the most when 260k sparse features collapse into 200 smooth dimensions trained on only ~20M tokens.

Average-pooled corpus-trained Word2Vec + logistic is a well-known weaker baseline for this competition (~0.96-0.97): mean pooling discards term frequency and word order, and 200d CBOW embeddings trained on this modest corpus capture far less discriminative signal than NB-weighted 200k-dim TF-IDF bigrams plus char n-grams, so it should regress meaningfully from the 0.9799 sparse-linear blend.

The char-level NB-LogReg should add modest complementary signal for obfuscated toxicity and the simplex can downweight it if unhelpful, but 10%-holdout tuning and rare-label noise cap the gain to a small improvement.

C=0.1 over-regularized the 60k-feature sparse model; C=4/liblinear is the canonical setting for this exact word+char TF-IDF setup in public kernels (~0.985 standalone), so branch A improves substantially and the 0.5/0.5 rank blend with branch B lifts roughly half that gap, gaining ~0.004 AUC.
fastText is likely a bit weaker than the tuned TF-IDF branches but architecturally diverse, so an equal rank blend should add a small AUC gain while rare-label noise keeps it modest.

The char-NB branch adds a mostly complementary view, but it is correlated with the existing char/word TF-IDF branches and the equal 1/3 rank blend dilutes A/B, so expect only a small mean-AUC gain if it finishes within budget.

Per-label blend tuning on a 16k holdout gains very little (branches are similarly strong and weights land near 0.5, with noisy selection on rare labels threat/identity_hate that have only ~48/140 holdout positives), while dropping the 100% refit means both branches train on 10% less data — a small systematic AUC loss that likely just outweighs the tuning gain for a near-neutral-to-slightly-negative net.

NB log-count-ratio weighting is a well-known boost for linear TF-IDF models (it's exactly what makes branch B strong), and should help branch A's word features and likely the char n-grams too, though the fixed low C=0.1 limits the gain; expect a modest improvement in the rank-averaged blend to ~0.981.

A 0.01 min_df requires roughly 3,128 documents, aggressively removing lower-frequency toxic terms and n-grams—especially signals for rare labels—so underfitting should outweigh any regularization benefit.

Per-label balanced undersampling drastically shrinks the fitting set (especially for rare labels like threat/identity_hate, where only ~2x positives remain), losing negative-class information and degrading ranking quality slightly; AUC is fairly robust to class-reweighting so the drop should be small (~0.002 AUC), though rare-label noise makes the exact number uncertain.
Cosine/Rocchio centroids keep obvious lexical signal but lose the discriminative reweighting and rare-label context handling of the logistic/NB-logreg models, so mean AUC should regress modestly.

char_wb restricts n-grams to within-word boundaries (no cross-word noise) and matches the setup used in the classic high-scoring kernels for this competition, so branch A should improve slightly; since it's blended 50/50 with unchanged branch B, expect a small net gain of roughly +0.0005-0.001 AUC.
ComplementNB retains strong lexical ranking but loses the discriminative LR/NB-LogReg weighting, so AUC should fall modestly, especially on broader toxic/insult labels.

Crushing 60k TF-IDF features to 32 SVD components destroys most discriminative lexical signal, dropping branch A from ~0.975 to ~0.94 AUC; the 50/50 rank blend with the unchanged fastText branch then lands noticeably below the current 0.9734.

Collapsing all tokens outside a 2k DF vocabulary into one raretoken removes the medium/rare lexical and char-ngram signals that drive toxic, insult, threat and especially identity_hate AUC, so both branches and their rank blend should regress moderately.

Keeping English stop words lets high-frequency function words occupy slots in the 10k-feature cap, displacing some informative rare terms, while adding a few weakly useful tokens like 'you'/'your' — the two effects roughly cancel, giving a negligible, very slightly negative change in mean column-wise AUC.
Raw logit averaging removes the calibration-equalizing rank transform, letting the more extreme NB-LogReg branch dominate ordering and likely costing a small AUC amount.
Switching char_wb to char mainly adds space-crossing n-grams that dilute the fixed 50k char vocabulary, so branch A is roughly flat to very slightly worse and the rank-average halves that impact.

Scratch fastText with no subwords/pretraining, 256-token truncation and only 5 epochs should be weaker than the NB-logreg word-bigram branch, especially on rare labels, so the equal rank blend with the unchanged TF-IDF branch drops modestly despite some diversity.

Only the LR half of the 50/50 blend changes; keeping the top 128 ANOVA features should remove mostly redundant low-F histogram bins and slightly reduce LR variance while the NN/TTA path stays essentially unchanged, so I expect a very small gain rather than a large shift.
Label smoothing should modestly reduce the tiny-data CNN's overconfident errors; because the CNN is blended 50/50 with unchanged logistic regression, the overall gain should be small.

With only 10 samples per class, joint multinomial softmax shares statistical strength across classes and produces better-calibrated probabilities for log loss; OvR's independent binary fits yield less calibrated, noisier scores that the simple power/floor calibration only partially repairs, so a modest regression (~10-15%) over the strong 0.045 baseline is expected.

The bagged MLP should add modest nonlinear diversity to an already strong LR model, while the CV w=0 fallback and coarse blend grid limit downside; expect a small log-loss gain rather than a large shift.

Averaging the five validated fold models should keep almost all of the full-data signal while smoothing overconfident high-C probabilities, giving a small log-loss gain rather than a meaningful regression.

Adding complementary geometric descriptors (size, aspect ratio, Hu moments, compactness) to the 192 pre-extracted features with CV-tuned regularisation typically gives a modest log-loss gain on this dataset, with per-fold scaling and C-selection containing overfitting risk.

PCA-95 should mostly discard redundant/noisy histogram-contour directions while leaving the discriminative high-variance structure intact, giving a small denoising gain for the fixed-C logistic model.

Averaging 5 stratified-fold logistic regressions is classic CV bagging: each fold model sees 80% of data (slightly weaker individually than the full fit), but probability averaging reduces variance on a 99-class problem with only 10 samples/class, typically yielding a small (~1-3%) log-loss improvement over a single full-data fit.

The NN's feature branch (MLP on the 192 descriptors) plus silhouette CNN with rotation TTA should reach ~0.15-0.25 holdout log loss, and a 50/50 arithmetic blend of two decorrelated models both better than ~0.25 typically beats the 0.124 LR baseline by 10-25%, landing near 0.09-0.11.

Post-hoc power/temperature calibration fitted on OOF predictions typically gives a small but real log-loss gain for an already reasonably-calibrated logistic regression (sharpening plus a uniform floor reduces overconfident errors); LR's baseline calibration limits the upside to roughly 2-4%, and the OOF-vs-full-fit confidence mismatch is minor at 990 samples.

CV over the C grid on this small 990x192 dataset with 10 samples/class typically selects a much larger C (weakly regularized multinomial logit is near-optimal for these clean descriptors), cutting log loss from ~0.124 to roughly 0.05-0.07; procedure matches the spec and easily fits the time budget.

Geometric image descriptors (Hu moments, solidity, eccentricity, etc.) carry real species-discriminative signal complementary to the precomputed shape/margin/texture vectors, so logreg on the augmented standardized matrix should improve modestly, though gains are limited by the untuned C=1.0 linear model and potential noise/scale mismatch in the new features.
Stronger L2 shrinkage should reduce overfitting and overconfident errors in this 990-row, 99-class problem with correlated features, yielding a modest log-loss improvement.

Dropping the full-data refit means the submitted model trains on only 80% of the data (8 vs 10 samples per species), which with 99 classes and 240 features measurably hurts a logistic regression's calibration, so log loss regresses modestly despite the 'validated model' rationale.

The ensemble keeps the same strong LR as a component and learns leakage-free OOF weights, so it should mostly retain LR with small LDA/kNN contributions for a modest calibration/variance gain, limited by correlated linear models and coarse kNN probabilities.

HistGradientBoosting on only ~990 samples with 99 classes overfits and emits overconfident, peaky probabilities; trees are known to badly underperform well-regularized multinomial logistic regression on this small dense-descriptor leaf dataset, so log loss will rise sharply from ~0.061 to roughly 0.4-0.6.

The calibrated linear SVM should have similar classification strength to logistic regression, but its cross-validated Platt probabilities are likely somewhat less accurate for multi-class log loss, slightly weakening the soft-voting ensemble.

RF vote-fraction probabilities are coarser and less calibrated than HGB's soft log-loss outputs, so swapping one of four uniformly-weighted members likely causes a small log-loss regression, partly offset by freeing the tiny early-stopping split.

With only ~10 training leaves per species, a 95k-parameter sklearn MLP plus tiny noisy early-stopping validation is likely to overfit/be overconfident versus the linear model, and OOF uniform shrinkage only partly repairs the log loss.
Cross-validating C should select a slightly better regularization level than the fixed C=1.0 and improve probability calibration modestly, with little runtime or pipeline risk.

The 48 classical CV features (Hu moments, contour scalars, radial histogram) are largely redundant with the provided shape/margin/texture descriptors but add some complementary global shape signal; with standardization and L2-regularized multinomial logistic regression on only 1584 samples, this typically yields a small log-loss gain rather than overfitting, while the unrelated mlflow/psutil additions are inert.

CV-tuning C over a wide grid with proper stratified folds typically finds better regularization than the untuned C=1.0 on this small 990x192 dataset, giving a solid log-loss improvement at negligible runtime cost.
Soft probability averaging should keep the strong LR/LDA signals while KNN/HGB add enough nonlinear diversity to fix some confusable species, though the weaker HGB/KNN limit the gain.
OOF validation should select a small shrinkage that mitigates rare severely overconfident mistakes, with only a modest penalty on well-classified samples.

Fixed 90% shrinkage toward identity discards genuine correlation structure among the 192 correlated histogram descriptors (only ~10 samples per class), whereas Ledoit-Wolf 'auto' typically adapts to a less extreme value, so expect a modest regression in log loss.

Each 64-dim family LDA is well-conditioned with 990 samples, and equal-weight probability averaging of three complementary, decorrelated views typically reduces variance and overconfident errors relative to a single joint LDA, yielding a modest log-loss improvement despite losing cross-family covariance.

PCA at 90% variance discards some discriminative signal while lbfgs LR with tuned C already handles correlated features well, so dimensionality reduction likely causes a small log-loss regression rather than an improvement.

LDA with shrinkage is a classic strong fit for the 192 correlated Gaussian-like leaf descriptors and consistently beats multinomial logistic regression on this benchmark (typical log loss ~0.02-0.04 vs ~0.06), so expect a large improvement.
PCA(0.95) is unsupervised and may discard or dilute low-variance margin/texture cues for similar species, so the calibrated logistic model should stay close but likely regress slightly.

Shrinkage LDA is a strong classic on these 192 leaf descriptors, but its decision scores are less well-calibrated than tuned logistic regression, and scalar temperature only partially compensates, so expect a modest regression from the 0.0452 baseline.

Mixing in a 0.005 uniform prior barely changes confident correct predictions (log penalty ~0.005) but rescues rare near-zero probabilities on wrong cases, so net effect on log loss is a very small improvement, likely well under 1%.
Dropping Nyström landmarks from 512 to 384 modestly lowers kernel rank/capacity and changes the landmark subset, likely blurring a few fine species distinctions despite similar runtime and coverage.
Shrunk LDA should exploit the 192 discriminative descriptors better than fixed-C logistic on 10 samples/class, giving sharper mostly-correct posteriors, with some calibration risk limiting the gain.

Fold-local scaling is equivalent for the final fit, but CV should pick a less-regularized C than 1.0 and sharpen mostly-correct probabilities; the coarse 3-fold search and confusable similar species keep the gain moderate rather than near-zero.

OOF temperature scaling on logistic regression logits typically yields a small log-loss gain (a few percent) by correcting over/under-confidence without changing class rankings; tiny 990-sample data and a single scalar make overfitting risk minimal.

Nyström RBF features give the linear classifier a nonlinear kernel-like representation that typically cuts log loss substantially on this dataset (leaf classification responds well to RBF kernels), with some residual gap due to fixed C=1 and no tuning/ensembling.

The added temporal, request-form, pronoun, reciprocity/gratitude, and threshold/ratio history features are largely complementary to the existing TF-IDF/metadata blocks, with low overfitting risk, so a small AUC gain is most likely.

Random forests handle high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF poorly: with ~8000 mostly-noise features and max_features='sqrt', splits concentrate on weak single-word signals, the ~9 strong numeric features get diluted, and probabilities from tree leaf fractions are coarse and uncalibrated — linear models are the well-established stronger choice for this exact sparse-text regime, so expect a sizable AUC drop from 0.671 to roughly 0.60-0.63.

Random forests handle the 9 numeric features fine but split poorly on 5000 sparse high-cardinality TF-IDF columns (each rare unigram is nearly useless as an axis-aligned split), so the dominant text signal is largely lost; expect holdout/leaderboard AUC to drop well below the 0.748 logistic baseline despite the giver_known indicator and ensemble averaging.
Replacing discriminative TF-IDF unigrams with 50 unsupervised LDA topics loses lexical signal, so the model falls back mostly to requester-history features and AUC should drop moderately.

The supervised OOF logistic-regression text logit is a much stronger predictive signal than 20 unsupervised LDA topic proportions, so replacing it removes most of the text signal; modest gains from topic×metadata interactions won't compensate, yielding a small regression in AUC.
Likely near-neutral to slightly negative: dropping the absolute timestamp removes a little in-window temporal ranking signal, while UTC hour/weekday are noisy and add feature dilution for LightGBM.

The HGB on requester-history/time/text-stat features captures non-linear signals the linear model misses, and rank-averaging with a CV-selected weight is a low-variance blending scheme that typically adds 1-2% AUC on this RAOP dataset, with small risk of regression since w* can fall back to pure LR if the tree adds nothing.

A fully grown forest with sqrt feature sampling will underuse the sparse TF-IDF signal and overfit individual terms, likely losing several AUC points to the regularized linear model despite better nonlinear use of metadata.

Bag-of-subreddits encodes which communities the requester was active in (e.g., prior RAOP/assistance subreddits), a known predictive signal in the Althoff et al. analysis that is complementary to the existing count features; binary IDF-weighted presence should give a modest AUC lift without overfitting given min_df=5.

giver_username_if_known is the classic RAOP leakage feature: it is non-'N/A' almost only for successful requests, so the 0/1 flag identifies a large fraction of test positives with near-perfect precision, letting the logistic model rank those rows at the top and lifting AUC from ~0.66 to ~0.85.

The stack should modestly beat the linear baseline by keeping the TF-IDF text signal while letting LightGBM capture nonlinear requester-history interactions, though gains are limited by the small dataset and compressing text to one OOF logit.

The added dense time, text-statistic, and zero-inflated requester-history features should add complementary signal to TF-IDF/metadata with little overfitting risk; MLflow logging should not affect predictions.

ExtraTrees with sqrt feature sampling will mostly split on noisy sparse TF-IDF, rarely see the nine numerics, and underperform a regularized linear model on high-dimensional text, so AUC likely drops moderately.

Removing the 5k unigram TF-IDF block discards the strongest discriminative text signal for this task; frozen MiniLM embeddings plus 9 behavioral covariates underperform a regularized linear model over sparse word features on ~4.5k short documents, so AUC likely drops several points despite the variance-reduction rationale.

Document-level length, gratitude/please flags, money/link mentions and VADER sentiment are known predictive signals on RAOP that length-normalized TF-IDF misses; appending ~22 scaled dense features to a linear model on 5.7k rows typically adds ~1.5-2 AUC points without overfitting risk.

Dropping TF-IDF text removes the dominant predictive signal in RAOP; the nine requester-history features alone are weak (Althoff's analysis still showed narrative/text factors matter most), so a metadata-only logistic typically lands around 0.60-0.62 AUC, well below the 0.65 text+meta model.
Self-trained averaged Word2Vec likely dilutes rare/title-specific lexical signal that TF-IDF preserves, while metadata and text-stats remain, so expect a modest AUC regression rather than a gain.

Frequent bigrams and a larger TF-IDF vocabulary should recover some phrase-level signal, but gains stay modest because C=0.3 and the existing engineered phrase statistics already capture part of that signal.

On RAOP the requester-history features (account age, RAOP activity, karma, subreddit breadth) carry most of the stable signal, while TF-IDF+SVD text adds variance and generalizes poorly across the 2010-2013 split; dropping it typically yields a modest AUC gain for metadata-only GBMs (~0.64-0.67).

Random forests on dense SVD-reduced TF-IDF features typically underperform a tuned LightGBM on small noisy tabular data like RAOP; expect a modest AUC regression of roughly 0.01-0.02, though the model family swap should still land in the low 0.60s and easily fits the time budget.

MiniLM sentence embeddings add complementary semantic signal to unigram TF-IDF on this small text dataset, typically yielding a modest AUC gain for logistic regression, though the dense scaled 384-dim block limits the upside.

Adding bigrams, lowering min_df to 2, expanding to 100k features, and unicode accent stripping enriches the dominant text signal on RAOP; logistic regression on sparse TF-IDF handles the wider vocabulary well, typically adding 1-2% AUC over a unigram/5k baseline despite untuned C.
The added length/readability/lexicon features are low-risk and partly orthogonal to unigram TF-IDF plus requester history, so they should give a small AUC lift under L2 regularization.

SVD-300 preserves most TF-IDF signal and LightGBM can exploit nonlinear interactions with the numeric history features, typically giving a small AUC gain over plain logistic regression on this dataset, though CV-based early stopping on ~4.5k samples adds some variance.

Swapping an 8-column quantile spline (which captures the multi-year trend in success rates) for 2 annual Fourier features loses trend information while adding only weak seasonality; with 5000 TF-IDF features dominating, the effect is small and likely slightly negative.
Weaker L2 regularization should let informative TF-IDF terms contribute more strongly, producing a modest AUC gain despite some increased overfitting risk.

Timestamp carries a modest known signal in RAOP (success rates drifted over the 2010-2013 collection window), and a smooth quantile-spline encoding lets the linear model capture that drift with little overfitting risk, so a small AUC gain is expected.

Distance-weighted kNN with cosine metric on ~7k-dim sparse TF-IDF features suffers from curse-of-dimensionality and noisy neighbors on this small imbalanced dataset, typically scoring well below a regularized linear model on RAOP (kNN baselines land around 0.55-0.60 AUC vs 0.65 for logistic regression).

KNN on 9 metadata features is a weaker learner than CatBoost for this small tabular signal (curse of dimensionality, no feature weighting, smooth probability averaging), so its half of the 50/50 blend drags the combined AUC down modestly from 0.645.
Weaker L2 should let normalized TF-IDF lexical signal contribute against the scaled metadata, giving a small blend AUC gain despite some overfitting risk.
Absolute request date likely has only a weak smooth trend after text/history features, and the few regularized spline columns should give a tiny AUC bump with minimal overfit risk.
BernoulliNB binarizes away TF-IDF magnitudes and continuous requester-history signal, so ranking should regress modestly versus regularized logistic despite remaining usable presence cues.
The absolute-date spline is a weak temporal/base-rate signal added to an already regularized linear model, so it should move rankings only slightly with a tiny positive gain.

Adding binary subreddit-participation features (a known informative signal from the RAOP paper) with L2-regularized logistic regression should give a modest AUC lift; the removed holdout split doesn't affect the final full-data fit, and MLflow instrumentation is functionally inert.

CatBoost on the nine history features should add a small nonlinear metadata signal mostly complementary to the text-dominated logistic model, but the fixed 50/50 blend and weak metadata keep the gain modest.

Adding bigrams typically gives a small AUC bump on this RAOP TF-IDF+LR setup, but the shared 5000-feature budget (truncated by raw term frequency) dilutes unigram coverage, capping the gain; the tracking/holdout-removal changes don't affect predictions.
Author attribution is a stylometry task where function/stop words are strong style signals; removing them from the word view slightly degrades log loss despite redundancy with char_wb n-grams.

Stacking the TF-IDF LR with two diverse multinomial NB models (word and char counts) via a log-linear meta-learner on log-OOF probabilities is the classic winning recipe for this competition; NB adds complementary signal to LR, and the geometric-blend meta-model typically cuts log loss by ~5-8% over the single LR baseline.
Stop-word removal should mostly strip redundant/downweighted function-word mass from the word models while char and meta features still preserve style, giving the stack a small net gain.

Level 1 is unchanged, and a strongly regularized linear combiner over already-informative OOF probabilities should be a bit better calibrated and less fold-noise-driven than the LightGBM stacker, giving only a small gain.

Punctuation usage (Poe's dashes/semicolons, Lovecraft's comma-heavy clauses, fragment-ending marks) is genuinely author-discriminative in this corpus, so stripping it removes real stylistic signal from the case-sensitive char block; the word block is nearly unaffected and the vocabulary-shrinkage regularization benefit is small, yielding a modest net regression in log loss.

OOF stacking of word/char LR (C=10) plus tuned word/char MultinomialNB with a log-prob LR meta-learner is a well-known recipe on Spooky Author; diversity from NB and stronger regularization tuning typically cuts log loss from ~0.44 to ~0.40, with the 10-minute budget comfortably met by parallel folds.

L2-regularized LR on 130k TF-IDF features already handles the high dimensionality well with ~19.6k examples; chi2 selection to 10k mostly keeps frequent word n-grams and discards many individually weak but collectively useful char n-grams, slightly hurting LR calibration, and the re-tuned NB blend only partly compensates, so expect a small regression (within noise, roughly 0.360–0.366).

Function words are useful authorship-style signals here, so removing them from word TF-IDF/counts likely hurts NB and slightly hurts LR despite the intact char block; blending can only partly compensate.
Cross-validation is likely to select a moderately larger C (around 3–10), yielding a modest gain in fit and probability calibration over C=1 while remaining within the runtime budget.
Diverse OOF word/char LR+NB predictions plus stylometric meta-features should beat the single C=1 LR, but the weaker NB/meta signals cap the gain at a modest log-loss improvement.

Cross-boundary char n-grams plus preserved capitalization add strong author-style signals (punctuation-in-context, casing habits) that char_wb misses, and the extra ~300k sparse features are well within LR's capacity and the time budget, so a modest log-loss gain is expected.

MultinomialNB on count n-grams is a strong, decorrelated model for this classic competition; an OOF-selected arithmetic blend with the TF-IDF LR (which can fall back to w=1.0 if NB is poor) typically drops log loss from ~0.43 to ~0.39-0.40, a 6-9% improvement.

Stopword removal discards function-word usage which is itself a strong author-style signal and breaks many informative word-bigrams, so fastText likely loses discriminative features and log loss worsens slightly.

Class imbalance is mild (40/31/28), so oversampling only slightly reweights priors; fastText softmax probabilities shift marginally toward minority classes, yielding a small net effect likely near-neutral to slightly positive on log loss.

ComplementNB on word/char TF-IDF is a strong, well-calibrated complement to LR for this dataset (classic winning-ensemble component), and the OOF-selected convex weight will fall back to w~1 if NB adds nothing, so expect a modest log-loss gain with little downside risk.

Tuned MultinomialNB should run quickly, but its independence assumptions and less-calibrated probabilities on high-dimensional TF-IDF features typically yield substantially worse log loss than tuned logistic regression.
Dropping char_wb n-grams removes useful author-specific morphology/stylometric signal, so the word-only NB-SVM should be a modest log-loss regression despite lower runtime.

ComplementNB is a solid text classifier but produces overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities compared to the ratio-weighted logistic NB-SVM head, so log loss typically degrades substantially (from ~0.41 toward ~0.50) on this dataset.

CV-selecting C directly on log loss typically finds a better regularization point (often C~3-10) than the arbitrary C=1.0 for this TF-IDF+LR setup, yielding a modest improvement of roughly 0.005-0.015 in log loss; the MLflow additions are telemetry-only and don't affect the metric.

MultinomialNB on sparse TF-IDF/char n-grams usually keeps decent accuracy but is overconfident and miscalibrated under log loss, so confident EAP/MWS mistakes should raise log loss versus the tuned linear LR baseline.

fastText's softmax probabilities are poorly calibrated and its bag-of-ngram model underperforms tuned TF-IDF + logistic regression on this small sentence-level task; known fastText results on Spooky Author are typically ~0.5-0.6 log loss vs ~0.43 for the current pipeline, with the 1e-6 fill for missing classes adding further loss.

5-fold CV selection of C over a sensible grid typically picks a slightly stronger/weaker regularization than the default C=1.0 (often C=2-4 helps this TF-IDF+LR setup), yielding a small but real improvement over the hard-coded baseline; the parallelization and mlflow additions don't change the predictions.

NB count-ratio weighting plus C=4 one-vs-rest should exploit author/style cues better than plain multinomial TF-IDF LR, with moderate gain because independent probabilities are renormalized rather than jointly calibrated.

Scaled stylometric features (punctuation density, word-length stats) carry genuine author signal for Poe/Lovecraft/Shelley and are a standard small boost to TF-IDF+LR; with only 14 MaxAbs-scaled columns vs ~100k TF-IDF dims the effect is modest but positive, roughly a 1% log-loss reduction.

NB-log-ratio feature weighting with OVR liblinear logistic (the classic NBSVM trick) is a well-documented improvement over plain multiclass LR on this TF-IDF setup, typically cutting log loss from ~0.44 to ~0.36-0.38 on Spooky Author Identification.
C=0.25 adds moderate L2 shrinkage on sparse word/char n-grams, likely reducing overconfident mistakes and improving log loss slightly without runtime risk.

Char_wb (2,5) TF-IDF alone retains substantial style signal (affixes, punctuation, word-boundary fragments), but dropping the word unigram/bigram block removes the strongest discriminative signal (author-specific vocabulary like Lovecraft's archaisms and Poe's lexical tics), so NB-logistic log loss should regress moderately from 0.518 to roughly 0.57-0.59.

The NB-ratio feature reweighting is a weak heuristic on this data; plain one-vs-rest logistic regression on word+char TF-IDF is the well-established strong baseline for Spooky Author (typically ~0.40 log loss), so removing the ratio scaling should improve substantially over the current 0.518.
C=4 to C=2 slightly strengthens L2 in a p>>n TF-IDF logistic model, likely improving calibration/logloss a bit; added telemetry is metric-neutral.

NB log-ratio weighting is a strong text prior that should emphasize author-indicative word/char n-grams over plain TF-IDF logistic regression, while normalized OvR logistic probabilities remain usable for log loss, so expect a solid but not SOTA improvement.
Function words (stop words) are among the strongest stylistic signals for authorship attribution; deleting them degrades both word n-gram and char_wb features, so log loss should regress moderately.
Stronger L2 should slightly reduce variance from correlated sparse n-grams while temperature rescaling preserves confidence, yielding a near-neutral to tiny log-loss gain.

Switching char_wb to char lets n-grams span word boundaries, which typically adds noise for author-attribution TF-IDF models on this dataset; expect a small regression in log loss while the rest of the pipeline (unchanged refit-on-all behavior) keeps the score close to 0.432.

NB log-ratio feature weighting with one-vs-rest logistic usually improves discrimination for short author-styled text, though independent OvR probabilities are a bit less calibrated than the multinomial softmax, so the gain should be modest rather than dramatic.
Reducing L2 regularization from C=1 to C=4 should let discriminative word/char n-grams contribute more, giving a modest log-loss gain with limited overconfidence risk.
One-parameter temperature calibration on a stratified holdout should slightly improve log loss for a somewhat miscalibrated TF-IDF logistic model, with limited risk and only small refit mismatch.

Log1p target with LightGBM typically gives a small RMSE gain on skewed fare data (trees fit the bulk better, less tail-dominated gradients), though the expm1 inverse adds slight bias and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows dilutes any gain, so expect roughly 1% improvement.

Quadrupling training data from 1M to 4M rows reduces model variance with unchanged features and hyperparameters, yielding a modest but real RMSE improvement (early stopping will use more/all of the 1000 trees on the larger sample); the mlflow logging and n_jobs/datetime tweaks only affect wall-clock, not predictions.

Airport-proximity features are a well-known strong signal for NYC taxi fares (JFK flat-fare zone, airport surcharges); six cheap vectorized haversine features let LightGBM carve out airport trips, giving a modest but real RMSE gain with no runtime or leakage risk.
log1p stabilizes the multiplicative fare noise and should help most valid rows slightly, with only a small expm1/Jensen underprediction penalty and little effect on the corrupt-row floor.

The unconstrained ensemble already learns a largely monotone distance response, so the constraint changes little; it only prunes spurious non-monotonic splits in sparse regions, yielding a tiny generalization gain (~0.1-0.3% RMSE) with no runtime cost.

Log1p target reduces the influence of the right-skewed fare tail on squared-error gradients and matches the roughly multiplicative fare structure, typically yielding a small holdout/submission gain for GBDT on this dataset; the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows (mean-fare fallback) caps any improvement, so expect a modest drop from ~4.126 to ~4.09-4.11.

Removing the train/inference mismatch helps slightly, but in-sample encodings leak each training row's own fare into its key statistics, making the TE features look stronger during training than at test time; with m=20 smoothing the effects roughly cancel and likely net to a small regression (~4.21 RMSE vs 4.179).

Log1p fitting optimizes relative/multiplicative error and expm1-backtransformed predictions are biased low (Jensen), underpredicting the heavy right tail of large fares that dominate raw-space RMSE, so the graded RMSE likely degrades slightly; effects are modest since features, cleaning, and the invalid-row mean-fare rule are unchanged.

Airport-distance features are a well-known, reliable win for this dataset (JFK flat-rate and EWR surcharge trips become easy to isolate), and LightGBM can exploit them immediately with unchanged hyperparameters; expect a modest but real RMSE gain, limited by the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor in the graded test set.

On the ~2.8% corrupt test rows, LightGBM now predicts the conditional mean of the matching corrupt training population given hour/weekday/year/passenger_count instead of the valid-row global mean, which is strictly closer to the MSE-optimal prediction and shaves a little off the ~2.1 RMSE floor; valid-row predictions are essentially unchanged, so only a small overall gain.
Quadrupling the clean sample should modestly reduce variance and use more boosting iterations, but identical features/hyperparameters and the corrupt-row RMSE floor cap the gain.
Leakage-safe route/cell fare means should add toll/airport signal and trim a few tenths of RMSE, though the corrupt-row floor limits the overall gain.

Log1p training optimizes log-space RMSE, so back-transformed predictions approximate the conditional geometric mean and systematically underpredict the high fares that dominate dollar-space RMSE (Jensen bias, no correction applied); the variance-stabilization benefit on the mild, $500-capped skew doesn't offset this, giving a small regression of roughly 1%.

Manhattan distance and bearing add genuine signal beyond haversine (grid-aligned travel and direction-dependent tolls) and LightGBM exploits them well, but they are partially redundant with the raw coordinates and existing distance, so expect only a modest ~1-2% RMSE improvement; runtime impact is negligible.

Distance-to-airport/Manhattan features let the trees carve out flat-fare JFK trips and airport pricing regimes that raw coordinates capture poorly; this is a well-known effective feature for this competition and typically yields a solid single-digit RMSE gain, though the ~2.8% corrupt-test-row floor (~2.1 RMSE) caps total improvement.

L1 is robust to the heavy fare tail but targets conditional medians while grading is RMSE; after the existing fare/coordinate cleaning and with large leaf samples, this metric-objective mismatch likely causes a small RMSE regression rather than a gain.

Log1p training optimizes relative/log-space error and expm1 gives a median-like, slightly low prediction on the raw RMSE metric; with invalid-row fallback unchanged this likely causes a small regression rather than a gain.

L1/MAE training is misaligned with RMSE and tends to fit the conditional median, underpredicting the right-skewed legitimate high fares; robustness to a few bad labels likely does not offset that bias.
Huber with delta=1 is too median-like for dollar fares and mismatches the RMSE objective, likely underpredicting large/noisy fares that also appear in the graded sample, causing a slight regression.

Log-target training optimizes a different loss than raw-dollar RMSE and the expm1 back-transform is biased low (geometric vs arithmetic mean), systematically underpredicting expensive rides; with no bias correction this typically costs ~1% on raw RMSE despite the nicer target distribution.

Airport distance/flag features are a well-known strong signal for this dataset (JFK flat fares, LGA/EWR surcharges), and LightGBM can exploit them directly; they should cut error on the ~97% valid rows substantially (roughly 3.6→3.45 RMSE there), while the ~2.8% corrupt test rows impose an irreducible floor, capping the overall gain at a few percent.

Quadrupling the training sample from 1M to 4M rows lets LightGBM fit the fare surface more finely (especially with 63 leaves and min_child_samples=100), which on this dataset typically buys a few percent RMSE improvement, comfortably within the 10-minute budget for 10 histogram features.
5-fold averaging should reduce model variance slightly with identical features/hparams, but the fixed corrupt-row floor and highly correlated fold models cap the gain.

Leak-free smoothed pickup-cell fare should add a modest location prior beyond raw coordinates/distance, but ~100m cells are sparse in 1M rows and invalid test rows are unchanged, so expect only a small RMSE gain.

Snapping coordinates to a 0.01-degree (~1 km) grid destroys fine-grained distance and location precision that the GBM relies on for short/medium trips; the route-encoding pooling benefit doesn't compensate, so RMSE regresses moderately.

RMSE rewards the conditional mean, while L1/MAE is more median-leaning and can underpredict skewed high fares; RMSE early stopping limits damage, so expect a small regression rather than a robustness win.

L1 loss fits conditional medians, which is slightly misaligned with the RMSE metric; robustness to surviving outlier fares may offset some of that, so expect a small net regression of a few tenths of a percent.

Airport-distance features are among the highest-value known features for NYC taxi fare prediction (JFK flat-fare trips and airport surcharges); LightGBM can exploit them well, giving a solid but not dramatic RMSE improvement over the 4.137 baseline on the same 1M-row sample.
L1/conditional-median training underpredicts the right-skewed high-fare tail and fits large errors slower at the same learning rate, so RMSE should modestly worsen despite early stopping on RMSE.

Rounding coordinates to a ~1 km grid discards fine-grained pickup/dropoff location signal that LightGBM exploits for fare variation within neighborhoods; the unrounded haversine distance preserves trip length, so the regression should be small but real (well under 1%).

L1 (median) objective typically degrades RMSE vs L2 (mean) objective since RMSE rewards conditional means; fares are right-skewed so median-targeted predictions are biased slightly low, though the corrupt-row RMSE floor limits the damage.
The rotated L1 grid distance is a physically relevant NYC street-distance proxy that should complement haversine slightly, giving a small RMSE gain with negligible runtime risk.

Conservative OOF-smoothed directional route means should help common/airport OD pairs, but 0.01-degree routes are sparse with 1M rows and the corrupt-row fallback leaves a hard RMSE floor, so expect only a modest gain.

A Manhattan-grid distance rotated 29° (NYC street orientation) adds genuinely useful geometric signal beyond haversine for fare prediction, so LightGBM should gain modestly, though correlation with the existing distance feature and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows cap the improvement; the MLflow logging additions are best-effort wrapped and shouldn't affect the run within budget.

Doubling the training sample from 1M to 2M rows (same pipeline, still well within the time budget) reduces model variance and typically yields a modest RMSE gain of ~1.5-2.5%, though the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows limits the overall improvement.

Airport-route is a well-known strong signal in this dataset (JFK flat-fare trips and airport surcharges), and encoding it as a LightGBM categorical should capture the fare premium without hurting other splits; expect a modest but real RMSE drop of roughly 2% from 4.138.

LightGBM on raw features + per-char f_27 is the well-known baseline for TPS May 2022 and plateaus around 0.972-0.975 AUC, while the tuned SiLU MLP at 0.9866 exploits the smooth feature interactions better; declaring the letter columns categorical helps slightly but won't close the gap, so this is a regression.

Quantile one-hot should modestly help by giving integer/count features exact categorical embeddings, robustifying heavy-tailed numerics, and easing nonmonotone threshold learning, while 10-bin coarseness and unchanged f_27 encoding cap the gain.

Full-rank PCA preserves information, but after standardization the unsupervised whitening likely rotates away from the meaningful raw axes and amplifies low-variance/noise directions, giving little extra conditioning benefit for linear leaves and a small AUC regression.

The ten positional character features carry most of f_27's signal, while the nearly unique complete strings make the smoothed target encoding collapse toward the prior and leave an approximately numerics-only model.

Full-string target encoding is likely too sparse/high-cardinality and only captures marginal string effects, while dropping the ten positional character columns removes interaction information LightGBM was using, so I expect a mild AUC regression.

The explicit additive sums give LightGBM direct access to important diagonal interactions that are awkward to approximate with axis-aligned splits, while the threshold indicators should add a smaller secondary gain.
The logistic model is much weaker on the interaction-heavy/f_27 structure, so an equal 50% rank blend likely drags the strong LightGBM ranking down slightly despite added diversity.

The scaled/checkpointed MLP should be trainable and competitive, but ordinal per-character f_27 and lack of tree-style interaction splitting should underperform the tuned LightGBM baseline by roughly 1%.
A small ordinal-encoded MLP on raw tabular features should underfit the interactions and categorical structure that LightGBM exploits, despite enough epochs to converge.

Linear leaves add high per-leaf variance with tiny linear_lambda, extrapolate poorly on heavy-tailed f_28, and impose meaningless linear trends on ordinal f_27 codes, likely offsetting any oblique-boundary gain.
The unique-letter count of f_27 is a known weakly informative aggregate for this dataset; LightGBM can partially infer it from the 10 per-char columns, so expect only a tiny AUC bump (~+0.0001).

These three sums are the known planted additive interactions in TPS May 2022; giving axis-aligned trees the exact diagonal boundary directions provides a real but modest AUC gain (~+0.002), since deep trees could already approximate them imperfectly.

f_27 is a ~10-char string with near-row-level cardinality, so native categorical splits mostly memorize training strings with no holdout/test overlap (26^10 space) while discarding the positional letter signal that drives this dataset; the model effectively falls back to numeric + letter-count features, losing several AUC points and risking a slow high-cardinality categorical build.

Adjacent-character bigrams add a modest amount of f_27 sequence signal beyond unigrams/counts, while 676-way native categorical features are feasible for LightGBM at 800k rows, so I expect a small AUC gain rather than a large jump.

Linear PCA rotations add almost nothing to axis-aligned trees that already see the raw f_00..f_15, while the mined pairwise products encode nonlinear interactions trees cannot easily split out, so swapping products for PCs likely loses most of the small gain the products provided, landing near the raw-feature baseline.

The per-position ordinal encoding of f_27 preserves character identity at each of the 10 positions, which is highly informative in this dataset (interactions with f_27 characters are a known signal); hashing whole strings into 64 buckets destroys positional structure and merges distinct codes into ~64 colliding groups, so LightGBM loses most of the f_27 signal, costing roughly 1.5-2 AUC points.

ExtraTrees with random split thresholds cannot exploit the additive feature interactions in this synthetic dataset nearly as well as gradient boosting, and known TPS-May-2022 results put bagged/tree ensembles ~0.02-0.04 AUC below tuned LightGBM; the run should finish in budget since the CV fits are concurrency-capped, but the model swap itself is a clear regression.

An sklearn MLP (256,128) with adam and constant LR on the same per-char ordinal features typically lands just below tuned LightGBM on this dataset (~0.973-0.977) — it can learn multiplicative interactions but optimizes less sharply than GBDT with ordinal-encoded characters and heavy-tailed f_28, so a small regression from 0.9781 is most likely.

Order-invariant letter-count and distinct-character features expose aggregate f_27 information that is difficult for position-wise categorical splits to reconstruct, likely yielding a modest AUC gain without materially affecting runtime.

The full 10-character f_27 sequence is extremely high-cardinality, so its frequency is nearly constant and discards the useful per-position letter signal, effectively leaving a mostly numeric-feature model.

Letter-frequency counts and unique-char count of f_27 are well-known informative features for TPS May 2022 (the string encodes interaction structure beyond per-position identity), so they should give a small but real AUC gain over the 0.97696 baseline while keeping runtime essentially unchanged.

TPS May 2022 is known to contain real multiplicative feature interactions, and gain-ranked screening on 150k rows reliably surfaces the strongest ones; adding 25 such product features to the unchanged LightGBM pipeline should give a small but real AUC lift (~+0.001), limited by the fact that deep trees already capture some interactions.

Refitting on all 800k rows with rounds scaled to 3333 (early stopping never fires, best_iter=3000) adds ~11% more training signal; the mild overfitting risk of no eval_set is offset by more data, typically yielding a small AUC gain of ~0.0002-0.0005.

Declaring the ten f_27 per-position codes as categorical lets LightGBM use many-vs-rest partitions instead of threshold splits on meaningless alphabetical order; with 26 categories (below max_cat_threshold=32) this typically yields a small but real AUC gain (~0.001) on this dataset, with comparable runtime.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is a known informative aggregate for this competition (the label depends on character-level patterns in f_27), and adding it as one extra column to a tree model that already sees per-position ordinals gives a small but real lift with negligible risk of harm or runtime impact.

TPS May 2022 is dominated by higher-order feature interactions; max_depth=2 caps each tree at pairwise interactions and boosting is additive so it cannot recover them, causing a large AUC drop from 0.982 to roughly 0.90.

The CPU MLP's 0.9822 is unusually strong for this dataset (it learns the f_27 and numeric interactions well); a modestly-configured LightGBM (num_leaves=31, max_bin=63, 600 trees) without feature engineering typically lands around 0.970-0.975 on TPS May 2022, so the swap is likely a small regression.

LightGBM gbdt with default-ish params (31 leaves, max_bin 63, no subsampling, 600 iters) on raw numerics + per-char ordinals is a solid fit for this threshold/interaction-heavy synthetic data but slightly weaker than the tuned 0.9822 MLP; expect a small regression to ~0.980 within the time budget.

Coarse quartile coding throws away within-bin continuous information that LightGBM’s finer histogram splits were exploiting, so with an already underfit/high-capacity baseline AUC should regress modestly despite intact f_27 and integer features.

Dropping num_leaves from 127 to 7 restricts each tree to ~depth-3 interactions; since this dataset's signal lives in higher-order feature interactions (especially f_27 character combinations), 3000 shallow trees will underfit relative to the baseline, costing roughly 1.5-2 AUC points.

num_leaves=4 forces near-stump trees that cannot capture the deep feature/f_27 character interactions driving this dataset's signal, so despite 3000 boosting rounds the model underfits severely and AUC drops substantially from 0.9915.

A single linear sum of three continuous features is nearly redundant for gradient-boosted trees, which can already approximate additive interactions via splits; it may offer a tiny ranking benefit but any change will be within run-to-run noise of the 0.99147 baseline.

A linear sum of three features already present adds almost no information for axis-aligned GBDT splits; trees can approximate it from the components, so the score will be statistically unchanged (within seed/split noise), at most a negligible wobble around 0.97692.

A time-bounded CPU MLP on scaled numerics plus ordinal f_27 characters should underperform the tuned LightGBM, since trees capture the synthetic threshold/category interactions more efficiently under the same 90/10 protocol.

Treating each nominal character-position code as categorical lets LightGBM partition letters directly rather than relying on arbitrary ordinal thresholds, likely yielding a modest AUC gain within the runtime budget.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is a well-known informative signal for this competition (character repetitions encode state information beyond per-position values), and adding it as one extra feature to an unchanged LightGBM setup should yield a small but real AUC gain.

With ~90% white pixels already predicted near-perfectly, most residual squared error sits on thin strokes/edges; up-weighting dark targets redirects gradient signal there (like oversampling the rare foreground) and the slight loss of background precision costs little, so unweighted RMSE should improve a few percent, though the dark bias on ambiguous stain-vs-text pixels caps the gain.

The wall-clock budget yields roughly 4-5x more optimizer steps (~8-10k vs 2000) with the cosine schedule still annealing LR to ~0, and since the baseline was clearly undertrained (2000 steps in ~1 min), longer training of this small U-Net on abundant random crops should cut RMSE by roughly 10-15% to about 0.014, with minimal timeout risk since CSV writing was already accommodated.

L1 vs L2 on this near-binary denoising task is close to a wash: RMSE is L2-matched which favors MSE, but L1's constant gradients sharpen outputs on confident paper/text pixels and are robust to stain outliers, empirically (EDSR, Zhao et al.) giving a slight RMSE edge even under a squared-error metric; with only 2000 steps and a strong baseline (0.01655), expect a small ~1-2% improvement.
Zero-mean input-only brightness/contrast jitter should mildly regularize gray-level overfitting on the ~100 paired scans while eval stays unmodified; clipping and fixed steps keep the gain small.

Training is unchanged so the delta is purely inferential: the two extra scaled views are individually slightly worse (resampling blur at 0.75x, out-of-distribution stroke widths) but their errors are only partially correlated with the 1.0x view, so equal-weight averaging reduces flat-region/stain variance a bit more than the added edge-blur bias, yielding a small ~1% RMSE gain at negligible time cost.

With only 2000 steps over ~12M distinct crops the baseline is underfit rather than overfit, so p=0.2 channel dropout at the bottleneck mostly slows convergence and adds a BatchNorm/dropout train-eval mismatch, giving a small regression roughly within seed noise.

Dropout2d(p=0.1) after BN in every block of a small MSE-regression U-Net adds gradient noise and a mild train/test variance shift against the frozen BN running stats; with a fixed 180 s training budget this slows convergence slightly and the baseline shows no strong overfitting to correct, so expect a small regression (~2-3%) rather than a gain.

The extra resolution level roughly doubles the receptive field (~41→89px), giving the net enough context to distinguish large faint stains from text, which should outweigh the ~25% step reduction under the fixed 180s wall-clock budget; expect a modest net RMSE improvement.

A 23-px median background channel gives the small U-Net explicit low-frequency stain/shading context its limited receptive field struggles to compute, a well-known help for this task; the diff is implemented correctly (2-ch input, crops/flips, predict path), so expect a solid ~8-12% RMSE improvement within budget.
The deeper U-Net and 256px crops add useful page-level context and reduce crop-boundary mismatch, but the same pixels-per-step and short fixed schedule keep the gain modest.

The U-Net was trained with random h/v flips so it is approximately flip-equivariant; averaging 4 flipped TTA passes reduces prediction variance and typically yields a small but consistent RMSE gain (~1.5-2.5%) with no downside risk.

The wall-clock budget (180s) with an equivalent cosine-to-zero LR schedule should yield roughly as many or somewhat more optimizer steps than the original fixed 2000 on a typical GPU, so convergence is the same or slightly better, giving a near-neutral to small improvement in RMSE.

The score is RMSE and the clean targets have no label outliers, so replacing the matched L2 loss with near-L1 Charbonnier under the same LR/schedule is more likely to slightly hurt RMSE than help despite sharper edges.

Training with extra injected Gaussian noise (σ=0.05, ~3x the baseline RMSE) but inferring on un-augmented test images creates a noise-level mismatch: the learned MMSE denoiser assumes stronger corruption than is present, so it over-smooths/snaps gray antialiasing and faint structures toward the binary prior, and with ~105 large images yielding ~30k+ distinct crops the baseline's overfitting is mild, so the regularization benefit is outweighed by the distribution shift.

GroupNorm removes the crop-vs-full-page running-statistics mismatch (BN stats are also noisy after only 2000 short training steps) and adapts normalization per test page, which should give a small net gain, though most of the effect is likely within seed noise since batch-32 BN was already working reasonably well.
