SSIM+L1 (Zhao et al.) is a well-validated restoration loss that produces sharper, higher-contrast outputs than MSE, which suits near-binary document targets and typically yields a small RMSE gain too, though the benefit is bounded because RMSE is natively matched to L2 and training is short (2000 steps), so expect only a few-percent improvement with some seed noise.

8-fold dihedral TTA averaging is a well-established, near-free variance reduction for image regression; even without rot90 in training augmentation it typically yields a modest (~2%) RMSE gain, and runtime stays trivially within budget.

The evaluation metric is L2/RMSE, and MSE training directly optimizes it (conditional mean); a pure SSIM loss trades absolute-intensity accuracy for structural agreement—Zhao et al. themselves note L2-trained nets still win on PSNR/RMSE while SSIM-trained nets win on SSIM—so expect crisper strokes but slightly biased flat-region intensities, giving a modest ~4-8% RMSE regression.

Residual (DnCNN-style) prediction with a linear, zero-initialized head removes sigmoid saturation on the dominant near-white background and starts from the identity mapping, giving faster, better convergence within the same fixed 2000-step budget — a well-established gain over direct image regression, typically in the 5-10% relative range for this task.

Under Adam the sqrt(MSE) transform is nearly scale-neutral, so the only real effect is the 0.1-weighted SSIM term, which slightly biases optimization away from the MMSE optimum that the RMSE metric rewards; expect a sub-1% regression, well within run noise.

Identity-initialized residual prediction removes sigmoid saturation and lets the U-Net learn sparse noise corrections while preserving the input, so RMSE should drop moderately; clamping limits unbounded-output risk.

With only 105 real training images, adding 804 diverse synthetic corruptions of the same clean targets acts as a strong regularizer and usually improves generalization, though the imperfect hand-crafted noise model (especially full-image blur) and 88% synthetic sampling dilution cap the gain to a few percent.

4.5x more Adam steps with the cosine schedule stretched to match should noticeably improve convergence of this undertrained small U-Net; random 128px crops + flips from 105 images provide enough data variety that overfitting risk at 9k steps is low, so expect a solid but diminishing-returns gain (~8-12% RMSE reduction), with wall-clock still fine since 2k steps was far under budget.

Dihedral-8 TTA is a variance-reduction win for a small patch-CNN denoiser (text scans have no privileged orientation, and transpose inverses are exact), typically shaving ~2-4% off RMSE; inference cost grows 8x but only over 39 full images per epoch plus 29 test images, well within budget.

L1 trains toward the conditional median while RMSE rewards the conditional mean, so the objective is slightly misaligned with the metric; robustness to large stain residuals and constant-gradient pushes toward the near-binary targets partly offset this, but a small net RMSE regression (~2%) is the likeliest outcome with short CPU training and cosine decay limiting late-stage jitter.
The loss change is compute-neutral; upweighting rare dark glyph pixels should reduce stroke/edge errors more than it risks over-darkening easy background, giving a small RMSE gain.
Dark ink/edge pixels likely carry most residual error; normalized target-weighted MSE should recover them while leaving easy background nearly intact, giving a small net RMSE gain.

Residual prediction with zero-initialized output conv starts training from the identity (a strong prior since clean≈noisy for most pixels) and removes the sigmoid's asymptotic saturation that prevents outputting exact 0/1 intensities, typically yielding a solid RMSE gain for denoising within the same fixed step budget.

The evaluation metric is RMSE, which is dominated by large residuals; switching the training objective from MSE to L1 down-weights exactly those large errors, so the L1-trained U-Net should achieve slightly worse RMSE despite similar perceptual quality (typically a few percent regression when train/eval objectives are mismatched this way).

Zero-init residual (identity) output starts training at the noisy-input RMSE instead of sigmoid's ~0.5 saturation, converging much faster within the short 2000-step budget, and inference-time [0,1] clipping replaces the sigmoid's bounding role, so final RMSE improves modestly.

Halving NAFNet width from 16 to 8 quarters capacity (~620k→~155k params); with a fixed 2000-step budget on ample patch data the model is capacity-limited rather than overfit, so denoising quality typically degrades ~0.5-1 dB, i.e. a ~8-10% RMSE regression to roughly 0.0185-0.0195.

Unweighted MSE is exactly the evaluation metric, so the current model already approximates the conditional-mean optimum; reweighting by (3-2y) biases predictions toward black in ambiguous stain/text regions (weighted optimum = mu - 2sigma^2/(3-2mu)), and with ~88% of pixels being white background even small extra background error offsets gains on ink, so expect a modest regression of roughly 1-2%.

The closing-based illumination-normalization channel (I/background) is a strong, well-matched prior for this dataset's stains/wrinkles that the small UNet can exploit immediately with identical crops/flips and no train/test shift, while the same 2,000 updates, loss and capacity mean a modest but real gain rather than a large one.

Only the final 1x1 conv+sigmoid leaves autocast; bf16 quantization of the output contributes <0.001 RMSE on top of 0.0162, so removing it yields at most a ~0.1% improvement — effectively unchanged (and a strict no-op if the run executes on CPU where autocast is already disabled).
Four-view flip TTA should slightly reduce prediction variance and edge artifacts, but flips were already training augmentations so the gain is small.

NAFNet's residual formulation (zero-init scales start as identity), SimpleGate/channel-attention blocks, and LayerNorm make it a stronger and faster-converging denoiser than the plain BN U-Net at the same 2000-step budget, while its 1x1-conv/width-16 design is ~5x cheaper in FLOPs than the baseline U-Net so it comfortably fits the CPU time budget; expect a solid but not dramatic RMSE gain given the very short from-scratch training.

The Stanford Dogs/competition images are ImageNet-1k training images for exactly these 120 synsets, so the fb_in22k_ft_in1k head has effectively been trained on the target label set and distribution; its dog-restricted, temperature-calibrated softmax should be at least as good as the frozen-feature LR, and the holdout-tuned blend (with w=0 as a safe fallback, so downside is ~nil) should cut log loss by roughly 15-25% with only a tiny holdout-overfitting risk from the 77-point grid.

PCA-256 keeps the high-variance directions where ImageNet-supervised ConvNeXt features concentrate breed-discriminative signal, while truncating mostly-noise low-variance components that L2 was already shrinking — a mild denoising/conditioning gain partly offset by losing some fine-grained low-variance cues; with C re-tuned on the same grid the net effect should be a small (~1%) log-loss improvement, roughly within noise of the 0.3096 baseline.

Mixup/CutMix are the core regularizers of the ConvNeXt recipe and typically help fine-grained 120-class fine-tuning; they soften overconfident predictions (well-aligned with log loss, and temperature scaling on clean val recalibrates), so a moderate ~4-6% log-loss improvement is expected despite the short 6-epoch schedule slightly slowing convergence.

With only ~77 images/breed fine-tuning a 28M model end-to-end, the default ImageNet (0.08, 1.0) crop scale adds meaningful regularization and matches the backbone's pretraining augmentation, which should reduce overconfident memorization and modestly improve log loss, though very tight crops inject some label noise so the gain is small rather than dramatic.

ConvNeXt-V2-L (IN-22k→IN-1k, ~89% top-1) is vastly stronger than ResNet-50 V1 (~76%), and since all 120 breeds are ImageNet classes, both its 1000-d log-probs and 1536-d pre-logit features are far more discriminative (~91-93% breed accuracy vs ~85%), which after LR recalibration should cut log loss from ~0.45 to roughly 0.25-0.31; the extended C grid guards against overconfidence, and runtime stays well within budget.

The 1000-d log-softmax block is a deterministic (mostly near-constant, standardization-amplified noise) function of the pooled vector, so dropping it removes collinear/noise dimensions without losing information the linear probe can't already extract — expect a small improvement in log loss, on the order of 0.005-0.01 absolute.

The exact closed-form ridge solve avoids any lbfgs under-convergence at high C on the 2560-d features and gives near-identical decision boundaries to LR, while explicit holdout temperature scaling directly optimizes log-loss calibration (decoupling sharpness from regularization), which should yield a modest log-loss improvement with no runtime risk since feature extraction is unchanged.

PCA to 128 components per block discards low-variance directions that a linear probe on strong frozen features (convnext/CLIP/DINOv2) actually exploits for fine-grained breed discrimination, and L2-tuned LogisticRegression on 10k images was not overfitting badly at 2560-d, so the compression likely costs a small amount of log loss rather than regularizing usefully.

ConvNeXt-Base pretrained on IN-22k and fine-tuned on IN-1k is a far stronger frozen feature extractor than IN1K-V1 ResNet-50 for fine-grained dog breeds (expect ~7-9 points higher linear-probe accuracy), and the matching 224px/0.875-crop transform plus holdout re-selection of C keeps calibration sound, cutting log loss roughly from 0.45 to ~0.33 with no plausible runtime or correctness risks.

Fine-tuning an ImageNet-22k ConvNeXt-Tiny end-to-end (even for only ~6 epochs with flip-TTA and temperature scaling) substantially outperforms frozen ResNet-50 features + logistic regression on this fine-grained task; ~83-87% val accuracy with validation-calibrated probabilities translates to roughly 0.32-0.36 log loss, with the 7-minute guard and OOM fallback keeping the run inside budget.

The 120 breeds are exact ImageNet classes, so the kept fc head's log-softmax injects a strong, well-regularization-friendly signal (trained on ~1300 imgs/class vs the probe's ~77) that a standardized linear probe can exploit with small weights; the pooled block is a superset of that info but L2 limits how well the probe decodes it, so adding head outputs plus proper scaling and holdout C-selection should give a modest but real log-loss gain (roughly 0.45 -> ~0.41).

Replacing ResNet-50-V1 features with L2-normalized concatenated features from ConvNeXt-in22k, OpenAI CLIP ViT-B/16, and DINOv2 ViT-B/14 (all far stronger fine-grained/dog-breed-discriminative encoders) with holdout-tuned C should cut log loss from ~0.45 to ~0.30; implementation (valid timm names, dual transforms, single-pass loader, block-wise normalization) is sound and fits the time budget.

Log loss rewards calibration, and dropping label smoothing 0.1 removes a strong calibration prior while focal loss's focus on hard/confusable examples encourages confident mistakes on ambiguous breeds; focal's vanishing gradient on easy examples only partly offsets overconfidence, so a modest regression is expected.

Dogs are literally an ImageNet subset, so the frozen conv1–layer3 features are already near-optimal; freezing them regularizes a 25M-param model on only ~10k images (better-calibrated probabilities, which log loss rewards) while layer4+fc (~15M params) still provides ample adaptation capacity, so a small improvement over full fine-tuning is likely, and reduced backprop keeps the run well within the time budget.

Horizontal-flip TTA with probability averaging is a well-established, low-risk win for frozen-feature + linear-head pipelines: the mirror view acts as an ensemble member that smooths per-class probabilities, typically shaving ~1.5-3% off multiclass log loss; the NUM_WORKERS=0 change only affects data-loading robustness, not the metric, and the extra test extraction is well within budget.

The augreg ViT-B/16 (in21k->in1k) features are strongly aligned with this task since ImageNet-1k itself contains ~120 dog breeds, while CLIP ViT-B/32 features are coarser (32x32 patches, contrastive generic objective) and known to linear-probe noticeably worse on fine-grained breed recognition (~75-80% vs ~86-88% top-1), so log loss should regress substantially though the run itself will complete fine.

PCA-256 on 2048-d GAP features retains the dominant discriminative subspace and cuts the probe's parameters ~8x (less overfitting at ~85 imgs/class), which typically gives a small log-loss gain; the upside is capped because fine-grained breed signal partly lives in low-variance directions that get truncated, and C=0.3 is no longer re-tuned for the new feature geometry, so the net effect is near-neutral to mildly positive.

DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings are substantially stronger than ResNet-50 ImageNet features for fine-grained breed discrimination (linear-probe top-1 gains of ~5+ points on Stanford Dogs), so the same LR+10-view-TTA pipeline should drop log loss from ~0.44 to roughly 0.26-0.30, with the C re-selection adding a small calibration benefit.

With ~9.2k samples vs 2816 dims the original problem is not ill-conditioned, so truncation to 256 components mostly discards fine-grained discriminative directions while whitening amplifies noisy low-variance retained components and inflates feature scale ~10x, making C=1.0 effectively far weaker regularization and worsening calibration — expect a modest log-loss regression, not a gain.

k-NN accuracy on these frozen features may be only mildly worse than LogReg, but its distance-weighted vote probabilities are coarse and near-zero (~9e-4 after smoothing) whenever the true breed has no neighbor among the 10 retrieved, and with 120 fine-grained classes that happens for ~10-15% of test images, each costing ~7 nats — log loss punishes this far more than the accuracy gap, roughly doubling the loss versus the well-calibrated linear head.

End-to-end fine-tuning with augmentation, label smoothing, warmup+cosine schedule should beat the linear probe on frozen features (better accuracy and reasonably calibrated softmax), and 10 epochs of ResNet-50 at bs=64 in fp16 fits the ~10-min budget, though gains are capped by the short schedule and ~76 images/class.

ViT-B/16 augreg (in21k->in1k) frozen features are far stronger than ResNet50-V1 for linear probing on the ImageNet-dogs subset (~89% vs ~82% linear-probe accuracy), so log loss should drop substantially; only mild risk that the untuned C=0.3 is suboptimal for the 768-d ViT feature scale.

10-view TTA (5 crops x hflip) with probability averaging is a reliable variance-reduction trick that almost always lowers log loss a few percent for frozen-backbone linear heads; the corner-crop/center-crop train-test mismatch slightly blunts the gain, so expect a modest ~3-4% improvement over 0.4529.

The ImageNet-22k-pretrained ConvNeXt features are stronger and complementary to ResNet-50, while per-block normalization prevents scale imbalance, so the concatenated linear classifier should substantially improve log loss.

The breed-to-ImageNet mapping matches with exact string equality, but torchvision's WEIGHTS.meta['categories'] entries are comma-separated alias strings (e.g. 'affenpinscher, monkey pinscher, monkey dog'), so the assert len(matches)==1 fails on the very first breed and the run crashes before any submission is written — the metric stays at the baseline level.
PCA-256 should retain the main feature subspace and fit faster, but with C fixed it likely discards some low-variance breed-specific directions, causing a small log-loss regression.

The pretrained ResNet-50 was optimized for average pooling before its classifier, so max-pooled features have mismatched, heavy-tailed statistics that are typically less linearly separable; expect a modest log-loss regression (a few points of accuracy), only partly offset by temperature recalibration.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 (80.9% vs 76.1% top-1) produces clearly more discriminative frozen features and the 232px resize preserves slightly more detail, typically giving a modest but real log-loss gain on fine-grained dog-breed transfer with the same logistic head.
C=0.3 was already holdout-tuned; tenfold stronger L2 makes the transferred head overly shrunk and underconfident, with the brief fine-tuning only partly compensating.

Dropping input resolution 224→192 shrinks dogs to ~86% of the backbone's trained pixel scale and discards fine-grained detail (ear/coat texture) that discriminates the 120 breeds, so the frozen features and LR-initialized head get modestly less discriminative; the brief last-block fine-tune can't recover the lost detail, yielding a small log-loss regression while still running well within budget.

PCA-256 keeps the roughly 119-dim breed-discriminative subspace of the ResNet-50 GAP features so the change is small, but truncation plus reusing the raw-feature-tuned C=0.3 costs a bit of fine-grained signal and calibration, yielding a slight log-loss regression.

Dropping input resolution from 224 to 192 preserves crop geometry but discards fine detail and shifts inputs off the pretrained ResNet-50's native scale, which typically degrades fine-grained breed discrimination modestly, raising log loss a few percent.

Swapping ResNet-50 IMAGENET1K_V1 for the much stronger V2 checkpoint (~5pt higher ImageNet top-1, better transfer features) with its matched 232px preprocessing should cut log loss roughly in proportion to the ~20% relative error reduction, landing near 0.36; the added MLflow/config scaffolding doesn't affect the metric.

Same frozen features and C=0.3 classifier; only held-out scalar logit calibration is added, which should slightly improve confidence calibration/log loss while the tracking and tempdir changes are prediction-neutral.
Low-learning-rate fine-tuning of only the final bottleneck should modestly improve the already strong frozen features while limiting overfitting.

Horizontal-flip TTA with probability averaging is a well-matched transform for dog breeds (left/right symmetric), so averaging two views of frozen ResNet-50 features through the same logistic regression typically yields a small but real log-loss reduction (~1.5–2.5%); the extra mlflow/psutil bookkeeping doesn't affect predictions and the single extra test pass on 1,023 images is trivially within budget.

For AUC, balanced undersampling of a logistic regression mostly just shifts the intercept, but here C is fixed so shrinking each label's training set (down to ~956 rows for threat, a ~167x cut) multiplies the effective L2 strength by the keep fraction, over-shrinking the rare-label models and throwing away >99% of the negatives that pin down the ranking, while both branches also share the same subset (more correlated errors in the blend); expect roughly neutral common labels and small AUC losses on threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic that pull the column mean down a few tenths of a percent.

Stacking the shared char_wb 2-6 features into NB-LogReg reproduces the well-known strong word+char NB-LogReg kernel; char n-grams add orthogonal signal that especially lifts the rare labels (threat, identity_hate), so branch B gains ~0.003 AUC and the fixed 50/50 rank blend captures roughly half of that, with modest runtime/memory risk only.

AUC is rank-based so balancing the class mix mostly shifts calibration, not ordering, for abundant labels (toxic/obscene/insult stay ~flat), but collapsing rare-label fits to ~1-3k rows against 60k-200k features (and computing NB ratios on ~500 negatives) sharply increases variance for threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic, and noisier OOF stack features compound this — net small regression, offset only by faster runtime.

Pure MultinomialNB on TF-IDF is a weaker, less discriminative branch than the NB-ratio + liblinear NBSVM, so the equal rank blend and OOF stack inherit a small but real AUC drop despite faster deterministic fits.

Mean-pooled Word2Vec + LR is a markedly weaker branch (~0.948-0.955 AUC) than the word+char TF-IDF branch it replaces (~0.976), and since the MLP now trains on the same 200-d embeddings it becomes highly correlated with branch A — two-thirds of the rank blend becomes one weak, redundant signal while only branch B (~0.979) remains strong, dragging the mean AUC down by roughly 0.003.

ROC AUC depends only on ranking, so 1:1 undersampling buys nothing (it mostly shifts intercepts), while discarding 84-99.7% of negatives raises variance of the LR weights and the NB log-ratios and silently increases effective L2 (C is not rescaled by sample size), hurting the rare labels most — threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic get fit on only ~1k-3k rows against 60k-200k features — so all three branches degrade slightly and the rank-average blend lands roughly 0.001-0.002 AUC below the full-data baseline.

Branch D is a genuinely decorrelated model class (shared-hidden-layer sparse MLP) but will be undertrained — the 690s epoch-start guard likely allows only 1-2 epochs after A-C finish, putting its held-out AUC near the 0.97 discard threshold; equal-weight rank averaging of a slightly weaker but diverse model with three strong linear branches historically nets a small gain on this task, offset by a real chance it is discarded (no change) or mildly dilutive, so the expected effect is a small positive (~+0.0005 AUC).

For AUC, balanced undersampling mostly shifts the intercept and leaves ordering nearly intact on abundant labels, but it discards 80-99% of negative-class information and makes the rare-label fits very high-variance (threat trains on ~956 rows against 200-250k features at C=4), so expect small losses concentrated in threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic that drag the column mean down a few thousandths.

Lowercasing and whitespace steps are no-ops (TfidfVectorizer already lowercases and splits on whitespace), but the de-obfuscation and URL/IP/timestamp canonicalization merge rare toxic variants into strong canonical tokens, reducing sparsity and slightly sharpening the linear models' features — typically a small net gain, partly offset by losing some emphasis signal from repeat-collapsing.

Feature-level stacking of B's OOF logits lets each branch-A classifier learn a near-optimal A+B combination per label (including cross-label signal that helps rare labels like threat/identity_hate), but the gain is capped because the unchanged 0.5 rank blend re-averages with B (now highly correlated with stacked A), and the /20 logit scaling plus strong C=0.1 regularization shrinks how much A can use the new columns — net effect a small positive, with the 30 extra liblinear fits still fitting inside the 15-min kill window.

The small multitask MLP should be competitive with the linear TF-IDF branches and add some nonlinear/label-sharing diversity, but it reuses branch A's features so the equal rank blend likely gives only a small lift.

Branch C (NB-LogReg over B's word 1-2grams + A's char_wb n-grams) is the classic stronger NB-logreg variant and should individually beat branch B, so replacing half of B's blend weight with C yields a small net gain; but C is highly correlated with B and A's weight drops from 1/2 to 1/3, capping the diversity benefit, so the improvement is modest (~+0.001 AUC). Runtime stays within budget since C's liblinear fits (max_iter=100, tol=1e-3) cost about the same as B's existing fits on a 25% wider matrix.

Holdout-fitted per-label weights should shift the blend toward the stronger NB-LogReg branch and capture genuine per-label branch-strength differences for the common labels, while the 0.5 shrinkage bounds the damage from noisy weight estimates on rare labels (threat, identity_hate) — net effect is a small positive gain on the order of a few ten-thousandths of AUC, though noise on the rare-label columns gives wide error bars.

Compressing 100k sparse n-grams to 300 dense LSA factors discards the discriminative long-tail n-gram signal that drives the strong baseline, and the damage is worst for the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) that dominate the column-mean noise — LSA+LogReg on this dataset typically lands around 0.95-0.96 mean AUC, a clear regression from 0.9798, with only speed/simplicity gained.

AUC depends only on ordering, and keeping all positives with a 10:1 negative cap mostly shifts intercepts for the linear branches while leaving the common labels (toxic essentially untouched, obscene/insult mostly kept) nearly unchanged; the effect concentrates on rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) where branch B's NB log-odds get noisier and fastText sees far fewer negatives, so a small net regression in the mean column AUC is more likely than a gain.

The single softmax fastText makes co-occurring toxicity labels compete (and fastText samples one label from multi-label lines), so branch F's per-label rankings should degrade slightly; with branches A/B unchanged and F only one-third of the rank blend, expect a small mean-AUC drop.

ComplementNB on raw word counts is a decent imbalanced-text baseline (~0.95-0.965 mean AUC historically on this dataset) but it discards the discriminative TF-IDF logistic models, the char n-gram view that catches misspellings, and the ensemble diversity — classic NB underperforms NB-LogReg/TF-IDF blends here by roughly 1.5-2.5 AUC points, so this 'simplification' is a clear regression.

Mean-pooled from-scratch Word2Vec + logistic is a well-known ~0.94-0.96 baseline on this task: it discards word order, IDF weighting, and char n-gram robustness to misspellings, and dilutes the rare-label signal (threat, identity_hate) that exact-token TF-IDF features capture sharply, so replacing the three-branch sparse ensemble regresses the metric by roughly 3 points despite the cleaner pipeline.

Averaged corpus-trained Word2Vec vectors with a linear head lose the fine-grained lexical signal that 200k-dim TF-IDF n-grams (especially char n-grams capturing slurs/misspellings) provide; this is a well-known result for this competition, where mean-pooled embedding + logistic baselines score ~0.93-0.95 vs ~0.98 for the TF-IDF blend, with the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) degrading most because their sparse cues are diluted by pooling.

Char-level NB-LogReg is a genuinely diverse third branch (different analyzer and model family from A's plain logreg and B's word NB-LogReg) and historically the second-strongest classic model on this task, so per-label simplex blending should add a small real gain (~+0.001) on the well-populated labels, partially offset by noisier weight tuning on the 10% holdout for rare labels (threat, identity_hate) and a coarser 0.1 grid; runtime stays within budget.

C=0.1 heavily underfit the 60k-feature sparse branch A, dragging the rank blend down; C=4 with liblinear is the standard config for exactly this word+char TF-IDF setup on this competition, bringing branch A to ~0.985 standalone and lifting the 50/50 rank blend by roughly +0.005 AUC, with liblinear easily fitting within the time budget.

A well-configured supervised fastText (dim=64, bigrams, 20 epochs) is a diverse but slightly weaker model (~0.972-0.977 standalone) than the linear TF-IDF branches; adding it as a 1/3-weight rank component to two correlated ~0.98 branches typically yields a small net AUC gain from error decorrelation, though rare-label noise (threat, identity_hate) caps the upside and a small regression is plausible.

Char-NB-LogReg (3-7g, 100k) is the classic third leg of this competition's linear trio; it adds a decorrelated feature view to the two word-dominant branches, and 3-way rank averaging of word-LR + word-NB + char-NB historically lands ~0.985 public LB versus ~0.980 for the two-branch blend, though gains are partly muted by noisy rare labels and the added char-vectorizer fit pushes runtime close to budget.

Dropping 10% of training data (no full-data refit) costs more AUC — especially on rare labels threat/identity_hate that lose ~10% of their few positives — than the small, holdout-noise-limited gain from per-label blend weights; the two branches are highly correlated so the blend AUC is flat in w, capping the upside while the data loss is certain.

Label-specific NB log-ratio weighting is a proven trick for linear TF-IDF models on this task (branch B already relies on it), and branch A's top-frequency word/char features have count mass large enough that the smoothing bias under rare labels is negligible, so branch A's solo AUC should rise slightly; the gain is partly offset by reduced diversity against the already-NB-weighted branch B and by C=0.1 not being re-tuned for the rescaled features, netting a small positive shift in the rank blend.

min_df=0.01 ≈ 3,127 docs, which collapses branch B's vocabulary (200k → ~10-25k ultra-common n-grams) and shrinks branch A's word/char vocabularies, deleting the mid-frequency slur/insult terms that carry most ranking signal—especially for rare labels like identity_hate/threat—while adding no new features, so the rank blend regresses moderately with no timeout risk.

Undersampling discards ~90-99% of negatives (threat drops to 956 rows), making branch B's per-label NB log-count ratios and both LR fits much noisier, and with C fixed the effective regularization rises sharply as n shrinks — hurting the rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) that dominate column-mean variance, for a modest net AUC regression despite the faster fits.

Cosine class-centroid (Rocchio-style) scoring keeps the strong lexical ordering so it stays around 0.95 mean AUC, but it discards the discriminative per-feature weighting LR learns, losing roughly 2-4 AUC points concentrated in the rare, few-positive labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) where noisy positive centroids hurt most.

char_wb concentrates the fixed 50k vocabulary on word-internal n-grams with boundary padding (better for slurs/obfuscations) instead of noisy boundary-crossing substrings, while cross-word phrase info is already covered by branch B's word bigrams — typically a tiny gain, within noise of the rare-label column mean.

ComplementNB retains useful word/char evidence, but replacing the discriminative LR and NB-LogReg heads with independent-feature NB scoring should lose ranking quality, especially on threat and identity_hate.

Crushing branch A's 60k sparse TF-IDF features to 32 SVD components destroys the rare-ngram signals that drive its high AUC (especially threat/identity_hate), turning the stronger branch (~0.975) into a weak one (~0.92-0.93), and the equal-weight rank average with the fastText branch (~0.965) lands well below the current blend.

Collapsing the long tail of rare-but-highly-discriminative tokens (slurs, obfuscated profanity, misspellings) into a single 'raretoken' destroys the exact surface features the char n-gram TF-IDF and fastText branches rely on for the rare labels (identity_hate, severe_toxic, threat), and this information loss outweighs any mild regularization benefit, so mean column-wise AUC drops modestly.

Keeping stop words adds back genuinely predictive pronouns ('you'/'your' are known toxicity signals in this dataset) while TF-IDF already downweights the non-informative ones, and the ~300 displaced rare content words are backed up by the char 2-6-gram features and the unchanged NB branch — so the blend moves by only a tiny, likely slightly positive amount.

The expit/logit blend is effectively margin averaging; the heavily regularized word+char branch (C=0.1) is down-weighted versus the less-regularized NB branch (C=4), losing some of the rank blend's calibration-robust complementary signal, so a tiny AUC regression is likely.

Switching char_wb to char lets 2-6-grams cross word boundaries, which with a fixed 50k feature cap dilutes the most informative within-word n-grams with noisier cross-boundary ones; effect is small (char_wb is marginally better for this task in classic kernels), so expect a tiny regression of roughly 0.0005 absolute AUC.

CPU fastText without pretrained or subword vectors is competitive but likely a bit weaker than per-label NB-logistic TF-IDF on rare labels, so the equal rank blend with the unchanged word+char branch slips slightly.

Keeping the 128 highest-F features removes mostly near-noise histogram tail bins and slightly reduces variance of the L2-regularized LR (which is fairly robust to redundant features anyway), and since the LR is only half of the 50/50 blend with the unchanged NN, the net effect on test log loss is a small improvement well under 1%, with negligible runtime cost.

Log loss is dominated by the overconfident-error tail, and label smoothing on a heavily-augmented NN trained with only ~8 images per class mainly tempers those overconfident mistakes (and improves calibration per Müller et al. 2019) while sacrificing little on the correct bulk; the unchanged LR half of the 50/50 blend dampens the effect, so expect a small net improvement rather than the larger regression the 0.9 confidence cap would cause in a near-separable regime.

OvR and multinomial give similar rankings/accuracy here and the tuned power+floor calibration absorbs the scale difference, but multinomial LR directly optimizes the joint cross-entropy that is being scored while OvR's 99 independent imbalanced binary fits produce slightly less log-loss-aligned probabilities that a 2-parameter global calibration cannot fully repair, so expect a small regression rather than a gain.

A 5-seed MLP bag on these informative 192 descriptors is a reasonably strong second model (OOF ~0.06-0.10), and blending it with the calibrated LR at a CV-selected weight typically yields a small genuine log-loss gain, while the w=0 fallback bounds the downside to roughly the current 0.0451.

Averaging the 5 fold models at the selected (likely high) C softens overconfident probabilities and gives bagging-style variance reduction that log loss rewards, typically outweighing the 80%-vs-100% per-model data loss, so a small improvement over the single full-data refit is expected.

The 21 geometric features are mostly redundant with the 192 purpose-built shape/margin/texture descriptors, but absolute size and Hu moments add a little complementary signal, and CV-selected C plus standardization keeps overfitting risk minimal—so expect a tiny improvement within noise, roughly 0.055-0.057.

PCA(0.95) retains most signal so the impact is small, but with only 10 samples/class the discarded low-variance directions still carry discriminative information (histogram-bin detail), and the isotropic L2 penalty on decorrelated, variance-ranked components effectively reweights regularization against the model; expect a modest regression rather than a gain since the fixed C=1.0 baseline was already well-regularized.

Averaging probabilities from five fold-models (each on 80% of data) versus one full-data fit is roughly neutral for a well-regularized convex linear model, but the averaging slightly softens overconfident predictions, which log-loss rewards, so expect a small ~1-3% improvement from 0.0882 to about 0.086.

The two-branch NN reuses the strong standardized descriptors and adds silhouette/TTA diversity, so the 50/50 probability blend should smooth the LR probabilities and correct some errors, with gain limited by the tiny per-class training set.

OOF-fitted temperature (power a) plus a small uniform floor reliably shaves a few percent off log loss for a slightly over/under-confident softmax LR; with only 2 grid-searched scalars chosen on 990 OOF points, selection noise/transfer gap is small, so expect a modest real improvement (~0.1244 -> ~0.119-0.120) with negligible risk of regression.

5-fold CV tuning of C on the 990x192 standardized descriptors reliably beats fixed C=1.0 (the grid almost certainly selects a larger C that sharpens well-calibrated probabilities without losing accuracy on this near-linearly-separable dataset), so expect a solid but modest log-loss drop from 0.1244 to roughly 0.10; the refit-on-all-data step adds a tiny extra gain, and the grid-search selection bias over 11 candidates is too small to cause a regression.

The ~27 geometric descriptors are largely redundant with the existing 64 shape descriptors (same binary masks), and L2-regularized LR at C=1.0 is robust to correlated additions, so the effect is near-neutral with a small net gain from complementary global-shape cues (Hu moments, eccentricity, solidity); implementation is correct and runtime is trivially within budget.

At ~96% test accuracy the current C=1.0 model is already well-shrunk and reasonably calibrated; 5x stronger L2 barely moves decision boundaries but softens confident correct predictions, and since errors are mild confusable-species mistakes (not catastrophic), the calibration cost on the 96% correct outweighs any small gain, so log loss rises modestly.

The submitted model is now trained on only 80% of the data (792 vs 990 samples, 8 vs 10 per class); for multinomial logistic regression in this regime the estimation-error component of log loss scales roughly as 1/n, so test log loss should worsen by roughly 10-20%, landing around 0.09-0.10 (essentially what the internal holdout already measures).

LR and shrinkage LDA are both strong and partially decorrelated on these 192 leaf descriptors, and OOF-optimized convex weights will down-weight the weaker kNN, so the blend should modestly beat LR alone (typically ~0.05 log loss on this dataset); implementation is leakage-safe and runtime is unchanged in order of magnitude.

HistGBM may fit some interactions, but with 99 classes and only ~10 examples each it drops CV/refit and is likely less calibrated than the tuned multinomial logistic model, so log loss should rise sharply.

Multinomial logistic regression is a well-calibrated, strong linear member on these 192 descriptors, while the Platt-sigmoid LinearSVC must calibrate 99 one-vs-rest problems on ~3 samples/class per fold (with class_weight distortion), yielding noisier, overconfident probabilities; uniform 4-way soft voting dilutes but doesn't erase the damage, so log loss rises modestly.

Only 25% of the uniform soft vote changes; RF trains on all 891 rows and its vote-fraction probabilities are conservative (helping log-loss's asymmetric penalty), replacing an HGB that either stops very early or overfits given its ~1-row-per-class early-stopping split, so a small improvement is likely, though the 99-row test set makes the outcome noisy.

A ~95k-parameter MLP on ~890 training samples (~8 per class) will heavily overfit and output overconfident probabilities; early stopping triggers on validation accuracy (not log loss), and the uniform shrinkage capped at alpha=0.5 only partially recalibrates, so the well-calibrated linear model's 0.124 log loss degrades to roughly 0.3-0.45.

5-fold OOF selection over the C grid will likely land below 1.0 (roughly 0.1-0.3 given only ~10 samples/class in 192 dims), improving calibration and decision-boundary generalization beyond what the uniform shrinkage alone fixes at C=1.0; selection noise across the 11 correlated grid points is small and 55 tiny multinomial LR fits with fold parallelism run in a couple of minutes, so expect a modest ~10-15% log-loss improvement to about 0.108.

The leaves are black on white, so `mask = img > 127` actually selects the background, making the contour scalars and 32-bin distance histogram near-constant canvas/border descriptors (zeroed out by StandardScaler), but the 7 Hu moments of the complement still encode real leaf-shape signal, giving regularized logistic regression a small net gain over the 192-descriptor baseline.

CV-tuning C (grid includes C=1.0, and neg-log-loss selection typically lands at a less-regularized C around 10-100 for 990 standardized samples) plus refitting on all data reliably shaves ~15-20% off the 0.1244 log loss without changing anything else in the pipeline.

Soft-voting adds shrinkage LDA (typically at least as strong as LR on these descriptors) plus decorrelated tuned-kNN and HGB; probability averaging is Jensen-bounded by the mean member loss and diversity usually nets a gain, but the weaker kNN/HGB members dilute LR's already-confident correct predictions, so expect only a modest improvement over 0.1244 rather than a large drop.

OOF-tuned shrinkage toward uniform is a safe one-parameter calibration that mainly rescues LR's overconfident wrong predictions; with the baseline already strong (0.124) the tail is thin, so the selected alpha (~0.03-0.08) yields a real but modest gain, with slight overshoot risk from OOF models being less calibrated than the full-data fit.

The pooled covariance is already estimated from ~890 residual degrees of freedom (192 dims), so Ledoit-Wolf 'auto' shrinkage is near-optimal; forcing shrinkage=0.9 discards most discriminative correlation structure, collapsing LDA toward a diagonal nearest-centroid rule with compressed whitening and softened logits, which should substantially raise multi-class log loss (roughly 0.36 → ~0.55-0.65).
Per-family shrunk covariance fits avoid noisy cross-family covariance estimation, and equal-weight probability averaging should smooth complementary descriptor evidence for a modest log-loss gain.

L2-regularized multinomial LR on 192 standardized descriptors already handles collinearity, so PCA(0.90) mainly discards some discriminative low-variance directions (~10% of variance), likely causing a modest log-loss regression; the unchanged C grid and fold-local CV keep the effect small.
CV-tuned shrinkage LDA should suit the 192 descriptors in a 99-class, ~10-examples-per-class regime, giving better-calibrated shared-covariance posteriors than the l2 logistic search.

PCA is an orthogonal rotation, to which L2-penalized logistic regression is nearly invariant, so only the truncated low-variance directions (~5% of variance) change the model; these mostly-noise contrasts still carry some discriminative signal, so perturbing an already well-tuned, temperature-calibrated 0.045 baseline should give a near-neutral to slightly worse log loss.

Shrinkage LDA is well suited to 10 training leaves per species and correlated descriptors, and with the same out-of-fold temperature calibration it should be somewhat better calibrated than fixed C=1 logistic regression.

With a well-calibrated model already at 0.094 log loss, mixing in 0.005 uniform mostly shrinks confident correct probabilities, adding ≈-log(0.995)≈0.005 to nearly every sample's loss, while the uniform floor (5e-5) rarely rescues catastrophically wrong predictions, so the score regresses slightly.
384 Nyström landmarks still cover the correlated 192-D descriptors and 99 classes, while dropping restandardized low-spectrum components should slightly reduce overfitting.

Shrunk LDA (lsqr, shrinkage='auto') is a famously strong fit for this dataset—the 192 descriptors are near-Gaussian and classes nearly linearly separable, and Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage handles the 192-dims-vs-10-samples-per-class covariance estimation—typically cutting log loss roughly in half versus default-C logistic regression; the implementation is correct (scaler fit only on train split for validation, refit on all data for submission, class-order alignment via classes_ vs sample columns) and runs in seconds.

3-fold CV will select a larger C (likely 10-1000) than the fixed 1.0; on these 192 descriptors a tuned multinomial LR typically cuts test log loss roughly in half (to ~0.05-0.08), and 16 small LR fits run in well under a minute so there is no budget risk.

OOF temperature scaling on a 99-class logistic regression trained on only ~990 samples reliably softens mildly overconfident logits, typically buying a few percent of log loss; the temperature is learned correctly on out-of-fold logits and the model/features are unchanged, so expect a small real improvement (~0.124 -> ~0.120), tempered slightly because T is learned on smaller fold models than the final full-data fit.
Nystroem RBF features should add useful nonlinear/prototype structure over the strong linear baseline, but untuned C=1 and post-embedding rescaling cap the gain.

The 31 added features are leakage-free and include several signals known to matter on RAOP (temporal decay via t_days, request length, gratitude/reciprocity markers, upvote ratio, first-person rate) that are invisible to the current TF-IDF+log1p-numeric linear model; with only 4k rows and C=0.3 the noisy weak features (hour/weekday bins, day-of-month) do little harm, so expect a modest ~+0.01 AUC gain.

Random forests on ~8000-dim sparse TF-IDF features with sqrt sampling rarely see the 9 strong numeric features per split (~10% of splits), so deep unpruned trees memorize noisy text splits and badly underperform the linear model on this small (~4k row) dataset; RF may partially recover the numeric-feature signal (~0.60) but the text block becomes pure variance.

Random forests on 5k sparse TF-IDF features (with sqrt feature sampling giving the 10 strong numeric/giver columns only ~1.4% of split candidates, and giver_known constant at test) typically lose several AUC points versus a linear model that aggregates all word signals, so the nonlinear gains on requester history won't offset the text degradation.

Swapping 5000 sparse TF-IDF unigram weights for 50 dense LDA topic proportions discards substantial discriminative text signal for a linear model on ~4.5k short posts; TF-IDF+LR is a strong, well-conditioned baseline, and generic 50-topic LDA typically loses several AUC points, so the metadata+topics model should land around 0.69-0.71, a clear regression from 0.748 (runtime and the added mlflow scaffolding are non-issues).

Replacing the supervised TF-IDF→LR out-of-fold logit with 20 unsupervised LDA topic proportions discards a directly target-optimized text signal; LDA on short Reddit posts yields noisy, weakly-predictive topics, so LightGBM recovers only part of the lost text AUC despite gaining interaction freedom with metadata, yielding a moderate regression from ~0.703 to ~0.687.

Swapping the raw epoch (a noisy timeline identifier the heavily-regularized LightGBM can only use to memorize period base rates) for stationary hour-of-day/day-of-week features removes mild temporal overfitting and adds a weak but real behavioral signal, so the effect should be small and slightly positive — only 1 of 12 level-2 columns changes and strong regularization (num_leaves=8, min_child=50, lr=0.01) bounds the delta either way.

The HistGBM on dense-only features is weaker than the TF-IDF+LR model but captures nonlinear interactions the linear model misses; CV-gated rank averaging (with tie-breaks favoring the LR, so worst case ≈ baseline) typically adds a small +0.003–0.006 AUC on this dataset, with some risk of the gain not transferring from OOF to test.

Random forests underperform regularized linear models on sparse high-dimensional TF-IDF text: with max_features='sqrt' over ~5k columns, most candidate splits are noisy unigrams, fully grown trees overfit ~3.2k training rows, and vote-fraction probabilities rank worse than LR's additive log-odds; the strong requester-history numerics will keep AUC in the mid-0.6s but below the 0.70 linear baseline.

Subreddit-identity features are a known predictive signal on RAOP (community/status history) that the 9 numeric counts only partially capture; a min_df=5 binary TF-IDF block adds mostly clean, low-noise features to a well-regularized linear model, so a small AUC gain (~+0.005-0.006) is likely, with slight overfitting/sparsity risk capped by idf weighting and min_df.

giver_known is a near-perfect label leak in train (sanity print will show pos_rate ~1.0) but the Kaggle test set has giver_username_if_known = 'N/A' for every row, so the flag is constant zero at inference; logistic regression dumps most weight onto the leak feature and shrinks the TF-IDF/numeric coefficients, leaving test rows ranked by heavily attenuated residual weights — local holdout AUC will look inflated (~0.99) while the graded test AUC drops from ~0.657 to roughly ~0.58.

Stacking the out-of-fold TF-IDF logit with the raw numerics and timestamp in a well-regularized LightGBM preserves the text signal while adding modest nonlinear calibration/interaction gains over the linear blend; 4k rows x 11 features with early stopping keeps overfitting and runtime risk low, so expect a small improvement (~+0.008 AUC) over 0.6573.

The added dense block (text-length stats, karma ratio, RAOP-history indicators, request-time features) matches the features shown predictive in the Althoff et al. paper, and such engineered metadata typically adds ~0.01-0.02 AUC to a TF-IDF+LR baseline on this dataset; the implementation is correct and leakage-free, and the MLflow wrapper is a no-op for the metric.

ExtraTrees with random thresholds and sqrt feature sampling (~73 of ~5.4k candidates per split) is a poor fit for high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF: most splits land on near-zero word features, drowning out the linearly-separable text signal that logistic regression exploits, so the model degrades to mostly the numeric/embedding signal — consistent with the well-known superiority of linear models over tree ensembles on sparse text — while bagging and min_samples_leaf=3 keep the drop moderate rather than catastrophic.

On RAOP, L2-regularized TF-IDF unigram LR on ~4.5k docs is a well-behaved, genuinely additive signal (specific request phrasing, gratitude/politeness markers) that a linear probe over 384-d MiniLM embeddings only partially recovers, so dropping the sparse block while keeping the same C=0.3 LR should cost roughly 0.01–0.02 AUC; the mlflow additions are telemetry-only and don't affect the model.

The engineered document stats (text length, gratitude/politeness flags, VADER sentiment, punctuation, pronoun rates, readability) are exactly the signals the Althoff et al. paper shows are predictive on this dataset and are largely invisible to length-normalized TF-IDF, so they should add a modest ~0.005-0.01 AUC on top of the 0.6497 baseline; redundancy with unigram TF-IDF (please/thank) and heavy regularization cap the gain, while the implementation is sound (shared scaler fit on train, no leakage, trivial runtime).

The TF-IDF text block is the dominant predictive signal in the current 0.650 model; the nine requester-history numerics (several of which are ~constant zero since every row is a first-time RAOP post) alone typically support only ~0.60-0.62 AUC, so removing text should regress the score by roughly 6%.

Mean-pooled Word2Vec (all tokens weighted equally, including stop words, trained on only ~1M tokens) loses the discriminative token-level signal that 5k-feature TF-IDF gives a linear model, and the existing 15 text-stats features already capture most of the coarse semantic signal, so expect a typical few-point AUC regression rather than an improvement.

Adding bigrams and raising the vocabulary cap to 60k typically recovers phrase-level signal (e.g., reciprocity/hardship idioms) on this dataset and yields a modest AUC gain of roughly +0.005-0.01; the fixed C=0.3 L2 penalty with min_df=2 keeps overfitting in check on 5.6k rows, lbfgs handles the ~60k sparse features well within budget, and the mlflow additions are exception-wrapped no-ops that cannot affect the metric.

Dropping the TF-IDF+SVD text representation removes genuine lexical signal (request wording, narrative, gratitude cues) that the 300-component SVD already compresses well at 5.7k rows; metadata-only GBM on the 9 requester-history features typically lands ~0.61-0.62 AUC on RAOP, so expect a modest regression despite lower variance and faster training.

Same 309-dim SVD/numeric design, but sklearn RF with sqrt per-split sampling should dilute the few strong requester-history features and is typically slightly weaker than CV-tuned LightGBM on this small noisy matrix.

Adding 384-dim MiniLM embeddings to TF-IDF+metadata typically gives a small semantic-signal boost on this small (~4k) dataset under L2-regularized logistic regression, and the 256-token truncation plus 4-thread CPU encoding keeps runtime safely within budget, but gains are modest because TF-IDF already captures most lexical signal and C=0.3 remains untuned.

Adding bigrams and expanding vocabulary from 5k to 100k TF-IDF features typically captures useful phrase-level signals (e.g., 'lost my job', 'no money') in this small-text dataset, and C=0.3 regularized logistic regression handles the wider sparse matrix without overfitting much, so a modest AUC gain of ~0.01-0.015 over the 0.6573 baseline is expected.

The added length, readability, pronoun, gratitude, hardship, money, and reciprocity features are mostly label-aligned and only partly redundant with unigram TF-IDF plus status numerics, so they should give the regularized linear model a small AUC bump with negligible runtime risk.

On this small (~4.5k train) sparse-text problem, linear models on full TF-IDF are a strong prior; compressing to 300 SVD components loses some lexical signal and gradient boosting on dense LSA features typically matches or slightly underperforms regularized logistic regression here, with early-stopped CV only partly offsetting overfitting, so I expect a small regression (~0.650 vs 0.6573).

The quantile spline on absolute time captures the known multi-year drift in RAOP success rates as the community grew, while the annual Fourier encoding collapses all years and retains only weak seasonal signal; since text and requester-history features dominate the model, the loss should be small but real.

C=0.3 heavily shrinks coefficients on ~5k TF-IDF features over ~4k training rows; relaxing to C=30 (still L2-regularized with lbfgs) lets sparse linguistic cues fit better with only moderate overfitting risk, so a modest AUC gain of roughly half to one-and-a-half percent relative is likely.

An 8-dimensional quantile-spline of calendar time adds only weak temporal-drift signal to an L2-regularized logistic model, so the effect should be near zero with a slight positive tilt from capturing long-run success-rate trends.

Distance-weighted KNN with cosine distance on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF (where the unnormalized numeric/subreddit blocks dominate distances) is a much weaker learner than regularized logistic regression on ~4k training rows, and 25-neighbor vote fractions also give coarser probability ranking, so a clear AUC regression is expected.

KNN (k=25, distance-weighted) on the 9 standardized requester-history features is a meaningfully weaker ranker than CatBoost on this small tabular metadata (roughly ~0.60-0.62 vs ~0.65-0.67 standalone AUC), so swapping it into the unchanged 50/50 blend with the TF-IDF logistic model drags the combined score down modestly, cushioned only by decorrelation with the logistic component.

C=0.3 over-shrinks the L2-normalized TF-IDF coefficients so the logistic model is dominated by metadata and largely duplicates the CatBoost half of the blend; C=30 (still L2-regularized) lets text signals contribute, diversifying the 50/50 blend for a modest AUC gain, with only mild overfitting risk given ~4.5k samples and 5k sublinear-TF features.

Adding 8 smooth spline basis features of request timestamp to a ~5000-feature TF-IDF logistic model is low-risk (L2 regularization shrinks useless features, constant extrapolation handles out-of-range test times); the documented slow decline in RAOP success rate over the community's lifetime gives a weak monotone ranking signal, so expect at most a marginal AUC gain around +0.002.

Binarizing TF-IDF and thresholding the numeric history features discards useful magnitude information, while BernoulliNB’s independence assumptions should rank requests somewhat less effectively than logistic regression.

The spline timestamp block adds only ~8 weak features to a 5k-dimensional, regularized linear model, so impact is near-neutral; long-term trends in community success rate may give a tiny lift, and the implementation quirks (MLflow logging, no holdout printout) don't affect the written predictions.

Requester subreddit identity is a documented, non-leaky signal on RAOP that complements text/karma features; a min_df=5 binary block under L2 (C=0.3) should add a modest AUC gain (~+0.008), while the MLflow/holdout-removal changes don't affect test predictions.

CatBoost on the 9 metadata features captures nonlinear/interaction effects that the linear model misses, and a 50/50 blend of two diverse, comparably-strong models (text+meta logistic ~0.657, meta-only GBM ~0.64-0.65) typically gains ~0.01 AUC; the implementation is correct, tree-invariant to the log1p/standardization, and runs well within budget, with only a small risk that the fixed 50% weight to the weaker meta-only model dilutes text signal.

Adding bigrams captures short phrases (e.g., 'no money', 'pay it forward') that carry signal for request success; the fixed 5000-feature budget trades away some rare unigrams but on RAOP text+LR this swap is typically a small net positive (~+0.005-0.01 AUC), and the pipeline otherwise trains on identical data with identical hyperparameters.
Authorship attribution relies partly on function-word/pronoun usage and stop-word bigrams; the char view only partially offsets that lost stylistic signal, so I expect a slight log-loss regression.

The count-based word/char NB OOFs add complementary style signals and the log-linear meta-LR can recalibrate their overconfidence; expect a few-hundredths log-loss gain, with fold-averaged test probs roughly replacing the removed full-data LR refit.

Function words are prime stylometric signal for authorship attribution (and sklearn's stop list includes archaic connectives like 'upon', 'thus', 'indeed' that are frequent and discriminative in these 19th-century authors), so both word-level base models lose some signal; the char_wb models and meta-features partially backstop this in the stacker, so the net regression is small (~+0.001-0.002 log loss).

The 12 OOF probability columns are already informative, calibrated, and highly correlated, leaving little beyond a linear combination for a level-2 learner; classic stacking practice (Wolpert/Breiman) and Kaggle experience show a regularized multinomial LR combiner matches or slightly beats a GBM stacker on log loss by avoiding fold-noise overfitting and producing smoother, better-calibrated probabilities, while the 16 meta-features add little nonlinear signal — so expect a small improvement (roughly within test-set noise, ±0.005), with identical level-1 inputs and trivial runtime.

Punctuation is a genuine stylometric signal here (Poe's dashes/exclamations, Lovecraft's comma-heavy clauses, Shelley), and classic authorship-attribution work relies on it; stripping it removes informative char n-grams from the dominant feature block, and the modest regularization/vocab-shrink benefit only partially offsets that, so I expect a small regression rather than the claimed improvement.

The stack adds model diversity (C=10 word/char LRs plus count-based NBs) and a tuned log-prob meta-learner, a classic recipe on this dataset that historically moves a 0.44 single-LR baseline to roughly 0.36-0.39; the runtime stays in budget with parallel folds and fast NB fits.

Chi2 selection to 10k columns is leakage-free and cheap, but L2-regularized LR already handles the 130k sparse TF-IDF features well, and discarding the mid-frequency character n-gram tail (ranks 10k-60k) likely removes some discriminative signal and slightly worsens LR calibration; the OOF blend-weight search partially compensates by shifting weight toward the untouched NB branch, bounding the regression to roughly 1%.

Authorship attribution is the canonical case where function words are discriminative (stylometry relies on them), so removing stop words loses real signal from both the word TF-IDF and NB blocks; the untouched char_wb block partially back-fills function-word usage patterns, keeping the regression small (~+0.002 log loss) rather than large.

The explicit 5-fold CV over Cs=[1,3,10,30,100] is functionally equivalent to the proposed LogisticRegressionCV and will most likely select a moderately larger C (~3-10) than the fixed C=1.0, since the high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF stack is slightly over-regularized at C=1; this typically sharpens predicted probabilities and improves log loss by ~0.01-0.02 on this dataset (0.432 -> ~0.416), with runtime of 25 parallelized sparse lbfgs fits staying within budget.

Diversifying into 4 OOF base models (LR word/char TF-IDF + NB word/char counts) plus 16 stylometric features with a regularized LightGBM stacker is a well-proven architecture on this dataset; it typically beats a single stacked-feature LR by ~0.05-0.07 log loss, and the implementation is leak-free, class-order-safe, and comfortably within the time budget.

Case-sensitive boundary-crossing char n-grams capture punctuation/capitalization author tics (semicolons, dashes, quoted speech) that char_wb misses, and LR handles the ~400k sparse columns fine, giving a modest but real log-loss gain.

MNB on count n-grams is reasonably strong (~0.47 solo) and decorrelated with TF-IDF LR, so an OOF-tuned arithmetic blend (with w=1.0 as a safe fallback) should shave roughly 0.015-0.02 off the 0.4323 LR-only log loss with negligible overfitting risk from the small 44-combo grid.

Stopword removal is good hygiene for topic classification but harmful for authorship attribution: function words ('the', 'and', 'of') and their bigrams are precisely the stylometric signal that distinguishes Poe/Lovecraft/Shelley, so fastText loses discriminative features and log loss should regress moderately (roughly +0.03-0.04), though fastText's multithreaded training noise means some variance around this estimate.

The class imbalance is mild (~40/31/29), so balancing mostly shifts predicted priors toward uniform; since the test set keeps the natural distribution, this miscalibrates the softmax probabilities (EAP over-discounted, minorities over-boosted), which typically costs ~0.01 in log loss while adding no new information.

ComplementNB on the same TF-IDF matrix is a strong, complementary text model for this task; an OOF-selected convex blend with LR typically cuts log loss ~2-3%, and the OOF weight selection safely falls back to w≈1 if NB adds nothing, so downside risk is minimal.

Tuned multinomial logistic regression is usually better calibrated than MultinomialNB on l2-normalized word+char TF-IDF, so alpha CV likely only partly offsets NB's independence/overconfidence penalty.

Character n-grams are a strong, largely orthogonal stylistic signal for author attribution (morphology, punctuation habits); published ablations on this dataset show dropping them from a TF-IDF linear/NB-SVM stack costs roughly +0.02-0.05 log loss, so the word-only model should regress moderately rather than improve.

Replacing the discriminative NB-SVM head (ratio-weighted logistic regressions, well-calibrated probabilities) with a generative ComplementNB on the same TF-IDF stack yields markedly overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities on ~100k sparse features, so 3-class log loss should regress from ~0.409 to roughly ~0.50 despite similar accuracy.

CV-selecting C by neg_log_loss on word+char TF-IDF typically shifts C from 1.0 toward ~3-10 for this dataset, giving a modest calibration/log-loss gain of roughly 0.01; worst case it reselects C=1.0 and matches the baseline, while the mlflow additions are inert, so a small improvement to ~0.415 is the honest expectation.

MultinomialNB on word+char TF-IDF historically lands around 0.48-0.55 log loss on this dataset versus ~0.42 for tuned logistic regression, because NB's overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities are heavily penalized under log loss (sharp wrong predictions cost more than calibrated moderate ones), so swapping LR for NB with light alpha=0.1 smoothing should regress the score despite faster training.

fastText with lr=0.5, epoch=25 and softmax will roughly match TF-IDF+LR accuracy on this stylistic 3-class task (~78-80%), but its probabilities are notably overconfident after 25 epochs, so errors are penalized harder; expect a modest log-loss regression from ~0.432 to ~0.48 on the graded subset.

5-fold CV over C in [0.25..8] optimizes exactly the graded metric and will likely pick C≈2-4 (slightly better calibrated than hard-coded 1.0) for a small real gain; the implementation is faithful and deterministic (joblib preserves fit results), fits the time budget, and residual risk is just CV-vs-1,958-row-grading-subset noise, so expect ~0.5-1% improvement with a chance of being essentially unchanged if CV selects C=1.0.

NB-SVM (per-class log count-ratio weighting + one-vs-rest logistic with renormalization) is a well-documented improvement over plain multinomial LR on word+char TF-IDF for this exact competition, typically shaving ~0.02 off log loss; implementation is correct, leakage-free, and cheap (3 binary fits on ~19.6k rows), so a modest but real gain is expected.

Punctuation counts are largely redundant with the char_wb n-gram TF-IDF block, and only 14 MaxAbs-scaled dense features join ~100k sparse ones, but sentence-length and word-length stats add a little genuinely new signal, so expect a negligible-to-tiny improvement in log loss.

The change swaps plain multinomial LR for the classic NB-SVM-style trick (per-class log-count-ratio weights on binary occurrence applied to the TF-IDF matrix, then one-vs-rest liblinear LR) — a well-documented upgrade for this exact competition that typically moves TF-IDF+LR from ~0.44 to the high 0.3s; the implementation is correct (smoothed ratios, correct positive-class column, clip+renormalize) and three sparse liblinear fits easily fit the time budget.

With ~20k samples vs ~100k sparse TF-IDF n-gram features, C=1.0 is weakly regularized, so quadrupling L2 strength (C=0.25) should soften overconfident test-set probabilities and yield a small log-loss gain, though the change is modest since both settings are in a reasonable regime.

Character n-grams alone capture much of the stylistic signal, but dropping word unigram/bigram features removes distinctive vocabulary cues, so the NB-logistic model loses calibration and log loss worsens moderately (roughly 5-10%).

Direct L2 logistic regression on the strong word+character TF-IDF representation should be better calibrated and less noisy than the NB-ratio reweighting, though fixed C and one-vs-rest limit the gain.

Halving C from 4 to 2 modestly increases L2 shrinkage on the highly correlated word+char TF-IDF features, which typically softens overconfident probabilities and yields a small log-loss gain; the effect is minor (<0.5%) since both values sit on a flat part of the regularization path, and the added tracking/timing code does not alter the model.

NB log-count-ratio feature weighting (NBSVM-style) on binary document presence is a well-established improvement over plain multinomial LR for short-text authorship tasks like this, typically shaving a few hundredths off log loss (~0.37 -> ~0.34); the implementation is correct (column-wise sparse scaling, proper OVR probability stacking/normalization), and three sequential liblinear dual fits fit comfortably in the time budget.

Function words and pronouns are classic high-signal stylometric features for author attribution; TF-IDF already downweights them, so removing them (plus all stop-word-containing bigrams and their char n-grams) mostly destroys discriminative signal while adding spurious content-word bigrams, yielding a modest log-loss regression.

With p>>n correlated TF-IDF n-grams, stronger L2 (C=0.25) shrinks noisy coefficient directions, and the temperature scaling (which can sharpen down to 0.25) largely compensates for the softer logits, so log loss should change little — likely a small improvement as regularization handles geometry while temperature handles calibration.

Switching char_wb→char mainly reshuffles which n-grams survive the 60k max_features cap: boundary-spanning n-grams largely duplicate signal already in word bigrams and dilute discriminative within-word morphology, so expect a near-neutral but slightly worse log loss; the telemetry/refactor changes don't touch the model.

The change is a faithful implementation of the classic NB-log-ratio feature weighting (Wang-Manning NBSVM trick) with OVR logistic regression, which reliably beats plain multinomial LR on n-gram TF-IDF author attribution by upweighting rare author-discriminative features; the renormalized OVR probabilities cost little calibration, and three liblinear fits run well within budget, so expect a modest improvement over 0.432.

Raising C from 1.0 to 4.0 lightens L2 regularization on high-dimensional sparse word+char TF-IDF features with ~19.5k training rows, which for this competition typically yields a modest log-loss gain (optimal C is generally in the low single digits to ~10); the removed holdout print and kept holdout fit don't affect the final refit-on-all-data submission.

Temperature scaling is a strict generalization of predict_proba (T=1 recovers it) fitted directly on the holdout log loss; with ~150k sparse TF-IDF features and only ~17.6k training rows the C=1.0 logistic model is somewhat overconfident, so a scalar T slightly above 1 should transfer a small calibration gain (~0.004-0.005 absolute) to the test set, with negligible overfitting risk since only one parameter is tuned on ~1958 validation samples and the model/features are unchanged.
The metric remains raw-dollar RMSE; training on log1p optimizes relative error and expm1 predicts geometric/median fares, slightly downweighting high-fare errors, so I expect a small regression.

Quadrupling the training sample (1M→4M rows) with identical features/hyperparameters should modestly sharpen LightGBM's leaf estimates, cutting the valid-row RMSE (~3.60) by roughly 1-1.5%, but ~2.8% of test rows are corrupt and pinned to the mean fare, contributing a fixed ~2.05 RMSE floor that dilutes the gain to ~0.9% overall (4.102→~4.06-4.07); the timestamp-format and n_jobs tweaks only keep the larger workload inside the time budget without changing results.

Airport distances should help capture JFK flat-fare and LGA/EWR surcharge trips, but raw coordinates already give LightGBM most of the spatial signal and the corrupt-row floor caps the gain, so expect only about a 1% RMSE drop.

log1p+expm1 without bias correction predicts a geometric/conditional-median-like fare rather than the RMSE-optimal dollar mean, and log-scale early stopping underweights high-fare and corrupt unpredictable rows, so I expect a small regression.

Distance is the dominant, genuinely monotone feature, so the constraint acts as a mild structural regularizer and should slightly improve generalization; but with 4M rows the unconstrained model already learns a near-monotone distance response, and the ~2.8% corrupt test rows predicted as mean fare dilute any gain, so expect only a small improvement (~0.3-0.4%) with negligible runtime cost.

Fitting squared loss on log1p(fare) and exponentiating without bias correction approximates the conditional median (geometric mean) of the right-skewed fare, which sits ~3-5% below the conditional mean that RMSE rewards; with 4M rows estimation variance is already tiny, so this systematic low bias slightly outweighs any variance-stabilization/outlier-robustness benefit, while the 2.8% corrupt test rows get the same mean-fare fallback and anchor the score, yielding a small net RMSE regression.

In-sample target encoding leaks each training row's own fare into its cell/route statistics (up to ~1/21 weight for rare route keys despite m=20 smoothing), so the trees over-rely on these features whose train-time predictive power doesn't transfer to val/test rows; the log-count 'mismatch' the change fixes is a monotone shift that trees are invariant to, so the net effect is a mild regression typical of dropping OOF encoding.

Optimizing MSE in log space optimizes relative error, not the raw-dollar RMSE being graded; expm1 back-transform yields geometric-mean-like predictions biased systematically low (no smearing/bias correction), which raw RMSE punishes most on the high fares that dominate squared error — the variance stabilization and outlier down-weighting help slightly but typically not enough to offset the bias, so a small (~1–2%) regression is expected.

Airport-distance features are a well-known win for this dataset (JFK flat-fare and EWR surcharge trips become trivially splittable), but with raw coordinates already available to the trees and a ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows, the gain is modest — expect local valid-row RMSE to drop ~0.1, translating to roughly 1-1.5% on the graded score.

Keeping corrupt-coordinate rows in training lets LightGBM learn NaN-branch predictions conditioned on year/hour/weekday/passenger_count (and any single valid endpoint) for the ~2.8% of unpredictable test rows, which modestly beats the global-mean fallback, while predictions for the 97% valid rows are essentially unchanged; the corrupt rows' high fare variance limits the gain to a small overall RMSE improvement.

Quadrupling the training sample to ~3.6M cleaned rows gives LightGBM a modest generalization gain (roughly 3-4% lower RMSE on predictable rows), but the ~2.8% corrupt test rows still get the mean-fare fallback, so the ~2.1 RMSE floor limits the overall improvement to about 2.5-3%; the I/O, float32, explicit datetime format, and n_jobs changes are metric-neutral.

Out-of-fold smoothed target encoding of pickup/dropoff cells and route keys is a proven high-value feature for this competition (captures tolls, JFK flat fares, typical route prices that haversine misses), likely cutting valid-row RMSE from ~3.6 to ~3.42, but the ~2.8% corrupt test rows impose a ~2.1 RMSE floor that dilutes the overall gain to roughly 4%, with minimal downside risk given the m=20 smoothing and log-count features.

L2 training on log1p(fare) fits conditional log-means, and expm1 without a Jensen/smearing correction is biased low for dollar RMSE (especially via the weak fallback model), so I expect a small regression.

Manhattan distance and bearing are genuinely informative for NYC fares (grid street network, direction-dependent tolls) and LightGBM exploits them beyond haversine, but the ~2.8% corrupt test rows scored by the unchanged fallback model cap the total gain, so expect only a modest ~1-2% overall RMSE improvement (roughly 3.6 -> 3.53 on valid rows).

Airport/landmark distance features are a well-established win in this competition (JFK flat-fare and airport surcharge regimes become trivially separable for GBDTs), typically shaving 3-6% off RMSE; gains are capped by the ~2.8% corrupt test rows predicted as the mean, which set an irreducible MSE floor.

L1 fits the conditional median, which sits below the conditional mean for the right-skewed fare distribution, adding a small systematic downward bias that RMSE penalizes; the robustness benefit is limited because min_child_samples=100 over ~3.6M clean rows already averages out rare glitched fares, and L1's constant-magnitude gradients converge slower within the same 1000-tree budget, while the ~2.8% corrupt test rows still get the mean-fare fallback unchanged.

log1p/expm1 without a smearing correction fits E[log fare], whose inverse is below E[fare] for right-skewed rides, slightly hurting RMSE; unchanged invalid-row fallback caps the effect to a small regression.

The metric is RMSE, which is optimized by conditional-mean (L2) predictions; with fares already clipped to (0,500] and corrupt rows dropped, the residual outliers L1 robustness protects against are limited, while L1's constant-magnitude gradients converge slower at the same lr/rounds (slight underfit) and its median-oriented predictions sit off the RMSE-optimal mean — early stopping on RMSE can't fix the objective mismatch, so expect a modest regression of a few percent.

RMSE is aligned with L2; Huber with delta=$1 is close to L1 for most residuals and should pull predictions toward a robust/median location, likely underpredicting high-fare rows on same-distribution validation/test data.

RMSE rewards the conditional mean in dollars; fitting log1p(fare) with L2 and back-transforming without a smearing bias-correction estimates the conditional median/geometric mean, systematically under-predicting — by a few percent, worst on the high-fare rides that dominate squared error — and with ~900k rows the variance-stabilization benefit won't offset that bias, so expect a small regression (~4.19-4.21) rather than an improvement.

Airport-distance and near-airport flag features are a well-established win for this dataset — they let the model isolate flat-fare JFK trips and surcharge-heavy EWR/LGA trips that raw coordinates + trip distance can't cleanly express, giving a modest real gain on the ~97% valid rows, but the ~2.8% corrupt test rows (handled by the unchanged fallback model) put a hard floor that dilutes the overall graded improvement to roughly 1%.

Quadrupling the training sample from 1M to 4M rows gives LightGBM meaningfully more signal with unchanged hyperparameters, typically shaving a few percent off the learnable part of the error; the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows stays fixed, so overall RMSE drops modestly from 4.138 to roughly 4.03, and 3.6M rows x 10 features trains well within the time budget.
5-fold bagging should slightly reduce model variance and reuse the holdout rows across folds, while the invalid-row mean override stays fixed, so expect a small RMSE improvement.

The OOF-smoothed pickup-cell mean fare is a strong leak-free local target encoding that captures effects (airport flat fares, neighborhood price levels) that axis-aligned lat/lon splits approximate only inefficiently, so it should cut valid-row RMSE a couple percent; the ~2.8% corrupt-test-row floor limits total graded gain, and the added mlflow logging is wrapped best-effort no-op code that doesn't affect training.

Snapping to a 0.01° grid destroys sub-km precision in distance_km (std ~0.3-0.4 km error, worst for short trips that can collapse to distance 0) that the tree model actively exploits, while providing no real pooling benefit since LightGBM already partitions space internally and the 0.01° route encoding is barely changed — expect a mild RMSE regression.

L1 boosting fits the conditional median while RMSE rewards the conditional mean; on right-skewed fares that mismatch usually costs ~1% RMSE despite outlier robustness, with RMSE-based early stopping limiting the damage (the 2.8% corrupt-row floor is unaffected).

L1 boosting fits the conditional median, which sits below the conditional mean for right-skewed fare distributions and is therefore systematically suboptimal under RMSE; the robustness to surviving outlier fares only partially offsets this median-vs-mean bias on the ~97% valid test rows, so a slight RMSE regression is expected.
