Airport-proximity features capture the distinct flat-fare pricing of JFK/LGA/EWR trips — historically one of the highest-value feature additions in this competition — and LightGBM with 1M rows has the capacity to exploit them, so expect a solid ~2-3% RMSE improvement (roughly 4.14 → ~4.02), bounded by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows that these features cannot help.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean, so switching to L1 (conditional median) typically degrades RMSE; with fares already filtered to (0,500] the outlier-robustness benefit is small, while the median of the right-skewed fare distribution sits below the mean, biasing predictions low and pushing RMSE up modestly (the ~2.8% corrupt test rows are unaffected as they still get the mean-fare fallback).

Rounding coordinates to ~1km grid cells discards fine-grained location information that the trees could exploit via their own splits, while the preserved continuous haversine distance and zone-level location effects keep the loss small — LightGBM gains little regularization benefit here since the test set is the same distribution as training, so expect a slight regression well within an order of run-to-run noise.

L1 trains toward the conditional median while RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean; since extreme fare outliers are already removed by the (0,500] cleaning, the robustness buys little and the median-vs-mean bias on the right-skewed fare distribution (plus slightly worse split choices for RMSE) modestly worsens RMSE, with early stopping on validation RMSE capping the damage.

Adding a rotated Manhattan-style grid distance gives LightGBM a more realistic street-network travel proxy that complements haversine distance, typically yielding a small RMSE gain, but the corrupt-row noise floor (~2.1) and already-informative coordinate/distance features cap the improvement at well under 1%.

The cross-fitted, smoothed directional route-mean encoding is leakage-safe and gives LightGBM the pickup×dropoff interaction signal (airport flat fares, tolls, typical route pricing) that axis-aligned splits on raw coordinates struggle to learn; smoothing=50 pushes rare routes to the global mean (harmless fallback), so a modest but real gain on the ~97% valid test rows is expected, partially masked by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows.

The grid-aligned Manhattan distance (rotated 29° to match NYC's street grid) correlates better with actual taxi routes than haversine alone and is a known-helpful feature for this dataset, giving a modest RMSE gain; the MLflow tracking additions are wrapped in try/except and don't affect model output or runtime materially.

Doubling the training sample from 1M to 2M rows gives LightGBM a modest learning-curve gain on the predictable rows (~2% better local RMSE), but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows dilutes this to roughly a 1-1.5% overall improvement; 2M rows still fits the time budget.

The 16-way airport-route categorical cleanly captures flat-fare JFK/LGA/EWR trips (a known strong signal the raw coords only partially encode), improving valid-row RMSE by roughly 0.15-0.25, but the ~2.8% corrupt test rows still get the mean-fare fallback, capping the overall gain at a few percent; the MLflow/progress additions are inert and runtime is unaffected.

Plain LightGBM on raw numerics + per-position f_27 encoding is the well-known ~0.975-0.978 baseline for TPS-May-2022: trees cannot easily reconstruct the letter-count structure of f_27 from ten per-position categoricals, and 2000 rounds underfits vs the 3000-round baseline the README says was still improving, so it likely lands below the surprisingly strong MLP's 0.9866 despite GBDTs being the standard tabular workhorse.

Quantile one-hot binning loses within-bin resolution per feature, but with 31 numeric columns the joint bin space keeps predictions fine-grained for AUC, while making the MLP robust to the heavy-tailed f_28 and heterogeneous marginals and giving it tree-like piecewise responses that suit this interaction-heavy dataset — so a small net gain over the 0.9866 baseline is likely, consistent with published results on binned numeric embeddings for MLPs.

PCA whitening is target-blind: with already-standardized, weakly correlated features it stays close to a signed axis permutation, per-leaf linear models span the same function class (only ridge shrinkage directions change), and the only real structural effect is smearing the discrete f_27 ordinal columns into dense PCs, which slightly dilutes their clean split structure — so expect near-neutral with a small negative tilt, well within run-to-run noise either way.
Whole-string f_27 is too sparse/ID-like, so the smoothed TE mostly collapses to the prior on holdout/test and discards useful position-wise character signal, giving a modest AUC drop.

f_27 strings are 10-char codes from a large alphabet and are essentially unique per row, so the OOF/test target encoding degenerates to the constant global prior (unseen strings -> prior; single-sample fits smoothed at m=20 to ~prior), which means the change effectively deletes the ten per-character signal columns that drive most of the baseline's AUC, leaving a numeric-only-plus-nunique model that scores around 0.973-0.975.

The added sums and ternary threshold indicators match the known additive generative interactions in this synthetic dataset (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26), which GBDT can only approximate crudely via many per-feature splits; giving them explicitly should let the trees nail the sharp decision boundaries and lift AUC modestly from the already-high 0.9915 baseline.

Equal-weight rank averaging with a much weaker partner hurts: standardized logistic regression on these interaction-driven features (even with the 3 additive sums) should reach only ~0.88-0.91 AUC, and its signal is largely subsumed by the 3000-tree LightGBM, so the 0.5-weight blend drags the ranking below the 0.9842 tree-only score rather than adding useful diversity.

A small CPU MLP on scaled features (including the 3 additive sums) will train fully within budget and capture the smooth additive interactions, but it underperforms GBDT on this dataset—especially extracting signal from the ordinal-encoded f_27 letters and sharp thresholds—so expect a modest regression from 0.9842 to roughly 0.972–0.975.

GBDT excels on this dataset's sharp f_27 character-position and numeric interactions; a small MLP on ordinal-encoded characters and heavy-tailed standardized numerics typically lands ~0.95-0.96 on TPS-May-2022, a clear regression from the 0.977 LightGBM baseline.

Linear leaves should modestly help on this dataset's additive/oblique boundaries (target ~ sums of continuous features crossing thresholds), standardization/float32 are split-neutral, and early stopping on the 80k holdout caps overfitting from noisy leaf regressions; the ~2x linear-tree slowdown is the main risk but early stopping plus a ~5-7 min baseline should still finish under the 15-min kill, so expect a small net gain rather than a failure.

The unique-letter count of f_27 is a known informative feature in TPS May 2022 (the target depends partly on character diversity in f_27), and it adds information not recoverable by trees from 10 independent per-position ordinal splits, so a small AUC gain of ~0.001 is expected with all else held fixed.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is a well-known genuine interaction in TPS-May-2022 (decision boundary along the sum), and f_02+f_21 / f_05+f_22 sums also carry signal; giving axis-aligned trees these directions typically yields a small but real AUC gain (~+0.0003-0.0005) with identical model/budget.

The raw 10-letter string is nearly unique per row (~800k distinct values), so with LightGBM's default min_data_per_group=100 no categorical split on f_27 is ever eligible — the new feature is effectively inert — while the 10 genuinely informative per-position letter columns are deleted, leaving only numerics + letter counts and costing real positional signal (interactions this dataset is known to hinge on).

Adjacent-char bigrams declared as native categoricals let LightGBM split directly on joint character pairs (a known useful interaction in TPS-May-2022's f_27), giving a small but real AUC gain over the deep ordinal-split baseline; the model could already approximate pairwise interactions via successive splits, so the improvement is modest (+~0.0005-0.001), with no runtime or unseen-category risk.

The gain-mined supervised products captured real multiplicative interactions worth a few 1e-4 AUC, while unsupervised PCA directions are linear rotations that axis-aligned trees can already approximate, so they add ~nothing and the score slips back toward the no-interaction baseline.

f_27 strings are nearly unique per row (~900k distinct 10-letter codes), so FeatureHasher on the whole string just assigns each row a pseudo-random bucket among 64; buckets mix many unrelated strings, carry no generalizable signal for test, and the 64 noise columns only dilute splits — effectively this deletes f_27, the dominant signal source (the per-position ordinals are what let trees exploit its letter interactions), leaving only numeric+product features which historically reach only ~0.86-0.89 AUC versus 0.9753 with f_27 encoded properly.

ExtraTrees' random thresholds and sqrt-feature splits are substantially less efficient than 3000-round LightGBM at learning this interaction-heavy tabular signal, likely causing a 2–3 point relative AUC regression.

The sklearn MLP should finish in time, but ordinal f_27 features, heavy-tailed f_28, large-batch constant-lr Adam for at most 40 epochs, and accuracy-based early stopping without refitting on the internal validation split likely underfit the fine tabular interactions relative to the 3000-tree LightGBM, giving a modest AUC regression.

Bag-of-letters counts and nunique capture order-invariant f_27 signal that per-position categoricals can only reconstruct with many splits; this is a known-useful feature family for TPS May 2022, so expect a small real gain (~+0.0002-0.0004 AUC), with minor sampling noise from colsample_bytree over more features.

The full 10-char f_27 sequence is high-cardinality and nearly unique per row, so its frequency is an almost-constant, signal-free feature; dropping the per-position categoricals effectively removes all f_27 information and leaves a numeric-only LightGBM (~0.90 AUC), a large regression from 0.9768.

Per-letter counts and the unique-character count of f_27 are known strong signals for this competition (the target depends partly on letter multiset properties) that the per-position ordinals only express through many tree splits, so giving LightGBM these aggregate features directly should yield a solid AUC gain of roughly +0.005-0.008 with negligible overfitting risk.

Explicit gain-mined pairwise products surface the multiplicative interactions this dataset was designed with, giving the trees easier splits for a small AUC bump (~+0.0005), though a 3000-tree GBM on 720k rows already captures much of this on its own, and the extra screening fit plus 25 columns still fits the time budget.

Early stopping should not fire, so best_iter is about 3000 and the refit uses roughly 3333 trees on all 800k rows; with holdout AUC still rising, the extra data and rounds should give a small positive AUC bump.

Declaring the ten 0-25 letter-code columns as native LightGBM categoricals lets it find optimal many-vs-rest letter partitions instead of threshold splits on arbitrary alphabetical order — a known modest gain on this competition where f_27 carries most signal — with identical deterministic encodings, no overfit risk at 800k rows, and comparable runtime.

Distinct-character count of f_27 is a famously strong aggregate feature in TPS May 2022 that per-position ordinal encodings only approximate poorly, so adding it should give LightGBM a small but real AUC gain over the 0.98175 baseline.

This dataset's signal depends on higher-order feature interactions; capping trees at depth 2 (4 leaves) restricts the model to main effects plus pairwise terms, so the ensemble underfits despite the full 3000 rounds and AUC drops roughly 1.5-2%.

CPU LightGBM with only 600 trees, 31 leaves, and coarse max_bin=63 is a decent but under-tuned config for this dataset (the README's own GBDT baseline used 3000 trees/127 leaves and was still improving), so it should land near typical GBDT scores around 0.980, a small regression from the MLP's 0.9822.

LightGBM with this weakened config (600 trees, only 31 leaves, coarse max_bin=63, no bagging) plus logloss-based iteration selection underfits the smooth feature interactions the tuned MLP captured; plain LightGBM on this dataset typically lands ~0.975-0.978, below the MLP's 0.9822.

Quartile-binning floats to 4 ordered codes discards fine-grained signal that a 3000-tree, still-underfit GBDT was actively exploiting (LightGBM's own 255-bin histograms are strictly richer), so added bias yields a modest AUC regression of roughly half a point; runtime and pipeline are otherwise unaffected.

Cutting num_leaves to 7 caps each tree at ~depth 3, and this dataset's signal lives in high-order interactions (especially within f_27's character positions), so even 3000 additive rounds at lr 0.05 won't fully compensate — the model underfits and AUC drops by roughly a percentage point.

4-leaf trees cap each tree at ~2-3 splits, so the model can only encode low-order interactions per round while this synthetic dataset's signal lives in higher-order feature interactions; since the 127-leaf run was still improving at 3000 rounds, the much weaker trees converge even slower and underfit, but boosting 3000 simple additive trees still preserves most of the ranking signal, so expect a moderate drop rather than a collapse.

A single additive sum of three existing numeric features adds almost no new information to gradient-boosted trees, which already capture such interactions via successive splits, so the score should stay essentially unchanged within run-to-run noise (possibly a negligible bump).

Adding a sum of three features already present is near-redundant for gradient-boosted trees (they can approximate additive combinations via splits), so the effect is within run-to-run noise; at best a marginal gain from giving axis-aligned trees a ready-made diagonal direction, hence a prediction of essentially unchanged AUC (~0.9769-0.9770).

A CPU MLP on raw numerics plus ordinal-encoded f_27 characters (no embeddings, no engineered interactions) should train ~25-40 epochs within the 420s budget and reach a respectable AUC, but on this interaction-heavy synthetic tabular dataset a plain MLP typically trails tuned gradient-boosted trees by roughly 0.01 AUC.

Treating the 26-letter codes as native LightGBM categoricals lets the split finder form arbitrary letter subsets per position instead of thresholding a meaningless ordinal code, which better captures letter-identity effects in f_27; with 800k rows there's plenty of data per category, so a modest AUC gain (~+0.001) is expected.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is a well-known informative feature in TPS May 2022 that trees cannot easily derive from per-position ordinals, so adding it should give a small but real AUC gain (~+0.001) without changing runtime materially.

Since ~90% of pixels are near-perfect white background, the unweighted loss dilutes gradients on strokes where squared error concentrates; darkness-weighted MSE reallocates capacity to stroke/edge pixels, and the sum/w.sum() normalization keeps the loss scale (hence LR dynamics) roughly unchanged — the main risk is a slight dark-bias on ambiguous pixels, but the net effect should be a small (~1-2%) RMSE improvement.

The time-based budget yields roughly 8-10k steps (4-5x the original 2000, minus in-loop eval overhead) with cosine LR still annealing to ~0, so the undertrained U-Net fits better; gains are modest because the small model and fixed features cap achievable RMSE and overfitting risk on 105 images is low.

L1 is a well-replicated stronger default for pixel-level restoration (Zhao et al. 2017): its constant-magnitude gradients avoid the late-training stall of L2 and stop the few large-residual stain pixels from dominating, so even under an RMSE metric a small net gain (~2%) is expected, though run-to-run seed noise makes the outcome uncertain.

With only ~105 training images reused for 16k crops, the large 5-level U-Net can overfit to scan-specific gray-level statistics; mild input-only brightness/contrast jitter regularizes against this and typically yields a small val/test gain, though the benefit is limited because train and test share the same synthetic noise process (no real exposure shift), so expect ~1% improvement rather than a large one.
Same trained weights; adding 0.75x/1.25x views to the existing flip ensemble should mildly cancel residual noise/edge errors, with gains capped by single-scale training.

Dropout2d on e2/e3 (including the e2 skip path) injects feature noise into a short 2000-step regression training where random crops+flips already regularize, so slower convergence likely outweighs any overfitting reduction, giving a small RMSE regression roughly within run-to-run noise.

Dropout2d after BatchNorm in every block slows convergence within the fixed 180s time budget and BN/dropout interaction degrades dense regression output; with only mild overfitting in the baseline (test RMSE already 0.0085), the regularization benefit won't offset the undertraining, giving a small regression.

The extra 1/8-resolution stage roughly doubles the receptive field (~41→~89px), which helps separate large-scale stains/wrinkles from text strokes, and 4x parameters still train fine under the wall-clock-bound cosine schedule; the ~25-35% fewer steps within the fixed 180s partially offsets the gain, so expect a modest improvement on an already-low 0.00866 RMSE.

A median-23 background channel gives the U-Net an explicit local illumination estimate, effectively normalizing background shade across images, which typically yields a modest but real RMSE gain for document denoising; with training steps unchanged (2000), expect ~4-7% improvement rather than a dramatic one.

The 5-level U-Net's much larger receptive field and 256px crops help remove large-scale stains (coffee/sun spots) that the 3-level net misses, at the same pixels-per-step, so a modest gain is likely — tempered by less crop diversity per batch (8 vs 32), BN on smaller batches, and only 105 training images.

4-way flip TTA averages out prediction variance in a model already trained with flip augmentation, typically yielding a small but real RMSE gain (~1-3%); the 4x inference cost is negligible since training dominates runtime.

The baseline's 2000 steps ran well under budget, so a 180s wall-clock loop with time-based cosine decay roughly doubles optimizer steps (~4k) on GPU; more training with proper LR annealing should modestly improve convergence and cut RMSE by a few percent, with validation overhead and possible slower hardware capping the gain.
Charbonnier optimizes robust absolute error rather than the graded squared error; it may sharpen strokes but should trade a little RMSE for lower MAE, so I expect a small regression.

Injecting fresh Gaussian noise into inputs only (targets stay clean) acts as ridge-like regularization that prevents memorizing the small training set's specific noise realizations and forces context-based reconstruction; the train/test noise-level mismatch (test has no extra Gaussian) costs a little over-smoothing, but with ~105 training images the variance reduction should slightly dominate, giving a small net RMSE improvement at zero wall-clock cost.
GroupNorm should remove the crop-trained versus full-page BatchNorm statistics mismatch with little capacity or optimization cost, giving a small RMSE improvement rather than a large change.

SSIM+L1 typically trades a tiny bit of MSE-optimality for sharper stroke edges and better stain/shading structure, and in practice the Zhao et al. composite lands very close to (often slightly better than) MSE-trained RMSE on denoising; with the same architecture, data, and short 2000-step schedule, I expect a small ~1-2% improvement rather than a large swing.

The 8-fold dihedral TTA is implemented correctly (proper inverse transform ordering, per-transform padding/cropping) and averaging over rotations/flips reduces prediction variance; since training only included flips (not rot90), the rotated views add partially decorrelated errors, yielding a modest but reliable ~2-3% RMSE improvement with negligible runtime cost.

The graded metric is RMSE, whose optimum is the conditional mean that MSE directly targets; pure SSIM optimizes a different structural objective, and Zhao et al. (2017) show pure SSIM training loses roughly 0.5–1 dB PSNR (~6–12% RMSE) versus L2, so a moderate single-digit-percent RMSE regression is expected despite stable training and unchanged runtime.

Residual (DnCNN-style) prediction with zero-init final conv gives the network an identity shortcut and removes sigmoid saturation near the mostly-white background, which typically speeds convergence substantially in a short 2000-step run; expect a solid but not dramatic RMSE gain (~15%), with low regression risk since clamping and TTA are preserved.

Under Adam the sqrt(MSE) rescaling is nearly scale-invariant, so the real effect is the modest 0.1-weight SSIM term, which acts mostly early/mid training and nudges edge/background structure where the RMSE error mass concentrates, yielding a small (~1%) improvement with little risk of regression or timeout.

Document noise is sparse/localized so identity is a near-optimal init; residual (DnCNN-style) learning eases optimization substantially in a short 2000-step schedule, typically giving a high-single-digit RMSE improvement, with zero-init final conv stabilizing early training and clamp preserving output bounds.

Synthesizing 630 extra pairs from the clean targets with stains/shading/speckle roughly matches the real corruption and gives the small U-Net ~7x more diverse training signal (better background cleaning, less overfitting to 105 images), while real pairs anchor the mapping; the whole-image Gaussian blur is a partial distribution mismatch that likely caps the gain at a modest ~3% improvement.

4.5x more Adam steps (9,000 vs 2,000) with the cosine schedule stretched accordingly lets the small U-Net converge more fully; with random 128px crops over 105 images overfitting risk is low, so a modest ~9% RMSE gain is expected, and 9k steps of a tiny model on GPU should still fit within ~10 minutes.

Dihedral-8 TTA is correctly implemented (all 8 distinct transforms with exact inverses, including transpose views handled on padded multiples of 8), and averaging 8 consistent prediction maps reduces prediction variance for this U-Net denoiser, typically yielding a modest ~1-3% RMSE improvement without touching training.

Since grading is RMSE, swapping the directly-aligned MSE objective for L1 (which fits the conditional median, not the mean) usually costs a small amount of RMSE; L1's robustness to large stain residuals and constant gradients partially offset this, so I expect only a modest single-digit-percent regression.

The mild 3:1 foreground weighting should reduce under-reconstructed ink pixels while background remains abundant enough to stay accurate, giving a small net RMSE gain despite slight objective/metric misalignment.

The weighted objective no longer matches the unweighted RMSE metric: it biases predictions darker wherever the input-to-target mapping is ambiguous (stains, stroke edges), inflating error on the numerically dominant white background, so gains on rare ink pixels likely don't fully compensate — expecting a small net regression.

Residual prediction with a zero-initialized head starts training at the identity (RMSE ≈ noise level instead of sigmoid's ~0.5-everywhere output) and removes sigmoid saturation at the near-white/near-black extremes that dominate document pixels, which is a well-established win for denoising and matters a lot in a short 2000-step run; only inference-time clamping remains, so expect a moderate (~5-8%) RMSE improvement with identical compute.

Training with L1 optimizes the conditional median rather than the mean, so under an RMSE evaluation it typically scores slightly worse than MSE training; the model and budget are unchanged, so expect a small regression on the order of a few percent.

Zero-initialized residual head starts training at the identity (a strong prior for denoising), and removing the sigmoid eliminates vanishing gradients at the dominant near-0/near-1 document intensities, so the same 20-epoch budget converges faster and to a better optimum — a well-established gain (cf. DnCNN-style residual learning), with clipping at inference handling the now-unbounded output.

Halving BASE_CH cuts parameters ~4x; with only 2000 training steps over abundant pixel data the model is capacity-limited rather than overfitting, so expect mild underfitting and a modest RMSE increase, though the low complexity of document denoising keeps the regression small and runtime safely within budget.

Upweighting dark clean pixels is mismatched with unweighted RMSE: it may sharpen faint strokes but biases ambiguous pixels toward black and trades off dominant background accuracy, likely causing a slight regression.

The 31x31 grey-closing background-division channel is the classic, highly informative feature for this task (it erases stains/shadows while preserving text), and the raw channel is retained so information is only added, so with the unchanged 2000-step budget the UNet should reach a moderately better RMSE; the forced-CPU execution with 8 pinned threads plus the extra closing preprocessing adds runtime but should still finish inside the 15-minute hard kill.

The fp32-head edit is numerically inert (weights stay fp32, and under the added runtime.toml's CPU-only setting autocast is already disabled, so the new block changes nothing), so barring a CPU-timeout the score is unchanged modulo hardware-numerics noise, ~0.0162.
Correct four-flip self-ensembling should reduce small view-dependent padding/pooling errors, but gains are limited because training already used random horizontal/vertical flips.

NAFNet's residual (dirty + delta) formulation, zero-init residual scales, SimpleGate gating, and channel attention give a better inductive bias and faster, more stable convergence than the plain BN U-Net at the same 2000-step budget, typically worth ~8-12% RMSE on this task; main risk is wall-clock since runtime.json forces CPU, but the width-16 NAFNet is ~10x fewer FLOPs than the baseline U-Net so it should still finish.

The frozen trunk was fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k, whose 120 dog classes exactly match this label set and whose training data overlaps the Stanford Dogs images, so the pretrained head is a strong, well-calibrated second linear classifier on the same features; blending with holdout-tuned weight/temperature (with w=0 as a safe fallback) should give a modest but real log-loss gain over the pure LR baseline.

PCA-256 (unwhitened) keeps the bulk of feature variance while decorrelating inputs, so lbfgs converges much better within max_iter=1000 and the L2 penalty acts on a cleaner 256-d space; with C re-tuned on the same holdout this typically yields a small denoising/conditioning gain for linear probes on frozen features, though fine-grained signal lost in discarded low-variance components caps the improvement at a few percent.

Mixup/CutMix with the standard ConvNeXt recipe values is a sound regularizer for 120 confusable classes on ~8k images and typically improves log loss via better-calibrated, less overconfident predictions; gains are capped at a few percent because the 6-epoch schedule is short for prob=1.0 mixing, but temperature scaling on the clean val split and unchanged architecture keep the risk of regression low.

Widening RandomResizedCrop to the ImageNet-standard (0.08, 1.0) matches the backbone's pretraining augmentation and adds much-needed regularization/view diversity for ~69 train images per class, which should reduce overconfident errors and modestly lower log loss, though the 6-epoch budget caps the gain.

ConvNeXt-V2 Large (IN-22k->IN-1k, ~88.6% top-1) is a vastly stronger feature extractor than ResNet-50 V1 (~76%), and since the 120 dog breeds are a subset of ImageNet synsets, both its pooled features and its 1000-d log-probs are directly far more discriminative, so the identical linear-probe pipeline should drop log loss from ~0.45 to roughly ~0.30 (the extended C grid adds a small extra gain); runtime stays within budget on a datacenter GPU.

The 1000-d log-softmax block is a deterministic function of the pooled vector, so it adds no new information; ~880 of those columns are near-constant on all-dog images and StandardScaler inflates them into unit-variance noise dims that waste the L2 budget — dropping them should give a small but real improvement in log loss, with identical runtime behavior and no failure risk.

Ridge decision boundaries on strong frozen features are typically on par with logistic regression, and explicit holdout temperature scaling of the scores usually beats LR's predict_proba calibration for log loss (C-selection is only a crude implicit calibration knob), so I expect a small improvement, limited by mild selection noise from the ~1380-sample holdout and possible coarse T-grid mismatch on test.

PCA-128 keeps the dominant variance but fine-grained breed-discriminative directions often live in the low-variance tail that gets truncated, and the L2-regularized LR on 2560-d was not badly overfit to begin with, so expect a small regression in log loss (roughly +0.01) rather than a gain from denoising.

ConvNeXt-Base with ImageNet-22k pretraining is a far stronger frozen feature extractor than ResNet-50 IMAGENET1K_V1 for this task (the 120 breeds are literally ImageNet classes), and the holdout re-selection of C preserves calibration for the new feature scale, so log loss should drop from ~0.45 to ~0.29; the extra mlflow/TMPDIR/fork changes are infra-neutral and runtime stays well within budget.

End-to-end fine-tuning of an ImageNet-22k-pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny (whose pretraining includes these very dog-breed classes) is far stronger than frozen RN50 features + logistic regression for 120-class fine-grained recognition, and augmentation, flip TTA, label smoothing plus validation-tuned temperature scaling further cut log loss; the 6-epoch schedule (~144 steps/epoch at batch 64 with bf16) fits the 7-min guard on a modern GPU, with early-stop risk only mildly degrading the result, so expect ~0.27-0.31 vs 0.4515.

All 120 breeds are native ImageNet classes (and the test images are ImageNet-derived), so the previously discarded fc head contributes log-prob features from a classifier trained on ~10x more labeled data for exactly these classes; combining standardized pooled+logprob features with holdout-selected C should cut log loss from ~0.45 to roughly 0.33-0.36, with mild risk only from the C grid ceiling and extra fit time.

Replacing ResNet-50-V1 features with complementary IN22k-supervised (ConvNeXt-B), CLIP ViT-B/16, and DINOv2 ViT-B/14 features substantially strengthens the representation for fine-grained breed discrimination (DINOv2/CLIP linear probes are far better on dogs than RN50-V1), and block-wise L2 normalization plus a holdout-tuned C makes the LR ensemble effective, so log loss should drop from ~0.45 to ~0.30 with no realistic runtime risk (~10k images, 3 frozen backbones, well within budget).

Focal loss is a reasonable calibration tool versus plain CE, but here it replaces label smoothing (which is already well-suited to log loss), and its hard-example emphasis plus reduced effective gradient late in training—under an LR/schedule tuned for CE in a short 10-epoch run—typically yields comparable or slightly worse NLL, so I expect a modest regression around 3-5%.

Freezing conv1-layer3 still leaves layer4+fc ample capacity, and on this tiny ImageNet-dog subset it should act mainly as a regularizer/calibrator rather than remove needed features, giving a small log-loss gain.

Horizontal-flip TTA on test images averages two quasi-independent probability estimates per image, reducing prediction variance and improving calibration; dog photos are near bilaterally symmetric so flipped views stay in-distribution for the ImageNet-pretrained ViT, giving the usual small but reliable log-loss gain (~2%), while the NUM_WORKERS=0 change only affects data-loading robustness, not the metric.

The current augreg ViT-B/16 is ImageNet-21k-pretrained and fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k, whose label set literally contains these 120 dog breeds, so its frozen features are near-optimally tuned for this task; CLIP ViT-B/32 features are less fine-grained (contrastive image-text training, coarser 32x32 patches) and a fixed C=0.3 linear probe on them typically lands well below supervised ImageNet features on Stanford Dogs, so log loss should regress substantially (roughly 0.51 to ~0.8).

PCA-256 on dogs-only ResNet-50 GAP features should retain ~85-90% of variance and most breed-discriminative signal (120 classes fit comfortably in 256 dims), while denoising and better-conditioning the 120-class logistic probe; the main risk is that C=0.3 was tuned on raw 2048-d features and isn't re-tuned, but the 8x dimensionality cut roughly compensates, so I expect a small net log-loss improvement (~1-2%), with the diff itself being bug-free (PCA fit on train only, view order preserved through reshape, PCA cost negligible within budget).

DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings are far stronger than supervised ResNet-50 features for fine-grained breed discrimination (linear-probe accuracy on Stanford Dogs typically jumps ~5 points), which should cut log loss roughly 30% from 0.438 to ~0.30, with the holdout-based C re-selection and identical 10-view TTA preserving calibration and adding marginal gains; runtime is well within budget since only ~113k frozen ViT-B forwards are needed.

With n=9199 vs d=2816 and C=1.0, the baseline logistic regression is a near-MLE fit, so PCA-256 mainly trades a small truncation bias (deep-feature spectra decay fast, and fine-grained breed cues partly live in mid/low-variance directions) against mild denoising, decorrelation, and much better lbfgs conditioning/convergence; these effects roughly cancel with a slight net edge to the PCA-whitened model, so expect a near-neutral outcome with a small (~1%) log-loss improvement, well within budget since PCA on 10k x 2816 takes seconds.

k-NN votes on ~77 images/class in a 120-way fine-grained task yield coarse, miscalibrated, often confidently-wrong probabilities (distance weighting sharpens them further) that log loss punishes harshly, so replacing the discriminatively trained linear probe should regress substantially from ~0.54 to roughly ~1.0 despite equal runtime.

End-to-end fine-tuning with a sane recipe (warmup+cosine, label smoothing 0.1, RRC/flip augmentation) directly optimizes log loss and typically adds several top-1 points over frozen ResNet-50 features on Stanford Dogs within 10 epochs, and ~1,440 fp16 steps fits the time budget; label smoothing keeps probabilities calibrated, so log loss should drop from ~0.453 to ~0.34-0.36.

Swapping ResNet50-V1 features for augreg ImageNet-21k ViT-B/16 pooled features gives a much stronger linear probe on fine-grained dog breeds (typical top-1 jump ~84%→90%+), cutting log loss by roughly 30%; C=0.3 was tuned for ResNet features so the LR head may be slightly suboptimal but should still work well on the normalized 768-d ViT features.

The training path is untouched and the only effective change is 10-view (5-crop + hflip) TTA with probability averaging, a well-established variance-reduction trick that improves log loss for frozen-feature linear probes; the corner crops overlap the training center-crop view substantially (16px shifts), so gains are moderate (~5-10% relative), while the added mlflow telemetry is best-effort no-op and the 10x test forward passes still fit the time budget.

Concatenating a stronger, architecturally distinct ConvNeXt-Tiny (IN22K→IN1K) feature block with per-block L2 normalization should clearly improve the linear probe on this fine-grained, ImageNet-overlapping task (typically ~20-27% log-loss gain), while C=1.0 on normalized features is a reasonable if untuned choice and runtime roughly doubles but stays within the budget.

The breed→ImageNet mapping uses exact string equality, but torchvision's category names contain comma-separated aliases (e.g., 'affenpinscher, monkey pinscher, monkey dog'), so `assert len(matches)==1` fails on the very first breed, crashing the run before any submission is written — the graded score stays at the baseline.
The PCA step is correct and fast, but keeping C=0.3 while hard-truncating 2048 features to 256 PCs should discard some low-variance breed signal and slightly underfit, so log loss rises a little.

ResNet-50 was trained with average pooling, so swapping to max pooling yields off-distribution, sparser, higher-variance descriptors that typically degrade a linear probe modestly (a few accuracy points); the temperature calibration and fixed C=0.3 limit but don't eliminate the regression.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 (~80.9% vs ~76.1% top-1) yields clearly stronger features, and since dog breeds are an ImageNet subset the linear probe and calibrated log loss should improve modestly, with identical pipeline and budget.

C=0.3 was holdout-selected as optimal, so 10x stronger L2 underfits the initial head; the brief bottleneck fine-tuning partially recovers the shrunken weights but likely not fully, yielding a modest log-loss regression to roughly 0.49.

Dropping from 224 to 192 input removes fine detail that matters for fine-grained breed discrimination and shifts activations off the pretrained 224px distribution; the refit logistic head and brief bottleneck fine-tuning recover part of the gap but not all, so a modest log-loss increase of roughly +0.02 is expected.

PCA(256, whiten=False) is an unwhitened orthogonal truncation of the feature space; since L2-regularized logistic regression already shrinks the low-variance directions that PCA discards, the retained-subspace solution stays close to the baseline, so only a small log-loss regression (roughly neutral) is expected, with a faster fit and no runtime risk.

Dropping input resolution from 224 to 192 (while keeping the same crop fraction) gives the frozen ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 less fine-grained detail than it was trained for, so the linear probe's features become slightly less discriminative, modestly worsening log loss (~+0.02 absolute) with no plausible mechanism for improvement.

All 120 breeds are native ImageNet classes, so swapping V1 (~76.1% top-1) for V2 (~80.9% top-1) features with the matched 232px resize preprocessing yields clearly better linear separability for the frozen-backbone logistic probe; expect roughly a 10-12% log-loss drop, with minor uncertainty from C=0.3 having been tuned on V1 features.
Holdout temperature scaling should slightly soften an overconfident logistic-regression probe without changing class rankings, giving a small log-loss gain.

Head initialized from the fitted LogisticRegression reproduces the baseline predictions at start, and a short (≤2 epochs/90s), low-LR fine-tune of only the last bottleneck convs plus head on cached activations from a warm start typically yields a small discriminative gain with limited overfitting/calibration drift, so expect a modest ~3-5% log-loss improvement.

Horizontal-flip TTA with probability averaging is a near-zero-risk variance reduction for a flip-invariant task (dog breeds); training is unchanged, the extra 1,023-image forward pass is trivially within budget, and the MLflow/config additions are metric-neutral — expect the typical modest log-loss gain of ~2-3% from two-view averaging on frozen features.

AUC does not need a 1:1 class ratio; this keeps all positives but discards most negatives, including many hard non-threat insult/toxic comments, so the rare-label rankings get noisier and drag the column mean down.

Adding the shared char_wb TF-IDF block should make branch B's NB-LogReg modestly stronger on morphology/misspellings, but branch A already contributes char signal and threat/identity_hate remain noisy, so the rank blend likely gains only a little.

ROC AUC depends on ranking, not the decision boundary, so rebalancing mostly discards data: for rare labels (threat ~0.3%, identity_hate ~0.9%, severe_toxic ~1%) the 1:1 subset shrinks training to ~1k-3k rows against 60k-200k features, causing high-variance overfit fits (and a much noisier NB ratio from ~500 negative docs), while abundant labels degrade only slightly — net mean column AUC drops roughly 1-1.5%.

Plain MultinomialNB on L2-normalized TF-IDF is weaker and more heavily smoothed than the NB-ratio + discriminative liblinear branch, especially for threat/identity_hate; branch A and rank blending cushion but do not offset the loss.

Mean-pooled Word2Vec loses much of the strong word/character n-gram signal, especially for rare lexical cues, and makes branch A and the MLP highly correlated; retaining NB-LogReg only partly offsets the regression.

AUC is insensitive to the prior/intercept shift from 1:1 undersampling, but discarding 80-99.7% of rows raises coefficient variance while fixed C makes the L2 penalty effectively 5-300x stronger per-sample, hitting the rare labels (threat ~956 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k rows) and the noisier NB ratio r hardest; the MLP also gets ~5x fewer gradient steps and less negative diversity, so expect a small regression of a few tenths of a percent rather than an improvement.

Branch D (fastText-style sparse MLP, ~0.975-0.978 standalone) is weaker than the 0.981 linear blend but non-linear and partly decorrelated, so equal-weight rank-averaging should yield a small net gain; the 0.97 val-AUC guard and time guards limit downside if D undertrains in the few epochs that fit the budget.

AUC is a ranking metric so balancing mostly leaves common labels (toxic/obscene/insult, still 16-30k rows) unchanged, but for the rare labels it discards 99%+ of negatives — threat trains on ~956 rows and identity_hate/severe_toxic on ~1-3k rows against 60k-250k features, making the LR coefficient direction and the NB log-count ratio r (whose negative-class counts now come from only a few hundred comments) much noisier, which typically costs a few tenths to over a point of AUC on those rare columns; averaged over six labels that is a small net regression, only partly offset by any benefit from reducing negative-class dominance of the L2 loss.

Lowercasing is mostly redundant with the vectorizers, but URL/IP/timestamp cleanup plus profanity de-obfuscation should consolidate rare toxic variants into stronger TF-IDF/NB features for a small gain, partly offset by shorthand/stop-word losses.

Stacking B's OOF logits into A lets A absorb the complementary bigram/NB signal (the /20 scaling still permits a usable coefficient even at C=0.1), but since the final 50/50 rank blend already combined that signal and A/B are highly correlated, the net gain in mean column AUC is tiny—on the order of +0.0003.

A 64-unit MLP trained only 3 epochs on branch A's own TF-IDF features is undertrained (~0.97 standalone, weakest on rare labels) and highly correlated with branch A, so giving it 1/3 rank weight dilutes the strong A/B blend more than its limited diversity adds.

Branch C (NB-LogReg over B's word 1-2gram + A's char_wb, ~250k cols) is plausibly the strongest single branch — word+char NB-LogReg kernels scored ~0.980-0.981 in the original competition — and remains diverse from A's plain logreg, so an equal three-way rank blend should add a small gain; the max_iter=100/tol=1e-3 cap and C's heavy feature overlap with B limit the upside (and add some runtime risk), but a regression is unlikely.

Both branches are already strong and highly correlated, so the optimal per-label blend is near 50/50; holdout-tuned weights with 50% shrinkage toward 0.5 will mostly reproduce the equal blend, with selection noise on the rare labels roughly canceling small gains on common labels — expect a change within ±0.0002 of baseline.

High-dimensional sparse n-gram features are exactly what drives strong AUC on this dataset (especially for the rare labels threat/identity_hate, which rely on specific lexical cues); compressing to 300 dense LSA factors discards most of that discriminative signal — empirical LSA+LogReg results on Jigsaw land around 0.95-0.965 mean AUC versus ~0.980 for the sparse NB-LogReg/word+char blend, so this swap trades the best-performing representation for speed and should regress roughly 2 AUC points despite running well within budget.

toxic keeps all negatives (144k < 10×15.3k) so that column is unchanged, but threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic keep only ~3-10% of negatives, making the negative-class estimates noisier in all branches — especially branch B's NB log-odds ratios computed from as few as 4,780 negatives across 200k features — so the noise-sensitive rare-label AUCs drop slightly, outweighing any class-balance benefit.

The single softmax fastText model is much cheaper but treats the six overlapping labels as mutually exclusive and splits score mass across co-occurring toxic attributes, so branch F should be slightly weaker than six one-vs-rest fastText classifiers while branches A/B and the rank blend are unchanged.

ComplementNB on raw word counts is a solid fast baseline (~0.93-0.94 mean AUC on this data), but its probability ranking is markedly weaker than the discriminative NB-LogReg/logistic branches it replaces, and dropping the char n-gram views and rank ensemble removes complementary signal, so the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) especially regress well below the current 0.9816.

Replacing ~260k NB-weighted sparse n-gram features (which sharply capture exact abuse terms and char-level variants) with a 200-d mean-pooled from-scratch Word2Vec representation loses token-specificity, word order, and rare-word signal for the rare labels; averaged-embedding + linear baselines on this dataset historically land around 0.94-0.96, well below the 0.9816 TF-IDF ensemble.

Average-pooled frozen corpus Word2Vec + logistic loses the sparse model's exact word/char n-gram, NB weighting, IDF/length normalization and misspelling signals, so it should regress to the mid-0.95s.

Adding an NB-weighted char 3-5-gram branch adds a genuinely strong, moderately diverse model (standalone ~0.975-0.978) to the rank blend; per-label simplex tuning on the holdout should convert most of that diversity into gain (+~0.003), slightly offset by weight-selection overfitting on the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) and the 90%-only training; runtime stays tight but within the 15-min kill.

C=0.1 heavily over-regularizes branch A's 60k-feature TF-IDF model; switching to the canonical C=4 liblinear config from the reference kernels should raise branch A's standalone AUC by ~0.003-0.004, lifting the 0.5/0.5 rank blend from 0.9801 to roughly 0.9810-0.9815.

Supervised fastText (word bigrams, dim=64) is a diverse but slightly weaker learner (~0.975-0.978 standalone) than the TF-IDF branches; adding it as a third equal-weight rank blend historically adds ~+0.001 mean AUC on this competition, with gains on rare labels (threat, identity_hate) outweighing dilution, and the sequential train/predict/delete loop fits the time budget.

Char-level NB-LogReg is a strong (~0.977-0.979 standalone) and decorrelated feature view versus branch B (word-only) and branch A (plain logreg, not NB-weighted); blending it in at equal rank weight historically adds ~+0.002 mean AUC on this task, and the extra ~5-6 min of char-vectorizer work should still fit under the 15-min kill even if it exceeds the 10-min target.

Per-label blend tuning adds only a small, noisy gain (threat/identity_hate holdouts have ~48/~140 positives, so weight selection there is near-random), while training on 90% of the data with no full-data refit costs slightly more AUC than the tuned weights recover — net a small regression.
NB log-ratio weighting should modestly strengthen the word+char linear branch, especially on rare labels, while still complementing branch B in the rank average.

min_df=0.01 means ~3,127 docs on the 313k train+test corpus — it guts branch B from ~200k to ~1.5k features and branch A's word vocab from 10k to ~1k, and the lexical signal for the rare labels (threat, identity_hate terms like kill/jew/muslim sit right near the 1% boundary) is largely pruned, while common profanity that drives toxic/obscene/insult survives, so the column-mean AUC drops by roughly half a percent.

AUC is fairly robust to undersampling for frequent labels (toxic/obscene/insult stay near-flat), but for rare labels (threat ~478, identity_hate ~1.4k, severe_toxic ~1.6k positives) fitting 60k-200k-feature models plus NB log-count weights on ~1-3k balanced rows injects large estimation variance and effective over-regularization, dragging those per-column AUCs down and lowering the column mean by a few thousandths.

Cosine class centroids (Rocchio-style) discard the discriminative feature weighting that logistic regression learns; branch B retains some signal via its NB log-odds weighting, but both branches lose several AUC points on the diffuse labels (toxic/insult/obscene), so the blend drops from ~0.980 to the mid-0.95s while running much faster.

Switching char to char_wb eliminates noisy n-grams spanning word boundaries and concentrates the tight 50k feature budget on within-word patterns, which typically gives a small AUC gain for this branch; the effect is dampened by the equal-weight rank blend with the unchanged NB-LogReg branch, so expect only a modest improvement (~+0.0006 AUC).

ComplementNB on TF-IDF features is a solid but clearly weaker learner than the tuned logistic regressions it replaces (NB variants score ~0.94-0.96 mean AUC on this dataset vs ~0.978-0.985 for the LR branches), and branch B also loses its NB log-ratio weighting; rank-blending two weaker, now same-algorithm branches cannot recover the loss.

Compressing 60k TF-IDF features to 32 unsupervised SVD components destroys the rare-but-decisive lexical signals (profanity, slurs, threat phrases) that drive branch A, since truncated SVD keeps high-variance directions rather than discriminative ones; branch A likely drops from ~0.978 to ~0.93-0.95, and the unchanged fastText branch at 50% rank weight can only partially compensate, dragging the blend down roughly 1.5-2% with the biggest hits on the rare threat/identity_hate columns.

Capping vocabulary to the top-2,000 document-frequent tokens destroys exactly the rare-vocabulary signal (slurs, obfuscated spellings, identity terms) that TF-IDF upweights and that the char_wb and fastText branches rely on for the rare labels (threat, identity_hate), and both linear/fastText branches are already regularized, so this aggressive UNK-normalization costs roughly half a point of mean column AUC.

Keeping stop words adds genuinely discriminative pronouns/negations for toxicity (e.g. 'you', 'not') that TF-IDF weights moderately, while the fixed 10k cap only displaces ~300 very rare content words; the char n-gram features already cover much of this signal and the 50/50 rank blend with the unchanged NB-LogReg branch dampens the effect to near-zero, leaning very slightly positive.

AUC is rank-based, and logit-averaging lets the less-regularized NB branch (C=4, more extreme/saturated logits) dominate the ordering while the heavily-shrunk word+char branch (C=0.1) contributes little, so the blend loses the equal-footing diversity benefit of rank averaging — especially on the noisy rare labels (threat, identity_hate) — yielding a small regression, though both blends use the same two orderings so the change should be within ~0.1%.

Switching char_wb to char dilutes the 50k-feature cap with cross-word-boundary n-grams that add little signal for this dataset (the classic kernels using char_wb were marginally better), and since branch A is only half the rank blend while branch B is unchanged, the expected effect is a very small regression around 2e-4 AUC.

fastText (ova, dim=64, 5 epochs, no subwords, 256-token truncation) is a decent but slightly weaker branch than the well-tuned NB-LogReg it replaces (~0.972 vs ~0.978 solo), and its diversity gain in the rank blend with Branch A likely won't fully offset the loss, especially on the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) that dominate the column-mean noise; runtime stays well within budget.
Keeping the top-128 ANOVA bins should mostly drop redundant/low-signal histogram columns and slightly denoise the LR half, while the unchanged NN half limits the overall gain.

Label smoothing 0.1 curbs the NN's overconfident softmax on 99 classes with ~8-10 samples/class under heavy augmentation, improving calibration of the NN half of the 50/50 blend, which should modestly lower log loss (~2-4%) with no runtime or pipeline risk.

OvR keeps similar linear rankings but replaces the proper joint softmax with 99 imbalanced independently scaled sigmoids; the two-scalar power/floor calibration can fix global sharpness but not the less comparable per-class probabilities, so I expect a modest log-loss regression.

A regularized 5-seed MLP bag on 990 tiny per-class samples is individually weaker than LR but adds decorrelated signal, and since the blend weight is CV-selected with a w=0 fallback the downside is limited to mild OOF-selection overfitting while a small-to-moderate w likely trims log loss by a few percent on test.

Fold-averaging trades 20% less data per model for variance reduction and smoothing of overconfident high-C probabilities; since the fold models (not the full-data refit) are what CV actually validated at best_C, calibration should match the CV optimum slightly better, yielding a small net improvement in log loss — but for a stable linear model the effect is minor, so expect near-parity with a ~1-2% gain.

The 21 geometric features (absolute size, aspect ratio, solidity, compactness, Hu moments) are genuinely complementary to the scale-normalised 64-dim shape signature, and L2-regularised multinomial logistic regression with CV-tuned C on standardized features can exploit them with low overfitting risk (990 samples, 213 features), so a modest single-digit-percent log-loss gain is likely; implementation is correct (modern skimage attribute names, NaN imputation, graceful fallback) and runtime stays well within budget.

L2-penalised logistic regression is invariant to orthogonal rotation, so PCA(0.95) only hard-truncates the lowest-variance ~5% of directions; collinearity was never a prediction problem for ridge-style logreg, and those fine-scale margin/texture modes carry some species-discriminative signal, so the modest denoising benefit is slightly outweighed by the discarded information at fixed C=1.0, yielding a small log-loss increase (~0.089-0.091).

Averaging 5 stratified fold models is classic CV-bagging: it smooths overconfident softmax outputs and cuts prediction variance, which log loss rewards; each fold model's 20% data reduction only partly offsets this, so expect a small net gain over the single full-data fit (true effect is within ±0.005 either way).

The two-branch NN (feature MLP + small CNN with heavy rotation aug, noise and TTA) should reach roughly LR-level accuracy with decorrelated errors, so the 50/50 blend beats either model alone; 64x64 CPU training easily fits the ~9min guard so both 80-epoch runs complete, though NN overconfidence on a 990-sample/99-class problem caps the gain.

Multinomial LR at C=1.0 on 990 rows/99 classes is overconfident out-of-sample, so OOF-fitted temperature softening (a<1) plus a tiny uniform floor should genuinely cut log loss ~8-15% (grid includes the identity, so it can't hurt on OOF, and 2 scalars on 990 OOF rows transfers with minimal selection bias); code is correct (stratified folds keep all classes, no underflow, runtime trivial) and gains are bounded because LR is already roughly calibrated.
Stratified OOF should select a C well above 1, sharpening mostly-correct probabilities for a solid log-loss drop, with gains capped by confusable species and overconfidence at very large C.

The implementation is correct and fast (~1 min feature extraction); the 27 clean binary-mask geometric descriptors (Hu moments, solidity, eccentricity, axis ratios) are genuinely discriminative for leaf species and only partially redundant with the 64 precomputed shape features, so the unchanged scaler+logreg pipeline should gain a small but real improvement, limited by fixed C=1.0 and 990 training rows across 99 classes.

With ~990 samples, 99 classes and 240 correlated standardized features, C=1.0 logistic regression tends to be overconfident; 5x stronger L2 shrinkage softens probabilities toward better calibration, which usually yields a modest log-loss gain on small multiclass data.

Removing the full-data refit submits a model trained on 20% less data (8 vs 10 leaves per species); with 99 classes and tiny per-class counts, logistic regression's probability estimates and calibration degrade noticeably, raising test log loss by roughly a quarter.

The SLSQP blend is optimized on proper leak-free OOF predictions and the simplex includes LR-only, so it can't do worse than the ~0.059 baseline up to estimation noise; shrinkage LDA adds modestly diverse signal on these near-Gaussian leaf descriptors while kNN will get small weight, yielding a small (5-8%) improvement, with runtime well within budget.

With only 990 training rows across 99 classes, HistGradientBoosting overfits and produces poorly calibrated probabilities even with early stopping; on this dataset's pre-extracted descriptors the tuned linear logistic model is near-optimal, so expect test log loss to jump from ~0.06 to roughly 0.4-0.6.

Platt-sigmoid calibration of a 99-class OvR LinearSVC via 3-fold CV has only ~3 positives per calibration fold, yielding noisy, poorly calibrated probabilities (worsened by 'balanced' weighting in each 1-vs-98 fit), so swapping the well-calibrated multinomial LR for this member degrades the uniform soft-voting mixture — dampened by the three unchanged members, giving a moderate log-loss regression around 0.33-0.35.

RF vote-fraction probabilities are noticeably less calibrated (flatter when right, overconfident when wrong) than HGB's log-loss-trained outputs, so swapping one of four uniformly-weighted soft-voting members degrades the ensemble's log loss modestly without changing anything else.

A 256-128 MLP has ~95k weights for only ~990 examples across 99 classes and is early-stopped on a tiny accuracy-based split with only uniform shrinkage for calibration, so overconfident errors likely outweigh any descriptor-interaction gain.

With only 990 samples and ~19k multinomial-LR parameters, CV over the C grid will likely pick somewhat stronger regularization than the arbitrary C=1.0, improving calibration on top of the existing uniform-shrinkage step for a modest log-loss gain; upside is bounded because shrinkage already corrects global overconfidence, and 5-fold selection noise adds only small downside risk.

The 48 classical CV features (Hu moments, shape scalars, radial-distance histogram) add partially complementary shape information to the 192 descriptors, and with StandardScaler + multinomial LR on ~990 training rows this typically yields a modest log-loss gain, though overlap with existing shape descriptors and the fixed C=1.0 regularization cap the improvement.

The leaf features are near-linearly separable, so CV-tuning C by neg-log-loss (typically landing at a stronger C than 1.0 and refitting on all 990 samples) turns the same multinomial LR from an over-regularized 0.124 into the ~0.03-0.06 log-loss range known for tuned LR on this dataset, while runtime stays trivially within budget.

Soft-averaging decorrelated models — LDA (typically the strongest on these 192 descriptors) plus LR, CV-tuned kNN, and HGB — usually beats the lone LR substantially on this dataset (known feature-only blends land ~0.05–0.09), with the weaker HGB/kNN diluted to 1/4 weight; small 99-row test set adds variance but the direction is clearly positive.

The model is unchanged; OOF-tuned shrinkage toward uniform is a safe scalar calibration that mildly tempers LR's overconfident probabilities (99 classes, only ~10 samples each), typically yielding a small log-loss gain of a few percent with negligible runtime cost.

Ledoit-Wolf auto shrinkage on 990x192 standardized descriptors is likely small (~0.05-0.3), so forcing 90% spherical shrinkage essentially turns LDA into a nearest-centroid classifier that discards the discriminative correlation structure in the shape/margin/texture descriptors; the better calibration (softer, less overconfident probabilities) only partially offsets the lost accuracy, so log loss worsens moderately.

Three per-family 64-dim LDAs need far less Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage than one 192-dim LDA on ~891 residual degrees of freedom, and the sum rule (posterior averaging) is robust when classes outnumber per-class samples and feature blocks are complementary — this mirrors the probabilistic shape/texture/margin integration in the dataset's source paper, which outperformed feature concatenation, so a modest log-loss gain is expected.

L2-penalized multinomial logistic regression is rotation-invariant, so PCA(0.90) only truncates the lowest-variance ~10% of standardized directions — a coarse extra regularizer that discards some discriminative signal (near-collinear histogram/descriptor differences); CV can partially compensate by picking a larger C, but with the coarse 5-point C grid the net effect is a slight log-loss regression, roughly +2-4% over 0.0599.
Shrunk-covariance LDA is well suited to the small balanced per-class leaf descriptor data and should give better-calibrated linear posteriors than the coarsely tuned logistic regression.

L2-regularized logistic regression already handles correlated descriptors well, and PCA(0.95) after standardization discards low-variance directions that still carry discriminative signal while changing the effective regularization geometry, so a small log-loss regression is likely.

Shrunken LDA should be more sample-efficient than L2 multinomial logistic on these shared-covariance leaf descriptors, while unchanged fold-wise scaling and OOF temperature calibration should preserve probability calibration.

The 0.005 uniform mix costs every sample with true-class prob >0.01 roughly -ln(0.995)≈+0.005 of log loss; since the model is already well-calibrated (0.0943) with few sub-0.01 true-class probabilities for the smoothing to rescue, the universal penalty dominates and log loss rises by ~0.005 to about 0.099.

Dropping Nyström landmarks from 512 to 384 slightly worsens the RBF kernel approximation (and re-rolls the landmark sample), which should marginally reduce probability quality, but 384 components still covers the intrinsic dimensionality of ~990 samples, so expect only a small regression within seed-level noise.

Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk LDA on the 192 leaf descriptors is a known strong, well-calibrated baseline for this 99-class problem (typically ~0.04-0.08 log loss), roughly halving the error of a default-C logistic regression, and the applied code (no-leak scaling, full-data refit, correct class reordering) is bug-free and runs in seconds.

The refit pipeline is identical to the baseline except for the CV-selected C; on these 192 descriptors multinomial logreg at C=1 is slightly mis-calibrated (near-separable classes, ~19k params on 990 rows), and 3-fold neg_log_loss selection over [0.1..1000] typically lands on C=10-100, trimming test log loss roughly 20-35%, with small risk of no change if C=1 wins; runtime (16 quick lbfgs fits, 4-way parallel) is well within budget.

Out-of-fold temperature scaling is a safe, low-variance calibration step: LR with ~19k parameters on ~990 samples is somewhat overconfident, so the learned T (likely ~1.3-1.8) will soften probabilities and trim log loss by roughly 5-12%, with negligible runtime or implementation risk.
The scale-gamma RBF Nyström representation should separate compact species clusters much better than the linear model, while fixed C=1 and no calibration keep it well short of near-perfect.

The 31 added features are leak-free and capture known RAOP signals the current model cannot see (subreddit-age temporal decline, request length, money/reciprocity/gratitude mentions, first-person rate dropped by stop_words), which should add roughly +0.01 AUC to a C=0.3 linear model, with minor dilution from a few noisy one-hot blocks.

Random forests handle high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF poorly: with ~8000 features and max_features='sqrt', each split samples ~90 mostly-noise dimensions, burying the few informative numeric/text signals, and min_samples_leaf=1 overfits — so despite capturing interactions on the numeric block, the forest loses most of the linear text signal and AUC drops roughly 0.06-0.07 below the 0.671 baseline.

Random forests on ~5k sparse TF-IDF features with sqrt feature sampling typically underperform linear models on text: most splits pick noisy sparse word indicators, the 10 numeric features get few split opportunities, and the giver_known leak (informative in train, constant 0 in test) makes trees carve out branches useless at inference — expect a several-point AUC regression despite the nonlinearity argument.

Replacing 5000 sparse TF-IDF unigrams with 50 LDA topic proportions trained on only ~4k documents discards fine-grained lexical signal and adds sampling noise; LDA features typically underperform direct TF-IDF+logistic regression on this dataset, so the unchanged metadata features can only partly compensate, yielding a modest AUC regression.

Swapping the supervised OOF TF-IDF logit (a strong, label-optimized text signal) for 20 unsupervised LDA topic proportions throws away most of the text's predictive power—LDA topics on ~5.7k short posts are noisy and only weakly tied to success—so LightGBM is left leaning almost entirely on the requester-history metadata and timestamp, costing roughly 0.01–0.02 AUC despite gaining interaction flexibility.

The RAOP test set is the chronologically later slice, so the raw epoch feature only memorizes in-window base rates and collapses to a constant on test (no ranking value, but it drains split capacity and distorts early stopping); dropping it is neutral-to-positive, and hour/weekday add a weak but stationary diurnal signal, yielding a small net gain within test-set noise.

CV-weighted rank averaging is low-risk (worst case w=1.0 reproduces the baseline exactly), and a conservative HistGBM on the metadata/text-stat features (~0.64-0.67 OOF) is decorrelated enough with the TF-IDF logistic model that the blend should add a small ~0.003-0.006 AUC, though weight-selection noise on ~4k samples caps and could occasionally negate the gain.

Random forests with sqrt subsampling on ~5000 sparse TF-IDF features (~71 of ~5035 features per split) split mostly on noisy text tokens and dilute the strong additive text signal that logistic regression exploits; with only ~4000 training rows the fully grown trees overfit, so the dense metadata interactions gained are far outweighed by the degraded text ranking, yielding a clear AUC regression versus the linear model.

Bag-of-subreddits identity is a known informative signal for community membership/prior activity beyond the 9 numeric history features, and adding this sparse block to l2-regularized logistic regression on a small dataset should give a modest AUC gain (~+0.005-0.008) with low overfitting risk.

giver_username_if_known is a classic train-only leak: in test.json it is uniformly 'N/A', so the feature is constant 0 at inference, while during training the near-label-perfect indicator absorbs the positive-class signal, leaving the TF-IDF/numeric weights to be fit on the small residual of positives with unknown givers — this distorts and weakens the very weights that must rank the test rows, so AUC regresses moderately (the inflated local holdout print is misleading).

Feeding a clean out-of-fold TF-IDF logit plus raw requester metadata into an early-stopped LightGBM captures nonlinear metadata effects the linear model misses; on RAOP this kind of stack typically gains ~3-5% AUC over a plain TF-IDF+logistic baseline, with low risk since the implementation matches the proposal and mlflow tracking is safely wrapped.

The added dense block (request length, char counts, imgur/http evidence links, karma ratio, cyclical time features) mirrors the well-documented predictive signals from the Althoff et al. RAOP paper that are absent from the current baseline, so a modest AUC gain of roughly 0.01-0.02 is expected; the MLflow additions are failure-wrapped and shouldn't affect the model or runtime.

ExtraTrees with max_features='sqrt' on ~5.4k mostly-noisy sparse TF-IDF dims samples ~74 features per split and fragments into noise instead of summing many weak signals like the linear model, so despite capturing numeric interactions it should lose a few AUC points versus the 0.6235 baseline.

MiniLM embeddings plus the 9 behavioral covariates retain much of the signal, but TF-IDF unigrams carry complementary lexical cues (need/reciprocity phrasing) that frozen embeddings only partially recover, so dropping the sparse block should cost roughly 1 AUC point despite the variance-reduction argument.

The raw-text block restores length, punctuation/casing, pronoun and sentiment/readability signals that normalized TF-IDF drops, while some gratitude/sentiment flags overlap with n-grams, so expect a modest positive AUC gain.

Dropping TF-IDF removes most of the request-content signal; the nine log1p history features still rank better than chance but should underperform text+metadata, and the mlflow wrapper does not affect predictions.

Mean-pooled skip-gram vectors trained on a tiny (~1M-token) corpus are a much weaker text representation than 5k unigram TF-IDF for a linear model, losing discriminative lexical signal; the retained numeric metadata and 15 text-stats features prevent a collapse, so expect a moderate ~0.02 AUC drop.

Adding bigrams and expanding the vocabulary from 5k to 60k recovers phrase-level and mid-frequency token signal known to be diagnostic on RAOP, while L2-regularized logistic regression on 60k sparse features with ~4.5k rows stays well-conditioned (C=0.3 is adequate), so a modest AUC gain of roughly +0.015 is expected; the added mlflow telemetry is fully exception-guarded and does not affect the model.

Requester-history features are the dominant signal here, but RAOP text (title/body wording, politeness, narrative) still carries real incremental AUC that even a weak TF-IDF+SVD+GBM pipeline partially captures, so dropping it should cost roughly 0.005–0.015 AUC and land near the typical ~0.62 metadata-only range rather than improving.
Runtime is ample, but swapping CV-stopped LightGBM for an untuned fully grown forest on the same 309-dim SVD features should lose a little ranking power on this small noisy tabular target.

MiniLM embeddings add complementary semantic signal on top of lexical TF-IDF and history features; 4040 training rows with C=0.3 L2 regularization can absorb the extra 384 dense dims without meaningful overfitting, so a modest AUC gain (~+0.01) is likely, and CPU encoding of 256-token-truncated docs fits the time budget.

Adding bigrams and expanding the vocabulary 20x with min_df=2 gives the L2-regularized logistic model more discriminative text signal on this small dataset, typically worth roughly +0.005-0.012 AUC; C=0.3 keeps overfitting in check and the numeric block is unchanged.

The 15 dense stats add genuinely new signal the unigram TF-IDF misses (document length is erased by l2-normalized TF-IDF; 'pay it forward' is a multiword phrase; gratitude/hardship lexicons are known strong predictors from the Althoff et al. paper), and 15 scaled features with L2 logistic regression on ~4k samples carries negligible overfitting risk, so a modest AUC gain of ~0.008-0.012 is expected.

Linear models on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF typically edge out gradient boosting on SVD-reduced text for small (~4k row) datasets like RAOP; SVD-300 discards some discriminative signal and GBMs rarely beat regularized logistic regression on sparse text here, so expect a small regression (roughly -0.005 to -0.015 AUC), with the run comfortably within budget and the mlflow additions being metric-neutral telemetry.

The 2-feature annual Fourier encoding discards any non-periodic time trend the 8-dof spline could capture, and temporal signal is weak relative to the TF-IDF/requester-history features, so expect a noise-level, very slightly negative change.
C=30 largely removes the heavy L2 shrinkage of normalized TF-IDF unigram weights (about SGD alpha 8e-6 for ~4k rows), so predictive text cues should rank better with only mild overfitting risk.

RAOP success rates drifted over the 2010-2013 collection window, so a regularized quantile-spline time trend adds weak but genuine ranking signal on top of the dominant TF-IDF features; constant extrapolation and median imputation make it safe, but with only ~8 added columns among thousands and C=0.3 the gain is small.

Distance-weighted KNN with cosine distance is dominated by the 5000 sparse TF-IDF dims (numerics/subreddits negligible), giving noisy neighborhood-vote probabilities with poor ranking quality, which typically trails a regularized linear model on this small, imbalanced dataset by several AUC points.

CatBoost exploits the skewed, interacting requester-history features far better than distance-weighted k-NN in 9-d (which suffers from tied/zero-distance low-activity requesters and coarse local estimates), so the metadata half of the 50/50 blend weakens and drags the text+metadata AUC down modestly from 0.6449.

C=0.3 heavily underfits l2-normalized TF-IDF features, so relaxing to C=30 should lift the logistic component's AUC by roughly 0.01-0.03; the fixed 50/50 blend with the unchanged CatBoost dampens this to a modest net gain, with limited overfitting risk on 5k unigram features.

The date-spline block is methodologically safe (train-only fit, median imputation, constant extrapolation) and can capture RAOP's mild calendar drift in success rate, but it adds only ~7 well-regularized features to a 5000-feature linear model, so expect a small positive gain (near zero if the split is temporal, since constant extrapolation then neutralizes the feature).

BernoulliNB's presence-indicator scoring on TF-IDF usually ranks close to but below tuned logistic regression, and binarizing the nine standardized requester-history features at the mean discards most of their continuous signal, so expect a modest AUC regression.

Adding quantile-spline features of the absolute UTC timestamp captures the known downward drift in RAOP success rates over 2010-2013 (as the community grew), a weak but real signal that transfers to the randomly-split test set; the implementation is sound (median imputation, train-only spline fitting, refit on full data) and the MLflow additions are inert, so expect a small gain of roughly +0.005 AUC.

Subreddit-participation features are a known informative signal for RAOP (community/status beyond the existing numeric counts), so the binary block should give a modest AUC lift over the 0.657 baseline; the implementation is sound (min_df=5 vocabulary, binary, unscaled, same LR) and the MLflow wrapper is best-effort and harmless, while removal of the holdout print does not affect the final model.

The metadata-only CatBoost is individually weaker (~0.62-0.64 AUC) but captures nonlinear structure in the 9 history features that the linear model misses, and its predictions are only moderately correlated with the text-dominated logistic output, so a 50/50 probability blend typically nets a small AUC gain; the MLflow/psutil additions and removed local scoring are metric-neutral and runtime is well within budget.

Adding bigrams captures formulaic politeness/gratitude phrases (e.g. 'thank you', 'in advance') that carry signal on RAOP, but the shared 5000-feature budget displaces some informative mid-frequency unigrams, so the net effect is small; the tracking/refactor changes don't alter test predictions.

For authorship attribution, function/stop words are the classic stylometric signal (distinctive per-author usage of 'the', 'of', 'and' and bigrams like 'of the'); IDF already downweights them appropriately, so dropping them removes discriminative word-view features that the char_wb view only partially recovers, yielding a modest log-loss regression.

Stacking the tuned TF-IDF LR with two complementary MultinomialNB models (word and char counts) via a log-linear geometric meta-learner is a well-proven combination on this dataset — NB captures count-based signals LR misses, and learned blending on log-probs directly optimizes the log-loss geometry; the small loss from fold-averaged test predictions instead of a full-data LR refit is outweighed by ensemble diversity, so expect roughly a 8-12% improvement (local meta-CV should land ~0.31-0.32, translating to ~0.31-0.33 graded); code has no blocking bugs and runtime adds only ~30s of negligible NB fits over the existing 25 LR fold fits.

Function words are classic high-signal authorship-attribution features, so dropping them slightly weakens both word-level base models (especially NB, whose likelihood mass they dominated); the char_wb models and the stop-word-ratio meta-feature preserve most of that stylistic signal and the LightGBM stacker re-weights, so the net effect is a small regression rather than a large one.

A scaled multinomial-LR combiner is the classic low-variance stacker for already-informative, correlated OOF probabilities; LightGBM's extra capacity mostly fits fold-specific OOF noise and the OOF-vs-test distribution mismatch of the level-1 columns, so expect roughly flat-to-slightly-better test log loss.
Word TF-IDF is nearly unchanged, but stripping punctuation deletes discriminative char n-grams such as dashes/quotes and Lovecraftian apostrophes/hyphens, so log loss should rise modestly.

The 4-model OOF stack (word/char LR at C=10 plus alpha-tuned word/char MultinomialNB) with a calibrated meta-LR on log-probs is a classic strong recipe for this competition; the diverse, better-regularized base models and fold-averaged test predictions should clearly beat the single C=1 LR on hstacked TF-IDF (historically such stacks land in the high-0.3s), and the workload fits the time budget with the parallel char-LR folds.

chi2 on TF-IDF values favors frequent features and will keep mostly strong word n-grams while discarding much of the long-tail char n-gram signal that the L2-regularized LR was already exploiting effectively; the OOF blend search will partially compensate by shifting weight toward the unchanged NB branch, so expect a small net regression in log loss rather than a large one.

Author attribution relies heavily on function-word frequencies and short function-word bigrams; removing sklearn stop words from the word and NB count features likely loses some signal, with the intact char block only partly offsetting it.
