Tuning C via 5-fold CV on this word+char TF-IDF setup reliably finds a less-regularized optimum (C≈10-30) than C=1, typically cutting log loss by ~0.03-0.05 absolute; the refit-on-all-data pipeline is otherwise unchanged, so a modest but real improvement is expected.

OOF stacking of complementary word/char linear and NB models plus stylometric features should improve calibration and model weighting over a single LR, though the n-gram views are correlated so the gain is moderate rather than SOTA.

Boundary-crossing, case-sensitive char n-grams are a known small win for author attribution (punctuation-in-context and capitalization style differ strongly between Poe/Lovecraft/Shelley), and L2-regularized LR tolerates the ~3-5x larger sparse feature space, so expect a modest ~0.01 log-loss gain.

NB-on-counts is a decent, decorrelated second model (~0.46-0.50 OOF alone), and OOF-tuned convex blending with LR (which includes w=1.0 as a fallback, so downside is bounded) historically gives a modest ~0.01-0.02 log loss gain on this dataset; mlflow plumbing is inert and runtime stays within budget.

Authorship attribution is a stylometric task where function words (including pronouns like 'I'/'my', which strongly mark Poe) are classic high-signal features, so stopword removal discards useful style information and slightly distorts bigrams, likely causing a small log-loss regression despite the content-word focus argument.

The imbalance is mild (max/min ~1.4x), so oversampling mainly shifts the effective prior from the natural 40/31/29 toward uniform; that miscalibrates fastText's softmax probabilities against the naturally distributed test set (EAP under-predicted, HPL/MWS over-predicted), which log-loss penalizes by roughly the prior-shift KL (~0.01-0.02 nats), while duplicated minority rows add no new information; training time stays trivially within budget.

ComplementNB on TF-IDF is a diverse, reasonably strong model for this task, and an OOF-tuned convex blend with LR typically yields a small calibration/variance gain (~0.005-0.008 log loss); risk of regression is low since the OOF sweep can fall back to w=1.0 (pure LR).

MultinomialNB is a reasonable text classifier but its probabilities are poorly calibrated (overconfident) on sparse TF-IDF features, which the log-loss metric punishes; even with alpha CV-tuned toward heavier smoothing, NB historically lands ~0.40-0.44 on this dataset versus ~0.35 for tuned logistic regression, so expect a moderate regression.
Dropping the char_wb 2-5 block removes subword/morphology cues that usually help separate these three authors, so the word-only NB-SVM should be a bit less calibrated and log loss should rise.

ComplementNB on the same word+char TF-IDF stack is a reasonable text classifier (~80% accuracy) but its softmaxed joint log-likelihoods are far more overconfident and poorly calibrated than the NB-ratio-weighted logistic head of the NB-SVM, and log loss heavily punishes the confident mistakes, so the score regresses from ~0.41 to roughly ~0.45-0.52.

On high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF features for this dataset, log-loss-optimal C is typically larger than the arbitrary C=1.0 (CV will likely land near 3-10), and selecting C by 3-fold stratified CV directly on neg_log_loss reliably shaves ~0.01 off log loss; the added mlflow logging is best-effort/no-op and does not affect the metric.

MultinomialNB on word+char TF-IDF is a solid text baseline but typically trails logistic regression on this competition, and its overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities (especially with light alpha=0.1 smoothing) are penalized under log loss, so expect a modest regression from ~0.425 to ~0.47.

fastText is essentially an unregularized bag/subword-ngram linear classifier; with lr=0.5 and 25 epochs on ~18k sentences it should be close to the TF-IDF baseline but a bit more overconfident, so log loss likely worsens slightly.

C=1.0 is over-regularized for this high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF setup; known results for word(1,2)+char_wb(2,5) TF-IDF + tuned LR on this dataset put optimal C around 4-8 with log loss ~0.38-0.40, so 5-fold CV selection should yield a solid but not dramatic improvement over the 0.432 baseline.

NB-SVM's per-class log-count-ratio weighting mimics Naive Bayes (which is strong on this competition) while retaining discriminative per-class logistic regressors, so it should beat the plain multinomial LR baseline by a few hundredths of log loss, though imperfect calibration of the renormalized binary probabilities caps the gain.

Length/punctuation stylometry (sentence length, semicolons, dashes) is genuinely discriminative for Poe/Lovecraft/Shelley and complements TF-IDF, but 14 dense features among ~100k+ sparse ones yield only a modest gain, so expect a small improvement over 0.4323.

NB log-count-ratio weighting (NBSVM-style) with per-class liblinear binary LRs sharpens class-discriminative TF-IDF features and typically trims ~0.01-0.015 log loss vs plain multinomial LR on this dataset, with renormalized binary probabilities staying well-calibrated; liblinear fits easily within budget.
Stronger L2 should mostly calibrate/soften overconfident sparse TF-IDF logits; C=0.25 is still weak enough to avoid major underfitting, so I expect about a 1% log-loss gain.

Word unigram/bigram TF-IDF carries the strongest lexical signal for separating these three authors (Lovecraft's distinctive vocabulary especially); char_wb 2–5 grams capped at 60k features captures style and partially covers words, but public ablations for this competition consistently show char-only models ~0.03–0.05 log loss worse than word+char combined, so dropping the word block should be a modest regression, with faster runtime well within budget.

Removing the NB log-odds reweighting strips a useful per-feature scaling that lets L2 logistic lean harder on author-distinctive terms, so plain one-vs-rest TF-IDF logistic should lose a bit of discrimination/calibration and land a few hundredths higher, around 0.54-0.55.

Halving C (4→2) only modestly increases L2 shrinkage on a large correlated TF-IDF feature space; log-loss curves vs C are typically flat in this range, with slightly stronger regularization usually giving a tiny calibration gain (~0.002) rather than a regression.
NB-weighted one-vs-rest logistic is typically a modest improvement over plain TF-IDF multinomial LR, but renormalized independent binary probabilities cap the calibration gain.

Function words are classic high-signal stylometric features for author identification, so stripping them removes discriminative word unigrams/bigrams and char n-grams (and creates spurious adjacent-word bigrams across gaps), modestly worsening log loss despite temperature recalibration.

With ~200k+ sparse correlated TF-IDF features and only ~19.5k rows, stronger L2 (C=0.25) shrinks noisy rare n-gram weights while the temperature rescale absorbs the smaller margin scale, so calibrated log loss should improve slightly.

Switching char_wb to char keeps nearly all within-word n-grams (spaces are already in the text) and adds cross-word transition n-grams, which typically gives a small boost for author-style attribution; the 60k feature cap and unchanged LR keep the effect modest, so expect roughly a ~1% log-loss improvement (0.432 -> ~0.428), with some risk it lands flat.

The NB log-count-ratio weighting (Wang & Manning trick) with one-vs-rest liblinear classifiers is a well-established improvement over plain multiclass LR on TF-IDF for this competition, typically worth ~0.02 log loss; the untuned C=1.0 and removed holdout printout don't affect grading, and 6 small liblinear fits are well within the time budget.
On this classic TF-IDF + LogisticRegression setup, C=1.0 is over-regularized; relaxing to C=4.0 typically reduces log loss by ~0.015-0.02, and the removed holdout print doesn't affect the submission.

Temperature scaling fit on the stratified holdout almost certainly lands near T slightly above 1 (C=1.0 LR on ~100k sparse features is mildly overconfident), which typically shaves a few thousandths off log loss; the 90%-fit to 100%-refit mismatch and small validation set limit the gain, and the implementation is correct with sane bounds, so expect a small improvement rather than a regression.

The metric is RMSE on raw dollars, whose optimal point prediction is the conditional arithmetic mean; training on log1p and inverting with expm1 yields the conditional geometric mean, which is systematically biased low (by roughly sigma_log^2/2 times the fare, worst on the expensive airport rides that dominate squared error), and without a smearing/bias correction this bias typically outweighs any variance-reduction benefit on a moderately skewed, already-cleaned target, so the graded RMSE should worsen slightly (the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows is unchanged since the mean-fare fallback is preserved).

Quadrupling the shuffled sample should cut LightGBM sampling noise and support more effective rounds, but identical features/hyperparameters and the unchanged mean-fare fallback for corrupt test rows limit this to a modest gain.

Airport-proximity distances are a well-known high-value feature for this competition (JFK flat-fare and EWR/LGA surcharge trips have distinct fare structure that radial distances capture far more efficiently than raw lat/lon splits), so the 6 added features should cut clean-row RMSE by ~0.1, worth roughly 2% overall given the ~2.8% corrupt-row floor; the diff is correctly implemented and adds negligible runtime.

L2 on log1p + expm1 yields a median-like (Jensen-biased-low) predictor for a raw-dollar RMSE metric, slightly underpredicting high-fare and corrupt-floor test rows; the homoscedasticity/outlier-downweighting benefits roughly cancel against that bias, giving a small net regression (~4.19 → ~4.21).

The monotone constraint on distance_km matches the true metered-fare structure and acts as a light structural regularizer on the dominant feature; coordinates remain unconstrained so localized non-monotonicities (e.g., JFK flat fares) are still fittable, and with 4M rows the variance reduction should yield only a small (~0.3-0.4%) RMSE improvement, no runtime cost.

Training on log1p(fare) reduces the influence of the extreme-fare tail and matches the multiplicative fare structure, typically giving a small dollar-RMSE gain on this dataset; the uncorrected expm1 back-transform introduces slight downward (Jensen) bias that caps the improvement at roughly 1-2%.

In-sample encoding leaks each row's own fare into its key statistics (real self-influence for the many low-count route keys despite m=20 smoothing), so the trees over-trust the TE features, fit noise, and early-stop sooner; the removal of the 0.8-count train/inference mismatch is only a minor offset, so expect a small net regression rather than an improvement.

Optimizing squared error on log1p(fare) is misaligned with the dollar-RMSE metric: it fits conditional geometric means, so expm1 back-transform systematically underpredicts the conditional mean (Jensen bias, no correction applied) and reallocates model capacity away from the high-fare absolute errors that dominate RMSE; variance stabilization and reduced outlier leverage only partly offset this, so expect a small regression of roughly +0.05 RMSE.

Airport-distance features are a classic, sound win for this dataset (JFK flat fare, EWR surcharge) and let trees isolate airport trips with single splits, but raw coordinates already let LightGBM carve out the airport regions fairly well, so the marginal gain is modest — roughly 0.03–0.05 RMSE (~1%) on the valid rows, with the ~2.8% corrupt-row floor and all other settings unchanged limiting the overall movement.

Letting LightGBM learn NaN-coordinate routing replaces the fixed global-mean fallback with corrupt-population conditional means (via hour/weekday/year/passenger_count) and gives real model predictions to test rows that only had bad passenger counts, which should modestly cut error on the ~2.8% corrupt rows; valid-row performance is essentially unchanged, so the net gain is small since corrupt fares remain largely unpredictable.

Quadrupling training rows with identical LightGBM setup typically cuts the clean-row RMSE from ~3.6 to ~3.45 (more data, same 1000-tree cap now binds), but ~2.8% corrupt test rows predicted as mean fare impose a floor, so the graded RMSE improves only modestly from 4.138 to roughly 4.01-4.03; the n_jobs/dtype/datetime-format changes are neutral performance-wise and keep runtime within budget.

Leak-free smoothed target encodings of ~1km endpoint cells and ~2km route keys capture airport flat fares, tolls and neighborhood fare offsets that raw coords + haversine only approximate through many splits; with proper OOF and m=20 smoothing the sparse route keys degrade gracefully to the global mean, so this should shave roughly 0.05-0.10 off the ~3.6 valid-row RMSE (worth ~1.5-2% overall given the ~2.8% corrupt test rows are an immovable mean-fare floor), and the pandas groupby/map work plus unchanged LGBM config adds negligible runtime.

Training on log1p optimizes relative error while the metric is dollar-space RMSE, and expm1 back-transform without a smearing/bias correction systematically underpredicts fares (Jensen's inequality, geometric vs arithmetic mean), so the slight variance-stabilization benefit is outweighed by a low bias of roughly $0.5-$1 per ride, giving a modest RMSE regression.

Manhattan-block distance and coordinate deltas are genuinely informative for grid-based NYC fares (trees cannot subtract raw coordinates themselves) and bearing captures direction-dependent toll effects, typically worth ~0.03-0.08 RMSE on valid rows; since the ~2.8% corrupt test rows are handled by the unchanged fallback model, that fixed error floor dilutes the gain to roughly 1-1.5% overall, with negligible runtime cost.

Airport/landmark haversine distances are a classic, reliably helpful feature for this competition — they let the trees isolate flat-fare JFK/LGA/EWR pricing regimes far more sharply than raw coordinates, giving a modest but real RMSE gain (~0.1-0.2) with negligible runtime cost and no risk from untouched code paths.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean, so an L1 objective fitting the conditional median adds systematic downward bias on the right-skewed fare distribution, while the robustness benefit is limited because cleaning already caps fares at $500 and large LightGBM leaves (4M rows, 63 leaves) dilute the few remaining outliers — expect a small RMSE regression, not an improvement.

Log1p training optimizes relative error and expm1 without a bias/variance correction approximates conditional medians, underpredicting higher fares; with dollar RMSE and the invalid-row fallback unchanged, this should slightly worsen RMSE.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean, so an L1 objective that fits conditional medians introduces a small downward bias on the right-skewed fare distribution; after the existing (0,500] fare filter the residual outliers are too rare for L1's robustness to compensate, so a slight regression is expected.

With delta=1.0 most residuals (typical |r|~$2-4 on a 3.6-RMSE fit) fall in the linear regime, so Huber behaves mostly like L1 and shifts leaf values toward the conditional median of a right-skewed fare distribution — slightly suboptimal under an RMSE metric whose optimum is the conditional mean; the robustness benefit against residual corrupt rows is heavily diluted by 1M training rows, min_child_samples=100, and the existing fare/bbox cleaning, while ~2.8% of the test floor is unaffected, so expect a small regression (roughly +0.02-0.03 RMSE on the valid-row component).

Log-space training mismatches the RMSE metric: squared error in log space optimizes relative error and downweights the high-fare tail that dominates raw RMSE, and without a Duan/smearing bias correction expm1 back-transform systematically underpredicts the conditional mean (Jensen's inequality), so a small regression on the raw-dollar RMSE is expected despite the nicer target geometry.

Airport distance/flag features are a well-established win for this task (JFK flat fares and LGA/EWR trips deviate from metered distance-based pricing), but raw lat/lon plus 1000-tree LightGBM already approximates airport zones, so the marginal gain is moderate — expect valid-row RMSE to drop ~4-5%, which after the ~2.8% corrupt-row floor translates to roughly a 2-3% overall improvement from 4.129 to ~4.02.

Quadrupling the training sample (1M->4M rows) modestly reduces LightGBM's estimation error and stabilizes early stopping, but with only 10 features the learning curve is already flattening and the ~2.8% corrupt test rows impose a fixed error floor, so expect roughly a 2% RMSE improvement to ~4.06 with no meaningful timeout risk.

5-fold bagging of the same LGBM config reduces prediction variance and typically gains ~1.5-2.5% on the modelable rows, but ~2.8% of the test set is unpredictably corrupt (mean-fare override, fixed error floor), diluting the graded gain to roughly 1-1.5%; per-fold data drop (90%->80%) is more than offset by ensembling, and runtime stays well within budget.

The leak-free, smoothed pickup-cell mean fare adds genuine neighborhood-level signal (airport flat fares, surcharges, typical fare levels) that axis-aligned trees on raw coordinates can't easily carve out at 100m resolution, so it should modestly reduce error on the ~97% valid rows; but the gain is diluted by the fixed ~2.8% corrupt-row floor (contributing ~4.4 MSE), yielding roughly a 1% overall RMSE improvement with low risk of harm thanks to OOF computation and smoothing.

Snapping adds ~0.3-0.5km noise to distance_km and removes sub-km coordinate resolution that let trees model within-cell fare variation, while the route encoding already pooled at 0.01-degree cells so it gains nothing — net loss of real signal yields a mild regression.

L1 fits the conditional median while RMSE rewards the conditional mean; with fares already cleaned to (0,500] the outlier-robustness benefit is small and the median-vs-mean bias on the right-skewed fare distribution typically costs ~0.5-1.5% RMSE, and early stopping on RMSE only partially compensates.

L1 loss fits conditional medians while RMSE rewards conditional means, so the objective is misaligned with the metric; the added robustness to the few extreme fares (up to $500) that survive cleaning only partly offsets this, and early stopping on RMSE limits the damage — expect a small regression of roughly 1%.

Airport-proximity distances are classic high-value features for this competition (JFK flat-fare trips have distinctive fares that raw coordinates only let trees approximate), so clean-row RMSE should drop from ~3.6 to ~3.5; with the ~2.8% corrupt test rows contributing a fixed error floor, overall RMSE improves modestly from 4.137 to ~4.05.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean, so switching to the L1 (conditional-median) objective typically degrades RMSE slightly despite outlier robustness; early stopping still selects on validation RMSE, which limits the damage to a small regression.

Rounding coordinates to 0.01° (~1 km grid) coarsens spatial resolution below what LightGBM's 255-bin histogram splitting already achieves, discarding fine-grained location signal (airport flat-fare zones, Manhattan micro-geography) while the preserved unrounded haversine distance keeps the dominant trip-length signal, so the change is a small information loss with negligible regularization benefit given 1.8M training rows and early stopping — expect near-neutral to slightly worse RMSE.
L1 boosts toward conditional medians; with right-skewed fares scored by RMSE that usually costs a little, while unchanged invalid-row mean predictions leave the error floor intact.

The rotated Manhattan (street-grid) distance is a genuinely informative fare proxy that complements haversine, but it is highly correlated with the existing distance feature, so LightGBM gains only a small incremental benefit — expect roughly a 0.5–1% RMSE improvement.

Cross-fitted smoothed OD-cell target encoding is leak-free and adds real signal (route/toll/airport effects that raw coords approximate poorly), but 0.01-degree cells over only ~830K training rows make most routes rare, so the smoothing=50 shrinkage limits the gain to a solid but modest improvement on the valid rows while the corrupt-row floor is untouched.

The Manhattan-grid distance rotated 29° aligns with NYC's street grid and is a slightly better proxy for road distance than haversine, giving LightGBM a modest gain on valid rows, while the ~2.8% corrupt test rows pinned to the mean cap the overall improvement; the added mlflow tracking is best-effort/no-op and doesn't affect the metric.

Doubling the training sample from 1M to 2M rows gives LightGBM modestly better tree structure and lower variance, typically yielding a small RMSE gain (a few hundredths) on this competition, while the unchanged pipeline and corrupt-test-row floor cap the improvement.

Airport trips (JFK flat-fare especially) have distinct fare structure that distance alone only partially captures; a route categorical lets LightGBM split on these directly, typically worth ~0.1-0.15 RMSE on the valid rows, while corrupt test rows and all other settings stay unchanged (the added mlflow/tracking code is instrumentation only and does not affect predictions).

Plain LightGBM on raw numerics + per-position f_27 categoricals is the well-known baseline for this competition and typically plateaus around 0.977–0.980 without f_27 engineered features (unique-char counts, interactions), whereas the current MLP already exploits smooth continuous interactions to reach 0.9866, so swapping to GBDT likely costs roughly half a point to a point of AUC despite being a solid, well-tuned tree config.

Decile one-hot encoding makes the MLP robust to f_28's heavy tail and gives it piecewise-constant response curves (a weak version of numeric embeddings known to help tabular MLPs), but 10 coarse bins lose within-bin resolution, so I expect only a small net gain over the 0.9866 baseline.

PCA whitening is an invertible full-rank transform so no information is lost and the per-leaf regressions get marginally better conditioning, but PCA axes are variance-driven (unsupervised), not target-driven: the 10 f_27 letter-ordinal columns and any axis-aligned threshold structure get smeared across dense principal components, forcing the greedy tree to rebuild with many oblique staircases what it previously split on directly, and with capacity already binding (3000 rounds, still improving) that search inefficiency likely costs ~0.002-0.004 AUC, outweighing the modest conditioning benefit given the tiny linear_lambda=0.01.

f_27 is extremely high-cardinality (most strings occur 1-2 times), so the m=20 smoothed TE collapses to ≈ the global prior and discards the per-position character signal that the ten per-character split columns exploit — effectively dropping f_27 and costing roughly 0.015 AUC.

The 10-character f_27 strings are essentially all unique across 900k rows (26^10 space), so the smoothed whole-string target encoding collapses to the constant prior on both train and test (test strings are all unseen -> prior), while the change deletes the 10 per-position letter columns that carry real signal — the model is left with numerics + nunique only, costing roughly 0.02 AUC.

The added sums and ternary indicators target the well-known additive interactions in this dataset (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) that form strongly class-separating clusters; giving LightGBM these explicitly removes the need for deep axis-aligned approximations and typically lifts AUC from ~0.991 to ~0.996 under unchanged training settings.

Logistic regression on raw/ordinal features is far weaker than LightGBM on this interaction-heavy synthetic data (likely ~0.93-0.94 AUC), and giving it 50% rank weight drags the strong 0.9842 model down; blends only help when partners are comparably strong with decorrelated errors, so a small regression is expected.

A small CPU MLP on raw numerics plus ordinal-encoded f_27 underfits the sharp high-order feature interactions that gradient-boosted trees exploit in this dataset, so it should land a modest ~1-1.5% AUC regression despite the best-checkpoint selection and LR decay.

This dataset's signal is dominated by high-order discrete interactions (integer features x f_27 characters) that GBDTs capture natively; a small 40-64-64-64-16-1 CPU MLP on standardized raw features typically underfits these patterns and lands around 0.95-0.965 AUC on TPS May 2022, well below the tuned LightGBM's 0.9770, despite the sane recipe (best-epoch selection, cosine decay) keeping the run stable and on time.

linear_tree=True with ~40 features makes each boosting round several times slower than the assumed 2x (per-leaf O(features^2) linear refits on 720k rows), and with no early stop in sight for the full 3000 rounds the run is very likely hard-killed at 15 minutes before any submission is written, so it is recorded as a failure rather than a marginal AUC change.

f_27_nunique adds a compact repeat-count signal that the ten per-position ordinal splits only approximate under feature subsampling, so it should give a small positive AUC bump with unchanged training.

These three sums match the dataset's known additive interaction directions, giving axis-aligned trees a direct split dimension they otherwise approximate only crudely — but with 3000 deep trees the baseline already partially captures them, so the gain is small and positive (roughly +0.0004 AUC), with negligible feature-dilution risk from 3 extra columns.

Collapsing 10 positional columns into one ~15k-cardinality string categorical destroys per-position generalization (the known core signal: position-specific letter sets generalize across all strings, including rare/unseen ones, while a full-string categorical must learn noisy per-string gradient stats with sparse repeats and LightGBM's default max_cat_threshold/min_data_per_group limits), and with colsample_bytree=0.8, 20% of trees now lose all positional f_27 signal instead of just some of 10 columns — letter counts/nunique and the categorical recover part of the gap, but per-position encodings consistently beat full-string categoricals on this dataset, so expect a modest AUC regression.

Adding adjacent-char bigrams of f_27 as native LightGBM categoricals can capture some local string-interaction signal the ordinal per-position splits miss, but most f_27 signal is already covered by per-char ordinals, letter counts, and nunique, so expect only a tiny AUC bump with negligible runtime cost.

PCA components are linear rotations of features LightGBM already sees, adding near-zero signal for axis-aligned trees while diluting colsample_bytree; the gain-mined pairwise products they replace carry genuine multiplicative interaction info (this dataset rewards interaction features), so expect a small regression of roughly 0.001-0.002 AUC.

Hashing the whole 10-char f_27 string into 64 buckets destroys all per-position letter structure, and since test strings are unseen random codes the buckets carry zero generalizable signal — the model effectively falls back to numeric features + mined products only, which is known to score around 0.80 AUC in this competition, a large regression from 0.975.

Swapping tuned LightGBM boosting for a 300-tree ExtraTrees bagging ensemble loses the sequential additive fitting that exploits f_27's letter interactions; RF-style models on TPS May 2022 typically land near 0.94-0.95 AUC, a clear regression from 0.978, though the run should still finish within budget.

sklearn's CPU-only MLP with just 40 epochs, 2 modest layers, and ordinal-encoded f_27 underfits the interaction-heavy tabular signal compared to the tuned 3000-tree LightGBM; NN baselines on this competition consistently trail GBDT by roughly 1-2 AUC points, though the run should finish within the time budget.

In TPS-May-2022 the target is largely driven by order-invariant letter counts in f_27 (the well-known key insight of this competition), so adding explicit per-letter count features gives LightGBM direct access to signal that 10 per-position categoricals can only approximate, typically worth roughly +0.004 to +0.007 AUC over a ~0.9768 position-only baseline; the nunique feature adds little extra since it's a function of the counts, and the vectorized featurization keeps runtime safely in budget.

The per-position f_27 letters carry most of the signal (interactions with numeric features), while the full 10-char sequence is nearly unique per row so its frequency is almost constant ~1, effectively reducing the model to numeric-only features which plateaus around 0.90-0.92 AUC.

Per-letter occurrence counts and the distinct-character count of f_27 are known informative aggregate signals for this competition's string-based interactions (they capture information the per-position ordinal encoding misses), so adding 27 cheap, non-noisy features to an unchanged LightGBM should give a small but real AUC gain, roughly +0.002 over the 0.97696 baseline.

Deep GBDTs already capture most pairwise interactions implicitly, but gain-screened standardized products of the 16 continuous features (a real interaction source in this competition) typically add a small amount of signal, so expect a modest AUC bump of roughly +0.001-0.0015 over the 0.9770 baseline; runtime cost is minor.

Refitting on 100% of rows with proportionally more trees (3333 vs 3000) helps slightly because the model was still improving at the 3000-tree cap and 11% more data plus ~11% more trees is a safe, mild step up; overfitting risk is low at lr=0.05, so expect a small positive gain of roughly +0.0004 AUC.

Treating each f_27 position as a true LightGBM categorical lets single many-vs-rest splits isolate letter subsets that ordinal thresholds need two+ splits to approximate, which typically yields a small AUC gain on this dataset; with 26 well-populated categories and 720k rows the partition statistics are stable, so the change is low-risk but the deep 3000-tree ordinal baseline already captures much of the structure, capping the upside at roughly +0.1-0.2% relative.

f_27_nunique is a known strong interaction signal in TPS May 2022 (class balance shifts sharply with distinct-character count) that axis-aligned trees cannot efficiently reconstruct from per-position ordinals, so adding it as a single cheap feature should give a modest but real AUC boost over the 0.98175 baseline within the same 3000-tree budget.

max_depth=2 caps each tree at about four leaves, and with the same 3000 rounds plus a baseline still improving on holdout, it likely underfits higher-order interactions; the engineered sum only partly compensates.

LightGBM is a strong fit for this interaction-heavy data and will train all 600 rounds within the 420s budget, but the specified config (num_leaves=31, max_bin=63, 600-round cap, no bagging/feature fraction) is a moderately weak GBDT that typically lands ~0.980-0.981 on TPS-May-2022 with per-char ordinal features, slightly below the MLP's 0.9822.

LightGBM on the same char-ordinal features is a natural fit for this competition, but the constrained config (600 trees, 31 leaves, max_bin=63, no row/col sampling, ordinal-encoded letters treated numerically) typically lands in the ~0.977-0.980 range on TPS-May-2022, slightly below the current MLP's 0.9822; runtime (~0.3-0.6 s/iter on 720k rows) fits the 480s budget with the deadline callback as a safe fallback.
Quartile-coding the float predictors discards within-quartile ordering and tail thresholds that the still-underfit LightGBM can exploit, so a small AUC regression is likely.

num_leaves=7 caps each tree at ~6 splits, severely underfitting the higher-order numeric and f_27 positional interactions that the 127-leaf trees exploit; 3000 rounds at lr 0.05 only partially compensates, so expect roughly a one-point AUC drop rather than a collapse, since main effects and low-order interactions are still captured.

Restricting to 4 leaves (≈3 splits per tree) prevents individual trees from encoding the higher-order feature/f_27 interactions this synthetic target is built on, and 3000 rounds at lr=0.05 with early stopping cannot fully compensate, so the model underfits and loses roughly 2 AUC points versus the 127-leaf baseline.
The added sum is largely redundant for GBDTs but gives axis-aligned trees an explicit oblique f_00/f_01/f_26 direction, so I expect a small positive AUC move.

A linear sum of three existing inputs is nearly redundant for deep (127-leaf, 3000-tree) LightGBM, which already captures additive structure via splits; any tiny gain from an easy split on the sum is offset by slight colsample_bytree dilution, so the score moves only within feature-ordering noise of ~±0.0002 AUC.

f_27 position interactions drive this dataset, and GBDTs exploit ordinal splits on them far more effectively than a small MLP fed raw ordinal-encoded letters; NN-without-embeddings baselines for TPS-May-2022 land in the mid-0.94s, several points below the 0.977 LightGBM score, even though the CPU training should comfortably finish ~50 epochs within the 420s budget.

LightGBM's native categorical splits find optimal bipartitions over the 26 letters per position rather than being constrained to threshold splits on an arbitrary alphabetical ordering, and f_27 characters carry strong signal in this dataset, so a small AUC gain is expected with low regression risk given ample rows per category.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is a well-known strong signal in this competition that the per-position ordinals cannot capture (trees can't count unique values across columns), so adding it gives a modest but real boost over the 0.97696 baseline while leaving everything else unchanged.

Up-weighting dark targets should recover some stroke/edge error while the median-background input and abundant white pixels keep background mostly stable, but the unweighted RMSE is background-dominated and target-dependent weighting can bias outputs darker, so I expect only a small net gain.

Time-boxed training gives roughly 5x more optimizer steps (~11k vs 2k) with cosine decay annealing to ~0 at the end, fixing the baseline's clear undertraining; expect a solid but diminishing-returns gain of ~7-10% to about 0.0148, with mild overfitting risk on the 105 train images capping further improvement.

L1 gives constant-magnitude gradients that avoid late-training stall and produce crisper stroke edges instead of hedged gray boundaries, which usually trims RMSE slightly even under an RMSE metric, though with only 2000 training steps the gain over the already-low 0.0166 baseline is modest.

Train and test noise come from the same synthetic generator, so input-only brightness/contrast jitter creates off-distribution inputs mapped to unchanged targets, adding conditional noise to the MSE regression and consuming capacity/optimization steps, while the regularization benefit is small since dense 256x256 patch supervision already limits overfitting — expect a slight RMSE increase, roughly within seed-level run noise.

Multi-scale averaging adds a little blur bias from the 0.75x/1.25x resize round-trips but slightly reduces prediction error in the dominant flat regions and on low-frequency stains, netting a very small RMSE gain over the already-strong 4-flip TTA baseline; runtime impact is negligible.

With only 2000 training steps, flip augmentation, random crops and BatchNorm, this small U-Net is not strongly overfitting, so channel dropout at e2/e3 (which also injects noise into the skip path to d2) mostly reduces effective capacity and slows convergence, likely producing a small RMSE regression rather than a generalization gain.

Dropout2d in every block slows convergence within the fixed 180s time budget and the BN+dropout variance shift hurts this dense regression task, so the already-low RMSE regresses slightly rather than gaining meaningful regularization on only ~134 images.

Quadrupling capacity and doubling receptive field (~41→~89 px) helps disambiguate noise blobs from punctuation and model large-scale stains, and since training is wall-clock-bounded the ~25% fewer steps within the cosine-annealed 180s only slightly offsets this; with 105 images + crop/flip augmentation a 1.95M-param regressor is far from overfitting, so a small net RMSE gain is expected.

A 23x23 median-filtered background channel is a well-known strong prior for this dataset: it explicitly separates low-frequency stain/fold structure from thin text strokes, letting the U-Net regress the clean background instead of having to estimate it internally, so with the same training budget RMSE should drop meaningfully (roughly 10-15%) with negligible runtime cost.

The 5-level U-Net's much larger receptive field (~500px context) helps remove large stains/wrinkles the 3-level net can't see, while pixels-per-step, steps, and optimizer are unchanged so optimization stays comparable; main risks are undertraining the ~16x larger parameter count in the same 2000 steps and BN with batch 8, but per-step gradient pixel count is identical and FLOPs grow only ~1.7x (fits the budget), so a moderate net improvement is expected.

The model is trained with random flips, so the four flipped predictions are near-equivariant and averaging them cancels residual per-pixel noise; this classic self-ensemble TTA typically yields a small (~2%) RMSE reduction on denoising tasks without any risk of regression, at negligible runtime cost.

On a GPU each UNet step takes only tens of ms, so the 360s wall-clock budget fits roughly 2-5x the original 2000 optimizer steps with the same cosine-to-zero LR shape; more steps on effectively unlimited random-crop data lets the model converge further, giving a modest RMSE gain limited by diminishing returns and no model-selection/early-stopping benefit.

The leaderboard metric is RMSE, which L2 directly optimizes (conditional mean); a Charbonnier loss optimizes a median-like estimator and down-weights high-error pixels, so even if reconstructions look sharper the squared-error metric typically degrades slightly, and with only 2000 short training steps the optimization benefits of L1-style losses are unlikely to overcome this loss/metric mismatch.

Injecting sigma=0.05 Gaussian noise (3x larger than the current RMSE) into training inputs creates a train/inference distribution mismatch: the model learns to over-smooth and its BatchNorm running statistics are calibrated to noisier inputs, so on noise-free-of-Gaussian test scans it blurs text edges slightly; the regularization benefit on ~64k already-diverse random patches is small and unlikely to offset this, so expect a mild regression of a few percent.

With batch 32 on 128x128 crops (~0.5M pixels/channel) BN's running statistics are already very stable and uniform crop sampling keeps them consistent with full-page statistics, so the mismatch GN fixes is tiny; meanwhile BN's optimization/regularization benefits in a short 2000-step run are roughly offset by GN's batch independence, making the change near-neutral with a slight risk of regression.

The graded metric is pixel RMSE, which plain MSE directly optimizes (it targets the posterior mean); switching to 0.84*(1-SSIM)+0.16*L1 favors sharper, structure-preserving, more contrasted outputs that deviate from the MSE-optimal mean, typically costing a few percent in RMSE even though perceptual edge quality improves, with only 2000 training steps there is little room for the new objective to compensate.

8-fold dihedral TTA averages out per-orientation prediction errors in a well-trained regression U-Net, typically yielding a modest ~2-4% RMSE reduction on denoising; training is unchanged so the gain comes purely from reduced prediction variance, with negligible runtime cost.

The graded metric is RMSE, which MSE optimizes directly; pure SSIM is invariant to local mean/contrast shifts (its luminance/contrast terms barely penalize small uniform intensity offsets in the mostly-white background), so with the same fixed training budget the SSIM-trained net will retain small systematic intensity deviations and slightly washed stroke amplitudes that inflate squared error — consistent with Zhao et al.'s own finding that L2 wins on PSNR while SSIM wins only on SSIM, so a moderate RMSE regression is expected.

Residual (DnCNN-style) prediction removes the saturating sigmoid over a mostly-white pixel distribution and starts from the identity mapping, giving better-conditioned gradients and faster convergence in a short 2000-step budget — a well-established win for denoising — so expect a modest ~4-6% RMSE improvement, with small risk the gain is limited since BatchNorm plus a learnable final conv already partially compensates for sigmoid saturation.

Replacing MSE with a per-batch RMSE anchor keeps the pixel-optimum (conditional mean) intact while the modest 0.1-weight SSIM term adds useful structural gradient signal at stroke edges and backgrounds (mixed L2+SSIM losses are known to be roughly PSNR-neutral-to-slightly-positive in restoration), so expect a small net gain well within seed noise; Adam largely absorbs the gradient rescaling from sqrt(mse) and the extra 7x7 conv is computationally negligible, so runtime is unaffected.

Residual prediction with an identity-initialized head removes sigmoid saturation at the dominant near-white/near-black pixel values, lets clamp(0,1) exactly pin the extremes, and starts training from the already-decent identity mapping, so the same 2000-step budget converges to a clearly better solution (DnCNN-style gains, ~10-20% RMSE reduction expected).

Adding ~630 synthetic pairs with plausible document-like artifacts (stains/shading/speckle) diversifies the small 105-image training set and acts as strong augmentation, likely improving generalization to test noise, though the synthetic noise distribution only roughly matches the real one and real pairs drop to ~14% of samples, capping the gain at a modest few percent.

The 2000-step baseline is undertrained, and stretching the cosine schedule over 9000 steps (4.5x more Adam updates with the same random-crop/flip augmentation) should converge to a noticeably better denoising optimum with little overfitting risk, though gains are sublinear so I expect only a mid-single-digit RMSE reduction; the run should still fit in ~7-9 minutes, so the 60-epoch config likely survives.
Dihedral self-ensembling should average out some prediction noise; flips match training augmentation while transposed views are only mildly out-of-distribution, so a small RMSE gain is likely.

L1 trains the network toward the conditional median while RMSE scores the conditional mean; with Adam's scale-invariance and near-deterministic clean targets the gap is small, so expect a roughly neutral-to-slightly-worse RMSE (1–3% regression), robustness to stain outliers partially offsetting the median/mean mismatch.
Upweighting rare dark/antialiased glyph pixels should sharpen text reconstruction and reduce the largest errors, with only a small risk of over-darkening background.

Ink and edge pixels contribute a disproportionate share of the MSE while being a small minority of pixels; up-weighting them 10x focuses the limited 2000 training steps on these hard regions, likely cutting stroke/edge error more than it costs on easy background, yielding a modest net RMSE gain — though the effect is small because background already dominates pixel count and the short schedule limits how much the reweighted objective can shift the solution.
Zero-initialized residual prediction starts from the strong identity baseline and avoids sigmoid saturation, likely giving faster convergence and a modest RMSE improvement.

RMSE is dominated by large residuals, and L1 training optimizes the conditional median rather than the mean, de-emphasizing exactly the severely corrupted pixels that drive squared error — so despite better outlier robustness, the metric mismatch should cause a slight regression (1–4%) over MSE-trained baseline, with run-to-run seed noise making a near-tie possible.

Residual (identity-plus-correction) parameterization starts training from the noisy image itself and avoids sigmoid saturation near the mostly-white background, which typically eases optimization and yields a modest RMSE improvement while leaving architecture, budget, and data unchanged.

Halving NAFNet width from 16 to 8 (~4x fewer params, ~150k) on an already tiny, briefly-trained (2000 steps) model adds bias faster than it helps via regularization on this low-overfit paired dataset, so expect a modest RMSE regression roughly consistent with a ~0.7-0.9 dB capacity loss.

Foreground weighting concentrates capacity on text/stroke pixels where nearly all the squared-error mass lives (white background is already trivially predicted), and the weight normalization keeps the loss scale/LR regime intact, so a modest RMSE gain is expected with only a small risk from slightly darker hedging on ambiguous edge pixels.

The closing-based background-normalization channel gives the U-Net explicit stain/illumination-invariant structure it would otherwise have to learn in only 2,000 updates, which typically yields a modest RMSE gain (MSE is dominated by background regions), though the 3-level network's receptive field already exceeds the 31px window so the information is in-principle redundant, capping the improvement.

Forcing the 1x1 conv + sigmoid head to fp32 removes only bf16 quantization noise (~0.001 std) at the output; against a 0.0162 RMSE this adds in quadrature to a negligible amount, so the score is essentially unchanged with a marginal improvement at best, and any residual difference is just seed-level training noise.

Flip-based TTA averages out per-view prediction noise from a model already trained with flip augmentation, typically yielding a modest ~1-3% RMSE reduction on denoising tasks without changing the underlying model capacity.

NAFNet's gated LN blocks, channel attention, and global residual (dirty + correction, no sigmoid) are a stronger, easier-to-optimize denoising formulation than the plain BN U-Net at similar parameter count, and residual learning suits this mostly-white-background task; gains are capped by the very short 2k-step schedule and the narrow 16-channel full-resolution stage, so expect a moderate (~10-15%) RMSE improvement rather than a large one.

The fine-tuned ImageNet-1k head restricted to the 120 dog classes is a genuinely strong second classifier on the same frozen features (trained on ~150k dog images with in22k pretraining), so a holdout-tuned temperature/mixture blend with a w=0 fallback should beat pure LR by a few percent; gains are capped because the holdout flatters the head (Stanford train images are ImageNet images it was fine-tuned on), biasing w a bit too high, but the log-loss mixture surface is flat enough that the downside is small.

The 256 leading PCs should retain the breed-discriminative subspace of these ImageNet-dog-tuned ConvNeXt features while dropping noisy low-variance directions and improving LR conditioning/calibration, so I expect a small gain; fine-grained low-variance signal loss keeps it modest.

Mixup/CutMix are the standard ConvNeXt regularizers and reliably help fine-grained transfer on small datasets, softening overconfident predictions on confusable breeds (good for log loss); even with only 6 epochs the pretrained backbone converges fine, and temperature scaling on clean val recalibrates, so expect a modest ~4% log-loss improvement.

The standard (0.08, 1.0) RandomResizedCrop is the augmentation recipe this backbone was pretrained/fine-tuned with and adds useful regularization for ~77 images/class; it typically yields a modest log-loss gain in transfer fine-tuning, though the short 6-epoch schedule limits how large the improvement can be.

All 120 competition breeds are ImageNet-1k classes, so swapping the 76%-top1 ResNet-50 for the ~87%-top1 ConvNeXtV2-Large (IN-22k pretraining, strong on fine-grained dogs) makes both the 1536-d features and the 1000-d log-prob block far more discriminative; the sklearn LR refit recalibrates them, which should cut log loss roughly 35-45% (≈0.25-0.30) with runtime still well inside the budget.

The 1000-d log-softmax block is a deterministic function of the pooled vector (linear fc + per-sample normalizer), so it adds essentially no information, and after standardization its near-constant non-dog columns become unit-variance noise that consumes L2 budget; dropping it gives a small but real log-loss improvement while the holdout-tuned C largely absorbs any residual difference.

Closed-form ridge should give nearly the same linear boundaries on these frozen features, while the joint alpha/temperature holdout search mainly improves probability sharpness/calibration for log loss.

Truncating each block to its top-128 PCs keeps most breed-discriminative variance while removing nuisance tail directions, and the 6.7x parameter cut plus flatter C response yields slightly better-calibrated probabilities, so log loss improves modestly; the effect is small because the frozen features are already strong and C is holdout-tuned, with some risk that subtle fine-grained cues in low-variance directions offset part of the gain.

ConvNeXt-Base pretrained on IN-22k and fine-tuned on IN-1k yields far stronger frozen features for fine-grained breed discrimination than ResNet-50 V1 (linear-probe accuracy typically jumps ~6-9 points on Stanford Dogs), and re-selecting C adapts to the new feature scale, so log loss should drop substantially while the ~4 extra logistic fits and 88M-param forward pass still fit within the time budget.

Fine-tuning ConvNeXt-Tiny (IN-22k→1k pretrained, whose 1k head already covers these exact dog breeds) with strong augmentation, flip TTA, and validation-fitted temperature scaling should substantially beat a frozen ResNet-50 linear probe — expecting ~85-88% accuracy and well-calibrated probabilities around 0.28-0.34 log loss, with the 6-epoch short schedule and 90% data usage keeping it from going lower.

The discarded ResNet-50 head is already a breed classifier trained on ~1300 ImageNet images per breed (~17x more than the competition's ~77/class), so its log-softmax outputs are extremely informative features; logistic regression can recalibrate/blend them with the pooled features, and standardization plus the lower C range suits the mixed-scale inputs, yielding a large log-loss drop (roughly 0.45 -> ~0.32) with extraction time unchanged.

Replacing a single RN50-V1 feature with concatenated L2-normalized ConvNeXt-IN22k + CLIP + DINOv2 features (all much stronger, complementary backbones, DINOv2 especially good for fine-grained breeds) plus a holdout-tuned C should lift linear-probe accuracy from ~85% to ~90-92% with well-calibrated LR probabilities, cutting log loss from ~0.45 to roughly 0.29-0.33.

Focal loss (gamma=2) was designed for extreme class imbalance and is roughly neutral on this balanced 120-way fine-grained task, while dropping label smoothing removes a calibration regularizer that directly helps log loss and upweighting hard/ambiguous look-alike examples risks overconfident test errors that log loss heavily penalizes, so a modest regression over the 0.660 baseline is most likely.

Since all 120 breeds are ImageNet classes, the frozen conv1–layer3 features are already dog-relevant, so restricting updates to layer4+fc curbs catastrophic forgetting/overfitting on ~85 imgs/class at lr=0.01 and should yield slightly better-calibrated probabilities, though gains are modest because layer4-only adaptation still leaves most capacity trainable.

Horizontal-flip TTA on a frozen ViT feature extractor with a linear head is a well-established, low-risk trick; dog poses are roughly flip-symmetric so the averaged probabilities are slightly better calibrated, typically shaving ~1-2% off multiclass log loss, while only doubling the cheap test-set extraction within budget.

All 120 breeds are ImageNet-1k classes, so the current augreg in21k->in1k ViT-B/16 features are directly tuned to separate them; CLIP ViT-B/32 features are weaker for fine-grained breed distinctions (typical Stanford Dogs linear-probe accuracy drops from ~85-88% to ~70-75%) and the 32px patches discard texture detail, so log loss should roughly double to around 1.1-1.3 despite identical probing pipeline.

PCA-256 keeps the breed-discriminative subspace (the ResNet-50 was ImageNet-trained on these very 120 breeds, so breed signal lives in top-variance directions) while discarding noise dims that were consuming the C=0.3 L2 budget, giving a small calibration/generalization gain; effect is modest because ridge on raw features already shrinks low-variance noise, and the un-retuned C caps the upside.

DINOv2 ViT-B/14 linear-probe embeddings are dramatically stronger than supervised ResNet-50 features for fine-grained classification (typically +5-8 points accuracy on ImageNet-dogs-style tasks), so the same LR + 10-view TTA pipeline with a re-tuned C should roughly halve the log loss, landing around 0.19-0.23; runtime and memory are well within budget at 224px fp16.

The premise is shaky (n≈9.2k > p=2816, so the head is not in a singular regime); PCA-256 truncation discards low-variance directions that carry fine-grained breed signal, and whitening inflates per-dimension feature scale ~37x, so fixed C=1.0 becomes effectively ~1000x weaker regularization, yielding less calibrated, overconfident probabilities — expect a modest log-loss regression despite the faster fit.
The frozen embeddings should give k-NN useful signal, but neighbor-vote probabilities are coarser and less calibrated than the discriminative logistic probe, leading to costly confident misses.

End-to-end fine-tuning of the ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 on 9.2k in-domain dog images (10 epochs, warmup+cosine, label smoothing, bs=64) comfortably fits the GPU budget and typically lifts top-1 from ~84% (linear probe) to ~88-89% with better-calibrated softmax, cutting log loss roughly 20-25%; main risks are mild overconfidence on errors and runtime, both modest here.

ViT-B/16 augreg in21k_ft_in1k is a far stronger pretrained model (~84-85% ImageNet top-1 vs ~76% for ResNet50-V1) and its 768-d pooled features with a linear probe typically jump Stanford Dogs linear-eval accuracy from ~82-85% to ~89-91%, which should cut log loss roughly 25-30%; C=0.3 transfers reasonably since 768-d L2-regularized LR is not very sensitive, and runtime stays well under budget.

10-view TTA (5 crops x flips) with probability averaging is a reliable variance-reduction trick for frozen-feature + linear-model pipelines; it typically buys 1-2% top-1 accuracy and a noticeably larger relative gain in log loss (~5-8%) by smoothing overconfident single-view errors, and the 10x test forward passes (only ~10k images) fit easily in the time budget.

ConvNeXt-tiny (IN-22k→IN-1k) is a far stronger feature extractor than ResNet-50 V1 for fine-grained dogs (these exact breeds are ImageNet classes), per-block L2 normalization conditions the features well for the linear probe and C=1.0 is a reasonable (if untuned) setting on unit-norm features, and concatenating diverse backbones typically adds a small boost over the better single model — expecting log loss to drop from ~0.453 to ~0.33–0.38, with mild risk from the fixed C being somewhat over-regularizing.

The blend adds the pretrained ImageNet head's dog-restricted, temperature-scaled probabilities — a strong, partially decorrelated signal since that head was trained on all ImageNet dog images (which include this competition's train and likely test images) — and the CV grid includes alpha=0 with validation/test sharing provenance, so a modest log-loss improvement is likely with low regression risk.

PCA-256 retains the dominant variance (>>120 classes, so class structure mostly survives), but it hard-discards low-variance directions that carry fine-grained breed signal and the fixed C=0.3 was tuned for raw 2048-d features, so the combined truncation+L2 shrinkage slightly underfits — expect a small log-loss regression of roughly +0.005 rather than a gain from denoising.

Global max pooling is valid but gives noisier, scale-shifted descriptors than the average pooling this ImageNet ResNet was trained for; with fixed C and no standardization I expect a small log-loss regression.

IMAGENET1K_V2 (80.9% vs 76.1% top-1) uses a modern training recipe that transfers markedly better, and since dog breeds are literal ImageNet classes the linear-probe features gain several accuracy points; temperature scaling on the holdout re-calibrates, so log loss should drop ~0.06, with only a small risk from the 232px resize changing feature statistics.

C=0.03 was already measured worse than C=0.3 on the stratified holdout (underconfident probabilities hurt log loss on these 2048-d features), and the brief low-LR fine-tune (conv lr 1e-4, ~2 epochs) only partially re-inflates the head, so the under-regularized-then-over-regularized gap mostly persists, yielding a modest regression.

Dropping input resolution from 224 to 192 removes fine-grained detail that distinguishes similar breeds (a resolution-sensitive task) and shifts features off the backbone's pretrained 7x7 operating point, so log loss should degrade modestly — roughly 3-6% — with only partial compensation from the brief bottleneck fine-tuning.

PCA-256 keeps the bulk of ResNet50 feature variance so LR accuracy is nearly unchanged, but truncation drops some low-variance fine-grained cues and C=0.3 (tuned on raw features) is slightly miscalibrated in the rotated PCA space, yielding a tiny log-loss regression; runtime stays well within budget.

Dropping input resolution from 224 to 192 moves away from ResNet-50's training resolution and discards fine-grained detail (ear/coat cues) needed to separate similar breeds, so frozen features become slightly less discriminative and log loss rises modestly, though the effect is limited because the crop fraction and backbone are unchanged.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 is a substantially stronger backbone (~80.9% vs ~76.1% top-1) trained with a better recipe, and its features consistently transfer better on fine-grained tasks like Stanford Dogs; with matched 232px preprocessing this typically cuts linear-probe log loss by roughly 10-18% versus V1 features, with only minor risk that the fixed C=0.3 is slightly mistuned for the new feature scale.

sklearn predict_proba is exactly softmax(decision_function), so the only delta is the val-tuned T; L2-regularized LR on frozen features is mildly under-confident, so a single scalar temperature (fit on ~1,380 val images, low overfitting risk, ranking unchanged) typically trims log loss ~1-2%, with gains capped because C=0.3 was already holdout-tuned.

The head is initialized exactly at the CV-tuned regularized LR optimum, so 2 epochs of SGD with weaker effective weight decay mostly adds overconfidence/overfitting on unaugmented cached features, while the conv updates (lr 1e-4, single bottleneck block, <=288 steps, frozen BN) are too small to yield compensating feature gains — expect a slight log-loss regression.

Horizontal-flip TTA with 0.5/0.5 probability averaging is a near-free variance reduction: ResNet-50 features aren't perfectly flip-invariant, so averaging two correlated views smooths per-image errors and typically cuts multiclass log loss by ~1-3% relative for a frozen-feature linear probe, with essentially no risk of regression since the flip preserves breed semantics and the C=0.3 classifier sees in-distribution features.

Balanced 1:1 undersampling discards most negative evidence and, with fixed C, makes the logistic fits and NB count ratios noisy—especially for threat and identity_hate—so rare-label AUC should decline.

Adding the shared char_wb 2-6 block to branch B's NB-LogReg is a classic improvement in these toxic-comment kernels (worth roughly +0.003-0.005 AUC standalone via morphology/obfuscation signal the word 1-2grams miss, including on the rare labels), but since the final score is a 50/50 rank blend with the unchanged branch A, only about half of branch B's gain transfers; the restructuring (fit-once char vectorizer, hstack, vectorized NB counts) is output-neutral, so expect a modest net improvement over 0.9805.

AUC only depends on ranking, and for regularized linear models balanced undersampling mainly shifts the decision threshold (remedy for calibration/F1, not AUC); it discards >99% of negatives for rare labels, so threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic models train on ~1-3k rows where per-sample effective regularization rises sharply and branch B's NB log-count ratios become noisy, costing a few thousandths of AUC on the rare (noise-dominant) columns while common-label columns barely move, netting a small mean regression despite faster fits.

Plain MultinomialNB on TF-IDF is substantially weaker than NB-weighted liblinear logreg (≈0.95 vs ≈0.98 mean AUC) and its overconfident, clipped logits weaken the OOF stack into branch A, so half-weighting it in the rank blend drags the 0.9798 baseline down to roughly 0.975.

Mean-pooling 200-dim Word2Vec destroys the token-level signal (slurs/profanity presence) that drives toxicity AUC, dropping branch A from ~0.972 to ~0.93; with the equal rank blend then putting 2/3 weight on the two weak, mutually-correlated embedding branches, the blend falls below branch B alone (~0.978) to roughly 0.971.

1:1 undersampling throws away 84-99.7% of the training rows; rare labels (threat: 478 positives -> 956-row fits) become high-variance and relatively over-regularized at fixed C, and branch B's NB log-ratio is estimated from only a few hundred sampled negatives, so per-label AUCs slip most on threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic — AUC's rank invariance prevents a collapse, but the lost negative-class information nets a small regression.

Branch D (fastText-style EmbeddingBag net on the same TF-IDF blocks) will individually reach ~0.973-0.978 held-out AUC within its 2-4 epoch/time-guarded budget — weaker than the 0.9810 linear blend but somewhat decorrelated as the only non-linear/shared-representation model, so an equal-weight rank average should add a tiny amount of signal (roughly +0.0003-0.0005 absolute), with the 0.97 sanity threshold and 690s epoch guard making a harmful or blown run unlikely.

1:1 undersampling discards 90-99.7% of negatives and shrinks per-label fit data 5-167x while C stays fixed, so effective regularization rises sharply and rare-label models (threat: ~956 rows vs 250k features) become noisy centroid-like rankers; AUC tolerates prior shifts but the lost negative-distribution information degrades ranking slightly across all six labels, with threat/identity_hate contributing most of the mean-AUC drop.

Lowercasing is already a no-op (vectorizers lowercase by default), but the de-obfuscation map and repeat-char collapse concentrate fragmented profanity/slur variants onto canonical tokens and char n-grams, transferring the strong learned LR weights to previously missed comments — a small net gain, especially on the noisy slur-driven labels (identity_hate, threat), with negligible runtime cost.

Stacking B's leakage-free OOF predictions (all six labels) into A gives A complementary bigram/NB signal plus exploitable label-correlation structure, yielding a small mean-AUC gain partially offset by reduced A-vs-B blend diversity; the 30 extra liblinear fits on the 200k matrix add ~3-5 min, keeping the run under the 15-min kill.

A 3-epoch sklearn MLP (64 hidden units, ~1875 Adam steps) on the same TF-IDF features as branch A will be notably undertrained (~0.965-0.970 solo AUC) and highly correlated with A, so forcing it to 1/3 of the rank blend dilutes the strong linear ensemble more than its limited nonlinear diversity adds, with the noise hitting hardest on the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) that dominate column-mean variance.

Branch C (NB-LogReg over B's 200k word 1-2-grams plus A's 50k char n-grams) is the classic strong word+char NB baseline, individually better (~0.984-0.985) than either current branch, so an equal three-way rank average should lift the blend — though the gain is capped by C's high correlation with B (shared word block, same NB+liblinear method) and early-stopped liblinear fits.

Both branches are strong, highly correlated linear models, so blend AUC is very flat in the mixing weight near 0.5; holdout-tuned per-label weights (shrunk halfway back to 0.5, which also neutralizes rare-label validation noise on threat/identity_hate) will at best add a tiny gain on the common labels, leaving the mean column AUC essentially unchanged.

300-dim LSA compression discards the rare, highly discriminative n-gram cues that drive threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic AUCs; dense low-rank LR typically trails the sparse high-dimensional TF-IDF ensemble on this task by roughly 2 points of mean AUC.

Downsampling negatives to 10:1 leaves 'toxic' untouched (negatives < 10x positives) and roughly preserves linear-model ranking, but it discards ~90%+ of negative evidence for severe_toxic/threat/identity_hate, noisifies branch B's NB log-odds (q estimated from only ~4.8k docs for threat) and starves fastText of hard negatives, so expect a small mean-AUC regression concentrated in the rare labels — near but below run-to-run noise magnitude.

A single softmax multi-label fastText splits probability mass across co-occurring labels (so toxic-looking negatives score nontrivially on severe_toxic/threat/identity_hate) and gives each label ~10x fewer focused gradient updates than six dedicated binary models, weakening branch F's per-column ranking — especially on the rare labels that dominate the column mean — which slightly drags the 1/3-weight rank average despite the nice speedup.

The current 0.9816 ensemble stacks TF-IDF logistic regression and NB-LogReg branches that are individually ~0.975-0.98; a single raw-count ComplementNB is a known decent-but-clearly-weaker baseline on this dataset (~0.95-0.96 mean AUC), since it loses the discriminative power of regularized logistic regression on TF-IDF word+char features, so this swap is a significant regression despite being faster and simpler.

Mean-pooled from-scratch skip-gram embeddings with a linear head is a well-documented weaker baseline on this competition (~0.93-0.95): unweighted averaging dilutes rare-token evidence critical for threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic, 200 dense dims cannot match ~260k sparse n-grams for surface-form abuse signals, and min_count=5 drops misspelled abuse variants that the char branches currently capture — so the single dense pipeline regresses clearly versus the tuned three-branch TF-IDF rank average.

Average-pooled, self-trained Word2Vec (CBOW, 200d, min_count=5) + logistic regression is a well-known weaker baseline for this task: mean pooling dilutes the highly predictive lexical/profanity signal, min_count=5 drops rare slurs/misspellings, and order-agnostic 200-dim means transfer less evidence than exact word/char n-gram matches — this family of models typically lands around 0.945-0.955 mean AUC versus ~0.98 for the sparse TF-IDF NB-LogReg/char blend it replaces.

A diverse char-level NB-LogReg is a classic complement to word-level NB and plain-LR branches in this competition and typically adds ~0.001-0.002 mean AUC to a rank blend, though the 3-way per-label weight search on a 10% holdout slightly overfits rare labels (threat, identity_hate), capping the net gain.

C=0.1 badly over-regularizes the 60k-feature word+char model (est. solo ~0.973-0.976, dragging the 50/50 rank blend below branch B's ~0.986); switching to the standard C=4/liblinear config makes branch A a ~0.985-0.986 model, and rank-averaging two comparably strong, mildly decorrelated linear branches lands near the classic ~0.987-0.988 blend, all well within the time budget since liblinear is fast on 60k sparse features.

fastText (dim=64, word bigrams, 20 epochs) is a decent but slightly weaker standalone model (~0.975-0.977 mean AUC) that is only moderately correlated with the two linear TF-IDF branches, so equal-weight rank averaging it in should add a small diversity gain of roughly +0.001 to +0.003 AUC, with minor downside risk concentrated in the noisy rare labels (threat, identity_hate).

A char-level NB-LogReg branch is a well-known diverse view in this competition (word NB-LogReg + char NB-LogReg blends historically gain ~+0.002-0.004 mean AUC); branch A's char features are capped/strongly regularized so branch C adds mostly complementary signal, and the rank-average blend should improve especially the rare labels (threat, identity_hate), while the added char vectorizer cost still likely fits inside the 15-min kill window.

Per-label weight tuning of two highly correlated linear branches has a flat AUC(w) curve and is estimated on a 16k holdout with only ~48 threat positives, so its realized gain is tiny, while training both branches on 90% instead of 100% of the data systematically costs a little on all six columns — the two effects roughly cancel with a slight net regression.

NB log-count-ratio weighting is a known small win for linear TF-IDF models on this dataset (helps rare labels like threat/identity_hate), so branch A alone should gain ~0.001-0.002 AUC; the equal-weight rank blend with the already-NB-weighted branch B transmits roughly half of that, though increased branch correlation slightly tempers the ensemble gain.

min_df=0.01 of ~313k docs ≈ 3,130 documents, which prunes the word/char/bigram vocabularies from tens/hundreds of thousands of n-grams down to roughly the top 1-3k most ubiquitous ones, destroying the mid- and low-frequency discriminative features (slurs, threat phrases, toxic bigrams) that drive especially the rare-label AUCs, so both branches — and their rank blend — degrade noticeably.

Balanced undersampling throws away most negatives, so common labels lose a little (~0.003 AUC) while rare labels (threat ~478, identity_hate ~1405, severe_toxic ~1595 positives) are fit on tiny balanced subsets with very noisy NB log-count ratios, dropping their column AUCs by ~0.01-0.02 — since the mean weights all six columns equally, the rare-label losses dominate and the overall score falls by roughly 0.008.

Swapping tuned logistic regression for a cosine class-centroid (Rocchio-style) classifier on identical features loses the discriminative per-feature weighting that drives this baseline, typically costing ~1.5-2.5 AUC points; the NB-weighted branch retains more signal than plain TF-IDF, so the blend lands around 0.96 rather than collapsing.

char_wb drops noisy cross-word-boundary n-grams and concentrates the 50k feature budget on within-word patterns (where obfuscated profanity signal lives), a small gain for branch A that is halved by the 50/50 rank blend with the unchanged NB-LogReg branch.

ComplementNB is a decent imbalanced-text classifier but consistently trails tuned logistic regression on TF-IDF AUC, and branch B additionally loses the discriminative logreg layer on top of the NB log-count ratios (ComplementNB approximates only the raw NB weighting), so expect a modest mean-AUC drop of roughly 0.7-1%, partially cushioned by the rank-average ensemble of the two feature views.

Crushing 60k sparse TF-IDF features into 32 SVD components discards most fine-grained lexical signal (especially for rare labels like threat/identity_hate), badly weakening branch A, and the equal-weight rank blend with the unchanged fastText branch then drags the overall mean AUC down by roughly 1.5-2%.

Collapsing every token outside the top-2000 DF vocabulary into a single 'raretoken' destroys exactly the rare-slur, misspelling, and leetspeak char-/word-ngram signal that branch A's char_wb features and fastText rely on (most impactful for identity_hate/threat, which drive the column-mean), while the existing max_features pruning and minCount=2 already handled true rare-word regularization, so the undifferentiated aggregate token is a weak proxy and the blend loses a small amount of ordering signal.

Keeping stop words lets second-person pronouns ('you', 'your') — strong signals for insult/toxicity — into the 10k word vocabulary while IDF downweights uninformative fillers, a tiny net gain for branch A that is then halved by the 50/50 rank blend with the unchanged NB-LogReg branch, so the overall effect is near noise but very slightly positive.

Logit-averaging lets the more extreme NB-LogReg probabilities dominate the per-column ordering, so the blend loses some of the complementary signal that the equal-weight rank average preserves; both combine the same two models so the effect is small, slightly negative (roughly a few ten-thousandths of mean AUC).

Switching char_wb to char swaps clean word-boundary n-gram markers for cross-word n-grams whose frequent space-containing tokens crowd the fixed 50k feature budget; the added short-phrase context roughly offsets the lost boundary signal, so branch A shifts only marginally and the 50/50 rank blend halves that, leaving the mean AUC essentially flat to very slightly lower.

fastText (dim=64, 5 epochs, no pretrained vectors, 256-token truncation) is a weaker standalone model (~0.965-0.970 mean AUC, especially on rare labels) than the NB-LogReg branch it replaces, so the equal-weight rank blend with the unchanged word+char branch lands between the two members and below the current 0.9801 blend of two comparably strong linear branches.

Dropping the lowest-F third of mostly redundant histogram bins slightly reduces LR variance in this 10-samples-per-class regime, but C=1.0 L2 already suppresses much of that noise and the LR is only half of the blend, so the net effect on the final log loss is small and only mildly positive (within noise of zero).

With only ~10 images per species and strong rotation/noise augmentation, the one-hot-trained NN saturates and makes overconfident errors; label smoothing caps the logit gap and improves the calibration that log loss rewards, giving a modest gain — tempered by the fact that TTA and the 50/50 blend with the already-well-calibrated LR already soften the NN, so the effect is small and comparable to single-run seed noise.

OvR turns each species into a highly imbalanced (10-vs-980) binary problem whose independently-scaled scores aren't comparable across classes; row-normalization plus a single global power/floor calibration cannot correct this per-class scale heterogeneity, whereas the multinomial softmax jointly optimizes exactly the scored cross-entropy, so log loss regresses moderately (roughly 15-30%), with runtime still trivially within budget.

A 5-seed bagged MLP(512) on the 192 descriptors is a decent complementary learner (expected OOF ~0.05-0.07 with different errors than LR), and since blending and calibration hyperparameters are CV-selected with a w=0 fallback, the blend should match or beat LR-only; typical LR+NN blends on this dataset cut log loss ~8-12%, tempered slightly by OOF selection noise.

Multinomial logistic regression is a stable, low-variance convex estimator, so bagging five fold models (each trained on only 80% of 990 rows) gives minimal variance reduction while losing the full-data refit's extra 20% of training data; the slight probability smoothing at high C only partly offsets this, so expect a near-neutral to slightly worse log loss.

The 21 geometric features add genuinely new discriminative signal (absolute size, aspect ratio, solidity, component count) that the scale-normalised shape descriptor lacks, and with per-fold scaling plus CV-tuned C the well-regularised logreg should exploit them for a modest log-loss gain despite only 990 training rows.

PCA(0.95) on standardized features keeps essentially all discriminative signal while truncating the ~5% of variance in noise-dominated, near-duplicate histogram-bin directions, acting as mild spectral regularization for the fixed C=1.0 logreg in this 990-sample/99-class regime — so the score should stay very close to baseline with a small improvement, though a small regression is also plausible since L2 already handles collinearity softly.

Averaging predict_proba over 5 stratified folds smooths overconfident/ambiguous predictions and reduces coefficient variance of the 219-dim logreg, which usually helps log loss modestly; this is only partly offset by each fold model seeing 80% of the data, so expect a small net improvement over the single full-data fit (0.0882 -> ~0.085).

The CNN+feature NN with rotation TTA should reach roughly LR-level accuracy (~90%) but be overconfident (solo LL ~0.3-0.5); 50/50 arithmetic averaging with the well-calibrated LR (0.1244) decorrelates errors and typically nets a modest log-loss gain to ~0.10, and the 9-min guard keeps both CPU training runs inside the budget even if the second run is slightly truncated.

OOF temperature/power + epsilon calibration is a low-capacity (2-scalar) post-hoc fix that reliably shaves a few percent off log loss for a moderately-overconfident LR baseline (softening plus uniform-mixing caps catastrophic tail errors), and the 990-sample OOF estimate should transfer to test with only mild attenuation since the full-data model is slightly better calibrated than the 80%-data OOF models.

C=1 heavily over-regularizes; with 192 near-separable standardized features, 5-fold OOF selection will pick a much larger C (likely 100-3000), and tuned multinomial LR on this dataset typically lands around 0.055-0.07 log loss versus 0.124 at C=1, roughly halving the error.
Geometric/Hu features should add a little complementary global-shape signal to the strong precomputed descriptors, but redundancy and fixed C=1 cap the gain.

With 990 rows, 99 classes and 240 correlated standardized features, C=1.0 is likely slightly under-regularized for log-loss calibration, so 5x stronger L2 should modestly shrink overconfident probabilities and improve test log loss by a few percent, while C=0.2 is not extreme enough to cause meaningful underfitting.

Removing the full-data refit means the submitted model trains on only 80% of the data (8 vs 10 samples per class); the validation-aligned rationale doesn't add information, so calibration/accuracy degrade modestly, raising log loss by roughly 5-8% with some split-dependent variance.

The OOF-weighted blend is leakage-safe with only 3 free parameters, LDA with shrinkage is a strong and diverse learner on these 192 descriptors, and kNN adds complementary structure, so SLSQP-blended probabilities should modestly beat tuned logistic regression alone (~10-15% typical ensemble gain), with little risk of regression since the LR-only solution is inside the feasible weight simplex.

With only ~10 samples per class across 99 classes, histogram gradient boosting (trained on an 85% split with noisy ~148-sample early-stopping validation) tends to be overconfident and poorly calibrated on this dataset, typically landing near 0.15-0.30 log loss versus the strong, CV-tuned, well-calibrated linear model at 0.061.

The linear SVM should separate about as well as softmax LR, but 3-fold Platt calibration with only a few positives per class and no full-data refit is likely a bit less calibrated, so as one uniform voter it slightly raises log loss.
