Random-forest vote-fraction probabilities are typically less calibrated than HGB's softmax outputs trained directly on log loss for this small 891-row, 99-class problem, so swapping one of four uniformly weighted members should mildly worsen the ensemble log loss (HGB's early stopping is noisy but still functional); effect is bounded since LR/LDA dominate the vote and only 25% of the mixture changes, though the 99-row test set adds substantial noise.

With only 990 samples across 99 classes, a ~95k-parameter sklearn MLP (no dropout, early stopping on a tiny non-stratified 10% validation split) will likely match LR's accuracy but produce overconfident, poorly calibrated softmax probabilities that the single uniform-shrinkage scalar cannot fix, so log loss moderately regresses despite the added nonlinear capacity.

On this small (990x192), highly informative feature set, C=1.0 over-regularizes multinomial LR; 5-fold OOF log-loss selection over the half-decade grid will typically pick C>1 (roughly 3-30), improving both fit and calibration, and with alpha re-tuned and C=1.0 inside the grid as a safety floor, a modest real gain (~15-25%) is expected with low regression risk.

The threshold polarity is inverted for this data (leaves are black on white, so mask>127 selects the background, not the leaf), so the largest 'external contour' is just the image frame: the 9 contour scalars and 32-bin distance histogram encode canvas dimensions (near-constant or pure noise w.r.t. species), leaving only the 7 background Hu moments with weak, highly redundant shape signal; L2-regularized logistic regression absorbs a few dozen standardized noise/redundant columns with only a slight degradation in calibrated log loss.

CV-selected C on the standardized 192-dim descriptors typically lands on noticeably stronger regularization than the fixed C=1.0, cutting overconfident probabilities; tuned multinomial LR on this dataset commonly scores ~0.06–0.08 vs ~0.12 for the untuned baseline, and refit=True still trains on all 990 rows so no data is lost.

Equal-weight soft voting forces two much weaker members (tuned KNN ~0.4 and small-data HistGB ~0.3 log loss) to dilute the strong, well-calibrated LR/LDA probabilities on the ~90% of easy test points, roughly tripling per-point loss there; the hedging benefit on rare catastrophic points only partially offsets this, so the blend lands above LR's 0.1244 and far above LDA alone (~0.06).

LR with C=1.0 on 192 features is overconfident on a 99-class problem with ~10 samples/class, so OOF validation will find a small positive alpha (~0.01-0.03): shrinkage barely hurts the confident-correct majority while substantially rescuing the few extremely-confident wrong predictions that dominate log loss; the CV-selected alpha keeps downside risk near zero, so expect a modest single-digit-percent improvement.

Ledoit-Wolf auto shrinkage on ~990 standardized samples with correlated histogram-like features likely selects very light shrinkage (~0.01-0.1), so fixing shrinkage=0.9 heavily damps noisy small-eigenvalue whitening directions—softening LDA's overconfident probabilities and improving log-loss calibration on unseen test rows, per classic regularized discriminant analysis behavior with only 10 samples per class; accuracy should hold roughly steady while overconfident errors get cheaper.

Each per-family 64-dim LDA is individually weaker than the joint 192-dim model, but with only ~10 samples per class the joint shrunk covariance adds little, and equal-weight averaging of the three complementary probability matrices softens overconfidence and decorrelates errors, which typically yields a modest log-loss improvement on this dataset.

Truncating to 90%-variance PCs is a crude spectral filter that the CV-tuned L2 penalty already approximates smoothly; the discarded low-variance components carry some fine inter-species signal (e.g., among similar Acer/Quercus species), so log loss should rise slightly, though re-tuned C keeps the regression modest.

LDA with CV-tuned shrinkage is a comparable linear softmax classifier on these 192 correlated descriptors, but as a generative model its probabilities are usually slightly less calibrated than logistic regression (which directly optimizes log loss), so expect a mild regression in the same ballpark.

After standardization, PCA(0.95, no whitening) is equivalent to ridge LR with the bottom ~5% variance directions (fine-grained contrast directions among correlated shape/margin/texture descriptors) truncated; with n=1584 >> p=192 the model is not variance-limited, so discarding those weakly-penalized but partly discriminative directions removes a little signal while gaining almost no denoising benefit, yielding a small log-loss regression that temperature scaling cannot recover.

LDA with Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage is well suited to these near-Gaussian margin/shape/texture descriptors with only 10 samples per class, and with the same OOF temperature calibration it typically matches or modestly beats regularized logistic regression on this dataset, so expect a small improvement in log loss.

For a well-calibrated logistic model, mixing toward uniform (floor 5e-5) adds roughly -log(0.995)≈0.005 loss to the vast majority of confident correct predictions while only rescuing true-class probabilities below ~5e-5, which are rare at this loss level, so log loss rises by approximately the 0.005 shrinkage penalty.

Dropping Nyström components from 512 to 384 is a minor capacity/regularization tweak on ~990 training samples; with the fixed seed the landmark subset changes arbitrarily, and 384 features slightly under-captures the kernel spectrum, so expect a near-neutral to very small regression in log loss (roughly within ±1-2%).

LDA with Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage is a famously strong fit for this dataset (192 nearly Gaussian-separable descriptors, 10 samples/class, 99 classes), typically cutting log loss roughly in half versus a fixed-C logistic regression while shrinkage keeps plug-in probabilities calibrated enough to avoid extreme-loss blowups.

3-fold CV selection of C on the 192 well-separated descriptors typically lands near C=1–10 and yields a modest log-loss gain over the fixed C=1.0 baseline (or no change if C=1.0 is re-selected), so expect a small improvement to roughly 0.11.

OOF-fitted temperature scaling corrects logistic regression's mild overconfidence on this small 99-class problem, typically yielding a small but real log-loss gain (a few percent), with low regression risk since the fold-model temperature transfers nearly optimally to the refit full-data model.

Nystroem RBF features with a sensible gamma=1/192 give logistic regression nonlinear decision power on the 192 descriptors; kernelized models on this leaf dataset typically roughly halve log loss versus linear LR (0.12 -> ~0.06), and C=1.0 with 512 components on 990 rows is unlikely to overfit badly.
The added block supplies known missing RAOP signals (time trend, request length, reciprocity/gratitude, prior-RAOP thresholds) with low overfitting risk, so a small AUC gain is likely.

Random forests are a poor match for ~8000-dim sparse TF-IDF: max_features='sqrt' shows each split only ~89 mostly-noise word features (the 9 strong numeric columns are rarely candidates), single-feature threshold splits cannot aggregate distributed text evidence the way a linear model does, and unpruned deep trees on ~3.2k rows overfit, so the forest lands near the meta-features-only benchmark (~0.62), clearly below logistic regression's 0.671.

Random forests systematically underperform regularized linear models on small (~4k row), high-dimensional (5k) sparse TF-IDF data: max_features='sqrt' rarely surfaces the informative rare-word columns and axis-aligned splits on sparse tf-idf values are weak, so the model effectively falls back to the ~10 numeric/giver features — losing most of the text signal that drives the logistic model's 0.748.

The predictive load is carried by the requester-history features (untouched), but swapping 5000 TF-IDF unigrams for 50 unsupervised LDA topic proportions discards discriminative word-level signal that a regularized linear model exploits well at 4.5k rows, so text's marginal AUC contribution shrinks — expect a modest regression, roughly 0.735-0.740.

The supervised TF-IDF logistic logit concentrates label-relevant text signal into one strong feature, whereas 20 unsupervised LDA topic proportions are individually weak/noisy and LightGBM must rediscover which narratives matter; topic×metadata interaction gains won't fully offset the lost supervised signal, so expect a modest AUC drop toward roughly metadata-plus-small-topic-bump performance.

Hour-of-day and weekday are stationary, genuinely (if weakly) informative signals for giver activity, while the raw epoch mostly lets trees memorize interval base rates; swapping them should be roughly neutral with a slight positive tilt from reduced overfitting, since neither feature set is a dominant driver of this model's AUC.

The GBM on the same dense features adds mild non-linear/interaction signal that is mostly redundant with the LR but somewhat decorrelated; rank-blending with an OOF-selected weight typically yields a small gain (+0.005–0.01 AUC) and the CV weight selection guards against regression, though the text TF-IDF signal (unseen by the GBM) still dominates, capping the upside.

Random forests are a poor match for ~5000-dimensional sparse TF-IDF text on ~4.5k rows: with max_features='sqrt' each split sees only ~71 random columns, so informative-but-sparse word features are rarely chosen and trees mostly re-split the few dense numeric metadata features, discarding most of the additive text signal that drives the logistic model's 0.70 AUC (the classic linear-model-beats-RF regime for sparse text), likely dropping to roughly the metadata-only level ~0.65-0.67.

Subreddit-membership history carries real signal about requester community embeddedness (known from the Althoff paper and prior solutions) that is only partially captured by the existing numeric counts; as a min_df=5 binary TF-IDF block under C=0.3 regularization it adds modest, mostly non-redundant information, yielding a small AUC gain of roughly +0.01 with little overfitting risk.

In the shipped test.json, giver_username_if_known is 'N/A' for every row (or absent entirely, in which case the fallback forces zeros), so giver_known is a constant-0 column at inference; its learned weight multiplies zero and test rankings are unchanged apart from negligible solver noise, leaving AUC at ~0.6573.

Proper OOF stacking of the TF-IDF logistic score with requester-history numerics under a heavily regularized, early-stopped, seed-averaged GBM typically adds ~1-2 AUC points over a linear blend on RAOP by capturing nonlinear interactions, with modest overfitting risk from the raw timestamp feature.

The added blocks (request-length stats, evidence/link indicators, [request] tag, RAOP-history indicators, karma ratio, posting-time features) are documented weak-to-moderate predictors on this dataset that are largely complementary to unigram TF-IDF and the existing counts, so with C=0.3 they should yield a small but real AUC gain rather than noise.

On ~5.4k mostly-sparse TF-IDF features, signal is a sum of many weak word effects that a linear model aggregates well but single-feature tree splits cannot; with max_features='sqrt' the word block is diluted and ExtraTrees effectively leans on the small numeric/embedding block plus noise, typically costing several AUC points versus TF-IDF logistic regression on small text datasets like RAOP.

Word TF-IDF carries substantial task-specific signal on RAOP (narrative, gratitude, and wording cues drive pizza success) that generic MiniLM embeddings only partially recover, so dropping the 5k sparse block loses more signal than variance and modestly lowers AUC despite the cleaner dense design.

Length-normalized TF-IDF discards document-length and style signals that are known predictors in the RAOP paper (narrative length, gratitude/politeness, sentiment), so adding ~20 scaled dense features (especially log word/char counts and VADER compound) should give a small but real AUC bump over 0.6497, though many flags (please/thank) are redundant with existing unigrams and LR capacity limits the gain.

TF-IDF text features are the primary signal in this competition (narrative content drives success in the Althoff analysis and in most public baselines); the nine requester-history features alone capture only 'status' and typically yield ~0.60-0.62 AUC, so dropping text should regress the graded AUC from ~0.650 to roughly ~0.61, and the temporal-drift rationale is weak because the train/test split here is random, not time-based.

Mean-pooled skip-gram vectors trained on this tiny ~5.7k-doc corpus lose the token-specific discriminative signal that TF-IDF + LR exploits (known small-data result: TF-IDF beats averaged Word2Vec), so the text block's contribution shrinks while the unchanged metadata/text-stats features keep the score from collapsing — a modest regression of roughly 1.5 AUC points.

Adding word bigrams and a 60k vocabulary recovers diagnostic phrase-level and mid-frequency token signal that unigram-5k misses, and L2 logistic regression at C=0.3 handles ~60k sparse TF-IDF features on ~4.5k rows without severe overfitting, so a small AUC gain is likely — though the gain is dampened because the existing handcrafted gratitude/reciprocity/hardship text stats already capture part of the phrase signal and C is untuned for the larger feature space.

The 9 requester-history features carry real but limited signal (~0.60-0.61 AUC standalone on RAOP); the current pipeline already controls text overfitting via SVD-300 + CV early stopping, so discarding the TF-IDF text removes the narrative/reciprocity lexical cues that Althoff et al. show add lift beyond metadata, costing a few AUC points.

On dense 300-dim SVD + scaled numeric features, an untuned RandomForest with sqrt feature sampling dilutes the signal concentrated in the top SVD components and typically trails a CV-tuned, early-stopped GBM by a few AUC points, so expect a modest regression to roughly 0.60-0.62.

Frozen MiniLM embeddings add complementary semantic signal beyond 5k unigram TF-IDF on this small (~4k train) dataset, which typically yields a modest ~0.01 AUC bump under strong regularization (C=0.3) with low overfitting risk, and CPU encoding of a few thousand truncated docs fits comfortably in the budget.

Bigrams plus a much larger TF-IDF vocabulary (min_df=2, 100k cap) typically add modest discriminative text signal on this small (~4k train) dataset, and L2-regularized LR handles the high-dimensional sparse matrix fine, but the strong fixed C=0.3 caps how much of the added capacity converts into test AUC, so expect only a small gain over 0.6573.

Handcrafted text stats (length, gratitude/reciprocity/hardship lexicons, first-person pronouns) are well-documented predictors on RAOP that capture signal the stop-worded unigram TF-IDF misses (e.g., 'please'/'thanks'/'I' are stop-words, and doc length is invisible to sublinear TF-IDF), and adding only 15 scaled dense features to a strongly regularized linear model carries minimal overfitting risk, so expect a modest ~0.01 AUC gain.

LightGBM can exploit nonlinear interactions in the 9 metadata features (strong signals per the RAOP paper) and CV early-stopping tunes rounds sensibly, but SVD-300 compression of sparse unigram TF-IDF loses some linearly-separable text signal that logistic regression exploits, so the two effects roughly offset with a small net gain on this small, noisy dataset.

Date features are only a marginal part of this model (TF-IDF + requester history dominate), and swapping the absolute-time spline for two annual Fourier terms trades away a weak long-term trend signal for a weak seasonal one, so expect a small regression well within noise (~±0.004 AUC).

With ~4k training rows and ~5k sparse TF-IDF features, C=0.3 is likely over-shrunk; C=30 is still moderate L2 for this feature scale, so the text cues gain ranking latitude with only mild overfitting risk, yielding a small expected AUC gain.

A quantile-spline of absolute request time only captures weak long-term drift in base success rate; adding 8 well-regularized columns to a ~7k-feature logistic model rarely moves AUC meaningfully, so expect essentially flat performance with a possible negligible gain from temporal base-rate drift.

KNN (k=25, cosine, brute force) suffers from distance concentration in the ~6k-dim sparse space and cannot reweight blocks like LR does — since TF-IDF rows are L2-normalized, the cosine distance is dominated by the standardized numerics and high-variance subreddit counts, so neighbors are selected mostly on requester activity/subreddit overlap, losing the text signal and the learned feature weighting that gave LR its 0.649; runtime is trivial (small pairwise distance computation), so no budget risk.

Distance-weighted KNN (k=25) on nine coarse, heavily skewed requester-history features is a markedly weaker tabular learner than 600-iteration CatBoost — its smoothed neighborhood estimates are dominated by clusters of first-time posters and yield a noisier, lower-AUC metadata signal, which drags the fixed 50/50 blend down even though partial decorrelation with the unchanged TF-IDF logistic half cushions the drop.

Reducing L2 shrinkage (C=0.3→30) lets the small-scale document-normalized TF-IDF features earn coefficients comparable in effect to the unit-variance metadata features, and unigram lexical signal (need/gratitude/reciprocity) is genuinely predictive in RAOP, so the logistic half of the blend should rank slightly better; gains are capped because the 50/50 CatBoost blend dampens the change and C=30 with 5k features on ~4k docs incurs mild overfitting, so expect a small net improvement rather than a large one.

Spline features on the raw UTC timestamp capture a known multi-year downward trend in RAOP success rates as the community grew, adding a weak but real signal; with only ~7 extra standardized columns under C=0.3 regularization among 5000 TF-IDF features, overfitting risk is minimal, so expect a small AUC gain of roughly +0.001-0.003.

Binarizing TF-IDF at 0 discards term-frequency/discriminative weighting that LR exploits, and thresholding standardized meta-features at the mean throws away the magnitude of the strong requester-history signals (karma, account age), so BernoulliNB's generative ranking should land a few points below the 0.654 logistic baseline despite NB being a reasonable small-data text classifier.

A spline on the UTC timestamp can capture the slow drift in pizza success rate over 2010-2013, adding a small real signal; with only ~7 well-regularized dense features appended to a 5000-dim sparse model, overfitting risk is minimal, so expect a tiny AUC gain rather than a regression.

Binary subreddit-membership features add complementary signal about requester community embeddedness beyond the aggregate counts (number_of_subreddits already included), and a min_df=5 sparse block is safe for the existing L2-regularized LR, so expect a modest AUC gain rather than overfitting.

The logistic score is dominated by the 5000 TF-IDF text features, so a CatBoost model trained purely on the 9 requester-history features (likely ~0.60-0.63 AUC alone) adds a fairly decorrelated nonlinear signal; a 50/50 blend of complementary text and metadata models on RAOP typically gains ~+0.005-0.012 AUC over the text-only LR, landing around 0.664-0.668 with moderate run-to-run/test variance.

With max_features capped at 5000, frequent bigrams (e.g. politeness/gratitude phrases) displace some low-value unigrams; bigram features are sparser and the unchanged C=0.3 regularization slightly under-fits them, so the net effect is a small, near-neutral gain in ranking quality typical for this dataset.

Authorship attribution relies heavily on function-word/style signals carried by stop-word unigrams and bigrams; the char_wb view only partially compensates, so removing them from the word view typically causes a small regression in log loss, roughly on the order of 1%.

Stacking the LR-TFIDF with two diverse count-based Naive Bayes models via a properly regularized log-prob meta-learner on clean 19.6k-row OOF predictions is a well-established modest win on this competition (decorrelated errors, low overfit risk with only 9 meta-features), typically worth ~0.01-0.015 log loss; fold-averaged test predictions roughly offset the loss of the full-data refit.
Stop-word removal should make the word-level models more content-focused while the character models and meta-features retain function-word style, giving the stack a modest gain.

A strongly regularized multinomial LR on 12 already-informative, correlated OOF probability columns plus 16 meta-features matches or slightly edges the overfit-prone LightGBM combiner on this small stack, so expect essentially the same test log loss with a small improvement within noise.

Punctuation is a genuinely discriminative stylometric signal for these three authors (Poe's dashes/semicolons, Lovecraft's comma-heavy style), and the case-sensitive char block currently exploits it; the word block barely changes, so stripping punctuation removes more author signal than edition/chunker noise, giving a small regression of roughly 0.008–0.01 log loss.

Diverse 4-model stack (word/char LR + tuned word/char NB) with a calibrated meta-LR on clipped log-OOF probabilities mirrors classic kernels that scored ~0.30-0.35 on this dataset, clearly beating the single word+char LR at 0.4386; fold-averaged test predictions and 12-feature meta-learner keep overfitting risk low.

LR with L2 on 130k TF-IDF features at 19.6k samples is not variance-limited, and chi2 selection to 10k discards many individually weak but collectively useful char n-grams, slightly degrading LR calibration; the OOF blend shifts weight toward the unchanged NB branch and absorbs part of the damage, so net effect is a small regression (~+0.005 log loss) rather than a gain.

Function words are the classic stylometric signal in authorship attribution (they're not noise here — Poe/Shelley/Lovecraft differ in their usage), so removing them slightly degrades both the word-TFIDF LR block and the count-based MNB; the OOF blend-weight search bounds the damage by shifting weight toward the char features, so expect a small regression rather than a large one.

5-fold CV over C will likely select a moderately larger C (around 3-10) than the fixed C=1.0, which typically yields a small log-loss gain for multinomial LR on sublinear TF-IDF features, while the featurization and refit-on-full-data flow are unchanged, so only a modest improvement is expected.

The 4-model stack (word/char LR at C=10 plus count-based NBs) adds genuine diversity over the single LR, the 16 style/meta-features carry real author signal, and a well-regularized LGBM meta-learner with early stopping typically nets a solid calibration gain; minor risks are no full-data refit of level-1 and LGBM calibration, but historically such stacks on this dataset land ~0.38-0.40 vs ~0.43 for the single LR baseline.

Uncapped boundary-crossing char n-grams (1,5) capture punctuation/capitalization style that is highly discriminative for Poe/Lovecraft/Shelley, and with min_df=2 plus C=1.0 LR the added ~350k sparse features historically improve this baseline by roughly 0.02-0.03 log loss rather than overfitting.

The OOF-tuned arithmetic blend should not hurt and count-MNB adds a little complementary lexical signal plus safer 1e-6 clipping, but it is largely redundant with the word TF-IDF block while LR+char remains dominant, so expect only about a 1% log-loss drop.

Authorship attribution is a stylometry task where high-frequency function words ('the', 'and', 'of') are among the strongest author fingerprints (Burrows/Mosteller-Wallace), so removing them strips discriminative signal and turns word bigrams into spurious content-word adjacencies; expect a modest log-loss regression of roughly 2-3%.

The class imbalance is mild (~1.4:1), so fastText isn't strongly biased; oversampling shifts learned priors toward uniform and duplicates minority rows (seen 25 epochs each), miscalibrating probabilities for log loss and causing a small regression.

ComplementNB on tf-idf is a strong, decorrelated second model on this competition; OOF-selected convex blending is downside-protected (worst case w≈1 recovers LR), and typically buys ~0.005–0.012 log loss over a tuned LR alone, so expect a modest improvement rather than a regression.

MultinomialNB on TF-IDF is a decent classifier for this task but its predict_proba outputs are notoriously overconfident/poorly calibrated, which log loss punishes heavily; public Spooky Author kernels consistently show tuned logistic regression (~0.33-0.36) beating tuned MNB (~0.42-0.48) on identical word+char TF-IDF features, so alpha tuning won't close the gap.

Character 2-5 grams carry strong stylistic/punctuation signal that separates these authors (esp. Poe vs Shelley), so dropping them loses discriminative power and calibration; word 1-2 grams retain most lexical signal, so expect a moderate regression, not a collapse.

ComplementNB is a solid text classifier but its raw probabilities are noticeably more overconfident than the C=4 regularized NB-ratio-weighted logistic (NB-SVM), and the near-balanced class counts negate its uneven-data advantage, so expect a modest log-loss regression; its predict_proba already sums to 1 so dropping renormalization is harmless.

For high-dimensional TF-IDF text features, CV over C typically selects a less-regularized value (roughly 3–30) than the default C=1.0, which usually buys a few thousandths of log loss; features and pipeline are unchanged, so expect a modest, reliable improvement rather than a large jump.

MultinomialNB's independence assumption is badly violated by the large correlated char n-gram block, producing overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities; historically on this dataset MNB-on-TFIDF runs ~0.08-0.12 log loss worse than tuned logistic regression, so expect a clear regression from 0.425 to roughly 0.50-0.52.

fastText with subword+bigram features reaches comparable accuracy to TF-IDF+LR on this dataset, but with lr=0.5 and 25 epochs its softmax outputs are sharply overconfident and poorly calibrated, which log loss punishes, so it typically lands around 0.45-0.55 versus the well-regularized LR's 0.432.

For sparse high-dimensional TF-IDF text features, C=1.0 is typically slightly over-regularized; CV will likely pick C=2-4, yielding a modest log-loss gain of roughly 0.005-0.012 over the current 0.4323.

NB-SVM (log-count-ratio weighting + per-class binary LR with C=4, then row renormalization) is a well-documented modest improvement over a single multinomial LR on TF-IDF text tasks, typically worth a few hundredths of log loss; the 1-vs-rest probabilities stay reasonably calibrated after normalization, so expect ~0.41-0.42 vs 0.4323.

Stylometric features (sentence length, punctuation rates) carry real authorship signal for Poe/Lovecraft/Shelley and are only partially redundant with char_wb n-grams, so MaxAbs-scaled dense features stacked onto TF-IDF typically give a small log-loss gain; but 14 dense columns vs ~100k+ TF-IDF dims means the effect is minor (fraction of a percent), with slight risk of being neutral.

NB log-count-ratio feature weighting with one-vs-rest binary LR (Wang & Manning NB-SVM-style) is a well-known strong upgrade over plain multinomial LR on TF-IDF for this competition, typically cutting log loss ~10-20% despite slightly rougher probability calibration.

Increasing L2 strength (C 1.0 -> 0.25) on high-dimensional sparse word+char TF-IDF softens overconfident LR probabilities, which typically yields a small log-loss gain on this dataset with negligible runtime change.

Dropping the word unigram/bigram block removes the strongest lexical signal for distinguishing these authors' vocabularies; char_wb 2-5 grams retain partial word/style information so the NB-logistic still works, but log loss should regress roughly 8-12% from 0.518 to ~0.57.

Plain TF-IDF + L2 logistic regression (OvR, renormalized) is much better calibrated for log loss than NB-log-ratio-reweighted features, which produce overconfident probabilities; standard TF-IDF+LR baselines on this dataset land near 0.33-0.36, so this should be a large improvement over 0.5177.

With ~120k correlated word/char TF-IDF features and only ~19.5k training rows (p >> n), modestly stronger L2 (C=4→2) slightly shrinks overfit coefficients; the C–log-loss curve is shallow in this region so expect a very small improvement, though it could plausibly be flat or slightly worse.

NB log-count-ratio weighting (Wang–Manning NBSVM-style) on binarized counts typically improves TF-IDF logistic-regression text classifiers by a modest but real margin over plain multinomial LR, so expect roughly a 0.03 log-loss gain (~0.369 → ~0.335), with some risk offset by one-vs-rest calibration being slightly worse than softmax.

Authorship attribution is a stylometric task where function words (the, of, and, etc.) are among the most discriminative features; TF-IDF already downweights them, so stripping them removes real signal from the word branch and mangles high-frequency char_wb n-grams, likely causing a small-to-moderate log-loss regression.

Quadrupling L2 strength (C=1.0→0.25) on ~150k highly correlated word/char TF-IDF features typically yields a small log-loss gain by shrinking noisy coefficients; temperature scaling already handles calibration so the effect is modest, likely improving 0.382 to ~0.378, with some risk of slight underfitting making it near-neutral.

Switching char_wb->char keeps punctuation and cross-word-boundary n-grams (char_wb's token pattern drops all punctuation), and punctuation/function-word adjacency patterns are classically discriminative for authorship attribution, so the char channel adds modest orthogonal signal atop the word TF-IDF; expect a small log-loss improvement of roughly 1%, though the effect is small enough that a near-neutral outcome is plausible.

NB log-count-ratio feature weighting (Wang-Manning trick) is a well-established upgrade over plain TF-IDF logistic regression for this competition, typically cutting log loss ~10-15%, and per-class binary LR probabilities with row renormalization remain reasonably calibrated for log loss.

Raising C from 1.0 to 4.0 weakens regularization on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF features, which typically reduces log-loss slightly for this competition's tuned logistic baselines, though gains are modest since C=1.0 is already near the optimum.

Temperature scaling is a single scalar tuned on a ~1.9k-row stratified holdout (low overfit risk), and multinomial LR on TF-IDF at C=1.0 is mildly overconfident, so the optimized T slightly softens predictions; it transfers well to the refit full-data model, typically yielding a small but real log-loss gain of ~0.005 (≈1%), with essentially no risk of regression.

RMSE rewards the conditional mean, but log1p training + expm1 inversion yields the conditional median/geometric mean, which sits a few percent below the mean for the right-skewed fare distribution — a systematic downward bias that is largest on expensive rides where dollar-scale errors dominate RMSE; the tail-downweighting and variance-stabilization benefits don't offset this, and the ~2.8% corrupt-row fallback is unchanged, so expect a small (~1%) regression to roughly 4.15.

Quadrupling the training sample (1M→4M rows) reduces variance and sharpens leaf estimates for the 1000-tree LightGBM, typically cutting RMSE on the ~97% valid-coordinate test rows by ~3% (≈3.60→≈3.48), but the fixed ~2.8% corrupt-row component still predicted as the mean fare is unchanged, damping the overall gain to roughly 2-2.5% (4.10→≈4.00); the 1000-tree/0.05-lr cap limits further improvement and the run fits comfortably in budget.

Airport-distance features are among the highest-value known features for this competition (JFK flat-fare trips and long airport rides break the pure distance-fare relationship, and radial distances are hard for axis-aligned GBM splits to reconstruct from raw coordinates), so clean-row RMSE should drop ~0.1-0.15; however the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows is unaffected, damping the overall gain to roughly 3% (4.19 -> ~4.07).

Training L2 on log1p optimizes log-space RMSE, and expm1 of those predictions approximates the conditional geometric mean/median, which is biased low for the dollar-scale RMSE that rewards the conditional mean; with 1M rows and min_child_samples=100 the raw-scale model already dilutes fare outliers, so the stabilization gain is small and the missing smearing/bias correction yields a slight RMSE regression (~4.22-4.26).

The fare-vs-distance relationship is already learned as nearly monotone from ~3.6M clean rows, and the unconstrained coordinate splits can partially reintroduce distance non-monotonicity anyway, so the constraint binds on few splits and acts only as a mild regularizer in sparse long-trip regions — expect a negligible change, very slightly positive, well within run-to-run noise.

Log-target training dampens the influence of the long right tail of fares (up to $500) on squared-error gradients, which typically yields a small dollar-RMSE gain on the ~97% valid test rows; this is partly offset by the lack of a smearing/bias correction (expm1 of the log-space optimum underpredicts the conditional mean), and the ~2.8% corrupt test rows pinned to the mean-fare fallback are unaffected, so the net effect is a modest improvement of roughly 1%.

In-sample encoding with m=20 smoothing keeps per-row leakage bounded (~1/(count+20), and most pickup/dropoff cells have hundreds of trips), while it removes a real train/inference mismatch: the log(0.8) offset on all three log_count features, noisier 80%-fold fare_mean stats, and the OOF artifact where singleton-route training rows collapse to the global mean but test rows get informative encodings; early stopping on the leakage-free validation set caps any overfitting, so the mismatch fixes should net a small (~0.4%) RMSE gain.

RMSE rewards the conditional mean, but exp(log-model) predicts roughly the conditional geometric mean; with no smearing/bias correction, predictions are systematically ~4-6% low (worst on high fares, which dominate squared error), and this bias outweighs any variance-stabilization benefit, so raw-scale RMSE should worsen slightly from ~4.18 to ~4.22.

Airport-distance features are a well-known win in this competition: they let the trees isolate JFK flat-fare and EWR-surcharge trips with single splits instead of approximating airport circles from raw coordinates, but the ~2.8% corrupt test rows (predicted as mean fare, ~2.1 RMSE floor) dilute the gain, so expect roughly a 0.1 improvement on valid rows translating to ~2-2.5% overall.

Replacing the global-mean fallback with model predictions helps on the ~2.8% corrupt test rows — most clearly the subset with valid coordinates but out-of-range passenger_count, which become fully predictable (RMSE ~3.6-5 instead of ~12.7), and the coordinate-corrupt rows gain a little from conditional means given year/hour — while valid-row predictions stay essentially unchanged, so overall RMSE improves modestly.

Quadrupling training rows (1M→4M) with identical features/hyperparameters reduces split variance and lets boosting use more of its 1000-tree budget, typically worth ~0.15-0.2 RMSE on the predictable rows; but ~2.8% of graded test rows are corrupt and floored at the mean-fare prediction, diluting the gain to roughly a 3-4% overall improvement (4.138 → ~3.98), with dtype/n_jobs/I-O changes being metric-neutral and runtime still within budget.

OOF-smoothed route/cell mean-fare encodings capture JFK flat fares, bridge/tunnel tolls and habitual route pricing that haversine distance cannot express, and are historically among the strongest features for this dataset; with proper 5-fold OOF computation (no leakage), m=20 smoothing and ~1M rows giving healthy per-cell counts, this should cut the valid-row RMSE from ~3.6 to ~3.35, while the ~2.8% corrupt test rows keep the mean-fare fallback and their fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor contribution, so overall RMSE drops from 4.138 to roughly 3.9 with negligible runtime cost.

Training on log1p makes the model optimize conditional-mean-of-log, so expm1 yields roughly the conditional median of fare, which is biased low versus the conditional mean that dollar-space RMSE rewards — underpredicting large fares (whose squared errors dominate RMSE) and lowering fallback predictions for corrupt test rows from ~11.35 toward ~9; the variance-stabilization benefit is real but typically smaller than this metric-mismatch bias, so expect a modest ~1-2% regression (4.13 -> ~4.19).

Manhattan distance and bearing are classic, genuinely informative features for NYC fares (street-grid distance and direction-dependent tolls) that LightGBM cannot easily reconstruct from raw coords with axis-aligned splits, so the ~97% valid test rows should see a modest holdout gain (~3.6 -> ~3.5 RMSE), while the corrupt-row fallback is untouched, netting roughly a 2% overall improvement.

Airport/landmark distance features are a well-established win in this competition — JFK/LGA/EWR trips have distinct flat-fare/surcharge regimes that raw-coordinate trees only approximate, typically worth ~0.1-0.15 RMSE here; gains are partly masked by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows predicted as the mean, and the vectorized haversine calls add negligible time.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean (L2); the (0,500] fare filter already removed the worst outliers, so switching to an L1/median fit mostly adds mean–median bias on skewed but legitimate fares (airport flat-fare/toll trips) and LightGBM's L1 with unchanged hyperparameters converges slightly worse — expect a small RMSE regression on valid rows while the corrupt-row mean-fare floor is unchanged.

Squared error on log1p(fare) optimizes the conditional geometric mean, so expm1-inverted predictions are systematically biased low versus the arithmetic-mean target RMSE rewards (no smearing/bias correction is applied), and downweighting high-fare outliers hurts since the test ground truth contains the same noisy tail; corrupt-row fallback is unchanged, so expect a small regression on the ~97% valid rows, roughly +0.05 RMSE.

RMSE is minimized by conditional-mean (L2) predictions; since fares are already clipped to (0,500] and grossly corrupt rows are dropped, L1's robustness benefit is small while its median-targeting and weaker constant-hessian optimization mismatch the RMSE metric — early stopping on RMSE and 5-fold averaging cushion but don't reverse a small expected regression.

With delta=$1 vs a ~$4 residual scale, Huber behaves mostly like L1, pulling leaf predictions toward the conditional median (below the right-skewed conditional mean) and introducing a downward bias that RMSE penalizes; early stopping on RMSE and outlier robustness only partly offset this, so a small regression is the most likely outcome.

RMSE on the raw dollar scale is minimized by predicting the conditional mean, but expm1 of a log-space L2 model approximates the conditional geometric mean (~3-4% low given residual log-sigma ~0.25-0.3), and with no bias-correction multiplier this systematic underprediction — largest on the high-fare rows that dominate squared error — typically outweighs the modest variance benefit of compressing the skewed tail, so a small regression is expected.

Airport-proximity features are a well-known high-value addition for this competition (JFK flat fares, airport surcharges) that axis-aligned LightGBM splits cannot easily derive from raw coordinates, so expect a moderate RMSE improvement on the ~97% of valid rows while the corrupt-row floor (~2.1) caps the total gain.

Quadrupling training data from 1M to 4M rows gives LightGBM a modest generalization gain (roughly 0.1-0.15 RMSE on valid rows, typical for this dataset's learning curve), but the ~2.8% corrupt test rows predicted as the mean fare create a fixed error floor that damps the graded improvement, so expect ~3% better RMSE around 4.01.

5-fold bagging of the same LightGBM slightly reduces prediction variance on the ~97% valid test rows (each model sees 800k vs 900k rows, but averaging 5 models more than compensates), giving a modest ~1% RMSE gain, while the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows is untouched.

A properly OOF-smoothed 100m pickup-cell mean fare gives LightGBM a fine-grained local fare prior (airport/flat-fare zones, borough and traffic effects) that raw coordinates and distance only coarsely approximate, so valid-row RMSE should drop ~0.15 while the ~2.8% corrupt-test-row floor is unchanged, yielding a modest overall gain.

Snapping coordinates to a 0.01° (~1 km) grid removes sub-cell distance and position precision that LightGBM currently exploits (distance_km noise σ≈0.4 km ≈ +0.3-0.5 MSE on valid rows), while the claimed pooling benefit is already provided by the existing 0.01°-cell route encoding, so RMSE should rise slightly from 4.126 to ~4.16.
L1 loss fits conditional medians and downweights the large positive fare errors that RMSE still penalizes, so outlier robustness is unlikely to offset the mean-vs-median mismatch.

L1 boosting converges to conditional medians, which on the right-skewed fare distribution biases predictions below the conditional mean (underpredicting legitimately expensive rides) — RMSE penalizes exactly those squared errors, so the modest outlier-robustness gain is outweighed by the train-objective/eval-metric mismatch, giving a small ~1% regression.

Airport-proximity features are a well-known high-value addition for this competition (JFK flat-fare trips are poorly captured by distance alone); radial distances to JFK/LGA/EWR let LightGBM cleanly isolate airport rides that raw rectangular lat/lon splits only approximate, typically worth ~0.2 RMSE on the valid rows here, while the ~2.8% corrupt test rows cap the total gain and the runtime cost is negligible.

L1 training converges to the conditional median, which sits below the mean for right-skewed taxi fares, while RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean — the median shift costs roughly delta^2/(2*RMSE), likely outweighing the modest outlier-robustness gain, though early stopping on validation RMSE limits the damage to a small regression.

LightGBM's default histogram binning (255 bins) already quantizes the ~2.5° coordinate range into ~0.01° buckets, so explicitly rounding to 2 decimals is nearly a no-op for split selection, and the dominant distance feature is preserved unrounded — expect essentially neutral RMSE.

L1 fits conditional medians, which are suboptimal for RMSE on this right-skewed fare target; robustness gains against noisy fares are real but typically outweighed, giving a small RMSE regression of roughly 0.05–0.10.

The 29°-rotated grid (Manhattan-style) distance is a better proxy for actual road distance than haversine — it captures the orientation-dependent detour factor that axis-aligned tree splits cannot synthesize from raw coordinate differences — so it should cut error modestly on valid rows; the gain is capped because LightGBM already exploits coords+haversine and ~2.8% corrupt test rows impose an irreducible ~2.1 RMSE floor.

The out-of-fold smoothed route target encoding adds genuine origin-destination signal (e.g., JFK flat-fare routes, corridor-specific fares) that axis-aligned trees with only 63 leaves can't fully extract from raw coordinates, but with 0.01-degree cells most route keys are seen only a handful of times in 900k rows, so the strong prior (weight 50) collapses most values toward the global mean; the ~2.8% invalid test rows still get the mean fallback, capping the overall gain to a small improvement.

A grid-rotated Manhattan distance captures street-network travel distance (and direction) better than haversine alone, and LightGBM can't easily reconstruct this rotated L1 norm from raw coordinates, so it should give a small but real gain on the ~97% valid rows while the ~2.8% corrupt-row floor stays fixed.

Doubling the training sample from 1M to 2M rows yields a small gain on the predictable rows (diminishing returns for LightGBM at this scale), while the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows stays fixed, so overall RMSE improves only slightly from 4.138 to ~4.11; the run still fits the 10-minute budget.

Airport routes (esp. JFK flat-fare and Newark toll-heavy trips, ~3-4% of rows) have fares poorly explained by distance/coords alone, so an explicit direction-aware airport-route categorical should cut error on those rows meaningfully; but the raw coordinates already let LightGBM partially learn airport regions and the ~2.8% corrupt test rows (predicted as the mean) are untouched, capping the overall gain at roughly 2%.

LightGBM on raw features with per-character categorical f_27 is a solid but well-documented ~0.972-0.975 public AUC on TPS-May-2022, whereas the current MLP exploits the smooth synthetic feature interactions better (0.9866), so the swap likely regresses by roughly 1.3%.

10-bin one-hot quantization coarsely discards fine-grained continuous information the MLP uses to resolve the smooth cross-feature interactions that dominate this dataset (GBDTs need far finer splits here), while the only clear benefit — fixing heavy-tailed f_28 under standardization — is a single feature, so a small net AUC regression is the most likely outcome.

After standardization all 40 columns have variance ~1 and the synthetic features are near-independent, so the PCA eigenbasis is essentially an arbitrary dense rotation that scrambles the per-position letter structure of f_27 (the competition's key signal) across every component; tree splits stop being axis-aligned with the true boundaries and need expensive staircases to recover them, while the linear leaves are already span-invariant to rotation, so nothing compensates within the fixed 3000-round budget.

Out-of-fold smoothed target encoding of the full f_27 string (thousands of recurring values, ~50 rows each) preserves nearly all of f_27's dominant string-level marginal signal in one low-noise, calibrated numeric feature that the linear-tree leaves can exploit far better than arbitrary ordinal letter codes, while the freed tree capacity partly offsets the lost position-by-numeric interaction detail — net a small gain of roughly +0.001 AUC, though a flat or slightly negative result is plausible if f_27's position-specific interactions with numeric features carry more weight than expected.
Full f_27 codes are effectively unique, so the smoothed encoding mostly collapses to the prior while discarding informative position-wise character features.

These sums (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26) are the known generative interactions in this dataset; axis-aligned trees approximate diagonal boundaries poorly, so handing LightGBM the sums and threshold indicators should give a real but modest AUC gain over the already-strong 0.9915 baseline, limited by the fact that 3000 deep trees already partially capture the boundaries and the f_27 signal is unchanged.

A plain logistic regression on raw numerics + ordinal-encoded f_27 will score far below LightGBM (~0.80 AUC vs 0.984) on this interaction-heavy dataset, and an equal-weight rank blend with such a weak, only modestly correlated partner will drag the strong model down by roughly 1.5-2 AUC points rather than adding useful diversity.

The small CPU MLP will easily fit in the time budget (~2-3 min for 80 epochs) and best-checkpoint selection guards against the aggressive lr=0.01 phase, but ordinal-encoded f_27 characters are a poor input representation for a network (no embeddings) and MLPs historically underperform GBDTs on this interaction-heavy dataset, so expect roughly 0.95-0.96 AUC versus 0.9842 for LightGBM.

A small CPU MLP on raw + ordinally-encoded f_27 features will underexploit the equality-type string interactions and multiplicative continuous interactions that LightGBM's splits capture naturally (heavy-tailed f_28 also survives StandardScaler as outliers), so it should land around 0.955-0.965, a modest regression from 0.9770.

Linear leaves match the oblique 'sum-crossing-threshold' boundaries in principle, but 3000 deep trees at lr=0.05 already approximate them well, so gains are marginal and partly offset by noisy near-OLS leaf fits (linear_lambda=0.01 is weak for 41-feature linear models on ~100-sample leaves, including ordinal letter codes) — expect near-parity with a slight edge, and ~2x runtime still fits the budget.

nunique(f_27) is a known strong signal in TPS-May-2022 that axis-aligned trees cannot easily reconstruct from per-position ordinal chars (it needs cross-column equality counts), so adding it as one cheap integer feature should give a small AUC gain of roughly +0.0015–0.002 with essentially no regression or runtime risk.

These specific sums match the known rotated interaction structure of TPS May 2022, giving axis-aligned trees a directly splittable discriminative direction they otherwise approximate with costly staircases; originals are kept, so a small AUC gain (~+0.001) with minimal regression risk.

The raw 10-letter f_27 string has on the order of 500k+ distinct values (mostly appearing once or twice), so LightGBM's native categorical handling (min_data_per_group=100 default) lumps nearly all of them into a single catch-all bin, rendering the new feature useless; the change therefore effectively deletes the 10 positional letter columns that carry the core interaction signal, leaving only numeric features plus bag-of-letter counts, which should cost roughly 2 AUC points.

Adjacent f_27 bigrams as native LightGBM categoricals capture pairwise character interactions that per-position ordinals and counts cannot express (a well-known win in this competition), while the deterministic 0-675 encoding and holdout early stopping keep overfitting risk low, so expect a modest but real AUC bump of roughly +0.001-0.002.

The target in this competition depends on multiplicative interactions among continuous features, so dropping the 25 gain-mined product features loses real signal that axis-aligned trees only imperfectly reconstruct, while PCA's linear (orthogonal) components add almost nothing for a tree model that already sees the raw f_00..f_15 columns — net a small regression of a few thousandths of AUC.

Hashing the entire 10-char string into 64 buckets turns f_27 into a near-random 64-way one-hot (full strings are effectively unique), destroying the per-position character signal that drives f_27's well-known predictive power in this competition, so the model degrades to roughly its numeric-features-only performance (~0.96 AUC) plus a little noise from 64 useless sparse columns.

Swapping the well-tuned LightGBM (0.9781) for 300 unpruned ExtraTrees loses boosting's clear edge on this interaction-heavy synthetic tabular data (ET typically lands ~0.955-0.965 here), and the added 5-fold cross_val_predict of deep min_samples_leaf=1 forests greatly inflates wall-time and peak memory (real timeout/OOM risk under the 15-min kill) while contributing nothing to the final test predictions.

A shallow sklearn MLP on standardized raw features will train fine within budget, but with f_27 reduced to 10 arbitrary ordinal columns (no embeddings/one-hot) and no engineered interactions it underfits the categorical-interaction-heavy signal that the tuned 3000-tree LightGBM captures, so AUC should drop from ~0.978 to the mid-0.96 range.

The target in TPS-May-2022 is known to be generated largely from order-invariant letter-count information in f_27, so giving LightGBM direct per-letter counts (plus nunique) lets trees split on the true signal with single thresholds instead of approximating it from 10 positional categoricals, yielding a modest but reliable AUC gain (~+0.0005) with no runtime risk; public notebooks with exactly this engineering scored around 0.977-0.978.

The full-string frequency is a many-to-one hash that cannot identify which letters the string contains, so it discards essentially all of f_27's per-position categorical signal (the dominant non-numeric information in this dataset); the model effectively degrades to numeric-features-only performance around 0.94-0.95 AUC, with frequency contributing near-zero signal since signature popularity does not determine machine state.

Letter-frequency and distinct-character counts expose order-invariant signal in f_27 that the per-position ordinal encoding only captures through many hard tree splits; in this competition such count features reliably add roughly +0.01 AUC to a positions-only LightGBM baseline, with negligible runtime cost.

TPS-May-2022 has genuine multiplicative interactions among f_00..f_15 that axis-aligned GBDT splits approximate inefficiently, so gain-screened z-score products (a sound, deterministic selection on 150k rows) should give the unchanged main model a small but real lift of roughly +0.0005 to +0.001 AUC, with minimal runtime cost and little overfitting risk since early stopping is retained.

Refitting on 100% of data with n_estimators scaled by 1/0.9 is a standard, safe heuristic that adds 80k rows and ~333 extra trees (justified since holdout AUC was still improving at 3000), yielding a small positive gain; but with 720k rows already the learning curve is flat, so the improvement is marginal (~+0.0003 AUC) with essentially no overfitting risk.

Many-vs-rest categorical partitioning lets each split isolate arbitrary letter subsets per position (the true signal in f_27) instead of needing multiple ordinal thresholds, typically yielding a small AUC gain on this dataset with negligible runtime cost.

The count of distinct characters in f_27 is a known strong signal in this competition that trees cannot easily derive from the 10 per-position ordinal columns (set cardinality needs many splits), so exposing it directly should give a small but real AUC bump over the already-strong 0.9818 baseline; gains are limited because the per-character columns plus 3000 trees already capture part of this information.

Depth-2 trees restrict the ensemble to main effects and pairwise interactions, but this dataset's signal depends on higher-order feature interactions that the current 127-leaf trees capture, so AUC should drop by roughly 2-3 points despite the engineered sum feature partially compensating and the faster rounds not helping within the fixed 3000-tree budget.

A single modest-capacity LightGBM (31 leaves, 600 trees, max_bin=63, no subsampling) on raw features + f_27 char ordinals typically lands around 0.977-0.980 on TPS-May-2022, slightly below the current well-trained MLP's 0.9822, and it comfortably fits the time budget so no deadline truncation is expected.

LightGBM (31 leaves, 600 rounds) on raw numerics + per-char f_27 ordinals is a standard ~0.978-0.981 approach for this competition, but the smooth interaction-heavy generator is slightly better fit by the current MLP, so expect near-parity with a small regression; scaling is harmless to trees and the run fits easily in the time budget.

Quartile-coding the float sensors keeps only coarse order and discards within-quartile/interaction detail that the still-underfit GBDT was exploiting; integer and f_27 features should prevent a collapse, so expect a moderate AUC regression.

num_leaves=7 restricts each tree to shallow interactions (depth ~3); the 3000 boosting rounds at lr=0.05 partially compensate by composing many simple trees, but the high-order feature interactions in this dataset are captured less precisely, yielding a modest underfitting drop of roughly 0.004 AUC.
Cutting to 4 leaves makes each tree only a depth-3 rule; with the deeper model still improving at the 3000-tree cap, this should underfit feature interactions and modestly lower AUC.

f_00+f_01+f_26 matches a genuine additive interaction in this synthetic dataset; giving LightGBM the sum directly makes the diagonal boundary easier to learn than approximating it with many splits, yielding a small positive gain on an already-high 0.9915 baseline, with minimal regression risk since it's just one extra column.

LightGBM with 3000 deep trees already captures additive interactions of f_00/f_01/f_26 via axis-aligned splits, so an unthresholded linear sum is nearly redundant; expected effect is within run-to-run noise (feature fraction sampling shifts slightly), likely a negligible change around ±0.0001 AUC.

A CPU-trained MLP on ordinal-encoded f_27 positions with no embeddings or engineered interactions, capped at 420s (roughly 25-40 epochs after CSV loading), underfits the discrete feature interactions that LightGBM exploits via splits, so it should land in the typical plain-MLP range of ~0.955-0.963 AUC, a ~2% regression from 0.9770.

Treating the f_27 char columns as categorical lets LightGBM find arbitrary letter subsets per split instead of threshold splits on the meaningless alphabetical ordinal order; with 800k rows and only 26 categories per position the per-category statistics are robust, so this standard trick should give a small but real AUC gain with no runtime risk.

The unique-character count of f_27 is a known weakly-useful signal in TPS-May-2022 that axis-aligned trees can't easily reconstruct from the 10 per-position ordinals, so adding it explicitly should give a small, near-certainly non-negative bump over the 0.97696 baseline.

Error is dominated by the sparse dark/edge pixels (90% of pixels are near-trivial white background), and up-weighting darkness redirects gradient there with ~4x stroke weight while background keeps ~0.8x; because the 36 pages repeat 2-4x and every test scan re-uses a train page, targets are near-deterministic given the input, so the calibration bias a weighted loss would normally introduce is small — expect a modest net gain of a few percent, tempered by slight background degradation from capacity shift.

Training budget grows from ~2000 steps to roughly 10-13k steps (5.5 min at ~35-40 steps/s on GPU) with the cosine schedule still fully annealing to ~0, and since the test scans are re-noised copies of the same 36 training pages, the extra optimization on this tiny U-Net should measurably lower RMSE with diminishing returns, giving roughly a 10-15% improvement over 0.01611.

The metric is RMSE, so MSE training is metric-aligned (conditional mean is the MSE-optimal predictor); on this near-deterministic mapping the ambiguity L1's robustness could exploit is small, while L1's median-seeking adds squared-error bias on uncertain stroke-edge/stain pixels — the cited L1 benefits in the literature are mostly optimization-related and largely neutralized by Adam's gradient normalization, so expect a small regression of roughly 1-2% rather than a gain.

With only ~105 training scans of 36 repeated pages, input-only contrast/brightness jitter mirrors the real global-tint/fading noise and regularizes memorization of per-scan gray levels, likely giving a modest RMSE gain; the mild train/test distribution shift from aggressive jitter (p=0.8, ±0.1 brightness) caps the improvement.
Extra mild scale views should average out a little stain/stroke error, but single-scale training and fixed page geometry keep the gain marginal.

All 29 test scans are re-noised copies of the same 36 training pages, so page memorization is directly rewarded; Dropout2d(0.2) at the deep levels (which also feeds the skip path) impedes that memorization, slows the already short 2000-step training, and adds a dropout/BatchNorm train-eval variance shift, so a small RMSE regression is more likely than a generalization gain.

Dropout2d slightly reduces effective capacity and slows the fixed-time fit; because test scans reuse training page content, some page-specific memorization is beneficial, so a modest RMSE regression is likely.

The 4-level U-Net doubles receptive field (~89px), which helps distinguish mid-size stains/wrinkles from text strokes, and since training at 180s is already near convergence the ~25% fewer steps cost little; capacity gains also help because test pages are re-noised copies of train pages, so expect a modest ~3-5% RMSE improvement.

The median-background channel gives an explicit local illumination/stain reference, making stained paper whitening and text normalization much easier; fixed training steps and capacity keep the gain moderate rather than dramatic.

The 5-level U-Net's much larger receptive field and ~15x capacity should better remove global tints/large stains and memorize the 36 reused pages (which reappear in test), while 8x256x256 keeps pixels-per-step and BN statistics healthy and runtime stays well within budget; risk of mild undertraining at fixed 2000 steps caps the expected gain to roughly 10%.
4-way flip TTA averages out prediction noise in a roughly flip-equivariant U-Net, typically giving a small but real RMSE gain (~1-3%) on denoising, with negligible runtime cost.

The 180s wall-clock budget fits roughly 4.5k-6k steps of this small U-Net (vs 2000 in the baseline) with LR still cosine-annealed to zero, and since test pages are re-noised copies of training pages the extra optimization/memorization should modestly reduce RMSE; run still finishes well under 10 minutes.

The grading metric is L2, and the conditional mean (what MSE trains for) is exactly the L2-optimal predictor; switching to Charbonnier pushes toward the conditional median and down-weights the large stain/stroke errors that dominate the squared error, so RMSE should regress slightly — Adam's gradient normalization keeps the change small, but the loss/metric mismatch is the dominant effect here since the baseline is already near-converged and stable.

The test scans are re-noised copies of the same 36 clean training pages, so 'overfitting to training noise' is not the real bottleneck (page memorization actually helps), while injecting sigma=0.05 Gaussian noise creates a train/test input mismatch (test images carry only stain/tint noise) that biases the residual U-Net toward slight over-smoothing and consumes part of the short 2000-step budget on an irrelevant denoising sub-task, yielding a small net regression.

With batch 32 over 128x128 crops, BN statistics are estimated from ~500k pixels per channel and crop-vs-full-page activation distributions are both dominated by white background, so GN's consistency advantage is minimal here, while BN's faster optimization in a short 2000-step schedule gives it a slight edge — expect a small regression, roughly within noise.

MSE is metric-aligned, but SSIM+L1 has the same clean-image minimizer and weights sparse stroke/stain structure much more strongly; for this ink-sparse task expect a small (~0.2 dB) RMSE gain, not a regime change.

8-fold dihedral TTA on an MSE-trained U-Net is a standard low-risk variance reducer: the model was already trained with flip augmentation so flipped predictions are in-distribution, rot90 predictions are slightly weaker individually but averaging 8 correlated outputs still cuts noise and border artifacts modestly, typically yielding a ~1-2% RMSE improvement on this denoising task with negligible runtime cost.

RMSE is minimized by the posterior mean, which MSE training directly targets, while pure SSIM trades per-pixel fidelity for structural/contrast agreement — Zhao et al. show SSIM losses win on SSIM/perceptual metrics but slightly lose on PSNR/RMSE — and SSIM also tolerates small uniform intensity offsets in the 83%-white background that directly inflate RMSE, so expect a modest (~10%) regression with unchanged runtime.

Residual (DnCNN-style) prediction with a linear head and zero-init final conv acts like adding a global skip connection: the model starts at the identity and only learns the noise correction, avoiding sigmoid saturation on the 83%-white background, which improves gradient flow and convergence within the fixed 2000-step budget; clipping at inference also truncates overshoot near white, so expect a modest but real RMSE gain (~5-8%), not a regression.

The graded metric is RMSE and the baseline already optimizes it directly; swapping MSE for sqrt(MSE) is a monotone reparametrization that Adam largely normalizes away, while the 0.1-weighted (1-SSIM) term trades a little pixel fidelity for structural sharpness, which typically costs a small amount of RMSE (~1-2%) on a denoising task where the model is already near page memorization.

Residual prediction with zero-init final conv starts training from the identity (already near-optimal since targets are 83% white and noise is a sparse additive corruption), removes the sigmoid saturation floor that systematically penalizes pure-white pixels, and is a well-established denoising win (DnCNN) at negligible instability risk, so expect a modest ~5-8% RMSE improvement.

Synthetic stain/shading/speckle corruption of the exact clean pages that reappear (re-noised) in test adds targeted noise diversity to a tiny 105-image dataset and should reduce overfitting, but the ~7x dilution of real noisy samples (only 105/735 ≈ 14% of crops are real) plus imperfect noise modeling (blurred text, no wrinkles, mild shading range) caps the gain at a modest single-digit RMSE improvement.

4.5x more Adam steps with the cosine schedule stretched to full decay fixes clear underfitting at 2,000 steps, and because test scans are re-noised copies of the same ~36 training pages, extra fitting (even page memorization) helps rather than hurts; expect roughly a 10% RMSE drop with wall-clock still under ~10 min on GPU.

Dihedral-8 TTA on a converged denoising U-Net typically shaves ~1% off RMSE by averaging out flip/rotation-dependent errors; training was flip-augmented so 4 of 8 views are in-distribution, transposed views are slightly OOD (vertical text) but still locally plausible, and inference cost (39 small images) rises 8x yet stays trivial against the 20-epoch training budget.

MAE optimizes the conditional median, not the mean, and its constant gradient under-weights the large stain residuals that dominate squared error, so RMSE (the actual metric) should regress slightly; the effect stays small because clean targets are nearly deterministic given the repeated pages and Adam partially normalizes gradient-scale differences.

Since targets are deterministic the weighted loss has the same optimum, but with ~83% white pixels the unweighted MSE wastes most gradient on trivial background; upweighting ink 3x redirects limited training capacity to text strokes/antialiased edges where most of the residual error lives, giving a small RMSE gain at the cost of negligible background degradation.

Ink is only ~5% of pixels but dominates the squared error, and since Adam is invariant to global loss scale the reweighting purely shifts capacity onto strokes/edges; the systematic darkening bias of target-weighted MSE only affects genuinely ambiguous pixels (few, since stains are visually distinguishable from ink), so unweighted RMSE should improve modestly.

Residual prediction with a zero-initialized head starts training at the identity mapping (already near-optimal since noise is a sparse darkening correction) and removing the sigmoid eliminates saturation on the 83% pure-white target pixels, so with only 2000 short training steps the model converges to a visibly better solution; compute and wall-clock are essentially unchanged.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean that MSE trains for; L1 drives predictions toward the conditional median, which is slightly misaligned with the metric and typically costs a few percent in RMSE despite being more robust to large stain residuals, so I expect a small regression within run-to-run noise levels.

Residual (identity-plus-zero-init-delta) prediction is the classic DnCNN-style parameterization: it removes the sigmoid's asymptotic saturation on the 83% pure-white background pixels, starts training from an already-good identity mapping, and converges faster within the fixed 2000-step budget, typically yielding a modest (~5-15%) RMSE gain with low risk since clipping at inference still bounds outputs.

Halving NAFNet widths cuts parameters ~4x; with only 2000 training steps on 36 repeated pages the compact model still learns the dominant background-whitening/stain-removal mapping, but slightly underfits fine text-stroke detail, so a small RMSE regression (within run-to-run noise) is expected, with CPU runtime comfortably in budget.
Mild 3:1 foreground weighting should reduce over-whitened stroke/faint-text errors that dominate RMSE without badly biasing the mostly white background.

The illumination-normalized second channel is a sound, functionally correct feature, but the applied diff also adds execution.json forcing CPU with only 8 intra-op threads; 2000 UNet updates at ~350 GFLOPs/step need roughly 25-60 min on 8 CPU cores, so the run is hard-killed at 15 min before writing any submission and the effective score stays at the parent baseline.

Running only the final 1x1 conv + sigmoid in fp32 removes negligible bf16 output quantization (<0.2% RMSE effect), and under the added CPU-only runtime config autocast is already disabled so it is a literal no-op; same model, schedule, and data give an essentially unchanged RMSE of ~0.0162.

The 4-view flip TTA is correctly implemented (pad-after-flip, crop, unflip, float32 averaging, .copy() for negative strides) and should modestly reduce prediction variance for a ~1-3% RMSE gain since the model was already flip-augmented; the added runtime.json forces CPU-only execution, but the dominant cost (2000 training steps) is unchanged and the 4x inference overhead adds only ~1 minute, so the run still completes within the budget.

The residual NAFNet should remove tint/stains and preserve ink better than the plain sigmoid U-Net, but the very small width-16/single-block design and same 2k-update budget cap the gain; CPU forcing mainly affects runtime.

The frozen backbone's own ImageNet-1k head is a linear readout of the exact same features, but trained on 1.28M images whose 120 dog synsets match this label set exactly (and Stanford Dogs/Kaggle images largely come from IN-1k train, so the head has seen most of these images), making it a strong, partly decorrelated second classifier; blending it with the LR probabilities with weight and temperature tuned on the same holdout (where w=0 recovers the current 0.31 solution, capping downside) should cut test log loss by roughly 15-25%.

Unwhitened PCA is only an orthogonal rotation plus truncation of the lowest-variance 75% of feature directions; with C re-selected on the same holdout the effect is small, but for a 120-way fine-grained task some breed-discriminative signal (look-alike terrier/spaniel pairs) lives in those discarded low-variance directions, so a slight log-loss regression is more likely than a gain.

Mixup/CutMix at ConvNeXt-recipe strength is a well-matched regularizer for 120 confusable classes on ~8.3k images and yields softer, instance-dependent uncertainty that log loss rewards (temperature scaling on clean val handles global calibration); the prob=1.0 setting risks slight underfitting in only 6 epochs, capping the gain at a modest ~2-3%.

With only ~77 labeled images per class and a 28M-param backbone fine-tuned for 6 epochs, the standard (0.08,1.0) crop range adds useful regularization and matches the ConvNeXt pretraining distribution, likely giving a small log-loss gain; this is partly offset by noisy near-empty crops in short training and by the small 1023-image test set making the result noisy, so I expect only a modest improvement over 0.4471.

ConvNeXt-V2 Large pretrained on ImageNet-22k yields far more discriminative frozen features for these 120 ImageNet dog breeds than ResNet-50 V1 (linear-probe accuracy roughly 84% -> 91-92%), and the extended C grid improves calibration, so log loss should drop ~30% while staying well within the time budget.

The 1000-d log-softmax block is a deterministic linear function of the pooled vector, so it adds no information but ~1000 collinear/near-constant columns that StandardScaler inflates to unit-variance noise; removing it gives the L2-multinomial LR a homogeneous 2048-d space with less estimation variance and cleaner C selection, yielding a small log-loss improvement (the retained pooled features already contain the discriminative ImageNet-breed directions).

Ridge decision boundaries on strong frozen features are comparable to LR's, but explicit holdout temperature scaling directly optimizes calibration for log loss and the closed-form solve avoids lbfgs under-convergence at high C, yielding a small improvement; holdout overfitting across the 63-pair grid keeps the gain modest.
PCA to 128 dims/block likely discards some low-variance fine-grained breed cues while the tuned L2 linear probe was already managing overfitting, so I expect a small log-loss regression.

ConvNeXt-Base pretrained on ImageNet-22k and fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k (which contains these very dog breeds) yields far more discriminative frozen features than ResNet-50-V1 (ImageNet top-1 86.8 vs 76.1), and the holdout re-tuning of C adapts regularization to the new feature scale, so linear-probe accuracy should rise from ~84% to ~90% with a corresponding large log-loss drop; the ~350MB download and unchanged cheap extraction fit the time budget.

Fine-tuning an ImageNet-22k ConvNeXt-Tiny (whose pretraining includes these very dog breeds) with augmentation, label smoothing, flip-TTA and validation-based temperature scaling should reach ~88-91% accuracy and well-calibrated probabilities, roughly halving the frozen-ResNet50+logreg log loss; main risks are the 7-minute guard truncating the 6-epoch cosine schedule and first-run weight download, both of which still leave a clearly better model.

The ImageNet fc head is a breed classifier pretrained on ~1300 images/class for these exact 120 classes, so its log-probs add strong, well-calibrated signal the linear probe can't learn from 77 images/class alone; StandardScaler makes the two feature blocks commensurate and holdout-tuned C keeps regularization sane, so log loss should drop meaningfully (roughly 0.45 -> ~0.38), with minor risk that the capped C grid (max 0.1) slightly over-regularizes on standardized features.

Replacing IN1K ResNet-50 features with L2-normalized concatenation of three stronger, diversely-pretrained backbones (ConvNeXt-B IN22k, CLIP ViT-B/16, DINOv2 ViT-B/14 — each individually a better linear-probe on fine-grained dogs) plus holdout-tuned C on normalized features should cut log loss from ~0.45 to ~0.30; main risk is the ~1.1GB weight download and 5 LR fits squeezing the 10-min budget, not the metric.

Focal loss's (1-p_t)^2 factor shrinks gradients 2-4x during mid-training (effective LR cut over a fixed 10-epoch cosine schedule) and stops pushing confidence on already-correct examples, while classes here are nearly balanced so its hard-example emphasis addresses no real problem — net effect is slightly underfit, less-confident probabilities and a small log-loss regression versus label-smoothed CE.

Dog breeds are literal ImageNet classes so pretrained low/mid-level features transfer nearly optimally; freezing conv1-layer3 removes most of the overfitting/forgetting risk on ~9k images while layer4+fc still adapts the discriminative stage, typically yielding slightly better-calibrated log loss than full fine-tuning in a 10-epoch budget, with only a small accuracy-loss risk.

Horizontal-flip TTA on a frozen augreg-pretrained ViT (trained with flips, so mirrored features are in-distribution for the linear probe) is a low-risk variance reduction that typically shaves ~1-3% off multiclass log loss; the NUM_WORKERS=0 change affects only runtime, not the metric.

CLIP ViT-B/32 features are strong, but the coarser patch grid and image-text objective should be less aligned with these exact ImageNet dog-breed classes than the in21k+in1k ViT-B/16, so the unchanged linear probe likely regresses moderately.
PCA-256 is a valid denoising step but hard-truncates low-variance breed-specific directions while reusing C tuned for raw 2048-D features, so I expect a near-neutral to slightly worse log loss.

DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings are dramatically stronger than ResNet-50 ImageNet features for fine-grained breed discrimination (validated at exactly 256-resize/224-crop resolution in the DINOv2 paper), and the same TTA + LR pipeline with re-tuned C should cut log loss from ~0.44 to roughly 0.30.

With n=9199 vs p=2816 and mild C=1.0 the baseline LR is already well-conditioned, so the main effects are (a) truncation to 256 PCs, which keeps nearly all between-class structure (rank<=119) but discards some fine-grained signal, and (b) whitening+L2 acting as an anti-ridge that shrinks high-variance (most discriminative) directions more; net effect is near-neutral with a slight negative lean, roughly 0.545-0.55 log loss.

k-NN(10) on these ImageNet-supervised frozen features typically trails a linear probe by a few accuracy points, and its coarse distance-weighted vote probabilities are far worse calibrated for log loss than logistic regression (which directly optimizes a regularized version of the metric): in ~2800-d space distances concentrate so weighting is near-uniform, giving ~k/10-style probabilities capped near 0.8-0.9 on correct images and a 1e-3-smoothed floor (~7 nats each) for the several percent of test images with no true-breed neighbor, roughly adding 0.2+ nats over the 0.54 baseline.

End-to-end fine-tuning of ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 on Stanford Dogs-style data reliably beats frozen features + logistic regression (~84% vs ~77% top-1), and label smoothing 0.1 plus cosine decay keep probabilities calibrated for log loss; the short 10-epoch schedule with warmup is stable and fits the time budget, though it limits further gains, so expect log loss to drop from ~0.45 to roughly 0.30-0.35.

ViT-B/16 (augreg, in21k→in1k) is a far stronger frozen feature extractor than ResNet-50 V1 for fine-grained dog breeds (linear-probe accuracy typically jumps ~6-10 points on Stanford Dogs), so log loss should drop substantially despite the untuned C=0.3; expected ~0.30-0.35 vs 0.453.

Standard 10-crop TTA (FiveCrop+hflip) with probability averaging reliably reduces variance and overconfident errors on log loss vs single center-crop, typically a few percent gain for ImageNet-frozen features; training path is unchanged and test cost is trivial (10x on only 1,023 images), so risk of regression or timeout is minimal.

Adding frozen ConvNeXt-Tiny (in22k->in1k, a stronger and architecturally distinct backbone whose features are complementary to ResNet-50) with per-block L2 normalization reliably helps this exact fine-grained setup, typically cutting log loss ~12-18% versus the single-backbone baseline; runtime stays within budget and the C=1.0 default on normalized features is reasonable, so the main risk is only modest tuning suboptimality rather than regression.
