The blend adds genuinely complementary signal (the pretrained fc head was trained on these very ImageNet dog synsets, many test images included) while selecting only two scalars on an internal split caps the downside near the baseline; expect a modest log-loss gain of ~5-8%, assuming the engineer implements alias-aware category matching since literal exact-match normalization would crash the assert on comma-joined ImageNet category names like 'affenpinscher, monkey pinscher, monkey dog'.

PCA to 256 dims keeps most variance but discards low-variance directions that carry fine-grained breed-discriminative signal, and C=0.3 was tuned on raw 2048-d features, so log loss likely regresses modestly despite faster fitting.

Global max pooling produces noisier, sparser descriptors that discard the spatial-averaging signal GAP provides; linear probes on frozen ImageNet backbones are typically slightly better with average pooling, and the fixed C=0.3 (tuned for GAP features) won't fully compensate, so expect a modest log-loss regression.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 (80.9% vs 76.1% top-1, longer training with modern recipe) yields notably more discriminative frozen features for these exact ImageNet dog classes, and the matched 232px eval preprocessing keeps train/test consistent, so a ~10% log-loss improvement is expected with no runtime risk.

The 10x stronger L2 shrinks the probe, but the subsequent 2-epoch head+last-bottleneck fine-tuning partially washes out the init difference; residual effects lean negative because the holdout already selected C=0.3 over C=0.03 for these features, the final model ends slightly less well-fit, and the smaller head weights also weaken gradient signal into the fine-tuned conv block — so expect a small regression, not a wash or a gain.

Dropping input resolution from 224 to 192 mismatches the ImageNet-pretrained backbone's native scale and loses fine-grained detail that discriminates look-alike breeds, so frozen features and the briefly fine-tuned head both get slightly weaker; the run is otherwise identical and ~25% faster, so it stays well within budget with a modest log-loss regression.

PCA-256 keeps most variance so the effect is small, but C=0.3 was tuned on raw 2048-d features and fine-grained breed signal partly lives in the discarded low-variance directions, so the truncated, un-retuned linear classifier should land roughly neutral-to-slightly-worse than the 0.4287 baseline.

Dropping from 224px to 192px moves away from ResNet-50's native training resolution and discards fine detail critical for fine-grained breed discrimination (look-alike terrier pairs), so frozen features become less discriminative and log loss—sensitive to confident errors—degrades moderately, though adaptive pooling keeps the pipeline fully functional.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 weights (~80.9% vs 76.1% ImageNet top-1, better training recipe) yield substantially more discriminative frozen features for these 120 ImageNet dog classes, and the matched 232px preprocessing aligns with the checkpoint's eval protocol, so the same logistic head should cut log loss meaningfully; minor risk that C=0.3 is slightly off-optimal for the new features caps the gain.

The only modeling change is a holdout-fitted scalar temperature applied to identical features/classifier; a regularized logistic regression with log-loss-tuned C is already near-calibrated, so temperature scaling (typically T~1.1-1.4 for such overconfident linear heads) yields a small but real log-loss gain of roughly 0.005-0.01 nats, with negligible runtime overhead and no correctness bugs in the diff.

Warm-starting the head from the tuned LogisticRegression weights and unfreezing only the last bottleneck's convs with conservative LRs (1e-4/1e-3) for ≤2 epochs is a low-risk partial fine-tune: conv adaptation to the 120-class task should yield a small gain, while SGD diffusion around the well-regularized head solution and sharpening risk on the small 1023-image test set keep the improvement modest and preclude a large one.

Horizontal-flip TTA with probability averaging on frozen ResNet-50 features reliably gives a small log-loss gain (typically 2-4%) by reducing crop/orientation variance; training and classifier are unchanged, and the extra test pass (1023 images) plus mlflow overhead fit easily in the time budget.

1:1 undersampling mostly shifts the intercept (AUC-neutral) for common labels, but for threat (956 rows), identity_hate (~2.8k) and severe_toxic (~3.2k) it discards >98% of negatives and, with unchanged C, drastically weakens effective regularization so the 60k/200k-feature logistic models overfit tiny subsets and the NB ratio r is estimated noisily; both branches use the identical seed so the rank blend cannot average out this noise, yielding a modest regression concentrated in the rare, high-variance columns.

Adding char_wb 2-6 features to the NB-LogReg branch (a well-known gain in this competition, ~+0.002-0.004 AUC for that branch via subword/obfuscated-profanity signal) improves the 50/50 rank blend by roughly half that, since branch A and the blending are unchanged.

ROC AUC is threshold- and prevalence-insensitive, so fixing the 'boundary pulled toward majority' buys almost nothing for a linear model's ranking, while the change throws away 80-99.7% of the training rows per label and, worse, computes branch B's NB log-count ratios on tiny balanced subsamples — for rare labels the +1 smoothing on ~1k rows compresses the NB weight range and zeroes all features absent from the subsample, degrading rare-label columns; this propagates into branch A via the OOF stack, so expect a small net regression (roughly -0.002 absolute) with extra variance from the noisy threat/identity_hate columns.

Plain MultinomialNB on TF-IDF word n-grams scores only ~0.95 mean AUC here versus ~0.978 for the NB-LogReg hybrid, and since its rankings are highly correlated with branch A's logistic model, the equal-weight rank average gets dragged below branch A alone (~0.976) to roughly 0.969-0.970; the weaker MNB OOF stack features also slightly reduce branch A, and there is no timing/format risk since MNB fits in seconds deterministically.

Mean-pooled corpus-trained Word2Vec vectors discard the exact-token signal (slurs, obfuscated profanity, char patterns) that drives TF-IDF branches on this task — branch A drops from ~0.975 to ~0.94 and the undertrained 3-epoch MLP on 200-d dense inputs lands similarly (~0.94); since both weak branches share the same embeddings they are correlated, so the equal-weight rank blend drags the unchanged strong NB-LogReg branch (~0.980) down to roughly 0.973-0.975, with the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) losing the most column AUC.

AUC is insensitive to the intercept/calibration shift that class-balancing fixes, but 1:1 undersampling throws away 81-99.4% of negatives — for threat only 478 negative docs remain, making the NB log-count ratios and per-label coefficients much noisier, while sklearn's unrescaled C makes the effective L2 penalty far stronger (and the MLP gets ~6x fewer adam updates) — so rare-label rankings (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) degrade slightly while common labels are nearly unaffected, netting a small regression of roughly 0.002-0.004 absolute.

Branch D is a weaker-but-decorrelated model (shared-hidden-layer sparse MLP on TF-IDF) added at 1/4 rank weight to three strong linear branches; such diversity typically lifts mean AUC slightly, while the 0.97 val-AUC gate and time guards mean the worst realistic case is falling back to the unchanged 0.9810 blend, so expected outcome is a small net gain.

Keeping all positives but only 1:1 sampled negatives removes useful negative evidence; with C and NB ratios left tuned for full data, common labels are near-neutral while rare noisy labels (threat/identity_hate) likely lose AUC.

Lowercasing/whitespace steps are no-ops (TfidfVectorizer already lowercases and splits on whitespace), but URL/IP/timestamp unification frees slots in the tightly capped vocabularies and the repeat-collapse plus de-obfuscation consolidate sparse profanity/slur variants into high-count canonical tokens — which should slightly help the noisy rare-label columns (identity_hate, severe_toxic) that dominate the column mean — netting a small positive, partly offset by minor losses from shorthand merging (u→you becomes a stopword in branch A) and rare regex false positives like 'a55 road'.

The OOF stack is leakage-safe and gives branch A a small boost (mainly on rare labels like threat/identity_hate via B's NB view), but the /20 scaling keeps the 6 extra columns weak against 60k TF-IDF features and the final blend already contains B at 0.5 weight, so added correlation between branches caps the net gain at a small positive; the 30 extra liblinear fits on the 200k matrix should still fit the ~10-min budget.
The undertrained but multi-task nonlinear MLP should be close to branch A and diverse enough that an equal rank blend with the two linear TF-IDF branches adds only a tiny AUC gain.

Branch C is the classic strong word+char NB-LogReg config (individually likely the best of the three branches at ~0.984-0.985); although it is highly correlated with branch B, adding it at equal rank weight to the blend historically lifts mean AUC by a few thousandths on this dataset, and the max_iter=100 cap keeps runtime inside the budget.

The two branches are highly correlated linear models, so the rank-blend AUC is very flat in the mixing weight; holdout-fitted per-label weights (shrunk 50% toward 0.5) capture small genuine per-label branch-strength differences on the common labels while noise on the rare labels is bounded by shrinkage, netting a negligible change within a few 1e-4 of the 0.97980 baseline.

Compressing 100k sparse TF-IDF n-grams (plus losing all char n-grams) to 300 unsupervised LSA factors discards the fine-grained rare-token signal that drives threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic rankings, so per-label AUCs drop several points despite better conditioning — a clear regression from the 0.9798 sparse ensemble.

Keeping all positives with a 10:1 negative cap leaves toxic unchanged and should mostly shift class priors rather than rankings; rare labels get a less swamped fit but lose some negative coverage, netting a near-flat tiny gain.

Switching branch F from six independent binary fastText models to a single 7-class softmax model hurts per-column rankings: with softmax (not ova), fastText samples one random label per multi-label row per epoch, so co-occurring labels actively compete (probability mass is split and non-target true labels are pushed down) and rare labels like threat/identity_hate get a fraction of their previous effective training updates; this slightly degrades F's AUC, and since F carries 1/3 weight in the unchanged rank average with branches A and B, the blend regresses modestly (though the single-pass training comfortably fits the time budget).

Swapping three discriminative TF-IDF/NB-weighted logistic branches for a single generative ComplementNB on raw counts drops the LR refit, IDF/sublinear weighting, and char n-gram coverage that drive the 0.982 score — pure count-based NB variants historically land around 0.93-0.95 mean AUC on this competition, so this is a large regression (roughly -4 points) despite the faster, more stable closed-form training.

Unweighted mean-pooled from-scratch Word2Vec (20M-token corpus, 200d) loses TF-IDF's importance weighting and exact-match signal for slurs/misspellings captured by word+char n-grams; known w2v-mean+LR baselines on this task land ~0.95-0.96 versus ~0.982 for the sparse ensemble, so this is a substantial regression, especially on the rare labels.

Averaged corpus-trained Word2Vec vectors with a linear head discard word order and dilute rare slur tokens in long comments, and on this task such mean-pooled embedding models consistently score ~0.95-0.965 mean AUC versus ~0.98 for word+char TF-IDF n-gram linear models, so this replaces a strong surface-matching system with a weaker representation despite its semantic generalization.

A full-strength char_wb 3-5g NB-LogReg (100k features, C=4) adds genuinely diverse signal — branch A's char part is weak (50k features under C=0.1 sag) and branch B is word-only, and word+char NB blends were a classic ~+0.002-0.004 gain in this competition; the simplex search subsumes the old 2-way blends so holdout AUC is non-decreasing, with only minor transfer noise on rare labels (threat) from the 10% holdout, netting roughly +0.0015 mean AUC.

C=0.1 sag over-regularized branch A; C=4 liblinear matches the reference kernels (~0.9855 standalone on this exact word+char TF-IDF set), and rank-averaging it with the equally strong NB-LogReg branch (~0.985) yields blend synergy lifting the mean column-wise AUC from 0.9801 to ~0.986.

A supervised fastText branch with this config is individually a bit weaker than the two TF-IDF linear branches (~0.965-0.970 standalone) but only moderately correlated with them, so an equal-weight 3-way rank blend nets a small positive gain, tempered by extra noise on the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) that dominate the column mean.

Char-level NB-LogReg (3-7 grams, 100k features) is a well-documented strong, decorrelated branch for this competition — likely at or above branch B's standalone strength — so adding it as an equal third rank-average member to the existing word-based blend should yield a modest gain of roughly +0.002-0.003 AUC, and the extra char vectorizer plus 6 liblinear fits should still finish within the 15-minute hard limit.

Dropping 10% of training data (no full-data refit) costs a little AUC, especially on rare labels, and per-label weights tuned on a small holdout (~48 threat, ~140 identity_hate positives) are noisy and roughly cancel any genuine blending gains, so the net is a small regression from 0.98013.

NB log-count-ratio weighting is a proven boost for linear TF-IDF models on this task (branch B already uses it); applying it to branch A's word+char features should lift branch A by ~0.002 AUC (mainly on rare labels where the NB prior counteracts the strong C=0.1 regularization), which carries roughly +0.001-0.0015 through the equal-weight rank blend, with runtime and memory essentially unchanged.

min_df=0.01 on ~313k docs requires ~3,128-document frequency, which (given max_features picks top-by-count first) shrinks branch B from 200k to roughly ~8k ultra-common n-grams and branch A's word vocab from 10k to ~3-4k, discarding the rare-but-highly-discriminative slurs and phrase bigrams that drive AUC on the rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic), so the rank blend regresses by a few tenths of an AUC point.

Balanced undersampling leaves slope estimates roughly unbiased (so abundant labels like toxic/obscene/insult barely move), but rare labels collapse to tiny fits — threat trains on 956 rows, severe_toxic on ~3.2k — inflating coefficient variance and NB count-ratio noise exactly where the column mean is most sensitive, so mean AUC drops a few thousandths while runtime stays well within budget.

Cosine class-centroid (Rocchio-style) classifiers are substantially weaker than tuned logistic regression on TF-IDF features—especially for rare labels like threat/identity_hate where centroid pooling is crude—so replacing both branches' logreg heads should drop mean AUC from ~0.980 to roughly ~0.95 (the implementation is correct, fast, and the logit-blend reduces to averaging the raw cosine-difference scores, so no artifacts; the loss is purely classifier quality).

char_wb spends the 50k char features on within-word/padded-boundary n-grams rather than cross-word space n-grams, which should slightly help profanity/slur substrings; branch B and rank blending are unchanged, so expect a small positive mean-AUC bump.

ComplementNB is a generative model that ranks noticeably worse than discriminative logistic regression on TF-IDF features in this competition (typical CNB kernels score ~0.96-0.97 vs ~0.979-0.980 for NB-LogReg/LR), so both branches degrade, and the blend loses further power because both branches become the same classifier family with less diversity; complement smoothing helps rare labels only partially, so expect roughly a 0.008 absolute AUC drop.

Crushing 60k sparse TF-IDF features to 32 dense SVD components keeps the coarse profanity direction (so toxic/obscene survive) but destroys the rare lexical cues (slurs, threat phrases) that drive the threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic rankings, dropping branch A from ~0.978 to ~0.93-0.94 and dragging the equal-weight rank blend with the unchanged fastText branch down well below the current 0.9734.

Truncating to a 2,000-token vocabulary (UNK elsewhere) destroys exactly the long-tail lexical signal that char_wb n-grams and fastText rely on for the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) and for obfuscated/unusual insults; common profanity labels degrade little, but the column mean drops roughly half a point since linear TF-IDF already regularizes sparsity natively and gains nothing from this collapsing.

Keeping stopwords spends ~300 of the 10k word-vocab slots on high-frequency function words, displacing only tail-frequency content terms with little signal, while regaining discriminative pronouns like 'you/your' (strong insult cues); char n-grams and the unchanged NB branch already cover most of this, so the blend shifts negligibly, if anything slightly up.

The two branches are miscalibrated relative to each other (heavily regularized C=0.1 sag vs C=4 liblinear NB-LogReg), so in logit space the more confident NB branch's wider-spread logits dominate the blend, reducing the diversity benefit that the equal-weight rank average captured; since AUC only cares about column-wise ordering and both single branches likely score slightly below the rank blend, expect a very small regression, with rare noisy labels (threat, identity_hate) adding variance but no systematic gain.

Plain char n-grams can cross whitespace/punctuation, but with a 50k cap and an overlapping word-bigram NB branch this mostly adds high-frequency/low-IDF boundary-spanning n-grams, leaving the rank blend almost unchanged to very slightly worse.

A from-scratch fastText model (dim 64, no subwords, 256-token cap, 5 epochs) is a clearly weaker branch than NB-LogReg on this task (~0.965 vs ~0.9775 standalone), so an equal-weight rank blend with the strong word+char branch gets dragged slightly below the original 0.98013 blend, with decorrelation between model families limiting the damage to a couple tenths of a point.

k=128 mostly drops constant/near-constant histogram bins that StandardScaler already zeroed out, so the L2-regularized multinomial LR is barely affected; the small variance reduction is roughly neutral-to-slightly-positive, and the unchanged NN plus 50/50 blend halves whatever tiny delta remains.

Label smoothing (eps=0.1) bounds the NN's logit gaps under heavy rotation/noise augmentation, reducing overconfident errors that log loss punishes most, so the NN half of the 50/50 blend should be better calibrated; the gain is modest because the unchanged LR carries half the weight and smoothing slightly lowers confidence on already-correct predictions.

OvR replaces the jointly-fitted softmax (which directly optimizes the scored cross-entropy) with 99 extremely imbalanced (7-vs-700) independent binary fits whose renormalized scores are less well calibrated in relative ordering; the power/floor calibration layer absorbs the confidence-scale difference but not this degradation, so expect a modest log-loss regression of roughly 10-20%, with runtime still trivially within budget.

The OOF-guarded blend (w=0 fallback) can only help on the training CV, and a well-regularized 5-seed MLP bag usually adds enough decorrelated signal to LR on these 192 descriptors for a small real gain, but the 99-row test set and selection on the same OOF keep the expected improvement modest and partly noise-dominated.

Averaging the five fold models trades a little per-model data (80% vs 100%) for variance reduction and, crucially for log loss, softens the rare overconfident wrong predictions that dominate the loss at high C; with highly correlated fold models and only 99 test rows the effect is small, so expect a modest improvement within noise.

The 21 geometric features add genuinely new information (absolute size, aspect ratio, solidity, Hu moments) missing from the scale-normalised shape descriptor, and CV-tuned C with only 21 extra columns on 891 rows keeps overfitting risk minimal, so a small improvement is expected — though with only 99 test rows the result is noise-dominated and could easily land anywhere in roughly 0.050–0.060.

Unwhitened PCA is just an orthogonal rotation plus truncation of the bottom ~5% variance directions; L2-penalized logistic regression already shrinks those collinear/low-variance directions, so the change is near-neutral with a slight regression expected from discarding fine discriminative detail in the histogram-bin difference directions (a single full SVD on 891x219 adds negligible compute, well within budget).

Averaging 5 stratified-fold logreg models trades ~20% data per model for variance reduction and softer (less overconfident) probabilities, which by Jensen's inequality typically nets a small log-loss gain in this 10-samples-per-class, 219-dim regime; the 99-row test set adds noise, so expect only a modest (~2-4%) improvement.

The LR baseline (0.124) is already very strong; a from-scratch CNN+MLP trained on only ~890 samples across 99 classes will overfit despite augmentation and likely reach ~0.6-1.2 standalone log loss, and a 50/50 arithmetic blend with such a weaker model drags the true-class probabilities down (bounded improvement impossible, bounded regression up to 0.124+ln2≈0.82), so the blend should land around 0.4-0.55 — a large regression.

The model is unchanged, but LR probabilities here are mildly overconfident (192 features, ~9 samples/class), so power/temperature scaling plus a small uniform floor tuned on 891 OOF predictions should transfer reasonably well to the 99-row test set and shave roughly 10% off the log loss; risk is small since the grid includes the identity (a=1, eps=0) and OOF overfitting with 2 scalars is negligible.

CV over the C grid will pick a substantially larger C than the over-regularized C=1 (typical optimum ~100-1000 for standardized leaf descriptors), cutting OOF log loss roughly 25-35%, so the refit model should score near 0.09 on the 99-row test set, though the tiny test set makes the exact value noisy.

The 27 geometric descriptors are largely redundant with the provided shape/margin/texture vectors but add complementary global shape info (aspect ratio, circularity, Hu moments) as standardized, regularized inputs, so the L2 logreg should gain slightly without instability; the mlflow wrapper is fully exception-guarded and the feature extraction is numerically safe, so the run completes and yields a modest log-loss improvement.

C=0.2 shrinks logits (~x0.6-0.75), softening probabilities; since the C=1.0 model is already ~96% confident-correct on the 99-row test, the small penalty added to ~95 confident correct rows likely slightly outweighs the calibration gain on the ~3 errors, giving a mild log-loss regression (high variance from 99-row grading).

Removing the full-data refit means the submitted model is trained on only 80% of the data (~7 vs ~9 examples per class); for a multinomial logistic regression on 240 features with 99 classes this loses calibration and accuracy, so leaderboard log loss should regress modestly from ~0.081 to roughly ~0.10, while runtime slightly decreases.

LR and shrinkage LDA are both strong, mostly complementary linear models on these 192 descriptors, and SLSQP OOF weight learning will downweight the overconfident distance-weighted kNN, so the convex blend should modestly beat the single LR (typical 10-20% log-loss gain on this dataset), though with only 99 test rows a single flipped confident prediction could swing the result by ~0.01-0.02.

HistGBM likely regresses: after its 15% early-stopping split many classes have only ~7–8 training rows, while min_samples_leaf=10 forces impure leaves and hurts calibrated rare-class probabilities; the tuned linear model is already extremely strong.

Multinomial softmax LR is a naturally well-calibrated, strong member on these 192 descriptors, whereas per-class Platt-sigmoid calibration of an OVR LinearSVC with only 3 folds and ~9 samples/class yields noisy, flatter probabilities; swapping it into the 4-way uniform average likely degrades calibration slightly, so a modest log-loss regression (roughly +0.01-0.03) is expected.

RF's deep-tree vote-fraction probabilities are typically less calibrated than HGB's log_loss-optimized outputs, and uniform soft voting only dilutes (not eliminates) this; the swap likely costs a small amount of log loss, with high variance since the 99-row test set (1 sample/class) makes single confident errors swing the score by hundredths.

A single 256x128 MLP (~95k params) on 891 samples across 99 classes (~9/class) overfits despite early stopping and light weight decay; the retained uniform-shrinkage step only corrects global overconfidence (alpha just grows), so the well-calibrated linear baseline's ranking advantage is lost and log loss roughly doubles, with extra variance from the tiny 99-row test set.

CV-selected C (likely ~0.6-2.5, since the log-loss-optimal regularization for this small 891x192/99-class problem sits near 1) modestly improves probability calibration over the arbitrary C=1.0, but the existing OOF uniform-shrinkage already absorbs much of the mis-calibration and the 99-row test set plus selection noise cap the gain, so expect a small real improvement rather than a large one.

The images are black leaves on white backgrounds, so thresholding >127 masks the background, not the leaf: the largest 'contour' is just the image frame, making most of the 9 scalars and the 32-bin histogram near-constant canvas geometry (largely zeroed by StandardScaler); only the 7 log-Hu moments of the negative space (plus any scan-size/species batch correlation) add weak signal, so the already-strong 192-feature logistic regression improves only marginally, with a small chance of being flat or slightly worse.

CV-tuned C (10-fold stratified, neg-log-loss grid) on standardized features almost surely selects a better-regularized C than the arbitrary 1.0 — typically worth a 10-20% log-loss reduction on this 891x192/99-class problem; everything else (scaler, features, final full-data refit, submission format) is unchanged, and 250 fast lbfgs fits easily fit the time budget, though the 99-row test set adds noise.

Soft-voting adds shrinkage-LDA (typically the strongest single model on these leaf descriptors, ~0.05-0.08 log loss) plus CV-tuned kNN and HGB to the LR baseline; probability averaging hedges individual model errors and the data-adaptive CV/early-stopping fixes keep it valid, so the ensemble should clearly beat the 0.1244 LR baseline, landing near the ~0.06-0.09 range typical for feature-only ensembles on this dataset, though HGB's weaker calibration on 891 samples caps the gain.

OOF will likely select a small alpha (~0.01-0.03) because fold-models make some overconfident errors, but the 0.124 test loss over 99 rows implies no catastrophic (p<1e-4) test mistakes, so uniform shrinkage mostly multiplies well-predicted rows by (1-alpha), adding roughly alpha to the loss for a slight regression (with some chance alpha=0 and the score is unchanged).

Ledoit-Wolf 'auto' will pick only mild shrinkage here (~792 within-class degrees of freedom for 192 features), so forcing shrinkage=0.9 collapses LDA toward a spherical nearest-centroid rule that discards most whitening of the correlated margin/shape/texture histograms; that typically costs some discrimination, and with only 99 test rows the log loss is dominated by a few samples, so a modest regression is expected (high variance either way).

Splitting into 64-dim descriptor families imposes a sensible block-diagonal covariance constraint (cross-family correlations are near-zero by construction), cutting estimation noise with only ~9 samples/class, and arithmetic averaging of the three posteriors softens LDA's overconfident plug-in probabilities, which mainly reduces the log-loss penalty from confident errors while accuracy stays comparable.

PCA(0.90) is largely redundant with the L2 shrinkage the tuned logistic regression already applies to these correlated descriptors, so the only real effect is truncating the low-variance tail — which still carries some species-discriminative signal — yielding a near-neutral but slightly worse log loss on the 99-row test set.
Shrunk LDA is a strong stable linear generative model for these descriptors and log-loss-tuned shrinkage should calibrate probabilities somewhat better than the logistic baseline.

PCA(0.95) on the standardized descriptors retains most structure but hard-truncates low-variance directions that carry fine discriminative detail separating confusable species (e.g., Quercus/Acer variants); since the L2-regularized, temperature-calibrated logistic baseline is already near-optimal, the added bias likely causes a small log-loss regression that the refit scalar temperature cannot fully offset.

Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage LDA is a famously strong match for these highly correlated 192 leaf descriptors (near-linearly-separable classes with ~9 samples each), and with the same fold-safe scaling and scalar temperature calibration it typically edges out tuned logistic regression on log loss, though LDA's overconfidence keeps the gain modest.

Mixing with a 0.005-weighted uniform only helps examples whose true-class probability is below 1/99≈0.0101; the baseline score of 0.0943 (avg p_true≈0.91) rules out such catastrophic errors (even one p≈1e-4 error would exceed the total loss budget), so every test row's loss simply rises by ≈-log(0.995)≈0.005, giving ≈0.0943+0.005=0.0993, a ~5% regression.

With random_state=0 the 384 landmarks are a subset of the 512, so this is a strictly lower-rank RBF approximation; the added kernel-approximation bias for C=1.0 logistic regression should slightly outweigh any regularization benefit, giving a small (~2-4%) log-loss regression, though within landmark-sampling noise.

Shrunken LDA (lsqr, Ledoit-Wolf 'auto') is a famously strong fit for the 192 correlated leaf histogram descriptors with ~9 samples/class, typically beating fixed-C logistic regression (CV log loss ~0.03-0.08 vs ~0.12-0.2 for LR), so on this 99-row test split it should cut log loss roughly in half; the code change is correct (classes_ alignment, no-leak scaling, deterministic, fast), with residual risk only from LDA's occasionally overconfident errors on the small test set.

GridSearchCV will likely pick a larger C (10-100) that sharpens mostly-correct predictions on these near-separable standardized descriptors for a modest log-loss gain, though CV/test mismatch on the 99-row test set could erase it; fold-local scaling is irrelevant since refit=True refits on all data identically to the baseline.

Scalar temperature fitted on out-of-fold logits reliably improves calibration of an already-strong multinomial LR (which tends to be overconfident here), typically shaving ~5-12% off log loss with negligible runtime cost; gain is modest because LR is near-calibrated and T is transferred from weaker fold models to the full-data model.

Nyström RBF features (512 components, gamma=1/192 on standardized descriptors) make the 99 leaf classes near-linearly separable, and this kernelized-LR recipe is well documented to roughly halve log loss versus linear LR on this dataset; C=1.0 is untuned so calibration isn't optimal, the 99-row test adds variance, but a large improvement is expected and runtime is trivially within budget.

The new dense block adds genuinely complementary signal — the t_days time trend (success rate declined over the subreddit's life), request length, reciprocity/gratitude phrase flags (multi-word patterns invisible to unigram TF-IDF), and first-person rate (tokens removed by stop_words) are all documented RAOP drivers — while 31 extra features pose negligible overfitting risk for a C=0.3 logistic model on ~8k features, so expect a modest ~+0.008 AUC gain.

Random forests consistently underperform regularized linear models on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF: with ~8k sparse features and max_features='sqrt' (~89 candidates/split), the strong numeric and text signals are rarely in any candidate set, fully-grown trees (min_samples_leaf=1) overfit noise on ~2.3k samples, and leaf-frequency probabilities give a worse ranking than logistic regression's additive scores, so expect a sizable AUC drop from 0.671 to roughly 0.60.

Random forests with max_features='sqrt' on 5k sparse TF-IDF columns see mostly random word features at each split (~71 of 5010 candidates, so numeric columns appear in only ~12% of nodes), badly underusing the text signal that the linear model aggregates across all features; the Kaggle RF benchmark used metadata only, not TF-IDF, so expect a classic linear-beats-forest regression of roughly 0.07-0.10 AUC despite better nonlinear handling of the nine requester-history variables.

Replacing 5000 sparse TF-IDF weights with 50 LDA topic proportions compresses away the specific lexical signal (narrative keywords, phrasing detail) that the linear model exploits for ranking; topic features retain broad themes but typically lose several AUC points versus unigram TF-IDF on this dataset, so expect a moderate regression to roughly 0.70 despite clean, in-budget implementation.

Swapping the supervised TF-IDF+LR logit (which carries most of the text signal, ~0.66+ AUC alone) for 20 unsupervised, noisy LDA topic proportions forces LightGBM to relearn the text-outcome mapping from only 2878 rows; the metadata columns keep the score from collapsing but the lost discriminative text signal outweighs any narrative×metadata interaction gains, giving roughly metadata-plus-weak-topics performance (~0.66-0.68).

The train/test split here is an interleaved re-split of the original Kaggle training data (2878+1162=4040), so the raw epoch is not a non-transferable period ID — it captures RAOP's well-documented secular decline in success rate as the subreddit grew, a real signal that transfers fine to interleaved test rows; hour-of-day and weekday are genuine but weak effects in this dataset, so swapping a moderately useful trend feature for two weak cyclical ones should cost a few thousandths of AUC, with the rest of the pipeline unchanged.

Rank-blending the LR (AUC ~0.70) with a GBM on the ~30 dense metadata/time/text-stat features (likely ~0.63-0.66 alone) adds modest decorrelated nonlinear signal, and since w=1.0 would exactly recover the baseline ordering, CV weight selection makes a small gain (~+0.005 AUC) likely and a regression unlikely.

Random forests with fully grown trees consistently underperform regularized linear models on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF: they aggregate thousands of weak text features poorly (sqrt feature sampling, few useful splits per tree), overfit with min_samples_leaf=1 giving noisy leaf probabilities, and lose the additive text signal that drives the LR's 0.70 — the RF will mostly exploit the numeric metadata (~0.63-0.66 territory), so expect a regression of several AUC points.

Bag-of-subreddits adds genuine but weak signal about requester community embeddedness (complementing the existing subreddit-count feature), and the strongly regularized logistic model can absorb ~1-3k extra sparse binary features with minimal overfitting risk, yielding a small AUC gain.

giver_username_if_known is post-outcome leakage: it is filled almost exactly when the train label is True, but the column is absent from test.json so the feature is all zeros there; the model refit on train dumps most weight onto this leaky indicator, shrinking the text/numeric coefficients that alone determine test ranking, so the holdout print will look great (~0.9) while the graded test AUC drops well below the 0.657 baseline.

Proper OOF stacking of a text logit with raw requester-history numerics under a well-regularized LightGBM (capturing non-linear effects the linear log1p+scaled LR misses) should add roughly 2 AUC points on this small dataset, with low implementation risk and runtime far under budget, though timestamp noise and small-sample variance cap the expected gain.

The added dense block captures well-documented RAOP signals missing from the baseline (text length, request-time trend/hour/day, prior RAOP activity indicators, karma ratio), which for this dataset typically add a few hundredths of AUC to a TF-IDF+numeric logistic model; scaling is handled correctly and the MLflow wrapper is failure-safe, so a modest improvement from 0.657 to roughly 0.675-0.68 is expected.

ExtraTrees splits on single features with random thresholds, which works poorly on 5k sparse TF-IDF dimensions where signal is spread across linear word combinations; nonlinear gains on the 9 numerics and 384 embedding dims won't offset this, so expect a moderate AUC regression versus the linear model.

TF-IDF lexical cues (e.g., 'broke', 'pay it forward', 'job') are the strongest signal block on RAOP; frozen MiniLM embeddings plus the nine behavioral numerics capture only part of that, so dropping the 5k unigram block loses ~0.015-0.02 AUC despite reduced variance, and the added mlflow/psutil instrumentation is metric-neutral and safely wrapped.

The added document statistics (especially length, punctuation/caps, money mentions, and sentiment) are well-established predictors for RAOP per the Althoff et al. paper and are genuinely complementary to length-normalized, punctuation-stripped TF-IDF, so a modest but real AUC gain is expected; some features (please/thank flags) are redundant with unigrams, capping the upside, while runtime and dependency risks are negligible.

TF-IDF text carries most of the predictive signal for RAOP (narrative/plea wording); a 9-feature metadata-only logistic regression typically lands near 0.60-0.62 AUC on this dataset, so removing text should regress the graded score despite better variance properties.

Replacing 5,000 discriminative TF-IDF token features with 200 mean-pooled Word2Vec vectors trained on a tiny (~4k document) corpus discards token-level signal and conflates the text, so the logistic model falls back mostly on the unchanged metadata + text-stats blocks, costing roughly 3 AUC points.

Adding bigrams and expanding the TF-IDF vocabulary from 5k to 60k (min_df=2) recovers diagnostic phrases like 'pay it forward' that the unigram model misses; with C=0.3 lbfgs logistic regression on ~2.9k samples this typically yields a modest AUC gain of ~0.01 without overfitting, and the mlflow additions are telemetry-only with no modeling effect.

Text (gratitude, narrative, length, reciprocity phrasing) carries the dominant predictive signal in RAOP — per Althoff et al.'s own ablations, status/history features alone score well below the combined model — so dropping TF-IDF/SVD for 9 behavioral columns should lose roughly 2 AUC points despite lower variance.

Random forest on the same 309-dim SVD features is robust and runs well within budget, but bagged deep trees with sqrt feature subsampling typically rank slightly worse than early-stopped gradient boosting on dense SVD text features, so expect a small AUC regression (roughly -0.005 to -0.015) rather than an improvement.

MiniLM sentence embeddings add complementary semantic signal to unigram TF-IDF on this small dataset, typically worth ~0.02 AUC; runtime is fine (~4040 short docs on 4 CPU threads), and the scaled dense block integrates cleanly with L2-regularized logistic regression, though untuned C=0.3 caps the gain.

Adding bigrams and expanding the TF-IDF vocabulary from 5k to 100k typically captures predictive phrases (e.g. 'pay it forward', 'lost my job') on RAOP, and C=0.3 L2 regularization keeps the wider feature space from overfitting, so expect a modest ~1.5 AUC-point gain over 0.6573.

The 15 dense text stats add genuinely complementary signal: request length and reciprocity/'pay it forward' phrases are known strong RAOP predictors, and first-person pronouns plus 'please' are removed by sklearn's english stop words so the TF-IDF never sees them; standardized log-scaled features appended to a 5000-dim sparse model carry negligible overfit risk, so a modest ~1-2% AUC gain is expected.

SVD-300 preserves most TF-IDF signal and LightGBM with CV early stopping can exploit non-linear metadata/text interactions the linear model misses, giving a modest expected gain on this small, noisy dataset (typical RAOP GBM-on-SVD results land ~0.66-0.68), with runtime well under budget.

The cubic spline on absolute time captures multi-year drift in success rates plus seasonality, while a single annual sin/cos pair only models seasonality and wraps all years together, discarding trend; date features are minor relative to text/history, so expect a small regression rather than a large change.

Weakening L2 100x (C 0.3→30) on ~2.9k noisy documents with ~5k sparse TF-IDF features mostly frees the model to fit low-frequency token noise; AUC is usually flat-to-declining past the regularization optimum, so expect a small test-ranking regression with no runtime/convergence risk.

Absolute request time carries weak real signal (RAOP success rate drifted as the community grew), and 8 standardized spline features on 2878 rows is too small to overfit, so a small AUC bump is likely; extrapolation='constant' caps any harm if the split is temporal.

KNN with cosine distance on ~5k-dimensional sparse TF-IDF vectors from only 2878 training points suffers from the curse of dimensionality — neighbor similarity is noisy and dominated by incidental word overlap, and distance-weighted label fractions over 25 neighbors produce a much weaker ranking than a regularized linear model, though the shared text/numeric signal keeps it well above random (~0.58 vs 0.649).

Distance-weighted KNN on nine skewed requester-history features should be a weaker, lumpier metadata ranker than CatBoost, and at 50% blend weight it slightly drags down the unchanged TF-IDF logistic model.

Raising C from 0.3 to 30 relieves excessive shrinkage of small-valued TF-IDF coefficients, letting lexical need/reciprocity signals contribute to the logistic half; with ~2.9k samples and 5k features this typically sits near (not far past) the AUC-optimal regularization, so the 50/50 blend gains modestly, though mild overfitting risk caps the improvement.

RAOP success rates declined over the community's lifetime, so a smooth date spline adds a real but modest signal on top of text/history features; with only 8 standardized spline columns added to a regularized LR on a random train/test split, expect a small AUC gain (~+0.005) with negligible overfitting or runtime risk.

BernoulliNB's binarization discards TF-IDF magnitudes and collapses the nine informative numeric history features to above/below-mean indicators, and its independence assumption typically underperforms even modestly regularized logistic regression on this sparse text+metadata task, so a modest AUC regression is expected.

The 8 spline features on the UTC timestamp can capture the mild downward drift in pizza success rate over the subreddit's history, which transfers under a random train/test split and adds a tiny ranking signal to a heavily regularized 5000-feature model; the MLflow logging and suppressed holdout scoring don't affect final predictions.

Binary subreddit-membership indicators add genuine, mostly orthogonal signal about requester community engagement (e.g., assistance/gifting subreddits) beyond the activity-volume numerics, and L2 regularization at C=0.3 safely shrinks the rare min_df=5 features, yielding a small AUC gain rather than noise-driven regression; removing the holdout print does not change the final model, which was already refit on all data.

CatBoost on the 9 requester-history features is a decent standalone model (~0.62-0.64 AUC since karma/activity are strong RAOP signals) and adds nonlinear interactions the linear model misses; the fixed 50/50 blend slightly dilutes the dominant text signal but on net should give a small AUC gain, with runtime and implementation posing no risk.

Adding bigrams under the same 5000-feature cap swaps only the least-frequent unigram tail for a few hundred common bigrams (e.g. 'pay it forward', 'would really appreciate'), which usually adds a small amount of signal for logistic regression on this dataset; the removed holdout and added mlflow telemetry don't affect predictions, so expect a minor AUC bump within noise.

Function-word signal is already captured by the char_wb (2,5) view, so dropping stop words mostly trims high-frequency, low-IDF redundancy in the word view and refocuses the L2 budget on content words and cross-gap bigrams — a small net gain on 17.6k rows, with the lost stylometric bigram cues ('of the', 'it was') only partially offsetting it; effect size is near test-set noise, so only a modest improvement is expected.

Stacking adds two diverse, strong base learners (NB on word counts is historically at least as good as TF-IDF LR on this task, ~0.31-0.33 alone) with a learned geometric meta-blend on log-probs, which classically cuts log loss ~10-15% vs the single LR; fold-averaged test predictions keep meta-train/test scales consistent, risk of overfitting the 9-feature meta-learner is negligible, and runtime stays well under budget.

Function words are a genuine author-discriminating stylometric signal (and sklearn's list even removes archaic connectives like 'thereupon'/'wherein' that mark Poe/Lovecraft), so both word-level base models should degrade slightly; the char_wb models and meta-features still carry style cues and the LightGBM stacker dampens the damage, so the net regression is small (~+0.002 log loss).

With 4 strong, highly correlated base models, the 12 OOF probability columns already carry nearly all the signal, so a low-capacity regularized multinomial logistic combiner should match or slightly beat the LightGBM stacker by avoiding fold-noise overfitting and producing smoother, better-calibrated probabilities; the 16 meta-features retain most of their (modest) value linearly after scaling, so I expect a small ~1% log-loss improvement, well within the run budget since LR trains in seconds.

Train and test are a random split of the same editions, so punctuation is genuine transferable signal here (semicolons skew MWS 32/19/14%, apostrophes mark HPL dialect like o'/an', quotes skew EAP/HPL 17/6%); stripping it destroys high-signal case-sensitive char n-grams that word features cannot recover, so the small vocabulary/regularization benefit should be outweighed and log loss worsens modestly.

Stacking two C=10 TF-IDF logistic regressions with tuned word/char MultinomialNBs via 5-fold OOF and a log-prob meta-learner is the classic strong recipe for this competition; it adds model diversity and better regularization than the single C=1 LR, so the meta-CV (a good proxy since the graded test is a same-distribution 10% split) should land around 0.38-0.40 vs the current 0.4386, with minor test-set variance risk.

Keeping the top 10k chi2 columns retains the strong author cues (character names, Lovecraft dialect spellings, punctuation-style char n-grams) while dropping ~120k noisy/redundant tail features, giving the C=1.0 multinomial LR (currently ~390k coefficients for 17.6k rows) a mild variance reduction that typically translates to a ~1% log-loss gain; the OOF blend-weight search re-tunes anyway, limiting downside, so expect a small improvement within test-set noise.

Function words are classic discriminative stylometric features for authorship attribution (Poe/Shelley/Lovecraft differ in function-word usage), so removing them slightly hurts both the word-TF-IDF LR and the count NB; the char_wb block partially compensates, keeping the regression small (~1%).

CV over C on this word+char TF-IDF LR setup typically selects C≈3-10, which modestly reduces log loss vs the under-regularized C=1.0 default; train/test are iid so the gain transfers, though the small 1958-row test adds noise, so expect a small real improvement (roughly -0.01 log loss).

OOF stacking of diverse LR/NB text models plus informative punctuation/stylometry meta-features with a LightGBM meta-learner is a well-proven recipe on this dataset, typically cutting log loss ~10-15% below a single TF-IDF LR (0.43 -> ~0.37-0.38); the implementation is correct, leakage-free, and fits the time budget, with ±0.01 test-set variance.

Switching char_wb->char plus case-sensitivity and no feature cap adds author-discriminative punctuation/capitalization-in-context features (EDA shows strong per-author punctuation/case habits), which LR on TF-IDF typically converts into a modest log-loss gain; runtime and memory stay fine, though min_df=2 rare n-grams add some noise so the gain is moderate, not dramatic.

Blending count-based MultinomialNB with the TF-IDF LR is a classic complementary pairing on this dataset; the OOF-tuned weight can only pick pure LR in the worst case, and in practice NB's differently-calibrated probabilities typically shave ~0.015-0.02 off log loss, though NB's overconfidence and small-test variance cap the gain at a few percent.

fastText's uniform n-gram averaging lets high-frequency stopwords (~40% of tokens) dilute the dominant content-word signal (character names like raymond/arkham/dupin, author-specific vocabulary, dialect spellings) that transfers perfectly in this same-novel random split; removing stopwords concentrates the sentence vectors on discriminative tokens and creates cleaner content-content bigrams, which should outweigh the loss of pronoun/function-word stylometric cues (partly redundant with kept punctuation and names), yielding a modest log-loss improvement within run-to-run noise from multithreaded training.

The imbalance is mild (40/31/29), so oversampling adds little discriminative signal but shifts the learned priors from the natural distribution toward uniform; since log loss is calibration-sensitive and the test set keeps the natural distribution, the resulting prior miscalibration (on the order of KL(natural||uniform) ≈ 0.01 nats, plus slight overfitting to duplicated minority rows over 25 epochs) should produce a small regression rather than an improvement.

ComplementNB on the same non-negative TF-IDF should be weaker but mildly complementary, and the OOF sweep including w=1.0 likely picks an LR-heavy blend that shaves about 1% off log loss with little downside.

MultinomialNB is a reasonable text classifier but its independence assumption is badly violated by overlapping char n-grams, yielding overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities that log loss punishes heavily; even with CV-tuned alpha it typically lands around 0.44-0.48 on this dataset versus ~0.35 for tuned logistic regression, so this is a clear regression.
Dropping char_wb n-grams removes punctuation/morphology cues (semicolons, quotes, Lovecraft apostrophes) that complement the word/name features, so log loss should rise modestly.

ComplementNB on the same word+char TF-IDF stack will reach comparable accuracy but emits the classic overconfident, poorly-calibrated Naive Bayes probabilities (softmax over complement log-count scores), which multiclass log loss punishes heavily relative to the ratio-weighted logistic (NB-SVM) head, so the score regresses from ~0.409 to roughly 0.55-0.65.

3-fold CV selection of C directly optimizing neg_log_loss will likely pick C≈3-10 (typical optimum for high-dimensional TF-IDF logistic models), yielding a small log-loss improvement over the arbitrary C=1.0; gains are bounded by 3-fold selection noise and the small 1,958-row graded test, and the mlflow telemetry is model-neutral.

Keeping the same TF-IDF/style features should stay fast, but MultinomialNB double-counts correlated char n-grams and alpha=0.1 is overconfident under log loss versus calibrated softmax logistic regression.

fastText supervised on Spooky Author typically lands around 0.42-0.48 log loss — its subword/bigram features capture author cues well, but its softmax probabilities are less calibrated than tuned TF-IDF + logistic regression, so expect a modest regression from 0.4323 rather than an improvement.

5-fold CV over the C grid (which includes the old C=1.0) should reliably pick a slightly less-regularized value (likely C≈2-4), which typically shaves ~0.005-0.007 off log loss for TF-IDF+LR on this dataset; the run fits in budget via 4-way joblib parallelism and mlflow is failure-guarded, so the only real risk is CV noise picking a marginally suboptimal C, which still won't be worse than 1.0 by much.

NB-SVM (per-class log count-ratio weighted TF-IDF + binary logistic per class) is a classic strong text-classification baseline that reliably beats a single multinomial LR on small datasets like Spooky Author by roughly 0.03-0.06 log loss, with negligible runtime cost.

Punctuation counts (semicolons, quotes) and sentence-length stats carry genuine per-author signal only partially redundant with char n-gram TF-IDF, so the 14 scaled style features should give a small log-loss improvement (~0.5%) with negligible runtime cost and no implementation risks.

NB log-count-ratio feature weighting (Wang & Manning style) on TF-IDF with binary OvR liblinear logistic models is the classic strong recipe for this competition and typically beats plain multinomial LR on word+char TF-IDF by ~0.05-0.07 log loss; renormalization of independent binary probabilities costs little calibration-wise, so expect ~0.38 vs 0.441.

Stronger L2 (C 1.0->0.25) on high-dimensional sparse word+char TF-IDF shrinks overconfident coefficients toward the class prior, which usually improves probability calibration and log loss slightly on this dataset; the effect is modest since features and solver are unchanged, with some risk of mild underfitting offsetting the gain.

Char_wb (2,5) fragments still capture much of the style signal (punctuation, dialect spellings, even name fragments like 'perdi'/'arkh'), so the drop is modest rather than catastrophic, but removing whole-word unigram/bigram features loses the clean, high-weight near-deterministic cues (character names, distinctive vocabulary) that word TF-IDF provided, so log loss should regress by roughly 5-10% over the 0.5177 baseline.

Plain one-vs-rest logistic regression on word(1-2)+char_wb(2-5) sublinear TF-IDF is a strong, well-calibrated baseline for this dataset (~0.40-0.45 log loss), while the NB log-ratio reweighting with C=1.0 inflates the scale of rare discriminative features, weakening their effective L2 penalty and producing overconfident errors, so removing it should moderately improve the score.

Halving C from 4 to 2 modestly strengthens L2 shrinkage over ~120k correlated word/char TF-IDF features on 17.6k short texts, which typically softens overconfident probabilities and yields a small log-loss gain, but the effect is near noise-level for a 1,958-row test set.
NB log-odds weighting should modestly help this small author-attribution task by boosting rare author-specific word/char cues, while one-vs-rest plus row renormalization is roughly neutral.

Function words are a primary stylistic signal in authorship attribution (their frequencies and char n-grams distinguish Poe/Shelley/Lovecraft), so removing sklearn stop words strips discriminative features and corrupts bigrams into spurious adjacencies; TF-IDF's idf already downweights them, so the strong content cues (character names etc.) keep the loss near baseline but moderately worse, ~0.42 vs 0.382.

Stronger L2 (C=0.25) on high-dimensional correlated word+char TF-IDF typically reduces coefficient variance and improves log loss slightly, while the temperature step rescales logits so the net effect is small; expecting a modest improvement within noise.

Switching char_wb to char lets n-grams span word boundaries, capturing spacing/punctuation transition patterns that differ by author (e.g., Lovecraft's dialect apostrophes, semicolon usage); on this dataset the two analyzers typically perform very similarly with a slight edge to plain char, so expect a small improvement over 0.4323, well within noise given the 1,958-row test set.

NBSVM-style log-count-ratio reweighting of the word+char TF-IDF columns with per-class liblinear LR is a well-known small-data text trick that typically improves calibration over plain multinomial LR by a few percent on this dataset; the implementation is correct and fast, with ~±0.01 noise from the 1,958-row test set.

With ~200-300k sparse TF-IDF features and 17.6k same-distribution training rows, C=1 is somewhat over-regularized for log loss; raising C to 4 reduces coefficient shrinkage toward the typical optimum for this pipeline (small gain, not a regime change), while the removed holdout print and unchanged seed/features mean the submission differs only through the C value.
The scalar holdout temperature leaves ranking unchanged and should only mildly soften an already decent multinomial LR, giving a small calibration gain.

RMSE rewards the conditional mean in dollars; training on log1p and inverting with expm1 yields the conditional geometric mean, which is systematically biased low for this right-skewed fare distribution, and log-scale splits under-weight the expensive airport/long trips where the largest squared errors live — the ~2.8% corrupt-row floor is unchanged, so expect a small regression of roughly 1% (about +0.04 RMSE), with variance stabilization on the tail only partially offsetting the objective-metric mismatch.

Quadrupling the training sample (1M→4M rows) is the only substantive change and typically cuts GBM RMSE on the valid rows by ~3-4% of MSE; after adding back the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows, overall RMSE drops from 4.10 to roughly 4.00, while the MLflow/timestamp/n_jobs edits don't affect model quality.

Distances to JFK/LGA/EWR are a classic high-signal feature for this dataset (flat-fare airport trips, sharper location splits than raw coords alone), so LightGBM should cut valid-row RMSE by roughly 4-5%, which translates to ~3% overall after the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows.

L2 on log1p targets estimates the conditional geometric mean (~median), and expm1 without a bias/smearing correction systematically underpredicts dollar fares — the loss is misaligned with the dollar-RMSE metric, so the slight robustness gain against fare outliers is outweighed by the downward bias on typical and expensive rides (including the corrupt rows now predicted nearer the median than the mean), nudging RMSE up ~1-2%.
The distance monotonicity prior is mostly already learned from coordinates and should only lightly regularize the dominant feature, while the fixed mean-fallback corrupt rows cap any overall gain.

Fares are already cleaned of extremes and L2 on raw dollars is aligned with the RMSE metric; log1p training makes expm1 predictions approximate the conditional geometric mean (median), which under-predicts high fares and downweights the long trips that dominate dollar MSE, so expect a small (~1% on valid rows, ~0.7% overall) regression rather than a gain.

In-sample encoding leaks each training row's own fare into its key statistics (materially for the many rare ~2km route keys despite m=20 smoothing), so the GBDT over-trusts the TE features and generalizes slightly worse; this leakage typically outweighs the modest benefit of removing the 80%/100% log-count and mean-noise train/inference mismatch, giving a roughly neutral-to-slightly-worse RMSE within run-to-run noise.

Fitting L2 loss on log1p(fare) optimizes relative error, not dollar RMSE; expm1 of the log-space mean is the conditional geometric mean, which underpredicts the conditional arithmetic mean (Jensen bias, several percent on high fares), and with no smearing/bias correction the resulting underprediction of expensive trips — whose squared errors dominate RMSE — outweighs modest gains on short fares, so a small regression is expected.

Airport-distance features let the trees isolate JFK flat-fare and EWR-surcharge trips (~8% of rows with atypical fare behavior) with single splits, cutting valid-row RMSE from ~3.6 to ~3.45-3.5; the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows is unaffected, so the graded score improves only modestly from 4.138 to ~4.02.

The ~2.8% corrupt test rows come from the same population as corrupt training rows; their baseline per-row error (~12.5 when predicting the global mean 11.3) exceeds the overall fare std (~9.8), implying their fares are systematically shifted (likely higher, e.g. GPS-dropout long trips), so training with NaN-coordinate features lets LightGBM route these rows toward high-fare leaves and approximate their conditional mean, cutting their MSE contribution by roughly a third (2.1 -> ~1.7 floor) while leaving the ~3.6 RMSE on valid rows essentially unchanged.

Quadrupling the random sample should modestly reduce LightGBM variance and support more effective boosting rounds, but unchanged features and the fixed mean-fare predictions for corrupt test rows cap the gain.

Out-of-fold smoothed target encodings of ~1km endpoint cells and ~2km route pairs add toll/JFK-flat-fare/local-mean signal that raw coordinates + haversine cannot express, likely improving valid-row RMSE by ~0.15-0.20, but the ~2.8% corrupt test rows pinned at the mean fare dilute the graded gain to roughly 3% (4.138 -> ~4.00); the implementation is leak-free and runtime impact is negligible.
Log-space training fits a downward-biased geometric-mean fare and downweights costly airport/long-tail rides; without a bias correction, raw-dollar RMSE should rise slightly.

Manhattan-block distance and bearing are genuinely informative for NYC fares (street grid, direction-dependent tolls) and GBDTs benefit from explicit geometry features, but they are deterministic functions of coordinates the model already sees, and the ~2.8% corrupt test rows still go through the unchanged fallback model, so expect only a small gain on the valid-row portion — roughly 0.03 RMSE overall.

Distance-to-airport/Manhattan features are a well-established, high-value addition for this dataset (JFK flat-fare and airport surcharge regimes), typically cutting valid-row RMSE by ~5% (3.6 -> ~3.42); the ~2.8% corrupt test rows scored as mean fare are unaffected, dampening the graded gain to roughly 3-4%.

RMSE is minimized by predicting the conditional mean; switching to an MAE objective fits conditional medians, which for the right-skewed fare distribution systematically underpredicts, and the <=500 cap already removed the worst outliers, so L1's robustness buys little while the median-vs-mean bias costs roughly 0.1-0.15 RMSE.

The metric is raw-dollar RMSE, which the baseline already optimizes directly; training on log1p(fare) makes expm1-inverted predictions approximate the conditional geometric mean, systematically shrinking high-fare predictions (the metric mismatch of fitting RMSLE-style loss against an RMSE metric), so after re-mixing with the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows the overall score regresses slightly, on the order of 1-2%.
MAE training pushes leaves toward conditional medians; after cleaning the extreme-fare noise is rare, so robustness gains little while median-vs-mean skew should slightly hurt RMSE.

With delta=1.0 versus a ~$3.6 residual scale, most training rows fall in Huber's linear regime, making the fit L1-like: it pulls predictions toward the conditional median (underpredicting the right-skewed high fares that RMSE punishes most) and converges slower within 1000 capped-gradient trees; the reduced influence of corrupt rows only partly offsets this, so a mild RMSE regression is expected.

RMSE rewards the conditional mean on the dollar scale; log1p+expm1 predicts roughly the conditional median (systematically low on high fares, no bias correction) and reweights the loss toward relative error, so the small-tail stabilization is likely offset by median-vs-mean bias — expect roughly neutral to a slight regression.

Airport-proximity features are the classic high-value addition for this dataset: ~5.5% of test rows touch JFK/LGA/EWR with fares (JFK flat $45/$52 by year, EWR ~$71) that raw axis-aligned coordinate splits can only approximate, so explicitly giving the tree radial distances and near flags should cut error on those rows substantially (roughly halving airport-row RMSE), while the ~2.8% corrupt-row floor and all other behavior stay unchanged — a modest but real overall gain, with negligible runtime cost.

Quadrupling training rows 1M→4M with identical features/hyperparameters should modestly reduce valid-row RMSE (~3.62→~3.47 via learning-curve gains), which after adding the fixed ~2.8% corrupt-row floor (predicted at the unchanged mean fare) yields graded RMSE ≈4.01; runtime (~3.6M rows LightGBM, early-stopped) stays well within budget, and risk of regression is minimal since more data with the same GBDT setup is near-monotonically helpful.

5-fold bagging averages 5 models trained on overlapping 80% subsets, which reduces prediction variance and typically yields a modest RMSE gain over a single 90/10-split model despite each fold seeing slightly less data; the improvement is dampened because ~2.8% of test rows are unpredictable (fixed MSE floor from the mean-fare override), so the overall graded RMSE drops only ~1-2% from 4.138 to roughly 4.07-4.08.

The OOF-smoothed pickup-cell mean fare is leak-free and captures airport/neighborhood fare levels (JFK/LGA flat fares, Manhattan vs outer boroughs) that axis-aligned splits on raw lat/lon only approximate coarsely, giving a small but real gain on the ~97% valid rows; the ~2.8% corrupt-row mean-fare floor and the inert mlflow additions are unchanged, so the overall improvement is diluted to under 1%.

Snapping coordinates to a 0.01° (~1 km) grid destroys sub-kilometer precision in the raw coordinates and haversine distance — the dominant signal for the many short Manhattan trips — while the route encoding is essentially unchanged (rounding vs floor only shifts the same 0.01° cell partition by half a cell), so the model loses fine spatial resolution and RMSE regresses by roughly 3-5%.

L1 loss bounds the influence of the heavy right tail of atypical/extreme fares that L2 leaf means chase, typically yielding a small RMSE gain on this skewed, quantized fare data, while early stopping still monitors RMSE and the ~2.8% corrupt-row floor is unchanged — so expect a modest improvement of roughly 0.02 RMSE.

L1 training fits the conditional median rather than the mean, and on the right-skewed fare target that usually costs a little on an RMSE metric; robustness to the few surviving extreme fares (~0.04% above $100) recovers only part of that, while early stopping on RMSE keeps the model near its best-RMSE point, so expect a small regression of roughly 1%.

Airport-proximity features capture the large flat-fare JFK/LGA/EWR component (~5-6% of trips) that raw lat/lon only approximates with axis-aligned splits, likely cutting valid-row RMSE ~2-3%, but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows (predicted at mean fare, untouched by this change) dilutes the overall gain to roughly 1.5-2%; runtime impact is negligible (six vectorized haversine calls on 1M rows).

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean, so switching to the L1 (conditional median) objective on a right-skewed fare target systematically underpredicts high-fare rows in the identically-distributed test set; early stopping on RMSE and the reduced influence of training-set fare outliers only partly offset this, so expect a small regression rather than an improvement.
Rounding coordinates to ~1 km removes some fine pickup/dropoff resolution the trees can use, while keeping exact haversine distance should limit the damage to a small RMSE increase.

L1 fits the conditional median, which sits systematically below the mean for the right-skewed fare distribution, biasing predictions low and inflating squared error on the 97% valid test rows, while the robustness-to-outliers benefit is minimal because cleaning already removed fares >500 and extremes are ~0.04% of rows; RMSE-monitored early stopping mitigates but cannot remove this structural misalignment with the metric, so expect a modest regression from 4.138 to roughly 4.20-4.26.

The 29°-rotated Manhattan (street-grid) distance is a better proxy for metered driving distance than straight-line haversine and is a nonlinear combination axis-aligned trees cannot reconstruct from raw coordinates, so it should give a small real gain on valid rows; but ~2.8% of graded test rows are corrupt and pinned to the mean fare (a ~2.1 RMSE floor contributing ~26% of total MSE), which dampens any model improvement, so overall RMSE drops only slightly from 4.138 to ~4.12.

Leakage-safe (OOF, smoothed) directional route-mean target encoding is a proven feature family for this exact competition — it captures route-specific fare levels (airport flat fares, toll crossings, common Manhattan routes) that raw coordinates + haversine only partially express, and the heavy shrinkage (50) plus min_child_samples=100 keep rare-route noise from hurting; the ~2.8% corrupt test rows still get the mean-fare fallback so the floor is unchanged, capping the overall gain at a modest ~2%.

The rotated Manhattan-grid distance is a classic, mildly informative NYC taxi feature that complements haversine (LightGBM already has raw coords, so the gain is small, ~1-2% on valid rows, dampened by the ~2.8% corrupt-row floor); the MLflow instrumentation is metric-neutral overhead that fits the budget.

Doubling the training sample from 1M to 2M rows (same pipeline, seed, features, hyperparameters) gives LightGBM modestly better generalization on this distance-dominated problem, but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt test rows and diminishing returns of added data cap the gain at roughly 2%, and the 2M-row run still fits comfortably in the 10-minute budget.

Airport flat fares (JFK/LGA/EWR) are a strong known signal affecting ~5.5% of test rows; the GBM already partially learns airport regions from raw coordinates, so the explicit categorical route feature yields a real but modest gain of roughly 0.03-0.04 RMSE, with no runtime or compatibility risk.

LightGBM with categorical letter columns is a strong, natural fit and should land in the same ~0.983-0.987 band as the MLP on raw features, but the 2000-round cap (baseline notes show AUC still improving at 3000 rounds) slightly under-trains it, so expect a small regression within noise.

Standardization already neutralized the scale/outlier issues binning claims to fix, while 10 quantile bins discard within-decile resolution on the continuous features whose smooth interactions drive the signal, so the MLP loses a small amount of ranking information (roughly a few thousandths of AUC) despite the nicer per-bin response curves.

The features are essentially uncorrelated after standardization, so full PCA whitening is a near-arbitrary rotation that smears the strong axis-aligned per-position f_27 letter signals (positive rates 0.1-1.0 per letter) across 41 dense components, making each greedy split far less informative within the fixed 3000-tree budget, while the per-leaf linear regressions are rotation-invariant and therefore provide no compensating gain.

f_27 behaves like an ID (671k distinct strings in 800k rows, mean frequency ~1.2, max 10, and 72% of test strings unseen), so a whole-string target encoding with m=20 shrinkage collapses nearly every value to the prior — the OOF/full-train encoding is statistically honest but carries almost no signal, while deleting the 10 per-position character columns removes what the EDA identifies as the most informative feature group (position letters span 0.10-1.00 positive rates); the model is left with only the numeric interaction signal (historically ~0.92-0.94 for this dataset), so expect a large regression of roughly 0.05 AUC.

f_27 is nearly unique per row (671k distinct strings in 800k rows, 72% of test strings unseen), so the smoothed OOF target encoding collapses to the global prior for most train rows (singletons get enc=prior out-of-fold) and for 72% of test rows, making f_27_te almost constant, while the removed per-position character columns carry strong signal (e.g., position 6 positive rates from 0.10 to 1.00 across letters) that LightGBM was exploiting — the model effectively falls back to numerics + f_27_nunique only, a clear regression.

These sums encode real additive interactions known for this dataset (tail regions with extreme positive rates, decent support of a few percent of rows) that axis-aligned trees approximate only inefficiently, so handing them to LightGBM explicitly should yield a small but genuine AUC gain over the already-high 0.9915 baseline, with limited headroom capping the improvement.

Logistic regression on ordinal-encoded f_27 plus raw features captures only the weak linear signal (~0.70-0.75 AUC) since the dominant effects (distinct-letter count, categorical letter effects, continuous interactions) are not linearly accessible, and a 50/50 rank blend with such a much weaker, same-feature model acts mostly as injected ranking noise, dragging the 0.984 LGBM down by roughly 2-3 AUC points (a blend partner would need ~0.81+ AUC at equal weight just to break even).

A small MLP on ordinally-encoded f_27 positions cannot recover the letter-identity/distinct-letter-count interaction signal that GBDT exploits via axis splits (the key structure of this dataset), so it typically lands ~2-4 AUC points below the 0.9842 tree baseline, with extra downside risk if the 8-minute guard truncates the cosine schedule mid-training.

A small MLP on standardized raw features and ordinal-encoded f_27 underfits the sharp categorical/interaction structure (per-letter effects, count tails) that LightGBM exploits naturally; the run fits in budget but typical naive-MLP results on this competition land ~0.94-0.96, a clear regression from 0.977.

Linear leaves make each round strictly more expressive (piecewise-linear logits fit the oblique, sum-of-features boundaries better than staircases) and the unchanged 100-round early stopping on the i.i.d. holdout protects against the extra variance, so expect a small AUC gain; standardization/float32 is neutral for tree splits, and the improvement is bounded because the key f_27 structure (distinct-letter count) is still not engineered, while 2x-ish slower training still fits the budget.

The distinct-letter count of f_27 is a known strong signal in this competition (positive rates ~9% for 2-3 distinct, ~48% for 4-6, ~91% for 7-8) that axis-aligned trees cannot reconstruct from per-position ordinal columns, so adding it as an explicit feature should give a clear AUC boost, roughly from 0.977 to ~0.987.

The three targeted additive sums give axis-aligned trees direct access to diagonal decision boundaries that this interaction-heavy synthetic target is known to contain, so they should add real signal on top of the 0.9770 baseline, but the gain is bounded (~+0.002-0.003 AUC) because deep 127-leaf trees already approximate such boundaries, the strong f_27 distinct-count signal remains unexploited, and 3000-tree models extract most of what these linear combinations offer.

f_27 is near-unique (671k distinct strings in 800k rows; 72% of test strings unseen in train), so as a native categorical it can only memorize noise and routes most test rows down default branches, while deleting the 10 per-position ordinal columns removes the core positional-letter signal (e.g., position-6 rates spanning 0.10-1.00); retained letter counts, nunique, and numerics prevent a full collapse but can't recover position-specific interactions.

Adding adjacent-bigram categorical features gives LightGBM direct access to pairwise letter interactions in the pivotal f_27 column that ordinal per-position splits only approximate inefficiently, and with 720k training rows the ≤300 categories per bigram have enough support to mostly help rather than overfit — but the per-position, count, and nunique features already capture most of the f_27 signal, so the gain should be small (~+0.0004 AUC), with mild feature-pool dilution and rare-pair noise capping the upside.

PCA components are linear rotations of raw features already given to LightGBM, so they add essentially no usable signal for axis-aligned trees (and slightly dilute feature sampling), whereas the removed top-25 pairwise products explicitly encoded the multiplicative interactions this dataset's signal is built on — expect a small regression back toward the no-interaction-feature baseline (~0.974).

Hashing the whole near-unique f_27 string (671k distinct values, 72% of test strings unseen in train) into 64 buckets produces pure-noise one-hot features and destroys the dominant per-position-letter and distinct-letter-count signal, so the model falls back to essentially numeric-only performance around 0.93 AUC.

Bagged fully-grown ExtraTrees with random thresholds models the interaction-driven, per-position-letter signal much less efficiently than 3000-round gradient boosting (no boosting of residuals, ordinal letter splits wasted, no nunique-style features either way), which on this synthetic TPS dataset historically costs ~0.02-0.035 AUC versus a LightGBM baseline, and the added 5-fold cross_val_predict (≈5 total fits) pushes wall-clock close to the hard limit but should still complete and yield a submission.

sklearn's MLP (short 40-epoch Adam run, no embeddings/one-hot) must decode the nominal f_27 letters and their equality/count structure from raw ordinal scalars plus handle heavy-tailed f_28, and on this interaction-heavy tabular dataset such a plain MLP reliably trails a well-regularized LightGBM by several AUC points despite better native handling of multiplicative continuous terms.

The data card shows f_27 distinct-letter count is a dominant grouped signal (positive rate ~9%/48%/91% across nunique bands) that per-position categoricals can only reconstruct via expensive pair interactions a 127-leaf tree struggles to learn, so handing LightGBM explicit letter-count and nunique numeric features should add real signal (matching known competition results where these features gained ~+0.002 AUC), with only minor dilution risk from the larger feature pool under colsample_bytree=0.8.

The full-sequence frequency is essentially noise (670k distinct strings in 800k rows, so almost all values are 1) and carries no target signal, while the deleted per-position letter categoricals were the most informative feature group (per data card, position letters drive positive rates from 0.10 to 1.00); the model falls back to numeric-only interactions, which support roughly ~0.91 AUC versus the 0.9768 baseline.

The EDA shows distinct-letter count in f_27 is a dominant grouped signal (positive rate ~9% at 2-3, ~48% at 4-6, ~91% at 7-8 distinct letters) that per-position ordinals only capture indirectly via deep tree splits; adding f27_nunique and per-letter counts gives LightGBM direct split access to it, which in this competition historically yields a solid AUC gain of roughly +0.005, with negligible runtime cost and no risk to the pipeline.
