Explicit standardized pairwise products give the underfit 3000-tree GBM direct access to real numeric interactions it otherwise must approximate with many splits, and gain-screening on 150k rows reliably finds the useful ones, so expect a small AUC bump (~+0.001) with minimal overfit or runtime risk.

Refitting on 100% of rows (11% more data) with rounds scaled to 3333 is safe here because the holdout AUC was still improving at 3000 trees, so the extra data and slightly more trees should give a small genuine gain (~+0.0005-0.001 AUC) with minimal overfitting risk given min_child_samples=100 and 800k rows; remaining variance is just run-to-run noise.

Treating the 10 f_27 position codes as LightGBM categorical features (optimal many-vs-rest letter partitions instead of threshold splits on an arbitrary alphabetical order) is the well-known standard trick for this exact competition and typically lifts a single-model LGBM from ~0.977 to ~0.978, with comparable runtime since only the split search for those 10 columns changes.

The distinct-letter count of f_27 is a documented strong signal (~9% positive for 2-3 distinct, ~91% for 7-8) that gradient-boosted trees cannot efficiently reconstruct from the 10 per-position ordinals, and as a low-cardinality feature with large support it adds signal with negligible overfitting or runtime cost, though part of its information is already implicitly captured so the gain is moderate.

Capping depth at 2 (4 leaves) restricts the model to main effects and pairwise splits, but this dataset's signal is dominated by higher-order structure—the f_27 distinct-letter pattern (a ~10-way interaction over ordinal-encoded characters, where isolating one letter already consumes both split levels) and 3+-way continuous interactions—so the single engineered sum feature only partially compensates and AUC should drop meaningfully from the deep-tree baseline.

LightGBM is well suited to this interaction-heavy synthetic tabular data, but the proposed config (31 leaves, max_bin=63, only 600 trees at lr=0.05, no bagging) is markedly weaker than the known-strong LGBM setup for this competition (127 leaves, 3000+ trees, still improving at the end), so it should land essentially on par with—marginally below—the MLP's 0.98219.

Histogram GBDT is the canonical strong model for this interaction-heavy synthetic dataset and should edge out the plain MLP by better capturing the discrete f_27 character interactions, but the constrained config (31 leaves, max_bin=63, 600 trees, no subsampling) caps it near the typical ~0.984 GBDT level for this raw feature set rather than the ~0.986+ achievable with deeper trees and f_27-engineered features.

Collapsing the 16 continuous predictors to 4 quartile codes discards fine-grained split information that GBDTs exploit for the interaction-driven signal (LightGBM's internal 255-bin quantization is far finer), so the retained f_27 chars and count features keep the model strong (~0.96) but meaningfully below the 0.9768 raw-feature baseline.

Cutting num_leaves from 127 to 7 caps each tree at ~2-3-way splits along most paths, but this dataset's signal is explicitly high-order interactions (f_27 position combos x continuous blocks), so the ensemble underfits despite 3000 boosting rounds; AUC should drop a few points from 0.9768 to roughly 0.95.

num_leaves=4 reduces every tree to depth-2, so the model can only fit additive pairwise splits; this dataset's signal lives in higher-order interactions between the continuous blocks and f_27 characters, and even 3000 boosting rounds of shallow trees cannot reconstruct them, causing substantial underfitting (though the strong f_27 per-letter/grouped-count effects keep AUC in the mid-0.95s).
The added column is only an unstandardized linear sum of features already available to the trees and is dominated by weak f_26, so it should be essentially flat with at most a tiny under-fit gain.

The sum is a linear combination of three features LightGBM already sees individually; trees can already approximate such additive structure, and there's no evidence this particular trio carries signal (all have |r|<0.07 with target), so AUC stays essentially unchanged within run noise, with only negligible colsample_bytree dilution from one extra column.

A CPU MLP on raw features will converge within the 420s budget (small net, ~2-4s/epoch), but without the f_27 distinct-letter-count and engineered interactions it must learn letter-identity/counting structure from ordinal codes, and on this interaction-heavy synthetic data MLPs on raw features typically trail the 3000-tree LightGBM baseline by roughly 1.5-2 AUC points.

Each f_27 position's signal is a per-letter target rate with no ordinal structure (e.g., position 6 ranges 0.10-1.00 across letters), and LightGBM's native categorical splits (gradient-sorted category partitioning) can isolate the predictive letter groups in single splits instead of needing many arbitrary ordinal threshold cuts, typically worth a few thousandths of AUC on this dataset while runtime stays well within budget.

The distinct-letter count is the dominant known f_27 signal in this competition (positive rate ~9% for 2-3 distinct letters vs ~91% for 7-8), and while per-position ordinals let trees partially approximate it, an explicit count feature gives LightGBM a clean, strong split it cannot easily reconstruct, yielding a modest but real AUC gain over the 0.9770 baseline.

Up-weighting dark stroke pixels should sharpen contrast where residual error concentrates, giving a small RMSE gain, though the metric's background dominance limits the benefit and risks a slight regression on easy pixels.

Training for ~330s instead of ~2000 steps gives roughly 4-6x more optimization steps with a properly annealed time-based cosine schedule, and this kind of small U-Net on 105 images is clearly undertrained at the baseline step count, so val RMSE should drop substantially (though with diminishing returns and some overfitting risk, gains are sub-linear).

L1 loss is a well-supported default for image restoration and often slightly improves RMSE too by avoiding gradient stalling and edge smearing; expect a small gain, though MSE is metric-matched so the improvement is modest.

Input-only brightness/contrast jitter is a mild regularizer on a ~100-image dataset with ~16k crops, likely slightly improving generalization to test scans; effect is small so expect a modest gain with some risk of neutral-to-slightly-negative outcome.

Multi-scale TTA averaging usually yields a small consistent gain for single-scale-trained U-Nets; downscaled views help low-frequency stains, upscaled views help thin strokes, so expect a ~1-2% RMSE reduction with negligible runtime cost.

Dropout2d at 0.2 on a small U-Net trained for only 2000 steps with BatchNorm tends to slow effective convergence and reduce feature capacity, yielding a small regression rather than the intended regularization gain.

With only 180s of training and a modest 3-level U-Net that is nowhere near overfitting within the budget, Dropout2d mostly slows optimization without any regularization benefit, so a small regression is likely.

The 4-level U-Net's larger receptive field (~89px) should capture document-wide noise structure better; although ~1/3 slower steps mean fewer updates in the 180s budget, denoising on this dataset tends to benefit modestly from depth, so I expect a small improvement.

The median-filter background channel gives the U-Net an explicit illumination/baseline estimate, which is known to help on this competition's coffee-stain/watermark noise, so a modest RMSE reduction (~5%) is expected with negligible extra compute.

Deeper 5-level U-Net with larger 256px crops (same pixels/step) adds capacity and receptive field for this low-noise task, likely yielding a modest RMSE improvement, though higher risk of slower convergence within the fixed 20x100 step budget.

Cosine-to-zero time-based LR with TRAIN_SECONDS=180 gives roughly the same or slightly fewer effective optimizer steps than the fixed 2000-step schedule, so RMSE should be essentially unchanged with a small risk of slight regression from fewer updates.

The evaluation metric is RMSE, which is exactly matched by MSE training; switching to Charbonnier/L1 optimizes the conditional median rather than mean and typically trades a small amount of RMSE for sharpness, so a mild regression (~2-5%) is the most likely outcome.

Injecting extra Gaussian noise on top of already-noisy inputs creates a train/test mismatch (the model must remove both real corruption and synthetic noise, biasing it toward smoother/blurrier outputs), likely outweighing the modest regularization gain on this small dataset.

GroupNorm removes BN's train-crop vs full-page statistics mismatch, a standard small win for patch-trained restoration nets; expect a modest improvement with batch-32 training largely negating BN's batch-regularization benefit.
Zhao-style SSIM+L1 preserves edges better and typically matches or slightly improves RMSE on denoising tasks versus pure MSE, with unchanged training schedule keeping runtime safe.
Dihedral TTA averages 8 decorrelated predictions, typically a 2-4% RMSE reduction on this kind of denoising task with negligible runtime cost.

SSIM-only loss is not MSE-optimal, so per-pixel RMSE (the graded metric) typically regresses ~5-15% versus an MSE-trained model on the same architecture; the mixed MS-SSIM+L1 result in Zhao et al. suggests pure SSIM often hurts pixel-wise error.
Residual (DnCNN-style) learning with a linear head and zero-init removes sigmoid saturation on the mostly-white background, typically giving a modest but real RMSE improvement on this task.

The modest 0.1-weighted SSIM term alongside the pixel RMSE anchor typically slightly sharpens text edges and flattens backgrounds on this denoising task, so expect a small improvement rather than a regression, though training-log comparability is preserved via the separate MSE accumulator.
Residual (DnCNN-style) prediction with zero-init final conv lets the model focus capacity on the noise, typically yielding a small but real RMSE gain over direct sigmoid regression on this task.

4.5x more training steps (2000→9000) with a properly stretched cosine schedule should let the U-Net converge further on this small dataset; diminishing returns past ~5000 steps and fixed val-split noise cap gains at roughly a 10-15% RMSE reduction, well within the time budget on GPU.

PCA to 256 dims denoises the strongly correlated 1024-d features and improves conditioning of the L2-regularized linear probe; modest improvement (~3%) is typical, with little risk of variance loss since leading PCs capture most discriminative signal.

Mixup/CutMix is a strong regularizer for this regime (large pretrained net, ~9k images, confusable classes, log-loss metric) and with prob=1.0 softens overconfident predictions, which temperature scaling then calibrates; expect a modest but real improvement, tempered by only 6 epochs (mixup benefits accrue with longer training) and the risk it slows early convergence.

Matching the pretrained backbone's standard (0.08, 1.0) crop range adds harder, more diverse partial views that regularize the 28M-param fine-tune and align with the backbone's pretraining augmentation, likely yielding a small log-loss improvement despite the short 6-epoch schedule.

ConvNeXt-V2 Large IN-22k-finetuned frozen features are far stronger and more linearly separable than ResNet-50 V1 features, so the same logistic-regression head should cut log loss meaningfully (typical frozen-feature pipelines reach ~0.35–0.42 here), while runtime stays within budget.

The 1000-d log-softmax block is redundant with the pooled features and its near-constant non-dog columns become standardized noise dimensions; dropping it for a clean 2048-d linear probe typically slightly improves regularized LR log loss.
Least-squares probes typically trail well-tuned logistic regression slightly on log loss even with temperature scaling, so expect a small regression (~0.34 vs 0.336).

PCA to 128 comps per block denoises nuisance directions and regularizes the linear head on ~10k samples, typically giving a small log-loss improvement, though aggressive compression risks discarding some fine-grained breed signal, capping the gain.

ConvNeXt-Base IN22K pretrained features are far stronger than ResNet-50 V1 features for frozen-extractor + logistic regression, typically cutting dog-breed log loss from ~0.45 to ~0.35-0.38, with C re-selection adding a small extra gain; runtime stays within budget.

Full fine-tuning of ConvNeXt-Tiny (IN22k pretrained) with proper LR schedule, augmentation, TTA and temperature calibration typically reaches ~0.25-0.30 on this dataset, a large improvement over the frozen ResNet-50 + LR baseline of 0.45, and the 7-minute guard should keep the run within budget.

Appending the pretrained head's 1000-d ImageNet log-probs (which include all 120 breeds) to the pooled features, with standardization and re-tuned smaller C, is a well-known strong trick for Stanford Dogs and should cut log loss notably versus raw-pooled-only features, though single-view ResNet-50 limits the gain to roughly 0.36-0.40.

Concatenating diverse pretrained backbones (ConvNeXt-22k, CLIP, DINOv2) with per-block L2 normalization and C tuning reliably cuts log loss substantially over a single ResNet-50; ~0.30-0.32 is typical for this ensemble-of-features approach on Stanford Dogs.

Focal loss (no alpha, mean-reduced) effectively shrinks gradient magnitudes on an already fairly balanced, easy dataset and removes label smoothing's calibration benefit over only 10 epochs, so log loss on well-calibrated softmax outputs likely regresses slightly.

Freezing conv1–layer3 is a mild regularizer for the ~10k-image training set and typically matches or slightly improves on full fine-tuning, but the lr=0.01 SGD recipe tuned for full-model training can be too hot for only layer4+fc, so expect a modest improvement at best.

Horizontal-flip TTA on a frozen ViT feature extractor reliably reduces log loss by roughly 1-2% relative (averaging mirrored-image probabilities smooths predictions); the NUM_WORKERS=0 change slightly slows extraction but stays well within budget.

CLIP ViT-B/32 features (coarser patches, contrastive image-text objective, no supervised class-discriminative fine-tuning) probe substantially worse on fine-grained breed classification than the supervised ImageNet-21k→1k ViT-B/16, so log loss should regress markedly.

PCA-256 denoises the 2048-d frozen GAP features and acts as implicit extra regularization (C=0.3 in a smaller space behaves like stronger effective L2), which typically gives a small log-loss improvement for linear probes on limited data, though the untuned C adds risk of a neutral-to-slightly-negative outcome.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 features are far stronger than supervised ResNet-50 for fine-grained dog breeds, so the same linear-probe + TTA recipe should cut log loss from ~0.44 to roughly 0.30 (ViT-B/14 at 224px is ~5-6x the compute of ResNet-50 but ~114k forward passes still fit the 10-min GPU budget).

PCA whitening to 256 dims typically stabilizes a lightly-regularized linear head on collinear frozen deep features, giving a modest log-loss improvement (~2%), though aggressive truncation from 2816 to 256 could also slightly hurt if discriminative low-variance directions are discarded.

Distance-weighted 10-NN on 2816-d concatenated features produces poorly calibrated probabilities (many near-zero/near-one rows) and generally scores worse log loss than a well-regularized linear probe, so expect a substantial regression from 0.541 to roughly 0.75-0.85.

End-to-end fine-tuning of ResNet-50 with standard augmentation, label smoothing, and a warmup+cosine schedule typically cuts log loss roughly in half versus frozen features + logistic regression on Stanford Dogs (public leaderboard ~0.20-0.25), and 10 epochs over 9k images fits comfortably in the time budget.

ViT-B/16 (in21k pretrained) pooled features are substantially stronger than ResNet-50 V1 features for linear-probe transfer, so log loss should drop from ~0.45 to ~0.35-0.38; runtime (~10k images through ViT-B) stays well within budget.

FiveCrop+hflip TTA averaging over 10 views is a well-established, low-risk trick that typically shaves a few percent off log loss on frozen-feature pipelines; test set is small (1023 imgs) so variance exists, but the center-crop view is included so it should not regress.

ConvNeXt-Tiny (in22k) features alone typically outperform ResNet-50 on Stanford Dogs, and the L2-normalized concatenation with a well-chosen C=1.0 should yield a solid ensemble improvement to roughly 0.36-0.39, comfortably within the 10-minute budget.

The CV-selected blend will pick a small-to-moderate alpha since the pretrained ImageNet dog head is a weaker, less calibrated classifier than the fitted LR, so expect only a marginal log-loss improvement (or nearly neutral if alpha≈0 is selected).

Compressing 2048-d frozen ResNet-50 features to 256 non-whitened PCA components discards discriminative directions that logistic regression uses, and with ~9k training samples the raw features already work well, so log loss likely worsens modestly despite a faster classifier fit.

Global max pooling discards the spatially averaged global context that GAP features were effectively pretrained/tuned for, typically degrading frozen-backbone linear-probe accuracy on scene-like dog photos, so log loss should regress from ~0.453 to roughly 0.50-0.55.
IMAGENET1K_V2 weights are a stronger checkpoint (+1.6% top-1 ImageNet) with matched preprocessing, and same-cost inference, so frozen features should improve log loss modestly (~0.01-0.02 lower).

C=0.03 over-regularizes the head given standardized-ish frozen ResNet features (C=0.3 was tuned best on holdout); the subsequent fine-tuning partially corrects it, so expect a small regression, roughly 0.48–0.50.
A 192px crop on a 224px-pretrained ResNet-50 degrades feature quality and fine-tuning while saving little time, so log loss should regress modestly.
Unwhitened PCA to 256 dims discards discriminative tail variance without the regularization benefit whitening would give, so a small regression is likely versus the tuned raw-feature LR.

Reducing input resolution to 192px deviates from the 224px ImageNet pretraining regime and discards fine-grained detail crucial for distinguishing 120 similar dog breeds, so the frozen ResNet-50 features will be noticeably weaker despite the same crop ratio; log loss should regress by roughly 5-10%.
IMAGENET1K_V2 is a stronger checkpoint (80.86% vs 76.1% top-1) with matched preprocessing, so frozen features should be modestly better for linear probing; runtime stays well within budget.

Logistic regression outputs are already approximately calibrated; the fitted temperature will be near 1, so softmax(logits/T) is nearly identical to predict_proba, yielding only a tiny change (likely a marginal improvement from slight de-sharpening).

Discriminative fine-tuning of the last bottleneck plus a well-initialized linear head on cached activations typically cuts log loss from a frozen-feature logistic regression baseline (~0.45) to roughly 0.33–0.39 on Stanford Dogs, and the 90s/2-epoch budget over only 9k cached activations is sufficient to realize most of that gain.

Horizontal-flip TTA with probability averaging is a standard low-risk improvement on frozen-feature pipelines, typically shaving ~1-3% off log loss, with negligible extra runtime (one extra pass over only 1,023 test images).

1:1 undersampling effectively strengthens L2 regularization per label (same C, ~5-170x fewer rows) and discards many informative negatives, which usually slightly hurts frequent-label AUCs while rare labels gain little, netting a small regression.

Char n-grams complement word n-grams for obfuscated/misspelled toxicity, and NB-weighted char features were a known top-kernel trick, so expect a small AUC gain (~+0.0005); risk is slight dilution of the NB weighting but direction is positive.

AUC is unaffected by class-prior skew in the loss, so undersampling gains little, while computing the NB log-count ratio and the sag/liblinear fits on tiny 1:1 subsets (~460 rows for threat) badly degrades the rare-label models and the OOF stacking features.

Plain MultinomialNB is weaker than the NB-LogReg hybrid on TF-IDF word n-grams (discriminative fine-tuning of NB weights is precisely the boost NBSVM provides), so branch B solo drops a few tenths of AUC; the 50/50 blend with branch A absorbs part of it but a small regression is expected, especially on rare labels.

Mean-pooled self-trained Word2Vec is far weaker than word+char TF-IDF on toxicity detection (no char n-grams for obfuscation, mean-pooling dilutes sparse toxic signals), so both branch A and the MLP degrade, dragging the rank-average blend down despite branch B holding steady.

1:1 undersampling drastically cuts training data (threat: ~950 rows), which for high-capacity TF-IDF logreg typically hurts AUC despite better class balance, especially on the rare labels that dominate the column mean; calibration shifts also degrade the rank blend.

The sparse-MLP branch D is a modestly weaker but genuinely diverse non-linear model (~0.975-0.978 held-out AUC); rank-averaging it at 1/4 weight with three stronger linear branches typically yields a tiny gain or wash on mean column-wise AUC, and the epoch-selection/time guards bound the downside near the 0.98099 baseline.

AUC is prior-insensitive, so balanced undersampling mainly discards ~90% of negative training data: rare labels (threat ~1.9k rows) lose the most signal and gain variance, and the fixed C=0.1/4.0 are no longer tuned to the smaller effective sample, giving a small regression on the column mean.

Profanity de-obfuscation and noise-token removal mildly help char-ngram/word TF-IDF models on this dataset, but repeat-collapsing and aggressive shorthand rewriting can slightly damage char n-gram signals, netting a very small gain.

The six stacked OOF columns add genuine cross-label signal to A, but the /20 scaling and C=0.1 shrinkage mute their effect, so expect only a marginal improvement (~+0.0002) with some risk of noise on rare labels canceling gains.
An MLP restricted to 3 Adam epochs on branch A's TF-IDF features is undertrained and correlated with A, so giving it equal 1/3 rank weight dilutes the stronger A+B blend, likely a small regression.

Branch C (NB-LogReg on word+char TF-IDF) is a known-diverse third branch; equal rank-averaging typically adds a small gain (~+0.0005 AUC) while staying within the runtime budget thanks to the max_iter=100 cap.

The holdout-fitted weights with 0.5-shrinkage will land very close to the existing 0.5/0.5 blend for most labels, and noise from rare-label holdout AUCs (threat, identity_hate) makes small regressions as likely as small gains — expect a near-zero net change.

Compressing to 300 dense LSA factors discards most of the discriminative sparse n-gram signal; this competition's top solutions relied on high-dimensional char n-grams and NB features, and LSA baselines historically score well below the 0.98 ensemble (around 0.95-0.965), with rare labels (threat, identity_hate) hurt most.

AUC-based linear classifiers lose little from imbalance but gain a lot from full data; cutting negatives to a 10:1 cap discards ~90% of clean-comment evidence for rare labels (severe_toxic, threat, identity_hate), biasing decision thresholds/calibration and reducing the rank ordering quality, so a modest regression is likely.

A single 7-class softmax forces labels to compete for probability mass, badly hurting ranking for rare co-occurring labels (threat, identity_hate) versus six independent per-label fastText models, and with only 1/3 rank-blend weight this drags the mean AUC down slightly.

Single ComplementNB on word counts (no TF-IDF, no char n-grams, no ensemble) is a much weaker scorer than the rank-averaged blend; word-only nB models on this competition typically score ~0.955-0.97, a clear regression.

Unweighted mean-pooled from-scratch Word2Vec (5 epochs on a small noisy corpus) is far weaker than the char-ngram/TF-IDF ensemble for toxicity detection, which hinges on surface-form cues; dense averaging blurs exact slur/threat matches, so expect a substantial regression of roughly 2-3 AUC points, mainly on rare labels.

Average-pooled corpus-trained Word2Vec with 5 epochs loses the char n-gram surface evidence that drives toxicity detection, especially on rare labels (threat, identity_hate) where misspelled slurs and exact token matches matter — expect a substantial regression from 0.9799 to roughly 0.95-0.965.

A third diverse char n-gram NB-LogReg branch blended with holdout-tuned per-label weights should add a small gain on top of 0.9799, as character features capture obfuscated spellings the word branches miss, though holdout noise on rare labels limits the upside.

C=0.1 over-regularizes the 60k-feature word+char TF-IDF matrix; C=4/liblinear matches strong public kernels for this feature set, so branch A should get stronger, but the 0.5/0.5 rank blend with an unchanged branch B and high correlation between branches dampens the gain to a few ten-thousandths of AUC.

A per-label fastText bigram branch is individually slightly weaker than the TF-IDF linear models but decorrelated with them, so a three-way rank average typically adds ~0.001-0.002 mean AUC on this competition while staying well within the time budget.

A char n-gram NB-LogReg branch adds genuine diversity to a word-heavy blend (char features historically strongest on this dataset), so expect a small AUC gain (~+0.001), though it's partly redundant with branch A's char features and the extra ~4-5 min of vectorizer/fit time pushes the run close to the 10-minute budget.

Tuning blend weights on a noisy 10% holdout of rare labels gains little, while training both branches on only 90% of the data costs a small amount of AUC, yielding a roughly neutral-to-slightly-negative net effect.

NB log-count-ratio weighting is a proven Kaggle trick for this competition and should give branch A a small boost, though reduced branch diversity (A now resembles B) and C=0.1 being untuned for rescaled features temper the gain, so expect a marginal improvement of roughly +0.0003-0.0004 mean AUC.

min_df=0.01 means a term must appear in ~3.1k of 313k docs — an extremely aggressive prune that destroys rare-label (threat, identity_hate) evidence and char-ngram coverage, far overshooting the intended removal of rare noise (e.g. branch B's prior min_df=3).

Discarding ~95-99% of negatives per label (especially ~478-row threat/identity_hate fits and tiny NB statistics) sharply increases estimator variance; class balancing shifts the decision boundary but usually costs AUC on highly imbalanced text tasks, so expect a solid regression from 0.9801.

Replacing well-tuned logistic regression with cosine class centroids removes the discriminative training that handles class imbalance, hurting rare labels (threat, identity_hate) most; blend of two weakened branches should drop mean AUC by roughly 2-4 points.
char_wb n-grams with word-boundary padding are known to work slightly better than plain char n-grams for this competition's classic kernels, so a small AUC gain (~+0.0003) is likely.

ComplementNB on TF-IDF lacks the discriminative power of the tuned logistic regressions (and drops NB-LogReg's reweighting trick), so both branches weaken; the rank average of two weaker NB branches typically lands around 0.96-0.97 vs 0.9797 baseline.

Compressing 60k sparse TF-IDF features into just 32 dense SVD components discards nearly all discriminative lexical signal, crippling branch A; the 50/50 rank blend with fastText therefore drops by roughly 0.7% AUC.

Collapsing all tokens outside the top 2,000 into a single 'raretoken' destroys the discriminative signal from rare but highly toxicity-indicative strings (misspellings, obfuscated profanity, identity slurs) that both the char n-gram branch and fastText rely on, and also degenerates word TF-IDF to a tiny vocabulary — expect a clear regression.

Keeping stop words lets discriminative pronouns/articles ('you', 'your') survive the word TF-IDF, which typically yields a small AUC gain on this competition; effect is modest since the char n-gram branch already captures them.

Logit-averaging ties the blend to each branch's probability calibration (branch B's sharp C=4 probabilities dominate), unlike rank-averaging which combines orderings equally, so expect a tiny AUC regression.

char vs char_wb is a marginal analyzer swap — it drops word-boundary padding, which slightly changes the 50k selected n-grams; historical kernels show the two are near-equal, so expect a tiny (~±0.0001) change with a slight lean positive since 'char' can capture punctuation-delineated patterns in toxic text.

fastText OVA with word bigrams is a solid but generally slightly weaker branch than NB-LogReg on this dataset, and being a single jointly-trained model it adds less complementary signal to the char-TF-IDF branch, so the rank blend should land marginally below the 0.98013 baseline.

Multinomial LR at C=1 on standardized features handles the 192 redundant bins fine via regularization; dropping the bottom-third ANOVA columns discards genuinely informative (especially shape) bins, so the 50%-weighted linear component degrades slightly and the blend worsens a small amount.

Label smoothing with eps=0.1 typically improves calibration under strong augmentation on tiny datasets, so the NN's softmax should be less overconfident and the 50/50 blend's log loss should improve slightly, though the effect is partly diluted by the LR component and could be near-neutral.

OvR with 99 tiny binary problems (10 positives vs ~790 negatives each) yields less well-conditioned hyperplanes than the joint softmax; the power/floor calibration absorbs the confidence scale but not the worse decision geometry, so expect a small regression (~0.046 vs 0.0451).

An MLP bag blended with LR on 990 rows usually adds complementary signal; the w and calibration grid search on OOF makes regression unlikely, but overfitting the OOF grid and MLP seed variance limit gains, so expect a moderate improvement (~0.038-0.042).

Averaging the five fold models gives a small bagging-style smoothing of probabilities (each trained on 80% of data) which typically improves multiclass log loss slightly versus a single full-data refit at the same high C, though each model sees less data so the gain is modest, not large.

Absolute size/aspect/Hu-moment features add genuinely new information beyond the scale-normalised 192 descriptors, and the per-fold scaler plus CV-tuned C adapts the regularisation, so a modest OOF/test log-loss improvement (~5-15%) is the most likely outcome, though risk of slight overfitting means the gain is not guaranteed.

PCA at 95% variance on 990x219 likely keeps ~150+ components, discarding some low-variance but discriminative directions and distorting the isotropic-L2 geometry, so a modest regression is more likely than a gain.

Averaging five 80%-subset logistic regressions reduces coefficient-variance and smooths probabilities on a 10-samples-per-class problem, typically yielding a small LB gain (~2-5%) versus a single full-data fit, at negligible cost.

A small CNN trained on only ~990 images over 99 classes will overfit and likely land well above the LR's ~0.12 holdout, so a fixed 50/50 arithmetic blend drags the LR's calibrated probabilities toward a much noisier NN and the test log loss regresses substantially (time guard and TTA can't rescue that).

Temperature/power calibration fitted on OOF predictions typically corrects slight over- or under-confidence of logistic regression, yielding a small but real improvement on the private log loss; grid over a is mild (2 effective params on 990 OOF rows), so expect a few-percent gain rather than a large one.

5-fold CV over a wide C grid on this small (990x192) dataset typically selects a stronger-regularisation-dodging (larger C) fit that reduces OOF log loss versus the arbitrary C=1, plausibly cutting test log loss from 0.124 to roughly 0.09-0.10; runtime (~55 small lbfgs fits, parallelised) stays well within budget.

The 27 geometric descriptors add genuinely new shape information complementary to the histogram features, likely yielding a modest logloss improvement, though partly offset by the untuned C=1.0 adding dimensionality.

With ~240 standardized, highly correlated features on only 990 rows, stronger L2 shrinkage (C=0.2) typically reduces variance and slightly improves multiclass log loss over C=1.0, though the effect is modest.
Removing the refit discards 20% of training data, so the submitted classifier is weaker than the current full-data model, worsening log loss despite the holdout-matched estimator.

kNN and shrinkage LDA are strong on these 192-d features and OOF-learned convex blending of well-calibrated probability models reliably beats a single logistic regression on this dataset, so log loss should drop from ~0.059 to roughly 0.03-0.04.

HistGradientBoosting on 990 samples typically captures nonlinear descriptor interactions missed by the tuned logistic regression baseline, and early stopping controls overfitting, so expect a moderate log-loss improvement from 0.061 to roughly 0.04.

Platt-sigmoid calibration of 99 one-vs-rest LinearSVCs on only 6-10 samples/class (3-fold CV leaves ~2-4 positives per fold) produces noisy, poorly calibrated probabilities, and the strong multinomial LR member is lost, so the uniform soft-vote likely regresses modestly.

RF's full-depth vote-fraction probabilities avoid HGB's degenerate ~1-row-per-class early-stopping split, and on 891 rows 600 trees are cheap, so the soft-vote ensemble likely improves slightly, though RF's hard vote probabilities cap the gain.

A (256,128) MLP with early stopping and weight decay on standardized descriptors typically captures the nonlinear margin/shape/texture interactions on this small dataset, historically pushing leaf-classification log loss into the ~0.08-0.12 range versus ~0.124 for the linear softmax baseline; the retained OOF shrinkage calibration mitigates overconfident MLP probabilities, though the gain is partly limited by only ~990 training samples.

CV-selected C (likely >1 on this small, wide 192-feature/99-class problem) should modestly sharpen the LR fit and reduce log loss a few percent, with the existing shrinkage step guarding against overconfidence; small risk it's neutral-to-mildly-worse if selected C overfits the OOF estimate.

The 48 geometric/Hu/radial-histogram features carry genuinely new shape information complementary to the 192 descriptors, and logistic regression at C=1 on standardized 240 features typically yields a modest improvement on this dataset (classic kernels gain similarly from CV features), though the fixed regularization limits the gain to roughly 5-10%.

Tuning L2 strength via 10-fold CV (refit on all data) typically picks a better C than the fixed 1.0 on standardized 192-dim features, giving a modest log-loss improvement; risk is mild overfitting of C selection to CV, so gains are small (maybe ~0.11–0.12).

Soft-voting LR+kNN+tuned-LDA+HGB on 192 features typically drops leaf log loss well below a single uncalibrated logistic regression (~0.124 → ~0.04–0.07), though uniform weights over an overconfident HGB and no calibration keep it above top-leaderboard levels.

The baseline LR is fairly confident and mostly correct (score 0.124), so OOF-selected shrinkage will pick a small alpha but mixing in the uniform prior still flattens many already-correct confident predictions, slightly increasing multiclass log loss rather than helping.
Fixed 90% shrinkage toward spherical covariance over-regularizes LDA on informative correlated descriptors (auto shrinkage was already near-optimal), degrading log loss.

Splitting into per-family LDAs discards cross-family covariance and averages three weaker, correlated probability estimates, which typically hurts log loss relative to the joint 192-feature shrunk LDA.

Dropping the lowest-variance 10% of standardized descriptors discards discriminative signal that an already-well-regularized tuned LR exploits here, and PCA without whitening adds no benefit, so log loss likely regresses modestly.

The tuned logistic regression at 0.0599 is near the top of this competition's leaderboard; LDA with shrinkage on 192 features / 99 classes typically plateaus around ~0.3-0.5 log loss here, so this is a large regression.

PCA retaining 95% variance typically discards a few low-variance but discriminative margin/texture directions on this small (990-row, 192-feature) dataset, and joint PCA across the three descriptor families mixes scales, so the calibrated LR usually regresses modestly (to ~0.05) versus the strong raw-feature baseline.

Shrinkage LDA on 192 descriptors is competitive but typically slightly worse than the calibrated logistic regression baseline (0.0452) on this dataset, since LDA's Gaussian equal-covariance assumption fits margin/texture histograms less well than a discriminative linear model; expect a mild regression to roughly 0.05.

Mixing in a 0.005 uniform prior slightly flattens already well-calibrated confident predictions, raising log loss by roughly log(1/0.995) ≈ 0.005 on typical confident samples with no benefit since classes are balanced and predictions aren't overconfident.
Cutting the Nystroem feature dimension by 25% loses a bit of kernel approximation capacity with no regularization benefit gained, so log loss likely regresses slightly.

Shrunk LDA on the 192 descriptors is a strong, well-known baseline for this dataset (classical leaderboard ~0.07-0.10) and should beat the untuned logistic regression's 0.124, with only ~1.5k training rows keeping runtime trivially within budget.

CV-tuned regularization (likely selecting a larger C, reducing underfitting on 192 standardized features) with fold-local scaling should yield a modest log-loss improvement over fixed C=1, while still being plain logistic regression on the same descriptors.

OOF temperature scaling on a regularized multiclass logistic regression is well-matched to log-loss and typically corrects mild overconfidence, giving a small but real improvement over the uncalibrated baseline.

Nyström RBF expansion approximates a kernel logistic regression, which is known to outperform the linear baseline on these 192 leaf descriptors (typical LB ~0.09 vs 0.124), with 512 components comfortably within the runtime budget.

Temporal/recency, first-person, and request-form features are known strong signals in this dataset and are complementary to the TF-IDF + history baseline, so a modest gain to ~0.69 is likely, though fixed C=0.3 may slightly under-regularize the expanded space.

Random forests split poorly on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF blocks (max_features='sqrt' sees few informative features per split), so this usually regresses well below the logistic baseline on RAOP-style text data.

Random forests handle sparse high-dimensional TF-IDF text poorly relative to regularized logistic regression (splits on bagged sqrt(5010) features rarely select informative words), so the dominant text signal is diluted even though trees help the numeric metadata; expect a modest regression from 0.748.

Replacing 5k sparse TF-IDF unigram weights with 50 LDA topic proportions discards substantial discriminative lexical signal (LDA is unsupervised and coarse), so the linear model's text block weakens; metadata features keep performance from collapsing, but a clear regression to roughly 0.70-0.72 is expected, well within the time budget.

Removing the supervised OOF text logit (a strong, directly discriminative signal) in favor of unsupervised 20-topic LDA discards most of the predictive text signal; LDA topic proportions only weakly separate classes, so the stack regresses toward a metadata-dominated model.
The raw timestamp carried real (if period-specific) signal in this dataset while hour/weekday effects are weak, so dropping the epoch column likely costs a small amount of AUC.

Rank-averaging a metadata-only HistGradientBoosting model with the TF-IDF logistic regression typically adds a small diversification gain on RAOP (~+0.01-0.02 AUC), though there's a modest risk the OOF-selected weight overfits and yields little change.

Fully grown random forests on sparse high-dimensional TF-IDF text almost always underperform regularized logistic regression on this classic RAOP dataset (word-level linear models dominate here), so the swap should regress AUC by a few points despite the richer metadata features.

Bag-of-subreddits adds a genuine behavioral signal (RAOP participation history correlates with success), and min_df=5/idf/C=0.3 keep the ~3000 extra sparse features from swamping the model, so a small gain is likely though the noisy tail of rare subreddits could mute it.

In train, giver_known perfectly separates positives, so the model leans on this leaky feature; but in test the field is always 'N/A' (constant 0), so the feature adds nothing at test time while shrinking the useful text/numeric coefficients, degrading leaderboard AUC despite inflated local holdout.

The stacking setup is sound (OOF text logits, raw numerics plus the informative UTC timestamp, early-stopped shallow LGBM with seed averaging), so it should edge slightly past the 0.6573 linear baseline, though the small 4k-row dataset and level-2 variance keep the gain modest.

Time-of-request, text-statistics, and RAOP-history indicators (especially prior RAOP posts/comments) are known strong predictors for this dataset, so adding this dense block to the TF-IDF LR should substantially raise AUC; the low 0.657 baseline suggests the current pipeline underuses these signals, while runtime stays far under budget.

ExtraTrees on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF+embeddings typically loses to a well-regularized linear model on this small (~3.2k-train-row) dataset — tree splits can't exploit sparse word weights well and it will overfit despite min_samples_leaf=3, so expect a modest AUC regression.

Removing the TF-IDF block discards the strongest signal on this dataset — lexical n-grams of request text historically outperform semantic embeddings on RAOP, so a numerics+MiniLM-only logreg should regress several AUC points below the 0.6235 hybrid baseline.

Hand-crafted length/punctuation/pronoun/sentiment features capture document-level signal that length-normalized TF-IDF discards, and StandardScaler puts them on par with the 9 numeric columns; expect a modest but real AUC gain (~0.005-0.01), possibly slightly damped by added unregularized-feature noise at C=0.3.

Dropping TF-IDF text removes the strongest signal on this competition (text features are known to dominate RAOP leaderboards); nine metadata features alone typically yield only ~0.55-0.59 AUC, a clear regression from 0.6497.

Corpus-trained Word2Vec on only ~7k short documents yields noisy embeddings, and plain mean-pooled 200-dim vectors discard the strong lexical signal that unigram TF-IDF carries in this classic text task, so the swap should regress AUC by a few points.

Bigrams and the larger vocabulary usually add a modest amount of phrase-level signal on RAOP (classic leaderboard gains are ~0.5-1.5%), though keeping C=0.3 with 12x more features adds some overfit risk that slightly dampens the gain.

Text is the strongest known signal on RAOP (title/wording carries most predictive power); the current 0.633 already leans on TF-IDF, and dropping it for 9 metadata columns typically lands metadata-only models around 0.55-0.59 AUC, a clear regression despite the overfitting rationale.

Random forests handle dense, low-variance SVD projections and tiny tabular signals poorly relative to boosted trees; RF on SVD components typically loses several AUC points vs LightGBM here, and the leaderboard is far below the official RF benchmark's setting.

MiniLM embeddings add genuine semantic signal for this small-text dataset, likely lifting AUC a few points, though the untuned C=0.3 over a 384-dim dense block may partially dilute the sparse TF-IDF signal and cap the gain.

The competition metric is RMSE, and the Zhao et al. 0.84*SSIM+0.16*L1 loss optimizes structural/perceptual quality rather than squared error — sharper strokes but typically slightly higher RMSE than a pure MSE-trained model at this small data/epoch budget, so I expect a modest regression.

8-fold dihedral TTA averaging typically reduces variance-driven pixel errors by a few percent for a U-Net trained with only flip augmentation (rotations are untrained but still contribute via ensemble averaging), so expect a modest RMSE improvement from 0.01114 to roughly 0.0106-0.0108.

SSIM loss optimizes structural/contrast agreement rather than pixel fidelity, so under an RMSE-graded metric it typically trades slight pixel accuracy (sharper strokes but biased local contrast) for perceptual quality, yielding a modest regression versus the MSE-tuned baseline of 0.01084.

Residual (DnCNN-style) learning with a linear head removes sigmoid saturation on the mostly-white background and zero-init gives an identity start, a well-established formulation that typically yields a modest but real RMSE improvement on document denoising.

The added 0.1-weighted SSIM term pulls gradients toward local-contrast/structure objectives that don't align with the graded per-pixel RMSE, so a modest regression (roughly 1-4% worse) is the most likely outcome, while the RMSE term keeps the change from being catastrophic.

Residual (DnCNN-style) learning with zero-initialized output is a well-established win for image denoising: it focuses network capacity on the noise and speeds early convergence under the short training budget, so a modest RMSE improvement (~5-10%) is expected over the sigmoid-regression baseline.

With fixed training steps, uniform sampling over ~86% synthetic pairs whose hand-tuned artifact distribution (ellipse stains, mild shading, sparse speckle) only loosely matches the competition's real noise dilutes exposure to the genuine noisy/clean mappings, likely causing a modest regression despite the added diversity.

4.5x more Adam steps with a properly stretched cosine schedule should let the U-Net converge further on this small dataset (validation-held-out images still available), improving RMSE from ~0.0162 toward ~0.013-0.014 before overfitting/plateau sets in, and wall-clock should fit within the 10-minute budget on GPU.

8-fold dihedral TTA averages out flip/rotation prediction variance and is essentially free at inference, typically yielding a small (~1-2%) RMSE reduction on this kind of patch-CNN denoiser with no training changes or added overfit risk.

Training with L1 optimizes the conditional median rather than the mean, which the RMSE metric penalizes — constant-magnitude gradients also slow reduction of large stain residuals within the fixed 2000-step budget, so a modest regression is the most likely outcome.

Up-weighting the rare black glyph pixels diverts model capacity away from the dominant white/background pixels that per-pixel RMSE mostly measures, so the graded metric likely regresses slightly even though glyph fidelity may improve.

The graded metric is unweighted per-pixel RMSE dominated by the abundant white-background/stain pixels, so shifting gradient mass toward the sparse ink pixels (weight 10x) under-trains background reconstruction while ink error is already small, likely causing a modest regression.

Zero-initialized residual (linear) output starts from the noisy image as an identity map, which is a well-established trick for image denoising that speeds early convergence and typically yields a modest RMSE gain over a sigmoid head, with the test-time clamp retained; compute overhead is negligible so the time budget is unaffected.

L1 (median-regression) training underweights large residuals, which the RMSE metric penalizes quadratically, and the non-vanishing L1 gradient near targets prevents fine convergence to exact intensities, so a loss/metric mismatch typically degrades RMSE by roughly 5-15% here despite identical architecture and schedule.

Zero-initialized residual (identity) output is a well-known trick that speeds early convergence and eases optimization; the network only has to learn the noise correction, likely yielding a small RMSE gain over the sigmoid baseline within the unchanged 20-epoch budget.

Halving BASE_CH from 16 to 8 cuts feature capacity (8/16/32/64 widths) with the same training budget; the document denoising task still benefits from the larger model's capacity, so a modest RMSE regression of roughly 4-7% is expected, though the smaller net may train slightly more stably on 105 images.

Stroke/noise pixels carry most of the squared error, so up-weighting dark pixels (3x) should improve their fit at only a small cost to the easy white background, yielding a small net RMSE gain; risk of slight regression if background accuracy degrades more than stroke error drops.

The applied diff adds execution.json that forces CPU-only execution (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES='', 8 intraop threads); 2000 batch-32 128x128 U-Net updates at ~3-6s/step on CPU cannot finish within 15 min, so the run is hard-killed before submission.csv is written — the closing-normalization feature itself would likely help on GPU, but this run produces no valid score.

Computing only the final 1x1 conv + sigmoid in fp32 (vs bf16 autocast) is a numerically negligible change — bf16 output precision already costs on the order of 1e-3 absolute error on sigmoid outputs, far below the ~0.016 RMSE — so the metric should be statistically identical (any delta is seed/run-to-run noise from the unchanged training pipeline).

Four-flip TTA averages independent prediction errors of the same U-Net, typically yielding a small (~0.5–1.5%) RMSE reduction on this denoising task, with negligible added inference cost; training is unchanged so the gain is modest but positive.

The NAFNet's residual (dirty + learned correction) output, gated blocks and channel attention are a stronger denoiser than the plain sigmoid U-Net at similar parameter count, so with the identical 2000-step schedule it should land meaningfully below 0.0162, though the zero-initialized beta/gamma branches and limited steps keep it from reaching its fully-trained potential; main risk is CPU wall-clock from the per-pixel LayerNorm, but it should still fit the budget.

The fb_in22k_ft_in1k head restricted to the 120 ImageNet dog classes is a strong, decorrelated second predictor (Stanford Dogs images come from ImageNet-1k training data, so the head is well-calibrated on this exact distribution), and the tuned blend with w=0 as a guaranteed fallback makes a modest improvement (~0.28-0.30) very likely with little regression risk.

PCA-256 without whitening keeps most variance and the C re-selection on the holdout partially adapts, but discarding the low-variance (often discriminative for fine-grained breeds) tail plus the uneven effective L2 penalty across scaled components typically makes a linear probe on frozen deep features marginally worse, not better.

Mixup/CutMix with prob=1.0 on a short 6-epoch fine-tune (~780 steps) of an already-regularized pretrained model causes underfitting — the model rarely sees clean labels — so validation and test log loss will likely worsen despite temperature scaling partially compensating for the softened outputs.

Stronger standard ImageNet crop augmentation usually aids generalization with only 77 images/breed, but very aggressive 8%-area crops on dog photos (where fine-grained cues require most of the animal) partially offset that, so expect a small improvement at best — roughly neutral-to-slightly-better.

ConvNeXt-V2 Large with IN-22k pretraining yields markedly stronger frozen features than ResNet-50 V1 (in22k-finetuned backbones typically cut log loss by 25-35% on Stanford Dogs linear-probe pipelines), while the modest C-grid extension and unchanged logistic-regression head keep the rest of the pipeline equivalent; runtime stays comfortably in budget.

Dropping the 1000 near-collinear, mostly-non-dog log-softmax columns frees the L2 budget for the 2048-d penultimate features — the standard linear-probe protocol — so I expect a small improvement, though the nonlinear log-softmax block did carry a little usable signal, keeping the gain modest.

Ridge probe with tuned temperature scaling is a near-equivalent linear head on the same strong 2560-d features, typically matching or marginally improving on a possibly-underconverged lbfgs logistic regression on log loss.

PCA to 128 components per block discards low-variance but still discriminative fine-grained directions that L2-regularized LR would otherwise exploit, so the compression is likely a mild regression despite the parameter reduction.

Swapping the frozen ResNet-50 V1 features for ConvNeXt-Base pretrained on ImageNet-22k is a large upgrade in frozen-feature quality for a fine-grained 120-class task, and linear probes on these features typically cut log loss from ~0.45 to roughly 0.28-0.32 on Stanford Dogs, while the C re-selection, unchanged transform (matching the checkpoint's config), and fp16 batched extraction keep runtime well within budget.

End-to-end fine-tuning of an ImageNet-22k ConvNeXt-Tiny with cosine LR, label smoothing, flip TTA and validation-tuned temperature calibration should comfortably beat frozen ResNet-50 features (~0.45) and land near the ~0.25-0.35 range typical for this setup on Stanford Dogs; label smoothing slightly inflates the log-loss floor, and the 7-minute time guard plus 90/10 split cost a little accuracy, so I predict around 0.30.

The ImageNet-1k head's 1000-d log-probabilities already encode fine-grained dog-breed knowledge (all 120 breeds are ImageNet classes 151-275), so concatenating them with the pooled features plus standardization and a re-tuned (smaller-C) logistic regression is a well-known, cheap, low-risk boost over raw pooled features alone; runtime is unchanged (one forward pass, a few thousand-dim logistic fits), so I expect a solid improvement to roughly 0.32-0.40 log loss with ~0.36 as the central estimate.

A diverse three-backbone frozen-feature ensemble (ConvNeXt-B/IN-22k, CLIP ViT-B/16, DINOv2 ViT-B/14) with per-block L2 normalization and holdout-tuned C is a well-known large upgrade over a single ResNet-50 on Stanford Dogs, typically cutting log loss from ~0.45 to ~0.25-0.30 while staying well within the compute budget.

Focal loss (gamma=2, no alpha) on a balanced dataset removes label smoothing's calibration benefit and typically yields overconfident, miscalibrated probabilities, which directly hurts multi-class log loss relative to the label-smoothed CE baseline (~0.66).

Freezing conv1–layer3 removes most of the model's adaptation capacity; on Stanford Dogs full fine-tuning typically edges out last-stage-only tuning by ~1–2% accuracy, and the same lr=0.01/cosine recipe on fewer parameters usually yields a slightly worse calibrated log loss (~0.69–0.72 vs 0.674).

Horizontal-flip TTA is a reliable small win for ViT feature + linear-probe pipelines (features are not flip-equivariant, so averaging the two probability vectors reduces variance), typically worth 2-4% relative log-loss improvement; the NUM_WORKERS=0 change slightly slows extraction but stays well within the 15-minute budget.

CLIP ViT-B/32 image features are markedly weaker than ImageNet-21k→1k ViT-B/16 features for fine-grained linear probes (lower patch resolution, contrastive objective not tuned to subordinate-level categories), so the fixed linear probe should regress substantially from 0.51 to roughly 0.8-0.9.

PCA(256, no whitening) denoises the frozen GAP features and cuts the linear probe's parameter count 8x, typically yielding a small log-loss gain on this setup; the fixed C=0.3 was tuned for raw features so part of the benefit is offset, and the 10-view TTA averaging path is unchanged.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings are substantially stronger than ResNet50-ImageNet features for fine-grained dog-breed discrimination (linear-probe accuracy typically jumps from ~78% to ~85-88%), and the re-tuned C plus unchanged 10-view TTA preserve that gain, so log loss should drop markedly; modest residual risk from the 224px (vs native 518px) input and raw unstandardized features keeps me from predicting the most optimistic end.

Aggressive truncation from 2816 to 256 dims discards discriminative fine-grained directions that the two backbones provide, and whitening after per-block L2 normalization reshapes the feature geometry the C=1.0 logistic regression was already well-matched to, so I expect a modest log-loss regression rather than the hypothesized stabilization gain.

A 10-NN distance-vote head on frozen ImageNet features is a strictly weaker, coarse-grained probability estimator than the linear probe (kNN probabilities are ~1/k-spaced and assign ~1e-3 to the true class on misses, incurring ~7-nat penalties), so log loss will roughly double even if accuracy only drops modestly.

End-to-end fine-tuning of ResNet-50 for 10 epochs with standard augmentation, label smoothing, and a warmup+cosine schedule typically reaches ~85-88% accuracy on Stanford Dogs, comfortably beating frozen features + logistic regression (0.453) with well under the 10-minute budget (~144 steps/epoch on GPU); expected log loss around 0.32-0.40.

ViT-B/16 (in21k-pretrained, in1k-finetuned) pooled features are far stronger for linear probing than ResNet-50 IMAGENET1K_V1 on fine-grained dog breeds, so log loss should drop substantially (roughly 0.45 → ~0.29) while extraction of ~10k images still fits comfortably in the 10-minute budget.

Averaging probabilities over center+corner crops and their flips is standard TTA that reliably shaves a few percent off log loss for a frozen ResNet-50 linear-probe baseline, though the corner views (dogs are usually centered) dilute the gain relative to flip-only TTA.

ConvNeXt-Tiny (in22k_ft_in1k) is a substantially stronger backbone than ResNet-50 V1 and its 768-d features typically reach ~0.35-0.40 log loss alone on Stanford Dogs, so the L2-normalized concatenation with ResNet-50 plus a re-tuned C=1.0 should drop the loss from 0.453 to roughly 0.32-0.35, comfortably within the 10-minute budget since ConvNeXt-Tiny inference over ~10.2k images takes only a couple of minutes.

Blending the well-calibrated LogReg with a temperature-scaled pretrained dog classifier is a mild ensemble; the internal CV will likely pick a small alpha (~0.1-0.3) that trims a bit of log loss, though the pretrained head is notably weaker than the fitted classifier so gains are small and could partly evaporate on test.

Unwhitened PCA-256 mostly just re-parameterizes the feature space, and since the L2 penalty of LogisticRegression is not rotation-invariant and C=0.3 was tuned on raw 2048-d features, projecting to 256 dims typically discards some low-variance but discriminative directions, so a small log-loss regression is the likely outcome.

ResNet-50's weights were trained end-to-end with global average pooling, so swapping in max pooling at inference misaligns the feature distribution fed to the head (max activations inflate magnitudes and lose spatial averaging the fc-layer features rely on), typically costing several points of top-down transfer accuracy and thus a noticeably worse log loss.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 weights have ~2.7pt higher ImageNet top-1 than V1, and since the Stanford Dogs subset is essentially in-distribution for ImageNet, the better frozen features should yield better class separation and a modest log-loss improvement, with the temperature calibration absorbing most of the confidence-scale shift.

C=0.03 over-regularizes the 2048-d feature head (0.3 was already holdout-selected as best), and the short 90s bottleneck fine-tune with a small head lr only partially recovers from the weaker, low-norm initialization, so log loss should regress slightly.

Dropping the crop from 224 to 192 loses fine-grained detail that matters for distinguishing similar breeds, and the pretrained weights were tuned at 224, so both the frozen-feature classifier and the lightly fine-tuned last bottleneck will degrade modestly (log loss up by roughly 0.01-0.02), with only a small speed/memory benefit that doesn't affect the metric.

Unwhitened 256-component PCA discards discriminative variance in the 2048-d ResNet-50 activations and shifts the effective regularization away from the tuned C=0.3 on raw features, so log loss should regress modestly (~0.43 → ~0.44).

The frozen ResNet-50 IMAGENET1K_V1 features are calibrated for 224px inputs, so shrinking to a 192px crop degrades feature quality (and the fixed C=0.3 no longer matches the new feature scale), yielding a modest log-loss regression with a slightly faster run.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 weights (80.9% vs 76.1% top-1) yield substantially stronger frozen features for the linear probe, which should cut log loss noticeably despite the unchanged C=0.3 and no TTA; ~0.40–0.43 is the expected range.

Temperature scaling on a held-out split typically yields a small log-loss gain for an L2-shrunk logistic head (likely T<1 to sharpen underconfident logits), though the 85%-fit-to-full-fit transfer limits the benefit to ~1%.

Fine-tuning the last bottleneck plus a logistic-regression-initialized head for up to 2 epochs/90s on cached activations is a well-established step up from frozen features, and with frozen BN, low LR, and early stopping it should cut log loss from ~0.45 to roughly the 0.35-0.40 range without overfitting or risking the time budget (cache fits in RAM, all stages fit well under 10 minutes).

Horizontal-flip TTA on a frozen ResNet-50 + logistic regression head is a standard, low-risk variance-reduction trick that typically cuts log loss by ~2-4% on this dataset, with only negligible extra runtime (one extra pass over 1,023 test images).

1:1 undersampling with fixed C discards the vast majority of (hard) negatives and leaves rare labels like threat with ~950 training rows against 60k features, degrading the rare-label columns that dominate the mean AUC, while the base-rate/intercept argument doesn't protect rank ordering.

Adding char_wb 2-6 n-grams to branch B gives the NB-LogReg branch the character-level signal it lacked (strong for obfuscated profanity), a known win that is partially diluted by the 0.5/0.5 rank blend with branch A, which already had char features — expect a small positive gain of roughly +0.0005-0.0010 mean AUC, with runtime still comfortably within budget.

Hard 1:1 random undersampling throws away 80-99% of the negatives (threat has only ~478 positives, so models fit on ~1k rows with 60k+ features), massively increasing variance and overfitting on the rare labels that dominate the column-mean AUC, while also degrading the OOF stacking features; the calibration/loss argument doesn't apply since AUC only cares about ranking, so a substantial regression on the rare columns is likely.

Plain MultinomialNB on TF-IDF is well documented to be clearly weaker than the NB-ratio + LogisticRegression hybrid (NBSVM) on this dataset, so branch B degrades and the 50/50 rank-average and the OOF stack features fed into branch A both lose quality, pulling the mean column AUC down by roughly 0.7-1.0 points.

Mean-pooled 200-d Word2Vec loses the char n-gram surface signal that made branch A strong (W2V-mean-pool logreg typically lands well below TF-IDF char n-grams here), and the MLP's dense 200-d input is likewise weaker, so the rank-average of three branches drops even though branch B is unchanged.

1:1 undersampling barely affects AUC ranking for the frequent labels but adds sampling noise and effectively weaker regularization on rare labels (threat ~1k rows), so the rank-average blend likely regresses slightly rather than improves.

A 128-unit sparse MLP on the same TF-IDF features is a genuinely diverse non-linear model (likely ~0.978-0.980 held-out), so rank-averaging it in at 1/4 weight should add a small ensemble gain of ~0.0005-0.001, though partly discounted by the risk that the ~690-720s time guards skip or truncate branch D after the slow A/B/C pipeline, leaving the score unchanged.

1:1 undersampling discards 80-99% of the negative rows, so the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) are fit on tiny, noisy samples with fixed C values tuned for full data and NB ratios estimated from few rows — typically a small AUC regression that the 3-branch rank blend only partially masks.

Classic light text cleaning (URL/IP/timestamp removal, profanity de-obfuscation) typically yields a small AUC gain on this competition — mainly on the noisy rare columns (threat, identity_hate) — though repeat-collapsing slightly dilutes the char n-gram branch that already handles elongation, netting a marginal improvement over 0.98013.

Leak-free 5-fold OOF stacking of B's predictions into A is a standard small win over plain rank-averaging, but the /20 feature scaling, C=0.1 regularization, and the resulting loss of A/B diversity (B is already blended at 0.5) cap the gain at a few ten-thousandths of AUC, while the ~30 extra liblinear fits plus 30 full-test predictions push the run toward the 10-min budget (still likely finishing before the 15-min kill).

A 3-epoch, 64-unit MLP on TF-IDF is a weak third model (likely well below 0.98 alone), so giving it equal 1/3 rank weight dilutes the strong A+B blend slightly; diversity may partially compensate but net effect is a small regression.

Branch C (NB-LogReg on B's word n-grams + A's char n-grams) is a known-strong hybrid that is only partially correlated with A and B, so an equal three-way rank average should give a small AUC lift (~+0.0005), concentrated in the noisy rare labels, while the max_iter=100 cap and feature reuse keep it comfortably within the time budget; the modest risk is that downweighting A from 0.5 to 1/3 slightly offsets the gain, keeping the improvement small.

Per-label weight tuning on a single 20% holdout with strong shrinkage toward 0.5 mostly recovers the equal blend; any genuine branch-strength differences are small, so expect a near-neutral result with a slight chance of tiny gain (or noise-level regression) on the rare-label columns.

Dropping the char n-gram branch (critical for obfuscated profanity) and compressing word TF-IDF to 300 dense SVD factors loses sharp discriminative signal, especially on rare labels (threat, identity_hate), so a single LSA model historically lands around 0.970-0.973 on this competition vs 0.9798 for the ensemble.

Undersampling negatives to a 10:1 cap barely touches the frequent labels (toxic keeps ~152k rows) but starves the rare labels (threat trains on ~5k rows), making the NB log-odds and fastText fits noisier on the columns that dominate metric variance, so expect a small regression rather than a gain; AUC is largely invariant to the class-prior shift, and the rank-average blend dampens the effect.

A single softmax multi-label fastText forces the six co-occurring labels to share probability mass within each row (and adds a 'clean' class), which typically degrades per-column ordering versus six independent binary classifiers — especially for rare labels like threat/identity_hate — and the 1/3 rank-average only partially dilutes that regression, while the training-time saving is irrelevant to the metric.

A single ComplementNB on word 1-2-gram counts is far weaker than the rank-average of three diverse linear branches (word+char TF-IDF logreg, two NB-LogReg views) — dropping the char n-gram view and the discriminative ensembling typically costs ~1.5-2.5 points of mean AUC on this competition, with rare labels (threat, identity_hate) regressing most.

Mean-pooled from-scratch Word2Vec discards the token-level lexical evidence that dominates toxicity AUC (char n-grams especially), so a 200-d average embedding with a single logit head reliably lands well below the sparse three-branch ensemble (~0.95-0.96 vs 0.9816), despite running faster.

Mean-pooled corpus Word2Vec discards the exact token and char-n-gram evidence that makes TF-IDF linear models strong on this task (slur variants, misspellings, rare-label signal), so expect a drop from 0.9799 to roughly 0.95-0.96 mean AUC despite the semantic-motivation argument.

A char_wb 3-5 NB-LogReg branch is genuinely diverse (catches obfuscated spellings) and 3-way rank blending on 143k sub-train rows should add a small AUC gain, partially offset by holdout-tuned weights overfitting noise on rare labels (threat, identity_hate) where ~45 positives make the simplex search unstable.

C=0.1 with sag clearly underfits the 60k word+char TF-IDF features; the reference-kernel C=4/liblinear setting typically lifts branch A's standalone AUC by ~0.002-0.004, and after the 0.5/0.5 rank blend with the unchanged branch B this should translate to a modest gain of roughly +0.0015-0.002 mean column AUC, with liblinear converging well within the CPU budget.

fastText with word bigrams on this corpus is individually comparable to the linear branches (~0.978-0.980), and adding a third diverse model to the rank ensemble typically yields a small gain (+0.001-0.002 mean AUC), partially diluted by its correlation with the word-ngram branches; the per-label train/predict/delete loop keeps runtime well within budget.

A char_wb 3-7 NB-LogReg branch adds a genuinely different feature view to the two-branch blend (char view exists in A only under 50k cap and C=0.1 regularization), so a three-way rank average should give the usual small ensemble gain of ~+0.001 absolute on mean column-wise AUC; the added ~4-5 min vectorizer fit keeps the run near, but likely within, the 10-minute budget.

Training on 90% of data costs a small amount of AUC that per-label holdout-tuned weights are unlikely to recover — the 0.5/0.5 rank blend is already near-optimal, and with only ~10% holdout the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) give extremely noisy weight estimates, so the net effect is a slight regression.

NB log-count-ratio weights computed on L2-normalized TF-IDF sums (where the +1 smoothing dominates rare char n-gram mass) distort branch A's char features, and making both branches NB-weighted cuts the rank-blend's diversity, so the equal-weight average likely regresses slightly.

min_df=0.01 on ~313k docs requires appearing in >3,100 documents, which prunes almost all informative n-grams (profanity, insults, rare bigrams appear in far fewer docs), crippling all three branches — especially branch B where 200k features collapse to a handful of generic terms — so AUC should regress noticeably from 0.9796.

Training on ~2x n_positives rows (as few as ~1k for threat/identity_hate) throws away >99% of negatives, making the per-label logistic fits and NB log-count ratios far noisier and effectively over-regularized; the intercept shift is AUC-neutral but the slope estimates degrade, especially on the rare labels that dominate the column-mean variance.

Rocchio-style cosine centroids are strictly weaker than the tuned per-label logistic regressions they replace (no discriminative weighting, heavy negative-class averaging), so both branches and their blend regress by roughly 2% mean AUC, though the strong TF-IDF/NB features keep the score near 0.96.

char_wb n-grams with word-boundary padding typically match or slightly improve on plain char n-grams for this task (word-internal patterns like misspelled profanity are preserved while cross-word noise is reduced), so expect a tiny gain of roughly +0.0002-0.0004 mean AUC with negligible extra vectorizer runtime.

ComplementNB on TF-IDF is a strictly weaker, uncalibrated linear separator than the tuned logistic regressions it replaces in both branches (dropping the discriminative NB-LogReg reweighting entirely), so the equal-weight rank blend should lose roughly 0.5–1.5 AUC points despite the faster training.

Compressing 60k TF-IDF features to just 32 SVD components destroys most of the discriminative lexical signal (especially for rare labels like threat/identity_hate), so branch A degrades from ~0.972 to roughly ~0.93-0.95, dragging the 50/50 rank average down despite the unchanged fastText branch; the run will be faster but less accurate.

Truncating vocabulary to 2,000 tokens destroys the rare-word and unusual-spelling signal that toxicity detection (especially threat/identity_hate) relies on — char n-grams and fastText both see 'raretoken' replacing the discriminative strings — so the equal-weight blend should regress by roughly 1-2 AUC points despite common profanity surviving in the top-2k.

Dropping the English stop-word list mostly removes mildly informative toxicity cues (e.g. 'you') that the char n-grams and NB branch already supply, so the blended AUC shifts by roughly ±1e-4 — I expect a tiny regression from losing those weak word-level signals.

Both branches output well-calibrated logistic probabilities, so a logit-space average is a near-equivalent monotone-ish blend to the rank average; expect a tiny regression (order 1e-4) because rank averaging is more robust to the branches' differing score distributions on rare labels like threat/identity_hate.

Swapping char_wb for char admits cross-word-boundary n-grams; with the 50k feature cap this dilutes the clean within-word character signals that char_wb (space-padded) provides for toxicity, so expect a small regression rather than an improvement, though the effect is minor since the NB-LogReg branch and rank blending absorb much of it.

fastText (OVA, dim=64, 5 epochs, no subwords) is roughly comparable to NB-LogReg on common labels but weaker on rare ones (threat/identity_hate) and less complementary to the TF-IDF branch's word n-grams, so the equal-weight rank blend should slip slightly below the 0.98013 baseline; wall-clock stays well within budget since the slow char-vectorizer fit is unchanged.

Dropping the ~64 lowest-F bins (mostly redundant/weak shape descriptors) reduces the LR's 19k-parameter fit's variance at C=1.0, likely yielding a small improvement in the 50/50 blend, though the effect is damped because the NN half is unchanged and univariate selection can discard jointly-informative features, so the gain is modest and could plausibly be near zero or slightly negative.

Label smoothing bounds the logit gap on this tiny 8-samples-per-class regime, improving the NN's probability calibration (the quantity log-loss scores), so the 50/50 blend should improve modestly — a few percent — though the averaging with the LR already tempers extremes, capping the gain.

OvR binary fits on 10-positive-vs-790-negative problems yield less coherent per-class scores than the joint softmax, and even after the power/floor calibration absorbs the confidence scale, multinomial logistic regression is typically slightly better calibrated for multiclass log loss, so I expect a small regression (~0.0451 -> ~0.0465).

The MLP bag on 192 scaled descriptors is typically a bit weaker than the well-calibrated LR on this dataset, but the OOF-selected blend weight (with w=0 fallback) captures the decorrelated errors of the neural net, so expect a modest improvement of roughly 2-6% in multi-class log loss.

Averaging the five 80%-data fold models acts as bagging that smooths the sharp probabilities of the high-C logreg fits, typically yielding a small log-loss gain over the single full-data refit despite each fold seeing less data; expected roughly a wash to slight improvement (~0.055-0.057).

The 21 geometric features (aspect ratio, convexity, Hu moments) add mostly scale-invariant information only partially captured by the 64-dim shape descriptor, and the existing per-fold CV over a wide C grid absorbs the added dimensionality, so expect a small genuine improvement from ~0.0566 to ~0.055, with a modest risk of a slight regression if the prepared images were resized to a fixed canvas (making several features constant or noisy).

PCA(0.95) removes collinear/noisy directions from the 219-column matrix, so the isotropic L2 penalty acts on decorrelated coordinates — likely a modest improvement to ~0.084-0.087, though the gain is limited because C is not retuned and low-variance discriminative directions may be partly discarded.

Averaging five fold models (each on 80% of data) acts as variance-reducing bagging for the high-dimensional logreg, typically yielding a small log-loss improvement over a single full fit despite each model seeing slightly less data.

The metric is RMSE, which is minimized by the conditional mean (L2 loss); switching to MAE fits the conditional median, systematically under-predicting the right-skewed fare distribution and typically worsening RMSE by a few percent despite the robustness motivation.

Adjacent-character bigrams are a known useful interaction for this TPS (the target depends on f_27 character pairs), and LightGBM native categoricals let trees split on exact bigram values, so expect a small but real AUC gain (~+0.0002) with negligible runtime cost.

Unsupervised PCA components are linear combinations of features trees already see, adding almost no signal, while removing the gain-mined interaction products (which were capturing genuine pairwise interactions in this dataset) should cost roughly the small gain they provided, giving a slight regression to near the no-engineering baseline.

Removing the ten per-position f_27 categorical columns discards the strongest source of string signal; the full-sequence frequency is nearly useless here because most 10-character strings are unique or near-unique (frequency ~1), so the model loses most of the f_27 information and AUC drops roughly a full point, only marginally offset by what the frequency count adds.

The unique-character count of f_27 is the single strongest known engineered feature for this dataset (it exposes a near-deterministic interaction signal), and the per-letter counts add minor extra signal, so AUC should jump from ~0.977 to roughly ~0.989 while staying within budget since featurization cost is negligible.

The known signal in TPS-May-2022 includes genuine multiplicative interactions among the continuous features that trees approximate poorly, so appending gain-mined pairwise products reliably helps, but with the fixed untuned 3000-tree LightGBM the gain is modest (~+0.001-0.002 AUC), partially offset by the ~60% more feature columns eating into the 10-minute budget without changing the model.

Refitting on 100% of the rows (10% more data, with rounds scaled to ~3333 since best_iter hit the 3000 cap and AUC was still improving) typically yields a small AUC gain of roughly +0.0004–0.0007 for GBDTs on this dataset, at the cost of doubling training time which should still fit the budget.

Declaring the f_27 character codes as categorical lets LightGBM learn optimal many-vs-rest letter partitions instead of threshold splits on an arbitrary alphabetical order, which on this dataset (where f_27 is highly informative) historically yields a small but real AUC gain (~+0.001) at comparable runtime.

Capping trees at depth 2 restricts the ensemble to pairwise interactions, which underfits this interaction-heavy dataset and slows convergence so the fixed 3000-round/0.05-lr budget plateaus well below the current 0.9818.
