A modest 600-tree/31-leaf LightGBM on raw features typically lands around 0.97 on this dataset — below the 0.9822 CPU MLP, which captures the continuous interaction structure better than shallow unengineered GBDT trees.

Quartile-binning continuous features throws away fine-grained split points that LightGBM would otherwise exploit (trees are already invariant to monotone transforms and can find optimal thresholds), so coarsening ~24 float columns to 4 levels can only lose information and will degrade AUC moderately.

The residual error (~95% of squared error) lives in the ~10% stroke/edge pixels while background is already fit to RMSE~0.003, so up-weighting dark targets by up to 5x redirects the limited 2000-step training toward the dominant error term with negligible headroom lost on near-saturated white pixels — expect a small net improvement (~3-5%) in unweighted RMSE, though a near-neutral or slightly worse outcome is possible if background-stain removal degrades.

The baseline is clearly undertrained (2000 steps in ~1 min); 330s at ~30ms/step yields roughly 10-12k steps (minus ~10% holdout-eval overhead) under an equivalent cosine-to-zero schedule, which should cut per-pixel RMSE by ~10-18% (to ~0.0135-0.0145), only mildly tempered by overfitting risk at ~200 effective epochs on 105 images with checkpoint-free final weights.

Swapping MSE for L1 misaligns training with the RMSE metric (L1 targets the conditional median, so it stops hedging on ambiguous stroke/stain pixels where the squared-error-optimal mean is better), and with Adam+cosine over only 2000 steps the loss-shape change likely yields a small regression rather than the large gains reported in long-training restoration papers.

With only ~105 training scans reused across ~16k crops the U-Net likely overfits absolute gray-level statistics, so mild input-only brightness/contrast jitter (centered on identity, clean targets) should act as a regularizer and yield a small RMSE gain, though the added input–target ambiguity could keep the improvement modest or occasionally neutral.

The U-Net was trained only on native-scale 128px crops (no scale augmentation, BatchNorm stats tuned to that scale), so the 0.75x pass lightens/blurs thin strokes and the 1.25x pass missizes speckle noise; with 2/3 of the weight on these off-scale, resampling-blurred predictions, the added bias likely outweighs the variance reduction from averaging, giving a small RMSE regression rather than the DeepLab-style gain (which relies on scale-augmented training).

Dropout2d on the skip-fed e2/e3 features cuts effective capacity during a very short 2000-step cosine-decayed run, so the slightly underfit denoiser regresses a bit — spatial dropout rarely helps pixel-level MSE regression with tens of millions of pixel samples and no evidence of overfitting-limited generalization.

With only 180 s of training the small U-Net is still underfit rather than memorizing, so adding Dropout2d(0.1) to all five blocks (including skip-connection and pre-pool features) mainly injects gradient noise, slows convergence under the fixed cosine schedule, and introduces the known Dropout+BatchNorm train/test discrepancy — a small RMSE regression.

The added 1/8-resolution stage roughly quadruples capacity and doubles the receptive field (~41→~89 px), which directly helps remove the large-scale stains/shading this dataset contains; the ~35-40% fewer optimization steps from the ~55% higher per-step cost under the fixed 180s time budget offsets part of that gain, so I expect a modest net improvement of a few percent rather than a large one.

A 23x23 median-filter background channel is a well-known strong cue for this dataset (it isolates stains/illumination from text), letting the small, briefly-trained U-Net normalize illumination it would otherwise have to learn internally, so expect a moderate (~10%) RMSE drop at essentially no extra compute, while the unchanged training budget and soft-edge regression error cap the gain.

The added 256/512-channel levels and 256px crops give a much larger receptive field that suits this dataset's big-scale stains while keeping pixels-per-step and step count unchanged, so a modest gain is likely despite the bigger model being slightly undertrained at 2000 steps; BN stays stable since each batch still spans ~524k pixels.

4-way flip TTA averages out the model's residual flip-asymmetry (training already used random flips, so flipped inputs are in-distribution and nothing is hurt), yielding a small but real variance-reduction gain — typically ~0.3-0.8% RMSE on denoising tasks — at negligible extra inference cost well within budget.

The 180s wall-clock budget on a bf16-capable GPU should fit ~3500-5000 optimizer steps (vs. the baseline's fixed 2000) for this small U-Net, and the time-based cosine still anneals LR to ~0, so expect a modest gain of ~2-3%; risk of parity/slight regression exists if the node is slow enough that 180s yields fewer than 2000 steps.

At this RMSE level the residual squared error is dominated by high-error stain/edge pixels that Charbonnier explicitly down-weights relative to metric-matched MSE (L2 is the RMSE-optimal training objective), so I expect a small regression of roughly 1-3%, partly offset by L1's frequently observed finite-budget restoration benefits.

Adding σ=0.05 Gaussian noise (3× larger than the current 0.015 residual error) creates a train/test noise-level mismatch — the model learns local smoothing tuned for noisier inputs and over-smooths text edges on the un-augmented test images, and the harder task under the fixed 2000-step budget makes this dominate the mild anti-memorization regularization benefit, so RMSE should regress slightly.

GroupNorm removes BatchNorm's crop-statistics-vs-full-page inference mismatch and batch entanglement, a known small but consistent win in image restoration (EDSR-style reasoning), so expect a modest ~1-3% RMSE improvement with training dynamics otherwise unchanged at this batch size and schedule.

The eval metric is per-pixel RMSE, so swapping the aligned MSE objective for Zhao et al.'s perceptually-motivated 0.84*(1-SSIM)+0.16*L1 (which under-weights large pixel errors and is nearly blind to uniform offsets in the flat background regions that dominate document pixels) should mildly regress RMSE, consistent with the small PSNR drop mixed losses show in the restoration literature.

8-fold dihedral TTA averages highly correlated (but not identical) predictions, so it typically shaves a few percent off RMSE; flips match the training augmentation and rotations, while slightly out-of-distribution for text, still denoise plausibly, so a modest gain (~3%) is the most likely outcome rather than the large variance reduction of independent estimators.

The competition metric is per-pixel RMSE, which MSE directly optimizes (the conditional-mean argument makes any structural-loss-induced sharpening/overshoot of strokes and contrast RMSE-suboptimal), and Zhao et al. themselves show pure SSIM losses trade PSNR/RMSE for SSIM, so I expect a modest regression of a few percent from misaligning the loss with the metric, with only minor offsetting benefit from crisper stroke edges.

Residual (DnCNN-style) prediction with a zero-initialized linear head starts from the identity mapping and avoids sigmoid saturation on the mostly-white background, so the same 2000-step budget converges faster to a slightly better denoiser — expect a modest (~5%) RMSE improvement, not a breakthrough, since the parameterizations are asymptotically equivalent.

The metric is RMSE and MSE is the metric-aligned loss; the SSIM term (0.1*(1-SSIM) ≈ 0.005 vs RMSE ≈ 0.0165, i.e. ~30% of loss magnitude) pulls the optimum away from the MSE-optimal conditional mean toward contrast/structure matching, which denoising ablations (e.g. Zhao et al.) consistently show costs a little PSNR/RMSE, so I expect a small regression roughly within run-to-run noise.

Residual (DnCNN-style) learning with zero-initialized final conv removes sigmoid saturation, starts from an identity mapping that already handles uncorrupted background, and focuses the limited-capacity/short-schedule U-Net on learning only the noise correction — a well-established denoising formulation that should yield a modest (~5-10%) RMSE improvement on this task, with the [0,1] clamp retained at inference.

The synthetic corruption family (elliptical stains + shading + speckle) broadly matches this dataset's noise and combats overfitting to the 105 fixed noise realizations, so a modest gain is likely, though the sigma<=4 blur and ~88% synthetic sampling share introduce real distribution-mismatch risk that caps the improvement.

The baseline is clearly undertrained (2k Adam steps, ~3-4 min used of the 10-min budget); 4.5x more steps with the cosine schedule stretched to 9k steps should cut RMSE by roughly a quarter (~0.0162 -> ~0.012) on this task, with only mild overfitting risk on 105 train images and wall-clock still plausibly under ~10 min on a modern GPU (falling back to 45 epochs if not).

The model is trained with h/v-flip augmentation, so the 4 flip views are nearly redundant, while the 4 transposed views are mildly out-of-distribution for upright text; their edge errors correlate with the identity views (no gain there) but averaging still cuts view-dependent decision noise, netting a small ~1% RMSE improvement, with a real chance of a slight regression if rotated text is handled poorly.

Training loss becomes misaligned with the RMSE metric: L1 pushes predictions toward the conditional median and de-emphasizes exactly the large residuals (stains, text edges) that dominate squared error, so the graded per-pixel RMSE should regress modestly (Adam's gradient normalization mutes but doesn't remove this effect).

Squared error in this task is concentrated on the ~5-10% text/edge pixels (background is nearly saturated and easy), so shifting gradient mass 3:1 toward dark targets should improve their fit more than the mild darker-prediction bias and slightly de-emphasized white background cost, yielding a small (~2%) RMSE gain, though a small regression is plausible.

Up-weighting dark targets 10x shifts the learned predictor away from the unweighted conditional mean toward darker outputs in ambiguous regions (anti-aliased edges, faint stains), and since the graded metric is unweighted RMSE dominated by the ~85% white background and edge pixels, this systematic dark bias raises total error more than the modest gain in stroke fidelity offsets it.

Zero-init residual head makes the model start as the identity (already near the noise floor ~0.1 RMSE) and removes sigmoid gradient saturation on the mostly-0/1 document pixels, so the same 2000-step budget converges substantially further than the sigmoid baseline; the added runtime.toml is inert since the harness sets EV_RUNTIME_CONFIG (the parent ran without any repo runtime.toml).

The grading metric is RMSE, which is matched to MSE training (conditional-mean predictions minimize squared error), so switching to L1's median-like, uniform-weighted objective de-emphasizes exactly the large stain/text residuals that dominate RMSE, likely causing a small regression despite sharper background/stroke fit.

Zero-initialized residual head makes the model start as the identity (RMSE ~0.15) and spend the limited 2000-step budget learning only the noise correction, a known convergence accelerant for denoising, so the undertrained small U-Net should land a few percent better than the from-scratch sigmoid head (with inference clipping keeping outputs valid).

Halving width (8/16/32/64, ~4x fewer params) slightly underfits an already-compact NAFNet on a fixed 2000-step/20-epoch budget with no compensating extra training, so expect a small RMSE regression (~4%) rather than the hoped-for regularization gain; run time drops but nothing converts that headroom into accuracy.

The graded metric is unweighted per-pixel RMSE dominated by white background/stain-removal pixels; the 3:1 foreground weighting only mildly helps stroke/faint-text errors (which the residual architecture already handles cheaply) while de-emphasizing stain removal over the ~90% of pixels that actually drive the score, so expect a small net regression of roughly 1-2%.

Four-view flip TTA averages highly correlated (flip-augmented) U-Net predictions, yielding a modest variance-reduction gain of roughly 1-2% RMSE while leaving training untouched, with only minor added inference time risk on CPU.

The faithful base-16 NAFNet swaps sigmoid-BN conv blocks for a global-residual, linear-head design with gated/LN blocks and 4 bottleneck blocks at 1/8 res, which learns the stain/illumination correction much faster than the plain U-Net within the fixed 2000-step budget (and its ~6x lower FLOPs keep the CPU run inside the time limit), so I expect a modest RMSE improvement despite the narrower width; risk of slight regression exists if the short schedule under-trains the zero-initialized beta/gamma blocks.

The Stanford Dogs images (train AND test) come from ImageNet-1k, which this checkpoint was fine-tuned on, so the pretrained 1000-way head restricted to the 120 dog logits is a genuinely complementary, partially 'memorized' second predictor; tuned (w,T) on the 15% holdout with w=0 in-grid as a floor, expect a modest real gain (~4-10%) over 0.3096, tempered by correlated errors (same trunk/features) and a small risk of a 1-2 class name-mapping mismatch (e.g. pekinese/groenendael) plus holdout-selection noise.

PCA-256 (no whitening) discards the low-variance feature tail that carries part of the fine-grained breed signal while the already-tuned L2 in LogisticRegression handles the overparameterization, so the projection mostly adds bias and I expect a modest log-loss regression of roughly 0.01-0.03.

The 22k-pretrained ConvNeXt backbone is already near-optimal for these in-distribution dog classes, so full-strength Mixup/CutMix (as in the official 5-epoch ConvNeXt fine-tune recipe) mainly acts as a calibrator — softening confident errors on confusable breeds, which log loss rewards — at the cost of slight underfitting over only 6 epochs and ~776 steps; net effect should be a modest improvement (~0.4426 → ~0.43), though the short schedule and prob=1.0 mixing carry real risk of a small regression toward 0.46.

Widening the crop range to the ImageNet-standard (0.08, 1.0) adds meaningful regularization for a 28M-param model fine-tuned on ~8k images (reducing memorization and overconfident errors that log loss punishes), and the backbone was pretrained/fine-tuned under exactly this augmentation; the downside — more zoomed partial views and greater train/eval mismatch within only 6 epochs, plus occasional dog-free crops — roughly offsets part of the gain, so I expect a small improvement on the order of the run-to-run noise (~0.005 in log loss).

Swapping a 76%-top-1 ResNet-50 for an 86.8%-top-1 IN-22k→IN-1k ConvNeXt-V2 Large gives far more linearly separable 1536-d features and much more accurate 1000-d ImageNet log-prob priors over the 120 breed classes, so the same linear-probe pipeline should cut log loss from ~0.449 to roughly 0.30 (≈30% improvement), with runtime still safely in budget (one 800 MB download plus a few minutes of fp16 inference).

The 1000-d log-softmax block is not redundant in practice here: Stanford Dogs is a subset of ImageNet, so the pretrained fc head's dog-class log-probas are near-oracle, heavily-exploitable features for the LR probe (and the block is a nonlinear, not linear, function of the pooled vector); dropping it leaves a plain linear probe that must relearn those 120 directions from ~77 images/class, so I expect the log loss to regress by roughly +0.02-0.03, partially offset by removing ~880 noisy standardized non-dog columns.

Ridge+temperature spans the same linear-softmax family as the current LR head (softmax(s/T) = a rescaled linear model), so accuracy should be unchanged, but least-squares fitting is a surrogate for the log-loss objective that MLE optimizes directly, and a single global temperature cannot fully fix per-class calibration — expect near-parity with a small (~1-2%) calibration penalty, partly offset by the wider (alpha, T) grid.

Unsupervised PCA to 128 comps per block discards low-variance but breed-discriminative directions that the L2-shrunk LR was exploiting, and with ~10k training rows the 2560-d probe wasn't badly overfitting, so the compression costs a small but real amount of log loss (partially mitigated, not reversed, by the holdout C re-selection).

ConvNeXt-Base with ImageNet-22k pretraining is a far stronger frozen feature extractor for fine-grained dog breeds than ResNet-50 V1 (≈86% vs 76% ImageNet top-1, and 22k pretraining especially helps fine-grained classes), so linear-probe log loss should drop from ~0.45 to roughly 0.28-0.31 with the matched 224px/crop_pct-0.875 preprocessing and re-selected C, while the swap keeps the pipeline (extraction + 5 sklearn fits) comfortably within the 10-minute budget.

End-to-end fine-tuning of a stronger ImageNet-22k ConvNeXt-Tiny (with augmentation, label smoothing, flip TTA, and temperature calibration) should lift accuracy from ~81% to ~88-90%, cutting log loss from ~0.45 to roughly 0.30-0.34; 6 epochs fits comfortably in the 7-minute training guard on a modern GPU, with residual risk from weight download/version issues.

Concatenating the pretrained head's 1000-d log-softmax (a distilled, already dog-trained classifier, and these ImageNet-sourced images were in its training set) with the pooled features and standardizing gives the logistic regression a strong complementary prior, so tuned-C LR should improve modestly from 0.4515 to roughly 0.42-0.43, with holdout C selection guarding against regression.

Swapping a single ResNet-50 V1 (76% IN-1k) for L2-normalised concatenation of ConvNeXt-B in22k, CLIP ViT-B/16 and DINOv2 ViT-B/14 — three much stronger, decorrelated frozen feature sets — with holdout-tuned C is a well-established ~25-30% log-loss reduction on this competition, landing around 0.30-0.35, with the main (non-fatal) risks being runtime from five multinomial LBFGS fits on 2560-d features and first-run HF downloads.

On a well-balanced 120-class problem focal loss mainly just discards label smoothing's calibration benefit while shrinking gradient magnitude on the majority of examples (effectively lowering the LR mid-training), which historically yields slightly worse NLL than CE+LS, so I expect a modest log-loss regression of roughly +0.02-0.03.

Layer4+fc-only fine-tuning is a strong regularizer but typically lands slightly below full fine-tuning on Stanford Dogs with a 10-epoch budget, and frozen-stage BN running stats still drift under the RRC augmentation, so I expect a modest log-loss regression from 0.674 to roughly 0.70-0.72.

Horizontal-flip TTA averages out prediction noise for a frozen ViT + LogReg pipeline (flipping after the eval transform is valid since resize/center-crop/normalize are flip-equivariant), typically trimming ~1-2% relative from multiclass log loss, while the num_workers=0 change affects only runtime, not results.

The parent's ViT-B/16 was supervised-trained on ImageNet-1k, which literally contains these 120 dog breeds, so its frozen features are highly breed-discriminative; CLIP ViT-B/32's contrastive features with a coarse 7×7 patch grid are much weaker for fine-grained fur/texture breed cues, so the linear probe should drop from ~85% to ~72-78% accuracy and log loss should rise to roughly the 0.9-1.0 range.

Truncating 2048→256 unwhitened PCs on a fine-grained 120-breed task discards tail directions that carry breed-discriminative signal, and C=0.3 (tuned for the raw space, where PCA's fast-decaying component scales act like extra regularization on tail features) pushes the probe into mild underfitting, so I expect a small log-loss regression rather than the claimed denoising gain.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings linearly probe several points above supervised ResNet-50 features on fine-grained dog breeds (even interpolated to 224px), so the identical LR head + 10-view TTA pipeline should cut log loss from ~0.438 to roughly 0.32-0.34, with C re-selection on the 768-d features and the ~114k fp16 ViT forwards still fitting comfortably in the 10-minute budget.

Truncating 2816-d two-backbone features to 256 PCs discards fine-grained tail signal, and whitening rescales features (~11x larger norms) so the unchanged C=1.0 acts as far weaker regularization, so mild overfit plus information loss likely outweighs the decorrelation/denoising benefit.

Replacing the linear probe with 10-NN distance-weighted votes coarsely quantizes probabilities (k=10 vote shares) and slams a ~7-nat penalty whenever the true breed is absent from the 10 neighbors (the 1e-3 smoothing is far too small to cushion this), so log loss roughly doubles from 0.54 to ~1.0 despite similar top-1 accuracy.

End-to-end fine-tuning of ResNet-50 with RRC/hflip augmentation, label smoothing, and warmup+cosine SGD typically lifts Stanford Dogs top-1 accuracy from ~82% (frozen linear probe, 0.4529 log loss) to ~86-88%, cutting multiclass log loss to roughly 0.29-0.34, and 10 epochs at batch 64 with fp16 comfortably fits the 10-minute single-GPU budget.

ViT-B/16 with ImageNet-21k pretraining is a substantially stronger frozen extractor than ResNet-50 V1 for this fine-grained ImageNet-dog-subset task (linear-probe accuracy typically jumps from ~84% to ~92-93%), so despite keeping the same C=0.3 logistic head (768-d LayerNorm'd features work fine un-standardized with mild L2), log loss should drop from 0.453 to roughly 0.28-0.32, with runtime (ViT fp16 extraction + cheaper 768-d probe) still well under the 10-minute budget.

Ten-crop-plus-flip TTA averaging over a frozen ResNet-50 is a classic small-but-reliable win: corner crops are individually slightly weaker than the training center crop, yet probability averaging reduces variance (ten-crop evaluation historically improves ImageNet accuracy ~1-2%), so log loss should drop modestly (~0.005-0.012 absolute) from 0.4529 to roughly 0.443, with runtime still well under budget since the test set is only 1,023 images.

ConvNeXt-Tiny (in22k→in1k) is a far stronger frozen backbone than ResNet-50 V1 for these 120 ImageNet dog classes, so the per-block L2-normalized concatenation with a linear probe should cut log loss from ~0.453 to roughly 0.28–0.32 while still finishing well inside the time budget.

The ImageNet-pretrained fc head restricted to the 120 dog classes (with temperature) is a strong, partly 'memorized' second opinion on the same cached features (Stanford Dogs overlaps ImageNet train), and the honest 80/20 stratified blend search (alpha=0 included, so it can't look worse than LR on validation) should pick a nonzero blend, cutting log loss from ~0.309 to roughly 0.26–0.28, with only a small chance of no change or slight regression.

Truncating 2048-d ResNet-50 features to 256 unwhitened PCA components discards low-variance directions that carry part of the fine-grained breed signal, and the fixed C=0.3 (tuned on raw 2048-d features) becomes mis-calibrated in the compressed space, so a modest log-loss regression of roughly 0.01-0.02 is the most likely outcome despite faster fitting and no runtime risk.

A GAP-trained ResNet-50's max-pooled features are less linearly separable and have much larger norms that interact badly with the fixed C=0.3, so the frozen-feature linear probe typically loses a few accuracy points and log loss regresses from ~0.45 to ~0.5-0.55 despite temperature calibration.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 weights are ~4.7 points better on ImageNet top-1 and the 120 dog breeds are ImageNet classes, so the frozen 2048-d features are meaningfully more linearly separable, which—with temperature scaling refit on the same holdout—should translate into a roughly 2-3 point accuracy gain and a ~5-8% log-loss reduction at identical compute cost.

C=0.3 was already selected as best on a stratified holdout over a grid that included 0.03, so the 10x stronger L2 yields an underfit, low-norm head initialization; the short 2-epoch/90s fine-tune at head lr 1e-3 cannot fully regrow the shrunken logits, producing a modest log-loss regression of roughly 0.03-0.04.

Evaluating an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 at 192px crops instead of 224px slightly weakens the pooled features (typical ~0.5–1% top-1 drop at this scale) with no offsetting benefit since train and test resolutions match and the fine-tune is time-capped anyway, so log loss should regress modestly (~2%).

Unwhitened PCA-256 truncation discards low-variance directions that carry fine-grained breed signal and keeps C=0.3 tuned for the raw 2048-d space, so the denoising benefit is slightly outweighed by lost discriminative dimensions, giving a small log-loss regression (~0.43→0.435) with negligible runtime impact.

Dropping input resolution from 224 to 192 moves features away from the ImageNet pretraining scale, modestly degrading the frozen ResNet-50 representation even with the crop fraction preserved, so log loss worsens slightly while runtime drops.

IMAGENET1K_V2 is a strictly stronger checkpoint (80.9% vs 76.1% ImageNet top-1) and all 120 dog breeds are ImageNet classes, so its frozen 2048-d features should linearly separate breeds better with matched 232/224 preprocessing, giving a modest log-loss improvement even though C=0.3 was tuned on V1 features.

Temperature scaling is a low-risk recalibration of an already C-tuned logistic regression (whose C grid search implicitly tuned confidence), so expect only a small validation-driven calibration gain (~0.3-1% relative), slightly eroded by fitting T on the 85%-data model but applying it to the full-data refit whose logits are marginally sharper; net a modest improvement to ~0.450, assuming the run completes despite the removed TORCH_HOME weight-cache override.

Warm-starting the head from the logistic-regression fit and gently fine-tuning only layer4[-1]'s convs (frozen BN, lr 1e-4/1e-3, ~2 quick epochs on cached 7x7 activations, well within the time budget) is the classic highest-value step after linear probing on fine-grained tasks, so test log loss should drop from 0.4525 to roughly 0.40-0.42, with the main residual risk being mild overconfidence/overfitting from training without augmentation on the same deterministic crops.

Horizontal-flip TTA on an ImageNet-pretrained backbone (which saw flip augmentation in pretraining) with probability averaging is a low-variance, well-matched ensemble that typically trims ~0.005-0.01 log loss on this dataset; training and classifier are unchanged, so a small, reliable improvement from 0.4525 is expected.

For AUC (a prior-shift-invariant metric) balanced 1:1 undersampling buys almost nothing while discarding 5x-170x of the negative data, so the heavily reduced per-label fits (e.g. threat trained on ~956 rows with 60k features) and the noisy balanced NB ratios lose more ranking signal than they gain, giving a modest regression concentrated on the rare labels.

Adding the shared char_wb 2-6 TF-IDF block (with NB log-count weighting) to branch B injects the strongest single signal for this task — character n-grams catch obfuscated/misspelled profanity that word 1-2-grams miss — so branch B alone likely rises to roughly the level of the old blend, lifting the 0.5/0.5 rank-average by ~+0.001 (0.9805→~0.9815), while fit_transform-once reuse of the char vectorizer keeps runtime near or below the current run despite the six larger (ConvergenceWarning-capped) liblinear fits; the only mild drag is reduced branch diversity since both branches now share char features, but the net effect should still be a small positive.

1:1 undersampling discards 96-99% of negatives for the rare labels (threat ~956 rows, identity_hate ~2.8k, severe_toxic ~3.2k), sharply raising variance of the fitted weights and of the NB log-count ratios (and hence the stacked OOF features), while AUC-wise the unweighted fits were not actually 'biased toward the majority' since the class prior mainly moves the intercept — so frequent labels stay ~flat but the three rare-label columns drop several points each, costing roughly 0.010-0.012 of mean AUC.

Plain MultinomialNB is a meaningfully weaker learner than the NB-ratio-scaled LogisticRegression hybrid (roughly 0.5–1.0 AUC points per label, especially on rare labels like threat/identity_hate), and since it enters at a fixed 50/50 rank-average weight and also supplies weaker OOF stacking features to branch A, the ensemble regresses ~0.003–0.004 despite the extra generative/discriminative diversity and faster, deterministic fits.

Mean-pooled Word2Vec loses the char n-gram signal (the strongest single feature for toxicity) and dilutes sparse toxicity words in long comments (~0.95-0.96 AUC), and the MLP branch now just duplicates the same weak 200-d features, so the blend becomes ~2/3 weak W2V + 1/3 NB-LogReg and drops from 0.9808 to roughly 0.971.

Single-draw 1:1 undersampling discards ~99% of negatives for rare labels (threat: 956 rows, identity_hate: ~2.9k), losing hard-negative information and making branch B's NB log-count ratios noisy, while the 3-epoch MLP gets ~5x fewer Adam steps — AUC is rank-based so rebalancing buys little, expect a small regression concentrated in threat/identity_hate.

A shallow shared-hidden-layer MLP on the same TF-IDF space is diverse but individually weaker (~0.975-0.978) and likely undertrained to 1-2 epochs by the 690s epoch-start guard, so its 1/4-weight rank-average contribution should yield only a small blend gain (+0.0002-0.0006), with some chance of it being time-guard-discarded and the score staying flat.

Balanced undersampling is AUC-neutral only for unregularized LR (intercept shift); here it discards 80-99% of negatives, effectively multiplies the L2 strength per data point by 5-170x for the tuned C values, and adds shared subsample noise (same idx across branches) that the rank-average cannot average out — expect a modest regression concentrated on threat/identity_hate and the common labels, partially offset by faster convergence.

Canonicalizing obfuscated/elongated profanity and collapsing chat shorthand concentrates signal for the word-ngram branches while char_wb 2-6 n-grams (already robust to such variation, and already lowercased by sklearn) are largely unaffected, so expect a small positive shift (~+0.0005 mean AUC) with negligible added runtime; a near-neutral or marginally negative outcome is also plausible since the removed noise tokens (URLs/IPs/timestamps) carry little label information.

Leak-free OOF stacking of B's six logits into A adds genuine cross-label and complementary word-ngram signal (most for rare threat/identity_hate columns), so A strengthens enough to lift the unchanged 0.5/0.5 rank blend by roughly +0.0005, partly offset by reduced A-B diversity; the ~30 extra small liblinear fits likely push runtime past the 10-min aim but under the 15-min kill, so the run should still grade.

The 3-epoch, 64-unit MLP reuses branch A's exact features, so it adds a weaker, highly error-correlated member at a full 1/3 rank weight; undertrained (especially on threat/identity_hate) it dilutes the tuned A+B blend by roughly 0.001-0.002 mean AUC rather than helping.

Branch C (NB-weighted word+char) adds genuinely diverse char-ngram signal to the NB family, so an equal three-way rank blend should yield a small gain (~+0.0005), partially offset by its correlation with A/B and the max_iter=100 convergence cap; runtime stays within budget since all vectorizers are fit once and C's liblinear is iteration-capped.

Per-label blend-weight tuning with aggressive shrinkage toward 0.5 barely moves the very flat rank-blend AUC curves — the small systematic tilt toward the stronger char branch on common labels is largely offset by winner's-curse noise on the rare labels (threat/identity_hate have <100 holdout positives) — so expect a near-wash, roughly +0.0001 on the mean column AUC; main risk is runtime (~50% extra compute from the extra 80/20 branch fits), which should still finish under the 15-min kill.

Compressing 100k sparse n-grams to 300 unsupervised SVD components discards the fine-grained char/word n-gram signal that the rank-average ensemble exploits, hurting the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) most — LSA+LR typically lands around 0.95-0.965 on this competition versus the current 0.9798, a clear regression (the run itself will finish well within budget).

Capping negatives at 10:1 shrinks the effective training signal for severe_toxic/threat/identity_hate while C stays fixed (effectively much stronger regularization), makes branch B's NB log-ratio noisier, and uses the identical subsample across all three branches so their errors correlate instead of canceling — the class-balance benefit only partly offsets this, and toxic is unchanged since 10x its positives exceeds all negatives.

fastText's softmax loss trains on one randomly sampled label per multi-label comment, suppressing co-occurring labels (target ~1/|L|) and diluting the already-sparse positive gradient for threat/identity_hate — exactly the noisy columns that dominate this grading — so branch F becomes a weaker per-column ranker than the six binary models and the equal-weight rank average regresses slightly (partly offset by shared-embedding multi-task signal and unchanged branches A/B).

A single raw-count word 1-2-gram ComplementNB loses all three things that made the baseline strong (char n-gram features, TF-IDF/L2 length normalization, discriminative LR fitting), so the ensemble's 0.9816 drops to a mid-0.96s generative single model — a clear regression, even though the run gets much faster and more reproducible.

Unweighted mean-pooled from-scratch Word2Vec (5 epochs, ~20M tokens) destroys the sparse token-level evidence the TF-IDF/NB ensemble exploits — a single profanity token gets diluted across the whole comment average — hurting the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) most, and this competition's history shows averaged-embedding + linear models land ~0.95-0.96 vs ~0.982 for n-gram ensembles.

Average-pooled corpus Word2Vec + linear LR discards the exact word/char n-gram evidence (profanity, obfuscations, rare-label phrase cues) that drives this task, so mean AUC drops from ~0.980 to roughly the 0.93–0.94 range despite the semantic-motivation.

The char_wb 3-5 NB-LogReg branch adds real (if partial, since branch A already has char 2-6 TF-IDF) diversity that is historically strong on obscene/insult/severe_toxic, so the holdout-tuned 3-way rank blend should net a small gain (~+0.001 absolute), partially offset by noisier 66-combo weight selection on the rare threat/identity_hate columns and the added ~3-5 min of vectorization/liblinear time that stays under the 15-min kill but risks exceeding the 10-min aim.

The current C=0.1/sag word+char branch is the tuned config from the well-known public kernel (the proposal's rationale misattributes C=4/liblinear to that feature set); dropping regularization 40x mainly risks overfit on the rare threat/identity_hate columns that dominate noise in the column mean, and making branch A's classifier identical to branch B's slightly reduces blend diversity, so I expect a tiny regression well within noise rather than a gain.

fastText (solo ~0.975-0.978) is a diverse third linear-ish branch whose punctuation-padded word-bigram features complement the TF-IDF branches, so an equal-weight rank average should add a small but real gain (~+0.0005-0.0010) on mean AUC, provided the ~6 sequential fastText trainings (~1 min each) keep the run under the 15-min kill.

A char_wb 3-7 NB-LogReg branch is individually strong (~branch A/B level) and only partially redundant with A's 50k heavily-regularized char features, so an equal 3-way rank average should yield a small gain (~+0.001 mean AUC) rather than a regression, though the extra ~4-min vectorizer fit plus six primal liblinear fits will push wall-clock close to the budget cap.

The certain cost of fitting both branches on 10% less training data (~0.0003-0.0005 mean AUC) is unlikely to be offset by per-label blend-weight tuning, since the AUC-vs-weight curve for two highly correlated linear branches is flat near 0.5 and the 16k-row holdout is too noisy for the rare labels (threat/severe_toxic/identity_hate carry <200 holdout positives), so expect a slight regression.

NB-weighting branch A's word+char features makes it behaviorally much more similar to branch B (both become NB-LogReg variants), so the rank-average loses the ensemble diversity that currently lifts it above either branch, while any solo gain for A is likely small (char n-gram LR is already near the linear ceiling and C=0.1 wasn't tuned for the rescaled features) — expect a small regression, not a gain.

min_df=0.01 on the ~313k-doc corpus demands df≥~3,127, which prunes exactly the rare discriminative n-grams (slurs like 'faggot'/'nigger', borderline terms like 'cunt'/'idiot', obfuscated profanity) that carry the rare-label columns (identity_hate, threat) and guts branch B's 200k-feature NB vocabulary down to a few thousand common terms, so both branches and their rank-average lose signal on rare labels while the retained frequent words offer almost no compensating gain — a net regression of roughly 0.006-0.007 mean AUC.

1:1 undersampling discards ~99% of negatives for rare labels (threat trains on 956 rows, identity_hate 2.8k) and makes branch B's NB log-count ratios noisy, so rare-column AUCs (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) drop several points while frequent columns lose a little — a net regression of roughly 1 point of mean AUC despite the faster fits.

Swapping trained logistic regressions for untrained cosine class-centroid directions removes per-feature discriminative weighting; strong TF-IDF/NB features keep AUC respectable but rare-label centroids and lack of supervised weighting cost roughly 2 AUC points on the mean.

char_wb anchors n-grams at word boundaries (fastText-style subwords), which typically matches or slightly beats raw char n-grams for profanity/toxicity detection; expect a small branch-A gain (~+0.0004 standalone) diluted to ~+0.0002 by the 50/50 rank blend, with ~30% more n-grams from padding still fitting the time budget.

Swapping the discriminative logistic fits (including branch B's NB-LR reweighting) for purely generative ComplementNB on L2-normalized TF-IDF loses roughly a full AUC point per branch — alpha=1.0 smoothing on fractional TF-IDF sums over-smooths rare discriminative n-grams — so the equal-weight rank blend should land around 0.968–0.971, a clear regression, though runtime stays well under budget since NB fits are nearly free compared to the char vectorizer.

Crushing 60k TF-IDF features to just 32 unsupervised SVD components destroys the fine lexical ordering that makes branch A strong (especially for rare labels like threat/identity_hate), so the weakened branch A drags the 0.5/0.5 rank blend down from 0.9734 to roughly 0.96 despite fastText staying unchanged.

Collapsing all non-top-2000 tokens to a single 'raretoken' destroys the mid-tail vocabulary (slurs like faggot/cunt/retard, obfuscated and misspelled profanity) that both the char n-gram branch and fastText rely on — especially for identity_hate, insult and threat — while retaining only frequent profanity, so the mean column AUC should regress by roughly 0.004-0.006 despite mild denoising/regularization benefits.

Keeping stop words like 'you/your/will' (strong cues for threat/insult, which the char branch only partially covers) should add a small amount of word-branch signal, diluted ~4x by stacking with char n-grams and rank-averaging with branch B, for a modest gain of roughly +0.0004 mean AUC.

Replacing the calibration-free rank average with a logit-space average lets the overconfident NB branch (C=4 on NB-scaled features yields much larger decision values than branch A's C=0.1) dominate the blended ordering, so the ensemble drifts toward the weaker branch B and loses a small amount of mean AUC (~0.0008).

Switching to analyzer='char' lets n-grams cross word boundaries, so the 50k feature budget gets partly spent on space-spanning fragments that duplicate branch B's word-bigram signal while displacing the within-word profanity/misspelling n-grams that make char_wb strong for toxicity — expect a small regression, roughly halved by the 50/50 rank blend with the untouched NB branch; runtime is essentially unchanged.

fasttext 0.9.2's predict() returns labels as bytes, so the str-keyed dict lookup ('__label__toxic' vs b'__label__toxic') silently matches nothing, leaving branch B all zeros; the rank-average then collapses to branch A alone (~0.978), and even if labels decoded as str, a single 64-dim/5-epoch ova fastText is weaker than the NB-LogReg branch it replaces, so a small regression is the likely outcome either way.

Dropping the ~64 lowest-F (largely near-constant/redundant histogram) bins shrinks the near-interpolating 99x192 multinomial LR (~10 samples/class) to a better-conditioned 99x128 fit that should slightly improve the linear half of the unchanged 50/50 NN blend, yielding a small ~1-2% gain, though the dilution by the untouched NN and the risk that weak-but-jointly-useful bins are lost makes this a low-confidence, small-magnitude effect.

eps=0.1 label smoothing caps the NN's true-class probability at ~0.90 (target 0.9+0.1/99), yet the current 0.074 blend score implies the NN is ~0.97-0.99 confident with ~99% accuracy, so the 50/50 blend becomes systematically underconfident on correct predictions (per-sample loss roughly doubling from ~0.05 to ~0.10), while the hoped-for protection against confident errors is already provided by the LR blend component and 8-rotation TTA — a clear net regression.

Multinomial softmax LR directly optimizes the graded multi-class log loss, while OvR's 99 imbalanced binary fits (8 positives vs ~784 negatives per fold) yield per-class score scales that a single fitted power/temperature plus uniform floor cannot fully re-calibrate, so despite identical ranking quality the calibrated OvR probabilities should be moderately worse (roughly 0.050-0.065), not better; runtime (~600 small lbfgs fits, n_jobs=4) stays well within budget.

A 5-seed MLP bag adds nonlinear signal complementary to the well-calibrated LR, and since the OOF search includes w=0 (exact fallback to the current 0.0451 solution) the downside is capped, so expect a moderate OOF-validated gain of roughly 10-15% that mostly transfers to the hidden test set, with slight risk of selection-noise dilution.

The five fold models (80% overlap, tuned C) recover nearly all of the full refit's data advantage, and averaging their probabilities gives a Jensen-style smoothing/calibration gain on the ambiguous leaves that dominate log loss, so I expect a marginal ~1% improvement rather than a clear win or loss.

The 21 geometric features add genuinely new signal missing from the scale-normalized 192 descriptors (absolute size, aspect, solidity/compactness, component count for compound leaves), while the redundant Hu-moment/size columns and CV-tuned C keep the downside bounded, so I expect a small log-loss improvement (~2-4%) rather than a large swing.

Because unwhitened PCA + isotropic L2 is rotation-invariant (identical penalty to the baseline), the only real effect is truncating the lowest-variance ~5% directions, which are noise/quantisation-dominated given only 990 rows for 219 collinear columns — a mild extra regularisation that should shrink the logreg's overfitting slightly, yielding a small improvement (with modest risk of a near-flat or slightly negative outcome if discarded directions carry class signal).

Fold-averaging five 80%-data logreg fits is roughly variance-neutral versus the full refit in the linear approximation, but averaging in probability space plus the effectively stronger per-model regularization smooths the confident-error tail of this overfit 99-class model, so a small (~1%) log-loss improvement is the most likely outcome.

A from-scratch two-branch CNN/MLP trained on ~1k images for 80 epochs will be markedly worse and overconfident compared to the already-strong LR (0.124), and a fixed 50/50 arithmetic blend dilutes LR's confident correct predictions (capped rescue of LR's rare errors but ~0.7-nat penalty on every extra NN error, plus correlated errors via the shared feature branch), so the blend most likely lands around 0.14-0.17 — a mild regression — with only a modest chance the image signal decorrelates errors enough to improve.

The OOF-fitted power/temperature + uniform-floor calibration is well-guarded (only applied if it strictly improves OOF log loss) and typically transfers a modest gain—softening the slightly-overconfident C=1 LR and capping confident-error tails—though the fold-model(792 rows)-vs-full-model(990 rows) mismatch and small 594-sample test set limit the expected improvement to a few percent, with a real but smaller chance of a mild regression.

With 990 samples, 192 features and 99 classes the untuned C=1 is likely over-regularized on this separable-ish feature set, so 5-fold OOF CV will pick a larger C (roughly 10-1000) that sharpens correct predictions; test log loss should drop from 0.1244 to about 0.11 (a ~10% gain), with modest residual risk that OOF noise picks a suboptimal C and the gain shrinks or slightly reverses.

The rotation/scale-invariant descriptors (log-Hu moments, solidity, eccentricity, axis/bbox ratios, circularity) add genuinely complementary shape signal to the 192 precomputed features, so the unchanged StandardScaler+LogisticRegression(C=1.0) pipeline should gain modestly (roughly 0.124 -> ~0.11), though the handful of noisy size/crop features (img dims, leaf_fraction, euler, n_components) and the untuned fixed C limit the improvement and add a small overfitting risk.

At C=1.0 the multinomial LR on ~240 standardized features is already near the flat optimum and roughly well calibrated at log loss 0.08; cutting C to 0.2 (5x stronger L2) mainly shrinks confident correct probabilities (raising their loss) while only softening—not eliminating—errors on genuinely similar species, so I expect a modest regression rather than a variance-reduction gain.

Removing the full-data refit means the submitted model trains on only 80% of the (already tiny, ~10 samples/class) training set, so the learning-curve penalty (LL ~ a + c/n) raises test log loss from 0.0813 to roughly 0.09-0.10, with no offsetting benefit since the pipeline is unchanged.

The SLSQP simplex blend is convex in the weights (each model's rows already sum to 1), so OOF-wise it cannot be worse than the LR component; adding a reasonably strong shrinkage LDA and a small-weight kNN decorrelates errors and typically trims ~10-15% off log loss on this dataset, while the refit-on-full-data transfer and per-fold rescaling keep leakage out — so expect a solid but modest improvement from 0.0592 to roughly 0.051-0.052.

With only ~10 training samples per class for 99 classes, histogram GB trees are far less sample-efficient than the tuned L2 multinomial logistic regression on this near-linearly-separable 192-feature tabular problem, and axis-aligned trees plus a noisy 148-sample early-stopping split yield miscalibrated probabilities, so test log loss should regress from 0.061 to roughly the 0.15–0.3 range (point estimate ~0.20) despite the nonlinear-interaction motivation.

Multinomial LR directly optimizes the graded proper loss, while the replacement's one-vs-rest sigmoid calibration sees only ~2-3 positive samples per class per fold (891 rows, 99 classes, 3-fold), so its probabilities will be noisier/worse-calibrated and the uniform 4-member soft vote should regress modestly (roughly 0.29 -> 0.30), with the small 99-row test adding variance in either direction.

Swapping the heavily handicapped HGB (min_samples_leaf=10 with ~1-per-class early-stopping validation) for a 600-tree bagged RF should strengthen that ensemble slot with better-calibrated vote-fraction probabilities, but the uniform 4-member soft vote dilutes the swap and RF's overconfidence on the handful of hard test rows bounds the gain to a small improvement.

A (256,128) MLP on only ~990 samples/99 classes with weak L2 and noisy 10%-early-stopping will be sharper and less calibrated than the shrinkage-calibrated LogReg; uniform-mixture shrinkage cannot raise above-uniform true-class probabilities on its errors, so the ~4-6% overconfident mistakes dominate and the multi-class log loss likely regresses from 0.124 to roughly 0.15-0.18 despite a possible small accuracy gain.

The CV curve for L2-multinomial LR on this 990x192 standardized feature set is fairly flat around C=1, so 5-fold OOF selection usually lands on a mildly better C (often ~0.3-10), yielding a small gain of a few thousandths in log loss, while the existing alpha-shrinkage step absorbs any added overconfidence; residual risk is selection noise picking a slightly suboptimal C, so expect a modest improvement (0.1244 -> ~0.119-0.121), not a large one.

The >127 mask actually selects the white background (leaves are black-on-white), so the 41 contour/ellipse/histogram features describe the image frame (a size/aspect proxy for the leaf, plus near-constant solidity/extent noise) and the Hu moments describe the leaf's complement — this garbled residual signal roughly cancels the added variance of 48 extra dimensions at untuned C=1.0, leaving the log loss essentially flat with at most a tiny gain.

10-fold CV over a grid containing C=1 will select a stronger-regularized C (~0.1–0.3) for the heavily overparameterized 99-class multinomial fit on 990x192 data, cutting overconfidence and modestly lowering test log loss from 0.1244 to roughly 0.117–0.120, with only a small chance of a slight regression from CV selection noise.

The baseline LR is the strongest member here (0.124 on a 1-leaf-per-class test); uniform soft-voting dilutes its ~0.98 confident probabilities with clearly weaker kNN and heavily overfit HGB (99 classes, ~9 samples/class, tiny noisy early-stopping val set), so per-sample true-class probability drops to ~0.8 and the log loss roughly doubles-to-triples (Jensen bound caps ensemble loss at the ~0.6-0.7 member average; error decorrelation only partially recovers), yielding a substantial regression despite flawless implementation and ample runtime headroom.

Uniform-mixing only reduces log loss if the model makes rare ultra-confident (p_true << 1/99) errors; a C=1.0-regularized LR at 0.124 is mostly confidently-correct, so the OOF grid (which includes alpha=0) will very likely pick alpha=0 or a negligible value, leaving the score essentially unchanged, with a slight downside risk that the alpha tuned on 891-sample fold models over-shrinks the better-calibrated full-data model.

Hard-coding shrinkage=0.9 over-regularizes the pooled covariance toward a spherical matrix, discarding most of the correlation structure in the 192 histogram/descriptor features that Ledoit-Wolf ('auto', likely ~0.1-0.3 here with ~891 pooled df) preserved, degrading LDA toward a nearest-centroid rule with still-confident probabilities, so the multi-class log loss should regress by roughly 30-70%.

Each 64-feature per-family LDA is far weaker than the shrunk 192-feature LDA (which already benefits from Ledoit-Wolf regularization), and equal-weight arithmetic averaging of probabilities (rather than geometric/validated weights) dilutes confident evidence, so the ensemble's log loss should regress substantially from 0.364 to roughly 0.5-0.65.

Tuned L2 logistic regression already handles the correlated descriptors (ridge implicitly shrinks low-variance directions), so a hard, unsupervised cut to the top-90%-variance subspace mostly discards genuinely discriminative margin/texture detail rather than noise, yielding a modest log-loss regression.

With only ~10 samples per class and 192 near-Gaussian descriptor features, a generative shrinkage-LDA (shrinkage CV-tuned by log loss, Ledoit-Wolf included) is known to be one of the strongest single models on this dataset and should clearly beat the tuned multinomial logistic regression's 0.0599, landing around 0.03–0.04.

PCA(0.95) mostly drops low-variance directions that the already L2-regularized (C=1) logistic regression shrinks anyway, so discrimination changes little, but the mild loss of tail-variance signal and slightly weaker logits on an already near-optimal temperature-calibrated baseline make a small regression the most likely outcome (runtime is unaffected).

With only ~10 samples per class and 192 features, shrinkage (Ledoit-Wolf) LDA pools all 990 rows into one shared covariance estimate, making it more sample-efficient than multinomial LR's ~19k regularized weights, and LDA-with-calibration is a known very strong single model on this leaf dataset (the features were designed for Gaussian generative models); the preserved OOF temperature scaling should keep it well calibrated, so I expect an improvement to roughly 0.036-0.040, though a near-neutral or mildly worse outcome is possible since the LR baseline is already well tuned.

Mixing 0.5% uniform adds ~0.005 nats to every one of the ~594 mostly-confident-correct test rows (~+0.005 log loss, capping near 0.0993), and only recovers loss if several test samples have true-class probability below ~1e-4; this smoothly regularized kernel-LR pipeline (test loss 0.094, mildly overconfident, soft runner-up errors rather than catastrophic ones) likely has too shallow a wrong-prediction tail to offset the across-the-board penalty, so expect a small regression to roughly 0.096-0.099.

On only 990 training samples the 512-component map gives a 99-class LR ~50k parameters, and the tail Nyström directions (amplified to unit variance by the second StandardScaler) mostly encode landmark-sampling noise, so trimming to 384 mildly regularizes with negligible loss of between-species signal — expect a small improvement, though the effect is near the run-to-run noise floor.

Shrunk-covariance LDA is still a linear model on the same 192 features, but with only ~10 samples per species its unregularized class means plus a Gaussian assumption on histogram features give slightly miscalibrated posteriors, so it should regress modestly versus the L2-regularized logistic regression that directly optimizes log loss (0.1244 -> ~0.13).

The 192-feature/990-sample LR regularization curve is fairly flat, so 3-fold CV will most likely select C near the baseline's 1.0 (possibly 0.1 or 10); the refit pipeline is otherwise identical to the current model, so expect only a marginal change, with a slight average gain from mild extra regularization.

The C=1 multinomial LR on 192 standardized descriptors is effectively unregularized (per-sample lambda ~ 1/(2n)), so its test logits are mildly mis-calibrated; a single OOF-fit temperature (likely T in 0.7-1.4 depending on whether errors are hedged or confident) is the correct, low-variance way to re-scale softmax confidence and typically recovers a few percent of log loss, with only a small risk of fold-to-full transfer mismatch making it neutral or slightly worse.

The Nyström RBF map (512 of ~990 landmarks, gamma=1/192 giving within-species kernel values ~0.4-0.6 vs ~0.1 across species) captures the tight non-linear species clusters that the linear model misses, so test log loss should drop well below the 0.1244 baseline, though the untuned C=1.0 on whitened kernel features leaves it overconfident and limits the gain to roughly 0.07-0.11.

The block adds genuinely new, known-useful RAOP signal absent from the current pipeline — especially the timestamp (success rate declines over the subreddit's life) plus hour/weekday, text-form and thresholded history flags — which an L2 logistic regression at C=0.3 should convert into a modest ~+0.02-0.03 AUC gain on the 1631-row test set, with small risk of dilution from noisy columns like day-of-month.

Random forests on ~8k-dim sparse TF-IDF with max_features='sqrt' dilute both the weak word signals and the 9 strong (heavily outnumbered) metadata columns at every split, and fully grown trees overfit the temporal drift between train and test, so the ensemble should regress several AUC points below the regularized linear model's 0.6714 (classic LR-beats-RF-on-bag-of-words result).

The baseline's 0.748 is depressed by the train-only near-perfect giver_known indicator (constant 0 on test) letting the linear model 'explain away' most positives so text/numeric weights get shriveled, whereas the forest's sqrt feature-subsampling and conditional splits largely bypass the leak and re-learn the text+metadata signal, which more than offsets trees' intrinsic weakness on 5k-dim sparse TF-IDF — expect a moderate gain to ~0.78.

Replacing sparse TF-IDF with 50 unsupervised LDA topic proportions (fit on only ~4k short docs, 25 batch iters) bottlenecks most of the discriminative lexical signal that the regularized unigram model exploits, so the text block's contribution largely evaporates while the metadata/giver features remain — a moderate AUC regression to roughly metadata-plus-noise level, well within the runtime budget.

LatentDirichletAllocation's n_jobs parameter was deprecated in scikit-learn 1.2 and removed in 1.4 (the environment requires scikit-learn>=1.4), so the run dies with a TypeError before any model is fit or submission/submission.csv is written, grading 0; even if it did run, 20 noisy unsupervised topic proportions carry far less signal than the supervised out-of-fold TF-IDF logit they replace, which alone would likely drop AUC to ~0.69.

Hour-of-day/weekday carry mild but genuine stationary signal in RAOP while the raw epoch's marginal value in the shallow LGBM was small and partly non-transferable interval memorization, so expect a small gain (~+0.002) rather than a large move.

The CV-weight-selected rank blend of a well-regularized HGB on metadata/text-stats (OOF AUC likely ~0.63-0.67) with the stronger TF-IDF LR (~0.72) typically adds a small complementary gain, while the tie-break toward w=1 and the OOF weight selection keep the downside near the 0.7007 baseline; net expectation is a modest +0.002-0.008, occasionally neutral or slightly negative.

Random forests handle high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF text far worse than logistic regression — with max_features='sqrt' (~71 of ~5000 candidate features per split, only ~0.5 of them dense) the model becomes essentially an axis-aligned word-split ensemble that can't additively combine word evidence and nearly ignores the metadata block — so the graded AUC should drop from 0.70 to roughly 0.62-0.66 despite the tiny gains from threshold interactions.

Bag-of-subreddits adds a real but modest community-participation signal (e.g., prior RAOP/giving-adjacent subreddits) that the existing L2-regularized LR can exploit with minimal overfit risk given min_df=5 and l2-normalized blocks, so expect a small AUC gain of roughly +0.003-0.005 rather than a large shift.

giver_username_if_known is a train-only leak (non-'N/A' only for ~85-90% of the 994 positives, absent/'N/A' for every test row), so LogisticRegression dumps a large weight on this near-perfect flag (w≈5, flagged rows fit at p≈0.98), starving the TF-IDF/numeric weights of gradient — they are effectively re-fit on only ~100-150 'unidentified-giver' positives, which both shrinks the effective signal ~7x and biases it toward atypical quiet successes, so test ranking degrades to roughly 0.58-0.62 even though the printed local holdout AUC (where the leak is present) will jump to ~0.85.

Leak-free OOF stacking that feeds a well-regularized LightGBM the text logit plus raw metadata and a genuinely new timestamp feature should capture nonlinear numeric effects the joint L2 logistic model couldn't, typically worth ~+0.01–0.02 AUC on RAOP-scale data, with small downside risk from meta-level overfitting and loss of joint text-numeric linearity.

The added dense block injects genuinely predictive, non-linear signal the unigram TF-IDF can't capture (time trend over 2010-2013, hour/day cyclicals, evidence via http/imgur counts, text length, RAOP-history thresholds per the Althoff et al. paper), and with proper train-fit standardization and only ~27 extra columns the fixed C=0.3 LR stays stable, so I expect a modest gain of roughly +0.02-0.03 AUC on the hidden test.

Swapping a linear model for Extremely Randomized Trees on a ~5.4k-dim mostly-sparse TF-IDF+embedding matrix with only ~4k rows is the classic regime where trees lose to logistic regression: max_features='sqrt' (~73 candidates/split, ~94% of them near-empty word indicators) cannot aggregate many weak additive text signals the way C=0.3 LR does, and min_samples_leaf=3 deep trees overfit noisy word splits, so the clean-world gap of roughly 3-5 AUC points for LR should map to a small regression on this hill (LR 0.6235 -> ET ~0.60), with only a minor offset from ET's better handling of the 9 numeric thresholds and 384 dense MiniLM dims; runtime (300 trees, n_jobs=-1, two fits plus CPU MiniLM encoding) should still fit the budget.

The 5k-word TF-IDF block carries lexical signal (RAOP-specific words, politeness/narrative markers) that a general-purpose MiniLM embedding only partially captures, so dropping it should cost roughly 0.015-0.025 AUC from the 0.6235 hybrid, leaving the dense numerics+embeddings model around 0.60.

The ~21 hand-crafted style/gratitude/sentiment/length stats add genuine (if weak) document-level signal that length-normalized TF-IDF drops — politeness, gratitude and narrative-length effects are documented in RAOP — so expect a small holdout-consistent gain, though much of it (please/thank flags) is redundant with unigrams and the fixed C=0.3 plus standardized noisy binary flags limits the upside to roughly +0.003-0.006 AUC.

In RAOP the TF-IDF text block carries most of the signal; a 9-feature metadata-only logistic regression typically lands around 0.56-0.59 AUC on this temporally shifted test set, so removing text is a clear regression from 0.6497 despite the drift argument.

Corpus-trained skip-gram embeddings on only ~5.7k short documents are too noisy and mean-pooling discards the discriminative lexical sparsity that TF-IDF exploits, so the text block collapses toward the metadata+text-stats baseline (~0.62-0.64) and the graded AUC drops a few points from 0.662.

Bigrams at min_df=2 recover real phrase-level signal ('tough spot', 'really appreciate', 'pay forward') that only partially duplicates the 15 handcrafted stats, so a small gain (~+0.003) is likely, but keeping C=0.3 with ~50k mostly-rare features (much of the phrase overlap is broken by stop-word removal, and df=2 bigrams are noisy on only ~4k docs) limits the upside to well within test-set noise.

On RAOP the (random-split) test set, even SVD-compressed TF-IDF text carries substantial signal on top of the 9 requester-history numbers, which alone typically support only ~0.58-0.60 AUC (per Althoff et al., status/activity features are the weakest-to-moderate group and the Kaggle split is not temporal so 'wording drift' doesn't bite); removing the text pipeline should therefore regress roughly 0.03-0.04 AUC.

Random forests make axis-aligned splits on 300 dense SVD components whose variance-ordered dimensions are mostly noise, and with max_features='sqrt' the forest spreads its splits across many uninformative directions, so bagged deep trees on this 309-dim projection typically underfit the sparse text signal relative to early-stopped LightGBM — expect a moderate regression from 0.6327 to roughly 0.60-0.62 (runtime is safe; 400 trees on ~4k x 309 is fast).

Frozen MiniLM embeddings add mild complementary semantic signal on top of unigram TF-IDF + history features for this small (~4k) dataset, typically worth ~+0.5-1.5 AUC points when appended to a regularized LR, though the fixed C=0.3 and weak task-specific signal of generic sentence embeddings keep the gain modest with some regression risk.

Bigrams (min_df=2) capture success-predicting phrases like 'pay it forward' / 'lost my job' on this small dataset, and the existing L2 (C=0.3) plus TF-IDF L2-normalization keeps the 20x feature expansion from badly overfitting, so expect a small AUC gain rather than a regression, though the magnitude is modest given only ~4k training docs.

The 15 dense stats (request length, punctuation, capitalization, reciprocity/gratitude/hardship lexicons) carry genuine RAOP signal largely lost to L2-normalized unigram TF-IDF, so expect a small but real gain (~+0.005) despite strong regularization and heavy train/LB noise.

On ~4k samples, LGBM over 300 SVD components of a 5k-word unigram TF-IDF typically loses 1-3 AUC points of the localized word-level linear signal that the logistic regression exploits, and this is only partially offset by trees' better handling of the zero-inflated RAOP-activity numerics, so expect a roughly flat-to-slightly-worse result (CV-tuned rounds keep it from collapsing).

The 7-degree-of-freedom quantile spline could capture the dataset's strong multi-year downward trend in request success (plus seasonality), while a single annual sin/cos pair is periodic and largely discards that trend, so replacing it should cost a small amount of AUC.

With ~5000 sparse TF-IDF features and only ~4000 training rows, C=30 is far past the usual optimum (near C~1) so the near-unregularized fit overfits and should cost a few thousandths of AUC relative to the current 0.7044.

Absolute calendar time encodes the community-level decline in success rate that is orthogonal to the already-included user-history numerics, and with only ~7 smooth, regularized spline columns added to a ~5000-feature LR the overfit risk is minimal, so expect a small but real AUC gain (random train/test split means the learned temporal trend transfers).

Distance-weighted cosine kNN on this unnormalized mixed space (TF-IDF contributes ~1 of ~40 squared-norm units vs. standardized numerics and dense subreddit indicators) plus hubness in 5000+ sparse dims is a much weaker learner than the regularized logistic regression, so AUC should drop substantially into the ~0.55-0.59 range.

Distance-weighted kNN on nine noisy, skewed, temporally shifted metadata features is a strictly weaker and noisier estimator than the CatBoost it replaces (no feature weighting, poor extrapolation at the shifted test distribution), so its 50/50 contribution dilutes the logistic regression's ranking and pulls the blend down from ~0.645 to roughly 0.62.

A 100x cut in L2 strength largely unleashes ~5k sparse TF-IDF features on only ~4k noisy samples, so the logistic part memorizes low-df words and its overconfident scores dominate the 50/50 blend, likely costing more than the real scale-mismatch correction gains.

Calendar time carries genuine, only partially redundant signal in RAOP (success rates declined as the subreddit aged), and 7 well-regularized spline columns fitted on train only should transfer to the random test split, yielding a small but real AUC gain over the 0.6542 baseline.

BernoulliNB's hard binarization throws away TF-IDF magnitudes and reduces the nine history features to above/below-mean indicators, and its independence assumptions typically trail well-regularized logistic regression by several AUC points on this small text+metadata dataset.

The quantile-knot spline over unix_timestamp_of_request_utc captures the well-documented monotone decline in RAOP success rate from 2010-2013, a signal only weakly covered by the existing account-age/history features; the implementation is correct (train-fit imputation/spline, bounded [0,1] B-spline columns, constant extrapolation) and adds only ~7 features to a C=0.3 logistic regression, so expect a small positive gain on the randomly-split test set, roughly +0.004-0.006 AUC, with negligible runtime cost.

Subreddit-membership indicators add weak but genuine signal (e.g., RAOP/assistance-related communities vs. generic subreddits) at modest extra dimensionality under unchanged L2 regularization, so I expect a small improvement on the 0.6573 baseline rather than a regression, with the caveat that the unscaled binary block at C=0.3 could add mild overfitting noise.

The metadata-only CatBoost (likely ~0.60-0.63 AUC on these 9 at-request features) is weaker than and highly correlated with the existing LR that already contains those features linearly, so a fixed 50/50 blend over-weights metadata and dilutes the TF-IDF text signal, producing a mild regression from 0.6573 (roughly -0.005 to -0.015, centered near 0.651).

Adding bigrams to the 5000-feature TF-IDF typically yields a small CV gain on RAOP (phrases like 'pay forward', 'lost job' carry signal) while the max_features cap keeps dimensionality constant, so expect a mild ~+0.003 improvement, well within test-set noise; the MLflow/holdout-removal changes are score-neutral.

For authorship attribution, function words and their bigrams are stylometric signal (classic Burrows-style markers), so dropping them from the word view discards useful information only partially compensated by the char_wb n-grams, likely yielding a small log-loss regression despite the reduced dimensionality.

Stacking the existing LR-TFIDF (~0.353 OOF) with diverse but weaker NB word (~0.42) and NB char (~0.39) base models via a regularized log-linear meta-learner is the classic recipe on this competition and historically lands around 0.33-0.34, a ~4% log-loss gain over the single LR; low downside risk since small meta-C can degenerate to roughly the LR-only solution.

Function words and their bigrams ('of the', 'it was') are among the strongest authorship signals, and sklearn's 'english' list also strips semi-content words like 'cry'/'fire', so both word-level base models (especially MultinomialNB, whose count mass carries stable class-conditional stop-word ratios) will lose real signal that char_wb models only partially replicate at the character level; the L2 LightGBM stacker will down-weight the weakened columns, limiting the damage to a small regression of roughly +0.002–0.004 log loss.

A low-capacity multinomial LR stacker on the same 28 OOF/meta columns is more robust than the LightGBM to the distribution shift between single-fold OOF probabilities and 5-fold-averaged test probabilities (where tree thresholds can misfire) and to fold-specific noise, so I expect a small improvement of roughly 0.002 in log loss, though the nonlinear use of meta-features by the GBM makes a neutral-to-slightly-worse outcome plausible.

Punctuation (semicolons, dashes, quotes, ellipses) is a genuinely discriminative, transferable stylometric signal in this within-corpus random train/test split — train and test come from the same authors/editions, so 'editorial noise' still generalizes — and stripping it mainly deletes informative case-sensitive char (1,5)-gram features (word block is essentially unchanged since the default token pattern already ignores punctuation), so I expect the log loss to regress by roughly 0.01.

OOF stacking of diverse word/char TF-IDF LRs (C=10) plus tuned MultinomialNB base models with a log-prob meta-learner is a known-strong recipe for this dataset (meta CV ~0.36-0.37), and the fold-bagged test predictions should land well below the current under-regularized hstack LR baseline of 0.4386, with NB and parallel fold-fits keeping the run inside the 10-minute budget.

Dropping ~92% of the stacked word+char TF-IDF columns removes the redundant-n-gram averaging that the L2-regularized LR exploits, so the LR branch's OOF log loss worsens slightly; the NB blend-weight search re-optimizes toward NB and absorbs part of the damage, leaving a small net regression (~+0.003 log loss) on the graded test.

In authorship attribution, function words and their bigrams are among the strongest stylometric signals, so stripping 'english' stop words from the word-level TF-IDF and NB count features should slightly hurt LR and noticeably hurt NB (the char_wb block only partially compensates and the blend-weight search can only mitigate, not reverse, the loss), yielding a modest log-loss regression of roughly 1-3%.

Honest 5-fold CV over C∈{1,3,10,30,100} on ~19.5k TF-IDF rows will most likely pick C≈3–10 (the loss-vs-C curve is flat with a mild optimum above 1), yielding a small regularization-tuning gain of ~0.004–0.008 log loss over the fixed C=1 baseline on the 1,958-row graded split; there is a real chance it picks C=1 (no change) or a weaker-regularized C that slightly overfits, so the expected effect is a modest improvement, not a large one.

Proper 5-fold OOF stacking of four diverse text models (LR word/char TF-IDF, MNB word/char counts) plus stylometric meta-features with a LightGBM meta-learner is the classic recipe on this competition and historically drops log loss from a ~0.43 single stacked-LR to roughly 0.37-0.40; the correctly implemented OOF protocol and early-stopped level-2 keep overfitting in check, so expect a solid ~10% relative improvement on the graded subset, with small-test-set variance the main uncertainty.

Cross-word-boundary, case-preserving, uncapped char n-grams capture strong stylometric signal (punctuation-in-context, spacing, capitalization, function-letter habits) that the frequency-capped intra-word char_wb block misses — historically worth several points of log loss on this exact task — so expect a drop from 0.432 to roughly 0.37–0.38, with only mild overfitting risk since min_df=2, sublinear TF-IDF and L2 (C=1) keep the ~350k sparse features in check.

MNB on word counts has decorrelated errors vs the TF-IDF LR, and an OOF-tuned probability blend (small grid, ~19.5k rows) reliably buys ~0.01-0.015 log loss here (classic NB+LR ensemble effect), so I expect ~0.42 vs 0.4323, with modest noise from the ~1,958-row graded split; runtime (~6 LR fits) should stay under 10 min.

Function words are the canonical stylometric signal for authorship attribution (and sklearn's aggressive 318-word list even removes genre-relevant content words like 'fire', 'cry', 'found'), so dropping them removes discriminative unigram/bigram/char-ngram features and splices together artificial bigrams across the gaps, making the log loss slightly worse despite shorter documents and faster training.

Log loss on a test set with the natural EAP-heavy distribution is a proper scoring rule, so retraining fastText on uniformly oversampled data systematically shifts its learned priors from (0.41/0.30/0.29) toward uniform — a guaranteed first-order regression bounded by the marginal KL of ~0.012 nats — and the mild 40/31/29 imbalance means the small gains from extra minority-class updates cannot offset that prior mismatch, yielding a slight worsening from 0.6072 to roughly 0.612.

ComplementNB on the same TF-IDF is a clearly weaker but decorrelated model (OOF ~0.45 vs LR ~0.37), so the OOF sweep will pick w near 0.8-1.0, yielding either a small ensemble gain (~0.001-0.004 log loss) or a fallback to pure LR (w=1.0) that exactly reproduces the parent's 0.3548; expected value is a marginal improvement, with a small chance of a tiny regression from overconfident NB folds on the 1,958-row graded subset.

MultinomialNB's independence assumption double-counts the massively correlated word- and char-TF-IDF blocks and yields poorly calibrated probabilities on short sentences, so even with tuned alpha it typically lands ~0.40-0.44 on this task versus ~0.355 for the discriminative, C-tuned logistic regression — a clear regression, not an improvement.

Character n-grams carry most of the stylistic signal in this competition (char TF-IDF linear models outperform word-only ones), so removing them from the NB-SVM stack should degrade log loss from ~0.409 to roughly 0.44-0.45.

Plain ComplementNB (default norm=False) on the heavily-smoothed L2-TF-IDF stack lacks the one-vs-rest logistic calibration that makes NB-SVM strong, so expect a regression from 0.409 to roughly NB-level ~0.45-0.48.

3-fold CV log-loss selection will most likely pick C≈3.16 over the untuned C=1.0, which on high-dimensional sparse word+char TF-IDF typically yields a small genuine gain (~0.003–0.008 log loss), partially muted by noise on the ~1,958-row graded test set, so expect a modest improvement to roughly 0.421–0.423.

MultinomialNB's independence assumption double-counts the heavily correlated char/word n-gram blocks, producing overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities that are penalized under log loss — expect roughly a 0.04-0.05 regression versus the logistic regression baseline (0.425 → ~0.47), consistent with this competition's history where MNB TF-IDF baselines trailed LR by a wide margin.

fastText with word bigrams + char subwords (minn=2, maxn=5) historically lands ~0.38-0.42 log loss on this competition, modestly edging out an untuned word+char TF-IDF/LogisticRegression baseline (~0.43), though the dim=100 averaging bottleneck and lack of IDF weighting keep the gain small and a slight regression is possible.

C=1.0 is already near-optimal for word+char TF-IDF logistic regression on this data, so 5-fold CV over a tight grid most likely selects C≈1–2 and yields only a marginal (~1%) log-loss improvement, with a real chance of a near-identical score if C=1.0 is reselected.

NB-SVM's per-class log-count-ratio weighting is a proven strong upgrade over plain multinomial LR on this competition's TF-IDF features (historically worth ~0.01-0.02 log loss), though the gain is partly offset by one-vs-rest probability renormalization being less calibrated than softmax and mild C=4 overfit risk on the ~120k-dim stack.

The 14 stylometric features add genuine (mostly length/punctuation-rate) signal that L2-normalized TF-IDF partially destroys, at negligible variance cost with ~19k samples under fixed L2 regularization, so expect a small improvement of roughly 0.002-0.003 log loss; the features are largely redundant with char n-grams so the gain is modest, and slight regression is possible but unlikely.

This is the classic NBSVM/NB-ratio reweighting (jhoward-style one-vs-rest liblinear LR on TF-IDF multiplied by per-class log occurrence ratios), which historically beats plain multinomial TF-IDF LR on this exact competition by ~0.03-0.05 log loss; the implementation is faithful (binary occurrence matrix, +1 smoothing, per-class reweighting of train/test, row normalization), fits comfortably in the time budget, so I expect an improvement from 0.441 to roughly 0.39-0.41.

C=1.0 sits near the flat optimum for TF-IDF (sublinear, min_df=2, L2-normalized) logistic regression, so quadrupling L2 strength to C=0.25 likely underfits the redundant word+char n-gram stack slightly (~+0.003-0.005 log loss), a small regression on the ~1,958-row holdout.

Dropping the word 1-2 gram TF-IDF block removes the strongest lexical signal (distinctive author vocabulary), leaving char_wb 2-5 fragments which capture style only partially, so the char-only NB-logistic should regress log loss by roughly 8-12% relative to 0.5177.

Removing the NB log-count-ratio reweighting turns the hybrid into plain one-vs-rest L2 logistic regression on the same word+char TF-IDF; this ablation typically costs a small amount of log loss (~0.01-0.02) because the NB transform acts as a helpful author-specific feature prior, so expect a modest regression from 0.5177 to roughly 0.53 with identical runtime and output format.
