The only functional change is halving C (4.0→2.0) in both fits; the log-loss-vs-C curve for word+char TF-IDF LR is flat near its optimum, and slightly stronger L2 on ~150k correlated n-gram predictors typically trims a few ten-thousandths of log loss (the mlflow/telemetry additions and dtype tweak don't affect predictions), so expect a marginal ~0.001 improvement, essentially neutral.

The NB log-ratio rescaling mainly helps word-count features, while here it is stacked onto char n-gram TF-IDF where multinomial LR is already strong, and the one-vs-rest binary sigmoid + renormalization is typically worse calibrated for 3-class log loss than the softmax baseline, so I expect a modest regression (~+0.01 log loss) rather than an improvement.

Function words and their character n-grams are strong stylometric signals for authorship (TF-IDF's IDF already downweights them, so removal mostly destroys informative char-branch signal like ' the '/punctuation transitions rather than noise), so stripping English stop words before both vectorizers should modestly worsen log loss.

Cutting C from 1.0 to 0.25 pushes an otherwise near-optimal L2 point into mild underfitting on the high-dimensional word+char TF-IDF representation; the fitted temperature absorbs most of the global confidence shrinkage but cannot recover the slightly degraded decision boundaries, so I expect a small log-loss regression on the ~1,958-row graded test (well within its sampling noise, so a near-flat or marginally better result is plausible).

Cross-word 'char' n-grams are largely redundant with the word (1,2) bigram features and, under the 60k max_features cap, displace the discriminative within-word patterns that 'char_wb' captured, so I expect a small log-loss regression (~+0.005) from 0.4323; the removed holdout and added MLflow telemetry do not affect the graded model.

NBSVM-style per-class log-count-ratio scaling of the same word+char TF-IDF matrix is a well-validated boost for linear text models (Wang & Manning; jhoward's NB-SVM), and OVR binary-LR stacking is asymptotically calibrated for 3 classes, so I expect a modest log-loss gain (~0.43 -> ~0.42) despite mild risk from untuned C=1, TF-IDF-sum-based ratios, and slightly weaker effective regularization.

Raising C from 1.0 to 4.0 weakens L2 regularization on a ~150k-feature TF-IDF stack fit on only ~18k rows, making the already-well-fit logistic model more overconfident, which typically nudges 3-class log loss up slightly (~+0.004) on a flat regularization path; the removed holdout print has no effect on grading.

Temperature scaling fitted on the held-out 10% flattens the mildly overconfident high-dimensional TF-IDF logistic regression (train acc ~0.97 vs val ~0.85 implies T* likely ~1.1-1.2), which typically trims ~0.004-0.006 log loss; estimation noise on ~2k validation rows and transfer to the full refit limit the gain, so expect a small but real improvement rather than a large one.

RMSE rewards the dollar-scale conditional mean, but log1p-training + expm1 yields a median/geometric-mean-like estimate biased low by roughly sigma^2/(2(1+m)) (~$0.4-0.5 given the ~$3.5 conditional noise), a systematic bias that slightly outweighs the mild variance-stabilization benefit of the multiplicative error model, since the capped/cleaned fare tail is not extreme enough for log-space fitting to help.

4x more training rows with unchanged capacity/early-stopping typically cuts the valid-row RMSE from ~3.6 to ~3.45 (variance reduction), which after the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row floor maps to graded RMSE ≈ 3.95 (~3.7% better), assuming the ~4M-row LightGBM run stays inside the 15-minute kill limit.

Airport-distance features let the trees cheaply isolate JFK/LGA/EWR trips (e.g. the ~$52 JFK flat fare) that raw-coordinate splits only partially capture, giving a real but modest gain on the ~97% of test rows with valid coordinates (~3.6 → ~3.5 clean RMSE), which maps to roughly 4.19 → ~4.12 overall given the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows; compute cost is negligible, so the run stays well within budget.

L2 on log1p makes expm1 outputs estimate the conditional median/geometric mean rather than the RMSE-optimal conditional mean, so predictions run systematically ~2-6% low (notably the ~2.8% NaN-coordinate test rows, whose learned default drops from the ~$11.5 mean fare toward the ~$9 geometric mean), and the second-order MSE penalty (~0.5-1% on clean rows) plus the dampened fit of genuinely expensive trips is unlikely to be offset by the modest outlier-robustness gain, giving a small regression from 4.19 to roughly 4.22-4.25.

The constraint encodes genuinely correct domain knowledge on the dominant feature and regularizes the sparse long-trip region, but with 4M rows the ensemble already learns a near-monotone distance response (and the small true non-monotonicity at near-zero distances slightly offsets the gain), so expect only a noise-level improvement of roughly 0.1-0.2%.

The metric is plain dollar-RMSE, which is minimized by the conditional mean, but log1p-space squared-loss training (with a plain expm1 inverse and no smearing/mean correction) yields roughly the conditional geometric mean, so predictions systematically under-predict fares by ~exp(sigma_log^2/2)-1 (~2-4%); this Jensen-gap bias (~0.1-0.3 added MSE on the ~97% valid rows, i.e. +0.01-0.04 overall RMSE) is only partially offset by robustness to residual high-fare outliers, and early stopping now optimizes the wrong (log-scale) objective, so I expect a small regression from 4.126 to ~4.15.

Replacing OOF with in-sample encoding lets each training row's own fare leak into its route/cell fare_mean features (worst for the many low-count route keys, which the trees can isolate via log_count≈log1p(1)), inflating the model's reliance on the encodings so that predictions on the leak-free val/test encodings degrade — an effect that typically outweighs the modest consistency gain from removing the ~log(0.8) count offset and OOF noise, so I expect a slight RMSE regression from 4.179 to about 4.20.

With RMSE on the dollar scale the optimal prediction is the conditional mean, but log1p-training + expm1 yields approximately the conditional median, a systematic ~4-6% under-prediction (no exp(σ²/2) bias correction applied), and NYC fares are additive in dollars (base + per-mile + surcharges), so the multiplicative reweighting toward cheap rides slightly hurts; the robustness gain from taming the right tail only partially offsets this, netting a small regression of roughly 0.05 RMSE.

Airport-distance features let the trees isolate flat-rate JFK and Newark-surcharge trips with single splits, typically cutting valid-row RMSE by ~0.2 (3.6→3.4), which after the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor translates to roughly a 3-4% overall RMSE improvement (~4.14→~3.99).

The ~2.8% corrupt test rows (which contribute ~4.5 of the 17.1 total squared error) are now predicted by a model that trained on that population — it learns their subgroup mean and time/passenger covariates instead of the global valid-row mean, and passenger-count-only-invalid rows regain full coordinate-based predictions — while the ~2.8% NaN rows in training barely perturb LightGBM's splits on valid rows, so the net effect is a modest gain on the order of 2-5% RMSE.

4x more training rows with identical features/hyperparameters should cut the clean-row RMSE ~3-4% (from ~3.6 to ~3.5), which after dilution by the ~2.8% corrupt-row error floor (~26% of total MSE, unchanged) yields roughly a 2-3% overall RMSE improvement, while the usecols/float32/explicit-format tweaks and n_jobs=4 keep I/O and training (est. ~5-8 min total) inside the budget; float32 binning and the unchanged seed make the pipeline otherwise score-neutral, with the main residual risk being runtime rather than accuracy.

Correctly out-of-fold smoothed target encodings of route/endpoint cells add toll, airport-flat-fare and route-level signal that raw coords + haversine cannot express, typically worth ~0.1-0.2 RMSE on the clean rows (3.62 -> ~3.45-3.5), which after the fixed ~2.1 floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows lands near 4.05; leakage-free construction and m=20 smoothing make a regression unlikely, though sparsity of 0.02-degree route keys at 1M rows caps the gain.

Training on log1p(fare) makes both models predict ~conditional medians instead of the conditional means that RMSE rewards, so the skewed fare distribution (and especially the weak-feature fallback model, where median≈8.6 vs mean≈11.3) gets systematically under-predicted; the Jensen-gap bias (~4-5% of fare on valid rows, ~2.6 dollars on the 2.8% fallback rows) adds roughly 1% MSE that the modest robustness/variance-stabilization gains only partially offset, yielding a slight regression from 4.129 to about 4.16.

Manhattan grid distance and bearing are genuinely informative on top of haversine + raw coordinates (trees can't easily derive the L1/grid adjustment themselves), so expect a modest ~0.08-0.12 RMSE gain on the ~97% valid test rows, diluted to roughly 2% overall by the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row noise floor; training cost stays within budget and the unchanged fallback keeps the invalid rows' contribution constant.

Airport/Manhattan distance features are a proven, low-risk addition for this competition: they let the trees isolate JFK/LGA/EWR flat-fare and Manhattan regimes the raw coordinates capture only via many splits, likely cutting clean-row RMSE from ~3.60 to ~3.48-3.50, which after dilution by the ~2.8% corrupt test rows' fixed ~$12 error (floor ~2.1) yields roughly 4.00-4.03 versus 4.104, i.e. a ~2% improvement with negligible added runtime.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean, so swapping L2 for L1 makes the model predict conditional medians, which systematically under-predicts on the right-skewed fare distribution (conditional mean-median gap of roughly $1-1.5); the robustness gain on the already-cleaned (0,500] fares is small, so the added bias squared inflates MSE on the ~97% valid rows and worsens total RMSE from ~4.10 to ~4.25-4.35.

Training on log1p(fare) optimizes relative error and inverts to the conditional geometric mean, so without a smearing correction the model systematically underpredicts fares by roughly 3-5% and reallocates capacity away from expensive rides, which slightly worsens a raw-scale RMSE that squared loss on raw fares was already metric-aligned to optimize.

L1 fits the conditional median rather than the mean, and since fare distributions are right-skewed this adds a systematic low bias that RMSE punishes (early stopping on RMSE only picks the iteration count, not the quantile being fit), so the score regresses slightly despite L1's robustness to residual label noise.

alpha=1.0 makes Huber nearly an L1 objective, pulling predictions toward the conditional median of a right-skewed fare distribution and adding a systematic underprediction bias that the RMSE metric punishes quadratically, while the robustness benefit is small since cleaning already removed the worst label outliers.

Fitting log1p(fare) makes the model approximate the conditional median (expm1 of the mean-log) rather than the conditional mean that raw-scale RMSE rewards, and it under-weights dollar errors on expensive rides while the expm1 back-transform adds a ~3-5% under-prediction bias with no smearing correction, so clean-row RMSE should regress slightly (3.6 → ~3.65), diluted by the fixed ~2.1 invalid-row floor into roughly 4.13 → 4.18.

Airport distances/near-flags are a proven signal for NYC fares (JFK flat fare) and should cut clean-row RMSE by ~1.5-2%, but the gain is diluted to ~1.4% overall because ~26% of total MSE sits in the ~2.8% corrupt-coordinate test rows handled by the unchanged fallback model.

Quadrupling the random training sample (1M→4M) modestly cuts LightGBM's estimation variance on the ~97% of test rows with valid coordinates (valid-row RMSE ~3.6→~3.5) while the ~2.8% invalid-row mean-fare floor (~2.1 RMSE contribution) stays fixed, yielding roughly 4.14→~4.02 overall, and reading 4M CSV rows plus histogram LightGBM on ~3.6M×10 features fits the 10-minute budget with early stopping capping trees.

Averaging 5 fold-models trained on 80% subsets reduces prediction variance and the larger 200k-row eval sets make early stopping more stable, so the modelable (valid-row) portion of the test set improves ~0.5-1% (e.g. ~3.60 -> ~3.57 RMSE), which after mixing with the unchanged ~2.8% invalid rows predicted at the mean gives roughly 4.14 -> 4.11; the mean-fare override and data floor are untouched, per-fold training data is only slightly smaller (800k vs 900k), and runtime (~5 folds x <1000 trees with early stopping) stays within the 10-minute budget.

The leak-free OOF pickup-cell target encoding adds exactly the signal the baseline lacks — local fare level (JFK/LGA flat fares, Manhattan vs. outer boroughs) beyond raw coordinates — which should cut clean-row RMSE from ~3.56 to ~3.44, though the ~2.1 RMSE corrupt-row floor absorbs part of the gain, yielding roughly a 2-3% overall improvement; the implementation is correct (proper OOF for train, full-data encoding for test, smoothing 30) so regression risk is low.

Snapping to 0.01° adds ~0.4 km RMS noise to the dominant distance_km feature and pools away within-cell position that trees could exploit, while the route encoding already pooled at the same 0.01 scale (so it gains nothing), yielding a modest regression from ~4.13 to ~4.2.

L1 loss fits conditional medians rather than means, so on the right-skewed fare distribution predictions are biased low and tail errors grow, worsening RMSE even though early stopping still selects on RMSE.

L1 loss targets the conditional median while RMSE rewards the conditional mean; fares are right-skewed so median-fitting systematically under-predicts (and LightGBM's L1 leaves converge slowly at lr=0.05), costing roughly 0.1-0.2 RMSE on valid rows on top of the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor, only partially offset by outlier robustness.

Airport-anchor distances (especially the JFK flat-fare region) are a well-known effective feature for this dataset, but the gain is diluted by the ~2.8% corrupt test rows that set a fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor and by the model already partially learning airport zones from raw coordinates, so expect a small improvement of roughly 0.05-0.10 RMSE.

Switching to regression_l1 makes the model predict the conditional median, which under-predicts the right-skewed fare distribution (mean > median), so RMSE — an L2 metric aligned with the previous objective — degrades modestly (roughly +0.1 on the ~3.6 valid-row RMSE, ~4.25 overall).

LightGBM's adaptive histogram binning (max_bin=255, roughly equal-frequency) already pools raw coordinates at ~100-300m resolution in dense Manhattan, so rounding to 2 decimals (~1km grid) mostly discards fine-grained location signal (airports/tolls are preserved, but sub-km neighborhood effects are lost) while adding little regularization benefit beyond what min_child_samples and early stopping already provide — expect a small regression, not an improvement.

Switching to regression_l1 makes the model estimate the conditional median rather than the mean, and since fares are right-skewed (tolls, waiting time) the predictions become systematically low, which RMSE punishes; the fixed ~2.8%-corrupt-row error floor dilutes the effect, so expect a modest regression from 4.138 to roughly 4.2-4.26 rather than an improvement.

A rotated Manhattan/grid travel-distance proxy is a genuinely complementary signal to haversine for NYC street fares, typically shaving ~0.05-0.15 RMSE on valid rows, but the gain is diluted by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the ~2.8% corrupt test rows, so expect a modest improvement from 4.138 to roughly 4.05.

A correctly cross-fitted, heavily smoothed (prior weight 50) directional route-mean target encoding adds real route-level signal (airport flat fares, toll crossings) for the sizable share of rides on well-populated 0.01-degree routes that raw coordinates + haversine only partially capture, so expect a modest improvement of roughly 0.08-0.10 graded RMSE (valid-row RMSE ~3.6→~3.5) with the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor unchanged; leakage-free OOF construction and negligible runtime cost make regression unlikely, though heavy shrinkment caps the gain.

The 29°-rotated Manhattan grid distance is a classic high-value feature for NYC taxi fares (street-grid distance predicts the meter better than haversine), so expect a ~3% gain on the ~97% of valid test rows, which after the ~2.1 RMSE floor from corrupt rows dilutes to roughly a 2-3% total improvement (4.138 → ~4.03); the MLflow/tracking diff is score-neutral.

Doubling the training prefix from 1M to 2M rows gives a typical log-scale learning-curve gain of only ~0.03–0.05 RMSE on the ~97% of valid test rows, which is diluted by the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row floor, so the graded RMSE should drop slightly from 4.138 to about 4.11, with read/featurize/LightGBM time roughly doubling but still finishing well inside the 10-minute budget.

The airport_route categorical lets LightGBM directly capture JFK flat-fare and Newark-surcharge patterns that raw coordinates/haversine only learn imperfectly, so the ~5% airport trips get more accurate predictions; expect a small gain on the valid rows, partially diluted by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows.

LightGBM with this config (near the README's known-good baseline, plus native categorical handling of the f_27 letters) is the stronger learner on interaction-heavy mixed-type tabular data like TPS May 2022, so it should land slightly above the small from-scratch MLP's 0.9866 — but since both use identical raw features with no engineered interactions, the gain is likely only a few tenths of an AUC point (with real risk of a near-tie or small regression if the MLP already sits near the no-FE ceiling).

Quantile one-hot binning gives this underfitting small MLP a GBDT-like piecewise inductive bias (LightGBM on the same features beats the MLP by ~0.003 AUC), handles f_28's heavy tails and non-monotone integer/count effects directly via first-layer bin weights, at only ~10% irreducible within-bin resolution loss on the continuous columns — so I expect a small gain (~+0.001), with a real chance it lands neutral or slightly negative; runtime/memory (~1 GB dense matrix, marginally wider first layer) stay well within the 10-minute budget.

TPS-May-2022 features are nearly uncorrelated, so full-rank PCA is essentially an arbitrary random rotation (whitening adds nothing since inputs are already unit-variance), smearing the axis-aligned character/numeric interaction signal that LightGBM's greedy axis-aligned splits and leaf models exploit, so AUC regresses from 0.9786 to roughly 0.97.

f_27 is a near-unique high-cardinality string (most strings appear once), so the m=20 smoothed whole-string target encoding collapses to the prior for the vast majority of rows and carries almost no signal, while discarding the ten per-position letter columns removes the real positional string signal — the model falls back to roughly numerics-only performance (~0.96) instead of the current 0.9786.

f_27 strings are near-unique at 800k rows, so the smoothed OOF target encoding collapses toward the prior for most rows and cannot replace the ten per-position ordinal columns, whose well-pooled marginal and char×numeric interaction signal is worth roughly 0.002–0.003 AUC; keeping only f_27_nunique plus a nearly-constant TE column yields a net small regression to about 0.990.

These are the competition's well-known 'magic' interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26 threshold indicators); adding them to an LGBM on this dataset historically lifts AUC from ~0.991 to ~0.997-0.998, and trees learn them easily via the ternary indicators, so a large gain is expected within the unchanged runtime budget.

A logistic regression on the same 44 raw/ordinal columns is far weaker (~0.88-0.91 AUC, no interactions, no unique-char signal) and its errors overlap heavily with signal LightGBM already captures, so a 50/50 rank average dilutes the strong model's ranking and drops graded AUC by roughly 0.006-0.010.

A ~12k-parameter MLP on standardized raw features cannot match a 3000-tree/127-leaf LightGBM on this interaction-heavy tabular problem (trees natively capture the axis-aligned threshold/interaction structure that made this dataset famous), so expect roughly a 0.8–1.5 AUC-point regression to ~0.974 despite proper training, checkpointing, and the same features.

A small MLP on standardized raw features captures the smooth additive/interaction signal but handles the 10 ordinal-encoded f_27 positions poorly (per-letter categorical effects and unique-character-count structure that tree splits exploit), so it should land well below the 0.977 LightGBM baseline, around the mid-0.94s, while easily fitting the CPU/time budget.

The dataset's key interactions are indeed sum-of-features thresholds, so linear leaves should sharpen those oblique boundaries somewhat (leaves average ~5k samples, so the 41-dim leaf fits are stable), but split finding is still axis-aligned, the unique-character structure of f_27 is unaffected, and LightGBM linear trees historically give only marginal gains at a large (possibly budget-breaking) runtime cost — so expect a small gain, with real risk of a 15-minute kill.

The unique-character count of f_27 was one of the few consistently valuable engineered features in TPS May 2022 (a symmetric summary trees can't cheaply synthesize from the 10 per-position ordinals), so it should add a small but real gain of roughly +0.002–0.004 AUC on top of the 0.97696 baseline, with the model, split, and runtime essentially unchanged.

These are exactly the well-known TPS-May-2022 'magic' interaction sums (i_00_01_26, i_02_21, i_05_22); since axis-aligned trees can't represent diagonal sum boundaries, feeding the raw sums to LightGBM historically lifts AUC from ~0.977 to roughly 0.983-0.985 (the unique-character-count feature, not included here, would be needed for the ~0.99 regime), so I expect a solid but partial gain of about +0.006.

Deleting the 10 per-position character columns removes most of f_27's real signal, and LightGBM cannot recover it from the ~800k-cardinality whole-string categorical (max_cat_threshold=32 and mostly singleton strings below min_child_samples=100 make such splits nearly always invalid), so AUC falls back toward numeric + letter-counts + nunique (~0.975-0.985), with a substantial training-slowdown/timeout risk on top.

The 9 adjacent-character bigram categoricals are mostly redundant with signal the model already captures (per-position ordinals + letter counts + nunique), since this dataset's known interactions are mainly among numeric features, so expect a tiny positive bump at best (~+0.0002 AUC) with slight risk of noise dilution.

The 16 continuous features are near-independent, so PCA(8) components are arbitrary ~equal-variance rotations that add essentially no signal trees can't already get from the raw columns, while removing the gain-mined product interactions (which likely contributed a small real boost) and mildly diluting colsample_bytree, so the score should regress slightly toward the raw-feature baseline.

f_27 is near-unique per row (~1M distinct strings), so hashing the whole string into 64 buckets produces quasi-random one-hot noise that destroys the per-position letter signal trees were exploiting; the model falls back to numeric + mined products only, roughly 0.02-0.03 AUC below the 0.97527 baseline.

ExtraTrees with sqrt feature subsampling and random thresholds is a weaker learner than the 3000-round LightGBM on this interaction-heavy dataset, and Kaggle TPS May 2022 forests typically trail tuned GBDT by ~0.008-0.01 AUC on the raw features, so expect a solid regression to roughly 0.968-0.972 (with some risk the 3x-repeated fitting work pushes the run near the wall-clock limit).

A 40-epoch sklearn MLP with only 256/128 ReLU units and ordinal-encoded f_27 characters is both undertrained and poorly suited to the non-monotonic per-letter lookup signal that LightGBM's 3000 trees exploit fully, so despite standardization and partial interaction learning it should regress from 0.978 to roughly 0.96.

Letter-count/unique-count features are the canonical next step for TPS-May-2022: trees cannot count distinct letters from per-position categoricals, so the 27 bag-of-letters features unlock genuinely expressible signal (the pre-interaction-era public notebooks with letters+nunique sat around ~0.98), giving a solid but partial gain (~+0.005) since the largest known jump (+~0.018, to ~0.995) came from numeric interaction sums that are deliberately not added here; runtime stays within budget.

The change deletes the ten per-position letter columns, which carry most of f_27's signal (per-position letter effects plus unique-letter-count structure worth ~0.025 AUC over numeric-only), and replaces them with a single full-string frequency that only weakly proxies those effects, so AUC should fall back to roughly the numeric-only LightGBM level (~0.950-0.955) plus a small frequency boost.

The unique-character count of f_27 is a well-known strong signal in TPS-May-2022, and explicit per-letter counts spare the trees from having to learn cross-position aggregates via splits, so this should add a solid but modest ~+0.004 AUC over the 0.97696 baseline (with a small risk of slightly longer training time from 27 extra columns, still within budget).

The known real interactions in TPS-May-2022 pair low-index continuous features with f_19–f_28 (e.g. f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26), none of which are in the mined f_00..f_15 product set (which is mostly integer features), so the 25 gain-ranked products add almost no information a 3000-tree, 127-leaf GBDT can't already express — expect a change within run-to-run jitter (~±0.001), with a slight positive tilt because the model is still underfitting at 3000 trees; runtime should stay under the 15-min kill.

Since early stopping never fires (best_iter=3000 → refit with 3333 trees on all 800k rows vs 3000 trees on 720k), stage 2 recovers the 10% held-out rows and adds boosting rounds in a regime where holdout AUC was still improving, so expect a small, reliable gain of roughly +0.0003–0.0004 AUC (data scaling ~+0.0002, extra rounds ~+0.0001–0.0002) with essentially no overfitting risk since more data accompanies more rounds.

Native categorical splits let LightGBM form arbitrary letter subsets per f_27 position instead of alphabetical threshold intervals; with 26 low-cardinality levels and 3000 trees the ensemble could already approximate subsets, so expect only a small gain (~+0.001 AUC) rather than a step change.

The distinct-character count of f_27 was one of the single highest-value engineered features in this exact competition — a cross-position combinatorial signal that per-character ordinal columns cannot express in shallow tree splits — so adding it to the 0.98175 baseline should yield a solid but partial gain (~+0.005 AUC), well short of the ~0.995 full-feature-engineering ceiling since per-letter counts, pairwise position features, and richer interactions remain excluded.

Capping trees at depth 2 (4 leaves) cuts per-tree capacity ~30x versus the current 127-leaf trees while keeping the same 3000-round/0.05-lr budget, and since the baseline's holdout AUC was still improving at 3000 rounds (no overfitting), the ensemble will underfit the higher-order f_27/feature interactions and lose a few thousandths of AUC, despite faster training and native pairwise-interaction coverage.

A 600-round, 31-leaf LightGBM on raw features plus f_27 ordinals is a materially under-trained, no-feature-engineering GBDT (this competition's no-FE GBDT plateau is ~0.975 at full convergence, with 0.98+ requiring engineered interactions), so it should land around 0.971-0.975 — a clear regression from the MLP's 0.9822, while still finishing comfortably inside the time budget.

On TPS-May-2022, GBDTs without engineered features (especially the f_27 unique-character count) plateau around ~0.96 AUC — structure the parent MLP apparently approximates implicitly to reach 0.9822 — and the modest 600-tree/31-leaf/max_bin=63 budget sits below even the 3000-tree no-FE ceiling, so expect a clear regression of roughly 2%.

Collapsing the float predictors (including high-value ones like f_21/f_28/f_24) to 4-level quartile codes destroys within-bin resolution that LightGBM's 255-bin splits would otherwise exploit, so a large share of the continuous-feature signal is lost while f_27/integer features remain intact — expect a clear ~1%+ AUC regression.

Cutting num_leaves 127→7 (~depth-3 trees) at fixed 3000 rounds/lr=0.05 leaves the ensemble badly underfit on this interaction-heavy dataset (pairwise sensor interactions, f_27 cross-position structure), and since the baseline was still improving at 3000 iterations the capacity loss cannot be compensated, yielding a solid regression to roughly ~0.969-0.971; runtime actually shrinks, so the run completes safely.

num_leaves=4 turns each tree into a near-additive 3-split stump, crippling the model's ability to express the pairwise/interaction structure this dataset's signal (and the per-character f_27 effects) depends on, so despite 3000 boosting rounds at lr=0.05 the AUC should regress by roughly 0.003-0.004 from 0.9915 to ~0.987-0.989.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is one of the known planted interactions in TPS-May-2022 (the (f_00+f_01, f_26) structure); giving LightGBM this rotated projection captures the diagonal/band boundary far cheaper than axis-aligned staircasing, historically worth roughly +0.001-0.002 AUC over a chars+nunique baseline, at negligible runtime cost.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is a well-documented genuine interaction in TPS-May-2022 (the 'V-shape' sum), so exposing it explicitly to LightGBM should yield a real but modest gain of roughly +0.003–0.004 AUC over the 0.9769 no-feature-engineering baseline.

A small CPU-trained MLP (50-epoch cap, 420s budget, no feature engineering) can partially learn this dataset's interaction signal but will land a few thousandths below the 3000-tree LightGBM baseline (~0.977), since it lacks the engineered interactions (e.g., f_27 unique-count) and is compute-limited, yielding roughly ~0.972 AUC.

Letter codes at each f_27 position are nominal, so LightGBM's native categorical (subset) splits should capture per-letter and letter-pair effects more efficiently than order-imposing numeric thresholds — a small typical gain (~+0.0002-0.0004 AUC), partly damped because 3000 trees with 127 leaves can already approximate nominal splits from integer codes.

The distinct-character count of f_27 is the classic high-value engineered feature for TPS May 2022 — a 10-way interaction over the character positions that the baseline's trees can't efficiently learn from the ordinal columns alone — historically worth roughly +0.003–0.005 AUC on this exact setup, while the unchanged LightGBM config and fixed seed keep run time and noise essentially the same.

Stroke/edge pixels carry the large majority of the residual squared error and the short-schedule U-Net is underfit on them, so up-weighting dark targets should sharpen stroke geometry for a small net RMSE gain, partially offset by the objective-mismatch bias that darkens ambiguous background-adjacent pixels (which are only weight-1 in the metric).

The baseline is clearly undertrained (2000 steps, ~30-60s of the budget), so ~5-10x more steps under a fully time-annealed cosine schedule should cut RMSE by roughly 10-20% (to ~0.013-0.014), with only mild overfitting risk given the small U-Net and heavy random-crop/flip augmentation over 105 images.

Restoration literature (Zhao et al.) shows L1 usually beats MSE slightly even on PSNR/RMSE metrics thanks to non-vanishing gradients and crisper stroke edges, but the RMSE-vs-MAE objective mismatch, the heavy-white-background pixel distribution, and the short 2000-step schedule cap the gain to a ~1-2% RMSE reduction (within run-to-run variance, could land near-neutral).

With only ~105 train pairs seen ~44x per pixel by a ~10M-param U-Net, gray-level overfitting is the main failure mode, and input-only brightness/contrast jitter regularizes toward structure-based denoising; the gain is modest because BatchNorm already absorbs much of the global tone shift and the fixed 2000-step budget means the harder augmented task converges slightly less, so I expect a small improvement (~1-2%) rather than a large one, with real risk of a neutral-to-slightly-negative outcome.

The model was trained only at native scale, and the 0.75x/1.25x views require bilinear resampling of the prediction maps back to (h,w), which low-passes the sharp text-stroke edges that dominate per-pixel RMSE (a blur round-trip of a text page alone costs ~0.01-0.03 RMSE); unlike flip TTA, these scale-view errors are systematic (blurred edges) rather than independent, so averaging 12 views instead of 4 should degrade, not improve, by roughly 15-25%.

With only 2000 training steps, Dropout2d (p=0.2) mostly reduces effective capacity and slows convergence rather than curbing overfitting, and dropping e2 also corrupts the skip connection while the known dropout-BatchNorm variance shift miscalibrates eval-time statistics, so a small regression is the most likely outcome.

In a fixed 180-second training budget on an image-to-image MSE regression task, Dropout2d on every block (including the e1/e2 skip-connection sources) mostly adds gradient noise and degrades precise pixel reconstruction rather than fixing overfitting that BatchNorm and random crops already partly control, so I expect a small regression on the order of 1-3%.

The 4th level quadruples capacity and grows the receptive field from ~41px to ~89px (useful for large stains) at only ~30-35% higher step cost, so despite ~25% fewer steps in the fixed 180s time budget the extra context should yield a small RMSE gain (~2-3%), well within run-to-run variance of either sign.

A 23x23 median-filter background channel hands the U-Net an explicit stain/illumination estimate (a classic top-performing trick in this competition), making background recovery nearly free so the fixed 20x100-step budget converges to visibly lower error; small risks (border artifacts, dense-text background bias) shouldn't outweigh the gain, so I expect roughly a 20-25% RMSE reduction from 0.01625 to about 0.0125.

The 5-level U-Net (~16x params, ~2x FLOPs/step, still fits the budget at same pixels/step) has a much larger receptive field that should better capture the large-scale stain/wrinkle noise, and 256px crops make the new deep levels meaningful, so I expect a modest ~5% RMSE gain, tempered by fixed 2000-step budget, batch-8 BN noise, and mild overfit risk on 105 images.

4-way flip TTA acts like a tiny ensemble on a flip-augmented (hence near-flip-symmetric) U-Net, so the four un-flipped outputs are highly correlated and averaging trims only ~1-3% of RMSE (0.01624 -> ~0.0159), with negligible 4x inference cost well inside the budget and essentially no risk of regression.

A 360s wall-clock budget almost certainly yields several-fold more optimizer steps than the current 2000-step schedule (the small UNet at batch 32/128px runs ~10-40ms/step on GPU, so the baseline trains only ~30-90s and is undertrained), and the cosine-to-zero LR over the full budget lets it converge further; expect ~10-20% RMSE reduction, partly eroded by validation passes eating into the budget and mild overfitting on 105 images, while total runtime (~420-500s) should still finish within the limit.

The metric is RMSE, which the conditional-mean (MSE-trained) predictor directly optimizes; Charbonnier's bounded gradients systematically under-weight the high-error stain/edge pixels that dominate squared error and push edge predictions toward the median (more binary) instead of the gray mean, so I expect a modest regression (~0.1–0.3 dB equivalent), not the improvement the SR-literature motivation suggests.

σ=0.05 injected noise is large relative to the current 0.0152 error, so under the fixed short training budget the model must spend capacity removing a corruption type absent at test time (train/test input mismatch, mild over-smoothing near text edges), which likely slightly outweighs the genuine anti-memorization benefit on this small dataset.

GroupNorm removes BatchNorm's mismatch between batch statistics estimated on 128x128 crops of an 87.5%-synthetic mixture and the running statistics applied to full real test pages (the classic crop-train/full-image-infer BN weakness), so I expect a small but real RMSE gain of ~2-3%, partially offset by GN's typically marginally slower convergence in this short 2000-step schedule.

The graded metric is per-pixel RMSE, for which MSE is the matched (proper) loss; Zhao et al.'s SSIM+L1 composite is a perceptual objective that in their own paper trades PSNR/RMSE for structural quality, and here it de-emphasizes the flat white background pixels that dominate the RMSE computation, so I expect a small (~2-4%) regression from 0.02767 to roughly 0.0285 despite identical architecture, data, and budget.

8-fold dihedral TTA is a low-variance ensembling trick that typically cuts RMSE a couple percent on patch-regression U-Nets; the gain is partly diluted because flips/rot180 are already in-distribution from training augmentation and rot90 views are slightly out-of-distribution for upright text, but averaging still reduces prediction variance, and the extra ~1 min of forward passes fits the time budget.

The graded metric is per-pixel RMSE, for which MSE is the matched loss; pure SSIM (Zhao et al.) consistently costs a few tenths of a dB PSNR on denoising, and computing the blur(x^2)-mu_x^2 variance terms under bfloat16 autocast near white backgrounds (true variance ~1e-4 vs bf16 rounding ~2e-3, C2=9e-4) adds noisy/unstable gradients, so I expect a moderate regression (~10-25%) rather than an improvement.

Residual (DnCNN-style) learning with zero-init output starts the model at the identity (noisy input is already a decent estimate), removes sigmoid saturation exactly on the dominant near-white background where gradients were shrinking, and the inference-time clamp forgives noise over-estimation, so with identical capacity/schedule it should converge faster and cleaner, cutting RMSE by roughly 8-13%; risks are minor (bf16/fp32 promotion is unchanged and TTA algebra stays correct since subtraction is per-view).

The metric is RMSE, so MSE was already the matched objective; replacing it with sqrt(MSE) shrinks the pixel-gradient ~10-25x under Adam (amplifying the SSIM term's effective weight late in training), and SSIM is nearly blind to the flat, low-contrast stain shifts this task needs removed while pushing edge sharpening/overshoot, so a small regression (roughly 1-4%) is the most likely outcome, well within the time budget.

Residual (DnCNN-style) learning with zero-initialized head starts at the noisy-input identity, converges faster under the tight epoch budget, and avoids sigmoid saturation on the predominantly-white background, so a modest ~4% RMSE improvement is the most likely outcome.

Synthetic stain/shading/speckle corruption approximates the real artifact process and multiplies noise realizations per document (curbing memorization of image-specific artifacts), so despite diluting the 105 real pairs to ~1/7 of sampled crops under the fixed 2000-step budget, the shared denoising structure should transfer and give a modest generalization gain; a small regression is possible if the synthetic noise mismatch dominates.

Stretching the same recipe from 2,000 to 9,000 steps with the cosine schedule annealed over the full run gives a converged LR-to-zero model that should cut RMSE by roughly 10-15% on this small U-Net denoiser (random crops/BN limit overfitting), with residual risk that only ~45 epochs fit the 10-minute budget.

Averaging over the 8 dihedral transforms is a variance-reducing ensemble at inference: the 4 flip variants align with the flip augmentation already used in training (so inverse transforms are exact and predictions consistent), the 4 transposed variants add mild diversity, and typical dihedral-TTA gains for a fully-convolutional denoiser are ~1-3% relative RMSE, while the 8x forward-pass cost (~1600 extra full-image passes for validation plus 232 for test) stays well within the 10-minute budget on GPU.

MSE training directly matches the RMSE evaluation and its quadratic gradient weighting concentrates capacity on the high-residual stain/edge pixels that dominate squared error, while L1's constant gradient magnitude shifts optimization toward the abundant easy background pixels, so a small regression of a few percent is the most likely outcome.

The eval is unweighted per-pixel RMSE dominated by the ~90% white-background pixels, so shifting the loss toward black targets (weight 3) mostly biases the sigmoid outputs darker on easy constant-black strokes while slightly degrading the majority white pixels, giving a small net regression rather than the hoped-for edge-accuracy gain.

The graded metric is unweighted RMSE, and in this dataset most squared error sits on white-target pixels (residual stains, noisy background) whose gradients get diluted ~1.6x by the weight normalization, while the extra 10x emphasis goes to hard, capacity-limited ink/edge pixels — an objective mismatch that should trade away more stain/background accuracy than it recovers on text, yielding a mild regression.

Zero-init residual (identity) prediction removes sigmoid saturation on near-bimodal 0/1 document pixels, lets the small U-Net learn only the stain/noise correction instead of regenerating text, and converges faster within the fixed 2000-step budget, so validation/test RMSE should drop modestly (~5-10%) despite inference clamping.

RMSE rewards the conditional mean, which MSE trains directly; L1 pushes predictions toward the conditional median, giving modest gains on easy background pixels but larger squared errors on the hard, uncertain corruption pixels that dominate RMSE, so a small regression (~2-5%) is the most likely outcome given the heavy-tailed residual distribution and short 2000-step training schedule where loss-induced bias, not capacity, differentiates the two.

Zero-initialized residual head starts at the identity (RMSE ≈ noisy-vs-clean), passes sharp text through untouched via the input skip so the network only has to learn stain removal, which typically converges faster and with less regression-to-mean blur than a from-scratch sigmoid head within this 2000-step budget.

Dropping BASE_CH 16→8 cuts parameters ~4.5x (roughly 500k→115k); with the fixed 2000-step budget the network is still capacity/optimization-limited on this task, so expect a modest RMSE regression of ~5-8% rather than a regularization gain, though the residual global connection keeps the degradation contained.

The 3:1 foreground weighting shifts the training objective away from the conditional mean that plain MSE (identical to the graded unweighted RMSE) would converge to: the weighted-optimal predictor is biased dark on ambiguous stroke-edge pixels (e.g. p=0.5 maps to ~0.25, raising their squared error ~25%) while giving less gradient to the majority-white background, so the loss/metric mismatch should regress per-pixel RMSE by a few percent despite better stroke emphasis.

The closing-based background-division channel hands the U-Net an illumination/stain-normalized input (background ~1, text dark), removing a major smooth-background error source for near-zero compute cost, so with the same 2000-update budget I expect a solid but partial gain (~5-10% lower RMSE), not a transformation, since text-edge reconstruction still dominates the residual error.

The only systematic effect is removing bf16 quantization of the sigmoid output (ULP ~2^-8 near 1.0 gives ~1e-3 RMS noise on the mostly-white pixels, ~0.2% of the 0.01624 RMSE in quadrature), while the fp32 last-layer training-path change shifts the trajectory only marginally, so expect a tiny improvement of roughly 0.1-0.3%.

Four-view flip TTA averages out prediction noise and filter asymmetries of a flip-augmented U-Net, typically yielding a small (~1%) RMSE reduction at negligible extra inference cost, though vertical flips of text make the gain modest.

The small NAFNet (similar ~600k params, ~6x fewer MACs, deeper /8 pyramid, global residual without sigmoid, no BN train/eval mismatch) should roughly match or slightly beat the BN-ReLU U-Net at this fixed 2000-step budget — larger receptive field helps stain removal and residual output avoids sigmoid saturation, while zero-init beta/gamma warm-up and thinner 16-ch full-resolution capacity cap the gain, so I expect a small improvement (~0.0158 vs 0.01624), with genuine risk of parity or a slight regression.

The competition's images are Stanford Dogs, i.e. ImageNet-1k train images, so the fb_in22k_ft_in1k head has literally been fine-tuned on these exact pictures with the exact 120 breed labels; after temperature-tuning and holdout-tuned blending (w=0 in the grid caps the downside) it should land around 0.20-0.26 — bimodal, ~0.15-0.20 if memorization is strong, ~0.29-0.30 if it isn't.

Hard-truncating the 1024-d ConvNeXt features to the top-256 PCs discards low-variance directions that a holdout-tuned L2 logistic regression would already softly shrink (and fine-grained breed cues leak into the tail), so expect a small log-loss regression (~0.005 absolute) rather than a gain; PCA fit/transform costs only seconds so runtime stays well within budget.

Full-strength mixup/cutmix (prob 1.0, alpha 0.8/1.0) on only a 6-epoch fine-tune is aggressive — timm's own short fine-tune recipes weaken mixup to 0.1 — so the model slightly underfits; temperature scaling absorbs most of the calibration/hedging benefit, leaving a small net regression in log loss.

Lowering min_scale to 0.08 makes ~30% of training views heavily zoomed (often cropping out the head/ears that carry the discriminative fine-grained cues) in a whole-object task evaluated with full-view center crops over only 6 epochs, so the added augmentation diversity likely fails to outweigh the label noise and train/test view mismatch — a small log-loss regression.

ConvNeXt-V2 Large (in22k→in1k, ~87% ImageNet top-1 vs ResNet-50's 76%) yields far more discriminative frozen features plus its own strong 1000-d dog-breed logits, lifting linear-probe accuracy on this fine-grained task from roughly ~83% to ~90% and cutting log loss by about a third (0.449→~0.30), while the fp16 forward pass over 20.5k images stays well within the runtime budget.

The 1000-d log-softmax block is not mere noise: ~118 of its columns are the pretrained ImageNet classifier's dog-breed logits (Stanford Dogs is a subset of ImageNet), effectively distilling an ~85%-accurate breed classifier into the linear head for free, which a 9k-sample L2-regularized LR on 2048 pooled features alone cannot fully relearn; dropping it should cost roughly 0.04-0.06 log loss despite the collinearity/noise-dimension concerns.

Ridge+temperature spans the same softmax-linear family as LR and gains a decoupled holdout-tuned temperature, but the ±1 least-squares surrogate slightly misfits per-class score scales and is outlier-sensitive, so expect an essentially-wash-to-slightly-worse log loss (~1-2% regression).

PCA to 128 non-whitened components per block is a lossy compression that discards low-variance but discriminative directions needed for fine-grained 120-breed separation, while the existing tuned-C L2 regularization already controls overfitting, so I expect a small regression (~0.336 -> ~0.347) rather than a gain.

convnext_base.fb_in22k_ft_in1k is a much stronger backbone than ResNet-50 V1 (~86% vs ~76% ImageNet top-1) and has explicitly seen all 120 dog breeds during in1k head training, so its 1024-d pooled features linearly probe Stanford Dogs at roughly 90% accuracy (vs ~82% for the ResNet-50 probe behind the 0.4515 baseline), cutting log loss by about a third; the holdout-based C re-selection preserves calibration, the transform (224, crop_pct 0.875, ImageNet stats) matches the checkpoint, and the ~2-4x heavier extraction plus 5 logistic fits still fit comfortably within the 10-minute budget, so the main risks (350MB HF download availability, minor bilinear-vs-bicubic resize mismatch) are small.

Fine-tuning an ImageNet-22k ConvNeXt-Tiny for 6 epochs with label smoothing, flip-TTA and temperature calibration should lift top-1 accuracy from ~82% (frozen ResNet-50 + LogReg) to ~88-91%, cutting log loss from 0.45 to roughly 0.28-0.32; the 7-minute guard only mildly reduces epochs on slower GPUs, so a large improvement is the likely outcome.

The ImageNet-trained head is itself a strong 120-breed classifier (all competition breeds are ImageNet classes), so appending its 1000-d log-softmax to the pooled features injects prior knowledge a 9.2k-sample linear probe can't learn alone; standardization plus re-tuned C should recover most of that benefit, plausibly ~0.45→~0.40, though 880 near-noise non-dog columns, a C grid capped at 0.1, and five 3048-d lbfgs fits (runtime risk) temper the expected gain.

Concatenating three diverse, stronger-than-ResNet50 frozen backbones (IN-22k supervised ConvNeXt-B, DINOv2, CLIP) with per-block L2 normalization and holdout-tuned C decorrelates errors and should lift linear-probe accuracy from ~80% to ~92%, cutting log loss from 0.45 to roughly 0.25-0.30 while staying well within the compute budget.

On this balanced 120-class dataset focal loss (γ=2) removes label smoothing's calibration benefit, shrinks gradient magnitude on the easy majority (tunnel effect, effectively under-training within 10 epochs), and yields overconfident wrong predictions on confusable breeds — confident mistakes are exactly what log loss punishes, so I expect a regression from 0.66 to roughly 0.72–0.78.

Dog breeds are already ImageNet classes, so full fine-tuning exploits well-matched mid-level features and, at only 10 epochs with augmentation+label smoothing, is more likely under- than overfitting; freezing conv1-layer3 (trainable params drop to ~15M, still ~60% not 'a sixth') removes capacity, so layer4+fc-only typically loses a few top-1 points and log loss regresses ~0.03-0.08, while the still-updating BN running stats in frozen layers add mild train/test mismatch.

Hflip TTA averages two fairly-correlated but decorrelated-error views of each test image (the augreg model was pretrained with flip augmentation, so flipped features remain in-distribution), which typically smooths overconfident probabilities and yields a modest ~1-2% relative log-loss reduction on a 0.51 baseline.

The 120 dog breeds are ImageNet-1k classes, so the current ViT-B/16 (in21k→in1k fine-tuned) features are near-ideal for a linear probe (~85% acc, 0.51 LL), whereas CLIP's contrastive B/32 features with a coarse 49-token patch grid and no label-taxonomy specialization should drop linear-probe accuracy to roughly ~70%, about doubling the log loss despite CLIP's robustness advantages, which don't help on this in-distribution fine-grained task.

Truncating to 256/2048 PCs discards low-variance directions that still carry fine-grained breed signal, and layered on top of an already-tuned L2 (C=0.3, no retuning, no whitening) it acts as extra un-tuned regularization, so the calibrated log loss should regress slightly rather than improve.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 features are dramatically stronger than supervised ResNet-50 features for fine-grained dog-breed discrimination (linear-probe accuracy typically jumps from ~80% to ~88-90% on Stanford Dogs), so log loss should fall from 0.438 to roughly 0.28-0.33 (~0.30 point estimate) with the same LR head + 10-view TTA; compute (~19.4k ViT-B/14 @224 forwards in fp16, ~5x R50 FLOPs) and the C re-selection both fit comfortably in the 10-minute budget, with the main residual risks being the one-time weight download and the mild handicap of running DINOv2 at 224 rather than its native 518 resolution.

PCA-256 with whitening acts as a mild regularizer on the highly collinear 2816-d concatenated features and lets lbfgs converge cleanly (the raw 2816-d fit is likely near the iteration cap), so I expect a small log-loss gain, though truncation may discard some fine-grained low-variance signal, capping the improvement at a couple percent.

k-NN's discrete distance-weighted votes give similar top-1 accuracy but much poorer calibrated probabilities on a 120-class fine-grained problem — images whose 10 neighbors are all from a confusable breed get ~9e-4 true-class probability (≈7.0 log-loss each after the 1e-3 mix) and many correct cases sit at ~0.4-0.9 confidence — so log loss should roughly double versus the well-regularized linear head (0.54 → ~0.85-1.0).

Fine-tuning the full network on a 120-way task the ImageNet backbone was essentially pretrained on (dog breeds are ImageNet classes) should add a few accuracy points over the frozen-feature linear probe, and label smoothing keeps wrong-prediction probabilities tame, so log loss should improve modestly from 0.453 to roughly 0.40-0.42 — though the gain is capped because the frozen baseline already exploits that pretraining overlap, and the ~0.105-per-correct-sample label-smoothing floor plus 10 short epochs make parity or slight regression plausible.

ViT-B/16 with in21k pretraining and in1k fine-tuning (which includes these exact 120 breeds) yields far more linearly-separable fine-grained features than ResNet-50 V1, so the identical logistic-regression head should lift probe accuracy from ~80% to ~87-89% and cut log loss by roughly a third; the untuned C=0.3 and no standardization add mild overconfidence risk but are unlikely to outweigh the feature-quality gain, and ViT-B extraction at ~4x ResNet FLOPs still fits the 10-minute budget.

Probability-averaging over 10 correlated but diverse views (5 crops × flips) is a classic variance-reduction ensemble that typically trims ~1-1.5% off log loss for a frozen ResNet-50 classifier; corner crops are slightly out-of-distribution for the center-crop-trained LR, capping the gain to a modest improvement over 0.4529.

ConvNeXt-Tiny (in22k_ft_in1k) features are far stronger than ResNet-50 V1 for this ImageNet-derived dog task, and per-block L2 normalization plus a concatenated 2816-d linear probe should cut log loss substantially (to roughly 0.30-0.34), well within the time budget since it only adds one frozen inference pass.

The Stanford Dogs images are ImageNet-train images that the frozen ResNet-50 head has essentially memorized, so blending the CV-tuned, temperature-scaled 120-dog pretrained logits (high alpha) with the linear probe should cut log loss from ~0.31 to roughly 0.15-0.22 (point estimate ~0.19), with the alpha=0 fallback capping downside.

Un-whitened PCA truncation to 256 of 2048 dims discards low-variance directions that carry fine-grained breed-discriminative signal (Norfolk vs Norwich-type distinctions), while C=0.3 was already tuned for the full raw features, so the added bias likely outweighs the mild denoising/regularization benefit, yielding a modest log-loss regression.

ResNet-50 was trained with global average pooling, so max-pooled descriptors are noisier and differently scaled (C=0.3 was tuned for GAP features), and GAP almost always beats GMP for frozen-feature linear probing; expect a modest log-loss regression of roughly 3-4%.

IMAGENET1K_V2 ResNet-50 weights (80.9% vs 76.1% ImageNet top-1) are trained with a stronger recipe and consistently yield more discriminative frozen features for linear probing, so the logistic head should lose less log loss (roughly a 5-7% relative gain), while the existing temperature calibration on the holdout keeps the sharper predictions from being overconfident.

C=0.3 was already holdout-selected over 0.03 for this exact feature set, and while the 2-epoch/90s bottleneck fine-tune will partially wash out the more-shrunk head (underconfident heads catch up quickly via larger gradients), the fixed fine-tune budget means the C=0.03 initialization ends the run slightly further from the optimum in both head and conv tuning, yielding a small log-loss regression.

Dropping the crop from 224 to 192 shrinks objects to ~0.86x the scale the pretrained ResNet-50 filters (and frozen BN statistics) were trained on and discards fine-grained detail critical for 120-breed discrimination, and the short last-block-only fine-tune can only partially re-adapt, so log loss should regress by a few hundredths despite faster feature extraction.

Non-whitened PCA to 256 of 2048 dims discards low-variance directions that carry fine-grained breed signal, and the C=0.3 tuned for raw features is mismatched to the rescaled PCA space, so the pipeline should regress log loss modestly (roughly 0.429 → ~0.45).

Dropping the input from 224px to 192px (with IMAGENET1K_V1 weights trained at 224) degrades the frozen ResNet-50 features for fine-grained breed discrimination — a 6x6 instead of 7x7 feature grid and a ~14% scale mismatch — costing a few accuracy points and raising log loss by roughly 5%, only partially offset by the classifier being refit on the same lower-resolution features and slightly softer predicted probabilities.

The IMAGENET1K_V2 checkpoint has ~4.7pt higher ImageNet top-1 than V1 and Stanford Dogs is an ImageNet subset, so its frozen 2048-d features should be meaningfully more linearly separable for the 120 breeds, cutting log loss by roughly 8-10% even with the C=0.3 that was tuned on V1 features.

Temperature scaling only recalibrates the softmax of an already-regularized logistic regression (whose predict_proba is softmax(decision_function)), so the validation-tuned T (likely near 1) should transfer only a tiny gain to test log loss — second-order at best, with some risk of ~0 if T≈1.

Two epochs of low-lr fine-tuning of the last bottleneck (with a well-regularized LR-init head, frozen BN, and deterministic crops) is one of the most reliable small wins over a linear probe — expect a few hundredths of log-loss improvement — though the weakly-regularized CE refit of the head over only ~288 steps adds some overconfidence risk, so the gain is modest rather than large.

Horizontal-flip TTA on dog images (breed is mirror-invariant) averages two correlated probability estimates, typically yielding a small but consistent ~1-2% relative log-loss reduction for a frozen-backbone linear probe; cost is one extra test pass (1023 images), well within budget.

Keeping C fixed while cutting per-label training rows 5x (toxic) to 163x (threat) massively strengthens effective L2 regularization and makes branch B's NB log-count ratios noisy (threat: 490 sampled negatives), so the rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic) lose several thousandths of AUC each while the frequent labels stay roughly flat — the rank-average blend cannot undo this, yielding a net regression of ~0.004 mean AUC despite the intercept-shift argument being AUC-neutral in principle.

Char 2-6-gram features carry strong per-label signal (obscenity, rare slurs) that branch B's word-only NB-LogReg currently lacks, so B strengthens and drags the 50/50 rank blend up (~+0.001), but the gain is dampened by feature redundancy with branch A (which already uses the identical char block) and by normalize() already de-obfuscating much of what char n-grams would capture, so expect a modest improvement to ~0.9813 rather than a large jump, with a small risk of timeout-adjacent runtime growth from six liblinear fits on a ~136M-nnz matrix.

AUC is threshold-free so class imbalance mostly hurts calibration, not ranking; aggressive 1:1 undersampling discards most negatives and leaves tiny fits for rare labels (threat: 956 rows, severe_toxic: 3190, identity_hate: 2810) with 60k-200k features, adding variance that degrades the rare columns (and the OOF stack features) that dominate the column mean.

MultinomialNB is essentially the NB-weighting half of the current NB-LogReg branch with the discriminative layer removed, so branch B weakens on its own (hardest on rare labels like threat/identity_hate where Laplace smoothing shrinks informative n-gram weights), and while its more generative error profile adds some diversity, the 50/50 rank blend and the OOF stack features fed to branch A both lose more from the weaker component than they gain from decorrelation, netting a ~0.003 AUC regression.

Mean-pooled self-trained Word2Vec (200-dim, 5 epochs on ~20M tokens) + linear/MLP heads is far weaker than the char+word n-gram branch it replaces (char n-grams are key for profanity/obfuscation and rare labels), so two of the three blended branches drop to ~0.95-0.96 while branch B stays ~0.978, dragging the equal-weight rank average down to roughly 0.971-0.976 despite the modest transductive benefit of embedding test-set tokens.

1:1 undersampling throws away most of the negatives (threat drops to ~956 training rows, severe_toxic ~3.2k) and effectively strengthens the L2 penalty relative to the (sum-form) data term, so the rare-label columns regress meaningfully while frequent labels are roughly neutral; the rank-average blend loses a few thousandths, giving ~0.976 vs 0.9808.

Branch D (a 128-unit shared-hidden MLP on the union TF-IDF features) is the only non-linear, multi-task model in the blend and should add a small diversity gain on the noisy rare columns, but its rank-128 bottleneck, 90%-data fit, and equal 1/4 weight against three strong linear branches cap the upside at a few ten-thousandths, with modest dilution/skip risk (time guards, 0.97 sanity floor) roughly offsetting.

AUC is prior-invariant for well-specified models, so balancing buys little, while discarding 80–99% of the negatives (threat trains on just 956 rows) destroys hard-negative information and inflates variance in all three branches at once — expect roughly a 0.003–0.008 mean-AUC regression, centered near -0.005.

Profanity de-obfuscation plus elongation-collapsing concentrates the word-TFIDF/NB-LogReg signal for the noisy sparse labels (threat, identity_hate) where the char n-gram branch was already robust, so the 50/50 rank blend should see a small net gain (~+0.001-0.002), with URL/timestamp scrubbing roughly neutral; slight offsetting risk from lost char-ngram expressiveness (e.g. '!!!!' runs).

The stacking idea itself is sound but only worth ~+0.0005 if it finishes; the real problem is compute — the OOF loop turns branch B's 6 liblinear dual fits into 36 (30 extra fits on ~128k×200k plus 30 test-set multiply/predict passes over 153k rows plus per-fold r recomputation), adding roughly 6–10 minutes to a pipeline already near ~10 minutes with the 4-minute char vectorizer still to come, so the run is very likely hard-killed at 15 minutes before submission.csv is ever written, recording a failed run (score 0) rather than a metric change.

A 3-epoch, 64-unit MLP on branch A's own 60k features will be an undertrained, A-correlated model (weak especially on rare labels like threat/identity_hate), so giving it equal 1/3 rank weight dilutes the strong A+B blend slightly rather than adding diversity — expect a small regression of ~0.001 in mean AUC, with runtime still fitting under the kill limit.

Branch C (NB-weighted word 1-2-gram + char_wb n-grams) is a genuinely diverse, roughly peer-strength linear model — char n-grams with NB weights were a known strong signal in this competition — so an equal three-way rank blend should add a small gain (~+0.0005), modestly offset by C's high correlation with B (shared 200k word block) and the max_iter=100 convergence cap, which the baseline's own experiments suggest has little AUC effect.

Per-label validation-tuned blend weights (with 0.5 shrinkage toward equal) capture a small genuine signal on the well-populated labels (toxic/obscene/insult) while the shrinkage limits damage from noisy rare-label argmaxes (threat/identity_hate have only ~100-300 holdout positives), so the net effect over the already near-optimal 0.5/0.5 rank average is a tiny +0.0002-ish gain; secondary risk is the extra ~half-pass of vectorizer fitting plus 12 more liblinear fits pushing runtime from ~8min toward the 10-min guideline, though it should still finish before the 15-min hard kill.

Compressing 100k word n-grams to 300 dense SVD components discards the char n-gram signal and the low-variance directions that carry rare-label (threat/identity_hate) discrimination, so the single LSA+LogReg model loses ~0.02 mean AUC versus the two-branch sparse ensemble despite its denoising motivation.

Undersampling to 10:1 leaves 'toxic' untouched but discards 90-97% of negatives for the rare labels (threat, identity_hate, severe_toxic), thinning the NB log-count ratios and raising fit variance, so those noisy columns wobble slightly down on net even though training gets faster and better-conditioned; the three correlated branches share the same subsample, so the blend absorbs rather than cancels the error.

A 7-class softmax forces the six toxicity labels to compete for probability mass with __label__clean, so per-column scores are distorted by the shared normalizer (multi-label positives like obscene+insult get deflated on the toxic/severe/threat columns), whereas the current six one-vs-rest fastText models directly optimize each column's ranking; expect a slightly weaker branch F diluted into the 1/3 rank average, i.e. a small regression (~-0.2 to -0.4%), with the consolation of a much shorter runtime.

For binary labels ComplementNB's ranking score is essentially plain MNB (X·log-count-ratio plus a length term), i.e. the 'NB' half of branch B without the logistic refit, without TF-IDF/sublinear damping, without char n-grams, and without the 3-branch ensemble — each of which is worth AUC on this task — so expect a solid regression from 0.9816 to roughly 0.95, with the rare labels (threat, identity_hate) and obfuscation-sensitive labels (obscene) hit hardest; runtime is safely within budget.

From-scratch Word2Vec (only ~22M tokens, 5 epochs) with unweighted mean pooling discards the exact surface-form and char-n-gram matching that drives this metric — diluting rare-label signal (threat, identity_hate) and missing obfuscated profanity — so a single dense LR head should land around 0.955-0.968, a clear regression from the 0.9816 TF-IDF ensemble.

Average-pooled, corpus-trained Word2Vec (small ~22M-token corpus, min_count=5, order-agnostic mean) throws away the exact lexical and char-n-gram evidence (slurs, obfuscated profanity) that drives toxicity AUC, so a per-label logistic regression on the 200-d mean vector should land around 0.94-0.96 mean AUC — a clear regression from the ~0.98 n-gram rank-blend, consistent with historical results where even attention-LSTMs with huge pretrained embeddings only marginally beat linear n-gram models.

The new char_wb 3-5 vectorizer alone costs ~2.5 min to fit plus ~1.5-2 min to transform on ~300k docs (the README already flags the existing 4-min char vectorizer as the budget-dominant cost and warns against adding vectorizers), and the six dual-liblinear fits run on matrices with ~5-7x branch B's nnz — branch B already maxes its 1000-iteration cap — adding roughly 8-14 min to an ~8-10 min pipeline, so the run is very likely hard-killed at 15 minutes with no submission written (if it did finish, the three-way tuned blend would only gain ~+0.001-0.002).

The rationale misattributes configs: C=0.1/sag is actually the proven reference setting for this exact word+char TF-IDF branch, while C=4/liblinear is tuned for the NB-ratio-weighted features of branch B; without that feature scaling, 40x weaker regularization overfits the rare labels (threat ~478 pos, identity_hate ~1.4k pos), dragging branch A down ~0.001-0.003 mean AUC, which the 0.5/0.5 rank blend with the unchanged branch B dampens to roughly -0.001.

A fastText word-bigram embedding classifier (~0.979-0.981 standalone on this dataset with the given preprocessing/hyperparameters) is genuinely diverse from both TF-IDF linear branches, so an equal-weight 3-way rank average should net a small ~+0.001 gain, partially capped by equal weighting on a slightly weaker third model, rare-label (threat/identity_hate) noise, and a tight-but-feasible wall-clock budget.

Branch C adds a second full char n-gram pipeline over the same ~313k docs (vectorizer fit ~4-5 min + transform ~2 min + 6 primal liblinear fits) on top of a run that already sits near the 10-min aim with the char fit as its dominant cost, so the total lands ~16-19 min and is hard-killed at 15 min before submission.csv is written — the graded score collapses to 0 (had it fit, the extra char-NB view would likely have added only ~+0.001 AUC to the rank blend).

The two branches are highly correlated so the true gain from per-label weights over 0.5/0.5 is tiny (~+0.0002), while training on 90% of data and noisy holdout tuning on rare labels (threat has only ~50 holdout positives) costs a similar amount, netting a very slight regression.

Per-label NB log-count-ratio reweighting is a proven booster for sparse linear toxic-text models (especially the noisy rare columns threat/identity_hate) and pairs well with the strong C=0.1 regularization, but making branch A NB-weighted like branch B reduces blend diversity and C=0.1 is no longer tuned for the rescaled features, so the net effect is a small positive gain (~+0.0005 AUC).

min_df=0.01 on the ~313k-doc corpus requires ~3,127 document occurrences, wiping out rare-but-highly-discriminative profanity, slurs, and misspellings: branch B's 200k word/bigram vocabulary collapses to a few hundred function words and branch A's char n-grams lose the rare tail that gives them misspelling robustness, so the equal-weight rank blend regresses by roughly 1-1.5 AUC points (with rare labels like identity_hate hurt most), though runtime only gets faster.

Discarding 81-99% of negatives per label (threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic trained on only ~1-3k rows) inflates coefficient variance and removes hard negatives from both branches, so the blend loses roughly 1 AUC point overall despite the faster, still-completing run.

Cosine class-centroid (Rocchio) classifiers lose the discriminatively-trained per-feature weights of logistic regression, especially hurting rare labels (threat, identity_hate) whose positive prototypes are estimated from a few hundred docs, so despite the same TF-IDF/NB features and blend the mean AUC should drop from ~0.980 to ~0.96.

char_wb spends the 50k feature budget on word-boundary-padded within-word n-grams (stronger profanity/obfuscation signal, less cross-word filler) and typically edges out plain 'char' on this dataset, so branch A should gain ~0.0008 AUC, roughly halving to ~+0.0004 after the 50/50 rank blend with the unchanged NB branch.

ComplementNB is a generative log-count-ratio linear scorer that lacks the discriminative training of the tuned LRs it replaces (and drops branch B's NB-weighted-LR trick), so both branches lose several thousandths of AUC — especially on rare labels like threat/identity_hate — leaving the rank-average blend around ~0.974 despite the retained word/char feature diversity and much faster fit.

A 32-component unsupervised SVD is a severe rank bottleneck on branch A's 60k TF-IDF features (a linear model on SVD output is just a linear model constrained to a 32-dim subspace), destroying much of the lexical discriminative signal — especially for rare labels like threat/identity_hate — so branch A drops from ~0.97 to roughly 0.91-0.93 and the 50/50 rank blend falls to about 0.95-0.96 despite the unchanged fastText branch (runtime actually shrinks, so no timeout risk).

Collapsing every token outside the top-2k document-frequency vocabulary into a single 'raretoken' guts the char n-gram branch's core strength (obfuscated/misspelled profanity and rare slurs), strips mid-frequency toxicity words (cunt, faggot, nigger, moron...) that the rare-label columns depend on, and makes both blend branches near-duplicates on a ~2k-word language, so mean AUC drops from ~0.973 to roughly 0.96 despite common profanity (fuck, shit, stupid) surviving the cutoff.

sklearn's English stop list removes highly toxic-predictive tokens like 'you', 'your', 'not', 'will' (directed attacks: 'fuck you', 'I will kill you'), so keeping them should add real signal to the word block at the cost of only ~200 displaced tail words under the 10k cap — a small gain, heavily diluted by the unchanged char n-gram and NB branches in the 50/50 rank blend.

Logit-space averaging lets the overconfident, saturation-prone NB branch (C=4, logits clipped at ±27.6) dominate rows where branch A's opinion is drowned out, losing rank averaging's calibration robustness, so expect a small regression of a few ten-thousandths of AUC.

char n-grams spanning word boundaries mostly add high-frequency low-signal features that crowd the fixed 50k budget (redundant with branch B's word bigrams for phrase signal) while char_wb's word-bounded n-grams are the battle-tested config for catching obfuscated profanity, so branch A degrades slightly and the 50/50 rank blend dips by a few ten-thousandths.

fastText (dim=64, 5 epochs, no subwords, train-only text) is a slightly weaker and less-tuned word-bigram model than the proven NB-LogReg branch it replaces — the 64-dim bottleneck and few epochs hurt rare labels (threat, identity_hate) — so the unchanged 50/50 rank blend with branch A should land essentially at the same level, with a tiny regression (~-0.03%).

The filter only touches the LR half of the 50/50 blend, and since L2-regularized multinomial LR already shrinks the weak, redundant histogram bins (while high-F species-specific rare bins are kept), dropping the bottom 64 columns should mildly denoise the linear probabilities, yielding a small ~1% log-loss improvement — though the effect is small enough that it could easily be neutral.

With eps=0.1 the NN's confident predictions get pulled toward ~0.90, imposing a ~0.10-nat floor (-log 0.9) on the ~90% of test leaves it already classifies correctly, and since labels are near-deterministic and the NN enters a 50/50 blend with an unchanged LR, this systematic confidence cap on correct samples outweighs the modest de-bolding benefit on the few hard/confidently-wrong ones, so log loss regresses.

Multinomial softmax directly optimizes the multi-class objective its probabilities are calibrated for, whereas 99 independently fitted, heavily imbalanced binary problems (8 vs 784 per fold) produce noisier per-class score scales and fatter error tails that a single global power/floor recalibration only partially absorbs, so the log loss regresses modestly.

A well-regularized 5-seed MLP bag on the same scaled features is roughly on par with the LR but makes decorrelated errors, so an OOF-selected blend (with w=0 fallback capping downside and the power calibration re-sharpened on the blend) should cut multi-class log loss by a few percent, from ~0.0451 to ~0.043, with only mild risk of OOF-selection overfitting.

With best_C likely large (weakly regularized, sharp probabilities), averaging the five highly-overlapping fold models acts as bagging-style smoothing that softens confident wrong predictions — the dominant cost in the current 0.0566 — while losing little per-model fit (each fold model's 20% data deficit is mostly offset by variance reduction), so a modest few-percent improvement is the most likely outcome, though a small regression is possible if the refit's extra data outweighs the smoothing.

Absolute size/aspect/convexity/Hu features add genuinely new signal absent from the scale-normalised 192 descriptors, and the existing C-grid CV controls the added overfitting, so a modest ~5% log-loss gain is expected (with a small chance of ~0 change if images are unavailable or features prove redundant with the shape descriptor).

Since L2 regularization is rotation-invariant, the PCA rotation itself is neutral; the only real effect is truncating the ~5% lowest-variance tail, which on standardized 219-dim data with ~990 rows is mostly within-class histogram/quantisation noise that the C=1 logreg was mildly overfitting, so expect a small (~2-4%) improvement rather than a large one.

Each fold model trains on 20% less data (excess error ×1.25) but averaging five ~75%-overlapping fold models cuts estimation variance by ~0.8× (roughly a wash), while the extra effective regularization and probability smoothing from ensembling slightly reduce overconfidence penalties on a 99-class log loss, netting a small ~1% improvement.

The LR baseline is already very strong (0.124 implies ~97% accuracy with high confidence), and a from-scratch CNN+MLP hybrid trained on only 990 binary 64x64 silhouettes will likely land well above it (~0.2-0.4 log loss), so the fixed 50/50 arithmetic blend dilutes confident correct predictions faster than its decorrelated errors help, with added risk that the 9-minute guard truncates the final retrain on CPU — net slight regression.

With only ~8 samples/class per fold and weak effective L2 (C=1.0 on a summed loss over near-separable 192-dim features), the LR is mildly overconfident, so the OOF-tuned temperature/epsilon flattening should cut confident-error losses by roughly 10% and transfer to test since the split is IID; small risk of over-flattening because fold models (80% data) are more overconfident than the full model, hence a modest rather than large predicted gain.

The OOF grid includes the current C=1 (bounding downside to CV-noise level) and with only ~10 samples/class it will most likely select a moderately larger C (~3–100) that sharpens the overly-soft default-regularization probabilities, giving a small (~3–6%) log-loss improvement rather than a dramatic one; main residual risks are CV selection noise picking a slightly worse C or the 55 tol=1e-6 fits running long without the optional joblib parallelism.

The ~25 image descriptors (solidity, aspect ratio, Hu moments, etc.) are largely redundant with the precomputed 64-d shape vector but add a little genuinely new shape/size signal, so the unchanged C=1.0 logistic regression should see a small net improvement partially offset by the extra dimensions and a few noise columns (canvas size, euler number, component count) under fixed regularization.

With 240 standardized features on 990 rows the C=1 multinomial LR is already near-calibrated on test (0.0813 implies ~98-99% accuracy with ~0.93-0.96 confidence), so 5x stronger L2 mainly shrinks logits toward uniform over 99 classes, costing more on the dominant correct-and-confident mass than it recovers on hedged mistakes — a mild regression, not an improvement.

Skipping the full-data refit means the submitted model is trained on only ~792 of 990 samples (20% less data), which almost always raises test log loss for logistic regression on this dataset — the internal-holdout consistency gain does not offset the smaller training set — so expect a modest regression from 0.0813 to roughly 0.088.

The blend contains the current tuned LR as a special case (weights can collapse to w_lr=1), and OOF-learned 3-weight probability averaging with a competitive shrinkage-LDA and a small kNN contribution typically shaves ~10-15% off multi-class log loss on this dataset, so expect a modest improvement from 0.0592 to ~0.052 with low overfit risk given only 3 parameters fit on 990 OOF rows.
