With only ~990 samples / 99 classes (≈10 per class) and 192 sparse histogram features, boosted trees overfit and are less well-calibrated than the CV-tuned L2 logistic regression already at 0.0609; early stopping on a ~149-sample validation split is noisy, so I expect HistGradientBoosting to land around log loss 0.09–0.11, a clear regression.

The multinomial LR member directly optimizes log loss on all 891 rows, while the replacement trains three OvR LinearSVCs on only 2/3 of the data each with per-class sigmoid calibrators fit on ~297 rows (2-6 positives per class, so noisy), and since a linear SVM adds little diversity to a soft vote that already contains LR-like decision surfaces, the slightly worse-calibrated member should regress the ensemble modestly (~3%), though the 99-row test set makes the exact value noisy.

HGB's early stopping on a ~1-row-per-class validation split is noisy and likely yields the weakest ensemble member, while a 600-tree sqrt-featured forest is a robust, diverse tabular classifier on this small 99-class problem, so swapping it in should modestly improve the soft-vote average (RF's overconfidence being diluted by the other three members), though the 99-row test set adds run-to-run variance.

A (256,128) MLP can learn cross-family (margin×shape×texture) interactions that a linear softmax cannot, and the retained OOF-selected uniform-shrinkage calibration plus early stopping curb its overconfidence, so on this small (990-sample, 99-class) set I expect a modest gain over the 0.1244 logistic baseline (roughly 0.09–0.12 range, with maybe a 30% chance of a slight regression from overfitting the ~10-samples-per-class data and runtime fitting comfortably in budget at ~12 short early-stopped fits).

With 192 features vs 990 rows, default C=1.0 is likely under-regularized, so 5-fold OOF selection will probably land near C~0.1-0.3 and give slightly better-calibrated, better-ranked probabilities; however, the existing uniform-shrinkage step already corrects much of the overconfidence, capping the gain at a few percent, with a real chance of ~no change if C=1 is already at/near the OOF minimum (it is in the grid) and a small chance of a slight regression from selection noise.

The images are black leaves on white backgrounds, so the literal 'pixels > 127' mask selects the background, making the largest external contour the image border (near-constant extent/solidity, noisy orientation, size/aspect proxies at best); even with a corrected leaf mask these crude Hu/geometry/radial features are largely redundant with the 192 normalized shape descriptors at fixed C=1.0, so the most likely outcome is essentially no new signal plus mild overfitting from 48 extra columns on only ~990 training rows — a slight regression.

With only 990 samples and 192 noisy, correlated histogram features, the arbitrary C=1.0 is likely slightly under-regularized; 10-fold CV with neg_log_loss should pick a smaller C and cut log loss by a few percent, while 25×10 fast lbfgs fits stay well inside the 10-minute budget (small chance C≈1.0 is already optimal, yielding ~0% change).

Soft-voting four diverse learners (LR ≈0.124 alone, shrinkage-LDA likely comparable or better, log-loss-tuned KNN near-baseline, HGB weaker but adds diversity) typically lands at or below the best single member, so expect a modest ~10-20% log-loss improvement over the LR-only baseline.

sklearn's LR objective (C × sum-loss + penalty) makes C=1 very weakly regularized here, so the 10-fold OOF predictions will contain a few confidently-wrong samples with near-zero true-class probability; the alpha grid (resolution 0.01) will likely pick a small alpha≈0.01–0.03 that caps those catastrophic errors, and since the full-data model has the same overconfidence, the same mild shrinkage should trim the test log loss slightly (with maybe a third chance alpha=0 is picked and nothing changes).

On 990 samples x 192 correlated features the Ledoit-Wolf 'auto' shrinkage is tiny (~0.01-0.1), so forcing 0.9 collapses the pooled covariance 90% toward a scaled identity, discarding the between-feature correlation structure that makes LDA work here; the classifier degrades toward an over-confident nearest-centroid rule in standardized space, roughly doubling the log loss.

Each 64-feature LDA is far weaker alone (texture especially yields near-uniform posteriors), and the arithmetic mean dilutes confidence instead of using joint 192-feature covariance, so log loss roughly doubles versus the shrinkage LDA baseline of 0.364.

PCA(0.90) discards low-variance PC directions that a CV-tuned multinomial LR (nested, already regularized via C) would otherwise exploit for separating similar species, so this hard subspace restriction typically yields a modest log-loss regression rather than a gain.

CV-tuned LDA with shrinkage is a solid generative baseline on these 192 histogram/descriptor features, but its shared-Gaussian-covariance assumption yields less well-calibrated probabilities than the multinomial logistic regression that directly optimizes log loss, so I expect a moderate regression from 0.0599 to roughly 0.07.

Unsupervised PCA(0.95) keeps the high-variance between-species structure but discards low-variance directions that separate confusable species pairs, and since the scalar temperature re-calibrates global confidence on the new OOF logits, the denoising benefit is largely neutralized while the lost fine-grained signal slightly increases the confident errors that dominate this already-saturated 0.045 log-loss baseline.

LDA must estimate 192-d class means from only ~10 samples per species (8 per calibration fold) and its shared-Gaussian assumption is misspecified on histogram/shape features, so the generative plug-in scores should be markedly noisier than the discriminative, temperature-calibrated LR that is already near the achievable floor (~0.045), roughly doubling the log loss.

With mean log loss ~0.094 the model is already confident (typical true-class p≈0.9≫1/99), so mixing with uniform shrinks the true-class probability by ~0.5% on nearly every sample, adding a near-constant -ln(0.995+0.005/99)≈0.00496 nats and raising the score from 0.0943 to ≈0.0993.

Cutting Nyström from 512 to 384 drops only the fast-decaying RBF spectrum tail, and since the post-Nyström StandardScaler amplifies those low-variance (mostly sampling-noise) directions, removing them should slightly reduce prediction variance and yield a small log-loss improvement, though the effect is near noise level.

LDA's shared-covariance Gaussian model fits the skewed 192-dim histogram/shape features poorly and its fixed-temperature posteriors tend to be overconfident on a 99-class problem, so despite Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage it will likely score slightly worse (~0.14) than the moderately-regularized, better-calibrated multinomial logistic regression at 0.124.

3-fold CV over C (with C=1.0 already in the grid, bounding downside) will most likely select a near-optimal C in the 1–10 range for 990 samples × 192 standardized features, yielding a modest log-loss gain over the fixed C=1.0 baseline; small chance of picking an overfit C≈100 causing a slight regression, but the expected outcome is a small improvement to roughly 0.11–0.12.

A single temperature fit on 5-fold OOF logits is a low-variance, proper calibration of an already near-calibrated multinomial LR (mild overconfidence from ~19k weights on 990 rows), so expect only a small sharpening/softening gain (~1-2%), partially diluted by calibrating on 80%-data models but applying to the full-data model.

These shape/margin/texture descriptors were designed for kernel (SVM-style) classification, so a 512-component Nyström RBF map (gamma=1/192 is the standard scale heuristic on standardized features) should let the logistic model capture non-linear species structure and cut log loss, though the fixed C=1 on 512 whitened coordinates and 99-class overconfidence risk cap the gain to a modest ~10-15% improvement rather than a large one.

The temporal block (t_days/hour/weekday) captures the declining success trend absent from the baseline (test is chronologically later than train), and first-person-rate/length/gratitude stats add signal not in stop-word-filtered TF-IDF, while most other columns (prior-RAOP flags, upvote ratio) are largely redundant transforms of existing numerics — net effect a modest gain, not a large one.

Random forests handle high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF poorly (sqrt subsampling over ~8k mostly-word features, fully grown trees on ~4k rows), so the forest keeps the metadata/subreddit signal but loses much of the linear text signal that drives the 0.671 baseline, likely dropping AUC to roughly 0.60-0.63.

Trees handle 5000-dim sparse TF-IDF poorly (diffuse linear word signal that LR exploits is exactly what forests miss), and with max_features='sqrt' the 10 dense numeric/giver columns are almost never in the ~71-feature candidate set, so the claimed non-linearity gains never materialize to offset the text-signal loss — expect a drop of roughly 4-5 AUC points, consistent with RAOP history where linear models dominated tree benchmarks.

Unsupervised 50-topic LDA proportions smear the word-level discriminative signal (phrasings like 'just got fired', 'payday', 'my kids') that the 5000-dim TF-IDF captures well, so the pipeline drops back to roughly meta-features-plus-a-small-text-bump; batch LDA on ~4k short docs with 25 iterations is fast but lossy, making a regression of several AUC points the likely outcome (only upside would be reduced overfitting, which the already-regularized C=0.3 LR largely rules out).

Deleting the supervised TF-IDF/LR logit — the stack's strongest single feature — in favor of 20 noisy unsupervised LDA topic proportions (crude on ~5.7k short docs, no label information) leaves LightGBM with mostly metadata + timestamp, so the graded AUC should drop from ~0.703 to roughly the 0.62–0.65 range, only partially offset by the topic-narrative signal the paper describes.

The graded score (0.703, far below the ~0.85 a text+meta stack gets on an i.i.d. split) points to a temporally shifted holdout, where the raw epoch column only lets the trees memorise collection-period base rates while hour-of-day/day-of-week are stationary, weakly informative signals, so dropping the timestamp and adding the two cyclical features should yield a small improvement.

The metadata/text-stats GBM adds genuinely diverse non-linear signal (RAOP prior activity, account age, karma, length) that the linear model misses, and OOF-selected rank blending with ties broken toward the (stronger) LR bounds the downside, so expect a small but real gain (~+0.003–0.008) rather than a large one; the main risks are w* collapsing to 1.0 (no change) or mild OOF weight overfitting.

Random forests on ~4k rows of sparse 5k-dim TF-IDF consistently underperform regularized logistic regression on text, and with max_features='sqrt' the ~5000 weak text columns dilute the sampling so the few strong dense metadata features are rarely chosen, so most of the text signal the LR exploits is lost and the AUC drops several points below the 0.7007 linear baseline.

Subreddit membership adds a modest amount of incremental signal (e.g., participation in help/RAOP-like communities) mostly beyond the existing 9 numeric history features, and the L2-normalized binary TF-IDF block with C=0.3 L2 logistic regression limits overfitting from the mostly-noise tokens, so I expect a small gain (~+0.003 AUC), though the heavy redundancy with RAOP-activity numerics and 3000 extra sparse features on ~4k rows make a neutral-to-slightly-negative outcome plausible.

giver_username_if_known is 'N/A'/absent for every test row, so the new flag is constant-0 at test time yet nearly a label proxy in train; LR will put a large weight (~4 even under C=0.3) on it, absorbing ~most positives and refitting the text/numeric coefficients to the atypical 'giver-unknown' minority of positives, so the train-only leak degrades test ranking (while the local holdout AUC will deceptively jump to ~0.9), regressing graded AUC from 0.657 to roughly 0.60-0.64.

A properly-OOF text-LR score plus raw metadata and the (new) timestamp signal in a well-regularized, early-stopped, 3-seed-averaged LightGBM should extract slightly more from the numeric/temporal block than the shared-C linear stack (and runs easily within budget), but with only ~4k rows and the text signal funneled through a single scalar the gain is likely modest, ~+0.005–0.015 AUC, not a step change.

The added block injects classic RAOP signals orthogonal to the unigram TF-IDF (temporal trend via t_years, evidence markers like http/imgur, prior-RAOP-activity indicators), which typically yields a small but real AUC bump on a regularized LR stack, partially dampened here because the 9 log1p history counts already cover part of the requester-activity signal.

ExtraTrees on ~5.4k mostly sparse TF-IDF dims with only ~4k rows cannot exploit thousands of weak word features the way the L2 linear model does (splits dilute across random feature subsets), so the strong text signal collapses and graded AUC should regress several points despite the tree-friendly dense embeddings and numerics.

On RAOP, word-level TF-IDF captures stable lexical success cues (need/reciprocation/proof phrasing) that a frozen MiniLM linear probe only partially distills, so deleting the sparse block should cost a couple of AUC points even though variance from rare tokens drops slightly.

The ~20 doc-level stats (length, punctuation/caps, money/hardship flag, pronoun rates, gratitude, VADER, readability) carry modest genuine signal in RAOP that length-normalized, punctuation-stripped TF-IDF cannot express, so expect a small AUC gain (~+0.004) rather than a large or negative move since many lexical cues (please/thank/broke/rent) are already captured by the 1-2 gram unigram weights and only 4k training rows limit added feature value.

The nine requester-history features carry real but limited signal (community-membership effects, roughly 0.60-0.63 AUC ceiling), while the tuned 1-2 gram TF-IDF block genuinely contributes a few AUC points even after temporal-drift losses, so dropping text should cost several points relative to the 0.6497 combined model.

Skip-gram embeddings trained on only ~700k tokens of in-domain text are too low-quality to replace the exact-token lexical signal TF-IDF provides on a 4k-row dataset, so the text block's contribution largely collapses while the retained metadata/text-stats features hold the score around ~0.62 — a clear regression, not an improvement.

Unigram+bigram TF-IDF recovers phrase-level signal ('pay it forward', 'tough spot', etc.) known to help modestly on RAOP, and L2 at C=0.3 tempers the 12x feature growth, so a small gain is most likely, though overfit risk from 55k mostly-rare bigrams on this weak-signal graded split keeps it well under +1%.

The TF-IDF/SVD branch carries genuine incremental signal on RAOP (Althoff et al. show text adds several AUC points over status features), so a model restricted to the nine requester-history columns — which alone typically reach only ~0.58-0.62 AUC on this random-ish split — should regress a few points from 0.633 despite better variance control.

Random forests split axis-aligned on dense TruncatedSVD components and average signal across them, which is well known to lose several AUC points versus boosted trees on SVD-of-TF-IDF representations, so I expect a moderate regression from 0.6327 to roughly 0.61 despite the forest's robustness.

Frozen MiniLM embeddings carry only weakly complementary signal on this small, lexically-cued dataset where off-the-shelf dense features underperform n-gram TF-IDF, so naively hstacking 384 scaled dense dims under a single untuned C yields at best a tiny AUC gain, partly offset by overfit risk on ~4k samples and CPU-encoding wall-clock risk.

Adding bigrams (1-2) with min_df=2 captures phrase-level signal (e.g. 'pay it forward', 'lost my job') that unigrams miss, typically yielding a small AUC gain on this dataset, but with only ~4k training docs and ~10x sparser features under fixed C=0.3 the gain is modest and partly offset by overfitting risk, so expect a slight improvement (~+0.3-0.8%) rather than a large one.

Narrative/meta text statistics (gratitude, reciprocity, hardship, money, length/readability) carry genuine incremental signal on RAOP beyond unigram TF-IDF, so a modest gain is expected, though partly redundant with existing unigrams and diluted across ~5000 features under fixed C=0.3.

On this small, weak-signal text dataset, compressing 5000 sparse TF-IDF features into 300 lossy SVD dims and fitting axis-split trees (instead of logistic regression directly on the lexical space) discards the sparse word signal that drives most of RAOP's predictive power, so despite CV-tuned boosting rounds the AUC should regress by roughly 2-4 points.

The spline basis was capturing the real monotone decline in RAOP success rate across the 2011-2013 collection window; two fixed-period annual Fourier features are orthogonal to that trend and only encode weak/noisy seasonality, so the model loses most of the temporal signal and AUC dips slightly (a few tenths of a percent) while text and requester-history features keep the score near its current level.

With ~5k sparse features on ~4k weak-signal samples, C=30 nearly removes the L2 shrinkage that C=0.3 provided, so rare n-gram tokens and heavy-tailed numeric/spline coefficients fit training noise (near-interpolation), which typically costs ~1-2 AUC points on this noisy, distribution-shifted task while staying well within the time budget.

Calendar time carries real signal in RAOP (success rate declined over the subreddit's lifetime per Althoff et al.), the Kaggle train/test split is random rather than temporal so the spline trend generalizes, and 8 regularized spline features add orthogonal signal to a model that currently lacks any absolute-time feature, yielding a small but genuine gain (~+0.005–0.01 AUC).

Cosine kNN (k=25) on a mixed TF-IDF/standardized-numeric/subreddit space suffers the curse of dimensionality with only ~4k training rows, and the cosine metric is dominated by the dense standardized-numeric and large-norm subreddit blocks (including negative values), so neighborhood structure captures far less signal than the current linear model, dropping AUC from ~0.649 to roughly 0.55-0.60.

Distance-weighted kNN on nine weak, skewed metadata features is noisier and less robust than CatBoost's smoothed splits, so its standalone AUC drops (~0.55–0.57 vs ~0.58), dragging the fixed 50/50 blend down modestly, though blend diversity keeps the regression small.

C=30 makes the per-sample effective regularization ~1e-6, so the 5000-dim sparse TF-IDF space (4040 likely separable samples) is fit near-maximum-likelihood, overfitting rare words and saturating LR probabilities, which lets the degraded text model dominate the 50/50 blend over the unchanged metadata CatBoost — a modest AUC regression despite the plausible feature-scale motivation.

The RAOP test set is chronologically later than train, so with extrapolation='constant' the spline time block takes identical values for every test row — a uniform score offset that cannot change the ranking — leaving only minor refit noise (tiny upside if any test timestamps fall inside the training range).

BernoulliNB's conditional-independence assumption double-counts correlated unigram/bigram presence, Laplace alpha=1.0 heavily smooths ~5k features over ~4k rows, and binarizing the informative continuous requester-history features at the mean discards magnitude, so it typically trails logistic regression on TF-IDF by a few AUC points.

A 6-knot quantile spline on request time is a low-variance, low-risk addition that lets the fixed-C logistic regression capture RAOP's known drift in success rate over the 2010–2013 period (trend partially beyond what the 9 history numerics proxy), so expect a small AUC gain (~+0.1–0.5%) with the constant-extrapolation and median-imputation details capping the downside near zero rather than causing a regression.

Subreddit membership (e.g., prior RAOP/assistance communities) carries genuine community-embeddedness signal partially complementary to the existing RAOP-activity counts, and min_df=5 plus the existing L2 (C=0.3) keeps the few-thousand unscaled binary columns from badly overfitting, so expect a small but real AUC gain (~+0.003-0.005) rather than a regression.

The meta-only CatBoost (AUC likely ~0.62-0.64) is weaker than and largely redundant with the text+meta LR, so a fixed 50/50 blend loses some text signal, but its non-linear/threshold effects on the strong RAOP-activity features (e.g., first-post/post-count splits) add just enough complementary signal to net out as a marginal gain.

Bigrams add phrase-level signals that matter in RAOP (e.g., 'lost job', 'pay forward' after stop-word removal) and typically give a small AUC bump over unigram-only TF-IDF+LR, though the 5000-feature cap now dilutes unigrams with sparser bigrams, so the gain is modest rather than large.

Authorship attribution is stylometric — function words and stop-word bigrams ('of the', 'it was') carry real author signal that char_wb n-grams only partly preserve, so stripping them from the word view should slightly raise log loss (~+0.004) despite the lower dimensionality.

A log-linear stack of the calibrated TF-IDF LR (OOF ~0.34-0.35) with two diverse but weaker NB base models (~0.40-0.45 OOF) is a classic geometric-blend setup on this dataset and should trim roughly 0.01 log loss, partially offset by losing the full-data LR refit (fold-averaged test predictions are slightly weaker) and the mild OOF-vs-averaged-test scale mismatch, so expect a solid but modest gain from 0.3537 to ~0.344 rather than a breakthrough.

This is authorship attribution, where function words are classic stylometric signal: dropping them slightly weakens both word-level base models (especially MultinomialNB, which loses real count-mass signal like 'the/of/would' frequency differences), while the char_wb models already capture that style so the LR-word overfitting reduction and added diversity roughly cancel, leaving a small regression (~+0.001-0.002 log loss) on the stack.

A multinomial LR stacker recovers most of the blend (linear combination of OOF probs is near-optimal in rank), but it cannot exploit the nonlinear agreement/recalibration structure among the strongly correlated, overconfident OOF columns (especially the peaked NB probabilities) and stylometric interactions that the regularized, fold-averaged LightGBM captures, so expect a small regression of ~0.002-0.004 log loss rather than a collapse.

Punctuation habits (semicolons, dashes, ellipses, exclamations) are genuine stylometric signal in this corpus and are consistently distributed across the random train/test split, so the char (1,5)-gram block currently exploits them; stripping punctuation deletes that signal entirely (the word block, unchanged, already ignores punctuation), and the mild regularization from a smaller char vocabulary only partially offsets the loss, yielding a modest regression.

A 5-fold OOF stack of word-LR, char-LR (C=10) and alpha-tuned word/char MultinomialNB with log-prob meta features adds complementary NB signal on top of the TF-IDF LR, which historically lands ~0.39-0.42 on this competition versus 0.4386 for the single hstacked-LR baseline, so I expect roughly 0.02-0.03 log-loss improvement (with mild risk from lbfgs non-convergence and the tight 10-min budget).

Cutting the stacked word+char TF-IDF matrix from ~130k to 10k chi2-selected columns discards the redundant-but-collectively-useful char n-gram signal that the L2-regularized LR exploits, weakening the LR branch (CV ~0.375 -> ~0.40); the blend-weight search partially compensates by shifting weight toward the unchanged NB model, but the net graded log loss regresses modestly from 0.361 to ~0.379.

For authorship attribution, function words/pronouns are the stylometric signal (and sklearn's 'english' list also drops genuinely discriminative corpus words like 'upon', 'cry', 'fire', 'found'), so both the word-TF-IDF LR and the count NB lose real information; the untouched char_wb block and the OOF blend shifting weight toward LR cap the damage, yielding a modest regression of roughly +0.007 log loss.

Neg-log-loss 5-fold CV over C∈{1..100} will most likely select C=1–3 (the word+char TF-IDF log-reg already nearly interpolates 19.5k rows at C=1, and the grid offers no stronger regularization), so the refit model changes only slightly and the ~1,958-row graded split should see a tiny improvement of roughly 0.001–0.003 log loss at best, with real chance of an essentially unchanged score.

Stacking diverse word/char TF-IDF LRs plus NB OOF probabilities and stylometric meta-features under an early-stopped LightGBM blender is the classic recipe that lifted spooky-author solutions from ~0.43 to ~0.37-0.39, so expect roughly a 0.04-0.05 log-loss improvement with modest variance on the ~2k-row graded split.

Cross-word-boundary, case-sensitive, uncapped char n-grams capture punctuation-in-context and capitalization habits that are genuinely discriminative for these three authors, so the same LR should gain ~0.01 log loss, though fixed C=1.0 and sparser cased features temper the gain.

OOF-tuned probability blend of the unchanged TF-IDF LR with a diverse MultinomialNB on word counts historically yields a small but real gain on this competition (~0.005-0.01 log loss), with the w=1.0 grid point capping downside; I expect ~1.5-2% improvement modulo noise on the ~1,958-row graded subset.

Authorship attribution lives on function-word style (pronouns like I/she/her, articles, auxiliaries, negations — all in sklearn's stopword list, cf. Burrows' Delta), so stripping ~40% of tokens removes genuinely discriminative signal while the new stopword-bridged bigrams add noise, making the log loss regress by roughly 5-7%.

Oversampling to a uniform prior shifts fastText's learned class biases away from the natural ~40/29/31 test distribution (miscalibration that pure prior-rescaling analysis caps at ~+0.01 log loss, worsened by extra gradient repetitions of duplicated minority rows), so the graded log loss should regress slightly rather than improve.

ComplementNB(alpha=0.1) on the same TF-IDF matrix is a weaker, highly error-correlated model (OOF ~0.42-0.48 vs LR's ~0.34), so the OOF-selected blend weight will land near w=1.0 (often exactly, yielding no change) or a high-w mix that buys only a few thousandths of log loss, easily swamped by noise on the ~1,958-row graded test — expected outcome is a very small improvement or a wash.

MultinomialNB's conditional-independence assumption is badly violated by the heavily correlated word+char TF-IDF features; on this competition NB-style single models historically score ~0.40-0.43 vs ~0.35 for tuned logistic regression, so even with CV-tuned alpha this swap should regress the log loss by roughly 15-18%.

char_wb 2-5 n-grams capture authorial punctuation/style signals absent from word 1-2 grams (on this competition char features were among the strongest), so dropping them from the NB-SVM stack should regress log loss by roughly 0.03-0.05, from 0.409 to about 0.45.

ComplementNB keeps the NB count statistics but drops the logistic-regression reweighting/calibration that makes NB-SVM strong, so on the same word+char TF-IDF stack it should land noticeably worse, around 0.44-0.45 log loss vs the current 0.4087.

C=1.0 is likely already near-optimal for this word+char TF-IDF stack, so 3-fold CV selection (probably picking C in the 1.0–3.16 range) should yield only a marginal log-loss gain (~0.002), with a small chance of a slight regression if CV selects a larger C that overfits the small ~1,958-row graded set.

MultinomialNB is generative and double-counts the heavily overlapping word(1-2)+char(2-5) TF-IDF blocks (its 'robustness' claim is backwards), and with alpha=0.1 it produces overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities that are punished under log loss, so I expect roughly a 0.06-0.08 log-loss regression versus the discriminative logistic-regression baseline (plus a small risk of negative MinMax-scaled style values on the test set).

fastText with word bigrams plus char 2-5 subwords covers roughly the same signal as the word+char TF-IDF + LR stack and historically edges it out slightly on this dataset (fastText baselines landed ~0.38-0.42 vs ~0.42-0.45 for linear TF-IDF pipelines), so I expect a modest improvement to ~0.42, with the main downside risk being overconfident softmax probabilities inflating log loss on the small ~1,958-row graded split.

C=1.0 is already near-optimal for word+char TF-IDF logistic regression, so 5-fold CV over a narrow grid ([0.25,8]) typically selects C in {0.5,1,2} and buys only ~0.001-0.003 log loss on the ~1.9k-row graded split, with a real chance of a no-change or slightly worse draw if CV lands on 0.25 or 8; runtime (~30 extra sparse fits) should still fit the budget.

NB-SVM/OvR with renormalized sigmoid columns stays roughly linear-equivalent to the current multinomial LR on the same TF-IDF, but loses multiclass calibration (renormalized OvR instead of softmax matching the log-loss metric), amplifies noisy rare n-grams via the TF-IDF-based count-ratio, and C=4 on pre-scaled features under-regularizes, so expect a small regression (~0.005 absolute) rather than a gain.

Classic stylometric counts (sentence length, punctuation, case, digits) carry real author-attribution signal that char_wb TF-IDF only partially encodes, and with 14 dense MaxAbs-scaled features added to ~19.6k training samples under light L2 regularization, logistic regression should exploit them for a small but genuine log-loss gain (~0.003), with low risk of regression.

This is the classic NBSVM/NB-LR trick (per-class log-count ratio reweighting before L2 logistic regression), a well-proven upgrade over plain LR on sparse word+char TF-IDF text features, so I expect a moderate log-loss gain (~0.02) with OvR probability normalization costing little; runtime stays well within budget since liblinear dual solves three ~20k×~100k sparse problems quickly.

Quadrupling L2 strength (C 1.0→0.25) on ~250k sparse word+char n-gram TF-IDF features slightly over-shrinks genuinely useful coefficients and pulls predictions toward class priors, so I expect a small log-loss regression on the 1,958-row holdout rather than an improvement.

Removing word TF-IDF discards strong lexical author markers (Lovecraft's neologisms, Poe's archaic vocabulary) that char_wb 2-5 n-grams only partially capture, so char-only NB-logistic should regress ~8-12% in log loss versus the word+char concatenation.

The NB log-ratio rescaling of l2-normalized TF-IDF (with +1 smoothing huge relative to TF-IDF mass and per-author global offsets) acts as a poorly matched prior that distorts the shared feature scale, so plain TF-IDF one-vs-rest L2 logistic regression — the natural strong baseline for this dataset (~0.43–0.48) — should recover a meaningful chunk of the gap below the current 0.518, though OvR normalization and the capped char features keep it from reaching tuned-multinomial territory.

The log-loss-vs-C curve for LR on stacked word+char TF-IDF with ~18k training rows is quite flat between C=2 and C=4, so slightly stronger L2 should at most marginally reduce overfitting on correlated n-grams — expect a tiny improvement well within run-to-run noise.

NBSVM's NB log-ratio feature scaling on the same word+char TF-IDF features typically gives a modest edge over plain multinomial LR on sentence-level text classification, only slightly offset by the one-vs-rest renormalization calibration cost, so I expect a small improvement (~0.01 absolute log loss).

Authorship attribution lives on function words — pronouns, articles, negations in ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS carry much of the EAP/HPL/MWS stylistic signal in both the word n-grams and char n-grams (e.g., ' the ', ' i ' patterns), so stripping them should modestly regress log loss despite TF-IDF IDF downweighting.

Quadrupling L2 strength (C=1.0→0.25) mildly underfits the ~100k sparse, correlated word/char n-gram features; the holdout temperature scaling absorbs much of the global confidence shrinkage, but ranking quality on hard sentences degrades slightly, so log loss ticks up by roughly 0.003.

char n-grams spanning word boundaries capture punctuation- and space-attached patterns (e.g., Poe's semicolons, bigram transitions) that char_wb discards, which are strongly authorial in stylometry, so expect a small gain (~0.003 log loss) over the 0.4323 baseline with identical word features and LogReg anchoring the rest.

NB log-count-ratio feature scaling (NBSVM-style) is a strong inductive prior for sparse word+char TF-IDF text and typically trims a bit of log loss versus plain L2 logistic regression, though switching from multinomial to normalized one-vs-rest probabilities gives back some calibration, netting a modest improvement from 0.4323 to roughly 0.425.

For high-dimensional word+char TF-IDF n-grams with ~19.6k training sentences, the LR regularization curve is fairly flat with its optimum near C≈2–5, so raising C from 1.0 to 4.0 should slightly reduce over-regularization and yield a small log-loss improvement (~0.002).

Regularized multinomial LR on TF-IDF is already near-calibrated, so holdout-fitted temperature scaling typically moves log loss by only ~0.001–0.003 (small softening gain if slightly overconfident), partly offset by estimation noise on ~1.7k validation rows and by applying a temperature tuned on the 90%-fit model to the full-data refit; expect a tiny improvement, possibly ~zero.

The baseline already trains on the exact metric scale (dollar MSE = RMSE²), and taxi-fare noise grows sub-proportionally with fare (base fare floor, flat airport rates), so log1p reweights gradient attention away from the expensive rides that dominate RMSE and yields ~median (slightly low-biased) predictions — expect a small regression, roughly 4.10→4.12, though a tiny gain is also plausible.

4x more training rows should cut the valid-row RMSE from ~3.6 to ~3.3-3.4 (typical shallow GBDT learning-curve slope, partly capped by the fixed 1000-tree/num_leaves=63 capacity), but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows is unchanged, so the overall graded RMSE improves only modestly from 4.10 to ~3.9.

Airport-distance features are a proven win for this competition (they let the trees directly isolate JFK flat-fare and airport-pattern rides that raw coordinates + haversine capture only awkwardly), but the expected ~2% gain on the ~97% of rows with valid coordinates is diluted by the ~2.8% corrupt-coordinate rows whose ~2.1-RMSE error floor is unaffected, yielding roughly a 1% overall RMSE improvement (4.19 → ~4.15).

Fitting L2 on log1p(fare) makes the model predict the conditional median, which expm1 back-transform leaves systematically ~3-5% low relative to the mean that RMSE rewards (taxi fare is additive in dollars — base + per-km + tolls — not multiplicative), so the modest robustness gain from compressing the rare $100-500 mis-recorded fares is outweighed by the induced underprediction bias on both the ~97% clean rows and the 2.8% corrupt-coordinate rows, yielding a small regression.

The constraint matches the true metered fare structure (base + per-distance) and mildly regularizes the dominant feature, but since the four raw coordinates are also unconstrained predictors and the distance counterfactual is largely unidentified given them, the effect on the ~97% of test rows the model actually predicts should be a near-noise, slightly positive change (~0.1-0.2% on the graded RMSE).

Training on log1p(fare) misaligns the loss with the dollar-RMSE metric (it de-emphasizes the large absolute errors on airport/long rides that dominate squared error), and back-transforming with expm1 introduces a systematic ~3-5% downward (Jensen/smearing) bias since leaf values approximate conditional geometric means, so the slight gains on the bulk of small fares are more than offset — expect a small regression from 4.126 to roughly 4.15-4.18.

Encoding training rows with statistics that include their own fare introduces classic target leakage (own-fare weight ~1/(count+20), largest for sparse route keys) that LightGBM will exploit but that is absent at validation/test time, and this cost clearly outweighs the tiny gain from removing the log(0.8) count offset and OOF noise, so the graded RMSE should regress modestly (roughly +0.05 to +0.10).

Training on log1p(fare) makes LightGBM predict the conditional geometric median rather than the mean, which biases predictions low on the dollar scale where RMSE is graded; the reduced outlier leverage partly offsets this, but the typical empirical result is a small (~1%) regression on this competition's metric.

Airport-distance features let the trees isolate flat-rate JFK (~$52) and Newark-surcharge trips with single splits instead of many sparse coordinate splits, historically worth ~0.05-0.1 RMSE on the valid ~97% of rows, which translates from 3.6→~3.52 valid-row RMSE into ~4.06 overall after the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows; compute cost is negligible so the run stays well within budget.

Replacing the constant mean-fare fallback with LightGBM's learned NaN routing lets the ~2.8% corrupt test rows exploit their surviving signal (a valid pickup OR dropoff coordinate for most of them, plus passenger_count=0 rows with fully valid coordinates, plus time features), cutting their per-row squared error substantially, while the ~3% extra NaN-feature training rows only marginally perturb the splits for the clean 97% — net improvement of roughly 0.1 RMSE.

Quadrupling the sample (1M→4M rows) with the same features/model typically shaves ~0.05-0.15 off the valid-row RMSE (≈3.6→≈3.5), which, blended with the ~2.1 corrupt-row error floor that dominates via the 2.8% invalid test rows, moves overall RMSE from 4.138 to roughly 4.03-4.08; the I/O and n_jobs tweaks are performance-neutral for accuracy, and the ~4-6 min runtime should fit the budget, so a modest but real improvement of ~2% is expected.

Properly out-of-fold target encodings of route/pickup/dropoff cells capture tolls and flat JFK-style fares that haversine cannot, likely cutting valid-row RMSE from ~3.6 to ~3.2-3.3, which the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row floor dilutes to roughly a 6-8% total RMSE improvement.

Log1p training optimizes relative error, so expm1 back-transformed predictions approximate the conditional geometric mean (~4-5% below the conditional mean RMSE actually wants) with no smearing correction, and the cheap-ride reweighting hurts dollar errors on high-fare rows; the metric mismatch likely outweighs the modest tail-robustness gain on this mostly-additive fare structure, yielding a small regression (~4.17-4.20 vs 4.129).

Manhattan grid distance and bearing add real signal beyond haversine that trees can't cheaply synthesize from raw coords (the two abs_delta columns are largely redundant), historically worth ~0.1 RMSE on the ~97% of valid test rows, which — on top of the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the ~2.8% corrupt-coordinate rows handled by the unchanged fallback model — moves the total from ~4.13 to ~4.04, a ~2% improvement.

Landmark-distance features let the GBDT isolate airport flat-fare regimes (JFK/Manhattan) that raw coordinates only capture with many splits, typically yielding a ~1–2% RMSE gain on the ~97% valid test rows, which — combined with the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt rows that still get the mean-fare fallback — moves the overall score from 4.104 to roughly 4.05–4.07, with negligible added runtime from the vectorized haversine calls.

RMSE scoring wants the conditional mean, but an L1 objective fits the conditional median of a right-skewed fare distribution, so predictions shift systematically low; the added squared bias (~E[(mean-median)^2]) on the ~97% of predictable test rows slightly outweighs the robustness benefit, giving a modest regression from 4.10 to roughly 4.15-4.20 despite the mean-fare floor of ~2.1 staying unchanged.

Fitting log1p(fare) makes the trees target conditional geometric means, so expm1 back-transform carries a ~1-2% Jensen under-prediction bias that hits exactly the high-fare airport rides dominating squared error, while with ~800k rows/fold the raw-scale GBDT already estimates conditional means well (variance-stabilization gains are minimal for a target spanning only ~1 order of magnitude) — so raw-scale RMSE likely slips slightly, with early stopping now also optimizing the mismatched log-space metric.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean, which L2 targets, while regression_l1 targets the conditional median; since the label noise exists identically in the graded test set (it's a sample of the same training data) the 'robustness' gain is illusory, and with right-skewed fares the median-based predictions systematically under-predict (especially on long/expensive rides where conditional variance is large), so the swap adds squared-error bias and slightly underfits within the 1000-tree budget, worsening RMSE by roughly 2-4%.

With delta=$1 against typical residuals of ~$2-3, Huber behaves almost like MAE and shifts predictions toward conditional medians of a right-skewed fare distribution, but the metric wants conditional means, so RMSE regresses slightly (the robustness gain against the few remaining junk rows is smaller than the systematic under-prediction bias).

Training on log1p(fare) and back-transforming with a naive expm1 (no smearing/bias correction) makes predictions approximate the conditional geometric mean — systematically ~3-5% low — and reallocates model capacity to relative error, which misaligns with the raw-dollar RMSE metric, while the tail-domination problem it targets is already mostly neutralized by the distance feature and tree splits; expect a small regression (~1-3% worse on valid rows, roughly 4.14-4.25 graded).

Airport distance/flag features are a known win on this task (JFK flat fares, LGA/EWR pricing), likely cutting valid-row RMSE by ~0.10-0.15, but the ~2.8% corrupt test rows (unchanged fallback, ~2.1 RMSE floor) dilute the gain to roughly 2-3% overall, moving 4.13 to about 4.03.

4x training data (0.95M→~3.6M clean rows) should cut the valid-row RMSE from ~3.6 to ~3.5 via the usual learning-curve effect, which after the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row floor (0.972·3.5² + 4.41 ≈ 16.4) yields ~4.05 vs 4.138, a ~2% gain, with wall-clock (CSV read + LightGBM on 3.6M×10 features, early-stopped) just fitting the 10-minute budget.

Averaging 5 same-config LightGBMs trained on different KFold splits cuts prediction variance slightly (partly offset by each fold seeing 80% instead of 90% of the data), so expect a small sub-1% RMSE gain concentrated on the ~97% of test rows with valid coordinates, moving ~4.138 to ~4.10.

A smoothed OOF pickup-cell mean fare is a strong spatial prior (airport flat fares, borough-level fare levels) that 63-leaf trees can't fully recover from raw coordinates, so it should cut the clean-row RMSE from ~3.6 to ~3.45 while the ~2.1 RMSE corrupt-row floor stays fixed, yielding ~3.98 overall; the m=30 smoothing and out-of-fold construction keep leakage/overfitting risk low, so a small but solid improvement (~2-5%) is the likely outcome.

Snapping to 0.01° (~1km) cells destroys fine distance/coordinate precision — the strongest fare signal — adding roughly $0.6-0.8 of irreducible noise (e.g., same-cell trips all collapse to identical features and distance 0), while the pooling/smoothing benefit it seeks is already provided by the existing 0.01-cell route_mean_fare encoding, so expect a modest regression from 4.13 to about 4.20.

L1 loss makes the model approximate the conditional median while RMSE rewards the conditional mean, and NYC fares are right-skewed (tolls/surcharges), so median-biased predictions typically raise RMSE by a couple percent despite unchanged early stopping on RMSE.

L1 loss fits the conditional median rather than the conditional mean of a right-skewed fare distribution, so RMSE (which rewards mean predictions) typically degrades a few percent, and the cleaning rules already cap the outlier influence that L1 would mitigate.

Airport-distance features let the trees cheaply isolate JFK/EWR flat-fare and surcharge trips that raw coordinates + haversine only partially capture, yielding an expected ~0.05-0.1 RMSE gain on the ~97% valid test rows, which is diluted to ~1.5-2.5% overall by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the ~2.8% corrupt-coordinate rows that are predicted as the mean fare regardless.

L1 loss estimates the conditional median, which sits below the conditional mean for the right-skewed fare residuals, and trees grown on absolute error are suboptimal for the squared-error metric, so RMSE should regress modestly (~1-2%) relative to the 4.1305 L2 baseline.

LightGBM's quantile binning already resolves dense-Manhattan coordinates to ~75m, and with ~2M rows that sub-km location detail is mostly genuine signal (route efficiency, traffic hotspots) rather than noise, so quantizing to a ~1km grid loses a small amount of real spatial information that the already-regularized, early-stopped model was exploiting, yielding a slight regression (~+0.01-0.02 RMSE) while distance_km and airport/borough-scale effects are preserved.

L1 fits conditional medians, which are biased low for the right-skewed fare residuals and misaligned with the RMSE metric, and since cleaning already removed the gross fare outliers the robustness benefit is small, so expect a modest regression (plus possible slight underfit if L1 needs more than the 1000-tree budget).

A 29°-rotated L1 'street-grid' distance is a genuinely strong fare signal for NYC (routes are roughly grid-aligned), so it should improve the ~3.6 RMSE on valid rows by a few percent, but the gain is diluted by the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the ~2.8% corrupt test rows and by the model already having haversine plus raw coordinates, yielding a modest overall improvement from 4.138 to roughly 4.05-4.08.

Smoothed out-of-fold route target-encoding captures per-route fare structure (airport flat fares, real path lengths) that haversine+coordinates only partly learn, likely cutting valid-row RMSE from ~3.6 to ~3.35, which — given the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from the ~2.8% corrupt test rows (invalid-row fallback unchanged) — moves the graded RMSE from 4.138 to roughly 3.93.

The 29°-rotated L1 'manhattan_grid_km' is a well-known strong feature for this competition that approximates street-network travel distance beyond what haversine + raw coordinates give the trees, typically worth ~2-4% RMSE on valid rows (partially masked in the graded score by the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor), so expect roughly 4.14 -> ~4.03.

Doubling the random training sample (1M→2M rows) reduces LightGBM's clean-row error modestly (learning-curve effect, roughly 1-2% on the ~3.6 clean RMSE), which after the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor compounds to about -0.03 graded RMSE, while the extra ~1-2 minutes of CSV read and training time still fits comfortably in the 10-minute budget; early stopping on a now-200K-row holdout keeps the fit stable, so a small, safe improvement from 4.138 to ~4.10 is expected.

The airport_route categorical encodes the flat-fare JFK (~$45-52) and EWR/LGA trip structure that axis-aligned coordinate splits learn only inefficiently; roughly 6% of valid trips are airport trips whose per-row error should drop noticeably, but the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows is unchanged, so the overall RMSE improves only ~2% (valid-row RMSE ~3.61 -> ~3.5).

On TPS-May-2022 raw features, gradient-boosted trees are the known strong baseline (~0.991-0.992 AUC vs ~0.987 for a small MLP): they capture the feature interactions the synthetic generator embedded, handle the nominal f_27 letters natively, and 2000 lr=0.05 rounds on 720k rows comfortably beats the 60-epoch 64-wide MLP despite being slightly under-converged relative to the 3000-round version.

One-hot quantile bins let the first layer directly represent the non-monotone effects of the 12 integer count columns (f_07-f_18) and restore resolution lost to f_28's heavy tail under standardization, while the 10-bin coarseness costs little on the smooth float columns, so the small undertrained MLP should gain a modest ~+0.002 AUC (characters stay as ordinals, so most of the hard work is unchanged).

PCA whitening is unsupervised and re-aligns the low-cardinality, high-signal axes (f_27 character ordinals, integer features) into dense principal-component mixtures that axis-aligned LightGBM splits can no longer isolate with single thresholds; the linear-tree leaves only absorb the purely linear part of the signal, so the boosted tree structure — which carries most of the AUC on this interaction-heavy dataset — has to rebuild raw-feature-aligned partitions through many oblique splits, a net regression of roughly 0.3–0.5 AUC points despite the better-conditioned leaf regressions.

In this dataset f_27 strings are essentially unique row identifiers (10-20 letters per position → ~4e10 possible strings), so a smoothed target encoding of the full string collapses to a near-constant column equal to the prior for train (out-of-fold), validation, and test rows, deleting all f_27 signal; the score regresses to the numeric-only LightGBM baseline (~0.003-0.006 AUC below the current per-character-ordinal model).

f_27 is near-unique (hundreds of thousands of distinct strings, most appearing once or twice), so a m=20-smoothed out-of-fold target encoding collapses to the global prior for almost every row and carries essentially no signal, while deleting the ten per-position ordinal columns removes genuinely informative features — a net AUC regression of roughly 0.001–0.0015.

These are the well-known 'magic' interactions of TPS May 2022 (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26 with those exact thresholds) that expose the synthetic generator's near-deterministic diagonal rules — axis-aligned trees can't efficiently learn them from raw features, and public notebooks showed this exact engineering lifts a single LGBM from ~0.9915 to ~0.9950 AUC.

A logistic regression on these raw/ordinal features reaches only ~0.88-0.90 AUC (the real signal here is nonlinear: unique-char structure, interactions), and its signal is essentially a subset of what the LightGBM already captures, so an equal 50/50 rank blend dilutes the strong model rather than adding complementary signal, dropping the graded AUC from ~0.9842 to roughly 0.978-0.980.

A ~12k-parameter MLP on standardized features can exploit the three precomputed additive sums and smooth continuous signals, but the ordinal-encoded f_27 characters and step-like interaction structure favor tree splits, so it should land slightly below the 3000-tree LightGBM (~0.981 vs 0.984), with best-epoch checkpointing preventing a larger collapse.

On this dataset MLPs only beat GBDT when given engineered interactions/unique-char features; a small 64-unit MLP on the same 40 raw/ordinal columns will land around 0.968-0.973, a modest regression versus the 3000-tree LightGBM baseline of 0.97696.

The dataset's known oblique structure (targets driven by sums of feature pairs/triples crossing ~±5 thresholds) is exactly what linear leaves represent efficiently, so a modest gain is likely, but 43-feature near-unregularized (linear_lambda=0.01) per-leaf WLS fits on ~100-sample leaves add overfit variance and the ~2x slowdown risks the 10-min budget, tempering the expected improvement.

The count of unique characters in f_27 was one of the strongest known engineered signals in TPS May 2022 — it correlates strongly with the target and is very hard for trees to synthesize from the ten per-position ordinals — so adding it should lift the single-LGBM baseline from ~0.9770 to roughly ~0.981.

These three sums are exactly the continuous interaction features discovered in TPS-May-2022 EDA (the 'i_02_21', 'i_05_22', 'i_00_01_26' directions, where target=1 concentrates in the tails of the sums); feeding raw sums lets axis-aligned LightGBM split directly on these diagonal boundaries that 3000 trees could otherwise only approximate, so expect a solid but partial gain (~+0.003–0.004 AUC) since the other big interaction signals (unique-character count of f_27, integer-feature interactions) remain absent.

f_27 is a near-unique row identifier (~700k+ distinct 10-char strings in 900k rows), so the raw-string categorical carries no transferable signal while giving LightGBM ~700k bins whose O(#categories) split search at every node of 3000 trees x 127 leaves (plus sorting per node) blows the 15-minute wall-clock budget — the run is hard-killed before writing a submission; even in the unlikely event it finished, dropping the 10 per-position encodings alone would cost ~0.002 AUC.

Adjacent-character bigrams as native categoricals let a single split express pairwise f_27 position interactions, which is cheap and safe with ~720k rows, but a 127-leaf/3000-tree ensemble can already approximate those interactions via successive ordinal splits and this competition's real interaction gains were mostly among the numeric features, so expect only a small (+0.0002–0.0006) AUC improvement, with a modest chance of a neutral or slightly negative result.

The gain-mined products captured real pairwise-interaction signal in this dataset (trees learn products poorly on their own), while PCA components are near-arbitrary linear mixtures of the already-present raw f_00..f_15 (the interaction signal is quadratic, not low-rank linear), so swapping them in loses the interaction gain and yields a modest regression back toward the raw-feature baseline.

Hashing the whole 10-char f_27 into 64 buckets destroys the per-position letter signal (and adds ~random collision features), leaving the model effectively numeric+products only, which for this dataset scores around 0.95 — a clear regression from 0.9753.

The mandated 5-fold cross_val_predict multiplies an already ~10-minute 300-tree fully-grown ExtraTrees fit on 900k rows by ~5x compute (and ~25-30GB of tree nodes, risking OOM), so the run is hard-killed at 15 minutes before submission/submission.csv is ever written — a failed run scored 0 — and even if it squeaked through, sqrt-feature ExtraTrees would only reach ~0.96 vs the 0.978 LightGBM.

A quick sklearn MLP (256,128, ~40 epochs, constant LR, ordinal-encoded f_27, no unique-character-count or engineered interaction features) historically lands ~0.968–0.975 AUC on TPS-May-2022 raw features — slightly below a fully-trained 3000-tree LightGBM (0.978) which captures the discrete/mean-shift structure the undertrained MLP only partially learns — and it should still finish in ~5 minutes, so expect a modest regression of roughly half a percent relative.

The unique-character count and per-letter occurrence counts of f_27 are known to be among the strongest signals in TPS May 2022 (the label depends heavily on the multiset of letters), so adding these 27 order-invariant features to the existing per-position codes should lift LGBM AUC from ~0.977 to ~0.990 while costing negligible runtime.

The 10 per-position categorical letters carry most of f_27's signal (tree-learnable letter-repetition structure behind the famous unique-character-count effect), while a full-string frequency feature is only a noisy proxy for low unique-char strings (most rows have frequency 1), so removing the letters costs roughly 1+ AUC points that the frequency count only marginally offsets.

The unique-character count of f_27 was one of the strongest known signals in this competition (duplicate letters are rare and highly informative), and per-letter counts give the trees multiplicity information that per-position ordinals cannot easily synthesize with axis-aligned splits, so adding these 27 low-cost integer columns should yield a modest, reliable gain of roughly +0.002 AUC over the 0.97696 baseline with negligible runtime overhead.

This dataset's known continuous interactions are mostly sum/difference (diagonal) structure, so z-scored pairwise products capture it only partially via their s²/d² component; a gain-based screen of 120 products will include a few genuinely useful pairs (e.g., around f_02/f_21, f_05/f_22, f_00/f_01/f_26) but most of the 25 add little beyond what 3000 trees already learn from raw features, and the remaining boost levers (f_27 unique-char count, exact-form interactions) are untouched — expect a small ~+0.002 AUC gain (0.977→~0.979), with modest risk of dilution and runtime headroom still fitting the ~10-minute budget.

Refitting on the full 800k rows (11% more data) with proportionally scaled trees (~3333) should yield a small AUC gain since stage 1 was still improving at 3000 trees (undertrained, no overfit risk from dropping early stopping at this constant trees-per-row ratio), typically worth +0.0002–0.0004 on this dataset.

LightGBM's optimal many-vs-rest partitioning of the 26 letters per f_27 position removes the arbitrary alphabetical ordering that threshold splits impose; the per-position letter effects in this dataset are not alphabetically monotonic, so this is usually a small positive tweak (~+0.0003-0.0005 AUC) with early stopping limiting the extra overfitting risk from the more flexible splits.

The unique-character count of f_27 is the single most famous engineered feature for TPS-May-2022 (a planted signal in the synthetic generator); public experiments (e.g., Ambrosm's EDA/GBDT notebooks) showed it alone lifts a raw-feature LGBM from ~0.981-0.982 to ~0.989-0.990 AUC, and it is information trees cannot easily reconstruct from the ten per-position ordinal columns, so I expect roughly +0.006-0.008 here with negligible added runtime.

max_depth=2 caps each tree at ~4 leaves/pairwise interactions, and since the baseline is still underfitting at 3000 rounds with 127-leaf trees, the ~30x capacity reduction plus loss of the higher-order structure (unique-character counts, multi-feature interactions beyond the one engineered sum) that deep trees were partially learning makes this a clear regression of roughly 0.004-0.005 AUC.

On TPS-May-2022, GBDT on raw numeric + f_27 ordinal features (no engineered products/sums/unique-count features) plateaus around 0.976-0.978 AUC — and this config (600 trees, 31 leaves, max_bin 63) is weaker than typical — so it should regress below the current MLP's 0.9822, which benefits from the smooth interaction structure of this synthetic dataset.

TPS-May-2022's signal lives largely in smooth float-sum/product interactions where the converged MLP excels, so a modest 600-tree/31-leaf/max_bin=63 LightGBM on the same raw features (also undertrained vs the 3000-tree baseline whose AUC was still improving) should regress to roughly the ~0.95-0.96 raw-GBDT level.

Quartile-coding the ~16 float predictors caps each at 4 levels / 3 split points, destroying within-quartile resolution that a 3000-tree, still-improving (early stopping never fired) LightGBM was exploiting for fine-grained and interaction signal, so expect a modest regression of roughly 0.004-0.006 AUC while integer and f_27 character signal is preserved.

This dataset's signal is heavily interaction-driven and the 127-leaf model is still underfitting at 3000 rounds, so cutting capacity to 7-leaf stumps-like trees removes the ability to express multi-feature interactions, yielding a clear AUC regression (roughly 0.977 → ~0.971) though the run stays well within budget.

This dataset's signal is dominated by feature interactions (the competition's stated theme), and 4-leaf trees can only express coarse main effects plus weak, piecewise pairwise interactions; 3000 rounds at lr=0.05 cannot compensate for the lost per-tree interaction capacity, so the ensemble underfits relative to the 127-leaf baseline and AUC should regress by roughly half a point (≈0.9915 → ≈0.9865) rather than improve.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is the well-known 'magic' interaction for TPS May 2022 (these three continuous features share a target-correlated latent shift, so their sum is far more separable than the individuals); giving LightGBM this explicit diagonal feature should add roughly +0.002 AUC over the 0.99147 baseline, with only a small chance the effect is ~neutral.

f_00+f_01+f_26 is a genuine three-way interaction in this dataset's generating process (known tail effect beyond roughly ±5), so giving LightGBM the raw sum lets it capture with two splits what it otherwise approximates poorly with axis-aligned splits on the individual columns — a real but modest gain (~+0.001-0.002 AUC) since the effect only touches ~1% of rows and the 3000-tree ensemble already recovers part of it.

This dataset's signal is dominated by multiplicative/interaction effects and f_27 structure that boosted trees split on naturally, while a small raw-feature MLP (no engineered interactions or embeddings, ~420s CPU cap, ~20-50 epochs) historically tops out around 0.96-0.97 on TPS-May-2022, so replacing the 0.977 LightGBM with this MLP should regress AUC by roughly 0.008-0.012.

LightGBM's native categorical splits partition each f_27 position into arbitrary letter subsets instead of arbitrary ordinal ranges over the meaningless A-Z codes, capturing per-letter target rates more directly with the same capacity, so expect a small positive gain (~+0.001 AUC) with negligible runtime or overfitting risk at ~26 low-cardinality categories.

The unique-character count of f_27 is the best-known engineered feature for TPS May 2022 — it encodes class-conditional string diversity that axis-aligned trees cannot recover from the ten per-position ordinals — and historically adds roughly +0.002–0.003 AUC to a single LightGBM at this baseline level (~0.977), with essentially no risk of regression or runtime cost.

Weighting the loss by target darkness moves the trained predictor away from the RMSE-optimal conditional mean (darker outputs on ambiguous stroke-edge and faint-stain pixels, less pressure to clean large white/stain regions that the unweighted metric counts equally), so the sharpening benefit on the ~5% ink pixels is likely outweighed by a small net regression on per-pixel RMSE.

The baseline is undertrained (2000 steps ≈ 1 min); ~330 s of GPU time yields roughly 5-7x more optimizer steps with the LR annealing to ~0, and since test scans are re-noised copies of the same 36 training pages, longer training of the small U-Net reliably lowers per-pixel RMSE (eval overhead every 100 steps slightly reduces effective step count, and mild overfitting to noise realizations caps the gain, so expect a solid but not dramatic ~10-15% improvement).

The metric is RMSE, so MSE-trained L2 is metric-matched: in ambiguous stain-over-text regions the MSE optimum hedges gray while the L1 optimum commits to the median, and Zhao et al. themselves found L2 best on PSNR for denoising (L1's edge is an SSIR/sharpness and long-schedule result), so I expect a small regression (~+2%) rather than the claimed improvement.

Mild brightness/contrast jitter is benign-to-helpful here: it mirrors the dataset's real global-tint/fading noise mode and regularizes a tiny 36-page dataset, so I expect a small (~2%) RMSE gain, partly offset by 80% of training crops being slightly off the test intensity distribution within the fixed step budget.

The model was trained only at 1x on near-binary targets, so the 0.75x/1.25x round-trips (antialias bilinear) effectively low-pass the averaged prediction by ~0.4-0.5 px and present scale-mismatched inputs; the extra blur raises error on ink-stroke edges (which dominate this RMSE) more than the variance-reduction helps on broad stains, so flip-only TTA likely remains better and the score should regress a few percent.

With only 2000 optimizer steps the U-Net is closer to underfit than overfit, and Dropout2d placed before the next blocks' BatchNorms creates a train/eval variance shift, so the added regularization slightly slows convergence and yields a small RMSE regression (~+0.5-1%) rather than a generalization gain.

With a fixed 180-second wall-clock budget a small U-Net is still converging, so channel dropout mainly slows fitting rather than preventing harmful overfitting — especially since test scans are re-noised copies of the same 36 training pages, where memorizing page content actually helps — yielding a slight RMSE regression (~1-3%).

The 4th level adds capacity and doubles the receptive field (~89px), which helps with the heterogeneous multi-scale noise (global tint, large stains), and although the ~30% higher per-step cost cuts the number of optimization steps under the fixed 180s budget, thousands of steps remain plenty for the model to converge on only 36 underlying pages, so a modest net improvement of a few percent is expected.

The 23x23 median-filter channel explicitly exposes the slow-varying stain/fold/tint background, turning the task into near-background-subtraction (a known strong trick for this competition), so the small U-Net reaches lower error within the same short 2000-step budget; the diff is correctly implemented (consistent full-image bg computation before cropping, proper 2-channel flips and padding), so runtime stays well within budget and a solid ~25% RMSE reduction is expected, though not more since the baseline can already partly infer background from its receptive field.

A 5-level U-Net with 256px crops gives ~2x the receptive field and ~14x the parameters for roughly 2x the per-step compute (same pixels/step), which should meaningfully improve removal of large-scale stains/tint while still fitting the wall-clock budget; the same 2000-step training schedule limits the gain to a modest ~8% RMSE reduction.

The model is trained with random h/v flips, so its four flipped predictions are highly correlated but not identical; averaging them in TTA cancels prediction noise for a small, consistent RMSE gain (~1-2% relative) at negligible extra inference cost (batched into one forward pass), with no risk of timeout since only ~230 extra image-forwards are added.

A 180s wall-clock budget on a modern GPU yields roughly 2-4x the baseline's 2000 optimizer steps (small ch=32 U-Net at ~20-50ms/step) under a full cosine decay to zero, and since all 29 test scans are re-noised copies of the same 36 training pages, the extra training/memorization should cut per-pixel RMSE by ~5-10% (0.01626 -> ~0.0150).

The graded metric is RMSE, so MSE is the matched training loss; Charbonnier/L1 equal-weights all pixels and de-prioritizes the high-error stain/stroke pixels that dominate the squared error, and in this short 2000-step budget (where the page-memorization optimum is the same for both losses) that typically costs a small amount of RMSE — likely a 1-4% regression, partly within single-seed noise.

The injected i.i.d. Gaussian noise (sigma=0.05, ~3x the current 0.015 RMSE and unlike the structured stain/wrinkle/tint test noise) dominates the training loss with an auxiliary denoising task that doesn't exist at inference, diverting the small U-Net's limited capacity and biasing it toward low-pass behavior that slightly blurs text strokes, while the regularization benefit is modest because random 128x128 crops are already diverse and the real generalization gap is across structured noise types — so I expect a small regression rather than the claimed robustness gain.

BatchNorm→GroupNorm removes the crop-batch-vs-full-page statistics mismatch (and adds per-sample robustness to globally tinted pages) in this restoration U-Net, which typically yields a small gain, but with batch 32 BN was already well-behaved and both are norm layers, so expect only a ~1-2% RMSE improvement rather than a large shift.

The composite SSIM+L1 loss optimizes structure rather than the graded RMSE: SSIM relatively downweights errors in bright (white-background) regions that dominate the pixel-wise squared error, and the literature consistently shows SSIM-trained restorers trade a few tenths of a dB of PSNR (i.e., ~3-6% higher RMSE) for perceptual sharpness, so a modest regression is the most likely outcome despite crisper strokes.

Only 4 of the 8 dihedral views (identity/flips) match the flip-only training augmentation; the rot90/rot270 passes are out-of-distribution for a U-Net that has learned an upright text-layout prior, so their grayer, less-confident stroke predictions dilute the confident upright predictions when averaged, and the resulting pull of saturated 0/1 outputs toward gray hurts RMSE more than the modest variance reduction from ensembling helps.

The graded metric is per-pixel RMSE, which the MSE loss matches directly; a pure SSIM loss down-weights luminance bias and edge/contrast fidelity (as in Zhao et al., where SSIM-only training hurt PSNR/RMSE), so the sharp-looking but pixel-biased outputs will land a modest regression on this already-heavily-memorized task.

Residual (DnCNN-style) learning with a zero-initialized linear head removes the sigmoid's saturation/quantization near the mostly-white background (letting untouched pixels pass through exactly) and lets the small U-Net spend capacity on the noise itself, a well-established formulation for this exact competition that should cut RMSE by roughly 15-25% with identical compute and no new failure modes.

The graded metric is pure RMSE, and swapping the direct MSE objective for sqrt(MSE)+0.1*(1-SSIM) is Adam-scale-neutral on the pixel term but adds a misaligned structural proxy (SSIM's luminance/contrast invariance plus bf16-autocast cancellation noise in its variance estimates) that nudges gradients away from pixel-error minimization, so I expect a small regression on the order of 1-3% rather than an improvement.

DnCNN-style residual learning with zero-init (identity start) is well-suited to this mostly-darkening stain/tint noise: the global skip preserves text strokes directly and the model only learns the brightness correction, which converges faster than sigmoid-bounded direct regression under the fixed 2000-step budget, yielding a moderate RMSE improvement.

Synthetic stain/shading/speckle corruption multiplies noise realizations per clean page ~7x in a tiny 36-page dataset, regularizing the noisy-to-clean mapping and improving robustness to the test set's re-noised pages; the modest distribution mismatch (lighter corruption, whole-image blur) and ~7x dilution of real-pair exposure temper the gain to a few percent, with the 2000-step budget easily absorbing the ~30s generation cost.

4.5x more optimization steps with a correctly stretched cosine schedule lets the underfit small U-Net converge further, and because test scans are re-noised copies of the same 36 training pages, the extra training (including page memorization) translates into genuinely lower test RMSE, with only mild diminishing returns; wall-clock should still fit (fallback to 45 epochs if tight), so expect roughly a 10-17% RMSE reduction from 0.01624.

Dihedral-8 averaging cancels the model's one-sided stroke-edge biases (flips/rot180 are in-distribution since training used h/v flips) and adds ensemble diversity from the four transposed views, which are mildly out-of-distribution for sideways text and only slightly worse, so expect a small net RMSE improvement (~1-2%) rather than the large gain full-TTA gives on orientation-augmented models.

The metric is RMSE, which MSE training directly optimizes; switching to L1 downweights exactly the large stain/stroke-boundary residuals that dominate RMSE and pushes predictions toward the conditional median instead of the error-minimizing mean, so I expect a small regression (~3%) rather than an improvement.

Squared error is concentrated on the ~5% ink/stroke pixels, so tripling their gradient share should sharpen glyph reconstruction and trim total RMSE slightly, though the unweighted metric and mild underfitting of stain-removal background keeps the gain small (~1%).

The graded metric is unweighted RMSE dominated by the ~95% white/stain background pixels, so reweighting the training loss 10:1 toward the ~5% ink pixels optimizes a different objective than the metric: stroke sharpness gains are limited (stroke cores are already near-black), while the effectively down-weighted background/stain whitening (weight ~0.53x) should degrade slightly, yielding a small regression from 0.01603 to roughly 0.0166.

Zero-init residual head makes the net start as the identity and learn only the noise correction (tint/stains), avoiding sigmoid saturation on the ~83% pure-white targets and converging faster within the fixed 2000-step budget — a standard denoising win worth roughly 8-15% RMSE; the main risk is the diff's CPU-only/8-thread runtime.toml slowing training toward the 15-min kill, but as a runtime (non-ML) setting it should be inert under the harness's EV_RUNTIME_CONFIG, so I predict the run completes with a ~0.014-0.0145 RMSE.

The metric is RMSE, so swapping MSE for L1 creates a loss-metric mismatch: L1 underweights the large stain/stroke residuals that dominate squared error (and pushes toward the conditional median rather than mean), and although L1's constant gradient better saturates the ~88% pure white/black pixels, the net effect of losing quadratic pressure on heavily corrupted regions should be a modest regression of roughly 3-4%.

Zero-initialized residual head starts at the identity (already far better than a random sigmoid) and learns the mostly-additive darkening correction without sigmoid saturation, so it converges faster within the fixed 20-epoch budget to a slightly lower RMSE, though both parameterizations end near the same capacity/noise floor.

Halving BASE_CH cuts parameters ~4x while keeping steps fixed, and since test scans are re-noised copies of the same 36 train pages (where extra capacity aids memorizing crisp clean strokes), the thinner 8/16/32/64 NAFNet should slightly blur stroke reconstruction and raise RMSE by a few percent, though the smaller net easily fits the CPU time budget.

The eval is unweighted per-pixel RMSE, and under plain MSE the rare ink pixels already carry a large share of the loss (bigger errors), so upweighting them 3x mostly introduces an objective mismatch (biasing ambiguous dark regions darker and reallocating gradient away from stain-removal background) for a likely small net regression.

The applied diff pins execution to CPU with only 8 intraop threads (execution.json + configure_execution force CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=""), and retaining 2,000 batch-32 128x128 U-Net updates is ~700 TFLOPs of fp32 compute — roughly 20-60 minutes on 8 CPU cores — so the run is hard-killed at 15 minutes mid-training, never writes submission.csv, and is recorded as a failure; the graded RMSE therefore stays at the parent's 0.01624 (the closing-normalization channel is a sound idea that would likely improve RMSE ~15-20% if the run actually executed on GPU within budget).

The runtime config forces CPU execution where autocast/AMP is already disabled, so computing the final 1x1 conv + sigmoid in float32 is a numerical no-op; with the same seed and schedule the pipeline reproduces the parent run's fp32 result (~0.01624) essentially exactly (the only scenario with a real effect, bf16 output quantization ~0.001 RMSE on GPU, does not apply here).

Four-view flip TTA on a U-Net already trained with flip augmentation averages four highly correlated denoising estimates, trimming the variance component of the error for a typical ~1.5-3% RMSE gain; the main risk is the new CPU-only runtime.json (13 threads, CUDA hidden) slowing the unchanged 2000-step training past the 15-min kill, but assuming the run completes like the parent, expect ~0.0159.

The faithful NAFNet keeps the identical 2000-step/batch-32 training recipe but swaps in a global residual (clean = dirty + correction) with a linear output and channel attention, which suits this mostly-white, perturbation-style noise slightly better than the plain sigmoid U-Net (offset partly by zero-init beta/gamma warm-up and the halved base width), so expect a modest improvement to ~0.0155 — with the real risk being the runtime.json-pinned CPU/13-thread run, whose ~130 TFLOP training load lands near the 10-15 minute budget but should still finish and grade.

The fb_in22k_ft_in1k head was fine-tuned on these very ImageNet images, so its 120-dog-class softmax (temperature-tuned) is a strong, partially decorrelated second predictor; the holdout grid includes w=0 so it can't regress much, and blending with the frozen-feature LR should net a moderate ~5-10% log-loss gain over 0.3096.

Unwhitened PCA-256 discards ~768 low-variance directions that can carry fine-grained breed signal, while the holdout-tuned L2 in the current LR already controls overfitting on the 1024-d features, so expect a small log-loss regression (~1-2%) rather than an improvement.

Mixup/CutMix's smoothing over confusable breeds aligns well with log loss on a small 120-class dataset, so I expect a modest improvement, though the 6-epoch fine-tune limits gains since mixup slows convergence and temperature scaling already captures part of the calibration benefit.

With only 6 epochs of fine-tuning and an eval-time center crop (~0.58 area fraction) that the current (0.35, 1.0) crop range closely matches, dropping the min scale to 0.08 shifts most training views to zoomed, often part-only crops that are ambiguous for look-alike breeds and slow convergence under the fixed short cosine schedule, so I expect a small log-loss regression (~+0.01) rather than a generalization gain; temperature scaling already absorbs most calibration benefit.

ConvNeXt-V2 Large (IN-22k→IN-1k) frozen features are far stronger and more linearly separable for these 120 ImageNet dog classes than ResNet-50 V1 (IN-1k top-1 ~88% vs ~76%, plus 22k pretraining on fine-grained breeds), so linear-probe accuracy should rise from ~84% to ~89-90%, cutting log loss by roughly a third to ~0.31 while compute (~69 GFLOPs/img × 10.2k images, fp16) and the six LR fits on 2536-d features stay comfortably inside the 15-minute budget; main residual risks are the ~800 MB HF download time and slight overconfidence on look-alike breed pairs, which the strongly-regularized C grid partially mitigates.

The 1000-d log-proba block is not free redundancy: it hands the L2-regularized LR the pretrained ImageNet dog-classifier (trained on ~17x more per-class data than the 9,199 train images, and nearly identical to the 120 target breeds) at an L2 cost of ~1 per class direction, which a small-C probe on raw pooled features cannot cheaply replicate from ~77 samples/class, so dropping it should regress log loss by a couple of points; the near-constant non-dog columns add some noise but the holdout C search limits that harm, and blending two comparable, differently-erring predictors (probe + pretrained logits) typically improves log-loss calibration.

Ridge+temperature spans the same softmax-of-linear-scores family, but squared-loss fitting plus a single global temperature cannot match multinomial LR's directly log-loss-aligned, per-class adaptive calibration on 120 confusable breeds, so a small regression (with per-class score-scale mismatch and holdout-selected T applied to the full refit) is the most likely outcome.
