PCA-128 per block retains most of the dominant (breed-related) variance of dog-only features and cuts overfitting, but for a 120-class fine-grained task the ~119-dim class-mean span plus nuisance (background/pose) variance competes for the top-128 slots, so low-variance directions carrying look-alike-breed signal are discarded; with the C grid and pipeline otherwise unchanged I expect the information loss to slightly outweigh the mild regularization/calibration benefit, giving a small regression of roughly +0.005 log loss.

ConvNeXt-Base with in22k pretraining (which saw far more dog breeds) gives frozen 1024-d features substantially more discriminative than ResNet-50 V1's, and the holdout re-tuned C compensates for the layer-normed feature scale, so log loss should drop from 0.45 to roughly 0.28-0.34 (probe accuracy ~85% to ~90-92%), with mild risk of a smaller gain if the C grid caps below the optimum or the 5 logistic fits push runtime.

End-to-end fine-tuning of an ImageNet-22k ConvNeXt-Tiny on this same-pool 90/10 re-split should lift accuracy from ~87% (frozen linear probe) to ~90-93%, and hflip TTA plus validation-fitted temperature scaling should cut log loss from 0.45 to roughly 0.30-0.36 (point estimate 0.33), with residual risk that a short 6-epoch schedule, label smoothing, or the 7-minute training guard leaves it closer to the baseline.

The pretrained fc head's log-softmax adds a nonlinear, well-calibrated (and partly memorized, since Stanford Dogs is an ImageNet subset) breed signal on top of the pooled features that logistic regression can learn to blend with its own linear separator, yielding a modest log-loss gain that is slightly damped by the heavier C-grid and the amplification of near-constant non-dog log-prob dims under standardization.

Swapping ResNet-50 V1 features for an L2-normalized concat of ConvNeXt-B/in22k, CLIP ViT-B/16 and DINOv2 ViT-B/14 — all markedly stronger and more diverse frozen extractors on this ImageNet-dog subset — with holdout-tuned C should cut the log loss from ~0.45 to roughly 0.30-0.33 (a ~25-35% relative gain), while extraction (~50 GFLOPs/img over ~10k images) and five LogReg fits on 2560-d features stay within the 10-minute budget; main residual risks are mild CLIP weakness on fine-grained breeds and noisy holdout C selection on 1,380 rows, neither of which should overturn the improvement.

Focal loss mainly helps under extreme class imbalance, which this near-balanced 120-class set lacks, while dropping label smoothing removes the calibration/overconfidence protection that log loss on a small 1,023-image test set rewards, so a few highly confident mistakes on look-alike breeds should push the loss modestly above the 0.660 baseline.

Layer4+fc-only tuning keeps ImageNet's already dog-tuned early features but forfeits the mid-level adaptation that full fine-tuning uses to separate confusable breeds on ~9k images, so I expect a modest regression (roughly 0.69-0.73) rather than an improvement, with the same 10-epoch recipe.

Horizontal-flip TTA averages two correlated but non-identical views of each test image under a flip-augmented (augreg/in1k) ViT-B/16, which typically yields a small, consistent log-loss reduction (~0.5-1.5%) without touching training; the NUM_WORKERS=0 change affects only runtime, which stays well within budget.

The current ViT-B/16 was fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k, which literally contains these 120 dog classes, so its frozen features are near-optimal for the linear probe, whereas CLIP ViT-B/32's contrastive image-text features with a coarse 7x7 patch grid are markedly weaker for fine-grained breed discrimination (ImageNet linear-probe gap ~20 points vs an ft-in1k ViT-B/16), so log loss should roughly double from ~0.51 to ~1.0; runtime is safe (B/32 is faster than B/16 and LogReg converges on 768-d features).

PCA-256 on dog-only ResNet-50 GAP features should retain ~85-90% of variance while cutting the 245k-parameter probe to ~31k, so the denoising/overfitting reduction likely yields a small log-loss gain, though the fixed C=0.3 (tuned on raw features) and loss of low-variance fine-grained directions keep it near-neutral rather than a clear win.

Frozen DINOv2 ViT-B/14 embeddings are markedly stronger than supervised ResNet-50 features for fine-grained dog breeds (linear-probe accuracy roughly 84%→89-90%), so log loss should drop from ~0.44 to ~0.33, modestly tempered by 224px pos-embed interpolation, the 0.875 crop recipe, and residual overconfidence risk that the holdout-C selection and TTA averaging only partly mitigate.

Whitening rescales per-dim std from ~0.027 to 1 (~1400x higher effective C for the fixed C=1.0 LogReg) in an overparameterized, near-separable regime, so the head interpolates and becomes overconfident while PCA truncation also drops fine-grained tail directions — both raise log loss on a metric dominated by confident errors.

A k=10 distance-weighted k-NN head yields sparse vote distributions, so for the ~10-20% of test images whose true breed is absent from the 10 nearest neighbors the (smoothed) probability is ~9e-4, costing ~7 nats each, while even correct images only get a ~0.4-0.8 vote share — unlike the dense, well-calibrated logistic regression, this roughly triples the log loss despite comparable accuracy.

End-to-end fine-tuning of the ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 (whose pretraining data already covers these exact 120 dog breeds) with RRC/hflip augmentation, label smoothing, and warmup+cosine SGD should lift test accuracy several points over the frozen-feature logistic probe and cut log loss by roughly a quarter (10 epochs on 9.2k images fits comfortably in the time budget), with label smoothing keeping overconfidence from inflating the loss on the small 1,023-image test set.

ViT-B/16 (21k-pretrained, 1k-fine-tuned) pooled features are far more linearly separable for these ImageNet dog classes than ResNet-50 V1 features, so the same linear probe should lift accuracy from ~86-88% to ~92-93% and cut log loss from 0.453 to roughly 0.30-0.35, only mildly tempered by C=0.3 not being retuned for the 768-d feature scale.

Averaging probabilities over 10 highly-correlated views (including the exact baseline center crop and its flip) reduces prediction variance and softens confident errors on the small 1,023-image test set, which typically yields a ~1-3% relative log-loss gain for frozen-feature linear probes, partially offset by the 8 corner/flip views being slightly off the center-crop distribution the logistic regression was fit on.

ConvNeXt-Tiny (in22k_ft_in1k) frozen features are substantially stronger than ResNet-50 V1 for fine-grained dog breeds, and per-block L2-normalized concatenation acts as a two-backbone ensemble, so log loss should drop from 0.453 to roughly 0.32-0.36 (well within the time budget since extraction only adds ~1-2 min).

The temperature-scaled ImageNet dog-head restricted to the 120 breeds is a genuinely diverse complement (it was trained on ~150k dog images vs the LR's 9.2k, and many Stanford Dogs images were in ImageNet training), so the guarded alpha/T grid search — which includes alpha=0, capping downside — should capture a modest calibration/blend gain of roughly 0.01 log loss over 0.3093, partly offset by the 80%-LR selection bias and grid overfitting on 1,840 validation rows.

Truncating 2048-d ResNet-50 features to 256 unwhitened PCA components discards low-variance directions that still carry fine-grained breed-discriminative signal, and C=0.3 was tuned for the raw feature scale, so a modest log-loss regression (~+0.01 absolute) is the most likely outcome; runtime impact is negligible and the pipeline stays deterministic.

ResNet-50's features were trained to be read out by average pooling, so swapping in global max pooling yields less robust descriptors and inflates feature magnitude (making the hardcoded C=0.3 effectively under-regularized), which historically costs a few percent on fine-grained linear probes — a modest log-loss regression despite the temperature recalibration.

IMAGENET1K_V2 (ResNet-strikes-back recipe, ~80.9% vs 76.1% top-1) should yield modestly more separable 2048-d features for these literally-in-pretraining dog classes, and since the temperature is refit in-run the calibration stays consistent; same one-pass cost keeps runtime well under budget, so expect a small log-loss improvement (~0.43) with only minor risk of regression if V2 features transfer slightly worse to linear probing.

C=0.3 was already holdout-selected over 0.03 for these 2,048-d frozen features, and the brief seeded 2-epoch fine-tune only partially washes out the shrunken, underfit head initialization (conv adaptation and batch order are unchanged), so expect a small log-loss regression of roughly +0.01–0.03.

Dropping the crop from 224 to 192 (~14% smaller linear scale, 6x6 instead of 7x7 layer4 maps) loses fine-grained texture detail that a 224-pretrained ResNet50 needs for look-alike breeds; the 2-epoch/90s fine-tune cap was never time-binding, so the compute savings buy nothing and the logistic-regression head is re-fit on slightly weaker features, yielding a modest log-loss regression (~+0.02-0.03).

Unwhitened PCA-256 discards 1792 tail directions of the ResNet-50 features that likely carry some fine-grained breed-separating signal (confusable pairs dominate log loss), and C=0.3 was tuned for the raw feature scale, so the pipeline should slightly underfit and regress the log loss by ~0.005-0.01, though the effect is partly offset by the extra regularization acting like a stronger prior on a heavily overparameterized linear probe.

Dropping the frozen ResNet-50 input from 224px to 192px coarsens the ImageNet-pretrained features (6x6 instead of 7x7 pooled map) and loses fine-grained detail critical for look-alike breeds, so the retrained linear probe regresses log loss by roughly 4-7% despite the preserved crop geometry and unchanged training setup.

IMAGENET1K_V2 is a markedly stronger checkpoint (80.9% vs 76.1% ImageNet top-1) trained on these very dog classes, so its frozen 2048-d features plus the matching 232/224 preprocessing should yield a solid linear-probe improvement (roughly 3 points accuracy, ~0.04 lower log loss), with the fixed C=0.3 and telemetry/config changes adding negligible risk.

Temperature is a safe, near-no-op post-hoc calibration for an already holdout-tuned C=0.3 logistic regression (2048-d features, ~31 params/sample hints at mild residual overconfidence), so expect only a small log-loss improvement (~0.5% relative), with the 85%-fit-to-100%-refit transfer and the small 1,023-image test set adding noise in either direction.

Gentle last-bottleneck fine-tuning warm-started from the logistic-regression head is a well-proven upgrade over linear probing on Stanford Dogs (cache/BN-frozen/short-SGD design is sound, fits the time budget, and should complete both epochs), so expect a solid but modest log-loss gain from 0.4525 to roughly 0.40-0.42, partially tempered by slight overconfidence on the small 1,023-image test set.

Horizontal-flip TTA on a frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 almost always yields a small log-loss gain by softening confident errors; the gain is capped because the logistic regression was trained on single-view features, so expect a modest ~0.005 absolute improvement rather than a large one.

For AUC, balancing a logistic fit mostly shifts the intercept (no benefit) while discarding 83–99% of negatives at fixed C, which strengthens effective L2 regularization 5–170x, starves the rare-label NB log-count ratios of negative data (threat: 478 negatives), and adds subsampling variance — so threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic columns regress the most and the mean column-wise AUC drops roughly 0.008 from 0.9805.

Stacking the shared char_wb 2-6 block onto branch B upgrades the weaker word-only NB-LogReg branch (char n-grams + NB weighting are the classic strong combo here, especially for threat/identity_hate), which should lift the 0.5/0.5 rank blend by ~+0.0005 despite slightly reduced branch diversity, while the single-pass fit_transform restructuring frees roughly the time the six heavier (~136M-nnz) liblinear fits add, keeping the run under the 15-minute kill.

ROC AUC is threshold-free, so rebalancing the class prior mostly shifts intercepts and buys little for logistic-regression ranking, while 1:1 undersampling discards 5x-167x of the training rows (only 478 negatives remain for threat, 1,405 for identity_hate), starving the models of hard-negative information and simultaneously degrading branch B's OOF stacking features — expect a net regression of roughly 0.01 mean AUC, concentrated in the rare labels that carry equal weight in the column mean.

MultinomialNB on TF-IDF is a strictly weaker ranker than the NB-LogReg hybrid (alpha=1.0 smoothing over 200k features flattens rare-feature weights, and losing the discriminative correction hurts rare labels like threat/identity_hate most), so branch B's standalone AUC drops ~1.5-2 points, which the fixed 50/50 rank blend and the now-weaker OOF stack features into branch A cannot recover — a net regression of roughly 0.25-0.3% despite MNB's greater decorrelation from branch A.

Frozen mean-pooled word2vec (trained on only ~20M corpus tokens, no fine-tuning) yields a much weaker branch (~0.95 AUC vs ~0.98 for the char/word TF-IDF branch it replaces), and the MLP on the same 200-d embeddings is highly correlated with it, so the 1/3-equal rank blend — despite branch B surviving — drops roughly a full AUC point from 0.9808 to ~0.970.

Fitting on 1:1 subsamples discards 81-99% of the negatives and, with C held fixed (sklearn's penalty is not rescaled by n), over-regularizes the fits 5-167x, so the rare columns (threat with 956 rows, identity_hate with 2,810) lose the most AUC while the frequent columns lose ~0.003-0.005 from data loss; the NB log-count ratios get noisier and the 3-epoch MLP is left with only ~380 Adam steps, and since all three rank-averaged branches degrade together the blend cannot recover, yielding roughly -0.009 mean AUC.

The time guards mean D will realistically get only 1-2 epochs on the same TF-IDF features as A/B/C, so it lands slightly below the linear branches (val ~0.978-0.980, above the 0.97 keep-threshold) and its rank-average contribution at 1/4 weight is near-neutral: modest non-linearity diversity gain mostly offset by undertraining and high feature overlap, with a meaningful chance D is time-skipped (score unchanged) and a small risk the extra ~2-3 min pushes past the kill.

1:1 undersampling discards 90-99% of the negatives — including nearly all the hard 'toxic-but-not-this-label' examples that define each column's AUC — so threat/severe_toxic/identity_hate rankings degrade (insults and profanity outrank true threats/hate), and since all three branches share the same subsample the errors are correlated and the rank-blend can't cancel them; only runtime improves.

Applying consistent train+test noise removal (IPs/URLs/timestamps), repeat-collapse, and profanity de-obfuscation mainly helps the word-level NB branch and rare profanity-driven labels (obscene/insult/identity_hate) by merging rare obfuscated variants into high-frequency forms, while the char n-gram branch loses only a little intensity gradation; net effect should be a small positive (~+0.0004 absolute), though with meaningful probability of a near-neutral or tiny negative outcome.

Clean OOF stacking (no leakage) gives branch A genuine cross-label signal that notably helps the rare columns (threat/identity_hate) while the /20-scaled logit features keep A mostly A-like, so the 50/50 blend should gain a few ten-thousandths; no new information enters the ensemble and part of the gain is offset by reduced A-B diversity, so expect a small positive move (~+0.0005) rather than a jump, with a secondary risk that the 30 extra liblinear fits push wall-clock toward the 15-min kill.

A 3-epoch, 64-unit MLP on branch A's features yields a genuinely weaker third ranking (especially on the rare threat/identity_hate columns where its shared representation has barely learned label-specific cues), and the untuned equal 1/3 rank weight dilutes two strong, well-matched linear branches — so the mean column-wise AUC regresses by roughly 0.002 despite the added nonlinearity/diversity.

Branch C is a feature-superset NB-LogReg (B's word 1-2-grams plus A's char_wb n-grams, with the same max_iter=100 liblinear behavior branch B already uses), so it should be at least as strong as B individually and add partially decorrelated char-level signal to the blend; an equal 1/3 rank average of three correlated-but-diverse linear branches typically gains ~+0.0005-0.0015 mean AUC on this competition, and runtime stays within budget since the expensive vectorizers are fit only once.

Holdout-tuned per-label weights (coarse 0.05 grid + 0.5-shrinkage) will reliably tilt the common labels (toxic/obscene/insult, thousands of holdout positives) toward the stronger char-n-gram branch A, while shrinkage bounds the noise-driven damage on threat/identity_hate (~96/~280 holdout positives), so expect a small net gain of ~+0.0002-0.0004 mean AUC (quadratic loss means moving halfway to the optimum captures ~75% of the potential gain); the extra ~3-5 min of holdout vectorizer/model fits should still finish under the 15-min kill but pushes near the soft 10-min target.

Compressing 100k sparse word n-grams into a rank-300 linear subspace (while dropping char n-grams, NB weighting, and the two-branch ensemble) throws away most of the task-specific lexical signal — LSA-LR is strictly a rank-constrained linear model, so AUC drops across all columns and collapses hardest on the rare threat/identity_hate labels, landing well below the 0.9798 sparse ensemble.

Subsampling to 10:1 discards ~90-97% of negatives for the rare labels (threat keeps ~5k of 160k rows, severe_toxic/identity_hate ~10%), so all three branches lose the hard negatives that define the top of those AUC rankings (toxic is untouched since its ratio already exceeds 10:1, and obscene/insult keep >half their data), producing a small mean-column regression concentrated in threat/severe_toxic/identity_hate despite the faster runtime and rank-based blending absorbing calibration shifts.

A single softmax over 7 mutually-exclusive classes forces the six label probabilities to share a normalized mass (a toxic+obscene+insult comment splits its score ~3 ways), scrambling per-column orderings relative to six dedicated binary fastText models — the rare-label sharing benefit doesn't offset this, so branch F weakens slightly and the equal-weight rank blend (2/3 unchanged A+B) regresses by a small amount.

A single raw-count word 1-2-gram ComplementNB is essentially plain multinomial-NB scoring (double-counts overlapping n-grams, no IDF/length normalization, no char n-grams for obfuscated profanity), so it lands well below the 3-branch TF-IDF logistic/NB-LR rank blend — expect roughly a 0.015-0.02 absolute mean-AUC drop to ~0.964, a clear regression despite the speed and robustness gains.

Unweighted mean-pooled from-scratch Word2Vec (200d, 5 epochs) discards the sparse word/char-n-gram evidence that makes this dataset nearly lexical — diluting profanity in long comments, dropping rare/obfuscated slurs via min_count=5 — so the single lbfgs LogReg head should land around 0.95-0.96 mean AUC versus the 0.9816 three-branch ensemble, a clear regression.

Mean-pooled corpus-trained Word2Vec loses the exact-token and char-n-gram precision that makes TF-IDF linear models excel at toxicity detection (obfuscated profanity, rare-label lexicons like threat/identity_hate), so a single 200-d average-embedding logistic regression drops the mean column-wise AUC from ~0.980 to roughly 0.92-0.94; the run itself easily fits the time budget.

A char 3-5 NB-LogReg branch is genuinely diverse from the word-NB and word+char-logreg branches (obfuscated-profanity signal), and per-label simplex-tuned rank blends historically add ~+0.001 mean AUC on this competition; however, part of the holdout-tuned gain (especially on ~48-positive threat in the 10% holdout, where the 66-combo search can overfit) won't transfer, and the added ~3-4 min of char vectorization plus six liblinear fits eats most of the runtime headroom — net expectation is a small, likely +0.0005-0.0010 improvement over 0.97987 rather than a large jump or a regression.

C=0.1 with n≈160k is mildly over-regularized for the 60k-feature TF-IDF stack, so C=4 liblinear should give branch A a small lift on the frequent labels, but the C-vs-AUC curve is a broad plateau, rare labels (threat/identity_hate) may offset part of it, and the 50/50 rank blend with the already-C=4 branch B halves (and partially de-diversifies) the gain — net a tiny improvement of roughly +0.0003 on the mean column AUC.

fastText word-bigram classifiers are individually a bit weaker than the TF-IDF branches but decorrelated, so an equal 1/3 rank-average should add a modest ensemble gain (~+0.001-0.002 mean AUC, concentrated in the stronger columns), assuming the extra ~4-6 minutes of sequential per-label training keeps the total run under the 15-minute kill limit (borderline but plausible at thread=4, dim=64).

A char_wb 3-7-gram NB-LogReg is a strong (~0.980 solo) and genuinely decorrelated third feature view (branch A's char block is capped at 50k under C=0.1, branch B is word-only), so an equal three-way rank average typically buys ~+0.001 mean AUC on this competition; the main risk is runtime (a second char vectorizer fit plus primal liblinear fits likely pushes the run to ~11-14 min), but it should stay under the 15-min kill.

The per-label weight tuning gains little (0.5/0.5 rank-average of two similar linear branches is already near-optimal, and holdout tuning on rare labels like threat/identity_hate with ~48/140 positives is noisy), while training both branches on only 90% of the data with no full refit — especially losing ~10% of the few hundred threat/severe_toxic/identity_hate positives — costs slightly more, yielding a small net regression.

Label-specific NB log-count scaling on branch A mostly acts as an implicit regularization relaxer (the per-label prior-shift term multiplies features by ~2.2-5.8, raising effective C of 0.1 toward 0.5-3.4), which should help the underfit rare-label columns (threat/identity_hate/severe_toxic) while strong profanity n-grams get correctly boosted; expect a small net gain (~+0.0003-0.0008) that partially survives the rank average, partly offset by reduced A/B diversity and double-counting of IDF-like downweighting on common n-grams.

min_df=0.01 (~3,127 of 313k docs) is ~1000x more aggressive than the old min_df=3 and slashes the vocabularies from 10k/50k/200k to roughly 1k/12k/2k features, deleting the rare discriminative n-grams (slurs, threat words like 'kill you', 'nigger', 'fag', 'idiot') that carry the rare labels, so threat and identity_hate AUC drop several points while toxic/obscene/insult degrade mildly — a clear net regression from 0.9796.

Per-label undersampling discards 90–99.7% of negatives (threat: only 956 fit rows), starving the rare columns of the other-toxic negatives that teach them to separate e.g. threats/identity-hate from generic toxicity, so the equal-weight blend regresses to roughly 0.965–0.969.

Rocchio-style class centroids replace discriminatively trained logistic regressions, losing the ability to suppress non-discriminative and correlated features, which hurts most on rare/noisy labels (threat, identity_hate) and subtle cases; prototypes of profanity still capture obvious cases, so a large but not catastrophic regression of roughly 2-4% mean AUC is expected.

char_wb n-grams (word-boundary-padded, less diluted by cross-space junk under the 50k cap) are typically slightly stronger than raw char n-grams for logistic regression on this dataset — a small solo gain for branch A diluted to a few ten-thousandths by the 50/50 rank-average with the unchanged NB branch; runtime is comparable or slightly faster since char_wb emits fewer n-grams per document.

Replacing the discriminative LR / NB-LogReg fits with generative ComplementNB linear scoring (further diluted by alpha=1.0 smoothing on small-magnitude l2-normalized TF-IDF masses) typically costs ~0.4-0.8 AUC points per branch on this dataset; the two-branch rank blend recovers a little, but the net result is a clear regression from 0.9797 to roughly 0.974.

Compressing the 60k word/char TF-IDF space to just 32 SVD components destroys most label-specific lexical signal (especially for rare threat/identity_hate) in branch A, and since AUC blending can't recover lost ordering information, the 50/50 rank average is dragged down toward the fastText branch's level — a clear regression from 0.9734.

Collapsing all tokens outside the top-2,000 df vocabulary into one 'raretoken' destroys the char n-gram branch's main strength (rare/obfuscated profanity and slurs) and the memorization signal that rare labels (threat, identity_hate, insult) depend on, leaving only frequent-word style plus a weak rare-token-density feature — a clear regression of roughly 0.005-0.010 mean AUC despite mild regularization benefit.

Keeping stop words restores predictive pronouns/negations ('you', 'not') that sklearn's list also over-prunes ('name', 'system'), a small known win for toxicity word features, but the effect is heavily diluted by the dominant char n-grams and the 50/50 rank blend with the unchanged NB branch, so expect only a tiny gain (~+0.0003 absolute).

Logit-averaging weights branches by confidence, and the C=4 NB-LR branch's much wider (often saturated) logits dominate the blend, pulling the ensemble away from the stronger char-n-gram branch that the calibration-free rank average balanced evenly, so mean AUC should dip slightly (order of 4e-4) below 0.98013.

char_wb n-grams respect word boundaries and are the standard, slightly stronger choice for capturing profanity variants; switching to 'char' spans whitespace, wastes more of the 50k feature cap on generic cross-word fragments, mildly weakening branch A, with the regression diluted but not erased by the 50/50 rank blend with the unchanged NB branch.

The replacement fastText branch (word bigrams, rank-64 joint ova model, 5 epochs, no TF-IDF/NB weighting) is roughly comparable to but likely slightly weaker than the per-label NB-LogReg it replaces on this dataset, so the 50/50 rank blend with the unchanged word+char branch should land within ~±0.0005 of the current score, with a small expected dip (~-0.0003) since the NB-ratio reweighting was particularly strong for the rare labels; runtime drops well within budget with no crash risk (k=-1 list predict and ova handling are correct for fasttext 0.9.2).

Dropping the weakest third of the 192 histogram bins (many near-constant or redundant) should modestly reduce the variance of the already-regularized multinomial LR on ~9 rows/class, and since the LR only carries half the 50/50 blend weight, the expected gain is small (~1-3% log-loss improvement), with genuine risk of a near-zero or slightly negative outcome given the tiny 99-row test set and noisy F-statistics at 9 samples per class.

The 0.0744 blend implies both models are already ~0.97+ confident and correct on ~90% of the 99 test leaves, so eps=0.1 smoothing caps the NN's probability near ~0.9 and adds ~0.03-0.05 log-loss on every easy sample, far outweighing the small calibration gains on the handful of uncertain Quercus/Acer-type leaves (errors here are already moderately confident, not saturated), yielding a net regression to roughly 0.09-0.11.

Multinomial softmax is the better-specified model for log loss; OvR's 99 imbalanced binary fits (9 pos vs ~880 neg) produce overlapping high scores for similar species (e.g. Quercus group) with per-class score-scale mismatch that the single global power/floor calibration can only partly absorb, so OOF and test log loss should regress moderately (roughly 0.05-0.08 vs 0.045) despite identical geometry of the rest of the pipeline; runtime (~600 small lbfgs fits, n_jobs=4) stays well within budget.

The 5-seed MLP bag on ~891 rows/99 classes will be clearly weaker and more overconfident than the tuned LR, so the OOF search most likely picks only a small w (or falls back to w=0); on the near-saturated 99-row test the blend's confident disagreements with LR plus selection noise over 33x more (alpha,w) candidates and re-fitted sharpening make a mild regression (~0.045 -> ~0.048) the most likely outcome, with the w=0 fallback capping the downside.

Averaging the five CV-fold logreg models acts as bagging/calibration smoothing on the few confusable-species rows that dominate the residual log loss, and best_C was tuned by OOF for exactly this 80%-data configuration, so a small net gain is expected despite each fold model seeing ~20% less data than the removed full refit.

The 21 image-derived descriptors (absolute size, aspect ratio, solidity, Hu moments) add genuinely complementary signal to the scale-normalised 192 features, and the unchanged 5-fold OOF selection over a wide C grid bounds overfitting risk, so a modest log-loss improvement is expected — though with only 99 test rows (one per species) the gain will be smaller and noisier than the OOF delta.

For L2-regularized logistic regression a full PCA is just a rotation (penalty-invariant), so the only real effect is truncating the ~5% lowest-variance tail — mostly within-class noise/quantization directions given between-species variance dominates — which acts as mild extra regularization on a 219-feature model with only ~9 samples per class, yielding a small expected gain (~2%) that stays within the noise of the 99-row test set; a small regression is also plausible.

Each fold model trains on 20% less data and five near-identical linear models are highly correlated (75% training overlap), so bagging gains little while giving up the full-data refit — a small regression, further magnified by the tiny test set.

The augmented two-branch CNN+MLP (images + same 192 features, TTA, strong regularization, full-data refit) should land near LR quality with partially decorrelated errors, so a 50/50 blend typically buys a modest log-loss gain (~0.09-0.12), though the tiny 9-samples-per-class data and 99-row test leave real risk of a flat-to-slightly-worse outcome.

The OOF-fitted power/temperature + uniform-floor calibration targets exactly this model's dominant loss source — confident errors on confusable species from a near-interpolating overparameterized LR — so mild hedging should transfer to test as a small gain, though the fold-model (713 rows) vs full-model (891 rows) miscalibration mismatch and good-row flooring costs keep the improvement marginal (roughly no-change to -5%, small chance of slight regression).

With only ~9 rows per class and 192 standardized features, C=1 (effective ridge λ≈1/n) is already at or beyond the overfitting point, so the 5-fold OOF log loss should rise monotonically over the C≥1 grid and the selection will land on the grid floor C=1, reproducing the parent's model (only tighter lbfgs tolerance changes it in the 4th decimal) — i.e., a no-op despite the extra CV compute; any residual risk (grid lacks C<1, so it can only pick equal or weaker regularization) tilts slightly toward unchanged-to-worse, not better.

The ~27 image-derived descriptors are largely redundant with the 64-dim contour shape features (all geometrically derivable from the outline) but give the linear model directly accessible shape summaries (solidity, eccentricity, Hu moments), so expect a small gain partially offset by overfit risk (27 extra features, ~9 rows/class, fixed C=1.0) and edge cases in the >50%-coverage polarity flip.

With ~9 training rows per class and 240 standardized, highly correlated features, the C=1.0 multinomial logistic regression is mildly overconfident/overfit (near-separable training set), so 5x stronger L2 shrinkage should slightly reduce multi-class log loss on the 99-row test, though the tiny test set makes the delta noisy and a small regression is plausible.

Removing the full-data refit submits a model trained on only ~80% of the data (~7 vs 9 samples per class), which degrades generalization of the regularized multinomial LR and raises expected log loss from 0.0813 to roughly 0.09-0.11 (matching its internal holdout level), a clear regression despite the estimator-matching rationale.

The OOF-learned convex blend keeps the already-strong tuned LR dominant while distance-weighted kNN and shrinkage LDA add complementary signal, which on this feature set typically trims multi-class log loss by ~10-20%; the SLSQP weight fitting on 891 OOF rows guards against over-weighting the weaker members, though the tiny 99-row test set adds variance in either direction.

On only 891 samples with 9 per class across 99 species, an untuned multiclass HistGradientBoosting (trained on just 85% of data, early-stopped on a noisy ~134-sample validation split with 1-2 samples per class, no rollback to best iteration) tends to overfit and emit overconfident probabilities — tree ensembles historically score ~0.1-0.2 where tuned logistic regression scores ~0.06-0.09 on these pre-extracted leaf features — so I expect the log loss to roughly double from 0.0609 to ~0.11.

The multinomial LR member directly optimized the proper scoring loss on the full 891 rows, while the replacement is a one-vs-rest LinearSVC trained on only 2/3 of the data per calibration fold with Platt sigmo人 fits seeing ~3 positive samples per class — noisier, less calibrated probabilities — so the 4-member uniform soft vote should regress modestly (diluted by the unchanged kNN/LDA/HGB members).

The early-stopped HGB is handicapped here (min_samples_leaf=10 vs ~8 samples/class in its one-vs-all trees, plus a ~100-row noisy validation split), so it emits diffuse probabilities that dilute the trio's confident correct predictions; a 600-tree fully-grown RF yields sharper, generally more accurate vote fractions with no validation-split dependency, which on log loss should net a modest improvement (~0.29→~0.26), though the 99-row test set makes the magnitude uncertain and a small regression is possible.

A ~95k-parameter (256,128) MLP trained on only 891 samples (99 classes, ~9 each) with a noisy 80-sample accuracy-based early-stopping split and weak L2 (1e-4) will overfit and be less calibrated than the well-shrunk linear baseline that already sits at ~0.124; the OOF-selected uniform shrinkage only partially compensates, so I expect the multi-class log loss to roughly double.

The 5-fold OOF selection (7-8 samples/class per fold, no shrinkage in the criterion) will almost certainly pick stronger regularization than C=1 (likely C≈0.3-0.316), which dulls the sharp, near-memorized probabilities on this duplicate-heavy 99-row test set that produce the current 0.124, and the re-tuned alpha shrinkage only partially compensates — so a mild regression (~+5-20%) is the most likely outcome, with ~20% chance of an identical score if C_best=1.0 and a smaller chance of a wash or tiny gain if C_best>1.

The 48 CV features (Hu moments, size/shape scalars, radial histogram) are largely redundant with the existing 64 shape descriptors and add noise-prone entries (Hu-7 sign flips, discontinuous ellipse orientation) under a fixed C=1.0, so with only ~9 samples/class and a tiny 99-row test set I expect a small, uncertain net gain — a slight improvement on average, but easily neutral or mildly negative.

10-fold stratified CV with neg_log_loss over a dense C grid (which includes 1.0) picks a better-regularized multinomial LR and refits on all data — on this classic 192-feature leaf dataset, tuned-C logistic regression reliably cuts log loss ~10-20% versus fixed C=1 (tuned LR is a known ~0.09-0.11 solution vs ~0.12-0.13 untuned), and the ~250 warm-started lbfgs fits parallelized over folds finish comfortably inside the 10-minute budget; main risk is the tiny 99-row test set adding variance, but the expected direction is a modest improvement.

The baseline LR is already strong (0.124) and uniform soft voting dilutes it with weaker members — especially HGB on a 99-class/~9-samples-per-class problem (plus distance-weighted kNN), whose flatter probabilities raise loss on the many easy points far more than hedging recovers on the few hard ones, so expect roughly 0.18-0.25.

The convex OOF loss vs alpha will almost certainly be minimized at alpha=0 (or a knife-edge 0.01) since C=1 regularized LR's OOF errors are rarely extreme enough (p_true<1e-4) for uniform-mixing to pay off; the final 9-samples-per-class model is already confident and near-perfect on this easy 99-row test, so any alpha>0 just dilutes correct predictions, giving ~0.1244 (no change, most likely) to ~0.134 — i.e., zero-to-small regression.

With n=891 vs p=192, Ledoit-Wolf 'auto' shrinkage is near zero, so forcing 0.9 replaces the well-estimated pooled covariance with ~90% identity, collapsing LDA toward a nearest-centroid rule that discards the strong margin/shape/texture correlation structure — log loss should roughly double on these 99 confusable species.

Arithmetic averaging of three 64-feature per-family LDAs discards the multiplicative cross-family evidence of the 192-feature model (which is already ~0.36 and benefits from shrinkage handling the pooled covariance), so the diluted, less confident averaged probabilities will most likely regress the log loss to roughly 0.40-0.48.

Unsupervised PCA retaining only 90% of variance (likely ~60-70 of 192 components, no whitening) discards low-variance but species-discriminative directions and distorts the effective L2 penalty across unequal-variance PCs, so the already-well-tuned logistic regression likely regresses modestly on this tiny 99-row test set, with sizable per-row score noise.

With only ~9 samples/class and 192 features, shrinkage-regularized LDA (a known top-tier model on this exact leaf-features dataset) is far more sample-efficient than over-parameterized multinomial LR — its shared shrunken covariance should resolve the handful of ambiguous test leaves better and more confidently, cutting log loss by roughly a third, though the tiny 99-row test set adds noise around that estimate.

PCA(0.95, no whitening) drops the low-variance directions that carry fine margin/texture distinctions between morphologically similar species (e.g., the many Quercus/Acer pairs) and re-weights L2 shrinkage against subtle signals; with the baseline already near-saturated and properly temperature-calibrated on only 99 test rows, flipping a couple of borderline predictions hurts more than the mild variance reduction from halving the coefficient count helps, so I expect a small regression (~0.05 rather than 0.045).

Swapping the near-interpolating, temperature-calibrated LR (already near-perfect at 0.045 on a 99-row test, so little headroom) for shrinkage LDA imposes a shared-covariance Gaussian assumption that fits these heteroscedastic histogram features poorly, so a few extra confusions among similar species (Quercus/Acer pairs) with still-confident scores likely raise log loss to roughly 0.06-0.07.

Mixing with uniform multiplies each true-class probability by 0.995 and adds 0.005/99, which helps only samples where the model put <~1% on the true class (break-even at p≈0.0101) but adds ~0.005 nats to every confident sample; with a 0.094 baseline almost all mass sits in confident predictions, so average loss rises by ~0.005 (to ~0.099), a ~5% regression.

With 891 training samples and gamma=1/192, the RBF-Nystroem spectrum is largely captured by a few hundred components, so cutting 512→384 mostly coarsens the kernel approximation without meaningfully reducing overfitting under the existing L2 (C=1.0) regularization, yielding a small log-loss regression on the 99-sample test set.

Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk LDA is a generative linear classifier well suited to this many-class, ~9-samples-per-class regime (where generative models tend to beat discriminative ones) and its data-driven shrinkage directly fixes the baseline's untuned regularization, so a modest log-loss improvement (with some overconfidence risk on borderline species) is the most likely outcome.

CV-tuning C with neg_log_loss (pipeline refit on all data, only C differs from baseline) will most likely pick a mildly better-regularized C than 1.0 for this 192-feature/891-sample/99-class problem, yielding a small calibration gain (~5-10%); a tie (C=1.0) or slight regression on the tiny 99-row test set is also possible, so the expected effect is a modest improvement.

The OOF-fit temperature (likely T≈1.1–1.4) softens the mildly overconfident multinomial-LR logits in this feature-rich, sample-poor regime, trimming the heavy penalty on confidently-wrong test rows while barely hurting the ~98% confident-correct rows, so expect a small but real log-loss improvement (~0.005 absolute) rather than a regression; the change is correctly implemented (decision_function columns aligned, exact log-loss objective, softmax at T) and runs in seconds, well under budget.

An RBF kernel (gamma=1/192 ≈ 'scale', 512 Nyström components on ≤891 rows) captures the nonlinear same-species similarity in the margin/shape/texture descriptors that the linear baseline cannot — kernel models are historically much stronger than linear on this dataset — so I expect a moderate log-loss improvement, tempered by real overconfidence risk from the spectrum-whitening second scaler plus untuned C=1.0 on 512 features with only ~9 samples/class and a tiny 99-row test set where a few confidently wrong rows could swing the score; compute cost is trivial and the code is bug-free, so no timeout/crash risk.

The 31 dense features add genuinely new signal absent from the current pipeline — especially absolute request time (t_days, capturing the documented decline in success rate over the subreddit's life) and request-form features (length, gratitude/reciprocity flags from the Althoff et al. analysis) — and hstacking 31 standardized columns onto the existing sparse blocks with C=0.3 L2-regularized LR is a low-risk change with negligible runtime cost, so a modest gain of roughly +0.03 AUC (0.671 -> ~0.70) is the expected outcome, though the redundant history flags may dilute part of the gain.

Fully-grown random forests on ~8k sparse TF-IDF/subreddit features with only ~2.3k training rows overfit and cannot exploit the linear additive structure of text that regularized logistic regression thrives on, so AUC typically regresses several points on this dataset.

Random forests are markedly weaker than regularized logistic regression on ~5k sparse TF-IDF columns at n≈2.9k (sqrt feature sampling almost never considers the 10 dense columns, so the touted numeric non-linearities never materialize), and the near-leaky giver_known indicator (≈perfectly predicts the label in train, all-zero in test) lets trees carve the ~80% of positives with a known giver into pure leaves, so test-time rankings come from the thin hard-positive region — a solid regression from 0.748 to roughly 0.65–0.70, not the improvement the change argues for.

Replacing 5000 discriminative TF-IDF unigram weights (which carry the word-level narrative and edit-'thanks' leakage signal) with 50 unsupervised, only-partially-converged LDA topic proportions discards most of the text block's discriminative information while leaving the metadata block unchanged, so the linear model should regress to roughly the metadata-plus-weak-topic level around 0.70-0.72.

Deleting the supervised OOF text logit removes the single strongest predictive signal in the stack; 20 coarse unsupervised LDA topics on short documents carry far less label-relevant text information (and only marginally add narrative/metadata interactions), so the score should fall back to near metadata-only levels, roughly 0.64-0.67.

On this (almost certainly random) re-split of the 4040-row RAOP train set, the raw epoch timestamp carries the documented decline in success rate across the 2011-2013 collection window and almost certainly helped the level-2 trees; dropping it loses more (a few thousandths of AUC) than the small stationary hour-of-day/weekday signal adds, so expect a slight regression to ~0.701.

The dense-only HGB (time trend, RAOP history, text stats; likely ~0.63-0.66 OOF) adds a partly decorrelated signal to the text-dominated LR, and rank-averaging with a CV-chosen weight (with w=1, i.e. pure LR, in the grid bounding the downside) typically buys a few thousandths of AUC on this dataset, though the 1162-row test set makes the realized delta noisy.

Random forests handle high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF poorly — fully grown trees (min_samples_leaf=1) overfit the ~2300-row training split and sqrt feature sampling can't exploit the many weak additive word signals that logistic regression sums, so the text-driven ranking degrades even though tree splits capture some metadata interactions.

Subreddit membership carries genuine community-type signal (e.g. prior RAOP/assistance activity) only partially redundant with the existing RAOP-history counts, and the binary+idf, min_df=5, L2-regularized block is low-variance, so I expect a small gain (~+0.005) that transfers imperfectly to the temporally shifted test set.

giver_username_if_known is a near-perfect target leak on train but absent (all zeros) on test, so logistic regression crowd-out shrinks and biases the real TF-IDF/numeric coefficients — trained effectively on only the ~150-200 'uncovered' positives — degrading test ranking from 0.657 to roughly 0.60-0.63.

The OOF text-logit → LightGBM stack preserves the baseline's text signal while letting conservative, early-stopped trees (plus the new raw timestamp) capture nonlinear/interaction effects in the skewed requester-history metadata that the jointly-fit linear model handles poorly, so on this small random-split dataset I expect a modest ~+0.005–0.015 AUC gain rather than a regression, with low overfit risk from seed averaging and the 11-column bottleneck.

The added time-trend (success rate declined over the subreddit's life), text-length/evidence stats, and history indicators are classic paper-derived signals that are only partially redundant with the existing TF-IDF + log-count blocks, so with C=0.3 they should yield a small but real gain (~+0.01 AUC) with low risk of regression since the pipeline, scaling, and leakage handling are all correct.

Tree ensembles are markedly weaker than regularized logistic regression on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF text: with max_features='sqrt' (~74 of ~5.4k features per split) splits concentrate on the 393 dense embedding/numeric columns, so most of the word-level signal that drives the current 0.6235 is discarded, and the period-specific interactions ET does learn are unlikely to transfer to the (evidently shifted) grading test — expect a solid regression to roughly 0.56-0.60.

On this 2.9k-sample task the sparse unigram TF-IDF block captures lexical cues (specific vocabulary of successful requests) that generic frozen MiniLM embeddings only partially encode, so dropping it should cost roughly 0.02 AUC despite the variance argument; the MLflow addition is score-neutral.

The ~24 doc-level stats add genuinely new signal that TF-IDF discards (stop-word removal kills pronoun rates, L2 normalization kills length, tokenization kills '!'/'?'/ALL-CAPS), so a regularized LR on 2.9k rows should squeeze out a small gain, but noisy/correlated features (VADER on Reddit slang, readability, a money regex that false-fires on 'rent' inside 'parent/current') cap it at roughly +0.003-0.006, with a modest chance of a flat or slightly negative result.

Dropping the TF-IDF text block removes the model's strongest signal (request wording/narrative, which typically drives RAOP AUC into the mid-0.60s); the nine requester-history numbers alone — dominated by prior RAOP activity and karma, heavily zero-inflated — historically cap out around 0.59-0.61, so this should be a clear regression from 0.6497 despite the drift argument.

Mean-pooled Word2Vec trained on only ~4k documents yields noisy, weak embeddings that lose the discriminative lexical cues TF-IDF captured (and add 200 noisy dense dims to a ~2.9k-row logistic fit), so the text block's contribution shrinks while the unchanged metadata/stats block anchors the score, producing a modest regression from 0.662 to roughly 0.645–0.655.

Uni+bigram TF-IDF typically adds a little phrase-level signal on RAOP, but with only ~2.9k training rows, fixed C=0.3 and many noisy min_df=2 bigrams, expect only a small LB gain (with real risk of a flat or slightly negative outcome).

On RAOP the TF-IDF/SVD text block carries genuine, non-redundant signal beyond the nine requester-history columns (the paper's core finding is that narrative wording drives success), so a metadata-only LGBM retains only ~60-70% of the current model's lift over chance, dropping AUC from 0.633 to roughly 0.58.

Fully-grown random forests over 300 dense LSA components (many low-variance noise directions) with no depth/min-sample regularization typically rank slightly below a regularized, early-stopped LightGBM on this small, temporally shifted test set, so expect a modest AUC regression (~0.62 vs 0.633), with model-swap noise on n=1162 of the same order.

Frozen MiniLM embeddings carry only weak signal for RAOP success, and because the 384 standardized dense columns (row norms ~20 vs ~1 for L2-normalized TF-IDF and ~3 for the 9 numeric features) receive ~100-400x weaker effective L2 regularization at the unchanged C=0.3, the fit tilts heavily onto an overfit-prone embedding block, diluting the TF-IDF/numeric signal that produced 0.657.

Bigrams add some genuinely predictive phrases (payback promises, hardship narratives) and L2 logistic regression degrades gracefully on the wider sparse matrix, so a small gain is likely, partly offset by added variance from min_df=2 with ~100k features on only 2878 training rows.

The 15 standardized length/style/lexicon stats (title/body length, punctuation, upper-case, gratitude/reciprocity/hardship) add signal not fully captured by L2-normalized TF-IDF (e.g., document length, shouting, readability), and with only 15 extra columns on ~2.9k rows the overfit risk under C=0.3 is small, so expect a modest AUC gain of roughly +0.002–0.005, though much of the lexicon signal is redundant with existing unigrams, keeping the gain small.

Replacing logistic regression on raw TF-IDF with LightGBM over a 300-component SVD usually loses several points on small text problems (trees approximate dense linear text structure poorly, and LSA discards discriminative directions), and the random-fold CV early stopping likely overfits relative to this evidently shifted evaluation set, only partly offset by better nonlinear handling of the 9 numeric features.

The flexible quantile-knot spline over request time can capture the well-documented monotone decline in RAOP success rate as the community saturated, while a single annual sin/cos pair can only encode seasonality (weak/noisy over just ~2.8 years of data), so swapping it in should lose that small trend signal and produce a mild regression on the order of a few thousandths of AUC, roughly at noise level.

Raising C from 0.3 to 30 nearly removes the L2 penalty, so with only 2878 weak-signal training rows the rare-word TF-IDF coefficients and heavy-tailed standardized numeric/spline features are essentially unregularized; near-separation overfits these noisy cues, and the heavy shrinkage at C=0.3 was likely closer to (or past) the optimum, so I expect a modest AUC regression of roughly 0.005-0.015 rather than an improvement.

RAOP success rates declined steadily over the 2010–2013 calendar window, so a quantile-knot spline of the request timestamp adds a genuinely new ~0.58–0.60-AUC trend signal mostly uncaptured by the existing text/history/subreddit features, at only ~7 extra regularized columns (negligible overfit/timeout risk) — expect a small positive gain of roughly +0.005–0.012 AUC.

Cosine kNN on this mixed space is dominated by the unnormalized numeric/subreddit blocks (TF-IDF rows are unit-norm and contribute only ~5-10% of vector energy), so neighborhoods reflect activity-profile clusters rather than lexical signal, losing most of the linear text separability that gave LogisticRegression its 0.649 — expect a clear regression to roughly 0.57-0.61 despite trivial runtime.

KNN (k=25, distance-weighted, Euclidean) on 9 standardized heavy-tailed metadata features suffers from the curse of dimensionality with only ~2.3k training points, so it will be a noticeably weaker and noisier metadata model than the depth-5 CatBoost it replaces, dragging the fixed 50/50 blend down modestly (a small regression, not a collapse, since the TF-IDF logistic regression still carries most of the signal).

Raising C 100x effectively removes L2 regularization for a ~2900-sample fit over thousands of sparse TF-IDF features, letting the logistic component overfit (near-separable text data) and degrading the 50/50 blend despite the unchanged CatBoost half.

The 0.654 baseline is far below the ~0.85 a TF-IDF+LR normally gets on a random RAOP split, implying the harness split is temporal (test requests post-date the training window); with extrapolation='constant' every test row then receives identical spline values, so the new block adds no ranking signal on test — only small retrained-coefficient perturbation and slight dilution of the genuinely useful features, i.e., roughly zero-to-slightly-negative change.

Binarize=0 collapses sublinear TF-IDF weights and the standardized activity features into mere presence/above-mean indicators, and BernoulliNB's independence assumption double-counts the highly correlated requester-history block, so the generative model should rank clearly worse than the regularized logistic regression baseline of 0.654.

The spline over unix_timestamp_of_request_utc adds the documented 2011→2013 decline in RAOP success rate — a signal absent from the baseline's TF-IDF + 9 requester-history features — and since the 2878/1162 split is random over the same time window (train sample shows shuffled dates), the properly fit-on-train date block should yield a small real gain (~+0.005–0.015 AUC), with the MLflow scaffolding and removed holdout print having no effect on the graded submission.

The subreddit block adds a little genuine signal (prior RAOP/assistance-community activity) that partially survives the strong L2 (C=0.3), but most of it is redundant with the existing numeric history features, so expect only a marginal, noise-level gain.

The metadata-only CatBoost (likely AUC ~0.58-0.61 on this test set) is blended at a heavy fixed 50/50, diluting by half the TF-IDF text signal that drives the 0.657 logistic regression, while adding little new information since the LR already includes those same nine numeric features — so the probability average should land slightly below the current score, around 0.645.

Switching to (1,2)-grams keeps the same 5000-feature TF-IDF budget (so unigrams still dominate, with only the most frequent content bigrams like 'pay forward'/'lost job' entering), which historically yields a small, noisy AUC gain on this tiny 2878-sample corpus; the mlflow/tracking and removed-holdout changes in the diff do not alter the model's predictions, so expect roughly +0.003 with high variance around the 0.6573 baseline.

For authorship attribution, function words and their bigrams carry real stylometric signal, and since char_wb n-grams never cross word boundaries they cannot replace the lost stop-word bigram features, so dropping them should slightly (not catastrophically) worsen log loss.

A correctly-calibrated OOF stacking of complementary MultinomialNB word/char bases under a log-linear meta-learner typically buys ~1-3% relative log-loss over a single strong word+char LR on this dataset, while replacing the full-data LR refit with fold-averaged test predictions is roughly neutral (matching the OOF scale), so expect a modest improvement from 0.3537 to ~0.346.

Function words are among the strongest authorship cues in this stylometry task (sklearn's list even removes 'upon', 'shall', 'whither'), so dropping them degrades the word-level LR and MNB base learners more than the extra diversity vs. the unchanged char_wb models helps the LightGBM stacker, producing a small regression on the 1,958-row graded set.

A strongly regularized multinomial-logistic combiner is the textbook stacker for correlated OOF probability columns; with only ~87 parameters on ~14k rows it cannot fit fold noise the way the early-stopped, subsampled 3000-tree LightGBM can, so I expect it to land within a few thousandths of the current 0.2986, most likely a small improvement (~0.297–0.298), though the delta is near noise since the two stackers' predictions will be highly correlated.

Punctuation is genuinely discriminative here (semicolon presence 14/19/32%, quotes 17/6/13%, apostrophes 16/9/7% across EAP/HPL/MWS) and transfers to the test set because train/test are a random split of the same source texts, so the char n-gram block loses real authorial signal that the speculative regularization benefit from a smaller vocabulary only partly offsets — a small regression of roughly +0.01 log loss.

The stacking ensemble (better-tuned C=10 word/char LRs plus tuned NB models, combined via a log-prob meta-learner) is historically worth ~0.06 log loss over a C=1 hstacked LR on this competition (~0.44 -> ~0.36-0.38), with the main risks being the 10-minute budget from parallel char-LR folds and small-test noise, so I predict ~0.37.

Chi2 pruning ~130k TF-IDF columns to 10k discards the weak, distributed char-n-gram style signal that L2-regularized LR exploits well (and favors rare class-pure fold noise), so LR's OOF likely degrades slightly; the re-tuned NB blend weight cushions most of it, leaving a roughly neutral-to-marginally-worse score (~0.363) with the 1,958-row test set adding ±0.003 of effectively random swing.

Authorship attribution is the classic case where function words carry signal (sklearn's aggressive English list even removes discriminative items like 'seemed', 'upon', pronouns), so the word-count MultinomialNB degrades noticeably and the TF-IDF LR loses syntax bigrams like 'of the' that the char_wb block (which keeps style but not word order) cannot replace; the re-optimized blend weight just shifts toward LR, forfeiting most of the NB boost, yielding a small net regression while runtime stays well within budget.

The feature pipeline and final all-rows refit are unchanged, so only C differs; on word+char TF-IDF with ~110k sparse features the CV curve over [1,3,10,30,100] is flat-to-mildly-better around C=3-10, so the most likely outcome is a few thousandths of log-loss improvement (with real chances of a no-op if CV picks C=1 or a tiny regression if it picks C>=30), and the explicit 25-fit joblib CV plus refit should still finish well inside 10 minutes.

Blending two TF-IDF LRs with complementary NB models and stylometric meta-features via a properly OOF-validated LightGBM meta-learner is a known strong recipe on this dataset (historically ~0.38-0.40 vs ~0.43 for a single concatenated LR), so I expect roughly a 0.03-0.04 absolute drop with modest run-to-run variance on the 1,958-row test set, and the ~4-6 min runtime fits the budget.

Cross-boundary char n-grams, case patterns, punctuation 1-grams (strong author cues per the data card) and dropping the 60k cap add real stylistic signal that transfers to the same-novel test split, so L2 logistic regression should gain ~0.01 log loss despite mild extra overfit risk at fixed C=1.0 and ~1.7x more nonzeros (still well within the time budget).

5-fold OOF-selected blend of the unchanged LR with a word-count MultinomialNB (whose OOF log loss ~0.46-0.48 is weaker but decorrelated thanks to count-vs-TFIDF and no char features) typically buys a small ~0.004-0.008 log-loss gain; the weight grid includes w=1.0 so the downside is bounded, but NB/LR errors are correlated enough that the improvement is modest, not large.

Authorship attribution signal lives largely in high-frequency function words (pronoun/auxiliary/preposition rates are classic stylometric cues: EAP's 'I', MWS's 'he/she/her', etc.), so stripping sklearn's 318 stopwords deletes those discriminative word/bigram/char-ngram features while leaving only content words and punctuation — the classic 'stopword hygiene' rationale that helps topic classification actively hurts style classification, so I expect the log loss to regress from 0.605 to roughly 0.64-0.65.

Balancing the training file without any prior correction makes the softmax learn uniform 33/33/33 priors instead of the natural 40/31/29; since log loss is a proper scoring rule on the natural-distribution test set, this miscalibration (Jensen gap of the prior reweighting is ~0.01 for this mild imbalance) plus extra overfitting from duplicated minority rows should cost a bit more than it gains in minority-class accuracy — expect a small regression from 0.607 to ~0.617.

ComplementNB on the same TF-IDF is a weaker (~0.42-0.45 OOF) but diverse model, so the OOF-swept convex blend will land at w≈0.7-0.9 and shave a few thousandths off the tuned LR's log loss (0.3548 → ~0.351), with modest risk of no change (w=1.0) or small test-set noise on 1,958 rows.

MultinomialNB's conditional-independence assumption double-counts the heavily overlapping word/char n-grams, producing overconfident, miscalibrated probabilities, so even with CV-tuned alpha it typically scores ~0.42-0.46 log loss on this dataset versus 0.355 for the tuned logistic regression — a clear regression, though it trains far faster and stays well within the time budget.

char_wb 2-5 grams carry strong, complementary authorial signal (punctuation habits like semicolons/quotes/apostrophes, dialect spellings, morphology) that word 1-2 grams miss, and with a random train/test split there is no domain shift to justify preferring 'cleaner' word features, so removing the char block should regress log loss from ~0.409 to roughly 0.43-0.44.

Replacing the NB-ratio + per-class logistic-regression hybrid with a single generative ComplementNB head removes the discriminative calibration step: pure NB on correlated word+char TF-IDF features is a well-known weaker, less calibrated linear baseline for log loss (typical ~1.2x worse than NB-SVM/LogReg on this dataset), so expect a regression from 0.409 to roughly 0.45-0.52; the code itself is valid, fast, and deterministic, so the run will complete under budget.

C=1.0 is already near-optimal for this word+char TF-IDF stack, so 3-fold log-loss CV will most likely pick C≈1–3.16 and yield only a small gain (~0.003–0.008 log loss); with 1,958-row test noise the expected outcome is a modest ~1% improvement, with real chance of ~0% change or a slight regression if CV lands on a neighboring C.

MultinomialNB's independence assumption double-counts the heavily correlated word+char n-gram blocks and yields overconfident, poorly calibrated probabilities (which log loss punishes), so on this dataset NB typically scores ~0.06-0.10 worse than the discriminative LR baseline of 0.4253; the MinMax-scaled style features also become near-negligible under NB.

fastText with word bigrams plus 2-5 char subwords spans nearly the same feature space as the word(1-2)+char(2-5) TF-IDF/LR baseline and historically lands in the same ~0.41-0.43 band on this competition, with the low-rank averaging acting as a useful regularizer and subwords covering the 2% OOV test tokens, so expect a small, uncertain improvement rather than a step change.

C=1.0 sits near a shallow optimum for this TF-IDF+LR setup, so 5-fold CV will most likely pick C in [1,4] and yield only a marginal test-log-loss gain (~0.002-0.005), with a small chance of picking a mildly worse C and a tiny regression.

NB log-count-ratio weighting sharpens the strong word-level class cues (character names, Lovecraft dialect) and effectively rebalances the word block against the char block that dominates the TF-IDF mass, so the per-class binary LRs (C=4) should edge out the multinomial LR; the gain is partly offset by one-vs-rest probability renormalization and noisier NB ratios on non-binarized sublinear TF-IDF char features, netting a modest improvement from 0.4323 to roughly 0.425-0.427.

Sentence length and punctuation-count features carry genuine author signal (MWS semicolons/longer sentences, HPL apostrophes) that L2-normalized TF-IDF largely discards, so LR should gain a small amount (~0.003 absolute) as seen in this competition's history, though char 2-5 grams already capture part of it, limiting the improvement; risk of a near-zero or slightly negative result exists but is lower.

NBSVM-style class-specific NB log-ratio scaling of the existing word+char TF-IDF is a proven small boost for sparse high-dim linear models (helps rare but diagnostic n-grams like author names/dialect spellings), so I expect a modest improvement over the 0.4413 multinomial-LR baseline, partly offset by one-vs-rest probability calibration noise and slightly sharper (riskier) confidence under log loss; runtime (3 liblinear dual fits on ~10M nnz) should fit the budget.

With ~130k sparse word+char n-gram features but only 17.6k training rows, quadrupling L2 strength (C 1.0→0.25) should mildly reduce overfitting to isolated lexical fragments, giving a small log-loss improvement on the 1,958-row test set, though the effect is near the paired-noise floor so it could also be roughly neutral.

Dropping word TF-IDF removes strong lexical cues (character names like raymond/dupin/arkham, dialect words) that char n-grams only partially recover via fragments, so the char-only NBSVM-style model should regress modestly from 0.518 to roughly 0.55 log loss.

Removing the NBSVM-style NB log-count ratio reweighting leaves plain L2 logistic regression (C=1.0) to learn author evidence directly from ~130k sparse word+char TF-IDF features on only 17.6k sentences; on small text datasets this ablation typically costs a few hundredths of log loss, so I expect a modest regression from 0.5177 to roughly 0.54.

Halving C (4→2) doubles the L2 penalty on ~90k highly correlated word/char n-gram features fit to only 17.6k rows; this mild tightening typically trims a few thousandths of log loss (or is ~neutral), so I expect a small improvement to ~0.368.

Swapping tuned multinomial LR for one-vs-rest NB-weighted LR on identical word+char sublinear TF-IDF features is roughly a wash on this authorship task (char n-grams already capture the style cues the NB ratios amplify), while one-vs-rest row-normalized probabilities and NB-amplified confidence typically cost a little log-loss calibration, so a small regression (~+0.003) is the most likely single outcome; run-to-run noise on 1,958 test rows makes ±0.01 plausible in either direction.

Function words are a core stylometric signal for authorship attribution (and TF-IDF's IDF weighting already discounts them), so stripping English stop words from both the word- and char-TF-IDF branches should remove discriminative style cues and modestly regress log loss, with only partial offset from freeing char-ngram feature slots for content n-grams.

C=0.25 sits below the broad optimum (~0.5–1) for word+char TF-IDF logistic regression on 17.6k rows; the fitted temperature absorbs most of the uniform logit shrinkage, leaving a small second-order underfitting penalty (~+0.005 log loss), though tamer char-ngram overfitting gives a modest chance of a slight gain.

Switching to analyzer='char' spends the 60k feature cap on cross-word/space n-grams that largely duplicate the existing word (1,2) TF-IDF signal while crowding out char_wb's complementary within-word morphology features, so I expect a small regression (higher log loss, ~+0.002 absolute).

The NBSVM-style log-count-ratio feature reweighting (Wang & Manning) is a well-known strong linear baseline for small sparse text problems: it boosts near-deterministic author cues (character names, dialect n-grams) that transfer across this random train/test split, so the three one-vs-rest liblinear L2 fits should land slightly better than the multinomial LR (~0.42 vs 0.432), with only mild risk from the heuristic stacking/normalization of the three binary probabilities and the unusual application of the ratio to L2-normalized sublinear TF-IDF (which usually shrinks the NBSVM gain).

The word(1-2)+char(2-5) TF-IDF space is ~130k features vs only 17.6k training rows, so C=1.0 is already near the L2 optimum; raising C to 4.0 under-regularizes and sharpens (overconfident) probabilities on rare noisy n-grams, so the 1,958-row test log loss should regress slightly (~+0.003 absolute, well within the 10-min budget since runtime is unchanged).

Temperature scaling is a safe monotone recalibration of the same model: the L2-regularized TF-IDF logistic regression is only mildly overconfident, so the fitted T (likely ~1.05–1.2) should give a small (~0.001–0.005) log-loss gain, partly offset by holdout noise and the 90%-fit vs full-refit mismatch, with essentially zero risk of a large regression.

Training on log1p(fare) makes the trees target the conditional geometric mean, so expm1-inverted predictions run ~4% low with no exp(σ²/2) bias correction, and since metered fares are additive (base + per-mile/minute) rather than multiplicative, the dollar-scale RMSE on the ~97% valid rows should degrade slightly (~1% MSE), leaving the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor untouched for a net small regression from 4.10 to ~4.14.

Quadrupling the sample (1M→4M) with the same features/model should cut the learnable-row RMSE from ~3.6 to ~3.4 while the ~2.1 irreducible floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows (mean-fare predicted) stays fixed, so overall RMSE drops from 4.10 to roughly 3.95-4.00 (~3% improvement), with the explicit-format timestamp parse and n_jobs fix being result-neutral.

Airport-distance features are the classic win for this task: they let single splits isolate the ~5.5% of trips touching JFK/LGA/EWR (JFK flat fare ~$52, EWR surcharge) whose fare structure raw coordinates + haversine only partially capture, so the valid-row RMSE (~3.6) should drop ~2%, which after the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows translates to a total improvement from 4.19 to roughly 4.14 (about 1-1.5% better, essentially free in runtime).

Fitting L2 on log1p makes the model output the conditional median (expm1 of E[log1p]) rather than the conditional mean that raw-scale RMSE rewards, so typical and especially long/expensive trips are systematically underpredicted; the data is already outlier-cleaned (fares capped at 500), so the usual robustness benefit of the log target is small and does not offset the median-vs-mean bias (plus early stopping now optimizes log-space RMSE and NaN-feature test rows get a ~$9 geometric-mean prediction instead of ~$11), yielding a modest ~1-2% RMSE regression.

The fare-distance relation is genuinely non-decreasing, so the constraint acts as a mild correct regularizer on the dominant feature, but with 4M training rows the unconstrained ensemble already learns an almost monotone distance response in dense regions (and coordinate splits remain unconstrained, letting the model express any true non-monotonicities like airport flat fares), so the effect should be at the noise level — a tiny improvement of ~0.1-0.2% on the valid rows, diluted further by the ~2.8% fixed mean-fare-fallback floor in the graded RMSE.

expm1 back-transform returns the conditional median (~3-5% low-biased vs the mean RMSE wants) and log-space splitting/early stopping optimizes relative instead of absolute dollar errors, while the variance-stabilization benefit is marginal with 3.6M training rows — so expect a slight regression of roughly 1%.

Replacing 5-fold OOF encodings with in-sample ones lets each training row's own fare leak into its *_fare_mean features (self-weight up to ~1/(c+20)≈4.8% on the many sparse route keys), which gradient boosting reliably over-exploits and early stopping only partially curbs; that small but certain leakage harm should slightly outweigh the genuine but second-order gain from removing the ~log(0.8) log_count offset and the OOF noise mismatch, so I expect a marginal regression of roughly 0.005-0.015 RMSE.

The metric is RMSE on the raw dollar scale, but log-target training optimizes relative error: it systematically predicts near the conditional geometric rather than arithmetic mean (a ~1-3% downward bias) and underweights the expensive airport/long rides whose large dollar errors dominate squared loss, so with the data, features and corrupt-row floor unchanged I expect a small regression from 4.18 to roughly 4.20-4.23.

Airport-distance features let the trees isolate flat-fare JFK/EWR rides (~5.5% of trips) with single splits instead of many sparse coordinate splits, giving a modest RMSE gain on the ~97% predictable rows (local ~3.6 -> ~3.5) that is diluted to ~1-2% overall by the irreducible ~2.1 corrupt-row floor; risk of regression is low since the features are strictly informative and everything else is unchanged.

Only ~2.8% of test rows change behavior (invalid coordinates/passenger counts), switching from the global-mean fallback (~11.3) to LightGBM's NaN-branch prediction conditioned on calendar features; the README's own decomposition (floor ~2.1 from these rows + ~3.6 on the rest vs current 4.138) implies a subpopulation mean offset of only ~$2, so capturing it fully saves ~0.1-0.15 in overall MSE (~0.3-0.5% RMSE), valid-row predictions are essentially unchanged, and the realistic outcome is a marginal improvement to ~4.12.

3.9x more training rows with the same features/hyperparameters gives a modest, near-monotone gain (clean-row RMSE ~3.62 -> ~3.52, slightly dampened by the 1000-tree cap binding instead of early stopping), which against the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row floor moves the graded RMSE from 4.138 to about 4.06, while the usecols/dtype/format I/O speedups and n_jobs=4 keep the ~4-6 minute run safely inside the 10-minute budget.

The out-of-fold smoothed cell/route target encodings add real signal the baseline lacks (JFK flat fares, bridge/tunnel tolls, location-level fare priors) and the implementation is leak-free and fast, but the benefit is damped by m=20 shrinkage on sparse cells, overlap with what the trees already learn from raw coordinates, and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the ~2.8% corrupt test rows, so expect a modest ~0.1 RMSE gain (4.14 → ~4.04), not a large one.

Training on log1p(fare) makes both models approximate conditional medians instead of the conditional means that dollar-space RMSE rewards: the effect on the well-conditioned main model is near-neutral, but the weak-featured fallback (and high-fare rows) systematically under-predicts after expm1 with no smearing correction, so the graded RMSE should regress slightly from 4.13 to roughly 4.17-4.19.

Manhattan distance and bearing are classic additive features for this task (typically 3-4% off valid-row error), but the model already has raw coordinates and the ~2.1 RMSE floor from the ~2.8% corrupt test rows dilutes the overall gain to roughly 2%, giving ~4.03.

Distance-to-JFK/LGA/EWR/Manhattan features are the classic high-value addition for this task (airport flat-fare regimes, ~5.5% of trips), reliably improving the model's own RMSE by roughly 2% on valid rows, which after dilution by the ~2.8% corrupt-row floor baked into the 4.104 score yields a modest ~1.5% overall gain at negligible compute cost.

RMSE is minimized by the conditional mean, but the MAE objective makes LightGBM fit the conditional median, which systematically under-predicts the right-skewed fare distribution (and since the graded test is drawn from the same heavy-tailed data, there is no robustness payoff), so expect a modest regression of roughly 1-3% on the valid rows (3.6 -> ~3.7), diluted to ~4.19 overall by the fixed corrupt-row floor.

Training on log1p(fare) makes LightGBM leaves estimate geometric rather than arithmetic means, so back-transformed predictions are systematically ~3-5% low (unsmearinged retransformation bias, biggest on the cheap-ride bulk) and early stopping now optimizes log-space rather than dollar RMSE; with an already-cleaned target and RMSE grading, this typically costs a few hundredths of RMSE, only slightly damped by the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row floor.

With an RMSE metric, L1 training drives the trees toward conditional medians, which sit below conditional means for the right-skewed fare distribution (tolls, surcharges, airport flat fares), so predictions get biased low and the long-tail rides are systematically underfit — robustness to the few residual outliers is worth less than this median-vs-mean shift, so RMSE should regress slightly (early stopping on RMSE limits the damage).

Huber with delta=$1 sits deep in its linear regime given typical residuals of $2-4 (valid-row RMSE ~3.6), so training becomes nearly MAE-like and drives predictions toward conditional medians of a right-skewed fare distribution, which systematically under-predicts the mean and inflates the RMSE metric; early stopping on RMSE only partially mitigates, and the corrupt rows Huber would guard against are already dropped by cleaning.

Training on log1p(fare) makes the model approximate the conditional median rather than the RMSE-optimal conditional mean, so expm1 back-transformation systematically under-predicts (~3% low) and reweights the loss away from high-fare rows whose dollar errors dominate the squared metric, giving a modest RMSE regression from 4.13 to about 4.20 despite the nicer-shaped target.

Airport distances/flags expose the JFK flat-fare and EWR/LGA surcharge regimes that raw coords + haversine only partially capture, typically worth ~2-4% on the clean rows (which dominate the 4.129 score), while the ~2.8% corrupt-row floor and fallback path are untouched; runtime cost of 12 extra columns is small, so expect a modest, reliable gain to roughly 4.00-4.05.

Quadrupling the sample (1M→4M rows, same features/early stopping) trims the model-error component on valid rows from ~3.6 to ~3.45-3.5 while the ~2.1 corrupt-row floor is unchanged, so total RMSE improves modestly from 4.138 to about 4.00 (and the run should still fit the 10-minute budget).

Averaging 5 fold-models trained on 80% subsets cuts prediction variance (each model slightly weaker from 780k vs 878k rows, but diversification more than compensates), yielding a typical ~1-2% gain on the 97% clean test rows that is diluted by the fixed ~2.8% corrupt-row mean-fare floor, so overall RMSE should edge down from 4.138 to roughly 4.10; runtime (~4.4x single-model compute with early stopping) stays within budget.

A properly out-of-fold, smoothed pickup-cell target encoding adds a strong spatial fare prior (airport flat fares, neighborhood congestion/toll effects) that 63-leaf trees can't cheaply learn from raw coordinates, so valid-row RMSE should drop ~1.5-3%, diluted to ~2% overall by the fixed ~2.1 RMSE floor from the 2.8% corrupt test rows.

Snapping to a 0.01° grid (~1 km) injects ~0.4-0.5 km of quantization noise into the dominant distance signal for the many short trips (median ~2-3 km), and destroys sub-cell spatial detail trees currently exploit in dense Manhattan, while the route encoding is already 0.01-cell based so it gains nothing — expect a small regression from 4.13 to roughly 4.20.
