regression_l1 makes the model predict conditional medians, which undershoot the conditional means of the right-skewed (toll/surcharge-tailed) fare distribution, and with a large cleaned sample and RMSE-based early stopping that systematic bias costs more than the robustness to the few remaining fare outliers, so RMSE should regress by roughly 1%.

Switching to regression_l1 makes the model predict conditional medians instead of means; fares are right-skewed even after cleaning, so predictions will systematically under-predict by ~$0.5-1, and since the graded metric is RMSE (matched to L2), this adds a bias term that outweighs the modest robustness gain against the rare >$100 fares, worsening RMSE by roughly 2%.

Airport anchor distances are the classic next signal for this task (JFK flat fare, LGA/EWR fare patterns affect ~5.5% of test trips, plus landmark anchoring for all trips), the vectorized haversine calls add negligible runtime, and LightGBM with early stopping safely absorbs 6 more features — expect a modest ~2% RMSE improvement from 4.137 to ~4.05, diluted by the ~2.8% corrupt test rows that are unaffected by features.

regression_l1 makes the model predict conditional medians, which sit below the conditional means of the right-skewed fare residuals, so RMSE (a mean-optimal metric) worsens by ~1-2% on the ~97% valid test rows while the mean-fare fallback rows are unchanged; robustness gains are negligible since fares >$100 are only ~0.04% of cleaned rows.

LightGBM's internal 255-bin quantile binning already discretizes coordinates (to ~100m in dense Manhattan), so 2-decimal rounding mostly just discards sub-km resolution (blurred airport/toll boundaries, coarser street-grid geometry correction) while the pooling 'regularization' benefit is largely redundant with min_child_samples=100 and early stopping; the dominant haversine signal is unchanged, so expect an essentially flat, very slightly worse score.

L1 trains the conditional median while RMSE rewards the conditional mean, and taxi fares are right-skewed, so the L1 model will systematically under-predict and (with sign-gradients at lr=0.05) likely underfit slightly, giving a modest RMSE regression of ~2-3% despite early stopping on validation RMSE.

The 29°-rotated L1 street-grid distance is a classic strong fare proxy that trees cannot efficiently synthesize from raw coordinates and haversine alone, so adding it as a numeric feature should yield a small but real RMSE gain (~2% on the predictable rows, diluted by the ~2.8% corrupt test rows and the already-present airport/haversine features), with negligible compute cost and no risk to the runtime budget.

The leakage-safe, cross-fitted route-mean encoding adds genuine OD-pair signal for popular routes (airport corridors, dense Manhattan pairs) that trees can't efficiently learn from raw coordinates, but smoothing=50 at ~1km cells leaves most routes (avg N≈3) shrunk almost to the global mean, so expect a modest clean-row RMSE gain (~3.6→~3.45) that is diluted by the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row floor, landing near 4.01 versus 4.138.

The 29°-rotated Manhattan distance is the classic NYC path-distance signal that complements haversine (which underestimates grid travel), so it should shave ~0.05–0.08 RMSE off the ~3.6 clean-row error; the fixed ~2.1 corrupt-row floor dilutes this to roughly a 1% improvement on the graded 4.138.

Doubling the randomly-ordered training prefix from 1M to 2M rows is a pure sample-size increase (data card confirms the head is representative), which typically yields a small ~0.5-1% learning-curve gain on the ~97% of test rows the model can fit (≈3.60 -> ≈3.58 valid-row RMSE), diluting to ≈0.02 overall RMSE given the ~2.1 floor from corrupt test rows, while runtime only roughly doubles and stays comfortably inside the 10-minute budget; removed holdout print and MLflow logging do not affect the model.

The airport_route categorical isolates the JFK/LGA/EWR flat-fare structure (≈5.5% of test rows) that haversine+coordinates only partially capture, so expect a modest gain on valid rows (~3.61→~3.50) diluted by the ~2.1 RMSE corrupt-row floor, landing near 4.04 overall.

LightGBM at these settings is the standard strong baseline for this dataset and its native split-based interaction discovery (plus proper categorical handling of the f_27 letters) should edge out the small MLP by ~0.002 AUC, though the 4-thread run may hit the 9-minute guard before 2000 rounds, capping the gain slightly.

This dataset's signal lives in fine-grained interactions among the continuous columns (sums/products that the first linear layer computes exactly from raw inputs), so collapsing 31 numeric features to 10 quantile bins discards within-bin resolution for little gain — the marginals are weak (|r|<=0.13), so per-bin flexibility adds little — and the ~2.4x wider first layer slows epochs enough to risk the 9-minute guard; expect a small regression of roughly -0.001 to -0.002 AUC.

The 31 numeric columns are nearly uncorrelated, so full-rank PCA is essentially an arbitrary rotation that smears individually meaningful split axes and the 45° pair-sum interactions across all 41 PCs, and it also dilutes the per-position f_27 ordinal effects into mean+contrast mixtures; the small gains (a first PC proxying the mean char code / distinct-letter signal and better-conditioned leaf ridge fits) should not fully offset this, so I expect a modest regression of roughly 0.001-0.002 AUC.

f_27 is nearly unique per row (671k distinct strings in 800k rows, max count 10, 72% of test strings unseen), so a whole-string smoothed target encoding collapses to ~the prior and carries almost no generalizable signal, while the deleted 10 per-position ordinals encode one of the strongest signals in the data (e.g. position-6 letter positive rates span 0.10–1.00), leaving essentially a numeric-features-only LightGBM at roughly 0.94 AUC — a clear regression of ~4%.

f_27 is near-unique (670k distinct strings in 800k rows, 72% of test strings unseen), so with m=20 smoothing the OOF target encoding collapses to the global prior for ~70% of train rows and ~72% of test rows, adding almost no signal, while the removed ten per-position ordinal columns are dense, generalizable features (position 6's letters alone span 0.10–1.00 positive rate) — a clear regression of roughly 0.005–0.007 AUC to about 0.985–0.986.

These are the competition's famous 'magic' interactions (f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22, f_00+f_01+f_26 thresholded into ternary indicators) — diagonal half-plane signals that axis-aligned trees approximate poorly even with 3000 trees — historically worth roughly +0.0005–0.0015 AUC on a strong LGBM baseline, so I expect a solid but modest gain to ~0.9922 rather than the 0.993+ range that required many more engineered features and ensembling.

Logistic regression on this interaction-driven dataset captures only the weak marginal linear signal (max single-feature |r|=0.13, rest <0.07; the additive sums are redundant for a linear model), giving a standalone holdout AUC of roughly 0.64-0.70, and a 50/50 rank-average injects that weak model's noise into the 0.984 LGBM ranking, dropping the blend AUC to roughly 0.91-0.93.

TPS-May-2022 is the rare tabular dataset where MLPs beat GBDTs (the smooth sum/stripe interaction structure is NN-friendly), and the key magic sums are already in the 43 features, so a sound Adam+cosine recipe with best-epoch checkpointing should land around 0.986-0.991 despite the modest 64-wide capacity and slightly aggressive lr=0.01 — a modest gain over the 0.98416 LightGBM baseline.

A tiny 12k-parameter MLP with ordinal (not one-hot/embedded) letter encodings and only 60 CPU epochs cannot match 3000 boosted trees on this interaction-heavy tabular problem, so expect a modest regression to roughly 0.965-0.972 AUC.

TPS-May-2022's signal is known to live in oblique boundaries (sums of continuous features) that constant-leaf trees approximate with staircases, so piecewise-linear leaves should yield a real but modest gain (~+0.003); the main risk is the much slower per-tree linear refits, but with lr=0.05 and high per-tree capacity the holdout AUC should plateau well before 3000 rounds, letting 100-round early stopping keep the run inside the 15-minute kill limit.

The distinct-letter count of f_27 is the strongest known engineered feature for this competition (positive rate swings from ~9% for 2-3 distinct letters to ~91% for 7-8), and since counting distinct letters across 10 ordinal positions is hard for axis-aligned trees to reconstruct implicitly, adding it as an explicit column should add a solid few thousandths of AUC (~+0.005-0.007) on top of the 0.97696 baseline.

These are exactly the three 'hidden' additive interactions this TPS was built around (f_00+f_01+f_26, f_02+f_21, f_05+f_22 show near-monotonic target-rate curves); adding their raw sums to LightGBM historically lifts AUC from ~0.977 to ~0.985-0.988, so expect roughly +0.009 absolute (~+0.9%).

f_27 is nearly unique per row (72% of test strings unseen in train), so a single ~600k-cardinality categorical gives ~zero out-of-sample signal (smoothed singleton stats, unseen codes fall to the default branch, min_child_samples=100), while deleting the 10 per-position ordinal columns removes the strongest fine-grained f_27 signal that counts+nunique cannot replace — an estimated ~0.005-0.008 AUC regression (with added runtime risk from huge-bin histogram/split-finding costs).

The nine bigram columns are deterministic functions of the already-present per-position ordinals (no new information for a 127-leaf, 3000-tree GBDT that can already express pairwise interactions), but native categorical grouping gives the still-improving-at-3000-trees model a slightly cheaper path to those combos, so I expect a tiny gain (~+0.0002) with real chance of a flat or marginally negative noise-level outcome.

PCA components are variance-driven linear mixes of already-present raw columns and add essentially no information to axis-split trees, so the swap mostly forfeits the mined products' modest real interaction signal (especially count-feature joint tails), yielding a small regression from 0.97527.

f_27 is nearly unique per row (72% of test strings unseen), so hashing the whole string into 64 pseudo-random buckets destroys all per-position letter and unique-count signal — the dataset's most informative feature group — leaving the model at roughly numeric-features-only performance (~0.90 vs 0.975), with the 64 near-noise bucket columns adding at best mild overfitting.

The single fully-grown 300-tree ExtraTrees fit on 800k rows already consumes most of the 10-minute budget (per the change's own sizing), and the added 5-fold cross_val_predict refits that ensemble ~4x more BEFORE submission.csv is written, so the run is hard-killed at 15 minutes and recorded as a failure (no submission, AUC 0) — and even if it squeaked under the kill, sqrt-feature ExtraTrees would land around 0.965, well below the 0.978 LightGBM baseline.

A small (256,128) sklearn MLP capped at ~40 epochs captures the linear character-sum signal and some smooth cross-terms but underfits the fine-grained threshold/interaction structure that 3000 LightGBM trees exploit (0.9781 baseline), so expect a modest regression to roughly 0.97.

The distinct-letter count of f_27 is a known strong signal (positive rate jumps from ~9% for 2-3 distinct letters to ~91% for 7-8) that a tree ensemble cannot easily reconstruct from the 10 per-position categoricals, so adding the 27 order-invariant count features should lift the LGBM AUC by roughly +0.003, from ~0.9768 to ~0.980.

The full-string frequency is nearly constant noise (670k distinct strings in 800k rows, max count 10, ~72% of test strings unseen), so this change effectively deletes the per-position f_27 categorical group — the most informative feature family (position 6 alone spans 0.10→1.00 positive rate) — leaving the booster with numeric-only signal, which on this interaction-heavy dataset historically plateaus around AUC ≈ 0.90.

The distinct-letter count of f_27 is the competition's known 'magic' feature (positive rate ~9%/48%/91% across nunique buckets) and is hard for trees to reconstruct from 10 positional ordinals, so adding it (plus largely-redundant per-letter counts) should lift AUC by roughly +0.005 over 0.97696 at negligible compute cost since the new columns are tiny-cardinality integers.

The mining pool f_00–f_15 excludes the columns where this dataset's real interactions live (f_19–f_28, f_29/f_30 pairs, and f_27-derived signals), and z-scored products are the wrong functional form for the known sum/threshold-style interactions, so the 25 appended columns are essentially noise that dilutes a fixed 3000-tree budget — a wash to a tiny regression (plus some runtime risk from ~1.6x more features).

Refitting on the extra 10% of rows with a proportionally scaled round count (3333 vs 3000) is a standard mild win — the baseline was still improving at iteration 3000, so more data plus slightly more trees should add a small ~+0.0003–0.0006 AUC gain with negligible overfit risk since early stopping never fired.

The alphabetical code order is arbitrary relative to the per-letter positive rates, so native categorical splits (optimal letter subsets per position) should be strictly more efficient than threshold splits; deep 3000-tree ensembles already approximate subset partitions, so expect only a small gain (~+0.001 AUC), with mild risk that cat_smooth/min_data_per_group regularization and split-heuristic quirks mute it to ~zero.

The distinct-letter count of f_27 is a strong monotone grouped signal (≈9% positive for 2-3 letters vs ≈91% for 7-8) that trees cannot cheaply reconstruct from the 10 per-position ordinals, so adding it as a single split-friendly feature should yield a genuine but modest gain (~+0.002 AUC) over the 0.98175 baseline, consistent with TPS-May-22 community results.
